app.text: Volume calculators (Material Volume, Structure Bedding, Bedding & Shading) show weight: tons, no allowance = yd³ × density (t/yd³); with compaction allowance = yd³ × (1 + allowance) × density (allowance added first; default 15%, Bedding & Shading uses its own box). 1 ton/yd³ = 74.07 lb/ft³. Density presets (tons per yd³, verify with your supplier; from supplier conversion charts): 3/4" crushed rock 1.35; Pea gravel (1/4" rock) 1.40; Coarse sand (concrete sand) 1.485 (110 lb/ft³); Fine sand (mason sand) 1.431 (106 lb/ft³); Asphalt (hot mix) 1.96 (145 lb/ft³); Road base (Class 2 / 3 / 6) 2.0. Rounded to one decimal, an exact half to even.
app.title: Weight in tons from a volume (material densities)

app.text: On a run, bedding used is calculated: footage × trench width × bedding thickness (yd³, or tons by the material's density), plus the compaction allowance (15% by default), always labeled an estimate. Pipe used comes from Pipe Installed footage. A run ended early is figured to its stop point. Job materials show Used / Ordered / Expected; Ordered = the PM's orders + delivery tickets.
app.title: Run bedding and backfill volumes on a run

app.text: The permit checks every air test against these unless the permit sets its own: O2 minimum 19.5%; O2 maximum 23.5% (oxygen-enriched air is a fire hazard); LEL maximum 10%; H2S maximum 10 ppm (the OSHA construction limit, 8-hour average); CO maximum 25 ppm (the Cal/OSHA limit, lower than federal OSHA and NIOSH; NIOSH recommends 35 ppm and federal OSHA allows 50 ppm). Outside any limit: EVACUATE. Air test re-check: check-in is blocked when the last test is older than the permit's reminder minutes, or 20 minutes when blank. Emergency number default 911 (changeable).
app.title: Confined space gas limit defaults
app.table_source: app permit form labels (OSHA/NIOSH values as stated there)

app.text: California 811 (Gov Code 4216.2), as built in the app: call at least 2 working days before digging, the call day not counted ("Can dig from"); start work within 14 calendar days of the call ("Start work by"); a ticket is good for 28 days. Jobs in other states use that state's own numbers from the app's state table (Locates › Rules for the state). Working days are Mon–Fri except federal and California holidays as the 811 centers post them (New Year's Day, MLK Day, Presidents' Day, Cesar Chavez Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and the day after, Christmas; a Saturday holiday is the Friday before, a Sunday one the Monday after). Alerts at 7 days, 2 days and the day of expiry.
app.title: 811 locate ticket timing the app uses

app.text: Run Notes Delay reasons: Utility conflict, Waiting on inspector, Weather, Equipment down, Waiting on material, Waiting on survey / stakes, Traffic control, Other. Utility Found: Water, Gas, Electric, Telecom, Sewer, Storm, Abandoned line, Unknown. Rework reasons: Grade off, Damaged pipe, Failed test, Inspector call, Other. Daily report Delays & Extra Work kinds: Delay, Standby, Extra work; reasons: Weather, Utility conflict, Waiting on inspector, Waiting on materials, Design change, Owner-directed, Other. When a run note delay flows into the daily, Utility conflict, Waiting on inspector, Weather and Waiting on material map across; others become Other with the run note's reason kept in the detail.
app.title: Run Notes and daily report reason lists

app.text: Inspection and test types: Inspection, Pressure test, Mandrel test, CCTV inspection, Compaction test, Other; results Pass, Fail, Partial. Job book safety events: Near miss, First aid, Incident, Property damage, Stop work. Closeout checklist: Punch list clear, Restoration complete, As-builts sent, Final inspections done, Materials returned, Tickets reconciled, Owner sign-off. Default job plan categories: Demo, Excavation, Pipe Installed, Backfill, Restoration, Structures. Material types: Pipe, Bedding / Shading, Road base, Asphalt, Concrete, Fittings, Structures, Other. Concrete ticket uses: Encasement, Thrust blocks, Collars, Manhole base / bench, Pipe bedding (CLSM), Backfill (flowable fill), Curb / sidewalk / paving restoration, Other.
app.title: Inspection and test types, job book lists
app.table_source: app code PB_INS_KINDS, job book, PB_MAT_TYPES, ticket Use list

field.text: Most public sewer, storm and water work is bid as unit prices: the owner lists bid items with estimated quantities, the contractor bids a price per unit, and payment is for the actual measured quantity installed. Typical pipe bid items: linear feet of pipe by size, material and sometimes depth range (for example '8 inch PVC SDR 35, 0 to 10 ft deep'); manholes each, plus vertical feet over a base depth; services each; fittings by the each or by the pound (ductile fittings); rock excavation by the cubic yard; select backfill or stone by the ton or CY; pavement restoration by the SY or ton. The specs' 'Measurement and Payment' section says exactly how each item is measured (for example pipe measured along the centerline through manholes or from inside face to inside face). Read it before bidding and before measuring pay quantities. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Unit price contracts: how pipe work is paid
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: A basic way to build a unit price for pipe: cost per foot = (crew labor cost per day + equipment cost per day) / expected production in feet per day + materials per foot (pipe, gaskets, bedding, backfill, tracer wire) + trucking and disposal per foot + restoration per foot if included + overhead and profit markup. Example with round numbers: crew labor $4,000/day, equipment $3,000/day, production 300 ft/day gives $23.33/ft for labor and equipment; materials $18/ft; trucking $4/ft; subtotal $45.33/ft; plus 15% overhead and profit = about $52/ft. The production rate is the most sensitive number: at 200 ft/day the labor and equipment part becomes $35/ft. Use your own historical production by size and depth; DOT tables (for example WSDOT's sanitary sewer range of 200 to 400 LF/day) are only a sanity check.
field.title: Unit pricing: building a cost per foot
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Unit price contracts have estimated quantities, and actual quantities often differ. Many public contracts include a clause allowing a price adjustment when a major item's quantity changes significantly. On federal-aid highway contracts, 23 CFR 635.109 defines a significant change for a major item as an increase or decrease of more than 25% of the original contract quantity; the adjustment applies to the portion beyond that (on an increase) or is based on actual quantity (on a decrease). State and city contracts often follow a similar 25% rule, but terms vary. If a quantity is trending well over or under, notify the owner in writing early, track quantities daily, and know your cost on that item so you can show why the unit price should change. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Quantity overruns and underruns
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: 23 CFR 635.109, Standardized changed condition clauses (federal-aid highway contracts)

field.text: A differing site conditions (changed conditions) clause lets the contractor get more time or money when the site isn't as represented. On federal-aid contracts, 23 CFR 635.109 includes two types: physical conditions at the site that differ materially from those indicated in the contract (Type I, for example rock or groundwater where borings showed none, or utilities not shown), and unknown physical conditions of an unusual nature that differ materially from those ordinarily encountered (Type II). The clause requires prompt written notice to the engineer before the conditions are disturbed, so the owner can see them. Field steps: stop work in the affected area if possible, notify in writing right away, photograph and measure, record it in the daily report, track the extra cost separately (T&M), and keep doing unaffected work. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Differing site conditions
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: 23 CFR 635.109, Standardized changed condition clauses (federal-aid highway contracts)

field.text: A change order modifies the contract's scope, price or time. Typical flow: (1) a change arises (owner request, design error, unforeseen condition, RFI answer that adds work); (2) the contractor gives written notice within the contract's deadline (often days, not weeks); (3) the contractor prices the change (unit prices if applicable, a lump sum proposal, or time and materials if price can't be agreed); (4) the owner reviews and negotiates; (5) a signed change order (or a unilateral directive with the price to be settled later) adds the work. Do not proceed with extra work on a verbal OK unless the contract allows it and you document it the same day; get it in writing. Include time impact in the request, not just money, or you may waive it. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Change orders: the basic process
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: When extra work can't be priced in advance, it's usually done on time and materials (also called force account on public jobs). A good daily T&M ticket shows: date, project, change or work order number, and a clear description of the work and location (station); each worker's name, trade classification and hours (straight and overtime); each piece of equipment with ID, size, operating hours and standby hours; materials used with quantities (attach invoices); subcontractor and trucking costs; and the owner's representative's signature the same day. Pricing follows the contract: labor at actual wage plus burden, equipment at the contract's rate source (often the Rental Rate Blue Book or a state rate schedule), materials at invoice, plus the contract's markups. Photos before, during and after help. Unsigned or late tickets are the most common reason extra work goes unpaid. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Time and materials (T&M) or force account tickets
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Equipment on T&M or force account work is usually paid using a rate source named in the contract, such as the Equipment Watch Rental Rate Blue Book, a state DOT equipment rate schedule, or the contractor's actual rental invoices for rented equipment. Rates typically cover ownership and operating costs; the operator is paid separately as labor. Standby (equipment held on site for the extra work but not operating) is often paid at a reduced rate, commonly a fraction of the ownership portion without operating costs; the exact rule is in the contract. Record operating versus standby hours separately on every ticket, and get the owner to agree the equipment is being held for the change. Know your contract's rule before the work starts. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: T&M: equipment rates and standby
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Delays cost money and time, but only documented delays get compensated. Practices: give written notice of any delay within the contract's deadline; record in the daily report what work was delayed, why (owner, utility, design, permit, weather, differing condition), when it started and ended, and what crew and equipment were affected (idle, demobilized or reassigned); take dated photos; keep correspondence (RFIs, emails) that show the cause; update the schedule to show the impact on the critical path (a time impact analysis). Separate excusable delays (more time, maybe no money, such as unusually severe weather) from compensable delays (owner-caused: time and money) and contractor-caused delays. Concurrent delays complicate claims. Weather: many contracts allow time only for weather beyond normal for the season, often using historical weather data. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Delay documentation
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: The daily report is the most important project record for pay, claims and disputes. A complete daily report includes: date, weather (temperature, rain, conditions) and site conditions (wet trench, frozen ground); crew on site (names or counts by trade) and hours; equipment on site and hours (working, idle, down); work performed by location (stations, manholes, structures) and quantities installed (feet of pipe by size, structures, services, tons of stone); materials delivered; tests and inspections (who, what, result); visitors and owner instructions received; delays and their cause; extra work and T&M ticket numbers; safety items (toolbox talk, trench inspections, incidents, near misses); utility conflicts and locate ticket numbers; and photos. Write facts, not opinions, and write it the same day. Have it signed by the foreman or super. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Daily reports: what to record
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Photos are cheap insurance. Good practice: take pre-construction photos and video of the whole route (pavement condition, curbs, driveways, lawns, mailboxes, building foundations near the work) to protect against damage claims; photograph utilities as found (depth with a tape in the shot), unexpected rock and groundwater, differing conditions, every T&M item, test setups and gauges, and completed work before backfill (especially services and fittings for as-builts). Make sure photos carry date, time and location (GPS) data; include a station marker, stake or sign in the frame when you can. Store them by date and location so you can find them later. Many disputes are settled by whoever has the better photos. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Photos and video for the record
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Job costing tracks actual cost against the estimate, activity by activity, so you know where you're making or losing money while the job is still running. Set up cost codes that match how you estimated: for example mobilization, traffic control, 8 inch sewer pipe, 12 inch sewer pipe, manholes, services, rock excavation, dewatering, testing, restoration, and extra work (each change order its own code). Each day, the foreman assigns crew hours and equipment hours to cost codes and reports installed quantities. The office applies labor rates, equipment rates and material invoices. Then for each code you can compare cost per unit and hours per unit to the estimate. The value comes from accurate daily coding; if all hours go to one code, the report is useless. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Job costing: cost codes
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Labor cost in job costing is more than the hourly wage. Labor burden adds employer payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare, federal and state unemployment), workers' compensation insurance (which varies a lot by state and trade class), general liability tied to payroll, health insurance, retirement, union fringes where applicable, and paid time off. Burden as a percent of wages varies widely by company, state and union status; compute your own from actual costs rather than using someone else's percentage. For each crew, the daily labor cost = sum of (hours x wage x (1 + burden rate)) including overtime premiums. Use this burdened rate for estimates, T&M tickets (where the contract allows actual burden), and cost reports. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Job costing: labor cost and burden
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: To charge or estimate equipment fairly, figure cost per hour in two parts. Ownership costs (incurred whether it runs or not): depreciation (purchase price minus resale value, spread over expected life in hours), interest on the money invested, insurance, property taxes, storage and licensing. Operating costs (only when running): fuel, lubricants and filters, repairs and maintenance, tires or undercarriage, and wear parts like bucket teeth and cutting edges. Total hourly cost = ownership per hour + operating per hour; the operator's wage is separate labor. Example structure: a machine with $40/hr ownership and $35/hr operating costs $75/hr plus operator. Compare to rental rates: if the machine sits idle much of the year, renting may be cheaper; high utilization favors owning. Industry rate books (Rental Rate Blue Book, Corps of Engineers EP 1110-1-8) use the same structure.
field.title: Equipment cost per hour: ownership and operating
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Key performance indicators that owners and PMs use: Production: feet laid per day and per working hour, by pipe size and depth; structures per day; services per day. Labor productivity: man-hours per foot (or per unit), compared to estimate; production factor = earned hours (installed quantity x estimated hours per unit) / actual hours (above 1.0 is better than estimate). Cost: cost per foot by cost code versus estimate; equipment cost per foot. Schedule: percent complete versus planned; schedule variance (earned value minus planned value); percent plan complete for weekly commitments (Last Planner). Quality: test pass rate on first try (air, mandrel, pressure, bac-T), punch items per 1,000 ft. Safety: incidents, near misses, trench inspection completion. Track a few consistently rather than many sporadically. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: KPIs for pipe crews and projects
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Earned value compares what you planned, what you did and what it cost. Planned value (PV): budgeted cost of work scheduled to date. Earned value (EV): budgeted cost of work actually completed (installed quantity x budgeted unit cost). Actual cost (AC): what that work actually cost. Schedule variance SV = EV - PV (negative means behind). Cost variance CV = EV - AC (negative means over budget). Schedule performance index SPI = EV / PV; cost performance index CPI = EV / AC (below 1.0 is bad). Example: planned 2,000 ft by now at $50/ft (PV $100,000); installed 1,800 ft (EV $90,000); spent $99,000 (AC). SV = -$10,000 (behind), CV = -$9,000 (over), SPI 0.90, CPI 0.91. Estimate at completion is often projected as budget / CPI. Standard project controls method.
field.title: Earned value basics for PMs
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: A punch list is the list of incomplete or defective items to fix before final acceptance. For pipe projects typical items: manhole channels or benches rough or incomplete, rims not at final grade, frames not sealed, debris in lines (found on CCTV), failed or missing tests, valve boxes not centered or not to grade, hydrants not plumb or wrong height, tracer wire continuity failures, restoration (lawns, pavement cracks, curbs, driveways), missing marker posts, and cleanup. Best practice: walk the job with the owner, get one consolidated written list with locations, assign each item to a person with a date, close items with photos, and get sign-off. Don't let punch work drag on: it ties up retainage and the warranty start date. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Punch lists
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: As-builts record what was actually installed, for the owner to find and maintain it for decades. What to capture during construction (not from memory at the end): manhole and structure locations and rim and invert elevations as built; pipe sizes, materials and lengths between structures; service locations by station and offset from the downstream manhole, with depth, length and end location tied to permanent objects (two or three measurements from house corners, poles, hydrants); water valves, fittings, bends, hydrants and blow-offs with ties; utility crossings found with depths; changes from the plans (re-routes, grade changes, added fittings); abandoned lines. Many owners now want GPS coordinates. Keep a red-line set in the field and mark it daily. As-builts are usually required before final payment. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: As-built (record) drawings for utilities
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Typical closeout items on public utility projects: punch list complete and signed off; all test reports submitted and accepted (air, mandrel, vacuum, CCTV, hydrostatic, bac-T, compaction, concrete); as-built drawings; final quantities agreed and final pay application; change orders all executed; warranties and maintenance bonds (warranty commonly one year from acceptance, but check your contract); operation and maintenance manuals for valves, pump stations or equipment; lien waivers or releases from subs and suppliers; certified payrolls complete (on prevailing-wage jobs); permits closed (road, stormwater/SWPPP notice of termination, dewatering); site cleaned and restored; final acceptance letter from the owner; retainage released. Start collecting closeout documents during the job, not at the end. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Project closeout checklist
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: On most construction contracts the contractor bills monthly through a pay application listing quantities installed (unit price) or percent complete by line item (schedule of values). The owner often withholds retainage, a percentage of each payment held until completion; common amounts are 5 to 10%, sometimes reduced after a milestone (such as 50% complete), and many states limit retainage on public work by law. Tips: agree on measured quantities with the inspector before submitting; attach supporting documents (quantity sheets, test reports); bill stored materials only if the contract allows and with proper documentation; track what's billed versus earned so you're not overbilled or underbilled; and push for retainage reduction and release at the milestones the contract or state law allows. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Retainage and pay applications
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Federally funded or assisted construction contracts over $2,000 are generally covered by the Davis-Bacon and Related Acts, which require paying laborers and mechanics at least the locally prevailing wages and fringe benefits for their classification as set in the wage determination in the contract, and submitting weekly certified payrolls (the Department of Labor provides optional form WH-347). Many states have their own prevailing wage laws for state and local public works with different thresholds. Practical points: classify each worker correctly by the work actually done (an operator running a backhoe gets the operator rate that day), post the wage determination on site, keep payroll records, and pay apprentices only at apprentice rates if they're in a registered program. Errors can lead to back pay and debarment. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Prevailing wage and certified payroll
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: U.S. Department of Labor, Davis-Bacon and Related Acts

field.text: Public construction usually requires surety bonds. Bid bond: guarantees the low bidder will sign the contract and provide the required bonds; often 5 to 10% of the bid amount, as stated in the bid documents. Performance bond: guarantees the contractor completes the work per the contract (usually 100% of contract amount). Payment bond: guarantees subcontractors and suppliers get paid (usually 100%), because liens usually can't be filed on public property. On federal construction the Miller Act requires performance and payment bonds above a threshold (currently $150,000 under the Federal Acquisition Regulation); states have 'Little Miller Acts' with their own thresholds. Your bonding capacity depends on your financial statements, experience and track record with the surety. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Bonds: bid, performance and payment
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Requests for information (RFIs) ask the engineer to clarify the plans or specs; submittals give the engineer product data and shop drawings to approve before ordering. RFI tips: ask early (Last Planner guidance notes RFI turnaround can take two to three weeks), one question per RFI, reference the sheet and spec section, propose a solution, and note any cost or schedule impact. Submittal tips: submit complete packages for long-lead items first (precast structures, large pipe, valves, castings); highlight the exact model and options on product sheets; keep a submittal log with dates sent, returned and status; don't order or install unapproved material. Lean planning puts submittals and RFIs on the look-ahead as constraints with owners and dates. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: RFIs and submittals
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Lean Construction Institute Last Planner System (Mastt summary)

field.text: The preconstruction meeting (with owner, engineer, inspector, utilities and key subs) is the time to settle how the job will run. Topics worth covering for utility work: contacts and chain of command; work hours, traffic control and permits; utility conflicts and relocations by others, with dates; locate procedures and who calls 811; testing procedures, who witnesses and how much notice the inspector needs; submittal and RFI process; measurement and payment details (how pipe is measured, how rock is verified); change order and T&M procedures, including who can sign tickets; shutdown and tie-in procedures for water mains; stormwater and dewatering permits; property owner notifications; schedule and milestones; and safety requirements. Write the agreements in the meeting minutes and keep a copy on site. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Preconstruction meeting: what to settle
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: A good bid starts with an accurate takeoff from the plans: pipe length by size, material and depth range (measure from the profile, since depth drives cost); number and depth of manholes and structures; services, fittings, valves, hydrants; pavement and restoration areas; rock and unsuitable soil allowances from borings; dewatering needs; utility crossings (count them, each one slows the crew); traffic control phases; and test requirements. Check the bid form quantities against your own takeoff; differences reveal where the owner's estimate may overrun or underrun. Note risks in a bid notes sheet: deep sections, high groundwater, tight streets, many crossings, short work windows. Then build crew-day pricing for each section rather than one average rate for the whole job. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Bidding: quantity takeoff for pipe jobs
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: The geotechnical report (soil borings) tells you what you'll dig through and is a major source of risk. Look for: soil types by depth (sand, clay, rock), groundwater depth at each boring and the date measured (wet season versus dry), rock depth and type (with rock quality if cored), bearing values and recommendations for bedding, dewatering and shoring, and contamination notes. Compare boring locations to your pipe route and depths: borings far from the line or shallower than your trench leave gaps. Many contracts say the borings are for information only; know how your contract treats them, because that affects whether a differing site condition claim will hold. Price groundwater and rock risk where borings show them, and ask questions before bid day. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Bidding: reading the geotech report
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: On utility jobs, delays often come from others: precast suppliers, pipe deliveries, testing firms, paving subs, utility companies relocating their lines. Practices: confirm lead times at bid and order long-lead items right after approval; get delivery schedules in writing and confirm a few days ahead; set paving and restoration subs' dates as the pipe work nears completion, not after; schedule testing firms and the owner's inspector early; track utility relocations by others on the look-ahead with dates and contacts; hold weekly coordination meetings on bigger jobs. Lean planning's constraint log works well here: each constraint has an owner and a need-by date. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Subcontractor and supplier coordination
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Lean Construction Institute Last Planner System (Mastt summary)

field.text: Owning equipment makes sense when it's used most of the time; renting makes sense for occasional or specialized needs. To decide: compute your owning cost per year (depreciation, interest, insurance, taxes, storage, plus repairs) and divide by the hours you'll actually use it; compare to rental rates for the same hours (daily, weekly and monthly rental rates differ a lot, with monthly cheapest per day). Low utilization machines are often cheaper to rent; your core excavators and loaders that run every day usually favor owning. Also weigh: availability when you need it, breakdown risk and backup machines, mobilization costs, and cash flow. Track hours per machine per year with telematics or hour-meter logs so the decision uses real data. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Small business owner: own versus rent equipment
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Safety performance directly affects a contractor's costs and ability to win work. The Experience Modification Rate (EMR or mod) adjusts workers' compensation premiums based on your claims history compared to similar companies; 1.0 is average, below 1.0 lowers premiums, above 1.0 raises them. Many owners and general contractors require an EMR at or below a set value (often 1.0) to bid. A single serious trench injury can raise premiums for years and lead to OSHA citations. Investments that pay back: trench protection equipment, training for competent persons and operators, daily trench inspections recorded in writing, and near-miss reporting. OSHA penalties are adjusted annually for inflation; serious and willful trench violations bring significant fines. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Safety costs and EMR
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: A project schedule (often a CPM, critical path method, schedule) links activities in order with durations. The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities; any delay on it delays the whole job. For pipe projects, the critical path often runs through deep sections, structure deliveries, utility relocations by others, testing waiting periods (such as a 30-day wait for mandrel testing if specified), and paving windows. Update the schedule regularly (monthly or as the contract requires) with actual progress, and use it to request time extensions (time impact analysis shows how a delay pushed the finish). Float is the slack non-critical activities have; who owns float is set by the contract. A simple bar chart is fine for small jobs, but tie it to production rates. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Schedule basics for PMs: critical path
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Your own production history is more valuable than any published table. Record for each pipe run or day: pipe size and material, average depth, soil type, groundwater, shoring method, crew size, equipment, feet installed, working hours, and main delays. After a few jobs you'll see your real feet per day for, say, 8 inch PVC at 8 to 12 ft deep in clay with a box, which you can use to bid and schedule. Published ranges help as a check: WSDOT lists sanitary sewer at 200 to 400 LF/day and water main at 100 to 800 LF/day (normal 300); NCDOT uses 50 to 300 LF/day for pipe depending on project type. If your bid rate is outside these ranges, have a reason.
field.title: Production rate history: building your own database
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: WSDOT M22-31 Appendix 6 production rates

field.text: Sewer and water work happens in people's streets and yards. Good practice reduces complaints and claims: notify residents and businesses before work starts (door hangers with dates, contact number, what to expect); give advance notice of water shutoffs (utilities often require a minimum notice, check yours); keep driveways open or give notice and time windows when closing them; keep the site clean, sweep streets daily, control dust; restore mailboxes, lawns and landscaping promptly; take pre-construction photos; have a single contact person to handle complaints and log each one with what was done. On sewer service reconnections, coordinate timing so homes aren't without service unexpectedly. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Customer and public relations on utility jobs
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.text: Most public utility contracts include a warranty (guarantee) period, commonly one year from final acceptance (check your contract; some are longer or require a maintenance bond). During the warranty, the contractor must fix defects in materials and workmanship, such as trench settlement, leaking joints, failed pavement patches, broken valve boxes, or sewer defects found on a final CCTV or mandrel test (Berkeley County, for example, requires a final mandrel test in the 12th month). Practices: diary the warranty end date; walk the job before it ends with the owner; respond quickly to callbacks; and document repairs. Good compaction and restoration during the job are the best way to avoid warranty costs. Your contract and project specs govern; this is general practice, not legal advice.
field.title: Warranty period and callbacks
field.topic: Business, project management and job costing
field.source: Construction management practice (general; not legal advice; your contract governs)

field.note: Same facts as ca-cal-osha-trench-and-confined-3 (this ord), now a CA state card (state field, title starts with the state).
field.text: California's permissible exposure limits (Title 8 section 5155, Table AC-1) are stricter than federal for gases crews meet in manholes and vaults. Carbon monoxide: Cal/OSHA PEL 25 ppm 8-hour average with a 200 ppm ceiling (federal construction PEL 50 ppm; NIOSH REL 35 ppm, which many monitors use as the alarm). Hydrogen sulfide: Cal/OSHA 10 ppm 8-hour average, 15 ppm short-term (15-minute) limit, and a 50 ppm ceiling never to be exceeded; federal construction 10 ppm. Carbon dioxide: 5,000 ppm PEL, 30,000 ppm STEL. The confined space limits are the same in both systems: oxygen 19.5 to 23.5 percent and 10 percent of the LEL. The app's permit defaults (O2 19.5-23.5, LEL 10, H2S 10, CO 25) already use this CO limit everywhere; a company program may set stricter limits, and 15 ppm H2S is a 15-minute limit, not a working level. None of this is a go/no-go: the entry supervisor and the company program decide.
field.title: California confined space air limits: Cal/OSHA CO 25 ppm and H2S 10 / 15 / 50 ppm (8 CCR 5155), stricter than federal
field.topic: State safety plan: confined space
field.source: 8 CCR 5155 Table AC-1 (carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide rows); 29 CFR 1926.55 Appendix A; NIOSH Pocket Guide
field.edition: Title 8 section 5155 as posted on dir.ca.gov

field.text: Two California duties that come up on every incident. Reporting: a serious injury or illness or a death must be reported to the Cal/OSHA district office immediately, meaning as soon as practically possible and no later than 8 hours after the employer knows or should have known (8 CCR 342; 24 hours only with proven exigent circumstances). Serious injury or illness (8 CCR 330(h), Labor Code 6302) means inpatient hospitalization for other than observation or diagnostic testing, amputation, loss of an eye, or serious permanent disfigurement. Federal is 8 hours for a death and 24 hours for the others. Give the injured worker a workers' comp claim form (DWC-1) within one working day (Labor Code 5401). IIPP: every California employer must have a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program (8 CCR 3203) with training, hazard inspections and a way for workers to report hazards; inspectors ask for it along with the trench permit, the heat illness plan (8 CCR 3395) and the competent-person training record. Log the incident in the app's job book as a safety event (no medical details).
field.title: Cal/OSHA injury and illness reporting and the IIPP: what a foreman has to do
field.topic: Cal/OSHA (Title 8) rules for trenches and confined spaces in California

field.text: California is a state-plan state: Cal/OSHA (the Division of Occupational Safety and Health) inspects and cites private and public construction, not federal OSHA. The standards are Title 8 of the California Code of Regulations; numbers like 1926.652 are federal and do not appear on a California citation, which cites 1541.1, 1953, 3395 and so on. A 'serious' citation needs no injury, only a realistic possibility of death or serious harm. Common trench citations in California: no permit for a 5 ft trench (341), no protective system or a box used past its tabulated depth (1541.1), no ladder within 25 ft (1541(c)), spoil or equipment at the edge (1541(j)), no competent-person inspection (1541(k)), digging before the locate marks and positive responses were in (1541(b)), no heat illness plan or water and shade (3395). Keep on site: the 341 permit, tabulated data for the box, the IIPP, the heat plan, training records and the daily inspection log.
field.title: Cal/OSHA versus federal OSHA on a California job: who inspects and what they cite
field.topic: Cal/OSHA (Title 8) rules for trenches and confined spaces in California
field.source: Cal/OSHA enforcement practice; 8 CCR 341, 1541, 1541.1, 1950-1962, 3203, 3395

field.text: Title 8 section 1541(k) requires a competent person to make daily inspections of excavations, the adjacent areas and protective systems for evidence of possible cave-ins, failed protective systems, hazardous atmospheres or other hazardous conditions: before the start of work, as needed throughout the shift, and after every rain storm or other hazard-increasing occurrence; exposed employees must be removed from the hazard until precautions are taken (1541(k)(2)). Cal/OSHA expects proof: most California contractors keep a written daily trench inspection form (date, time, location, depth, soil type and the tests used, protective system and its tabulated data, water conditions, atmosphere, access, spoil, utilities, inspector's name). The competent person must be able to identify soil and protective system hazards and have authority to stop work and fix them. The app's daily report and run notes can carry the record (station range, depth, box type, soil type as classified, inspections done); the competent person's name should be on it.
field.title: Cal/OSHA competent person and daily trench inspection record in California
field.topic: Cal/OSHA (Title 8) rules for trenches and confined spaces in California
field.source: 8 CCR 1541(k); 8 CCR 1540 (competent person definition); Cal/OSHA trenching guidance

field.text: California specs say '95% relative compaction' instead of '95% of Proctor'. Relative compaction = in-place dry density divided by the maximum dry density from the named laboratory test, times 100. Caltrans uses California Test 216 for the maximum density (its own procedure, run differently from a Proctor test) and California Test 231 for in-place density and relative compaction with the nuclear gauge; many cities, the Greenbook (SSPWC) and geotechnical engineers specify ASTM D1557 (modified Proctor) as the reference instead. The percentage is only meaningful with its reference test named, because CTM 216 and D1557 can give different maximum densities for the same soil, so 95% against one is not the same as 95% against the other. Ask the inspector or the spec which curve the gauge is set to before you argue a failing test. Standard Proctor (ASTM D698) is rarely the reference in California.
field.title: What 'relative compaction' means in California specs (CTM 216 and 231 vs Proctor)
field.topic: California compaction specs: relative compaction, Caltrans 19 and 26, Greenbook 306
field.source: Caltrans California Test 216 and 231; ASTM D1557; Caltrans Standard Specifications sections 25 and 26 (acceptance under California Test 231)

field.text: Caltrans Standard Specifications section 19-3 (Structure Excavation and Backfill) governs backfill around culverts, pipes and structures on state work; 19-3.03E is the structure backfill subsection. Field rules: structure backfill is placed in horizontal layers of the thickness the section sets and compacted to at least 95 percent relative compaction, tested under California Test 231 against California Test 216; pipe bedding and the zone around culverts follow the pipe standard plans and the contract; slurry cement backfill is its own material in 19-3 and goes only where the plans or specs call for it (keep it fluid so it fills around the pipe and keep the pipe from floating); ponding and jetting are allowed only under the conditions the specification sets, and Caltrans' Construction Manual says ponding alone is not acceptable because it does not consolidate the fill uniformly. Layer thickness, the 95 percent zone under the roadway and test frequency are edition and contract specific: read the job's edition of 19-3 and 19-5 and the special provisions, and ask the resident engineer before the first lift goes in.
field.title: Caltrans structure and trench backfill compaction (Standard Specifications Section 19-3)
field.topic: California compaction specs: relative compaction, Caltrans 19 and 26, Greenbook 306
field.source: Caltrans Standard Specifications section 19-3 (19-3.03E structure backfill) as cited in Caltrans geotechnical specification notes; Caltrans Construction Manual section 4-19; California Test 216 and 231

field.text: Caltrans Section 26 (Aggregate Bases), 26-1.03D and E: if the aggregate base thickness shown is 0.50 ft or less, spread and compact it in at least one layer; if more than 0.50 ft, in at least two layers of approximately equal thickness; the compacted thickness of any one layer must not exceed 0.50 ft (6 inches); moisture must be uniform and enough to get compaction; compact each layer to at least 95 percent relative compaction, accepted under California Test 231. Section 25 (Aggregate Subbases) has the same rules: one layer at 0.50 ft or less, two or more layers above that, no compacted layer over 0.50 ft, and at least 95 percent relative compaction. Many city and county standards built on Caltrans copy these numbers for trench patches and road base under slabs. A plate compactor will not reliably make a 6-inch compacted layer of Class 2 base in one set of passes; use a roller or thinner lifts and test.
field.title: Caltrans aggregate base and subbase layers (Sections 26 and 25): 0.50 ft layers, 95 percent
field.topic: California compaction specs: relative compaction, Caltrans 19 and 26, Greenbook 306
field.source: Caltrans Standard Specifications sections 25-1.03 and 26-1.03D, 26-1.03E (2018 edition text)

field.text: In Southern California most city and county utility work is built under the Greenbook (Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction). In the 2021 edition trench backfill material is Section 217 and placement and densification are in Section 306 (Open Trench Conduit Construction, 306-12 Backfill and Densification). The Greenbook baseline is 90 percent relative compaction for mechanically compacted trench backfill unless otherwise specified, with density against ASTM D1557; nearly every agency supplement raises it to 95 percent in the upper part under pavement and sets the depth of that zone, so the city's supplement and standard drawing are the numbers that count. Lifts no thicker than the compactor can densify; jetting or flooding only for granular backfill and only when the Engineer approves it in advance, never for clay; bedding and pipe zone material per the agency's drawing, often sand or 3/4 inch crushed rock with a minimum sand equivalent; slurry cement backfill where the agency requires it under streets. Check the edition named in the contract: section numbers moved between editions.
field.title: Greenbook (Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction) trench backfill, Section 306
field.topic: California compaction specs: relative compaction, Caltrans 19 and 26, Greenbook 306
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 Sections 217 and 306-12 as adopted and amended by Southern California agencies (for example City of Corona amendments to 306-12.3.2); ASTM D1557

field.text: Many Southern California cities require sand-cement slurry (a controlled low strength material, CLSM) instead of compacted soil for trench backfill under pavement. Crews name it by cement content: 'one-sack slurry' is about 94 lb of cement per cubic yard (one sack of portland cement is 94 lb) and 'two-sack' about 188 lb, with sand, water and sometimes fly ash. It is deliberately weak so it can be dug up later; ACI 229 treats roughly 300 psi as the upper limit for later machine excavation, and one-sack mixes sit well under that. The Greenbook class name and strength for the job come from Section 201-6 and the agency's permit; order by that class. Placement: fill from the top of the pipe zone (or from the bedding if the agency allows and the pipe is restrained against flotation) to the bottom of the pavement section; no compaction; traffic plates until it sets; pavement patch the next day or per the permit. Order by the yard from ready-mix, allow for over-break, and keep the trench from floating the pipe by filling in lifts or weighting the pipe.
field.title: Slurry backfill in California streets: one-sack and two-sack sand-cement slurry
field.topic: California compaction specs: relative compaction, Caltrans 19 and 26, Greenbook 306
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) Section 201-6 (CLSM); ACI 229R; typical city encroachment permit conditions

field.text: A nuclear gauge test (California Test 231 or ASTM D6938) takes a few minutes per spot: the technician seats the gauge on a flat spot, drives the probe to the lift depth (6 to 8 inches typical), reads wet density and moisture, and compares dry density with the maximum from California Test 216 or ASTM D1557 for that soil (a new curve is needed when the material changes). Frequency is set by the agency; typical is one test per lift per 100 to 300 ft of trench and at every structure, plus wherever the inspector suspects soft spots. A failed test means the lift is reworked (add water if dry, aerate if wet, more passes, or thinner lifts) and retested; never bury a failed lift. Record station, offset, depth, result and retest on the daily report. Clean rock backfill has no density curve and is accepted by method (lifts and passes), not by gauge.
field.title: Taking and failing a density test in California: what the inspector does and what you do
field.topic: California compaction specs: relative compaction, Caltrans 19 and 26, Greenbook 306
field.source: Caltrans California Test 231; ASTM D6938; California agency inspection practice

field.text: Southern California specs and ready-mix tickets name concrete by Greenbook class, three parts: the first number is the minimum cement (cementitious) content in pounds per cubic yard, the letter is the combined aggregate grading from the Greenbook grading table, and the last number is the minimum 28-day compressive strength in psi. So 560-C-3250 is 560 lb of cement per cubic yard, grading C, 3,250 psi: the usual class for structures, manhole bases and collars, thrust blocks and pavement patches on many agency standards. 520-C-2500 (520 lb, 2,500 psi) is the usual curb, gutter, sidewalk and extruded curb class; 520-A-2500 uses the coarser A grading for concrete pavement. The letter is a grading, not a nominal top size by itself; A is coarser than C, and the sieve limits are in Greenbook Table 200-1.4. Agencies also use 'Class 2' aggregate base and 'one-sack slurry' from the same book. When a detail says 560-C-3250, order it by that name; the plant knows the mix. Caltrans uses 'minor concrete' and concrete designated by compressive strength instead.
field.title: Greenbook concrete class names: what 560-C-3250 means (SSPWC Section 201-1)
field.topic: California concrete and asphalt specs: Greenbook classes, Caltrans, city patches, opening to traffic
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) Section 201-1 class designations and Table 200-1.4 combined aggregate gradings, as restated in agency standards (for example City of Albany Technical Provisions Section 17)

field.text: Caltrans Standard Specifications Section 90 defines concrete differently from the Greenbook. Minor concrete (curb, gutter, sidewalk, minor structures, section 90-2) is specified by a minimum cementitious material content set in the specs and the item's own section, not by a strength you test. Concrete with a specified 28-day strength of 3,600 psi or more is 'designated by compressive strength' (90-1.01D), prequalified and sampled by the resident engineer's lab; concrete not designated by strength is controlled by cementitious content and the Section 90 tables. Supplementary cementitious materials (fly ash, slag) are required as a share of the cementitious content (90-1.02B) for durability and alkali-silica reaction control. Field items that follow: discharge from a truck mixer within 1 1/2 hours or 250 drum revolutions after the cement meets the aggregate, less when the concrete is 85 F or hotter; placement temperature limits; curing compound or water cure for the specified period. On a city job built to Caltrans specs, the ticket should show the mix number the engineer approved, not just a psi.
field.title: Caltrans minor concrete and structural concrete: what the numbers mean on a state job
field.topic: California concrete and asphalt specs: Greenbook classes, Caltrans, city patches, opening to traffic
field.source: Caltrans Standard Specifications Section 90 (90-1.01D, 90-1.02B, 90-2) as summarized in Caltrans Construction Manual section 4-90 (2019)

field.text: Caltrans Section 39 requires a tack coat before each hot mix asphalt lift and on the vertical faces of cold joints and trench patches, and gives the application rates in a table by the surface being covered (new HMA, existing or milled pavement, PCC) and the emulsion grade (Section 94 covers the emulsions). The residual rates are small fractions of a gallon per square yard, higher on milled or aged surfaces and lower on fresh HMA; take the number from the contract's table, not from memory, because the edition and the emulsion change it. Practical: a thin, even, unbroken film; no puddles and no bare streaks; let it break (turn from brown to black) before paving; protect it from traffic and tracking. Prime coat goes on aggregate base before the first lift only where the plans require it, at a heavier rate the engineer sets, and needs curing time before paving. City trench patch details copy these rules: 'tack all edges' means the sawcut faces and the existing surface the T-cut sits on.
field.title: Caltrans tack coat and prime coat: what the spec controls, check the rate in the contract
field.topic: California concrete and asphalt specs: Greenbook classes, Caltrans, city patches, opening to traffic
field.source: Caltrans Standard Specifications Sections 39 (tack coat) and 94 (asphaltic emulsions); check the contract edition for rates

field.text: The street's owner, not the pipe spec, sets the patch. Common Southern California patterns, each set by the specific city's standard drawing and the encroachment permit: a T-cut in which the final sawcut is set back beyond each trench wall onto undisturbed base (12 inches is common, some cities more, or to the lane line); full-depth asphalt replacement at least equal to existing plus an added inch, with a minimum thickness, over compacted base or slurry; temporary cold mix or steel plates allowed only for a limited time; a grind-and-overlay of the full lane or half street for cuts in pavement under a moratorium (streets paved within the last few years) or for many cuts in one block; slurry seal of the lane in some cities; and compaction and asphalt density testing by the city. Los Angeles, San Diego, Orange County cities and Caltrans each have their own detail; get it before the sawcut, because the T-cut width sets the asphalt tonnage and the moratorium rules can turn a patch into a lane overlay.
field.title: City trench patch standards in Southern California: T-cuts, moratoriums and the permit
field.topic: California concrete and asphalt specs: Greenbook classes, Caltrans, city patches, opening to traffic
field.source: Southern California city standard plans for pavement restoration and encroachment permit conditions (typical patterns; the specific city's drawing governs)

field.text: Hot mix can carry traffic once it has cooled enough that tires do not mark or shove it. Finish rolling must be done before the mat cools below the cessation temperature, about 175 F for conventional dense-graded mixes (Asphalt Institute guidance), and traffic can usually go on when the surface is below about 140 to 150 F, often 30 to 60 minutes after rolling for a thin trench patch and longer for thick lifts or hot days; many agencies simply say when the surface cools to ambient or to a set temperature, measured with an infrared thermometer. Warm mix cools faster. Do not let trucks turn or stop on a fresh mat; keep tack from tracking; set plates on cold patch where the permit allows if the mat is not ready at opening time. Chip seals and slurry seals have their own longer cure (hours to a day) and a speed limit at first. Check the permit's opening time; some cities require the lane open by a clock time no matter what, so plan the paving start from the opening time backward.
field.title: When traffic can go on an asphalt patch or new mat
field.topic: California concrete and asphalt specs: Greenbook classes, Caltrans, city patches, opening to traffic
field.source: Asphalt Institute and NAPA compaction guidance (cessation temperature); typical agency opening-to-traffic practice

field.text: Concrete: the spec sets an opening strength or time; pavement and driveway aprons commonly open at a stated strength around 2,500 to 3,000 psi shown by cylinders or a maturity meter, or after a stated time (several days for normal mixes, 1 to 3 days for high-early mixes), and light foot traffic and form removal come sooner; the numbers in the contract and the engineer's direction govern, not a rule of thumb. Curb and sidewalk take foot traffic the next day and no vehicles until the spec says. Flowable fill and one-sack slurry: excavatable mixes set in a few hours and can carry plates and light traffic the same day, pavement the next day when the surface is firm and no water bleeds up (NRMCA CIP 17; the mix and weather change this); do not pave over slurry that is still soft. Thrust blocks: pressure test only after the block reaches the strength or age the spec names, commonly 7 days or a stated psi. Manhole collars and frames set in concrete: no traffic until the spec time, usually 1 to 3 days or a high-early mix.
field.title: When traffic or loads can go on concrete, flowable fill and slurry backfill
field.topic: California concrete and asphalt specs: Greenbook classes, Caltrans, city patches, opening to traffic
field.source: ACI 325/330 practice; NRMCA CIP 17; typical utility and city specifications (the contract governs)

field.text: Tickets from a Greenbook-area plant show the mix by class and number, for example 560-C-3250 or '520-C-2500 P' (pea gravel pump mix), plus batch time, yards, slump ordered, water held out ('WH 5 gal'), air if specified, and admixtures (water reducer, accelerator, fiber). Checks before discharge: class matches the detail (a thrust block detail calling for 560-C-3250 cannot take 520-C-2500); batch time against the discharge limit (ASTM C94: 1 1/2 hours or 300 drum revolutions unless the purchaser allows otherwise; Greenbook also uses 90 minutes from the addition of water at the plant, and the Engineer can shorten it in hot weather); slump within the spec range before adding any held-out water, and add only what the ticket allows, once, mixed in for at least 30 revolutions; temperature under the hot-weather limit the spec sets; and that the driver has not added water on the way. Photograph the ticket and attach it in the app's field ticket with the Use (thrust block, collar, manhole base) so the yardage lands on the right job line.
field.title: Reading a Southern California ready-mix ticket for a utility pour
field.topic: California concrete and asphalt specs: Greenbook classes, Caltrans, city patches, opening to traffic
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) Section 201-1 (as restated in agency technical provisions); ASTM C94; app field tickets

field.text: In California construction stormwater is covered by the State Water Board's Construction General Permit (CGP), Order 2022-0057-DWQ, adopted September 8, 2022 and effective September 1, 2023, not EPA's permit. Coverage is required for projects that disturb 1 acre or more of soil, or less than 1 acre when part of a larger common plan of development; linear underground and overhead utility projects (pipelines) are covered too, as LUPs, by disturbed area. The owner's Legally Responsible Person (LRP) files the Notice of Intent and the permit registration documents (SWPPP, site map, risk level) in the SMARTS online system before grading, pays the fee, and files a Notice of Termination when the site is finally stabilized. The contractor usually runs the SWPPP day to day, but the LRP holds the permit. Under 1 acre: the city's own erosion control and MS4 rules still apply (silt fence, inlet protection, no sediment in the street or storm drain). Discharges of sediment, slurry or washout can draw per-day penalties from the Regional Board and stop-work from the city.
field.title: California Construction General Permit: who needs coverage and who signs (CGP, SWRCB)
field.topic: California Construction General Permit (SWPPP) in plain words
field.source: California SWRCB Construction General Permit, Order 2022-0057-DWQ (adopted Sept. 8, 2022, effective Sept. 1, 2023)

field.text: The CGP requires two certified roles. A Qualified SWPPP Developer (QSD: a licensed engineer, geologist, landscape architect or holder of a listed erosion-control certification who has passed the state QSD training) writes and amends the SWPPP and sets the site's risk level, and under the 2022 permit stays involved for the life of the job with periodic site inspections. A Qualified SWPPP Practitioner (QSP: holds the state QSP certificate on top of a listed prerequisite certification; often the superintendent or a consultant; a QSD may act as QSP) implements it: the routine weekly inspections, the inspections before, during and after qualifying precipitation events, sampling where required, training the crew, and keeping the records in SMARTS. For a pipe crew the QSP is the person who tells you where the fiber rolls, inlet protection, stabilized entrance, concrete washout and stockpile covers go, and who signs off dewatering discharges. Any change to the site (new stockpile, new entrance, dewatering) goes through the QSP before it happens.
field.title: QSD and QSP: who writes and who runs the SWPPP on a California job
field.topic: California Construction General Permit (SWPPP) in plain words
field.source: California CGP (Order 2022-0057-DWQ) QSD/QSP provisions; CASQA guidance

field.text: The CGP sorts sites into Risk Level 1, 2 or 3 (Risk Type 1 to 3 for linear projects) from the site's sediment risk (soil erodibility, slope, rainfall) and the receiving water's sensitivity. The 2022 permit dropped the Rain Event Action Plan (REAP) and replaced it with inspections and actions keyed to a 'qualifying precipitation event' (QPE): a National Weather Service forecast with a 50 percent or greater chance of 0.5 inch or more of precipitation in a 24-hour period (it continues while each following day forecasts 0.25 inch or more). For a QPE: a QSP inspection within 72 hours before it starts (up to 120 hours ahead with a longer forecast), an inspection every 24 hours while it lasts, and a post-event inspection within 96 hours if the site rain gauge recorded 0.5 inch or more. Risk Level 2 and 3 sites also sample turbidity and pH at each discharging location once per 24-hour period against numeric action levels. All levels: inspections at least weekly, BMP maintenance, forecasts checked weekly, records in SMARTS. Discharging muddy trench water, sawcut slurry or concrete washout to a street or inlet is a violation at any level; retain and treat it on site, or haul it.
field.title: Risk levels, qualifying precipitation events and inspections under the 2022 California CGP
field.topic: California Construction General Permit (SWPPP) in plain words
field.source: California CGP (Order 2022-0057-DWQ) risk level, QPE and monitoring provisions; State Water Board 2022 CGP Qualifying Precipitation Event guidance

field.text: The BMPs a utility crew actually touches (names from the CASQA Construction BMP Handbook): stabilized construction entrance (rock pad or shaker plates) so trucks do not track mud; fiber rolls or silt fence downslope of spoil piles and along the trench line; storm drain inlet protection (gravel bags, filter inserts) at every inlet downstream of the work; stockpile management (cover or berm spoil and base piles, keep them off the gutter); dewatering through a filter bag or settling tank with the QSP's approval, never straight to a storm drain; concrete and slurry washout in a lined washout, not the trench or the street; street sweeping (not hosing) at the end of each day; spill kits on the crew truck for hydraulic oil and fuel; trash and debris contained (the 2022 permit added a specific trash prohibition); and tracking it all on the daily report. Inspectors photograph the gutter: if sediment is in the street, the crew failed, not the QSP.
field.title: Pipe crew BMPs that satisfy the California CGP and the city inspector
field.topic: California Construction General Permit (SWPPP) in plain words
field.source: CASQA Construction BMP Handbook; California CGP (Order 2022-0057-DWQ)

field.text: California's one-call law is Government Code 4216 to 4216.24. There are two regional notification centers: Underground Service Alert of Southern California (DigAlert, digalert.org) and USA North 811 (usanorth811.org) for the rest of the state; dialing 811 or going online reaches the right one. Process: (1) delineate (white-line) the dig area before you call (4216.2(a)); (2) file the ticket at least 2 working days before digging, not counting the day you call, and not more than 14 calendar days before (4216.2(b)) (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day); (3) operators mark their lines or report no conflict by the legal start date and post an electronic positive response you can check on the ticket (4216.3); (4) inside the tolerance zone (24 inches each side of the mark) find the line with hand tools, or vacuum excavation if the operator agreed, before any power equipment (4216.4); (5) the ticket is good for 28 days; renew by the end of the 28th day or stop digging (4216.2(e), (i)). Private lines past the operator's service point are not marked. This is a plain-language summary; the law and the center's excavator manual govern.
field.title: California 811: DigAlert and USA North, how a locate request works (Gov Code 4216)
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216, 4216.2, 4216.3, 4216.4 (as amended through Jan. 1, 2025); DigAlert and USA North 811 excavator guidance

field.text: Gov Code 4216.2(b): notify the regional notification center at least 2 working days and not more than 14 calendar days before you start digging; the day you call does not count. A working day is Monday to Friday, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., except state and federal holidays (4216(v)). The ticket is valid for 28 days from the date it is issued; if work continues past that, renew it online or by calling 811 by the end of the 28th day (4216.2(e)). If a ticket expires while work is going on, you must stop digging at once, get a new ticket, and wait for the operators to respond again before resuming (4216.2(i)). You may not start until every operator has responded and any required onsite meeting is done (4216.2(g)). If marks are no longer reasonably visible, re-notify the center and stop digging in that area until it is remarked; the operator has 2 working days to remark, and if your white lines have faded you re-delineate first (4216.3(b)). The notice period does not apply in an emergency as defined in 4216(f), but the center still takes an emergency ticket. The app's Locates screen shows Can dig from, Start work by and the expiry for these rules.
field.title: California ticket timing: 2 working days, 14 days ahead, 28 days valid (Gov Code 4216.2)
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216(v), 4216.2(b), (e), (g), (i), 4216.3(b); app Locates screen

field.text: Gov Code 4216.2(a): before notifying the regional notification center, the excavator must delineate the area to be excavated. If it is not delineated, an operator may choose not to locate and mark until it is. Delineate means to mark in white the location or path of the proposed excavation, following the Common Ground Alliance delineation guidelines (4216(d)); if white marks could be confused with traffic markings, flags, stakes or other markers may be used as long as the center is told. Use the standard white-lining symbols: dashes along a trench line, corners and 'X' marks for pits, arrows and 'TO' for a run. If a very long alignment cannot practically be painted, describe the limits precisely on the ticket and ask the center how it wants the area shown (map or electronic delineation). Why it matters: locators mark only within your delineation; a line outside it is legally unmarked, and digging there is digging without a locate. Keep the white lines visible while the ticket is open; when they fade and you need a remark, re-delineate first (4216.3(b)). On private property that needs no excavation permit, the same delineation rule applies when you contact the center (4216.2(d)).
field.title: Delineation (white-lining) is required in California before the call (Gov Code 4216.2(a))
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216(d), 4216.2(a), (d), 4216.3(b)

field.text: Gov Code 4216(u) defines the tolerance zone as 24 inches on each side of the operator's field marking: 24 inches each side of a single mark (treated as the centerline); 24 inches plus half the marked size each side when the mark states the size; or 24 inches outside each edge mark when the operator paints the outside edges. Inside that zone, 4216.4(a) requires you to find the exact location of the line with hand tools before any power-operated or boring equipment is used there, and to use reasonable care. Vacuum excavation may be used instead only if you told the center when you got the ticket and the operator agreed (an operator that objects says so in its positive response). Power equipment may remove pavement in the zone only if there is no known installation in the pavement. Treat every line as live, even if it looks abandoned (4216.4(a)(3)). If hand digging cannot find the line, ask the operator; it has one working day to give what it has (4216.4(b)). Marks show horizontal position only, never depth. Pothole every marked line your trench will cross before the machine gets there, support it, and keep a spotter on the bucket. Many states use 18 inches; California is 24.
field.title: California tolerance zone: 24 inches each side, hand tools or vacuum only (Gov Code 4216, 4216.4)
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216(u) tolerance zone definition; 4216.4(a) and (b)

field.text: Gov Code 4216.3(a): before the legal excavation start date each operator on the ticket must locate and mark its lines in the delineated area, give you what information it has on where they are, or tell you it has none there; known abandoned lines are marked with an A in a circle. 4216.3(c): each operator must also post an electronic positive response through the center before the legal start date, and the center must make those responses available to you on the ticket. 4216.2(g): except in an emergency, you may not begin until every operator on the ticket has done this and any required onsite meeting is complete. Before starting each area: pull up the ticket, confirm every listed operator shows marked or no conflict, and look for paint that matches. If an operator has not responded, or marks are missing where you expected a line, notify the center of the failure to respond (4216.3(d) requires this, with the ticket number) and do not dig there with a machine until it is resolved or the line is located by other means. A ticket with an unresolved operator is not a green light. Document the check (screenshot or note on the daily report).
field.title: Positive response in California: check every operator's status before you dig (Gov Code 4216.3)
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216.2(g), 4216.3(a), (c), (d); DigAlert / USA North 811 positive response systems

field.text: Gov Code 4216(j) defines high priority subsurface installations: natural gas pipelines with normal operating pressure above 60 psig, petroleum pipelines, pressurized sewage pipelines, electric supply lines, conductors or cables at 60 kV or more to ground, and hazardous materials pipelines that could endanger workers or the public if damaged. 4216.2(c): when your excavation is proposed within 10 feet of one, the operator must notify you and arrange an onsite meeting before the legal start date (or another agreed time); at the meeting you go over your methods and tools and the operator says what information and support it will give; you may not begin excavating until the meeting is complete. Cal/OSHA repeats the onsite meeting requirement in Title 8 section 1541(b)(1)(B). Expect: exact location by potholing, no machine digging in the tolerance zone, the operator's own clearance and support rules, possibly an operator standby, and a written record of the meeting. Damage to a high priority installation is a 911 call, not just a call to the operator (4216.4(c)(1)). If you get a high-priority notice and nobody has met you onsite, stop and call the operator before digging.
field.title: High priority subsurface installations in California: onsite meeting before you dig (Gov Code 4216(j), 4216.2(c))
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216(j), 4216.2(c), 4216.4(c)(1); 8 CCR 1541(b)(1)(B)

field.text: Gov Code 4216.4(c): if you discover or cause any damage to a subsurface installation, including a break, leak, nick, dent, gouge, groove or damage to the coating or cathodic protection, you must notify the operator immediately. If the damage is to a gas or hazardous liquid pipeline and any flammable, toxic or corrosive gas or liquid is escaping, or the damaged line is a high priority installation, you must immediately call 911 first, then the operator. You must also notify the regional notification center within 48 hours of the damage (4216.4(c)(3)). Steps at a gas strike: stop the machine and leave it where it is (do not restart engines near the leak, no phones or radios in the gas cloud); get everyone upwind and well back; keep the public and traffic away; no smoking, no sparks, no attempt to crimp, plug or bury the line; let the gas company shut it in. Nobody goes back into a trench near the leak. Afterwards: photos of the marks and the damage from a safe distance, the ticket number, and a damage report; the operator and the Dig Safe Board can investigate whether the ticket, marks and tolerance zone rules were followed. Report near misses to the foreman too.
field.title: Hit a gas line in California: what to do and who to call (Gov Code 4216.4)
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216.4(c)(1), (c)(2), (c)(3); 8 CCR 1541(b)(5); gas operator damage guidance

field.text: Electric strike: if the bucket contacts a live cable or duct, the operator stays on the machine and tells everyone to stay back at least 35 ft (utility guidance; the ground around the machine can be energized); back the bucket clear only if the machine can move safely; if the machine catches fire, the operator jumps clear with feet together and shuffles away, never touching machine and ground at once. Call 911 and the electric utility; a line at 60 kV or more is a high priority installation, so 911 is required by law for damage to it (Gov Code 4216.4(c)(1)). Notify the operator immediately for any damage, even a nick in the jacket (4216.4(c)(2)); a nicked conductor fails later. Fiber and telecom strikes are not an injury hazard but are expensive: do not pull or cut the cable, protect the ends, call the owner immediately; cut fiber can mean a large claim and a locate-ticket review. Water strike: shut the machine down, call the water utility, keep people out of the flooded trench (undermined walls), and expect the utility to control the shutdown. Every strike also goes to the regional notification center within 48 hours (4216.4(c)(3)).
field.title: Hit an electric line or fiber in California: operator stays put, everyone else back
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: Utility and OSHA guidance on electrical contact with equipment; California Government Code 4216(j), 4216.4(c)

field.text: Pipeline jobs outlast one ticket, so plan locates like materials. Practice that fits the California rules: file tickets by reach (manhole to manhole or by block) 2 working days ahead of when the crew will get there, never more than 14 calendar days ahead; keep a board or the app's Locates list with each ticket's area, start date and 28-day expiry; renew 2 to 3 working days before the 28th day so there is no gap, because an expired ticket means stop digging until a new ticket is answered (4216.2(i)); re-notify the center for a remark when paving, grading or rain wipes the paint and stop in that area until it is remarked (4216.3(b)); keep the white lines fresh as the work moves; check positive response each morning for the area you will open that day; and keep the dig footprint inside the delineated and ticketed area (service trenches and bore pits included). A ticket does not cover a new area added later; file a new one. The app alerts at 7 days, 2 days and the day of expiry.
