field.title: Long jobs and moving crews: keeping California tickets valid area by area
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216.2(b), (e), (i), 4216.3(b); field practice

field.text: 811 in California covers subsurface installations owned by operators that belong to the regional notification center, up to the point where the operator's responsibility ends (meter, property line or the connection point the operator sets). Not marked: the customer's own water and sewer services past that point, private gas after the meter, landscape lighting and irrigation, private fiber and site electrical to outbuildings, septic systems, abandoned lines nobody claims, and lines of small owners that are not members. Note also that nonpressurized sewer lines and storm drains are not 'subsurface installations' under Gov Code 4216(s), so they may not be marked at all. Treat the dig area as having unknown lines anyway: look for valve boxes, cleanouts, risers, pedestals and old trench scars; hire a private locating service with a sonde or electromagnetic locator for the private side; pothole before the machine. Marks never show depth; a line marked at the surface can be 6 inches or 6 feet down, so slow, thin cuts and a spotter are the rule near any mark.
field.title: What California 811 does not cover: private lines, depth, and lines nobody owns
field.topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
field.source: California Government Code 4216(q), (s) (member operator and subsurface installation scope); CGA best practices

field.text: California's Waterworks Standards, Title 22 section 64572, set the separation for new water mains, and the horizontal and vertical rules are different. Horizontal, parallel runs: at least 10 ft from any pipeline carrying untreated sewage (gravity sewer or force main), primary or secondary treated sewage, disinfected secondary-2.2 or secondary-23 recycled water, or hazardous fluids such as fuel, industrial waste or sludge; a new water main may not share a trench with any of these (64572(a)). At least 4 ft from a pipeline carrying disinfected tertiary recycled water or storm drainage (64572(b)). Vertical: in every case the water main must be at least 1 ft above the other pipe, and that vertical rule applies only when the two pipes are closer than 10 ft horizontally (64572(e)). The one line that goes below a water main is a raw-water supply line headed to a treatment plant: 4 ft horizontal and 1 ft below (64572(c)). All distances are outside of pipe barrel to outside of pipe barrel (64572(g)). This is not the Ten States 18-inch rule used in many other states; the water agency's standards can be stricter, and the stricter one governs.
field.title: California water main separation: 10 ft or 4 ft horizontal, 1 ft vertical with water on top (22 CCR 64572)
field.topic: California water and sewer separation (22 CCR 64572, DDW criteria)
field.source: 22 CCR 64572(a), (b), (c), (e), (g) (California Waterworks Standards, Water Main Separation)

field.text: 22 CCR 64572(d): where a new water main crosses a pipeline carrying any of the fluids in 64572(a) or (b) (sewage, force mains, recycled water, hazardous fluids, storm drain), the water main must cross at an angle of no less than 45 degrees to the other pipe and at least 1 ft above it, outside of barrel to outside of barrel, and no connection joint may be made in the water main within 8 horizontal ft of the pipeline it crosses. In practice: a full stick of water main centered on the crossing, no couplings, services or fittings in that 16 ft window, and skew crossings straightened to 45 degrees or better. The regulation does not provide for a water main crossing under a sewer or storm drain; if the profile shows the water main below, or less than 1 ft between pipe walls, or a joint inside the 8 ft, it needs an approved alternative before pipe goes in (next chunk). 64572(f): no new water main within 100 ft of a landfill, wastewater pond or hazardous waste site, or within 25 ft of a cesspool, septic tank, leach field, seepage pit, underground hazardous material tank or recharge site. If the plan violates any of this, it is an RFI before the trench is open.
field.title: Crossings under 22 CCR 64572(d): 45 degrees or more, water 1 ft above, no water main joint within 8 ft
field.topic: California water and sewer separation (22 CCR 64572, DDW criteria)

field.text: 22 CCR 64572(g): separation is measured from the nearest outside edge of each pipe barrel, not invert to invert. Top outside of the lower pipe = its invert + outside diameter - one wall (for 8 inch SDR 35 sewer, OD 8.40 in and wall 0.24 in: invert + 8.16 in = 0.68 ft). Bottom outside of the upper pipe = its invert minus its wall (8 inch C900 DR 18: wall 0.503 in = 0.042 ft; 8 inch ductile iron pressure class 350: 0.25 in plus lining). Example: sewer IE 100.00, water IE 101.60 above it: sewer top outside 100.68, water bottom outside 101.56, clearance 0.88 ft = 10.5 in, under California's 12 in and under the 18 in many agency standards use. Reading invert to invert (1.60 ft) would hide the problem. Check every crossing on the profile the same way, check the crossing angle (45 degrees minimum) and where the water main joints fall (none within 8 ft), and pothole the existing line: profiles show existing utilities as approximate. Use the app's calc for the arithmetic and the pipe table for walls.
field.title: Measuring the crossing clearance on a California profile: outside to outside, not invert to invert
field.topic: California water and sewer separation (22 CCR 64572, DDW criteria)
field.source: 22 CCR 64572(d), (g) applied to plan reading; pipe dimensions from ASTM D3034, AWWA C900 and AWWA C151

field.text: There is no automatic 'special construction' fix in 22 CCR 64572. The old DDW memo 2003-02 ('Criteria for the Separation of Water Mains and Non-Potable Pipelines') was withdrawn by the Division of Drinking Water in December 2017; do not use it. When 10 ft or 4 ft horizontal, 1 ft vertical with water on top, the 45 degree crossing or the 8 ft joint rule cannot be met, the water system must request an alternative under 22 CCR 64551.100: show the State Board it gives at least the same public health protection, and get written State Board (DDW) approval before it is built. DDW has a 'Main Separation Alternative Request' checklist for this. Agency standards typically use the sewer in pressure-rated gasketed PVC or fused HDPE with no sewer joint in the affected zone, a sleeve or encasement, and extra clearance; the numbers come from the agency's approved standard, not from Ask. A water main never runs through a sewer manhole. 64572(h) lets the State Board exempt a short replacement main (under 1,320 ft, same alignment, no more than 6 inches larger, sleeved or upgraded material). A profile that fails the regulation is an RFI to the engineer and the water agency before pipe goes in.
field.title: When the California separation can't be met: State Board approved alternative, not a field decision
field.topic: California water and sewer separation (22 CCR 64572, DDW criteria)
field.source: 22 CCR 64572(h); 22 CCR 64551.100; DDW letter to public water systems, Dec. 14, 2017 (superseding Guidance Memo 2003-02); DDW Main Separation Alternative Request checklist

field.text: OSHA's Appendix E to 1910.146 explains how sewer entry differs: the space rarely can be isolated (it is one piece of a continuous system), so the atmosphere can suddenly and unpredictably become lethally hazardous from upstream discharges beyond anyone's control; and sewer crews should keep contact with the weather service and emergency services to get warning of surge flow and flooding. The construction rule says the same thing in 1926.1204(e)(1): continuous monitoring where entrants work and an early-warning system for engulfment. So: a sewer permit space is never 'tested clean' once; monitoring is continuous with alarms at 19.5 percent O2, 10 percent LEL, 10 ppm H2S and 25 ppm CO (the Cal/OSHA limit; many meters ship at 35 ppm, so set them lower), or the company's stricter limits, the attendant watches flow and weather (rain upstream), entrants are harnessed on a retrieval line, and everyone exits on any alarm, rising flow or unusual smell. Forced ventilation runs for the whole entry. H2S deadens the nose at roughly 100 ppm, so a rotten-egg smell that fades is a warning, not relief. Treat every manhole as a permit space unless the competent person has evaluated it otherwise.
field.title: Sewer entries: why they are different (1910.146 Appendix E) and how crews handle them
field.topic: Confined space numbers for construction crews (29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA) in one place
field.source: 29 CFR 1910.146 Appendix E; 1926.1204(e)(1); NIOSH hydrogen sulfide guidance

field.text: OSHA's Table B-1 (Appendix B to Subpart P) gives the steepest slope allowed for excavations less than 20 ft deep, as horizontal to vertical: stable rock, vertical (90 degrees); Type A, 3/4 to 1 (53 degrees); Type B, 1 to 1 (45 degrees); Type C, 1 1/2 to 1 (34 degrees). Footnote 2: a short-term slope of 1/2 to 1 (63 degrees) is allowed in Type A only for excavations 12 ft or less deep; short term means open 24 hours or less; a short-term Type A cut deeper than 12 ft goes back to 3/4 to 1. Footnote 3: sloping or benching deeper than 20 ft must be designed by a registered professional engineer; since the table covers only less than 20 ft, exactly 20 ft and deeper is engineer-designed (the app's Trench Sloping screen says the same). Lay-back per side = depth x ratio: a 10 ft Type C trench lays back 15 ft each side. When there are signs of distress (fissures, slumping, bulging or heaving at the bottom, spalling, ravelling), the slope must be cut back at least 1/2 horizontal to 1 vertical flatter than the table (Appendix B (c)(3)). The OSHA library chunk for Appendix B (c) carries Table B-1 as text; this chunk is a plain-language copy of the official table, and the competent person picks the system.
field.title: Table B-1 maximum allowable slopes (OSHA 1926 Subpart P Appendix B), in words
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Table B-1 with footnotes 1-3 and paragraphs (b), (c)(3)

field.text: Appendix B Figure B-1 shows the only bench shapes OSHA allows without an engineer. Type A (cohesive, 1.5 tsf or more): simple bench or multiple benches with the overall profile inside 3/4 to 1; the bottom (first) bench is at most 4 ft high and benches above it at most 5 ft. Type B: single or multiple benches inside 1 to 1, each bench at most 4 ft, and only in cohesive Type B soil (no benching in granular Type B). Type C: no benching at all; slope it 1 1/2 to 1, shore it, or shield it. Benching from this figure is for excavations less than 20 ft deep; at 20 ft or deeper a registered professional engineer designs it. A bench cut taller than the figure allows, or a bench in Type C or in granular soil, is an unprotected vertical face. Because benching eats width (a 10 ft Type B trench needs 20 ft of lay-back plus the bottom), it is used in open ground, not streets. The competent person classifies the soil and picks the system; this is a word copy of a drawing, check the official figure.
field.title: Figure B-1 benching rules in words: 4 ft first bench, Type A and B only
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Figure B-1 (bench dimensions as summarized in OSHA's Trenching and Excavation publication and OSHA-based training material)

field.text: Appendix B Figure B-1 also shows two mixed shapes. (1) Unsupported vertically sided lower portion, Type A soil only: the bottom of the cut may stand vertical for at most 3.5 ft with the rest sloped at 3/4 to 1 when the whole excavation is 8 ft or less deep; for 8 to 12 ft deep the vertical part is still 3.5 ft maximum but the slope above must be 1 to 1. Type B and Type C get no unsupported vertical foot. (2) Supported or shielded vertically sided lower portion, all three soil types, 20 ft or less: a trench box or shoring in the bottom with sloping above at the soil's maximum slope (A 3/4:1, B 1:1, C 1 1/2:1), and the shield or support must extend at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side so material sliding down the slope cannot drop into the box. Separately, 1926.652(g)(2) allows digging up to 2 ft below the bottom of a shield when the shield is designed for the full depth and there is no sign of soil loss from behind or below it. Any other shape is an engineer's design or tabulated data under 1926.652(b)(3), (b)(4).
field.title: Vertically sided lower portion: 3.5 ft unsupported in Type A only, and shield plus slope (18 in rule)
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Figure B-1 (Type A, B, C vertically sided lower portion configurations); 1926.652(g)(2)

field.text: Appendix C gives timber shoring (crossbraces, wales, uprights) for trenches up to 20 ft deep without an engineer. Tables C-1.1 (Type A), C-1.2 (Type B) and C-1.3 (Type C) are for mixed oak or equivalent (850 psi bending); Tables C-2.1 to C-2.3 are the same layout for Douglas fir (1,500 psi). Each table runs by depth band (5 to 10, 10 to 15, 15 to 20 ft; over 20 ft, see note 1 and get an engineer) and trench width (up to 4, 6, 9, 12, 15 ft), and gives crossbrace, wale and upright sizes and spacings; 'close' means planks side by side, and tight sheeting (tongue and groove, 3 inch minimum, or steel sheets) is required in saturated or submerged soil. OSHA's own Example 1: a 13 ft deep, 5 ft wide trench in Type A, from Table C-1.1, arrangement B1: 4 x 4 crossbraces at 6 ft horizontal and 4 ft vertical, no wales, 3 x 8 uprights at 6 ft (skip shoring); three other arrangements are listed. The tables do not apply with equipment over 20,000 lb next to the trench, stored material or structures beyond a 2 ft soil surcharge, or crossbrace vertical loads over 240 lb per foot; then it is tabulated data or an engineer under 1926.652(c). Read the whole row before building from it.
field.title: How to use Appendix C timber shoring tables (Tables C-1.1 to C-1.3)
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix C, paragraphs (c), (d), (e), (g) Example 1, Tables C-1.1 to C-2.3

field.text: Appendix D covers aluminum hydraulic shores (speed shores) and waler systems for trenches up to 20 ft deep. Tables D-1.1 (Type A), D-1.2 (Type B) and D-1.3 (Type C) give, by depth and trench width, the cylinder size (2 inch, rated at least 18,000 lb, or 3 inch, 30,000 lb) and the maximum horizontal and vertical spacing of vertical shores; D-1.4 covers waler systems, and Type C always needs sheeting. OSHA's Example 1: 6 ft deep, 3 ft wide, Type A, from Table D-1.1: 2 inch cylinders at 8 ft on center horizontally and 4 ft vertically. Rules in the appendix: at least three evenly spaced shores in a group; plywood between shores only stops ravelling and is not structural; the tables do not apply with equipment over 20,000 lb next to the trench, crossbrace vertical loads over 100 lb per foot, or shoring only the lower part of a sloped trench unless the slope is flatter than 3 to 1 or members are picked for the full depth. Hydraulic shores are set and pumped from the top so nobody enters an unprotected trench to install them. Most crews use the shore maker's own tabulated data under 1926.652(c)(2), which must be on site; outside the table, it is tabulated data or an engineer.
field.title: How to use Appendix D aluminum hydraulic shoring tables (Tables D-1.1 to D-1.4)
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D, paragraphs (c), (d), (g) footnotes 2, 3, 6, 7 and Example 1, Tables D-1.1 to D-1.4

field.text: A trench box (shield) is used under 1926.652(c)(2) or (c)(3): the manufacturer's tabulated data (or a registered engineer's) sets the maximum depth by soil type, the allowable surcharge, whether stacking and spreader extensions are allowed, and the sloped-trench rules. Typical box data: a depth rating for Type A, B and C (deepest in A, shallowest in C), rated lateral pressure in psf, allowed spreader lengths, and notes that the rating assumes the box sits on the trench bottom (or up to 2 ft above it when designed for the full depth, 1926.652(g)(2)). The competent person checks: the data sheet is on site and matches this box and these spreaders; the trench depth plus any dig below the box is within the rating for the soil type they classified; surcharge from spoil and machines is within the data; no bent walls, cracked welds or damaged lifting eyes; the box is sized so people stay inside it; and where sloping is used above the box, it reaches at least 18 inches above the toe of the slope (Appendix B). Employees may not be in the shield when it is being installed, removed or moved vertically (1926.652(g)(1)(iv)). A box past its rating is no protection; stop and ask.
field.title: Trench box tabulated data: what it says and what the competent person checks
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(c)(2), (c)(3), (g)(1), (g)(2); Appendix B Figure B-1; shield manufacturer tabulated data (general)

field.text: Appendix A requires at least one visual and one manual test by the competent person. Visual: soil as dug (clumps = cohesive, runs = granular), layers and their dip, cracks and fissures, water seeping, previous excavation scars, vibration sources, surcharge. Manual tests: thumb penetration (indents only with great effort = about 1.5 tsf, Type A range; pushes in several inches easily = 0.5 tsf or less, Type C); pocket penetrometer or shearvane for a number; plasticity (roll a 1/8 inch thread 2 inches long without breaking = cohesive); dry strength; wet shake (dilatancy). Not Type A no matter how hard it feels: fissured soil, soil subject to vibration (traffic, pile driving, machines), previously disturbed soil (old trench backfill, fill), layers dipping into the cut at 4H:1V or steeper, and soil with seeping water. Granular soils such as gravel, sand and loamy sand are Type C (angular gravel, silt, silt loam and sandy loam can be Type B, so the competent person classifies them and treats doubtful soil as Type C); submerged soil or soil with freely seeping water is Type C; a layered deposit is classified by its weakest layer, except that layers may be classified individually where a more stable layer lies under a less stable one.
field.title: Appendix A soil tests in words: visual plus one manual test, and what rules out Type A
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A, paragraphs (b) definitions of Type A, B, C and (d) acceptance criteria (plain-language summary)

field.text: Top width = bottom width + 2 x depth x slope ratio. Examples for a 4 ft bottom: 6 ft deep Type A (3/4:1): 4 + 2 x 6 x 0.75 = 13 ft. 8 ft deep Type B (1:1): 4 + 16 = 20 ft. 8 ft deep Type C (1.5:1): 4 + 24 = 28 ft. 12 ft deep Type C: 4 + 36 = 40 ft. Type A short-term (1/2:1, 12 ft or less, open 24 h or less): 10 ft deep: 4 + 10 = 14 ft. Shield in the bottom with Type C slope above: in a 10 ft trench with a 6 ft tall box on the bottom, the box must stick up 18 inches above the toe of the slope, so the vertical side can be at most 4.5 ft and the slope covers the top 5.5 ft; at 1.5:1 that is 8.25 ft of lay-back each side, so the top width is the box's outside width plus about 16.5 ft. Excavated volume grows with the square of depth on sloped cuts, which is why boxes win in streets. Use the app's Trench Sloping calculator for the exact numbers; the competent person picks the system.
field.title: Worked trench widths: how much room sloping and benching take
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: Geometry from OSHA Appendix B Table B-1 slopes and Figure B-1 shield-and-slope rule; app Trench Sloping calculator

field.text: Approximate weights for solid-wall PVC gravity sewer pipe from a manufacturer's submittal table (pipe only; the maker's current sheet governs for lifting plans): SDR 35, ASTM D3034: 4 in (OD 4.215) about 1.1 lb/ft; 6 in (6.275) 2.4; 8 in (8.400) 4.3; 10 in (10.50) 6.7; 12 in (12.50) 9.6; 15 in (15.30) 14.4. Larger sizes are ASTM F679 PS 46: 18 in (OD 18.70) about 22 lb/ft; 21 in (22.05) 31; 24 in (24.80) 39; 27 in (27.95) 50. Per stick: multiply by 14 ft (common sewer length) or 20 ft: an 8 in 14 ft stick is about 60 lb, a 12 in 14 ft stick about 135 lb, a 15 in 20 ft stick about 290 lb, a 24 in 20 ft stick about 780 lb. SDR 26 (and F679 PS 115) is about one third heavier. Two people can handle 8 in and smaller; 12 in and up is a machine lift. Full skids: see trucks-capacity-22 for feet per truckload.
field.title: PVC SDR 35 sewer pipe weight per foot and per stick (ASTM D3034 and F679)
field.topic: Pipe weights per foot and per stick, and how to lift pipe
field.source: Manufacturer submittal weight table for ASTM D3034 SDR 35/26 and ASTM F679 PS 46/115 PVC sewer pipe (approximate weights per foot); Westlake and Lasco dimension sheets for OD and wall

field.text: Approximate weights for C900 PVC pressure pipe (cast iron OD, 20 ft laying length) from JM Eagle's Blue Brute submittal table: DR 18 (235 psi): 4 in (OD 4.80, wall 0.267) 2.6 lb/ft; 6 in (6.90, 0.383) 5.3; 8 in (9.05, 0.503) 9.2; 10 in (11.10, 0.617) 13.9; 12 in (13.20, 0.733) 19.7. DR 14 (305 psi): 4 in 3.2; 6 in 6.7; 8 in 11.6 (about 25 percent heavier than DR 18). DR 25 (165 psi): 4 in 1.9; 6 in 3.9; 8 in 6.7; 10 in 10.1; 12 in 14.4 (about 30 percent lighter than DR 18). A 20 ft stick: 6 in DR 18 about 105 lb, 8 in about 185 lb, 12 in about 395 lb. Other makers are within a few percent; use the sheet for the pipe on site. C900 is laid with a machine and a pipe sling or a rated pipe hook; the bell end is heavier, so balance the pick a little toward the bell. Keep gasketed bells out of the dirt when setting pipe down.
field.title: PVC C900 water pipe weight per foot: DR 18, DR 14 and DR 25 (AWWA C900, JM Eagle table)
field.topic: Pipe weights per foot and per stick, and how to lift pipe
field.source: JM Eagle Blue Brute C900 submittal and data sheet (approximate weight lbs/ft, DR 14, 18, 25), rev. 2017; AWWA C900 dimensions

field.text: Ductile iron is heavy. McWane Ductile's standard dimensions and weights table for Tyton (push-on) joint pipe, pressure class 350, 18 ft nominal laying length, average weight per foot including the bell, before cement lining: 4 in (OD 4.80, wall 0.25) 11.3 lb/ft; 6 in (6.90, 0.25) 16.6; 8 in (9.05, 0.25) 22.0; 10 in (11.10, 0.26) 28.4; 12 in (13.20, 0.28) 36.4; 16 in (17.40, 0.34) 58.8; 24 in (25.80, 0.43) 110.2. Per 18 ft stick: 4 in about 225 lb, 6 in about 300, 8 in about 395, 10 in about 510, 12 in about 655, 16 in about 1,060, 24 in about 1,985. Standard cement-mortar lining adds roughly 1 to 3 lb/ft depending on size; thicker pressure or special thickness classes weigh more, and 20 ft sticks weigh more per length. Use the maker's table for the pipe actually delivered. Never roll or drop DI into the trench: the lining cracks and the coating scars. Lift with a nylon sling around the barrel near the balance point or a rated pipe hook in the bell; chains scar the coating.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe weight per foot: pressure class 350 push-on, McWane table (add lining)
field.topic: Pipe weights per foot and per stick, and how to lift pipe
field.source: McWane Ductile submittal sheet, Tyton Joint Pipe standard dimensions and weights (PC 350, 18 ft); AWWA C151 nominal thicknesses

field.text: RCP weight comes from the concrete annulus at about 150 lb per cubic ft. ASTM C76 wall B minimum thickness is the inside diameter in feet plus 1 inch: 12 in pipe 2 in wall, 15 in 2.25, 18 in 2.5, 24 in 3, 30 in 3.5, 36 in 4, 42 in 4.5, 48 in 5, 60 in 6 (wall C is thicker and heavier, wall A thinner). Computed barrel weights: 12 in about 90 lb/ft; 15 in 125; 18 in 165; 24 in 265; 30 in 385; 36 in 525; 42 in 690; 48 in 870; 60 in 1,300. Producer catalogs run a little higher because of the joint: one producer lists B-wall pieces at 12 in 832 lb, 15 in 1,168, 18 in 1,504, 24 in 2,264, 30 in 3,240, 36 in 4,336, 42 in 5,488, 48 in 7,120, 60 in 10,360 (standard 8 ft pieces), so plan picks from the producer's sheet. Those loads are why RCP is a lift-chart job: check radius and over-the-side rating, use the cast-in lift holes or anchors with the right hardware or a rated pipe sling or C-hook, and keep people clear until the pipe is on the bedding. Elliptical-reinforced pipe goes in with the TOP mark up.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe weight per foot and per piece (ASTM C76 wall B)
field.topic: Pipe weights per foot and per stick, and how to lift pipe
field.source: ASTM C76 wall B thicknesses; weights computed at 150 pcf; County Materials reinforced concrete pipe catalog (B-wall weight per piece)

field.text: Solid-wall HDPE (PE4710) weight follows from OD and wall: for IPS DR 17, 6 in (OD 6.625, wall 0.39) about 3.2 lb/ft, 8 in (8.625, 0.51) about 5.4, 12 in (12.75, 0.75) about 11.7; DR 11 is about 50 percent heavier; maker tables land within a few percent of these. Steel pipe: weight in lb/ft = 10.68 x wall x (OD - wall), inches; a 12.75 in OD, 1/4 inch wall pipe is about 33 lb/ft bare, more with cement lining. Dual-wall corrugated HDPE and polypropylene (ADS N-12 type) and vitrified clay are not safe to estimate from a formula: corrugated pipe weight depends on the profile and makers do not publish it on every sheet, and clay pipe comes in short, heavy lengths; get the weight from the maker's sheet or the delivery ticket before planning a pick. For handling by hand, OSHA has no lifting weight limit; the NIOSH lifting equation starts at 51 lb for one person under ideal conditions and drops it for reach, twisting and frequency, so bending into a trench to place pipe is a two-person or machine job well below the numbers above.
field.title: HDPE, corrugated plastic, clay and steel pipe weights: what to compute and what to look up
field.topic: Pipe weights per foot and per stick, and how to lift pipe
field.source: Weights computed from standard dimensions (ASTM F714 / AWWA C906 HDPE, steel pipe formula); maker sheets for corrugated and clay pipe; NIOSH Revised Lifting Equation

field.text: Rules that keep pipe and people whole: rig from the pipe's balance point (about mid-length, a little toward the bell on bell-and-spigot pipe) with a nylon or polyester sling in a choker or basket; never lift gasketed pipe by a chain through the bell or by the bucket teeth; use rated pipe hooks, C-hooks or vacuum lifters for big pipe; two-point picks with a spreader for long flexible sticks (20 ft PVC and HDPE) so they do not whip or bow; tag lines to control swing; nobody under the load or between the load and the trench wall (1926.651(e)); set the pipe on the bedding, slack the sling, then the pipelayer approaches. Rigging is inspected before each shift and damaged slings are removed from service (1926.251). Check the excavator lift chart at the reach you will actually use (over the side, at the far point of the swing, bucket and rigging weight subtracted) against pipe weight; as an illustration only, a machine that lifts several tons close in at the tracks may be rated for a fraction of that at full reach over the side, and the chart for that machine is the only number that counts. Ask gives no go/no-go on a lift; the operator and competent person decide.
field.title: Lifting pipe right: slings, hooks, balance and the lift chart
field.topic: Pipe weights per foot and per stick, and how to lift pipe
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.251 rigging; 1926.651(e); ASME B30.9; excavator lift chart practice

field.text: Gray cement-looking pipe in an old water or sewer line (common in neighborhoods built from the 1940s to the 1970s) that is lighter than concrete, has a smooth or slightly chalky surface, and shows a fibrous, matted or stringy texture at a broken end or a cut face is asbestos-cement pipe (AC pipe, often called transite after a brand). Common sizes 4 to 36 inch in about 13 ft lengths, joined with cast iron or AC couplings and rubber rings; often tan or gray with faded stenciling. Do not cut, grind, snap, break, drill or abrade it dry, and do not dry sweep the dust: asbestos fibers are a cancer hazard, and OSHA (29 CFR 1926.1101) and Cal/OSHA (8 CCR 1529) treat AC pipe work as asbestos work with trained workers, wet methods, respirators, containment of cuttings and disposal as asbestos waste. A photo cannot confirm it; treat suspect gray pipe as AC until the owner's records or a lab says otherwise, stop and tell the superintendent.
field.title: Asbestos cement (AC, transite) pipe by eye: gray cement pipe, chalky, fibrous at a break, 1940s-1970s
field.topic: Replacement chunks with the words crews type (retrieval fixes)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1101; Cal/OSHA 8 CCR 1529; utility AC pipe guidance

field.text: A yellow plastic pipe (solid yellow, or black with yellow stripes) uncovered in a trench wall or bottom is almost always a gas line: yellow is the APWA color for gas, oil, steam and petroleum, and polyethylene gas mains and services run from 1/2 inch to 12 inch, sometimes with a tracer wire or yellow warning tape above. Nothing about a photo tells you whether it is live, abandoned or at what pressure; California law says to presume every line is active (Gov Code 4216.4(a)(3)). Stop digging near it, keep the bucket away, do not pull on it, hang on it or use it as a step, and do not try to cut or cap it. If it is not on your ticket, call 811 and the gas operator; if it was marked and you are inside the 24 inch tolerance zone with a machine, you are already outside the one-call law. Any contact, even a scrape of the pipe, is reported to the gas company at once (Gov Code 4216.4(c)(2)); escaping gas is a 911 call first (4216.4(c)(1)). Hissing, smell or dirt blowing: 911, everyone upwind, no ignition sources, no restarting the machine.
field.title: Yellow plastic pipe in the trench wall: natural gas, stop and call
field.topic: Replacement chunks with the words crews type (retrieval fixes)
field.source: APWA Uniform Color Code; California Government Code 4216.4(a)(3), (c)(1), (c)(2); gas operator guidance

field.text: Pipe bends (elbows, ells) are named two ways: by degrees or by the fraction of a full circle they turn. Quarter bend (1/4 bend) = 90 degrees; eighth bend (1/8 bend) = 45 degrees; sixteenth bend (1/16 bend) = 22 1/2 degrees; thirty-second bend (1/32 bend) = 11 1/4 degrees. Sewer and drain fittings (PVC, clay, cast iron DWV) use the fraction names; water fittings (ductile iron MJ, C900) use degrees. Telling them apart by eye: lay the fitting on the ground and sight the two legs; a sixteenth bend looks almost straight (a slight dog-leg), an eighth bend is an obvious half-right-angle, a quarter bend is a square corner; the degree or fraction is usually cast or printed on the fitting. A long-sweep quarter bend has a bigger radius than a standard one and takes more laying length. The app's fitting laying lengths list bends by degrees (90, 45, 22.5, 11.25).
field.title: Bend names by fraction: quarter bend 90, eighth bend 45, sixteenth bend 22.5, thirty-second bend 11.25
field.topic: Replacement chunks with the words crews type (retrieval fixes)
field.source: Plumbing and sewer fitting nomenclature (UPC/IPC DWV fittings; ASTM D3034 fittings)

field.text: Typical gravity sewer tolerances in specs: invert within about 0.02 to 0.05 ft (1/4 to 1/2 inch) of design at any point, no reverse grade, no standing water (bellies) on the CCTV, and alignment within about 0.1 to 0.2 ft; some agencies accept more on storm drain and less on flat sewers, and the number in the contract is the one that counts. A stick reading 0.03 ft high at the target may be inside tolerance by itself, but the next stick starts from it, so a run of high joints drifts out; fix it while the stick is still exposed rather than after backfill. How: lift the stick, scrape or add bedding under the bell and barrel (never under the bell alone, which leaves the barrel unsupported), re-set, re-home the joint and re-shoot. A low stick needs bedding added under its full length, not just shimmed. Re-check the laser setup and target height when several sticks read the same way: heat shimmer, a bumped laser or the wrong target height fool you. The spec and inspector govern.
field.title: Pipe laid high or low at the laser target: grade tolerance, when to pull the stick and re-lay
field.topic: Replacement chunks with the words crews type (retrieval fixes)
field.source: Common municipal specifications for gravity sewer line and grade tolerance; ASTM D2321 installation practice

field.text: Manhole spacing (distance between manholes, 'how far apart') under the Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities, chapter 30, section 33.1): not more than 400 ft for sewers 15 inches in diameter and smaller; not more than 500 ft for 18 to 30 inch sewers; up to 600 ft may be approved where adequate modern cleaning equipment is provided, and greater spacing may be permitted in larger sewers; and a manhole at every change of grade, size or alignment, at every intersection of sewers, and at the end of each line (terminal cleanouts are allowed only for special conditions and short runs under local rules). Local standards vary (many cities 300 to 500 ft; some allow 600 ft on large trunk sewers). A drop pipe is provided where the incoming sewer enters 24 inches or more above the manhole invert (section 33.2). Spacing is a design decision on the plans; the crew's job is to confirm each manhole station and the pipe length between structures (center to center) before laying.
field.title: How far apart manholes go, and where one is required (Ten States spacing rules)
field.topic: Replacement chunks with the words crews type (retrieval fixes)
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), chapter 30 sections 33.1 and 33.2, as adopted in state regulations (for example Virginia 9VAC25-790-350)

field.text: OSHA 1926.651(l): walkways or bridges with standard guardrails must be provided where employees or equipment are required or permitted to cross over excavations, and guardrails meeting 1926.502(b) (top rail 42 inches plus or minus 3, midrail, toeboard where things can fall) are required where the walkway is 6 ft or more above the lower level. Cal/OSHA's Title 8 section 1541(l)(1) says it directly: walkways or bridges with standard guardrails where people or equipment cross excavations over 6 ft deep and wider than 30 inches. A walkway is a built crossing (planked bridge, steel plate, engineered ramp) rated for the load and secured against shifting, not a loose board. Jumping a trench is a fall-into-excavation and cave-in exposure in one; crews walk around, use the walkway, or use the ladder down and up inside the protective system. Equipment crosses only on plates or ramps designed for it (1926.651(c)(1)(ii): structural ramps for equipment must be designed by a competent person qualified in structural design). Keep crossings away from spoil piles and off unsupported edges.
field.title: Crossing a trench: walkways and guardrails (1926.651(l)), never jump it
field.topic: Trench crossings, walkways, loads, traffic and public protection (OSHA 1926.651, 1926.501/502)

field.text: Fall protection applies at excavations too. 1926.501(b)(7)(i): each employee at the edge of an excavation 6 ft or more deep must be protected by guardrails, fences or barricades when the excavation is not readily seen because of plant growth or another visual barrier; (ii): each employee at the edge of a well, pit, shaft or similar excavation 6 ft or more deep must be protected by guardrails, fences, barricades or covers. Cal/OSHA 1541(l)(2) adds that wells, pits and shafts must be barricaded or covered and remote excavations get barriers. Manhole and vault openings get covers or barricades whenever unattended. Practical: barricade both sides of an open trench in a work area, cover bore pits and manhole excavations with plates or rated covers (marked, secured), fence pits left open overnight, and light them. People working at the edge of a deep excavation without a protective system below are the competent person's call; nobody works on the face above others unless the people below are protected from falling or rolling material (1926.652(f)).
field.title: Falling into pits, holes and shafts: covers and guardrails at 6 ft (1926.501(b)(7))
field.topic: Trench crossings, walkways, loads, traffic and public protection (OSHA 1926.651, 1926.501/502)

field.text: 1926.651(e): no employee may be underneath loads handled by lifting or digging equipment, and employees stand away from any vehicle being loaded or unloaded so spillage or falling material cannot hit them (operators may stay in cabs that are equipped to give adequate protection). On a pipe job that means nobody in the trench under the stick while the bucket swings pipe, boxes or bedding over them; set the pipe down on the bedding with people clear, then they move in. 1926.651(f): when mobile equipment is operated next to an excavation, or must approach the edge, and the operator does not have a clear and direct view of the edge, a warning system is required: barricades, hand or mechanical signals, or stop logs; if possible, grade the ground away from the excavation. Keep dump trucks backing to the edge on stop logs with a spotter, and keep the excavator's tracks far enough back that the wall does not carry its weight (the competent person sets the distance; the 2 ft rule in 1926.651(j)(2) is a minimum for spoil and equipment at the edge, not a machine setback for working loads).
field.title: Loads over the trench and equipment near the edge: 1926.651(e) and (f)
field.topic: Trench crossings, walkways, loads, traffic and public protection (OSHA 1926.651, 1926.501/502)

field.text: 1926.651(d): employees exposed to public vehicular traffic must be given and wear warning vests or other reflectorized or high-visibility garments (ANSI 107 Class 2 or 3 in practice). The traffic control plan (MUTCD Part 6, the California MUTCD, and the encroachment permit) sets the lane closure, tapers, buffer, flaggers and channelizers; the trench itself gets positive protection where traffic runs next to it (drums or barricades at least, barrier where the permit requires). Steel plates over open trenches in roadways at the end of the day: OSHA treats them as covers, which in a roadway must hold at least twice the maximum axle load of the largest vehicle expected to cross and be secured against moving (1926.502(i)); the road agency's encroachment permit sets the plate thickness by trench width, how far the plate laps past the edges, pinning and ramping. Never leave a trench open overnight with only cones. Pedestrian routes get a protected detour or a covered walkway.
field.title: Traffic next to the trench: vests, barriers and work zone rules (1926.651(d), MUTCD Part 6)
field.topic: Trench crossings, walkways, loads, traffic and public protection (OSHA 1926.651, 1926.501/502)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(d); FHWA MUTCD Part 6 and California MUTCD; Caltrans Encroachment Permits Manual section 602.1 (steel plate bridging); city encroachment permit conditions

field.text: Open excavations are an attractive nuisance and a liability. Common practice (city permits plus OSHA's rules for employees): backfill or plate trenches in streets and sidewalks before leaving; fence (6 ft chain link panels or orange safety fence per the permit) around excavations that stay open off-road, with no gap a child can get through; barricades with lights or reflectors where traffic or pedestrians pass (1926.600(a)(1) requires lights or reflectors, or barricades with them, on equipment left unattended at night next to a highway or an active construction area); cover manhole and vault openings with the lid or a rated cover, never plywood alone; pull ladders or block access so nobody climbs in; store spoil at least 2 ft back (1926.651(j)(2)) and away from sidewalks; post the contractor's emergency number. In the morning the competent person inspects before anyone enters (1926.651(k)): overnight rain, traffic vibration and vandalism change the trench.
field.title: End of day and the public: barricades, fencing, plates and lights around open excavations
field.topic: Trench crossings, walkways, loads, traffic and public protection (OSHA 1926.651, 1926.501/502)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.600(a)(1), 1926.651(j)(2), 1926.651(k); city encroachment permit and public safety practice

field.text: Compaction specs are written as a percent of a lab maximum dry density found by a Proctor test. Standard Proctor (ASTM D698, AASHTO T99) uses a lighter hammer and lower compactive effort; modified Proctor (ASTM D1557, AASHTO T180) uses a heavier hammer and more effort, giving a higher maximum density and lower optimum moisture. So '95% modified' is a harder target than '95% standard.' Each soil type on a job needs its own Proctor curve, giving maximum dry density (lb per cubic ft) and optimum moisture content (percent). Field density divided by lab maximum = percent compaction. Example: field dry density 112 pcf, lab max 118 pcf, compaction = 112 / 118 = 94.9%. Always know which Proctor the spec means and which curve the tester is using.
field.title: Proctor tests: standard versus modified
field.topic: Installation: compaction and density testing
field.source: ASTM D698 / D1557 test method scopes; standard soils practice

field.text: Soil compacts best near its optimum moisture content (from the Proctor test). Too dry: the soil won't densify no matter how much you run the compactor; add water evenly and mix. Too wet: the soil pumps, ruts and can't reach density; dry it by spreading and aerating, mixing with drier material, or replace it. Clays are very sensitive to moisture; clean stone and sand are much less so, which is one reason specs favor granular backfill under pavement. Specs often require moisture within a range such as optimum minus 2 to plus 2 percent (check yours). Testers report moisture with every density test, so if a test fails, look at moisture first. Don't flood trenches to settle backfill unless the specs allow water-settling for that material.
field.title: Moisture and compaction
field.topic: Installation: compaction and density testing
field.source: Standard soils compaction practice

field.text: The nuclear density gauge (ASTM D6938) is the most common field compaction test. It measures wet density and moisture in a few minutes, from which dry density and percent compaction are calculated. Direct transmission mode (probe pushed into a pre-drilled hole to the test depth) is used for soil lifts; backscatter mode for thin layers like asphalt. Because it contains radioactive sources, operators need training and a license from the NRC or an Agreement State, must wear a dosimeter badge, and must store and transport the gauge per regulations (it's a hazardous material for shipping). Keep the crew a few feet back while it's in use and never leave it unattended. Results depend on using the right Proctor value for that material.
field.title: Compaction testing: nuclear density gauge
field.topic: Installation: compaction and density testing
field.source: ASTM D6938 scope; NRC portable gauge licensing guidance

field.text: Other field density tests: Sand cone (ASTM D1556): dig a small hole, weigh the soil removed, fill the hole with calibrated sand from a cone to measure its volume, then dry a soil sample for moisture; slower but no radiation, often used to check a nuclear gauge. Rubber balloon (ASTM D2167): measures hole volume with a water-filled balloon. Dynamic cone penetrometer (DCP, ASTM D6951): a drop-hammer rod that measures penetration per blow; many agencies accept DCP blow counts as a quick check of trench backfill. Electrical and other non-nuclear gauges exist, but acceptance varies. Whatever the method, test each lift at the frequency in your specs (often per lift per so many feet of trench or per structure). Ask the inspector which methods and frequency they require before backfill starts.
field.title: Compaction testing: sand cone and other methods
field.topic: Installation: compaction and density testing
field.source: ASTM test method scopes; agency practice

field.text: Specs set how often backfill must be tested, often by lift and distance (for example one test per lift per 100 to 300 ft of trench, plus around each structure) or at the inspector's discretion; check your project specs. When a test fails: stop placing more lifts over it, find the cause (wrong moisture, lift too thick, wrong material, poor compactor coverage), rework the failed area (dig out if needed, adjust moisture, recompact), and retest. Document test locations by station, offset and depth or elevation, with pass/fail results, in the daily report; failed and retested locations should show both results. Backfilling over untested lifts can mean digging them back up at the contractor's cost.
field.title: Compaction test frequency and failed tests
field.topic: Installation: compaction and density testing
field.source: Common municipal specification practice

field.text: Matching the compactor to the soil and space saves time. Vibratory plate compactors work best on granular soils (stone, sand, gravel), in thin lifts. Rammers (jumping jacks) work on cohesive soils (clay, silt) and in tight areas like haunches and around structures; they compact by impact. Trench rollers (remote-controlled padfoot rollers) handle wider trenches and thicker lifts in cohesive soils. Excavator-mounted plate compactors (hoe-packs) and compaction wheels compact thicker lifts quickly without people in the trench, good for deep trenches. PPI notes Class I and II embedment compact best by vibration and Class III and IVA by impact; don't use impact tampers directly over plastic pipe until about 12 inches of cover. Make several overlapping passes per lift; more passes on a lift that's too thick won't reach the bottom.
field.title: Compaction equipment for trenches
field.topic: Installation: compaction and density testing
field.source: PPI conduitcalc: Compaction of Embedment Materials

field.text: ASTM C94 (ready-mixed concrete) generally requires discharge to be completed within 1-1/2 hours or before the drum has turned 300 revolutions after water was added to the cement, whichever comes first, unless the buyer allows otherwise. Adding water on site to raise slump is allowed only within limits (no more than the mix design's maximum water-cement ratio, and usually only once, with mixing after), and the ticket should record water added. Too much water weakens concrete and increases shrinkage cracking. For thrust blocks and manhole bases, check the delivery ticket for mix, strength, time batched and water added. Make test cylinders if the spec requires (ASTM C31) and check slump (ASTM C143).
field.title: Ready-mix concrete delivery time and water
field.topic: Concrete basics for utility crews
field.source: ACI 305 (hot weather) / ACI 306 (cold weather) concreting guides and ASTM C94 ready-mix spec, as commonly summarized

field.text: ACI 306 defines cold weather concreting conditions as air temperature that has fallen to, or is expected to fall below, 40 degrees F during the protection period. Fresh concrete must be protected from freezing until it reaches about 500 psi compressive strength (an ACI 306 benchmark), which takes longer in cold weather. Practices: don't place concrete on frozen ground or against frozen soil (common for thrust blocks; thaw or remove the frost first); use heated concrete, accelerators (non-chloride near reinforcing steel or ductile fittings if specs require), insulated blankets or enclosures; and allow more cure time before pressure testing water mains. Flowable fill also must be protected from freezing until it hardens (NRMCA). Check your specs for minimum placement temperatures.
field.title: Cold weather concrete
field.topic: Concrete basics for utility crews
field.source: ACI 305 (hot weather) / ACI 306 (cold weather) concreting guides and ASTM C94 ready-mix spec, as commonly summarized

field.text: ACI 305 covers hot weather concreting, which can cause fast setting, cold joints, lower strength and cracking. Practices: limit concrete temperature at delivery (many specs set a maximum around 90 to 95 degrees F; check yours); dampen the subgrade and forms (no standing water) so they don't suck water out; place and finish quickly; protect from wind and sun; cure promptly with water, curing compound or wet blankets; schedule pours in the cooler part of the day; and avoid adding extra water to fix slump (use a retarder or water reducer from the plant instead). Check the delivery ticket for batch time, since hot weather shortens working time.
field.title: Hot weather concrete
field.topic: Concrete basics for utility crews
field.source: ACI 305 (hot weather) / ACI 306 (cold weather) concreting guides and ASTM C94 ready-mix spec, as commonly summarized

field.text: Cutting concrete pipe, manholes, pavement and some other materials with saws or jackhammers creates respirable crystalline silica dust, which causes silicosis and lung disease. OSHA's construction silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153) Table 1 lists tasks with required controls; for handheld power saws cutting concrete or masonry, the main control is water delivered continuously to the blade, with respirator requirements depending on task duration and location (check Table 1 for your task). Other tasks like jackhammering and walk-behind saws have their own controls. Employers need a written exposure control plan. Practical: use wet cutting, don't dry-cut concrete pipe, keep others upwind, and wear the respirator the table calls for. Cutting PVC or ductile iron doesn't produce silica, but cement-lined DI does.
field.title: Silica dust from cutting pipe and concrete
field.topic: Confined spaces and silica (overview)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153, Respirable crystalline silica in construction (Table 1)

field.text: Main trench dewatering methods: Open pumping (sump pumping): dig a sump at the low end or below trench grade, line it with stone, and pump with a trash or submersible pump; works for light seepage and in clays and gravels where the walls stay stable. Well points: a line of small-diameter well screens jetted into the ground along one or both sides of the trench, connected by a header pipe to a vacuum pump; lowers groundwater in sands and silty sands; NCPI notes they should be close to the trench walls and sunk below the trench bottom, with spacing based on soil. Deep wells: larger wells with submersible pumps for deep cuts or large drawdowns in permeable soils. Choosing a method needs soil and groundwater information from borings; specialty dewatering contractors design larger systems.
field.title: Dewatering methods: sumps, well points and deep wells
field.topic: Groundwater and dewatering
field.source: NCPI Vitrified Clay Pipe Engineering Manual, Chapter 3 (dewatering)

field.text: Watch for these problems when dewatering pipe trenches: boiling or quick conditions in the trench bottom (sand bubbling up with water), which means the bottom is losing strength; walls sloughing or caving from seepage; pumped water carrying lots of fine sand, which means you're pulling soil and can undermine nearby pavement, utilities and buildings; settlement of nearby structures when groundwater is lowered in soft clays or organic soils; and pipe floating or shifting off grade. Responses: slow or reposition pumping, add filter fabric and stone, switch to well points, deepen sumps, use a stone foundation, and stop work if the trench is unstable. OSHA requires a competent person to monitor water removal (1926.651(h)). Document dewatering problems as possible differing site conditions.
field.title: Dewatering: signs of trouble
field.topic: Groundwater and dewatering
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Pump planning basics: estimate inflow from test pits or a short test excavation (watch how fast water rises); pick a pump with capacity to spare at the actual head (lift height plus friction in hoses), because pump curves drop off sharply with head; keep a backup pump on site for critical dewatering; plan fuel for overnight runs or use electric pumps with float switches; route discharge hoses safely across traffic and sidewalks (ramps or buried crossings); and plan where the water goes under your permits. Trash pumps handle solids; submersible pumps handle continuous seepage in sumps. Size hoses to limit friction losses. Field rule of thumb: dewatering is cheaper to plan than to fight after the trench floods.
field.title: Dewatering: pumps and planning
field.topic: Groundwater and dewatering
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: California non-exempt construction workers are covered by Wage Order 16 (construction, drilling, logging and mining) and Labor Code 512 and 226.7 (as of Nov 5, 2026). Meal: an unpaid, duty-free 30-minute meal period must start no later than the end of the 5th hour of work; a second 30-minute meal must start no later than the end of the 10th hour. Rest: a paid 10-minute rest break for every 4 hours worked or major fraction of 4 hours, in the middle of each work period where practicable; none is required if the whole day is under 3.5 hours. A missed, late or short break owes a premium of 1 extra hour of pay at the regular rate (one for meals and one for rests per day). Applies to hourly (non-exempt) employees; union crews may fall under a CBA exemption for meals and overtime. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California construction meal and rest breaks: the basic rule (Wage Order 16)
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: IWC Wage Order 16-2001 (8 CCR 11160), construction, drilling, logging and mining sections 10 and 11; Labor Code 512; Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. Supreme Court, 2012) S166350; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: A crew working 12 hours in California (Wage Order 16, non-exempt, no CBA exemption) is owed 3 paid 10-minute rest breaks and 2 unpaid 30-minute meal periods (as of Nov 5, 2026). Example, start 6:00 AM: rest 8:00; 1st meal 10:30 to 11:00 (must start by the end of the 5th hour of work, 11:00 at the latest); rest about 1:30 PM; 2nd meal 3:30 to 4:00 (must start by the end of the 10th hour of work, here 4:30 PM at the latest, since the first meal is not work time); rest about 5:30; quit 7:00 PM = 12 hours worked over 13 hours on site. Pay: first 8 hours straight time, hours 9 to 12 at 1.5x, any time over 12 at 2x. The 2nd meal can be waived only by mutual consent when the day is no more than 12 hours and the 1st meal was not waived; at 12.1 hours it cannot be waived. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: 12-hour shift break and lunch schedule in California (how many breaks for 12 hours)
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. Supreme Court, 2012) S166350; IWC Wage Order 16-2001 (8 CCR 11160), construction, drilling, logging and mining sections 3, 10, 11; Labor Code 510, 512; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Paid 10-minute rest breaks owed per day in California, from the Supreme Court's reading of "4 hours or major fraction" (as of Nov 5, 2026): under 3.5 h = 0; 3.5 to 6 h = 1; over 6 up to 10 h = 2; over 10 up to 14 h = 3; over 14 up to 18 h = 4. So: 3.5 h 1, 4 h 1, 5 h 1, 6 h 1, 6.5 h 2, 7 h 2, 8 h 2, 9 h 2, 10 h 2, 10.5 h 3, 11 h 3, 12 h 3, 13 h 3, 14 h 3, 14.5 h 4, 15 h 4, 16 h 4. Rest breaks are paid, count as hours worked (including for overtime), should fall near the middle of each 4-hour block where practicable, and cannot be stacked onto lunch or used to leave early unless the employee freely chooses that. The employee must be relieved of all duty and employer control during the break (no on-call or radio duty; Augustus v. ABM, 2016). Applies to non-exempt employees under Wage Order 16. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: How many rest breaks for an 8, 10, 12 or 16 hour shift: California rest break table (3.5 to 16 hours)
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. Supreme Court, 2012) S166350; IWC Wage Order 16-2001 (8 CCR 11160), construction, drilling, logging and mining section 11; DIR rest and meal period summary (rev. 1/2011); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California meal periods by hours worked in the day (as of Nov 5, 2026): 5 hours or less = no meal required; over 5 up to 6 hours = 1 meal, which may be waived by mutual consent; over 6 up to 10 hours = 1 meal, not waivable; over 10 up to 12 hours = 2 meals, the 2nd waivable by mutual consent only if the 1st was taken; over 12 hours = 2 meals, neither waivable. Each meal is at least 30 minutes, duty-free and unpaid; the 1st starts no later than the end of the 5th hour of work, the 2nd no later than the end of the 10th. Wage Order 16 sets no third meal. The employer must relieve the worker of all duty and let them leave; it need not police that no work is done, but must not discourage or pressure people to skip or shorten lunch. Put waivers in writing. Applies to non-exempt employees. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California meal period table by shift length and waivers (5, 6, 10, 12 hours)
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: Labor Code 512(a); IWC Wage Order 16-2001 (8 CCR 11160), construction, drilling, logging and mining section 10; Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. Supreme Court, 2012) S166350; DLSE Meal Periods FAQ; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: An on-duty meal period (eating while staying on duty, for example the only operator watching a pump or a flagger who cannot be relieved) is allowed in California only when the nature of the work prevents relief from all duty AND there is a written agreement; the employee can revoke the agreement in writing at any time. An on-duty meal is paid as hours worked. If the employer requires workers to stay on the job site during lunch, the lunch must be paid even if they do no work, and a suitable place to eat should be provided. Wanting to finish early is not a reason for an on-duty meal: working through lunch does not let a crew leave early unless a valid on-duty agreement applies. If the meal is not a proper off-duty meal and not a valid on-duty meal, the 1-hour meal premium is owed (as of Nov 5, 2026). For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Working lunch / on-duty meal period on a California job site
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: IWC Wage Order 16-2001 (8 CCR 11160), construction, drilling, logging and mining section 10(D); DLSE Meal Periods FAQ; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: If a California employer does not provide a required meal, rest or heat-illness recovery period, it owes the worker 1 additional hour of pay at the regular rate of compensation for each workday it happens (Labor Code 226.7). The regular rate includes non-discretionary bonuses and similar pay, not only the base wage. Per day the maximum is 1 premium for meal violations and 1 for rest violations (recovery periods follow the same section). A late meal (starting after the end of the 5th hour), a short meal (under 30 minutes) or a meal interrupted by work counts as not provided. Premiums are wages: they go on the pay stub and are owed on payday. They do not count as hours worked for overtime. Claims can go to the Labor Commissioner or court; the limit is generally 3 years (as of Nov 5, 2026). For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Missed break premium pay in California (meal, rest and heat recovery periods)
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: Labor Code 226.7; Wage Order 16 sections 10(F), 11(D); DIR rest and meal period summary (Murphy v. Kenneth Cole, 3-year limit); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California lets a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) replace some state rules for construction workers (as of Nov 5, 2026). Meal periods (Labor Code 512(e)-(f), Wage Order 16 section 10(E)): the state meal rules do not apply to a construction-occupation employee covered by a valid CBA that expressly provides wages, hours and working conditions, meal periods, final and binding arbitration of meal-period disputes, premium pay for all overtime hours, and a regular hourly rate at least 30% above the state minimum wage (2026: at least $21.97/h; 2027: at least $22.62/h). Overtime (Labor Code 514, Wage Order 16 section 3(H)): the same wages/hours/premium overtime/30% conditions remove the daily, weekly and 7th-day overtime rules. These exemptions do not mention rest breaks or heat recovery periods. Whether a CBA qualifies is a legal question: ask the union rep, HR or a labor attorney. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Union construction crews in California: CBA exemption from meal period and overtime rules
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: Labor Code 512(e)-(g), 514; Wage Order 16 sections 3(H), 10(E); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California rest breaks should come near the middle of each 4-hour work period "insofar as practicable"; the Supreme Court said rest breaks do not have to come before the first meal, and employers may deviate from the ideal timing when practical needs of the job require it. Wage Order 16 allows staggering rest breaks so equipment can keep running. A crew cannot be required to skip or combine rest breaks to leave early. The break must be a net 10 minutes of rest: walking time to a shade tent or rest area should not eat the 10 minutes, and the worker must be relieved of all duty (no radio duty or staying on call). Supervisors should not discourage breaks. The employer must authorize and permit them; if one is not provided the 1-hour rest premium is owed. Rest time is paid and counts toward overtime (as of Nov 5, 2026). For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Rest break timing, staggering, and can the crew skip breaks to leave early (California)
field.topic: Employment law: California meal and rest breaks (construction)
field.source: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. Supreme Court, 2012) S166350; IWC Wage Order 16-2001 (8 CCR 11160), construction, drilling, logging and mining section 11(A)-(D); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California overtime under Labor Code 510 and Wage Order 16 (as of Nov 5, 2026), for non-exempt workers: 1.5x the regular rate for hours over 8 in a workday and over 40 in a workweek; 2x for hours over 12 in a workday. The workday and workweek are fixed periods the employer sets (a 24-hour period and 7 consecutive days). The regular rate includes non-discretionary bonuses and shift differentials, not just base pay. Overtime is not stacked: an hour counted as daily overtime is not counted again toward weekly overtime. Overtime may be paid by the next regular payday after the period it was earned. Union crews under a qualifying CBA (premium overtime and a regular rate at least 30% above minimum wage) are exempt from these rules (Labor Code 514). Employees cannot be disciplined for refusing more than 72 hours in a week, except in an emergency. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California overtime and double time for construction workers (daily, weekly)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Labor Code 510, 514; Wage Order 16 section 3(A), (D), (E), (H); DLSE paydays FAQ; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: In California, when a non-exempt employee works all 7 days of the employer's workweek, the 7th consecutive day in that workweek is paid at 1.5x for the first 8 hours and 2x for every hour over 8 (Labor Code 510; Wage Order 16 section 3(A)) (as of Nov 5, 2026). The rule counts days within one fixed workweek, so 7 days in a row that span two workweeks do not trigger it. Example: Monday to Saturday 8 hours each, Sunday (7th day in the workweek) 10 hours: Sunday pays 8 hours at 1.5x and 2 hours at 2x, and the weekly hours over 40 are not counted twice. Wage Order 16 also allows jobs that need 7 or more consecutive days to accumulate rest days, as long as workers get the equivalent of one day off in seven each month. Union crews under a qualifying CBA may be exempt. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: 7th day rule in California (seventh consecutive day overtime)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Labor Code 510; Wage Order 16 section 3(A), (G), (H); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: An alternative workweek schedule (AWS) lets a California employer schedule up to 10 hours a day within a 40-hour week without daily overtime, for example four 10-hour days (Wage Order 16 section 3(B)-(C)) (as of Nov 5, 2026). Rules: the employer proposes it in writing, holds a meeting at least 14 days before the vote, and at least two-thirds of the affected work unit must approve it in a secret ballot before it starts; results go to the Division of Labor Statistics and Research within 30 days. Under an AWS, hours beyond the scheduled day (up to 12) and over 40 a week are 1.5x, and over 12 a day is 2x. Regular pay cannot be cut to adopt it. Wage Order 16 bars AWS days over 8 hours on public works contracts that would violate Labor Code 1810-1815. Repeal takes a petition by one-third and a two-thirds vote. Union crews follow their CBA. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Alternative workweek schedule (4x10s) in California construction
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Wage Order 16 section 3(B)-(C); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California reporting time pay (Wage Order 16 section 5) (as of Nov 5, 2026): if a worker reports for a scheduled day and is not put to work, or gets less than half the usual or scheduled day, the employer owes pay for half the scheduled day, at least 2 hours and no more than 4 hours, at the regular rate. Example: scheduled 8 hours, sent home after 1 hour: owed 4 hours (1 worked plus 3 reporting pay). If called back a second time in a day and given under 2 hours of work, 2 hours are owed. No reporting pay is owed when work can't start or continue because of threats to people or property, a public utility failure (power, water, gas, sewer), an act of God such as storms, or other causes beyond the employer's control, or if the worker leaves voluntarily. Being sent home for slow or poor work is not an exception. A CBA covering the crew controls unless it says otherwise. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Reporting time pay / show-up pay in California (sent home early, rained out)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Wage Order 16 section 5; DLSE Reporting Time Pay FAQ; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: A split shift is a workday interrupted by an unpaid, non-working period set by the employer that is longer than a normal meal period. In most California wage orders (Orders 1 to 15, section 4) a minimum-wage worker on a split shift is owed one extra hour at minimum wage, with pay above minimum wage counted toward it. Wage Order 16, which covers on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining, defines "split shift" but its minimum wage section has no split shift premium, so the premium generally does not apply to on-site construction work (as of Nov 5, 2026). Office and yard staff who fall under another wage order may be different, and local ordinances can add rules. Unpaid gaps still cannot be used to avoid the meal, rest or overtime rules. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Split shift premium: does it apply to California construction (Wage Order 16)?
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Wage Order 16 sections 2 and 4 (no split shift premium); DLSE Split Shift FAQ (Orders 1-15); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California counts as hours worked any time a worker is under the employer's control (as of Nov 5, 2026). Wage Order 16 section 5(A) says employer-required travel after the first place the employee must report is paid at the regular rate (or overtime rate when it applies). In practice: driving from home to the job site is a normal commute and usually unpaid, but if the employer requires the crew to meet at the yard and ride in the company truck, the ride from the yard to the site is generally paid (Morillion v. Royal Packing, Cal. Supreme Court 2000). Travel between job sites during the day is paid. Hauling tools or equipment, loading the truck, or picking up materials on the way is work. Overnight out-of-town travel is generally paid. Paid travel counts toward overtime. A CBA may set travel or subsistence pay on union jobs. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Travel time pay in California: yard to job site, between sites, out-of-town jobs
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Wage Order 16 sections 2, 5(A); Morillion v. Royal Packing Co. (2000) 22 Cal.4th 575; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California state minimum wage: $16.90/hour for all employers in 2026; $17.40/hour starting January 1, 2027 (announced by DIR on August 13, 2026) (as of Nov 5, 2026). Cities and counties can set higher rates and the highest one that applies where the work is done must be paid. Notable 2026 local rates: City of Los Angeles $18.42 (from July 1, 2026); unincorporated Los Angeles County $18.47 (July 1, 2026); Santa Monica $18.47; Pasadena $18.57; Malibu $17.91; West Hollywood $20.25; San Diego city $17.75; San Francisco $19.61; San Jose $18.45. Riverside County cities such as Beaumont have no local ordinance and use the state rate. Union and public-works jobs usually pay far above these, under a CBA or prevailing wage determination. Rates change Jan 1 and July 1; check the city's page. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California minimum wage 2026 and 2027, and local city rates in Southern California
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: DIR News Release 2026-66 (Aug 13, 2026); DOL state minimum wage table (updated Nov 5, 2026); LA County DCBA; Davis Wright Tremaine local rate summaries (Dec 2025, June 2026); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: In California a worker is non-exempt (gets overtime, meal and rest breaks) unless the employer proves an exemption (as of Nov 5, 2026). The executive, administrative and professional exemptions need BOTH a salary of at least 2 times the state minimum wage for full-time work ($70,304 a year / $5,858.67 a month in 2026; $72,384 a year / $6,032 a month in 2027) AND duties tests, including spending more than half the time on exempt work (managing, independent judgment, professional work). Job titles don't decide it. A working foreman who spends most of the day running equipment or laying pipe is usually non-exempt even if salaried. Superintendents and PMs who mainly manage may be exempt if paid the salary. Salaried non-exempt workers still get overtime. Federal law has its own, lower test; the stricter rule wins. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Exempt vs non-exempt in California: salary test 2026 and 2027 (foremen, supers, PMs)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Wage Order 16 section 1(A); DIR News Release 2026-66 ($72,384 for 2027); 2026 = 2 x $16.90 x 2,080; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California paydays (Labor Code 204; DLSE) (as of Nov 5, 2026): most non-exempt workers must be paid at least twice a month on regular paydays posted at the workplace. Wages earned on the 1st to 15th are due by the 26th; wages earned on the 16th to the end of the month are due by the 10th of the next month. Weekly or biweekly payrolls must be paid within 7 calendar days after the pay period ends. Overtime may be paid no later than the payday for the next regular pay period. Exempt executive, administrative and professional employees may be paid once a month. If payday falls on a holiday the business closes for, pay can go out the next business day. Late or short pay can lead to penalties under Labor Code 210. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California paydays and pay timing (how often construction workers must be paid)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: DLSE Paydays, pay periods and final wages FAQ; Labor Code 204, 210; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Every California payday the employer must give an itemized wage statement (Labor Code 226) (as of Nov 5, 2026) showing: gross wages; total hours worked (for non-exempt); piece-rate units and rates if paid by piece; all deductions; net wages; the pay period dates; the employee's name and last 4 digits of SSN or an employee ID; the employer's legal name and address; and every hourly rate in effect with the hours at each rate (straight, overtime, double time, meal/rest premiums). Paid sick leave available must also be shown (on the stub or a separate writing). Statements must be kept at least 3 years. Penalty for a knowing failure: the greater of actual damages or $50 for the first pay period and $100 for each later one, up to $4,000 per employee. Workers can ask to see their records. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Pay stub / itemized wage statement requirements in California (Labor Code 226)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Labor Code 226(a), (e); Labor Code 246(i); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California final pay (Labor Code 201, 202; DLSE) (as of Nov 5, 2026): if the worker is fired or laid off (including at the end of a job), all wages, including accrued vacation or PTO, are due immediately at the time and place of termination. If the worker quits with at least 72 hours' notice, pay is due on the last day; if they quit without notice, within 72 hours (mailed if they ask). The construction industry has no special exception (oil drilling, motion picture and seasonal cannery work do). Waiting time penalty (Labor Code 203): if the employer willfully fails to pay on time, the worker's daily wage keeps running for each day late, up to 30 days. No penalty if there is a good-faith dispute about the amount, but undisputed wages must still be paid without requiring a release. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Final paycheck in California when fired, laid off or quitting (end of job layoff)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: DLSE Paydays, pay periods and final wages FAQ; Labor Code 201-203; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California paid sick leave (Labor Code 245-249, as amended by SB 616) (as of Nov 5, 2026): covers employees who work 30 or more days for the same employer in California within a year, including part-time and temporary. Accrual: at least 1 hour per 30 hours worked; or front-load at least 40 hours or 5 days a year (with 24 hours/3 days by day 120 and 40 hours/5 days by day 200 for new hires). Use can start after 90 days of employment. Employers may cap use at 40 hours or 5 days a year and accrual at 80 hours or 10 days. Uses: own or family member's illness or care, preventive care, and safe-time for victims of violence. Paid at the regular non-overtime rate; not paid out at termination, but restored if rehired within 12 months. Construction workers under a qualifying CBA are exempt. Local ordinances (LA, San Diego, others) may give more. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California paid sick leave 2026: 40 hours or 5 days (construction workers)
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: DLSE California Paid Sick Leave FAQ (updated Dec 2025); Labor Code 245.5, 246; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California employers must keep accurate records for each non-exempt employee (Wage Order 16 section 6; Labor Code 1174, 226) (as of Nov 5, 2026): name, address, occupation; time records showing when each work period starts and ends, and meal periods (authorized rest breaks need not be recorded); total daily hours; wages paid each payroll period; and itemized wage statements. Records must be kept in English for at least 3 years at the workplace or a central location in California. Public works jobs also need certified payroll records (Labor Code 1776). Workers can request copies of their payroll records and personnel file (copies within 21 days for payroll records). Accurate daily time cards from the foreman (start, lunch out/in, quit) are the employer's main protection in break and overtime disputes. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California record keeping: time records, meal periods and how long to keep payroll
field.topic: Employment law: California pay, hours and overtime (construction)
field.source: Wage Order 16 section 6; Labor Code 226(b)-(c), 1174, 1198.5; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Cal/OSHA's outdoor heat standard (8 CCR 3395) covers every outdoor job in California, including trench and pipe crews (as of Nov 5, 2026). Water: fresh, pure, suitably cool and free, close to the work, at least 1 quart per worker per hour for the whole shift (or a way to refill it).
