Shade: when it is over 80 F the employer must keep shade up while workers are present, big enough for everyone on a rest, recovery or meal break to sit in it fully shaded; at or below 80 F shade must be provided on request. Cool-down: anyone can take a preventative cool-down rest in the shade when they feel they need it, for at least 5 minutes, and must be checked for symptoms. At 95 F or above, construction must also run high-heat procedures. A written Heat Illness Prevention Plan must be at the site. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California heat illness rules for construction: water, shade, 80 F and 95 F triggers
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: 8 CCR 3395 Heat Illness Prevention in Outdoor Places of Employment (Cal/OSHA); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: When it is 95 F or hotter, Cal/OSHA's heat standard requires extra steps for construction, agriculture, landscaping, oil and gas extraction and hauling of construction materials (as of Nov 5, 2026): effective communication so any worker can reach a supervisor (voice, radio or phone that works in the area); observing workers for alertness and heat symptoms by a supervisor watching 20 or fewer people, a mandatory buddy system, regular contact with anyone working alone, or another effective method; designating who will call 911 / emergency services; reminding everyone throughout the shift to drink water; and pre-shift meetings on these procedures and the right to cool-down rest. The extra 10-minute cool-down every 2 hours at 95 F is required for agriculture only, not construction. New workers on a high-heat job must be closely watched for their first 14 days, and everyone during a heat wave. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California high-heat procedures at 95 degrees for construction crews
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: 8 CCR 3395 Heat Illness Prevention in Outdoor Places of Employment (Cal/OSHA) subsections (a)(2), (e), (g); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: A "recovery period" is a cool-down break in the shade to prevent heat illness. In California it is paid time, and if an employer does not allow a recovery period required by a Cal/OSHA heat standard it owes 1 extra hour of pay at the regular rate for that day, the same as a missed rest break (Labor Code 226.7). A worker resting must be monitored and not ordered back to work until symptoms are gone. Signs of heat illness (confusion, vomiting, fainting, hot skin, stopping sweating) mean start cooling and call 911 under the site's emergency procedures; the heat plan must say how to give clear directions to the site. Supervisors and workers must be trained before working in heat. Indoor work (vaults, pump stations, shops) is covered by a separate rule, 8 CCR 3396, starting at 82 F indoors (as of Nov 5, 2026). See the first aid library for treatment. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Heat recovery period pay and heat emergencies in California
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: Labor Code 226.7; 8 CCR 3395 Heat Illness Prevention in Outdoor Places of Employment (Cal/OSHA) (d), (f), (h); 8 CCR 3396 indoor heat (2024); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Every California employer must have a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP, 8 CCR 3203) (as of Nov 5, 2026). It must name the person responsible; ensure workers follow safe practices; communicate with workers on safety (construction employers typically hold toolbox / tailgate meetings at least every 10 working days under 8 CCR 1509); do periodic inspections; investigate injuries; fix hazards in a timely way; and train workers when hired, when given new jobs and when new hazards come in. Construction contractors also need a Code of Safe Practices posted at each job. Since July 1, 2024 most employers also need a written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan and training (Labor Code 6401.9). Workers can report hazards without retaliation and can see the IIPP. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Cal/OSHA Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) and workplace violence plan
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: 8 CCR 3203, 8 CCR 1509; Labor Code 6401.9 (SB 553); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: If you are hurt on a California job (as of Nov 5, 2026): get first aid or call 911 for emergencies, then tell your supervisor or employer right away and in writing. The law gives 30 days from the injury (Labor Code 5400), but waiting can cause problems with the claim. The employer must give you a claim form (DWC-1) within 1 working day of learning of the injury. Fill out the employee section and return it; within 1 working day the employer completes its part, gives you a dated copy and sends it to the insurer. Within 1 working day of the form being filed, the employer must authorize medical treatment up to $10,000 while the claim is decided. If the claim is not denied within 90 days it is presumed accepted. Workers comp covers medical care, temporary and permanent disability pay and job retraining vouchers, no matter who was at fault. Help: DWC Information & Assistance officers. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: How long do I have to report a work injury in California (workers comp claim form DWC-1)
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: DWC Injured Worker Guide; Labor Code 5400, 5401, 5402; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: A California employer must report any serious injury, illness or death of an employee at work to Cal/OSHA immediately, meaning as soon as practically possible and no later than 8 hours after it knows (or with diligent inquiry would have known); up to 24 hours is allowed only in exigent circumstances (8 CCR 342). "Serious" is defined in Labor Code 6302(h) and 8 CCR 330(h): inpatient hospitalization of any length for other than medical observation or diagnostic testing, amputation, loss of an eye, or serious permanent disfigurement (the old over-24-hours test no longer applies). Reports are made by phone or Cal/OSHA's online system to the nearest district office. This is in addition to the workers comp claim form and the insurer's report, and to keeping the Log 300 injury records. Workers do not make this report, but anyone may file a safety complaint with Cal/OSHA (as of Nov 5, 2026). For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Employer reporting of serious injuries to Cal/OSHA (8 hours) and records
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status

field.text: California law bars retaliation (firing, demotion, cutting hours, threats, reporting immigration status) against workers who complain about unpaid wages, breaks or overtime, file a wage claim, report safety hazards or refuse unsafe work under Labor Code 6311, use paid sick leave, file a workers comp claim, or report suspected violations to a government agency (Labor Code 98.6, 1102.5, 6310, 132a) (as of Nov 5, 2026). A retaliation complaint with the Labor Commissioner must generally be filed within 1 year of the retaliatory act; workers comp discrimination (132a) goes to the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board. Federal OSHA's 11(c) complaint has a 30-day deadline and can be filed at the same time. Missing a deadline may still leave a lawsuit; ask an attorney. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Retaliation protections in California: safety complaints, wage claims, breaks
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: DLSE How to File a Retaliation Complaint (June 2026); Labor Code 98.6, 98.7, 1102.5, 6310, 6311, 132a; whistleblowers.gov; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California prevailing wage (Labor Code 1720-1861) (as of Nov 5, 2026): public works paid in whole or part with public funds over $1,000 (construction, alteration, demolition, installation, repair, maintenance) must pay at least the prevailing wage rates set by the DIR Director for each craft and county, including fringe benefits, holiday and overtime rates and travel/subsistence where listed. Workers are paid for the work they actually do (operating a backhoe = operator rate). Contractors and subs must register with DIR before bidding or working on public works over $25,000 (construction, alteration, demolition, installation, repair) or $15,000 (maintenance); the annual fee is $400 (one to three years at once; renew by June 30). Rates are on DIR's prevailing wage determination pages and must be posted at the site. Underpayment penalties run up to $200 per day per worker plus back wages. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California prevailing wage on public works: what it covers and DIR registration
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: DIR Public Works contractor registration page; DIR SB 854 fact sheet; DOL state prevailing wage table (2023); Labor Code 1725.5, 1771, 1775; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: On California public works, every contractor and subcontractor must keep certified payroll records (CPRs) for each worker: name, ID, craft, hours each day and week, rates and fringe benefits paid (Labor Code 1776) (as of Nov 5, 2026). CPRs must be submitted electronically to the Labor Commissioner through DIR's eCPR system at least monthly (at least once every 30 days while work is performed and within 30 days after the last day of work), or more often if the contract says so. Late filing can cost $100 per day up to $5,000 per project. Projects at or under the small-project limits ($25,000 construction / $15,000 maintenance) don't file eCPR but must keep records for 3 years. Public works overtime: over 8 hours a day or 40 a week must be paid at least 1.5x the basic rate, with a $25 per worker per day penalty for violations (Labor Code 1813, 1815). For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: California certified payroll (eCPR) and public works overtime
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: Labor Code 1771.4 (as amended 2023), 1776, 1813, 1815; DIR Certified Payroll Reporting page; DIR SB 854 fact sheet; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: On California public works contracts of $30,000 or more, every contractor and subcontractor in an apprenticeable craft must employ registered apprentices for at least 1 hour of apprentice work for every 5 hours of journeyman work, unless an exemption applies (Labor Code 1777.5) (as of Nov 5, 2026). Steps: send the contract award information (form DAS 140) to the apprenticeship committees for each craft; request apprentices with form DAS 142 at least 3 business days before they are needed; pay training fund contributions shown in the prevailing wage determination to the craft committee or the California Apprenticeship Council (form CAC-2). Apprentices are paid the apprentice rate only if they are registered in a state-approved program and work within the ratio; otherwise the journeyman rate is owed. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Apprentices on California public works (1 apprentice hour per 5 journeyman hours)
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: DIR Apprenticeship Requirements for public works page; Labor Code 1777.5; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: California presumes a worker is an employee unless the hiring business proves all three parts of the ABC test (Labor Code 2775, AB 5) (as of Nov 5, 2026): A, free from the company's control and direction; B, the work is outside the usual course of the company's business; C, the worker is customarily engaged in an independent business of the same kind. A laborer or pipelayer paid "1099" by a pipeline contractor almost never passes part B. For construction subcontractors, Labor Code 2781 uses the older Borello test only if all seven conditions are met: written subcontract; CSLB license covering the work; business license if required; own business location; authority to hire and fire; assumes financial responsibility (insurance, bonds, warranties); and an independently established business. Construction trucking has had a separate rule; check its current status. Misclassification can mean back wages, taxes and penalties. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).
field.title: Employee or independent contractor in California: the ABC test and construction subs
field.topic: Employment law: California heat, safety, injuries, public works and worker status
field.source: EDD DE 231G (rev. 9/2023); Labor Code 2775, 2781; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: PAGA (Private Attorneys General Act, Labor Code 2698): workers can sue for civil penalties for Labor Code violations on behalf of the state and other workers, after notice to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency; 2024 reforms let employers cut penalties by fixing problems (as of Nov 5, 2026). Discrimination: California's FEHA covers employers with 5 or more employees and bars harassment by anyone at workplaces with even 1 employee; complaints go to the Civil Rights Department, generally within 3 years. CFRA leave: employers with 5 or more employees must give up to 12 weeks of job-protected family and medical leave to workers with 12 months of service and 1,250 hours in the past year. Pregnancy disability leave is separate. These sit on top of the federal rules in the federal file. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the California Labor Commissioner (dir.ca.gov/dlse).

field.source: Labor Code 2698-2699.8 (2024 amendments); Gov. Code 12940, 12945.2, 12960; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: The federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) sets the floor in every state (as of Nov 5, 2026): minimum wage $7.25 an hour, and overtime of 1.5x the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek for non-exempt employees. A workweek is a fixed, recurring 168-hour period; weeks cannot be averaged. Federal law has no daily overtime, no double time and no 7th-day premium; those come from states (for example California, Alaska, Nevada, Colorado) or union agreements. The regular rate includes most bonuses and shift differentials. When state or local law sets a higher minimum wage or better overtime rule, the employer must follow the one that gives the worker more. Complaints go to the U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division (1-866-487-9243), generally within 2 years (3 if willful). For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Federal minimum wage and overtime (FLSA) for construction workers
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division; FLSA 29 U.S.C. 206, 207, 255; DOL state minimum wage table (Nov 5, 2026); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Federal law (FLSA) does NOT require employers to give meal periods or rest breaks to adult workers (as of Nov 5, 2026). Breaks are required only where state law (for example California, Oregon, Washington, Nevada, Colorado) or a union contract requires them. But if an employer does give breaks, federal rules decide whether they are paid: short breaks of about 5 to 20 minutes must be paid and counted as hours worked; a bona fide meal period, usually 30 minutes or more, can be unpaid only if the worker is completely relieved of duty (no eating at the controls, no watching the pump, no answering the radio). An "unpaid lunch" where the crew keeps working must be paid. So in a state with no break law, a 12-hour shift with no lunch is legal federally but all 12 hours must be paid, with overtime over 40 in the week. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Lunch and breaks under federal law (no federal meal or rest break requirement)
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: DOL WHD Fact Sheet 22 (Hours Worked); 29 CFR 785.18-785.19; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Under the FLSA (as of Nov 5, 2026): normal home-to-work commuting is not work time, even to a job site that changes, as long as it is in the normal area. Time counts once the first principal activity starts: if workers must report to the yard to load tools or get instructions, the ride from the yard to the site is work time, and so is travel between job sites during the day. A one-day assignment in another city: travel there and back is work time, minus the normal commute. Overnight travel: travel during the worker's normal working hours is work time, including the same hours on Saturday or Sunday; as a passenger outside normal hours it is not, but driving the company truck is. Paid travel counts toward overtime. States such as California can be stricter. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Federal hours worked: travel time, yard to site, between jobs, out of town (FLSA)
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: DOL WHD Fact Sheet 22; 29 CFR 785.33-785.41; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Federal hours-worked rules (as of Nov 5, 2026): "engaged to wait" is work time: a crew told to stand by at the site for the concrete truck, the inspector or the locate is on the clock. "Waiting to be engaged" (sent home and told to come back at 1 PM, free to use the time) is not. On call at the site or so restricted that the worker can't use the time freely is work time; on call at home with a phone is generally not. Pre- and post-shift tasks that are integral and indispensable to the job (fueling and greasing equipment, picking up the truck and tools, required safety meetings, putting on specialized protective gear that the job requires) are work time; changing into ordinary work clothes at home usually is not. Required training related to the job is work time. Union contracts can address clothes-changing time under FLSA section 3(o). For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Waiting time, on-call time and donning or doffing gear under federal law
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: DOL WHD Fact Sheet 22; Portal-to-Portal Act, 29 U.S.C. 254; 29 CFR 785.15-785.17, 785.24; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Under federal law, to be exempt from overtime as an executive, administrative or professional employee, a worker must be paid on a salary basis of at least $684 per week ($35,568 a year) and meet the duties test (as of Nov 5, 2026). The 2024 DOL rule that raised the threshold was vacated by a federal court in November 2024, so $684 is the federal level in effect. Duties matter more than titles: a foreman who mostly runs equipment or lays pipe is usually non-exempt; an executive must primarily manage, direct two or more full-time workers and have real say in hiring and firing. Blue-collar workers who do manual work are not exempt no matter the pay. Many states set higher salary levels (California $70,304 in 2026; Washington, New York, Colorado and others also higher); the stricter rule wins. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Federal exempt vs non-exempt: salary threshold $684 per week (FLSA)
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: DOL WHD overtime / exemptions; 29 CFR 541; Texas v. U.S. DOL (E.D. Tex. Nov. 15, 2024) vacating the 2024 rule; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: The Davis-Bacon Act covers federal contracts over $2,000 for construction, alteration or repair of public buildings or public works; the Related Acts apply the same rules to projects funded by federal grants, loans, guarantees or insurance (for example many water and sewer projects funded by EPA state revolving funds, and federal-aid highways) (as of Nov 5, 2026). Laborers and mechanics on the site must be paid at least the wage and fringe rates in the contract's wage determination (WD), found on SAM.gov, for the classification of work actually done, whatever their skill. A worker who does two kinds of work can be paid both rates only with accurate time records for each. If a needed classification is missing, the contractor requests a conformance through the contracting agency. The WD and the Davis-Bacon poster must be posted at the site. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Davis-Bacon prevailing wage on federal and federally funded construction
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: DOL WHD Davis-Bacon overview (2022); DOL government contracts construction pages; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Davis-Bacon details (as of Nov 5, 2026): wages are paid at least weekly. The fringe benefit amount in the wage determination can be met by contributions to bona fide plans (health, pension), paid at least quarterly, or by paying the difference in cash on top of the base rate. Contractors submit certified payrolls every week that work is done, with a signed Statement of Compliance; DOL's form WH-347 (OMB 1235-0008, expires 01/31/2028) is optional but the weekly payroll is not; electronic signatures are allowed. Apprentices may be paid less only if individually registered in an approved program and within its ratio. Overtime: the Contract Work Hours and Safety Standards Act requires 1.5x the basic rate over 40 hours a week on covered contracts over $100,000. False certified payrolls can bring criminal penalties; violations can mean withholding and debarment. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Davis-Bacon fringe benefits, certified payroll WH-347, apprentices and overtime
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: DOL Form WH-347 page; DOL WHD Davis-Bacon overview (2022); 29 CFR 5.5; 40 U.S.C. 3701-3702; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Under the OSH Act, workers have the right to (as of Nov 5, 2026): working conditions free of known serious hazards; training in a language and words they understand; required safety equipment, mostly provided at no cost; see and get copies of the injury log (OSHA 300) and their exposure and medical records; file a confidential complaint asking OSHA to inspect; take part in an inspection and talk to the inspector privately; and refuse work in good faith only when there is a real danger of death or serious injury, there's no time to get it fixed through OSHA, and the employer refused to fix it (ask first, don't just walk off unless the danger is immediate). In state-plan states (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada, Arizona and others) the state OSHA enforces equal or stricter rules. OSHA: 1-800-321-6742. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: OSHA worker rights on construction sites (federal)
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: OSHA Workers' Rights (OSHA 3021); 29 CFR 1977.12; OSHA State Plans page; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: If an employer fires, demotes, cuts hours, threatens or otherwise punishes a worker for raising a safety concern, reporting an injury, filing an OSHA complaint or taking part in an inspection, the worker can file a retaliation complaint under Section 11(c) of the OSH Act within 30 days of the adverse action (as of Nov 5, 2026). Truck drivers covered by the Surface Transportation Assistance Act (for example refusing to drive an unsafe or overweight truck, or over hours of service) have 180 days. File online (preferred), by phone to any OSHA area office or 1-800-321-OSHA, by mail, fax or in person; complaints can't be anonymous. In state-plan states a worker can file with both federal OSHA and the state plan (California's is 1 year with the Labor Commissioner). The clock starts when the action is taken and communicated. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: OSHA whistleblower complaint: 30 days to file for safety retaliation (Section 11(c))
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: whistleblowers.gov How to File a Whistleblower Complaint; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: The federal Family and Medical Leave Act (as of Nov 5, 2026) covers private employers with 50 or more employees for 20 or more weeks in this or last year. A worker is eligible after 12 months with the employer, 1,250 hours worked in the past 12 months, and working at a site with 50 or more employees within 75 miles (a construction company's employees on scattered job sites are usually counted at the office or yard they report to). Eligible workers get up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year for their own serious health condition, a family member's, a new child, or certain military family needs (26 weeks for caring for a servicemember). Health coverage continues and the worker returns to the same or an equivalent job. Many states (California CFRA, Washington, Oregon and others) give more, including paid leave. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: FMLA family and medical leave basics (federal)

field.source: DOL WHD FMLA (Fact Sheet 28 / elaws); 29 CFR 825.110-825.111; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Federal anti-discrimination laws enforced by the EEOC (as of Nov 5, 2026): Title VII bars discrimination and harassment because of race, color, religion, sex (including pregnancy, sexual orientation and gender identity) and national origin, at employers with 15 or more employees; the ADA bars disability discrimination and requires reasonable accommodation, also 15 or more; the ADEA protects workers 40 and older, 20 or more employees; the Equal Pay Act covers almost all employers. Retaliation for complaining is also illegal. A charge must generally be filed with the EEOC within 180 days, or 300 days where a state or local agency enforces a similar law (most states, including California). Many states cover smaller employers (California: 5 employees; harassment: 1). Report harassment under the company policy and keep notes. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.

field.text: Every employer in the U.S. must complete Form I-9 for each new employee, citizen or not (as of Nov 5, 2026). The employee fills out Section 1 no later than the first day of work. Within 3 business days of starting, the employee shows original, unexpired documents from the form's Lists of Acceptable Documents (one from List A, or one from List B plus one from List C) of their own choosing, and the employer completes Section 2. Employers may not ask for specific documents or more than the form requires; that can be discrimination. I-9s are kept for 3 years after hire or 1 year after the job ends, whichever is later. Some states and federal contractors require E-Verify. Ask cannot give advice about anyone's immigration status; questions go to HR or an immigration attorney. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.

field.source: USCIS I-9 Central; 8 CFR 274a.2; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Federal child labor rules for construction (as of Nov 5, 2026): under 14, no construction work. Ages 14 and 15 are barred from construction, transportation, public utilities and most jobs using power-driven machinery, ladders or scaffolds, and have hour limits (3 hours on a school day, 18 a school week, 8 on a non-school day, 40 a non-school week, 7 AM to 7 PM, 9 PM June 1 to Labor Day). Ages 16 and 17 may work in construction with no federal hour limits but not in Hazardous Occupations, which include: driving on public roads (HO 2, narrow exceptions at 17), power-driven hoisting equipment such as backhoes, excavators with lifting, forklifts, cranes, boom trucks and lifts (HO 7), circular saws and chop saws (HO 14), wrecking and demolition (HO 15), roofing (HO 16) and trenching and excavation, including work in trenches over 4 feet deep (HO 17). Registered apprentices and student-learners 16+ have limited exemptions. States often add rules. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Child labor rules for construction: minimum ages (federal)
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: DOL WHD Fact Sheet 43 (rev. Dec 2016); 29 CFR 570; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Anyone who drives a commercial motor vehicle that requires a CDL (for example a dump truck, lowboy or water truck over 26,000 lb) is covered by DOT/FMCSA drug and alcohol testing (49 CFR Parts 40 and 382) (as of Nov 5, 2026). Tests: pre-employment (drug), random, post-accident, reasonable suspicion, return-to-duty and follow-up. For 2026 the FMCSA minimum random rates are 50% of drivers for drugs and 10% for alcohol per year. Employers must check the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse before hiring and yearly. A positive test or refusal means immediate removal from safety-sensitive driving until the return-to-duty process with a Substance Abuse Professional is done. Marijuana is still prohibited under DOT rules even where states allow it. Non-CDL workers are tested only under company policy and state law. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Drug and alcohol testing for CDL drivers (DOT / FMCSA) on construction jobs

field.source: U.S. DOT ODAPC random testing rates (updated Jan 15, 2026); 49 CFR Part 382; checked 2026-11-05

field.text: There is no final federal OSHA heat standard (as of Nov 5, 2026). OSHA proposed a Heat Injury and Illness Prevention rule in 2024 (it would key on heat index triggers of 80 F and 90 F), and as of the latest status checked in 2026 it had not been finalized. Until then, federal OSHA cites dangerous heat under the General Duty Clause (Section 5(a)(1)) and runs a heat emphasis program, and recommends water, rest and shade, acclimatization of new workers, and a heat plan. Several states have their own enforceable heat rules: California, Washington, Oregon, Colorado (agriculture), Maryland, Nevada and Minnesota (indoor); see each state's file. Check osha.gov/heat for the current status of the federal rule. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.
field.title: Federal heat rule status and the OSHA General Duty Clause
field.topic: Employment law: federal rules (FLSA, Davis-Bacon, OSHA rights, leave, discrimination)
field.source: OSHA heat pages; Safety Regulatory status update (Mar 6, 2026; secondary); checked 2026-11-05

field.text: Federal OSHA reporting (as of Nov 5, 2026): an employer must report a work-related death within 8 hours, and any inpatient hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye within 24 hours, by calling OSHA (1-800-321-6742), the area office, or online (29 CFR 1904.39). Most employers over 10 employees keep the OSHA 300 log, 301 incident reports and post the 300A summary February 1 to April 30; records are kept 5 years. State-plan states have their own rules (California: serious injuries within 8 hours to Cal/OSHA). FLSA payroll records (name, hours each day and week, pay) must be kept at least 3 years, and time cards and rate tables at least 2 years. Workers comp claim deadlines are set by each state; see the state files. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the agency named above.

field.text: Quick facts for construction workers in Alaska (as of Nov 5, 2026). State labor office: Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development (https://labor.alaska.gov). Safety: Alaska runs its own OSHA state plan (AKOSH), covering private and public employers. Workers comp, reporting an injury: Give the employer written notice within 30 days of the injury. Tell the foreman or employer in writing as soon as possible and keep a copy. Federal law (FLSA wage and overtime rules, OSHA, Davis-Bacon on federally funded work) applies in Alaska too; where state and federal rules differ, the one that gives the worker more applies. Union agreements (CBAs) can change some rules where the state allows. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development.

field.text: Minimum wage in Alaska (as of Nov 5, 2026): $14.00 per hour from July 1, 2026, rising to $15.00 on July 1, 2027 (2024 Ballot Measure 1). Exempt salary must be at least 2x minimum wage for a 40-hour week. The federal minimum is $7.25; the highest of federal, state and local rates that applies where the work is done must be paid. Overtime in Alaska: Alaska has overtime by the day: 1.5x for hours over 8 in a day and over 40 in a week, for employers with 4 or more employees; a voluntary flexible 10-hour-day plan approved by the state is allowed. field.text: Final paycheck in Alaska (as of Nov 5, 2026): Fired or laid off: within 3 working days. Quit: by the next regular payday at least 3 days after notice. Late final pay can add a penalty of up to 90 days of wages. A layoff at the end of a job counts as a discharge in most states. Sick leave in Alaska: Yes (2024 Ballot Measure 1, from July 1, 2025): 1 hour per 30 hours worked; up to 40 hours a year at employers with under 15 employees and 56 hours at 15 or more. Unused sick leave usually does not have to be paid out at the end of the job unless company policy says so; vacation payout rules vary by state and policy. field.text: State prevailing wage in Alaska (as of Nov 5, 2026): Little Davis-Bacon Act (AS 36.05): public construction contracts over $25,000. The Department of Labor sets the rates (Laborers and Mechanics Minimum Rates of Pay, Pamphlet 600). Contractors file a notice of work and certified payrolls with the department during the job. On top of any state law, projects paid with federal money (for example EPA state revolving fund water and sewer jobs or federal-aid highways) carry federal Davis-Bacon wage determinations and weekly certified payrolls; when both apply, the higher rate for each classification must be paid. Workers are paid for the classification of work they actually do. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development.

field.text: Meal and rest breaks in Colorado (as of Nov 5, 2026): Colorado's COMPS Order covers most private employees including construction: a 30-minute uninterrupted, duty-free meal period when the shift is over 5 hours (if the job prevents it, an on-duty meal must be paid); and a paid 10-minute rest break for each 4 hours or major fraction (over 2 up to 6 hours = 1; over 6 up to 10 = 2; over 10 up to 14 = 3; over 14 = 4), in the middle of each work period where practical. A missed rest break must be paid as extra time worked. Heat illness rules in Colorado: No general heat standard for construction; Colorado's heat rule covers agricultural workers only. BOLI says overtime is due after 8 hours a day Monday to Friday, even under 40 hours in the week; on an established schedule of four 10-hour days (Monday to Thursday or Tuesday to Friday), after 10 hours a day; and for all hours worked on Saturdays, Sundays and six legal holidays (New Year's Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas). field.text: Quick facts for construction workers in Rhode Island (as of Nov 5, 2026). State labor office: Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training (https://www.dlt.ri.gov). Safety: Federal OSHA covers private employers (no state plan for private-sector work). Workers comp, reporting an injury: Give the employer notice within 30 days; claims within 2 years. Tell the foreman or employer in writing as soon as possible and keep a copy. Federal law (FLSA wage and overtime rules, OSHA, Davis-Bacon on federally funded work) applies in Rhode Island too; where state and federal rules differ, the one that gives the worker more applies. Union agreements (CBAs) can change some rules where the state allows. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training.

field.text: Meal and rest breaks in Rhode Island (as of Nov 5, 2026): A 20-minute meal period for a 6-hour shift and a 30-minute meal for an 8-hour shift (not required where fewer than 3 people are on the shift). No rest break law. Heat illness rules in Rhode Island: No state heat standard; federal OSHA rules apply (General Duty Clause, OSHA heat guidance: water, rest, shade, acclimatization). Breaks that are given and under about 20 minutes count as paid work time under federal law in every state. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training.

Breaks that are given and under about 20 minutes count as paid work time under federal law in every state. field.text: Minimum wage in Washington (as of Nov 5, 2026): $17.13 per hour in 2026; $17.73 on January 1, 2027 (announced September 30, 2026). Higher local rates include Seattle ($21.30 in 2026), SeaTac, Tukwila, Renton, Bellingham, Everett, Burien and unincorporated King County. Exempt salary 2026: $80,168.40 a year; 2027: $92,196 (51+ employees) or $82,976.40 (50 or fewer). The federal minimum is $7.25; the highest of federal, state and local rates that applies where the work is done must be paid. Overtime in Washington on private jobs: 1.5x over 40 hours a week; long workdays alone do not trigger overtime. Public works jobs are different: on work for the state, a county or a city, done by contract or subcontract, 8 hours is a day's work and time over 8 hours in a day is paid at 1.5x (RCW 49.28.010). A 4-10 schedule avoids overtime for the first 2 hours over 8 only under a voluntary agreement written, signed and dated with each worker for that project (or a union agreement), kept 3 years; on it, no more than 10 hours a day except in an extraordinary emergency (WAC 296-127-022, RCW 49.28.065). Saturday, Sunday and holiday work still follows the prevailing wage overtime rules, and hours over 40 in a week are always overtime. Prevailing wage and union jobs usually pay well above the minimum. For a specific case, ask HR, a labor attorney or the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries (L&I).

field.text: An excavator's lift chart (load chart) gives the rated load at combinations of lift point radius (horizontal distance from the swing centerline to the hook) and lift point height (above or below ground). Charts usually show separate columns for lifting over the front (or rear) and over the side; over the side is usually less because the machine is less stable that way. Ratings in many charts follow ISO 10567: the lesser of 75% of the static tipping load or 87% of the hydraulic lift capacity, and charts often mark which limit governs. The chart applies to the stated configuration (boom, stick, counterweight, shoe width, bucket or coupler on or off); subtract the weight of attachments, coupler and rigging if the chart says so. Always use the radius you'll actually reach, including when you swing the load to set it. Use the chart in your machine's cab or manual.
field.title: Excavator lift charts: how to read them
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: Excavators lift pipe, boxes and structures every day, so lift practice matters. Common rules from manufacturer manuals and safety guidance: lift only from the designated lifting point (lifting eye on the bucket linkage or quick coupler), never from bucket teeth or by wrapping slings around the bucket; use rigging rated for the load and inspected that shift; know the load weight (from delivery ticket or catalog) and check it against the lift chart at the working radius; keep the load low and swing slowly; use tag lines to control long pipe; never let anyone stand under the load or between the load and the trench wall or box; use the machine's lift mode or overload warning if it has one; work on level, firm ground; and use one designated signal person. OSHA's crane standard generally doesn't cover excavators lifting pipe, but OSHA rigging rules (1926.251) and the maker's limits still apply.
field.title: Lifting with an excavator: safe practice
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: OSHA 1926.251 requires that rigging equipment be inspected before use on each shift and as needed during use by a competent person, and that defective rigging be removed from service. Slings and hardware must have their rated capacity identified (alloy steel chain slings must carry a permanent tag with size, grade, rated capacity and maker). Quick daily check: Chain slings: tag present and legible, no stretched, nicked, gouged, bent or cracked links, no worn hooks. Wire rope slings: look for broken wires (OSHA 1926.251(c)(4)(iv): out of service if broken wires exceed 10 percent of the total wires in any length of eight diameters; ASME B30.9 for slings: ten randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay, or five in one strand in one lay), kinks, crushing, birdcaging, heat damage, corroded or damaged end fittings. Synthetic web and round slings: tag present, no cuts, tears, holes, melting, burns, chemical damage, broken stitching, or exposed red warning yarn. Remove damaged rigging and tag it 'do not use.'
field.title: Rigging inspection: before each shift
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.251, Rigging equipment for material handling

field.text: Hardware checks (per ASME B30.26 and maker guidance): Shackles: use only rated shackles with the working load limit (WLL) and maker marked; the pin must be the correct pin for that shackle, fully threaded in (screw pin) or secured (bolt type with nut and cotter); look for bending, cracks, wear, and opened-up jaw; never replace a pin with a bolt. Hooks: safety latch present and working (where required), no cracks, no twisting, no opening of the throat beyond the maker's limit; load seated in the bowl, not on the tip. Eyebolts and lifting eyes: rated, fully threaded in, shouldered type for angled pulls, loaded in line with the shank unless rated for angles. Remove anything bent, cracked, heat-damaged, welded on in the field, or unmarked. Exact removal criteria are in ASME B30.26 and the maker's literature.
field.title: Rigging hardware: shackles, hooks and eyebolts
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: ASME B30 series (B30.9 slings, B30.26 rigging hardware, B30.5 crane signals) as summarized in rigging industry guides

field.text: When a load hangs from two sling legs at an angle, each leg carries more than half the load. Leg tension = (load / number of legs) / sine of the angle between the sling leg and horizontal. Multipliers: legs at 90 degrees (vertical) = 1.000; 60 degrees = 1.155; 45 degrees = 1.414; 30 degrees = 2.000. Example: 4,000 lb pipe on a two-leg bridle at 45 degrees: each leg = 2,000 x 1.414 = 2,828 lb, so each leg and shackle must be rated for at least that. At 30 degrees each leg sees 4,000 lb, the full load. Avoid sling angles flatter than 30 degrees from horizontal; use longer slings or a spreader bar for long pipe. A choker hitch also reduces sling capacity (slings are rated lower in choker than in vertical; see the sling tag). Exact trigonometry.
field.title: Sling angles and leg loads
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Pipe handling practice from manufacturer guides: lift PVC, HDPE and coated pipe with nylon or polyester slings, not chains or wire rope that gouge the pipe; for long pipe (20 ft and up), use two slings spaced well apart or a spreader bar so the pipe stays level and doesn't bend or slip; check the sling hitch is snug so the pipe can't slide out; use a tag line to control swing and keep people out of the swing path; for RCP and large pipe use the producer's lifting device or rated pipe hooks; never lift pipe by inserting forks or hooks into a bell that can crack; lower pipe gently into the trench and never drop or roll it in. For unit-bundled pipe, follow the unloading instructions on the truck: don't cut bands while standing on the side the pipe can roll toward.
field.title: Lifting pipe: slings, spreader bars and tag lines
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: Use one designated signal person who the operator can see, and agree on signals before the lift. Standard crane hand signals (ASME B30.5), commonly used for excavators too: Hoist (raise load): forearm vertical, index finger pointing up, small horizontal circles. Lower: arm extended down, index finger pointing down, small circles. Swing: arm extended, point in the direction to swing. Stop: arm extended, palm down, hold. Emergency stop: arm extended, palm down, move hand rapidly back and forth. Raise boom: arm extended, fist closed, thumb up. Lower boom: arm extended, fist closed, thumb down. Dog everything (hold all motion): clasp hands in front of body. Use 'move slowly' by placing the other hand motionless near the signaling hand. Anyone may give the emergency stop. If the operator loses sight of the signal person, stop. Use radios when line of sight isn't possible.
field.title: Hand signals for excavators and cranes
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: ASME B30 series (B30.9 slings, B30.26 rigging hardware, B30.5 crane signals) as summarized in rigging industry guides

field.text: A daily pre-start check catches most breakdowns before they cost a day. Typical excavator walkaround (from operator manuals): engine oil, coolant and hydraulic oil levels; fuel and DEF level; look for leaks under the machine and at hoses, cylinders and swivel; check tracks (tension, broken shoes, loose bolts) or tires; grease boom, stick, bucket and coupler pins per the manual (many machines call for daily or every 10 hours on front linkage pins); check bucket teeth and cutting edge; quick coupler: locking pin engaged and working (do a coupler test by curling the bucket against the ground); check lights, horn, travel alarm and backup alarm; seat belt, mirrors, glass, wipers; fire extinguisher; air filter indicator; and walk the work area for hazards. Write defects on the daily report and don't run with safety defects. Check your machine's manual for exact items.
field.title: Excavator daily walkaround
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: Quick couplers let operators swap buckets fast but have caused deaths when attachments fell off onto workers in trenches. Safety practices from manufacturer and safety-agency guidance: use the coupler's locking pin or safety device every time; after each attachment change, do a physical check: curl the bucket fully, press it into the ground and move it to show it's locked, and get out to look if the coupler has no clear indicator; never let anyone stand within reach of the bucket while changing attachments or while swinging over the trench; keep the coupler and pins clean and maintained; know whether your coupler is manual, semi-automatic or fully automatic, and don't bypass alarms. Make sure the bucket and coupler weight is accounted for in the lift chart.
field.title: Quick coupler safety
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: Every machine has a maintenance schedule in its operator's manual, by hours on the hour meter. Typical structure (intervals vary by make, model and conditions, so use your manual): daily or every 10 hours: walkaround, fluid levels, grease front-end pins, drain water separator; weekly or about 50 hours: grease other points, check belts, battery, track tension; every few hundred hours: engine oil and filter (newer machines often around 500 hours, older ones 250), fuel filters; around 1,000 hours and up: hydraulic filters, final drive and swing oil, coolant checks; hydraulic oil change often several thousand hours, longer if oil analysis shows it's healthy. Severe conditions (dust, heat, hammer work) shorten intervals. Oil sampling (S-O-S or similar) catches wear early. Log every service by hour meter.
field.title: Equipment service intervals: the basics
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: Hydraulic hammers (breakers, hoe rams) are used for rock and concrete in trench work. Practices from manufacturer guidance: match hammer size to the carrier excavator's weight and hydraulic flow and pressure; grease the tool bushing frequently (often every 2 hours of hammering, per the maker) with chisel paste; keep the tool pressed firmly and perpendicular to the work; don't run the hammer blank (firing without contact) or pry with the tool; hammer in short bursts (makers commonly recommend no more than about 15 to 30 seconds in one spot before repositioning); check for loose bolts and hose wear daily. Hammer work shortens hydraulic oil and filter life; follow severe-service intervals. Protect workers from flying chips and noise.
field.title: Hydraulic hammers and attachments
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: Unloading is a common injury point. Practices from pipe makers and safety guidance: unload on level, firm ground; check the load for shifting before releasing any binders or straps, and release them from the side away from where pipe could roll; use a forklift with the right fork length or rated slings; never stand on or beside the load where pipe could roll or fall; for PVC unit bundles, lift units intact and don't stack more than the maker allows; inspect pipe and structures for shipping damage and note it on the delivery ticket before the driver leaves; check the delivery against the order (size, class, quantity). Keep the driver informed and out of the swing area. Store gaskets out of sunlight and away from oil.
field.title: Unloading pipe and materials from trucks
field.topic: Equipment, lifting and rigging basics
field.source: Industry practice / manufacturer operator manuals (check your machine's manual)

field.text: Under the Clean Water Act NPDES program, construction sites that disturb one acre or more (or are part of a larger common plan of development that will disturb one acre or more) generally need stormwater permit coverage, either EPA's Construction General Permit (in states where EPA is the authority) or a state permit. Coverage usually requires a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) describing erosion and sediment controls, inspections and stabilization, kept on site. Linear utility projects often count disturbed area along the route. The plan names who inspects and how often (EPA's CGP uses routine inspections at least every 7 calendar days, or every 14 days plus after storms of 0.25 inch or more; state permits vary). Check your state permit's exact requirements.
field.title: Stormwater permits for construction (SWPPP basics)
field.topic: Stormwater, erosion and sediment control
field.source: U.S. EPA NPDES stormwater program for construction activities (Construction General Permit)

field.text: Silt fence is a fabric barrier that slows runoff and lets sediment settle before water leaves the work area. Proper installation per EPA and state guidance: install along the contour, not up and down slopes; bury the bottom edge of the fabric in a trench (commonly about 6 inches deep) and backfill and compact it so water can't flow underneath; use stakes on the downslope side at the spacing the spec shows; turn the ends upslope (J-hooks) so water doesn't run around; don't use silt fence across concentrated flow channels or ditches (use check dams instead). Inspect after rain and remove sediment before it reaches about half the fence height (common state guidance; check yours). Compost filter socks or wattles are alternatives in some areas.
field.title: Silt fence and perimeter controls
field.topic: Stormwater, erosion and sediment control
field.source: U.S. EPA NPDES stormwater program for construction activities (Construction General Permit)

field.text: Storm drain inlet protection keeps sediment from entering storm sewers near the work: filter bags or inserts under grates, gravel and fabric barriers, or curb inlet filters, sized and maintained so they don't cause street flooding. Clean them after storms. Stabilized construction entrances (rock pads where vehicles leave the site) shake mud off tires; typical state details call for a pad of coarse stone over geotextile, with a minimum length and thickness specified (check your state detail), and street sweeping when mud gets tracked out anyway. On utility jobs in streets, the daily sweeping of mud off pavement is usually a permit condition. Check your SWPPP and local details.
field.title: Inlet protection and construction entrances
field.topic: Stormwater, erosion and sediment control
field.source: U.S. EPA NPDES stormwater program for construction activities (Construction General Permit)

field.text: Water pumped out of trenches usually carries sediment and must not be discharged muddy into storm drains, streams or wetlands. Common controls: pump into a dewatering filter bag (geotextile bag) placed on a vegetated or stable area, a sediment trap or basin, or portable settling tanks (frac tanks, weir tanks); for contaminated groundwater, treatment or disposal under a specific permit. Keep pump intakes off the trench bottom (on stone in a sump or a perforated barrel) to pump cleaner water. Many states require a separate dewatering permit or authorization under the stormwater permit, and some prohibit discharge to the sanitary sewer without the sewer authority's approval. Inspect discharge points for erosion. Check your permits before pumping.
field.title: Dewatering discharge and sediment
field.topic: Stormwater, erosion and sediment control
field.source: U.S. EPA NPDES stormwater program for construction activities (Construction General Permit)

field.text: Disturbed areas must be stabilized (seed and mulch, erosion blanket, gravel, pavement) promptly after work stops in that area; EPA's CGP requires stabilization to start immediately and be completed within a set time (generally 14 calendar days) when work has permanently stopped or temporarily stopped for a period, with state permits setting their own timelines. Concrete washout: wash out concrete truck chutes and tools only in a designated washout (lined pit or container) so high-pH wash water doesn't reach soil or storm drains. Also keep fuel and chemicals in secondary containment, have a spill kit, and dispose of trash daily. These are standard SWPPP items inspectors check.
field.title: Stabilization and concrete washout
field.topic: Stormwater, erosion and sediment control
field.source: U.S. EPA NPDES stormwater program for construction activities (Construction General Permit)

field.text: Rock is one of the biggest cost risks in pipe work. Estimating points: review borings for rock depth and type and how close borings are to your line; decide method by rock type and quantity (hammer for small or soft rock, ripping for weathered rock, drill and blast for long runs of hard rock, which adds blasting subs, permits, pre-blast surveys and vibration monitoring); expect production to drop sharply in rock; include over-excavation and extra bedding below the pipe; account for disposal and the large swell of blasted rock (about 65% in ProjectEngineer's table) when figuring haul-off; and read the contract's rock definition and pay method (unit price per CY with a pay line, or included in pipe price). Document rock daily with photos and measurements.
field.title: Estimating rock excavation
field.topic: Estimating and bidding risk items
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: Dewatering can range from a small trash pump to a full well point system, so estimate it from the borings and site. Consider: groundwater depth versus trench depth along the route, soil type (sands need well points; clays may only need sumps), length of time each section is open, pumps and backup pumps, fuel or power, hoses and discharge lines, filter bags or settling tanks, permit costs, monitoring labor (including nights and weekends), and specialty contractor quotes for well points or deep wells. If groundwater conditions aren't known, raise it before bid or carry an allowance and an exclusion. Poor dewatering also cuts pipe production, so include the productivity loss.
field.title: Estimating dewatering
field.topic: Estimating and bidding risk items
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: Traffic control is often under-priced on utility jobs. Include: devices (signs, cones, drums, barricades, arrow boards, message boards) by phase and duration, rented or owned; flaggers (two per one-lane two-way setup, plus relief for breaks) for every working hour; setup and takedown time each day; pilot cars or police officers if required; traffic control plan preparation and permit fees; night work lighting; and maintenance of devices (someone checking them). Production limits from work windows belong in the pipe price too. Check whether traffic control is a lump sum, a per-day item or included in other items.
field.title: Estimating traffic control
field.topic: Estimating and bidding risk items
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: Every pipe bid carries risk: unknown utilities, rock, groundwater, bad soil, weather, quantity changes, owner delays. Ways to handle it: identify and list risks for each job; price known conditions directly (do not hide them in contingency); carry a contingency in proportion to risk that isn't covered by contract clauses (differing site conditions, quantity variation); use clear qualifications and exclusions on private work; ask pre-bid questions to clarify unknowns; and know which risks the contract puts on you versus the owner. After the job, compare actual to estimate by cost code and update your production and cost database. General estimating practice.
field.title: Contingency, risk and bid notes
field.topic: Estimating and bidding risk items
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: Beyond direct costs, a bid needs: mobilization and demobilization (moving equipment, setting up field office or yard, initial traffic control and erosion control); job overhead (supervision, pickup trucks, small tools, temporary facilities, surveying if not provided, testing not paid by the owner, permits, insurance and bonds tied to the job); company overhead (office, estimators, accounting, yard) allocated as a percentage; and profit. Many public bid forms cap mobilization at a percentage of the contract (check yours). Markups vary widely by company and market; know your own overhead rate from your books rather than using a rule of thumb.
field.title: Mobilization, overhead and markup
field.topic: Estimating and bidding risk items
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: When the trench crosses or runs beside an existing utility (gas, water, electric duct, telecom, sewer), the exposed line must be supported and protected so it doesn't sag, break or get hit. OSHA 1926.651(b)(4) requires underground installations to be protected, supported or removed as necessary while the excavation is open. Common practices: support crossing pipes with a beam (timber or steel) across the trench and straps or slings at intervals; don't let a line hang unsupported over a long span; protect it from the bucket and from falling material; follow the owner's requirements (many gas and electric utilities have specific support details and must be present); and bed and backfill under and around the line carefully when closing the trench so it isn't left hanging on compacted backfill. Report any damage, even coating scrapes, to the owner.
field.title: Supporting exposed utilities across a trench
field.topic: Working around existing utilities
field.source: OSHA 1926.651(b)(4); utility owner practice

field.text: Besides water and sewer separation rules, utilities often require minimum clearances between your new pipe and their facilities, for example a set distance from gas mains, electric duct banks and telecom lines, both horizontally and at crossings, and extra clearance for HDD bores near existing lines. Typical requirements appear in the utility's design standards or in the plans' general notes; they may call for 12 inches or more at crossings, sometimes with insulation board or a concrete pad between. When a design crossing doesn't work in the field (the existing line is deeper than shown), stop and call the engineer and the utility owner. Pothole crossings ahead of the crew. Check your project specs and utility standards for exact clearances.
field.title: Clearances between new pipe and other utilities
field.topic: Working around existing utilities
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Trench and pipe work in summer carries heat illness risk, especially in deep trenches with little air movement and for new or returning workers who aren't acclimatized. OSHA's heat guidance centers on water, rest and shade: drink water often (OSHA suggests about one cup every 15 to 20 minutes during heavy work in heat), take rest breaks in shade, gradually build up workload for new workers over the first week or two, watch each other for signs (heavy sweating, dizziness, cramps, confusion, hot dry skin), and treat heat stroke as a 911 emergency (cool the person immediately). Plan heavy work for cooler hours. Several states have their own heat rules; check yours.
field.title: Heat illness on pipe crews
field.topic: Field safety: heat, swing radius, power lines, traffic
field.source: OSHA Heat Illness Prevention resources

field.text: Being struck by an excavator's counterweight or bucket is a leading cause of serious injury on pipe crews. Practices: barricade or mark the swing radius of the counterweight where people walk; never walk behind a working excavator; make eye contact and get the operator's acknowledgment before entering the swing area; operators stop all motion when someone enters; keep the top man in a defined safe spot; use a spotter when backing trucks and loaders, with backup alarms working (OSHA requires backup alarms or a spotter for equipment with an obstructed rear view under 1926.601 and 1926.602); and keep workers out of the trench while the box is moved or pipe is swung. Never ride on equipment or in buckets.
field.title: Excavator swing radius and struck-by hazards
field.topic: Field safety: heat, swing radius, power lines, traffic
field.source: OSHA 1926.600-602; common safety practice

field.text: Excavators, dump trucks raising beds, and pipe being lifted can contact overhead power lines, often fatally. OSHA's crane standard requires at least 10 ft clearance from lines up to 50 kV for cranes and derricks, more for higher voltages, and many companies apply similar rules to excavators lifting loads. Practices: survey for overhead lines before work starts; mark them with flags or goal posts; assign a spotter when working near them; contact the power company to de-energize, insulate or relocate lines when work must be close; never assume a line is insulated or dead. If contact happens, stay on the machine unless there's fire; if you must leave, jump clear with feet together and shuffle away. Keep everyone back from the machine.
field.title: Overhead power lines near excavation
field.topic: Field safety: heat, swing radius, power lines, traffic
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC power line clearance (as summarized)

field.text: Workers on foot in or near traffic are at risk from passing vehicles and from their own work vehicles backing. Practices: wear high-visibility apparel (OSHA 1926.651(d) requires it for workers exposed to vehicle traffic in excavations; MUTCD calls for ANSI/ISEA 107 Class 2 or 3 for workers in the right-of-way); set up the approved traffic control before work; keep a buffer space clear; face traffic when possible and have an escape route; use internal traffic control plans so dump trucks and equipment inside the work zone have defined paths and spotters; and limit people on foot near moving equipment. Night work needs Class 3 apparel and good lighting. Field and MUTCD practice.
field.title: Struck-by traffic: workers in the roadway
field.topic: Field safety: heat, swing radius, power lines, traffic
field.source: OSHA 1926.651(d); MUTCD Part 6

field.text: This first aid library gives pipe and utility crews plain-language general first aid steps taken from the American Red Cross, American Heart Association, Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons), OSHA, NIOSH/CDC and Mayo Clinic. It is general first aid, not a substitute for hands-on CPR/AED and First Aid certification; get trained and keep the card current. OSHA 29 CFR 1926.50 (in the OSHA library) requires provisions for prompt medical attention before a project starts, a person with a valid first aid certificate on site when a clinic or hospital is not reasonably accessible, first aid supplies, and eye and body flushing where corrosives are used. Three rules run through every chunk here: 1) get help first: call 911 or the site's emergency number, and on a confined-space permit use the app's EMERGENCY button; 2) never become the second victim: do not enter a trench, excavation, vault, manhole or confined space to rescue anyone without training, a protective system and the rescue plan, because would-be rescuers die this way; 3) follow the 911 dispatcher, your company's program and your competent person over anything written here. Where sources give different numbers, the chunk says so.
field.title: First aid library: what it is and is not
field.topic: First aid
field.source: American Red Cross, AHA, Stop the Bleed, OSHA 29 CFR 1926.50, NIOSH/CDC, Mayo Clinic (summarized)

field.text: Scene safety comes before first aid on any pipe job. The first person to reach an injured worker is often the next one hurt. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. On a confined-space permit, press the app's red EMERGENCY button, which dials the permit's emergency number. Shout for the foreman and anyone first-aid trained. 2. Stop and look before you move: moving equipment and swing radius, traffic in the work zone, trench walls and spoil piles, suspended loads, live power lines or a struck cable, gas alarms or a manhole or vault with bad air, running pumps or saws in the hole. 3. Shut down what you safely can: stop the excavator and other equipment near the edge, kill engines in or near the trench, stop traffic with your flagger, keep everyone else back. 4. Never enter a trench, excavation, vault, manhole or confined space to reach someone unless you are trained, the space has a protective system or tested air, and the rescue plan is in place. NIOSH reports that more than 60 percent of confined space deaths are would-be rescuers, and trench rescuers have been killed by a second wall collapse. 5. Put on gloves before touching blood. Then give first aid only where you are safe.
field.title: Scene safety first: don't become the second victim
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA trenching and confined spaces guidance; NIOSH confined space statistic as cited by UC Riverside EH&S

field.text: Calling 911 from a pipeline or utility jobsite goes faster when someone has the address ready. Steps: 1. Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. On a confined-space permit the app's EMERGENCY button dials the permit number and shows a 'Read this to the dispatcher' script with the address first. 2. Give the location first: the job's street address (the site address on the permit or job book), nearest cross street or intersection, landmarks, mile marker or station if on a highway, and which side of the road. Cell phone location can be off, so say it out loud. 3. Say what happened and how many are hurt: for example 'worker buried in a trench collapse, about 8 feet deep' or 'man down in a sewer manhole, gas suspected'. Say if a technical rescue (trench or confined space) or the power company is needed. 4. Say the person's condition: awake or not, breathing or not, heavy bleeding. 5. Tell them how the ambulance gets in: which gate or entrance, road closures, detours. 6. Send one person to the gate or road to meet and guide the ambulance, and clear a path for it. 7. Stay on the line and answer questions. Do not hang up until the dispatcher ends the call.
field.title: Calling 911 from a jobsite: what to tell the dispatcher
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Minneapolis 911 'What to say' guidance; common emergency dispatch practice

field.text: The red EMERGENCY button at the top of the Active Permit screen in The Pipelayer's Bible is the fastest way to get help during a confined space entry. Steps: 1. Press EMERGENCY. It opens the phone dialer with the permit's emergency number (911 unless the permit was changed). Confirm the call actually connected; opening the dialer does not prove it did. 2. Read the 'Read this to the dispatcher' text, address first, and give the headcount. 3. Use Text 911 if a call can't get through or you can't talk, and Text Contacts to reach others. The button does not push an alert to the foreman or office by itself; the company's Live now board shows EMERGENCY reported when the phone has signal. 4. The attendant stays outside and runs non-entry rescue (retrieval line, winch) if it is set up. Nobody enters without the trained rescue team and rescue plan. 5. When it is over, mark Activated by Mistake or Incident Resolved and add a note. Ending the incident is NOT permission to re-enter; a new air test and the entry supervisor decide that. This is general guidance; follow your permit's rescue plan.
field.title: The app's EMERGENCY button on a confined-space permit
field.topic: First aid
field.source: The Pipelayer's Bible app help (Active Permit EMERGENCY button)

field.text: A first aid kit on a pipe or utility job should be easy to reach, weatherproof and checked. Steps when someone is hurt: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious first, then grab the kit, gloves on. What to stock: 1. The American Red Cross basic kit list includes absorbent compress dressings, assorted adhesive bandages, adhesive tape, sterile gauze pads and roller bandages, antiseptic wipes, antibiotic and hydrocortisone ointment packets, an instant cold compress, an emergency blanket, a CPR breathing barrier, nonlatex gloves, tweezers, triangular bandages, a thermometer and first aid instructions. The Red Cross says to customize it. 2. For pipe work add bleeding control: a commercial tourniquet and hemostatic or plain packing gauze (Stop the Bleed kit), plus trauma shears. 3. Eye and skin flushing: OSHA 1926.50(g) requires quick drenching or flushing facilities where corrosives (including wet cement) may reach the eyes or body. 4. OSHA 1926.50 Appendix A points to ANSI Z308.1 for minimum kit contents; larger crews need more or larger kits. See the OSHA library for the rule text. 5. Know where the AED is, if your company provides one. Medicines in kits (aspirin, antihistamine) follow company policy.
field.title: First aid kit basics for a pipe crew
field.topic: First aid
field.source: American Red Cross recommended first aid kit list; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.50(d), (g) and Appendix A

field.text: Life-threatening bleeding can kill in minutes, before an ambulance reaches a jobsite. Signs: blood spurting or flowing steadily, blood pooling on the ground, clothing or bandages soaking through, a limb partly or fully cut off, or a person confused or passing out while bleeding. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Tell them 'severe bleeding'. Make sure the scene is safe (equipment stopped, out of the trench). 2. Put on gloves if you have them; don't delay long to find them. 3. Find where the blood is coming from. Open or cut clothing to see the wound. 4. Put a clean dressing, gauze or cloth over the wound and press down hard with both hands, using your body weight. 5. Keep pushing without letting up until the bleeding stops or EMS takes over. Do not lift the dressing to check; add more on top if it soaks through. 6. If pressure doesn't stop bleeding from an arm or leg, use a tourniquet. If the wound is deep or in the groin, armpit or neck, pack it. Stop the Bleed offers free or low-cost hands-on courses; take one.
field.title: Severe bleeding: recognize it and apply direct pressure (Stop the Bleed)
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons), as summarized in Florida DOH Stop the Bleed card

field.text: Wound packing is the Stop the Bleed method for deep wounds where a tourniquet won't work, such as the groin, armpit, neck or a large deep wound on the body or upper leg. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Gloves on if available. 2. Expose the wound and find the bleeding. 3. Push hemostatic gauze, plain gauze or the cleanest cloth you have straight into the wound, packing it tightly with your fingers until the wound is full. Keep feeding gauze in until no more fits. 4. Put both hands on top of the packed wound and press down hard with your body weight. 5. Hold firm, steady pressure until the bleeding stops or EMS takes over. The Stop the Bleed course teaches how long to hold; when in doubt, keep holding. 6. Don't pack wounds of the chest or belly that go into the body cavity; just cover them and hold pressure as told by the dispatcher. 7. Watch for shock and keep the person warm. Hands-on Stop the Bleed training makes packing far more effective.
field.title: Wound packing for deep bleeding wounds
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons), as summarized in Florida DOH Stop the Bleed card

field.text: A tourniquet stops life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg when pressure isn't enough or can't be held (for example an amputation from a pipe or bucket). Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Make the scene safe. 2. Place the tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the bleeding site, between the wound and the heart. Don't place it on a joint (elbow or knee); go above the joint if needed. Over clothing is acceptable if it is not bulky. 3. Pull the strap as tight as you can and fasten it. 4. Twist the rod (windlass) until the bleeding stops. It will hurt; that is expected. Lock the windlass in its clip so it stays tight. 5. Note the time it went on; write it on the tourniquet or the person's skin and tell EMS. 6. Don't loosen or remove it. Only medical staff remove it. 7. If bleeding doesn't stop, Stop the Bleed training teaches placing a second tourniquet above the first. Use a commercial tourniquet if available; improvised ones (belt, rope) often fail. Keep one in every truck's kit.
field.title: Tourniquet use for arm or leg bleeding
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons), as summarized in Florida DOH Stop the Bleed card; MedlinePlus traumatic amputation

field.text: A traumatic amputation (finger, hand, foot caught in a pipe, rigging or equipment) needs two jobs: save the person, then save the part. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Shut down the machine and lock it out before reaching in. 2. Control the bleeding first with hard direct pressure; use a tourniquet if pressure doesn't stop arm or leg bleeding. The person's life matters more than the part. 3. Treat for shock: lay the person down and keep them warm. 4. Save the part: if the cut end is dirty, remove debris and rinse it gently. Wrap it in a clean, damp cloth or gauze, seal it in a plastic bag, and set the bag in a container of ice water. 5. Don't put the part directly in water or directly on ice, and never use dry ice. If there's no cold water, keep it away from heat. 6. Send the part with the person to the hospital. Don't assume it's too small to save. 7. Don't push bones or tissue back into place, and look for other injuries. MedlinePlus notes a part that isn't cooled may only stay usable for about 4 to 6 hours. Amputations must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours (29 CFR 1904.39).
field.title: Amputation: control bleeding and save the part
field.topic: First aid
field.source: MedlinePlus (NIH) traumatic amputation

field.text: An impaled object, such as rebar, a grade stake, a nail or a metal shard stuck in the body, is acting like a plug. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Tell them what is stuck in the person and where. 2. Don't pull it out. Removing it can cause heavy bleeding. 3. Stabilize it so it can't move: build up bulky dressings or rolled cloth around the object and tape or wrap them in place. 4. Press around the object, not on it, to control bleeding. 5. If the person is pinned to something by it (for example fallen on vertical rebar), don't try to lift them off; support them and wait for EMS, who may cut the object. 6. Keep the person still and warm and watch for shock. 7. Objects in the eye: don't remove; see the eye injury chunk. General first aid; your First Aid course covers hands-on stabilization.
field.title: Impaled objects (rebar, stakes, metal) in a wound
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Standard first aid practice (American Red Cross / Mayo Clinic principles)

field.text: Crush injuries happen when a worker is pinned by a pipe stick, trench box, bucket, rolling equipment or a dropped load. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Tell the dispatcher the person is pinned, by what, and for how long. 2.
