Make the scene safe: stop and secure the machine (bucket down, brakes set, engine off), stop people from walking under suspended loads, and don't enter an unprotected trench. 3. Only move the object if it can be done safely and quickly with the right equipment and an operator and competent person directing it. Don't cause a second collapse or drop. 4. Medical guidance differs on releasing a person who has been pinned for a long time, because a crushed limb can release harmful substances into the blood when freed (crush syndrome). Tell the dispatcher how long and follow their and EMS instructions. 5. Control visible bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet. 6. Keep the person still if a spine injury is possible, keep them warm, and watch for shock. 7. Don't give food or drink. General first aid; guidance varies.
field.title: Pinned or crushed by pipe, equipment or a load
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic shock and spinal injury first aid; crush syndrome noted as varying in EMS guidance

field.text: Assume a spine injury after a fall into a trench, a struck-by blow from a bucket or pipe, or a vehicle hit, especially if the person has a head injury with changing alertness, severe neck or back pain, weakness, numbness or paralysis, loss of bladder or bowel control, or the neck or body is twisted oddly. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. 2. Keep the person still. Hold the head and neck in line with your hands, or put rolled towels or jackets on both sides of the neck. 3. Don't move the head or neck. Give first aid where they lie. Move them only if staying put is more dangerous (fire, traffic, a wall about to fall in, rising water), and only if you can do so without entering an unsafe trench. 4. Leave a hard hat on unless it blocks the airway. 5. If they stop breathing and you are trained, start CPR without tilting the head back; lift the jaw instead. 6. If they vomit, roll them onto their side with at least one helper, keeping head, neck and back in line.
field.title: Suspected spine injury: don't move them unless there's danger
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic spinal injury first aid

field.text: When a trench or excavation caves in on a worker, the first minutes are about getting real rescuers rolling without burying more people. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Say 'trench collapse, worker buried' and the depth so they send a technical trench rescue team. 2. Get everyone out of the trench and back from the edge. A second collapse is likely; walls next to a cave-in are often undercut. 3. Shut down equipment, pumps and vibration near the trench, and stop traffic close by. Keep spoil and heavy equipment away from the edge. 4. Do not jump in or send anyone in an unprotected trench. Workers digging by hand in an unshored trench have been killed by the next wall to fall. Rescue entry needs a protective system (shoring, a shield or sloping) installed by trained people. 5. Keep track of where the buried worker was last seen and tell rescuers. 6. If part of the worker is uncovered and can be reached from a protected position, keep the face and chest clear so they can breathe. 7. Send someone to meet the fire department at the road. Even partial burial is deadly: OSHA notes a cubic yard of soil can weigh as much as a car.
field.title: Trench collapse: buried worker response from outside the trench
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA Trenching and Excavation; NIOSH FACE trench collapse reports

field.text: Going in after a downed or buried coworker is the most common way one death becomes two or three on underground jobs. Steps if someone is down or buried: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. On a confined-space permit, press the app's red EMERGENCY button, which dials the permit's emergency number. 2. Stay out. NIOSH reports more than 60 percent of confined space deaths are would-be rescuers. In a NIOSH investigation of a utility vault, a worker who went in without testing or breathing protection to help a collapsed coworker died of hydrogen sulfide and oxygen deficiency. 3. Use non-entry rescue if it is set up: the attendant uses the retrieval line and winch or tripod already attached to the entrant's harness. 4. Ventilate the space from outside if you can do so without entering, and keep testing the air from outside. 5. Trench: don't enter without a shield, shoring or sloping installed. Wait for the technical rescue team. 6. Rescue entry is only for trained rescuers with the right respirators (SCBA for unknown or deadly air), a protective system and the written rescue plan. Your permit's rescue plan and competent person decide; this is general guidance.
field.title: Why you don't go in after a coworker: trenches, vaults, manholes
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH FACE report (utility vault hydrogen sulfide fatalities); NIOSH confined space statistic as cited by UC Riverside EH&S; OSHA confined spaces

field.text: Heat illness hits pipe crews working in trenches, on hot pavement and in heavy gear. OSHA says symptoms overlap, so don't try to figure out which heat illness it is: when in doubt, cool the worker and call 911. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Call immediately for confusion, slurred speech, fainting, seizures or unconsciousness. 2. Move the worker to shade or air conditioning, out of the trench if it can be done safely. 3. Cool them right away: cold water or ice bath immersion is the fastest method; otherwise remove outer layers and heavy protective clothing, put ice or cold wet towels on the head, neck, trunk, armpits and groin, and fan them. 4. Never leave the worker alone; heat illness can get worse fast. 5. New workers and anyone back from time off are at higher risk in their first days; take every symptom seriously and let them stop work. Warning signs to watch for in yourself and your crew: heavy sweating or hot dry skin, dizziness, nausea, headache, cramps, confusion, dark urine.
field.title: Heat illness: when in doubt, cool them and call 911
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA Heat-Related Illnesses and First Aid

field.text: Heat stroke is a medical emergency; NIOSH says it can be fatal if treatment is delayed, and body temperature can reach 106 F or higher within 10 to 15 minutes. Signs: confusion, altered behavior or slurred speech, loss of consciousness, seizures, hot dry skin or heavy sweating, very high body temperature, rapid heart rate. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious now. Stay with the worker until help arrives. 2. Move them to a shaded, cool area and remove outer clothing. 3. Cool them as fast as possible: immerse in a cold water or ice bath if you can (OSHA calls this the best method). Otherwise soak the skin and clothing with cool water, put cold wet cloths or ice on the head, neck, armpits and groin, and fan them. 4. Keep cooling until EMS takes over. 5. If they stop breathing, start CPR. 6. Don't give fluids to someone who is confused or not fully awake. Heat stroke can happen even if the person is still sweating.
field.title: Heat stroke: signs and emergency cooling
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Heat-related Illnesses; OSHA Heat-Related Illnesses and First Aid

field.text: Heat exhaustion signs: headache, nausea, dizziness, weakness, irritability, thirst, heavy sweating, raised body temperature and less urine. Heat syncope is brief fainting or dizziness from standing a long time or standing up fast in the heat. Steps for heat exhaustion: 1. Get help: get the worker to a clinic or emergency room; Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if medical care isn't available or they get worse (confusion or passing out means treat as heat stroke). 2. Someone stays with the worker. 3. Move them out of the heat and remove extra clothing, including boots and socks. 4. Cool them with cold compresses or have them rinse head, face and neck with cold water. 5. Encourage frequent small sips of cool water. Steps for heat syncope: 1. Sit or lie down in a cool place. 2. Slowly drink water, clear juice or a sports drink. If someone fainted, check for injuries from the fall, and any worker who doesn't come around quickly needs 911.
field.title: Heat exhaustion and heat fainting (syncope)
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Heat-related Illnesses

field.text: Heat cramps are muscle pain or spasms in the belly, arms or legs. Heat rash is red clusters of pimples or small blisters on the neck, chest, groin or elbow creases. Rhabdomyolysis (rhabdo) is muscle breakdown from heat and hard work: muscle pain or cramps, tea- or cola-colored urine, weakness, sometimes no symptoms. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if the worker is confused, faints or seems seriously ill. Rhabdo needs medical care right away. 2. Heat cramps: every 15 to 20 minutes drink water and have a snack or a drink that replaces carbohydrates and electrolytes (such as a sports drink). Avoid salt tablets. Get medical help if the worker has heart problems, is on a low-sodium diet, or the cramps don't go away within 1 hour. 3. Heat rash: move to a cooler, less humid area, keep the rash dry, use powder for comfort; don't use ointments or creams. 4. Rhabdo: stop work, drink more fluids (water preferred), go to the nearest medical facility and ask to have blood tested for creatine kinase (CK).
field.title: Heat cramps, heat rash and rhabdomyolysis
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Heat-related Illnesses

field.text: Cooling a heat-sick worker fast saves lives; on a jobsite use what you have. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for any sign of heat stroke (confusion, slurred speech, fainting). 2. Best: put the worker in cold water or an ice bath up to the neck, with someone holding them. A stock tank, tarp-lined trench box bottom or a large cooler filled with ice water can work if it is safe. OSHA calls immersion the best way to cool a worker fast in an emergency. 3. If no immersion is possible: strip heavy and outer clothing, soak the skin and clothing with cool water (water truck, hose, jugs), put ice packs or cold wet towels on the head, neck, armpits, groin and trunk, and fan hard. Keep re-wetting. 4. Move them to shade, an air-conditioned truck cab or building. 5. Keep cooling until EMS takes over; don't stop because they 'look better'. Plan ahead in hot weather: ice in the cooler, extra water, shade, and know who calls 911.
field.title: Cooling methods ranked for heat emergencies
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA Heat-Related Illnesses and First Aid; NIOSH Heat-related Illnesses

field.text: Heat acclimatization is the body getting used to heat, and OSHA notes many heat deaths happen in a worker's first few days on a hot job. NIOSH acclimatization schedules: 1. New workers: no more than 20 percent of the usual heat exposure (duration) on day 1, and increase by no more than 20 percent each day after. 2. Experienced workers returning to the heat: no more than 50 percent on day 1, 60 percent on day 2, 80 percent on day 3 and 100 percent on day 4. 3. A weekend off usually doesn't cause loss, but a week or more away can; acclimatization can often be regained in 2 to 3 days. Water: NIOSH recommends about 8 ounces (1 cup) every 15 to 20 minutes during work in the heat, which is roughly 24 to 32 ounces an hour. Drink before you're thirsty. NIOSH warns not to drink more than 48 ounces (1.5 quarts) an hour, because too much fluid can drop blood salt levels dangerously. For long shifts with heavy sweating, electrolyte drinks help. Rest in shade and watch your buddy. If anyone shows heat illness signs, call 911 for anything serious and start cooling.
field.title: Heat acclimatization and drinking water on the job
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH heat stress acclimatization recommendations; NIOSH heat stress hydration guidance (Pub. 2017-126)

field.text: Hypothermia happens when the body loses heat faster than it makes it, from long cold exposure, wet clothes, wind or working in cold water in a trench. Early signs: shivering, fatigue, clumsiness, confusion. Late signs: shivering stops, skin turns blue, pupils widen, pulse and breathing slow, loss of consciousness. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious right away. 2. Move the person to a warm place (heated truck, trailer, building). 3. Remove wet clothing gently. 4. Warm the center of the body first: chest, neck, head and groin, using dry blankets, clothing or skin-to-skin contact. 5. If they are awake and can swallow, give warm sweet drinks. Never give alcohol. 6. Keep them dry and wrapped, including the head and neck. 7. If they have no pulse or aren't breathing, start CPR. Handle a very cold person gently. Dress in layers, keep spare dry clothes and gloves in the truck, and take warm breaks.
field.title: Hypothermia: signs and first aid
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Fast Facts: Protecting Yourself from Cold Stress

field.text: Frostbite is freezing of skin and the tissue under it, most often the nose, ears, cheeks, chin, fingers and toes. Signs: numbness, aching, tingling or stinging, and bluish or pale, waxy skin. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for serious frostbite, or get the person to medical care; check for hypothermia too, which comes first. 2. Get into a warm room as soon as possible. 3. Don't walk on frostbitten feet or toes unless you must. 4. Rewarm the area in warm (not hot) water, or with body heat such as fingers tucked in the armpits. 5. Don't rub or massage the area; it causes more damage. 6. Don't use a heating pad, fire, engine exhaust, heater or radiator to rewarm; numb skin burns easily. 7. Don't rewarm if it could freeze again before reaching shelter. Prevention: dry gloves and socks, face and ear covering, and breaks out of the wind.
field.title: Frostbite: signs and first aid
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Fast Facts: Protecting Yourself from Cold Stress

field.text: Trench foot is injury from feet staying wet and cold for a long time, common when crews stand in water in a trench. NIOSH says it can happen at temperatures as high as 60 F if feet stay wet. Signs: red skin, numbness, leg cramps, swelling, tingling pain, blisters or ulcers, bleeding under the skin, and in bad cases gangrene (dark purple, blue or gray skin). Chilblains are itchy, red, inflamed patches or ulcers from repeated exposure of bare skin to cold just above freezing. Steps: 1. Get help: get medical care for trench foot or for skin that turns dark, blisters or ulcerates; Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if the worker is also hypothermic. 2. Trench foot: remove boots and wet socks, dry the feet, and avoid walking on them. 3. Chilblains: don't scratch, warm the skin slowly, keep blisters and ulcers clean and covered. Corticosteroid creams can ease itching. Prevention: dewater the trench, wear waterproof boots, and change into dry socks during the shift.
field.title: Trench foot and chilblains from wet, cold trenches
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Fast Facts: Protecting Yourself from Cold Stress

field.text: A worker who collapses in a manhole, vault, wet well, pit or deep trench should be treated as a bad-air event (hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, low oxygen or other gas) until proven otherwise. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. On a confined-space permit, press the app's red EMERGENCY button, which dials the permit's emergency number. Tell them 'worker down in a confined space, possible gas'. 2. Do not go in. Anyone entering without SCBA or supplied air and rescue training can drop within breaths, just like the first worker. 3. Attendant: start non-entry rescue with the retrieval line or winch attached to the entrant's harness, if it is rigged. 4. Keep others out and back from the opening. Keep the blower running, or start ventilation if it can be done from outside. 5. Test the air from outside with the four-gas meter and tell rescuers the readings. 6. Once the person is out in fresh air: check breathing, start CPR if they aren't breathing (use a breathing barrier), and give oxygen only if trained. 7. Anyone with even mild symptoms after exposure (headache, dizziness, nausea, eye irritation) needs medical evaluation.
field.title: Worker down in a manhole, vault or trench: suspected bad air
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH FACE report (utility vault H2S fatalities); OSHA confined spaces; OSHA hydrogen sulfide fact sheet

field.text: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is the 'rotten egg' sewer gas found in sanitary sewers, manholes, wet wells, lift stations and swampy or organic soils. Your nose is not a safe detector: OSHA warns that high concentrations deaden the sense of smell almost instantly. Effects: low levels irritate eyes, nose and throat; moderate levels cause headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and staggering; high levels cause rapid collapse, stopped breathing and death, possibly within a few breaths. NIOSH lists 100 ppm as immediately dangerous to life and health (IDLH). Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. On a confined-space permit, press the app's red EMERGENCY button, which dials the permit's emergency number. 2. Never attempt a rescue in an area that may contain H2S without the right respiratory protection (SCBA) and rescue training. 3. If you feel symptoms or the meter alarms, get out to fresh air now and warn others. 4. Once a victim is in fresh air, check breathing and start CPR if needed. 5. Rinse irritated eyes with clean water. 6. Everyone exposed needs medical evaluation; OSHA notes some effects can be delayed for hours or days.
field.title: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) exposure: sewer gas
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA Hydrogen Sulfide fact sheet

field.text: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas from gas- and diesel-powered cut-off saws, trash pumps, compactors, generators and equipment exhaust. It builds up quickly in trenches, pits, vaults and other low or poorly ventilated spots. Signs: headache, weakness or lightheadedness, nausea or vomiting, trouble breathing, confusion, blurred vision, drowsiness, loss of muscle control, passing out. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if anyone is confused, unresponsive or passed out. On a confined-space permit, press the app's red EMERGENCY button, which dials the permit's emergency number. 2. Shut off the engine if you can do it without entering bad air. 3. Get the person into fresh air only if you can do it safely from outside or from a protected, ventilated position. Don't go into the hole if others are dropping. 4. Anyone with symptoms goes to fresh air and gets medical care right away, even if they seem to recover; Mayo Clinic notes memory or movement problems can show up later. 5. Start CPR if they aren't breathing. 6. Don't let anyone back in until a meter shows the air is safe and the source is fixed. Keep engines out of the trench and downwind, and use a CO meter.
field.title: Carbon monoxide from saws, pumps and generators in trenches
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic carbon monoxide poisoning; OSHA confined spaces

field.text: Oxygen-deficient air happens when oxygen is used up or pushed out, for example by rust on steel, decaying organic matter, sewer gases, or gases like nitrogen, carbon dioxide or argon displacing air in a vault, tank, pipe or deep excavation. NIOSH and OSHA use 19.5 percent oxygen as the minimum safe level for entry (normal air is about 20.9 percent). Low oxygen gives little warning: poor judgment, clumsiness, then sudden collapse. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. On a confined-space permit, press the app's red EMERGENCY button, which dials the permit's emergency number. 2. Don't enter to rescue. A would-be rescuer breathes the same air and drops the same way. 3. Use the retrieval line and winch from outside if rigged, and ventilate from outside. 4. In fresh air, check breathing and start CPR if needed. Oxygen given by trained responders helps. 5. Anyone who felt dizzy or confused needs medical evaluation. Always test oxygen first, then flammables, then toxics before entry, and keep testing (see the confined space library).
field.title: Oxygen-deficient air: low oxygen in confined spaces
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH FACE report (utility vault); OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA confined spaces

field.text: Electric shock on a jobsite can come from a damaged cord, a struck cable, a pump, or a boom or load touching an overhead line. Rule one: don't touch the person until the power is off. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for any high-voltage contact, and call the power utility to cut the line. Say it is an electrical contact. 2. Turn off the power at the source if you can (unplug, breaker, disconnect). For high-voltage lines only the utility can. 3. Low-voltage only (a cord or tool): if you can't shut it off, push the source away with a dry non-conducting object (wood, plastic, cardboard) while standing on something dry. 4. High-voltage: stay well back: utility guidance says at least 35 ft and Mayo Clinic says at least 50 ft, so use 50 ft or more where you can, farther if wires are jumping or sparking; don't approach until the utility says the power is off. 5. Once safe, check breathing; start CPR and use an AED if they aren't breathing. 6. Cover burns loosely with sterile gauze or a clean cloth; don't remove clothing or clean the burn. Keep them warm. Every electrical shock victim needs medical evaluation; injuries inside the body can be worse than the skin shows.
field.title: Electric shock: person in contact with power
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic electrical burns first aid; OSHA downed electrical wires fact sheet

field.text: When an excavator boom, dump bed, crane or pipe load contacts an overhead power line, the whole machine and the ground around it can be energized. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious and call the power company to de-energize the line. 2. Operator: stay in the cab and don't touch anything. Try to move the boom or machine away from the line only if you can do it safely. Stay put unless the machine is on fire. 3. If you must get off (fire): jump completely clear without touching the machine and the ground at the same time, land with both feet together, and shuffle away in small steps, keeping your feet together and close to the ground. 4. Everyone else: stay back from the machine, load lines and the ground around it. Voltage spreads through the ground in rings, which is why stepping can kill. Don't touch the machine or anyone touching it. 5. Don't approach or touch an injured person until the utility confirms the line is dead. Then check breathing and give CPR as needed. 6. Never drive over a downed line. Prevention and clearance distances are in the field safety and OSHA libraries.
field.title: Equipment touching an overhead power line: what the operator and crew do
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA downed electrical wires fact sheet; Mayo Clinic electrical burns first aid

field.text: Hitting a buried electric cable with a bucket, probe bar, auger or shovel can energize the machine, tool and surrounding ground. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if anyone is hurt or there is fire or arcing, and call the electric utility and 811 to report the strike. 2. Operator: stay on the machine if it is safe; if you can, move the bucket away from the cable. Leave only if there's a fire, jumping clear with feet together and shuffling away. 3. Crew: everyone out of the trench and back from the machine and the strike. Don't touch the machine, tools or anyone in contact. 4. Keep everyone away until the utility confirms the cable is de-energized. 5. For anyone shocked, once power is off: check breathing, start CPR and use an AED if needed, cover burns loosely, and get them to medical care even if they feel fine. 6. Don't try to fix, cover or backfill the damaged cable. Follow your state one-call law and company procedure for reporting the damage.
field.title: Striking a buried electric cable while digging
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA downed electrical wires fact sheet; Mayo Clinic electrical burns; common one-call damage practice

field.text: Lightning is a real risk to crews in open cuts, on equipment and near pipe stockpiles. The National Weather Service says lightning victims do not carry an electrical charge, so you can touch them and help right away. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. 2. Move the victim to a safer place if you can; lightning can strike the same area again. 3. Check breathing. Cardiac arrest is the main immediate cause of death from lightning: start CPR if they aren't breathing and use an AED if one is available. 4. Check for burns and other injuries (falls, being thrown), and keep them warm. 5. Anyone struck needs medical evaluation even if they seem fine. Prevention: NWS says 'When thunder roars, go indoors.' Get out of the trench and off equipment and into a substantial building or a hard-topped vehicle; open equipment cabs, sheds and canopies are not safe. Stay inside until 30 minutes after the last thunder.
field.title: Struck by lightning: first aid and the 30-minute rule
field.topic: First aid
field.source: National Weather Service lightning safety (overview and brochure)

field.text: CPR keeps blood moving to the brain when someone's heart stops (after a collapse, electric shock, lightning or a bad-air rescue once they're out). Hands-only CPR is what the American Heart Association teaches the public for an adult who suddenly collapses. Steps: 1. Get help: check the scene is safe, tap and shout to see if they respond, then shout for help. Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious and send someone for an AED. 2. If they aren't breathing or are only gasping, start compressions. 3. Put two hands on the lower half of the breastbone in the center of the chest. 4. Push hard and fast: at least 2 inches deep, 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Let the chest come back up after each push. 5. Don't stop for more than 10 seconds. Swap with another person about every couple of minutes if you can. 6. Use the AED as soon as it arrives. 7. Keep going until EMS takes over or the person starts breathing. If trained, CPR with breaths uses 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Get certified in CPR/AED; hands-on practice matters.
field.title: Hands-only CPR for an adult who collapses
field.topic: First aid
field.source: American Heart Association CPR infographic and Heartsaver CPR AED summary (2025 Guidelines)

field.text: An AED is a portable device that checks the heart rhythm and gives a shock if needed. It talks you through each step. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Start CPR while someone brings the AED. 2. Turn the AED on and follow its voice prompts. 3. Expose the chest and wipe it dry if it is wet or sweaty. 4. Put one pad on the upper right chest and the other on the lower left side, a few inches below the left armpit (as shown on the pads). If pads might touch, put one in the middle of the chest and one on the back between the shoulder blades. 5. Plug in the pad connector if needed. 6. Make sure nobody is touching the person and say 'CLEAR!' while it analyzes. 7. If a shock is advised, make sure nobody is touching them, say 'CLEAR!', and press the shock button. 8. Right after the shock, or if no shock is advised, restart CPR starting with compressions, and follow the prompts. Move the person out of standing water before using an AED. Know where your company's AED is kept.
field.title: Using an AED (automated external defibrillator)
field.topic: First aid
field.source: American Red Cross AED steps

field.text: Choking means something is blocking the airway. Signs: hands clutched to the throat, can't talk, weak or no cough, noisy or squeaky breathing, lips or skin turning blue or gray. Steps: 1. Get help: have someone call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious while you help. If you're alone, give first aid first, then call. 2. If the person can cough forcefully, let them keep coughing. 3. If they can't cough, talk or breathe: give 5 back blows. Stand slightly behind, support their chest with one arm, lean them forward, and strike between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. 4. Then give 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind, put a fist just above the navel, grab it with your other hand, and thrust in and up. 5. Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until the object comes out. 6. If they become unresponsive, lower them to the ground, start CPR, and look in the mouth before breaths; remove an object only if you can see it. Mayo Clinic notes the Red Cross teaches back blows plus thrusts, some programs teach thrusts only; both are accepted. Alone and choking: thrust yourself over a chair back or tailgate edge.
field.title: Choking adult: back blows and abdominal thrusts
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic choking first aid (citing American Red Cross)

field.text: A fracture on a pipe job often comes from a fall into the trench, a pipe stick rolling onto a leg, or a hand caught in rigging. Signs: deformity, severe pain with movement or pressure, swelling, bone through the skin, numb or discolored fingers or toes beyond the injury. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for major trauma, a deformed limb, bone through the skin, heavy bleeding, numb or discolored fingers or toes, or a suspected break in the head, neck, back, pelvis or thigh. 2. Stop bleeding with pressure using a sterile bandage or clean cloth. 3. Keep the injured part still. Don't move the person unless you must, and don't try to straighten the bone or push a bone end back in. 4. If you're trained and help is far away, splint the area above and below the break. 5. Put ice wrapped in a cloth on the area; never ice directly on skin. 6. Treat for shock if they feel faint or breathe fast: lay them down, head slightly lower than the body, legs raised if that doesn't hurt the injury. Treat as a spine injury if the fall or blow could have hurt the neck or back.
field.title: Broken bones (fractures): first aid
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic fractures first aid

field.text: A splint holds a broken or badly hurt limb still to cut pain and further damage while waiting for or traveling to care. Mayo Clinic advises splinting only if you're trained and medical help isn't close. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious first. If EMS is coming soon, just hold the limb still and let them splint. 2. Splint it the way you find it. Don't straighten it. 3. Use something stiff: a board, folded cardboard, a rolled magazine, a rolled jacket, or a commercial splint. 4. Make it long enough to cover the joint above and below the break (for a forearm, from past the elbow to past the wrist). 5. Pad the splint with cloth for comfort. 6. Tie it on with strips of cloth, tape or triangular bandages above and below the injury, not over it. Snug, not tight. 7. Check fingers or toes before and after: if they get cold, pale, blue, numb or tingly, loosen the ties. 8. An arm can be supported in a sling against the body. Never splint the neck or back yourself; keep the person still.
field.title: Splinting basics for a suspected fracture
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic fractures first aid; standard first aid splinting practice

field.text: Sprains (stretched or torn ligaments, often an ankle rolled on uneven ground or rock) and strains (pulled muscles, often from lifting pipe or fittings) are among the most common pipe crew injuries. Steps: 1. Get help: get medical care right away if the person can't bear weight, the joint is unstable or numb, the skin changes color, there's pain directly over the bone, or it looks deformed (could be a fracture). Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if it came with a fall from height or other serious injury. 2. Rest: keep weight off it. Mayo Clinic suggests 48 to 72 hours or as a clinician advises. 3. Ice: 15 to 20 minutes at a time, 4 to 8 times a day for the first 48 hours, with a cloth between ice and skin. Don't ice more than 20 minutes at once. 4. Compression: wrap with an elastic bandage to limit swelling, not so tight it causes numbness. 5. Elevation: raise it above heart level when possible. See a doctor if it doesn't improve in 2 or 3 days. Report it to your foreman even if it seems minor.
field.title: Sprains and strains: R.I.C.E.
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic sprain first aid

field.text: A dislocation is when bones are forced out of position at a joint, such as a shoulder, finger, elbow or knee cap, often from a fall or a hand caught by a moving pipe. Signs: obvious deformity, severe pain, can't move the joint, swelling. Steps: 1. Get help: get medical care as soon as possible; Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if there's heavy bleeding, numbness, a cold or pale limb beyond the joint, or other serious injury. 2. Don't try to move the joint or force it back into place. That can damage nerves, blood vessels, muscles and ligaments. 3. Keep the joint still with a splint or sling in the position you found it. 4. Put ice wrapped in cloth on it to limit swelling. 5. Check fingers or toes past the injury for color, warmth and feeling, and tell EMS if they change. 6. Don't delay care; a dislocation can hide a fracture.
field.title: Dislocated joint: don't pop it back in
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic dislocation first aid

field.text: Thermal burns on pipe jobs come from cutting torches, HDPE fusion heater plates, hot tar or asphalt, exhaust parts and fires. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for a burn that is deep (dry, leathery, charred, white, brown or black), larger than about 3 inches across, on the face, hands, feet, groin or a major joint, wraps around a limb, or comes with smoke inhalation. Electrical, lightning and strong chemical burns always need emergency care. 2. Stop the burning: move away from the heat, put out burning clothing. 3. Minor burns: cool under cool (not cold) running water for about 10 minutes. 4. Remove rings, watches and tight items before swelling starts. Leave clothing that is stuck to the skin. 5. Cover loosely with a clean, dry cloth or sterile gauze. 6. Major burns: check breathing, raise the burned area above heart level if possible, and watch for shock (pale, cool skin, weak pulse); lay them down and cover with a clean sheet. 7. Don't use ice or very cold water, butter, oil or toothpaste, and don't pop blisters. Hot asphalt or tar: cool with water, don't peel it off; let medical staff remove it.
field.title: Heat burns: torch, hot pipe, fusion plate, exhaust
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic burns first aid

field.text: Chemical burns can come from PVC primer and solvent cement, fuel, acids and degreasers, pipe lubricants, line-marking or disinfecting chemicals (chlorine for water main disinfection). Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for large or deep burns, burns on the face, hands, feet, groin or a major joint, or if the person feels ill. If unsure whether a chemical is toxic, call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222, then 911 if needed. 2. Protect yourself: put on gloves. 3. Brush off any dry chemical before wetting it. 4. Remove contaminated clothing and jewelry. 5. Rinse the skin with running water for at least 20 minutes (Mayo Clinic; a shower or hose if available). Keep the chemical out of the eyes. 6. Cover loosely with gauze or clean cloth. 7. Rinse again for several more minutes if pain returns. 8. Watch for shock with a big burn. Take the container, label or Safety Data Sheet (SDS) to the hospital; the SDS first aid section has product-specific instructions. Rinse times differ between sources and products; follow the SDS and poison control.
field.title: Chemical burns on skin (solvents, primers, fuels, cleaners)
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic chemical burns first aid; Poison Help line

field.text: Wet cement, concrete, grout and mortar are strongly alkaline and can cause caustic cement burns: blisters, dead or hardened skin, or black or green skin, sometimes down to the bone. OSHA warns you cannot rely on pain to warn you, and burns can keep getting worse after contact ends. Kneeling in wet concrete or cement inside boots and gloves causes many of these burns. Steps: 1. Get help: OSHA advises anyone with a cement burn to see a health care professional immediately; Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for a large or deep burn. 2. Get out of the wet concrete and remove soaked clothing, boots, gloves, rings and watches. 3. Rinse the skin well with clean, cool water and wash with a pH-neutral or slightly acidic soap. OSHA says diluted vinegar or a buffering solution may help neutralize residue. 4. Don't use abrasives, waterless hand cleaners, or lanolin or petroleum jelly, which trap cement against the skin. 5. Cover loosely with a clean dressing. 6. Replace boots that cement got into and keep contaminated clothes away from street clothes. For cement in the eyes, see the eye flushing chunk.
field.title: Cement and concrete burns on skin
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA 3351 Preventing Skin Problems from Working with Portland Cement

field.text: A chemical splash in the eye, including wet cement, concrete, lime, solvent cement or chlorine, can cause permanent damage within minutes. Flushing right away matters more than anything else. Steps: 1. Get help: start flushing first, and have someone call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Every chemical or cement splash in the eye needs emergency or eye-specialist care after flushing. 2. Flush with clean, lukewarm water right away: eyewash station, bottle, hose on gentle flow, faucet or shower aimed at the forehead. Hold the eyelids open and roll the eye. 3. Flush for a long time: ANSI/OSHA eyewash guidance uses at least 15 minutes; Mayo Clinic says at least 20 minutes. Sources differ, so keep flushing at least 15 to 20 minutes and longer for cement or strong chemicals, or until EMS or poison control (1-800-222-1222) says stop. 4. Remove contact lenses if they don't come out with flushing. 5. Don't rub the eye and don't put anything in it except water or saline; no eye drops unless medical staff say so. 6. Take the product name, container or SDS to the hospital. OSHA 1926.50(g) requires flushing facilities where corrosives may reach the eyes.
field.title: Chemicals or wet concrete in the eye: flush now
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic chemical splash in the eye first aid; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.50(g); ANSI Z358.1 (15-minute flush, as commonly cited)

field.text: Dust, sand, grit and metal chips from cutting pipe, grinding or wind across the jobsite are common eye injuries. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious or get emergency care if an object is stuck in the eye, sticking out, or the eye was hit hard, cut or punctured, or vision changes. 2. Embedded or large object: don't try to remove it, don't press on the eye, and don't rub. Cover the eye loosely (a paper cup taped over it works) and keep the person still. 3. Loose dust or grit: wash your hands, then flush the eye with a gentle stream of clean, lukewarm water from an eyewash bottle, cup or faucet, holding the lids open. 4. To look for the speck, pull the lower lid down while they look up, then lift the upper lid while they look down. Flush it out; don't dig with fingers or tools. 5. Remove contact lenses before or during flushing. 6. Get medical care if flushing doesn't remove it, vision is affected, or pain, redness or the feeling of something in the eye lasts more than 24 hours. Metal from grinding can rust in the eye; have it checked.
field.title: Dust, grit or metal in the eye; embedded objects
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic foreign object in the eye first aid

field.text: A concussion is a brain injury from a hit to the head or a jolt that whips the head, such as being struck by a bucket, pipe or falling object, or a fall into a trench. Even a bump that seems minor can be serious. Common signs: confusion, nausea, balance problems, blurry vision, sensitivity to light and noise, dizziness. Danger signs that need emergency care right away (CDC): - a headache that gets worse and won't go away - weakness, numbness or poor coordination - repeated vomiting - slurred speech - drowsiness or can't be woken - one pupil larger than the other - seizures - can't recognize people or places, or more and more confused, restless or agitated - unusual behavior or passing out Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for any danger sign or loss of consciousness. 2. Treat as a possible spine injury; keep the head and neck still. 3. Control scalp bleeding with gentle pressure. 4. Don't let them go back to work or drive that day; have them seen by a doctor and keep someone with them.
field.title: Head injury and concussion signs
field.topic: First aid
field.source: CDC HEADS UP concussion fact sheet

field.text: Stings from bees, wasps, hornets and yellow jackets are common when clearing brush or digging into ground nests. Most cause only local pain and swelling. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for any sign of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), even one or two signs: trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, face, eyelids or throat, dizziness or fainting, weak fast pulse, hives, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. See the anaphylaxis chunk. 2. Move away from the nest to avoid more stings. 3. Scrape out any stinger left in the skin. 4. Wash the area with soap and water. 5. Hold a cold, damp cloth or ice wrapped in cloth on it for 10 to 20 minutes. 6. Raise the arm or leg if that's where the sting is. 7. Calamine lotion, a baking soda paste or hydrocortisone cream can ease itching; follow the label for over-the-counter antihistamines or pain relievers. See a doctor if swelling keeps spreading or the site looks infected. Workers with known sting allergies should tell the foreman where their epinephrine auto-injector is.
field.title: Bee, wasp and hornet stings
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic insect bites and stings first aid

field.text: Anaphylaxis is a severe, fast allergic reaction (to stings, foods, medicines or latex) that can kill. Signs: hives, itching or flushing, swelling of the face, eyes, lips or throat, wheezing or trouble breathing or swallowing, a weak fast pulse, nausea or vomiting, dizziness, fainting. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious right away. Don't wait to see if it gets better. 2. Ask if the person carries an epinephrine auto-injector (for example EpiPen or Auvi-Q). If they need it, ask if you should help. It is usually pressed against the outer thigh and held in place for several seconds; follow the instructions printed on the device. Only use one prescribed to them unless your company program says otherwise. 3. Have them lie on their back and stay still; loosen tight clothing and cover with a blanket. 4. If they vomit or bleed from the mouth, turn them on their side. 5. Don't give anything to drink. Antihistamine pills are too slow to treat anaphylaxis. 6. If they stop breathing, start CPR. They need the ER even if they improve, because symptoms can come back. Whether to give a second dose depends on the device instructions and the dispatcher.
field.title: Anaphylaxis: severe allergic reaction and epinephrine auto-injectors
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic anaphylaxis first aid; Mayo Clinic insect bites and stings

field.text: US venomous snakes include rattlesnakes, copperheads, cottonmouths (water moccasins) and coral snakes, found in brush, rock piles, pipe stockpiles and trench spoil. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious or get emergency medical care right away. Don't drive yourself; dizziness or fainting can happen. Don't wait for symptoms. 2. Stay calm and tell your supervisor. 3. If it's safe, take a photo of the snake from a distance. Never catch, trap or handle the snake, even a dead one or its head. 4. Sit or lie down with the bite in a comfortable, neutral position (not raised high or hung low) while waiting. 5. Remove rings, watches and tight items before swelling starts. 6. Wash the bite with soap and water and cover with a clean, dry dressing. 7. Mark the edge of the swelling or tenderness on the skin with a pen and write the time. Do NOT: use a tourniquet, cut the wound, suck out venom, apply ice or soak in water, use electric shock or folk remedies, drink alcohol, or take aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen.
field.title: Snakebites (US venomous snakes)
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Venomous Snakes: Symptoms and First Aid

field.text: Most spider bites are minor, but the black widow (shiny black, red hourglass on the belly) and brown recluse (brown, violin-shaped mark on the back) can cause serious illness. Both hide in stored pipe, fittings, boxes, gloves and boots left in the conex or truck. Steps: 1. Get help: get medical care right away for a suspected black widow or brown recluse bite, if you aren't sure what bit you, or for severe pain or belly cramps, a growing wound, red, purple or brown skin spreading around the bite, or streaks. Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious for trouble breathing or swallowing. 2. Clean the bite with mild soap and water. 3. Put a cool, damp cloth or ice wrapped in cloth on the bite for 15 minutes every hour. 4. Raise the bitten area if possible. 5. Over-the-counter antibiotic ointment and pain relievers can be used per the label. Black widow bites may cause belly pain, cramping, nausea, sweating and shaking. Brown recluse bites may start mildly then develop fever, chills and a sore with a dark center. A tetanus shot may be needed. Shake out gloves and boots before putting them on.
field.title: Spider bites: black widow and brown recluse
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic spider bites first aid

field.text: Poison ivy, poison oak and poison sumac cause an itchy, blistering rash from oil (urushiol) on the leaves, stems and roots, even in winter. Clearing right-of-way and digging through roots spreads it onto gloves, tools and clothing. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious or go to an ER for a severe allergic reaction (swelling, trouble breathing) or if the person has had a severe reaction before. 2. Rinse the skin right away with rubbing alcohol, a poison plant wash or a degreasing soap and plenty of water. Keep rinsing so the wash doesn't dry on the skin and spread the oil. 3. Scrub under fingernails with a brush. 4. Use wet compresses, calamine lotion or hydrocortisone cream for itching; an oatmeal bath may help. An antihistamine may help but can cause drowsiness (no driving or operating equipment). 5. Get medical care for a severe rash or one on the face or genitals. 6. Wash contaminated clothing, gloves and tools. Never burn brush that may contain these plants: NIOSH warns the smoke can cause serious lung reactions.
field.title: Poison ivy, poison oak and poison sumac
field.topic: First aid
field.source: NIOSH Fast Facts: Protecting Yourself from Poisonous Plants

field.text: Respirable crystalline silica dust comes from cutting concrete pipe, sawing pavement, chipping, jackhammering and handling some sands and stone. The serious diseases (silicosis, lung cancer, kidney disease) build up over years, so there's no first aid fix; the job is to stop exposure. First steps after a heavy dust exposure: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if someone has severe trouble breathing, chest pain or blue lips. 2. Move the worker out of the dust into clean air. 3. Eyes: flush dust out with clean water for several minutes; don't rub (see the eye chunk). 4. Skin: wash with soap and water. Change dusty clothes and don't blow them off with compressed air. 5. Coughing, wheezing or shortness of breath that doesn't settle: get medical evaluation. 6. Report it to the foreman so the dust controls (water on the blade, vacuum, respirator) get fixed before work resumes. OSHA's silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153, Table 1) sets the controls for each task and requires medical exams for workers who must wear respirators 30 or more days a year; see the silica library.
field.title: Silica dust exposure: first steps
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA Respirable Crystalline Silica in Construction (29 CFR 1926.1153)

field.text: Raw sewage contains bacteria, viruses and parasites that can cause stomach illness, hepatitis A, tetanus through cuts, and skin and eye infections. Pipe crews are exposed during sewer taps, bypass pumping, repairs and live connections. Steps after a splash or soaking: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if someone swallowed a large amount or is seriously hurt; otherwise see a doctor for any cut that got sewage in it or any illness afterward. 2. Wash exposed skin with soap and clean water right away; wash hands before eating, drinking, smoking or using a phone. 3. Flush splashes in the eyes, nose or mouth with clean water. 4. Clean any cut, put a clean dressing on it, and keep it covered; wear gloves over chapped or cut hands. 5. Change out of badly soiled clothing; keep work clothes separate and shower before going home. 6. Don't touch your face, eyes, nose or mouth until you've washed. Vaccines: CPWR guidance says sewer workers need up-to-date tetanus and diphtheria shots and should ask a doctor or nurse about hepatitis A vaccination. See a doctor if you aren't sure when your last tetanus shot was.
field.title: Sewage exposure: hygiene and when to see a doctor
field.topic: First aid
field.source: CPWR Hazard Alert: Biological hazards in sewage (NIOSH/NIEHS funded)

field.text: Used needles and syringes turn up in sewer manholes, storm drains, inlets, bypass pump strainers and excavated trash. A stick can carry hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV. The risk from one stick is usually low, but some treatments work best when started quickly. Steps: 1. Get help: report it to your foreman or supervisor right away and get to a doctor, clinic or ER the same day. Never decide on your own that you don't need care. 2. Wash it with soap and water. Don't squeeze it or use bleach or other harsh chemicals on it. 3. Cover it with a clean bandage. 4. Don't recap or throw the needle loose in the trash. If it can be picked up safely with pliers or tongs, put it in a hard plastic container with a lid for disposal per company or local rules. 5. Tell the medical provider how it happened, the type of needle, whether blood was visible and how deep the stick was. They may order tests, vaccines or medicines. 6. Report it in your company's injury process. Wear cut- and puncture-resistant gloves and use tools, not hands, to clear debris.
field.title: Needle-stick from sewer debris or trash
field.topic: First aid
field.source: MedlinePlus (NIH) exposure to blood or body fluids / needlestick instructions

field.text: Shock means the body isn't getting enough blood flow. It follows heavy bleeding, crush injuries, burns, severe allergic reactions and heat illness, and can kill even if the injury looks survivable. Signs: cold, sweaty, pale or gray skin, blue or gray lips or nails, fast heartbeat, fast shallow breathing, nausea, weakness, lightheadedness or fainting, confusion, anxiety or restlessness. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. 2. Control bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet. 3. If a head, neck or back injury is possible, don't move them unless they're in danger. 4. Otherwise lay them down and raise the legs slightly, unless that causes pain or trouble breathing. 5. Keep them still, loosen tight clothing, and cover them to keep warm (head, hands and feet too). If they're overheated, cool them instead. 6. For a severe allergic reaction, use their epinephrine auto-injector if available. 7. If they vomit and no spine injury is suspected, roll them on their side. 8. Don't give food or drink. 9. Start CPR if they stop breathing.
field.title: Shock (medical): signs and first aid
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic shock first aid

field.text: Fainting is a brief loss of consciousness, often from heat, standing a long time, pain, dehydration, low blood sugar or a heart problem. On a jobsite the fall itself can cause injury, especially near an open trench. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if the person doesn't come around within about one minute, isn't breathing, was hurt in the fall, has chest pain, or may have heat illness. 2. If you feel faint, sit or lie down right away, away from the trench edge, and don't stand up fast. 3. If someone faints, lay them on their back. If they're breathing and not injured, raise their legs about 12 inches and loosen belts and collars. 4. Check breathing; start CPR if they aren't breathing. 5. Treat any injuries from the fall; control bleeding with pressure. If they fell into a trench or from height, treat as a possible spine injury. 6. Don't help them up too fast; let them rest. In hot weather, cool them and give water once fully awake. Anyone who faints at work should be seen by a doctor and not drive or run equipment that day.
field.title: Fainting on the job
field.topic: First aid
field.source: Mayo Clinic fainting first aid; NIOSH heat syncope

field.text: Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can hit a worker with diabetes who skipped a meal, worked hard in the heat or took medicine without eating. Signs include shakiness, sweating, confusion or 'brain fog', irritability, and in severe cases not being able to stay awake. It can look like heat illness or being drunk. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if the person is confused and can't swallow safely, passes out, or doesn't improve. 2. If they're awake and can swallow, give fast sugar: CDC's 15-15 rule is about 15 grams of carbohydrate, such as 4 ounces (half a cup) of juice or regular (not diet) soda, 1 tablespoon of sugar or honey, 3 to 4 glucose tablets, or 1 tube of glucose gel. 3. Wait 15 minutes; if they have a meter and are still under 70 mg/dL, or still have symptoms, repeat. 4. Once better, have them eat a snack or meal with protein and carbs. 5. Never put food or drink in the mouth of someone who is unconscious or can't swallow; roll them on their side and call 911. Glucagon is used only by someone who knows how, from the person's own kit.
field.title: Diabetic emergency: low blood sugar
field.topic: First aid
field.source: CDC Treatment of Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia)

field.text: A seizure can cause shaking, stiffening, falling, staring or loss of awareness. Causes include epilepsy, head injury, heat stroke, low blood sugar, electrical shock and toxic gas exposure. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious if the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, another seizure follows, the person has trouble breathing or doesn't wake up, was injured, has never had a seizure before, has diabetes, is pregnant, or it happened in water. On a jobsite, also call if it may be from heat, a head injury, electricity or gas. 2. Stay with them and stay calm. Time the seizure. 3. Ease them to the ground and clear the area of tools, pipe and equipment; keep them away from the trench edge. 4. Put something soft and flat (a jacket) under the head, remove glasses, and loosen anything around the neck. 5. Gently roll them onto their side to keep the airway clear. 6. Don't hold them down, and don't put anything in their mouth. 7. Don't give food or water until fully alert. 8. Afterward, help them sit somewhere safe and explain what happened. Don't let them drive or run equipment.
field.title: Seizures: first aid
field.topic: First aid
field.source: CDC First Aid for Seizures

field.text: A stroke is a blood clot or bleed in the brain. Fast treatment saves brain function, so learn F.A.S.T.: - Face: ask the person to smile. Does one side droop or feel numb? - Arm: ask them to raise both arms. Is one weak or numb, or does it drift down? - Speech: ask them to repeat 'The sky is blue.' Is speech slurred, strange or hard to understand? - Time: call 911 right away, even if the signs go away, and note the time the first symptoms started. Other sudden signs: trouble seeing in one or both eyes, trouble walking, dizziness or loss of balance, sudden severe headache with no known cause, sudden confusion. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious immediately. Don't drive them yourself unless told to. 2. Write down the time symptoms began and tell EMS; it guides treatment. 3. Keep them safe and comfortable, sitting or lying, away from the trench and traffic. 4. Don't give food, drink or medicine. 5. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR. Stroke signs can look like heat illness or low blood sugar; treat it as an emergency either way.
field.title: Stroke: F.A.S.T. signs
field.topic: First aid
field.source: American Heart Association/American Stroke Association warning signs

field.text: A heart attack is a blocked artery to the heart. Warning signs (American Heart Association): - Chest discomfort in the center of the chest lasting more than a few minutes, or that goes away and comes back: pressure, squeezing, fullness or pain. - Discomfort in one or both arms, the back, neck, jaw or stomach. - Shortness of breath, with or without chest discomfort. - Cold sweat, nausea or lightheadedness. Women are more likely than men to have shortness of breath, nausea or vomiting, and back or jaw pain, though chest discomfort is still most common. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious right away; don't let them 'walk it off' or drive themselves. 2. Have them stop work and sit or rest in a comfortable position, out of the heat. 3. Give aspirin only if the 911 dispatcher tells you to and the person isn't allergic. 4. Send someone for the AED. 5. If they collapse and aren't breathing normally, start hands-only CPR and use the AED. 6. Send someone to meet the ambulance at the gate. Heat, heavy lifting and digging can trigger heart attacks in workers with heart disease.
field.title: Heart attack: warning signs and what to do
field.topic: First aid
field.source: American Heart Association warning signs of heart attack and stroke

field.text: After the injured worker is cared for, report the incident so it gets investigated and the hazard gets fixed. Steps: 1. Get help first: make sure 911 (or the site's emergency number) was called for anything serious and the person is in medical hands. On a confined-space permit, close out the EMERGENCY panel (Incident Resolved) only when it's over; that is not permission to re-enter. 2. Tell your foreman or superintendent right away, even for minor injuries. They notify the safety person and decide on OSHA reporting. 3. Secure the scene: keep the trench, equipment or area as it was if it is safe, and take photos. 4. In The Pipelayer's Bible, log it in the job book with Add Safety Event (Near miss, First aid, Incident, Property damage or Stop work). Describe what happened and the hazard; do not put medical details, diagnoses or treatment in it. Medical information goes through your company's confidential injury process. 5. Write down witnesses, time, location and what was done. 6. Fix the cause before work resumes, and talk it through at the next toolbox talk.
field.title: After an incident: reporting on the job and in the app
field.topic: First aid
field.source: The Pipelayer's Bible app help (job book Add Safety Event); common safety program practice

field.text: OSHA requires employers to report severe work injuries (29 CFR 1904.39): 1. A work-related fatality must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours. 2. An in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, an amputation, or the loss of an eye must be reported within 24 hours. 3. The clock starts when the employer learns about it (or learns it was work-related). 4. Report by phone or in person to the nearest OSHA Area Office, by the toll-free number 1-800-321-OSHA (1-800-321-6742), or with OSHA's online reporting form. If the Area Office is closed, use the toll-free number or the online form. 5. OSHA asks for the company name, the location and time of the incident, the type of event, the number of employees affected, their names and job titles, the contact person and phone number, and a brief description. In-patient hospitalization means a formal admission to a hospital, not just ER treatment. Getting help comes first: call 911 for anything serious. The foreman or superintendent usually makes this report through the company's safety person, so tell them right away. The full rule text is in the OSHA recordkeeping library. States with their own OSHA plans may have extra rules: California requires any serious injury, illness or death to be reported to Cal/OSHA within 8 hours (8 CCR 342).
field.title: OSHA reporting: hospitalization, amputation, eye loss and fatality
field.topic: First aid
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.39

field.text: A force main carries sewage under pressure from a lift (pump) station. Materials are usually ductile iron, PVC (C900) or HDPE. Differences from gravity sewer and water mains: thrust restraint is needed at bends like a water main; air release valves at high points must be sewage-rated (combination air valves designed for wastewater); separation from water mains still applies; ductile iron force mains often need a special lining (not standard cement) to resist hydrogen sulfide corrosion; force mains are hydrostatically tested like water mains (check spec pressure and allowance) but not disinfected; and they're often marked with green tracer wire and warning tape. Grade is less critical than gravity sewer, but avoid unnecessary high points, which trap air. Follow your project specs.
field.title: Sewage force mains: what's different
field.topic: Force mains, lift stations and bypass pumping
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Lift (pump) stations collect sewage in a wet well and pump it through a force main. Field crews typically build or set: the precast wet well (set level on a prepared base, often heavy, so lift planning matters), valve vault, pumps on guide rails, piping, check valves and isolation valves, electrical controls, and the generator or bypass connection. Watertight construction is critical: seal joints, use watertight pipe penetrations, and coat interiors if specified (hydrogen sulfide corrodes concrete). Wet wells are permit-required confined spaces; never enter without testing, ventilation and a permit. Startup includes testing pumps, floats and alarms with the owner. Follow the shop drawings and maker's instructions.
field.title: Lift stations: field basics
field.topic: Force mains, lift stations and bypass pumping
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: When connecting to or replacing an active sewer, flow must be bypassed around the work. Plan: measure or estimate peak flow (including wet-weather flow), choose pumps with capacity and backups, plug the upstream line or manhole, set suction hoses or pipes in the upstream manhole, run discharge lines (often fused HDPE or hard pipe across traffic with ramps or buried crossings) to a downstream manhole, and staff or monitor the bypass around the clock with alarms if it runs overnight. A sewage spill is a reportable violation in most states, so have a spill plan and someone watching levels. Many agencies require a written bypass plan submitted for approval. Test the bypass before cutting into the line.
field.title: Bypass pumping basics
field.topic: Force mains, lift stations and bypass pumping
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Pipe terms crews use. Bell: the enlarged end of a pipe that the next pipe's spigot slides into. Spigot: the plain end that goes into the bell. Gasket: the rubber ring that seals a bell and spigot joint. Homing mark (insertion mark): the line on the spigot showing how far to push it into the bell. Barrel: the main body of the pipe between the ends. Lay length: the effective length a pipe adds to the line when joined (shorter than overall length because of the bell). Stick or joint: one length of pipe. Invert: the inside bottom of the pipe. Crown: the inside top. Springline: the horizontal centerline (middle) of the pipe. OD and ID: outside and inside diameter. Nominal size: the name size (for example 8 inch), which may differ from actual OD or ID.
field.title: Glossary: pipe parts and pipe terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Pipe rating terms. DR or SDR (dimension ratio): outside diameter divided by wall thickness; lower number means thicker wall. Pressure class (PC): the working pressure rating of pressure pipe in psi (for example C900 DR 18 is PC 235). Pipe stiffness (PS): a gravity pipe's resistance to deflection, in psi at 5% deflection (PS 46, PS 115). Class (RCP): concrete pipe strength class I to V based on D-load. D-load: concrete pipe test load in pounds per foot of length per foot of diameter. Wall A, B, C: concrete pipe wall thickness options. CIOD or DIOD: cast iron or ductile iron outside diameter sizing (C900 PVC uses it so DI fittings fit). IPS: iron pipe size (steel pipe OD). DIPS: ductile iron pipe size (HDPE made to DI OD). PE 4710: a high-performance polyethylene material designation.
field.title: Glossary: pipe ratings
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Trench and backfill terms. Foundation: the soil below the bedding; replaced with stone if soft. Bedding: the layer the pipe rests on. Haunch or haunching: the material from the bedding up to the pipe's springline, worked under the pipe. Initial backfill: from springline to some distance over the crown (often 6 to 12 inches). Embedment: bedding plus haunching plus initial backfill, the 'pipe zone.' Final backfill: from the top of the embedment to grade. Select backfill: specified imported material. Native backfill: the dug material reused. Lift: one layer of backfill placed and compacted at a time. Proctor: the lab test giving maximum density and optimum moisture. Percent compaction: field density divided by Proctor maximum. Spoil: excavated material piled beside the trench.
field.title: Glossary: trench zones and backfill
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Grade and survey terms. Grade (slope): fall over distance, in percent or ft per ft. Benchmark (BM): a point of known elevation; TBM is a temporary benchmark. HI (height of instrument): elevation of the instrument's line of sight or laser beam. Backsight (BS): rod reading on a known elevation. Foresight (FS): rod reading on a point to find its elevation. Turning point (TP): a temporary point used to move the instrument. Station: distance along the centerline in hundreds of feet (12+50 = 1,250 ft). Offset: distance to the side of the centerline. Hub: a survey stake set flush with a tack or mark. Lath: a tall stake with markings next to a hub. Cut and fill: how far below (cut) or above (fill) the stake the design grade is. Cut sheet: a list of stakes with cuts. Flowline: the line of the inverts.
field.title: Glossary: grade and survey terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Sewer structure terms. Manhole (MH): an access structure on a sewer. Base: the bottom section of a precast manhole. Riser or barrel section: the cylinders stacked on the base. Cone: the tapering top section (eccentric or concentric). Flat top: a slab top for shallow manholes. Adjusting rings (grade rings): thin rings to set the frame height. Frame and cover (ring and lid): the casting at the top. Boot (flexible connector): the rubber seal where pipe enters the manhole. Channel (invert): the formed trough carrying flow through the manhole bottom. Bench (shelf): the sloped floor beside the channel. Drop manhole: a manhole with a drop pipe for a high inlet. Doghouse manhole: a manhole built over an existing pipe. Catch basin: a storm inlet with a sediment sump. Cleanout: a riser for rodding a line. Wye: a Y-shaped fitting for a branch connection.
field.title: Glossary: sewer structure terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Water system terms. Main: the distribution pipe in the street. Service: the small line from the main to a customer. Corporation stop (corp): the valve screwed into the main or saddle at the service tap. Curb stop: the service shutoff valve near the property line, with a curb box to grade. Meter pit or box: where the water meter sits. Saddle: a clamp on the main for a tap. Tapping sleeve and valve (TS&V): a split sleeve and valve for tapping a live main. Gate valve, butterfly valve: main line valves. Valve box: the adjustable cast iron box over a buried valve. Hydrant lead: the pipe from the main to a hydrant, with an auxiliary valve. Blow-off: a flushing outlet at a dead end or low point. ARV or air release valve: vents air at high points. Thrust block: concrete that resists water pressure force at fittings. Restraint: joint hardware that ties pipe together against thrust. Bac-T: bacteriological (coliform) test of new mains.
field.title: Glossary: water system terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Fitting terms. Bend (elbow, ell): changes direction; named by angle (11-1/4, 22-1/2, 45, 90 degrees). Tee: a straight run with a branch at 90 degrees. Cross: two branches opposite each other. Wye: a branch at an angle (usually 45 degrees), common on sewers. Tee-wye or sanitary tee: a branch fitting with a curved turn. Reducer: changes pipe size (concentric or eccentric). Coupling: joins two plain ends; repair coupling (slip coupling) has no center stop so it can slide over the pipe. Transition coupling: joins different materials or ODs. Cap: closes a spigot end; plug: closes a bell or opening. MJ (mechanical joint): bolted gland joint on DI fittings and valves. Push-on: gasketed bell joint pushed together. Solid sleeve: a long MJ coupling used to join two plain ends. Flange: a bolted face joint, used in vaults and pump stations.
field.title: Glossary: fittings
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Testing terms. Air test (low-pressure air test): pressurizing a plugged sewer section with air and timing the pressure drop. Vacuum test: pulling a vacuum on a manhole and timing the drop from 10 to 9 inches of mercury. Mandrel: a go/no-go gauge pulled through flexible pipe to check deflection (usually 5%). Deflection: the reduction in vertical inside diameter of flexible pipe under load, in percent. Hydrostatic test (hydro): pressurizing a water main with water and measuring make-up water. Make-up water (testing allowance): water added to hold test pressure. Chlorination: disinfection of new water mains. Residual: the chlorine left in the water after a contact time. CCTV: TV camera inspection of sewers. PACP: NASSCO's standard defect coding for sewer CCTV. Infiltration: groundwater leaking into a sewer. Exfiltration: water leaking out. I and I: infiltration and inflow (inflow is surface water entering through covers, roof drains or cross-connections).
field.title: Glossary: testing terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Safety terms. Competent person: someone trained to recognize trench hazards with authority to correct them. Protective system: sloping, benching, shoring or shielding that protects against cave-ins. Trench box (shield): a steel or aluminum box that protects workers inside but doesn't hold the walls. Shoring: supports (hydraulic, timber, screw jacks) that hold the trench walls. Sloping: cutting walls back at an angle. Benching: cutting walls in steps. Tabulated data: the maker's or engineer's tables for using a protective system. Type A, B, C soil: OSHA soil classes from most to least stable. Spoil setback: keeping spoil at least 2 ft from the edge. Tolerance zone: the hand-dig zone each side of a marked utility. Positive response: the system showing each utility's locate status. Confined space: a space large enough to enter with limited entry and not meant for occupancy. LEL: lower explosive limit. PPE: personal protective equipment.
field.title: Glossary: safety and excavation terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Equipment terms. Excavator (trackhoe): tracked digger with boom, stick and bucket; mini excavator under about 10 tons. Backhoe (loader backhoe): wheeled tractor with loader in front and hoe in back. Loader: wheeled or tracked bucket machine for moving material. Skid steer and compact track loader: small loaders. Quick coupler: device for fast attachment changes. Hoe-pack: excavator-mounted plate compactor. Hammer (breaker, hoe ram): hydraulic rock and concrete breaker. Lift chart: rated loads at radius and height. Rigging terms. Sling: chain, wire rope or synthetic strap for lifting. Hitch: how the sling is rigged (vertical, choker, basket). Shackle: U-shaped connector with a pin. WLL (working load limit): the most a piece of rigging should lift. Tag line: rope to control a load's swing. Spreader bar: beam that spreads sling points for long loads.
field.title: Glossary: equipment and rigging terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Contract terms. Unit price: payment per unit installed (per foot, each, ton). Lump sum: a fixed price for a defined scope. Bid item: a line on the bid form. Change order (CO): a signed change to scope, price or time. Field order or directive: an owner instruction to proceed, priced later. T&M (time and materials) or force account: payment for actual labor, equipment and materials plus markup. RFI: request for information. Submittal: product data or shop drawings for approval. Retainage: money held back from payments until completion. Pay app: monthly payment request. Schedule of values: breakdown of a lump sum for billing. Differing site condition: a site condition materially different from the contract documents. Liquidated damages (LDs): a set daily charge for finishing late. Substantial completion: when the work can be used for its purpose. Punch list: final list of items to fix. As-builts (record drawings): drawings of what was actually built.
field.title: Glossary: contract and business terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Production terms. Footage: linear feet of pipe installed. Feet per hour (ft/hr): footage divided by working hours. Cycle time: time for one repeat of an operation (one dig-swing-dump, or one pipe joint). Bottleneck: the slowest step limiting the whole crew. Production factor: earned hours divided by actual hours. Cost code: a category for tracking cost by activity. Burden: payroll costs on top of wages (taxes, insurance, benefits). Ownership cost: equipment costs whether running or not. Operating cost: equipment costs only when running (fuel, repairs, wear). Utilization: share of available time a machine is used. Look-ahead: a short-term schedule of upcoming work and its constraints. PPC (percent plan complete): share of weekly commitments completed. EV (earned value): budgeted cost of completed work. CPI and SPI: cost and schedule performance indexes.
field.title: Glossary: production and cost terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Soil terms. Clay: fine-grained, sticky, cohesive soil; holds a vertical cut short-term but weakens when wet. Silt: fine-grained, low cohesion, turns soupy when wet. Sand: granular, no cohesion, runs when dry or saturated. Gravel: coarse granular soil. Loam: mix of sand, silt and clay. Hardpan: very dense cemented soil. Fill: soil placed by people, often previously disturbed and less stable (OSHA can't classify it as Type A). Unsuitable material: soil the specs say must be removed (organic, wet, soft). Bearing capacity: how much load soil can carry. Unconfined compressive strength: a measure used to classify cohesive soils for OSHA (Type A is 1.5 tsf or more). Groundwater table: the level below which soil is saturated. Pumping or quick condition: soil losing strength from upward water flow. Swell: volume increase when dug; shrink: volume decrease when compacted.
field.title: Glossary: soil terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage

field.text: Storm drainage terms. Culvert: a pipe or box carrying a stream or ditch under a road or driveway. Headwall: a concrete wall at a culvert end that holds the slope and protects the pipe end. Flared end section (FES): a sloped metal or concrete end piece on a culvert. Wingwall: angled walls on a headwall. Riprap: large stone placed to prevent erosion at outlets. Energy dissipator: structure or riprap that slows outlet flow. Storm sewer: a piped drainage system with inlets and manholes. Inlet: a structure collecting surface water (curb inlet, grate inlet). Underdrain: perforated pipe in stone draining groundwater from under pavement. Detention basin: a pond that holds and slowly releases runoff. Retention basin: a pond that holds water without a regular outflow. Outfall: where a storm system discharges to a stream or ditch. Swale: a shallow grassed channel.
field.title: Glossary: storm drainage terms
field.topic: Field glossary
field.source: Field glossary compiled from industry standards and common usage
