field.text: Pipe slope (grade) is rise or fall divided by horizontal distance. As a decimal: fall / run. As a percent: fall / run x 100. Percent grade is the same number as feet of fall per 100 ft. Examples: 0.40% = 0.40 ft fall per 100 ft = 0.0040 ft per ft. 1.00% = 1 ft per 100 ft. 2.08% = 2.08 ft per 100 ft. To find slope from two inverts: (upstream invert minus downstream invert) / distance x 100. Example: upstream invert 102.36, downstream invert 100.00, 236 ft apart: 2.36 / 236 = 0.0100 = 1.00%. Pipe lasers take grade in percent (Spectra: a 1 ft rise over 100 ft equals 1.00%). Watch the sign: most lasers use plus for uphill from the laser and minus for downhill; gravity sewer shot upstream from the downstream manhole is usually entered as a positive grade.
field.title: Slope basics: percent, feet per 100 ft, and decimal
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Spectra Precision DG613 pipe laser setup guide

field.text: Plumbing and service lines are often given in inches per foot; mains in percent. Conversion: percent = inches per foot / 12 x 100 = inches per foot x 8.333. And inches per foot = percent x 0.12. Common values: 1/8 inch per foot = 1.04%; 3/16 inch per foot = 1.56%; 1/4 inch per foot = 2.08%; 1/2 inch per foot = 4.17%; 1 inch per foot = 8.33%. Going the other way: 0.40% = 0.048 inch per foot (about 3/64 inch); 1.00% = 0.12 inch per foot (about 1/8 inch); 2.00% = 0.24 inch per foot (about 1/4 inch). In feet per foot: 1/4 inch per foot = 0.0208 ft/ft. Exact math; no source dispute.
field.title: Slope conversions: inches per foot to percent
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Survey and grade work uses feet and decimal feet (tenths and hundredths), while tapes and tools often read inches. Inches to decimal feet: 1 inch = 0.083 ft; 2 = 0.167; 3 = 0.25; 4 = 0.333; 5 = 0.417; 6 = 0.50; 7 = 0.583; 8 = 0.667; 9 = 0.75; 10 = 0.833; 11 = 0.917; 12 = 1.00. Fractions: 1/8 inch = about 0.01 ft; 1/4 inch = about 0.02 ft; 1/2 inch = about 0.04 ft; 3/4 inch = about 0.06 ft. Decimal feet to inches: multiply the decimal by 12. Example: 0.37 ft x 12 = 4.44 inches, about 4-7/16 inches. A quick field rule: 0.01 ft is just over 1/8 inch, and 0.08 ft is about 1 inch. Exact math.
field.title: Feet and tenths to inches conversion
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: To find the pipe invert at any point along a straight run: invert at point = downstream invert + (slope as decimal x distance upstream from the downstream point). Example: downstream manhole invert out 100.00 at station 10+00, slope 0.50%, find the invert at station 11+75: distance 175 ft x 0.005 = 0.875 ft; invert = 100.00 + 0.88 = 100.88. To check a whole run: upstream invert = downstream invert + slope x length; if the plan shows MH 1 invert out 100.00, MH 2 invert in 101.20, length 300 ft, slope = 1.20 / 300 = 0.40%. If your computed slope doesn't match the plan slope, ask the engineer before laying; it usually means a length or elevation typo. Exact math.
field.title: Invert math: figuring the invert at any station
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Invert: the lowest inside point of the pipe, where water flows; plan elevations for gravity pipe are almost always inverts. Flowline: the line along the inverts, often used to mean the same as invert. Crown: the highest inside point of the pipe (inside top). Springline: the horizontal centerline of the pipe, halfway up. Outside top of pipe ('top of pipe') = invert + inside diameter + wall thickness. Bottom of pipe (outside) = invert minus wall thickness. Bottom of trench (top of bedding is the outside bottom of pipe) = invert minus wall thickness minus bedding depth. Example: 8 inch PVC SDR 35, invert 100.00, ID about 7.9 inches (0.66 ft), wall about 0.24 inch (0.02 ft), 6 inch bedding (0.50 ft): outside bottom about 99.98, trench bottom about 99.48, outside top about 100.68. Use the maker's exact dimensions for your pipe.
field.title: Pipe terms: invert, flowline, crown, springline
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: A cut sheet (grade sheet) lists, for each stake: station, offset distance and side, stake (hub) elevation, design invert elevation, and the cut (or fill) from the stake to the invert. Cut = stake elevation minus design invert. Example: stake at 12+50, 10 ft left offset, hub elevation 108.42, invert 100.95; cut = 7.47 ft, often written C 7.47 or C 7 ft 5-5/8 in (0.47 ft x 12 = 5.64 inches). Some sheets give cut to bottom of trench or to top of bedding instead; read the header. Always check the math on a few lines: stake minus cut should equal the invert, and inverts should change by slope times distance from stake to stake. Mark it if a stake is disturbed and get it reset; don't guess.
field.title: Cut sheets: reading a grade sheet
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Stationing measures distance along a pipeline or road centerline from a starting point. One station = 100 ft. 12+50 means 1,250 ft from the start (station 0+00). 12+50.75 means 1,250.75 ft. To get distance between two points, subtract: from 12+50 to 15+10 is 1,510 - 1,250 = 260 ft. Plans show manholes, fittings, services and crossings by station and offset. Stations increase in one direction, not necessarily downstream; check whether your sewer stationing runs upstream or downstream. When recording services or utility crossings in the field, write the station and offset (for example 'Sta 13+42, 6 ft R, 4 inch lateral, invert 101.15'); that's what the as-builts need. Exact convention used in US civil plans.
field.title: Stationing explained
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Grade stakes are usually set on an offset line, a set distance (often 5, 10 or 15 ft) to one side of the pipe centerline, so the excavator doesn't dig them out. Each offset stake is marked with station, offset distance and side (for example 'OS 10 ft L') and cut to invert or other reference. To set pipe from an offset stake: measure the offset back to the centerline at right angles, and transfer the grade with a level, laser or string line. Protect stakes with lath and flagging; note any disturbed stakes in the daily report and request resets. Reference points (RPs) for manholes are often two stakes at known distances so the manhole location can be found after excavation. Surveyors' practices vary; read the stake markings legend from your surveyor.
field.title: Offset stakes and why they're offset
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: To get elevations with a level or laser and rod: set up the instrument, take a backsight (BS) rod reading on a benchmark (BM) of known elevation. Height of instrument (HI) = BM elevation + backsight. Then any foresight (FS) reading gives elevation = HI - foresight. Example: BM elevation 105.20, BS 4.36, HI = 109.56; rod reads 9.12 on the pipe invert, so invert = 109.56 - 9.12 = 100.44. To find the rod reading you need for a design elevation: target rod reading = HI - design elevation; for design invert 100.50, rod should read 9.06. Always shoot the benchmark again at the end (closing) to make sure the instrument didn't move. Exact method.
field.title: Differential leveling: HI, backsight and foresight
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: When the benchmark is too far away or out of sight, use turning points (TP): from the first setup, take a foresight on a solid, stable point (a hub, a bolt, a rock), compute its elevation, move the instrument, then backsight that TP to get the new HI. Continue until you reach the work area. To check, run back to the original benchmark (or to a second known benchmark): the difference between the known and computed elevation is the closure error. For construction grade, an error of a few hundredths of a foot over a short loop is usually acceptable, but check your project's survey tolerance. Rules: turning points must not move (no soft dirt or loose gravel), keep backsight and foresight distances about equal to cancel instrument error, and hold the rod plumb. Standard surveying practice.
field.title: Turning points and closing a level loop
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: A benchmark (BM) is a point of known elevation used to control grades: a survey disk, a bolt on a hydrant, a chiseled square on a curb. Temporary benchmarks (TBMs) are set near the work by the surveyor for daily use. Field rules: get the benchmark list from the surveyor or plans; check two benchmarks against each other before trusting either; protect TBMs from being run over or dug up; re-check them if they're on something that can move (a hydrant that got hit, a fresh curb); and never set grade from an existing manhole rim or invert unless the plans say that's the control, because rims get adjusted. If two benchmarks disagree by more than a few hundredths, stop and call the surveyor. Standard practice.
field.title: Benchmarks and temporary benchmarks
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: A grade rod (grade pole) is used to check the trench bottom or pipe grade against a laser or string line. With a rotating laser above ground: set the laser at a known HI, compute the rod reading for each point (rod reading = HI - design elevation, or for trench bottom = HI - trench bottom elevation), and set the receiver on the rod to that reading. Then the rod reads 'on grade' when its foot is at the right elevation. With a fixed-length grade rod and a string or batter boards: the boards are set a constant height above invert (for example an even 10.00 ft) so the same rod length checks every point. Because grade changes along the run, rotating lasers set to the pipe's percent grade let one rod setting work along the whole run. Standard practice.
field.title: Grade rods and the fixed-target method
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Setting a pipe laser (summary of Spectra's DG613 guide): (1) Grade: enter the design slope in percent. (2) Elevation: decide beam height above invert; for 6 inch pipe and precast inverts the laser can sit right in the invert; for 8 inch, a mounting plate; for 10 to 15 inch pipe or flat manhole bottoms, an invert plate and fixed pole. Set beam height by top-pole scale or by rod on the laser (HI plus cut-to-invert, minus beam height, minus the beam offset given by the maker). (3) Line: center the laser over the pipe centerline (plumb bob, transit or over-the-top setup) and aim at a second control point; the farther the second point, the better the line. (4) Lay pipe with a target in each new stick, centering the bulls-eye. Check grade after the first 25 to 50 ft. Exact steps vary by model; follow your laser's manual.
field.title: Pipe laser setup in the manhole
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Spectra Precision DG613 pipe laser setup guide

field.text: Check a pipe laser's calibration periodically and whenever it's been dropped (from Spectra's guide): pick a fairly level area (no more than about 4 inches rise per 100 ft); mark points A and B about 100 ft apart; set the laser behind the lower point, let it warm up about 10 minutes, set grade to 0.000%, aim over A and B and read beam heights A1 and B1; move the laser behind B, aim back over B and A, and read B2 and A2. Error = (A2 - A1) - (B2 - B1). If the two differences match, it's in calibration. If the error is more than 0.02 ft per 100 ft (about 6.4 mm per 30 m), Spectra says send it to an authorized service center. Other makers use similar two-peg checks; follow your model's manual.
field.title: Pipe laser calibration check
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Spectra Precision DG613 pipe laser setup guide

field.text: When the laser spot on the target flames, bends or jumps, it's usually refraction from temperature differences in the pipe: sun-heated pipe in a cool trench, solvent fumes from glue, or cold pipe in a warm trench. Spectra notes it mostly affects the last 4 or 5 joints. Fixes: backfill as you go so pipe stays cool; lay small pipe with its sun-baked side down; run a blower once the run passes about 50 ft, aimed to make a corkscrew of fresh air, mounted on the side or invert (not the top); increase blower speed as the run gets longer; for 18 inch and larger pipe, put the nozzle low or use two blowers. If it won't clear, switch to an over-the-top setup. Also check the target is clean and the laser window isn't fogged.
field.title: Pipe laser problems: heat shimmer and fumes
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Spectra Precision DG613 pipe laser setup guide

field.text: After laying the first 25 to 50 ft, check that the pipe is actually on the design slope (Spectra recommends this): take a rod reading on the invert at the start and end of the laid pipe, compute the fall over the distance, and compare to design. Example: readings differ by 3.451 ft over 145 ft = 2.38%. If grade is off, find out why before laying more: wrong grade dialed, laser bumped, laser out of calibration, or a wrong benchmark. During the day, re-check grade on the last laid stick with a rod whenever the laser is disturbed. At the end of a run, shoot the invert where the pipe enters the upstream manhole and compare to plan. Record checks in the daily report. Many specs reject reverse grade or level spots outright.
field.title: Checking grade on laid pipe
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Spectra Precision DG613 pipe laser setup guide

field.text: Agencies set the allowed deviation from design line and grade for gravity sewers; check your project specs. A common municipal spec wording limits variance from established line and grade to 1/32 inch per inch of pipe diameter, not to exceed 1/2 inch, provided the variation doesn't create a level or reverse-sloping invert; for 8 inch pipe that's 1/4 inch. Other specs give fixed limits such as a few hundredths of a foot of grade and a few inches of line. Practically all specs reject reverse grade (water flowing backward) and many reject sags that hold water on CCTV beyond a set depth (often a fraction of an inch or a percent of diameter). Flat sewer grades (0.3% and less) leave little room; there, laser setup and calibration matter most. This chunk describes typical spec practice, not one standard.
field.title: Typical line and grade tolerances for gravity sewer
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Common municipal specification practice

field.text: The Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities) set minimum slopes for gravity sanitary sewers so flow reaches at least 2 ft per second (with Manning n = 0.013). Commonly cited minimums: 8 inch, 0.40%; 10 inch, 0.28%; 12 inch, 0.22%; 15 inch, 0.15%; 18 inch, 0.12%; 21 inch, 0.10%; 24 inch, 0.08%. Many states and cities adopt these or stricter values, and some require steeper slopes on the upper end of lines with low flow. These are design values: the field crew builds what the plans show. If plan slope is flatter than these minimums, it's usually been approved by the engineer, but it's worth raising if it looks wrong.
field.title: Minimum sewer slopes (Ten States Standards)
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), sewer design chapter

field.text: When sewer pipes meet at a manhole, design practice usually adds a small drop in invert across the manhole to make up for flow losses. Ten States Standards guidance: when a smaller pipe joins a larger one, set the invert of the larger pipe so the energy gradients match; an approximate method is to put the 0.8 depth point of both sewers at the same elevation, or match the crowns. Many cities' standards also specify a minimum invert drop across a manhole (for example about 0.1 ft for a straight-through run and more for bends or junctions); check your local standard details. The plans give 'invert in' and 'invert out' for each pipe; build the manhole channel to match those, not to an assumed drop.
field.title: Drops through manholes and matching crowns
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), sewer design chapter

field.text: Uni-Bell gives handy conversions for pipe joints: a 1 degree vertical direction change equals about a 1.75% change in slope (because tan 1 degree = 0.0175). Offset at the end of a stick from a joint deflection: offset = length x tan(angle); 1 degree over 20 ft is about 0.35 ft (4.2 inches), and over 10 ft about 0.175 ft (2.1 inches). Curve radius from joint deflection: R (ft) = 57.3 x lay length (ft) / degrees per joint. Example: 18 ft ductile iron at 3 degrees per joint gives R = 57.3 x 18 / 3 = about 344 ft. Use these to plan horizontal curves or small vertical changes with joint deflection within the pipe maker's limit.
field.title: Converting joint deflection to slope and offset
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Uni-Bell, Changing Direction: Axial Joint Deflection Explained

field.text: GPS machine control (also called GNSS or 3D machine control) uses satellite receivers on the excavator plus sensors on the boom, stick and bucket to compute the bucket tip's position and compare it to a 3D design model (surface, alignment or pipe profile). The operator sees cut or fill on a screen; with 'automatics' the hydraulics hold grade. Corrections come from a job-site base station or a network (RTK). Before use, the site must be localized (calibrated) to the project control points so GPS coordinates match the plan coordinates and elevations. Trimble-reported trials showed about 43% faster trenching with guidance and about 52% with automatics versus conventional methods (small sample). Good for digging trench bottom and bedding to grade with no grade checker in the hole.
field.title: GPS machine control: how it works
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Construction Equipment report on Trimble machine-control trials

field.text: GPS machine control is only as good as its setup. Daily checks: at startup, touch the bucket tip on a known checkpoint (benchmark or control hub) and confirm the screen elevation and position match within your tolerance; recheck after changing buckets (the bucket dimensions must be entered correctly), after any machine service affecting sensors, and if readings jump. Vertical GPS accuracy is typically worse than horizontal; RTK receiver specs are commonly around 1 to 2 cm horizontal and 2 to 3 cm vertical under good conditions, worse near tall buildings, trees or deep trench walls blocking satellites. On flat sewer grades, many crews use GPS for digging and an in-pipe laser or rod check for setting the pipe invert. Accuracy figures vary by manufacturer and conditions; check your system's specifications.
field.title: GPS machine control: daily checks and accuracy limits
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: GNSS receiver manufacturer specifications (typical ranges); field practice

field.text: A rotating (plane) laser set up above the trench sends a level or sloped plane of light across the job. A receiver on the excavator stick, or on a grade rod, tells the operator or grade checker whether they're on, above or below grade. For pipe trenches, set the laser to the pipe's percent grade along the alignment (dual-grade lasers set slope in two directions) so the receiver offset stays constant down the run. Common use: dig the trench bottom to grade with the stick receiver, then use the pipe laser or rod for final pipe invert. Check the laser's HI against a benchmark every setup and recheck if it's bumped or after wind or vibration. Laser range and accuracy vary by model; check the manual. Standard practice.
field.title: Rotating laser and machine receivers
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Before laying toward an existing structure, confirm the existing invert in the field: open the manhole, measure down from the rim to the invert of the pipe or channel at the tie-in point, and compute elevation (rim elevation from survey minus measured depth), or shoot it directly with a level and rod. Compare to the plan. If the existing invert is different from the plan by more than a small amount, the grade of your new pipe may change; call the engineer before laying, not after. Also pothole crossing utilities between your start and the tie-in to confirm no conflicts. Starting at the existing downstream structure and working upstream (laser in the manhole) avoids building a pipe that misses the tie-in. Standard practice.
field.title: Tying into an existing manhole or pipe
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Before lasers, grade was carried with batter boards and a string line, still used on short runs and repairs. Batter boards are set across the trench at intervals (often every 25 to 50 ft) with the top of each board a constant height above design invert; a tight string pulled over the boards along the centerline is then parallel to the invert. A grade rod of that fixed length, with a foot that sits on the invert, is held at each pipe; the pipe is on grade when the rod's top mark touches the string. Strings sag over long spans and boards get bumped, so check frequently. This method is also handy when a laser fails mid-run. Standard practice.
field.title: Laying pipe with a string line or batter boards
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Manhole rims are set to finished grade shown on the plans: flush with pavement in streets, often slightly above grade in yards or fields (local standards may call for a few inches above grade to keep surface water out), and to match final paving elevations after paving. Adjust with grade rings (concrete or HDPE adjusting rings) between the cone or top slab and the frame; local standards cap total ring height (often around 12 inches maximum, check yours). Use the rim elevation from the plans, not the existing ground, and if paving isn't final yet, set temporary and adjust later. Rims on a slope may need tilting to match the pavement cross slope. Record final rim elevations for the as-builts.
field.title: Manhole rim and frame elevations
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Common municipal standard details

field.text: Plan and profile sheets show the pipeline from above (plan view, with stations, offsets, manholes, services and utilities) and from the side (profile view, with existing ground, proposed ground, pipe slope and inverts). The profile usually lists for each segment: pipe size, material, length, and slope (for example '310 LF 8 inch PVC SDR 35 @ 0.40%'), and for each manhole: station, rim elevation, and invert in and out elevations by direction. Crossing utilities are drawn where they cross with their elevations (often approximate unless potholed). Read the grid: vertical scale is often exaggerated (for example 1 inch = 5 ft vertical versus 1 inch = 50 ft horizontal) so slopes look steeper than they are. Before laying, check that inverts, slope and length on the profile agree with each other.
field.title: Profile sheets: reading a sewer plan and profile
field.topic: Grade, survey and layout
field.source: Standard surveying and construction-staking practice (math worked here)

field.text: Pipe installation standards (ASTM D2321 for plastic gravity pipe, C1479 for concrete, AWWA C600 and C605 for water) use the same zone names. Foundation: the trench bottom below the bedding; only needs work if the native soil is soft, wet or rock. Bedding: the layer the pipe sits on, shaped or loosened so the pipe is evenly supported along its length. Haunching: the material from the bedding up to the pipe's springline (middle), placed and worked under the curve of the pipe; this is the most important zone for support. Initial backfill: from springline to a set distance above the crown (D2321 commonly 6 inches or more above the top of the pipe; specs vary, often 12 inches). Embedment means bedding plus haunching plus initial backfill. Final backfill: everything above the initial backfill to grade. Check your project details for the exact depths.
field.title: Pipe zone terms: foundation, bedding, haunching, initial and final backfill
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: ASTM D2321 (underground installation of thermoplastic pipe for sewers and gravity flow), as summarized by PPI and manufacturers

field.text: ASTM D2321 groups embedment soils into classes by how well they support plastic pipe. Class I: crushed stone or angular manufactured aggregate with few fines (best, needs least compaction effort). Class II: clean coarse-grained soils, such as clean gravels and sands (Unified Soil Classification GW, GP, SW, SP), with little fines. Class III: coarse-grained soils with fines, such as silty or clayey gravels and sands (GM, GC, SM, SC). Class IVA: fine-grained inorganic soils of low plasticity (ML, CL); usable only with care and good moisture control, and often limited by specs. Class IVB (high-plasticity clays and silts) and Class V (organic soils, peat) are not recommended for embedment. The lower the class number, the easier it is to get good support. Specs usually require Class I or II in the pipe zone. Summary based on D2321 as described by PPI and manufacturers.
field.title: ASTM D2321 embedment material classes
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: ASTM D2321 (underground installation of thermoplastic pipe for sewers and gravity flow), as summarized by PPI and manufacturers

field.text: PPI's summary of embedment compaction practice: minimum density of about 90% Standard Proctor ('moderate' compaction) is generally satisfactory, with the designer setting the final requirement based on cover, live load, groundwater and soil. Lift thickness in the pipe zone: Class I about 12 inches, Class II about 8 inches, all others about 6 inches. Place lifts evenly on both sides of the pipe and compact each one before the next. Don't use impact tampers directly over the pipe until about 12 inches of backfill covers it. Class I and II compact best by vibration (vibratory plates); Class III and IVA by impact (jumping jacks, rammers). Class II can be helped by slight wetting but don't flood the trench where native soil doesn't drain. Check density at the start to prove the method, then at random and whenever material changes. Your specs govern.
field.title: Embedment compaction: lifts and density for plastic pipe
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: PPI conduitcalc: Compaction of Embedment Materials

field.text: Haunching means filling and compacting the space under the lower curve of the pipe, from the bedding to the springline. It's where most pipe failures start when done poorly: voids under the haunches let flexible pipe deflect and rigid pipe crack. Method: place embedment in shallow lifts on both sides at the same time; work it under the pipe with a shovel, a slicing bar or tamping bar, or a narrow tamper (PPI notes haunching is best compacted by hand tampers or suitable power compactors); don't just dump stone over the top and hope it flows under. Keep the pipe on line and grade while haunching; watch the laser target or check grade after haunching. For large pipe, compact the haunches before placing the rest of the sidefill. Class I crushed stone flows into haunches much better than sand or native soil. Guidance from PPI and manufacturer installation guides.
field.title: Haunching: how to do it right
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: PPI conduitcalc: Compaction of Embedment Materials

field.text: Bedding gives the pipe a uniform, firm-but-not-hard support. Common guidance from ASTM D2321 and manufacturer guides: bedding at least about 4 inches thick in normal soil and about 6 inches in rock (check your specs; many call for 4 to 6 inches, some more for large pipe). Leave the middle third of the bedding under the pipe slightly loose (uncompacted) so the pipe settles into it evenly, and compact the outer parts. Dig bell holes at each joint so the pipe rests on its barrel, not on the bells; fill them after the joint is made. Don't bring pipe to grade by putting rocks, blocks or dirt clods under it (except approved temporary supports that are then removed or bedded around per specs). Fine-grade the bedding to the laser before setting each stick. Specs set the exact bedding thickness; check your project details.
field.title: Bedding: thickness and bell holes
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: ASTM D2321 (underground installation of thermoplastic pipe for sewers and gravity flow), as summarized by PPI and manufacturers

field.text: Trench width must leave room to place and compact embedment beside the pipe, but not be so wide that it adds load (for rigid pipe) or wastes material. ASTM D2321 is widely summarized as requiring a minimum trench width at the pipe zone of the greater of the pipe OD plus 16 inches, or 1.25 times the pipe OD plus 12 inches, unless the engineer approves otherwise. Example: 12 inch PVC (OD about 12.5 inches): OD + 16 = 28.5 inches; 1.25 x 12.5 + 12 = 27.6 inches; so about 28.5 inches minimum. Agency specs often set their own minimum and maximum widths (commonly a maximum at the top of pipe, beyond which a stronger pipe or bedding is required). For rigid clay and concrete pipe, NCPI warns that widening a 2 ft trench by 6 inches can raise load about 50%. Check your project specs.
field.title: Minimum trench width for plastic gravity pipe
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: ASTM D2321 minimum width rule as summarized by manufacturers; NCPI manual

field.text: If the trench bottom is soft, wet, organic or pumping (moves under foot or bucket), the pipe can't hold grade and will settle. Usual fix: over-excavate the unsuitable material (commonly 6 to 24 inches or as the engineer directs) and replace it with compacted crushed stone foundation, often wrapped in a geotextile fabric so fines don't migrate into the stone. In very poor ground, deeper over-excavation, a timber or concrete cradle, or piles may be designed. Dewater first; NCPI notes water must be removed before establishing a firm, unyielding foundation and bedding. Document over-excavation quantities daily (depth, length, stone tons) with the inspector, because unsuitable material removal is often a separate pay item or a change order. Check your specs for the pay item and method.
field.title: Foundation: soft, wet or unstable trench bottom
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: NCPI Vitrified Clay Pipe Engineering Manual, Chapter 3

field.text: When pipe is laid in rock, the rock must not touch the pipe. Common requirement in ASTM D2321 practice and agency specs: over-excavate rock below the pipe and replace with granular bedding, commonly at least 6 inches under the pipe (some specs ask more for large pipe), and keep rock points away from the sides. Remove loose boulders and rock larger than the spec allows from the embedment zone and from the first lift of final backfill so they don't fall on the pipe. Transitions from rock to soil along the trench need a gradual change in bedding so the pipe doesn't hinge. Document rock excavation (length, depth, method, hours of hammer or blasting) daily with photos, as it is often paid separately or as a differing site condition. Check your project specs for rock definitions and pay limits.
field.title: Rock in the trench bottom
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: ASTM D2321 (underground installation of thermoplastic pipe for sewers and gravity flow), as summarized by PPI and manufacturers

field.text: Final backfill fills the trench from the top of the initial backfill to subgrade or finished grade. Material: often excavated native soil if it meets specs (no large rocks, frozen lumps, debris or organics); under pavement, many agencies require imported granular backfill or flowable fill. Compaction: commonly 90 to 95% of standard Proctor (ASTM D698) outside pavement and 95% standard or a modified Proctor (D1557) percentage under pavement, in lifts typically 8 to 12 inches loose depending on the compactor; check your specs, which govern. Don't drop large rocks on the pipe from height; no heavy compaction directly over plastic pipe until enough cover is in place (PPI suggests about 12 inches before impact tampers). Keep moisture near optimum. Water-settling (jetting) is prohibited by many specs; use it only if approved.
field.title: Final backfill above the pipe zone
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: PPI guidance; common agency specification practice

field.text: Ductile iron and PVC water pipe designs reference AWWA standard laying conditions (in AWWA C150 for DIP and similar in C605 for PVC), as summarized by DIPRA: Type 1, flat-bottom trench with loose backfill; Type 2, flat-bottom trench with backfill lightly consolidated to the pipe centerline; Type 3, pipe bedded in at least 4 inches of loose soil, backfill lightly consolidated to the top of pipe; Type 4, pipe bedded in sand, gravel or crushed stone to a depth of one-eighth the pipe diameter (4 inch minimum), backfill compacted to top of pipe (about 80% standard Proctor); Type 5, pipe bedded to its centerline in compacted granular material (4 inch minimum under pipe), compacted granular or select material to top of pipe (about 90% standard Proctor). Higher type numbers support the pipe better and allow deeper cover. The design names the laying condition; check the plans.
field.title: AWWA standard laying conditions for water pipe (Types 1 to 5)
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: DIPRA / AWWA C150 standard laying conditions as summarized by ductile iron manufacturers

field.text: AWWA C600 covers installation of ductile iron water mains and C605 covers PVC and PVCO pressure pipe. Both cover inspection on delivery, trench preparation and bedding, laying and jointing, deflection limits, thrust restraint (blocks or restrained joints), backfill, hydrostatic testing, and connections. Key field themes: keep pipe interiors clean (cap ends overnight and plug the open end when work stops), keep water out of the trench, check the pipe and gaskets before laying, follow joint deflection limits, install restraint before testing, and test hydrostatically at the required pressure for at least 2 hours with make-up water within the allowable formula. Disinfection is under AWWA C651. Your utility's specs often add requirements, such as tracer wire, specific bedding, test pressures and valve spacing. Summary in plain words; refer to the standard and specs for the exact text.
field.title: AWWA C600 and C605: water main installation in brief
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: AWWA C600 and C605 scopes as summarized by DIPRA, Uni-Bell and utility specs

field.text: Water main and sewer specs require keeping the inside of the pipe clean. Practices: inspect each pipe before lowering and swab or blow out any dirt; keep end caps on until laying; at the end of each day, and whenever the trench is left, install a watertight plug in the open end of the line so groundwater, mud and animals don't get in (a common C600/C605 and utility requirement); don't use the pipe as a drain for trench water; in wet trenches, keep the plug on until the next joint is ready. For water mains, AWWA C651 stresses that preventing contamination during construction is the first step of disinfection; heavily contaminated pipe may need swabbing with hypochlorite solution. For sewers, debris left in the line shows up on CCTV and must be flushed out before acceptance.
field.title: Keeping pipe clean and plugging open ends
field.topic: Installation: embedment, bedding and backfill
field.source: AWWA C651 / C600 practice

field.text: Typical sequence for laying gasketed PVC sewer pipe (D3034) from manufacturer guides: start at the downstream manhole with the bell facing upstream; set the laser in the manhole on grade and line; dig the trench to grade below the pipe, place and shape bedding to the laser (leave the middle third loose, dig bell holes); clean the bell, gasket and spigot; check the gasket is seated in its groove; lube the spigot (and gasket if the maker says) with approved lube; lower the next stick, align it straight with the last one, and push the spigot in to the homing mark with a bar and block or a pipe puller; put the target in the bell and set grade; haunch and place initial backfill evenly on both sides before moving on, so the pipe can't move; recheck grade. Plug the open end at day's end. Follow your pipe maker's guide.
field.title: Step by step: laying PVC gravity sewer pipe
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Pipe manufacturer installation guides (Uni-Bell, DIPRA, ACPA member guides), summarized

field.text: Typical sequence for C900 PVC water main from manufacturer and AWWA C605 practice: inspect each pipe and gasket for damage; keep pipe ends capped until use; lay on a uniform bedding with bell holes; clean bell and spigot, confirm the gasket is properly seated (some gaskets are factory-locked), lube the spigot with NSF-61 lube; align and push home to the insertion mark (don't over-home); deflect at joints only within the maker's limit after the joint is assembled straight; install tracer wire on top of the pipe; install fittings with restraints or thrust blocks per plans; keep trench water out of the pipe and plug the open end when work stops; place embedment in lifts and compact. Pressure test, disinfect and bac-T test before service per specs and AWWA C651.
field.title: Step by step: laying C900 PVC water main
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Pipe manufacturer installation guides (Uni-Bell, DIPRA, ACPA member guides), summarized

field.text: Typical sequence for push-on ductile iron (AWWA C600 practice and maker guides): inspect pipe, lining and gaskets; install polyethylene encasement first if required (slide the tube on before joining); clean the bell's gasket seat and the spigot; seat the gasket fully in the bell (loop it in, then press it home so it's even all around); lube the inside face of the gasket and the spigot end with the maker's lube; align the pipe straight and push home with a bar, come-along or the bucket through a timber, until the spigot stripe reaches the bell face or as the maker shows; check with a feeler gauge if the maker suggests; deflect afterward within limits; restrain joints per plans; then complete polywrap overlap at the joint and backfill. Field-cut ends need beveling.
field.title: Step by step: laying ductile iron water main
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Pipe manufacturer installation guides (Uni-Bell, DIPRA, ACPA member guides), summarized

field.text: Typical RCP sequence from ACPA guidance and producer instructions: prepare bedding to grade, slightly loose under the middle third, with recesses for the bells; lay downstream to upstream with bells (grooves) facing upstream; lift with the producer's lift device or rated hooks; clean joint surfaces; place the gasket (lubricated per maker) on the spigot or the butyl sealant on the tongue or groove; lower the pipe and line it up just short of home; pull the joint home evenly with a come-along, pipe puller or winch anchored back on laid pipe (pushing with the bucket only through a timber and with care); check the joint gap is even all around and the pipe is on grade; plug lift holes; haunch and backfill evenly in lifts. Wrap joints with external joint wrap if specified.
field.title: Step by step: laying reinforced concrete pipe
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Pipe manufacturer installation guides (Uni-Bell, DIPRA, ACPA member guides), summarized

field.text: A rolled, pinched or displaced gasket is the most common cause of failed air and pressure tests. Causes: dirt or stones in the bell or on the spigot; no lube or too little; spigot not beveled after a field cut; pipe pushed home at an angle; gasket not fully seated before assembly (for loose gaskets); cold, stiff gaskets. Prevention: clean every bell and spigot, check gasket seating with your fingers all the way around, lube properly, bevel cut ends, align straight before pushing, push smoothly. If you feel unusual resistance or see the gasket bulge out, pull the joint apart and check. Some crews use a feeler gauge on push-on DI joints to check the gasket position all around after assembly, if the maker provides that procedure.
field.title: Joint problems: rolled or displaced gaskets
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Pipe manufacturer installation guides (Uni-Bell, DIPRA, ACPA member guides), summarized

field.text: Pushing a gasketed pipe too far (over-homing) or not far enough (under-homing) both cause problems. Over-homing PVC can bottom the spigot against the bell's end, leave no room for thermal movement, and crack the bell, especially in cold weather; push only to the homing mark. Under-homing leaves the gasket near the edge of the seal zone, so the joint may leak or pull apart when backfill or thrust moves the pipe. When you cut a pipe, re-mark the homing line at the same distance as the factory mark. When pushing with the excavator bucket, it's easy to over-home; push gently through a timber, watch the mark, and stop. Check marks again after initial backfill on the first few joints.
field.title: Joint problems: over-homing and under-homing
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Pipe manufacturer installation guides (Uni-Bell, DIPRA, ACPA member guides), summarized

field.text: To join different pipe materials or sizes, or repair a broken section: Flexible rubber couplings (with stainless steel shear bands for gravity sewers) join pipes of different ODs, such as clay to PVC; pick the coupling for the exact two ODs, and use a shear band where specs require so the joint can't shift. Repair (slip) couplings for gasketed PVC have no center stop, so you can slide them fully onto one pipe, set a replacement piece, then slide the coupling back across the joint; mark the centered position first. Ductile iron solid sleeves (long MJ couplings) and wide-range couplings or repair clamps are used on water mains. Check that couplings are rated for the pressure and the pipe material, and restrain them where thrust exists. Follow the coupling maker's torque values.
field.title: Transition and repair couplings
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Mechanical joint (MJ) fittings and valves seal by a gland pulling the gasket into the bell with T-bolts. Good practice from AWWA C600 and C111 guidance: clean and lube the gasket and spigot; slide gland and gasket on the spigot; insert the spigot fully and center it; push the gasket evenly into the bell; bring the gland up and insert bolts with nuts finger tight; tighten bolts in a crisscross pattern (bottom, top, then sides, like a car wheel) in stages so the gland stays parallel to the bell face, keeping the gap even all around; finish at the torque range C600 lists by bolt size (commonly cited: 5/8 inch bolts 45 to 60 ft-lb; 3/4 inch 75 to 90 ft-lb; 1 inch 100 to 120 ft-lb; 1-1/4 inch 120 to 150 ft-lb). Use a torque wrench. Wedge-action restraint glands have their own twist-off nuts for the wedge bolts.
field.title: MJ bolt tightening on ductile iron fittings
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: AWWA C600/C111 guidance as commonly summarized by ductile iron manufacturers

field.text: Gasketed plastic pipe uses elastomeric gaskets meeting ASTM F477 (for push-on joints in plastic pipe), with joint performance tested per ASTM D3212 for gravity sewer. Concrete pipe gaskets follow ASTM C443; ductile iron gaskets follow AWWA C111. Special gasket materials (nitrile or fluorocarbon) are used where pipe may contact petroleum or chemicals; standard SBR or EPDM gaskets can swell and fail in contaminated soil, so specs often require oil-resistant gaskets near gas stations or fuel lines. Care: store gaskets out of sunlight and away from heat, oil and ozone sources (electric motors), keep them clean, warm them in cold weather so they seat easily, and never reuse a damaged gasket. Many PVC pipes have factory-installed locked gaskets that shouldn't be removed.
field.title: Gaskets: types and care
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Cold weather changes how pipe behaves. PVC loses impact strength as temperature drops, so handle it with more care: don't drop it, don't let it bang during unloading, and inspect more closely for cracks. Gaskets get stiff: keep gaskets and lube warm (in the truck cab) so they seat and spread. HDPE gets stiffer and harder to bend, and fusion procedures may need adjustment or shelter per the maker. Frozen bedding or backfill must not be used; most specs prohibit placing pipe on frozen ground. Thaw or remove frost in the trench bottom. Protect concrete (thrust blocks, collars) and flowable fill from freezing. Water in test lines can freeze and burst pipe or fittings; drain test equipment overnight. Follow manufacturer cold weather guidance.
field.title: Cold weather pipe handling
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Matching the yard names to the D2321 classes for plastic pipe (the class definitions are already in the installation file; this is the cheat sheet). Class I: crushed angular stone with little or no fines, such as #57, #67, #78, #8, CA-7, CA-11, '3/4 clean', 'clean crushed', crushed RCA if clean; PPI describes it as generally manufactured aggregate. Class II: clean sands and gravels, often natural deposits, such as clean washed sand, concrete sand, pea gravel and clean screened pit gravel (GW, GP, SW, SP), with few fines. Class III: granular soils with fines, such as crusher run, 3/4 minus, DGA, Class 5, road base, dirty sand and silty gravel (GM, GC, SM, SC); these need more compaction effort and moisture control. Class IVA: silts and lean clays, rarely allowed. IVB and V: fat clay, organic soil, peat: never in the pipe zone. Your spec can be stricter, e.g. Class I only.
field.title: Which stone and soil names fall in which ASTM D2321 embedment class
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: PPI conduitcalc, Pipe Embedment Materials; ASTM D2321 as summarized by PPI and manufacturers (ADS embedment classes detail)

field.text: Angular crushed stone (Class I) interlocks: each piece has broken faces that bite into its neighbors, so it holds its position beside the pipe and gives high side support even with modest compaction. Rounded gravel and pea gravel (Class II) roll past each other; they flow into haunches easily but can shift under load, especially when wet or vibrated, and need compaction to reach comparable stiffness. PPI notes that after grain type, density has the greatest effect on embedment stiffness, and that smaller rock is easier to place in haunches. Practical choices: crushed stone for flexible pipe (PVC, HDPE, PP) in sewer and storm, deep cover, wet trenches and anywhere the spec says Class I; rounded or sand bedding is common for water, gas and conduits and where sharp stone could damage coatings or polywrap. Never let large angular rock bear on coatings, polyethylene encasement or tracer wire.
field.title: Angular crushed stone versus rounded gravel in the pipe zone
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: PPI conduitcalc, Pipe Embedment Materials; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: PPI guidance: the max aggregate size in the bedding, haunch and initial backfill should be compatible with pipe size, and smaller rock is easier to place in the haunches. Common limits seen in specs and maker guides (check yours): PVC sewer 4 to 15 inch, 3/4 inch to 1 inch max, which #57 or #67 meets; small services and laterals, 1/2 inch max (#7, #78, #8); larger flexible pipe, up to about 1 1/2 inch; ductile iron and concrete pipe, often up to 1 to 1 1/2 inch in the pipe zone, with no stones over 3 inches or so within a foot of the pipe in final backfill. Polywrapped DI and coated steel often require sand or fine stone against the wrap. Above the pipe zone, many specs keep rock over 6 inches out of the first 1 to 2 feet over the crown. Oversize stone point-loads pipe walls and gouges plastic.
field.title: Maximum stone size next to the pipe
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: PPI conduitcalc, Pipe Embedment Materials; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Migration is fine soil (fine sand, silt, dispersive clay) moving into the voids of coarser open-graded material like crushed rock. NCPI lists the drivers: gravity, water flow from dewatering, rising and falling groundwater, and permeable bedding acting as a French drain along the trench. When the stone's voids fill or the surrounding soil washes into the stone, the pipe loses side support and the surface can settle. PPI notes the risk is greater when groundwater flows from outside the trench toward the inside. NCPI test numbers: soil mixed into crushed rock started affecting support at 0 to 20 percent; at 20 percent soil, settlement rose about 20 percent; at 40 percent, about 200 percent; at 55 to 60 percent, about 800 percent. Field experience suggests migration can cut embedment stiffness about in half. Watch for it where clean #57 is placed against silt or fine sand in wet ground.
field.title: Soil migration: how fines wash into clean stone and pipe loses support
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; PPI conduitcalc, Pipe Embedment Materials

field.text: Options when clean stone sits against fine native soil in wet ground (NCPI and common practice): 1) Non-woven geotextile wrap ('burrito wrap') around the embedment, separating stone from trench walls and bottom. 2) A graded filter: a layer of sand or well-graded material between the fine soil and the stone, sized so each layer cannot wash into the next; NCPI says graded filters should be designed by a geotechnical engineer and are usually only practical for very large pipe. 3) A smaller or well-graded embedment that is filter-compatible with the native soil (for example #8 or a well-graded crushed material instead of #57). 4) Flowable fill, which has no voids so there is nothing to migrate into. 5) Trench dams or clay plugs to stop water running along the stone. Compact the bedding too: NCPI found compacted rock settled about 25 percent less than uncompacted.
field.title: Stopping migration: fabric wrap, graded filter, choke stone or flowable fill
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: A choke stone (choke course) is a smaller clean stone spread over a layer of large open stone to fill its surface voids and give a tight, walkable surface. Typical combos: #57 over #2 or #3 foundation stone in a soft trench bottom; #8 over #57 in permeable pavement and under paver bedding; #57 over quarry spalls or riprap-size rock for haul roads. Place a thin layer (often 2 to 4 inches), then work it into the larger stone with a plate compactor or roller so it locks in, not just sits on top. Purpose in pipe work: stop the bedding stone or sand above from falling into big voids below, provide an even grade surface for the pipe, and reduce point loads. A choke layer is not a substitute for geotextile where fine native soil can pump up from below; in that case use fabric under the big stone too.
field.title: Choke stone: what it is and how to place it
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: NCPI recommends a non-woven synthetic geotextile at the boundary between incompatible materials, wrapping the embedment. Steps: 1) Dewater and shape the trench. 2) Lay the fabric on the trench bottom and up both walls, with enough extra width to fold over the top with overlap (common practice: at least 12 inches overlap; trench perimeter plus overlap gives the roll width). 3) Place and compact bedding on the fabric. Keep loads off the bare fabric: NCPI says nothing heavier than a person should be placed on it, and protect it during compaction. 4) Lay pipe, place haunch and initial backfill stone. 5) Fold the fabric over the top, overlapping the edges, then place the next backfill. Overlap roll ends (often 1 to 3 feet). NCPI tests: geogrid cut settlement about 25 percent, thin fabric about 40 percent, thick fabric about 70 percent, but fabric only helped when the rock was compacted.
field.title: Geotextile wrap around pipe embedment ('burrito wrap') step by step
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; overlap widths from General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Open-graded aggregate is mostly one size range with few small particles and almost no fines: #57, #67, #8, #2. It has lots of voids (roughly 35 to 45 percent), drains fast, needs little compaction effort, and does not have a meaningful Proctor density (testing is by method spec or relative density). Dense-graded (well-graded) aggregate has every size from the top size down to dust in the right proportions so small pieces fill the gaps between big ones: crusher run, DGA, ABC, Class 5, Class 2, 3/4 minus. It compacts to a high density, carries traffic, and is tested with a Proctor and nuclear gauge, but drains slowly and is sensitive to moisture. Gap-graded material is missing a middle size. Use open-graded for drainage, bedding and wet foundation stabilization; dense-graded for base under pavement, structural fill and trench backfill that must not settle.
field.title: Open-graded versus dense-graded aggregate
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Fines are particles small enough to pass the #200 sieve (0.075 mm): silt and clay. The wash test (ASTM C117) reports them as percent passing #200. Rough meaning for granular material under the Unified Soil Classification: under 5 percent fines is 'clean' (GW, GP, SW, SP); 5 to 12 percent is borderline with dual symbols (like GW-GM); over 12 percent is silty or clayey (GM, GC, SM, SC). NCPI notes inundated gravels with more than about 12 percent fines lost strength and stiffness, and that the USCS boundary is 12 percent. Practical effects: more fines means better compaction density for base but slower drainage, more moisture sensitivity, frost heave risk and pumping under traffic when wet. Clean stone for drainage and Class I usually has under about 1 to 2 percent passing #200; dense-graded bases typically run 3 to 12 percent (MnDOT Class 5 3 to 10; Caltrans Class 2 up to 12).
field.title: Fines content: what 'percent passing #200' means and why it matters
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; MnDOT 3138; Caltrans Section 26; USCS (ASTM D2487) boundaries

field.text: A gradation report lists sieves from largest to smallest with 'percent passing' each one, next to the spec band. Sieves: 2, 1 1/2, 1, 3/4, 1/2 and 3/8 inch, then #4 (4.75 mm, about 3/16 inch), #8 (2.36 mm), #16, #30, #50, #100 and #200 (0.075 mm). Example #57 result: 1 1/2 inch 100, 1 inch 97, 1/2 inch 40, #4 6, #8 2, #200 0.8. Compare to the typical C33 #57 band (1 1/2 inch 100, 1 inch 95 to 100, 1/2 inch 25 to 60, #4 0 to 10, #8 0 to 5): every sieve is inside, so it passes. A number above the band means too fine on that sieve; below means too coarse. Read the #200 line first for drainage and frost questions, and the top sieves for oversize against your pipe's max stone size. Also check the date, the sample location and that the product name matches your ticket.
field.title: How to read a sieve analysis (gradation) report
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: ASTM C33 #57 band as commonly published (verify against your spec)

field.text: Many agencies require compacted crushed base (crusher run, DGA, Class 5, Class 2, CA-6) for the full depth or the upper few feet of trench backfill in roads, because native clay settles and clean stone has no Proctor target. To get density: place in lifts the compactor can handle (often 6 to 8 inches loose for a plate or jumping jack, up to 12 inches for a trench roller or hoe-pac on granular), keep the moisture near optimum (wet the pile if it is dry and dusty; let it drain if it is pumping), and compact each lift before the next. Typical requirements are 95 percent of standard or modified Proctor in the top few feet. Kentucky DGA, for example, is placed no more than 6 1/2 inches per lift without approval. Get tests at the frequency your permit requires, and keep base dry until paving to avoid pumping.
field.title: Dense-graded base as trench backfill under pavement
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: KYTC Section 302; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Backfilling the whole trench with #57 is fast and needs little compaction, but it has drawbacks inspectors raise: there is no Proctor density to test against, so acceptance is by method; clean stone placed loose can still settle a little and can let pavement edges ravel; the stone column becomes a French drain that collects groundwater and surface water and carries it along the trench, washing fines from the trench walls and soaking the subgrade under the road; and in clay areas it can act as a 'bathtub' that holds water under pavement and freezes. Some agencies allow it with geotextile wrap and a dense-graded cap; others ban it under roads. If you use clean stone, compact it in lifts with vibration, wrap it where the native is fine-grained, and install trench dams on slopes.
field.title: Clean stone as full-depth backfill: why some agencies ban it
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: A trench dam (trench plug, cutoff) is a short section of low-permeability material placed across the trench to stop groundwater from running along the stone bedding like a drain. Built from compacted clay, lean concrete, flowable fill or bentonite, it fills the full trench width from the bottom to above the stone, often 2 to 5 feet long. Common practice spacing: at manholes, at the bottom of steep runs, every few hundred feet on slopes, where the trench crosses a wetland or stream, and where the sewer leaves a high water table area. Why it matters: water running in the bedding carries fines away (migration and settlement), can drain wetlands or wells, and lets infiltration find pipe joints. Many specs and wetland permits require them with spacing set by grade. Show locations on the as-builts.
field.title: Trench dams, clay plugs and anti-seep collars in stone bedding
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Imported stone and base cost money for the material, the trucking and the haul-off of the native it replaces, so reuse native soil when the spec and the soil allow. Native usually works above the pipe zone when it is free of organics, debris, frozen lumps and large rock, and is within a few percent of optimum moisture so it can be compacted. Import is usually needed when: the spec requires select or granular backfill (often under paving); native is saturated clay, peat, or so wet it pumps; native contains rock over the spec limit for the first foot or two over the pipe; or density tests keep failing. Middle options: dry native by spreading it (if time and space allow), mix in lime or cement where approved, or use flowable fill in short critical sections such as under driveways. Record the reason and quantity of any import that is a pay item.
field.title: Native backfill or imported material: making the call
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: RCA is old concrete pavement, curb, slabs and structures crushed and screened into base or clean stone sizes (sold as crushed concrete, RCA Item 4, recycled Class 2, Class 5 (C), RCA #57). FHWA's user guidelines (FHWA-RD-97-148) report: being 100 percent crushed, it is very angular, with friction angles typically above 40 degrees and CBR from 90 to over 140, comparable to crushed limestone; crushed fines from air-entrained concrete absorb 4 to 8 percent water versus 2 percent or less for natural aggregate, so it needs more water to reach optimum; compacted unit weight is lower than natural stone, so a ton covers more volume. FHWA recommends crushing and screening to AASHTO M147 or ASTM D2940 base gradations and limiting asphalt (RAP) content to 20 percent. Good dense-graded base and backfill; clean RCA stone is used for some bedding where specs allow.
field.title: Recycled concrete aggregate (RCA, crushed concrete): properties
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 User Guidelines, Reclaimed Concrete Material in granular base

field.text: FHWA reports agencies have seen a white powdery precipitate (tufa, calcium carbonate) from RCA clog subdrains and blind geotextile filters; it forms when air's CO2 reacts with free lime in the concrete. The problem is not universal. RCA leachate is alkaline (pH can exceed 11), so some jurisdictions such as Ontario restrict stockpiling and placement near watercourses, and alkaline RCA in contact with moisture can corrode aluminum or galvanized steel pipe. FHWA recommendations: wash coarse RCA where subdrains are used, use RCA without much unhydrated cement or free lime, run leachate tests near drains, keep geotextile out of the base drainage path, remove reinforcing steel, and limit asphalt chunks to 20 percent. Field takeaways: do not use RCA as underdrain or French drain stone unless the spec allows it, keep it away from CMP and aluminum pipe, and watch for rebar pieces in the pipe zone.
field.title: Recycled concrete cautions: tufa clogging, high pH, galvanized and aluminum pipe
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148, Reclaimed Concrete Material (granular base and embankment guidelines)

field.text: RAP is milled or crushed old asphalt pavement (millings, grindings). FHWA guidance for granular base: CBR drops below what is expected for normal base once RAP exceeds about 20 to 25 percent of the blend, and drops almost in proportion to RAP content; blends up to 30 percent have been used. Asphalt coating hinders compaction, so density falls as RAP content rises; compaction improves with little or no water; nuclear gauges tend to overestimate density and moisture in RAP, so use a control strip and lab moisture checks. RAP blends can gain strength over time as the binder sets up, but can also creep, and stockpiled blends can harden into chunks. Asphalt adhesion makes finish grading hard. MnDOT caps composite bitumen at 3.5 percent in base. Uses: driveway and shoulder surfacing, haul roads, blended base where allowed. Generally not acceptable as pipe embedment.
field.title: Recycled asphalt (RAP, millings) as base or backfill
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148, Reclaimed Asphalt Pavement in granular base; MnDOT 3138

field.text: Steel furnace slag is a byproduct of steelmaking, heavy (specific gravity 3.2 to 3.6 versus 2.5 to 2.7 for normal stone) and hard. FHWA warns it can be volumetrically unstable: hydration of free lime and magnesia can swell it 10 percent or more. FHWA says avoid confined applications such as backfill behind structures, base or subbase confined by curb and gutter, and trenches, and avoid placing it below grade or where it may be submerged. It can also form tufa (calcium carbonate) that has clogged subdrains and outlets, and its leachate can exceed pH 11, corroding galvanized or aluminum pipe. Processed slag should be aged wet in stockpiles (often months) and expansion-tested (ASTM D4792). Air-cooled blast furnace slag is a different, more stable product used in many states as aggregate. If a ticket says 'slag', find out which kind before it goes in a trench.
field.title: Steel slag: keep it out of trenches and confined fills
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 User Guidelines, Steel Slag (granular base)

field.text: Flowable fill (CLSM, controlled low-strength material, also flow fill, slurry, K-Krete) is mostly sand or fly ash, a little cement and a lot of water. FHWA typical mixes per cubic yard: high fly ash mix about 2,080 lb fly ash, 104 lb portland cement and 50 gallons water; low fly ash mix about 300 lb fly ash, 100 lb cement, 2,600 lb sand and 60 gallons water. General range: 50 to 100 lb cement and 50 to 80 gallons water per CY. Georgia DOT: excavatable mix 75 to 100 lb cement (fly ash not specified), 15 to 35 percent air, wet unit weight 90 to 100 lb per cubic ft; non-excavatable mix 75 to 150 lb cement plus 150 to 600 lb fly ash, 5 to 15 percent air, 100 to 125 lb per cubic ft. Miami-Dade: 50 to 100 lb cement, 0 to 600 lb fly ash or slag, about 2,750 lb fine sand, max 500 lb water. Order by agency mix name or approved plant mix number.
field.title: Flowable fill mix designs: what is in it
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA, Fly Ash Facts for Highway Engineers, Chapter 5 Flowable Fill; Georgia DOT Standard Specification Section 600, Flowable Fill; Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Dept Specification 03375, Flowable Fill

field.text: If anyone may dig the trench again (most utility trenches), order excavatable flowable fill. FHWA: machine removal generally works up to about 100 to 200 psi; hand digging needs about 50 psi or less. Georgia DOT sets 28-day lab strength at 100 psi max for excavatable and 125 psi minimum for non-excavatable. Miami-Dade targets 100 psi at 28 days for excavatable. Strength keeps climbing for months, especially with high cement or Class C fly ash, so a 'flowable fill' made with extra cement for early strength can turn into concrete that needs a hammer. Some agencies also use a removability modulus (RE, from strength and unit weight; under 1.0 is considered excavatable). Tell the plant it must be excavatable.
field.title: Excavatable versus non-excavatable flowable fill (strength limits)
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA, Fly Ash Facts for Highway Engineers, Chapter 5 Flowable Fill; Georgia DOT Standard Specification Section 600, Flowable Fill; Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Dept Specification 03375, Flowable Fill

field.text: Timing (FHWA): high fly ash mixes with about 5 percent cement can support a person in about 3 to 4 hours, depending on temperature and humidity; equipment can usually cross within 24 hours; some low fly ash mixes with high-calcium fly ash set enough for street patching in 1 to 2 hours. Accelerated 'fast set' mixes exist for traffic areas. Miami-Dade requires the fill be left undisturbed until it reaches 250 psi on a hand penetrometer, and bans placement in rain or below 40 F. Georgia DOT requires it to be at least 50 F at delivery and protected from freezing for 36 hours. High-water mixes (around 10 inch slump) bleed and subside about 1/8 inch per foot of depth (FHWA); NRMCA cites up to about 1/4 inch per foot, so leave it a little high or top off. Cold, wet weather slows set a lot; plan plates or barricades until it is firm.
field.title: Flowable fill: set time, weather limits and when you can pave
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA, Fly Ash Facts for Highway Engineers, Chapter 5 Flowable Fill; Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Dept Specification 03375, Flowable Fill; Georgia DOT Standard Specification Section 600, Flowable Fill

field.text: Flowable fill weighs about 90 to 145 lb per cubic ft depending on the mix (GDOT, NRMCA), roughly double water, so empty pipe floats in it easily (see the pipe flotation chunk for the uplift math). Georgia DOT requires pipe to be restrained with straps, soil anchors or other approved means where flotation or misalignment may occur. Field methods: place the first lift only to about the pipe springline or less, let it stiffen (often an hour or more) to lock the pipe, then fill the rest; set sandbags, precast blocks or spoil piles on the pipe; strap the pipe to earth anchors or rebar driven into the trench bottom; fill plastic pipe with water during placement where allowed; pour from one side and watch the grade. Check grade and alignment after placement. Fluid fill also pushes hard on forms, trench boxes, bulkheads and manhole walls, so brace bulkheads and pour lifts against new structures.
field.title: Flowable fill: stopping pipe and structures from floating
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: Georgia DOT Standard Specification Section 600, Flowable Fill; NRMCA CIP 17 (unit weight); General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: FHWA lists the benefits: self-leveling and self-compacting with no compaction equipment; crews do not enter the trench to compact, which can cut shoring needs and trench width; delivered by ready-mix trucks and placed by chute, pump, bucket or conveyor; resists segregation; often cheaper than placing and compacting soil when the plant is close. Uses: very narrow trenches (microtrenching, conduit), backfill under pavement where settlement is not acceptable, around manholes, vaults and structures where compaction is awkward, under and around pipe crossings, filling abandoned pipes, tanks and manholes, and bedding for pipe and slabs. Downsides: cost per yard versus native, set time before paving, flotation of pipe, pressure on forms, hard to dig if over-strength, and high pH (corrosion check per ACI 229R). Always check the agency's mix and placement requirements.
field.title: When flowable fill beats compacted backfill in a trench
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA, Fly Ash Facts for Highway Engineers, Chapter 5 Flowable Fill

field.text: Segregation is when big and small particles separate, so one end of the pile is coarse and the other fine. It mainly hits dense-graded base (crusher run, DGA, Class 5) and multi-size stone. Causes: dumping from a height into a cone (large stones roll to the outside and bottom), pushing material up into a tall pile with a dozer, conveyor drop piles, and loading from the edge of a pile. Fixes: build piles in low layers rather than tall cones; dump trucks in adjacent piles and blend; load across the face of the pile, not from the toe edge; remix with a loader before loading out; avoid long chute drops. FHWA recommends radial stacking and remixing before load-out for recycled materials too. In the trench, segregated base gives rock pockets that will not compact and fine pockets that pump. Clean single-size stone (#57) segregates very little.
field.title: Stockpile segregation: keeping gradation even
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 (stockpiling RCM); General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Clean stone is only clean until a loader digs dirt into it. Rules: drop stone on pavement, a stone pad, plywood or geotextile, not on mud; keep the loader bucket a few inches above the ground when you get to the bottom of the pile; keep bedding stone piles away from spoil piles (and on the opposite side of the trench when possible); do not let rain wash spoil into stone piles; keep different products in separate piles or bins with clear signs (#57 vs crusher run look alike when wet); cover sand and screenings if they must stay dry; protect stockpiles from runoff with silt fence or sock and keep them out of streets and inlets per your stormwater permit. Contaminated or mixed material should be rejected or used above the pipe zone only. Check each delivery ticket for the right product before it is dumped, not after.
field.title: Stockpile contamination and handling on the jobsite
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec); EPA construction stormwater permit practice

field.text: Most crushed stone, sand and screenings contain crystalline silica (quartz), especially granite, traprock, sandstone and many sands. Breathing the fine dust causes silicosis, lung cancer and kidney disease. OSHA's construction silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153) sets a permissible exposure limit of 50 micrograms per cubic meter as an 8-hour average, with an action level of 25. Dust sources on utility jobs: dumping and spreading dry screenings or base, sweeping, compacting dry base, cutting pavement and concrete, and crushing on site. Controls: wet the material or the pile, use water on saws and cutters (Table 1 methods), keep cabs closed with filtered air, sweep with water or vacuums instead of dry brooms, stand upwind, and use respirators when Table 1 or air monitoring calls for them. Wet cement in flowable fill is also caustic: wear gloves and eye protection.
field.title: Silica dust from stone, sand and screenings
field.topic: Aggregates: pipe embedment, backfill, recycled materials and flowable fill
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153, Respirable crystalline silica in construction

field.text: Woven geotextile is made of flat slit-film or monofilament tapes woven like a tarp: high strength, low stretch (AASHTO M288 counts geotextiles with under 50 percent elongation at break as the woven type), lower water flow, and usually cheaper for a given strength. Typical use: separation and stabilization under stone on soft subgrade, haul roads, under base courses, silt fence. Non-woven is felt-like, made of needle-punched fibers: stretches more (50 percent or more elongation), conforms to rough surfaces, passes water well through its thickness, and filters fines. Typical use: wrapping underdrains and French drains, burrito wrap around pipe embedment, under riprap, behind walls, and as cushion over liners. NCPI specifically recommends non-woven fabric for embedment wrap. Field ID: woven looks like a plastic tarp you can see through when stretched; non-woven looks like felt and is sold by weight (4 oz, 6 oz, 8 oz per SY).
field.title: Woven versus non-woven geotextile fabric
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: Ferguson Waterworks, AASHTO M288-17 Geotextiles Technical Data Sheet; NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Separation: keeps two materials from mixing, such as stone pushed into soft clay or mud pumping up into base; this is the most common pipe and road use. Filtration: lets water through while holding soil back, such as around an underdrain or under riprap; the fabric's opening size must suit the soil. Drainage: thick non-wovens carry some water in their plane, but in practice drainage comes from the stone and pipe, not the fabric. Stabilization: on very soft wet ground, a strong woven fabric plus stone spreads loads so equipment can work; often paired with a geogrid. Reinforcement: high-strength fabrics or geogrids in walls and steep slopes (engineered). Protection or cushion: thick non-woven protects liners and coatings from sharp stone. AASHTO M288 groups applications as subsurface drainage, separation, stabilization, permanent erosion control (under riprap), silt fence and paving fabric. Ask: which function does the spec want? That decides woven or non-woven.
field.title: What geotextiles do: separation, filtration, drainage, stabilization, reinforcement, protection
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: Ferguson Waterworks, AASHTO M288-17 Geotextiles Technical Data Sheet; AASHTO M288 application categories; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: AASHTO M288 is the common spec for highway and utility geotextiles. It sorts fabrics into survivability classes based on how rough installation will be: Class 1 is for the most severe conditions (big angular stone, heavy equipment, rough subgrade), Class 2 is moderate, and Class 3 is the least severe. Each class has woven (under 50 percent elongation) and non-woven (50 percent or more) versions with minimum grab, tear, puncture and burst strengths.
