On top of survivability, each application sets hydraulic properties: apparent opening size (AOS) and permittivity for drainage and filtration based on the soil's fines (subsurface drainage fabrics are rated by the percent of soil passing the #200, for example under 15 percent fines). Supplier example: for stabilization and separation, a Class 1 might be a heavy woven or 8 oz non-woven, Class 3 a lighter woven or about 4.5 oz non-woven. Submit the data sheet showing the class and application the spec names.
field.title: AASHTO M288 survivability classes (Class 1, 2, 3) for fabric
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: Ferguson Waterworks, AASHTO M288-17 Geotextiles Technical Data Sheet

field.text: Common places geotextile shows up on sewer, storm and water jobs (check plans and spec): 1) Around pipe embedment where clean stone meets fine native soil in wet ground (non-woven burrito wrap, per NCPI). 2) Under foundation stone in soft trench bottoms, so stone does not punch into the mud (woven or heavy non-woven). 3) Around underdrain and French drain stone (non-woven filter). 4) Under riprap at outlets, headwalls and ditches (non-woven, usually Class 1). 5) Under base in trench patches and haul roads on soft subgrade (woven separation). 6) Under construction entrances. 7) Under and around stone pads for manholes and structures in soft ground. 8) As inlet protection and silt fence (erosion control fabrics). 9) Over detention chamber and infiltration stone beds (per manufacturer). Fabric is not usually placed directly around solid pressure pipe; it is a soil-to-stone separator, not a pipe wrap.
field.title: Where fabric goes in pipe and utility work
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Practical installation rules (check the spec and maker): lay fabric smooth without big wrinkles, in direct contact with the soil, and in the direction of fill placement so the next sheet's overlap is not peeled back. Overlaps: the North Carolina riprap guidance calls for at least 12 inches with anchor pins every 3 ft along overlaps and the upstream edge buried at least 12 inches; on soft subgrade, overlaps of 18 to 36 inches or sewn seams are common. Do not drive equipment directly on the bare fabric; push stone out onto it from already placed stone, keeping at least 6 inches or so of cover under tracks and tires. NCPI: nothing heavier than a person on bare fabric over pipe bedding. Patch tears with a piece that overlaps at least 12 inches all around. Keep rolls wrapped and out of sunlight; most fabrics lose strength from UV if left exposed for weeks. Do not drop riprap from height onto fabric; a 4 inch sand or gravel cushion may be needed for large stone.
field.title: Installing geotextile: overlaps, pins, cover and damage
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: North Carolina Erosion and Sediment Control Planning and Design Manual, Practice 6.15 Riprap (via CICA Center); NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: A filter fabric that is too tight, or the wrong fabric for the soil, can clog (blind) and stop water, which is worse than no filter. Causes: fine silt or clay soils caking against the fabric, fabric placed between two drainage layers where it catches fines from the water, iron or bacterial slime in groundwater, and calcium carbonate (tufa) from recycled concrete or steel slag, which FHWA reports has blinded geotextile filters and clogged subdrains. Tips: use non-woven needle-punched fabric with the AOS and permittivity the spec sets for the soil; do not wrap the perforated pipe itself in a fabric sock in fine silty soils unless the spec says to (wrap the stone envelope instead, so the larger fabric area handles the flow); keep RCA and slag out of drainage stone unless specifically allowed; make sure the fabric touches the soil without gaps (water piping along gaps carries soil). Flush underdrains from cleanouts after construction.
field.title: Fabric clogging (blinding) and filter mistakes
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 (RCA tufa blinding geotextiles); General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: A geogrid is an open plastic grid (biaxial square, triaxial triangular, or uniaxial long strips) that stone locks into. Biaxial and triaxial grids are used for base stabilization: placed on soft subgrade under a layer of crushed base, they confine the stone so it spreads load and resists rutting, which can reduce the thickness of base needed or let trucks work on soft ground. Uniaxial grids reinforce retaining walls (MSE walls) and steep slopes and are always engineered. In pipe and utility work, grids show up in haul roads and staging areas on soft ground, wide over-excavations under large pipe or structures, and pavement restoration over soft subgrade. A grid is not a filter: its openings are large, so where fine soil could pump up into the stone, put a non-woven or woven separator under the grid or use a composite product. NCPI's lab tests found a geogrid cut embedment settlement about 25 percent, less than fabric.
field.title: Geogrids: what they are and where they help utility crews
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: NCPI, Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Riprap is large rock placed to stop erosion at pipe outlets, ditches, channel banks, headwalls and slopes. It is specified by a median size, d50 (half the stones by weight are smaller), or by a weight range or a state class number. The North Carolina erosion manual explains: graded riprap is usually preferred over uniform riprap because it forms a denser, flexible cover; about half the weight should be larger than d50, the largest stone about 1.5 times d50, and smaller sizes down to about 1 inch to fill gaps. Stone should be hard, angular and durable, with a specific gravity of at least 2.5; field stone or quarry stone may be used. Angular stone locks together; rounded cobbles roll out under flow. Riprap is always placed on a filter layer (geotextile or graded stone) so the soil underneath cannot wash out through the voids.
field.title: Riprap basics: d50, gradation and why it must be angular
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: North Carolina Erosion and Sediment Control Planning and Design Manual, Practice 6.15 Riprap (via CICA Center)

field.text: VDOT-based classes per the Hampton Roads regional standards: Class AI dry riprap, 25 to 75 lb stones (about 10 percent may be under 25 lb, about 10 percent 75 to 100 lb); Class I, 50 to 150 lb, at least 60 percent over 100 lb; Class II, 150 to 500 lb, at least 50 percent over 300 lb; Class III, 500 to 1,500 lb, at least 50 percent over 900 lb. Dumped riprap: Type I (core riprap) 3/4 to 2 tons each, averaging about 1 ton; Type II (heavy) 3 to 10 tons, averaging about 4 tons. Erosion control riprap is sound shot rock at least 8 inches thick with no stone over 15 inches. Grouted riprap on slopes uses Class I sized stone with 1 part cement to 3 parts sand grout. Riprap goes on geotextile bedding per Section 200. Other states use different names, so match the plan's class to your state's table.
field.title: Riprap classes: Virginia Class AI, I, II, III and Type I, II
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: Hampton Roads Regional Construction Standards Section 414 Riprap (VDOT based)

field.text: Minnesota DOT standard riprap gradations (from the Minnesota Stormwater Manual), with max size and max weight: Class I, 6 inch, 15 lb; Class II, 12 inch, 120 lb; Class III, 18 inch, 400 lb; Class IV, 24 inch, 1,000 lb; Class V, 30 inch, 2,000 lb. Reading the gradation tables, the median (d50) works out to about half the max size: roughly 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 inches, or about 2, 15, 50, 120 and 250 lb. As a rule of thumb, Class I and II are used at small culvert outlets and ditches, Class III and IV at larger outfalls and stream banks, Class V for heavy flow. Layer thickness and filter requirements come from the MnDOT spec and plan detail, often about 1.5 to 2 times the max or d50 size. The d50 estimates here were read from the gradation table, not stated directly.
field.title: Riprap classes: MnDOT Class I to V
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: Minnesota Stormwater Manual, MnDOT standard riprap gradations

field.text: PennDOT R classes per NESL (top size and approximate working range): R-3, 6 inch (2 to 6 inch), creek and road banks and gabion fill; R-4, 12 inch (3 to 12 inch), heavier flow and channels; R-5, 18 inch (4 to 18 inch); R-6, 24 inch (6 to 24 inch), 'bumper rock' and creek bends; R-7, 30 inch (12 to 30 inch); R-8, 42 inch (15 to 42 inch), heaviest armoring. New York equivalents: fine stone fill (about R-3), light stone fill (R-4), medium stone fill (R-6), heavy stone fill (R-7 and R-8). North Carolina (NCDOT, per the NC erosion manual): Class A, 2 to 6 inch; Class B, 5 to 15 inch; Class 1, 5 to 200 lb; Class 2, 25 to 250 lb. NESL notes working ranges are approximate and the gradation spec governs on specified jobs. PennDOT gabion fill: 3 to 5 inch stone for baskets under 1 ft tall, 4 to 8 inch for 1 ft and over.
field.title: Riprap classes: PennDOT R-3 to R-8, NY stone fill, NC Class A, B, 1, 2
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: NESL, Rip rap sizes; North Carolina Erosion and Sediment Control Planning and Design Manual, Practice 6.15 Riprap (via CICA Center)

field.text: From the North Carolina erosion manual: minimum riprap thickness is 1.5 times the maximum stone diameter and never less than 6 inches; final thickness should also consider construction method, flow, maintenance and the consequences of failure. Each granular filter layer should be at least 6 inches thick. Key the toe into a stable foundation, excavated to about 1.5 times the design thickness and extending horizontally from the slope, so the blanket cannot be undercut. Many plans also express thickness as about 2 times d50 (NESL estimates use about twice the nominal stone size). A Kitsap County example for an outfall with severe turbulence used d50 = 8 inches with a minimum 1 ft thickness and recommended 16 to 24 inches in turbulent areas. The plan detail governs; if it is missing a thickness, ask before ordering.
field.title: Riprap thickness, toe key and filter layer
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: North Carolina Erosion and Sediment Control Planning and Design Manual, Practice 6.15 Riprap (via CICA Center); NESL, Rip rap sizes; Kitsap County Stormwater Manual, F.3.2 Riprap Filter Systems

field.text: Riprap needs a filter underneath so channel soil does not wash out through the voids, and the filter itself must not wash through the riprap. Granular filter rule (Kitsap County manual): a reasonably well-graded sand and gravel usually works if D15 of the filter is less than 5 times d85 of the protected soil; in their example, ASTM C33 #57 stone met the filter criteria, and very large riprap may need two filter layers. Fabric requirements in the North Carolina manual: for granular soils with 50 percent or less fines, open area no more than 36 percent; for other soils, apparent opening size no larger than the #70 sieve (0.21 mm) and open area no more than 10 percent; minimum 4 percent open area, opening no finer than the #100 sieve (0.15 mm), and permeability greater than the soil. In practice most specs call for an AASHTO M288 Class 1 non-woven under riprap.
field.title: Riprap filter: granular rule of thumb and fabric requirements
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: Kitsap County Stormwater Manual, F.3.2 Riprap Filter Systems; North Carolina Erosion and Sediment Control Planning and Design Manual, Practice 6.15 Riprap (via CICA Center)

field.text: From the North Carolina erosion manual and practice: place riprap right after the filter, to full thickness in one operation; avoid chutes or dumping methods that separate big and small stone; use selective loading at the quarry and controlled dumping to get a dense, well-graded mass with few voids; hand or bucket-place to break up pockets of small stone or clusters of big stone and to get a uniform surface. The finished surface should blend with the surrounding grade without an overfall or protruding rock that kicks flow. At outlets, place riprap before or with the pipe end so it is in place before the first runoff. Do not drop large stone from height onto bare fabric; lower it with the bucket or place a cushion layer. Do not push riprap down a slope with a dozer (it segregates and tears the fabric). Inspect after the first storms and replace displaced stone. Excavator thumbs or grapples make placement much faster.
field.title: Placing riprap: do's and don'ts
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: North Carolina Erosion and Sediment Control Planning and Design Manual, Practice 6.15 Riprap (via CICA Center); General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Clean, washed stone with almost no fines is the drainage standard. Common choices (check spec): #57 for most French drains, underdrains, foundation drains and stone envelopes around perforated pipe; #4, #3 or #2 for high-flow drainage blankets and soft ground; #8 where the native soil is finer and a smaller filter-compatible stone is needed, or as a choke over #57; sand filters where the soil is silty. CDOT's filter material classes all limit the #200 to 0 to 3 percent: Class A (3 inch top, 20 to 90 percent passing 3/4 inch, 0 to 20 percent passing #4), Class B (1 1/2 inch top, 20 to 60 percent passing #4, 0 to 10 percent passing #50), and Class C (3/4 inch top, 60 to 100 percent passing #4, 10 to 30 percent passing #50). Avoid RCA and steel slag in drains (tufa clogging, per FHWA) and avoid screenings and crusher run, which hold water.
field.title: Drainage stone: which sizes for which drains
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: CDOT Section 703 Table 703-10; FHWA-RD-97-148; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Clean #57 drains fast but has big voids, so silty fine sand or silt next to it can wash into the stone and eventually into the pipe through its perforations. The fix is a filter: either a non-woven geotextile around the whole stone envelope, or a two-stage drain where a sand filter (like CDOT Class C or a concrete sand) sits against the soil and the coarse stone sits around the pipe. Signs the filter is wrong: sediment coming out the drain outlet, sinkholes or settlement along the drain line, or a drain that stops flowing within a year. Size perforations to the stone (slots smaller than the stone's small sizes). For soils that are mostly clay, migration is less of a risk but water flow is slow, so drains are often designed with a sand or fabric interface and a larger collection area. The engineer's filter design governs; if field soils differ from the plans (for example a silt seam), call it in.
field.title: Matching drain stone to the soil: when #57 alone is not enough
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: CDOT 703 filter materials; NCPI migration guidance; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Backfill against walls, headwalls, box culverts and some vaults is often specified as free-draining granular material so water does not build up pressure behind the wall. Typical details: a zone of clean stone (#57 or similar) or a porous backfill gradation (for example Iowa DOT gradation No. 29 'porous backfill') against the back of the wall, wrapped in non-woven fabric where it meets native soil; weep holes or a perforated drain at the base leading to an outlet; and compacted granular or native backfill outside the stone zone. Compact in thin lifts with light equipment near the wall (heavy rollers close to a wall add pressure). Do not use clay or steel slag behind walls; FHWA warns steel slag can expand in confined fills behind structures. Check the plan detail for zone width, stone size and drain outlet location.
field.title: Free-draining backfill behind walls, headwalls and structures
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: Iowa DOT IM 209 (porous backfill gradation); FHWA-RD-97-148 steel slag; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: A stabilized construction entrance is a pad of large clean stone where trucks leave the site, so mud is knocked off tires before it reaches the street. Typical details in state erosion manuals (your permit and plan govern): coarse aggregate about 2 to 3 inches (often ASTM #1 or #2 or a DOT size; quarry spalls in the Northwest), at least 6 inches thick (often 8 to 12), full width of the exit and at least 50 ft long (some states 70 ft), on a woven geotextile so the stone does not sink into the subgrade. Top-dress with clean stone when the voids fill with mud; add a wash rack or tire wash if mud still tracks. Sweep (wet or vacuum, not dry, for silica and dust control) any tracked soil off the street the same day. For utility jobs moving along a street, each laydown yard or stockpile exit usually needs one.
field.title: Construction entrance stone (rock pad at the site exit)
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: EPA construction stormwater BMP practice and state erosion and sediment control manuals; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Gabions are wire mesh baskets filled with stone, used for retaining walls, channel lining, outlet protection and slope stabilization. Fill stone must be hard, durable and larger than the mesh openings so it cannot fall through; PennDOT (per NESL) uses 3 to 5 inch stone for baskets less than 1 ft tall and 4 to 8 inch stone for baskets 1 ft and taller, and R-3 riprap is commonly used as gabion fill. Fill in lifts about 1 ft deep, place stone by hand or carefully by bucket on the exposed faces for a tight face, and install internal cross ties (bracing wires) at each lift to stop bulging. Overfill slightly to allow for settlement, then close and lace the lid. Place geotextile behind and under gabions where they sit against soil. Weight for planning: gabion stone runs roughly 1.4 to 1.7 tons per CY of basket depending on voids; check the quarry.
field.title: Gabions and gabion fill stone
field.topic: Aggregates: geotextiles, geogrids, riprap and drainage stone
field.source: NESL, Rip rap sizes; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: You can estimate any clean stone's weight from two numbers. Solid rock (limestone, granite, traprock) has a specific gravity around 2.65, so solid rock weighs 2.65 x 62.4 = about 165 lb per cubic ft, or about 2.23 tons per cubic yard. A pile of clean stone like #57 is roughly 35 to 40 percent air (voids); NCPI measured about 40 percent porosity in uncompacted #67. At 40 percent voids: 165 x 0.60 = about 99 lb per cubic ft = 1.34 tons per CY. At 35 percent voids: about 107 lb per cubic ft = 1.45 tons per CY. That is why clean stone tickets usually run 1.35 to 1.5 tons per CY. Dense-graded base packs the voids with fines, so compacted it weighs more (about 1.75 to 1.95 tons per CY). Heavier rock (traprock, slag at SG 3.2 to 3.6) weighs more; RCA and lightweight aggregates weigh less. Wet material adds water weight.
field.title: Why stone weighs what it does: tons per cubic yard from rock density and voids
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Computed from specific gravity and void ratio; NCPI Soil Migration and Buried Pipe (porosity); FHWA-RD-97-148 (slag specific gravity)

field.text: Typical loose or as-delivered weights (check your supplier's scale data, they vary by rock and moisture): #57, #67 and other clean crushed stone, about 1.35 to 1.5 tons per CY (about 100 to 110 lb per cubic ft); a common estimating number is 1.4. #8 and small chips, about 1.3 to 1.45. Pea gravel, about 1.3 to 1.45. Large clean stone (#1 to #3), about 1.3 to 1.45. Concrete sand and fill sand, about 1.3 to 1.5 dry, more when damp; New Mexico's mining table uses 1.45 for sand and 1.42 for 1/4 to 2 inch gravel. Screenings and stone dust, about 1.3 to 1.5 loose. Aggregate Markets uses about 1.4 tons per CY as the general gravel figure. Rule of thumb in the field: 1 ton of clean stone is about 0.7 CY; 1 CY is about 1.4 tons.
field.title: Tons per cubic yard: clean stone, pea gravel and sand (typical values)
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: New Mexico EMNRD Mining and Minerals Division, conversion factors; Aggregate Markets, Choosing the right dump truck; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Dense-graded base (crusher run, DGA, ABC, Class 5, Class 2, CA-6, 3/4 minus) is the material where loose and compacted weights differ most. Typical: loose in the truck or pile about 1.4 to 1.6 tons per CY; compacted in place about 130 to 145 lb per cubic ft, which is about 1.75 to 1.95 tons per compacted CY (140 lb per cubic ft x 27 / 2,000 = 1.89). So one compacted yard of base takes about 1.3 loose yards. Estimate base by compacted volume times compacted unit weight: tons = sq ft x thickness in ft x lb per cubic ft / 2,000. If the lab Proctor is available, use its max dry density plus a few percent moisture for the in-place weight. New Mexico's mining table uses 1.25 tons per CY for base course measured loose, which shows how much the number depends on how it is measured; always ask whether a quoted factor is loose or compacted.
field.title: Tons per cubic yard: crusher run, road base and DGA, loose versus compacted
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Existing KB aggregate base math; NM EMNRD conversion factors; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Typical weights (vary a lot with moisture; use for rough planning only). Pit run and bank run gravel: New Mexico's mining table uses 1.62 tons per CY, heavier than screened gravel because sand fills the voids; field range about 1.5 to 1.8. Common fill dirt and loam: about 1.1 to 1.4 tons per loose CY when moist (New Mexico's table lists 0.8 for fill dirt and topsoil, likely dry and loose). Topsoil: about 1.0 to 1.3 loose and moist. Clay: about 1.1 to 1.5 loose, heavier wet. Bank (in place) soil weighs more per yard than the same soil loose because it swells when dug (clay roughly 20 to 40 percent depending on the reference, common earth about 25, sand and gravel about 12 percent; see the swell tables in the soils and materials math files). For haul-off, trucks usually weigh out on wet clay before they fill up; for light topsoil they fill up first.
field.title: Tons per cubic yard: pit run, fill dirt, topsoil, clay
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: New Mexico EMNRD Mining and Minerals Division, conversion factors; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Riprap: NESL uses about 1.5 to 1.7 tons per CY (1.6 for estimating) versus about 1.4 for typical aggregate; New Mexico's mining table lists riprap and gabion stone at 1.05, so ask the quarry how they measure. Recycled concrete (RCA): lighter than natural stone (FHWA notes lower compacted unit weight), roughly 1.2 to 1.4 tons per loose CY, so a ton covers more area. RAP millings: roughly 1.1 to 1.4 tons per loose CY, compacted more. Steel slag: specific gravity 3.2 to 3.6 versus 2.5 to 2.7 for normal rock (FHWA), so expect about 20 to 30 percent heavier per yard; if your tickets show slag, your tonnage per yard will be high. Flowable fill: about 90 to 145 lb per cubic ft depending on mix (GDOT, NRMCA), or about 1.2 to 1.95 tons per CY, but it is ordered by the cubic yard, not the ton.
field.title: Tons per cubic yard: riprap, recycled concrete, RAP, slag, flowable fill
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: NESL, Rip rap sizes; New Mexico EMNRD Mining and Minerals Division, conversion factors; FHWA-RD-97-148; GDOT Section 600

field.text: Formulas: cubic yards = tons / (tons per CY); tons = cubic yards x (tons per CY); cubic yards = cubic feet / 27; tons = cubic feet x lb per cubic ft / 2,000. Examples at 1.4 tons per CY for clean stone: a 22 ton load = 22 / 1.4 = about 15.7 CY; 15 CY = 15 x 1.4 = 21 tons; an 18 ton tri-axle load = about 12.9 CY. For compacted dense-graded base at about 1.9 tons per CY: an 18 ton load builds about 9.5 compacted CY. Coverage: 1 CY spread 1 ft thick covers 27 sq ft; 6 inches thick, 54 sq ft; 4 inches thick, 81 sq ft. So 1 ton of #57 (about 0.71 CY) at 6 inches covers about 38 sq ft. Always confirm the factor on your supplier's ticket or website; a 0.1 ton per CY error on 1,000 tons is about 50 CY.
field.title: Quick conversions: tons to yards and yards to tons
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data)

field.text: When figuring embedment or flowable fill per foot, subtract the space the pipe takes: area = 0.7854 x OD (ft) squared. Computed from typical ODs: 4 inch PVC sewer, ASTM D3034 (OD 4.215 in): 0.097 sq ft per ft (Sch 40 or perforated IPS, 4.5 in: 0.11). 6 inch D3034 (6.275 in): 0.215 (Sch 40, 6.625 in: 0.24). 8 inch PVC (8.4 in): 0.385. 10 inch PVC (10.5 in): 0.60. 12 inch PVC (12.5 in): 0.85. 15 inch PVC (15.3 in): 1.28. 18 inch PVC (about 18.7 in): 1.91. 24 inch ductile iron (25.8 in): 3.63. For corrugated HDPE and concrete pipe, use the maker's OD (bells and corrugations are bigger than the nominal size; 24 inch corrugated HDPE is about 28 inches OD, about 4.3 sq ft). Divide by 27 for CY per foot of pipe. For small pipe in a big trench the deduction barely matters; for large pipe in a tight trench it is a big share of the stone.
field.title: Pipe outside area to subtract from trench stone (table)
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Computed from published typical outside diameters (PVC sewer and C900, AWWA ductile iron)

field.text: Given: 300 ft of 8 inch PVC (OD 8.4 in = 0.70 ft), trench 3 ft wide, 6 inches of bedding below the pipe, stone to 12 inches over the crown. Stone depth = 0.5 + 0.70 + 1.0 = 2.2 ft. Area per ft = 3 x 2.2 = 6.6 sq ft, minus pipe 0.385 = 6.215 sq ft per ft. Volume = 6.215 x 300 = 1,865 cubic ft / 27 = 69.1 CY. Tons at 1.4 tons per CY = 96.7 tons. Add 10 percent for over-dig and waste = about 106 tons, or 6 loads at 18 tons (or 5 to 6 at 20 tons). If the trench is actually dug 3.5 ft wide, the stone goes to 7.7 - 0.385 = 7.3 sq ft per ft, about 18 percent more stone. Measure your actual bucket width and trench width, since a wider trench is the most common reason stone overruns.
field.title: Worked example: bedding stone for 300 ft of 8 inch PVC sewer
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data)

field.text: Given: 200 ft of 12 inch PVC (OD 12.5 in), trench 3.5 ft wide, 10 ft to trench bottom, 1 ft of pavement section on top (asphalt and base, figured separately). The spec requires compacted dense-graded base from trench bottom to subgrade. Backfill depth = 10 - 1 = 9 ft. Area = 3.5 x 9 = 31.5 sq ft minus pipe 0.85 = 30.65 sq ft per ft = 1.135 compacted CY per ft. For 200 ft: 227 compacted CY. At about 140 lb per cubic ft compacted (1.89 tons per CY): 227 x 1.89 = 429 tons; add 5 percent = about 450 tons, about 23 loads at 20 tons. Note: if you estimated with a loose factor (1.45 tons per CY) you would order only about 330 tons and run short by about 100 tons. Also plan the haul-off: the 227 bank yards of native that this replaces swell to roughly 280 to 320 loose yards.
field.title: Worked example: full-depth granular backfill under pavement
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data)

field.text: Given: 60 ft of trench bottom is soft; engineer directs 2 ft of over-excavation in a 4 ft wide trench, replaced with #57 (or #2 with #57 choke) wrapped in non-woven geotextile. Stone: 4 x 2 x 60 = 480 cubic ft / 27 = 17.8 CY x 1.45 tons per CY = about 25.8 tons, call it 27 to 28 tons with waste. Fabric: perimeter to wrap = bottom 4 + two sides 2 + 2 + top 4 = 12 ft plus about 1 ft overlap = 13 ft of fabric width per foot of trench. Area = 13 x 60 = 780 sq ft / 9 = 86.7 SY; add about 10 percent for end laps = about 95 SY (a 12.5 x 360 ft roll is 500 SY). Document the over-excavation daily (station limits, depth, width, stone tickets) and get the inspector's sign-off, because undercut and replacement is usually a separate pay item or a change.
field.title: Worked example: over-excavation foundation stone and fabric
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data)

field.text: Given: a 48 inch manhole on a precast base about 5.5 to 6 ft in outside diameter, with a spec calling for 12 inches of compacted crushed stone under the base extending 1 ft beyond it. Pad size about 8 x 8 ft square (or a 9 ft square to allow for a sloppy hole): 9 x 9 x 1 = 81 cubic ft / 27 = 3.0 CY x 1.45 tons per CY = about 4.4 tons. For a 72 inch manhole (base about 7.5 to 8 ft OD) on the same rule, 10 x 10 x 1 = 100 cubic ft = 3.7 CY = about 5.4 tons. In soft ground the engineer may require more depth plus fabric. Level and compact the pad carefully and check elevation with the laser or rod before setting the base; a base set on an uneven pad cracks or sets out of plumb. Add structure stone to the day's order so it is not robbed from the pipe bedding pile.
field.title: Worked example: stone pad under a manhole base
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data)

field.text: Sloped excavations take far more backfill than a trench box. Given: 8 ft deep cut, 4 ft bottom width, side slopes 1:1 from the bottom (Type B soil, no box), 8 inch PVC. Top width = 4 + 2 x 8 = 20 ft. Total area = (4 + 20) / 2 x 8 = 96 sq ft per ft. Embedment zone (bottom 2.2 ft): width at 2.2 ft = 4 + 4.4 = 8.4 ft; area = (4 + 8.4) / 2 x 2.2 = 13.6 sq ft, minus pipe 0.385 = 13.3 sq ft = 0.49 CY of stone per ft (versus 0.23 in a 3 ft box). Final backfill = 96 - 13.6 = 82.4 sq ft = 3.05 CY per ft. If final backfill must be imported base at 1.89 tons per compacted CY: about 5.8 tons per ft, 580 tons per 100 ft. Compare a 3 ft box trench: (8 - 2.2) x 3 = 17.4 sq ft = 0.64 CY per ft. Decide between box and slope with the backfill numbers, not just the dig time.
field.title: Worked example: sloped trench backfill quantities balloon
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data); OSHA Subpart P slope ratios

field.text: Given: 100 ft of 8 inch PVC under a street, trench 2 ft wide, flowable fill from trench bottom to 1 ft below finished grade, with the fill depth 3 ft. Area = 2 x 3 = 6 sq ft minus pipe 0.385 = 5.615 sq ft per ft. Volume = 5.615 x 100 = 561.5 cubic ft / 27 = 20.8 CY. Add 5 to 10 percent for trench overbreak and spillage: order about 22 to 23 CY. At 9 to 10 CY per mixer truck that is 3 trucks; stagger them so the first lift can stiffen around the pipe before the rest arrives (flotation). Check: trench walls wider than planned add up fast (a 2.5 ft actual width makes it about 26 CY before overage). Ask the plant about short-load charges, minimum order, and wait time charges, and confirm the excavatable mix by name or number.
field.title: Worked example: ordering flowable fill for a trench
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data); FHWA flowable fill guidance

field.text: Given: 500 ft of 4 inch perforated underdrain (OD about 4.5 in) in a trench 2 ft wide by 3 ft deep, filled with #57 and wrapped in non-woven fabric. Area = 2 x 3 = 6 sq ft minus pipe 0.11 = 5.89 sq ft per ft. Stone = 5.89 x 500 = 2,945 cubic ft / 27 = 109 CY x 1.4 tons per CY = about 153 tons, about 160 to 165 tons with waste (8 to 9 loads at 20 tons). Fabric: perimeter = bottom 2 + sides 3 + 3 + top 2 = 10 ft plus 1 ft overlap = 11 ft per ft; 11 x 500 = 5,500 sq ft / 9 = 611 SY, plus end laps about 10 percent = about 670 SY. Check the spec for whether the fabric goes around the whole stone envelope (common) or only on the trench walls, and the stone size (some use #8 or a sand filter instead of #57 in silty soils).
field.title: Worked example: underdrain stone and fabric
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data)

field.text: Given: plans show a riprap apron 10 ft wide by 15 ft long at a culvert outlet, d50 of 9 inches, thickness 2 x d50 = 18 inches (1.5 ft), on non-woven geotextile. Volume = 10 x 15 x 1.5 = 225 cubic ft / 27 = 8.33 CY. At 1.6 tons per CY (NESL's estimating number): 13.3 tons; add 10 percent waste = about 14.7 tons, so order 15 tons. NESL's method is the same: area x depth (ft) / 27 x 1.6, then add 10 percent. Fabric: 150 sq ft of apron plus about 12 inches extra on each side and the toe and keyed ends, about 12 x 17 = 204 sq ft = about 23 SY. If the apron has a toe key (often 1.5 times the riprap thickness deep), add that volume. Riprap tons per yard vary by quarry, so ask what factor they use.
field.title: Worked example: riprap apron at a pipe outlet
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: NESL, Rip rap sizes; Standard construction math (worked example; arithmetic exact, unit weights are typical values, use supplier data)

field.text: A good stone order includes: 1) Product by spec name, not just slang: '#57 washed crushed limestone, ASTM C33' or 'VDOT 21A' or 'Class 5 per MnDOT 3138', and whether recycled content is allowed. 2) Quantity in tons (or loads) and a daily schedule. 3) Truck type and any site limits (no semis, weight-posted streets, overhead lines, tight turnarounds); clean stone at about 1.4 tons per CY hits legal weight (often 18 to 22 tons on a tri-axle or quad) before the bed is full, which is why stone is sold by the ton. 4) Exact drop points: stationing or addresses, and whether to drop in one pile or tailgate-spread. 5) Contact name and phone for the driver. 6) Ticket requirements: job name, PO, product, net tons, DOT source approval number if needed. 7) Paperwork for the inspector: current gradation and Proctor report or DOT certification. Order the day before and confirm early in the morning; have the supplier drop where you will be working, not where you are now. Check every ticket's product name before the truck dumps.
field.title: Ordering aggregate: what to tell the supplier
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Keep every scale ticket and total them daily by product and location. Compare against what you should have used: tons per foot from your estimate times feet laid. Typical waste or overrun allowance: 5 to 10 percent for bedding and base, 10 percent for riprap (NESL uses 10 percent). If you are running much higher, common causes are: trench wider than planned (operator, bucket size, or sloughing walls), over-digging below grade, stone going into areas that should be native, stone left in the pile at the end or spread on the haul road, or tickets for loads that went to another job. If you are much lower, check that the bedding depth and cover over the pipe meet the spec. When stone is a pay item by the ton, the tickets are the pay record; get the inspector to initial them or log them daily, because missing tickets are hard to get paid for later.
field.title: Tracking stone: tickets versus placed quantity and waste factors
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: NESL, Rip rap sizes; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: How stone gets paid depends on the contract, so read the measurement and payment section. Common setups: 1) Incidental: bedding and backfill are included in the price per foot of pipe; extra stone because you dug wide is on you. 2) Paid by the ton from tickets, but only up to a 'pay limit': a maximum trench width (often pipe OD plus 1 to 2 ft, or a width shown on the detail) and a set depth below the pipe. Stone outside the limit is not paid. 3) Paid by the cubic yard computed from plan dimensions, not tickets. 4) Undercut and foundation stone: a separate unit price per ton or CY, paid only when the engineer directs it, measured before backfill. 5) Select backfill under pavement: separate item by the ton or CY within pay limits. Know your pay width before digging, size the bucket to it, and document any direction to undercut in writing the same day.
field.title: Pay limits for trench stone and backfill: what usually gets paid
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: Construction contract practice (your contract governs)

field.text: Flowable fill comes in standard concrete mixer trucks, usually 8 to 10 CY per load (some up to 11), with short-load fees below a plant minimum (often 3 to 5 CY). It can be chuted directly into the trench, pumped, or placed by bucket. Plan placement: have the trench ready, pipe restrained, bulkheads braced and traffic control set before the first truck; schedule trucks so a first lift can stiffen around the pipe before the next arrives; allow for wait-time charges if you hold trucks. Very fluid mixes run down the trench on grade, so build bulkheads (plywood, sandbags or a soil plug) at the ends of the pour. The mix is caustic like concrete: gloves, boots and eye protection. Truck washout goes into a lined washout container or pit, never into storm drains, ditches or the sewer, per your stormwater permit.
field.title: Ready-mix trucks for flowable fill: loads, timing and washout
field.topic: Aggregates: weights, estimating and ordering
field.source: FHWA flowable fill guidance (delivery by ready-mix trucks); General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: The stone size numbers crews use (#2, #57, #8 and so on) come from ASTM D448 (road and bridge) and ASTM C33 (concrete), which share one size table; AASHTO M43 uses the same numbers. Rule of thumb: the bigger the number, the smaller the stone. A single digit is one size band (#5 is 1 inch down to 1/2 inch). A two or three digit number blends the bands in its name, so #57 is #5 plus #7 (1 inch down to #4 sieve, about 3/16 inch) and #467 is #4 through #7. Every standard size is a clean, screened stone with almost no fines: the top sieve passes 100 percent (with a little oversize allowed on the next sieve up) and usually only 0 to 10 percent (0 to 15 for the biggest sizes) passes the bottom sieve in the name, with 0 to 5 percent on the next sieve down. Screenings (#10) are the exception. A size number tells you gradation only, not rock type or quality; washed vs unwashed, crushed vs gravel, and LA abrasion come from the spec and the quarry.
field.title: How aggregate size numbers work (#57, #8, #67 explained)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703

field.text: Nominal size ranges from the ASTM D448/C33 table: #1 is 3 1/2 inch down to 1 1/2 inch; #2 is 2 1/2 inch down to 1 1/2 inch; #24 is 2 1/2 inch down to 3/4 inch. Crews call these 2 inch stone, 3 inch clean, ballast-size or 'big rock'. Common uses (practice, check your spec): stabilizing a soft or pumping trench bottom before a choke layer of #57 goes on top; construction entrance pads (often 2 to 3 inch stone); subbase layers in permeable pavement; gabion and drainage blankets; some agencies use them for mass concrete. They are open-graded with large voids (roughly 40 percent), so fines from a mucky subgrade will push up into them unless you use a geotextile or a choke stone. Too big for direct contact with plastic pipe; do not use as bedding or haunch material.
field.title: #1, #2 and #24 stone: large clean stone (3 1/2 to 3/4 inch)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: From the ASTM D448/C33 size table: #3 is 2 inch down to 1 inch (clean, one size band). #357 is 2 inch down to the #4 sieve (about 3/16 inch), a blend of #3, #5 and #7, so it packs tighter than #3. Typical uses: #3 for drainage blankets, foundation stone under structures and pipe in wet ground, and backfill for subsurface drain fields; #357 is a large-aggregate concrete size used in mass or paving concrete in some regions, and sometimes as a coarse base. CDOT lists both No. 3 and No. 357 in its coarse aggregate table. For pipe work, #3 is foundation stone, not embedment: most plastic pipe makers limit particle size in the pipe zone to well under 2 inches. Check spec and pipe maker.
field.title: #3 and #357 stone (2 inch to 1 inch, 2 inch to #4)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; CDOT 703

field.text: ASTM D448/C33 nominal sizes: #4 is 1 1/2 inch down to 3/4 inch; #467 is 1 1/2 inch down to the #4 sieve. Field names: '1 1/2 inch clean', 'inch and a half washed', 'drain rock' in some areas. #4 is a uniform, very open stone used for drainage layers, French drains in heavy flow, foundation stabilization and some railroad and septic work. #467 is a common concrete coarse aggregate for footings and paving and is sometimes used as bedding for large concrete or ductile iron pipe where the spec allows bigger stone. For PVC and HDPE in the 4 to 15 inch range, most specs and manufacturers want smaller stone (3/4 inch to 1 inch max), so #4 is normally foundation stone rather than embedment. Check the pipe maker's max particle size.
field.title: #4 and #467 stone (1 1/2 inch to 3/4 inch, 1 1/2 inch to #4)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: ASTM D448/C33 nominal sizes: #5 is 1 inch down to 1/2 inch; #56 is 1 inch down to 3/8 inch. These are clean, fairly uniform 'inch stone' with no small chips. Uses: drainage stone, French drains, asphalt base mixes, some concrete and subbase work, and backfill around drain tile where a fast-draining stone is wanted. Because they lack the smaller sizes, they have bigger voids than #57 and are a little harder to compact into the haunches of small pipe. Some specs allow #5 or #56 as Class I embedment; many simply call out #57 or #67 instead. If a supplier is out of #57, ask the engineer before substituting #5 or #56; the gradation difference matters for migration and haunch support.
field.title: #5 and #56 stone (1 inch to 1/2 inch, 1 inch to 3/8 inch)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: #57 is 1 inch down to the #4 sieve (about 3/16 inch) per the ASTM D448/C33 table, a blend of #5 and #7. In most of the East, Midwest and South it is the default 'clean stone', '3/4 inch washed', 'pipe stone' or 'bedding rock' (people call it 3/4 inch because most of it looks that size). Uses: Class I pipe bedding and embedment for PVC, HDPE, DI and concrete pipe; foundation stone; drainage and French drains; underdrain trenches; manhole and structure bases; concrete coarse aggregate; permeable pavement reservoir layers. Its voids (roughly 35 to 40 percent) make it free-draining, which also means it can act as a drain along the trench and can let fines from surrounding soil migrate in. Compacts well with a plate or by working it into the haunches; get it under the pipe, not just beside it. Verify your spec's gradation band and whether it must be washed.
field.title: #57 stone: the workhorse (1 inch to #4, '3/4 inch clean')
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: ASTM D448/C33 nominal sizes: #6 is 3/4 inch down to 3/8 inch; #67 is 3/4 inch down to the #4 sieve; #68 is 3/4 inch down to the #8 sieve. #67 is the other big bedding stone: slightly smaller top size than #57, so it works into haunches of small pipe a little easier and many PVC specs prefer it for 4 to 12 inch sewer. It is also the most common concrete coarse aggregate in many markets and is used in asphalt. #6 is uniform and open, mostly asphalt and drainage. #68 carries more small chips and is used where a tighter, smaller stone is wanted (some DOTs, e.g. Virginia, list #68 for pipe bedding). NCPI test work notes uncompacted #67 has about 40 percent porosity, so it must still be worked and compacted. Check spec and pipe maker for allowed sizes.
field.title: #6, #67 and #68 stone (3/4 inch to 3/8 inch, #4 or #8)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; NCPI Soil Migration and Buried Pipe; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: ASTM D448/C33 nominal sizes: #7 is 1/2 inch down to the #4 sieve; #78 is 1/2 inch down to the #8 sieve (about 3/32 inch). Field names: '1/2 inch chip', 'half inch clean', '78s'. Uses: asphalt surface mixes, chip seals, some concrete block and precast work, and bedding for small diameter pipe (laterals, 4 and 6 inch services, small HDPE) where specs want a smaller stone that moves into the haunch easily. #78 has more small sizes than #7, so it packs tighter and is a bit less prone to letting fines migrate in. Both are still clean stone with almost no #200 fines. NCDOT lists a #78M size for asphalt and other uses. Use when the plan, spec or pipe maker calls for a max particle size of 1/2 inch.
field.title: #7 and #78 stone (1/2 inch to #4, 1/2 inch to #8)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; NCDOT Table 1005-1; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: #8 is 3/8 inch down to the #8 sieve per the ASTM D448/C33 table. Field names: 3/8 chip, 3/8 clean, 'crushed pea stone', 'birdseye' in some areas (not the same as rounded pea gravel). Uses: bedding for small pipe and services, the setting bed and joint fill for permeable pavers, choke course over #57 in permeable pavement, filter stone around perforated pipe in fine soils, chip seal, and asphalt. Because it is small and clean it flows into haunches easily but still needs to be worked under the pipe and compacted. In open-graded drainage systems #8 is often the layer that keeps sand from migrating into a #57 or #2 layer below it. Check the spec; some agencies call #8 'No. 8 coarse aggregate' and some use it as Class I bedding for HDPE storm pipe.
field.title: #8 stone: 3/8 inch chip (3/8 inch to #8), 'pea stone' crushed
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: From the ASTM D448/C33 size table: #89 is 3/8 inch down to the #16 sieve (about 1/20 inch), and #9 is #4 down to #16. These are the small chips at the fine end of the coarse sizes. Uses: chip seal and surface treatments, fine asphalt mixes, precast and block plants, some bedding for very small services, and filter layers. #9 is close to a coarse sand in feel. They are still washed, screened stone with low fines, unlike screenings (#10), which include the dust. For pipe zone material, a small size like #89 behaves more like a coarse sand: it places easily but drains less freely and is less resistant to washing if water runs along the trench. Use only where the spec allows.
field.title: #89 and #9 stone (3/8 inch to #16, #4 to #16)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: #10 in the ASTM D448 table is 'screenings': #4 sieve down to dust, the fine byproduct left after the coarse sizes are screened out. Names: stone dust, crusher dust, quarry dust, manufactured sand, rock fines, 'screenings', 'blue dust' (traprock regions), 'limestone fines'. Uses: paver and patio base leveling layer, setting bed under precast, backfill around small conduits in some specs, blending into base. It packs hard when compacted at the right moisture, but it holds water, is frost-susceptible, and washes out if water runs through it. Most pipe specs do not allow screenings in the pipe zone unless named. Safety: dry screenings are mostly crystalline silica dust in granite, traprock and sandstone; keep it damp when dumping, sweeping or cutting near it (OSHA 1926.1153).
field.title: #10 screenings, stone dust, quarry fines, crusher dust
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate sizes table (reproduced in Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C, ASTM D448-12); CDOT Section 703; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: The most common ordering mix-up. 'Clean', 'washed' or a number like #57 means screened stone with the fines removed: it drains, needs little compaction effort, and is used for bedding, drainage and foundation stone. 'Minus' (3/4 minus, 3/4-0, 1 1/2 minus, crusher run, road base, DGA, ABC, GAB) means the stone plus everything smaller down to dust: a dense-graded mix that compacts into a hard, tight layer with a Proctor density, but does not drain well. Use minus for road base, trench patches under pavement, pads and shoulders; use clean for pipe zones that call for Class I, drainage and wet trench bottoms. Some specs allow dense-graded base in the pipe zone (Class II or III behavior), but it must be compacted at the right moisture. When ordering, say both the size and clean vs minus, and quote the spec item number.
field.title: Clean (washed) stone versus 'minus' stone: 3/4 clean vs 3/4 minus
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: 'Crusher run' is unscreened crushed stone straight off the crusher, top size down to dust: a dense-graded base. Regional names: CR-6 (about 1 1/2 inch minus) and CR-8 (about 1 inch minus) in the Maryland area; 'quarry process' or 'QP', 'site pack', 'RC-6' or 'crusher run' in NJ/PA/MD; GAB (graded aggregate base) in Georgia, Maryland and other DOTs. The Hampton Roads (Virginia) regional standards define crusher run aggregate as crushed aggregate used for backfilling and bedding pipe and box culverts, meeting VDOT Section 205. Crusher run compacts hard and is common as trench backfill under pavement, base under slabs and patches, and driveway base. It is not free-draining and its fines can migrate into adjacent clean stone. Gradation and quality vary by state, so cite the state spec when ordering.
field.title: Crusher run, CR-6, CR-8, GAB, site pack, quarry process (Mid-Atlantic and Southeast names)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: Hampton Roads Regional Construction Standards Section 200 (VDOT 205/208 references); donsnotes aggregate terms; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: 21A and 21B are Virginia (VDOT Road and Bridge Specs Section 208) dense-graded aggregate base materials; Virginia localities' standards point to Section 208 for subbase and aggregate base. Both are crushed stone that passes 100 percent on the 2 inch sieve (21A 94 to 100 and 21B 85 to 95 percent on the 1 inch) graded down to dust. 21A carries more fines (minus #200 6 to 12 percent) so it compacts very tight and is common under pavements, shoulders and trench patches; 21B has fewer fines (4 to 7 percent) and drains a little better, so it is used where some drainage in the base is wanted. Section 208 lists other sizes too (such as 22). In Virginia, 'crusher run' sold by quarries is usually one of these. Check the current VDOT Section 208 table for the exact gradation bands and the plasticity limits before submitting.
field.title: 21A and 21B aggregate base (Virginia VDOT)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: VDOT Road and Bridge Specifications Section 208 as referenced in Hampton Roads Regional Standards; gradation ranges approximate from memory of VDOT table, verify; Carmeuse Virginia gradation chart (VDOT sizes)

field.text: DGA = dense graded aggregate. In Kentucky (KYTC Section 302) DGA and CSB (crushed stone base) are the two standard base courses; aggregate must meet Section 805. Single-lift limits: 6 1/2 inches compacted for DGA and 8 inches for CSB, otherwise place in two or more layers each at least 3 inches; density is checked against a control strip (lot average at least 98 percent of target, no single test below 95 percent), and fines must not be added to make density. Other regional names for similar dense-graded base: 'DGA' or 'I-3 / I-5' in New Jersey, '2A' or '2A modified' in Pennsylvania (PennDOT subbase No. 2A), 'Item 4' (NYSDOT subbase Type 2, also sold as RCA Item 4) in New York, '304' in Ohio. All are minus materials that compact tight and do not drain freely.
field.title: DGA and CSB (Kentucky), NJ DGA, PennDOT 2A, NY Item 4
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet Standard Specifications Section 302 (2026); regional names from General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: ABC = aggregate base course. It is the base name used by NCDOT (Table 1005-1 lists ABC and ABC(M), for aggregate base course and stabilization), Arizona (ADOT/MAG ABC), South Carolina and others. 'Road base' is the generic West and Mountain term for dense-graded crushed base, usually 3/4 inch or 1 inch minus. 'Flex base' is the Texas DOT name (Item 247 flexible base, graded by type and grade). Florida uses 'limerock base' and 'crushed concrete base'; Georgia uses GAB. All are minus materials meant to be compacted to a Proctor density at near optimum moisture. In utility work they show up as trench backfill under pavement, as the base course of trench patches, and as pads for structures. Order by the state spec item, since the gradation and plasticity rules differ by state.
field.title: ABC, road base, flex base, limerock (South and West names)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: NCDOT Table 1005-1 (aggregate designations); General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: In Minnesota and North Dakota 'Class 5' is the everyday name for dense-graded base. MnDOT spec 3138 (products with less than 25 percent recycled content), percent passing: Class 5 is 1 1/2 inch 100, 3/4 inch 70 to 100, 3/8 inch 45 to 90, #4 35 to 80, #10 20 to 65, #40 10 to 35, #200 3 to 10. Class 5Q is a coarser, more open version (check the current table). Class 6 is like Class 5 but tighter and cleaner (#4 35 to 70, #200 3 to 7). Recycled material is allowed and is labeled in the name: (B) bituminous, (C) concrete, (G) glass, e.g. Class 5 (BC). Limits: glass max 10 percent and 3/4 inch, brick max 1 percent, wood, plastic and other junk max 0.3 percent, composite bitumen max 3.5 percent. Used as trench backfill under roads, patch base and pads.
field.title: Class 5 and Class 6 aggregate base (Minnesota MnDOT 3138)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: MnDOT Specification 3138 (aggregate for surface and base courses), via MnDOT NRRA

field.text: In California, 'Class 2 base' or 'Class II AB' is the standard dense-graded base (Caltrans Standard Specs Section 26). 3/4 inch max grading, contract compliance percent passing: 1 inch 100, 3/4 inch 87 to 100, #4 30 to 65, #30 5 to 35, #200 0 to 12. The 1 1/2 inch max grading runs 2 inch 100, 1 1/2 inch 87 to 100, 3/4 inch 45 to 90, #4 20 to 50, #30 6 to 29, #200 0 to 12. Quality: R-value at least 78, sand equivalent at least 22 (25 operating range), durability index at least 35. Caltrans allows processed reclaimed asphalt concrete, PCC, lean concrete base and cement-treated base in Class 2, so 'recycled Class 2' is common. Many California cities require Class 2 base under trench patches and as trench backfill in the street section.
field.title: Class 2 aggregate base, 'Class 2 base' / 'Class II base rock' (California Caltrans)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: Caltrans Standard Specifications Section 26, Aggregate Bases (via MnDOT NRRA)

field.text: Colorado crews say 'Class 6' for the standard road base. CDOT Section 703 Table 703-2 lists aggregate base course Classes 1 through 7. Class 6 runs 1 inch 100, 3/4 inch 95 to 100, #4 30 to 65, #8 25 to 55, #200 3 to 12, liquid limit 30 max, PI 6 max: a 3/4 inch minus crushed base used under pavement, in trench patches and for pads. Class 3 is bank or pit run material (up to 6 inch top size, #200 max 20 percent), used as subbase and bulk fill. Class 5 and Class 7 are other gradations. CDOT also has filter material Classes A, B and C (all limit #200 to 0 to 3 percent) for drains. Confirm against the current CDOT Section 703 before you submit.
field.title: Class 6 road base and Class 3 pit run (Colorado CDOT)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: CDOT Standard Specifications Section 703, Tables 703-2 and 703-10

field.text: Illinois material names come from IDOT gradation numbers: CA = coarse aggregate, FA = fine aggregate. CA-6 is the common 'grade 8' or 'road base' dense-graded crushed stone, roughly 1 1/2 or 1 inch minus with fines, used for base, trench backfill under pavement and pads. CA-7 is a clean stone of about 1 inch down to the #4 sieve, similar to #57, used for bedding, drainage and concrete. CA-11 is a clean 3/4 inch stone similar to #67. CA-16 is a clean 3/8 inch chip similar to #8, used for small pipe bedding and asphalt. FA-1 and FA-2 are concrete sands; FA-6 is a fine 'trench backfill' sand in some Chicago-area municipal specs. Many Chicago-area sewer specs call CA-7 or CA-11 for bedding and CA-6 or FA-6 for trench backfill. Check the IDOT Article 1004 gradation table for exact bands.
field.title: CA-6, CA-7, CA-11, CA-16 and FA sand (Illinois IDOT names)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: IDOT gradation designations (Article 1003/1004) as commonly used by suppliers; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Indiana (INDOT) uses its own size numbers alongside the ASTM ones: #53 is the common dense-graded base (about 1 1/2 inch minus with fines), #73 is a smaller dense-graded base (about 1 inch minus), #2, #5, #8, #9, #11 and #12 are clean coarse sizes, and 93PG is pea gravel: generally uncrushed gravel with a maximum of 20 percent crushed particles. Iowa DOT uses gradation numbers: No. 14 'modified subbase' runs 1 1/2 inch 100, 3/4 inch 70 to 90, #8 10 to 40, #200 3 to 10; No. 12a granular subbase (crushed stone) runs 1 1/2 inch 100, 1/2 inch 40 to 80, #8 5 to 25, #200 0 to 6; No. 29 is porous backfill; No. 11 is granular surfacing and shoulder stone (used for Class A crushed stone surfacing). An Iowa note waives the #200 limit on gradation No. 2 (sand) when it is used for pipe bedding.
field.title: Indiana #53, #73, pea gravel 93PG and Iowa modified subbase / granular surfacing gradations
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: INDOT Aggregate Specification Chart; Iowa DOT IM 209 Aggregate Gradation Table

field.text: In Oregon and Washington, crushed rock is named by top size and bottom size: '3/4-0' (three-quarter minus, dense-graded with fines), '1 1/2-0', '1-0'; versus '3/4-1/4' or '3/4 clean' for screened stone without fines. WSDOT names: CSBC = crushed surfacing base course (about 1 1/4 inch minus), CSTC = crushed surfacing top course (about 5/8 inch minus), 'gravel borrow' and 'gravel base' (pit run type materials), 'select borrow', and 'ballast' (a coarse 2 1/2 inch minus base, not railroad ballast). 'Quarry spalls' are a 2 to 8 inch or so crushed rock used for construction entrances and soft ground. 'Drain rock' is clean 3/4 to 1 1/2 inch. In California and the Southwest 'base rock' or 'Class 2' is common. Always confirm the agency's gradation section (WSDOT 9-03).
field.title: 3/4-0, CSBC, CSTC, gravel borrow, ballast (Pacific Northwest and West names)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: WSDOT Standard Specifications Section 9-03 names; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Pea gravel is naturally rounded, water-worn gravel, usually about 1/4 to 3/8 inch (sometimes up to 1/2 inch), screened and often washed. INDOT's 93PG pea gravel is generally uncrushed gravel with no more than 20 percent crushed particles. Because the stones are round, pea gravel flows and self-levels almost like a liquid, which helps fill haunches, but it also rolls and shifts, has low friction, and gives less side support than angular crushed stone at the same density. Many sewer specs exclude it or list it as Class II (clean rounded gravel) rather than Class I; some allow it for small services and for water line bedding. Uses: drainage, play areas, landscape, around septic and drain tile, and some HDPE storm detention bedding where the maker allows. Ask: does the spec say crushed or angular? If yes, pea gravel is not acceptable.
field.title: Pea gravel: rounded stone and pipe bedding
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: INDOT Aggregate Specification Chart (93PG); ASTM D2321 class descriptions as summarized by PPI; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Railroad ballast is hard, angular, clean crushed stone (granite, traprock, quartzite or hard limestone/slag) graded in AREMA sizes such as No. 4A, No. 24 and No. 3, roughly 2 1/2 or 2 inch down to 3/4 inch or 1 inch. Railroads require tough stone (low LA abrasion) and very little fines so the track drains. For utility crews it comes up when crossing under or alongside track: the railroad permit usually requires you to restore the ballast section with matching material, keep fouled ballast (mixed with dirt) out of the track, and keep spoil and equipment off the ballast shoulder. Do not confuse it with WSDOT 'ballast', which is a coarse 2 1/2 inch minus road base, or with 'ballast' some suppliers use for any 2 inch stone. Railroad work also needs flagging and a railroad-approved work plan.
field.title: Railroad ballast versus road 'ballast'
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: AREMA ballast size designations as commonly summarized; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Bank run (bank-run gravel) and pit run are natural sand and gravel dug from a pit and loaded with little or no screening or crushing. Expect rounded stones, a wide size range, and a variable amount of silt and clay. CDOT's Class 3 base is defined as bank or pit run material with up to a 6 inch top size and no more than 20 percent passing the #200. A New Mexico mining conversion table uses 1.62 tons per cubic yard for pit run, heavier than screened gravel because the sand fills the voids. Uses: subbase, bulk fill, embankment, haul roads, backfill above the pipe zone where allowed. Problems: oversize cobbles that can damage pipe in the first foot of cover, wet pockets of fines, and variability load to load. Many specs call it 'select granular borrow' with limits on top size and fines. Get a sieve test from the pit before you rely on it.
field.title: Bank run, pit run, gravel borrow: unprocessed natural material
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: CDOT Section 703 Table 703-2; New Mexico EMNRD mining conversion factors; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: These are spec names, not standard products, so the definition is whatever the project spec says. Typical meanings: Common fill or common borrow: any soil free of organics, trash, frozen lumps and large rock, usable for embankment and general backfill. Select fill or select backfill: a better imported material with limits on top size (often 3 or 4 inches), fines content and plasticity, often a granular soil. Structural fill: material placed under buildings, slabs, footings or pavements, compacted to a high density (often 95 percent of standard or modified Proctor) and often limited to low plasticity (for example PI under 10 or 15) with a max top size. Granular borrow: sand and gravel with limited fines. Before ordering, read the spec's gradation and plasticity table, then ask the supplier for a current sieve and Proctor report on that exact product.
field.title: Select fill, structural fill, common fill and borrow: what the names usually mean
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: Concrete sand (ASTM C33 fine aggregate): a coarse, washed sand, the sand in ready-mix. C33 fine aggregate generally has a fineness modulus of about 2.3 to 3.1 and low fines; coarser and grittier than mason sand. Good bedding and haunch sand for water lines, gas and conduits, and the sand used to make flowable fill. Mason sand (ASTM C144): a finer, more uniform sand for mortar; C144 allows a larger share of fines than plaster sand, and one sand usually cannot meet both C144 and C897 plaster sand. Too fine and expensive for bulk backfill. Fill sand, utility sand, pipe sand, select sand: unwashed or lightly processed sand with some silt, sold for bedding services, backfill and leveling; quality varies a lot. Washed sand is any sand rinsed to remove silt and clay. For pipe zones, check the spec's limit on the #200 fines.
field.title: Concrete sand vs mason sand vs fill sand vs utility sand
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: STO Corp technical hotline TH 0603-S (ASTM C144 vs C897); ASTM C33 as commonly summarized

field.text: Clean sand is Class II material under ASTM D2321 (SW, SP), and many water, gas, electric and telecom specs require 'sand padding' around the pipe. Pros: no sharp edges against coatings, wraps and thin-wall pipe, easy to shovel into haunches, cheap where local. Cons: it washes out if groundwater runs along the trench, it can turn quick (flowing) in a wet trench bottom, it needs real compaction effort in thin lifts (check your spec's lift limit), and fine uniform sand can migrate into nearby stone. In a wet trench, many engineers switch to crushed stone or wrap the sand with fabric. Do not 'water settle' or jet sand unless the spec allows it; flooding can float pipe and soften the trench walls. Check whether your spec wants concrete sand, a named DOT sand, or just 'clean sand free of rock over 1/2 inch'.
field.title: Sand as pipe bedding: when it works and when it fails
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: PPI conduitcalc Pipe Embedment Materials; ASTM D2321 summary; General industry and supplier practice (varies by region, quarry and spec)

field.text: The Los Angeles abrasion test (AASHTO T 96 / ASTM C131) tumbles about 5,000 g of washed, dried coarse aggregate with steel balls in a steel drum for 500 revolutions, then sieves it on the #12 sieve. The percent lost to fines is the 'LA loss' or 'LA wear'. Lower is tougher. Typical losses per Pavement Interactive: hard igneous rock about 10, basalt 10 to 17, limestone 19 to 30, dolomite 18 to 30, quartzite 20 to 35, granite 27 to 49, gneiss 33 to 57, soft limestone and sandstone about 60. State limits for asphalt coarse aggregate run 25 to 55 percent loss, most 40 or 45; AASHTO limits SMA to 30. Base and bedding specs often allow a higher loss. Weak stone breaks down under rollers and traffic into fines, which hurts drainage and density. The test correlates with dust generation better than with field performance.
field.title: LA abrasion test in plain words (how tough the stone is)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: Pavement Interactive, Los Angeles Abrasion

field.text: Soundness tests check whether stone breaks down from weathering. The sulfate soundness test (AASHTO T 104 / ASTM C88) soaks the aggregate in sodium or magnesium sulfate and dries it, usually 5 cycles; salt crystals growing in the pores act like freezing water. The result is percent loss. Typical limits: ASTM C33 coarse aggregate for concrete commonly allows about 12 percent loss with sodium sulfate or 18 percent with magnesium sulfate; DOT base and drainage limits vary. The Micro-Deval test tumbles wet stone with steel balls and is a better predictor of breakdown in service; some states (Maine, for example) use it in place of LA abrasion. Shale, soft sandstone, chert and some porous limestones fail soundness and pop out or crumble. Why crews care: unsound stone turns to fines in the trench or base, clogs drains and loses support. Ask the quarry for its current DOT approval or test report.
field.title: Soundness, Micro-Deval and freeze-thaw durability of stone
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: Pavement Interactive (Micro-Deval note); ASTM C33/C88 limits as commonly summarized

field.text: Fractured faces (ASTM D5821): the count of broken (crushed) faces on gravel particles. Natural gravel is rounded; running it through a crusher breaks faces on it. Specs for crushed gravel base and bedding often require a minimum percent of particles with one or two fractured faces, so the material locks together instead of rolling. Quarried crushed stone is 100 percent fractured. Angular particles give more friction and support (crushed RCA, for example, has friction angles above 40 degrees per FHWA) but can scratch coatings; rounded particles flow and place easily but shift more. Flat and elongated particles (ASTM D4791) are slabby or long pieces that break under compaction and leave voids; asphalt specs limit them, and they matter less for bedding. When a spec says 'crushed stone' or 'angular', pit gravel without fractured faces does not meet it.
field.title: Fractured faces, angularity, flat and elongated pieces
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 (recycled concrete friction angle); ASTM D5821/D4791 as commonly summarized

field.text: 'Deleterious material' means anything in the aggregate that hurts performance: clay lumps and friable particles, shale, coal and lignite, chert that pops, soft particles, wood, roots, trash and organics. Specs limit each by percent. Fines tests you will see on a material report: wash loss or minus #200 (ASTM C117), the percent of silt and clay sized dust; sand equivalent (Caltrans Class 2 base needs at least 22), where a higher number means cleaner, less clayey fines; liquid limit and plasticity index (Atterberg limits), where a high PI means clayey, sticky fines that lose strength when wet (CDOT base classes cap LL at 30 or 35). Recycled products add limits for brick, asphalt, glass, wood and plastic (MnDOT caps wood, plastic and similar at 0.3 percent). In the field: stone that leaves a muddy film on your hand or makes muddy water may be out of spec for 'washed' or Class I.
field.title: Deleterious material, clay lumps, sand equivalent and plasticity (dirty stone)
field.topic: Aggregates: standard sizes, trade names and quality
field.source: Caltrans Section 26; CDOT 703; MnDOT 3138; ASTM C117 scope

field.text: Asphalt pavement (hot-mix asphalt, HMA, blacktop, bituminous concrete, 'hot mix', 'AC') is about 94 to 96 percent aggregate (crushed stone, gravel, sand, mineral filler) and about 4 to 6 percent asphalt binder by weight. The binder (asphalt cement, 'oil', 'AC', 'liquid asphalt') is the heavy black residue from refining crude oil; it is a thermoplastic: soft and sticky when hot, stiff when cold. Asphalt is flexible pavement: it bends over the base and spreads load through layers, so base and subgrade compaction under it matter more than with concrete. Coal tar is a different material used mainly in some sealcoats, and banned or restricted in several states and cities because of PAH content.
field.title: What asphalt is: binder, aggregate and 'blacktop'
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Performance Grade (PG) binders are named PG XX-YY. XX is the high pavement temperature in Celsius (7-day average max) the binder handles without rutting; YY is the low pavement temperature (negative) it handles without thermal cracking. PG 64-22 = good to 64 C (147 F) pavement temperature and down to -22 C (-8 F). Grades step in 6 C increments: highs 52, 58, 64, 70, 76, 82; lows -10, -16, -22, -28, -34, -40. Colder climates use lower 'low' numbers (PG 58-28, 52-34); hot climates and heavy, slow or standing traffic use higher 'high' numbers (PG 70-22, 76-22). The spread (high minus low) is the useful temperature interval; PG 64-22 is 86. Spreads of 92 or more usually need polymer modification.
field.title: PG binder grading explained (PG 64-22, PG 58-28, PG 76-22)
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: TxDOT, Asphalt Materials and Uses / PG binder FAQ

field.text: Polymer-modified binders add SBS (styrene-butadiene-styrene, the most common), SBR latex, ground tire rubber, or other modifiers so the binder resists rutting at high temperatures and stays flexible in cold. Premium grades like PG 76-22 or PG 70-28 essentially require polymer because of the elastic recovery and MSCR tests. 'Grade bumping' means raising the high-temperature grade one or two steps (e.g. PG 64-22 to 70-22 or 76-22) for heavy truck volumes, slow-moving or standing traffic like intersections, bus stops and toll plazas. PMA mixes are stiffer and stickier: they need higher mix and compaction temperatures, quicker rolling, and may pick up on rubber tires. Follow the supplier's temperature range.
field.title: Polymer-modified asphalt (PMA) and grade bumping
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: TxDOT, Asphalt Materials and Uses / PG binder FAQ

field.text: An asphalt emulsion is asphalt binder suspended in water with an emulsifier, so it can be sprayed or mixed without heating it to 300 F (applied around 140 to 160 F, or cooler for tack). It 'breaks' when the water separates out (turns from brown to black) and 'cures' as the water evaporates. Naming: C prefix = cationic (positive charge; no C = anionic); RS/MS/SS = rapid, medium or slow setting; 1 = low viscosity, 2 = high viscosity; h = harder residue; P = polymer; HF = high float. Examples: CRS-2 (chip seal), CSS-1h and SS-1h (tack coat, fog seal, slurry), CRS-2P (polymer chip seal), HFRS-2. Don't mix cationic and anionic products in the same tank. Emulsions must not freeze.
field.title: Asphalt emulsions: what RS, MS, SS, C and h mean
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: TxDOT, Asphalt Materials and Uses / PG binder FAQ

field.text: Cutback asphalt is binder thinned with petroleum solvent instead of water. RC (rapid curing) uses naphtha or gasoline-type solvent; MC (medium curing) uses kerosene-type; SC (slow curing) uses a heavier oil. The number (30, 70, 250, 800, 3000) is viscosity: lower = thinner, more solvent (MC-30 can be close to half solvent). MC-30 and MC-70 are traditional prime coats because they penetrate granular base; MC-250/800 and RC-250 appear in cold-weather chip seals and stockpile patch. The solvent evaporates as volatile organic compounds and is flammable, so cutbacks are banned or restricted seasonally in many ozone nonattainment areas (TxDOT, for example, restricts them in some areas during the summer ozone season). Emulsions have replaced most cutback uses.
field.title: Cutback asphalt: RC, MC, SC and why it's restricted
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: TxDOT, Asphalt Materials and Uses / PG binder FAQ

field.text: Prime coat is a low-viscosity asphalt (MC-30, or special prime emulsions) sprayed on a granular aggregate base before the first asphalt layer; it penetrates the top 1/4 to 1/2 inch, binds loose fines, waterproofs the base and helps bond.
