Typical rates are around 0.15 to 0.30 gal per sq yd and it needs time to cure (often 24 hours or more); many agencies now skip prime under thick asphalt. Tack coat is a thin application of emulsion or hot binder between asphalt layers, or onto concrete or milled surfaces, to glue the new lift to the old one so they act as one layer. They are not interchangeable: tack doesn't penetrate base, and prime is too slow and thin for bonding asphalt layers.
field.title: Prime coat vs tack coat
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: TxDOT, Asphalt Materials and Uses / PG binder FAQ

field.text: Tack coat bonds the new lift to the surface below so the layers carry traffic together. Without a good bond, layers slip: you get slippage cracks (crescent-shaped cracks where vehicles brake or turn), delamination, and pavement life can drop by a large fraction even when each layer is built right. Too much tack is also bad: it can bleed up through thin overlays and act as a slip plane. Surface must be clean and dry; sweep milled and dusty surfaces first (dust stops bond). Apply uniformly with a distributor spray bar with nozzles at the right angle and bar height for double or triple overlap, not a streaky hand wand, except on small patches. Tack all vertical edges of patches and cold joints.
field.title: Tack coat purpose and what happens without it
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: Pavement Interactive, The Right Tack to Take

field.text: Specs give tack as residual rate (asphalt left after water evaporates). PennDOT Pub 408 residual rates (gal per sq yd): new asphalt 0.03 to 0.05; existing asphalt 0.04 to 0.07; milled surface (asphalt or concrete) 0.04 to 0.08; portland cement concrete 0.04 to 0.07. Milled surfaces need more because tack runs into the grooves. Application rate = residual rate / residual content of the emulsion (from the bill of lading). Example: residual 0.06 with a 57 percent residue tack: 0.06 / 0.57 = 0.105 gal per sq yd shot. Diluted emulsion (e.g. an SS-1h with about 60 percent residue diluted 1:1 with water = about 30 percent) needs about twice the gallons. Check the rate by measuring gallons used over a known area; run a 100 ft test strip.
field.title: Tack coat rates: residual vs application rate
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: PennDOT LTAP Tech Sheet 189, Tack Coat (Pub 408 Sec 460 rates)

field.text: Emulsion tack goes on brown and turns black when it breaks (the water separates). Paving is normally done after the break, when the tack is tacky; timing depends on temperature, humidity and wind (minutes on a hot day, much longer in cool damp weather). Haul trucks and paver tracks pick up soft tack and carry it off ('tracking'), leaving bare spots and dirty streets. Non-tracking or 'trackless' tacks (hard-residue emulsions, often about 50 percent residue) break fast and resist pickup, and are now common on trench patch and overlay work. Hot-applied PG binder tack bonds immediately. Never pave on wet tack in the rain. Don't let traffic run on broken tack longer than necessary.
field.title: Tack coat breaking, tracking and non-tracking tack
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: PennDOT LTAP Tech Sheet 189, Tack Coat (Pub 408 Sec 460 rates)

field.text: Hot mix asphalt (HMA) is produced and placed hot, typically about 275 to 325 F at the plant (higher for polymer mixes), and must be compacted before it cools to about 175 F. Warm mix asphalt (WMA) uses additives (waxes, chemical surfactants, zeolites) or water foaming at the plant to coat and compact at lower temperatures; FHWA-cited products claim reductions of about 18 to 100 F. Cold mix is made with emulsion or cutback and can be stockpiled and placed cold; it is weaker and used for temporary patches. WMA accounted for about 41 percent of US mix tonnage in 2021 (NAPA). Spec rules for HMA usually apply to WMA, with adjusted temperatures from the mix design.
field.title: HMA vs WMA vs cold mix: what's different
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: FHWA Warm-Mix Asphalt technologies page

field.text: WMA lets plants produce and crews place mix about 30 to 100 F cooler than HMA (FHWA cites products ranging from about 18 F up to 100 F reduction). Field benefits: less smoke, odor and asphalt fumes for the paving crew; lower fuel use at the plant (reported 20 to 55 percent for some technologies); longer haul distances and more time to compact; easier compaction in cool weather (often used to extend the paving season); allows higher RAP content. Watch-outs: don't assume WMA can be placed at any temperature; minimum laydown and rolling temps still apply per the mix design; foamed WMA can be tender at first; and moisture damage potential is evaluated in mix design. Treat it like HMA for burns; it's still hot.
field.title: Warm mix asphalt (WMA) benefits in the field
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: FHWA Warm-Mix Asphalt technologies page

field.text: Cold patch is asphalt mix made with cutback or emulsion binder so it stays workable in a stockpile or bag for months and can be placed in cold or wet weather. Standard stockpile patch is cheap but soft; it shoves and pulls out under traffic. High-performance proprietary cold mixes (UPM-type and polymer cold mixes) cost more but bond better and last longer, some even in wet holes. Use for temporary trench patches, potholes and winter emergencies until hot mix plants reopen. Practices: clean out loose material and water, place in lifts no more than about 2 to 3 inches, overfill about 1/4 to 1/2 inch per inch of depth, compact with a plate, roller or truck tire, and check after traffic.
field.title: Cold patch (stockpile patch) and high-performance cold mix
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Superpave (Superior Performing Asphalt Pavements, from the 1990s SHRP research) is the mix design method most DOTs use. It picks a PG binder for the project climate and traffic, sets aggregate gradation and quality rules, and compacts trial samples in a Superpave gyratory compactor that kneads the mix like rollers and traffic. The mix is designed at a target number of gyrations (Ndesign, higher for heavier traffic) to reach about 4 percent air voids, with minimum VMA (voids in mineral aggregate, room for binder) and limits on VFA and dust-to-binder ratio. DOT mix names often include NMAS and traffic level, e.g. '12.5 mm Superpave, Level C' or 'SP-9.5'. The design sets binder content; plants and field tests check it.
field.title: Superpave mix design in plain words
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: The Marshall method is the older mix design system still used by many cities, counties, airports and parking lot specs. Samples are compacted with a drop hammer (commonly 50 or 75 blows per side, 75 for heavy traffic) and tested for stability (load the briquette breaks at, in lb) and flow (how much it deforms, in 0.01 inch), plus air voids (typically 3 to 5 percent) and VMA. Spec names like 'Marshall surface mix' or old local designations (e.g. 'I-2', 'S-III', 'Type C') come from this system. Results don't translate exactly to Superpave, so don't substitute one for the other without approval. In the field, both are hot mix: the placement and compaction rules are the same.
field.title: Marshall mix design in plain words
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Asphalt pavement is built in layers. Base course: the bottom asphalt layer, coarse aggregate (19 to 37.5 mm NMAS), placed thick; sometimes called 'black base' or asphalt-treated base. Binder course or intermediate course: middle layer, 12.5 to 25 mm NMAS. Surface course or wearing course: top layer, finer (9.5 or 12.5 mm), more binder, smoother and more watertight, sometimes with polymer and high-friction aggregate. Under these sits aggregate base and subgrade. A typical city street: 2 inch surface on 2 to 4 inch binder on 6 to 12 inches of aggregate base. Trench patches often match existing layers or follow a city detail like 3 inches binder plus 1.5 to 2 inches surface.
field.title: Asphalt mix types: base, binder, surface course
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: NMAS (nominal maximum aggregate size) is one sieve size larger than the first sieve that retains more than 10 percent of the aggregate. It names most Superpave mixes: 4.75 mm (thin leveling and sand mixes), 9.5 mm (3/8 inch, thin surface lifts, driveways), 12.5 mm (1/2 inch, most common surface), 19 mm (3/4 inch, binder/intermediate), 25 mm (1 inch, base), 37.5 mm (1-1/2 inch, thick base). Bigger NMAS = coarser, needs thicker lifts. Fine mixes look smooth and tight; coarse mixes look open. When a foreman asks 'what's a 9.5 versus a 12.5', the answer is the maximum stone size and the minimum lift thickness each one needs.
field.title: NMAS: nominal maximum aggregate size and mix names
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Asphalt compacts properly only when the lift is thick enough for the stones to reorient. NCAT research and many DOT specs recommend a compacted lift at least 3 times NMAS for fine-graded mixes and 4 times NMAS for coarse-graded and SMA mixes. Examples: 9.5 mm (3/8 inch) mix: about 1.1 to 1.5 inch minimum; 12.5 mm: 1.5 to 2 inches; 19 mm: 2.25 to 3 inches; 25 mm: 3 to 4 inches. Lifts that are too thin cool fast and don't hit density, with stones crushing under the roller; lifts that are too thick (more than about 3 to 4 inches for surface mixes in trench patches) are hard to compact all the way to the bottom with plate compactors. Check your spec's min and max per lift.
field.title: Lift thickness vs aggregate size (3x to 4x NMAS rule)
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Dense-graded mixes (most HMA) have a smooth gradation that compacts tight. Stone matrix asphalt (SMA) uses gap-graded coarse stone with stone-on-stone contact, rich polymer binder and fibers; very rut-resistant, used on highways, needs aggressive steel rolling and no pneumatic rollers. Open-graded friction course (OGFC) and porous asphalt have big connected voids (about 15 to 20 percent or more) to drain water; used on highways for spray reduction and in parking lots over a stone reservoir for stormwater. Porous pavement must not be sealcoated or covered with sediment, and is rolled lightly with static rollers. Patching porous pavement with dense mix kills its drainage; use matching mix.
field.title: Stone matrix asphalt (SMA), open-graded and porous mixes
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: RAP (reclaimed or recycled asphalt pavement) is millings and broken asphalt crushed and screened for reuse. Asphalt is the most recycled material in the US: NAPA's survey found about 95 percent of reclaimed asphalt was reused in 2021, 94.6 million tons, and the average mix contained nearly 22 percent RAP (up from 15.6 percent in 2009). RAP replaces virgin aggregate and binder, saving cost. Too much RAP stiffens the mix and can cause cracking, so specs limit content (often 15 to 30 percent in surface, more in base) or require softer binder or rejuvenators. Millings are also used as driveway and shoulder material. Keep RAP stockpiles separate from clean aggregate; don't use millings as structural trench backfill unless allowed.
field.title: RAP: recycled asphalt pavement in new mix
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: NAPA annual recycled materials and WMA survey (2021 data) via Pit & Quarry

field.text: Key terms on asphalt lab reports: Gmm (maximum specific gravity, 'Rice') = density of the mix with no air voids. Gmb (bulk specific gravity) = density of a compacted sample or core. Air voids = (1 - Gmb/Gmm) x 100. Lab design target is about 4 percent air voids; in-place after rolling is usually higher, about 6 to 8 percent. Percent compaction or density is usually reported as percent of Gmm (e.g. 93 percent of Gmm = 7 percent voids). VMA (voids in mineral aggregate) is the space between aggregate particles, filled with binder plus air; too low VMA means too little binder and a dry mix. Binder content (Pb) is percent by weight, usually 4.5 to 6.5 percent.
field.title: Asphalt volumetrics: Gmm, air voids, VMA in plain words
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: To check you're putting down the right thickness, compare tons placed to area paved. Spread rate (lb per SY) = tons x 2,000 / SY paved. Divide by 110 to get approximate compacted inches. Example: 18.5 tons placed on 150 ft x 12 ft = 200 SY: 18.5 x 2,000 / 200 = 185 lb per SY, / 110 = about 1.7 inches, short of a 2 inch spec (which needs about 220 lb per SY). Reverse it to plan trucks: 2 inch lift at 220 lb per SY means one 20 ton truck covers about 182 SY, or about 136 ft of 12 ft lane. Loose mat is about 20 to 25 percent thicker than compacted, roughly 1/4 inch per inch, so set the screed accordingly.
field.title: Asphalt yield check: spread rate in the field
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Each hot mix truck carries a weigh ticket: plant, mix type or mix ID (e.g. 12.5 mm SP surface, PG 64-22), net tons, truck number, time loaded and often temperature. Check the mix ID matches what the spec and permit require for that layer (base vs surface mixes get mixed up), and the tons for your yield log. Note load time: mix that sat too long or arrived crusted and cold should be rejected. Measure mix temperature in the truck or behind the screed with a probe or infrared gun; many specs reject loads outside a window (often below about 250 to 275 F or above about 325 to 350 F for HMA). Keep tickets for pay quantities and agency restoration records.
field.title: Asphalt plant ticket: what to check
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Typical HMA discharge temperatures with PG 64-22 are about 285 to 325 F, polymer-modified mixes often 300 to 340 F, and WMA about 225 to 275 F, but the supplier's mix design and DOT spec set the actual range (FHWA example spec: 165 C / 329 F maximum, placed within 10 C of target). Overheating above about 350 F ages and burns the binder (blue smoke, a dull, brittle mat). Mix that arrives too cold can't be compacted to density. Measure with a probe thermometer in the load or behind the screed; infrared guns read only the surface and can read cooler crust. Tarp loads in cool weather and on long hauls; most specs require tarps.
field.title: Asphalt mix temperature ranges at the plant and paver
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: Asphalt carries load by spreading it through layers onto the subgrade: surface and binder asphalt on top, then aggregate base (crushed stone, often 6 to 12 inches, compacted to 95 to 98 percent of Proctor), sometimes subbase, then compacted subgrade. A weak layer anywhere shows up on top as rutting, alligator cracking or settlement. On trench restoration, that means the trench backfill and base under the patch matter more than the asphalt itself; many agencies require flowable fill or compacted aggregate in the top few feet. Full-depth asphalt (asphalt directly on subgrade) is used in some designs. Match or exceed existing pavement thickness when patching.
field.title: Asphalt pavement design layers and base
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: On asphalt streets, cuts are restored with asphalt over a compacted or flowable-fill trench. On concrete streets (rigid pavement), restoration is concrete, usually full panels or to joints, with dowel bars drilled and epoxied into adjacent slabs, matching thickness (often 7 to 10 inches) and high-early mix if traffic must reopen. Composite pavements (asphalt overlay on old concrete) need the concrete replaced first, then the asphalt overlay. Brick and pavers are relaid on sand or mortar setting beds per detail. Asphalt opens to traffic as soon as it cools (often an hour or two); concrete needs strength time unless high-early. The agency's street cut permit specifies which.
field.title: Asphalt vs concrete pavement for utility cuts
field.topic: Asphalt materials: binders, emulsions, mixes, tack, quantities
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Standard asphalt overlay or paving sequence: 1) prep: patch failed areas, adjust manholes and valve boxes, clean; 2) mill (cold plane) to remove old surface to depth and restore cross slope; 3) sweep thoroughly; 4) tack coat at spec rate and let it break; 5) pave with the paver at a steady speed matched to truck delivery, screed set to depth and slope; 6) breakdown rolling right behind the paver while hot; 7) intermediate rolling for density; 8) finish rolling to remove marks while still warm; 9) joints compacted and sealed as required; 10) density tests (cores or nuclear gauge) and smoothness checks; 11) stripe and open after cooling. FHWA stresses steady trucks so the paver never stops and rollers never park on a fresh mat.
field.title: Paving process overview: mill, tack, pave, roll
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: Milling machines grind off old asphalt with a rotating drum of carbide teeth to a set depth (commonly 1.5 to 2 inches for mill-and-overlay, full depth for some reconstruction), conveying millings into trucks. Uses: remove deteriorated surface, keep curb reveal and drainage, match gutter lines, remove ruts, and create a keyed edge at overlay limits ('butt joint' or 'wedge mill'). Fine-tooth drums leave a smoother texture for thin overlays. Milled surfaces must be swept or vacuumed before tack, and get a higher tack rate. Mill-and-fill limits on trench restoration (e.g. mill 1.5 to 2 inches across the full lane) are common city requirements. Locate and mark manholes, valve boxes and shallow utilities before milling; drums destroy castings and lines.
field.title: Milling (cold planing) basics
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: The paver receives mix from trucks into the hopper, slat conveyors move it back to augers that spread it in front of the floating screed, which levels and pre-compacts the mat. Screed thickness and slope are set by the operator or automatic grade and slope controls (string line, ski, sonic or laser references). Keys to a smooth mat: constant head of material in front of the screed (auger about half to two-thirds buried), steady paver speed matched to supply (stop-and-go leaves bumps), trucks backing to the paver without bumping it, and not dumping the hopper wings into cold chunks every load. Heat the screed before starting. A typical overlay paver runs about 20 to 50 ft per minute.
field.title: Asphalt paver: screed, hopper and steady speed
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: Three rolling stages: Breakdown rolling right behind the paver, while the mat is hottest (often roughly 250 to 300 F for HMA), achieves most of the density, usually with a vibratory steel double-drum roller. Intermediate rolling follows to reach target density, with a pneumatic (rubber-tire) roller that kneads and seals the surface or with the vibratory roller in more passes. Finish rolling with a static steel roller removes roller marks and smooths the surface while the mat is still warm enough to work (above about 150 to 175 F). A tender zone, often around 190 to 240 F, makes some mixes shove under the roller; crews pause, then resume when it firms. Establish a rolling pattern on a test strip with a nuclear gauge.
field.title: Breakdown, intermediate and finish rolling
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: Pavement Interactive, Factors Affecting Compaction

field.text: Hot mix must be compacted before it cools to about 175 F (79 C), the commonly cited cessation temperature for dense-graded HMA (FHWA guideline specs say the required density should be achieved before the mat cools to 79 C). Below that the binder is too stiff and more passes just crack aggregate. Cooling time to 175 F depends heavily on lift thickness: Pavement Interactive's MultiCool examples show a 1 inch lift placed at 300 F cools in about 7 to 9 minutes, a 2 inch lift at 250 F in about 12 to 16 minutes, and a 4.2 inch lift in 39 to 54 minutes, with colder base and wind shortening it. Thin lifts in cool weather leave very little time; keep rollers tight to the paver.
field.title: Cessation temperature: when rolling stops working
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: Pavement Interactive, Factors Affecting Compaction

field.text: Steel double-drum vibratory rollers (tandem rollers): the main breakdown roller; vibration greatly increases density per pass. Static steel rollers (two-axle tandem or three-wheel): finish rolling and thin lifts. Pneumatic rubber-tire rollers (typically 7 to 11 tires): intermediate rolling, kneading and sealing the surface; tires must be hot or they pick up mix. Combination rollers: steel drum front, rubber tires rear. Small 'walk-behind' and 1 to 3 ton ride-on rollers and vibratory plates: trench patches, sidewalks, driveways. Keep drums wet with water or release agent, never diesel fuel, which softens the binder (FHWA guidance prohibits fuel oil). Drive wheel closest to the paver on the first pass.
field.title: Asphalt roller types and uses
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: For vibratory steel rollers, density depends on impact spacing: aim for about 10 to 14 impacts per foot (NAPA guidance). Impacts per foot = vibrations per minute / (speed in ft per minute). Example: 3,000 vpm at 250 ft per minute (about 2.8 mph) = 12 impacts per foot. Going faster spaces impacts too far and leaves ripples. Typical breakdown speed is about 2 to 3.5 mph. Use high amplitude for thick lifts and low amplitude for thin lifts (under about 1.5 inches), or roll static on very thin overlays and over bridge decks and near structures. Turn off vibration when stopped or reversing so the drum doesn't dig in. FHWA example spec caps vibratory speed around 4 km/h (2.5 mph).
field.title: Vibratory roller settings: frequency, speed and impacts per foot
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: General rolling practice: overlap passes by about 6 inches, keep the drive drum toward the paver, change direction smoothly and stagger stopping points so you don't leave a transverse bump, never turn or park on hot mat. FHWA example spec: initial rolling parallel to centerline, working from the low side or edges toward the center (or the crown). Longitudinal joints: on the hot side, roll with the drum overhanging the cold lane by about 6 inches, or roll the hot side with the drum about 6 inches off the joint and come back, pinching in; both methods are used. Transverse joints: roll across the joint first. Unsupported edges: keep the drum 2 to 3 inches in on the first pass to avoid pushing the edge.
field.title: Rolling patterns and joint rolling
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: Density is how tightly the mat is compacted, usually reported as percent of Gmm (theoretical max density). Common DOT targets are about 92 to 93 percent of Gmm minimum (about 7 to 8 percent air voids), with pay adjustments above or below; some agencies now push 93 to 94 percent. Research (NCAT and others) suggests each 1 percent increase in density can extend pavement life about 10 percent, because high air voids let water and air in, causing raveling, oxidation and stripping. Small trench patches often aren't tested by core but agencies may require nuclear gauge readings or a rolling pattern. Under-compacted patches look open, porous and wear quickly; over-rolled cold mat shows cracked aggregate.
field.title: In-place density targets for asphalt
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Cores: 4 or 6 inch diameter cylinders drilled from the compacted mat after rolling, tested in the lab for bulk specific gravity (Gmb) and compared with Gmm for percent density. They're accurate and the usual acceptance test; FHWA example spec takes four 6 inch cores per lot at random locations. Core holes must be dried and filled with hot mix or approved patch material and compacted. Nuclear density gauges (and non-nuclear electromagnetic gauges) give instant readings for setting rolling patterns and quality control; they must be correlated to cores for each mix. Gauges need a licensed operator, radiation safety training, and secure storage (nuclear gauges contain Cs-137 and Am-241:Be sources). Use backscatter mode on asphalt.
field.title: Cores vs nuclear gauge for asphalt density
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: Most specs limit asphalt paving by air or surface temperature and lift thickness. FHWA's sample guideline: minimum surface temperature 40 F for compacted lifts 4 inches (100 mm) or more, 47 F for 2 to 4 inches, and 50 F for lifts under 2 inches, measured as an average of three surface readings. Other common rules: air 40 F and rising, no paving on frozen, wet or frosty base, and seasonal dates for surface course (e.g. no surface course after mid-November). Thin lifts lose heat fastest, so cold weather is hardest on surface course and trench patches. Cold-weather tools: WMA, tarped loads, shorter hauls, thicker lifts, more rollers tight to the paver. Temporary cold patch or plates bridge winter until plants reopen.
field.title: Minimum paving temperatures and cold weather limits
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: When paving in cool conditions (roughly below 50 F, or windy): tarp every load and insulate truck beds; schedule the hottest part of the day; increase lift thickness where allowed (thicker lifts hold heat); keep roller passes right behind the paver with an extra breakdown roller; use WMA additives to extend compaction time; avoid leaving the hopper wings to cool (cold chunks); remove cold lumps rather than raking them in; preheat cold joints with an infrared heater; and check mat temperature constantly with an IR gun. Don't place mix on frozen ground or base with frost, standing water or ice; it won't bond, and the base will settle when it thaws. Many agencies require temporary patches over winter and final paving in spring.
field.title: Cold weather paving: practical tips
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: A T-patch (named for its cross-section shape) has the asphalt surface extend beyond the trench walls onto undisturbed, well-compacted base on both sides, typically 6 to 12 inches (some cities 12 to 24 inches), after a second sawcut. Reasons: trench edges get undermined and loosened during excavation; the wider top bridges the softer trench backfill; and the patch's joints sit on solid ground rather than directly over the trench wall where settlement concentrates. Some agencies also require an infrared seal or crack seal along the patch edges, or a full-lane mill and overlay when the cut is in new pavement (moratorium streets). Narrow slivers of old pavement left between patch and curb or joint (often under 2 to 3 ft) are usually required to be removed and included.
field.title: T-patch detail: why the patch steps out past the trench
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: In trench patches, compaction is often by vibratory plate or small walk-behind or 1 to 3 ton ride-on roller, which compacts much less per pass than a big roller. Practices: keep lifts thin (often 2 to 3 inches compacted per lift for plates); compact while the mix is hot, starting along the edges against the old pavement, then the middle; overlap passes; keep the plate moving; use more passes than you think; wet the plate base or roller drum with water or release agent, not diesel. Rake the loose mix about 1/4 inch high per inch of compacted thickness so it finishes flush. Hand-tamp corners and around castings. A depression after a few weeks almost always means the base or trench backfill below wasn't compacted.
field.title: Compaction of trench patch asphalt with plates and small rollers
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Infrared heaters warm existing asphalt to a workable temperature (often about 300 F at the surface, a few inches deep) in several minutes without burning it. The heated asphalt is scarified, rejuvenator and fresh hot mix are added, then it is raked and compacted, making a seamless repair with no cold joint. Uses: potholes, raised or sunken trench patch edges, settled areas around manholes and valve boxes, and sealing patch perimeters by reheating the seam. Some cities require infrared sealing of all utility patch edges. Limits: works on the top 1.5 to 2 inches; can't fix bad base or deep failures; overheating causes blue smoke and brittle binder. Keep propane equipment clear of gas meters and vents.
field.title: Infrared asphalt repair and infrared joint sealing
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: When a trench in traffic can't be closed the same day, steel road plates (commonly 1 inch thick, also 3/4 and 1-1/4 inch; sizes like 5x10, 6x10, 8x20 ft) span the cut. Common practices: extend at least 12 inches past the trench edges onto solid pavement on all sides, pin or shim so they don't rock or shift, and ramp the edges with cold patch (cold mix ramps about 12 to 24 inches wide per many permits) for high-speed traffic; some cities require recessed plates milled flush. Post 'Steel Plate Ahead' signs and check plates and ramps daily, especially after rain or snowplowing. Plates are slippery when wet. A 1 inch 8x20 plate weighs about 6,500 lb; lift with rated hardware.
field.title: Temporary steel plates over trenches in the road
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Joints are where most paving fails first. Longitudinal joint tips: overlap the new lift onto the cold mat by about 1 to 1.5 inches, bump back the excess with a lute (don't broadcast it across the mat), set the screed about 1/4 inch per inch high for roll-down, and roll to pinch the joint. Some specs require joint adhesive, notched wedge joints, or density at the joint. Transverse joints (end of day, start of new run): cut back to full-depth, straight, vertical face, tack it, start paver with screed on shims, and check with a straightedge. FHWA example guide: offset lift joints at least 6 inches from those below; keep top-course longitudinal joints on lane lines, not in wheel paths. Tack every cold vertical face.
field.title: Joint construction in asphalt paving
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: FHWA Hot Mix Asphalt Pavement construction guidelines (state spec review)

field.text: Crack sealing puts specialized hot-pour rubberized sealant (ASTM D6690 types) into working cracks that open and close with temperature, usually after routing a reservoir (e.g. about 3/4 inch wide by 3/4 inch deep) and cleaning with hot compressed air (heat lance). Crack filling puts asphalt emulsion or cheaper material into non-working or wide cracks to keep water out, typically without routing. Typical candidates are cracks about 1/8 to 3/4 inch wide; wider cracks may need patching or mastic. Cracks must be clean and dry; the overband should be thin and narrow (common spec max 2 to 3 inches wide) so it isn't slick or tracked. Sealant kettles run around 380 to 400 F; burns are serious. Seal in cool, dry months when cracks are open.
field.title: Crack sealing vs crack filling
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: A chip seal sprays hot binder or emulsion (CRS-2, CRS-2P, HFRS-2, or PG binder) onto the road, then immediately spreads a single layer of clean, uniform stone chips (often 3/8 inch) and rolls them in with pneumatic rollers to seat them. It seals the surface, adds skid resistance and extends pavement life on low to moderate volume roads. Keys: clean surface, correct binder rate so chips embed about 50 to 70 percent, chips spread within a minute or so of the binder, rolling right away, slow traffic (pilot car) and sweep loose chips after cure. Don't chip seal in cool or wet weather; many specs require 50 to 60 F and rising. Loose chips break windshields.
field.title: Chip seal (seal coat, oil and chip, tar and chip)
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: TxDOT, Asphalt Materials and Uses / PG binder FAQ

field.text: Slurry seal is a cold mix of fine aggregate, emulsion (often CSS-1h or quick-set), water, mineral filler and additives, spread in a thin layer (about 1/8 to 3/8 inch) by a special truck with a spreader box. It seals and refreshes surfaces on residential streets and parking lots, opening in a few hours. Microsurfacing is a stronger polymer-modified version that cures chemically and fast, can be placed in thicker passes and fills ruts, and can carry traffic in about an hour. Both need a structurally sound pavement; they don't fix base failures or settle utility patches. Utility patches made just before a city's slurry program should be flush and fully cured. Cape seal = chip seal topped with slurry.
field.title: Slurry seal and microsurfacing
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Fog seal is a light spray of diluted slow-set emulsion (SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1, CSS-1h) on an existing pavement to seal fine cracks, slow raveling and darken the surface; it can be slick until cured, so sand may be applied. Sealcoat (pavement sealer) is a thicker coating of asphalt emulsion or refined coal tar with fine sand and fillers, squeegeed or sprayed on parking lots and driveways every 2 to 4 years; it protects from oxidation and fuel but adds no strength. Coal tar sealcoats contain high levels of PAHs and are banned in some states and cities; asphalt emulsion sealers are the alternative. New asphalt usually should cure 30 to 90 days before sealcoating.
field.title: Fog seal and parking lot sealcoat
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: TxDOT, Asphalt Materials and Uses / PG binder FAQ

field.text: Throw-and-roll: clear water and debris, fill the pothole with cold patch slightly high, compact with truck tires or a plate; fast and good for emergencies, but often short-lived. Semi-permanent (recommended where time allows): sawcut or mill a square or rectangular area to sound pavement, remove loose material and water, tack the edges and bottom, fill with hot mix (or high-performance cold mix) in lifts, compact with a plate or roller from the edges in. Spray injection patchers blow emulsion and aggregate into the hole. Persistent potholes over utility trenches usually mean bad backfill or water entering the base; fix the cause.
field.title: Pothole repair: throw-and-roll vs semi-permanent
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Raveling is the loss of aggregate from the surface, starting with fines and progressing to larger stone, leaving a rough, pitted surface. Causes: low density (under-compacted, high air voids), mix placed too cold or segregated, low binder content or overheated binder at the plant, aged and oxidized pavement, dirty aggregate, or paving in cold weather. Common at patch edges and in areas compacted with small plates. Prevention: compact to target density while hot, avoid segregation, use correct mix temperature. Fixes: fog seal or slurry for minor raveling; mill and overlay for severe cases. Raveling at a fresh trench patch usually means the mix was cold or the patch wasn't compacted enough.
field.title: Asphalt defect: raveling
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Rutting is permanent depressions in the wheel paths. Mix rutting (narrow ruts with humps on the sides) comes from a mix that is too soft or rich: too much binder, too much fine or rounded sand, binder grade too low for heat and slow heavy traffic, or low air voids. Structural rutting (wide, dish-shaped) comes from weak base or subgrade, including poorly compacted trench backfill. Shoving is a ripple or bulge, usually at intersections, stop bars and steep grades where traffic brakes and accelerates; caused by unstable mix, poor bond (no tack), or tender mix rolled at the wrong temperature. Fixes: mill and replace with a stiffer mix or polymer binder; for structural ruts, repair the base.
field.title: Asphalt defect: rutting and shoving
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Segregation is separation of coarse stone from fines, leaving coarse, open, rocky patches that are porous and ravel early. Patterns tell the cause: end-of-load or truck-to-truck segregation (chevrons or spots at regular intervals) from truck loading or dumping the hopper wings too low; center streak behind the paver gearbox; edge streaks from auger runout; random spots from stockpile handling. Prevention: plant silo and truck loading in multiple drops, keep the hopper from running empty, fold wings sparingly, keep augers running steady with a consistent head, and don't broadcast raked material across the mat. Thermal segregation (cold spots) acts similarly; use material transfer vehicles or remixing.
field.title: Asphalt defect: segregation
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Bleeding or flushing is a shiny, black, sticky film of binder on the surface, usually in the wheel paths, slick when wet and soft in heat. Causes: too much binder in the mix, too much tack coat (especially under thin overlays), low air voids in the mix design, over-rolling with pneumatic rollers on a rich mix, excessive chip seal binder, or sealer applied too heavy. Fixes: blotting with hot sand or fine chips for minor cases; mill and replace for severe cases. On trench patches, bleeding at the edges often traces back to puddled tack or cutback in cold patch. Check tack application rates and keep tack out of puddles.
field.title: Asphalt defect: bleeding and flushing
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Alligator (fatigue) cracking: interconnected cracks forming small blocks like alligator skin in the wheel paths, caused by a pavement too thin or a weak base or subgrade (often wet); needs full-depth repair, not sealing. Transverse (thermal) cracks run across the road at intervals from cold-temperature shrinkage when binder is too stiff for the climate (low-temperature PG grade too high) or the pavement is aged. Block cracking: rectangular blocks from aged, oxidized binder. Reflective cracks mirror joints or cracks in old pavement below an overlay, like concrete joints under asphalt. Edge cracks and settlement cracks outline poorly compacted utility trenches. Seal working cracks; fix base failures.
field.title: Asphalt defect: alligator, thermal and reflective cracking
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Delamination is the top lift separating from the layer below, often coming off in sheets; slippage cracks are crescent-shaped cracks pointing in the direction of braking or turning traffic. Both point to poor bond: missing, too little or dirty tack, dust from milling, paving on wet surfaces, or a thin lift over a polished surface. Roller checking is short, fine transverse cracks in the mat surface during rolling, caused by tender mix, rolling too hot or with the wrong roller, or a mat moving on a slick (overtacked or wet) layer. Prevention: clean surface, correct tack rate, proper temperature and roller type. Severe delamination requires milling out the failed lift.
field.title: Asphalt defect: delamination, slippage and roller checking
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: A trench patch that settles (dips) within weeks to months almost always failed below the asphalt: trench backfill not compacted in thin enough lifts or at the right moisture, large rocks or frozen material in backfill, water draining into the trench through the bedding, or pipe bedding washout. A patch that humps or bulges can come from too much loose mix placed for roll-down, from frost heave in silty backfill, or from shoving of soft mix. Edge cracking and raveling at the patch outline mean poor joint compaction or no tack/seal. Agencies typically hold warranty on patches for 1 to 3 years. Documenting compaction tests, lift thicknesses and photos on the daily report protects the contractor.
field.title: Settled or humped trench patches: diagnosing
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Hot mix arrives around 275 to 325 F, crack sealant kettles and binder tanks run 300 to 400 F, and hot asphalt sticks to skin, holding heat, so burns are deep and fast. Prevention: long sleeves and pants, leather or heat-resistant gloves, safety glasses or face shield around kettles and spray bars, boots that cover the ankle (no low-top shoes), stay clear of truck tailgates and paver hopper when dumping, never put water into a hot kettle (steam eruption), and keep kettle lids closed. First steps for a burn: cool the area with cool running water for at least 20 minutes, don't peel asphalt off the skin (it removes skin), don't use solvent or ice, cover loosely and get medical care; large or facial burns need EMS.
field.title: Asphalt burns: prevention and first steps
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: NIOSH asphalt fume guidance as reported by Safety+Health magazine (NSC)

field.text: Asphalt fumes from hot mix, kettles and sealants can cause eye, nose and throat irritation, cough, headache, dizziness and nausea, and long-term exposure may cause bronchitis and skin problems. NIOSH's recommended exposure limit for asphalt fume is 5 mg per cubic meter as a 15-minute ceiling. Highway-class pavers built since the late 1990s have engineering controls (fume capture and exhaust over the auger and screed) under a NIOSH, industry and union partnership; keep those systems working. WMA reduces fumes noticeably. Other practices: stand upwind, don't overheat mix, minimize time over the hopper and screed, wash before eating, and change contaminated clothing. Burning cutbacks and solvents add more hazard.
field.title: Asphalt fumes and paver exhaust ventilation
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: NIOSH asphalt fume guidance as reported by Safety+Health magazine (NSC)

field.text: Milling machines, sawcutting asphalt and concrete, and jackhammering old pavement generate respirable crystalline silica, especially over concrete and with sandstone or granite aggregate. OSHA Table 1 (1926.1153) covers drivable milling machines when they use water spray with surfactant and the factory dust controls (no respirator required under those controls); small milling attachments and walk-behind mills need water or vacuum dust collection. Sweepers should use water. Milling machines, breakers and plate compactors are also high-noise; hearing protection is needed near them (OSHA's construction limit is 90 dBA for 8 hours, 1926.52; NIOSH recommends 85 dBA). Watch for struck-by risk from conveyors, backing trucks and rollers with blind spots; keep a spotter and back-up alarms working.
field.title: Silica and noise hazards on milling and paving crews
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 Respirable Crystalline Silica in Construction, Table 1

field.text: Paving crews work among backing dump trucks, rollers with poor visibility, pavers and traffic. Key practices: an internal traffic control plan so trucks back in a planned path; spotters with direct eye contact and agreed signals; nobody walks behind a backing truck or between truck and paver; rollers are a leading cause of run-overs and rollovers on slopes and edges, so wear seatbelts with ROPS, keep off unsupported edges and drop-offs, and set the brake when parked. High-visibility apparel (ANSI Class 2 or 3), and lighting for night work. Hot surfaces on screeds and rollers burn. Propane screed heaters: check hoses and connections, and shut off cylinders when not in use.
field.title: Asphalt paving work zone and equipment safety
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Common residential and light commercial sections (check local codes and the owner's spec): driveways 2 to 3 inches compacted surface mix (9.5 or 12.5 mm) on 4 to 8 inches of compacted aggregate base; parking lots 3 to 4 inches total asphalt on 6 to 10 inches base, more in truck lanes. Slope at least about 1 to 2 percent for drainage; flat spots puddle and ravel. Compact the base to spec and proof roll before paving; soft spots should be undercut and replaced. Fresh asphalt stays soft for days in summer heat: avoid parking heavy vehicles, turning tires in place, or using jack stands for a few days. Sealcoat only after the surface cures, often 30 to 90 days.
field.title: Asphalt driveway and parking lot paving quick facts
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Many cities restrict cutting newly paved streets for a period (a street cut moratorium, often 3 to 5 years) except for emergencies, and when cuts are allowed in new pavement they require more: wider T-patch or full-lane mill and overlay, matching mix, infrared joint sealing, pavement degradation fees, and longer warranties. Coordinate utility work before scheduled paving programs. On new pavement, take extra care with sawcut lines (parallel and perpendicular to the road), match the surface texture, and seal joints. Record restoration areas with GPS photos for the permit closeout. Check the agency's right-of-way rules before bidding; restoration costs can exceed the pipe work on short service cuts.
field.title: Asphalt restoration over utility cuts in new pavement (moratorium)
field.topic: Asphalt paving, patching, preservation, defects and safety
field.source: General asphalt industry practice (NAPA/Asphalt Institute/state DOT specs as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: When ordering ready-mix, give: job address and gate/access; pour time and spacing between trucks (e.g. first truck 7:00, then every 30 minutes); total yards and load size; mix by supplier mix number or psi class; slump (e.g. 4 inch); air (e.g. 6 percent); aggregate size (3/4 inch or pea gravel for pump); admixtures (non-chloride accelerator, retarder, fibers, hot water); placement method (chute, pump, buggy, bucket) and whether a pump is needed; and who signs tickets. Ask about short-load charges (often for loads under 4 to 6 yards), standby time charges (often after 5 to 7 minutes per yard), winter or Saturday charges. Confirm the order the afternoon before and call to hold or cancel early for rain.
field.title: Ordering ready-mix concrete: what to tell dispatch
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Order more than the neat calculated volume: about 5 to 10 percent extra for formed flatwork like sidewalk and curb, 10 to 15 percent or more for thrust blocks, encasement and bases poured against dug soil (over-dig and soft spots soak up concrete), and add pump line and hopper waste (often about 0.5 yard per pump setup). Running short mid-pour means a cold joint or a short load surcharge; ordering the last truck 'to finish' with a measured remaining volume is the standard move. Example: thrust blocks totaling 4.2 CY neat x 1.15 = 4.8, order 5 yards. Leftover concrete must go to a washout or approved spot, never in storm drains or ditches. Over-ordering a full yard is cheaper than a cold joint.
field.title: Concrete overage: how much extra to order
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Check every ticket before the truck discharges: supplier and plant; ticket number; date and time batched (the clock for ASTM C94's 90 minute / 300 revolution limit starts here; many DOTs allow 60 to 90 minutes, less in hot weather); truck number; job name/address; mix number or description (psi, cement type, aggregate, air); yards on this load and cumulative yards ordered/delivered; admixtures and doses; batch weights of cement, fly ash/slag, sand, stone and water; water withheld or 'water allowed on site' (gallons that can still be added without exceeding the design w/c); and signature lines for water added, time arrived, time started and finished discharge. If the mix number doesn't match the approved submittal, stop and call. Keep tickets with the daily report; inspectors and PMs need them.
field.title: Reading a ready-mix delivery ticket
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: ASTM C94 allows water to be added on arrival when slump is below spec, as long as the design maximum w/c and the max slump are not exceeded, followed by at least 30 revolutions at mixing speed, and generally only once before discharge begins. The ticket shows how many gallons can be added ('water allowed' or 'withheld'). Rules of thumb: add only what the ticket allows, never add water to a partially discharged load to 'loosen up the end', record gallons added and who authorized it on the ticket, and tell the tester (cylinders should be made after any water addition). Many specs require the inspector's approval. Unauthorized water is the most common reason for low cylinder breaks.
field.title: Adding water to ready-mix on site: the rules
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Slump cone: 12 inches tall, 8 inch base, 4 inch top; 5/8 inch bullet-nose rod. Sample per ASTM C172 and start within 5 minutes. Dampen cone and base, stand on the foot tabs. Fill in 3 layers of equal volume (first layer about 2-5/8 inch high, second to about 6-1/8 inch). Rod each layer 25 times spread evenly, penetrating about 1 inch into the layer below; do not tap the cone. Strike off the top, clean around the base, then lift straight up in 5 seconds plus or minus 2 with no twisting. Measure from the top of the cone to the displaced original center of the top, to the nearest 1/4 inch. Whole test from start of filling to lifting within 2-1/2 minutes. If it shears off sideways, retest.
field.title: Slump test procedure (ASTM C143) step by step
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ASTM C143 summary, SI Certs ACI field technician study page

field.text: Slump is a quick check of consistency and batch-to-batch uniformity, not strength. Typical ranges: 1 to 3 inch for slipform curb and paving; 3 to 5 inch for hand-placed curb, sidewalk, slabs, manhole collars; 4 to 6 inch for thrust blocks, encasement and footings; 5 to 7 inch for pumping; 8 inch plus or flowing only with a superplasticizer. Specs usually allow a tolerance (often plus or minus 1 inch, or 1.5 inches for higher slumps). Slump under about 1/2 inch or over about 9 inches means the test isn't meaningful. A load that comes in 2 inches higher than the previous one usually has extra water. Sudden slump loss in the truck can mean hot weather or an over-time load.
field.title: What slump numbers mean in the field
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ASTM C143 summary, SI Certs ACI field technician study page

field.text: Air content of fresh concrete is measured with a Type B pressure meter (ASTM C231) for normal-weight concrete: fill the bowl in 3 layers, rod 25 times each and tap the sides 10 to 15 times, strike off, clamp the lid, fill with water through petcocks, pump to initial pressure, release and read percent air. For lightweight or porous aggregate use the volumetric 'roll-a-meter' (ASTM C173). Typical spec for exterior concrete is about 5 to 7 percent, plus or minus 1.5. Air is checked on the first truck and at the cylinder sampling frequency. Low air risks freeze-thaw scaling; high air costs strength (about 5 percent per 1 percent of air). Pumping and over-vibration can reduce air.
field.title: Air content testing: pressure meter and volumetric
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: A proper sample is a composite from the middle of the load: take two or more portions at regular intervals during discharge from a truck mixer, not the first or last part, combine and remix in a wheelbarrow, and finish the composite within 15 minutes. Start slump, air and temperature within 5 minutes and molding cylinders within 15 minutes of getting the sample. Samples from the end of the chute after the first half yard or so are typical; on pumped work, specs may require sampling at the point of placement (end of the hose) because pumping changes slump and air. Shield the sample from sun, wind and rain. A sloppy sample taken from the first gush of a truck gives misleading results.
field.title: Sampling fresh concrete correctly (ASTM C172)
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Cylinders are 4x8 inch or 6x12 inch plastic molds (diameter at least 3 times max aggregate size). 4x8: fill in 2 layers, rod each 25 times with a 3/8 inch rod. 6x12: 3 layers, 25 strokes each with a 5/8 inch rod. Penetrate about 1 inch into the layer below, tap the mold 10 to 15 times after each layer to close rod holes, strike off level, cap with a lid. Mark each with ID, date, time. Mold on a level, firm spot where they won't be disturbed. A set usually means 2 or 3 cylinders per break age plus spares (e.g. one at 7 days, two or three at 28, one hold). Record slump, air, concrete and air temperature, truck and ticket number on the sample sheet.
field.title: Making concrete test cylinders (ASTM C31)
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ASTM C31 summary, SI Certs ACI field technician study page

field.text: Right after molding, cylinders must be stored for up to 48 hours at 60 to 80 F (68 to 78 F for mixes of 6,000 psi or more) in a moisture-tight setting, shielded from sun and radiant heat, with a min/max thermometer and the readings recorded. Use an insulated cure box with a heater or cooler as needed. Then transport to the lab within that window, cushioned and wrapped so they don't jar or dry out, within 4 hours of travel time. In the lab they're demolded and kept moist at 73.5 F plus or minus 3.5. Cylinders left on a truck dash, in a hot pickup bed, or frozen overnight will break low and can cause a costly and unnecessary investigation.
field.title: Initial curing of cylinders: the first 48 hours
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ASTM C31 summary, SI Certs ACI field technician study page

field.text: Lab break tests (ASTM C39) crush cylinders in a compression machine and divide the max load by the area for psi. A strength 'test' is the average of 2 6x12 or 3 4x8 cylinders from the same sample at the specified age, normally 28 days (sometimes 56 days for fly ash or slag mixes). 7-day breaks are an early warning only, typically about 65 to 75 percent of design, and can't be used to accept or reject concrete. Field-cured cylinders, kept beside the pour, show when the actual structure is strong enough to strip forms, backfill or load, but are not acceptance tests. Break reports also list fracture type; odd fracture patterns suggest bad capping or end prep.
field.title: Cylinder break tests: 7-day and 28-day
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: NRMCA Concrete in Practice CIP 9, Low Concrete Cylinder Strength

field.text: Under ACI 318 as summarized by NRMCA, concrete strength is acceptable when both: (1) the average of any 3 consecutive strength tests equals or exceeds specified strength f'c, and (2) no single test falls more than 500 psi below f'c (for f'c of 5,000 psi or less; above that, no test below 0.90 f'c). Example for 4,000 psi: tests of 4,250, 3,800, 4,100 average 4,050, all above 3,500, so acceptable. A single 3,400 test triggers an investigation. Statistically, about 1 test in 100 fails from normal variation. If testing procedures were bad, investigate cylinders before coring. If procedures check out, cores are taken (ACI accepts when 3 cores average at least 85 percent of f'c and none is under 75 percent).
field.title: Concrete strength acceptance: 3-test average and 500 psi rule
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: NRMCA Concrete in Practice CIP 9, Low Concrete Cylinder Strength

field.text: NRMCA lists the usual culprits for low strength results: improper cylinder handling, curing and testing (the main cause); cylinders initially cured above 80 F or allowed to freeze; left in the field extra days; damaged in transport; delayed stripping; bad capping; careless breaking. Concrete causes: extra water added on site from placement delays or slump requests, high air content, production errors. What crews can do: keep cylinders in a temperature-controlled cure box, record water added, make cylinders after any water addition, keep the sample representative, and get them to the lab on time. Use ACI Field Testing Technician Grade I certified people for acceptance testing.
field.title: Low cylinder breaks: common causes
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: NRMCA Concrete in Practice CIP 9, Low Concrete Cylinder Strength

field.text: Typical spec frequency (check yours): one set of strength cylinders per 50 to 150 cubic yards per mix per day, and at least one set per day for each class of concrete placed; slump, air and temperature with each set and whenever a load looks different. Many DOTs require tests on the first load of the day. Small quantities (thrust blocks under a few yards) are sometimes waived by the engineer with a certification from the supplier. Testing is usually by the owner's or contractor's QA lab; the crew's job is to call the lab ahead of time, give them safe access, provide a level spot for cylinders, and not let trucks discharge before the tester is ready if tests are required on that load.
field.title: Concrete testing frequency on utility jobs
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Place concrete as close to its final spot as possible; don't move it sideways long distances with vibrators or rakes, which separates paste from stone. Common practice limits free fall to about 3 to 5 ft unless the mix is designed for it or you use a drop chute or tremie, especially in narrow forms with rebar. Place in even lifts (often 12 to 18 inches in walls) and work each into the previous one before it sets to avoid cold joints. Truck chutes reach about 12 to 20 ft; beyond that use a pump, conveyor, buggy or crane bucket. Don't place on standing water, mud, frost or snow. Dampen dry subgrade (no puddles) so it doesn't pull water from the concrete.
field.title: Placing concrete: chutes, pumps, buckets and drop height
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Boom pumps (truck-mounted, 28 to 60+ meters) reach over obstacles and are fast; line pumps (trailer-mounted, hose laid on the ground) handle smaller volumes like sidewalk, footings and thrust blocks in tight spots. Line pumps usually need 3/8 inch pea gravel or pump mix with at least 5 inch slump; boom pumps handle 3/4 inch stone with a decent paste content. Before pumping, the line is primed with grout or slurry, which goes to waste, not into the structure. Safety: keep clear of the boom and outriggers, never stand at the hose end when starting or clearing a blockage (hose whip), observe power line clearance (concrete pumping industry guidance keeps the boom at least 20 ft from lines up to 350 kV, more for higher voltages), set outriggers on cribbing on firm ground away from trench edges.
field.title: Concrete pump basics: boom vs line pump
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Consolidation removes entrapped air pockets (not the tiny entrained air) and makes concrete fill around rebar and against forms. Internal (stick/spud) vibrator tips are typically 1 to 2.5 inch for utility work. Technique: insert vertically and quickly, let it sink by its own weight into the layer below by about 6 inches, hold for about 5 to 15 seconds until large bubbles stop rising and the surface shows a sheen, then pull out slowly (about 3 inches per second). Space insertions about 1.5 times the radius of action so circles overlap (commonly every 12 to 18 inches). Don't drag the vibrator, don't use it to move concrete, don't touch rebar or forms for long. Under-vibration causes honeycomb; over-vibration with wet mixes causes segregation.
field.title: Vibrating concrete: consolidation technique
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Order of operations for sidewalk, slabs and aprons: 1) place and spread with a come-along (not a garden rake); 2) strike off/screed with a straightedge or vibratory screed; 3) bull float or darby right away to embed stone and level; 4) wait for bleed water to disappear (never work it in); 5) edge with an edger along forms; 6) groove control joints with a jointer or plan to saw; 7) float with a magnesium or wood float (hand or power) to open the surface; 8) trowel only for interior surfaces, and steel trowel does not suit air-entrained exterior work; 9) broom finish for traction on exterior walks, ramps and aprons, pulled perpendicular to traffic; 10) cure immediately. Re-run the edger and jointer after brooming if lines got filled.
field.title: Flatwork finishing sequence: screed to broom
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: Portland Cement Association (PCA) concrete technology pages, summarized

field.text: Control joints make the inevitable shrinkage crack happen in a straight line. NRMCA guidance: space joints 24 to 36 times the slab thickness (about 8 to 12 ft for a 4 inch slab), never more than about 15 ft; keep panels square-ish (length no more than 1.5 times width); avoid L-shaped panels and line joints up with corners of openings and structures. Depth at least 1/4 of the slab thickness and never less than 1 inch (1 inch for a 4 inch walk, 1.5 inch for 6 inch). Sidewalks are commonly jointed at intervals equal to the walk width (e.g. every 5 ft on a 5 ft walk) per city detail. Joints can be tooled while plastic, formed with inserts, or sawed.
field.title: Control joints (contraction joints): spacing and depth
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: NRMCA Concrete in Practice CIP 6, Joints in Concrete Slabs on Grade

field.text: Sawcut as soon as the concrete can take the saw without the edges raveling or the blade dislodging stone, and before random cracks form. Early-entry dry-cut saws (Soff-Cut type) are typically used about 1 to 4 hours after finishing at a minimum 1 inch depth. Conventional wet saws are usually run about 4 to 12 hours after placing, sooner in hot, windy weather and later in cold weather or with slag, fly ash or retarders. Test with a short cut: if edges ravel badly, wait; if it cuts clean, go. Cutting too late (next day after a cold night) often finds cracks already formed. Use water or vacuum dust control per OSHA silica Table 1.
field.title: Sawcut timing for control joints
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: NRMCA Concrete in Practice CIP 6, Joints in Concrete Slabs on Grade

field.text: Construction joints are where one pour stops and the next starts (end of day, running short). Put them where a control joint would go; in slabs and pavement use smooth dowels or keyways per detail. Expansion or isolation joints let concrete move independently of something else: around manhole frames, valve boxes, poles, buildings, at curb returns, where sidewalk meets driveway or curb, and at fixed structures. They use full-depth premolded filler (asphalt-impregnated fiber board or foam, commonly 1/2 inch), set flush or just below the surface and often sealed. Many cities require expansion joints at intervals (e.g. every 40 to 100 ft) in curb and walk; follow the standard detail.
field.title: Construction joints, expansion joints and isolation joints
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: NRMCA Concrete in Practice CIP 6, Joints in Concrete Slabs on Grade

field.text: Curing keeps moisture in and temperature reasonable so cement keeps hydrating. Methods: wet curing (soaker hoses, sprinkling, ponding, wet burlap or curing blankets kept wet); covering with plastic sheeting (white in sun, black in cool weather, lapped and weighted, though it can leave mottled color); liquid membrane curing compound (ASTM C309, white-pigmented for sun, sprayed uniformly right after finishing when the sheen is gone, typically about 200 sq ft per gallon, check the label); leaving forms in place; and insulating blankets in cold weather. Curing compound may need to be removed before coatings or sealants. Uncured exterior flatwork can lose up to half its surface strength, scale and crack.
field.title: Curing concrete: methods
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Common guidance from ACI 308 practice and DOT specs: keep concrete moist and above about 50 F for at least 7 days for normal Type I/II concrete, or until it reaches about 70 percent of specified strength; about 3 days for high-early concrete; longer (10 to 14 days) for mixes with high fly ash or slag or in cool weather. Many DOT specs say 7 days for structures and pavement, or until cylinders reach a stated strength. Practical field rule: don't let fresh flatwork dry out in the first 24 hours under any conditions. In cold weather, curing and freeze protection run together; you can't wet cure below freezing, so use blankets plus curing compound or plastic.
field.title: How long to cure concrete
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: ACI 305 hot-weather risk is driven by concrete temperature, air temperature, humidity and wind together, not just heat. Evaporation rates above about 0.2 lb per sq ft per hour (from the ACI nomograph or an app/weather-station calculator) make plastic shrinkage cracks likely; low-bleed mixes crack at lower rates. Countermeasures: windbreaks and sunshades, fog misting above the surface (not puddling), evaporation retarder sprayed after screeding, place at night or early morning, cool the concrete (chilled water, ice), retarder or mid-range water reducer from the plant, dampen subgrade and forms, more finishers, and cure immediately. Plastic shrinkage cracks look like short parallel cracks 1 to 3 ft long appearing within hours.
field.title: Hot weather concreting: evaporation and plastic cracking
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: ACI 306 applies when the air is at or below 40 F during the protection period. Minimum concrete temperature as placed and maintained: 55 F for sections under 12 inches thick (slabs, collars, walls), 50 F for 12 to 36 inches (thrust blocks, bases). Minimum temperature as mixed: 60 F (under 12 inch) or 55 F (12 to 36 inch) when air is above 30 F; 65 F or 60 F at 0 to 30 F air; 70 F or 65 F below 0 F. Don't overheat; about 20 F above minimum is a practical max. Concrete must reach about 500 psi before it can survive one freeze, which most good mixes reach in about 48 hours at 50 F. Protection period at the minimum temperature: 2 days for unloaded, unexposed work and 3 days if exposed (1 and 2 days with accelerated, high-early set).
field.title: Cold weather concreting: ACI 306 temperatures
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ACI 306 cold weather tables as summarized by Cemstone Cold Weather Concrete guide

field.text: Never place concrete on frozen subgrade, frost, snow or ice, or against frozen soil (critical for thrust blocks and manhole bases): when the frost thaws the ground settles and the block loses bearing, and frozen ground also pulls heat from the concrete. Thaw the subgrade with ground heaters or insulated blankets, or remove frozen soil; the subgrade should be no more than about 20 F colder than the concrete. Protection: insulated curing blankets (overlap the edges and corners, which freeze first), heated enclosures (use indirect-fired heaters, since direct-fired heaters' exhaust CO2 causes surface dusting, and CO is a hazard in enclosures and trenches), hot water and heated aggregate at the plant, accelerators or Type III. Remove protection gradually: no more than a 50 F drop in 24 hours for thin sections, 40 F for 12 to 36 inch sections.
field.title: Cold weather: never pour on frozen ground; blankets and heat
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ACI 306 cold weather tables as summarized by Cemstone Cold Weather Concrete guide

field.text: US rebar size number = diameter in eighths of an inch for #3 through #8: #3 = 3/8 inch (0.375), 0.376 lb per ft; #4 = 1/2 inch, 0.668 lb per ft; #5 = 5/8 inch, 1.043 lb per ft; #6 = 3/4 inch, 1.502 lb per ft; #7 = 7/8 inch, 2.044 lb per ft; #8 = 1 inch, 2.670 lb per ft. Bigger bars (#9 to #18) are based on old square-bar areas (#11 is 1.41 inch). Standard stock lengths are 20, 40 and 60 ft. Example: 30 #4 bars at 10 ft = 300 ft x 0.668 = 200 lb. Metric soft-conversion marks: #4 = 13, #5 = 16, #6 = 19. Weights per CRSI standard tables.
field.title: Rebar sizes, diameters and weights
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ACI 318 cover and splice provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide; CRSI bar data

field.text: Most rebar is ASTM A615 Grade 60 (60,000 psi minimum yield). Grade 40 shows up in light incidental work; Grades 75, 80 and 100 where designers need fewer bars. ASTM A706 is low-alloy weldable rebar, required where bars are welded or for seismic detailing; don't weld A615 bars without engineer approval. Rolled-on bar markings in order: mill letter or symbol, size number (e.g. 5 or metric 16), type letter (S = A615 carbon steel, W = A706, SW = meets both, R = A996 rail steel, A = A996 axle steel), then grade by one continuous line or number (one line or '60' = Grade 60; two lines or '80' = Grade 80; no mark = Grade 40). Epoxy-coated (green or purple) and galvanized bars are for corrosion; patch coating damage per spec.
field.title: Rebar grades and bar markings
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ACI 318 cover and splice provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide; CRSI bar data

field.text: Cover is the clear distance from the bar to the concrete surface; it protects steel from rust and fire. ACI 318 baseline minimums for cast-in-place: 3 inches when cast against and permanently exposed to earth (footings, thrust blocks, bases poured against soil); 2 inches for formed surfaces exposed to weather or earth for #6 and larger, 1-1/2 inches for #5 and smaller; 3/4 inch for interior surfaces not exposed. Precast and DOT specs differ; bridge decks need more. Hold cover with chairs, bolsters or concrete dobies (not bricks, rocks or wood). Plastic-tipped chairs where surface is exposed. Inspectors measure cover before the pour; low cover is the main cause of rust spalling later.
field.title: Concrete cover over rebar (ACI 318 minimums)
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ACI 318 cover and splice provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide; CRSI bar data

field.text: Lap splices transfer force from one bar to another by overlap. Plans and details govern; ACI uses Class B splices (1.3 times the development length) by default. Field rule of thumb often seen on details for Grade 60 bar in normal concrete is about 40 to 48 bar diameters, e.g. #4 lap about 20 to 24 inches, #5 about 25 to 30 inches, #6 about 30 to 36 inches; top bars and epoxy bars need more. Stagger laps where possible. Tie bars at intersections (every intersection or per pattern) with tie wire so the mat doesn't shift. Minimum clear spacing between bars is the largest of 1 bar diameter, 1 inch, or 1.33 times max aggregate size. Clean bars of mud, oil and loose scale; tight mill scale and light rust are fine.
field.title: Rebar lap splices and placement basics
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
