field.source: ACI 318 cover and splice provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide; CRSI bar data

field.text: Welded wire reinforcement (WWR, mesh) is designated like 6x6-W1.4xW1.4 (old name 6x6-10/10): 6 inch spacing both ways, wire area 0.014 sq in. Heavier 6x6-W2.9xW2.9 (old 6/6) is common in driveways. Mesh does not prevent cracking; it holds cracks tight, and only if it is in the slab, usually in the upper half or middle third. Mesh lying on the subgrade does nothing; 'hooking' mesh up during the pour rarely works, so set it on chairs or use sheets instead of rolls. Lap sheets at least one wire spacing plus 2 inches per common practice. Many city sidewalk details use no mesh, just joints; others require it at driveways. Fibers may replace mesh with approval.
field.title: Welded wire mesh in slabs
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Forms must hold the concrete's liquid pressure without bulging, be tight enough to not leak paste, and be set to line and grade. Flatwork: 2x4 or 2x6 lumber or steel forms staked about every 3 to 4 ft and at joints, top set to grade with a string line, with flexible hardboard or steel for radii. Curb: steel curb forms or slipform machine. Manhole bases and collars: steel ring forms or plywood. Apply form release oil before rebar goes in. Walls and deep blocks: pressure rises with pour rate and slump (SCC and fast pours act like full liquid head, about 150 lb per sq ft per ft of depth), so use proper ties and bracing. Strip side forms on flatwork usually the next day; structural forms per spec or field-cured cylinder strength.
field.title: Formwork basics for curb, walks, collars and bases
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Precast (manholes, inlets, vaults, boxes, pipe, thrust-block alternatives) is made in a plant with controlled curing and higher strength (often 4,000 to 6,000 psi), arrives ready to set, needs no cure time on site and isn't weather-dependent, but needs crane capacity, exact base prep and lead time, and joints that must be sealed. Cast-in-place (CIP) fits odd shapes, field changes, tie-ins to existing structures, doghouse manholes over live pipes, and thrust blocks, but needs forms, testing, cure time and weather protection. Common hybrid: precast barrel sections on a cast-in-place base, or a precast manhole with a poured invert channel and bench. Check the spec for which is allowed.
field.title: Precast vs cast-in-place concrete for utility structures
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Non-shrink grout (ASTM C1107, cement-based) is a bagged mix that doesn't shrink as it cures, used for setting manhole frames and grade rings, pipe penetrations in structures, under base plates and equipment, anchor bolts, and filling lift holes. Mix with the exact water on the bag (measure it, don't eyeball), mix 3 to 5 minutes with a drill paddle, and place within its working time (often 15 to 30 minutes). Consistency can be plastic, flowable or fluid by water amount within the label range. Pre-soak the concrete surface to saturated surface-dry (no standing water). Keep it moist-cured and don't place it below the minimum temperature on the bag (often 40 to 45 F). Epoxy grouts are for high-strength, chemical or vibration loads.
field.title: Non-shrink grout: uses and mixing
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Masonry mortar types by minimum 28-day compressive strength (ASTM C270 property spec): Type M = 2,500 psi (proportions about 1 part portland : 1/4 lime : 3 sand), strongest, for below-grade masonry, foundations, manholes and structures in contact with soil; Type S = 1,800 psi (1 : 1/2 : 4-1/2), high bond, for below-grade and structural walls, common for brick manholes and setting grade rings; Type N = 750 psi (1 : 1 : 6), general above-grade use; Type O = 350 psi (1 : 2 : 9), interior non-load. Memory trick: every other letter of 'MaSoN wOrk'. Stronger is not always better for above-grade brick. Grout for filling block cells is a different material (ASTM C476).
field.title: Mortar types M, S, N, O (ASTM C270)
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: ASTM C270 mortar property and proportion tables as published by Engineering ToolBox

field.text: Older sewer systems have brick or block manholes laid in mortar; repairs and some new adjustments still use it. Use Type S or Type M mortar (or the manufacturer's sewer-rated mortar) for anything below grade or in contact with sewage. Wet brick before laying in hot weather so it doesn't suck water from the mortar. Full mortar joints, then parge (plaster) the outside with 1/2 inch of mortar to seal against infiltration. Hydraulic cement (fast-setting plug cement) stops active leaks in a few minutes; push it into the leak and hold. Corroded brick manholes often get a cementitious or epoxy liner. Don't use Type N or O mortar in manholes.
field.title: Brick and block manholes, and mortar work in sewers
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Shotcrete is concrete or mortar sprayed at high velocity onto a surface (ACI 506). Wet-mix: ready-mixed concrete is pumped and air added at the nozzle; higher production, less dust and rebound. Dry-mix (gunite): dry materials are blown through the hose and water added at the nozzle by the nozzleman; good for small repair jobs and stop-and-start work, more dust and rebound (often 15 to 30 percent on walls, more overhead). Uses: manhole and culvert rehab, shoring walls, slope protection, tunnel and vault repairs. Rebound and overspray are waste, not reusable. Certified nozzlemen (ACI) are often required. Silica dust and wet cement exposure are high; respirators, eye protection and full skin cover.
field.title: Shotcrete basics: wet-mix vs dry-mix
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Plastic shrinkage cracks: short, parallel, appear within hours on hot, windy days; caused by fast surface drying. Drying shrinkage cracks: run across slabs between joints spaced too far apart or cut too late. Settlement cracks: over poorly compacted trench backfill or around manholes and structures; these step or tilt. Crazing: fine map-like surface lines from finishing with bleed water or poor curing; cosmetic. Map cracking with gel staining: alkali-silica reaction. Corner cracks: at re-entrant corners of slabs and around manhole frames without isolation joints. Rust stains along cracks: corroding rebar with low cover. Hairline cracks under about 1/32 inch are usually not structural; growing, offset or wide cracks need an engineer's look.
field.title: Common concrete cracks and their causes
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Scaling is flaking of the top surface, usually 1/8 to 3/8 inch deep, almost always on exterior flatwork exposed to freeze-thaw and deicing salt. Causes: no or low air entrainment, finishing with bleed water, extra water, poor curing, salting in the first winter before the concrete has cured and dried (avoid deicers the first winter; use sand), and ammonium-based deicers. Spalling is deeper chunks breaking off, often from rusting rebar with low cover, joint edges loaded by traffic, or freezing in saturated concrete. Popouts are small cone-shaped pits from expansive aggregate particles near the surface. A penetrating sealer (silane or siloxane) in the fall helps new flatwork resist salt.
field.title: Scaling, spalling and popouts
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Honeycomb is a rough, stony area where mortar didn't fill between coarse aggregate, usually at form faces, around rebar and at the bottom of walls or blocks. Causes: under-vibration, stiff mix, rebar too congested for the aggregate size, leaky forms losing paste, dropping concrete too far. Bug holes are small surface pits from trapped air, mostly cosmetic. A cold joint forms when fresh concrete is placed against concrete that has already set, so the two don't knit; causes are delayed trucks, breakdowns, slow placement in hot weather. Prevent with steady truck spacing, retarders, vibrating new concrete into the previous lift. Honeycomb that exposes rebar or leaks must be chipped back to sound concrete and repaired.
field.title: Honeycomb, voids and cold joints
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: For spalls, honeycomb and damaged edges: sawcut the perimeter at least 1/2 inch deep (no feathered edges), chip out to sound concrete and at least 3/4 inch behind any exposed rebar, clean the rebar of rust, remove dust and loose material, pre-wet to saturated surface-dry or apply bonding agent or scrub coat per the product. Use a repair mortar suited to the depth (polymer-modified for thin repairs, concrete with pea gravel for deep ones), compact it well and cure it like new concrete. Vertical and overhead repairs need non-sag mortars. For cracks: epoxy injection for structural bonding of dry cracks, polyurethane injection for leaking cracks in manholes and vaults, and routing and sealing for moving cracks.
field.title: Concrete repair basics: patching and bonding
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Sawcut concrete pavement, curb and sidewalk in straight lines at the removal limits before breaking, usually full depth, to protect the remaining concrete and give a clean edge. Most city details require removal to the nearest joint or a minimum panel size rather than leaving small slivers; check the permit. Walk-behind saws with diamond blades cut about 4 to 6 inches deep per 14 inch blade, deeper with 20 to 36 inch blades. Break out with a hoe ram, skid-steer breaker or jackhammer, keeping away from the sawcut edge. Drill and epoxy dowels or tie bars into the existing concrete per detail when replacing pavement. Locate utilities before cutting; saws cut gas service lines and electric conduit as easily as concrete.
field.title: Concrete removal and sawcutting for utility work
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Wet cement forms calcium hydroxide with a pH of about 12 to 13, which causes alkaline chemical burns that often don't hurt for hours while damage continues; kneeling in wet concrete or concrete inside boots is the classic way crews get full-thickness burns. Prevention: alkali-resistant gloves (butyl or nitrile), long sleeves taped over gloves, pants taped over or tucked into waterproof boots, waterproof knee pads, eye protection, no rings or watches. If concrete gets in boots or soaks clothing, stop, remove it, and wash the skin with clean running water for at least 20 minutes. Don't use lanolin or petroleum jelly on exposed skin. Get medical care for any burn and bring the SDS. Wet cement also contains hexavalent chromium, which causes allergic dermatitis.
field.title: Wet concrete skin burns: prevention on the pour
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: National Precast Concrete Association, cement burns

field.text: Typical steps for replacing curb and gutter after a utility cut: sawcut at joints or at least the minimum replacement length per city detail (often a 5 to 10 ft minimum section or to the next joint); remove and dispose; compact base to spec (often 4 to 6 inches of aggregate base); set steel forms or slipform to string line, matching flow line grade so water doesn't pond; drill and epoxy dowels into existing curb ends if required; place 3,500 to 4,000 psi air-entrained concrete at low slump (about 2 to 4 inch); finish, edge and tool joints to match spacing (often 10 ft) with expansion joints at returns and structures; broom or light finish; cure with compound; protect from traffic until the specified strength or days.
field.title: Concrete curb and gutter replacement: field steps
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: For sidewalk and apron restoration: remove to the nearest joints (no small slivers), compact subgrade and 4 inches or so of aggregate base, set forms to line and grade with cross slope toward the street (commonly 1 to 2 percent; ADA limits running slope and cross slope on public walks to about 2 percent cross slope max), place 3,500 to 4,000 psi air-entrained concrete, typically 4 inches thick for walks and 6 to 8 inches at driveways and aprons (check detail), with expansion joints at curbs, buildings and driveways and control joints at walk-width spacing. Detectable warning panels at curb ramps per ADA/PROWAG. Broom finish, cure, barricade, and keep traffic off driveways about 7 days or per spec.
field.title: Sidewalk and driveway apron replacement: field steps
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Cast-in-place manhole bases: excavate to firm undisturbed soil or stabilize with stone, place a stone leveling course, form or use a precast base ring, and pour 3,000 to 4,000 psi concrete to the detail thickness (often 8 to 12 inches) with rebar if required. Set the first barrel section into the fresh base or on a keyway. Inverts (the flow channel) and benches are formed with concrete or grout after pipes are set: shape the channel to the full pipe diameter for at least half its depth (often up to the crown or springline per detail), slope the bench toward the channel (commonly about 1 inch per ft), and steel-trowel it smooth so solids don't hang up. Keep sewage out of fresh concrete until it has set.
field.title: Manhole bases and benches poured in place
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: When raising or lowering manhole frames in pavement, grade rings (precast concrete or HDPE/rubber) are set on the cone, sealed with mortar, butyl or a manufacturer's adhesive, and the frame set to finished grade and slope. The collar around the frame (often 12 to 18 inches wide, square or round per detail, full depth of pavement) is typically 3,500 to 4,500 psi air-entrained or high-early concrete, sometimes with rebar. Common failure points: loose rings, non-air-entrained concrete scaling, collars too thin, and pavement settling around a rigid collar. Use high-early mix when traffic must reopen quickly, and keep traffic off until opening strength. Some agencies require the collar finished slightly below the asphalt surface.
field.title: Manhole collars and frame adjustment concrete
field.topic: Concrete practice: ordering, testing, placing, curing, repair
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: ASTM C150 / AASHTO M 85 portland cement types: Type I = general purpose (sidewalk, curb, thrust blocks). Type II = moderate sulfate resistance, also moderate heat (II(MH)); most bags and silos in the US are dual-rated Type I/II. Type III = high early strength, ground finer, gains strength in days instead of weeks; used for fast turnaround, cold weather, precast. Type IV = low heat of hydration for massive pours like dams; rarely stocked. Type V = high sulfate resistance for soils or groundwater with high sulfate and some sewer and wastewater exposures. Your spec or the geotech report says which type; the ready-mix ticket or mix submittal shows what you actually got. Check the spec before substituting.
field.title: Portland cement types I, II, III, IV, V explained
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: Portland Cement Association (PCA) concrete technology pages, summarized

field.text: Type IL is portland-limestone cement (ASTM C595 / AASHTO M 240): regular portland clinker interground with extra limestone, up to 15 percent by weight (SCDOT spec says less than 15 percent). It cuts the carbon footprint by roughly 10 percent and has largely replaced Type I/II at many US plants since about 2021. In the field it places, finishes and gains strength about like Type I/II; some finishers notice slightly different bleed and set. Many DOTs now allow IL wherever Type I or II is specified (SCDOT does, and still allows fly ash or slag replacement with IL). If your spec still says 'ASTM C150 Type I/II only', get an approved substitution in writing before the pour.
field.title: Type IL portland-limestone cement (PLC, 'IL cement')
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: SCDOT Supplemental Specification, Type IL Portland-Limestone Cement (AASHTO M 240)

field.text: Blended hydraulic cements under ASTM C595 / AASHTO M 240 are portland cement combined at the mill with another material: Type IL = limestone, Type IP = pozzolan (usually fly ash or natural pozzolan), Type IS = slag cement, Type IT = ternary blend of two of those. A number in parentheses can show the percentage, e.g. IS(25) = about 25 percent slag. Blends usually set and gain early strength a bit slower, especially in cold weather, but often end up stronger and less permeable long term. ASTM C1157 is a separate performance spec (GU general use, HE high early, MS/HS sulfate, MH/LH heat). Ask the ready-mix supplier which cement is in your mix if early strength or cold weather matters.
field.title: Blended cements: IP, IS, IT and what the letters mean
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: Portland Cement Association (PCA) concrete technology pages, summarized

field.text: Fly ash is the fine ash captured from coal power plant stacks (ASTM C618). It acts as a pozzolan: it reacts with the calcium hydroxide that cement gives off and makes more binder. Class F (low calcium) is best for sulfate resistance and controlling alkali-silica reaction; Class C (high calcium) has some cementing ability of its own and gains strength faster. Typical replacement is about 15 to 25 percent of the cement, higher in some specs. Effects in the field: better workability and pumpability, less heat, slower set and slower early strength (watch cold weather and sawcut timing), denser concrete long term. Fly ash supply has tightened as coal plants close; harvested and blended ashes are now common. Follow your mix design.
field.title: Fly ash in concrete: Class F vs Class C
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Slag cement is ground granulated blast-furnace slag from iron making (ASTM C989, grades 80, 100, 120). It reacts with water and with the cement's calcium hydroxide, so it replaces part of the portland cement, commonly 25 to 50 percent, sometimes more for mass concrete or sulfate exposure. Benefits: lower heat, lower permeability, better sulfate and chloride resistance, lighter color. Drawbacks: slower setting and early strength, especially below about 50 F, so blankets, accelerators or reduced slag may be needed in cold weather, and saw cutting and form stripping may come later. A slag mix can look slightly green-blue on fresh breaks; that fades and is normal.
field.title: Slag cement (GGBFS) in concrete
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Silica fume (microsilica, ASTM C1240) is an extremely fine powder, about 100 times finer than cement, from silicon metal production. Usually 5 to 10 percent of cementitious material. It makes very dense, high-strength, low-permeability concrete used for bridge decks, parking garages, chemical-resistant or abrasion-resistant work, and some repair mortars. Field issues: it is sticky, needs a high-range water reducer, has almost no bleed water, so it is very prone to plastic shrinkage cracking. Cure immediately: fog, evaporation retarder, wet burlap right behind finishing. Don't wait for bleed water that never comes. Inhaling the dry powder is a respiratory hazard; follow the SDS.
field.title: Silica fume concrete
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Concrete does not dry to get hard, it hydrates: water chemically reacts with the cement to grow interlocking crystals (calcium silicate hydrate, the glue) and calcium hydroxide. That reaction needs water and warmth and gives off heat. Practical results: if the concrete dries out early, the reaction stops at the surface and you get weak, dusty, cracked concrete, which is why curing matters. Cold slows it; below about 40 F it nearly stalls, and if the water in fresh concrete freezes it expands and damages the paste. Hot speeds it up, shortens working time and can lower final strength. Initial set is when it stops being workable (often 2 to 6 hours); final set is when it is hard enough to walk on; strength keeps climbing for weeks.
field.title: Hydration: how concrete hardens (plain words)
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Typical strength gain for a normal Type I/II mix cured around 70 F: about 40 to 50 percent of the 28-day strength at 3 days, about 65 to 75 percent at 7 days, about 90 percent at 14 days, and 100 percent of design (f'c) at 28 days, with slow gain after that. High-early (Type III or accelerated) mixes can hit design strength in 3 to 7 days. Mixes with fly ash or slag gain slower early and may be specified at 56 days. Cold weather can double or triple the time. So a 3,000 psi thrust block cured at 50 F may only be around 1,500 to 2,000 psi at 7 days. Check the spec or engineer before pressure testing, backfilling heavy loads or stripping forms early.
field.title: Concrete strength gain over time (3, 7, 28 days)
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Water-cement ratio (w/c, or w/cm when fly ash or slag is counted) is pounds of water divided by pounds of cementitious material. Less water = stronger, less permeable concrete. ACI 211.1 typical 28-day strengths: non-air-entrained: 0.82 = 2,000 psi, 0.68 = 3,000, 0.57 = 4,000, 0.48 = 5,000, 0.41 = 6,000. Air-entrained: 0.74 = 2,000, 0.59 = 3,000, 0.48 = 4,000, 0.40 = 5,000. Example: a mix with 564 lb cement and 270 lb water has w/c 0.48. Specs for freeze-thaw, deicer salt or sulfate exposure often set a maximum w/cm like 0.45 or 0.40 regardless of strength. Every gallon of water added on site (8.33 lb) raises the ratio.
field.title: Water-cement ratio and strength table (w/c, w/cm)
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: PACA/NRMCA summary of ACI 211.1 w/cm vs strength table

field.text: Rule of thumb from PCA/NRMCA training: adding 1 gallon of water per cubic yard raises slump about 1 inch, cuts 28-day strength roughly 150 to 200 psi, raises shrinkage, and has about the same effect on strength as leaving out a quarter bag of cement. Example: 10 gallons dumped into a 10-yard truck is only 1 gallon per yard, but 20 gallons on a 4-yard load is 5 gallons per yard, which can drop a 4,000 psi mix toward 3,000 psi and push w/c over a 0.45 spec limit. Better options: order the right slump, ask the plant for a water reducer or superplasticizer, or let the driver add the withheld water allowed on the ticket. Any added water must be recorded on the ticket.
field.title: Why adding water on site weakens concrete
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: A cubic yard of normal concrete weighs about 3,900 to 4,000 lb (about 145 to 150 lb per cubic ft). A common 4,000 psi air-entrained mix has roughly 520 to 610 lb of cementitious material (about 5.5 to 6.5 'sacks' at 94 lb), 250 to 290 lb of water (30 to 35 gallons), about 1,700 to 1,900 lb of coarse aggregate (#57 or #67 stone, 3/4 to 1 inch), 1,100 to 1,400 lb of sand, 5 to 7 percent air, plus admixtures in ounces. Coarse aggregate is the backbone; sand fills voids; paste coats everything. Mix designs are submitted by the supplier with their history of test breaks. Field crews don't change proportions; changes go through the supplier and engineer.
field.title: Concrete mix design basics: what's in a cubic yard
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: 'Sack' or 'bag' means a 94 lb bag (1 cubic ft loose) of portland cement. A '5-sack mix' has 470 lb cement per cubic yard, a '6-sack' 564 lb, '6.5-sack' 611 lb, '7-sack' 658 lb. Older specs and foremen still order this way, but modern specs order by strength (psi), max w/cm, slump and air. As a rough guide only: 5 sack ≈ 2,500 to 3,000 psi, 5.5 to 6 sack ≈ 3,000 to 4,000 psi, 6.5 to 7 sack ≈ 4,000 to 5,000 psi, depending on water, aggregates and admixtures. 'Lean mix' or '2-sack' is low-cement fill concrete. When calling dispatch, give psi class, slump, air, aggregate size and any admixtures, and quote the supplier's mix number if you have it.
field.title: Sack mix, '6-bag mix', and old-school concrete terms
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Typical strengths (check plans, city standard details and DOT spec, which govern): 2,000 to 2,500 psi lean or 'mud mat' and pipe cradle in some details. 3,000 psi: thrust blocks, kickers, pipe encasement, manhole bases poured in place, valve pads, fence posts (many water utilities specify 2,500 to 3,000 psi for blocking). 3,500 to 4,000 psi air-entrained: curb and gutter, sidewalk, driveway aprons, manhole collars and grade ring collars exposed to traffic and salt. 4,000 to 4,500 psi: DOT structural concrete, concrete pavement patches, inlet tops. 5,000 psi and up: precast manholes, pipe, boxes. Flowable fill (CLSM) is not structural concrete, typically 50 to 150 psi so it can be dug later.
field.title: Concrete psi classes and common uses on utility jobs
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: For thrust blocks, kickers and anchor blocks at water main bends, tees and plugs, utilities commonly specify 2,500 to 3,000 psi concrete placed against undisturbed soil, with plastic or tar paper keeping concrete off the joints, bolts and fitting so the joint can be taken apart. Order a slump around 4 to 5 inches so it fills against the soil without heavy vibration; air is often not required below grade. For pipe encasement (under roads, shallow cover, crossing separation), 3,000 psi with 3/4 inch stone at 4 to 6 inch slump; tie pipe down or place in lifts so it doesn't float. High-early mix or extra cure days before pressure testing. Always use your utility's standard detail for block size and strength.
field.title: Thrust block and encasement concrete: what to order
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Air-entraining admixture (ASTM C260) creates billions of microscopic bubbles (about 4 to 7 percent of the volume for typical exposed concrete). When water in the concrete freezes and expands, the bubbles act as relief valves, preventing freeze-thaw cracking and salt scaling. Required for any concrete exposed to freezing and deicing salt: curb, sidewalk, driveway, paving, collars, exterior steps. Typical targets for 3/4 to 1 inch aggregate are about 5 to 7 percent, plus or minus 1.5 percent; smaller aggregate needs more air. Each 1 percent of extra air lowers strength about 5 percent, so too much is also bad. Do not hard-trowel air-entrained exterior flatwork; it can cause surface delamination. Air is checked on site with a pressure meter.
field.title: Air entrainment: why and how much
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: Portland Cement Association (PCA) concrete technology pages, summarized

field.text: Water-reducing admixtures (ASTM C494) let you get the same slump with less water, so you get stronger concrete without fighting the w/c limit. Type A normal water reducer cuts water about 5 to 10 percent. Mid-range reducers about 6 to 12 percent. Type F/G high-range water reducers, called superplasticizers or 'super P', cut water 12 to 30 percent and can turn a 3 inch slump into 8 inches or flowing concrete. HRWR slump boost wears off in about 30 to 60 minutes, so some are added at the jobsite by the driver per the supplier's instructions. Use these instead of adding water when you need more workability for pumping, tight rebar or encasement. Note the dose and time on the ticket.
field.title: Water reducers, mid-range and superplasticizers (HRWR)
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Accelerators (ASTM C494 Type C/E) speed setting and early strength for cold weather or fast turnaround. Calcium chloride is the cheapest and strongest, usually up to about 2 percent by weight of cement (the ready-mix plant calls it '1 percent' or '2 percent calcium'). Chloride rusts reinforcing steel, ductile iron and embedded metal, so ACI 318 limits chloride by exposure: 0.30 percent water-soluble chloride (by weight of cement) for reinforced concrete exposed to moisture (roughly a 0.5 percent CaCl2 dose), 0.15 percent where deicing salt, seawater or other chlorides reach it, and 0.06 percent in prestressed concrete; calcium chloride is not used with embedded aluminum. Near rebar, wire mesh, DI fittings and bolts, order a non-chloride accelerator (NCA). Accelerators are not antifreeze; still protect from freezing.
field.title: Accelerators and calcium chloride: rebar warning
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: ASCC article on calcium chloride in cold weather concrete (ACI 318 chloride limits)

field.text: Retarding admixtures (ASTM C494 Type B, or Type D water-reducing and retarding) slow setting, typically by 1 to 3 hours depending on dose and temperature. Used in hot weather, long hauls, big pours where you need to avoid cold joints, and for exposed aggregate finishes (surface retarder sprayed on top). Extended-set or hydration-stabilizing admixtures can hold concrete for several hours for very long hauls. Too much retarder can leave concrete soft for a day or more and delay sawcutting and stripping. If a load is retarded, the ticket should show it; plan finishing crew and saw timing accordingly. Don't use a retarder to justify exceeding the spec's discharge time limit without written approval.
field.title: Retarders and hydration stabilizers
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Fibers are mixed in at the plant to control cracking. Microfibers (polypropylene, commonly about 0.5 to 1.5 lb per cubic yard per the maker) reduce plastic shrinkage cracking in the first hours; they do not replace structural rebar. Macro synthetic fibers (typically 3 to 7.5 lb per CY) and steel fibers (often 25 to 60 lb per CY) add toughness and can replace light wire mesh in some slabs when the engineer approves. Fibers lower measured slump a bit, so ask for a water reducer rather than water. Fuzzy surfaces can show fibers; a quick pass with a torch or extra floating cleans them up. Fibers are useful for sidewalks, slabs on grade, shotcrete and patching. Check your spec before substituting fibers for mesh.
field.title: Fibers in concrete: synthetic, steel and what they do
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Coarse aggregate for concrete is usually #57 (1 inch to #4) or #67 (3/4 inch to #4) crushed stone or gravel; pea gravel (3/8 inch, #8) for pump mixes and thin sections. Max size should be no more than about 1/3 the slab thickness or 3/4 of the clear space between rebar. Sand is ASTM C33 concrete sand. Problems: alkali-silica reaction (ASR) when reactive aggregate meets alkali, causing map cracking and gel years later (controlled with fly ash, slag or low-alkali cement); D-cracking in pavement from freeze-susceptible stone; popouts from shale or chert particles near the surface; dirty or clay-coated aggregate weakens bond. Aggregate quality is the supplier's job, but popouts and ASR show up as warranty complaints.
field.title: Aggregates for concrete: sizes and problems
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Fresh concrete unit weight (ASTM C138) is measured by filling a known-volume bucket and weighing it, typically about 140 to 150 lb per cubic ft for normal-weight air-entrained concrete. Yield = total batch weight from the ticket divided by unit weight, converted to cubic yards; if a truck tickets 10 yards but yields 9.6, you'll run short. Higher air means lighter weight and more yield but lower strength. Lightweight concrete (expanded shale aggregate) is about 90 to 115 lb per cubic ft. Flowable fill is about 90 to 145 lb per cubic ft depending on mix (foamed, high-air excavatable mixes are lightest). If you're regularly short on yardage, ask the tester to run unit weight and compare to the batch weights before blaming over-dig.
field.title: Unit weight, yield and air in fresh concrete
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Fresh concrete temperature (ASTM C1064) is measured with a probe thermometer inserted at least 3 inches into a sample, read after about 2 minutes. Typical spec window: minimum about 50 F (higher in cold weather per ACI 306) and maximum about 90 to 95 F. Hot concrete loses slump fast, sets early, cracks more and ends up weaker. Cold concrete sets slowly and is at risk of freezing. Plants control temperature with heated water and aggregates in winter, and chilled water, ice or liquid nitrogen in summer. Record concrete temperature with each set of cylinders and on the pour log. If a load is outside the spec range, call the inspector before placing.
field.title: Concrete temperature limits at delivery
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Sulfates in soil or groundwater react with cement paste and cause swelling, cracking and softening. ACI 318 exposure classes S1 to S3 call for Type II, Type V, blended cement or SCMs, and lower w/cm (0.50 down to 0.45). In sanitary sewers, a different problem: hydrogen sulfide gas from sewage is converted by bacteria on the crown and walls of manholes and pipes into sulfuric acid, which eats concrete (microbial induced corrosion, crown rot). Signs: soft, pasty, rough concrete with exposed aggregate above the flow line, especially downstream of force main discharges and drop manholes. Remedies are liners, coatings, calcium aluminate cement or polymer concrete, and controlling turbulence and H2S.
field.title: Sulfate attack and sewer concrete corrosion
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: High-early strength concrete reaches useful strength in hours to a few days instead of 28 days. It is made with Type III cement, extra cement (7 to 8 sacks), lower w/c, accelerators (non-chloride near steel), heated materials, or blankets. Typical uses: concrete pavement patches and utility cut restoration that must open to traffic the same or next day (often specified as e.g. 3,000 psi in 24 hours, or 'opening strength' by maturity or cylinders), thrust blocks needed before pressure testing, cold weather work. Tradeoffs: shorter working time, more heat and shrinkage cracking, higher cost. 'Rapid-set' bagged products and calcium sulfoaluminate cements can open in 1 to 2 hours; follow the manufacturer's mixing water and temperature limits.
field.title: High-early strength concrete
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Self-consolidating concrete flows under its own weight, fills forms around tight rebar and levels itself without vibration. Measured by slump flow (spread diameter, often 20 to 30 inches) instead of slump, using the same cone. It uses high-range water reducers and viscosity modifiers so it doesn't segregate. Common in precast plants and for congested walls and encasements where vibrating is impossible. Field cautions: it puts full liquid pressure on forms (design forms for it), leaks through gaps, and must not be vibrated hard or it may segregate. Don't confuse SCC with simply adding water to get a 'soupy' mix; SCC is engineered and keeps its low w/c.
field.title: Self-consolidating concrete (SCC) and flowable mixes
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Concrete shrinks as it loses water: plastic shrinkage in the first hours when the surface dries before set, and drying shrinkage over weeks and months (roughly 1/16 inch per 10 ft of slab is a common figure). Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension (only about 10 percent of compressive strength), so when shrinkage is restrained by the subgrade, forms, pipes or adjoining slabs it cracks. That is why joints are cut to make the crack happen where you want it. More water, more cement paste, hot dry wind and poor curing all increase shrinkage. Rebar and mesh don't stop cracks; they hold cracks tight. Thermal contraction from temperature swings adds to it.
field.title: Concrete shrinkage and why it cracks
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Bleeding is water rising to the surface of freshly placed concrete as the heavier solids settle. Normal concrete bleeds for the first 1 to 3 hours depending on temperature and mix. If you float or trowel while bleed water is on the surface, you work water back into the top 1/8 inch, raising the surface w/c and causing dusting, crazing, scaling and delamination. Correct practice: screed and bull float, then wait until the water sheen is gone before edging, jointing and final floating. Never sprinkle dry cement ('dusting' or 'drying shake') to soak up bleed water; it makes a weak skin that peels. Low-bleed mixes (silica fume, high fines, cold air entrained) need prompt curing instead.
field.title: Bleed water: what it is and why not to finish into it
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: The maturity method (ASTM C1074) estimates in-place strength from temperature history. Sensors or loggers are tied to rebar or embedded in the pour, and temperature over time is converted to a maturity index; a lab calibration curve for that specific mix relates maturity to strength. DOTs increasingly use it to decide when concrete pavement patches can open to traffic, when to strip forms, or when to stop cold-weather protection, instead of breaking field-cured cylinders. Wireless sensors read through a phone app. It only works if the calibration mix matches what was delivered; big changes in w/c, air or cement need a new curve. It's especially useful in cold weather when field cylinders lie.
field.title: Concrete maturity method for early strength
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: Three different materials crews mix up: Flowable fill (CLSM, controlled low-strength material) is a soupy mix of sand, a little cement, fly ash and water, typically 50 to 150 psi so it can be re-excavated by machine (often specified under 150 to 300 psi max for excavatability); used for trench backfill under pavement, abandoning pipes and filling voids. Lean concrete (2,000 to 2,500 psi, low cement) is for mud mats, pipe cradles and fills that need to be firmer but not structural. Structural concrete (3,000 psi and up) is for thrust blocks, bases, collars and anything carrying load or exposed to weather. Ordering flowable fill for a thrust block or concrete for trench fill are both costly mistakes.
field.title: Flowable fill vs lean concrete vs structural concrete
field.topic: Concrete science: cements, SCMs, mix design, admixtures
field.source: General industry practice (ACI/PCA/NRMCA guidance as commonly taught); varies by spec

field.text: A French drain is a gravel-filled trench, usually with perforated pipe, that collects groundwater or soggy-yard water and carries it away by gravity. Typical residential numbers from a building-inspection guide: trench at least 12 inches wide (18 to 24 inches for heavy water), 18 to 24 inches deep for yard drains; slope at least 1% (about 1 inch per 8 ft), 1 to 2% preferred; 4-inch perforated pipe; line the trench with non-woven geotextile (not landscape weed fabric); 2 to 3 inches of washed angular stone (3/4 to 1-1/2 inch, like #57 clean rock) under the pipe; pipe with holes facing DOWN; backfill with the same stone; fold the fabric over the top with at least 6 inches of overlap. Outlet to daylight (most reliable), a dry well where soil drains, or a storm system with permit. Add cleanout risers every 50 to 100 ft on long runs.
field.title: French drain: what it is and how to build one
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: Jaspector, French Drains: Design, Installation, and Common Mistakes

field.text: Most failed French drains have one of these problems: wrong stone (stone with fines, crusher run, or round pea gravel and river rock that packs and clogs); no filter fabric around the stone, the main cause of early clogging; relying on a pipe sock alone as the filter in silty soil (socks blind off); flat spots or bellies where sediment settles; holes facing up; no cleanout to flush the line; no proper outlet or discharging onto a neighbor's property or into a sanitary sewer (not allowed); treating surface runoff as if it were groundwater (a French drain is slow; surface water needs a swale or inlet); and burying it with no record of where it runs. Before you backfill, shoot grades every 25 ft or so to prove the fall is continuous to the outlet, and take photos with a tape for the as-built.
field.title: French drain mistakes that make them fail
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: French Drains: Design, Installation, and Common Mistakes (Jaspector)

field.text: A curtain drain (interceptor drain) is a French-drain-style trench dug across a slope, UPHILL of what you are protecting (a house, a road cut, a septic field, a wet spot in a field), to catch groundwater moving downhill before it gets there. It runs roughly along the contour with just enough fall (commonly 0.5 to 1%) to an outlet at one or both ends. It should be deep enough to cut into the wet layer, often down to a less permeable layer such as clay or rock where the seepage is running. Build it like a French drain: fabric-wrapped clean stone, perforated pipe holes down, solid pipe from the last perforated section to the outlet, rodent screen at daylight. Some people also call an interior basement perimeter drain a 'curtain drain', so ask which one is meant. Septic setbacks from curtain drains are set by the health department.
field.title: Curtain drain / interceptor drain on a slope
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General drainage practice (NRCS subsurface drainage concepts, residential practice); terminology varies regionally

field.text: Footing drains collect groundwater at the base of a foundation so it does not build pressure against basement or vault walls. Common residential practice (IRC R405 style): perforated pipe or a gravel drain alongside the footing, with the pipe set on filter fabric at or below the top of the footing (never above the slab level it protects); clean gravel extending about 1 ft beyond the footing and about 6 inches above its top, covered with filter fabric so backfill fines can't get in; drain to daylight, a storm system where allowed, or a sump pit and pump. Commercial buildings and deep vaults follow the drawings, often with drainage board down the wall tied into the pipe. Never tie footing drains into the sanitary sewer (it is illegal infiltration in most cities). Check grade so the pipe never runs uphill, and put cleanouts at corners where the spec allows.
field.title: Foundation drains / footing drains around buildings and structures
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice based on IRC R405 foundation drainage provisions; check your code and drawings

field.text: Highway edge drains are perforated pipes (commonly 4 or 6 inch) in a narrow fabric-lined trench of permeable stone along the pavement edge or under the shoulder, draining water out of the base course. The weak point is almost always the outlet: solid (non-perforated) outlet pipe laid on a steady fall to the ditch, spaced at intervals set by the DOT detail (often a few hundred feet); a small concrete headwall or apron at the outlet so mowers don't crush the pipe; a rodent screen or flap; and an outlet marker post so maintenance can find it. Video inspections by DOTs have found many edge drain outlets crushed or buried right after construction. Field checks: no sags, outlet higher than ditch flowline, pipe not crushed by shoulder rollers, fabric overlapped on top before backfill. Follow your DOT's standard drawing for pipe type, stone and outlet spacing.
field.title: Pavement edge drains and underdrain outlets (DOT roadways)
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General DOT practice (FHWA pavement subsurface drainage concepts); spacing per your DOT standard

field.text: Common perforated drain pipes: single-wall corrugated polyethylene (cheap, flexible, often 4 to 6 inch, with or without a fabric sock; crushes under traffic and is hard to jet); dual-wall corrugated HDPE perforated (AASHTO M252 for 3 to 10 inch, M294 for 12 inch and up; stiffer, smooth inside); PVC perforated drain or sewer pipe (SDR 35 or ASTM D2729 thin-wall; smooth, easy to clean, holes usually in two rows at about 120 degrees apart); slotted pipe (narrow slots, better in sandy soils). Rules of thumb: put the holes down unless the spec or maker says otherwise; socks clog in silty soils, so a stone envelope wrapped in fabric is usually better; use solid pipe for the section that leaves the drained area and through any structure; under pavement or traffic, use dual-wall or PVC rated for the cover. Check the spec for perforation class and pipe standard.
field.title: Perforated drain pipe options: corrugated, PVC, socks and slots
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General industry practice; standards named are those commonly specified

field.text: Trench drains (channel drains, linear drains) are pre-sloped or neutral channels with a grate on top; slot drains have a narrow continuous slot instead of a grate. They catch sheet flow across a wide paved area such as a driveway apron, loading dock, parking garage or plaza. Grates and channels are rated by the European EN 1433 load classes (number = test load in kN): A15 pedestrian and bike paths; B125 walkways and car parking; C250 curb areas and car/truck parking; D400 roads and forklift traffic; E600 industrial, high wheel loads; F900 airports, docks, extreme loads. A drain maker's guide says use C250 or higher for channels up to 12 inches wide under AASHTO HS-20/HS-25 truck loads, E600 or higher for channels wider than 12 inches, and go up a class if loads are uncertain. The rating counts only when installed in the concrete surround the maker shows.
field.title: Trench drains and slot drains: load classes (EN 1433 A15 to F900)
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: Sioux Chief 865 Series load rating guide (EN 1433 classes)

field.text: Typical trench drain install (follow the maker's drawing for the load class): dig the trench wide and deep enough for the concrete surround (often around 4 to 6 inches each side and below for light classes, more for heavy); set channels on chairs, rebar or the maker's installation brackets, in sequence from the outlet upstream so the slope builds in the right direction; join sections with the supplied sealant if the drain must be watertight; set the top of the grate about 1/8 inch or so below the finished pavement so wheels hit concrete and water drops in, not above; keep grates locked in place during the pour so the channel doesn't float or squeeze in; pour and vibrate concrete fully under the channel haunches; tie into the outlet catch basin or pipe. Saw expansion joints in adjacent slabs where the maker requires. The pour is where most go wrong: floated channels and voids under the haunch.
field.title: Installing trench drains in concrete
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice from manufacturer installation guides; check your product's drawings

field.text: Smaller surface inlets: area drains and yard drains (round or square grates on PVC or HDPE drain basins, such as Nyloplast-style, or small precast boxes) for lawns, courtyards and parking islands; yard inlets (precast concrete boxes with a grate top, sized like a small catch basin) in grassed areas and backyards; drop inlets (a box set in a ditch or median with a grate on top, where ditch water drops in and goes into a culvert or storm pipe). DOT median and ditch drop inlets usually get a riprap or concrete collar so the ditch doesn't scour around the box, and a ditch block downstream so water doesn't bypass; TxDOT notes a 6-inch ditch block may not capture all flow, so a taller block may be needed. In lawns, set the grate about 1 to 2 inches below finished grade with a sodded or stabilized ring so water reaches it. Order grates rated for the traffic expected.
field.title: Area drains, yard inlets and drop inlets
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, storm drain inlets (drop inlets); general practice for yard drains

field.text: TxDOT compares the main street inlet types. Curb opening inlets: an opening in the curb face that depends on a gutter depression; self-cleaning, work on grade and in sags, don't catch bikes, but repeated asphalt overlays raise the gutter and shrink the opening. Grate inlets: used in sags, beside barriers, in V-gutters and ditches; easy to access but clog with debris and can trap bike wheels and wheelchairs. Combination inlets (curb opening plus grate): good in sags because the curb opening acts as overflow when the grate clogs; usually not worth it on a continuous grade. Slotted and trench (linear) drains: catch wide shallow sheet flow without a depression; slotted drains need enough slope to self-clean, are hard to install right, and collect debris in sags. Sag inlets are designed with a safety factor (about 2 for grates, which equals assuming 50% clogging).
field.title: Inlet types: curb opening, grate, combination and slotted (pros and cons)
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Section 5 Storm Drain Inlets

field.text: The throat is the opening in the curb face of a curb inlet, commonly about 4 to 6 inches tall; the length (often 5, 10 or 15 ft on DOT inlets) sets its capacity. A local gutter depression in front of the inlet lets water drop toward the opening and increases how much it catches. TxDOT's recommended depression depths: 0 to 1 inch in a traffic lane, 1 to 3 inches outside traffic lanes or in parking lanes, and 1 to 5 inches on lightly traveled city streets. Too deep is a hazard to cars and bikes. Field points: form the depression and transition exactly per the standard drawing; check the throat height after paving; every overlay that isn't milled first raises the gutter and cuts the throat, so mill at the curb line. Inlet lids and tops are often precast with the throat; confirm the plan inlet type number (for example a 10-ft curb inlet) before ordering.
field.title: Curb inlet throat, gutter depression and overlays
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Section 5 Storm Drain Inlets (depression depths, overlay note); throat dimensions are typical values

field.text: Grates and frames are mostly gray or ductile cast iron, or fabricated steel. Pick by load: heavy-duty (AASHTO H-20 / HS-20 or HS-25 rated) for streets and anywhere a truck can drive; light-duty for lawns and walkways only. Bike-safe grates have bars perpendicular to traffic or a vane or honeycomb pattern; parallel-bar grates trap wheels and are banned on many roads. Grates in sidewalks, crosswalks and accessible routes must meet ADA rules: openings no wider than 1/2 inch in the direction of travel, with long openings perpendicular to the main walking direction. Bolted or locking grates deter theft and keep grates in place under traffic or high flow. Set frames on full mortar or butyl and adjusting rings so they don't rock, and check that the grate sits flat in the frame. Order from the plan's casting number (for example a Neenah or EJ catalog number) or approved equal.
field.title: Storm grates and frames: load rating, bike-safe and ADA openings
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice; ADA 1/2-inch opening rule from the ADA Standards for Accessible Design (302.3); load terms per AASHTO

field.text: Inlet location rules from TxDOT: put inlets upstream of sag points, intersections, gore areas, superelevation transitions (where the cross slope flips), driveways, crosswalks and curb ramps so water does not run across them; capture 100% of gutter flow at intersections, ramps and crosswalks; space inlets so gutter flow (spread) doesn't get too wide. Sag inlets are the end of the line: if they clog, water ponds until it overtops the curb or crown, so flanking inlets are often added on each side about 50 to 100 ft from the low point on major roads and underpasses. Field tip: if grades change in the field (a sag moves because of a pavement change), tell the engineer; an inlet that ends up a foot from the actual low point can leave a permanent pond. Shoot the gutter flowline after curb is set to confirm the low point.
field.title: Where inlets go: upstream of crosswalks, sags and flanking inlets
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Section 5 Storm Drain Inlets

field.text: A catch basin has a sump: the floor is set below the outlet pipe (commonly 2 to 4 ft below, per local detail) so sand, grit and trash settle out before water goes downstream. Many cities also require a hood or trap on the outlet pipe (a cast iron or plastic elbow, 'snout' or bell hood) so floating oil, leaves and trash stay in the basin instead of going down the pipe. Sumps hold standing water, which can breed mosquitoes and freeze, and they must be vacuumed out regularly (see the cleaning chunk); when a sump fills more than about half way it stops trapping much. An 'inlet' without a sump has its floor shaped to the outlet pipe so it self-cleans. Build exactly what the detail calls for: putting a sump where the plan shows a flow-through inlet (or the reverse) changes maintenance and water quality credits.
field.title: Catch basin sumps, hoods and traps
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General municipal standard-detail practice

field.text: A headwall is a concrete wall at a culvert or storm pipe end that holds back the embankment, protects the pipe end, reduces erosion and improves inlet flow. Types: straight headwall (parallel to the road, for pipes in straight ditches), L-shaped or U-shaped endwalls, and headwalls with wingwalls flared out (often about 30 to 45 degrees) to guide water in and hold the slope. Many have a concrete apron and a cutoff wall or toe wall extending down below the apron (commonly 1.5 to 3 ft) so water can't undercut it. Precast headwalls save time; cast-in-place need footing, forms and rebar per the DOT standard. Field points: pipe end flush with or set into the wall as detailed; footing on firm undisturbed soil; weep holes if shown; backfill compacted in lifts behind the wall; riprap or apron at outlet. Use the DOT standard drawing for the pipe size and skew.
field.title: Headwalls, endwalls and wingwalls at culvert ends
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General DOT practice; dimensions vary by state standard drawing

field.text: A flared end section is a metal (galvanized steel or aluminum) or precast concrete piece that bolts or ties to the culvert end and flares out to match the ditch or slope, improving flow and protecting the fill. Install points: set on a compacted, shaped bed at the same line and grade as the pipe; connect to the pipe with the supplied connector bands, bolts or tie bolts (concrete FES are often joined with joint ties so they don't slide off); place the toe plate or cutoff wall at the end so water can't undercut; backfill and compact around it so the slope meets the edges; add riprap at the outlet per plan. Precast concrete FES are heavy (hundreds to several thousand pounds) so check the lift rating and use proper rigging. Inside the road clear zone, DOTs may require safety slope end sections with cross bars so a car can drive over them. Follow the DOT standard for the pipe size.
field.title: Flared end sections (FES) on culverts and storm outfalls
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General DOT practice; check your state standard drawings

field.text: Culvert material choices (see the pipe-concrete, pipe-hdpe and pipe-other-materials files for details): reinforced concrete pipe (RCP) and precast box culverts are strong, long-lasting and hydraulically smooth (Manning n about 0.013), but heavy and need good joints to stop soil loss. Corrugated metal pipe (CMP) in galvanized steel, aluminized Type 2 steel or aluminum is light and cheap, but corrugations are rough (n about 0.024 for annular) and inverts rust out or wear from abrasive gravel and acidic or salty water; paved inverts help. Corrugated HDPE and polypropylene (PP) with smooth interiors are light and corrosion-proof but depend on good backfill and need minimum cover and care with fire. Structural plate arches and 3-sided precast span bigger streams. Many DOTs pick material by service life tables based on soil and water pH, resistivity and abrasion.
field.title: Culvert materials: RCP, CMP, plastic and box culverts compared
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: Manning n values from ODOT Hydraulics Manual App. 8-A; other points general DOT practice

field.text: Culverts are sized by the engineer to pass a design flood (often the 10, 25, 50 or 100-year storm depending on road class and what floods if it fails) without the water upstream (headwater) rising too high over the road or flooding property. Key ideas: the headwater depth divided by culvert height (HW/D) is limited by DOT criteria; both inlet control and outlet control must be checked and the higher headwater governs; many agencies set a minimum size, commonly 15 or 18 inch under roads and 12 to 15 inch for driveways, so it doesn't plug with debris; outlet velocity is checked to size the riprap. Things in the field that change capacity: setting it lower or higher than plan, shortening or lengthening it, changing material (roughness), adding or removing a headwall or flared end, and leaving debris or sediment in it. Get approval before any of those changes.
field.title: Culvert sizing basics in plain words
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General DOT practice; inlet/outlet control from TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual

field.text: Inlet control means the entrance is the bottleneck: the barrel could carry more water than can squeeze in through the opening. It is common on steep culverts. What matters: the size and shape of the opening and how the inlet edge is built (square edge, beveled, headwall, flared end, projecting pipe). What happens downstream doesn't matter. Outlet control means the barrel or the downstream water is the bottleneck: the pipe can't carry all the water the inlet would accept. It is common on flat culverts or when the outlet is flooded (high tailwater). What matters: pipe size, length, roughness (smooth vs corrugated), slope, and tailwater, plus entrance losses. Designers compute the upstream water level (headwater) both ways and use the higher one. Field takeaway: on outlet-control culverts, swapping smooth pipe for corrugated, or a blocked outlet ditch, raises the water upstream.
field.title: Culvert inlet control vs outlet control in plain words
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Hydraulic Operation of Culverts

field.text: Culverts that carry streams with fish, or that are in waters regulated under Clean Water Act Section 404 and state stream rules, often must be set below the stream bed so natural bed material forms a continuous bottom through the pipe. Common rules (vary by state and agency): embed the invert some percentage of the rise (frequently around 20%, or a minimum depth like 1 ft) below the streambed; match the culvert slope to the stream; size the span to the bankfull width; and fill the bottom with streambed material. Bottomless arches and 3-sided boxes are used where possible. Work in the stream is often limited to low-flow seasons and needs a stream diversion or pump-around. Never swap a buried design for one at stream grade without approval; a perched outlet (pipe sitting above the stream) blocks fish and erodes the bed. Follow the permit conditions to the letter.
field.title: Culverts in streams: burying the invert and fish passage
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice; embedment values vary by state fish-passage and 404 permit conditions

field.text: An outfall is the point where a storm pipe or ditch discharges to a stream, pond, wetland, ditch or the sea. Construction points: set the outfall invert at or slightly above the receiving water's normal level (or as designed) so it doesn't fill with sediment or sit perched high above the bank; angle the pipe downstream rather than straight across the stream so it doesn't scour the opposite bank; build a headwall, flared end and riprap apron per plan; use a flap gate or duckbill check valve where the plans show (tidal areas, river backwater) so flood water doesn't back up into the system; screen or grate large openings where safety requires. Outfalls are permitted points under MS4 programs and many cities number and map them, so keep the as-built location and invert. Work below the high-water mark usually needs a 404/state permit.
field.title: Storm outfalls: what they are and how to build them
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice; MS4 mapping requirement per EPA Phase II small MS4 fact sheet

field.text: Typical state erosion control handbook rules (Tennessee) for a riprap apron at a pipe outlet: size for the 25-year, 24-hour peak flow or the pipe's design flow, whichever is greater. Read the apron length (La) and median stone size (D50) from the handbook table using the flow, pipe diameter (Do) and tailwater: low tailwater is less than half the pipe diameter deep (assume low on flat ground with no channel). Width at the pipe: 3 x Do. Width at the downstream end on flat ground: Do + La for low tailwater, Do + 0.4 x La for high tailwater. In a defined channel, carry the riprap across the bottom and up the banks to 1 ft above tailwater or top of bank. Maximum stone size 1.5 x D50; thickness 1.5 x maximum stone size (about 2.25 x D50), at least 6 inches. Build the apron at zero grade, straight, with no bend. If flows exceed the table, use a stilling basin or energy dissipator.
field.title: Riprap apron outlet protection: design rules
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: Tennessee Erosion and Sediment Control Handbook, Outlet Protection

field.text: Example using the Tennessee handbook rules: a 24-inch pipe (Do = 2.0 ft) discharges onto flat ground, so assume low tailwater. Suppose the handbook table gives an apron length La = 20 ft and D50 = 9 inches for your flow (always read your own table). Width at the pipe end = 3 x 2.0 = 6.0 ft. Width at the downstream end = Do + La = 2.0 + 20 = 22.0 ft. Maximum stone = 1.5 x 9 = 13.5 inches. Thickness = 1.5 x 13.5 = about 20 inches (1.7 ft). Volume of the trapezoid-shaped apron = average width (6 + 22) / 2 = 14 ft, x 20 ft long x 1.7 ft thick = about 476 cubic feet = about 17.6 CY. At roughly 1.4 to 1.7 tons per CY in place (check your supplier), order about 25 to 30 tons, plus geotextile with 1 ft overlaps under it. The plans or DOT standard govern if they differ.
field.title: Riprap apron worked example (24-inch pipe outlet)
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: Computed from Tennessee Erosion and Sediment Control Handbook, Outlet Protection rules; table values in the example are illustrative

field.text: When outlet velocity or flow is too high for a plain riprap apron, engineers use energy dissipators: riprap stilling basins (a scour hole lined with riprap where the jet drops and spreads); concrete impact basins (USBR Type VI style, the jet hits a hanging baffle wall); baffled aprons and chutes with concrete blocks for steep slopes; drop structures and drop manholes that step water down in stages; and plunge pools. FHWA's HEC-14 is the national design reference. Field points: build baffle heights, block spacing and basin floor elevations exactly to the drawing, since small changes affect performance; form and place reinforcing carefully (large impact basins carry high loads); place cutoff walls and riprap at the basin exit; and keep the outlet channel open. These are often in deep, wet excavations near water: shoring, dewatering and fall protection apply.
field.title: Energy dissipators at storm outlets: stilling basins, impact basins, drop structures
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice; FHWA HEC-14 is the standard reference for energy dissipators

field.text: A level spreader is a dead-level trench or lip across a slope that takes concentrated flow (from a pipe, swale or diversion) and lets it spill out evenly as sheet flow onto a stable vegetated area. Typical criteria from a nonpoint source manual: drainage area 5 acres or less; channel coming in at 1% or flatter; spreader at 0% grade; length at least about 2 ft per cfs (no more than 0.5 cfs per foot of level section); at least 6 ft wide and 6 inches deep below the lip; downslope area uniform, 10% or flatter, fully vegetated before use; and at least 100 ft of vegetated buffer before surface waters. Some states require much longer spreaders (for example around 10 to 13 ft per cfs for grass buffers), so check yours. The lip MUST be dead level; any low spot concentrates flow and gullies the slope. Set the lip with a laser or transit, and use a rigid lip (concrete, timber or stone) where spec'd.
field.title: Level spreaders: turning a pipe outlet into sheet flow
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: Level Spreader fact sheet (Geosyntec NPS manual); state length criteria vary

field.text: Quick contrast of storm pipe materials (details are in the pipe files): RCP (ASTM C76) is rigid, strong under shallow and deep cover, smooth (n about 0.013), heavy, and its gasketed or mortared joints control soil loss. Corrugated HDPE (AASHTO M294 / ASTM F2306) and polypropylene (ASTM F2764) dual-wall pipe are light, corrosion-proof, smooth inside (n about 0.012), flexible, and depend on embedment and compaction; they can float in wet trenches. CMP is light, rough unless paved or spiral-rib (n up to 0.024), and can corrode or abrade. PVC (ASTM D3034 / F679, profile wall F794) is common for smaller storm lines and roof leaders. Ductile iron is used where cover is very shallow or loads extreme. Selection usually depends on cover depth, loads, flow, corrosion and abrasion, cost, and agency approved-products lists. Follow the spec; substitutions need engineer approval.
field.title: Storm pipe materials quick contrast
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice; n values from ODOT Hydraulics Manual App. 8-A (concrete, corrugated) with smooth plastic typical value

field.text: Storm pipe joints are usually specified as soil-tight or watertight. Soil-tight joints keep backfill from entering the pipe but may leak water: split coupling bands on CMP, some bell-and-spigot plastic with no gasket, or RCP with mortar or mastic. Watertight joints use rubber gaskets and are lab-tested to hold pressure: for example corrugated HDPE and PP watertight joints are commonly tested to ASTM D3212 at 10.8 psi, and gasketed RCP to ASTM C443. Many agencies now require watertight joints, or soil-tight with a geotextile joint wrap, because leaking storm joints pull soil into the pipe and cause sinkholes. Field points: clean and lubricate gaskets, check the home mark on plastic pipe, don't 'stab' with a bucket without a sling or bar, and wrap RCP joints with fabric (often about 2 ft wide) where the spec says. Joints in high groundwater or fine sands need the most care.
field.title: Storm pipe joints: soil-tight vs watertight
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice; joint test standards named are those commonly specified (ASTM D3212, C443)

field.text: Roadside ditches and swales are lined to resist the water's velocity and shear: seed and mulch or sod for low velocities (roughly up to about 4 to 5 fps on good grass, less on sandy soil); erosion control blanket (straw or coconut) to protect seed until it grows; turf reinforcement mats (TRM, permanent synthetic mats) for higher flows where grass alone won't hold; riprap or rock lining for steep grades and high shear; and concrete or asphalt paved ditches for very steep or high-flow sections. Designers check shear stress or velocity (FHWA HEC-15 method). Field points: shape the ditch to the typical section before lining; key blankets and mats into anchor trenches at the top and at intervals; staple at the maker's pattern, usually denser on the upstream edges; overlap upstream piece over downstream (shingle with the flow). Rock check dams slow flow on long slopes.
field.title: Ditch and swale lining: grass, mats, riprap and concrete
field.topic: Drains, inlets, culverts, end treatments and outlet protection
field.source: General practice; FHWA HEC-15 is the standard reference for channel linings; velocity limits vary by state

field.text: All rock falls into three families, and each digs differently. Igneous rock formed from molten rock: granite, diorite, gabbro (coarse grained, cooled deep underground) and basalt, diabase ('trap rock'), rhyolite (fine grained, cooled at or near the surface). Usually hard, massive and abrasive; the hardest to rip; often needs blasting when fresh. Sedimentary rock formed from layers of sediment: shale and mudstone, siltstone, sandstone, conglomerate, limestone, dolomite, chalk, coal. Generally the most rippable, especially when thin bedded, fractured or weathered; but massive limestone and well-cemented sandstone can be very hard. Metamorphic rock is rock changed by heat and pressure: slate (from shale), schist, gneiss (from granite or sediments), quartzite (from sandstone), marble (from limestone). Rippability depends on foliation (layering) direction and spacing; quartzite is extremely hard and abrasive. The FHWA rippability guide makes the same ranking: igneous hardest, metamorphic variable, sedimentary most rippable.
field.title: Rock types met in excavation: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: FHWA Central Federal Lands geophysical methods manual, Determining Rippability of Rocks (citing Caterpillar Handbook of Ripping, 8th ed.); Standard geology and excavation practice

field.text: Granite (light colored, speckled, coarse crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica) and basalt or diabase ('trap rock': dark gray to black, fine grained, heavy) are typical hard igneous rocks. Fresh, unweathered, massive granite or trap often has compressive strength well over 15,000 psi and very wide joint spacing, so a hydraulic hammer makes slow progress and blasting or rock trenching is usually needed for long runs. Weathered granite near the surface becomes decomposed granite (DG, grus) that digs like dense sand. Granite contains a lot of quartz, so breaking, drilling and sawing it creates respirable crystalline silica dust: use water and the controls in OSHA Table 1 (see osha library). Trap and granite chips are very sharp; keep blasted or hammered fragments out of the pipe zone and bed pipe on at least the specified cushion of granular bedding. Building codes give crystalline bedrock a presumptive bearing of 12,000 psf.
field.title: Granite, basalt and trap rock in the trench (hard igneous rock)
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice; IBC/CBC Table 1806.2 (12,000 psf)

field.text: Limestone (gray to tan, fizzes strongly with dilute acid) and dolomite (similar but fizzes only weakly unless powdered) are common bedrock across the Midwest, Appalachian valleys, Texas Hill Country, Florida, Kentucky, Tennessee and Missouri. Thin-bedded or weathered limestone often rips or hammers out; massive limestone can need blasting. ProjectEngineer lists limestone swell at about 67%. Limestone dissolves in groundwater, creating karst: pinnacles and slots of rock with soft clay between (rock surface can jump 10 ft or more in a few feet of trench), solution channels, caves, and sinkholes. Karst problems for pipe work: sudden voids under the trench, clay-filled slots where you expected rock, water lost or gained suddenly, and new sinkholes triggered by leaking pipes, dewatering or concentrated stormwater. Bridge voids with concrete or flowable fill or graded stone as the engineer directs, and keep pipe joints tight to avoid washing soil into openings.
field.title: Limestone and dolomite: ledge rock, karst, sinkholes and voids
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: ProjectEngineer swell table; standard karst geology practice

field.text: Shale is thin-layered sedimentary rock made of clay and silt; mudstone and claystone are similar without the fine layering. Fresh shale is often rippable and can be dug with a rock bucket, but it varies from soft to hard. Key behaviors: slaking (it breaks down into flakes and mud when exposed to air and water cycles, so a trench wall or bottom that looked like rock turns to clay within days); some shales swell (expansive clay shales such as the Pierre and Bearpaw in the Plains, and others in Texas and Colorado); and slabs slide along bedding planes that dip toward the trench. ProjectEngineer lists shale and soft rock swell at about 65%. Practical tips: minimize the time trench walls and bottoms are exposed, keep water off the bottom, remove slaked material before bedding, don't reuse shale chips as embedment unless allowed, and watch for wedge failures along bedding and joints. Black shales may also contain pyrite that can produce acid drainage and sulfate attack.
field.title: Shale and mudstone: soft rock that slakes and swells
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: ProjectEngineer swell table; Standard geology and excavation practice

field.text: Sandstone is cemented sand; how hard it digs depends almost entirely on the cement.
