Poorly cemented sandstone crumbles in your hand and digs like dense sand; silica- or iron-cemented sandstone can be very hard and abrasive, wearing teeth and hammer tools fast. Conglomerate is cemented gravel and cobbles; it can break out into large blocks. ProjectEngineer lists sandstone swell at about 54%. Field notes: sandstone is often fractured in blocks along joints and bedding, so it may rip well; massive, quartz-cemented sandstone may need blasting. Water often flows along bedding planes and fractures in sandstone. Sandstone is mostly quartz, so drilling, hammering, sawing and blasting create respirable silica dust; control with water and follow OSHA Table 1 practices (see osha library).
field.title: Sandstone and conglomerate in excavation
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: ProjectEngineer swell table; Standard geology and excavation practice

field.text: Metamorphic rocks are common in New England, the Piedmont, the Appalachians, parts of the Rockies and the West. Schist: shiny with mica, splits along foliation; often weathers to slick micaceous soil; rippability depends on whether foliation is steep or flat relative to the ripper pull. Gneiss: banded light and dark, hard like granite, often massive; may need blasting when fresh. Slate: fine-grained, splits into flat plates; moderate hardness; slabs can slide into trenches along cleavage. Quartzite: extremely hard and abrasive (mostly quartz), hard on teeth and hammer tools; often requires blasting; high silica dust hazard. Marble: metamorphosed limestone, softer, fizzes with acid, can have karst-like solution features. Building codes put foliated rock (schist, slate) with sedimentary rock at 4,000 psf presumptive bearing, lower than crystalline rock, because it can split along planes.
field.title: Metamorphic rock: schist, gneiss, slate, quartzite, marble
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice; IBC/CBC Table 1806.2

field.text: Rock weathers from the top down, so most digs move from soil through a transition into fresh rock. Typical profile: residual soil (no rock structure left), saprolite (soil-like material that still shows the original rock's banding and structure; common in the Piedmont from Virginia to Alabama, often MH or SM with mica), weathered rock (partly decomposed, digs with effort, may rip), then fresh rock. Decomposed granite (DG) in California and the Southwest is granite weathered into a coarse sand. Logs describe weathering grades: fresh, slightly, moderately, highly, completely weathered. Problems: boulders of unweathered rock ('corestones') float within saprolite; the rock surface is irregular, so auger refusal at one boring means little at the next; relict joints in saprolite can slide in trench walls even when it looks like soil. Contract rock definitions matter here: weathered rock that a large excavator can dig is usually not pay rock.
field.title: Weathered rock, residual soil, saprolite and decomposed granite
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice

field.text: Field hardness checks help describe rock and predict wear and digging difficulty. Mohs hardness scale (1 softest to 10 hardest): talc 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, feldspar 6, quartz 7, topaz 8, corundum 9, diamond 10. Field tools: fingernail about 2.5, copper coin about 3.5, steel knife or glass about 5.5, steel file about 6.5. Quick tests: if a knife scratches it easily, it is soft (calcite, limestone, shale, gypsum); if the rock scratches glass or the knife, it contains quartz or feldspar (granite, quartzite, chert, hard sandstone) and will be abrasive on teeth, hammer tools, saw chains and drill bits. Geotech logs also use field strength terms based on a geologist's hammer: one blow breaks it (weak), several blows (strong), many blows or it rings (very strong). High quartz content also means more silica dust when broken.
field.title: Rock hardness: Mohs scale and quick field scratch tests
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Mohs scale (standard mineralogy); field rock description practice

field.text: Engineers use seismic refraction (P-wave velocity) to estimate rippability. FHWA's guide, citing the Caterpillar Handbook of Ripping, says above about 2,000 m/s (about 6,600 ft/s) a D9 dozer is not enough and a larger tractor is needed, and a D11 can still rip some rocks near 3,000 m/s (about 9,800 ft/s). Factors that make rock easier to rip: frequent fractures, faults and laminations, weathering, moisture, high stratification, brittleness, low strength. Harder to rip: massive rock with no planes of weakness, crystalline rock (igneous), high strength. Ranking: sedimentary most rippable, metamorphic variable, igneous hardest. Wyoming DOT cautions that velocity alone ignores hardness, weathering, joint spacing and dip, and that moisture and fractures affect velocity readings, so use it with borings and test pits. For utility trenches, the relevant machine is usually an excavator with ripper tooth or hammer, not a dozer, so treat dozer rippability as a relative guide.
field.title: Rippability and seismic velocity: when a dozer can rip and when to blast
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: FHWA Central Federal Lands geophysical methods manual, Determining Rippability of Rocks (citing Caterpillar Handbook of Ripping, 8th ed.); Wyoming DOT Rock Rippability research proposal

field.text: Main options and where they fit: (1) Rock bucket and big excavator: weathered rock, soft shale, caliche, frost; cheapest when it works. (2) Ripper tooth (single shank) on excavator: fractured or bedded rock; break, then dig with the bucket. (3) Hydraulic hammer (hoe ram): short runs, structures, service trenches, trimming after blasting, rock near utilities or buildings where blasting isn't allowed; slow in hard massive rock. (4) Rock trencher or rock wheel saw (chain or wheel with carbide teeth): long straight runs in moderate rock, makes a clean narrow cut and small spoil; limited depth and width. (5) Drill and blast: long runs of hard rock; fastest per foot but needs licensed blaster, permits, pre-blast surveys and vibration monitoring. (6) Non-explosive methods: expansive grout in drilled holes, hydraulic rock splitters, or plasma/pneumatic breakers near sensitive structures. Hammer care is in the equipment file; estimating rock is in the estimating file.
field.title: Rock excavation methods for pipe trenches: compared
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice; equipment manufacturer practice

field.text: Blasting is done only by a licensed blaster under OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart U and state and local rules. For pipe crews: expect a pre-blast survey of nearby buildings, wells and utilities; vibration and airblast monitoring with seismographs; limits on charge per delay set from distance (scaled distance) and a peak particle velocity limit in the specs (the USBM RI 8507 curve allows 0.5 in/s for plaster and 0.75 in/s for drywall homes at low frequency, up to 2.0 in/s above 40 Hz; specs commonly set 0.5 to 2 in/s, tighter near wells, pipelines and fresh concrete); blasting mats or backfill cover to control flyrock in trenches; and notice to residents and utility owners. On site: obey the blaster's warning signals and clearance zone, no radios or cell transmissions near electric caps if the blaster says so, never dig into or pick through rock where a misfire may remain until the blaster clears it, and check existing utilities for damage after shots. Blasted rock swells about 65% (ProjectEngineer) and needs over-excavation below grade for bedding.
field.title: Drilling and blasting for trenches: what the crew needs to know
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart U (blasting and use of explosives) scope; ProjectEngineer swell table; common blasting specification practice (limits vary); USBM RI 8507 (Siskind et al. 1980) safe vibration criteria; OSM 30 CFR 816.67

field.text: Where blasting is not allowed (near buildings, live gas, water mains, schools) or for small volumes, rock can be split without explosives. Expansive demolition agents (soundless chemical demolition grout) are mixed with water and poured into drilled holes (often 1.25 to 2 inch diameter at spacing set by the maker); they expand over hours to a day and crack the rock. Hydraulic rock splitters push wedges into drilled holes and split rock immediately. Both are slow but quiet, with no flyrock or vibration. Safety: expansive agents get very hot and can blow out of holes ('blowout') if used in hot weather or wrong hole size; wear eye protection and never look down a loaded hole. Wet expansive grout is caustic like cement. Follow the manufacturer's temperature charts, hole size and spacing, and keep people clear until cracking finishes. After splitting, remove with hammer and bucket.
field.title: Non-explosive rock breaking: expansive grout and hydraulic splitters
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Manufacturer practice for expansive demolition agents and hydraulic splitters (check product instructions)

field.text: Size terms (USCS practice): cobbles are about 3 to 12 inches; boulders are larger than 12 inches. Many contracts define 'rock' for pay as boulders over a set volume (often 1/2 to 1 CY) or over a size that can't be removed by the excavator bucket, plus ledge rock that requires hammering or blasting. Field rules: keep boulders and cobbles out of the pipe zone and usually out of the first 1 to 2 ft of backfill above the pipe (specs often limit stone size near pipe to about 1 to 3 inches and higher up to 6 to 12 inches); boulders sticking out of trench walls are struck-by hazards and must be removed or secured (OSHA 1926.651(j) requires protection from loose rock and soil); boulders in glacial till can be undermined and drop when you dig beneath them. Large boulders in spoil piles can roll back toward the trench; keep spoil 2 ft back. Measure, photograph and log boulders for pay or change orders.
field.title: Boulders and cobbles: definitions, handling and pay
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: USCS size definitions; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(j); common specification practice (size limits vary)

field.text: Whether rock is paid extra depends entirely on the contract's definition. Common forms: (1) Material that can't be removed by a specified excavator (for example a track excavator of a certain weight or horsepower with rock bucket) without ripping, hammering or blasting; (2) boulders over a set volume, often 1/2 or 1 CY; (3) material requiring drilling and blasting, or a hydraulic hammer of a specified size; (4) some contracts include all excavation, rock or not, in the pipe unit price ('unclassified excavation'). Pay limits usually set a maximum width (for example pipe OD plus 2 ft) and depth (for example 6 inches below pipe) for rock measurement. What to do: read the definition before digging, notify the engineer as soon as you hit rock, let them verify that the specified equipment can't dig it, and measure the rock surface and pay limits together daily. Without that, claims are hard to win. Contract governs; general guidance only.
field.title: Rock definitions in contracts: pay rock vs common excavation
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Common agency specification practice (contract governs; not legal advice)

field.text: Rock trenches are not automatically safe. OSHA lets stable rock be cut vertically, but rock that is fractured, weathered, bedded toward the trench, or loosened by blasting or hammering can drop slabs and wedges. Submerged rock that isn't stable is classed with Type C soil, and soil overburden above a rock cut still needs sloping, benching or shielding. Practices: scale loose rock off walls with the bucket before anyone enters; watch for open cracks parallel to the trench (tension cracks) and joints dipping into the trench; keep spoil back at least 2 ft; check walls after every blast, rain or freeze-thaw and at each shift; and protect workers from rock falling from the face (OSHA 1926.651(j)). The competent person decides whether the rock is stable; if in doubt, use a box or shoring. See the OSHA excavation library for the exact rules.
field.title: Rock trench wall and bottom safety
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P (stable rock definition, 1926.651(j)), plain-language summary; see osha library

field.text: Most rock contains crystalline silica (quartz): granite, sandstone, quartzite, chert, shale and slate in significant amounts; limestone and marble usually less. Hammering, drilling, sawing, crushing and blasting rock creates fine respirable dust that causes silicosis, lung cancer and kidney disease, often years later. OSHA's construction silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153) applies, and its Table 1 lists controls for tasks like handheld drills, jackhammers, rig-mounted rock drills, and hydraulic hammers on equipment: usually water sprays at the point of impact, dust collection, enclosed cabs with filtered air, and respirators for some tasks. Keep people out of the dust cloud, run water on the hammer point, and keep cab doors closed. See the osha silica library for task-specific requirements.
field.title: Silica dust from rock and concrete breaking
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica in construction (summary; see osha library)

field.text: Northeast and Great Lakes conditions crews commonly meet: glacial till (dense, with cobbles and boulders) over shallow bedrock ('ledge' in New England: granite, gneiss, schist), glacial outwash sands and gravels that carry lots of groundwater, varved lake clays in valleys (Connecticut and Hudson valleys, Great Lakes basins), and sensitive marine clays along coastal Maine and New Hampshire. Expect boulders in nearly every trench, rock surface that changes fast, perched water on till, and running sand in outwash. Frost depths are deep (often 4 to 6 ft or more for water mains), and frost-susceptible silts and tills heave pavement. Older cities (Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland) have thick urban fill with brick, ash and old foundations. Plan for rock and boulder pay items, dewatering in outwash, and frost-safe backfill under roads.
field.title: Regional US geology: Northeast, New England and Great Lakes (glacial ground)
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice (regional generalization; always use project borings)

field.text: Southeast conditions: The Piedmont (Virginia through the Carolinas, Georgia and Alabama) has red clay residual soils over saprolite and weathered rock (granite, gneiss, schist), micaceous silts (MH) that are slick and hard to compact, and corestone boulders; the rock line is irregular, so expect partial-face rock. The Fall Line separates it from the Coastal Plain, which has sands, silty and clayey sands, marine clays and high water tables; wellpoints and running sand are common. Florida and south Georgia: fine sands (A-3, SP), shallow water table, muck and peat in low areas, and limestone near the surface with karst sinkholes and solution cavities. Gulf Coast (Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, coastal Texas): soft clays, organic deltaic soils, high water tables, and fat expansive clays in places. Iron-cemented sandstone layers ('ironstone') occur in some Coastal Plain areas.
field.title: Regional US geology: Southeast Piedmont, Coastal Plain and Florida
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice; Georgia DOT lime guideline (Fall Line, micaceous soils) (regional generalization; always use project borings)

field.text: Texas and the Great Plains: much of Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, San Antonio and Austin areas have high-plasticity expansive clays (blackland prairie, gumbo, CH soils) that shrink and swell, plus limestone and chalk (Austin Chalk) and shale bedrock. Houston has soft to stiff clays, high groundwater and active faults. Oklahoma, Kansas and Nebraska: loess, clay soils and shale and limestone bedrock. Colorado Front Range (Denver area) and Wyoming, Montana and the Dakotas: bentonitic claystone and clay shales (such as the Pierre Shale) with very high swell, slaking shale, and sulfate soils that can heave lime- or cement-treated subgrades. West Texas and New Mexico: caliche, collapsible soils and sulfates. Utility implications: expansive clay demands select backfill and moisture control; sulfate testing before lime treatment; shale exposure time kept short.
field.title: Regional US geology: Texas, Great Plains and Front Range (expansive clay and shale)
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice (regional generalization; always use project borings)

field.text: Midwest conditions: glacial till plains across Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota and Wisconsin (lean clay tills with sand lenses and boulders), outwash sand and gravel along river valleys (water-bearing; wellpoints), and loess caps along the Missouri and Mississippi (Iowa, Nebraska, Missouri, Illinois, western Kentucky and Tennessee, Mississippi bluffs). Below the glacial deposits, bedrock is often limestone, dolomite and shale; karst is common in southern Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Tennessee and parts of Iowa, Wisconsin and Minnesota. River bottoms (the American Bottom near St. Louis, the Mississippi floodplain) have soft clays, silts and high groundwater, and the New Madrid area has liquefiable sands. Frost depth for water mains is often 4 to 6 ft or more in the northern Midwest. Typical crew issues: silty clay that pumps when wet, loess that stands vertical then collapses, karst voids, and outwash running sand.
field.title: Regional US geology: Midwest, Mississippi Valley and loess country
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Standard geology and excavation practice; Iowa Geological Survey loess review (regional generalization; always use project borings)

field.text: Southwest (Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Southern California, Utah): alluvial fan deposits with cobbles and boulders, caliche layers, collapsible soils that settle 2 to 3 ft when wetted (Caltrans), gypsum and sulfate soils, and deep water tables (though perched water sits on caliche). California: decomposed granite, alluvium, expansive clays in valleys, bay mud (very soft organic clay) around San Francisco Bay, and liquefiable sands near the coast and rivers. Pacific Northwest (Seattle, Portland): dense glacial till ('hardpan') and outwash in the Puget Sound area, soft lake and river silts, landslide-prone slopes, and basalt in eastern Washington and Oregon; Palouse loess in eastern Washington and Idaho. Rocky Mountains: shallow rock of every type, boulders and talus. Alaska: permafrost (frozen ground that thaws and settles when disturbed), glacial silt and very deep frost. Earthquake zones add liquefaction risk to saturated loose sands and silts.
field.title: Regional US geology: West, Southwest, Pacific Northwest, Alaska
field.topic: Geology and rock excavation for utility crews
field.source: Caltrans collapsible soil manual; Standard geology and excavation practice (regional generalization; always use project borings)

field.text: Wheel loaders (front-end loaders, rubber-tire loaders, 'the loader') move and load loose material. Rough classes: compact loaders with about 0.5 to 2 CY buckets; small to mid-size loaders about 2 to 4 CY (the common utility-job size, like 924/938/950 or 444/544/644 class); large loaders 5 CY and up for quarries and big stockpiles. On pipe jobs a loader feeds bedding stone to the trench, backfills, loads trucks from stockpiles, carries pipe on forks, and cleans up. Wheel loaders are fast between stockpiles and easy on pavement, but weak in soft ground. Quick couplers let them switch between bucket, forks and grapple. Carry loads low, about 12 to 18 in off the ground, when traveling, especially on slopes.
field.title: Wheel loader sizes and uses
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets (typical values)

field.text: Loader spec sheets give static tipping load, measured straight and at full articulation (full turn). With a bucket, rated operating load for wheel loaders is commonly 50% of the full-turn static tipping load (ISO 14397-1 / SAE practice). With pallet forks the rating is a higher percentage of the full-turn tipping load measured at the fork load center, commonly 80% on firm, level ground and 60% on rough terrain, so read the fork column, not the bucket column. A full bucket of wet clay or stone can be at or over rated load, so a bigger bucket doesn't always mean more production. Tipping risk rises when turning with a raised load, on slopes, and on soft ground. Forks: keep the load against the backrest, know the load center, and don't hang chains off the fork tips unless the maker allows it. Check your machine's load chart for the attachment you are using.
field.title: Wheel loader rated load and tipping
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: SAE J818 / ISO 14397 rating approach as summarized in manufacturer literature; check your machine

field.text: Track loaders (crawler loaders, 'a 953', 'a 963') are loaders on a crawler undercarriage. They push like a small dozer, dig and load from the bank, work in mud and on rough sites where a wheel loader would bog down, and many have a 4-in-1 (multipurpose) bucket that opens like a clam for grabbing, dozing and back-dragging. On utility work they excavate manhole pits, strip topsoil, backfill, spread stone and load trucks on tight or soft sites. They travel slowly, damage pavement with steel tracks, and their undercarriage wears fast if run at high speed or in reverse on hard ground. OSHA requires ROPS and seat belts on crawler loaders.
field.title: Track loaders (crawler loaders)
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; OSHA 1926.1000 and 1926.602(a)(2)

field.text: Bulldozers (dozers, crawler tractors, 'the cat') push material. Small dozers (around D3 to D5 size, about 18,000 to 30,000 lb) are common on utility and site jobs for stripping topsoil, spreading stone and backfill, building haul roads and pads, rough-grading easements and pushing spoil back into the trench; mid-size dozers (D6 class, about 45,000 to 55,000 lb) handle mass grading and pushing scrapers; large dozers (D8 and up) rip rock and do heavy push work. Low-ground-pressure (LGP) versions with wide tracks work in swamps and soft soil. Many now have GPS machine control for grade. Dozers should not backfill directly on pipe until the specified cover is in place; heavy tracks can crush or shift pipe.
field.title: Dozer sizes and uses on utility jobs
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets (typical values)

field.text: Common blades: straight (S) blade, short with no wings, for fine grading, leveling and general earthmoving; universal (U) blade, tall and curved with big side wings, for carrying large loads over long pushes; semi-universal (SU), a curved blade with short wings, a middle ground for varied material; angle blade, which pivots left or right to cast material to one side for backfilling, side-casting and cutting slopes; and the power-angle-tilt or 6-way (PAT, VPAT) blade on small dozers, adjustable for angle, tilt and lift from the cab, popular for finish grading and utility backfill. A blade too heavy for the dozer makes it nose-heavy and hard to control. Choose by material, push distance and how fine the grade must be.
field.title: Dozer blade types: S, U, SU, angle and 6-way
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Caterpillar blade selection guidance; industry practice

field.text: A ripper is a rear-mounted shank (single shank for hard rock, multi-shank for softer or layered material) that a dozer drags through rock, hardpan, frost or old pavement to break it up so it can be pushed or dug. Single-shank rippers on larger dozers can make some rock rippable that would otherwise need blasting. Rippability is judged from rock type, fractures and seismic velocity tests; makers publish rippability charts by dozer size. On utility jobs, ripping along the trench line ahead of the excavator can greatly speed digging in weathered rock and frost. Rip in first gear at low speed, keep tips and shank protectors replaced, and pothole and mark utilities first: a ripper shank hooks and pulls cables and pipes.
field.title: Dozer rippers
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Manufacturer literature (rippability charts); industry practice

field.text: Skid steer loaders (SSL, 'Bobcat') are small wheeled loaders that steer by skidding; compact track loaders (CTL) are the same idea on rubber tracks, with better flotation and traction and less damage to lawns. They're the utility crew's handy machine: moving bedding stone in tight spots, backfill and cleanup, carrying pipe on forks, grading yards and driveways, sweeping, and running attachments. Radial-lift arms give more reach at mid-height and are good for digging and grading; vertical-lift arms give more reach and capacity at full height, better for loading trucks and pallets. Rated operating capacities range from about 1,300 lb on small units to over 3,500 lb on large ones. Most are ROPS/FOPS-equipped with a seat bar or belt that locks out the controls when raised.
field.title: Skid steers and compact track loaders: what they do
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets

field.text: Rated operating capacity (ROC) is the load the machine is rated to lift and carry. Under the SAE J818 / ISO 14397 approach, wheeled skid steers are rated at 50% of static tipping load, and compact track loaders at 35% of tipping load (track machines are more stable, so the factor is lower; some older spec sheets used 50% for CTLs too, so compare carefully). Example: a CTL with 8,600 lb tipping load has an ROC of about 3,000 lb. The ROC assumes a standard bucket and load center; forks, grapples and long attachments move the load center forward and cut capacity. A pallet of pipe fittings or a stack of 6-in PVC can exceed ROC quickly. Don't add counterweight beyond what the maker allows to beat the rating.
field.title: Skid steer and CTL rated operating capacity (ROC)
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: SAE J818 rating method as summarized in industry guides; manufacturer spec sheets

field.text: NIOSH has documented many skid-steer deaths where the operator was crushed between the lift arms or bucket and the machine frame, usually after leaving the seat or reaching outside the cab with the arms raised, or after a bypassed seat-bar or interlock let the controls move. Practices from NIOSH and maker manuals: enter and exit only with the bucket flat on the ground and the engine off, or use the lift-arm support device if the arms must be up for service; never bypass the seat bar, seat switch or interlocks; keep the seat belt and seat bar down; never reach out of the cab while the engine runs; carry loads low and travel straight up and down slopes with the heavy end uphill; and don't let anyone stand near the raised bucket or ride on the machine.
field.title: Skid steer safety: crush points and leaving the seat
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: NIOSH Alert: Preventing Injuries and Deaths from Skid-Steer Loaders (summary); manufacturer operator manuals

field.text: Attachments that pay off on pipe and site work: pallet forks (pipe, fittings, manhole adjusting rings); grapple bucket (debris, logs, broken concrete); 4-in-1 bucket; auger (fence posts, sign posts, test holes); hydraulic breaker (concrete and asphalt patches); trencher (shallow conduit, irrigation, electrical); cold planer (milling asphalt around patches and structures); angle broom or pickup sweeper (street cleanup, required by many permits); vibratory roller or plate compactor attachments (patches and small areas); landscape rake and tiller (lawn restoration); and snow pushes. High-flow attachments (planers, mulchers, some trenchers) need a high-flow machine; check gpm and psi. Every attachment changes the ROC, so check its weight.
field.title: Skid steer and CTL attachments for utility work
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer attachment catalogs

field.text: Motor graders (blades, maintainers, 'the grader') have a long moldboard (commonly 12 to 14 ft on construction graders) mounted under the frame between the front and rear axles, letting them cut and spread thin layers to tight grade. Uses: fine grading subgrade and base before paving, building road crowns and cross slopes, cutting and cleaning ditches (moldboard tipped up on the bank), spreading aggregate base, and maintaining haul roads. Many have front blades, rear rippers or scarifiers, articulated frames and GPS or laser grade control. On utility jobs a grader usually shows up for road restoration and base prep rather than the pipe work itself. A grader is not for heavy pushing or digging; that's a dozer's job.
field.title: Motor graders: what they do on utility and site jobs
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer literature

field.text: Scrapers (pans, 'earthmovers') load, haul and spread dirt in one machine. Types: open-bowl single-engine scrapers usually push-loaded by a dozer; twin-engine (tandem-powered) scrapers that self-load better and climb grades; push-pull scrapers that hook together to help each other load; and elevating scrapers with a paddle elevator that self-load and spread smoothly. Heaped bowl capacities run roughly 11 CY on small models up to about 44 CY on the largest twin-engine models. Scrapers are economical for mass grading over haul distances of roughly a few hundred feet up to around a mile or so; shorter is dozer work, longer is truck work. They're common on subdivision and highway jobs and rare on trench work. Haul roads need maintenance by a grader and water truck to keep cycle times fast.
field.title: Scrapers: open bowl, elevating and push-pull
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets (typical values)

field.text: Match the compactor to the soil. Smooth-drum vibratory rollers: granular soils (sand, gravel, crushed stone base) and mixed soils; Bomag guidance puts the limit at roughly 10% cohesive (clay) content. Padfoot (tamping foot) vibratory rollers: cohesive and mixed soils, up to roughly 50% cohesive content; the pads knead and compact from the bottom up and top down. Sheepsfoot rollers: static (no vibration), often towed, for clay and silt; many passes needed. Pneumatic (rubber-tire) rollers: kneading action for granular base and asphalt, also good for proof rolling to find soft spots. For trenches: vibratory plates on granular, rammers (jumping jacks) on cohesive and in tight areas, and remote trench rollers (padfoot) on wider trenches. Use test strips and density tests to confirm.
field.title: Compactor types: which roller for which soil
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Stormwater/GX Contractor 'How to Select a Soil Roller' (Bomag, Caterpillar, Volvo guidance)

field.text: Vibratory compactors shake the drum or plate at a set frequency (vibrations per minute, vpm, or hertz) and amplitude (how far the drum moves, in inches or mm). Rule of thumb from roller makers: granular material or thin lifts get high frequency and low amplitude; cohesive material or thick lifts get low frequency and high amplitude. Volvo notes most vibratory soil compactors offer settings from about 1,200 to 2,500 vpm, and units 7 tons and up often have two amplitudes from about 0.015 to 0.080 in. Caterpillar's travel-speed rule is about one impact per inch (25 mm) of travel: too fast leaves washboarding, too slow wastes time. If the roller starts bouncing violently ('double-jumping' or decoupling) the material is at max density for that setting; drop to low amplitude. Running vibes in static is pointless on soil.
field.title: Vibration frequency and amplitude basics
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Stormwater/GX Contractor 'How to Select a Soil Roller' (Caterpillar, Volvo, Bomag guidance)

field.text: Loose lift thickness has to match the compactor or the bottom of the lift won't reach density no matter how many passes. Typical ranges (your spec and test strip govern): rammers (jumping jacks) about 4 to 6 in, up to 8 to 10 in on large rammers in cohesive soil; light vibratory plates about 4 to 6 in of granular; heavy reversible plates about 8 to 12 in of granular; walk-behind and remote trench rollers about 6 to 12 in; ride-on vibratory smooth-drum rollers 8 to 12 in on most DOT embankment specs, thicker on rock fill with big rollers; padfoot rollers about 6 to 12 in in clay. Many DOT and city specs simply say 8 in loose lifts for embankment and 6 in in the pipe zone. In the pipe zone, check the pipe spec: impact tampers are kept off plastic pipe until about 12 in of cover.
field.title: Lift thickness by compactor (typical guidance)
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; compactor manufacturer guidance; DOT specifications (typical; check yours)

field.text: Pneumatic-tired rollers (rubber-tire rollers) have staggered rows of smooth tires (often 7 to 11) that knead the surface; ballast and adjustable tire pressure change the contact pressure. They're used on granular base, chip seal and asphalt (to seal the surface), and for proof rolling. Proof rolling means running a heavy rubber-tired vehicle, often a loaded tandem dump truck or a heavy pneumatic roller, slowly over subgrade or backfilled trench while an inspector watches for rutting, pumping or deflection (soft spots). Many specs call for proof rolling backfilled trenches under paving. Soft spots get undercut and replaced or recompacted before base goes down. Check your spec for the vehicle weight, tire pressure and acceptance limits.
field.title: Pneumatic rollers and proof rolling
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Industry practice; DOT specifications (typical)

field.text: Telehandlers (telescopic handlers, reach forklifts, 'lull' after a brand) are rough-terrain forklifts with a telescoping boom. Uses: unloading pipe and precast, setting manhole sections on smaller jobs, moving pallets and fittings, and placing material over obstacles. Each telehandler has a load chart by boom angle and extension; capacity drops fast as the boom extends. Stabilizers (outriggers) if equipped raise capacity; frame leveling (sway) should be done only with the boom low. Operators need forklift training under OSHA 1926.602(d) and 1910.178. When a telehandler is configured with a winch and hook to hoist and move a suspended load, OSHA treats it as a crane (1926.1400(c)(8)); fork-mounted lifting jibs without powered hoisting fall under the attachment's own load chart. Use only maker-approved attachments with their charts.
field.title: Telehandlers on utility sites
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: OSHA 1926.1400(c)(8); OSHA interpretation letter June 21, 2012; manufacturer operator manuals

field.text: Telehandler tip-overs happen when the boom is extended with a load on uneven or soft ground, when the operator levels the frame with the boom raised, when driving with the load high, or when the load is heavier than the chart at that extension. Practices: know the load weight; read the load chart for the exact attachment; level the frame before raising the boom; set stabilizers on firm ground or pads; travel with the boom retracted and the load low; drive straight up and down slopes with the load uphill; watch the load moment indicator if fitted; keep the seat belt on, and if it starts to tip, stay in the cab, brace and lean away (don't jump). Never lift people except on an approved platform used per the maker.
field.title: Telehandler stability and tip-overs
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; ANSI/ITSDF B56.6 (summary)

field.text: Rollers and compactors kill operators by rolling off embankment edges, trench edges and slopes, and kill ground workers by running over them, especially when backing. OSHA ROPS rules now cover compactors manufactured after July 15, 2019, and many older ones have ROPS: wear the seat belt so you stay inside the protective zone. Practices: keep the drum back from unsupported edges (rule of thumb at least the drum width, more on soft edges), roll edges with the drum parallel to the edge only after the edge is confined, mark drop-offs, and never jump from a tipping roller. OSHA 1926.602(a)(9) requires a horn on bidirectional machines like rollers and a backup alarm or spotter when the rear view is obstructed. Keep walkers clear of the drum.
field.title: Compactor rollover and runover hazards
field.topic: Heavy equipment: loaders, dozers, graders, scrapers, compactors
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1000(a), 1926.602(a)(9); industry practice

field.text: Excavators are sorted by operating weight. Common US usage (makers draw the lines a little differently): mini or compact excavator, under about 6 metric tons (roughly 13,000 lb), e.g. 1 to 5 ton machines; midi excavator, about 6 to 10 tons (13,000 to 22,000 lb), like the 8-ton class; standard or full-size, about 10 to 45 tons (22,000 to 100,000 lb), with the 20-ton (320/210/220 class) and 30 to 36-ton machines being the workhorses for mainline sewer and water; large or mass excavation machines, 45 tons and up. Crews also call them hoes, trackhoes, diggers or by model number (a '320', a '35 Deere'). Size choice is driven by depth, the box and pipe weight you must lift, and how much room you have on the street. Check the spec sheet for your exact machine.
field.title: Excavator size classes: mini, midi, standard, large
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets

field.text: Rough maximum dig depths with a standard boom and stick (long sticks add a few feet, short sticks lose some): 1-ton mini about 5 to 7 ft; 3-ton mini about 9 to 10 ft; 5-ton about 11 to 12.5 ft; 8-ton midi about 14 to 15.5 ft; 14-ton about 17 to 19 ft; 20 to 23-ton class (a '320' or '210' size) roughly 20 to 23 ft; 30-ton class roughly 23 to 25 ft; 36 to 50-ton class roughly 24 to 27 ft. Big machines often get heavy-duty short sticks, so depth doesn't always grow with weight, and exact figures change with model year, boom and stick, so read your machine's spec sheet and working range diagram. Plan pipe work at least 2 to 4 ft shallower than max depth: at full reach the machine digs slowly, can't curl a full bucket and lifts poorly, and a trench box and bedding stone add depth.
field.title: Excavator dig depth by size (rough ranges)
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Cat model specs as compiled by Heavy Equipment Guide; mini/midi ranges from manufacturer spec sheets (typical)

field.text: Mini excavators (about 1 to 6 tons) are used for service laterals, water services, potholing around utilities, tight backyards, hand-dig assist and cleanup. Most have a dozer blade (backfill and stabilizer), rubber tracks (won't tear up pavement or lawns), and many are zero-tail-swing. A 3 to 4-ton mini usually tows behind a 3/4 or 1-ton pickup on a tag trailer, but check machine plus trailer weight against your truck's towing rating and whether the combination needs a CDL (combined gross over 26,000 lb with a trailer over 10,000 lb). Limits: they tip easily when lifting over the side, have small lift capacity, and most only dig 8 to 12 ft. Always lift over the blade end with the blade down when you can; lift charts are higher there. Keep the seat belt on: minis roll over on slopes and trench edges.
field.title: Mini excavators on utility work
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; FMCSA CDL class definitions (49 CFR 383.91) summarized

field.text: Midi excavators (about 13,000 to 22,000 lb, the 7 to 10-ton class) fill the gap between minis and 20-ton machines. They're popular for water and gas services, storm inlets, short sewer runs, and tight streets where a 20-ton machine would block the lane. They typically dig 13 to 16 ft, often come with a blade, and many are reduced or zero tail swing. Most need a tag trailer with a 1-ton dually or medium truck, or a gooseneck; watch trailer and towing ratings. Lifting is the weak spot: a light 8-foot trench box plus a stick of pipe may be over the chart at working radius. Compare the lift chart with your heaviest box, plate or structure before choosing a midi for mainline work.
field.title: Midi excavators (6 to 10 ton class)
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets

field.text: Tail swing is how far the counterweight sticks out past the tracks when the house rotates. Conventional machines swing well outside the track width, which is a struck-by and property-damage hazard on streets. Zero tail swing (ZTS) machines keep the counterweight inside the track width; reduced tail swing (RTS) or short-radius machines (often marked 'SR' or 'CR' in model names) swing only a few inches past. Pros: you can work with one lane closed, beside a wall, a building or traffic barrier, and the operator doesn't hit things behind him. Cons: less counterweight means lower lift capacity over the side, a heavier front end, and cramped cabs on small models. Even with ZTS the front (boom and bucket) still swings: barricade the work zone anyway.
field.title: Zero tail swing and reduced tail swing excavators
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer literature

field.text: Crawler (track) excavators are the standard for pipe work: more stable when lifting, better flotation in mud, can travel over spoil and rough ground. Steel tracks (triple-grouser shoes) grip best and last in rock; rubber tracks or rubber pads on steel shoes protect pavement but cost more and wear faster. Wheel (rubber-tire) excavators drive between sites at 20 to 25 mph, work well on city streets and paved areas, and use outriggers and/or a blade for stability; lift charts are given with outriggers up and down, and the difference is large. Wheel excavators usually can't work steep or soft ground. Shoe width matters too: wide (pad) shoes for soft ground, narrow shoes for rock and steep side slopes. Lift charts change with shoe width and undercarriage, so read the right column.
field.title: Tracks versus wheels on excavators
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer literature

field.text: Common buckets: general purpose (GP) or digging bucket with teeth for most soils; heavy-duty and severe-duty or rock buckets with thicker wear plates, side cutters and penetrating teeth for rock, cobbles and frost; trenching buckets, narrow and deep for small pipe and services; ditch cleaning or grading buckets, wide with a smooth edge and no teeth, for shaping ditch slopes, fine grading and stripping (tilting versions for slopes); clean-up buckets for bedding stone; skeleton (sifting) buckets to separate rocks from backfill; V-buckets for ditches; and clamshell buckets for digging inside manhole boxes or shafts. Use a smooth-edge bucket or bolt-on edge when digging near marked utilities or shaping bedding. Bucket weight counts against your lift chart.
field.title: Excavator bucket types for trench work
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer attachment catalogs

field.text: Pick bucket width from the trench width the spec calls for at the top of pipe, not the biggest bucket that fits. Typical widths: minis 12 to 36 in; 8-ton class 18 to 42 in; 20-ton class 24 to 48 in (60 in cleanup); 30 to 36-ton 30 to 60 in. Bucket width is measured across the cutting edge; teeth and side cutters can add 1 to 4 in, so the real trench comes out wider. Common pipe-spec trench widths are pipe OD plus 1 to 2 ft (check the plans and pipe standard). If you are using a trench box, the box inside width must clear the bucket and the pipe with room to work; a box about 1 ft wider than the wider of the pipe or bucket is a common target. Overcut trench means more stone, more spoil and, for rigid pipe, more load on the pipe.
field.title: Bucket width for trenching: matching the trench
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; trench box selection guidance (Equipment World)

field.text: Quick couplers (quick attach, QA) let the operator swap buckets without driving pins. Types: manual pin-grabber (hooks over the bucket's pins, locked with a pin or screw); hydraulic pin-grabber (cab switch, with a mechanical or gravity safety latch that should hold the front pin even if pressure is lost); wedge-lock couplers that pull a wedge against dedicated bucket brackets; and tilt couplers or tiltrotators with standardized S-type interfaces (S40, S60, S70, S80) common in Europe. ISO 13031 is the international safety standard for excavator quick couplers and calls for a positive locking system and a way to confirm lock. A coupler must match the pin diameter, pin spacing and stick width of the attachment; adapters add weight and length. Coupler weight reduces lift capacity and digging force a little.
field.title: Quick coupler types: pin grabber, wedge, tilt
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: ISO 13031 (title and scope, public summaries); manufacturer coupler manuals

field.text: A thumb clamps material against the bucket so the excavator can pick up pipe, rocks, logs, broken concrete and debris. Mechanical (fixed or stiff-arm) thumbs are pinned at set positions; you curl the bucket against them. Hydraulic thumbs run off an auxiliary circuit and can be closed with the load at any bucket position; progressive-link thumbs follow the bucket through its arc. Pin-on thumbs mount on the main bucket pin and work well with couplers. On pipe jobs a thumb is handy for unloading pipe and placing structures, but never pick plastic pipe with a thumb hard enough to crush or gouge it; use slings or a pipe grab. Keep the thumb folded when trenching close to utilities, and remember thumb weight cuts lift capacity.
field.title: Excavator thumbs: hydraulic and mechanical
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer attachment literature

field.text: A tiltrotator mounts between the stick and the attachment so the bucket can tilt (typically about 40 to 45 degrees each way) and rotate 360 degrees. On pipe and utility work it lets the operator dig around crossing utilities, shape bedding, square up manhole excavations and set pipe without repositioning the machine; many add a gripper for picking pipe and small structures. Downsides: costly, add weight (cutting lift capacity and dig depth slightly), more hydraulic maintenance, and need operator training. They're common in Scandinavia and spreading in North America on 6 to 30-ton machines. Many use S-type quick couplers top and bottom; confirm both locks every time, just like a standard coupler.
field.title: Tiltrotators on excavators
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Manufacturer literature; trade press (typical values)

field.text: Choosing a tool for rock in the trench: a rock bucket with penetrating tips handles rippable rock, frost and soft shale; a single-shank ripper tooth on the excavator rips layered or weathered rock so the bucket can follow, and is cheaper and faster than hammering where it works; a hydraulic hammer (breaker, hoe ram) is for hard rock, boulders and concrete; blasting is used for long runs of hard rock where allowed. A common sizing rule of thumb is a hammer weighing roughly 1/10 of the carrier's weight, but always match the maker's carrier range and the machine's auxiliary flow and pressure. Wet or frozen ground and old concrete pipe encasement often need a hammer. Track production (feet per hour) for each method in your rock to choose next time. Breaking concrete makes silica dust: use water and follow Table 1.
field.title: Rock: hammer, ripper tooth or rock bucket?
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer hammer sizing charts (typical)

field.text: Excavator-mounted compaction lets you compact backfill from the top without people in the trench. Vibratory plate (hoe-pack, plate compactor attachment) runs off the auxiliary hydraulics; it works best on granular backfill and needs the right flow and case-drain line per the maker. Compaction wheels (sheepsfoot-type wheels pinned to the stick) have no hydraulics; the operator presses and rolls them along the trench, and they work well in cohesive (clay) backfill. Both can compact thicker lifts than hand equipment, but only to what the maker and your spec allow; many specs still limit loose lift thickness (often 8 to 12 in for embankment, sometimes thicker with test strips). Keep wheel and plate off the pipe until the minimum cover in the pipe spec is in place, and never compact against an unsupported trench wall with workers below.
field.title: Excavator compaction plates and compaction wheels
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer attachment manuals; pipe installation specs (check yours)

field.text: Example using a made-up chart (always use the one in your cab): a 20-ton machine, standard stick, 31.5 in shoes, bucket removed. At 15 ft load radius and 0 ft load point height the chart shows 13,200 lb over the front and 9,400 lb over the side; at 20 ft radius it shows 8,900 front and 6,300 side; ratings marked with an asterisk are hydraulic-limited, unmarked are tipping-limited. Load: a 16-ft by 8-ft steel trench box weighing about 6,500 lb (check the box tag) plus about 300 lb of chains, plus a 1,200 lb bucket and coupler left on. Total about 8,000 lb. That works at 15 ft over the side (9,400) but fails at 20 ft over the side (6,300). So pull the box closer, lift over the front (tracks lined up with the load), or take the bucket off if the chart assumes no bucket.
field.title: Reading an excavator lift chart: worked example
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Worked example built on standard lift-chart practice (ISO 10567 rating method); values illustrative only

field.text: In plain words: OSHA's crane rule (29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC, starting at 1926.1400) lists excavators, power shovels, wheel loaders, backhoes, loader backhoes and track loaders as excluded, and says they are still excluded when used with chains, slings or other rigging to lift suspended loads. The rule text puts no conditions on that exclusion, so an excavator setting pipe, boxes or manholes doesn't need a certified crane operator under Subpart CC. What still applies: the rigging rules in 1926.251; equipment rules in 1926.600 to 602, including the power line clearance in 1926.600(a)(6); the manufacturer's lift chart and operator manual; and the general duty to keep workers out from under loads. Machines that are cranes (boom trucks, truck cranes) and forklifts or telehandlers rigged to hoist with a winch and hook are covered. State plans can be stricter; check yours.
field.title: Excavator lifting and OSHA: is it a crane?
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes

field.text: OSHA 1926.1424 requires crane swing-radius barriers, and while excavators are outside that rule, the struck-by and crushing hazard is the same, so most contractors barricade or mark the area the counterweight sweeps. How: set cones, delineators, caution tape or a rope line at the counterweight's tail-swing distance plus a buffer (often 2 to 3 ft) on the sides and rear, wherever people walk; keep material stockpiles and pipe out of the pinch zone between the counterweight and anything fixed (a wall, truck, pole, box or pipe stack), since workers get crushed there. Rule for the crew: no one enters the swing area until the operator has seen them, stopped, and set the controls or lowered the lockout lever. Operators: look before every swing, and stop when you lose sight of a crew member.
field.title: Swing radius barricades around an excavator
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: OSHA 1926.1424 concept applied by industry practice; field safety practice

field.text: Every modern excavator has a hydraulic lockout lever (safety lever, pilot shutoff, 'gate' or armrest lift-up) that kills the hydraulic controls. Use it every time: before anyone approaches the bucket to hook rigging, change teeth or check grade; before you reach out of the cab or get out; and when traveling on a trailer. Before leaving the seat: lower the bucket or attachment to the ground, set the lockout lever, idle down and shut off, and take the key if the machine will be unattended (OSHA 1926.600(a)(3) requires blades and buckets lowered or blocked when not in use or under repair). Many injuries come from an operator bumping a joystick while leaning out to talk or while a laborer hooks a sling. Rigging hookups: operator hands off the joysticks, lever up, bucket still.
field.title: Excavator safety lever (lockout) and leaving the seat
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.600(a)(3); manufacturer operator manuals

field.text: Long-reach excavators have a much longer boom and stick (often 50 to 70 ft reach on a 20 to 35-ton base) for dredging ponds, cleaning ditches and canals, and digging deep structures from the bank. On pipe jobs they're sometimes used to reach across a creek or set a box from far back. Trade-offs: small bucket, slow cycle, very low lift capacity at reach, and big tipping risk if the operator swings a full bucket out at full length; the long boom also makes power lines a bigger hazard. Don't use a long-reach machine to lift pipe or boxes unless its own lift chart (specific to that front) allows it. Demolition high-reach machines are a separate class with their own counterweights and charts.
field.title: Long-reach and high-reach excavators
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer literature

field.text: A backhoe loader (backhoe, rubber-tire hoe, 'JCB' or 'Case' after the brands) has a front loader bucket (typically about 1 to 1.5 CY) and a rear hoe on a swing frame with stabilizers. Common 14 to 15-ft class machines dig about 14 to 15 ft with a standard dipper and about 17 to 19 ft with an extendahoe (telescoping stick). They drive on roads at about 20 to 25 mph, which makes them good for water service crews, repair crews and municipal work. Limits: the hoe swings only about 180 degrees, lift capacity is modest, and they're less stable than a tracked excavator on uneven ground. Set both stabilizers and lower the loader bucket before digging, and never travel on a slope with the loader bucket raised.
field.title: Backhoe loader basics
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets (typical values)

field.text: Backhoe loader practices from operator manuals: set the stabilizers down on firm ground (pads on asphalt to avoid punching through) and lower the loader bucket so the front tires are just off the ground or loaded, before digging; dig with the seat facing the hoe and the parking brake set; don't swing a loaded bucket downhill on a slope; when roading, raise and lock the stabilizers, put on the boom/swing transport lock, lower the loader bucket to carry height, and turn on lights and beacon; and keep your seat belt on. Backhoes are covered by OSHA's ROPS rules as wheel tractors or loaders, and many rollovers happen while traveling on slopes or banks with the boom swung to the side. Never use the loader bucket as a work platform or to lift people.
field.title: Backhoe safety: stabilizers, boom lock and road travel
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; OSHA 1926.1000 (ROPS)

field.text: Track parts a mechanic or dealer will name: track shoes (pads, grousers; single, double or triple grouser), track chain or links held together by pins and bushings, the sprocket (drive) at the final drive end, the front idler with the recoil spring and grease track adjuster behind it, bottom (track) rollers carrying the machine weight, top (carrier) rollers holding up the upper track, and track guards that keep the chain on the rollers. The swing bearing and swing drive turn the house. The center joint (swivel) passes hydraulic oil to the travel motors. Final drives have their own gear oil. Knowing the names helps when you report a problem, for example 'loose shoe bolts on the left track, oil weeping from the right final drive'.
field.title: Excavator undercarriage terms crews use
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer service literature

field.text: Hammers, plate compactors, augers, tiltrotators and hydraulic thumbs run off the excavator's auxiliary circuits. Check the attachment's required flow (gpm) and pressure (psi) against the machine's settings; too much flow overheats and damages the attachment, too little makes it weak. Many machines have selectable modes (one-way flow for hammers, two-way for thumbs and augers) and the dealer can set flow and relief pressure. Some attachments need a case drain line straight to tank. Before connecting: relieve pressure per the manual, wipe couplings clean, connect, then check for leaks at idle. Hammer work needs a return filter and a shorter oil change interval. A blown aux hose sprays hot oil at high pressure; never feel for leaks with your hand (injection injury).
field.title: Excavator auxiliary hydraulics for attachments
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Manufacturer attachment and operator manuals

field.text: Practices from operator manuals and field experience: work with the tracks perpendicular to the trench so the idlers and sprockets are away from the edge and the final drives are on solid ground; keep the machine back from the edge far enough that the track load doesn't collapse the wall (soil surcharge also affects the trench protective system); on slopes, travel straight up and down, not across, with the bucket low and the boom pointed downhill when descending; don't swing a loaded bucket downhill on a side slope; build a level bench to work from; and spread the tracks to the wide setting if the machine has variable gauge. Wet clay and frozen ground fail without warning. Seat belt on: a sliding or tipping machine throws an unbelted operator out under the ROPS.
field.title: Excavator working on a slope or trench edge
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; field practice

field.text: Before hauling an excavator, know its shipping weight (operating weight plus or minus bucket and attachments), transport height with the boom folded, overall length, and track width. Many 20-ton machines ship around 10 to 10.5 ft wide and 10 ft tall on the deck, which is wider than the 8.5-ft legal width, so they usually need an oversize permit; 30 to 36-ton machines are heavier and often need a lowboy with more axles and an overweight permit too. Minis and midis usually fit within legal width. Low the boom, curl the stick under, set the bucket on the deck and lock the swing. Measure the actual loaded height on the trailer; height limits and bridge clearances vary by state and route.
field.title: Excavator transport dimensions to know
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; federal 102-inch width limit (23 CFR 658.15); state permit rules vary

field.text: For setting pipe with an excavator: hook to the designed lift eye on the coupler or bucket linkage, never to teeth or by wrapping a choker around the bucket; use a nylon sling or pipe tongs sized for the pipe; balance the stick so it hangs level for alignment with the bell; swing slowly and keep the pipe low; let the top man or pipe layer control it with a tag line or hand guidance only when it's lowered near grade, never stand between the pipe and the box or trench wall while it's moving; push home with the bucket only through a timber header or bar per the pipe maker, never by pushing directly on the pipe end. The operator must see the layer or have a signal person. Check the stick weight from the delivery ticket against the lift chart at the reach to the laying spot.
field.title: Pipe laying with an excavator: lift points and control
field.topic: Heavy equipment: excavators and backhoes
field.source: Industry practice; pipe manufacturer installation guides; OSHA 1926.251 rigging

field.text: Grease keeps pins and bushings from galling. Typical practice from operator manuals: grease boom, stick, bucket and coupler pins on excavators every 8 to 10 hours (daily) and after washing or working in water or mud; new machines and new buckets may need it more often; loader linkage and articulation joints daily or per manual; swing bearing and swing gear per manual (often weekly or 250 hours). Use the grease the maker specifies, commonly an NLGI #2 EP lithium-complex grease, often with moly for pins. Lower the attachment to the ground and lock out the controls first; wipe each fitting; pump until old grease and dirt purge out of the joint; replace broken zerks. Hammer tools use chisel paste. Over-greasing sealed fittings (some swing bearings) can blow seals.
field.title: Greasing heavy equipment: how and how often
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals (typical intervals)

field.text: Daily fluid checks: engine oil (dipstick, machine level, engine off for several minutes); hydraulic oil (sight glass, with cylinders in the position the manual shows, often bucket and stick curled in and on the ground); coolant (at the overflow tank, never open a hot radiator cap); fuel and DEF; and on some machines, transmission oil at operating temperature. Weekly or per manual: final drives, swing drive and axle oils. Use the specified oils: Tier 4 engines with a DPF usually require low-ash oil (API CK-4 or the maker's spec) and ultra-low-sulfur diesel (15 ppm). Keep fill caps and funnels clean; dirt in hydraulic oil ruins pumps. Note oil added on the daily report; rising consumption warns of a leak or engine wear.
field.title: Checking fluids on heavy equipment
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; EPA nonroad diesel ULSD requirement (summary)

field.text: Tier 4 Final machines over about 75 hp mostly use SCR, which injects DEF (a 32.5% urea and water solution) into the exhaust to cut NOx; low DEF first reduces engine power (derate) and can eventually limit the machine to idle. DEF freezes at about 11 to 12 F and expands up to about 7% when frozen, so don't fill tanks to the top in winter; onboard heaters thaw it once the engine runs, and never add anything to thaw it. Store between about 12 and 86 F; heat shortens its roughly 12-month shelf life. Keep DEF clean: dedicated jugs, nozzles and funnels, closed transfer systems, never tap water, never fuel in the DEF tank (or DEF in the fuel tank, which ruins the fuel system). DEF caps are usually blue.
field.title: DEF (diesel exhaust fluid) handling
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Equipment World, 'How to handle DEF in freezing temperatures'; Genie Tier 4 overview

field.text: Tier 4 diesel engines collect soot in a diesel particulate filter (DPF) and burn it off by regeneration. Passive regen happens on its own during normal hard work when exhaust is hot. Active or automatic regen: the engine raises exhaust temperature (often by injecting extra fuel) while you keep working. Parked or manual regen ('park and burn'): when the dash asks, park in a safe spot, set the controls, and start the regen; it can take around 30 minutes. Practices: don't shut the engine off mid-regen unless it's an emergency; park away from dry grass, fuel, wood and people, since exhaust parts get very hot; use the inhibit switch only when necessary (like near flammables) and run the regen soon after; long idling builds soot faster. Use low-ash oil and ULSD or the DPF clogs with ash.
field.title: DPF regeneration on Tier 4 machines
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Genie (Terex) Tier 4 overview; manufacturer operator manuals

field.text: Track tension is set by grease in the track adjuster cylinder near the front idler. To check an excavator: swing the house 90 degrees, use the boom to lift one track off the ground, run it a few revolutions to clear dirt, stop it and set the lockout lever, then measure sag at the lowest point the way your manual says (from the bottom of the track frame or a roller to the top of the shoe). Specs and the measuring point vary widely by make and model, so use the number in your operator manual. Add grease to tighten; open the relief fitting slowly (a turn or so, never remove it) to loosen, wearing eye protection because grease is under very high pressure. Set tension in the conditions you're working in; mud packing tightens tracks. Too tight wears pins, bushings and sprockets fast; too loose throws tracks.
field.title: Track tension: checking and adjusting
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Equipment World, 'How to properly adjust the track tension on your crawler excavator'; manufacturer manuals

field.text: On tracked machines the undercarriage often accounts for a large share (commonly cited around half) of maintenance cost. Wear items: pins and bushings (track 'stretch' or pitch), sprocket teeth, idlers, bottom and top rollers, shoe grousers. Slow wear by: keeping tension correct; cleaning packed mud and rock out of the undercarriage daily, especially before freezing nights; minimizing high-speed travel and reverse travel; turning gradually and alternating turn direction; using the narrowest shoe that gives enough flotation; working up and down slopes rather than across; and keeping the idler forward when digging so the sprocket isn't taking the digging load where the manual says so. Dealers measure undercarriage wear with gauges and ultrasonic tools; schedule a check every few hundred hours.
field.title: Undercarriage wear and how to slow it
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer undercarriage guides; industry practice

field.text: Cold start practices for diesel equipment: plug in block heaters and hydraulic tank heaters overnight when below freezing; use winter-blend diesel (No. 1 blended with No. 2 or treated fuel) to prevent gelling, and drain water separators; wait for the glow plug or intake grid heater light before cranking; crank in short bursts (often no more than about 30 seconds, then rest); don't use ether on engines with glow plugs or grid heaters, as it can explode. After starting, idle a few minutes, then run at moderate rpm and cycle the hydraulics slowly (boom, stick, bucket and swing through partial strokes) to warm the oil before working hard; cold hydraulic oil is thick and can starve pumps and blow hoses. Clean ice from tracks and steps, and use three points of contact getting on.
field.title: Cold weather starting and warm-up
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; industry practice

field.text: Idling burns roughly 0.5 to 1.5 gallons per hour on mid-size equipment, adds engine hours (lowering resale and moving up service), and on Tier 4 machines builds soot that forces more regens. Some places limit idling by law. California's off-road diesel regulation limits idling to 5 consecutive minutes, with exceptions for doing the machine's work (like powering a crane or pump), service and repair (including filter regeneration), safety checks, warm-up to maker temperature, and some queuing; medium and large fleets need a written idling policy. Many cities, states and project specs have similar rules. Most new machines have auto-idle and auto-shutdown settings: use them. Shut down when waiting on trucks, inspectors or pipe for more than a few minutes, unless heat or cold makes the cab necessary.
field.title: Idling rules and why to cut idle time
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: CARB In-Use Off-Road Diesel idling FAQ; industry practice

field.text: OSHA requires vehicles on a jobsite to be checked at the start of each shift (1926.601(b)(14)): service and parking brakes, tires, horn, steering, coupling devices, seat belts, operating controls and safety devices, plus lights, wipers and defrosters where needed; fix defects before use. For earthmoving machines check also: fluid levels and leaks, tires (cuts, pressure) or track condition, bucket or blade cutting edges and teeth, pins and keepers, articulation lock removed for work and stored, backup alarm and horn working (1926.602(a)(9)), ROPS undamaged with no unauthorized welding or drilling, seat belt working, fire extinguisher charged, mirrors and cameras clean, steps and handholds clean. Write it down; many companies use daily inspection forms in the app.
field.title: Pre-shift inspection for loaders, dozers and rollers
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(14), 1926.602(a)(9); manufacturer operator manuals

field.text: Rollovers are a leading cause of operator deaths in construction equipment. OSHA requires rollover protective structures (ROPS) on scrapers, wheel loaders, rubber-tired dozers, wheel tractors, crawler tractors and loaders and motor graders (1926.1000), and on compactors and skid steers manufactured after July 15, 2019; sideboom pipelayers are excluded. Seat belts must be provided on earthmoving equipment with ROPS (1926.602(a)(2)), and the ROPS only protects you if the belt keeps you inside it. Most excavators also have ROPS-certified cabs. Never remove, weld on or drill a ROPS (it must be remounted with equal-quality bolts or welds if removed, and carry its label). If the machine starts to roll: stay in the seat, belt on, hold the wheel or armrests, lean away from the fall. Don't jump.
field.title: Rollovers, ROPS and seat belts
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety

field.text: Crush and pinch points on and around machines: between an excavator counterweight and a wall, truck, pole, pipe stack or another machine; between the bucket or attachment and the trench box or pipe; between a loader's lift arms and frame (OSHA requires scissor points on front-end loaders that endanger the operator to be guarded, 1926.602(a)(10)); in a skid steer's lift arm zone; at articulation joints on loaders, graders and ADTs (engage the articulation lock before service); and between a dump body and frame. Rules: stay out of any space that can close; make eye contact with the operator before entering the work area; operators stop and lock out when someone approaches; never reach into a machine while it's running; block raised parts before working under them (1926.600(a)(3)).
field.title: Swing and pinch points around equipment
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.600(a)(3), 1926.602(a)(10); field practice

field.text: Backing kills: workers are struck by backing dump trucks, loaders and rollers every year, often in work zones. OSHA requires a backup alarm audible above surrounding noise, or a signal person who says it's safe, for vehicles and earthmoving equipment with an obstructed rear view (1926.601(b)(4), 1926.602(a)(9)(ii)). Practices: plan traffic so trucks back as little as possible (drive-through loading, turnaround areas); use one designated spotter who stays visible to the driver in the driver's mirror and out of the vehicle's path; agree on hand signals or radios first; driver stops if he loses sight of the spotter; spotters never walk backward behind a moving vehicle or stand between a vehicle and a fixed object; everyone wears high-visibility clothing; and cameras and proximity sensors help but don't replace a spotter.
field.title: Backing equipment and using a spotter
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(4), 1926.602(a)(9)(ii); field practice

field.text: Every machine has large blind areas where the operator can't see a person on foot, even with mirrors: close behind and beside dump trucks (the passenger side most of all), behind an excavator's counterweight and on the side opposite the cab, in front of a loader bucket when raised, and around rollers and dozers close to the machine. NIOSH has published blind-area diagrams for common construction machines showing how big these zones are. Practices: walk around the machine before moving it; know your machine's blind areas and keep ground workers out of them; assume the operator can't see you unless you've made eye contact; add mirrors, cameras and proximity alarms; and set up a work-zone plan (internal traffic control) that separates people on foot from equipment paths.
field.title: Blind spots on heavy equipment
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: NIOSH construction equipment visibility research (summary); field practice

field.text: Machine-operator rules near buried lines: confirm the locate tickets are active and marks are visible before digging; know your state's tolerance zone (often 18 to 24 in either side of the marks) and expose lines there by hand or vacuum excavation; use a smooth-edge bucket and dig in thin cuts as you approach; have a spotter watch for warning tape, sand bedding or a line; and don't swing a ripper, hammer or auger in the zone. If you hit a gas line: stop the machine and shut it off if safe (no sparks), get everyone away and upwind, call 911 and the gas company, don't try to crimp or plug it, and keep people and traffic out. If you hit an electric line: stay on the machine unless there's fire, warn people away, and call the utility. Report every strike to the one-call center and owner.
field.title: Working near buried utilities with equipment
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Common Ground Alliance best practices (summary); state one-call laws (vary)

field.text: OSHA rules for parking: set the parking brake whenever equipment is parked, and chock wheels and set the brake when parked on an incline (1926.600(a)(3)(ii)); fully lower or block blades, buckets and dump bodies when not in use, with controls in neutral, engine stopped and brakes set (1926.600(a)(3)(i)); and equipment left near a highway or active work at night needs lights, reflectors or lighted barricades (1926.600(a)(1)). Good practice: park away from trench edges and out of traffic lanes, on firm level ground; let turbo engines idle a few minutes to cool before shutdown; close windows and lock the cab and fuel cap to stop theft and vandalism; take keys; and drain air tanks and refuel at end of day in cold weather to reduce condensation in the tank.
field.title: Equipment parking and end-of-day shutdown
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.600(a)(1), (a)(3); manufacturer manuals

field.text: Slips and falls getting on and off machines are among the most common equipment injuries. Rules: face the machine and keep three points of contact (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand) on steps and handholds; don't jump off; don't climb with tools or a coffee in your hand (hand them up or use a bag); keep steps, tracks and handholds clean of mud, grease and ice; use the designated steps, not tracks or tires, when possible; and don't use controls or the steering wheel as a handhold. Wear boots with good tread. When fueling or greasing at height on large machines, use the maker's platforms or a ladder, not the tracks.
field.title: Three points of contact and climbing on equipment
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; industry practice

field.text: Equipment hydraulics run at roughly 3,000 to 5,000+ psi. A pinhole leak can inject oil under the skin (injection injury), which looks minor but needs emergency surgery within hours; tell the ER it's a high-pressure injection. Never feel for leaks with your hand; use cardboard or wood. Before working on hydraulics: lower attachments to the ground, shut down, and relieve pressure by cycling the controls with the key on (engine off) per the manual; the accumulator and tank may still hold pressure. Replace hoses that are rubbed through, bubbled, kinked or weeping at the fittings; route and clamp hoses away from pinch points. Hot oil burns too: let the machine cool before opening the hydraulic tank, and open caps slowly.
field.title: Hydraulic hose and pressure safety
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; medical guidance on injection injuries (summary)

field.text: Machine fires usually start from fuel or hydraulic oil spraying on a hot turbo or exhaust, or from dry debris (grass, leaves, paper) built up around the engine and DPF. Prevention: blow out or clean the engine compartment and belly pans regularly, especially after work in brush; fix leaks right away; check that hoses and wires aren't rubbing; don't park a hot machine on dry grass; stay with the machine during a parked regen; and fuel only with the engine off. Keep a charged fire extinguisher on the machine (many owners and specs require one) and know how to use it. If a fire starts: lower the attachment, shut down, get off, use the extinguisher only if it's small and you have a clear exit, and call 911.
field.title: Fire prevention on heavy equipment
