field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; insurer loss-control guidance (summary)

field.text: OSHA's general rules require that only employees qualified by training or experience operate equipment and machinery (1926.20(b)(4)), and forklift and telehandler operators need specific training and evaluation (1926.602(d) and 1910.178). Crane operators need certification under 1926.1427. Excavator, loader and dozer operators don't need a federal certificate, but employers should train on the specific machine: the operator manual, controls, lift charts, attachments, inspections and the site's hazards. Many contractors use NCCER heavy equipment programs, union apprenticeship, or dealer training, and document a hands-on evaluation. Truck drivers need the right CDL class and medical card. Keep training records; inspectors and insurers ask for them after incidents.
field.title: Operator training and qualifications
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety

field.text: When a machine bogs down: stop spinning tracks or wheels before you dig deeper. Excavators can usually walk themselves out by planting the bucket ahead and pulling while tracking, or by pushing the boom down to lift a track and placing mats or timber under it. Use crane mats or timber mats to cross soft ground. When pulling a stuck machine with another machine, use rated recovery straps or chains and shackles hooked to the maker's tow points (never to the bucket teeth or ROPS), keep everyone well clear of the line (a broken strap or chain whips back and can kill), pull slowly in a straight line, and use a spotter. Snatch-pulling with chains is dangerous. In deep mud, call for a winch or a bigger machine rather than risk a rollover.
field.title: Mud, soft ground and getting a machine unstuck
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; industry practice

field.text: Equipment on street jobs adds struck-by risks for both workers and the public. Practices: keep the excavator's counterweight and boom inside the closed lane and the work zone; a reduced or zero-tail-swing machine helps; never swing over an open traffic lane; use a flagger or a stop for truck entry and exit; trucks enter and leave the work zone in the direction of traffic; keep beacons and lights on; turn the machine so the operator can see traffic when possible; and stop work if traffic control is knocked down. Equipment left near traffic overnight needs lights, reflectors or lighted barricades (1926.600(a)(1)) and should be parked behind barrier or well off the road. MUTCD and the traffic control plan set the layout.
field.title: Working near traffic with equipment
field.topic: Heavy equipment: maintenance, operation and safety
field.source: OSHA 1926.600(a)(1); MUTCD Part 6 (summary); field practice

field.text: Steel trench boxes (shields) are sold by panel length, height and wall thickness. Common lengths 16, 20 and 24 ft (shorter 8 to 12 ft boxes for services and tight spots), heights often 4, 6, 8 and 10 ft for stacking. Wall thickness: lightweight steel about 4 in, heavy-duty 6 in and up, some 8 in. Depth ratings vary widely by maker, size and soil type (one trainer quotes roughly 15 to 20 ft for 4-in walls and 20 to 30 ft for 8-in walls, but treat those as illustrations only); the actual rating is on the box tag and in the maker's tabulated data by soil type. Choose a box about 4 ft longer than the pipe stick and about 1 ft wider (inside) than the wider of the pipe or bucket. Aluminum boxes are light enough for small machines but dent and cost more; use them for shallow, small-pipe work.
field.title: Trench box sizes and depth ratings
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Equipment World, 'A Guide to Trench Boxes'

field.text: Box weight decides what machine can handle it. Typical ranges (check the tag): an 8 ft by 16 ft lightweight steel box about 4,000 to 6,000 lb; an 8 ft by 20 ft heavy box about 8,000 to 12,000 lb; aluminum 4 ft by 8 ft boxes a few hundred pounds. Spreaders (struts) hold the panels apart and set the inside width; they're pinned in collars or adjustable, and come in many lengths. Spreaders must be the maker's parts at the approved lengths and positions in the tab data; never substitute pipe or timber. A bent spreader or cracked panel is structural damage: take the box out of service until the maker or an engineer approves repair. Lift with all four lift points using a rated chain bridle and keep the spreader pins and keepers in.
field.title: Trench box weights and spreaders
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Manufacturer catalogs (typical ranges); Equipment World trench box guide

field.text: Boxes are moved by lifting with a chain bridle on the lift lugs or by dragging forward with the bucket or a chain on the drag lugs as the dig advances. OSHA requires that no one be in the shield while it's installed, removed or moved vertically (1926.652(g)(1)(iv)). Rules from OSHA and tab data: dig no more than 2 ft below the bottom of the shield, and only if the shield is rated for the full trench depth and there's no sign of soil loss behind or below it; keep the box from shifting sideways; stack boxes only with the maker's stacking pins or connectors and within tab data. Workers climb out or move to a protected section before the box is pulled. Backfill the gap under and behind the box as it's pulled so soil doesn't cave behind the pipe.
field.title: Moving a trench box: pulling, dragging and stacking
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652(g); Equipment World trench box guide

field.text: Slide rail systems use steel posts (rails) set at the corners or along the trench, with heavy steel panels that slide down the rails in channels as the excavator digs, pushing each panel down in steps. They give a wide-open working area free of cross spreaders (or with high spreaders) for big manholes, lift station pits, vaults and pipe with many crossing utilities, and they can be installed around existing utilities where a box can't drop in. Configurations include single-bay, multi-bay linear runs and four-sided pits. They're installed and removed per the maker's procedure, under tabulated data or an engineer's design, by a trained crew, and usually rented with field support. They need a large excavator to push and pull the panels.
field.title: Slide rail shoring systems
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Manufacturer literature (typical); OSHA 1926.652(c) (manufacturer tabulated data)

field.text: Hydraulic shores (speed shores, hydraulic trench jacks) are aluminum cylinders with rails or plates that are lowered into the trench from the top and pumped tight against the walls with a hand pump (usually water/glycol or hydraulic fluid). Used for utility trenches, service connections, and spot repairs, especially where crossing utilities prevent a box. Spacing (vertical and horizontal) and whether you need sheeting (fin-form plywood or aluminum sheeting) depend on soil type and depth in Appendix D of Subpart P or the maker's tab data. Install and remove from the top with the tool, keeping workers out of unprotected trench; remove from the bottom up while leaving the top shore in until the end. Check pressure and for leaks daily.
field.title: Aluminum hydraulic shores
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D (summary); manufacturer tabulated data

field.text: Manhole boxes (four-sided boxes, pit boxes) are square or rectangular shields, often 8 ft by 8 ft up to 12 ft by 12 ft or more inside, sometimes with a cut-out or knock-out panel for the pipe to pass through. They're stacked for depth and lifted as a unit with a four-leg bridle. Alternatives for manholes and vaults: slide rail pits, stacked trench boxes set end to end with end panels, or steel or aluminum modular panel systems. Size the inside dimension to the manhole base diameter plus working room (a 48-in manhole base is about 5 to 6 ft OD, so an 8 ft by 8 ft box is common). Pipe entering a box sits in the gap between panels or through the cut-out: keep that gap within the maker's tab data.
field.title: Manhole boxes and shoring for structures
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Manufacturer catalogs; industry practice

field.text: Trenchers cut narrow trenches continuously. Walk-behind chain trenchers dig about 4 to 6 in wide and up to about 3 ft deep for irrigation, electrical and small water services; ride-on and compact trenchers dig deeper and wider; large track trenchers dig 1 to 3 ft wide and 5 to 10 ft or more deep for drain tile, fiber, pipelines and rock cutting with carbide teeth; wheel (rockwheel) trenchers cut rock and pavement; microtrenchers saw a 1 to 2-in slot in pavement for fiber. Trenchers are fast on long runs of small conduit but leave a narrow trench that's hard to bed and compact around pipe. Hazards: entanglement in the moving chain (deaths happen), utility strikes, and buried flying debris; keep everyone clear of the boom and spoil auger.
field.title: Trenchers: chain, wheel and micro
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets (typical values)

field.text: Directional drills are classed by thrust/pullback and torque, and the dividing lines vary by source. A common breakdown: mini (small) rigs under about 40,000 lb pullback (many under 20,000 lb) and under about 4,000 ft-lb torque, for cable, fiber, gas and water services and small pipe on bores of a few hundred feet; midi rigs about 40,000 to 100,000 lb and 4,000 to 20,000 ft-lb, for conduit bundles and pipe up to roughly 12 to 24 in on bores up to roughly 1,000 to 2,000 ft; maxi rigs over 100,000 lb and 20,000 ft-lb, for large pipe (roughly 24 to 48 in and up) and river crossings of several thousand feet. Mud pump capacity scales with rig size, from well under 100 gpm on minis to several hundred gpm and more on maxis. Modern rigs push these limits. Size the rig to the pullback force the product pipe needs plus a margin, and the reamer to the pipe.
field.title: HDD rig sizes: small, medium, large
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: The Driller, 'What size HDD rig' (classification from industry sources)

field.text: A directional drill spread besides the rig: a mud (fluid) mixing system and tank with mixing hopper; a mud recycling system on larger bores (shakers, desanders, desilters) so drilling fluid is reused; a vacuum excavator to suck up returns at entry and exit pits; drill rods (pipe) and a rod loader; reamers and swivels for pullback; a walkover locator or wireline steering tool; fusion machine for HDPE; and a water source. Typical small-rig crew: operator, locator, and a laborer handling rods and fluid. Pothole every utility the bore crosses and watch for inadvertent returns (frac-outs). Drill rigs need electrical strike protection: grounding stakes, a voltage alarm (strike alert) and ground mats where the operator stands.
field.title: HDD support equipment and crew
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Industry practice; HDD equipment maker literature

field.text: Two main pipe bursting setups: pneumatic bursting uses an air-driven hammer (percussive bursting tool) pushed by a compressor and pulled forward by a constant-tension winch through the old pipe; static bursting uses a hydraulic puller in the exit pit that pulls a string of linked rods and a bursting or splitting head through the old line (splitters with blades cut ductile iron and steel). The new pipe, usually fused HDPE, follows behind. Static pullers are rated by pull force (often tens of tons to over 100 tons) and cause less vibration near structures; pneumatic tools work fast in brittle clay and cast iron. Equipment also includes rod pushers, expander heads, bypass pumps, and a fusion machine. Pits need shoring.
field.title: Pipe bursting equipment: static and pneumatic
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: NASTT pipe bursting guidance (summary); manufacturer literature

field.text: Auger boring (jack and bore) machines sit on a steel track in the launch pit, jacking a steel casing forward with hydraulic cylinders while a rotating auger string inside carries spoil back to the pit. Machines are sized by casing diameter (roughly 4 in up to 60 in or more) and thrust (hundreds of tons on large units). Support gear: track sections, casing and auger segments (often 10 or 20 ft), a cutting head, a steering head or water level for grade on longer bores, a crane or large excavator to set casing and augers, and a welder to weld casing joints. The thrust block at the back of the pit must take the full jacking force. Keep everyone clear of the rotating auger and drive; entanglement is a serious hazard.
field.title: Auger boring machines
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer literature

field.text: Vacuum excavators (vac trucks, hydrovacs) loosen soil with pressurized water (hydro-excavation) or compressed air (air excavation) and suck the spoil into a debris tank. Truck-mounted units commonly have debris tanks of a few yards up to 10 to 15 CY plus several hundred to 1,500 gallons of water; trailer units are smaller for potholing. Ditch Witch guidance: keep pressure at or below 2,800 psi for soft excavation, reduce pressure when using heated water, keep the wand moving, and hold the nozzle about 8 in from the utility. Hydro works in hard soil, clay and cobbles; air works in softer soil, avoids slurry and leaves dry spoil you can reuse as backfill. Hydro slurry must go to an approved disposal site. Use a rotating or zero-degree nozzle per the maker, never point it at people.
field.title: Vacuum excavation equipment: hydro and air
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Ditch Witch, 'Hydroexcavation best practices'

field.text: Pump types used on pipe jobs: self-priming centrifugal trash pumps (2, 3, 4 and 6-in) handle muddy water with solids up to roughly a third to half of the suction size, and are the workhorse for sumps; automatic-priming 'dri-prime' or vacuum-assisted pumps for well points and running dry; electric submersible pumps that sit in a sump or well and push water up (no suction lift limit); and diaphragm pumps for low flow of thick muddy water. Suction lift is limited by atmospheric pressure (theoretical about 33.9 ft at sea level; practical about 15 to 25 ft depending on the pump and altitude), so set suction pumps low or use submersibles in deep pits. Pump curves drop as total head rises. Discharge to a sediment bag or tank, not straight to a storm drain.
field.title: Dewatering pumps: trash, submersible, diaphragm
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Industry practice; pump manufacturer curves (typical)

field.text: A well point system has small-diameter well points (screens about 1.5 to 2 in diameter, a few feet long) jetted with water into the ground along the trench, connected by swing pipes to a header pipe running along the surface, and a vacuum-assisted well point pump pulling water through them. Spacing is set by the dewatering designer from the soil and the drawdown needed; points are commonly a few feet apart (closer in fine sands, farther in coarse sands), sunk below trench bottom and close to the trench. Because suction lift is limited, one stage lowers water only about 15 to 18 ft at best; deeper cuts need a second stage or deep wells. They work in sands and silty sands; clay doesn't drain and clean gravel may need too much water. Install days ahead so the water table drops before digging, run 24/7 with a standby pump, and check discharge permits.
field.title: Well point systems: equipment and layout
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Industry practice; dewatering contractor literature (typical values)

field.text: Support equipment: towable generators (power pumps, tools, job trailers; size to the starting load of the biggest motor, often 2 to 3 times its running amps), light towers for night work and traffic control (aim lights away from drivers), and air compressors for pneumatic tools, piercing tools and pneumatic bursting (rated in cfm at a pressure, e.g. 185 cfm at 100 psi). All are engines: keep them out of trenches, pits and manhole openings and downwind of workers to keep carbon monoxide out of confined spaces; ground generators per the maker and use GFCI protection for cord tools (OSHA 1926.404). Fuel them only when shut down and cool, with a spill kit and secondary containment where required.
field.title: Generators, light towers and compressors on site
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Industry practice; OSHA 1926.404 (GFCI) summary

field.text: Piercing tools ('moles', 'hogs', impact moles) are air-driven torpedoes that pound through soil to make a small bore, typically 2 to 6 in, under sidewalks, driveways and lawns for water services, gas services and conduit. They run from a 185-cfm class compressor with a lubricator, launched from a small pit and aimed with a sighting frame; they can't be steered, so they drift in rocky or mixed soils and can surface or hit utilities. Typical runs are 20 to 60 ft. Pothole every crossing utility and the exit point first. Pull the service line in behind the tool or with the tool reversed. Keep the air hose connections pinned (whip checks) and stand clear of the launch pit during launch.
field.title: Pneumatic piercing tools (moles) for services
field.topic: Heavy equipment: shoring, trenchers, trenchless, vac and dewatering equipment
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer literature

field.text: Common dump trucks (payloads vary with state law, axle spacing and truck tare weight; check yours): single-axle dump, about 5 to 8 CY and roughly 5 to 8 tons payload, for small jobs and city work; tandem (10-wheeler), about 12 to 18 CY and roughly 12 to 15 tons legal payload under the bridge formula, more where state law allows; tri-axle (tandem with a lift or pusher axle), about 15 to 20 CY and roughly 16 to 23 tons depending on the state; quad-axle (two lift axles), roughly 22 to 27 tons in states that allow it; super dump or Super 10 (trailing axle), roughly 19 to 26 tons, up to about 28; semi end dump, about 22 to 37 CY and roughly 22 to 26 tons; belly dump and side dump trailers, about 22 to 26 tons. Weight usually limits you before the bed is full with stone, wet clay or asphalt. See the truck capacity file for details.
field.title: Dump truck types and typical capacities
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Industry practice; trucking and aggregate supplier guides (typical ranges)

field.text: On the Interstate system federal limits are 80,000 lb gross, 20,000 lb on a single axle and 34,000 lb on a tandem axle (two or more axles more than 40 in and not more than 96 in apart), and the Federal Bridge Formula, W = 500 x [ (L x N) / (N - 1) + 12N + 36 ], limits weight on any group of axles by the number of axles (N) and the distance between the outer axles (L, in feet). That's why spreading axles out (lift axles, trailing axles) raises legal payload. States set limits on non-Interstate roads, some have grandfathered higher limits, and many post lower limits on local roads and bridges, plus spring frost laws. Overweight means fines, damaged roads and longer stopping distances. Check your state DOT's limits and get the scale ticket.
field.title: Truck legal weight: federal limits and bridge formula
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: FHWA Bridge Formula Weights

field.text: A Super Dump (often called a Super 10) is a tandem dump with a load-bearing trailing axle behind the bed that's flipped down for travel and folded up over the bed when dumping. By stretching the length between outer axles, it raises the bridge-formula gross weight. Custom Truck's figures: a standard tandem with 22-ft spacing is limited to about 52,500 lb gross; adding a pusher axle (4 axles at 22 ft) about 56,500 lb; a Super Dump with 4 axles over 34 ft about 64,500 lb; and with three pushers plus the trailing axle (7 axles over 34 ft) up to the 80,000 lb maximum. Payload is gross minus the truck's own weight. Advantage on utility jobs: near-semi payloads with the maneuverability of a straight truck. Rules vary by state.
field.title: Super 10 / super dump: why the trailing axle matters
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Custom Truck One Source, 'What are Super Dumps'

field.text: End dumps (semi end dumps) raise the whole trailer box to dump out the tailgate; they carry big loads but are tall and tippy when raised, so dump only on firm, level ground, never with the trailer twisted or in high wind, and keep away from power lines. Belly dumps (bottom dumps) open gates under the trailer to lay a windrow while moving; great for spreading stone or base on long runs, no tipping hazard, but they don't handle sticky clay or large rock well and can't dump into a hole. Side dumps tip the tub sideways; they unload fast, are stable, and handle rock and big chunks, but need room to the side. On trench jobs, end dumps and tandems usually haul spoil; belly dumps deliver bedding or base on long open runs.
field.title: End dump, belly dump and side dump trailers
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Industry practice

field.text: Dump trucks tip over when dumping on soft or uneven ground, with sticky material hanging in the top of the bed, with a twisted frame on end dumps, or in wind. They also hit power lines with the bed up and drive off with the bed raised into bridges and wires. Practices: dump on firm, level ground; check overhead before raising; keep people out of the area beside the truck while dumping; lower the bed fully before moving; never get under a raised bed without the permanently attached body prop locked in place (OSHA 1926.601(b)(10)); tailgate trip handles must keep the driver in the clear (1926.601(b)(12)); and use a spotter when backing to a trench or paver. Haul trucks loaded by excavators need a cab shield or canopy (1926.601(b)(6)).
field.title: Dump truck rollover and raised-bed hazards
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(4), (b)(6), (b)(10), (b)(12); industry practice

field.text: Off-road haul trucks carry dirt and rock on large sites. Articulated dump trucks (ADTs, 'artics', 'rock trucks'), with a pivot between cab and body and all-wheel drive, typically carry about 25 to 45 tons (for example 25, 30, 40-ton classes) and handle mud, grades and rough haul roads; they're common on big sewer interceptors, subdivisions and dam or pond work. Rigid-frame haul trucks start around 40 tons and go to hundreds of tons in mining; they need good haul roads. Off-road trucks aren't street legal and usually exceed road weight limits, so crossing public roads needs a permit or flagging. Haul road rules: maintain roads with a grader and water truck, post speed limits, use berms on drop-offs, and keep light vehicles off haul routes or use radios.
field.title: Articulated and rigid haul trucks
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Industry practice; manufacturer spec sheets (typical values)

field.text: Example: a 30-ton excavator with a 2.0 CY bucket loads wet clay into tri-axles. Fill factor for clay about 0.85, so 1.7 loose CY per pass. Wet clay weighs roughly 1.4 tons per loose CY (check your material), and the tri-axle's legal payload is about 18 tons, so the truck holds 18 / 1.4 = 12.9 LCY by weight, even though the bed would hold more. Passes = 12.9 / 1.7 = 7.6, round to 8. Excavator cycle 20 seconds, so load time = 8 x 20 = 160 s = 2.7 min. Truck cycle: wait and spot 1, load 2.7, haul 6 miles at about 30 mph = 12, dump 2, return 10 = 27.7 min. Trucks needed = 27.7 / 2.7 = about 10 to keep the excavator loading nonstop. On a pipe crew the hoe lays pipe half the hour, so 4 to 6 trucks is often plenty.
field.title: Truck counts: worked example with weight check
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Standard cyclic estimating method (equipment production texts); values illustrative

field.text: A digging cycle is load bucket, swing loaded, dump, swing back. Rough cycle times for a well-matched machine in common earth at 90 degrees of swing, from manufacturer handbooks and field timing: small and mid excavators about 13 to 20 seconds in easy conditions; 20 to 36-ton machines about 15 to 22 seconds loading trucks at shallow depth. Cycle time grows with depth (a 12 to 20-ft sewer trench often runs 25 to 40 seconds or more), with wider swing angles (180 degrees adds several seconds), hard or sticky material, a trench box in the way, and tight spoil placement. Loading over the side into trucks parked at the right height and angle is fastest. Time 10 to 20 real cycles with a phone stopwatch on your job and use that average, not handbook numbers.
field.title: Excavator cycle times: what's typical
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Manufacturer performance handbooks (typical ranges); field practice

field.text: Fill factor is how full the bucket actually gets compared with its rated heaped capacity. Typical values published in manufacturer performance handbooks and estimating texts: moist loam or sandy clay about 100 to 110%; sand and gravel about 95 to 110%; hard, tough clay about 80 to 90%; well-blasted rock about 60 to 75%; poorly blasted rock about 40 to 50%. Loose stockpiled stone loaded by a loader is often near 95 to 100%. Sticky wet clay may fill well but won't dump clean, costing time. Deep trench digging with long reach usually fills less than shallow loading. Use the low end for estimating, and check it on site by counting passes per known truck load (scale tickets divided by passes).
field.title: Bucket fill factors by material
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Caterpillar Performance Handbook fill-factor table as reproduced in construction equipment texts

field.text: Equipment trailers: tag trailers (bumper-pull or pintle) for minis, skid steers and compact equipment, often 10,000 to 25,000 lb capacity; tilt-deck or beavertail trailers; goosenecks; lowboys (low deck about 18 to 24 in high) with a removable gooseneck (RGN) so equipment drives on from the front, used for 20-ton and larger excavators, dozers and loaders; and multi-axle lowboys with jeeps and boosters for 40 to 80-ton loads. The low deck keeps tall machines under height limits. Know the trailer's rated capacity, deck height, and the loaded height and width before you go; the driver needs the right CDL class and the tractor must be rated for the gross combination weight.
field.title: Lowboy and equipment trailers
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Industry practice

field.text: Federal law sets a 102-in (8.5-ft) maximum vehicle width on the national truck network; anything wider needs a state oversize permit. Height limits are set by states (commonly 13.5 ft in many eastern states and 14 ft or more in many western states), and length limits vary too. Loads over legal axle or gross weights need overweight permits, usually for 'non-divisible' loads like a single excavator (you can't haul extra material or attachments on a permitted load in most states unless allowed). Permits specify route, travel times (often daylight only, no holidays or rush hour), signs and flags, and escort vehicles above set widths. Each state on the route needs its own permit. Get permits before loading, and carry them in the truck.
field.title: Oversize and overweight permits: the basics
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: 23 CFR 658.15 (width); state DOT permit rules (vary)

field.text: Loading and unloading is where many machines tip off ramps. Practices: park the trailer on firm, level ground with the truck parked and wheels chocked; clean mud, ice and snow from ramps and tracks; set ramp spacing to the machine's track or wheel width; use a spotter who stands to the side, never in front; drive up straight and slowly, never turn or steer on the ramps; for excavators, back on with the boom toward the rear (or as the manual says), use the bucket low to balance at the crest, and swing only when fully on the deck; center the load to get correct axle weights; lower the attachment to the deck, lock the swing and lockout lever, shut down and take the key. Wear the seat belt while loading, and never jump if it starts to tip.
field.title: Loading equipment onto a trailer safely
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Manufacturer operator manuals; industry practice

field.text: Federal cargo securement rules for wheeled or tracked equipment weighing 10,000 lb or more (excavators, loaders, dozers, rollers): lower and secure accessory equipment like the boom, bucket or blade to the trailer; lock or restrain articulated machines so they can't pivot; use at least four tiedowns, placed as close as practical to the front and rear of the machine or at the maker's tie-down points; and restrain the machine against moving sideways, forward, backward and upward. The aggregate working load limit of the tiedowns must be at least half the cargo weight under the general rules. Use rated chains and binders, check them after the first few miles, and protect chains where they cross sharp edges.
field.title: Tying down equipment for transport (49 CFR 393.130)
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: 49 CFR 393.130 (Cornell LII text); 49 CFR 393.106 aggregate WLL rule

field.text: Water trucks spray haul roads and work areas for dust (often required by air permits and city permits), add moisture to backfill and embankment to reach optimum moisture for compaction, wash streets and fill test water or tanks. On-road water trucks commonly carry about 2,000 to 4,000 gallons; off-road water wagons and pulls carry about 5,000 to 20,000 gallons. Water weighs 8.34 lb per gallon, so 4,000 gallons is about 33,000 lb; partly full tanks slosh and can push the truck over on turns and slopes, so baffled tanks matter. Filling from a fire hydrant usually needs a city hydrant meter and a backflow preventer. Don't over-water clay backfill: it pumps and fails density.
field.title: Water trucks: dust control and compaction water
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Industry practice

field.text: Common cranes on utility work: boom trucks (straight telescoping boom on a commercial truck) for setting manholes and small precast; knuckle-boom (articulating) cranes on delivery trucks for unloading pipe and precast; rough-terrain (RT) cranes, four-wheel-drive with outriggers, for site lifts of structures, wet wells and large pipe; truck cranes and all-terrain cranes that drive to site for big picks like lift stations and box culverts; and crawler cranes for long-term heavy work like sheet piling. Cranes fall under OSHA Subpart CC: certified operator, qualified rigger and signal person, a ground conditions review, power line planning, inspections and a load chart for the configuration. Excavators lifting pipe are excluded, but a boom truck setting manholes is a crane.
field.title: Crane types used on utility and pipe jobs
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC (1926.1400 scope, 1926.1427 operator qualification) summarized

field.text: A crane's load chart only works if the crane is level and the outriggers are fully supported. Setup basics: OSHA 1926.1402 requires ground that, with supporting materials (blocking, mats, cribbing), meets the maker's specs for support and levelness, and the controlling entity must tell the crane user about known hazards under the setup area like voids, tanks and utilities. Sizing a pad: required area = outrigger force divided by allowable ground bearing pressure. Example: 40,000 lb outrigger load on soil good for 2,000 psf needs 20 sq ft, about a 4.5 ft by 4.5 ft mat. Never set an outrigger near a fresh trench, backfilled excavation, manhole or over a vault; backfilled trenches are soft. Extend outriggers per the chart (full, mid or retracted) and level within the maker's limit.
field.title: Crane setup, outriggers and mats
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: OSHA 1926.1402 (summary); DICA crane pad sizing method (CICA)

field.text: OSHA's equipment rule (1926.600(a)(6)) says equipment working near power lines must keep at least 10 ft from lines rated 50 kV or below, and 10 ft plus 0.4 in per kV above 50 kV for higher voltages, unless lines are de-energized and visibly grounded or insulating barriers are up; in transit with the boom lowered, 4 ft below 50 kV and 10 ft from 50 to 345 kV. Cranes under 1926.1408 must plan a 20-ft zone for lines up to 350 kV, or use the Table A distances once the voltage is confirmed by the utility: 10 ft up to 50 kV, 15 ft to 200 kV, 20 ft to 350 kV, 25 ft to 500 kV, 35 ft to 750 kV, 45 ft to 1,000 kV. Treat every overhead line as energized until the owner says otherwise. Use a dedicated spotter when close.
field.title: Power line clearance for cranes and equipment
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear

field.text: Vacuum lifters (vacuum lifting attachments) grab pipe, precast and plates with a rubber-sealed pad and a vacuum pump; they hang from an excavator or crane hook or mount on a coupler. Advantages: no slings under the pipe, no one in the trench to unhook, fast handling of large-diameter PVC, HDPE, ductile and concrete pipe. Requirements: pads sized for the pipe diameter and weight, a clean, smooth, dry contact area, a vacuum reserve tank so the load holds briefly if the pump stops, and gauges and alarms that warn on low vacuum. ASME B30.20 covers below-the-hook lifting devices including vacuum lifters. Never let anyone under or beside a vacuum-held load; a lost seal drops it instantly. Rough or wet concrete, coatings and grooved pipe may not seal.
field.title: Vacuum lifters for pipe
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: ASME B30.20 scope (summary); manufacturer manuals

field.text: Other pipe handling gear: pipe grab or pipe grapple attachments (coupler-mounted, often rotating, with padded jaws) that clamp pipe sticks so the operator can lay pipe without slings; C-hooks and pipe hooks that go inside the pipe end for lifting short or heavy pieces; pipe tongs (scissor clamps) for small pipe; spreader bars for long sticks to prevent bending; and padded slings or wide nylon slings for plastic and coated pipe. Use only gear rated for the pipe weight and type and marked with its rated load. Check rubber pads on grabs so they don't scratch PVC or damage ductile iron lining. Below-the-hook devices must be inspected and marked under OSHA rigging rules and ASME B30.20.
field.title: Pipe grabs, pipe hooks and C-hooks
field.topic: Heavy equipment: trucks, hauling, cranes and lifting gear
field.source: Industry practice; ASME B30.20 (summary); OSHA 1926.251

field.text: A septic system (onsite wastewater treatment system, OWTS, OSS, 'private sewage system') treats household sewage on the lot where there's no public sewer. Basic parts: the building sewer from the house; a buried watertight septic tank where solids settle to the bottom as sludge, grease and light material float to the top as scum, and bacteria partly break down the waste; and a drainfield (leach field, absorption field, soil treatment area) where the clarified effluent soaks into unsaturated soil, which does most of the real treatment by filtering and by microbes. Variations add a pump tank, pressure distribution, a mound, a sand filter or an aerobic treatment unit where the soil is poor, shallow or wet. Systems are permitted and inspected by the county or state health department (or state environmental agency), not by the sewer utility. Rules differ a lot by state and county, so always work to the approved permit design.
field.title: How a septic system works (onsite system overview)
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA septic system guidance (archived 'proper care' page); EPA mound and ATU fact sheets

field.text: Septic tanks are sized by bedrooms (a stand-in for flow), not bathrooms. Examples from state rules: Washington (WAC 246-272A-0232) requires at least 1,000 gallons liquid volume for a single-family home with 4 or fewer bedrooms, plus 250 gallons for each extra bedroom (5 bedrooms = 1,250 gal, 6 = 1,500 gal). North Carolina (15A NCAC 18E .0801) also sets a 1,000 gallon absolute minimum for any septic tank, 1,000 gal for 4 or fewer bedrooms and 1,250 gal for 5, and for larger flows uses formulas such as V = 2Q for design flows up to 600 gpd. North Carolina doubles the required tank size when a grinder or sewage lift pump sits upstream of the tank. Many states use 1,000 gal as the floor for a 3-bedroom house; some older rules allowed 750 or 900 gal. Commercial tanks are sized from design daily flow (Washington: 3 times design flow for nonresidential). Check your state and county code for the exact table.
field.title: Septic tank sizing: gallons by number of bedrooms
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: Washington WAC 246-272A-0232; North Carolina 15A NCAC 18E .0801

field.text: Inside a septic tank, the inlet and outlet have baffles or sanitary tees so incoming flow doesn't stir up the sludge and scum, and so only the clear middle layer (effluent) leaves the tank. The inlet tee directs flow downward; the outlet tee draws from below the scum layer. Washington requires at least two compartments, with the first holding one-half to two-thirds of the total volume (a two-compartment tank or two single tanks in series). North Carolina allows two tanks in series or one two-compartment tank, and when tanks are in series the first tank's outlet uses a sanitary tee reaching 25 to 50% of the liquid depth. Field points: set the tank level so the inlet sits higher than the outlet (commonly about 2 to 3 inches drop across the tank per manufacturer); never leave a tank without its outlet baffle, because solids will carry into and clog the drainfield; and check that baffles are in place before backfill.
field.title: Septic tank compartments, baffles and sanitary tees
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: Washington WAC 246-272A-0232; North Carolina 15A NCAC 18E .0801; common tank manufacturer practice

field.text: An effluent filter (outlet filter, 'Zabel' or 'Polylok' type screen) is a slotted cartridge set in the tank's outlet tee that stops suspended solids from leaving the tank and plugging the drainfield or pump. North Carolina requires an approved effluent filter in the outlet of the final compartment of every septic tank. Many states now require them on new systems. Maintenance: the cartridge is pulled and hosed off back into the tank (inlet side) during pumping or inspection, typically every 1 to 3 years or per the maker; a clogged filter backs sewage up into the house, which is a common 'my septic backed up but the tank isn't full' call. Bring the filter handle up under an access riser so it can be reached without digging. Wear gloves and eye protection; effluent carries pathogens.
field.title: Septic tank effluent filters (outlet filters)
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: North Carolina 15A NCAC 18E .0801; general onsite practice

field.text: Access risers bring the tank manholes up to grade so the tank can be pumped and inspected without digging. Lids must be secured (screwed down, locked or too heavy for a child) because people, especially children, have fallen into septic tanks and drowned or been overcome by gases. Septic tanks and pump chambers contain hydrogen sulfide, methane and low oxygen; a tank is a permit-required confined space for workers. Never enter a septic tank, even an 'empty' pumped one, or lean in head-first to look; work from outside with tools. Keep open tanks barricaded and covered when you step away. Methane is flammable, so no smoking or open flame near an open tank. Concrete tank lids can crack and collapse; don't drive over a tank unless it's rated for traffic.
field.title: Septic tank risers, lids and safety (falling in, sewer gas)
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: General onsite safety practice; OSHA confined space principles

field.text: EPA guidance: a household septic tank is typically pumped every 3 to 5 years, but the right interval depends on household size, tank size and water use, so have it measured. EPA's trigger: pump when the bottom of the scum layer is within 6 inches of the bottom of the outlet, or when the top of the sludge layer is within 12 inches of the outlet. Pumpers (septage haulers) measure layers with a sludge judge or stick. Pump through the main manhole (not just the small inspection port) so the whole tank can be cleaned, and check baffles and the effluent filter at the same time. Additives and yeast aren't a substitute for pumping. Septage is hauled to a treatment plant or permitted land-application site under state rules.
field.title: When to pump a septic tank (pumping interval and scum/sludge rule)
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA archived septic 'proper care' guidance; UGA Extension (2025)

field.text: EPA recommends a conventional household septic system be inspected by a septic professional at least every 3 years. Alternative systems with pumps, float switches, electrical controls or mechanical parts (mounds with pump chambers, ATUs, sand filters, drip systems) should generally be inspected once a year, and many states require a maintenance contract for them. An inspection typically checks: liquid level in the tank (high level can mean a clogged outlet or failing field), scum and sludge depths, baffles and filter, signs of leaks or roots, pump and alarm operation, and the drainfield surface for wet spots or odor. Many counties also require an inspection at property sale ('time of transfer'). Keep a record and a sketch of where the tank and field are.
field.title: Septic system inspection frequency
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA archived septic 'proper care' guidance

field.text: A conventional drainfield is a set of shallow trenches (often 18 to 36 inches wide and 18 to 36 inches deep, set by state rule) with perforated distribution pipe (usually 4 inch) laid level in washed gravel or stone, or in plastic chambers, with a separation layer (geotextile, untreated paper or straw per code) and soil cover on top. Effluent flows by gravity or by a pump to the trenches and soaks into the trench bottom and sidewalls. The key design numbers are the soil loading rate (gallons per day per square foot, from the perc rate or soil texture) and the vertical separation from the trench bottom to the seasonal high water table or bedrock (often 2 to 4 ft, varies by state). Field rules: keep trench bottoms and pipe level, never install in wet soil (smearing the trench walls seals them), scarify smeared surfaces, and keep heavy equipment off the field area.
field.title: Drainfield (leach field) basics: trenches, gravel and pipe
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: General onsite practice; state onsite codes vary

field.text: Plastic leaching chambers (arched, open-bottom units such as Infiltrator-type chambers) replace gravel and pipe in many drainfields. They're light, avoid dirty rock fines, and leave an open infiltrative surface; many states give a trench-length reduction for approved chambers, others don't. Install per the maker: level trench bottom, chambers interlocked end to end, end caps, inspection ports, and careful backfill so equipment doesn't crush them. A distribution box (D-box) splits gravity effluent evenly among trenches. It must sit level on firm, undisturbed or compacted base (a settled D-box sends all flow to one trench and overloads it); speed levelers or flow- equalizer inserts on the outlets fine-tune the split. Drop boxes are used on sloped sites to load trenches in series. Check the D-box and outlets during inspections.
field.title: Gravelless chamber drainfields and distribution boxes
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: General onsite practice; chamber manufacturer guidance

field.text: A perc test measures how fast water soaks into soil, reported in minutes per inch (MPI). Example procedure (Butler County, Iowa): dig three holes 4 to 12 inches in diameter and about 36 inches deep across the proposed field area; roughen the sides, remove loose dirt and put 2 inches of gravel in the bottom; presoak with 12 inches of water for at least 4 hours (overnight in clay); start the test 15 to 30 hours after presoak began; set water about 6 inches above the gravel and read the drop every 30 minutes (every 10 minutes in fast sand) for about 4 hours; MPI = time interval divided by the drop. Average the final rates, but if holes differ by more than 20 MPI, design for the slowest. Also bore one 6 ft hole in the field center to look for rock or water. Many states now rely on a soil evaluation instead of, or with, a perc test.
field.title: Perc test (percolation test) procedure and minutes per inch
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: Butler County (Iowa) Environmental Health, Perc Test Directions

field.text: Many states have replaced or supplemented perc tests with a soil evaluation by a licensed soil scientist, sanitarian or site evaluator. A backhoe digs a test pit (soil profile pit), often 5 to 8 ft deep or to a limiting layer, and the evaluator logs each horizon: texture (sand, loam, clay), structure, color, and redoximorphic features (mottling, gray or rust spots) that mark the seasonal high water table. The shallowest limiting layer (seasonal saturation, bedrock, hardpan or very slow soil) sets how much vertical separation is available and whether a conventional field, a shallow or pressure system, or a mound is needed. Crew tips: make pits safe (slope or bench them, keep spoils back, never enter a deep pit that isn't protected per OSHA), dig where the evaluator flags, and backfill and mark pits afterward. Soil tests in frozen or very wet ground may not be accepted.
field.title: Soil evaluation and profile pits for septic design
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: General onsite practice; OSHA excavation rules for test pits

field.text: A mound (Wisconsin mound) is a raised absorption bed built of clean sand fill on top of the natural ground, used where the site can't take a conventional field: slowly permeable soils, shallow soil over bedrock, or a high water table. Effluent goes from the septic tank to a pump (dosing) chamber, then is pumped under pressure in small doses several times a day through small perforated pipes in a gravel bed on top of the sand. The sand treats the effluent before it reaches the native soil. EPA's fact sheet lists limits such as at least 10 inches to seasonal high water, 2 ft to creviced bedrock and 1 ft to non-creviced bedrock under the mound, a maximum site slope of 25%, and no siting in floodplains, drainageways or depressions. Mounds cost much more than conventional fields, need a pump and power, and must be protected from traffic.
field.title: Mound septic systems: when they're used
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA Mound Systems fact sheet; Purdue Extension ID-163

field.text: Purdue Extension's mound construction steps (Indiana practice): fence the mound area plus 50 ft downslope and keep vehicles off before, during and after construction; install any upslope curtain drain; mow and cut trees at ground level, leaving stumps; install the feedline first, below frost (about 40 inches in Indiana) or sloped to drain back to the dose chamber; plow 7 to 8 inches deep along the contour, throwing furrows upslope; never work wet soil (if a sample rolls into a 1/8 inch ribbon it's too wet). Place specified medium sand, keeping at least 6 inches of sand under tracks; shape side slopes 3:1; lay at least 6 inches of washed stone, Sch 40 PVC laterals with holes facing down, 2 inches of stone over the pipe and a fabric barrier; then at least 6 inches of subsoil cap (about 1 ft at the center) and 6 inches of topsoil, and seed. Long axis follows the contour.
field.title: Building a mound system: site prep and construction steps
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: Purdue Extension ID-163, Mound Systems for On-Site Wastewater Treatment

field.text: Pressure-dosed systems (mounds, pressure distribution, sand filters, drip) use a pump tank or dosing chamber after the septic tank. Purdue guidance for mounds: the pump chamber at least the size of the septic tank, with about one day of reserve storage above the alarm; pump set 6 to 8 inches above the floor on blocks; a high-water alarm float about 3 inches above the pump-on float, on a separate fused circuit from the pump; house sewer at 2% slope and gravity effluent line at 1%. EPA's mound fact sheet adds: check the pump, floats and alarm yearly, calibrate pumps with event counters and run-time meters, flush laterals yearly, and consider standby power. Field tip: a homeowner silencing an alarm and ignoring it is the classic failure; the alarm means the pump or float has quit and storage is filling.
field.title: Pump tanks, dosing chambers and high-water alarms (septic)
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: Purdue Extension ID-163; U.S. EPA Mound Systems fact sheet

field.text: An aerobic treatment unit (ATU, 'aerobic septic', package plant for a house) blows air into the sewage so oxygen-using bacteria break it down faster and more completely than in a septic tank. Typical home units handle 400 to 1,500 gpd, often with a pretreatment (trash) tank, an aeration chamber and a clarifier. Effluent then goes to a drainfield or drip field, or in some states to surface spray after disinfection. NSF/ANSI Standard 40 Class I certification (per EPA's fact sheet) means the unit met effluent limits of 25 mg/L CBOD5 and 30 mg/L TSS (30-day averages; 40 and 45 mg/L 7-day), pH 6 to 9, with a noise limit of 60 dBA at 20 ft (6 m) in testing. ATUs are used on small lots, poor soils and near sensitive waters because cleaner effluent allows smaller or shallower fields where the code permits. They need electricity (EPA lists about 2.5 to 10 kWh per day for suspended-growth units).
field.title: Aerobic treatment units (ATUs) and NSF/ANSI Standard 40
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA Wastewater Technology Fact Sheet: Aerobic Treatment; NSF wastewater program update (NMED, 2010) for NSF/ANSI 40 Class I limits

field.text: EPA's ATU fact sheet recommends inspections about every two months and servicing quarterly, usually through a maintenance contract with a trained provider (many states require one for the life of the system). Sludge is typically wasted every 8 to 12 months. A new unit needs 6 to 12 weeks to grow its biomass. Common problems: blower or aerator failure (the unit turns septic and smells), clogged pumps or lines, motor or control failures, corroded parts, and process upsets from grease, chemicals, bleach, hydraulic surges or neglect, which send solids out to the field. Signs: alarm light, no air hum, gray-black or smelly effluent, chlorinator out of tablets on spray systems. Use only the disinfection tablets the maker specifies (pool chlorine tablets are not interchangeable). Field crews: never shut off the breaker to an ATU for long periods.
field.title: Aerobic treatment unit maintenance and common failures
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA Wastewater Technology Fact Sheet: Aerobic Treatment

field.text: Where soil is shallow or effluent must be cleaner, state codes allow advanced (alternative) systems. Pressure distribution: a pump doses small perforated laterals so effluent spreads evenly over the whole field instead of overloading the first few feet of a gravity trench. Sand or media filters (single-pass or recirculating sand filters, textile or peat filters) polish septic tank effluent before it goes to the soil. Drip dispersal: a pump, filters and controls push effluent through small pressure-compensating drip tubing laid 6 to 12 inches deep, good for slopes, thin soil and odd-shaped lots. Constructed wetlands and evapotranspiration beds are used in some regions. All of these need pumps, controls, alarms and routine service, and usually a state-listed product and a licensed installer and maintainer. Install exactly per the approved design and maker's manual.
field.title: Advanced onsite options: sand filters, drip, pressure distribution
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA septic system types guidance; state onsite codes

field.text: Setbacks keep septic systems away from drinking water and neighbors. They vary widely, so use your county's table. Example (Kern County, California, Environmental Health): water supply wells 50 ft from the building sewer, 100 ft from the septic tank, 100 ft from the disposal field and 150 ft from a seepage pit; streams 50 ft from the tank and 100 ft from the field; buildings 5 ft from the tank and 8 ft from the field; property lines 5 ft from the tank and field; domestic water lines 5 ft from the tank and field; pressure public water mains 25 ft. Virginia's waterworks rule requires water mains to be at least 10 ft horizontally from septic tanks and drainfields. Other common items: 10 ft from foundations, setbacks from slopes and cut banks, and larger setbacks in sole-source aquifer or shellfish areas. Mark setbacks in the field before digging.
field.title: Septic setbacks: wells, streams, property lines, water lines
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: Kern County (CA) Public Health septic setback table; Virginia 12VAC5-590-1150

field.text: Signs of failure: sewage backing up into the house or slow drains throughout; gurgling; wet, spongy or bright-green soggy areas or surfacing sewage over the drainfield or tank; sewage odors outside; high liquid level in the tank after pumping; and bacteria or nitrate in a nearby well. Common causes: tank never pumped so solids carried into and clogged the field (biomat buildup), too much water (leaky toilets, which EPA notes can waste up to 200 gallons a day; laundry all on one day; roof drains or sump pumps routed to the system), crushed or compacted pipes from vehicles, roots, a settled distribution box, a missing outlet baffle, failed pumps or alarms, and a field built in soil that was too wet or too shallow. Surfacing sewage is a public health hazard and must be reported to the health department; repairs usually need a repair permit.
field.title: Signs of a failing septic system and common causes
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA archived septic 'proper care' guidance; general onsite practice

field.text: Per EPA guidance: don't park or drive on the drainfield; plant only grass over it and keep trees at the distance a septic professional recommends so roots stay out; keep roof drains, sump pumps and other rainwater away from the field, since saturated soil can't take effluent. Spread out water use (EPA puts average indoor use near 70 gallons per person per day), fix leaks, and use high-efficiency fixtures. Don't flush wipes, grease, paint, solvents, medicines or 'flushable' products; limit garbage disposal use. For construction crews working near an existing system: locate and flag the tank and field first, keep tracked equipment, spoil piles and material laydown off them, don't route a trench through the field, and don't regrade over it. Compaction from one pass of loaded equipment can ruin a field.
field.title: Drainfield do's and don'ts (protecting the leach field)
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: U.S. EPA archived septic 'proper care' guidance

field.text: Onsite systems are regulated by states, usually delegated to county or district health departments (in some states the environmental agency). Typical sequence: application with a site plan; soil evaluation or perc test by a licensed evaluator or engineer; a design sized to bedrooms or flow; construction permit; installation by a state- or county-licensed installer; inspection before backfill (the inspector wants to see the tank, pipe, D-box and trenches or bed open); and an operation permit or final approval. Repairs, replacements, additions of bedrooms and connecting a new building often need a new permit. Large systems (often over a few thousand gallons per day) may be permitted by the state environmental agency or EPA's Underground Injection Control program. Never cover work before it's inspected; covered work may have to be dug up.
field.title: Septic permits: health department, installers and inspections
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: General onsite practice; state onsite codes

field.text: Field practice for septic and pump tanks (check the maker and permit): set the tank on a level, compacted base of sand or fine gravel on undisturbed soil, never on rock points or soft fill; check the inlet is higher than the outlet as the maker shows; use watertight joints and seals at pipe penetrations (flexible boots, not mortar alone), and seal riser joints; water-test or vacuum-test the tank if the code requires (many states do for new tanks). Backfill evenly in lifts so a plastic or fiberglass tank isn't pushed out of round; fill plastic tanks with water as you backfill when the maker says so. In high groundwater, empty tanks float: use anti-flotation deadmen or straps, or keep the tank full. Building sewer to the tank commonly runs at 1/4 inch per foot (2%), with a cleanout near the house.
field.title: Installing a septic tank: bedding, watertightness and flotation
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: General onsite practice; Purdue Extension ID-163 (2% house sewer)

field.text: When a property connects to public sewer, the old septic tank must be properly abandoned under the local health or plumbing code. Common requirements: have the tank pumped by a licensed hauler; then remove the tank, or crush or break the bottom so it can't hold water, and fill it with sand, gravel or other approved material; remove or fill the lids so no one can fall in; and get the abandonment inspected or documented. Cesspools and seepage pits are handled the same way. The new building sewer is connected to the public lateral, bypassing the tank; don't leave the old tank in line as a 'grease trap'. Septic tank effluent pumped into a public sewer without approval can be a violation. Keep the abandonment record with the sewer connection permit.
field.title: Abandoning a septic tank when connecting to public sewer
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: General local health/plumbing code practice

field.text: Onsite systems are designed for peak daily flow, not average use. Common design values: North Carolina uses 120 gallons per day per bedroom (or 60 gpd per person) for dwellings; EPA's Wisconsin mound fact sheet uses up to 150 gpd per bedroom (a 3-bedroom house = 450 gpd). Actual average use is lower (EPA puts indoor use near 70 gallons per person per day), which gives a safety margin. Commercial flows come from state tables (per seat, per employee, per site). Example: 4-bedroom house at 120 gpd per bedroom = 480 gpd design flow; drainfield area = design flow divided by the soil loading rate, so at 0.6 gpd per square foot the field needs 800 sq ft of trench bottom (check how your state counts sidewall and chamber credits). These are design numbers; the field crew builds the approved plan.
field.title: Septic design flow: gallons per day per bedroom
field.topic: Onsite wastewater: septic systems, drainfields, mounds and ATUs
field.source: North Carolina 15A NCAC 18E .0801; U.S. EPA Mound fact sheet; EPA proper care guidance

field.text: STEP (septic tank effluent pump) and STEG (septic tank effluent gravity) sewers keep a septic tank (interceptor tank) at each home and send only the settled liquid to the public collection line. Solids stay in the tank and are pumped out every several years by the utility or owner. STEP uses a small effluent pump (often a filtered turbine pump in the tank or a separate chamber) to push effluent into a small-diameter pressure main; STEG lets effluent flow by gravity in small pipe that can follow the ground with fewer manholes and flatter or variable grades because there are no solids to carry. Texas rules require a STEP pressure main to reach at least 1.0 ft/s once a day (lower than the 3.0 ft/s for grinder systems, since effluent has few solids). Pros: small shallow pipe, low I/I. Cons: tanks to maintain, odor and H2S from septic effluent, and corrosion at discharge points.
field.title: STEP and STEG systems (septic tank effluent pump / gravity)
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Texas 30 TAC 217.97 (pressure sewers); Pumps & Systems on low-pressure sewers

field.text: A low-pressure sewer (LPS) uses a grinder pump station at each home or small group of homes: a basin (often 50 to 100+ gallons usable) with a grinder pump that chops solids and pumps raw sewage into a small-diameter pressure main (often 1.5 to 4 inch) laid shallow, following the ground, often by directional drilling. Used where gravity sewer would be very deep, on hilly or rocky ground, waterfronts, and low-density areas. Pump types: progressing cavity (semi-positive displacement, about 11 gpm at high heads, good for residential) and centrifugal grinders (higher flow). Pipe is commonly HDPE DR 11, PVC SDR 21 or Sch 40 PVC rated at least 160 psi. Mains need flushing connections at ends, junctions and about every 1,000 ft on long runs, air release at high points, curb stops at each service and isolation valves for sections. Each station needs power from the home and an alarm.
field.title: Grinder pump low-pressure sewer (LPS) basics
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Pumps & Systems, Understanding the design benefits of low pressure sewer systems; Texas 30 TAC 217.97

field.text: Texas pressure sewer rules (30 TAC 217.97) give a good example of state criteria: collection pipe at least 1.5 inch; service pipe at least 1.25 inch for one dwelling unit, 1.5 inch for multiple units; grinder system mains must hit at least 3.0 ft/s once a day and stay between 2.0 and 8.0 ft/s; each discharge has a check valve, union and full-closing gate or ball valve (check valve upstream); where a service is buried less than 30 inches, add a check valve and shutoff at the main. Isolation valves at main intersections, both sides of stream crossings and at least every 2,500 ft, in locked boxes with position indicators. Air release valves at every high point (odor control within 50 ft of buildings). Pipe at least ASTM D2241 Class 200 PVC; discharge pipe rated 2.5 times max design pressure. Each single-home wet well needs at least 100 gallons of reserve above the alarm.
field.title: Pressure sewer rules: pipe size, velocity, valves, reserve storage
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Texas 30 TAC 217.97, Pressure Sewers

field.text: Field points for grinder pump stations (check the maker's manual and utility detail): set the basin plumb and level on compacted bedding; anchor against flotation with a concrete collar or ballast where groundwater is high (Texas rules require buoyancy protection); keep the top of the basin above grade so surface water can't run in; use the maker's inlet grommet for the building sewer; install the discharge with the check valve and shutoff (and curb stop at the property line) per detail; run the dedicated circuit and a control panel with a high-level audible and visual alarm (Texas requires panels at least 2 ft above the ground floor elevation served); rail systems make pump pulls easier than flexible hose. Startup: fill with clean water, cycle the pump, confirm alarm, and check that the run time matches expected flow. Tell owners not to flush wipes, grease or rags, which jam grinders.
field.title: Installing grinder pump stations: field checklist
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Texas 30 TAC 217.97; Pumps & Systems low-pressure sewer article; common manufacturer practice

field.text: A vacuum sewer uses a central vacuum station that holds the mains at about 16 to 20 inches of mercury (in. Hg) below atmospheric. Each house (often two per pit) drains by gravity to a valve pit. When about 10 gallons collect in the sump, a pneumatic interface valve opens with no electricity; atmospheric air pushes the sewage slug into the main at roughly 15 to 18 ft/s, and the valve stays open a few seconds longer to admit air (about 2 parts air to 1 liquid). Sewage travels to the station's collection tank and is pumped on to a gravity sewer or plant. Mains are typically 4 to 10 inch PVC (SDR 21, Class 200, gasketed); service laterals 3 inch; building sewers 4 inch. Good for flat, high-groundwater, coastal or rocky areas where deep gravity sewers are costly. One station serves many homes, so the station needs standby power and alarms.
field.title: Vacuum sewer systems: how they work
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Vacuum Sewers Design and Installation Guidelines (PDH Engineer 2007, based on AIRVAC practice)

field.text: Vacuum mains are laid in a sawtooth profile: long runs sloped at least 0.20% toward the station, with 'lifts' (short steep rises made of two 45 degree fittings) to gain elevation so the pipe can stay shallow. The profile keeps an open air path over the liquid so vacuum reaches every valve pit. Guideline lift heights: 1.0 ft for 3 to 4 inch pipe, 1.5 ft for 6 to 8 inch, 2.0 ft for 10 inch; several small lifts are better than one big one, and the guideline cites at least 50 ft at 0.20% before a lift. Total static loss is held to about 13 ft and friction loss to about 5 ft. Recommended main capacities: 4 inch about 80 homes, 6 inch 210, 8 inch 420, 10 inch 750 (at 0.5 gpm per home). Grade matters as much as on gravity sewer: a sag in the wrong place fills with liquid and blocks the air path. Follow the system supplier's profile drawings exactly.
field.title: Vacuum sewer installation: sawtooth profile, lifts and slopes
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Vacuum Sewers Design and Installation Guidelines (PDH Engineer 2007)

field.text: Vacuum mains are tested under vacuum rather than air pressure. The guideline's daily acceptance test: hold the section at 22 in. Hg for 2 hours after a 15-minute stabilization, with loss limited to 1% per hour (about 1/2 in. Hg per hour). Test each day's work so leaks are found while the trench is fresh. Division (isolation) valves are typically placed every 1,500 to 2,000 ft and at branches, rated to hold 24 in. Hg, so sections can be isolated to find leaks or problems. Valve pits are tested too, and the interface valve and controller are adjusted at startup. Common field problems: a leaking joint or cracked fitting (the station runs constantly), a waterlogged line from a stuck-open valve, or a sag that traps liquid. Use the supplier's test procedure and record vacuum readings.
field.title: Vacuum sewer testing and division valves
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Vacuum Sewers Design and Installation Guidelines (PDH Engineer 2007)

field.text: Lagoons are common in small towns because they're simple and cheap to run. Types (Oregon operator study guide): facultative ponds about 3 to 6 ft deep, with an aerobic top layer where algae make oxygen, a middle zone, and an anaerobic sludge layer on the bottom, and very long detention (often 1 to several months); aerated lagoons, partial-mix about 8 to 15 ft deep and complete-mix about 10 to 15 ft, with blowers or surface aerators; anaerobic ponds for strong industrial waste (odor risk); and shallow polishing ponds at the end. Facultative ponds are commonly loaded at about 15 to 35 lb BOD per acre per day, depending on climate. Some lagoons discharge under an NPDES permit; others are 'total containment' or irrigation systems with no stream discharge. Lagoon dikes and liners are earthwork: compaction and liner integrity specs matter.
field.title: Wastewater lagoons (stabilization ponds): types and depths
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Oregon water operator guide 10.3: Stabilization Ponds and Aerated Lagoons

field.text: Keep lagoon water at least about 2 to 3 ft deep so cattails and tules can't root (they breed mosquitoes and cause short-circuiting). Mow dikes, repair erosion and wave damage, add riprap where needed, and trap burrowing animals (muskrats, nutria) that tunnel through dikes. Unexplained level drops may mean seepage through the liner, which can violate groundwater rules. Measure sludge depth at least yearly with a sludge judge from a boat; sludge builds up near the inlet and cuts detention time. Spring and fall turnover can bring up odors; gray or black water with rotten-egg smell means overloaded septic conditions. Algae leaving the pond show up as suspended solids, and ammonia removal drops in cold water. Detention example: 15 acres x 5 ft deep = about 24.4 million gallons, which at 0.25 MGD is about 98 days. Use a boat with a buddy and life jackets.
field.title: Lagoon operation problems: weeds, dikes, sludge, odor
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Oregon water operator guide 10.3

field.text: Terms vary by city, but generally: the building drain is the piping inside the building; the building sewer runs from about 2 to 5 ft outside the foundation (per plumbing code) to the public sewer or to the property line; the lateral (service connection, house connection) is the pipe from the main to the property line or easement; and the main (collector) is the public sewer in the street. Ownership and maintenance responsibility differs: many utilities make the owner responsible for the whole line from house to main, including the tap; others own from the main to the property line or to a cleanout at the right-of-way. Plumbing permits and inspections usually cover the building sewer; the sewer utility controls the connection to the main (tap permit, inspection, fees). Check the local sewer use ordinance before digging in the street.
field.title: Building sewer vs lateral vs main: who owns what
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: General plumbing code and sewer use ordinance practice

field.text: Plumbing codes set minimum slope for building drains and building sewers. Common values (IPC-style, check your adopted code): pipe 2 1/2 inch and smaller at least 1/4 inch per foot (2.08%); 3 to 6 inch at least 1/8 inch per foot (1.04%); 8 inch and larger at least 1/16 inch per foot. Many utilities require 4 inch building sewers at 1/4 inch per foot (2%) anyway, and 6 inch for commercial or multifamily. Minimum building sewer size is commonly 4 inch for a single-family house (some codes allow 3 inch). Too flat and solids strand; very steep is usually fine on a building sewer but can cause problems at the connection. Use long-sweep fittings, avoid 90 degree short bends underground, bed it like a main, keep the pipe on a uniform grade, and keep cover enough to prevent freezing and crushing. See grade-survey files for slope conversions.
field.title: Building sewer slope and size (1/4 inch per foot rule)
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: International Plumbing Code (slope table) and common utility standards, as commonly summarized

field.text: Plumbing codes and utility details require cleanouts on building sewers so lines can be rodded or jetted. Common rules (check your code): a cleanout at or near the junction of the building drain and building sewer (often within a few feet outside the wall); at each aggregate change of direction over 135 degrees; at intervals not over about 100 ft on straight runs of building sewer; and a property-line or right-of-way cleanout where the utility's maintenance responsibility begins. Two-way cleanouts allow rodding toward the house and toward the main. Cleanout risers are the same size as the line up to 4 inch. In driveways and sidewalks, cap the riser and protect it with a cast iron box so it isn't crushed. A missing or broken cleanout cap is a big inflow source: replace it with a watertight cap. See structures-manholes-11 for mainline cleanouts.
field.title: Cleanouts on building sewers and laterals: spacing and placement
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Plumbing code practice as commonly summarized; I/I guidance (Clermont County)

field.text: When a new service connects to an existing main (more detail in water-appurtenances-9), typical utility rules: get the tap permit and schedule the utility's inspector; use an approved tap saddle (gasketed strap-on, clamp-on or insert type made for the pipe material and size) or cut in a wye with approved repair couplings; core the hole with a hole saw or coring machine sized to the saddle, never break it with a hammer ('hammer taps' crack pipe and leave jagged edges); make the tap in the upper half of the pipe, commonly between the 10 and 2 o'clock positions or at about 45 degrees above springline, so the lateral doesn't sit in flow; nothing may protrude into the main; keep taps a minimum distance from joints and from other taps (often 2 to 3 ft); don't tap into a manhole unless allowed, and then only through a core and boot above the bench. Retrieve the coupon from the main.
field.title: Tapping an existing sewer main for a lateral: rules
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Common sewer utility tap specifications

field.text: A backwater valve (backflow valve, check valve for sewer) has a flapper that lets flow out of the building but closes if the public sewer surcharges, so sewage doesn't come up floor drains and basement fixtures. Plumbing codes (UPC/IPC) require an approved backwater valve when fixtures sit on a floor level lower than the rim of the next upstream manhole cover on the public or private sewer. Only fixtures below that elevation drain through the valve; upper floors must bypass it so they keep draining and venting. Cleanouts for lines passing through the valve are labeled 'backwater valve downstream' (UPC). The valve must stay accessible for cleaning (usually in a pit with a cover or a clean-out box); a flapper jammed with debris doesn't protect anything. Many cities offer rebates for backwater valves in basement-flooding areas.
field.title: Backwater valves: when the plumbing code requires them
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: IAPMO Code Spotlight (UPC backwater valve provisions); city backwater valve guidance

field.text: Restaurants and food service must keep fats, oils and grease (FOG) out of the sewer. Two families: Hydromechanical grease interceptors (HGI, 'grease trap') are small units inside the building, rated by flow (common ratings 7 to 100 gpm) with grease capacity of at least 2 lb per gpm, need a vented flow-control fitting on the inlet, and hold water only a few minutes. Gravity grease interceptors (GGI) are large in-ground tanks (often 500 to 5,000+ gallons, sized for about 20 to 30 minutes of retention) outside the building, usually two compartments with manholes for pumping. Connect only grease-laden fixtures (pot sinks, pre-rinse, floor drains in food prep, dishwashers as allowed); never toilets or urinals; food grinders only through a solids interceptor. Hot water over 140 F can re-melt grease through small units. Local FOG ordinances set which type and size is required.
field.title: Grease interceptors vs grease traps (FOG separators)
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Open Exam Prep Journeyman Plumber guide 6.3 (ASME A112.14.3 / IAPMO Z1001 summaries)

field.text: Most FOG programs require pumping a grease interceptor when floating grease plus settled solids reach 25% of the liquid depth (the '25% rule'); past that, flow speeds up and grease washes out to the sewer.
