Pumping is by a licensed grease hauler; the owner keeps manifests and a maintenance log for the city's pretreatment or FOG inspector, and many cities set a maximum interval (often 30 to 90 days) regardless. Biological additives and enzymes that just move grease downstream are often banned. Construction points: set gravity interceptors level, watertight and anti-floated; use traffic-rated covers in drives; provide a sampling point or tee on the outlet if the ordinance asks; and install so every compartment can be reached by a vacuum truck. FOG is a leading cause of blockages and sanitary sewer overflows.
field.title: Grease interceptor maintenance: the 25% rule and FOG programs
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Open Exam Prep Journeyman Plumber guide 6.3; common municipal FOG ordinances

field.text: Sewer use ordinances often require industrial and commercial users to install a sampling (control, monitoring) manhole on their building sewer so the city's pretreatment staff can observe, sample and measure the discharge. Example (Moses Lake, WA code): when the director requires it, the industrial user installs a control manhole on the building sewer at its own expense, built to approved plans, safely located, and kept safe and accessible at all times, and the user maintains it. Typical details: located on the user's private line after all process flows join and before any domestic flow is added, a smooth channel or flume (Parshall or Palmer-Bowlus) for flow metering, room for an automatic sampler, and a lockable cover that city staff can reach without entering the building. Build the channel smooth and level so meters read correctly.
field.title: Sampling manholes (control manholes) for industrial users
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Moses Lake (WA) Municipal Code 13.05.100 Control Manholes; common pretreatment practice

field.text: Under the Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities, 2014): public gravity sewers carrying raw sewage are at least 8 inch; slopes are set so velocity is at least 2.0 ft/s flowing full with Manning n = 0.013 ('self-cleansing velocity'). Beyond the 8 to 24 inch minimums in grade-survey-18, the table continues: 36 inch 0.046 ft per 100 ft and 42 inch 0.037. Flatter slopes may be allowed where flow depth is at least 0.3 of the diameter at design average flow and the owner gives written maintenance assurance. Where velocity exceeds 15 ft/s, special provision against erosion and displacement is required (Illinois 35 IAC 370, a Ten States-based rule, uses the same 15 ft/s). Sewers 24 inch and smaller must be straight between manholes, checked by laser or lamping. These are design rules; crews build the plan grade and should raise anything that looks flatter than minimum.
field.title: Gravity sewer design basics: 8 inch minimum, 2 ft/s, Manning n
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities, 2014) as summarized; Illinois 35 IAC 370.320 (Ten States-based)

field.text: Ten States Standards (2014, chapter 11) size new sewers and plants on 100 gallons per capita per day plus industrial and big institutional flows, times a peaking factor from a curve (peak hourly flow can be roughly 2.5 to 4 times average for small areas, less for large ones). Sewers are designed to carry peak flow flowing full or at a set depth. Wet weather equalization should be considered where peak hourly flow is 3 times design average or more. For construction acceptance, Ten States sets an infiltration/exfiltration leakage limit of 100 gallons per inch of diameter per mile per day, tested with at least 2 ft of positive head. Example: 8 inch x 0.5 mile x 100 = 400 gpd allowable for that section. Treatment plant loads use 0.17 lb BOD and 0.20 lb suspended solids per person per day. Local agencies often use their own unit flows (per dwelling unit or acre).
field.title: Sewer design flows: 100 gallons per capita per day and peaking
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards) 2014, 11.243, 11.253, 33.94

field.text: Ten States Standards (2014) manhole rules beyond spacing and drops (see structures-manholes-6 and -8): minimum inside diameter 48 inches; minimum clear access opening 24 inches; flow channels shaped to the full crown height of the outlet pipe so surcharged flow stays in the channel; benches sloped at least 1/2 inch per foot (4%) toward the channel; and no lateral may discharge onto the bench, it must enter at channel level or by a drop. Manholes in areas of H2S get corrosion protection (lining or coating). Watertight manholes and flexible pipe connectors are standard (ASTM C923 boots). Where a manhole sits in a flood area or low spot, use watertight bolted covers and consider venting. A larger diameter (60 or 72 inch) is common for big pipes, multiple connections or inside drops; check your agency's standard detail.
field.title: Manhole design details: 48 inch diameter, 24 inch opening, bench slope
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards) 2014, sections 34.1-34.8

field.text: An inverted siphon (depressed sewer) carries a gravity sewer under a stream, canal, large culvert or utility by dipping down and back up; it flows full under pressure from the upstream head. Ten States Standards require at least two barrels, a minimum pipe size of 6 inch, and a velocity of at least 3.0 ft/s at design average flow, with inlet and outlet structures arranged so normal flow goes to one barrel and higher flows spill over to the others, and so each barrel can be taken out of service for cleaning. Siphons collect grit and grease at the low point, so they need regular flushing or jetting access, and upstream structures may release H2S where flow drops in. Build to exact grade at the inlet and outlet structures; a mistake there changes how the barrels share flow. Stream crossings also need at least 1 ft of cover in rock, 3 ft in other material.
field.title: Inverted siphons (depressed sewers) under streams and obstacles
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards) 2014, sections 35 and 36.11

field.text: A typical system goes from building laterals to 8 inch collectors in residential streets, to larger sub-mains and trunk sewers that drain whole neighborhoods (often 15 to 48 inch), to interceptors: large sewers (often 36 inch up to tunnels several feet in diameter) built along rivers or shorelines to intercept flow from many trunks, and historically from combined sewer outfalls, and carry it to the treatment plant. Interceptors are often deep, built in tunnels or by microtunneling, and owned by a regional sewer authority or district rather than the city. Field points: work on or near a live interceptor needs bypass plans sized for large wet-weather flows, H2S and confined-space controls, and coordination with the authority; connections to an interceptor usually require a manhole and a separate permit. Concrete interceptors are prone to crown corrosion (see H2S chunks).
field.title: Interceptors and trunk sewers
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: General collection system practice

field.text: Beyond the basics in force-mains-lift-stations-1, Ten States Standards (2014, section 49) set: cleansing velocity of at least 2 ft/s at design pumping rate, with about 8 ft/s as a recommended maximum (head loss, valve wear); minimum 4 inch diameter for raw sewage force mains; air relief valves at high points (vacuum relief where needed); the force main enters the receiving manhole with a smooth transition no more than 1 ft above the flow line, and that manhole gets corrosion protection; enough cover or insulation to prevent freezing; pipe and joints of water-main strength, designed for water hammer and cyclic surges; at least 10 ft horizontal separation from water mains; force mains that could be confused with potable mains must be identified; design Hazen-Williams C of 100 for unlined iron or steel and up to 120 for PVC, PE or lined ductile iron. Long force mains with long detention generate H2S.
field.title: Force main design rules: velocity, size, air valves, termination
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards) 2014, section 49

field.text: Ten States Standards (2014, chapter 40) lift station rules that crews and inspectors see on plans: at least two pumps, and with any one out of service the rest must handle peak hourly flow; raw sewage pumps pass 3 inch solids with suction and discharge openings at least 4 inch; wet well sized so fill time at average flow doesn't exceed 30 minutes (limits septic conditions); wet well floor sloped at least 1:1 to the hopper; ventilation of 12 air changes per hour continuous or 30 intermittent in wet wells; structures protected from the 100-year flood and operable in the 25-year flood; flow metering at stations of 350 gpm or more; alarms for power failure, high water, pump failure and unauthorized entry, sent to a 24-hour staffed location where available; and emergency pumping capability (generator, portable pump with a force main connection, or dual power feeds) unless storage prevents overflow. Wet wells are confined spaces.
field.title: Lift station design rules: pumps, wet well, ventilation, alarms, power
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards) 2014, sections 41-47

field.text: I/I is clean water that gets into sanitary sewers and takes up capacity. Inflow is stormwater that enters fast, directly, during rain: roof downspouts, foundation drains and sump pumps tied to the sanitary sewer, storm drain cross-connections, area drains, missing cleanout caps, and holes or vents in manhole lids. Infiltration is groundwater that seeps in more slowly through cracked pipe, failed joints, bad laterals and leaking manholes, and is worst when groundwater is high. Effects: sewer overflows to streams and backups into basements; the plant treats clear water as sewage, raising costs and rates; and pipes and pump stations must be built bigger. Private laterals, foundation drains and sump pumps can contribute more wet-weather flow than the public mains. New construction defects (unsealed joints, broken pipe, unplugged stubs, open manhole joints) become tomorrow's infiltration, which is why sewers are tested.
field.title: Inflow vs infiltration (I/I): what's the difference
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Clermont County (OH) Water Resources I/I FAQ; Open Exam Prep collection system rehabilitation

field.text: A sewer system evaluation survey (SSES) ranks I/I fixes by pairing several methods. Flow monitoring: portable meters in manholes record flow, compared against rainfall, to find which basins respond to rain (inflow) or run high in dry weather (infiltration). Smoke testing: non-toxic smoke blown into manholes comes up through broken pipes, open cleanouts, roof drains and illegal connections; notify residents and the fire department first. Dye testing: dye poured into a roof drain, catch basin or yard drain shows up in a downstream sanitary manhole if they're connected. CCTV and manhole inspections find cracks, leaking joints, roots and running infiltration. Night flow measurements (when use is low) show infiltration. Owners are often told to disconnect downspouts and sump pumps and send them at least 5 ft from the foundation, and to repair laterals.
field.title: Finding I/I: flow monitoring, smoke testing, dye testing, CCTV
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Clermont County (OH) Water Resources I/I FAQ; Open Exam Prep collection system rehabilitation

field.text: A combined sewer carries sewage and stormwater in the same pipe (common in older Northeast and Great Lakes cities); a separate system has a sanitary sewer and a storm sewer. A combined sewer overflow (CSO) is a designed relief point where, in heavy rain or snowmelt, flow above capacity discharges to a river at a permitted outfall. EPA's report to Congress counted 746 communities with combined systems, 9,348 CSO outfalls, and about 850 billion gallons of untreated sewage and stormwater discharged a year. A sanitary sewer overflow (SSO) is any release of raw sewage from a separate sanitary system (manhole overflows, pump station spills, broken force mains); EPA estimates 23,000 to 75,000 SSOs a year releasing 3 to 10 billion gallons, from wet-weather I/I, blockages (often FOG and roots) and mechanical failures. SSOs that reach waters of the U.S. are prohibited unless authorized by an NPDES permit and must be reported.
field.title: Combined vs separate sewers; CSO vs SSO
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: U.S. EPA Report to Congress fact sheet on CSOs and SSOs (2004); EPA SSO page (archived)

field.text: EPA's 1994 CSO Control Policy (made binding on CSO permits by Clean Water Act section 402(q) in 2000) requires combined-sewer communities to carry out nine minimum controls: proper operation and maintenance; maximum use of the collection system for storage; review of pretreatment requirements; maximizing flow to the plant; no dry-weather overflows; control of solids and floatables; pollution prevention; public notification of CSOs; and monitoring. They must also develop and carry out a long-term control plan (LTCP) with modeling, public input, priority for sensitive areas, alternatives and an implementation schedule. LTCP projects are what crews end up building: deep storage tunnels, storage tanks, sewer separation (new storm or sanitary pipe), green infrastructure, and plant expansions, often under a consent decree schedule. Dry-weather overflows are always violations.
field.title: CSO Control Policy: nine minimum controls and long-term control plans
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: U.S. EPA NPDES Inspection Manual, chapter 12 (CSO/SSO)

field.text: On sewer jobs, contractors cause SSOs by plugging lines without bypass, undersizing bypass pumps for rain, pumps running out of fuel, breaking a force main or lateral, or debris (rock, concrete, grout) left in a live line that later blocks it. Under the Clean Water Act and state rules, sewage spills that reach surface water or a storm drain are violations and usually must be reported to the state agency and the utility quickly (many states require notice within 24 hours or sooner; check yours). Practices: written bypass plan with backup pumps, float alarms and someone watching; check weather; plug and protect live lines while working; clean out construction debris and use debris traps or screens in the downstream manhole; keep a spill kit, plugs and a vacuum truck contact; and if a spill happens, stop the flow, contain it (berms, blocking storm inlets), recover what you can, and call the owner right away.
field.title: SSOs during construction: preventing and reporting spills
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: U.S. EPA SSO page (archived); common state SSO reporting practice

field.text: In sewage with no oxygen (long force mains, flat or slow sewers, wet wells with long holding time, septic tank effluent, warm weather), bacteria in the slime layer turn sulfate into sulfide. Turbulence at force main discharges, drops, hydraulic jumps and junctions releases it as H2S gas. In the pipe crown and manhole walls above the water line, Thiobacillus bacteria convert H2S into sulfuric acid, which attacks the cement paste in concrete, forming soft gypsum and ettringite that wash away, leaving exposed aggregate and rebar. This crown corrosion can destroy concrete pipe and manholes in years. A two-year study cited by MSW Management found 5.4% material loss and a 13% strength drop in untreated concrete. H2S is also deadly to workers (see first_aid-25). Sulfide control is usually worth it where anaerobic detention exceeds about 2 hours.
field.title: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) in sewers: where it forms and why it eats concrete
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: MSW Management, 'Conquering corrosion in concrete pipes' (2017); Ten States Standards 2014

field.text: Ways owners fight H2S: Design: keep velocity up, avoid long wet-well holding times, use smooth force main discharges (Ten States: no more than 1 ft above the flow line), drop structures that limit turbulence, and ventilation. Materials: PVC, HDPE, vitrified clay and fiberglass don't corrode from acid; concrete pipe and manholes get PVC or HDPE liners (T-lock), epoxy or calcium-aluminate coatings, or sacrificial concrete; ductile iron force mains get special linings. Chemicals: calcium nitrate, iron salts, magnesium hydroxide, hydrogen peroxide or oxygen injection, dosed upstream of the problem point; MSW Management describes a calcium nitrate program dosed at a wet well. Odor control at manholes: carbon filters, biofilters, sealed lids. Crews tying into a corroded manhole should expect soft concrete and loose steps; test the air and don't trust steps.
field.title: Controlling H2S odor and corrosion in collection systems
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: MSW Management (2017); Ten States Standards 2014 section 49.3; general practice

field.text: Fats, oils and grease from kitchens cool and stick to pipe walls, collecting debris and hardening into deposits that narrow the pipe, and with wipes and roots form blockages that cause backups and SSOs. FOG also coats lift station wet wells and floats, causing pump failures. Hot spots are downstream of restaurant clusters, apartment complexes and flat or sagging sewer sections. Utilities fight it with FOG ordinances (grease interceptors, pumping logs, inspections), public education ('can the grease'), and frequent jetting of hot spots. When jetting or CCTV finds heavy grease, crews may use root and grease cutters; never use solvents. On new construction, sags ('bellies') are where grease and solids settle first, which is one reason CCTV acceptance checks for ponding. Never pour concrete washout, grout or slurry into a sewer: it hardens like grease, only worse.
field.title: FOG (fats, oils and grease) blockages in sewers
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Common municipal FOG program practice; EPA SSO causes

field.text: Main trenchless rehab families (see trenchless-basics-4 and -5 for bursting and CIPP steps): CIPP lines the pipe with resin-soaked felt cured in place; for round but deteriorated pipe; small diameter loss; laterals reinstated from inside. Sliplining pushes or pulls a smaller new pipe into the old one and grouts the annulus; cheap for long runs but loses significant diameter, and laterals are excavated. Pipe bursting breaks the old pipe outward and pulls in HDPE of the same or larger size; needs pits and can heave nearby utilities. Fold-and-form inserts a folded thermoplastic liner and rounds it with heat and pressure; for round pipe with moderate damage. Spiral wound liners are machine-wound strips, good for large pipe and live flow, with some diameter loss. Chemical grouting seals leaking joints but adds no strength. Point repairs fix isolated defects. Choice depends on pipe condition, size, depth, flow and laterals.
field.title: Sewer rehab methods compared: CIPP, sliplining, bursting, fold-and-form
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Colorado operator guide: Collection System Rehabilitation

field.text: Sliplining field practice (common spec practice, check yours): CCTV and clean the host pipe, cut protruding taps and roots, and pull a test mandrel or proving section through to confirm the liner will pass. Dig an insertion pit long enough for the liner's bend radius (fused HDPE strings) or for jointed sections (pushed segmental PVC, fiberglass or HDPE with flush joints). Bypass flow, push or pull the liner in with a nose cone, without exceeding the maker's allowable pull force. Brace the liner against flotation, then fill the annular space with low-density cellular grout in stages so grouting pressure doesn't collapse the liner (watch the maker's pressure limit). Seal ends at manholes. Reconnect laterals by excavating and using saddles or tees. Sliplining reduces diameter but a smooth liner often carries similar flow because of the lower roughness. CCTV after.
field.title: Sliplining: insertion pits, annular grout and laterals
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Common sliplining specification practice; Open Exam Prep rehab guide

field.text: Manholes are major I/I and corrosion points. Inflow fixes: solid or gasketed covers, inflow dishes under vented lids, and raising covers out of low spots. The frame-to-chimney joint is the most common leak; repair with internal rubber chimney seals or external wraps, and replace broken adjusting rings. Leaking barrel joints and pipe penetrations are sealed with chemical grout (polyurethane or acrylamide injection) or hydraulic cement. Corroded cones and barrels from H2S get a cementitious or calcium aluminate liner (spray or spin-cast), 100% solids epoxy or polyurethane coatings, or a full structural liner (fiberglass insert, CIPP manhole liner); new precast can get cast-in PVC or HDPE liner sheet. Coatings fail mostly from bad prep: blast or high-pressure wash to sound concrete, stop infiltration first, respect the maker's dryness and temperature limits, and spark (holiday) test finished epoxy and plastic linings. Inverts and benches are rebuilt with grout. Manhole rehab is confined-space work.
field.title: Manhole rehab: frame seals, I/I fixes, coatings and liners
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Open Exam Prep collection system rehabilitation guide; Biogenic sulfide corrosion (Wikipedia) for CAC and epoxy; general practice

field.text: Not every defect needs a full-length liner. Sectional (point) CIPP liners, a few feet long, are pulled in on a packer and cured over a single crack, hole or bad joint. Test-and-seal chemical grouting uses a packer to isolate each joint, air-test it, and inject grout if it fails; it stops leaks but adds no strength. Excavated spot repair replaces a short section with new pipe and approved repair couplings (shear-banded flexible couplings). Lateral work: protruding (hammer) taps are cut back with a robotic cutter; broken or offset connections are fixed with a top hat or T-liner (lateral-to-main connection liner); roots at connections are cut then grouted or lined, since cutting alone invites regrowth. After any CIPP, every live lateral must be reinstated by robotic cutter and confirmed by CCTV before flow is returned; a missed lateral backs sewage into a house.
field.title: Spot repairs, sectional liners, grouting and lateral reinstatement
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Colorado operator guide: Collection System Rehabilitation

field.text: Sewer CCTV inspection uses a crawler or push camera to record the inside of a pipe; utilities increasingly require it coded to NASSCO's PACP (Pipeline Assessment Certification Program). PACP is a standard defect-coding system: the certified operator assigns a code to each observation, enters qualifiers (clock position, percentage, length), and assigns a condition grade. Defects fall into four families: structural (cracks, fractures, breaks, holes, deformation, joint offsets), operation and maintenance (roots, grease, debris, deposits, infiltration, obstructions), construction features (taps, connections, intruding seals), and miscellaneous (water level, camera underwater, survey abandoned). Companion programs cover manholes (MACP) and laterals (LACP), both requiring PACP certification first. PACP certification takes a NASSCO-approved training course plus an exam, and certificates must be renewed; check NASSCO for current requirements. See testing-sewer-11 for CCTV acceptance of new sewers.
field.title: CCTV inspection and NASSCO PACP coding basics
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: NASSCO PACP Condition Grading System (2023); Envirosight 'What is PACP'

field.text: Each PACP defect gets a condition grade from 1 to 5, rated the same regardless of pipe size or material (NASSCO: a grade 4 hole is a grade 4 hole). Grade 5 is the most severe. Commonly cited NASSCO meanings: 5 = immediate attention, pipe has failed or will likely fail within about 5 years; 4 = poor, severe defects likely to become grade 5 in about 5 to 10 years; 3 = fair, moderate defects that will keep deteriorating (about 10 to 20 years); 2 = good, defects that have not begun to deteriorate; 1 = excellent, minor defects, failure unlikely in the foreseeable future. Check the current PACP manual for exact wording. Structural and O&M grades are reported separately. The Quick Rating is a 4-character score: highest grade found and how many times, then the next highest grade and its count (e.g. 5241 = two grade 5 defects and one grade 4; counts over 9 use letters). Averages can hide a single severe defect.
field.title: PACP condition grades 1 to 5 and quick rating
field.topic: Sewer collection systems: small-community systems, laterals, gravity design, I/I, overflows, corrosion, rehab, CCTV
field.source: NASSCO PACP Condition Grading System (2023); common PACP summaries

field.text: A municipal wastewater treatment plant (WWTP, WRRF, POTW) treats sewage in stages. Preliminary treatment (headworks): screens remove rags and debris, grit chambers settle sand and gravel, and flow is measured. Primary treatment: primary clarifiers settle out heavier solids and skim floating grease. Secondary (biological) treatment: microorganisms eat dissolved and fine organic matter in activated sludge basins, oxidation ditches, SBRs, trickling filters or lagoons, then secondary clarifiers settle the biomass. Advanced or tertiary treatment where the permit demands it: nutrient removal (nitrogen and phosphorus), filtration. Disinfection: chlorine (then dechlorination) or UV light before discharge to the receiving water. Solids handling: sludge is thickened, stabilized (digesters), dewatered and hauled or land-applied as biosolids. The NPDES permit sets what the effluent must meet.
field.title: Wastewater treatment plant process train (overview)
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General wastewater treatment practice; operator study guides

field.text: Headworks protect everything downstream. Bar screens (mechanically cleaned, or manual bar racks) catch rags, wipes, sticks and plastics; modern plants add fine screens (openings often 1/4 inch down to a few millimeters) because wipes wrap pumps and clog equipment. Screenings are washed, compacted and landfilled. Grit removal (aerated grit chambers, vortex grit units, detritus tanks) settles sand, gravel, coffee grounds and eggshells that would wear pumps and fill tanks; grit is washed and landfilled. Flow is measured with a Parshall flume or meter. Headworks are also where H2S and odors are worst, so they're often enclosed with odor control, and they're hazardous (H2S, methane, confined spaces, rotating equipment). Construction tie-ins at a headworks are done under the plant's lockout/tagout and bypass procedures, often at night during low flow.
field.title: Headworks: bar screens, fine screens and grit removal
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General wastewater treatment practice

field.text: Primary clarifiers (primary settling tanks) are large round or rectangular tanks where flow slows down for roughly 1.5 to 2.5 hours so settleable solids sink and grease floats. A sludge collector (rotating rake arms in round tanks, chain-and-flight in rectangular) scrapes settled primary sludge to a hopper for pumping, and a skimmer removes scum. Typical removals are on the order of 50 to 70% of suspended solids and 25 to 40% of BOD, which lightens the load on secondary treatment. Effluent leaves over weirs around the edge, which must be level for even flow. Some smaller plants (extended aeration, oxidation ditches, lagoons) have no primaries. Work in or around empty clarifiers is confined-space and fall-hazard work, and drained tanks can float in high groundwater; never drain one without the engineer's OK.
field.title: Primary clarifiers and primary treatment
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General wastewater treatment practice (typical design ranges)

field.text: Activated sludge mixes wastewater with a concentrated population of bacteria (mixed liquor) in aerated basins, then settles the biomass in secondary clarifiers and returns most of it (return activated sludge, RAS) to the basin, wasting the excess (WAS). Typical operating numbers from an operator study guide: MLSS about 1,500 to 3,500 mg/L for conventional plants (MBRs 8,000 to 12,000); food-to-microorganism ratio (F/M) about 0.2 to 0.5 lb BOD per lb MLVSS per day (extended aeration 0.05 to 0.15); solids retention time (SRT/MCRT) 5 to 15 days conventional, 20 to 30+ for extended aeration; dissolved oxygen target about 1.5 to 2.5 mg/L (2.0 common setpoint), with nitrification stopping below about 1.0 mg/L; RAS rate 25 to 100% of influent flow. Blowers and diffusers supply the air and are usually the plant's biggest power use.
field.title: Activated sludge basics: MLSS, F/M, SRT and dissolved oxygen
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Oregon operator guide 11.1: Activated Sludge Process Control

field.text: Common secondary processes: Conventional plug-flow and complete-mix activated sludge with primary clarifiers. Extended aeration: long aeration time and SRT (20 to 30+ days), low sludge production, robust nitrification; common in package plants for small towns and subdivisions. Oxidation ditch: an oval racetrack channel with brush, disc or jet aerators, long SRT, MLSS about 3,000 to 5,000 mg/L. Sequencing batch reactor (SBR): fill, react, settle and decant in the same tank, so no separate clarifiers or RAS pumps. Membrane bioreactor (MBR): membranes replace clarifiers, producing very clear effluent (under 0.1 NTU) at higher power cost. Fixed-film options include trickling filters and rotating biological contactors (RBCs), and hybrids (IFAS, MBBR) put plastic media in aeration tanks. Each has its own piping, diffuser and equipment layout that crews build to shop drawings.
field.title: Activated sludge variations: oxidation ditch, SBR, MBR, extended aeration
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Oregon operator guide 11.1

field.text: Secondary clarifiers settle the activated sludge so clear effluent goes over the weirs and the sludge returns to the basins. Operators track settleability with the sludge volume index (SVI): about 80 to 150 mL/g is ideal, above 150 means bulking sludge that won't settle (often filamentous bacteria from low DO, low F/M, septic influent or nutrient shortage), and below 80 suggests old, dense sludge and pin floc. Brown, thick foam (Nocardia/Microthrix) is linked to long SRT, warm water and high FOG; white frothy foam to very young sludge or detergents. A clarifier losing its sludge blanket sends solids out and can break the permit. Construction points: clarifier weirs must be set level within tight tolerance, and drive mechanisms, scum troughs and baffles are installed to the manufacturer's tolerances.
field.title: Secondary clarifiers, sludge settling (SVI), bulking and foaming
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Oregon operator guide 11.1

field.text: Many permits now limit ammonia, total nitrogen and phosphorus because nutrients cause algae blooms and low oxygen in rivers, lakes and bays. Nitrification: bacteria convert ammonia to nitrate in aerated zones; it needs long SRT, DO above about 1 to 2 mg/L, enough alkalinity and warmer water (it slows sharply in cold weather). Denitrification: other bacteria convert nitrate to nitrogen gas in anoxic zones (mixed, no air) using BOD or added carbon such as methanol; internal recycle pumps send nitrate back to the anoxic zone. Biological phosphorus removal uses an anaerobic zone ahead of aeration so certain bacteria take up extra phosphorus, which leaves with the waste sludge. Chemical phosphorus removal adds alum or ferric salts to precipitate it. Designs with names like MLE, A2O, Bardenpho and 5-stage combine these zones. Upgrades often mean new baffle walls, mixers, recycle pumps and chemical feed.
field.title: Nutrient removal: nitrogen and phosphorus (BNR)
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General wastewater treatment practice; Open Exam Prep activated sludge guide

field.text: Before discharge, treated effluent is disinfected to kill pathogens (permits set E. coli, fecal coliform or enterococci limits). Chlorination uses sodium hypochlorite (common now for safety) or chlorine gas in a contact tank built with baffles for plug flow; then dechlorination with sulfur dioxide or sodium bisulfite removes the residual because chlorine is toxic to fish (permits often limit total residual chlorine to near non-detect). Ultraviolet (UV) disinfection passes effluent past banks of UV lamps in a channel, leaving no residual and no chemicals, but needs clear water and clean lamp sleeves. Peracetic acid and ozone are used at some plants. Safety: chlorine gas is deadly (one-ton cylinders, leak detectors, SCBA); hypochlorite and bisulfite cause chemical burns and must never be mixed with acids. Crews working in chemical buildings need the plant's chemical safety briefing.
field.title: Wastewater disinfection: chlorination, dechlorination and UV
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General wastewater treatment practice

field.text: Raw sludge is mostly water, so plants thicken and dewater it to cut hauling costs. Operator guide figures: gravity thickeners (mostly primary sludge) reach about 6 to 10% total solids; dissolved air flotation (mostly waste activated sludge) about 3.5 to 5.5%; gravity belt or rotary drum thickeners about 4 to 7%. Dewatering cake solids: belt filter press about 18 to 28%; decanter centrifuge about 22 to 32%; plate-and-frame press about 35 to 50%; sand drying beds about 20 to 60% depending on weather. Polymer is added to make solids clump. For a sense of volume: going from 4% to 25% solids cuts the total wet weight by 84% (100 tons becomes 16 tons). Dewatered cake goes to a landfill, land application, composting or drying. Dewatering buildings have H2S and ammonia odors and slippery polymer spills.
field.title: Sludge thickening and dewatering: percent solids by method
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Virginia operator guide 3.5: Solids Thickening, Digestion & Biosolids

field.text: Anaerobic digesters are heated, sealed tanks where bacteria break down sludge without oxygen, cutting volume, odor and pathogens and making biogas. Operator guide numbers: mesophilic digesters run at about 95 F (35 C), with temperature changes held to no more than about 1 F per day and hydraulic retention of 15 to 30 days; thermophilic digesters run at 131 to 140 F (55 to 60 C) for 10 to 15 days. Volatile solids destruction is about 45 to 60%. Biogas is about 60 to 70% methane and 30 to 35% CO2, with H2S from 100 to 5,000 ppm. Operators watch the volatile acid to alkalinity ratio (about 0.05 to 0.15 healthy; above about 0.5 is a soured digester). Aerobic digesters (aerated tanks) are used at smaller plants. Digester covers, gas piping, flame traps, waste gas burners and boilers are specialty work.
field.title: Anaerobic digesters: temperature, retention time and gas
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Virginia operator guide 3.5

field.text: Digester gas (biogas) is mostly methane, which is explosive between about 5% (LEL) and 15% (UEL) in air, so digester areas use Class I, Division 1 electrical equipment, no smoking or hot work without a permit, flame arresters on gas lines, and gas detection. H2S in digester gas runs from 100 to 5,000 ppm; the operator guide notes an OSHA ceiling of 20 ppm and IDLH of 100 ppm, with loss of smell above 100 ppm. Oxygen below 19.5% is an asphyxiation hazard. Digesters, wet wells, clarifier tunnels, pipe galleries and channels are confined spaces: 4-gas monitoring, forced ventilation, permits and trained attendants. Other plant hazards: drowning in open tanks and channels (life rings, rails), chemical storage (chlorine, caustic, ferric, polymer), rotating equipment (lockout/tagout), and sludge contact (pathogens; wash and keep tetanus shots current).
field.title: Digester gas and plant hazards: methane explosion range, H2S
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Virginia operator guide 3.5; OSHA confined space principles

field.text: Treated sewage sludge applied to land is regulated as biosolids under EPA's 40 CFR Part 503. Class A biosolids meet strict pathogen limits (fecal coliform below 1,000 MPN per gram of solids, or Salmonella below 3 per 4 grams) through processes like heat drying, pasteurization (above 70 C for at least 30 minutes) or thermophilic composting; they can be sold or given away with no site restrictions. Class B biosolids (fecal coliform geometric mean below 2 million MPN per gram) come from processes like mesophilic digestion (15 days at 35 C), aerobic digestion (40 days at 20 C) or lime stabilization (pH 12 for 2 hours) and may go only to agricultural, forest or reclamation sites with restrictions: public access 30 days to 1 year, grazing 30 days, and long waits before harvesting food crops (14 to 38 months depending on crop). Vector attraction reduction is also required. States add their own rules.
field.title: Biosolids: Class A vs Class B (40 CFR Part 503)
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Virginia operator guide 3.5 (summarizing 40 CFR Part 503)

field.text: EPA's secondary treatment regulation (40 CFR 133.102) sets the minimum effluent quality for publicly owned treatment works: BOD5 30-day average 30 mg/L and 7-day average 45 mg/L; suspended solids 30-day average 30 mg/L and 7-day average 45 mg/L; at least 85% removal of BOD5 and suspended solids on a 30-day average; pH 6.0 to 9.0. The permitting authority may use CBOD5 instead (25 mg/L 30-day, 40 mg/L 7-day, 85% removal). Waste stabilization ponds and some trickling filter plants can get adjusted limits. These are floors: many NPDES permits are stricter because of water quality, with limits on ammonia, nitrogen, phosphorus, chlorine residual, bacteria and metals. Field relevance: I/I that dilutes influent can make the 85% removal rule hard to meet, which is one reason utilities push I/I reduction.
field.title: Secondary treatment standards: 30/30/85
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: 40 CFR 133.102 (eCFR via Cornell LII)

field.text: The Clean Water Act (CWA, 1972 amendments to the Federal Water Pollution Control Act) makes it illegal to discharge pollutants from a point source into waters of the United States without a permit. Key pieces that touch underground utility work: the NPDES permit program (section 402) for treatment plant discharges, CSOs, industrial discharges and stormwater, including construction stormwater general permits; the national pretreatment program for industrial users of sewers; secondary treatment standards for POTWs; Section 404 permits from the Army Corps of Engineers for dredge and fill in wetlands and streams (stream crossings, trench spoil in wetlands); and state water quality standards and 401 certification. Penalties can be civil and criminal, and citizens can sue. Sewage spills, muddy dewatering discharges and filling wetlands without a permit are the CWA violations crews most often cause.
field.title: Clean Water Act basics for utility crews
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General Clean Water Act summary; NMED NPDES fact sheet

field.text: Under the CWA, discharging pollutants to waters of the United States requires a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit, issued by EPA or an authorized state. Permits last at most 5 years (they can be administratively continued if the holder reapplied on time). They contain effluent limits of two kinds: technology-based limits (what treatment can achieve, such as secondary treatment standards) and water quality-based limits (tighter limits where needed to protect the receiving water); plus monitoring and reporting (discharge monitoring reports, DMRs), and special conditions (sewer overflow reporting, pretreatment, biosolids). Individual permits are site-specific; general permits cover a category (like construction stormwater) and you get coverage by filing a notice of intent (NOI). Draft permits get at least a 30-day public comment period. Dewatering discharges on sewer jobs may need NPDES coverage too.
field.title: NPDES discharge permits: what they contain
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: New Mexico Environment Department NPDES fact sheet (2024)

field.text: EPA sets national wastewater rules, but most day-to-day permitting and enforcement is done by states. As of the New Mexico Environment Department's fact sheet, 47 of 50 states are authorized to run the NPDES program; in the others (New Mexico is one) EPA issues permits directly. The state agency is usually called the Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ), Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), environmental management, natural resources, or a water board. For sewers, the state agency typically reviews and approves plans for new sewer extensions and pump stations (often against Ten States Standards or its own design rules), issues construction or extension permits, sets SSO reporting rules, and inspects plants. County health departments handle septic systems. Local utilities enforce sewer use ordinances, pretreatment and connection rules. Know who signed your plans' approval letter.
field.title: Who enforces: EPA, state environmental agencies and authorized states
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: NMED NPDES fact sheet; Ten States Standards 2014 (state adoption)

field.text: The national pretreatment program keeps industrial pollutants from passing through or upsetting sewer plants and from contaminating sludge. Under 40 CFR 403.8, a POTW (or group under one authority) with total design flow over 5 million gallons per day that receives industrial pollutants must run an approved pretreatment program; smaller POTWs can be required to if problems warrant. Program elements: legal authority (a sewer use ordinance) to permit and control industrial users, entry rights, penalties of at least $1,000 per day per violation, inspecting and sampling each significant industrial user (SIU) at least once a year, slug-discharge control plans, local limits, an enforcement response plan, and yearly public notice of users in significant noncompliance. SIUs (40 CFR 403.3(v)) include categorical industrial users, users discharging an average of 25,000 gpd or more of process wastewater (not counting sanitary, cooling and boiler water), users contributing 5% or more of the plant's hydraulic or organic capacity, and others the control authority designates.
field.title: Industrial pretreatment programs: who needs one
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: 40 CFR 403.8 (eCFR via Cornell LII); SIU threshold per 40 CFR 403.3 as commonly summarized

field.text: Under 40 CFR 403.5(b), no one may put these into a public sewer: anything that creates a fire or explosion hazard, including wastes with a closed-cup flashpoint below 140 F (60 C); corrosive discharges with pH below 5.0 (unless the system is designed for it); solid or viscous substances that obstruct flow; pollutants in amounts that interfere with treatment; heat that raises the plant influent above 104 F (40 C) or inhibits biology; petroleum, cutting or mineral oils in amounts that cause interference or pass-through; pollutants that release toxic gases or fumes that endanger workers; and trucked or hauled waste except at designated points. Local ordinances add more (FOG limits, no stormwater, no construction dewatering without a permit). For crews: don't pump trench water, concrete washout, slurry, fuel-contaminated water or drilling fluid into a sanitary sewer without the utility's written permission.
field.title: What can't go down the sewer: pretreatment prohibitions
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: 40 CFR 403.5(b), via NOAA lab waste training page

field.text: A consent decree is a court-approved settlement, usually between EPA and the Department of Justice (often with the state) and a utility that violated the Clean Water Act, typically for repeated SSOs, CSOs or plant permit violations. It commits the utility to a schedule of fixes, often over 10 to 25 years and billions of dollars in big cities: sewer rehab and replacement, I/I reduction, pump station and force main upgrades, CSO tunnels and storage, plant expansions, plus programs like CMOM, FOG control and SSO response, with stipulated penalties for missed deadlines and regular progress reports. For contractors, consent decree work means fixed milestone dates that can't slip, heavy documentation, and strict SSO prevention and reporting during construction, since a spill on a consent decree project can trigger penalties for the owner. Administrative orders (AOs) are a lighter version issued by EPA or the state.
field.title: Consent decrees: what they mean for sewer and water projects
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General EPA/DOJ municipal enforcement practice; EPA NPDES Inspection Manual ch. 12

field.text: CMOM (capacity, management, operation and maintenance) is EPA's framework for running a sanitary sewer system to prevent SSOs; it shows up in NPDES permits, state rules and consent decrees. Typical elements: a mapped and inventoried system (GIS of pipes, manholes, pump stations); a cleaning and inspection schedule (jetting, root control, CCTV, manhole inspections); hot-spot cleaning for FOG and roots; a FOG program; pump station O&M with alarms and backup power; capacity assessment and hydraulic modeling; I/I studies and rehab; an overflow emergency response plan with SSO reporting; new-construction standards and inspection so new sewers don't add problems; staff training; and periodic self-audits. Contractors see CMOM in the form of strict testing and CCTV acceptance of new sewers, as-built and GIS data requirements, and bypass and spill plans.
field.title: CMOM programs for sanitary sewers
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: U.S. EPA SSO and CMOM program guidance, as commonly summarized

field.text: Plant upgrades are built while the plant keeps treating sewage, so the permit can't be broken during construction. Typical contract rules: a sequence of construction approved by the owner and sometimes the state; shutdowns and tie-ins only at approved times (often low-flow nights), with temporary bypass pumping or temporary treatment; the plant operators, not the contractor, operate existing valves, gates and equipment; lockout/tagout coordinated with plant staff; confined space entry under the owner's and contractor's programs (wet wells, channels, digesters, galleries); hot work permits near digesters and gas lines; drained tanks checked for flotation; and immediate reporting of any spill or upset. Watch for live process piping with sludge, gas and chemicals; label and verify before cutting. Respect the plant's safety orientation, PPE and chemical rules.
field.title: Working at an operating treatment plant: construction rules
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: General plant construction contract practice

field.text: Small communities and subdivisions often use package plants (factory-built steel or concrete extended aeration, SBR or MBR units), lagoons, or recirculating media filters rather than full-size plants. Package plants arrive as tanks with blowers and controls; crews set them on a slab, anchor them against flotation, connect influent, effluent, air and sludge piping, and build headworks screens and disinfection. Lagoon systems are cheap to run but struggle with ammonia in winter and algae solids; common upgrades add aeration, attached-growth media in the lagoon, a submerged attached-growth reactor or filters, or convert to a mechanical plant (see sewer-collection lagoon chunks). In Oregon's operator classification, non-aerated lagoons are Class I at any flow, aerated lagoons Class I up to 1 MGD. Small plants still need an NPDES or state discharge permit and a certified operator.
field.title: Small-town treatment: package plants and lagoon upgrades
field.topic: Wastewater treatment plants and wastewater regulation (Clean Water Act, NPDES, pretreatment, consent decrees)
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Oregon operator guide 10.3; general practice

field.text: Atterberg limits describe how a fine-grained soil changes with water content. Plastic limit (PL): the moisture at which the soil stops crumbling and starts to roll into a 1/8 inch thread; below it the soil is semi-solid. Liquid limit (LL): the moisture at which the soil starts to flow like a thick liquid (lab cup or cone test). Plasticity index (PI) = LL minus PL: the range of moisture over which the soil is plastic (moldable). Shrinkage limit (SL): below this, drying causes no more shrinkage. Results are percent water by dry weight. Rules of thumb: PI 0 = non-plastic (sands, most silts); PI under about 7 = slightly plastic; 7 to 17 = medium; over 17 to 20 = highly plastic, likely to swell and shrink. LL 50 is the USCS line between low (L) and high (H) plasticity. Lab tests are ASTM D4318 / AASHTO T 89 and T 90.
field.title: Atterberg limits: liquid limit, plastic limit, plasticity index (LL, PL, PI)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard soil mechanics definitions (ASTM D4318 scope); plasticity ranges are common practice, vary by reference

field.text: Field meaning of the lab numbers: If natural moisture is near or above the liquid limit, the soil is soft or soupy, flows into the trench and can't be compacted until dried; this is common in silts and soft clays below the water table. If natural moisture is near the plastic limit, cohesive soil is stiff and holds a cut, and compaction is usually workable. If moisture is well below the plastic limit, clay is hard, digs in chunks and clods, and needs water added and mixed to compact. High PI (over about 20) means slick when wet, shrinks and cracks when dry, swells when wetted, and is very sensitive to moisture during compaction. Low PI silts have a tiny workable window: a little rain turns them from firm to pumping. Liquidity index (moisture minus PL, divided by PI) near 1 means the soil is near liquid; near 0 means near its plastic limit.
field.title: What plasticity and liquid limit mean in the trench
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard soil mechanics practice

field.text: Expansive soils contain smectite clay minerals (montmorillonite, bentonite and others) that swell when wet and shrink when dry. Geology.com notes expansions of 10% or more are not uncommon, and ASCE has estimated about 1/4 of US homes have some expansive-soil damage; damage in a typical year exceeds that from floods, hurricanes, tornadoes and earthquakes combined. They are found in every state, especially Texas, Colorado Front Range, the Great Plains, the Gulf Coast and parts of California. Field signs: CH or A-7-6 soil, very sticky and shiny when cut, wide polygonal shrinkage cracks in dry weather, popcorn-textured surface crust, slickensides, cracked slabs and curbs nearby. Problems for utilities: heave and settlement cycles move shallow pipe, crack rigid pipe and joints, push on manholes, and lift pavement patches; dry cracks let water flow along the trench. Specs often require removing expansive soil from the pipe zone and under pavement, using non-expansive select fill, lime treatment, and trench plugs.
field.title: Expansive clay and swelling soil: signs and why it matters for pipe (bentonite, gumbo, montmorillonite)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Geology.com, Expansive Soil and Expansive Clay (H. King; ASCE and USGS map I-1940 cited)

field.text: Practical tips for trenching in expansive clay (follow the geotech report and specs first): don't let the trench bottom dry out and crack or get soaked by rain; cover or excavate and pipe the same day. Over-excavate and replace with granular or select non-expansive fill where specified; the swell can push back up through thin bedding. If reusing clay as backfill (only where allowed), compact it slightly wet of optimum and at moderate density as the geotech directs; very dry, very dense clay swells more when it later gets wet. Place trench plugs (clay, flowable fill or concrete) so stone bedding doesn't feed water along the line to swelling clay. Keep spoil away from the edge; dry clay looks stable but drops blocks along shrinkage cracks. Clean the bucket and padfoot often; wet fat clay sticks and slows production. Lime or cement treatment can reduce swell where engineered.
field.title: Working in expansive clay: backfill, moisture and trench tips
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard practice for expansive soils; Geology.com expansive soil mitigation summary; National Lime Association

field.text: Collapsible soils are dry, loose soils with an open structure held together by weak bonds (clay or carbonate cement or capillary suction) that suddenly lose volume when wetted, loaded or both. Caltrans lists wind-blown deposits (loess, dune sand, volcanic dust), alluvial fan and mudflow deposits, colluvium at the base of slopes, some residual soils, gypsum and salt-cemented sands, and even deep compacted fills. Collapse settlements of 2 to 3 feet are common in the southwestern US; about 15 feet occurred at a canal in the San Joaquin Valley. Warning signs: low dry density (Clevenger: under 80 pcf means large settlement risk, over 90 pcf small), honeycomb or pinhole structure, dry desert soil that stands vertically, distressed pavement near leaks or irrigation. Utility risk: a leaking water main, sewer or water-settled backfill can trigger collapse under the pipe, nearby slabs and roads. Mitigation: remove and replace with compacted fill, prewet with surcharge, compact new fill wet of optimum, avoid jetting or flooding trenches.
field.title: Collapsible soil: ground that settles when wetted (hydrocollapse, alluvial fans, loess)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Caltrans Geotechnical Manual, Collapsible Soil (2026)

field.text: Organic material in or under the pipe zone keeps compressing as it is loaded and keeps settling as it rots, so grade is lost after the job is accepted. Sources: buried topsoil layers, old swamp or pond bottoms, peat and muck (PT), organic silt and clay (OL, OH), stumps, roots, logs, sawdust and old wood fill. National Lime Association guidance also notes that organic content above about 1 to 2% can keep lime-treated soil from gaining strength. Field ID: dark color, musty or sulfur smell, fibers and roots, light weight, spongy. Most specs call organic soils unsuitable: remove to firm mineral soil and replace with stone or select fill, often with geotextile. Don't mix topsoil into trench backfill; strip and stockpile it separately for restoration. In deep organic deposits, also test air for methane and hydrogen sulfide, which can collect in low trenches and structures.
field.title: Organic soil, buried topsoil and wood: why it is unsuitable
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Common agency specification practice; National Lime Association Technical Brief (organic content limit)

field.text: Frost heave happens when water is drawn up to a freezing front and forms ice lenses that lift the ground; on thaw the soil turns to mush and loses strength. It needs three things: freezing temperatures, frost-susceptible soil and a water supply. The Corps of Engineers says inorganic soils with 3% or more finer than 0.02 mm are generally frost susceptible, and ranks them: F1 gravelly soils with 3 to 20% finer than 0.02 mm; F2 sands with 3 to 15%; F3 gravels over 20%, sands over 15% (except very fine silty sands), and clays with PI over 12; F4 (worst) all silts including sandy silts, very fine silty sands over 15% finer than 0.02 mm, clays with PI under 12, and varved clays with non-uniform subgrade. Pipe impacts: heave lifts shallow services, valves, curb boxes and manhole frames and breaks pavement patches. Use clean, non-frost-susceptible backfill (washed sand, clean gravel) in the frost zone under pavement and at structures; keep water mains below design frost depth.
field.title: Silt and frost heave: frost-susceptible soils (USACE frost groups F1 to F4)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: UFC 3-130-03 / TM 5-822-5 frost design soil classification (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers)

field.text: A quick condition (boiling, quicksand) happens when groundwater flows upward through sand or silt with enough force to cancel the weight of the grains. The soil loses all strength and behaves like a thick liquid. Soil mechanics puts the critical upward gradient at about 1 (roughly 1 foot of head loss per foot of soil travel) for most sands. It shows up when the trench or pit bottom is below the water table and pumping is from inside the excavation, especially in fine uniform sand and silt (SP, SM, ML). Signs: sand bubbling or 'boils' in the bottom, bottom rising or going soft, sumps filling with sand, pipe and boxes settling or floating, cloudy pumped water. Responses: stop digging deeper, lower the water outside the trench first (wellpoints or wells), pump from sumps below grade wrapped in fabric and stone, add a stone working mat, and stay out of an unstable trench. A quick or heaving bottom also undermines trench box and shoring support.
field.title: Quick condition, boiling and heave in the trench bottom
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard soil mechanics (critical hydraulic gradient); dewatering practice

field.text: Piping is erosion that starts where seepage exits (a trench wall, the bottom of a pit, an outfall) and works backward, washing out fines and forming tunnels or voids. Fine sand, silt, loess and dispersive clays are most vulnerable. In utility work it shows up as: sinkholes over sewer and storm lines where soil washes into open joints or broken pipe; voids beside manholes; muddy discharge from dewatering pumps (you are pumping the ground out from under nearby pavement and footings); and water running along crushed stone bedding. Prevention: keep pump intakes in fabric-wrapped stone sumps, use filter-compatible bedding or geotextile between fine soil and open-graded stone, build trench plugs where specified, make tight joints, and backfill and compact around structures carefully. If pumped water is carrying sand, slow down, rework the sump or switch to wellpoints, and watch for settlement of anything nearby.
field.title: Piping and internal erosion along pipe trenches
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard geotechnical practice (piping and filter criteria)

field.text: Running sand means dry or saturated cohesionless sand (and silty sand) that flows into the excavation as fast as you dig it out. Dry, clean sand runs at its angle of repose (very roughly 1.5:1 in loose sand); saturated fine sand below the water table can flow like liquid under the box. It is always treated as OSHA Type C, and the competent person decides on the protective system. Field tactics: lower the water table ahead of the dig (wellpoints are the usual tool in sand), use a trench box with full-depth sheeting or a slide-rail or sheet-pile system that keeps soil from running under or between panels, keep the bucket and box moving together, minimize open trench length, and place bedding and backfill right away. Don't let anyone enter a trench where sand is flowing into the bottom. Watch for loss of ground and settlement of pavement and nearby utilities behind the box, and fill voids.
field.title: Running sand and flowing ground: what to do
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard excavation practice; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P (see osha library for Type C rules)

field.text: Caliche (calcrete, calcic hardpan) is a shallow soil layer cemented mostly by calcium carbonate, sometimes with gypsum, silica or iron. It forms in dry climates as carbonate leached from upper soil is redeposited lower down. Common in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Nevada and Southern California. It starts as grain coatings and nodules and can grow into a continuous layer over a meter thick, usually hardest at the top. Field ID: white to tan, chalky to rock-hard, fizzes with dilute acid or strong vinegar. Excavation: thin or poorly cemented caliche digs with a rock bucket and teeth; hard caliche may need a ripper, hydraulic hammer, rock trencher or saw, and slows production sharply. It blocks water, so trenches can pond and soils above can be perched. Spoil comes out in slabs and hard chunks; screen or crush before reuse as backfill, and keep chunks off the pipe. Check whether your contract pays caliche as rock or as common excavation.
field.title: Caliche: hard cemented layer in desert soils (calcrete)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Geology.com, Caliche (H. King); USGS Calcic Soils and Calcretes in the Southwestern United States

field.text: Hardpan is a general field word for very dense or cemented soil that digs much harder than the soil above it: glacial till compacted by ice, caliche in the desert, iron-cemented layers (ironstone) in the Southeast, clay pans and fragipans (dense, brittle subsoil layers common in the East and Midwest). ProjectEngineer lists hardpan swell at about 50%, higher than common earth, because it breaks into chunks. Field notes: excavators with good teeth usually handle it, but production drops; very hard pan may need a ripper tooth or hammer. Water perches on top of hardpan, so trenches can be wet even when the water table is deep. It holds steep cuts when dry and intact, but once broken it is just dense soil; OSHA classification depends on strength and fissuring, not the name. Contracts usually treat hardpan as common excavation, not rock, unless the rock definition says otherwise; read it before arguing.
field.title: Hardpan, fragipan and cemented soils
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: ProjectEngineer swell table; standard excavation practice

field.text: Glacial till is soil dropped directly by glacier ice: an unsorted mix of clay, silt, sand, gravel, cobbles and boulders. It covers much of the northern US (New England, New York, the Great Lakes states, upper Midwest, northern Plains, Pacific Northwest). Lodgement till was overridden by ice and is very dense (hardpan, SPT N often over 50) and digs like soft rock; ablation till is looser. Typical USCS: SM, SC, GM, GC, ML or CL with boulders. Field realities: boulders and cobbles slow production, damage buckets and can't touch the pipe; dense till may stand steeply but sand and gravel lenses within it can run and carry water under pressure; perched water sits on top of dense till. Backfill: till can make decent backfill if the oversize stone is removed and moisture is right, but it is often too wet and silty to compact. Boulder removal and disposal should be in your bid and documented daily.
field.title: Glacial till: dense mixed soil with cobbles and boulders
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard glacial geology and excavation practice

field.text: Loess is wind-deposited silt from glacial outwash, found along the Missouri and Mississippi river valleys (Iowa, Nebraska, Missouri, Illinois, Kansas, western Tennessee and Mississippi), the Palouse of Washington and Idaho, and parts of Alaska. The Iowa Geological Survey reports loess forms about 38% of Iowa's land surface and reaches well over 60 ft thick along the Missouri River. Properties: tan to buff, uniform floury silt (ML, A-4), low density, relatively high permeability. It stands in near-vertical cuts when dry, but it can collapse suddenly when saturated, settle under foundations, and erode severely. Zones near perched water can be 'loess mush' close to the liquid limit. Utility notes: vertical faces look solid but slab off when wetted or vibrated; leaking pipes and water-settled backfill can trigger collapse; control surface water and spoil runoff; backfill needs close moisture control and is frost susceptible.
field.title: Loess: wind-blown silt that stands vertical and collapses when wet
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Iowa Geological Survey, Engineering geology of loess review (Misc. Pub. 18)

field.text: Fill is anything placed by people: old trench backfill, road embankment, graded lots, demolition rubble, cinders, ash, slag, foundry sand, brick, glass, wood and household trash. In older cities, several feet of mixed urban fill over native soil is normal. Why it matters: it is previously disturbed, so OSHA Subpart P will not let it be Type A; it is variable over short distances; voids and debris cause sudden caving and settlement; old backfill around existing utilities can run into your trench. It is often unsuitable as backfill (debris, organics, oversize, poor compaction) and may be contaminated (ash, cinders and historic fill can carry metals and petroleum). Field tips: look for color and texture changes, bricks, asphalt layers, wood; dig test holes at crossings; expect old pavement layers and abandoned pipes; segregate debris; report odors, staining, drums, tanks or ash to the super before continuing.
field.title: Fill and urban fill: old trench backfill, rubble and debris
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (previously disturbed soil); DASNY contaminated soil guidance (historic fill)

field.text: Signs the soil may be contaminated (from agency soil-management guidance): fuel or solvent odor (gasoline, diesel, heating oil, sweet chemical smell); dark, black, green or rainbow staining; soil wet with product; rainbow sheen on water in the trench; a sheen when a soil sample is shaken in a jar of water; photoionization detector (PID) readings above background; buried tanks, drums, pipes leading nowhere, asbestos pipe or debris; historic fill such as ash, cinders, slag, dredged sediment or railroad ballast. High-risk locations: old gas stations, dry cleaners, rail yards, plating shops, landfills, and along old fuel lines. Actions: stop digging in that area, get people out of the trench and upwind, notify the super and the engineer, keep the material separate, stockpile it on poly sheeting (DASNY guidance uses 6 mil) and cover it, and don't discharge water from the trench without approval. Test the air: contaminants can create toxic or flammable atmospheres in a trench.
field.title: Contaminated soil signs in the trench: odor, staining, sheen, drums, tanks
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: DASNY, Guidance for Contaminated or Impacted Soils (2020); OSHA 1926.651(g) hazardous atmospheres

field.text: Once contamination is suspected, who to call depends on the state and contract. Typical requirements: notify the owner's engineer right away; for petroleum free product or saturated soil, many states require a spill report within hours (New York, for example, requires a call to the spill hotline within 2 hours of discovery per DASNY guidance); the owner's environmental consultant samples soil and water; only trained workers (OSHA HAZWOPER, 29 CFR 1910.120) handle known hazardous waste; disposal goes to an approved facility with manifests. Keep a written record: location, depth, what you saw and smelled, PID readings if taken, photos, time notified and who. Unexpected contamination is usually a differing site condition, so the daily record supports a change order. Don't bury it back, haul it to your yard, or spread it on site without written direction. Your contract and state rules govern; this is general guidance.
field.title: Contaminated soil reporting and paperwork
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: DASNY, Guidance for Contaminated or Impacted Soils (2020); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120 scope; contract practice

field.text: Moisture content (water content, w) is the weight of water divided by the weight of dry soil, as a percent. Example: a sample weighs 120 lb wet and 100 lb oven-dry, so w = 20 lb / 100 lb = 20%. Because it is based on dry weight, clays can exceed 100% (peat can exceed several hundred percent). Typical natural moisture: clean sand and gravel above the water table a few percent; silts and lean clays 15 to 30%; fat clays 30 to 50% or more. Tested by oven drying (ASTM D2216), by nuclear gauge in the field, by microwave or by a calcium carbide 'speedy' tester. Optimum moisture (from the Proctor test) is the water content that gives the highest dry density for a given compactive effort. A soil can look damp but be well dry of optimum, or look fine but be wet of optimum and pump. Always compare field moisture to the Proctor optimum for that specific soil.
field.title: Soil moisture content: what the percent means
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard soil mechanics (ASTM D2216 scope); typical ranges vary by soil

field.text: Fixing moisture for compaction (the compaction file covers Proctor testing): Signs of too dry: soil won't stick together when squeezed, dust, clods that don't break down, density fails even after many passes. Fix: add water with a water truck or hose in light passes and mix with the bucket or a disc before compacting; let clays soak (temper) for hours or overnight because water enters clay slowly. Signs of too wet: soil leaves a wet smear on your hand, pumps or weaves under the compactor, footprints squeeze water, ruts. Fix: spread and turn it to dry in sun and wind, blend with drier soil or granular material, use lime or cement to dry it (only where allowed), or haul off and import. Hand squeeze test: near optimum, most soils form a ball that holds shape and breaks into a few pieces when dropped; if it oozes water it is wet; if it won't form a ball it is dry (except clean sand and gravel, which never ball).
field.title: Optimum moisture in the field: too wet, too dry, how to fix
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard compaction practice; National Lime Association (drying with lime)

field.text: Caterpillar's earthwork reference tables give bank and loose weights and the load factor (loose volume x load factor = bank volume): Clay, natural bed: 3,400 lb/BCY, 2,800 lb/LCY, LF 0.82 (about 22% swell). Clay, wet: 3,500 / 2,800, LF 0.80 (25%). Clay and gravel, dry: 2,800 / 2,400, LF 0.85 (18%). Earth, dry packed: 3,200 / 2,550, LF 0.80 (25%). Earth, loam: 2,600 / 2,100, LF 0.81. Gravel, pit run: 3,650 / 3,250, LF 0.89 (12%). Sand, damp: 3,200 / 2,850, LF 0.89 (12%). Sand, wet: 3,500 / 3,100, LF 0.89. Sand and gravel, wet: 3,750 / 3,400, LF 0.91. Sand and clay, loose: 3,400 / 2,700, LF 0.79. Crushed stone: 4,500 / 2,700, LF 0.60 (67%). Topsoil: 2,300 / 1,600, LF 0.70 (43%). Swell % = (1 / LF - 1) x 100. Cat warns weights vary with moisture, grain size and compaction; test your own material. Other references (ProjectEngineer) give clay swell near 40%; see the materials-math file.
field.title: Swell and load factors by soil: Caterpillar bank and loose weights
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Caterpillar, Earthwork Volumes Reference Tables (material weights and load factors)

field.text: Converting between bank and loose volume: Load factor (LF) = 1 / (1 + swell). Swell = 1/LF - 1. Void % in the loose material = swell / (100 + swell) x 100. Caterpillar's table: 10% swell = LF 0.909; 20% = 0.833; 25% = 0.800; 30% = 0.769; 40% = 0.714; 50% = 0.667; 60% = 0.625; 65% = 0.606; 70% = 0.588. Example: a 12 CY tandem heaped with soil at 25% swell carries 12 x 0.80 = 9.6 bank CY. To haul 300 BCY of that soil: 300 / 9.6 = 31.25, so 32 loads (always round up). Weight check: at 2,700 lb per LCY (wet earth, Cat), 12 LCY = 32,400 lb = 16.2 tons, which can exceed a tandem's legal payload; wet clay and rock often max out on weight before volume. Compute the weight, not just the yards.
field.title: Swell, voids and load factor math (Cat table)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Caterpillar, Swell & Void Percentage, Load Factors (math worked here)

field.text: Shrink is the volume loss from bank (in place) to compacted fill. Typical estimating ranges: sand and gravel 5 to 15%, common earth and loam 10 to 20%, clay 10 to 25%, but it depends on how dense the bank soil was and how hard you compact. Research for Wisconsin DOT measured compacted-to-bank 'expansion' factors of 1 to 15% for sands, about 12% for silts, and minus 5 to plus 9% for clays (meaning some over-consolidated clays ended up less dense compacted than in the ground, so they did not shrink at all), while crushed aggregates expanded 27 to 60%. Rock always bulks: blasted rock placed as fill takes more room than in the ground. Practical rules: dense glacial till or overconsolidated clay may give little or no shrink; loose sandy or disturbed ground shrinks more; for pipe backfill balance, also subtract the pipe and imported bedding volume. Track actual truck counts and in-place volumes to build your own factors.
field.title: Shrink factor: bank to compacted yards and why it varies
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Wisconsin DOT research 0092-22-05 (earthwork expansion factors) research brief; estimating ranges are general practice

field.text: Approximate in-place (bank) unit weights from Caterpillar's table, converted from lb per bank CY: dry clay 3,100 lb/CY (115 pcf); natural clay 3,400 (126 pcf); wet clay 3,500 (130 pcf); dry packed earth 3,200 (119 pcf); loam 2,600 (96 pcf); dry gravel 2,850 (106 pcf); pit-run gravel 3,650 (135 pcf); dry sand 2,700 (100 pcf); wet sand 3,500 (130 pcf); wet sand and gravel 3,750 (139 pcf); topsoil 2,300 (85 pcf); solid crushed-stone source rock 4,500 (167 pcf). A common design assumption for trench backfill load on pipe is 120 pcf (about 1.6 tons per bank CY). Saturated soils are heavier (125 to 135 pcf typical) and submerged soil effectively weighs about 62.4 pcf less because of buoyancy. Organic soils and peat can be 60 to 90 pcf. Use actual lab or scale data when it matters (crane picks over a trench, shoring design, truck weights).
field.title: Soil unit weights: how heavy is dirt (lb per cubic foot, tons per yard)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
