field.source: Caterpillar, Earthwork Volumes Reference Tables (material weights and load factors) (conversions: lb/CY / 27 = pcf); typical design values are common practice

field.text: The water table (groundwater table, phreatic surface) is the level where soil pores are fully saturated and water stands in an open hole. Field signs: water seeping in from the walls at a consistent level, soil color changing from brown to gray or blue-gray, mottled orange-gray soil just above (the zone the water table moves through seasonally), wet sand starting to flow. In borings, water level is recorded during drilling and again after some time (often 24 hours) because clays take a long time to fill a hole; MaineDOT boring logs carry a note that groundwater fluctuations may occur due to conditions other than those at the time of measurement. Water tables are highest in late winter and spring and after wet periods, and lowest in late summer and fall, often varying several feet. Near rivers, lakes and tidal areas, the water level follows them. A boring drilled in August may show dry ground where you will have water in April. Price and plan dewatering with that in mind.
field.title: Groundwater table: reading it in the field and in borings
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: MaineDOT boring log key (groundwater note); standard hydrogeology practice

field.text: Perched water is a local saturated zone sitting on top of a low-permeability layer (clay lens, dense till, caliche, rock, or an old pavement or slab) above the true water table. You dig through wet sand, hit dry clay, and below that the soil is dry again. It drains out over hours or days once cut, but can flood trenches suddenly and soften the soil it sits on. Artesian (confined) water is groundwater trapped under pressure beneath a confining layer (clay or rock); when you dig or drill through the cap, water rises above the bottom, sometimes above ground. In a trench bottom it can cause blowouts, boiling and heave, especially if the clay cap left below the trench is thin. Signs from borings: water that rises in the hole well above where it was first hit, or notes like 'artesian' or 'flowing'. If the geotech report mentions confined aquifers, ask how thick the cap must stay and plan relief wells before digging.
field.title: Perched water and artesian water: surprises in the trench
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard hydrogeology and excavation practice

field.text: Bearing capacity is the pressure soil can carry without failing or settling too much, given in pounds per square foot (psf) or tons per square foot (tsf; 1 tsf = 2,000 psf). Ultimate capacity is the failure load; allowable bearing is ultimate divided by a safety factor (often 3). It depends on soil strength, density, depth, footing width and groundwater (submerged soil carries roughly half). Field relevance: manhole and vault bases, thrust blocks (see the thrust-restraint file for tables), crane and outrigger pads near trenches, and heavy equipment on soft ground. Soft clay and saturated silt may carry under 1,000 psf; dense sand and gravel 3,000 psf or more; sound rock much more. Quick field checks: a pocket penetrometer reading in tsf on undisturbed clay (unconfined strength), or a T-bar or probe rod for soft spots; then confirm with the engineer. Wheel and outrigger loads near a trench edge also add surcharge to the walls.
field.title: Bearing capacity basics: what soil can hold under pipe, structures and equipment
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard foundation engineering practice

field.text: When there is no geotech data, building codes allow presumptive allowable bearing values (IBC and California Building Code Table 1806.2): crystalline bedrock 12,000 psf; sedimentary and foliated rock 4,000 psf; sandy gravel and gravel (GW, GP) 3,000 psf; sand, silty sand, clayey sand, silty gravel and clayey gravel (SW, SP, SM, SC, GM, GC) 2,000 psf; clay, sandy clay, silty clay, clayey silt, silt and sandy silt (CL, ML, MH, CH) 1,500 psf. Lateral bearing (psf per foot of depth): 1,200, 400, 200, 150 and 100 for the same classes. Sliding friction coefficients: 0.70, 0.35, 0.35, 0.25; clays use cohesion of 130 psf instead. Organic soils and peat get no value; they require an engineer. Utility standards (thrust block tables) use their own, sometimes lower, values. These are conservative building numbers, not a substitute for the project geotech report.
field.title: Presumptive load-bearing values from the building code (IBC/CBC Table 1806.2)
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: California Building Code / IBC Table 1806.2, Presumptive Load-Bearing Values

field.text: Some clays have special traps. Sensitive (quick) clay: soft marine or lake clay that loses most of its strength when disturbed; a firm-looking bank turns to liquid when dug or vibrated. Found in glacial marine deposits (for example parts of Maine, New Hampshire, the St. Lawrence and Champlain valleys, and Alaska). Varved clay: thin alternating layers of silt and clay laid down yearly in glacial lakes (New England, Great Lakes, Hudson Valley); the silt partings carry water, so walls slough in sheets, and the Corps of Engineers puts varved clays in frost group F3 or F4. Dispersive clay: sodium-rich clay that deflocculates in fresh water and erodes into tunnels (piping); common in parts of the Great Plains and West; signs are cloudy water in puddles that won't clear and tunnel erosion on slopes. All three need extra caution in trench walls and pipe zone, and the geotech report should flag them.
field.title: Sensitive clays, varved clays and dispersive clays
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: Standard geotechnical practice; UFC 3-130-03 (varved clay frost groups)

field.text: Quick strength checks for cohesive soil (not for sand): Pocket penetrometer: push the spring-loaded tip into a fresh, undisturbed face to the mark; it reads unconfined compressive strength in tsf. OSHA uses 1.5 tsf and up for Type A and 0.5 tsf or less for Type C cohesive soil (see osha library for the rule and Appendix A tests). Take several readings on fresh faces, not dried or smeared surfaces. Torvane: twists into the soil and reads shear strength (roughly half the unconfined strength). Thumb test: Type A cohesive soil can be indented by the thumb but only with very great effort; Type C is easily penetrated several inches. MaineDOT's log key ties consistency to strength: very soft (fist easily penetrates) under 250 psf shear; soft (thumb easily penetrates) 250 to 500; medium stiff 500 to 1,000; stiff (thumb indents with great effort) 1,000 to 2,000; very stiff (thumbnail indents) 2,000 to 4,000; hard (thumbnail with difficulty) over 4,000 psf.
field.title: Soil strength field checks: pocket penetrometer, torvane, thumb test
field.topic: Soils: behavior, problem soils, moisture, volume and groundwater
field.source: MaineDOT Key to Soil and Rock Descriptions; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A

field.text: The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS, ASTM D2487 lab / D2488 field) gives every soil a two-letter group symbol. First letter = main soil: G gravel, S sand, M silt, C clay, O organic, PT peat. Second letter = a modifier: W well graded, P poorly graded, M silty fines, C clayey fines, L low plasticity (liquid limit under 50), H high plasticity (liquid limit 50 or more). First split: coarse-grained if more than 50% stays on the No. 200 sieve (grains you can see); fine-grained if 50% or more passes the No. 200. Coarse soils are gravel if more than half the coarse part stays on the No. 4 sieve (about 3/16 inch), otherwise sand. There are 15 groups: GW, GP, GM, GC, SW, SP, SM, SC, ML, CL, OL, MH, CH, OH, PT. Geotech reports, boring logs and pipe specs (ASTM D2321 embedment classes) all use these symbols.
field.title: USCS soil classification: how the system works (GW GP GM GC SW SP SM SC ML CL OL MH CH OH PT)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary)

field.text: For gravels and sands, the percent passing the No. 200 sieve (fines: silt and clay) sets the second letter. Less than 5% fines: clean, classed on gradation only (GW, GP, SW, SP). More than 12% fines: classed by what the fines are (GM, GC, SM, SC). Between 5% and 12% fines: borderline, given a dual symbol such as GW-GM (well-graded gravel with silt) or SP-SC (poorly graded sand with clay). If a sand has more than 15% gravel, the name adds 'with gravel' but the symbol does not change. Field meaning: 'clean' material (under 5% fines) drains freely and compacts with vibration; once fines pass about 12%, the soil starts acting like its fines, holding water and getting moisture sensitive. Pipe specs often cap fines for embedment (ASTM D2321 Class II is clean, Class III allows more fines).
field.title: USCS fines content: clean, dirty and dual symbols (5% and 12% rule, GW-GM, SP-SM)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); Wikipedia USCS

field.text: Well graded means a good spread of particle sizes so small grains fill the gaps between big ones; it packs dense and strong. Poorly graded means mostly one size (uniform, like beach sand or pea gravel) or gap graded (sizes missing). The lab checks two numbers from the gradation curve: coefficient of uniformity Cu = D60/D10 and coefficient of curvature Cc = (D30 squared)/(D10 x D60). GW needs Cu of 4 or more and Cc between 1 and 3. SW needs Cu of 6 or more and Cc between 1 and 3. Fail either and it is GP or SP. Field feel: well-graded gravel looks like a mix of stone sizes with sand between; poorly graded looks like one size of marble. Poorly graded rounded gravel (pea gravel) rolls and shifts under pipe unless confined, which is why many specs prefer angular, well-graded crushed stone for bedding.
field.title: Well graded vs poorly graded: Cu and Cc (GW SW GP SP gradation criteria)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Wikipedia USCS (ASTM D2487 criteria)

field.text: GW (well-graded gravel, gravel-sand mix, little or no fines) and GP (poorly graded gravel, little or no fines; pea gravel, uniform washed stone, some river gravel). Field ID: grains clearly visible, gritty, no stickiness, water drains straight through, won't hold a ball. Trenching: no cohesion, so walls ravel and run, especially when dry or saturated; often OSHA Type C, use a box or slope. Groundwater flows fast through it, so dewatering needs volume. Backfill and bedding: excellent; GW is a top material for bedding, haunching and backfill under paving (ASTM D2321 Class I or II depending on angularity and fines). GP rounded gravel can shift; compact it with vibratory plates or rollers in lifts. Compaction: little sensitivity to moisture, vibration works best. Building code presumptive bearing for GW/GP is 3,000 psf. Watch for oversize cobbles in pit run near pipe.
field.title: GW and GP: gravels in the trench (well graded gravel, poorly graded gravel, pea gravel, pit run)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); CBC/IBC Table 1806.2; Standard geotechnical and pipe installation practice (varies by spec)

field.text: GM (silty gravel, gravel-sand-silt mix) and GC (clayey gravel, gravel-sand-clay mix) are gravels with more than 12% fines. Field ID: gravel visible, but the fines coat your hands; GM fines are dusty and non-sticky and dry to powder; GC fines are sticky when wet and form hard clods when dry. Trenching: GC can stand for a short time thanks to clay binder; GM sloughs more, especially when wet. Both often OSHA Type B or C depending on cohesion, water and fissures. Backfill: good to fair; usable as trench backfill and often as select fill, but moisture matters more than clean gravel, especially GC. Keep it near optimum moisture and compact in thinner lifts. GM fines can be frost susceptible. Presumptive bearing (building code) for GM/GC is 2,000 psf. Many specs accept GM/GC above the pipe zone but not as embedment for flexible pipe without approval.
field.title: GM and GC: silty gravel and clayey gravel (dirty gravel, bank run with fines)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); CBC/IBC Table 1806.2; Standard geotechnical and pipe installation practice (varies by spec)

field.text: SW (well-graded sand, gravelly sand, little or no fines) and SP (poorly graded sand, uniform; beach sand, dune or blow sand, mason sand). Field ID: gritty between fingers, individual grains visible, won't hold a ball when dry, crumbles when wet, no ribbon. Trenching: no cohesion; dry sand runs, saturated sand flows (running sand, quick condition below the water table). Typically OSHA Type C. Uniform fine SP below the water table is the classic boiling bottom; plan wellpoints. Backfill: very good for pipe embedment and backfill when free of organics; compacts well with vibratory plates and rollers and with water in some specs (jetting or flooding only if allowed). SP is harder to get to high density than SW and can rut under equipment. Presumptive bearing 2,000 psf in building codes. Clean sand is not frost susceptible unless it contains more than a few percent of very fine grains.
field.title: SW and SP: clean sands (concrete sand, mason sand, beach sand, blow sand)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); CBC/IBC Table 1806.2; Standard geotechnical and pipe installation practice (varies by spec)

field.text: SM (silty sand, sand-silt mix) and SC (clayey sand, sand-clay mix) have more than 12% fines. These are some of the most common native soils crews dig. Field ID: SM feels gritty with a floury dust, dries to a weak crumb, shows quick water on shaking (dilatancy); SC feels gritty but sticky, makes a short ribbon, dries to firm clods. Trenching: SC can stand short-term; SM caves when wet or vibrated and pumps under traffic when saturated. OSHA Type B or C, depending on strength, fissures and water. Backfill: fair to good above the pipe zone; SM is moisture sensitive and can be hard to compact if wet (it bleeds and pumps). Compact in 6 to 8 inch lifts near optimum moisture. SM with lots of fine silt is frost susceptible. ASTM D2321 puts SM/SC in Class III embedment, which needs more compactive effort than Class I/II. Presumptive bearing 2,000 psf.
field.title: SM and SC: silty sand and clayey sand (dirty sand, sandy loam)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); CBC/IBC Table 1806.2; Standard geotechnical and pipe installation practice (varies by spec)

field.text: ML is inorganic silt and very fine sand, rock flour, silty or clayey fine sand of low plasticity (liquid limit under 50, plots below the A-line or PI under 4). Field ID: smooth and floury, not gritty; dry lumps crush easily to powder (low dry strength); wet pat shows water on the surface when shaken and goes dull when squeezed (rapid dilatancy); can't roll a thread, or thread crumbles. Trenching: may stand when damp from apparent cohesion, then collapses as it dries or gets wet; turns to soup with water and vibration. Silt is often OSHA Type B or C. Backfill: poor; very moisture sensitive, narrow window around optimum, pumps under compactors, and highly frost susceptible (USACE frost group F4). Many specs reject ML for structural backfill under paving. Erodes easily: protect spoil piles and inlets. Presumptive bearing 1,500 psf.
field.title: ML silt: inorganic silt, rock flour, very fine sand (soupy when wet)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice; UFC 3-130-03 frost groups

field.text: CL is inorganic clay of low to medium plasticity (liquid limit under 50, plots above the A-line with PI over 7): lean clay, sandy clay, silty clay, gravelly clay. CL-ML is the borderline zone with PI of 4 to 7. Field ID: sticky when wet, makes a ribbon of 1 to 2 inches, rolls into a 1/8 inch thread, dry lumps are hard to crush with fingers (medium to high dry strength), little or no water shows on shaking. Trenching: holds a near-vertical cut short term; can be OSHA Type A if unconfined strength is 1.5 tsf or more and not fissured, disturbed or wet, but often Type B. Gets slick and weak when wet. Backfill: fair; compacts with sheepsfoot or padfoot, not plates; needs moisture near optimum and thin lifts. Wet CL ruts and pumps; dry CL forms clods that leave voids. Frost group F3 (PI over 12) or F4 (PI under 12). Presumptive bearing 1,500 psf.
field.title: CL lean clay: low to medium plasticity clay, sandy clay, silty clay
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice; UFC 3-130-03 frost groups

field.text: MH is inorganic silt with a liquid limit of 50 or more, plotting below the A-line: elastic silt, micaceous (mica-rich, shiny flakes) or diatomaceous fine sandy or silty soil. Common in weathered rock residual soils (for example Piedmont saprolite in the Southeast) and some volcanic soils. Field ID: feels smooth and springy or spongy, low to medium dry strength (higher than ML), slow or no dilatancy, thread is soft; mica flakes glitter in sunlight. Trenching: walls can look stiff but slough when wet; mica soils are slick. Backfill: poor; hard to compact, rebounds under compactors (elastic), moisture sensitive. Lime does not work well on very micaceous soils (Georgia DOT recommends cement instead). Usually rejected for structural backfill; may be used as general fill outside paved areas if specs allow. Presumptive bearing 1,500 psf.
field.title: MH elastic silt: high liquid limit silt, micaceous or diatomaceous soil
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice; Georgia DOT Guidelines for Lime Stabilization

field.text: CH is inorganic clay of high plasticity (liquid limit 50 or more, above the A-line): fat clay, gumbo, bentonitic clay, blackland clay. Field ID: very sticky and greasy when wet, sticks to boots and buckets, shiny when cut with a knife, long ribbon over 2 inches, rolls into a tough thread, dry lumps are very hard (can't break by hand), no dilatancy. Wide shrinkage cracks in dry weather. Trenching: stands well when dry and intact, but fissured CH (blocky, slickensided) can drop slabs without warning; it may not qualify as OSHA Type A when fissured. Very slick when wet. Backfill: poor; very hard to compact, shrinks and swells with moisture, can heave pavement and push on pipe and structures. Most specs prohibit CH within the pipe zone and under pavement; haul off and import select fill, or lime-treat if allowed. Frost group F3. Presumptive bearing 1,500 psf.
field.title: CH fat clay: high plasticity clay, gumbo, expansive clay
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice; UFC 3-130-03 frost groups

field.text: OL is organic silt or organic silty clay of low plasticity; OH is organic clay of medium to high plasticity, or organic silt with liquid limit 50 or more. Lab test: if the liquid limit after oven drying is less than 0.75 times the undried liquid limit, the soil is organic. Field ID: dark brown to black or dark gray, musty or rotten smell (stronger when heated or freshly dug), spongy feel, may contain roots, shells, fibers; lighter in weight than mineral soil. Common in marshes, old ponds, river backwater and buried topsoil. Trenching: weak, compressible, often wet; treat as OSHA Type C. Backfill and foundation: unsuitable; compresses and keeps settling as organics decay, so pipe goes off grade. Standard response is remove and replace (over-excavate to firm material, replace with stone or select fill, often over geotextile). Never use as backfill under paving or structures.
field.title: OL and OH: organic silt and organic clay (black, smelly, spongy)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); Wikipedia USCS (organic criterion); Standard geotechnical and pipe installation practice (varies by spec)

field.text: PT is peat and other highly organic soil: mostly plant matter, dark brown to black, fibrous or mushy (muck), very spongy, often saturated, with a strong organic or sulfur smell. It can hold several times its weight in water. Trenching: almost no strength; walls flow, bottom won't support a person or pipe, and it may generate methane or hydrogen sulfide in low areas, so test the air in deep trenches in organic ground. Thrust block tables give peat and muck a bearing value of zero. Pipe in peat: remove and replace to firm bottom when depth is reasonable; deeper deposits may need a designed foundation (stone mat with geotextile, timber or concrete cradle, piles, or floating with lightweight fill). Spoil is wet, heavy to haul, and often must be dried or disposed of separately. Peat compresses greatly under new fill load, so expect settlement of backfill and pavement over it. Document quantities removed for pay.
field.title: PT peat and muck: highly organic soil in the trench
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); Oregon DOT / VCMWD thrust tables (peat = 0 psf); Standard geotechnical and pipe installation practice (varies by spec)

field.text: Fine-grained soils are sorted on the plasticity chart: plasticity index (PI) on the vertical axis, liquid limit (LL) on the horizontal. A vertical line at LL = 50 splits low (L) from high (H) plasticity. The A-line (PI = 0.73 x (LL - 20)) splits clays (above) from silts and organic soils (below). Rules: CL plots above the A-line with PI over 7; ML plots below or has PI under 4; CL-ML is the hatched zone with PI 4 to 7. CH is above the A-line at LL 50 or more; MH and OH are below. Field meaning: high PI clays (CH) swell, shrink and are slick and hard to compact; silts near or below the A-line lose strength quickly when wet and are frost-prone. Your geotech report or lab sheet will list LL, PL and PI for each sample; use them with this chart to see why a soil behaves the way it does.
field.title: USCS plasticity chart: A-line, low vs high liquid limit (CL vs ML, CH vs MH)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Caltrans, Unified Soil Classification System chart (ASTM D2487 summary); standard ASTM D2487 plasticity chart (A-line equation)

field.text: The AASHTO system (AASHTO M 145) is the one most state DOTs use for road subgrade and embankment. It runs from A-1 (best) to A-7 (worst), plus A-8 for peat in some versions. Granular groups (35% or less passing No. 200): A-1 (stone fragments, gravel, sand), A-3 (fine sand), A-2 (silty or clayey gravel and sand). Silt-clay groups (more than 35% passing No. 200): A-4 and A-5 (silty soils), A-6 and A-7 (clayey soils). Granular groups rate excellent to good as subgrade; silt-clay groups rate fair to poor. In the A-2 subgroups the last digit tells you the fines: 4 and 6 mean LL 40 or less, 5 and 7 mean LL 41 or more; 4 and 5 mean PI 10 or less, 6 and 7 mean PI 11 or more. A-7 splits into A-7-5 and A-7-6 by PI versus LL minus 30. Each soil also gets a group index (GI) in parentheses, for example A-6(12); higher GI means a weaker subgrade. DOT specs often name allowed backfill by AASHTO group, such as 'A-1 or A-3 only'.
field.title: AASHTO soil classification: A-1 to A-7 overview (highway subgrade system)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: AASHTO M 145 classification table as summarized by Wikipedia (AASHTO Soil Classification System)

field.text: A-1 is the top AASHTO group: well-graded stone fragments, gravel and sand with few fines and low plasticity. A-1-a: 50% max passing No. 10, 30% max passing No. 40, 15% max passing No. 200, PI 6 max; mostly stone or gravel with or without binder (crusher run, dense graded aggregate, good bank run). A-1-b: 50% max passing No. 40, 25% max passing No. 200, PI 6 max; mainly coarse sand with or without binder. Rated excellent to good subgrade. Field use: preferred trench backfill under pavement and for structural fill; compacts readily with vibratory equipment and holds up when wet. Roughly lines up with USCS GW, GP, SW, GM (low fines). Many DOT 'select granular backfill' or 'Type A backfill' specs are written around A-1 material. Check your spec's exact gradation.
field.title: AASHTO A-1-a and A-1-b: stone fragments, gravel and sand
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: AASHTO M 145 classification table as summarized by Wikipedia (AASHTO Soil Classification System)

field.text: A-3 is fine sand: 51% or more passing the No. 40 sieve, 10% or less passing No. 200, and non-plastic (NP). Typical examples are beach sand, desert blow sand, and stream-deposited fine sand with little silt or clay. Rated excellent to good subgrade when confined. Field notes: drains well and is easy to compact with vibratory plates or smooth-drum vibratory rollers and water, but it has no cohesion, so it ruts under tires, shoves under traffic until confined, and runs or boils below the water table. Roughly USCS SP (sometimes SP-SM). Florida and Gulf and Atlantic coastal plain jobs see a lot of A-3. Often allowed as pipe embedment and backfill in DOT specs; check gradation limits and fines.
field.title: AASHTO A-3: fine sand (non-plastic, blow sand, beach sand)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: AASHTO M 145 classification table as summarized by Wikipedia (AASHTO Soil Classification System)

field.text: A-2 is granular soil (35% or less passing No. 200) with too many or too plastic fines to be A-1 or A-3. Subgroups by the fines: A-2-4 (LL 40 max, PI 10 max) and A-2-5 (LL 41 min, PI 10 max) have silty fines; A-2-6 (LL 40 max, PI 11 min) and A-2-7 (LL 41 min, PI 11 min) have clayey fines. Rated excellent to good overall, but A-2-6 and A-2-7 behave more like clay when wet. Roughly USCS GM, GC, SM, SC. Field notes: A-2-4 is a common, workable backfill that compacts well near optimum moisture; A-2-6 and A-2-7 need tighter moisture control, padfoot compaction, and can soften with water. Many DOT 'select fill' specs allow A-2-4 but limit A-2-6/A-2-7. Check the spec.
field.title: AASHTO A-2 subgroups: A-2-4, A-2-5, A-2-6, A-2-7 silty or clayey gravel and sand
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: AASHTO M 145 classification table as summarized by Wikipedia (AASHTO Soil Classification System)

field.text: A-4 and A-5 are silt-clay soils with more than 35% passing the No. 200 sieve and low plasticity (PI 10 or less). A-4: LL 40 or less, typically non-plastic to moderately plastic silty soils, sandy silt, silty loam. A-5: LL 41 or more, typically elastic silts and micaceous or diatomaceous soils. Both rate fair to poor as subgrade. Field notes: A-4 is very common, looks fine when dry but loses strength fast when wet, pumps under traffic, and is frost susceptible; compaction requires tight moisture control (often within 2% of optimum). A-5 is springy and hard to compact. Roughly USCS ML, MH and some SM with high fines. Many specs exclude A-4/A-5 from structural backfill under pavement, or allow it only with approval, drying or lime/cement treatment.
field.title: AASHTO A-4 and A-5: silty soils (fair to poor subgrade)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: AASHTO M 145 classification table as summarized by Wikipedia (AASHTO Soil Classification System)

field.text: A-6 and A-7 are clayey soils with more than 35% passing No. 200 and PI 11 or more. A-6: LL 40 or less; moderately plastic clay, typically shows high volume change between wet and dry. A-7: LL 41 or more; highly plastic clays. A-7 splits: A-7-5 has PI of LL minus 30 or less (elastic, often with silt and moderate swell); A-7-6 has PI greater than LL minus 30 (fat, highly plastic, often high swell). Both rate fair to poor as subgrade. Roughly USCS CL (A-6), CH and MH (A-7). Field notes: sticky, hard to compact, very moisture sensitive, high shrink-swell potential, slow to drain; DOTs commonly require removal, lime treatment, or capping with select fill under pavement. Use padfoot or sheepsfoot rollers and thin lifts if it must be reused.
field.title: AASHTO A-6 and A-7 (A-7-5, A-7-6): clayey soils
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: AASHTO M 145 classification table as summarized by Wikipedia (AASHTO Soil Classification System)

field.text: The group index is a number in parentheses after the AASHTO group, such as A-4(5) or A-7-6(25). It is computed from the percent passing No. 200, liquid limit and plasticity index; more fines and higher plasticity give a higher number. GI of 0 is the best soil within a group; values of 20 or more indicate very poor subgrade. A-1, A-3 and most A-2-4/A-2-5 soils have GI of 0. Field use: when a lab sheet or DOT soil survey gives A-6(15) versus A-6(4), the first is noticeably worse: wetter, weaker, harder to compact and more likely to be called unsuitable. Engineers use GI with pavement design; crews mainly use it as a quick red flag that a soil will need treatment, removal or careful moisture control.
field.title: AASHTO group index (GI): what A-6(12) means
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: AASHTO M 145 group index concept as described in DOT soil survey practice

field.text: ASTM D2488 is the field (visual-manual) version of USCS. With a handful of soil, water and a pocket knife you can classify most soils well enough for trench decisions. Steps: (1) estimate percent gravel, sand and fines by eye (fines are grains you can't see individually); (2) for coarse soils, judge grading and whether fines are silty or clayey; (3) for fine soils, run dry strength, dilatancy (shake), toughness (thread) and plasticity tests, and smell for organics; (4) note color, moisture (dry: dusty; moist: damp, no visible water; wet: visible free water), structure (fissured, layered, blocky, slickensided), cementation and reaction to acid (caliche). Write it in the log as group name plus symbol in parentheses, such as 'lean clay with sand (CL), brown, moist, stiff'. OSHA also requires at least one visual and one manual test to classify soil for protective systems (see OSHA Subpart P Appendix A in the osha library).
field.title: Field identification of soil: visual-manual tests every foreman can do (ASTM D2488)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A

field.text: Dry strength test (ASTM D2488): form a ball of soil about 1/2 to 1 inch across, let it dry completely (sun, dash heater or oven), then try to crush it between thumb and finger. Results: none (crumbles to powder at the slightest pressure) = silt or very fine sand (ML) or silty sand; low (crumbles with light pressure) = ML or MH; medium (breaks into pieces with considerable finger pressure) = CL or CL-ML; high (can't crush between fingers, breaks between thumb and a hard surface) = CL or CH; very high (can't break between thumb and hard surface) = CH, fat clay. Natural dry clods from the spoil pile work too, but caliche, carbonate cement or iron can give false high readings; test with acid or check for cementation.
field.title: Dry strength test: crush a dry lump to tell silt from clay
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice (dry strength terms summarized)

field.text: Dilatancy or shake test (ASTM D2488): make a pat of soil about the size of a golf ball, wet enough to be soft but not sticky. Hold it in an open palm and shake it horizontally, tapping the side of that hand with the other hand several times. Watch for water to appear on the surface (glossy, livery look), then squeeze the pat between fingers and see if the water disappears and the pat stiffens or cracks. Results: rapid (water appears quickly, disappears quickly on squeezing) = silt, very fine sand, ML or SM; slow (water appears slowly) = ML, MH or lean clay with silt; none (no visible change) = clay, CL or CH. A soil that shows rapid dilatancy will lose strength fast with vibration and water, will boil in a wet trench bottom and pumps under compactors.
field.title: Shake test (dilatancy): how to spot silt in the field
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice (dilatancy test summarized)

field.text: Thread test (toughness and plasticity, ASTM D2488): take a moist ball of soil (about the consistency of putty) and roll it on your palm or a flat surface into a thread 1/8 inch (3 mm) across. If it rolls that thin without crumbling, ball it up and roll again, losing moisture each time, until the thread crumbles at about 1/8 inch (this is near the plastic limit). Judge: can't roll a 1/8 inch thread at any moisture = non-plastic (silt, sand); thread barely holds and is weak and soft = low plasticity (ML, MH); thread holds, lump is medium stiff = medium plasticity (CL); thread rolls many times, lump is stiff and hard to deform when near the plastic limit = high plasticity (CH). High toughness clay will hold a vertical cut when intact but is the hardest to compact and swells the most.
field.title: Thread test (toughness and plasticity): roll a worm to judge clay
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice (toughness and plasticity terms summarized)

field.text: Ribbon test (USDA/NRCS texture by feel): take about two teaspoons of soil, add water drop by drop and knead until it is like putty. Squeeze: if it won't hold a ball, it is sand. If it balls, push it out between thumb and forefinger into a flat ribbon of even thickness over your finger until it breaks under its own weight. No ribbon: loamy sand. Weak ribbon (under 1 inch): sandy loam if very gritty, silt loam if very smooth, loam if in between. Medium ribbon (1 to 2 inches): sandy clay loam (gritty), silty clay loam (smooth), clay loam (neither). Strong ribbon (over 2 inches): sandy clay (gritty), clay (very smooth), silty clay (neither). Crew use: long ribbon = clay that holds a cut but is hard to compact and swells; short or no ribbon = sand or silt that caves. OSHA lists ribbon/plasticity tests among acceptable manual tests (see osha library).
field.title: Ribbon test: soil texture by feel (sandy loam, clay loam, clay)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Virginia Association of Soil and Water Conservation Districts, Key to Soil Texture by Feel (USDA/NRCS method)

field.text: Extra tricks for classifying soil in the field: Bite or grit test: a tiny bit between the front teeth; sand grates sharply, silt feels gritty but fine, clay feels smooth and sticky (spit it out; skip it in contaminated or sewage areas). Wash test: rub wet soil on your hand; sand and silt rinse off easily, clay smears and needs scrubbing. Jar test: fill a clear jar one-third with soil, top with water, shake hard, let stand; sand settles in under a minute, silt in about an hour, clay can take a day or more; the layer thicknesses give rough percentages. Smell: musty or rotten-egg odor suggests organic soil or peat; a fuel or solvent smell means possible contamination (stop and report). Acid test: a drop of dilute hydrochloric acid (or strong vinegar) fizzes on caliche, limestone and calcareous soil. These are aids for the competent person and the foreman, not a substitute for a lab or the geotech report.
field.title: Other quick field tests: grit bite test, wash test, jar settling test, smell and acid
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Standard soils field practice (ASTM D2488 adjunct methods; USDA texture methods)

field.text: Four systems show up on pipe jobs and they answer different questions. USCS (GW...PT): engineering behavior; used in geotech reports, boring logs, and pipe embedment specs. AASHTO (A-1...A-7): road subgrade quality; used in DOT specs and soil surveys. USDA texture (sandy loam, clay loam...): agriculture and NRCS soil surveys (Web Soil Survey); useful for a first look before borings. OSHA Type A/B/C (Subpart P Appendix A): only for picking slopes and protective systems; based on unconfined strength, granular vs cohesive, fissures, water and disturbance. Rough cross-walk: clean gravels and sands (GW, GP, SW, SP, A-1, A-3) are OSHA Type C when cohesionless; silty and clayey soils (SM, SC, ML, CL, A-2-4 to A-6) are usually Type B; stiff, intact, unfissured clays (CL, CH) may be Type A, but water, vibration, fissures or prior disturbance downgrade them. A USCS symbol never sets the OSHA type by itself; the competent person decides on site.
field.title: How USCS, AASHTO, USDA texture and OSHA soil types relate
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Synthesis of ASTM D2487, AASHTO M 145, USDA NRCS texture and OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A

field.text: General ranking for trench backfill (check your spec, which governs): Best: GW, GP, SW, crushed stone, A-1, A-3; drain well, compact with vibration, little moisture sensitivity; first choice for bedding, haunching and backfill under paving. Good: GM, GC, SP, SM with low fines, A-2-4, A-2-5; usable native backfill if kept near optimum moisture and placed in lifts. Fair: SM and SC with higher fines, CL, A-2-6, A-2-7, A-4, A-6; often allowed above the pipe zone outside pavement; needs moisture control, padfoot compaction and thin lifts. Poor: ML, MH, CH, A-5, A-7; usually rejected under pavement and near structures; haul off, dry or lime/cement treat. Unsuitable: OL, OH, PT, topsoil, frozen soil, debris, trash, cobbles and boulders over the spec size, and contaminated soil. ASTM D2321 embedment classes (Class I crushed stone to Class IV fine-grained) follow similar logic for plastic pipe; see the embedment files.
field.title: Backfill suitability by soil group: what you can put back in the trench
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Synthesis of ASTM D2321 class concept, AASHTO subgrade ratings and common agency specification practice

field.text: Pick the compactor for the soil, not just the trench width. Granular soils (gravel, sand: GW, GP, SW, SP, A-1, A-3): vibration rearranges grains; use vibratory plates, reversible plates, smooth-drum vibratory rollers, or vibratory plate attachments on the excavator. Cohesive soils (clay and clayey mixes: CL, CH, SC, GC, A-6, A-7): need kneading and impact; use jumping jacks (rammers), padfoot or sheepsfoot trench rollers, or padfoot wheel attachments; plates mostly bounce on clay. Silts (ML, SM with high fines): narrow moisture window; rammers or padfoot rollers in thin lifts, and stop if the soil starts pumping or bleeding water. Lift thickness is usually 6 to 12 inches loose depending on equipment and spec; thinner for hand-operated machines and cohesive soil. Vibration from large rollers can damage shallow pipe; keep heavy vibratory compaction off until the minimum cover in your spec is reached.
field.title: Matching compaction equipment to soil type (plate, jumping jack, padfoot, smooth drum)
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: Standard compaction practice; equipment manufacturer guidance (check your spec)

field.text: How soils are described in boring logs and inspection reports: order is usually consistency or density, color, moisture, group name and symbol, then extras. Moisture: dry (dusty, dry to touch), moist (damp, no visible water), wet (visible free water, usually below water table). Color clues: gray, blue-gray or green-gray means soil that stays saturated with little oxygen (often at or below the water table); orange and gray mottling means the water table rises and falls through that zone; black or dark brown can mean organics; red, brown and yellow mean oxidized, well-drained soil. Structure: stratified (layers over 1/4 inch), laminated (thinner layers), fissured (cracks), slickensided (shiny polished fracture planes; slabs can fall), blocky, lensed (pockets of other soil), homogeneous. Cementation: weak, moderate, strong. These words matter for OSHA too: fissured or slickensided clay is not Type A.
field.title: Soil description words on logs: color, moisture, consistency, structure
field.topic: Soils: USCS and AASHTO classification and field identification
field.source: ASTM D2488 visual-manual procedure as summarized by University of Alabama CE 340 lab notes; standard soils practice; soil color practice (USDA)

field.text: A geotechnical (geotech, soils) report usually has: project description; field exploration (number, location and depth of borings, test pits, probes); lab testing (moisture, gradation, Atterberg limits, Proctor, strength, corrosivity); subsurface conditions summary (soil layers, rock, groundwater); and recommendations (excavation and shoring, dewatering, pipe bedding and foundation, backfill and compaction, reuse of excavated soil, pavement section, thrust or bearing values). The appendix holds the boring location plan, boring logs, test pit logs, lab summary sheets and the legend or key to symbols. For the foreman: read the boring location plan against your line and depths, the logs nearest your work, the groundwater section (with dates), and the recommendations for bedding, unsuitable soils, reuse of spoil and dewatering. Flag anything that doesn't match what you dig, write it down with station and depth, and tell the super; that record supports differing site condition claims. Bid-side review is in the business-pm file.
field.title: Geotechnical report: what is in it and which pages a foreman should read
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Standard geotechnical report practice

field.text: A boring log is a vertical record of one hole. Typical columns left to right: depth (ft) and elevation; sample number and type (D or SS split spoon, U or ST thin-wall Shelby tube, R rock core, A auger cuttings); blow counts for each 6 inch push of the split spoon and the N-value; recovery (inches of sample recovered); graphic log (symbols or hatching for each soil); description (density or consistency, color, moisture, soil name, USCS symbol, notes like 'with cobbles', 'organic odor', 'fill'); lab results (moisture %, LL/PL, % fines); and remarks (water levels, drilling method such as HSA hollow stem auger, casing, refusal). Lines between layers show where the soil changes; a dashed line means the change was gradual or estimated. The header lists date drilled, rig and hammer type, ground surface elevation and water level readings. Always read the legend sheet that goes with the logs, because abbreviations vary by firm and DOT.
field.title: How to read a boring log: columns, symbols and what they mean
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: MaineDOT, Key to Soil and Rock Descriptions and Terms (boring log key, 2020); standard boring log practice

field.text: The Standard Penetration Test (SPT, ASTM D1586) drives a 2 inch outside diameter split-spoon sampler into the bottom of the boring with a 140 lb hammer falling 30 inches. Blows are counted for each of three 6 inch increments; the N-value is the sum of the second and third increments (the first seats the sampler). Example: blows 4-6-8 give N = 14 blows per foot. Higher N means denser or stiffer soil. Logs may show 'WOH' (sampler sank under weight of hammer) or 'WOR' (weight of rods) for very soft soil, and '50/3' meaning 50 blows drove only 3 inches (very dense or rock). Hammer type matters: automatic hammers deliver more energy than older safety hammers, so engineers correct to N60 (60% energy): N60 = N x (hammer efficiency / 60%). Automatic hammers commonly run about 80 to 90 percent efficient, so a field N of 20 is roughly N60 = 27 to 30; the log or report states the efficiency used. Crews mainly use N to judge digging difficulty and stability, not to design.
field.title: SPT N-value: the Standard Penetration Test explained
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: MaineDOT, Key to Soil and Rock Descriptions and Terms (boring log key, 2020); ASTM D1586 scope (summarized)

field.text: MaineDOT boring log key, N in blows per foot. Granular soil (sand, gravel, silt): very loose 0 to 4; loose 5 to 10; medium dense 11 to 30; dense 31 to 50; very dense over 50. Cohesive soil (clay): very soft under 2 (WOH or WOR); soft 2 to 4; medium stiff 5 to 8; stiff 9 to 15; very stiff 16 to 30; hard over 30. Field meaning: very loose to loose sand or soft clay at pipe depth means the trench bottom likely won't support pipe without a stone foundation, walls will move and boxes will settle; medium dense or stiff is normal workable ground; very dense sand, hard clay or glacial till (N over 50) digs slowly and may need a bigger machine or a ripper tooth. Very soft clay (N under 2) below the trench can squeeze up (bottom heave) in deep cuts. Other agencies use slightly different breakpoints; use the legend for your report.
field.title: SPT N-value to density and consistency (loose sand, soft clay, very dense)
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: MaineDOT, Key to Soil and Rock Descriptions and Terms (boring log key, 2020)

field.text: Refusal means the drill could not advance any further with the method in use. Spoon or sampler refusal is commonly recorded when it takes 50 blows (some agencies use 100) to drive the spoon less than 6 inches, written like '50/2' (50 blows for 2 inches). Auger refusal means the auger stopped turning or advancing. Casing refusal is similar for driven casing. Refusal can mean bedrock, but it can also be a boulder, cobble layer, cemented hardpan, caliche, buried concrete or old foundations. The only way to know it is bedrock is rock coring below the refusal depth (an 'R' run with recovery and RQD). For bids and claims, note whether the report confirms rock by coring or just reports refusal; 'auger refusal at 8 ft' in a glacial till area may be boulders, and the next boring 300 ft away may be different. Rock lines drawn between borings on profiles are interpretations, not measurements.
field.title: Refusal on a boring log: auger refusal, spoon refusal and what it doesn't tell you
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: MaineDOT, Key to Soil and Rock Descriptions and Terms (boring log key, 2020) (logs record casing refusal in notes); standard drilling practice (refusal criteria vary by agency)

field.text: When drillers reach rock, they may core it with a diamond bit, recovering a cylinder of rock (NQ core is about 1.9 inches across). Logs report: run length, recovery (percent of the run recovered; low recovery suggests soft seams, voids or broken rock), and RQD. Rock Quality Designation (RQD) = total length of intact core pieces longer than 4 inches divided by the run length, as a percent. MaineDOT ratings: very poor 25% or less; poor 26 to 50%; fair 51 to 75%; good 76 to 90%; excellent 91 to 100%. Also listed: rock type, weathering (fresh, slightly, moderately, highly, completely weathered), hardness, fracture spacing and dip, and sometimes compressive strength. Field meaning: low RQD, highly weathered rock may rip or hammer out reasonably; high RQD, fresh, hard rock (granite, quartzite, massive limestone) means hammering will be slow and blasting or a rock trencher may be cheaper on long runs.
field.title: Rock core and RQD on boring logs (rock quality designation)
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: MaineDOT, Key to Soil and Rock Descriptions and Terms (boring log key, 2020)

field.text: Test pits (test holes) dug with the excavator show far more than a boring: actual digging difficulty, wall stability, boulders, groundwater inflow rate, fill and debris, and existing utilities. Use them at known trouble spots, at crossings, where borings are far apart, and where the geotech report says 'variable'. Record station and offset, depth, each soil layer (USCS name, color, moisture), water depth and inflow after 15 to 30 minutes, cave-ins, boulders and their size, and take photos with a tape or rod for scale. Treat a test pit as an excavation: OSHA rules apply once anyone goes in, and over 5 ft needs protection; you can log most of it from the surface. Probe rods (a 1/2 inch steel rod pushed by hand) quickly find soft zones in a trench bottom: if it pushes in easily more than about 6 inches, the bottom is likely soft. Backfill and compact test pits that are in the future road or pipe path.
field.title: Test pits and probing: checking ground before and during the job
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Standard geotechnical and excavation practice; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652 (5 ft protective system rule)

field.text: Unsuitable material is soil the specs say can't stay under the pipe or be used as backfill. Common definitions include organic soil, peat, muck, topsoil, soft or saturated soil that won't support the pipe or won't compact, high-plasticity clay (CH, A-7) under pavement, frozen soil, debris, trash, rubble, stumps and roots, rocks over the size limit, and contaminated soil. Who decides: normally the engineer or inspector in the field, not the crew. Process: stop when the bottom is soft or the material looks unsuitable, show the inspector, agree on how deep to go and what to replace it with, and log it. Pay: many contracts have a unit price for 'unsuitable material removal' or 'foundation stone' per CY or ton, with a pay limit (trench width and depth below grade); work outside those limits or without approval may not be paid. Log station range, depth below pipe, width, tons of stone and truckloads hauled every day, with photos and the inspector's initials. See also the embedment file for foundation stone details.
field.title: Unsuitable material: definition, removal and pay
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Common agency specification practice (check your specs)

field.text: Over-excavation (undercut, remove and replace) means digging below the planned trench bottom or subgrade to take out bad soil and replacing it with better material. Typical pipe foundation undercut is 6 to 24 inches or as directed, replaced with crushed stone (often #57, #4 or 2 to 3 inch stone, sometimes called foundation stone, ballast or rip-rap base for very soft ground) wrapped in non-woven geotextile so fines don't pump into the stone. In deeper soft zones, a bridging lift of large stone pushed into the soft soil with the bucket, then smaller stone on top, gives a working platform. For structures (manholes, vaults), the undercut is usually wider than the base by at least the depth of the undercut on each side so load spreads into firm soil. Under pavement and slabs, specs or the geotech may call for 1 to 3 ft of undercut with select fill and geogrid. Compact the replacement in lifts and check grade before pipe goes down. Don't over-excavate without approval if you want it paid.
field.title: Over-excavation and replacement: how deep and with what
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Common agency specification and geotechnical practice (depths vary; follow plans and engineer direction)

field.text: Lime treats clay soils by reacting with water and clay minerals. Two uses: modification (quick drying and lower plasticity so wet clay can be worked and compacted; effects within hours to a couple of days) and stabilization (long-term strength gain over 28 days or more). National Lime Association guidance: soils with at least 25% passing the No. 200 sieve and a PI of 10 or more are candidates; organic content over about 1 to 2% can stop strength gain, and soluble sulfates over 0.3% need special precautions. The lab sets the minimum lime content (the dose that holds pH 12.4, ASTM D6276) and field specs typically add 0.5 to 1 percentage point for variability. Field doses of about 4 to 6% by dry weight mixed 6 to 12 inches deep are common, but the spec or geotech sets the number. High-PI clays may need two mixing passes with a mellowing period between (length set by the DOT spec, often 1 to 3 days). Many specs stop lime work in cold weather (around 40 F) because the reaction nearly stops. Not effective on very micaceous soils (cement works better) or clean sands with no clay.
field.title: Lime stabilization of clay: drying wet soil and cutting plasticity
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: National Lime Association, Technical Brief: Mixture Design and Testing Procedures for Lime Stabilized Soil (2006); Georgia DOT lime guideline (micaceous soils); doses are typical practice, check spec

field.text: Hydrated lime (calcium hydroxide) is a fine dry powder, very dusty; spread dry with special equipment or as slurry. Quicklime (calcium oxide) comes as pebbles (about No. 4 to 3/4 or 1 inch per Georgia DOT); less of it is needed because it contains no water, but it reacts violently with water, generating heat, and must be fully slaked; unslaked pebbles can swell later and damage pavement. Georgia DOT warns quicklime is very caustic and can cause severe skin burns. Safety for crews: wear goggles, gloves, long sleeves and a respirator or dust mask when spreading or mixing; keep lime off wet skin and out of boots; wash exposed skin promptly; flush eyes with water for at least 15 minutes and get medical care if lime gets in eyes; stay upwind; don't spread in strong wind near homes, cars or traffic. Lime dust is also tough on equipment air filters. See the first aid file for chemical burns.
field.title: Quicklime vs hydrated lime: handling and safety (chemical burns)
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Georgia DOT Geotechnical Manual 4.5.33, Guidelines for Lime Stabilization; lime product safety practice

field.text: Portland cement can stabilize a wider range of soils than lime: sands, silty soils, low-plasticity clays and micaceous soils. Cement-modified soil uses a small dose (commonly about 2 to 5% by dry weight) to dry and stiffen wet soil and cut plasticity; soil-cement or cement-treated base uses more to make a hard, bound layer: PCA's typical ranges run from about 3 to 5% for well-graded gravel (A-1-a) up to 10 to 16% for clays (A-7), with sands and silts in between; the lab mix design sets the dose. Georgia DOT points to cement (around 6%) for very micaceous soils where lime fails. Unlike lime, cement starts hydrating immediately, so mixing, compaction and finish grading must happen within a short window (often about 2 hours; check the spec), followed by curing (moist or sealed). Cement-treated soil is brittle and can crack. Safety: wet cement and cement-soil mixes are caustic (pH about 12 to 13) and cause chemical burns through clothing and boots; wear gloves, long sleeves and eye protection and wash off promptly. Dust contains respirable silica concerns when dry-mixing.
field.title: Cement stabilization and cement-modified soil
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Georgia DOT Geotechnical Manual 4.5.33, Guidelines for Lime Stabilization; Portland cement soil stabilization practice (PCA guidance, percentages vary; mix design governs)

field.text: Soils containing soluble sulfates (gypsum, sulfate-rich clays in parts of Texas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Nevada, California and other arid areas) can react with lime or cement and water to form expansive minerals (ettringite and thaumasite). The treated layer heaves weeks or months later, buckling pavement and lifting structures. National Lime Association guidance flags soluble sulfate levels above 0.3% (about 3,000 ppm) for special precautions; many DOTs require a sulfate test before lime or cement treatment and use extended mellowing, extra water, or a different treatment where sulfates are high. Field signs of sulfate soils: white crystalline crusts or veins (gypsum) in the soil, white efflorescence on spoil as it dries. If you see these and the plans call for lime or cement treatment, ask whether sulfate testing was done.
field.title: Sulfate heave: when lime or cement makes clay swell
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: National Lime Association, Technical Brief: Mixture Design and Testing Procedures for Lime Stabilized Soil (2006) (sulfate threshold); standard DOT practice

field.text: Geosynthetics help on soft ground. Geotextile (fabric): separation and filtration; keeps soft soil from mixing into stone and stone from punching into soil. Non-woven fabric is usually used around pipe foundation stone and drains; woven fabric under roads for strength. Geogrid: an open plastic grid that interlocks with aggregate to provide lateral restraint and spread load; little deformation needed to work. Caltrans guidance: consider geosynthetics for soft subgrades such as CL, CH, ML, MH, OL, OH and PT with CBR under about 3, R-value under 20, or undrained shear strength under 2,000 psf; for very soft ground (CBR under 2) put down at least 6 inches of aggregate as the first lift over it. Geogrid alone is only suitable if the stone meets filter criteria against the subgrade; otherwise use a geotextile, or both. Installation: clear sharp objects, pull taut and wrinkle-free, overlap at least 2 ft (more in very soft ground), and patch damage with a piece overlapping at least 3 ft beyond the hole.
field.title: Geotextile and geogrid for soft trench bottoms and subgrades
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Caltrans, Subgrade Enhancement Geosynthetic Design and Construction Guide (2013)

field.text: When the trench bottom or haul road is too soft for normal compaction (it pumps, the plate sinks, the probe rod goes in easily), a bridging lift builds a platform. Common practice: lay geotextile on the soft soil where specified, dump coarse crushed stone or shot rock (2 to 6 inch or larger) from the edge and push it out with the bucket rather than driving on the fabric, track or tamp it in without vibration that liquefies the soil, then choke the surface with smaller stone (for example #57) and continue with normal bedding. Static compaction or light passes often work better than heavy vibration on wet silt and clay, which can turn it to soup. In the trench, also keep the water pumped below the working level. Document the extra stone and depth with the inspector, since it is usually extra pay. For roads and yards, Caltrans suggests a first lift of at least 6 inches over geosynthetic on very soft subgrades.
field.title: Bridging lifts and working platforms on soft ground
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Standard construction practice; Caltrans, Subgrade Enhancement Geosynthetic Design and Construction Guide (2013) (initial lift)

field.text: Specs usually allow native soil as trench backfill above the pipe zone if it meets requirements (no organics, debris, oversize stone; moisture can be brought near optimum; reaches density), and require imported select material under pavement or where native is unsuitable. Field checklist before reusing spoil: (1) What is it? Run the quick field tests and compare to the geotech's description; (2) Is moisture workable today, or will it pump? (3) Will it pass density? Do a test section and get early tests; (4) Is it frost susceptible under pavement in a cold climate? (5) Any boulders over the spec limit (often 3 to 6 inches within 1 to 2 ft above pipe; larger allowed higher up)? (6) Any contamination signs? Importing costs trucks and material but reduces failed tests and settlement call-backs. Changing from native to import because native won't work is a cost item; get it in writing from the engineer.
field.title: Native soil vs imported backfill: making the call in the field
field.topic: Soils: geotech reports, borings, unsuitable material and stabilization
field.source: Common agency specification practice (limits vary; check your specs)

field.text: A drainage area (watershed, catchment, sub-basin) is all the land that drains to one point, such as an inlet, a culvert or a pond. Its boundary is the drainage divide: the ridge line where water on one side goes one way and on the other side goes the other. On a contour map, draw the divide by starting at the point of interest and going uphill perpendicular to the contours, following high points and ridges. Things that matter for runoff: area (acres), how much of it is paved or roofed (impervious), soil type, slope, and the longest flow path. Off-site water coming onto a job from upstream is the most common surprise: if a ditch, pipe or road crown sends water toward your trench or pond, it counts. In the field, watch where water actually goes in the first rain and tell the engineer if it doesn't match the drainage map.
field.title: Drainage areas and watersheds: reading where water comes from
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: General hydrology practice

field.text: The rational method estimates the peak flow off a small drainage area: Q = C x i x A, where Q is peak flow in cubic feet per second (cfs), C is the runoff coefficient (fraction of rain that runs off, 0 to 1), i is rainfall intensity in inches per hour for a storm lasting as long as the time of concentration, and A is the drainage area in acres. In US units the conversion factor is about 1 (1 acre-inch per hour = 1.008 cfs), so it is ignored. TxDOT limits it to areas up to about 200 acres with no significant flood storage, and uses a minimum time of concentration of 10 minutes. Assumptions: rain is uniform over the whole area and duration, runoff is proportional to intensity, the peak happens when the whole area is contributing, and storage is ignored. It is used for inlets, storm sewers, ditches and small culverts. Bigger or complex areas use NRCS (TR-55/TR-20) or other models.
field.title: Rational method (Q = CiA): what it is and when it applies
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Ch. 4 Section 12 Rational Method

field.text: TxDOT's runoff coefficient table for urban areas (pick within the range; higher for steeper, tighter soils and bigger storms): downtown business 0.70 to 0.95; neighborhood business 0.30 to 0.70; single-family residential 0.30 to 0.50; attached multi-unit residential 0.60 to 0.75; suburban residential 0.35 to 0.40; apartments 0.30 to 0.70; light industrial 0.30 to 0.80; heavy industrial 0.60 to 0.90; parks and cemeteries 0.10 to 0.25; playgrounds 0.30 to 0.40; railroad yards 0.30 to 0.40; asphalt streets 0.85 to 0.95; concrete streets 0.90 to 0.95; brick streets 0.70 to 0.85; drives and walks 0.75 to 0.95; roofs 0.75 to 0.95. Your local drainage manual may have its own table, which governs on that job.
field.title: Runoff coefficient C: urban land uses and pavements
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Table 4-10 Runoff Coefficients (urban)

field.text: TxDOT runoff coefficients for pervious areas: lawns on sandy soil, flat (2%) 0.05 to 0.10, average (2 to 7%) 0.10 to 0.15, steep (over 7%) 0.15 to 0.20; lawns on heavy (clay) soil, flat 0.13 to 0.17, average 0.18 to 0.22, steep 0.25 to 0.35. Unimproved land: sand or sandy loam 0 to 3% slope 0.15 to 0.20, 3 to 5% 0.20 to 0.25; black or loessial soil 0 to 3% 0.18 to 0.25, 3 to 5% 0.25 to 0.30, over 5% 0.70 to 0.80; deep sand 0.05 to 0.15; steep grassed slopes 0.70. For rural watersheds TxDOT builds C by adding four parts (relief, soil infiltration, vegetal cover, surface storage). Field note: compacted construction sites and frozen ground behave much more like pavement than lawn, which is why runoff during construction can surprise you.
field.title: Runoff coefficient C: lawns, bare ground and soils
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Tables 4-10 and 4-11 Runoff Coefficients

field.text: Most drainage areas are a mix of surfaces, so a weighted (composite) C is used: multiply each sub-area by its C, add them up, and divide by the total area. Example: 1.2 ac pavement at 0.90 + 0.3 ac roof at 0.90 + 1.0 ac clay lawn at 0.20 = (1.08 + 0.27 + 0.20) / 2.5 ac = 1.55 / 2.5 = composite C of 0.62. Many manuals also bump C up for rarer storms because more of the rain runs off when the ground is already wet: a common set of frequency factors is about 1.1 for the 25-year, 1.2 for the 50-year and 1.25 for the 100-year storm, with C times the factor not allowed to exceed 1.0. Not every agency uses these factors (TxDOT's rational method section doesn't list them), so use what your local manual says.
field.title: Composite runoff coefficient and adjusting C for big storms
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Composite C computed; frequency factors are common textbook/manual practice, not universal

field.text: Example: a 2.5-acre site with composite C = 0.62 (from the composite C example). Time of concentration is computed as 7 minutes, but the agency minimum is 10 minutes, so use 10. From the local IDF curve (NOAA Atlas 14), suppose the 10-year, 10-minute intensity is i = 5.5 inches per hour (read your own location's value; it varies a lot). Q = C x i x A = 0.62 x 5.5 x 2.5 = 8.5 cfs. In gallons per minute: 8.5 cfs x 448.8 = about 3,830 gpm. Compare to pipe capacity: an 18-inch RCP at 0.50% slope carries about 7.4 cfs flowing full (see the Manning example), so it's too small; a 24-inch at 0.50% carries about 16 cfs. This is why a small change in area, C or slope in the field can matter. Leave design to the engineer; use this to sanity-check and to explain why a pipe size was chosen.
field.title: Rational method worked example: peak flow from a small site
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Computed from Q = CiA (TxDOT HDM) and Manning's equation; intensity value illustrative

field.text: Rainfall intensity (i) in the rational method comes from an IDF curve: Intensity-Duration-Frequency. For a given return period (say the 10-year storm), short storms are more intense than long ones: a 5 or 10-minute burst might be several inches per hour, while the 24-hour average for the same frequency is under an inch per hour. The duration used equals the time of concentration of the drainage area. In the US the standard source is NOAA Atlas 14 (Precipitation Frequency Data Server), which gives depths and intensities for any location; TxDOT requires Atlas 14 on all projects, and if older IDF values are used and NOAA's numbers are higher, the designer must document extra freeboard. Many cities publish their own IDF tables. Intensity is in inches per hour, depth in inches; don't mix them. Newer atlas updates and climate-adjusted values are adopted by some agencies.
field.title: Rainfall intensity and IDF curves (NOAA Atlas 14)
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Ch. 4 Section 12 (NOAA Atlas 14 requirement)

field.text: Time of concentration is how long it takes water to travel from the farthest point of the drainage area (in travel time, not distance) to the inlet, culvert or point you're designing. It matters because the rational method uses the rain intensity for a storm lasting Tc: short Tc means higher intensity and higher peak flow. NRCS TR-55 adds up segments along the flow path: sheet flow (thin flow across the surface at the top of the path, limited by NRCS to 300 ft, and by many localities to 100 ft), then shallow concentrated flow (in small rills and gutters), then channel or pipe flow (computed with Manning's equation). Paving, curbs and pipes shorten Tc, which raises peaks; that's one reason development increases flooding. Many agencies set a minimum Tc (TxDOT uses 10 minutes; Iowa DOT uses 5 minutes for intake spacing).
field.title: Time of concentration (Tc) in plain words
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: HydroCAD Tc notes (TR-55 method); TxDOT HDM minimum Tc; Iowa DOT Design Manual 4A-6

field.text: The Kirpich formula is a quick Tc estimate for small rural watersheds with defined channels: Tc (minutes) = 0.0078 x L^0.77 x S^-0.385, where L is the flow length in feet and S is the average slope in ft/ft (fall over length). Example: L = 1,000 ft with 20 ft of fall, so S = 20 / 1,000 = 0.02. L^0.77 = about 204; S^-0.385 = about 4.5; Tc = 0.0078 x 204 x 4.5 = about 7.2 minutes. If the agency minimum is 10 minutes, use 10 minutes for intensity. Many manuals multiply Kirpich Tc by a factor for paved or grassed surfaces, and many prefer the TR-55 segment method instead, so check which method your local manual requires. Use it as a field sanity check, not for design.
field.title: Kirpich formula for time of concentration: worked example
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Kirpich formula (standard hydrology texts); example computed

field.text: A '100-year' storm or flood does not happen once every 100 years. It has a 1% chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year (USGS calls it the 1% annual exceedance probability event). Likewise a 10-year storm is 10% per year, a 25-year 4%, a 50-year 2%, a 500-year 0.2%. Each year starts fresh, so two 100-year floods can happen back to back. Over a longer period the odds add up: USGS notes about a 26% chance of at least one 100-year flood during a 30-year mortgage. By the same math, a 10-year storm has about a 41% chance of happening at least once during a 5-year job, and a 25-year storm about 64% over 25 years. That's why erosion controls, pump-arounds and open trenches need a plan for storms bigger than you expect.
field.title: Storm return periods: what a 10-year or 100-year storm really means
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: USGS Water Science School, Floods and recurrence intervals; additional probabilities computed as 1-(1-p)^n

field.text: Design storms are set by the local agency or DOT and vary, but a common pattern is: street inlets and gutter spread checked for the 10-year storm on through roads (Iowa DOT: 10-year on continuous grades, 50-year at sag points on major roads, and a 100-year check that keeps one 12-ft lane open each direction on freeways); local storm sewers 2 to 10-year; culverts 10 to 100-year depending on road class and what floods if they overtop; detention ponds often control the 2, 10 and 100-year peaks back to pre-development rates; emergency spillways for the 100-year or larger; riprap outlet aprons often the 25-year (Tennessee handbook uses the 25-year, 24-hour storm). Water quality practices are sized for a small frequent storm (often around 1 inch). Your project's drainage report says what storm each piece was designed for.
field.title: Typical design storms for drainage features
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Iowa DOT Design Manual 4A-6 Table 1; Tennessee ESC Handbook outlet protection; other values typical practice

field.text: Manning's equation estimates gravity flow in pipes and channels: Q = (1.486 / n) x A x R^(2/3) x S^(1/2), with Q in cfs, A flow area in sq ft, R hydraulic radius (A divided by wetted perimeter; for a full round pipe R = D/4) in ft, S slope in ft/ft, and n the roughness. The app's calculators include Manning's full pipe. Typical n values from Oregon DOT's hydraulics manual: concrete pipe 0.011 to 0.015 (0.013 normal); corrugated metal 2-2/3 x 1/2 inch annular 0.024; helical CMP depends on size, from about 0.013 at 12 inch up to 0.024 over 48 inch; smooth plastic 0.011 to 0.015; corrugated plastic (corrugated inside) 0.024; coated cast iron about 0.013. Doubling roughness halves capacity at the same slope. A pipe flows most at about 93% full, not completely full, but designers use full-flow capacity as the standard check.
field.title: Manning's equation for storm pipes: formula and roughness n
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: ODOT Hydraulics Manual Appendix 8-A (Manning n); Manning's equation standard form

field.text: Example: 18-inch pipe (D = 1.5 ft) at 0.50% slope (S = 0.005), flowing full. Area A = 3.1416 x 1.5^2 / 4 = 1.767 sq ft. R = D/4 = 0.375 ft, so R^(2/3) = 0.520. S^(1/2) = 0.0707. For RCP, n = 0.013: Q = (1.486 / 0.013) x 1.767 x 0.520 x 0.0707 = about 7.4 cfs, velocity V = Q / A = about 4.2 ft/s. Same size and slope in corrugated-interior pipe, n = 0.024: Q = 7.4 x 0.013 / 0.024 = about 4.0 cfs, about 46% less. A 24-inch RCP at 0.50% carries about 16 cfs (5.1 ft/s). Lessons: substituting a rougher pipe can cut capacity in half; capacity goes with the square root of slope, so cutting slope from 0.50% to 0.25% drops capacity about 29%; and going up one pipe size gives a big jump.
field.title: Manning's worked example: 18-inch RCP vs corrugated pipe
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Computed with Manning's equation; n values from ODOT Hydraulics Manual App. 8-A

field.text: For an open ditch, use the flow area and wetted perimeter of the shape. Example: trapezoidal grass ditch, 2 ft bottom width, 3:1 side slopes, flowing 1 ft deep, slope 1% (S = 0.01). Top width = 2 + 2 x 3 x 1 = 8 ft. Area A = (2 + 3 x 1) x 1 = 5.0 sq ft. Wetted perimeter P = 2 + 2 x 1 x square root of (1 + 3^2) = 2 + 6.32 = 8.32 ft. R = 5.0 / 8.32 = 0.60 ft, R^(2/3) = 0.71. Grass mowed to about 2 inches at 0.7 to 1.5 ft depth: n about 0.035 to 0.05 (ODOT); use 0.035. Q = (1.486 / 0.035) x 5.0 x 0.71 x 0.1 = about 15 cfs; velocity = 15 / 5 = 3.0 ft/s, OK for good grass. Tall grass (n 0.07 or more) would carry about half that at the same depth, so the water rides higher. Clean, recently dug earth: n about 0.016 to 0.020. Riprap: n much higher and varies with depth.
field.title: Manning's for ditches and swales: worked example
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Computed with Manning's equation; n values from ODOT Hydraulics Manual App. 8-A

field.text: Storm sewers are usually designed for a minimum velocity of about 2 to 3 ft/s flowing full (many manuals use 3 ft/s for storm, 2 ft/s for sanitary) so grit and sand don't settle and build up; flat storm pipes fill with sediment and lose capacity. Maximum velocities in pipes are often limited to around 10 to 15 ft/s (some say 20) to limit abrasion, especially with sandy runoff and CMP inverts, and to reduce energy at outlets. Ditches and swales: bare soil may erode at 1.5 to 3 ft/s, good grass holds roughly 4 to 6 ft/s, turf reinforcement mats more, riprap more still; designers check shear stress (FHWA HEC-15). Outlet velocity sets riprap apron size. In the field: a pipe laid flatter than plan loses velocity and silts up; steeper than plan increases outlet velocity and erosion. Check your local drainage manual for its numbers.
field.title: Velocity limits in storm pipes and ditches
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: General practice from state DOT drainage manuals; values vary by agency

field.text: The hydraulic grade line is the level water would rise to in a standpipe at any point in a storm system: in a pipe flowing partly full it is the water surface; when the pipe flows full under pressure (surcharged), the HGL is above the pipe crown and water rises up in the manholes and inlets. The energy grade line is the HGL plus the velocity head (V squared over 2g). Designers calculate the HGL backward from the outlet (starting at the tailwater, such as the pond or stream level) through every pipe and structure, adding friction losses and junction/bend losses, and make sure the HGL stays below the inlet grates and manhole rims, often with about 1 ft of freeboard. If it rises above a grate, water pops out and floods the street. Field impact: changing inverts, pipe size, junction shapes or the outlet elevation changes the HGL, so get approval first.
field.title: Hydraulic grade line (HGL) and energy grade line (EGL) in plain words
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: General hydraulics (FHWA HEC-22 concepts); freeboard values vary by agency

field.text: Spread is the width of water in the gutter measured from the curb face out into the road; encroachment is how far it reaches into the travel lanes. Inlets are spaced so spread stays within limits. Gutter flow uses a modified Manning equation (Iowa DOT form): Q = (0.56 / n) x Sx^1.67 x SL^0.5 x T^2.67, with Q in cfs, Sx gutter cross slope (ft/ft), SL longitudinal slope (ft/ft), T spread in ft, n for the gutter (troweled concrete 0.012, smooth asphalt 0.013, rough asphalt 0.016, broom-finished concrete 0.016; add 0.002 where sediment builds up on flat gutters, per FHWA HEC-22).
