Iowa DOT criteria: freeways no lane encroachment for the 10-year on grade, and one 12-ft lane open each direction in the 100-year check; primary highways 45 mph and up no encroachment in the 10-year on grade and 3 ft at sags in the 50-year; under 45 mph, 3 ft in the 10-year. Local streets follow city criteria.
field.title: Gutter spread: what it is and allowable limits
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Iowa DOT Design Manual 4A-6, Calculating spread and checking intake location

field.text: Example with the gutter flow equation Q = (0.56 / n) x Sx^1.67 x SL^0.5 x T^2.67: rough asphalt gutter n = 0.016, cross slope Sx = 2% (0.02), longitudinal slope SL = 1% (0.01), allowable spread T = 8 ft. Sx^1.67 = about 0.00147; SL^0.5 = 0.10; T^2.67 = about 256. Q = (0.56 / 0.016) x 0.00147 x 0.10 x 256 = 35 x 0.0377 = about 1.3 cfs. So that gutter can carry only about 1.3 cfs before water spreads 8 ft into the road; the next inlet must go where the accumulated runoff reaches about 1.3 cfs (plus any bypass from upstream inlets). Because spread goes up with flow to roughly the 3/8 power, doubling the flow widens spread only about 30%, but flattening the grade or the cross slope widens it noticeably. Field point: building the gutter flatter than plan (for example 1.5% instead of 2% cross slope) increases spread and ponding.
field.title: Gutter spread worked example
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Computed from Iowa DOT Design Manual 4A-6 gutter flow equation

field.text: Handy conversions for drainage numbers: 1 cfs (cubic foot per second) = 448.8 gallons per minute = about 0.646 million gallons per day. 1 cubic foot = 7.48 gallons; 1 gallon = 0.1337 cubic feet. 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft. 1 inch of rain on 1 acre = 3,630 cubic feet = about 27,150 gallons. 1 acre-inch per hour = 1.008 cfs (why the rational method Q = CiA needs no conversion in US units). 1 acre-foot = 43,560 cubic feet = about 325,850 gallons. Slope: 1% = 0.01 ft/ft = 1 ft per 100 ft = about 1/8 inch per foot. A pump rated 500 gpm moves about 1.1 cfs. Water weighs about 62.4 lb per cubic foot (8.34 lb per gallon), so 1 ft of water depth = about 0.433 psi, and 1 psi = 2.31 ft of head. Metric: 1 cfs = 28.3 liters per second.
field.title: Stormwater unit conversions crews use
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: Standard unit conversions (computed)

field.text: The rational method gives only a peak flow and is used for small areas (TxDOT up to about 200 acres) such as inlets, storm sewers and small ditches. NRCS methods (TR-55, TR-20, and software like HydroCAD, HEC-HMS) use a curve number (CN) based on soil hydrologic group (A sandy to D clay) and land cover, plus a 24-hour design storm, to produce a full runoff hydrograph: peak flow AND total volume over time. Hydrographs are needed to size detention ponds and underground storage, since storage depends on volume, not just peak. A higher CN means more runoff (pavement about 98; woods on sandy soil can be in the 30s). Many state and local manuals specify which method to use for which job. For crews, the takeaway is that pond and storage outlet sizes come from a routed hydrograph, so small field changes to storage volume or orifice size change the results.
field.title: Rational method vs NRCS (TR-55) methods: which is used when
field.topic: Stormwater hydrology and hydraulics in plain words
field.source: General hydrology practice; rational method area limit per TxDOT HDM

field.text: The federal Clean Water Act makes it illegal to discharge pollutants from a point source (a pipe, ditch or channel) into waters of the United States without a permit. Section 402 created the NPDES permit program (National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System). Stormwater was brought in through the 1987 amendments: Phase I (1990) covered large and medium cities (MS4s), many industries, and construction disturbing 5 acres or more; Phase II (1999) added small MS4s and construction disturbing 1 acre or more. Most states run NPDES themselves under EPA authorization (so you deal with the state environmental agency), and EPA runs it in a few places. The three stormwater permit families are construction (CGP and state equivalents; see erosion-sediment-control for SWPPP basics), industrial (MSGP), and municipal (MS4). Violations can bring fines per day per violation, so take inspections and records seriously.
field.title: Clean Water Act and NPDES: why stormwater is regulated
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General summary of the Clean Water Act NPDES program; MS4 phases per EPA fact sheet

field.text: An MS4 (municipal separate storm sewer system) is a publicly owned storm sewer network (city, county, DOT, university, military base) that collects runoff and usually discharges it untreated to streams and lakes. Phase I (1990) covers medium and large MS4s, generally serving 100,000 people or more. Phase II covers small MS4s: all those inside Census-defined urbanized areas (50,000+ people) are automatically covered unless waived, and others can be designated by the permitting authority. Each MS4 holds an NPDES permit and must run a stormwater management program. For contractors this means the city or DOT you work for is itself under a permit, so it will push requirements down to you: erosion control inspections, no illicit discharges, post-construction BMP standards, and as-built and maintenance records for any stormwater facilities you build.
field.title: MS4 permits: Phase I and Phase II storm systems
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: EPA Stormwater Phase II Final Rule Fact Sheet 2.0, Small MS4 Overview

field.text: EPA's Phase II rule requires each small MS4 program to cover six minimum control measures: 1) public education and outreach about polluted runoff; 2) public participation and involvement; 3) illicit discharge detection and elimination (mapping the storm system and outfalls, banning non-stormwater discharges by ordinance, finding and stopping them); 4) construction site runoff control for projects disturbing 1 acre or more, including erosion and sediment controls, control of construction wastes like building materials, chemicals and litter, site plan review and inspections; 5) post-construction runoff control for new development and redevelopment disturbing 1 acre or more, using structural and non-structural BMPs (like grassed swales and porous pavement) and ensuring long-term maintenance; 6) pollution prevention and good housekeeping for city operations, such as street sweeping, reduced salt and pesticide use, and frequent catch basin cleaning. Items 3, 4 and 5 are the ones crews feel directly.
field.title: MS4 six minimum control measures
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: EPA Stormwater Phase II Final Rule Fact Sheet 2.0, Small MS4 Overview

field.text: Storm drains go to streams, not a treatment plant, so only rain belongs in them. Things utility crews commonly get cited for: sawcutting slurry and core drilling water (high pH, fine solids; vacuum it up); concrete and mortar wash water (use a washout); muddy trench dewatering water without a filter bag or settling tank; chlorinated water from flushing or disinfecting new water mains (must be dechlorinated, typically with sodium thiosulfate or ascorbic acid tablets or diffusers, and often pH and turbidity checked, before reaching a storm drain or stream; follow your state's discharge rules); hydrostatic test water; fuel, hydraulic oil and grease leaks; paint, solvents and form oil; sewage from bypass pumping spills; and tracked mud. Cities' illicit discharge ordinances let them fine the contractor. Keep spill kits on trucks, block inlets near the work with inlet protection, and report spills per your SWPPP.
field.title: Illicit discharges: what crews must not put in a storm drain
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General practice under MS4 illicit discharge programs; dechlorination methods common industry practice

field.text: Permanent stormwater facilities (ponds, underground storage, bioretention, permeable pavement, separators) are usually required by the MS4's post-construction rules, and the owner must prove they were built as designed and will be maintained. Typical closeout items: an as-built (record) survey of pond grades, storage volume, outlet structure orifice sizes and elevations, pipe inverts and spillway elevations, certified by an engineer or surveyor; cleaning out construction sediment from forebays, Isolator Rows, sumps and pipes; stabilizing the drainage area; inspection by the city; and a recorded operation and maintenance (O&M) agreement or plan naming who maintains it and how often. Contractors are often held up on final payment or certificate of occupancy until these are done, so build to exact elevations, take photos before burying anything, and keep delivery tickets for stone, media and fabric.
field.title: Post-construction BMPs: as-builts, certification and maintenance agreements
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General practice under MS4 post-construction programs; Ohio EPA bioretention O&M plan requirement

field.text: Most drainage design rules come from the state DOT drainage or hydraulics manual (for example TxDOT Hydraulic Design Manual, Iowa DOT Design Manual Chapter 4, Oregon DOT Hydraulics Manual) and from city or county stormwater manuals for private development. They typically set: design storms for each feature, rainfall data source (often NOAA Atlas 14), runoff method and coefficients, minimum Tc, pipe minimum sizes, slopes and velocities, Manning n values, gutter spread limits, inlet types and spacing, culvert headwater limits, outlet protection, approved pipe materials, and standard drawings. Many are built on FHWA Hydraulic Engineering Circulars: HEC-22 (urban drainage), HDS-5 (culverts), HEC-14 (energy dissipators), HEC-15 (channel linings). State stormwater BMP manuals cover ponds, infiltration and bioretention. On a job, the contract spec says which manual governs; on DOT projects that's the DOT's, inside city limits it may be the city's.
field.title: State DOT and local drainage manuals: what they cover
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General practice; examples drawn from TxDOT, Iowa DOT and ODOT manuals cited elsewhere in this file set

field.text: Placing fill, riprap, headwalls, outfalls or culverts below the ordinary high water mark of streams, or in wetlands, usually needs a Clean Water Act Section 404 permit from the US Army Corps of Engineers (often a Nationwide Permit for utility lines, outfalls or road crossings) plus a Section 401 water quality certification from the state; many states add their own stream crossing or public waters permits, and fish and wildlife agencies may set work windows when you can't be in the water. Typical conditions: limits on the area of disturbance, pump-around or cofferdam to work in the dry, restore stream bed and banks, no equipment in flowing water, turbidity control, and specific culvert embedment for fish passage. Read the actual permit conditions before mobilizing; working outside the authorized footprint is a violation even if the work is good.
field.title: Working in streams and wetlands: Section 404 and state permits
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General summary of CWA Section 404/401 permitting; conditions vary by permit and state

field.text: Routine inspection items for storm systems (for owners, or for a contractor's pre-acceptance walk): inlets and catch basins: grate seated and bolted, no cracks, sump depth of sediment, trash, pipe connections intact, frame and adjusting rings sound, no settlement around the box; manholes: steps, cone and chimney, infiltration stains, roots, sediment in channel; pipes (CCTV or look through): sags holding water, joint gaps or soil coming in, cracks, crushed or deflected plastic or CMP, rust-through inverts; culverts: ends not crushed or buried, inlet not blocked by debris, outlet not perched or scoured; outfalls: erosion, undermined headwall or apron, missing riprap, flap gate working, dry-weather flow (possible illicit discharge); ponds and storage: outlet orifices clear, trash racks, spillway, embankment seepage or animal holes, sediment depth in forebay or Isolator Row. Record findings with photos and locations.
field.title: Storm structure and outfall inspection checklist
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General inspection practice for MS4 and DOT drainage maintenance

field.text: Catch basins and inlet sumps are cleaned mostly with vacuum trucks (combination jet-vac units like Vactor or Aquatech) or clamshell trucks. Common practice: clean when the sump is about half full of sediment (beyond that it stops trapping and starts flushing material downstream), or on a set schedule (often yearly, more in commercial and winter-sanding areas, as MS4 permits require 'frequent catch basin cleaning'). Steps: set traffic control; open the grate with a proper hook or lifter (they are heavy; use your legs, not your back); vacuum from the surface without entering; break up packed material with the jet wand; check the outlet pipe and hood; look for illicit discharge signs (odors, oil sheen, dry-weather flow); log depth removed. Don't jet sediment downstream into the pipe without catching it at the next structure. Entry into a basin is a confined space.
field.title: Catch basin cleaning with a vac truck
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General practice; MS4 good housekeeping measure per EPA small MS4 fact sheet

field.text: Hydro-jetting cleans pipes by pushing a nozzle upstream with high-pressure water; rear-facing jets pull the hose forward and scour debris back toward the downstream manhole where the vacuum hose picks it up. Typical technique: set up at the downstream structure; put a hose guide or roller at the manhole opening so the hose doesn't rub through on the frame; send the nozzle upstream and pull back slowly in passes (don't outrun the water, slow down at blockages so forward jets open them); vacuum material as it arrives; repeat until clean water returns. Pressures for cleaning commonly run about 1,000 to 1,500 psi, with blockages sometimes needing up to about 5,000 psi; flow (gpm) does most of the moving of debris in large pipe. Pick the nozzle for the job: general cleaning, penetrating, root-cutting or large-diameter culvert nozzles. Storm chambers and Isolator Rows need the maker's specified nozzle.
field.title: Jetting storm and sewer pipes: technique
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: Utility Contractor magazine, 10 Expert Tips to Ensure Safe Sewer Cleaning; technique general practice

field.text: Safety points for jet-vac work from industry guidance: open the upstream manhole first so the vacuum draws fresh air through the line, not sewer gas; never run a high-pressure nozzle outside the pipe, since it can whip like a loose fire hose and cut skin; keep the distance from the nozzle tip to the hose connection about 1.5 times the pipe diameter so the nozzle can't turn around in the pipe and come back out; don't free-spool, use a nozzle skid and hold the nozzle back when starting; replace worn hose, since it wears every pass; learn the boom on your specific truck and watch for overhead lines; set cones front and back with working flashers and keep noise low enough to hear traffic; wear waterproof gloves, boots, eye protection and hard hat; wash before eating, cover cuts, and keep hepatitis A and B shots current per CDC advice. Vac debris tanks can hold gases; don't put your head in the tank.
field.title: Jetter and vac truck safety
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: Utility Contractor magazine, 10 Expert Tips to Ensure Safe Sewer Cleaning

field.text: Material vacuumed from catch basins, storm pipes, separators and ponds is usually wet sediment mixed with trash, oil and road grit. Typical handling: decant free water at an approved location (often a sanitary sewer connection with the sewer authority's permission, or a decant facility), never back into the storm system or onto the ground; let solids drain at a lined drying pad or roll-off; dispose of solids at a landfill that accepts them, which may require testing (often for petroleum, metals, or a paint filter test for free liquids), especially from gas stations, industrial sites and separators; oil and absorbent pads go to a licensed waste hauler. Some states classify street and catch basin waste specially, with reuse options. Keep load tickets and disposal receipts, since MS4 and BMP maintenance records often require them. Pond dredging over a certain volume may need its own permit.
field.title: Disposing of storm cleaning debris and vac truck spoils
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General practice; disposal rules vary by state solid waste agency

field.text: Many road sinkholes start at a storm pipe or culvert. Water leaking through cracks, holes or separated joints carries soil into the pipe (and water running along the outside of the pipe washes fill away). Over months or years a void grows above the pipe; pavement can bridge it for a while, then collapses, sometimes under a vehicle. MnDOT's example: a 6-ft box culvert under a county road caused a collapse that closed the road. Warning signs: repeated patches in the same spot, cracked or dipping pavement, a small hole that turns out to be the top of a large void (the surface hole may be upstream of the actual pipe defect), rust-through at the bottom corners of CMP, separated joints, soil piles inside the pipe on CCTV, and new holes or erosion on the road embankment. Treat any small hole over a pipe as a possible large void: barricade, don't drive over it, and get the pipe inspected.
field.title: Sinkholes over storm pipes: leaking joints and soil loss
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: MnDOT, Look under the pavement (HydInfra culvert inspection article)

field.text: Ways crews and designers stop joints from pulling soil in: use watertight gasketed joints (or soil-tight joints with geotextile joint wraps on RCP, often about 2 ft wide centered on the joint, where specs allow); push joints fully home and check the gap, since an open joint in fine sand or silt will eat soil for years; keep pipes on line and grade so joints don't open from deflection; use proper embedment so the pipe doesn't settle and pull apart; where open-graded stone bedding is used in fine soils, wrap it with filter fabric so the native soil doesn't migrate into the stone and leave voids; build trench plugs or clay dams across the stone bedding at intervals on steep pipes so the trench doesn't become a drain carrying soil along the outside of the pipe; seal pipe connections at structures with boots or grout. Joint problems found on CCTV before acceptance are much cheaper to fix than a sinkhole later.
field.title: Preventing soil loss into storm pipes
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General practice; joint wrap widths vary by agency spec

field.text: 'Piping' in geotechnical terms is internal erosion: water seeping through soil picks up fine particles, opening a small channel that grows into a tunnel. In stormwater work it shows up as: pond embankments leaking along the outlet pipe (wet spots, boils or muddy water coming out at the downstream toe); trenches where water runs along the stone bedding and washes out the backfill, causing settlement over the pipe; behind headwalls where water gets around and under; and around dry wells or drains where fines wash into stone. Prevention: compact backfill well around pipes through embankments, use anti-seep collars or sand filter diaphragms as detailed, trench plugs in steep or high-groundwater trenches, filter fabric between fine soils and stone, and watertight joints. Muddy seepage at the toe of a pond embankment is an emergency sign; clear water seepage still needs watching. Report it to the engineer and owner right away.
field.title: Piping failures in ponds, embankments and along pipe trenches
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General geotechnical and dam safety practice

field.text: Infiltration trenches, chambers, dry wells, bioretention and permeable pavement fail mainly from clogging. Causes: construction mud washing in before the site was stabilized; compacted or smeared bottom from equipment; no or poorly maintained pretreatment (full forebays, Isolator Rows, sumps); dirty stone with fines; fabric on the trench bottom (Minnesota says no fabric on infiltration trench bottoms); fine sediment from winter sanding; and groundwater higher than assumed. Signs: water standing more than 48 to 72 hours after rain in an observation well or the surface, overflow during small storms, mosquitoes. Fixes depend on where the clog is: vacuum the surface (permeable pavement), replace the top fabric layer and stone (trenches have a separate top fabric for this reason), scrape and replace media (bioretention, sand filters), JetVac the Isolator Row. A bottom clog usually means digging it out and rebuilding, so prevention during construction is everything.
field.title: Why infiltration systems clog and what to do
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General practice; fabric note from Minnesota Stormwater Manual; drawdown targets from Ohio EPA bioretention

field.text: Typical culvert problems found in inspections: corroded or abraded inverts on CMP (rust-through along the bottom, often the first 10 to 20 ft at each end), which let water out under the pipe and lead to voids; separated or offset joints that pull in fill; crushed or bent ends from mowers, plows and vehicles; deflection (out-of-round) in flexible pipe that was poorly backfilled; perched outlets where the stream cut down below the pipe; scour holes and undermined headwalls or aprons at the outlet; piping along the outside of the pipe; blockage by debris, sediment, ice or beaver dams; and overtopping in storms bigger than design. Repairs range from invert paving and lining (sliplining, CIPP, spray-applied liners) to joint sealing or full replacement. When replacing, match the design capacity, inlet edge and invert elevations, and check whether fish passage or 404 permit rules now apply.
field.title: Common culvert failures
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: General DOT culvert inspection practice; MnDOT HydInfra inspection article

field.text: Empty pipe in a flooded trench floats if the water it displaces weighs more than the pipe plus anything holding it down. Water weighs 62.4 lb per cubic foot, so uplift per foot of pipe = 62.4 x the pipe's outside cross-section area. Example: a 48-inch (4 ft OD, roughly) pipe displaces about 3.1416 x 4^2 / 4 = 12.6 cubic feet per foot, about 784 lb of uplift per foot. Corrugated HDPE weighs only a small fraction of that, so an empty HDPE storm line or storage gallery can pop out of the trench in one storm. Large CMP floats too; even concrete vaults and manholes can float when empty in high groundwater. Prevention: keep dewatering running until enough backfill is on (for plastic pipe often at least about 1 to 1.5 diameters of cover, per maker), backfill as you go, plug and partially fill pipes with water where allowed, use the engineer's anti-flotation measures (concrete collars, extended bases), and don't leave long stretches of empty pipe bedded but unbackfilled overnight in rain.
field.title: Pipe flotation in wet trenches and storm storage (buoyancy)
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: Uplift computed from water weight; cover guidance general manufacturer practice

field.text: Pipe outlets and outfalls erode when water leaves faster than the ground can handle: scour holes form at the end of aprons, headwalls get undermined, channels downstream cut deeper, and riprap gets washed out or was too small. Inspect after the first few significant storms on a new project and after any big storm (the Tennessee handbook says to inspect outlet protection after heavy rains and repair immediately). Look for: stones moved or missing, fabric showing, a scour hole at the end of the apron, water going around the side of the riprap, the outlet pipe end hanging out over a hole, cracks or tilt in the headwall. Repairs: replace with larger stone if the original size was moving, extend the apron, add a cutoff/toe trench filled with stone, regrade and reline. Repeated failure means the design flow or velocity was underestimated, so tell the engineer instead of just adding stone each time.
field.title: Outfall and outlet erosion: inspect after storms and repair
field.topic: Stormwater regulations, inspection, maintenance and failures
field.source: Tennessee Erosion and Sediment Control Handbook, Outlet Protection (maintenance); general practice

field.text: Underground storage systems hold runoff under parking lots and open space. Detention systems store water and let it out slowly through an outlet control (orifice, weir) to cut peak flows; they may be lined (impermeable liner or watertight vault) so none soaks in. Retention or infiltration systems store water and let it soak into the native soil, reducing the volume that leaves the site; they need permeable soil, separation from groundwater and bedrock (often 2 to 3 ft or more, per state rules) and pretreatment so they don't clog. Many systems do both: infiltrate some and release the rest. Types: plastic chambers, modular crates/tanks, large-diameter pipe galleries (CMP, HDPE, RCP), precast concrete vaults, dry wells and stone infiltration trenches. Before building, know which kind yours is, since stone, fabric, liners and outlet elevations all depend on it.
field.title: Underground stormwater systems: detention, retention and infiltration explained
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General stormwater practice; separation distances vary by state manual

field.text: Stormwater chambers are open-bottom, arch-shaped corrugated polypropylene or polyethylene units laid in rows in a bed of clean stone. Water enters through a manifold or header pipe, fills the chambers and the stone voids, then soaks into the soil below or drains out through an outlet. Common brands include ADS StormTech (SC-160LP, SC-310, SC-740, SC-800, DC-780, MC-3500, MC-4500, MC-7200) and Cultec. An Isolator Row is one row at the inlet wrapped with special fabric so most sediment is trapped in that row, where it can be jetted out, instead of spreading through the whole bed. Chambers are flexible structures: their strength depends on the stone around them and the cover over them, so the maker's installation guide controls lifts, equipment and cover depth. ADS requires the contractor to inspect units and follow its guide; many jurisdictions want a pre-construction meeting with the maker's rep.
field.title: Plastic stormwater chambers (StormTech, Cultec type): what they are
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: ADS StormTech installation guides (SC/DC, MC-3500/4500)

field.text: StormTech guides name four backfill layers. A, foundation stone: clean, crushed, angular stone (AASHTO M43 sizes listed in the guide) from the subgrade up to the chamber feet; depth set by the site engineer, with a minimum of about 6 inches on smaller SC/DC chambers and 9 inches on MC-3500/MC-4500, compacted with two full passes of a vibratory compactor on MC systems. B, embedment stone: the same clean angular stone around and between chambers up to the chamber top; no compaction required. C, initial fill: from the top of the embedment stone to a minimum depth above the chambers (MC guide: 18 inches for MC-3500, 24 inches for MC-4500), granular well-graded soil or processed aggregate; compaction starts once that minimum cover is reached, in lifts of 12 inches max, to at least 95% Proctor (well-graded) or 95% relative density (processed aggregate). D, final fill: from the top of C to finished grade, native soil or pavement section per the plans. Check the exact numbers in your model's guide.
field.title: StormTech chamber backfill layers A, B, C and D
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: ADS StormTech SC/DC and MC-3500/4500 installation guides

field.text: Typical chamber sequence (follow the maker's guide for your model): 1) excavate to subgrade; protect it from compaction and silt if it is an infiltration system; get engineer approval of the bottom. 2) place non-woven geotextile over the subgrade and up the excavation sides. 3) place and level foundation stone (layer A) to grade. 4) lay woven geotextile strips under Isolator Rows. 5) set chambers in rows per the shop drawing, joining as the maker shows, with end caps, manifolds and inlet tees; inspect each unit. 6) spot stone along the chamber centerline, then place embedment stone evenly in lifts (about 12 inches max) so stone levels on both sides of a row never differ much; gaps between rows and to the perimeter commonly 12 inches max on SC models. 7) wrap the stone with geotextile over the top. 8) place initial fill and compact once minimum cover is in. 9) set inspection ports and the outlet structure. 10) final fill and paving.
field.title: Chamber system installation sequence
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: ADS StormTech installation guides

field.text: Chambers are crushed or pushed out of line by equipment more than anything else. StormTech rules (exact numbers in each guide's equipment table): no equipment on bare chambers or on embedment stone; place stone with an excavator or stone conveyor working from outside the bed; small dozers push cover stone only after the guide's minimum stone cover is placed, pushing parallel to the rows; for MC-3500/MC-4500 the guide wants about 36 inches of cover over the entire bed before excavators work on it (keep them off the bed when possible), 24 inches before dump trucks dump over chambers, and 18 inches (MC-3500) or 24 inches (MC-4500) before rollers, dynamic force only, parallel to the rows. SC and DC models have their own tables. Maximum cover limits apply too (MC guide: 8.0 ft for MC-3500, 7.0 ft for MC-4500). Fence off the bed and brief every operator before the stone goes in.
field.title: Equipment over chambers: what can drive on them and when
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: ADS StormTech MC-3500/MC-4500 Installation Guide, Table 2 and Figure 2; SC/DC guides

field.text: Chamber systems use two different fabrics, and mixing them up is a common inspection fail. Non-woven geotextile (for StormTech MC systems, ADS 601T or approved equal) wraps all the clean stone: over the subgrade, up the excavation walls, and over the top of the embedment stone, so native soil doesn't migrate into the stone voids. Woven geotextile (ADSPLUS woven, AASHTO Class 1 woven) goes in one continuous strip under each Isolator Row between the foundation stone and the chambers, extending past the chamber feet (about 6 inches on MC); it's woven so a JetVac nozzle can scour sediment off it without tearing it, and StormTech only permits JetVac cleaning on rows with that woven fabric. Some Isolator Row Plus designs also have fabric at the inlet end cap. Lap seams as the guide shows and keep fabric clean until covered.
field.title: Geotextile in chamber systems: woven under Isolator Row, non-woven wrap
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: ADS StormTech MC-3500/4500 installation guide; StormTech Isolator Row O&M

field.text: StormTech Isolator Row maintenance: inspect every 6 months the first year, then at least annually, adjusting to how fast sediment builds. Inspect from the surface: remove the inspection port cap and use a flashlight and stadia rod to measure sediment depth, recording it in a log; you can also look through the upstream manhole with a mirror or camera. Clean when average sediment reaches about 3 inches. Cleaning is by JetVac: a fixed culvert-type nozzle with rear-facing jets (effective spread at least 45 inches) is run through the row from the upstream manhole, making passes until the backflush water runs clean, while a vacuum truck sucks the sediment out of the manhole sump. ADS suggests a maximum nozzle pressure of about 2,000 psi and Isolator Row lengths of about 200 ft or less for easy maintenance, since JetVac reels vary in length. Inspection ports are often 4 to 8 inch risers in a traffic-rated box with a concrete collar in pavement. Manhole entry is a confined space.
field.title: Chamber inspection ports and Isolator Row maintenance
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: ADS StormTech Isolator Row Plus O&M Manual

field.text: Modular storage crates are stackable plastic modules (often over 90% open void) assembled into a big block underground. For infiltration the block is wrapped in non-woven geotextile and set on a level stone or sand base; for detention or rainwater harvesting it is wrapped in an impermeable liner (often 30 to 40 mil PVC or HDPE, welded or taped seams) with protective geotextile on both sides. Install points: level, compacted base is critical because modules carry load through their columns; place modules per the layout with ties or clips; protect the wrap at corners; backfill the sides with stone or select fill in thin lifts compacted carefully (sidewall soil holds the block); keep equipment off until the maker's minimum cover is reached (commonly 12 to 24 inches depending on module strength and load); respect maximum cover too. Inspection and cleanout ports go in as detailed. Use the maker's guide; module strengths vary a lot.
field.title: Modular tanks and crates (StormTank, Aquacell, R-Tank type)
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice from manufacturer installation guides; check your product

field.text: Pipe galleries are rows of big pipe (often 36 to 120+ inch CMP, corrugated HDPE or RCP) connected by headers or manifolds at each end, laid side by side in a stone or soil envelope. Detention galleries have solid pipe with watertight joints; infiltration galleries use perforated pipe surrounded by clean stone and fabric. Install points: level bedding to exact grade (many are laid flat or at a very slight slope); spacing between barrels per the maker (often around half the diameter or a set minimum like 12 to 24 inches) so you can compact backfill between them; compact backfill evenly in lifts on both sides of each pipe up to the springline and above; respect minimum cover before equipment crosses. Empty large plastic or metal pipe floats: plan for groundwater and storms during construction (see the floatation chunk). Get the maker's layout drawing and assembly instructions for fittings and bulkheads.
field.title: Large-diameter pipe storage galleries (CMP, HDPE, RCP)
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice from manufacturer guides (Contech, ADS); check your system's drawings

field.text: Concrete storage vaults (precast modular box sections, large three-sided or four-sided units, or cast-in-place) give strong, watertight storage under heavy traffic with little cover. Field points: subgrade and base stone level and compacted per the precast maker; set sections in order with joint sealant (butyl or gasket) and grout or wrap joints as specified; check access hatches and openings line up with the plan; build interior baffles, weirs and orifices to exact elevations; vacuum or water test if specified. Pieces can weigh 20 to 50+ tons, so a lift plan, a crane sized for the radius, and a qualified rigger and signal person are needed. Empty vaults in high groundwater can float: the engineer checks buoyancy and may add a base extension or anti-flotation slab; don't remove dewatering until enough backfill is on. Treat entry as a permit confined space.
field.title: Precast concrete stormwater vaults
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice; weights vary widely by size, check the precaster's submittal

field.text: Detention systems release water through an outlet control structure, often a manhole or box with a baffle wall or riser containing one or more orifices (round holes or plates) and weirs (notches or overflow crests), plus an emergency overflow. The orifice size and invert elevation set how fast water leaves, which is what the permit approved. Field rules: build orifice diameters and inverts exactly to plan (a 2-inch orifice drilled 3 inches, or set 0.2 ft low, changes the release rate); use the specified plate material (often stainless or aluminum) bolted and sealed so water can't leak around it; install trash racks or hoods over small low-flow orifices so they don't clog; check weir crest elevations with a level; keep the outlet pipe slope per plan. Small orifices clog easily, so maintenance must check them after storms. Most jurisdictions require a certified as-built survey of the outlet before final approval.
field.title: Outlet control structures: orifices, weirs and why elevations matter
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General stormwater practice

field.text: A dry well is an underground structure that takes roof or surface runoff and lets it soak into the ground: a perforated precast concrete ring or a plastic dry-well tank, or a stone-filled pit, surrounded by clean stone wrapped in non-woven fabric. Typical practice: put it in permeable soil with enough separation above seasonal high groundwater and bedrock (often 2 to 4 ft or more by local rule); keep setbacks from foundations (commonly at least 10 ft), septic systems and wells; pretreat (gutter screens, sumps, a catch basin) so it doesn't clog; provide an overflow; and provide a cover or inspection port for cleaning. Under EPA's Underground Injection Control program, a stormwater dry well that is deeper than it is wide at the surface, or uses subsurface distribution, is generally a Class V injection well, so states may require inventory or registration and prohibit wells where spills could reach groundwater. Check state and local rules.
field.title: Dry wells for stormwater: construction and rules
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice; Class V classification per EPA UIC program (summarized, not fetched); check state rules

field.text: Minnesota Stormwater Manual material specs for infiltration trenches: a 1 to 4 ft deep bed of double-washed stone, 1.5 to 3.0 inch size, uniform (uniformity coefficient 2 or less) with about 40% voids; non-woven geotextile (MnDOT Type I) on the trench sides with 12-inch overlaps and a separate top piece that can be replaced when the surface clogs; NO fabric on the trench bottom, since fabric there clogs and stops infiltration. The bottom gets one of: 6 to 8 inches of clean sand (1 to 2% fines or less), 3/8 inch pea gravel, 6 to 12 inches of fine filter aggregate, or about 12 inches of gravel or sand in cold climates. A surface layer of about 3 inches of river stone or pea gravel over fabric finishes the top. Pretreatment: a grass filter strip at least 20 ft wide around the trench. Place material so it does not compact the bottom.
field.title: Infiltration trench specifications
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Minnesota Stormwater Manual, infiltration media and material specifications

field.text: Infiltration systems (trenches, chambers, bioretention, permeable pavement) fail early when the native soil bottom is compacted, smeared or silted during construction. Ohio EPA's rules for bioretention apply to all of them: dig only when the soil is dry; excavate from the edge or on protective mats, keeping tracked and wheeled equipment off the bottom; rake the final surface with the bucket teeth, and till or scarify any smeared or compacted areas once dry; if those protections aren't followed, do infiltration tests after excavation. Keep sediment out: build the practice after the drainage area is stabilized, or route runoff to a temporary sediment basin. If the area has to serve as a sediment trap during construction, keep the trap bottom at least 12 inches above the final floor, then dig out to grade after the site is stable. Ohio says a fabric cover or perimeter barrier alone is not enough protection.
field.title: Building infiltration practices without ruining the soil
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Ohio EPA Rainwater and Land Development, 2.9 Bioretention (construction section)

field.text: Clean, uniform stone has about 40% voids (the Minnesota manual uses 0.40 for 1.5 to 3 inch washed stone; #57 is often taken as 0.35 to 0.40, check your design). Water storage in a stone bed = length x width x depth x void ratio. Example: an infiltration trench 100 ft long, 4 ft wide, 4 ft deep of stone: 100 x 4 x 4 = 1,600 cubic feet of stone x 0.40 = 640 cubic feet of water. At 7.48 gallons per cubic foot, that's about 4,790 gallons. For chamber systems, total storage = chamber volume + stone void volume around and over them; makers publish storage per chamber including stone. Don't count soil fill or sand over the system as storage. If the stone delivered has fines, void space and infiltration both drop, which is one reason inspectors reject dirty stone.
field.title: Storage math: how much water clean stone holds
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Computed; void ratio from Minnesota Stormwater Manual infiltration specs

field.text: Handy volume numbers for storage questions: 1 acre = 43,560 square feet. One inch of runoff over one acre = 43,560 / 12 = 3,630 cubic feet = about 27,150 gallons. So if a 2-acre parking lot that sheds about 90% of its rain gets a 1.5-inch storm, the runoff volume is about 2 x 3,630 x 1.5 x 0.9 = 9,800 cubic feet (about 73,300 gallons). Many state water quality volumes (WQv) are based on the first 1 inch (or 1.2 inch, or 90th percentile storm) of runoff from impervious area. Converting to stone: 9,800 cubic feet of water needs about 9,800 / 0.40 = 24,500 cubic feet of stone storage (about 907 CY of stone) if storing it all in stone voids. These are rough checks for the field; the engineer's design volume governs.
field.title: Runoff volume math: 1 inch of rain on 1 acre
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Computed (unit conversions); WQv concept general stormwater practice

field.text: Every underground storage product has a minimum cover (for traffic and construction loads) and a maximum cover (soil weight), measured from the top of the chamber, crate or pipe to finished grade or to the bottom of pavement as the maker defines it. StormTech MC guide examples: MC-3500 minimum 18 inches and maximum 8.0 ft; MC-4500 minimum 24 inches and maximum 7.0 ft; in unpaved areas where rutting may occur, cover is increased to about 30 inches. SC and DC chambers and other brands have their own minimums and maximums in their guides. Shallow pavement sections over storage often need the full depth of the C layer compacted before paving. If grades change in the field and cover goes below the minimum or above the maximum, stop and call the engineer and the manufacturer before paving or filling.
field.title: Cover depth over underground storage and paving on top
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: ADS StormTech MC-3500/MC-4500 Installation Guide, Figure 2

field.text: A dry detention pond (detention basin) is empty between storms: it fills during a storm and drains out through an outlet structure over hours to a couple of days, cutting the peak flow downstream. A wet pond (retention pond, wet detention) holds a permanent pool of water all the time, with storage above it; the permanent pool lets sediment and pollutants settle and gives better water quality. Both usually have: a sediment forebay at each inlet (a smaller cell that traps coarse sediment for easy cleanout), an outlet structure with orifices and weirs, an emergency spillway sized for big storms, and access for maintenance equipment. Infiltration basins hold water and let it soak in with no surface outlet except overflow. Extended detention ponds hold the water quality volume longer (often 24 to 48 hours). The plan sheet names the type and the permanent pool elevation; build the outlet and spillway elevations exactly.
field.title: Detention ponds vs retention (wet) ponds
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General stormwater practice (state BMP manuals); drawdown times vary by state

field.text: Pond and basin embankments are small dams. Field points: strip topsoil and roots under the embankment footprint; cut a core trench or keyway into firm soil along the centerline when the plans show it, filled with compacted clay; build the fill in thin lifts (often 6 to 8 inches loose) of the specified soil at the specified moisture and compaction (often 95% standard Proctor), with density tests; keep rock, roots and frozen soil out. The pipe through the embankment is the classic failure point: water seeps along the outside of the pipe and carries soil (piping). Use watertight joints, compact backfill around the pipe by hand-operated equipment in thin lifts, and install the anti-seep collars or the filter diaphragm (a sand zone around the pipe that catches migrating soil) exactly as detailed. Seed and protect slopes right away, and keep trees off the embankment. Large ponds may be regulated as dams by the state.
field.title: Building pond embankments and outlet pipes so they don't leak or fail
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice (NRCS pond and dam guidance concepts); check your plans and state dam safety rules

field.text: Bioretention cells (rain gardens) pond runoff over an engineered soil and plants. Ohio EPA specs as an example: ponding depth 18 inches or less, 12 inches or less preferred; ponded water drains within 24 hours, ponding plus the top 24 inches of media within 48 hours; media at least 2 ft thick, blended by volume 70 to 90% sand, 5 to 20% topsoil, 0 to 10% compost, with clay 10% or less, organic matter 1.5 to 5%, phosphorus 40 mg/kg or less, and long-term permeability 1 to 5 inches per hour, tested once per 100 CY; place in 8 to 12 inch lifts lightly soaked, overfill about 5% for settling. Below: 3 inches of #8 pea gravel choker (no fabric between media and stone), then about 12 inches of #57 or #67 washed stone with at least 3 inches above and below a 6-inch-plus perforated underdrain, holes down, no sock, with a capped cleanout riser. 2 to 3 inches of shredded hardwood mulch on top. Overflow riser at the max ponding elevation.
field.title: Bioretention and rain gardens: typical specs
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Ohio EPA Rainwater and Land Development, 2.9 Bioretention

field.text: A vegetated (grass) swale is a shallow, broad, grass-lined channel that carries runoff slowly so sediment settles and some water soaks in; typical design traits are a flat bottom (often 2 to 8 ft wide), gentle side slopes (3:1 or flatter for mowing), a longitudinal slope roughly 1 to 4% (check dams on steeper ones), and low velocities so the grass isn't flattened. A bioswale (dry swale, bio-filtration swale) adds engineered soil media and often an underdrain under the channel, so it filters and infiltrates more, like a linear bioretention cell. Wet swales intentionally hold water in low soils. Field points: grade the section and slope to plan; don't compact the bottom; stabilize with sod or blanket immediately since swales erode before grass is established; keep construction sediment out; build check dams with level tops and armored downstream faces. Maintenance: mow to the specified height, remove sediment, fix bare spots.
field.title: Bioswales and vegetated swales
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice from state stormwater manuals; dimensions vary by state

field.text: Permeable pavement lets water through the surface into a stone reservoir below. Minnesota manual typical sections: pervious concrete sits directly on an AASHTO #57 stone reservoir (or per hydraulic design); porous asphalt uses about 1 inch of #57 as a choker over a reservoir of #2, #3 or #5 stone; permeable interlocking concrete pavers (PICP) sit on about 2 inches of #8 bedding and joint stone over 4 inches of #57 base on a #2, #3 or #4 subbase. Reservoir thickness comes from structural and storage design. Options: a 6 to 12 inch sand filter layer (required in Minnesota if the system is used to meet permit requirements), non-woven geotextile (AASHTO M288 Class I or II) as a separator, a 4 to 6 inch perforated underdrain, an impermeable liner (30 mil PVC or similar) where infiltration isn't allowed, and a lockable perforated observation well. All stone must be washed free of fines.
field.title: Permeable pavement: the layered section underneath
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Minnesota Stormwater Manual, specifications for materials under permeable pavement

field.text: Permeable pavement clogs fast if it gets mud on it. During construction: build it last or keep it covered, route construction traffic around it, never stockpile soil or mulch on it, keep the stone clean before paving, and don't seal or overlay it. Maintenance per the Minnesota manual: vacuum or regenerative-air sweep at least twice a year (typically April after winter and November after leaf fall), more if sediment builds up, and keep records; on PICP, replace joint aggregate removed by sweeping with the same material; minimize winter sand and salt; and maintenance agreements should prohibit resealing, resurfacing and power washing (which drive fines down). Keep adjacent landscaping stable so soil doesn't wash onto the pavement. A simple field check: pour a bucket of water on the surface; if it puddles and runs off instead of disappearing, it is clogged and needs vacuuming.
field.title: Permeable pavement: construction protection and maintenance
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Minnesota Stormwater Manual, operation and maintenance of permeable pavement; construction points general practice

field.text: Sand filters treat runoff by passing it through a bed of sand, usually after a sedimentation chamber that removes coarse grit first. Types: surface sand filters (an open basin with a sand bed), underground sand filters in a concrete vault (DC-style three-chamber), and perimeter or Delaware sand filters (long narrow trenches along a parking lot edge with grated covers). Typical design traits: sand about 18 inches deep of clean concrete sand (ASTM C33), over gravel and a perforated underdrain, with the filter draining down within a day or two. Field points: build chamber walls, weirs and underdrain elevations to plan; use the specified washed sand; keep construction runoff out until the site is stabilized (construction mud ruins the sand). Maintenance: remove sediment from the settling chamber; when the filter drains too slowly, scrape and replace the top few inches of sand (often about 2 to 3 inches); remove trash. Underground units are confined spaces.
field.title: Sand filters for stormwater (surface, underground and perimeter)
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice from state stormwater manuals; dimensions vary

field.text: Hydrodynamic separators (Vortechs, Downstream Defender, CDS, Stormceptor type) are manhole-style structures that make incoming water swirl so grit settles to the sump and a baffle holds back oil and floating trash. Contech's Vortechs guide: inspect twice a year (spring and fall), more often where there is equipment washing or winter sanding, and keep a log (often a permit condition). Clean when sediment is within 12 to 18 inches of the dry-weather water surface; measure with a stadia rod from the opening down to the sediment top and the water surface, lowering the rod gently so you don't push into the sediment. Clean in dry weather with a vacuum truck (a clamshell bucket misses a lot). Use absorbent pads for oil (cheaper to dispose of than oily water), clean spills right away, net floating trash. Entry is usually unnecessary; if someone must go in, pump out all water and follow confined space entry rules. Reseat covers securely.
field.title: Hydrodynamic separators (swirl separators): how they work and cleaning
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: Contech Vortechs operations and maintenance guide

field.text: Permanent inlet filters (catch basin inserts) are baskets, bags or trays hung under the grate, often with absorbent media for oil, used as pretreatment on parking lots and at gas stations. They work only if emptied: when full they either bypass dirty water or block the inlet and flood the street, so most makers say inspect at least quarterly and after big storms, and replace absorbent media when saturated. These are different from the temporary inlet protection used during construction (covered in erosion-sediment-control). Oil-water separators (gravity separators with baffles or coalescing plates) are used where fuel or oil spills are likely, such as fueling areas and maintenance yards; they need routine oil skimming and sludge pumping by a licensed hauler. Field installation: set frames and inserts to the maker's fit for the specific grate size; confirm the overflow path is open.
field.title: Inlet filters, catch basin inserts and oil-water separators
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice; check the product's maintenance manual

field.text: Almost every stormwater practice that stores, filters or infiltrates water needs pretreatment upstream to catch sediment, trash and oil first; otherwise the expensive part (stone bed, sand, bioretention media, chambers) clogs and has to be dug up. Common pretreatment devices: sediment forebays on ponds and basins; Isolator Rows on chamber systems; deep-sump catch basins with hoods; hydrodynamic separators; grass filter strips (Minnesota uses at least 20 ft for infiltration trenches); stone diaphragms or pea gravel strips at pavement edges; and gutter guards or leaf screens on roof drains to dry wells. Crews matter here: build pretreatment devices first and to the right elevations, keep them clean during construction, and clean them out at the end of the job before turnover. Many owners refuse acceptance if the forebay or Isolator Row is full of construction mud.
field.title: Pretreatment: why forebays, Isolator Rows and sumps matter
field.topic: Underground stormwater storage, infiltration and surface BMPs
field.source: General practice; filter strip width from Minnesota Stormwater Manual

field.text: Quick pick for trench backfill. Granular soil (sand, gravel, #57 stone, crusher run, clean rock): vibratory plate. Most plates are effective on about 8 inch lifts; bigger reversible plates handle much thicker lifts (up to about 30 inches on the largest). Cohesive soil (clay, silt, 'dirt' with fines): jumping jack/rammer for small narrow trenches and tight spots, or a trench roller for longer runs with lifts up to about 18 inches. Triple-shaft reversible plates can also work cohesive soil. Steep grades favor trench rollers, which climb better than plates. Wrong machine for the soil means lots of passes and failed density tests: a plate on wet clay just shakes it, a rammer on clean stone just kicks it around. Lift thickness on your spec still rules; these are machine capabilities, not spec allowances.
field.title: Which compactor for which soil and lift: plate, jumping jack or trench roller
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: For Construction Pros: Get compaction in a tight spot; Compact Equipment: tips for selecting a plate compactor

field.text: A forward plate (single-direction, 'small plate', 'wacker plate') is the light end of compaction: roughly 100 to 300 lb, centrifugal force up to about 4,500 lb, running around 5,700 vibrations per minute. Makers rate them for thin granular layers, about 8 to 12 inches of sand or gravel (many specs and test strips hold forward plates to about 4 to 8 inch loose lifts), and covers roughly 1,000 to 3,200 cu ft per hour. Plates run about 13 to 26 inches wide across the range. Good for: bedding stone, sidewalk and driveway base, pipe zone stone after cover, small asphalt patches (models with a water tank). Not for: thick lifts, wet clay, or tight trenches where you cannot turn it around, since it only travels forward. Most forward plates have sealed exciter bearings with no oil to check. Specs vary by model; check the maker's sheet.
field.title: Forward plate compactor (single-direction plate): sizes and best use
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Compact Equipment: tips for selecting a plate compactor

field.text: Reversible plates (two-way plates, 'reversibles', 400 to 1,000+ lb class) put far more energy in the ground than forward plates: centrifugal force up to about 21,000 lb at a lower 3,000 to 4,000 vibrations per minute, with two exciter shafts instead of one. They compact medium to deep granular lifts, roughly 16 to 32 inches on the larger machines, at about 1,600 to 4,600 cu ft per hour. Because they go forward and back by moving the handle, they are the usual choice inside trench boxes, along walls and around structures where there is no room to turn. Triple-shaft models can handle some cohesive soil. Reversible exciters typically need regular oil checks, unlike sealed forward plates. Bigger machines may have a remote control (up to about 100 ft) and a compaction meter. Always confirm lift thickness against your spec, not just the machine's capability.
field.title: Reversible plate compactor: when to step up from a forward plate
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Compact Equipment: tips for selecting a plate compactor; For Construction Pros: Get compaction in a tight spot

field.text: Two numbers on a plate spec sheet matter: centrifugal force (how hard it hits, in lb or kN) and frequency (vibrations per minute, vpm, or Hz). Higher frequency does NOT mean more compaction force. Lower frequency with higher amplitude reaches deeper and suits medium to thick lifts; higher frequency suits thin lifts and fine material. Aggregate 1 inch and smaller compacts better with a higher-frequency unit. Plate width affects production and whether it fits between the pipe and the trench wall or box. When renting, tell the counter: soil type, lift thickness, trench width and whether it is asphalt. A compaction indicator light (on some models) tells you when the material has stopped getting stiffer so you quit passing before you over-work it.
field.title: Plate compactor frequency vs force: what the numbers mean
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Compact Equipment: tips for selecting a plate compactor; For Construction Pros: Get compaction in a tight spot

field.text: A rammer (jumping jack, jack, 'jumper', trench tamper) compacts by impact: an engine drives a spring-loaded foot up and down. Typical 60 kg class example, Wacker Neuson BS60-4s: about 156 lb operating weight, about 680 blows per minute, 11 x 13.2 inch shoe, travels about 23 to 28 ft per minute, 4-stroke gas engine (Honda GX100 or Wacker WM 100), 3.2 quart fuel tank, about 0.23 to 0.31 gal per hour, stroke at the foot about 2.2 to 3.1 inches. The BS50 is about 140 lb and the BS70 about 177 lb with the same 11 inch shoe. Rammers are the go-to for clay and silt (cohesive) backfill, haunches, around manhole barrels and in narrow trenches. Older and some current models are 2-stroke or oil-injected 2-stroke; check which you have before fueling.
field.title: Jumping jack / rammer (trench tamper): specs and how it works
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Wacker Neuson BS50/BS60/BS70 rammer spec sheet (Durante Rentals); For Construction Pros: Get compaction in a tight spot

field.text: Rammer technique: run at full throttle (half throttle makes it bounce and beat you up); let it pull itself forward, guiding it, not pushing; overlap passes; work thin lifts (commonly 4 to 8 inches loose for cohesive soil; your spec governs). Around pipe, tamp both sides evenly so the pipe is not shoved off line or grade, and keep the shoe off the pipe itself; many specs and pipe makers say no impact compaction directly over plastic pipe until there is about 12 inches of cover. Around manholes and structures, work in rings and do not hammer against fresh grout or boots. Transport and store per the manual: many rammers must be stood upright or laid only on a specified side, or oil and fuel get into the cylinder and air filter. Wear steel toes; rammers hop sideways on hard spots.
field.title: Running a rammer: technique in trenches and around pipe
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: General industry practice; Wacker Neuson BS50/BS60/BS70 rammer spec sheet (Durante Rentals)

field.text: Trench rollers (remote padfoot rollers, 'trench compactor', Rammax, Wacker RTx, Bomag BMP) are for cohesive backfill in trenches and larger confined areas. Drum widths run about 22 to 34 inches; Wacker's RTx converts between 22 and 32 inches. Example RTx-SC3: about 3,200 to 3,300 lb, 7,700 to 15,400 lbf centrifugal force, 41.7 Hz, 1.5 mph, about 20 hp diesel, climbs 45 to 50% grades. They can handle lifts up to about 18 inches. One maker says 99% of trench roller use is in cohesive soil; with padfoot drums they work granular soil too, but a reversible plate is more productive there. Low frequency/high amplitude, separate drive, and they turn in their own length. Lift thickness still per your spec and test results.
field.title: Walk-behind and remote trench rollers: sizes and lift depth
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: For Construction Pros: Get compaction in a tight spot; Wacker Neuson RTx-SC3 trench roller spec sheet (Durante Rentals)

field.text: Remote trench rollers keep the operator out of the trench, but the machine can crush someone against a trench wall or box. Wacker's SC3 infrared remote needs line of sight to receiver eyes on the machine; it stops travel and vibration if line of sight is lost or if the operator comes within about 3 ft (1 m) of the receiver eyes. A third eye on top keeps contact when working inside shoring. Rules: nobody in the trench ahead of or beside the roller; operator stands on the ground outside the trench where they can see the whole path; never defeat the proximity or line-of-sight stop; check the remote stop works at the start of each shift; keep the roller off the trench edge and away from the toe of the spoil pile; and use the lifting eye with rated rigging to set it in and out of the trench.
field.title: Remote-control trench roller safety: line of sight and stop zone
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Wacker Neuson RTx-SC3 trench roller spec sheet (Durante Rentals); General industry practice

field.text: When backfilling inside a trench box, compaction happens in a confined space with the box moving up as you go. Practices: use a reversible plate, rammer or remote roller sized to fit between pipe and box wall; compact in lifts as the box is raised so the shield never sits above uncompacted void (dragging the box can pull embedment and shift pipe); keep workers inside the box while compacting, never in the gap between box and trench wall; place backfill evenly on both sides of the pipe; and check the pipe with the laser target after compacting the first lifts at the haunches. For deep trenches, many crews compact upper lifts from above with an excavator-mounted plate (hoe-pack) or compaction wheel so nobody is in the trench at all. Follow your competent person's shoring plan.
field.title: Compacting inside a trench box or shoring
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Protect new pipe during compaction: compact haunches and side fill in equal lifts on both sides so the pipe is not pushed sideways or floated off grade; keep plates and rammer shoes off the pipe; get the cover depth your spec or the pipe maker requires before running compaction equipment over the top (often around 12 inches over plastic pipe for hand-held impact tampers, more for heavy rollers and hoe-packs; check your spec and pipe maker); and do not drive loaded equipment over shallow pipe. Re-shoot grade on the last few sticks after backfill compaction; if pipe moved, uncover and reset. With PVC and HDPE, too much side compaction can squeeze the pipe out of round vertically, too little leaves it free to deflect later and fail the mandrel test.
field.title: Compacting beside and over new pipe without damaging it
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Big plates, rollers and hoe-packs shake more than the trench. Watch: fresh concrete, grout and mortar at manholes and thrust blocks (keep vibratory equipment back until it has cured enough; check your spec); adjacent house foundations, old brick sewers, clay laterals and AC water pipe that can crack; utilities crossing the trench (hand-tamp around them, do not run a roller over a shallow crossing); and building owners near the job (vibration complaints and claims; some jobs require pre-construction surveys or vibration monitoring). Switch to a smaller plate or rammer, use static passes, or lighten the lift near sensitive items. If a manhole barrel joint opens or a lateral cracks, it is far cheaper to find it now than on the camera inspection.
field.title: Vibration near structures, fresh concrete and old pipe
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: For hot mix patches over a trench, use a forward plate with a water tank (keeps mix from sticking) and rounded plate edges; look for a tubeless water system. Practices: compact while the mix is hot, starting at the edges against the cut line and working in; overlap passes; do not stop the plate in one place on hot mix (it dents); and finish with a small roller on bigger patches. For pavers, a urethane or rubber pad on the plate keeps from chipping the stones. Hot mix is placed around 275 to 325 F (check the mix design and your DOT); hot mix and the plate's exhaust can burn, so wear long sleeves and boots and keep the tank water away from the engine. Do not use a wet plate on base stone; water tanks are for asphalt.
field.title: Plate compactor on asphalt patches and pavers
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Compact Equipment: tips for selecting a plate compactor; General industry practice

field.text: Compaction is done when the material stops getting denser, not after a fixed number of passes. Signs with hand-guided machines: the plate starts to bounce or 'hop' and moves faster across the lift; footprints and plate marks stop deepening; a probe rod or your boot heel no longer sinks. Some plates and rollers have meters (Wacker's Compatec, compaction indicator lights) that show relative stiffness. If it never firms up: lift too thick, material too wet or too dry, wrong machine for the soil, or soft subgrade pumping underneath. Too many passes on dry granular material can loosen the top. Your density tests (nuclear gauge or similar) are the real answer; use them early on a new material to learn how many passes it takes, then keep the crew consistent.
field.title: How many passes: knowing when the lift is done
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Compact Equipment: tips for selecting a plate compactor; Wacker Neuson RTx-SC3 trench roller spec sheet (Durante Rentals); General industry practice

field.text: Hand tools still matter in the pipe zone. A hand tamper (flat steel tamping plate on a handle, 8x8 or 10x10 inch) or a tamping bar (narrow butt end) works embedment under the haunches of small pipe where a plate cannot reach. Shovel slicing (pushing a shovel blade down into the stone along the pipe sides) works stone into the haunch before mechanical compaction. Keep hand tamping on the stone, not on the pipe. A narrow 'haunching' tamper or a short bar helps under bells and fittings. Pneumatic backfill tampers ('pogo' air tampers) run off a compressor and fit narrow trenches and around structures. Pick tools with solid handles; cracked wood handles must be replaced.
field.title: Hand tampers and tamping bars for haunches
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: General industry practice; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.301 hand tools

field.text: Daily: check engine oil (4-stroke) or premix (2-stroke) per the manual; check the air filter, which clogs fast in dust (blow out or replace; never run without one); check the exciter oil level on reversible plates if the maker calls for it (sealed forward plates need none); look at the shock mounts, belt and belt guard, and the base plate for cracks; check the handle vibration isolators; and on rammers check the bellows/boot for tears and the shoe bolts. Clean caked material off the plate base; it adds weight and throws off vibration. Use the lifting point or lift bail with rated slings; never lift by the handle. Follow the maker's service intervals; equipment with big air filters and easy-open covers costs less downtime.
field.title: Compactor daily checks and maintenance
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: Compact Equipment: tips for selecting a plate compactor; General industry practice

field.text: Hazards with plates, rammers and rollers: carbon monoxide from gas engines in trenches, pits and manholes (CO collects low; use a gas monitor and ventilation, or electric/battery or diesel remote equipment with good airflow; NIOSH warns small gas engines can build deadly CO in minutes even with openings); hand-arm vibration (rotate operators, use machines with isolated handles, keep hands warm and dry); noise (wear hearing protection; gas plates and rammers are loud enough at the operator to need it, and OSHA's limit is 90 dBA for 8 hours); crushed feet and shins (steel toes, keep feet back from plate edges and rammer shoes); and trench hazards (never enter an unprotected trench to compact). Do not refuel a hot engine in the trench; shut it off and refuel up top.
field.title: Compaction equipment safety: vibration, CO, noise, feet
field.topic: Tools: compaction equipment (plates, rammers, trench rollers)
field.source: NIOSH/OSHA/CPSC/EPA alert: CO poisoning from small gasoline-powered engines and tools (NIOSH 96-118); OSHA 29 CFR 1926.52 occupational noise exposure; General industry practice

field.text: The handheld cut-off saw (power cutter, quickie saw, chop saw, demo saw, Stihl TS or Husqvarna K series) is the pipe crew's main cutting tool for concrete pipe, ductile iron, manhole openings and pavement edges. Common blade sizes are 12, 14 and 16 inch; usable cut depth is roughly 4, 5 and 6 inches respectively (check your model). Power options: 2-stroke gas (most common), electric (indoors, but cords and water need GFCI), battery (short cuts, no exhaust) and hydraulic (runs off a power unit or excavator circuit, good in trenches since there is no engine exhaust at the saw). Wet kits feed water to the blade for dust control. They take abrasive or diamond blades only; toothed wood or carbide blades are prohibited on these saws because of kickback and thrown tips.
field.title: Handheld cut-off saw (quickie saw, chop saw, demo saw): basics
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (cutting blades); SafeWork NSW safety alert: safe use of hand-held cutting saws; General industry practice

field.text: Every cut-off blade is marked with a maximum RPM. The blade's rated speed must be equal to or higher than the saw's spindle speed shown on the saw's plate. Husqvarna warns many blades made for stationary saws have lower speed ratings and must not go on a handheld saw. An over-speed blade can fly apart. Other blade rules from the manual: use the correct arbor size (use the right bushing, not a loose fit); check blades for cracks, missing segments or broken pieces before mounting and often during use; never use a damaged blade or one that wobbles; run each new blade at full throttle for about a minute (away from people) to test it; and use only blades meant for the material. OSHA's abrasive wheel rule also requires ring-testing and close inspection of abrasive wheels before mounting, and wheels must fit the spindle freely without forcing.
field.title: Blade RPM rating: never run a blade on a faster saw
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (cutting blades); OSHA 29 CFR 1926.303 abrasive wheels and tools

field.text: Diamond blades come in three rim styles. Segmented (gaps between segments): for hard, abrasive work like concrete, concrete pipe, block, brick and asphalt; medium to hard bond; long life; faster but rougher cut; common on 12 inch and larger saws. Turbo rim (continuous wavy rim): faster cutting with a cleaner edge on concrete, brick, pavers and limestone; can run wet or dry; air through the turbo pattern helps cooling; common on grinders and small saws. Continuous rim (smooth rim): for dense, brittle material like tile, porcelain, granite and glass where you need chip-free edges, usually wet. For pipe crews, a quality segmented general-purpose or concrete blade is the everyday blade; get an asphalt blade for pavement. Never use a diamond blade on PVC or HDPE: heat melts the plastic onto the blade and it can kick back.
field.title: Diamond blade types: segmented, turbo and continuous rim
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Benchmark Abrasives: complete guide to diamond blades; Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (cutting blades)

field.text: The bond is the metal matrix holding the diamonds, and matching it to the material matters. Rule: hard material needs a soft bond; soft, abrasive material needs a hard bond. A soft bond wears faster and keeps exposing fresh diamonds, which is what you need on cured concrete, granite and hard stone. A hard bond resists wearing away too fast on crumbly or sandy abrasive material like asphalt, green (fresh) concrete, block and limestone. Wrong bond symptoms: a hard-bond blade on hard concrete glazes (diamonds stop being exposed, it quits cutting and gets hot); a soft-bond blade on asphalt or green concrete wears away very fast. Blade boxes usually say 'cured concrete', 'asphalt/green concrete' or 'general purpose'; buy for the main material you cut.
field.title: Diamond blade bond: hard bond vs soft bond
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Blades Direct: diamond blade bond types

field.text: Abrasive (composite, resin-bonded) cut-off wheels are the traditional way to cut ductile iron and steel pipe in the field, and they cut concrete too, but wear down quickly so cut depth shrinks as the wheel gets smaller. Husqvarna's manual says abrasive blades may be used only without water on its K760; water and moisture weaken the resin bond. Store abrasive wheels dry and flat, and do not use a wheel that got wet, was dropped or is chipped. Metal cutting throws sparks, so keep fuel, gas lines, solvent and dry grass away and have an extinguisher ready. Diamond blades rated for ductile iron (metal-cutting diamond) are also sold and last much longer than abrasive wheels. Check the blade label says it is rated for the material and the saw's RPM.
field.title: Abrasive cut-off wheels: for ductile iron and steel
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (cutting blades); OSHA 29 CFR 1926.303 abrasive wheels and tools; General industry practice

field.text: Wet blades need water to cool them; running a wet-only blade dry overheats the segments and can crack the core or throw a segment. Dry blades are designed to cut dry with air cooling (cut in short passes, let it spin free to cool), but 'dry blade' does not mean dry cutting is legal: OSHA's silica rule calls for water fed continuously to the blade for handheld saws cutting concrete and masonry, unless you follow an exposure assessment route instead. Water also lubricates the cut, reduces reactive force and kickback and reduces fumes. Practical: hook up the saw's wet kit (pressurized tank or hose), adjust flow so slurry forms, and keep the water running for the whole cut. Clean up slurry before it dries, because dried slurry turns back into dust.
field.title: Wet vs dry diamond blades and water for dust
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1; SafeWork NSW safety alert: safe use of hand-held cutting saws; General industry practice

field.text: If a diamond blade stops cutting, sparks a lot, smells hot or the segments look smooth and shiny, it has glazed: the bond is not wearing to expose new diamonds. Causes: bond too hard for the material, saw underpowered for the blade, too little feed pressure, or running a wet blade dry. Fix by dressing the blade: make a few cuts in a soft abrasive material such as a dressing stone, cinder block or a piece of asphalt or sandstone to open up the segments. If it keeps glazing, switch to a softer-bond blade.
