Other warning signs: blade wobble or out-of-round from too much feed pressure (back off; if it continues, replace the blade), cracks in the core, missing segments, or undercutting where the steel core wears faster than the segments in abrasive asphalt or base (asphalt blades often have undercut protection segments).
field.title: Glazed or slow diamond blade: dressing it and other fixes
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (cutting blades); Blades Direct: diamond blade bond types; General industry practice

field.text: Kickback is the saw being thrown up and back at the operator, usually in a split second. It happens when the blade slows or stops from pinching, binding or friction, especially in the upper front part of the blade (the kickback zone). Cutting with the lower half of the blade pushes the saw forward and away; cutting with the upper half drives it up and back toward your face and neck. Rules: never cut with the upper quadrant; keep the guard set so it blocks the front and upper quadrant and never pull it back past its stop; start the cut at full speed and enter gently without twisting; ease off at the end of the cut; hold the saw with both hands, firm footing, below shoulder height, never over-reaching; stand out of line with the blade; and do not move the saw while the blade is still spinning.
field.title: Cut-off saw kickback: the upper quadrant
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: SafeWork NSW safety alert: safe use of hand-held cutting saws; Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (kickback and pipe cutting)

field.text: Most cut-off saw injuries on pipe jobs come from the cut closing on the blade. Support the pipe so the cut stays open as you go: set it on timbers on both sides of the cut with the cut line overhanging slightly, chock it so it cannot roll, and use wedges if needed. Pipe lying on the trench bottom, or a bell end, can sag and pinch the blade near the end of the cut. Cut in stages around the pipe rather than one deep plunge; rotate the pipe or move around it. Never have a helper hold the pipe by hand across from the blade. SafeWork NSW reported a worker who cut his neck when the saw kicked back cutting a concrete stormwater pipe that was only chocked, not supported, and was cut in one full cut instead of gradual sections.
field.title: Pinching when cutting pipe: support it so the cut opens
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: SafeWork NSW safety alert: safe use of hand-held cutting saws; Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (kickback and pipe cutting)

field.text: Field-cutting reinforced concrete pipe: (1) mark the cut line all the way around (wrap a strap or use a pipe marking band so it is square); (2) set the pipe on timbers, chocked, cut line clear of supports so the cut opens; (3) use a sharp segmented diamond blade with the wet kit running (OSHA Table 1 requires continuous water for handheld saws on concrete); (4) score the line about 1/2 to 1 inch deep all the way around first, then deepen in passes, lower blade quadrant only; (5) the reinforcing steel will cut with the diamond blade, but slows it, so let it cut; (6) keep the off-cut supported so it does not drop and pinch the blade; (7) clean up slurry and dress sharp edges. Exclusion zone around the saw. Check the pipe maker and spec on whether field-cut ends need patching or a special joint.
field.title: Cutting concrete pipe (RCP) step by step
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: SafeWork NSW safety alert: safe use of hand-held cutting saws; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1; General industry practice

field.text: Ductile iron (DI) is usually cut with an abrasive or metal-rated diamond blade on a cut-off saw, or with a rotary/milling pipe cutter on bigger jobs. U.S. Pipe's steps: measure from the factory spigot end, mark several points around the pipe and scribe a square line (a non-square cut can leak, especially deflected). For cuts near the bell or on 14 inch and larger pipe, check the spigot OD at the cut with a diameter tape in hundredths against the maker's tolerance; order 'gauged pipe' (green stripe) where you know you will cut big pipe. After cutting, bevel the outside of push-on spigots and grind sharp edges so they do not cut the gasket, and put a new insertion mark on. Cement-lined DI throws silica dust when cut, so use water and Table 1 controls.
field.title: Cutting ductile iron pipe in the field
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: U.S. Pipe TYTON JOINT submittal and assembly instructions; McWane Ductile: chamfer or beveling ductile iron pipe; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1

field.text: After field cutting DI, remove the sharp edge. A chamfer just knocks off the sharp corner (file or grinder) and is enough for a mechanical joint (MJ) fitting or valve. A push-on joint (Tyton type) needs a real bevel: McWane says bevel the outside of the cut end about 1/4 inch at roughly 15 to 30 degrees with a portable grinder. A beveled end also works in an MJ. AWWA C600 says cut ends and rough edges should be ground smooth and push-on cut ends beveled per the maker. U.S. Pipe suggests using a shop-made bevel template as a guide. Then measure and paint a new insertion (home) mark at the maker's depth so you can see the joint is fully homed. Paint or coat bare iron per your spec.
field.title: Bevel vs chamfer on cut ductile iron
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: McWane Ductile: chamfer or beveling ductile iron pipe; U.S. Pipe TYTON JOINT submittal and assembly instructions

field.text: Cut PVC sewer and water pipe with a fine-tooth hand saw, a reciprocating saw, a wheel-type plastic pipe cutter or a guided pipe saw (for example a saw-and-bevel tool sized to the pipe). Keep the cut square: wrap a strap or paper band to mark it, or use a cutter that tracks around the pipe. Do not use a diamond blade on plastic: Husqvarna warns heat melts plastic onto the blade and can cause kickback. Abrasive wheels also melt and grab PVC. In cold weather PVC gets brittle; support it well and avoid impact. After cutting, deburr inside and outside, bevel the spigot like the factory end, clean off shavings, and re-mark the insertion line before assembling.
field.title: Cutting PVC pipe: saws, square cuts and no diamond blades
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (cutting blades); General industry practice

field.text: A field-cut gasketed PVC spigot must be beveled before it goes in a bell, or the square edge can roll or cut the gasket. Use a beveling tool (hand bevel, power bevel attachment) or a grinder/rasp to copy the factory bevel, typically around 15 degrees and down to roughly half the wall thickness; match the factory end and the maker's instructions. Then mark the insertion line: measure the factory spigot's distance from end to its insertion mark and copy it. Uni-Bell explains why the line matters: it shows the bevel has passed the gasket, and it prevents over-insertion, which leaves no room for thermal movement and can stress or leak the bell when deflected. After assembly the line should still be visible; with two lines, the one nearest the end should be hidden and the farther one visible.
field.title: PVC spigot bevel and new insertion line after a cut
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association: gasketed PVC pipe, the importance of insertion lines; General industry practice

field.text: A snap cutter (soil pipe cutter, chain cutter, 'snapper') wraps a chain fitted with cutting wheels around brittle pipe and squeezes until the pipe snaps clean along the line. Ratchet and lever versions handle about 1-1/2 to 6, 8, 12 or 15 inch pipe; hydraulic versions (example Wheeler-Rex 4 to 24 inch cast iron, concrete and tile cutter) use a remote hand pump and need only 2 to 3 inches of clearance to wrap the chain, handy for pipe in place in a trench. Use them for cast iron soil pipe, vitrified clay, concrete and other brittle pipe. They do not work on ductile iron (it bends instead of snapping), PVC or HDPE. They make no dust compared with sawing, a plus for silica. For AC (asbestos-cement) pipe, snap cutters are a common non-dust method, but follow your asbestos plan and rules.
field.title: Snap cutters for cast iron, clay and concrete pipe
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Wheeler-Rex 4-24 in. cast iron, concrete and tile snap cutter product page (Pollardwater); General industry practice

field.text: Beyond saws, iron and steel pipe can be cut with: wheel cutters (multi-wheel ratchet or hinged cutters that are rotated a short arc back and forth, good in tight trenches; common for cast iron, steel and some DI up to about 8 to 12 inch); rotary or milling cutters (clamp-on machines, often pneumatic or hydraulic, that travel around the pipe and leave a square cut and sometimes a bevel; used on larger DI and steel and where sparks or dust are an issue); and clamshell lathes for big-diameter cold cutting and beveling. Advantages over a cut-off saw: square cut, no kickback, less dust and sparks. Drawbacks: setup time and cost. Keep cutting wheels sharp and the right type for the material; dull wheels flare the pipe end.
field.title: Wheel cutters and rotary pipe cutters for iron and steel
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Walk-behind saws (flat saws, street saws, 'push saws', slab saws) cut pavement and slabs in straight lines for trench cuts and patches. Classes: entry level up to about 13 hp for short, shallow cuts; mid-size about 13 to 35 hp; large 35 to 65 hp or more for heavy pavement, often diesel for torque. Electric models (about 4 to 5 hp) work in enclosed areas. Example blade-to-depth figures from makers: 16 inch blade cuts about 5-3/4 inch deep; 20 inch about 7-1/2 to 7-3/4 inch; larger saws run 12 to 36 inch blades for about 4.6 to 15 inch depth. Rule from one supplier: if you cut deeper than 4 inches three or four days a week, look at a 35 to 65 hp saw. Check the guard size limit on your saw before mounting a bigger blade.
field.title: Walk-behind concrete and asphalt saws: sizes and depth
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: For Construction Pros: selecting concrete cutter applications

field.text: Walk-behind saw tips: match the blade to the saw's horsepower and RPM, because a blade built for a 65 hp saw will glaze on a 13 hp saw and blade speed ratings must suit the arbor speed; blade life is measured in inch-feet (length of cut times depth), useful for estimating blades on a job; run water continuously (built-in tank and pump on mid and large saws) since a hot blade warps and cuts crooked, and OSHA Table 1 requires integrated water for walk-behind saws; cut in passes on deep cuts rather than forcing full depth; keep a chalk line or pointer on the line; and raise the blade before moving or turning. Early-entry (green) saws cut fresh concrete control joints within hours and are not a substitute for a full-depth pavement saw.
field.title: Walk-behind saw practice: blade match, water and production
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: For Construction Pros: selecting concrete cutter applications; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1

field.text: Pavement cuts for utility work: cut full depth of the asphalt or concrete so the piece breaks out clean and the remaining edge is not undermined; most specs want straight, neat vertical cuts, often set back 1 ft or more beyond the trench wall after backfill for the final patch (check your agency's restoration spec). Composite pavement (asphalt over old concrete) needs the deeper saw or two passes. Locate first: shallow utilities, traffic loops, streetlight conduits and water services can be in the cut line. Keep the slurry out of storm drains (inlet protection, vacuum it up). Mark cut lines with paint or chalk, and set traffic control before sawing in the road. A cut-off saw is fine for short cuts, but a walk-behind saw gives straighter, deeper cuts with less operator strain.
field.title: Saw-cutting pavement for a trench or patch
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: OSHA's construction silica rule (1926.1153) Table 1 says what to do for each tool so you do not have to measure dust. Handheld power saws, any blade size, cutting concrete, block, brick, stone or concrete pipe: use a saw with built-in water delivery that feeds water continuously to the blade, and maintain it per the maker. Outdoors: no respirator needed for 4 hours or less a shift; over 4 hours, a respirator with APF 10 (for example a fitted half-mask N95 class or better under a respirator program). Indoors or in an enclosed area: APF 10 respirator regardless of time. Handheld saws cutting fiber-cement board (blade 8 inches or smaller), outdoors only: dust collector meeting the maker's airflow with a 99% filter, no respirator. If you cannot follow Table 1 exactly, you must assess exposure instead.
field.title: OSHA silica Table 1: handheld cut-off saws in plain words
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1

field.text: More Table 1 entries (1926.1153). Walk-behind saws: integrated water to the blade; outdoors no respirator required; indoors or enclosed, APF 10 respirator. Drivable saws (outdoors only): integrated water, no respirator. Rig-mounted core saws and drills: integrated water to the cutting surface, no respirator. Handheld and stand-mounted drills, including impact and rotary hammer drills: a commercial shroud or cowling with dust collection (airflow per the maker, 99% filter, filter cleaning), and clean holes with a HEPA vacuum, not by blowing; no respirator required. Dowel drilling rigs for concrete (outdoors only): shroud and dust collection with HEPA hole cleaning, and an APF 10 respirator. All equipment controls must be maintained so they actually work (water flowing, shrouds intact, filters clean).
field.title: OSHA silica Table 1: walk-behind saws, core drills and drills
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1

field.text: Table 1 (1926.1153) for breaking and grinding. Jackhammers and handheld chipping tools: water spray or stream at the point of impact, or a shroud with dust collection; outdoors, no respirator for 4 hours or less a shift and APF 10 over 4 hours; indoors or enclosed, APF 10 always. Handheld grinders (not mortar removal), outdoors: integrated water or a shroud with dust collection (25 cfm per inch of wheel diameter, 99% filter), no respirator; indoors, APF 10 over 4 hours. Walk-behind milling machines and floor grinders: water or the maker's dust collection, no respirator. Cleanup rules: no dry sweeping or dry brushing where it raises silica dust unless wet methods or HEPA vacuums are not feasible, and no compressed air to clean clothes or surfaces unless the dust is captured. PEL is 50 micrograms per cubic meter (8-hour), action level 25.
field.title: OSHA silica Table 1: jackhammers, grinders and cleanup
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1

field.text: Hand breakers come in classes by weight: light chipping hammers (about 10 to 20 lb) for trimming and chipping; 30 to 40 lb demolition breakers for light slabs and walls; 60 lb paving breakers for sidewalks, curbs and thin pavement; and 90 lb paving breakers for heavy concrete and rock, used downward only. Power types: pneumatic (most powerful for weight, needs a tow-behind compressor; older planning rule: breaker weight in lb roughly equals cfm at 90 psi, which is conservative; many current 60 to 90 lb breakers use roughly 40 to 70 cfm, so check the tool's rating); electric (35 to 70 lb class, plug-in, no compressor, needs a big enough generator and GFCI); hydraulic (runs off a power pack or excavator auxiliary, no engine exhaust at the tool, good power-to-weight); and battery breakers for small jobs. For large areas, a hoe ram on the excavator beats any hand tool.
field.title: Jackhammers and breakers: sizes and power types
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: For Construction Pros: match air compressor selection to your pneumatic tool needs; General industry practice

field.text: Hydraulic breakers, cut-off saws, chainsaws, pumps and drills (Stanley/Epiroc and others) run off a power unit or a machine's auxiliary circuit. They are rated by HTMA tool type: Type I about 4 to 6 gpm, Type II about 7 to 9 gpm, Type RR about 9 to 10.5 gpm and Type III about 11 to 13 gpm, all at about 1,500 psi nominal with system relief around 2,100 to 2,250 psi (2,000 psi on some classes), maximum return back pressure 250 psi and 25 micron filtration. Match the tool's type to the power source: too much flow overheats and over-speeds the tool; too little makes it weak. Stanley says do not run the tool with oil hotter than 140 F. Power units are sold by flow, for example 5 to 8 gpm or 8 to 12 gpm at 2,000 psi. Connect and disconnect with the flow off and couplers clean.
field.title: Hydraulic hand tools: HTMA flow classes and power units
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Stanley (Epiroc) hydraulic tool manual: HTMA/EHTMA requirements

field.text: Jackhammer practice: let the tool's weight do the work, do not lean on it or ride it; take bites 3 to 6 inches back from the edge so pieces break off rather than burying the bit; if the bit sticks, stop and free it with a bar, never pry with the breaker; keep feet clear of the bit; lift with legs, and use two people to move 90 lb breakers in and out of trenches. Equipment: tools must be locked to the hose or whip with a positive locking connector, and impact tools need a retainer clip or latch so the bit cannot shoot out (OSHA 1926.302). Shut off air and bleed the line before changing bits. Wear hearing and eye protection, steel toes and anti-vibration gloves, and use water spray for silica. Watch for buried utilities, rebar mats and voids under slabs.
field.title: Running a jackhammer safely
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.302 power-operated hand tools; General industry practice

field.text: A hammer drill (chuck-type) is light-duty for small holes in masonry. A rotary hammer uses a piston to hit the bit and takes SDS bits. SDS-plus (10 mm shank) covers about 3/16 to 3/4 inch bits, good for anchors and small holes. SDS-max (18 mm shank) covers about 1/2 to 1-3/4 inch bits, plus carbide core bits about 3 to 6 inch, and chisels; spline-drive tools are similar in size to SDS-max. A demolition hammer (demo hammer) has chisel mode only, no drilling, for chipping concrete, cutting out around pipes at manholes and breaking small areas. For more than a couple of square feet of concrete, step up to a jackhammer. Silica: OSHA Table 1 drills need a shroud with dust collection and HEPA hole cleaning.
field.title: Rotary hammers, hammer drills and demo hammers: which is which
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: Home Fixated: SDS Plus vs SDS Max; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1

field.text: Core drills cut round holes in precast manholes, vaults and walls for new pipe connections and boots. Rig-mounted core drills bolt or vacuum-mount to the wall and use diamond core bits (common sizes up to 12 to 24 inch or more) with water feed; this is the clean way to add a connection to an existing manhole instead of breaking out with a hammer. Practices: core diameter per the boot or connector maker (for example the gasket's required hole size); anchor the rig solidly (anchor bolt or vacuum base on a smooth surface) since a bit that binds will spin the drill; run water continuously (OSHA Table 1: rig-mounted core drills need integrated water, no respirator); keep the core from dropping inside onto anyone; and GFCI any electric drill near water. Locate rebar and joints first if you can.
field.title: Core drills for manhole connections and wall penetrations
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1; General industry practice

field.text: Pipe crews use chainsaws for clearing right-of-way, cutting roots in the trench, timber cribbing and blocking. The big hazard is kickback: when the upper quarter of the bar nose (the kickback zone) touches wood or another object, the saw is thrown up and back toward the operator. Pinch kickback happens when the wood closes on the top of the chain and pushes the saw straight back; pull-in happens when the bottom of the chain pinches and yanks the saw forward. Defenses: a working chain brake (test it before each use), low-kickback chain and bar, a sharp chain set to the right tension, full throttle when cutting, both hands on the saw with thumbs wrapped, and never cutting above shoulder height. Do not cut roots that are tangled with buried utilities until they are located and exposed.
field.title: Chainsaws on utility jobs: kickback and the chain brake
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Chainsaw PPE: chainsaw chaps or pants (cut-resistant), hard hat, eye protection (safety glasses plus face screen), hearing protection, gloves and sturdy boots (cut-resistant boots preferred). Safe use: start the saw on the ground or held firmly with the chain brake on, never drop-starting; keep bystanders back at least two tree lengths when felling and well clear when bucking; watch for spring poles and limbs under tension; plan a retreat path; shut off or engage the brake when carrying; refuel with the engine off and cool, away from sparks; and keep the chain sharp because a dull chain makes you push and raises kickback risk. 2-stroke saws use premix (STIHL specifies 50:1). Felling near power lines, roads or buildings is a job for a trained arborist.
field.title: Chainsaw PPE and safe use
field.topic: Tools: saws, blades, breakers, drills and pipe cutting
field.source: STIHL MS 261 instruction manual: mixing fuel; General industry practice

field.text: Plugs used on sewer and storm work: mechanical test plugs (rubber gasket squeezed by a wing nut or bolt; small sizes, cleanouts and pipe ends; sized to the exact pipe ID); single-size inflatable plugs (rubber bladder for one pipe size, used for air tests and blocking); multi-size inflatable plugs (one plug covers a range like 6 to 12 inch; must be inflated to a higher pressure; check the tag for the range); test balls (round inflatable balls, common in smaller lines and laterals); flow-through or bypass plugs (hollow core with a hose connection so you can test, bypass a little flow or attach a gauge); and blocking plugs for holding back flow during repairs. Every plug has a tag listing size range, inflation pressure and maximum back pressure. Match the plug to the pipe's actual inside diameter and condition.
field.title: Pipe plug types: mechanical, inflatable, test balls and flow-through
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: PlugCo inflatable pipe plug safety manual (2021); General industry practice

field.text: Inflatable plugs can blow out of a pipe like a cannon ball. Key rules from PlugCo's safety manual: only trained crews use them; stop flow before installing; measure the pipe ID and use the right size, never a different diameter; clean the pipe and plug (no solvents on the plug); never inflate a plug outside the pipe; inflate to the rated pressure on the tag, no more and no less, using a control with a relief valve and a calibrated gauge, never straight off a compressor without one; brace or block the plug whenever there is back pressure; use an extension inflation hose so you inflate and deflate from outside the danger zone; never stand in front of, beside or above a plug under pressure; release back pressure before deflating; never lift or pull a plug by its hose. Treat the manhole as a confined space.
field.title: Inflatable plug safety rules
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: PlugCo inflatable pipe plug safety manual (2021)

field.text: Back pressure is the pressure pushing on the back of the plug from water (or test air) behind it. Water head converts at 0.433 psi per foot. Example: a plug holding back a line that is 10 ft deep in water sees about 4.3 psi. The force on the plug is pressure times the pipe's inside area: an 8 inch pipe has about 50.3 sq in, so 5 psi pushes about 250 lb; a 24 inch pipe has about 452 sq in, so 4.3 psi pushes about 1,950 lb, close to a ton. During an air test at 4 psi, a 12 inch plug (113 sq in) takes about 450 lb. That is why plugs must be rated for the back pressure (on the tag), inflated to the right pressure and braced, and why nobody stands in line with them. Always add groundwater head to any test pressure when checking a plug's rating.
field.title: Back pressure on a plug: head of water and force
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: PlugCo inflatable pipe plug safety manual (2021); General industry practice

field.text: When a plug holds back pressure or flow, back it up mechanically. Common methods: a brace or 'plug bar' from the plug's lifting ring or yoke to the opposite manhole wall; timber struts wedged across the manhole; a chain or cable from the plug's eye tied off to a fixed point at the top (keeps it from traveling down the line); or plug yokes made for the purpose. Large plugs (PlugCo recommends water rather than air inflation on its biggest sizes) and plugs in steep lines need extra bracing. Seat the plug fully inside the pipe wall, centered and parallel, not half in the manhole, and use a protective sleeve if the pipe has debris or sharp edges that cannot be cleaned. Check the plug tag values match site conditions; if they do not, do not use it.
field.title: Blocking and bracing plugs in manholes
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: PlugCo inflatable pipe plug safety manual (2021); General industry practice

field.text: A sewer air test kit usually has: two or more plugs (one with a through-port for air and gauge); a control panel or test box with a shutoff valve, a pressure regulator, a relief valve (commonly set so the line cannot exceed about 9 to 10 psi; your spec sets the number) and a test gauge (typically 0 to 10 or 0 to 15 psi, readable to 0.1 psi; some specs require larger dials or digital gauges); air hoses long enough to keep the panel and the operator at the surface away from the manhole; and an air source (small compressor, oil-free). Some kits add a separate gauge for plug inflation. Before the test, check the gauge is calibrated (many agencies want a recent certificate), soap-test the hose connections and plug seals, and confirm the relief valve works. The procedure itself is in your spec and in the sewer testing chunks.
field.title: Low-pressure air test rig: what is in the kit
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Vacuum testing precast manholes needs: a vacuum test head (a ring with an inflatable seal that sits in or on the top of the cone, frame or riser, sized to the opening); a vacuum pump or venturi run off a compressor; a vacuum gauge reading inches of mercury (Hg), usually with a shutoff valve right at the head; inflatable or mechanical plugs for every pipe and stub entering the manhole, braced so the vacuum cannot pull them in; and a stopwatch. Tips: seal the head on a clean, smooth surface (grout or chipped tops leak); plug and brace all pipes before pulling vacuum; check the gauge is calibrated; keep everyone's hands and tools clear of the head; release vacuum slowly before removing the head. Spec values and times are in ASTM C1244 tables and your local spec.
field.title: Manhole vacuum test equipment
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: A mandrel (go/no-go gauge, 'pig') is pulled through flexible pipe to check it has not deflected more than allowed. Types: fixed-size mandrels (one size, usually 9 or more fins/legs, made for one pipe size and material); adjustable mandrels (fins or interchangeable legs set to different sizes, so one body covers several pipe sizes); and proving-ring mandrels that come with a ring to verify the mandrel's size before use. Pull by hand with a rope from manhole to manhole (many specs ban winches or mechanical pullers because they can force it through), with a tag line behind so you can pull it back if it hangs. A mandrel that stops at a spot marks deflection, a protruding service, debris or a bad joint; mark the distance on the rope and dig or camera it. Mandrel size is set from the pipe's base ID per your spec.
field.title: Deflection mandrels: types and how to pull them
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: A mandrel is a measuring tool, so treat it like one. Before testing, check the size with its proving ring (it should just pass through) or measure across the fins with calipers; adjustable mandrels must be set to the right legs for the pipe size, SDR and spec percentage. Inspectors often check it on site. Look for bent fins, which can make it pass when it should not, or fail when it should pass. Make sure the mandrel is for the pipe you laid: PVC SDR 35 and SDR 26 have different inside diameters, and profile wall, HDPE and PP pipes have their own base IDs. Clean and dry it after use, store it in its case, and keep the pull ropes in good shape. Record pipe size, mandrel size and stations on the test log.
field.title: Mandrel care and verifying the size
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Two kinds of sewer camera. Push (pushrod) cameras: a camera head on a semi-rigid cable pushed by hand; mostly used for pipe under about 6 inches (laterals, services, building drains); typical cable lengths 100 to 300 ft; some have self-leveling heads that keep the picture upright; good for checking a lateral, finding a blockage or locating a lateral's route. Crawlers (tractor cameras): a wheeled camera on a tether, driven from a truck or portable reel; for mainline sewer, storm drains and larger pipe; pan-and-tilt heads look up laterals and at joints; some systems run thousands of feet. New-sewer acceptance video is usually done with a crawler by the agency or a CCTV contractor following NASSCO PACP coding and your spec's speed and reporting rules.
field.title: Sewer cameras: push cameras vs crawlers
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: Varco Pumper: comparing pushrod and crawler inspection cameras; General industry practice

field.text: Most push cameras have a sonde (small transmitter) in or behind the camera head, commonly 512 Hz, which a walk-over locator can find from the surface. Use it to find a lateral's route and depth, a sag, a break or the spot where a camera stops. Set the locator to the sonde frequency, walk the line, find the peak signal and the two 'ghost' null points ahead and behind; the sonde is midway, and most locators read depth. Depth readings get less reliable near metal, rebar, other utilities and deep lines. Mark the spot with paint and the camera's footage counter reading. The footage counter is the distance from the launch point along the cable, not straight-line distance; calibrate it to a known length if you rely on it.
field.title: Locating with a camera sonde
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: A butt fusion machine has: a carriage with clamps and pipe-size inserts that hold and align both pipe ends; a facer (rotating blades that trims both ends flat and parallel); a heater plate (Teflon-coated, electrically heated) that melts the ends; a hydraulic or manual system that moves the carriage and applies pressure; and often a datalogger that records temperature, pressure and times for each joint. Machines run from about 2 inch hand machines to 65 inch fusion units. Setup: level the machine, support the pipe on stands or rollers so it slides freely (drag pressure must be measured and added to fusion pressure), keep pipe ends clean, and use a shelter or end caps to keep wind and dust off in bad weather. A generator sized for the heater and hydraulic unit is needed.
field.title: HDPE butt fusion machine: parts and setup
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Per the Plastics Pipe Institute municipal guidance, the heater plate surface must be 400 to 450 F (204 to 232 C). Check it with a surface pyrometer or temperature-indicating crayons, not just the dial thermometer, on both faces. Bring the faced pipe ends into full contact with the heater at fusion pressure, and on larger sizes hold that until a slight melt shows all the way around; then drop to drag pressure to let heat soak. Heat soak continues until the specified minimum bead forms on both sides; PPI recommends a minimum heat soak of 4.5 minutes per inch of pipe wall thickness. Then pull the heater fast, join at fusion pressure, and hold for the full cooling time. Pressure, bead size and times come from ASTM F2620, the pipe maker and the machine's chart.
field.title: Butt fusion heater temperature and heat soak
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: Plastics Pipe Institute municipal advisory board: butt fusion heating/melt procedure

field.text: Field checks for good HDPE butt fusion: wipe the heater faces with a clean, lint-free cotton cloth (no synthetic rags) before each joint; re-face if the ends are touched or dirty after facing; check high-low alignment after facing (commonly no more than 10% of wall); measure drag pressure for each joint and add it to the gauge pressure; do not open the heater-to-join window slowly (seconds count); never cool joints with water or air; and keep the joint clamped and unstressed for the full cooling time. A good bead is double-rolled, uniform all around, and the V between the beads does not go below the pipe surface. Cold, windy weather needs a shelter, longer heat soak per your procedure, and checking heater temperature more often. Many utilities require a datalogger printout per joint.
field.title: Butt fusion field checks and common mistakes
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Electrofusion joints (couplings, saddles, tapping tees, reducers) have heating wire built into the fitting. A control box (processor) feeds a set voltage for a set time; 39.5 volts is the most common input voltage, though makers use values from about 8 to 48 V. Most modern processors read the fitting's barcode (ISO format) and set the time automatically, with temperature compensation; some log each joint. Fittings usually have fusion indicators (small pins that pop up) to show heating happened. The processor needs a generator big enough for the fitting; large couplings draw a lot of power, and an undersized or poorly regulated generator can abort or under-fuse the joint. Use the maker's clamps to hold pipe and fitting still, and leave clamps on through the cooling time on the label.
field.title: Electrofusion processor and generator basics
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: Electrofusion welding overview (Wikipedia); General industry practice

field.text: Most bad electrofusion joints come from prep, not the box. Requirements: cut the pipe square; mark the pipe slightly past half the coupling length; scrape the entire fusion zone with a proper rotary or hand scraper to remove the oxidized skin and expose fresh material all the way around (sandpaper, rasps or emery cloth are not acceptable); clean with the approved wipe (typically isopropyl alcohol, 90% or better) and let it dry; do not touch scraped surfaces; insert to the mark and clamp. Uneven scraping leaves gaps that weaken the joint. Other causes: pipe moved during fusion or cooling, out-of-round pipe (use rerounding clamps), water in the joint, wrong fitting size, or a second fusion cycle on a fitting when the maker does not allow it.
field.title: Electrofusion failures: scraping and contamination
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: Electrofusion welding overview (Wikipedia); General industry practice

field.text: A wet tap (hot tap) connects a new branch to a live water main without shutting it down. Equipment: a tapping sleeve (bolted around the main) with an outlet; a tapping valve bolted to the sleeve outlet; and a tapping machine (Mueller CL-12 and others) with a shell cutter and a pilot drill, mounted on the valve. The pilot drill centers the cut and holds the cut-out coupon ('cookie') so it comes back out through the valve. Water Online says mismatched sleeve, valve and machine is the most common problem, so use matched equipment; the sleeve's branch ID should be at least 0.25 inch larger than the nominal branch so the shell cutter clears, and there must be enough travel to cut and fully retract so the valve can close. Small service taps use a different drilling machine with corporation stops.
field.title: Tapping machines and wet taps: the equipment
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: Water Online: making successful wet taps

field.text: Before tapping: block solidly under the sleeve and valve so the main is not loaded; align the machine adapter flange parallel and centered with the valve; hydrostatically test the sleeve and valve assembly before cutting (Water Online says do not use an air test); confirm travel and clearance measurements. Some utilities set further rules; Tucson Water, for example, requires the main purged of air and at least 40 psi (or operating pressure) before tapping, requires the cutter to retain the coupon, and does not accept size-on-size taps on 12 inch and larger pipe. After the tap, retract fully, close the valve, remove the machine and turn the coupon in if required. Clean and disinfect parts that contact potable water per your utility. Only experienced tappers should run the machine.
field.title: Wet tap checks: test, support, coupon and size limits
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: Water Online: making successful wet taps; Tucson Water standard 1407: taps into water lines

field.text: U.S. Pipe's methods for pushing Tyton push-on DI home: bar method for 3 to 6 inch (a bar used as a lever against a block at the bell face); backhoe method for 8 to 64 inch (guide the spigot in by hand, put a timber header between the pipe end and the bucket, and push steadily; do not slam it home, which can crack lining at the back of the socket); come-along (chain hoist) method for 3 to 64 inch in tight spots: two 3/4 to 2 ton hoists with about 24 ft of chain and two bell choker slings for 3 to 24 inch, and two 2 to 4 ton (minimum) hoists for 30 to 64 inch. Push until the first painted stripe disappears into the bell and the second is about flush with the bell face. Keep hands out of the bell and off the spigot while pushing.
field.title: Homing ductile iron: bar, bucket and come-along
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: U.S. Pipe TYTON JOINT submittal and assembly instructions

field.text: Other homing tools: a bar and wood block (the classic for small PVC; pry against the block on the bell end, never on the pipe end directly); pipe pullers and jacks (a cable or chain anchored back several joints and pulled with a lever or ratchet, so the force goes in line with the pipe and does not push laid pipe out of grade); and the excavator bucket with a timber block for large PVC, DI and RCP. For concrete pipe, makers sell internal and external pullers (for example a come-along with a cross-beam inside the pipe), which keep joints straight. Rules: push straight in line, never at an angle; stop at the insertion mark and do not over-home; shoot grade on the laid pipe after pushing; and keep people out from between the bucket and the pipe.
field.title: Pipe pullers and homing tools for PVC and concrete pipe
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: For water main pressure tests you need: a test pump (hand pump for short sections, gas or electric piston pump for longer ones) connected at a tap or blowoff; a calibrated pressure gauge in the range of the test (test pressure roughly in the middle third of the dial is easiest to read; many specs want 2 or 5 psi divisions or a digital gauge, and some want a calibration certificate); a measured makeup water source (a calibrated tank or meter so you can measure 'leakage' per AWWA C600/C605); and valves to isolate the pump. Place the gauge at the lowest point or correct for elevation (0.433 psi per foot). Bleed all air first. Keep people away from thrust blocks, plugs, caps and bolted joints while under pressure, and never tighten joints under pressure.
field.title: Hydrostatic test pump and gauge setup
field.topic: Tools: pipe plugs, test gear, cameras, fusion, tapping and pullers
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Size a generator from the tools that run at the same time. Running watts keep a tool going (volts times amps on the nameplate: a 12.5 amp, 120 V saw is 1,500 W). Starting (surge) watts are the short spike to start a motor, which can be up to 6 times running for 1-1/2 to 3 seconds. Rough multipliers: universal-motor tools (drills, circular saws, grinders, small cut-off saws) about 2 times running; capacitor-start motors (air compressors, pumps, table saws) about 3 times; some heavy-start motors about 6 times. Method: add the running watts of everything that runs together, except the tool with the biggest starting watts; add that tool's starting watts; then add 25% so the generator is not maxed out. If several motors start often, add their starting watts. Check your own nameplates.
field.title: Generator sizing: running watts vs starting watts
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Norwall PowerSystems: sizing guide for portable generators

field.text: Example: a 1 hp electric air compressor (about 1,200 W running, 3,600 W starting), a submersible sump pump (about 500 W running, 1,700 W starting), a 15 amp electric demo hammer (about 1,800 W running, 3,600 W starting at 2 times) and two 400 W LED work lights (800 W). Biggest starting load is 3,600 W (call it the compressor). Running watts of the others: 500 + 1,800 + 800 = 3,100 W. Total: 3,100 + 3,600 = 6,700 W, plus 25% = about 8,400 W. So an 8 to 10 kW generator, not a 5 kW one, if all of it runs together. If you stagger starts (start the compressor first, then the pump), you can get by smaller, but pumps on float switches start on their own. Method from Norwall's guide; tool wattages vary, so read the nameplates.
field.title: Generator sizing worked example for a pipe crew
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Norwall PowerSystems: sizing guide for portable generators

field.text: OSHA 1926.404(f)(3) says a portable generator's frame does not have to be driven to a ground rod, and the frame can serve as the grounding electrode, when: the generator only powers equipment mounted on it and/or cord-and-plug tools plugged into its own receptacles, and the metal parts of that equipment and the receptacle grounding terminals are bonded to the generator frame. Vehicle-mounted generators can use the vehicle frame as the ground under similar conditions with the generator frame bonded to the vehicle frame. If the generator feeds a temporary panel, a building or a structure's wiring, normal grounding rules apply (often a ground rod; get an electrician). Never cut off the ground pin on a plug or use a cheater adapter.
field.title: Generator grounding on the job site (OSHA)
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.404 wiring design and protection

field.text: OSHA 1926.404(b)(1): all 120-volt, single-phase, 15 and 20 amp receptacles that are not part of a building's permanent wiring and are used by workers must have GFCI protection, or the employer must run an assured equipment grounding conductor program. Exception: 2-wire, single-phase portable or vehicle-mounted generators rated 5 kW or less whose circuit conductors are insulated from the frame. The assured grounding program needs a written plan kept on site, a competent person, a visual check of cords and tools before each day's use, and continuity and terminal tests before first use, after repair, after damage (like a cord run over) and at least every 3 months, with test records. Practical: use GFCI cords or GFCI outlets on the generator, and push the test button each day, especially around pumps and water.
field.title: GFCI protection and assured grounding on construction sites
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.404 wiring design and protection

field.text: Long, skinny cords starve tools and burn up motors. Voltage drop rises with amps and length. A common target is 5% drop or less, and even a 12-gauge cord at 100 ft carrying a full 15 amps is right at about 5%. Rules of thumb: use 12-gauge for 15 amp tools on runs up to about 100 ft, 10-gauge for longer runs or heavy loads (pumps, demo hammers, compressors); keep cords as short as practical; unroll reels fully (coiled cords heat up); and do not run several big tools on one cord. Use heavy-duty, hard-service outdoor cords (SJOW/SOOW type), 3-wire with ground. A tool that bogs, a motor that runs hot or a cord that feels warm is a sign the cord is too small or too long. Basis: 120 V, NEC Chapter 9 Table 9 values.
field.title: Extension cords: gauge, length and voltage drop
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Pro Tool Reviews: extension cord size chart (NEC Ch. 9 Table 9 basis); General industry practice

field.text: Cords on pipe jobs get run over, buried and dragged through water. Before each day's use (required under an assured grounding program), check for: cuts or crushed spots in the jacket, exposed inner conductors, missing or bent ground pins, cracked plug or connector bodies, taped repairs (electrical tape is not a permanent fix on a hard-service cord), and burn marks. Take damaged cords out of service. In use: do not run cords through doorways or across roads without protection (cord ramps), keep connections out of puddles and trench water (hang them up), never pull a cord out by the cable, never lift or lower a submersible pump by its cord, and keep cords away from hot engine parts and sharp trench box edges. Power off before unplugging a running pump.
field.title: Cord and plug damage: inspect before use
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.404 wiring design and protection; General industry practice

field.text: Gas and diesel generators make carbon monoxide (CO), a colorless, odorless gas that can kill fast. NIOSH and OSHA warn small gasoline engines can build dangerous CO in minutes even in areas that seem ventilated, and that open doors, windows and fans do not guarantee safety. Generator placement: outdoors, downwind and away from the trench, manhole openings, pits, building doors, windows and air intakes; never in a trench, excavation, manhole, vault, tunnel or enclosed trailer. CO is about the same weight as air but collects in low, still spaces like trenches. Refueling: OSHA 1926.302 requires fuel-powered tools to be stopped before refueling; let the engine cool, keep fuel away from sparks, and do not refuel in the trench. Use CO monitors when people work near running engines.
field.title: Generators and carbon monoxide: placement and refueling
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: NIOSH/OSHA/CPSC/EPA alert: CO poisoning from small gasoline-powered engines and tools (NIOSH 96-118); OSHA 29 CFR 1926.302 power-operated hand tools

field.text: Gas-powered tools used in trenches, pits and manholes are a known CO killer: cut-off saws, plate compactors, rammers, trash pumps, pressure washers and small generators. NIOSH case examples include a worker who passed out using an 8 hp gas pump in a large room with doors open, and a plumber poisoned by a gas concrete saw in a basement with doors, windows open and a fan running. Controls: keep engines out of the hole (set pumps on the bank and run hose down; set generators away from the trench); use electric, battery, hydraulic or pneumatic tools in confined or low areas; ventilate with a blower drawing fresh air from away from exhaust; wear a personal CO monitor with alarm; and get out at the first headache or dizziness. Remember an excavator or truck idling at the trench edge adds CO too.
field.title: CO from gas tools in trenches and manholes
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: NIOSH/OSHA/CPSC/EPA alert: CO poisoning from small gasoline-powered engines and tools (NIOSH 96-118); Texas Dept. of Insurance fact sheet: CO from gasoline-powered engines and tools

field.text: CO exposure limits: OSHA PEL 50 ppm (8-hour average; Cal/OSHA PEL 25 ppm, lower than federal OSHA and NIOSH); NIOSH REL 35 ppm (8-hour) with a 200 ppm ceiling; NIOSH IDLH (immediately dangerous to life or health) 1,200 ppm. Many 4-gas monitors alarm at 35 ppm by default (check your company's settings). Symptoms: headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, chest pain and confusion; then vision problems, poor judgment and unconsciousness. Because confusion comes early, people often do not realize they are being poisoned. If someone has symptoms: get them to fresh air, shut off the engine if it is safe to do so, call 911, do not let them drive, and do not go back in until the area is ventilated and a monitor reads safe. Never enter a trench or manhole to rescue someone who collapsed without testing the air and proper equipment.
field.title: Carbon monoxide numbers and symptoms
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: NIOSH IDLH documentation: carbon monoxide; Texas Dept. of Insurance fact sheet: CO from gasoline-powered engines and tools

field.text: Tow-behind compressors are rated by cubic feet per minute (cfm) delivered at 100 psi; most air tools run at 90 psi. An old planning rule says a breaker's weight in pounds roughly equals its cfm (90 lb breaker about 90 cfm, 60 lb about 60 cfm); that's conservative, and many current paving breakers use roughly 40 to 70 cfm, chipping hammers about 20 to 40 cfm. Read the tool's rated air consumption. A 185 cfm compressor (the common rental size) typically runs two 90 lb breakers or two to three 60 lb breakers, or a breaker plus a clay spade. Add up every tool that runs at once; if demand exceeds supply, tools hit weak and the compressor runs flat out. Altitude cuts output; check the maker's chart at high elevation. Hose length and fittings also cost pressure at the tool.
field.title: Air compressor sizing: CFM vs tool demand
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: For Construction Pros: match air compressor selection to your pneumatic tool needs; Compact Equipment: tips for operating a tow-behind air compressor and pneumatic tools

field.text: A whipping air hose can break bones or kill. OSHA 1926.302: pneumatic tools must be fastened to the hose with a positive locking connection so they cannot come loose; impact tools need a retainer so the bit cannot fly out; and hose over 1/2 inch inside diameter must have a safety device (excess-flow or pressure-reducing valve) at the source or branch line that cuts flow if the hose fails. Whip checks (safety cables) go across every hose connection, compressor to hose and hose to hose and hose to tool. Pressure drops the farther the tool is from the compressor and at every fitting, so use one long hose rather than several short ones joined, and size hose up on long runs (two 90 cfm breakers at about 150 ft from a 185 cfm compressor will likely run short). Inspect hoses and couplings every day.
field.title: Air hose, whip checks and the OSHA safety valve rule
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.302 power-operated hand tools; Compact Equipment: tips for operating a tow-behind air compressor and pneumatic tools

field.text: Running a tow-behind compressor: park on level ground, chock the wheels, keep hatches and doors closed while running; start, let the engine warm up before loading, and check the gauge (about 50 to 70 psi right after start on the unit described by Compact Equipment, rising to operating pressure); open the service (discharge) valve slowly to protect hoses and tools; drain the water trap or separator every day; fill the fuel tank at the end of the day to cut condensation in the tank; check oil, coolant and air filter (dusty jobs clog filters fast); and inspect hoses, tools and running gear before use. Air tools need oil, so use an in-line lubricator or oil the tool per the maker. In freezing weather, moisture in the line freezes tools and couplings; drain often and use the maker's anti-freeze method.
field.title: Tow-behind compressor daily operation
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Compact Equipment: tips for operating a tow-behind air compressor and pneumatic tools; General industry practice

field.text: OSHA 1926.302(b)(4): compressed air used for cleaning must be reduced to less than 30 psi, and only with effective chip guarding and PPE (the 30 psi limit does not apply to cleaning concrete forms, mill scale and similar). Never blow dust off clothing or skin with air; air can enter the body through cuts and cause injury. On silica jobs (cutting concrete, block, cement-lined pipe), the silica rule forbids using compressed air to clean clothes or surfaces where it adds to exposure unless the dust cloud is captured by ventilation or there is no alternative, and restricts dry sweeping. Use a HEPA vacuum or wet methods instead. For blowing out drilled holes, Table 1 calls for HEPA vacuuming, not air.
field.title: Compressed air for cleaning: 30 psi and silica
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.302 power-operated hand tools; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1153 respirable crystalline silica, Table 1

field.text: A centrifugal trash pump can only lift water so far on the suction side, because atmospheric pressure (about 33.9 ft of water at sea level) is what pushes water up the suction hose. Practical maximum suction lift for self-priming trash pumps is about 25 ft at sea level, and it drops roughly 1 ft for every 1,000 ft of elevation as air pressure falls, plus more with warm water. In real trench work, plan on much less (often 15 to 20 ft) because output drops sharply as suction lift rises: the closer the pump is to the water, the more gpm it moves. Keep suction hose short (long suction hose adds friction and causes cavitation) and check it for holes and worn couplings, since any air leak kills the prime. If the water is too deep to reach, lower the pump on a bench in the excavation (with ventilation for exhaust) or use a submersible. Hot water can flash to vapor under suction.
field.title: Trash pump suction lift and placement
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Physics of suction lift (atmospheric pressure vs elevation); Equipment World trash pump guidance; general pump-maker practice

field.text: Trash pumps are named by port size: 2, 3, 4 and 6 inch. Typical maximum ratings for gas trash pumps (vary by maker and model): 2 inch roughly 150 to 220 gpm, 3 inch roughly 250 to 400 gpm, 4 inch roughly 400 to 560 gpm, with maximum heads often around 80 to 100 ft. Those are best-case numbers at near-zero head; real output at your total head (suction lift plus discharge height plus hose friction) is much less, so read the pump curve. Solids size is limited by the pump design and strainer, roughly up to a third to half of the port size on true trash pumps (bigger pumps pass bigger solids); for heavy mud and thick slurry use a diaphragm pump. Do not pump fuel, solvents or corrosives. Pick a pump with spare capacity and keep a backup on critical dewatering.
field.title: Trash pump sizing: gpm, head and solids
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Manufacturer trash pump spec sheets (ranges across common 2-4 inch models); general dewatering practice

field.text: Electric submersible pumps sit in a sump in the water, so there is no suction lift limit and no engine exhaust in the hole, a plus in trenches. Practices: dig a sump below trench grade and set the pump on a block or in a perforated bucket or screen wrapped in stone so it does not suck mud and fines (pumping fines can undermine the pipe bedding); use a float switch so it cannot run dry; power it from a GFCI-protected circuit and a generator big enough for its starting load (often about 3 times running watts); never lift, lower or drag it by the power cord, use the lifting rope or chain; keep the cord connection up and out of water; and route discharge to an approved sediment control, not straight to a storm drain or stream. Check the pump curve for the head you need.
field.title: Submersible pumps in trenches and sumps
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Norwall PowerSystems: sizing guide for portable generators; General industry practice

field.text: Suction hose must be rigid, reinforced (non-collapsible) hose rated for vacuum, with a strainer on the end, and as short as possible; a collapsing or leaking suction hose stops the pump. Discharge hose is usually layflat (cheaper, rolls up) or rubber for rough use. Hose size should match or exceed the pump port; going down a size raises friction a lot on long runs. Couplings: cam-lock (cam and groove) fittings are common; make sure the cam arms are closed and pinned, and use whip checks or tie-downs on pressurized discharge lines where a coupling failure could whip. Lay discharge hose where it will not be run over (or use hose ramps across roads), and keep discharge under control so it does not erode the bank or flood the street.
field.title: Pump hose: suction, discharge and couplings
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Light towers (light plants) light night work. Typical units have 4 lamp heads on a telescoping mast around 20 to 30 ft, metal halide or LED, with a diesel generator. Setup: level the trailer on firm ground, put down all outriggers or stabilizers before raising, look up for overhead power lines before raising (the mast must stay well clear of lines; check OSHA clearance distances), check the wind rating and lower the mast in high wind, and lock the mast winch. Aim lights down onto the work and away from oncoming traffic and nearby homes. Keep the unit out of the swing radius and outside the trench zone. Refuel with the engine off. LED towers use less fuel and start instantly; metal halide lamps need a cool-down before restarting.
field.title: Light towers: setup and safety
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Heaters are used to thaw ground, warm workers, protect fresh concrete and cure. OSHA 1926.154: supply enough fresh air for workers (mechanical ventilation if needed) and extra ventilation in confined spaces for combustion and safety; solid-fuel salamanders are banned in buildings and on scaffolds; keep heaters at least 10 ft from tarps and canvas and fasten coverings so wind cannot blow them into the heater; set heaters level; keep combustibles back the listed clearance (example: radiant heaters 36 inches sides and rear); and oil-fired heaters need a flame-failure safety shutoff. Propane and kerosene heaters make CO and use up oxygen, so never run them in a manhole, vault, trench under a tarp or closed trailer without testing the air. Ground-thaw blankets or hydronic heaters avoid open flame.
field.title: Job site heaters: OSHA rules and CO
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.154 temporary heating devices; General industry practice

field.text: A 4-gas monitor (multi-gas meter) reads oxygen (O2), combustible gas as % of the lower explosive limit (LEL), hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and carbon monoxide (CO). Common default alarm points (check your meter and company program): O2 low 19.5%, O2 high 23.5%; LEL 10%; H2S 10 ppm; CO 35 ppm (the app's permit uses 25 ppm everywhere, which is the Cal/OSHA limit, so set the CO alarm to 25 ppm or lower to match the permit). These line up with OSHA's confined space hazard limits for O2 and LEL. Sewers and manholes can hold H2S (rotten egg smell that you stop smelling at high levels), methane, low oxygen and CO from engines. Wear the meter in the breathing zone, or sample ahead with a pump and tube before entry. Some meters add sensors for other gases. The atmospheric testing order and entry limits are in the confined space chunks.
field.title: 4-gas monitor basics: what it reads and typical alarms
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: OSHA's bulletin on gas monitors, based on ISEA guidance: do a bump test (function check) or calibration check before each day's use, following the maker's instructions. A bump test briefly exposes the sensors to known test gas high enough to set off all alarms; it proves gas reaches the sensors and the alarms work, but does not prove accuracy. A calibration check compares the reading to the gas cylinder's concentration (usually acceptable within about 10 to 20%, per the maker). Full calibration adjusts the meter to a certified, NIST-traceable gas. If the meter fails a bump test or calibration check, do a full calibration before use; if it fails full calibration, take it out of service. Use in-date gas cylinders and keep records of bumps and calibrations; many docking stations do this automatically.
field.title: Gas monitor bump test and calibration
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA Safety and Health Information Bulletin: verification of calibration for direct-reading portable gas monitors

field.text: Sensors drift and get damaged. OSHA's bulletin lists causes: catalytic LEL sensors poisoned by silicones (some sprays and lubricants), hydride gases, halogenated hydrocarbons or sulfides; electrochemical toxic sensors upset by solvent vapors or corrosive gases; high concentrations of target gas; extreme temperature, humidity or dust; drops, shock and vibration; and normal aging. Test the meter's function again whenever any of those happen. When sampling a manhole or vault from the top with a pump and tube, let the sample draw long enough to clear the tube (makers commonly suggest about 2 minutes plus roughly 1 to 2 seconds per foot of tube; follow your meter's manual), and test top, middle and bottom. Keep the inlet filter clean and dry; water sucked into the pump kills it.
field.title: Gas monitor care: sensor damage and sampling
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA Safety and Health Information Bulletin: verification of calibration for direct-reading portable gas monitors; General industry practice

field.text: For vertical entries like manholes, a tripod with a retrieval winch (or a davit arm) lets the attendant pull an entrant out without going in. OSHA's permit space rule says each entrant wears a chest or full-body harness with a retrieval line attached, the other end attached to a mechanical device or fixed point outside the space, and a mechanical device must be available to retrieve people from vertical permit spaces more than 5 ft deep (1910.146(k)(3); the construction rule 1926 Subpart AA has parallel requirements). OSHA's interpretation allows entrants on one line only if each can be removed individually. Practices: set tripod legs on solid ground with chains or foot pads locked, center it over the opening, inspect the winch, cable and self-retracting lifeline before each use, and practice a rescue with the crew.
field.title: Confined space tripod and retrieval winch
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA interpretation letter 2013-02-25 on 1910.146(k)(3) retrieval systems; General industry practice

field.text: OSHA's construction noise limit (1926.52, Table D-2) is 90 dBA for 8 hours, with allowed time cut in half for every 5 dB louder: 95 dBA for 4 hours, 100 dBA for 2 hours, 105 dBA for 1 hour, 110 dBA for 30 minutes, 115 dBA for 15 minutes or less. Impact noise should not exceed 140 dB peak. Above these levels a continuing hearing conservation program is required. Many pipe crew tools are loud enough to reach these limits quickly (cut-off saws, jackhammers, hoe rams, rammers, plates, compressors, trash pumps), and NIOSH recommends a lower 85 dBA limit. Practical rule: if you have to shout to be heard at arm's length, wear earplugs or muffs. Double up (plugs plus muffs) for long jackhammer or saw work. Insert foam plugs properly: roll, pull the ear up and back, hold until it expands.
field.title: Hearing protection around saws, breakers and compactors
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.52 occupational noise exposure; General industry practice

field.text: Eye injuries on pipe jobs come from saw and grinder particles, breaker chips, rebar and wire ends, splashing slurry, wet cement (alkaline, causes chemical burns) and pressurized air or water. Wear safety glasses or goggles marked Z87+ (impact rated) at all times on the crew; add a face shield over glasses for cut-off saws, grinders and breaking; use goggles (not just glasses) for dust, slurry and cement work; and tinted lenses only in daylight. A face shield alone is not primary eye protection. Keep an eyewash bottle in the truck, and for cement or chemical splashes flush for at least 15 minutes and get medical care. Helpers standing near the saw or breaker need the same protection as the operator.
field.title: Eye and face protection for cutting and breaking
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Basic work zone equipment for a pipe crew: traffic cones (28 inch minimum with reflective collars for most roads and for night; check MUTCD and your agency), drums, Type I/II/III barricades, vertical panels, advance warning signs on stands (ROAD WORK AHEAD, ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD, FLAGGER symbol, END ROAD WORK), STOP/SLOW paddles (flagger), high-visibility apparel (Class 2 or 3), arrow boards or flashing lights for lane closures, sign weights or sandbags, and steel plates and ramps for trench crossings. Inspect devices for reflectivity and damage, and replace dirty or broken ones; many agencies grade devices as acceptable, marginal or unacceptable. Spacing, taper lengths and layouts are in the traffic control chunks; the approved traffic control plan governs.
field.title: Traffic control equipment: what the crew truck carries
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Shovels on a pipe crew: round-point (digging shovel) for digging, breaking into soil and general backfill; square-point (flat shovel) for cleaning trench bottom to grade, scooping stone and shaping bedding; trenching shovel (narrow blade, about 4 to 6 inch wide) for cleaning narrow trench bottoms and digging bell holes; drain spade (sharpshooter, long narrow blade) for clay, small hand trenches and potholing around utilities; and scoop shovels for loose stone and spoil. Long handles give leverage and save your back; D-handles work better in tight spaces. Fiberglass handles hold up better than wood in the wet. For locating near marked utilities within the tolerance zone, hand dig carefully with blunt or rounded tools, prying and scraping rather than stabbing. Air or vacuum excavation is safest near gas and electric.
field.title: Shovels for pipe work: which one for what
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Other hand tools: digging bar (spud bar, 'San Angelo' bar, typically 5 to 6 ft, about 15 to 20 lb) with a chisel or point end for breaking hard ground, rock and roots and prying pipe or castings, and often a tamping end on the other side; pick (pick and point) for hard ground and rock; mattock (adze blade plus pick or axe blade) for roots and hardpan; grub hoe for clearing; and pry bars for shifting pipe and manhole lids. Use a bar with both hands, feet set, and never stand under or in front of the bar when prying a heavy load. Keep striking ends dressed (no mushroomed heads) and replace cracked handles. Near marked utilities, do not drive a bar or pick blindly; probe gently with a fiberglass or blunt probe rod.
field.title: Digging bars, picks, mattocks and tampers
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.301 hand tools; General industry practice

field.text: Pipe crew hand tools: pipe wrenches (12 to 48 inch) for fittings and threaded pipe, aluminum ones are lighter for big sizes; chain tongs and strap wrenches for turning pipe and couplings without crushing; torque wrench or ratchet with the right socket for MJ bolts (tighten in a star pattern to the maker's torque); valve keys (T-handle, 5 to 10 ft or adjustable) for operating gate valves through valve boxes; curb stop keys; manhole hooks, lid lifters and magnetic lid lifters so nobody lifts a 100+ lb cover by hand at the rim; and come-alongs. OSHA 1926.301 bans wrenches with sprung or worn jaws that slip. Never use a cheater bar on a pipe wrench beyond the maker's rating, and pull toward you with footing set rather than pushing.
field.title: Pipe wrenches, chain tongs, valve keys and lid lifters
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.301 hand tools; General industry practice

field.text: OSHA's hand tool rule for construction (1926.301) is short: employers may not issue or allow unsafe hand tools; adjustable, pipe, end and socket wrenches cannot be used when the jaws are sprung (bent or worn) to the point that they slip; impact tools such as drift pins, wedges and chisels must be kept free of mushroomed heads; and wooden handles must be free of splinters and cracks and kept tight in the tool. In practice: do a quick look at hand tools when you load the truck each morning; grind off mushroomed heads on chisels, bars and drift pins (wear eye protection; mushroomed metal flies off when struck); replace loose or cracked shovel, pick and sledge handles rather than taping them; and tag and remove broken tools so they do not go back on the truck.
field.title: OSHA hand tool condition rules
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.301 hand tools

field.text: Battery (cordless) tools now include cut-off saws, demo hammers, rotary hammers, band saws, pipe cutters, plate compactors, rammers, light towers and pumps on the bigger 36 to 80 V class platforms. Pluses: no exhaust (so no CO in trenches and manholes), no cords to trip on or drag through water, quieter, instant start. Minuses: run time (bring spare batteries and a charger on the generator or truck inverter), cold weather cuts capacity (keep batteries warm in the cab), and high cost. Pick one platform for the crew so batteries interchange. Battery safety: keep packs out of water, do not use damaged, swollen or dropped packs, charge only with the maker's charger, store away from heat, and do not throw lithium-ion packs in the trash. Battery cut-off saws still need water for silica.
field.title: Cordless battery tools on the pipe job
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Most cut-off saws, chainsaws and some rammers and pumps run 2-stroke engines on premix. STIHL specifies 50:1 (gasoline to 2-cycle oil): 2.6 oz of oil per 1 gallon, 6.4 oz per 2.5 gallons, 12.8 oz per 5 gallons. Pour oil in the can first, then gas, close and shake. Mix only what you will use in a few days and never more than about a 30-day supply (premixed canned fuel lasts longer). Use the oil and ratio your engine's maker specifies; some older or other-brand tools call for 40:1 or 32:1. Wrong mix: too little oil scores the piston and seizes the engine; straight gas in a 2-stroke can ruin it in minutes. Label cans clearly (2-STROKE MIX vs GAS vs DIESEL); putting premix in a 4-stroke rammer or straight gas in a saw is a common crew mistake. Open shaken cans slowly, away from ignition.
field.title: 2-stroke fuel mix ratios: getting premix right
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: STIHL MS 261 instruction manual: mixing fuel; General industry practice

field.text: Dust kills small engines. Cut-off saws, plates, rammers and generators working in concrete and soil dust need air filter attention every day, sometimes several times a day: tap out or blow out foam and paper pre-filters (away from people, not with compressed air on your clothes), replace paper elements when clogged or damaged, and wash and re-oil foam elements per the maker. Cut-off saws often have a multi-stage filter; wet cutting cuts dust into the filter as well as the air. Signs of a clogged filter: loss of power, black smoke, hard starting. Never run an engine without its filter or with a torn one; dust gets past and wears the piston and rings fast. Keep the filter cover seal clean when you change it so dust cannot bypass.
field.title: Air filters on saws and compactors in dust
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Blade change on a cut-off saw: stop the engine and remove the spark plug wire or battery; lock the spindle (pin or lock button) and loosen the arbor bolt with the maker's wrench; check the inner and outer flange washers are clean, flat and undamaged; make sure the blade's arbor hole matches the spindle (use the correct bushing ring, never a loose fit); mount the blade with its rotation arrow matching the saw's rotation; tighten to the maker's spec; and confirm the blade RPM rating is equal to or higher than the saw's spindle speed. Check the guard is in place and adjusted. Then run the new blade at full throttle for about a minute with nobody in line with it, per Husqvarna, to check it. Never mount a toothed (wood or carbide) blade on a cut-off saw.
field.title: Changing a cut-off saw blade
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: Husqvarna K760 power cutter operator's manual (cutting blades); SafeWork NSW safety alert: safe use of hand-held cutting saws; General industry practice

field.text: Common fuel problems on small engines: stale gas (gasoline breaks down in weeks to months; ethanol blends absorb water and can gum carburetors), water in fuel, and wrong fuel. Tips: buy fresh fuel and use it within the time your engine maker recommends, or use a stabilizer or premixed ethanol-free canned fuel for tools that sit; check your manual for the maximum ethanol content allowed (many small engines limit it, often to 10%); drain or run dry tools that will sit for weeks; keep approved, labeled cans closed and in the shade; check 4-stroke oil level every day before starting (plates, rammers, pumps, generators, light towers); and keep diesel and gas cans different colors (yellow for diesel, red for gas is common). Refuel with the engine off and cool, never in a trench.
field.title: Small engine fuel and storage tips
field.topic: Tools: generators, compressors, pumps, gas monitors, hand tools and upkeep
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.302 power-operated hand tools; General industry practice

field.text: Typical pipe laser numbers, using Spectra's DG613/DG813 as an example: grade range -12% to +40%; accuracy about 1/16 inch at 100 ft (1.5 mm per 30 m) along the beam; self-leveling across the whole grade range with automatic cross-axis leveling; beam range up to about 500 ft (150 m) in good conditions; line (side-to-side aiming) range about 20 degrees; waterproof and dustproof to IP68 (can sit in a flooded manhole invert); operating temperature about -4 F to 122 F; NiMH battery about 40 hours (red) or 30 hours (green). Remote control range is roughly 425 ft by radio over the top and 500 ft infrared down the pipe. Grade is entered in percent, so convert from ft per ft or inches per foot first (0.0040 ft/ft = 0.40%). Other brands are similar; check your model's sheet.
field.title: Pipe laser specs: grade range, accuracy and beam range
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: Spectra Precision DG613/DG613G/DG813 pipe laser data sheet
