field.text: Pipe lasers come in red (600 to 680 nm) and green (510 to 570 nm) beams. Green looks much brighter to the human eye, so crews find it easier to see on the target in daylight at the trench end, in bright sun at the pipe end and on long runs; it costs more and eats batteries faster (Spectra's green model is rated 30 hours vs 40 for red). Use the matching target color (green targets for green lasers). Beam visibility tips: shade the target; clean the target face and the laser window; keep the beam out of hot exhaust and solvent fumes; run a blower on long runs to stop shimmer; and on long runs use a target with a larger face. Laser safety: pipe lasers are Class 2 or 3R (under 5 mW); do not stare into the beam or point it at people's eyes.
field.title: Red vs green beam pipe lasers and seeing the beam
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: Spectra Precision DG613/DG613G/DG813 pipe laser data sheet; General industry practice

field.text: Each setup: let the laser settle and finish self-leveling (most flash or beep while leveling; do not trust the beam until it is steady); confirm the grade on the display matches the cut sheet, including the sign (downhill negative on some models if you set up at the upstream end; most setups are at the downstream manhole shooting upgrade); set the line to the second control point and lock it; check beam height above invert with a rod; shoot the first pipe and check its invert with a level and rod before going on; and recheck after any bump, after lunch or a long break, and when temperature changes a lot. If the laser goes out of level it should stop or flash; never keep laying on a flashing beam. Keep the remote handy so you are not climbing into the manhole to adjust.
field.title: Pipe laser before-you-lay checks
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Pipe laser targets fit inside the pipe and show where the beam hits. Types: fixed targets sized for a pipe (6, 8, 10, 12 inch and up), adjustable targets with legs or a spring frame, and 'over the top' or rod targets for setups above the pipe. The target's center must sit on the pipe's centerline at the right height for your beam setup (beam at invert height plus offset, or centered in the pipe). Put the target at the same spot in every stick (usually at the spigot end of the pipe being laid, or the bell end per your crew's method) and keep it square to the beam. Clean targets of mud and glue. A target that is tipped, set for the wrong pipe size, or not seated in the invert gives false grade. Make sure the target matches the beam color.
field.title: Pipe laser targets: sizes and placement
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: A rotary (rotating, plane) laser spins a beam to make a level or sloped plane over the site. Types: horizontal self-leveling (level plane only; good for structure pads, manhole bases, grading); single-slope (one axis can be sloped); dual-slope or dual-grade (both axes sloped, used to set a plane matching the pipe's grade along the trench); and interior or line models. Beams are usually infrared (invisible, used with receivers, longer range) or red/green visible. Uses: digging trench bottom to grade with a stick receiver, checking bedding with a rod and receiver, setting manhole inverts and pads, and grading restoration. Set it on a stable tripod away from equipment vibration and traffic, check the HI on a benchmark each setup, and recheck if it is bumped.
field.title: Rotary laser types and uses on a pipe job
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: A receiver ('eye', detector) finds the rotating laser beam and shows on grade, high or low with arrows, lights and beeps. Rod receivers clamp to a grade rod; machine receivers mount on the excavator stick or dozer blade and show the operator a display in the cab. Most have accuracy (deadband) settings, often fine, medium and coarse (fine might be around 1/16 inch, coarse around 1/4 inch or more; check your model): use coarse for digging, fine for checking final subgrade or pipe. Clamp the receiver square on the rod at the right reading, plumb the rod with a rod level, and read the on-grade line at the receiver's marked notch. Machine receivers need the stick plumb when reading, unless the system has a tilt sensor. Check against a known point at startup.
field.title: Laser receivers: rod and machine eyes, accuracy settings
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Optical levels sit on a tripod and you read a rod through the scope. A builder's level (dumpy level) is leveled by hand with screws and a bubble vial and stays level only as long as you keep the bubble centered. An automatic level has a compensator (a pendulum prism) that keeps the line of sight level once the circular bubble is roughly centered, which is faster and more forgiving; it is the common survey-grade optical level on construction sites. Both need regular checks. Lasers make it a one-person job, but an optical level is cheap, needs no batteries, works in sun and fog where a laser receiver may struggle, and is the standard backup for checking a laser or shooting benchmarks. Always read the rod at the center cross-hair, not the stadia hairs above and below.
field.title: Builder's level vs automatic level vs laser
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: Jerry Mahun, Open Access Surveying Library: level check and adjustment; General industry practice

field.text: Check an automatic level for collimation (is the line of sight truly level?) with a peg test: set two points about 75 to 100 ft apart; set up near one point and read both rods (one short sight, one long sight); move to near the other point and read both again. If the instrument is perfect, the elevation difference between the points comes out the same both ways; any difference shows collimation error, which a shop or the manual's adjustment fixes. Compensator check: sight a rod and note the reading, gently press down on the front of the scope (the reading moves), then release; the cross-hair should return to the original reading. Or tilt slightly with a leveling screw and see if the reading holds. A sticky compensator means the level cannot be trusted. Balance backsight and foresight distances in daily work to cancel small errors.
field.title: Checking an automatic level: peg test and compensator check
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: Jerry Mahun, Open Access Surveying Library: level check and adjustment

field.text: Tripod setup: spread the legs to a stable stance with the head roughly level; push each foot firmly into the ground (step on the foot pads); on pavement, use a tripod star or chain so legs cannot slide. Tighten leg clamps. Mount the instrument hand-tight, center the bubble with the leveling screws, and on an optical level focus the eyepiece on the cross-hairs first, then focus on the rod and check there is no parallax (cross-hairs do not move against the rod when you move your eye). Keep the setup out of equipment paths and away from the trench edge, and do not lean on or bump the tripod. In sun and heat, shade the instrument; on hot days the air near the ground shimmers, so keep sights shorter. Check your HI on a benchmark whenever the setup might have moved.
field.title: Setting up a level or laser on a tripod
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Grade rods (level rods, story poles) come as telescoping fiberglass or aluminum rods, 13 to 25 ft, graduated in feet, tenths and hundredths (engineer's rod) or feet, inches and eighths (architect's rod). Use the scale that matches your cut sheets; most civil plans and grade sheets are in decimal feet. A rod must be plumb: use a rod level (circular bubble) or rock the rod slowly toward and away from the instrument and take the lowest reading. Make sure telescoping sections are fully extended and locked at the button; a section that slipped down an inch reads every shot wrong. Keep the foot clean of mud, set it on the exact point (pipe invert, hub, top of stake), and use a fixed-length grade pole with a foot for checking laid pipe invert.
field.title: Grade rods: types and keeping them plumb
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: On an engineer's rod each foot is split into tenths and hundredths. The red numbers mark whole feet; the black numbers mark tenths (1 through 9). Each tenth is split into 10 hundredths by black bars; the 'E' shapes on many rods cover 0.05 ft, with the points of the E at 0.01, 0.03 and 0.05. Read feet, then tenths, then count hundredths: a cross-hair two bars above the 4 at the 6 ft mark reads 6.42. On a grade rod with a receiver, set the receiver's on-grade notch at the reading you want. Common mistake: mixing up 0.1 ft with 1 inch (0.1 ft = 1.2 inches); another is reading the wrong foot mark when it is hidden. Call readings back to the instrument person to confirm.
field.title: Reading a tenths rod (engineer's rod)
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Tapes used by pipe crews: carpenter's tapes in feet and inches (fine for cutting pipe if the plans are in inches); engineer's tapes in feet, tenths and hundredths (match decimal-feet cut sheets and stationing; 25 ft pocket or 100 to 300 ft fiberglass/steel reels); and diameter (pi) tapes that read diameter directly when wrapped around a pipe, graduated in hundredths of an inch. U.S. Pipe recommends a diameter tape graduated in 100ths to check DI spigot diameter where you plan to cut near the bell or on 14 inch and larger pipe. Long tapes: pull taut, keep them straight and off obstacles, and avoid kinks; fiberglass stretches less with heat than steel but can stretch under hard pull. Do not use a steel tape near overhead lines or energized equipment.
field.title: Tape measures on the pipe job: tenths, inches and diameter tapes
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: U.S. Pipe TYTON JOINT submittal and assembly instructions; General industry practice

field.text: String line (mason's line, grade string) is still used for batter boards, curb and structure layout, and short pipe runs. Use braided or twisted nylon mason's line in a bright color (pink, yellow); braided holds tension and resists fraying, twisted is cheaper. Pull it tight with a line winder, line blocks, pins or nails; a long span sags in the middle, so support it every 25 to 50 ft with batter boards or stakes set to grade, and check sag with the rod. Wind and a bird landing on it move it, and crews bump it, so recheck often. A line level hung on the string is only rough and not accurate enough for pipe grade. Batter board method details are in the grade and survey chunks.
field.title: String lines: types, tension and sag
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: A total station measures horizontal angles, vertical angles and distance electronically, so it can give coordinates and elevations of any point it sees. Distances are measured to a prism on a pole or, on reflectorless models, straight off a surface. Robotic total stations track the prism so one person can stake out. Common uses on utility jobs: staking manholes, offsets and structures; as-builting inverts and rims; and checking GPS or machine control. Setup: over a known control point (with backsight to another control point) or by resection from two or more known points. Always shoot a check point after setup and every so often. Accuracy depends on the instrument (angle accuracy is commonly 1 to 5 arc-seconds) and the setup. Elevations from a total station are usually less precise than a good level over long sight lines.
field.title: Total station basics for crews
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: A GPS (GNSS) rover on a pole gives position and elevation using RTK (real-time kinematic) corrections from a base station on a known point or from a network (VRS/NTRIP over cellular). Corrections arrive by radio or internet. A FIXED solution means the receiver resolved the carrier-phase ambiguity: typical accuracy about 1 to 2 cm (0.03 to 0.07 ft) horizontal and 2 to 3 cm (0.07 to 0.10 ft) vertical in open sky. A FLOAT solution is only about 0.1 to 0.5 m (0.3 to 1.6 ft) and must never be used for grade or stakeout. Single-base RTK is reliable within roughly 20 to 30 km (12 to 19 miles) of the base. Vertical is the weak direction, which matters on flat sewer grades: many crews use GPS for location and the laser or level for invert grade.
field.title: GPS rover basics: RTK, fixed vs float
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: Swift Navigation glossary: what is RTK

field.text: Rover habits: start each day by shooting a known control point or benchmark and compare (record the difference); make sure the job file has the right coordinate system and site calibration (localization) the surveyor set up, or points can be off by feet; keep the pole bubble centered and the rod height entered correctly (a wrong rod height is a common elevation bust); wait for a fixed solution and watch the precision readout (HRMS/VRMS) before taking a shot; expect worse results near tall buildings, trees, under bridges, in deep trenches and next to excavator booms (multipath and blocked sky); and store points with good descriptions for as-builts. Never stake critical grade on a float solution. If the base gets bumped or moved, all its shots after that are suspect.
field.title: GPS rover field practice: checks and site calibration
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: Swift Navigation glossary: what is RTK; General industry practice

field.text: A plumb bob (brass or steel bob on a string) is still the simplest way to drop a point from the surface down into a trench or manhole: hang it from a string stretched between offset stakes or from a laser's centering mark, let it stop swinging (dip it in a bucket of water if wind makes it swing), and mark the point below. Used to set the pipe laser over the line, to transfer centerline from batter boards to the trench bottom, and to check manhole steps or frames are centered. Many pipe lasers have a top plumb mark or a down-pointing laser plumb. A torpedo level or a 2 to 4 ft level on the pipe gives a quick slope check, and digital (smart) levels can read percent grade directly, but neither replaces a laser or rod shot for true invert grade.
field.title: Plumb bob and transferring line down a trench or manhole
field.topic: Tools: survey and laying instruments (lasers, levels, rods, GPS)
field.source: General industry practice

field.text: Quick planning numbers (legal payload depends on your state, axle spacing and the truck's empty weight; check your scale tickets). Single-axle dump: about 5 to 8 CY, 5 to 8 tons. Tandem (10-wheeler): about 12 to 18 CY, 12 to 15 tons (more where state law allows). Tri-axle: about 15 to 20 CY, 16 tons in strict bridge-formula states up to about 22 to 23 tons where state law allows. Quad-axle: about 18 to 22 CY, 18 to 27 tons. Super dump / Super 10 / Super 18 (trailing axle): about 18 to 22 CY, 19 to 26 tons, up to about 28. Semi end dump: about 22 to 37 CY, about 22 to 26 tons. Belly dump: about 20 to 26 CY, about 22 to 26 tons. Side dump: about 20 to 31 CY. Articulated haulers: 25 to 60 tons. Roll-offs: 10 to 40 CY. Mixers: 8 to 11 CY concrete. Water trucks: 2,000 to 4,000 gal. Rule: loads = whichever is less, the heaped yards or legal tons divided by tons per loose yard.
field.title: Truck capacity cheat sheet: how many yards and tons each truck hauls
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Summary of the chunks in this file (manufacturer specs, trade press, FHWA)

field.text: Dump body size is quoted two ways. Struck (water level) capacity is the box filled level with the top of the sides: length x inside width x side height / 27. Heaped capacity adds a pile above the sides; off-road makers (Cat, Volvo, Deere) rate bodies 'heaped SAE 2:1', a pile sloping 1 ft up for every 2 ft in. Example: a Load King 16 ft body, 88 in inside width, 48 in sides (sold as '16 CY'): 16 x 7.33 x 4.0 / 27 = 17.4 CY struck; a 2:1 heap on that box adds about 3.4 CY, so roughly 20.8 CY heaped. A 10 ft single-axle body, 86.5 in wide with 29 in sides: about 6.5 CY struck, about 8.3 heaped. Real loads are rarely heaped on the road: loads must not spill (tarp laws), and most materials hit the weight limit first. Ask the seller whether a 'yard' rating is struck or heaped, and with or without sideboards.
field.title: Struck vs heaped capacity: how dump body yards are rated
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Custom Truck One Source Load King LK-16 and LK-10 spec sheets; Volvo CE and Cat spec pages (SAE 2:1 heap); volumes computed

field.text: A single-axle dump (one steer axle, one drive axle, often a 33,000 lb class or lighter chassis) carries a 10 to 12 ft body. Load King's 10 ft body is rated 'up to 7 CY' (86.5 in wide, 29 in sides; about 6.5 CY struck by the numbers). Smaller landscape bodies, like Rugby's 9 to 12 ft bodies, are 2 to 4 CY. Typical legal payload is roughly 5 to 8 tons, set by the axle ratings and the 20,000 lb federal single-axle limit on the drive axle. Weight governs for stone: 7 tons of #57 at about 1.4 tons per CY is only 5 CY. Use for: city work, small service and lateral jobs, hauling a few yards of bedding, cold patch and topsoil, and tight streets where a tandem won't fit. Check the door sticker (GVWR) and weigh it loaded; an overloaded single axle is the most common overweight ticket on small crews.
field.title: Single-axle dump truck capacity (5 to 8 yard dump)
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Custom Truck LK-10 spec sheet; Rugby Manufacturing body chart; FHWA axle limits; industry practice for payload

field.text: A tandem dump (steer axle plus two drive axles; 'ten-wheeler', 'tandem axle dump') usually carries a 14 to 18 ft body, about 12 to 18 CY struck; a common 16 ft body with 48 in sides is about 16 to 17 CY struck and about 20 heaped. Legal gross is set by the bridge formula: about 51,000 to 54,000 lb for 3 axles 20 to 24 ft apart (Custom Truck cites 52,500 lb at 22 ft). With a typical empty weight of about 25,000 to 28,000 lb, legal payload is roughly 11.5 to 14.5 tons under the bridge formula, more where state law allows. So a tandem weighs out at about 9 to 10 CY of stone or wet clay. Break-even is about 14 tons / 17 CY = 0.8 tons per CY, so only mulch, chips or light dry topsoil fill it by volume; loam and dirt weigh out first. Planning numbers: 13 to 14 tons per load, about 10 loose CY of spoil per load (about 8 bank CY at 25% swell).
field.title: Tandem dump truck (10-wheeler) capacity: yards and tons
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: FHWA Bridge Formula (computed); Custom Truck One Source super dump article (52,500 lb at 22 ft); Load King LK-16 spec; tare weights are industry typical

field.text: A tri-axle is a tandem dump with one lift (pusher or tag) axle added, 4 axles total. Bodies are usually 16 to 18 ft, about 15 to 20 CY struck. Payload depends heavily on the state. Under strict bridge-formula rules a 4-axle truck 22 to 24 ft long is limited to about 56,500 to 58,000 lb gross; Equipment World reported tri-axles limited to about 16 tons under federal and Texas bridge-formula law. States with higher straight-truck limits allow more: a Pennsylvania hauler reported 73,280 lb gross on a 4-axle unit and tri-axles netting about 47,000 lb (23.5 tons). Typical range: 16 to 23 tons. At #57 stone (about 1.4 tons per CY) that's about 11.5 to 16.5 CY, so weight governs before the bed is full. The lift axle must be down and loaded to count; check your registration and state DOT.
field.title: Tri-axle dump truck capacity: how many yards and tons
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Equipment World, 'Superdump solution'; ForConstructionPros, 'How to Specify Your Best Dump Truck' (Taylor Services, PA); FHWA bridge formula (computed)

field.text: A quad-axle dump is a tandem with two lift axles, 5 axles total, common in the Northeast, Pennsylvania, New York and other states whose straight-truck limits reward extra axles. Bodies run about 18 to 20 ft, roughly 18 to 22 CY struck. Under the federal bridge formula, 5 axles spread about 24 to 26 ft are limited to about 63,000 to 64,000 lb gross, roughly 14 to 16 tons of payload after a 32,000 to 35,000 lb truck. Where state law allows more gross on straight trucks, quads often scale about 22 to 27 tons. That's the number to ask your hauler for: tons per load on your route. At #57 stone (about 1.4 tons per CY), 25 tons is about 18 CY. Quads are longer and turn wider than tandems; plan the backing route to the trench and the dump spot.
field.title: Quad-axle dump truck capacity (quad, 5-axle straight truck)
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: FHWA Bridge Formula (computed); state limits vary (industry practice); see trucks-capacity worked examples

field.text: A Super Dump has a load-bearing trailing axle (Strong Industries' 'Strong Arm') hinged behind the body: down for travel, raised over the body to dump. It stretches the outer axle spacing to about 34 ft, raising bridge-formula gross: about 64,500 lb with 4 axles and up to 80,000 lb with 7 axles (steer, three pushers, tandem drive, trailing axle). Strong Industries says super dumps carry legal payloads of 19 to 26 tons, and the trailing axle adds up to 14,000 lb (7 tons) of allowable weight. A 7-axle super dump typically carries about 26 tons, roughly the same as a semi end dump, but turns and backs like a straight truck. Bodies are usually 18 to 22 CY. Raise the trailing axle and check overhead before dumping. Common names: super dump, Super 10, Strong Arm, trailing-axle dump.
field.title: Super dump / Super 10: payload with a trailing (Strong Arm) axle
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Strong Industries, superdumps.com; Custom Truck One Source; ForConstructionPros (26 tons on a 7-axle super dump)

field.text: 'Super 16' and 'Super 18' are trade names for super dumps, counted by tires. A Super 18 usually has a steer axle, three steerable pushers, a tandem drive and a trailing axle: 7 axles, 80,000 lb gross. Equipment World described a Texas fleet's 'Super 18s' with a 20,000 lb set-forward steer, three 8,000 lb pushers, 46,000 lb tandem drives and a trailing axle rated up to 13,000 lb, hauling up to 28 tons legal. A FleetOwner story had a paver going from 23.5 tons of asphalt to 25.5 tons with Super 18s. A Super 16 typically has one fewer pusher, so slightly less payload. 'Super 10' is the tandem with a trailing axle. Exact names vary by region and builder, so ask the hauler 'how many tons legal on this route?' and go by the ticket. All need firm, level ground to dump, and the trailing axle must be up before the body is raised.
field.title: Super 16 and Super 18 dump trucks: what the names mean
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Equipment World, 'Trucks: Superdump solution'; FleetOwner, 'Paving the way'

field.text: Michigan has the heaviest truck limits in the US, grandfathered under the 1982 federal 80,000 lb standard. Michigan limits axle loads, not gross weight: by statute, 18,000 lb per axle when axles are 9 ft or more apart, 13,000 lb when 3.5 to 9 ft apart, and 9,000 lb when closer. So Michigan dump trucks and gravel trains (straight trucks and doubles with many lift axles, 'centipedes') carry big payloads, often well over 30 tons on the heaviest combinations, spread over many lightly loaded axles. MDOT calls 164,000 lb theoretical (few trucks reach it) and compares one 11-axle Michigan truck at 154,000 lb with two federal 5-axle trucks (160,000 lb on 10 axles): about 13,000 vs 17,000 lb per axle. Michigan's frost laws cut these limits in spring. Out of state, the 80,000 lb federal limit and the bridge formula apply on the Interstate. Ask the hauler for legal tons on your route.
field.title: Michigan trucks: 164,000 lb, 11 axles and multi-axle gravel trains
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: MDOT Truck Weight brochure; Michigan Vehicle Code MCL 257.722; The Autopian (Michigan 164,000 lb explainer)

field.text: A truck and pup is a dump truck pulling a dump trailer ('pup'), common in the West, especially California. A transfer is a dump truck pulling a separate trailer box that rolls into the truck body to dump ('transfer dump', 'slam-door transfer'); a trade article describes one hauling two 10-CY loads per trip. Typical combined legal payload is about 24 to 26 tons where the combination meets the 80,000 lb gross and bridge-formula spacing: roughly 10 to 14 CY in the truck plus 10 to 14 CY in the pup or trailer box. They haul semi-sized loads but each box dumps like a short body, which is handy on streets and tight sites. The downsides are backing a trailer to a trench or paver and needing room to drop or swap the pup. Ask the hauler whether the price is per load, per ton or per hour, and for the legal tons on your route.
field.title: Truck and pup / transfer dump: truck plus trailer capacity
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: ForConstructionPros, 'How to Specify Your Best Dump Truck' (transfer, two 10-yd loads); industry practice for payload

field.text: End dumps ('semi end dump', 'end dump trailer', 'half round') are tractor-trailers whose tub tips up to dump out the back. Lengths are commonly 26 to 40 ft; 34 to 39 ft is typical for aggregate and dirt. Capacity varies with length, side height and shape: a 35 ft half-round with 57 in sides lists 36.9 CY at about 8,600 lb empty; deeper 'hi-cube' tubs go higher for light material. Typical range for dirt and stone: about 22 to 37 CY. Frameless trailers are lighter (more payload); framed ones are stiffer and more stable on rough ground. Legal payload on a 5-axle 80,000 lb rig is about 22 to 26 tons; one hauler reports a 39 ft frameless netting about 48,000 lb (24 tons). For dirt at about 1.3 tons per CY that's about 18.5 CY, so weight governs well before the tub is full. Biggest hazard: tip-over when dumping on soft or uneven ground.
field.title: Semi end dump trailer capacity: half round, frame and frameless
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: ITAG Equipment listing (2019 Travis 35 ft, 36.9 CY, 8,600 lb); ForConstructionPros (39 ft frameless nets about 48,000 lb); FHWA 80,000 lb

field.text: Belly dumps ('bottom dumps', 'cans') dump through gates under the trailer while moving, laying a windrow. Single trailers are about 36 to 46 ft, roughly 20 to 26 CY on tandem or tri-axle trailers; 'doubles' (two bottom dumps pulled together) carry more where state law allows. Legal payload on an 80,000 lb tractor-trailer is about 22 to 26 tons; Equipment World cites belly and end dump trailers hauling up to 24 tons. Best for free-flowing material on long runs: base course, sand, bedding stone, pipe-zone stone spread along an open trench line, and fill on embankments. Not good for sticky clay (it bridges over the gates), large rock or dumping into a hole. Gates can jam with frozen material. Check the windrow size with the spreading crew; a full can dumped at speed makes a long, low pile.
field.title: Belly dump / bottom dump trailer capacity
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Equipment World ('belly-dump and end-dump trailers up to 24 tons'); dealer listings (Ranco 23 to 24 CY trailers); industry practice

field.text: Side dumps tip the tub sideways with hydraulic cylinders, and they are much harder to tip over than end dumps because the center of gravity stays low. SmithCo's SX3-4234 tri-axle is listed at 23 CY water level and 31 CY heaped; its lifting third axle gives a shorter turning radius than a standard 40 ft tandem. One side-dump train operator reports running about 150,000 lb, possible only where state law allows multi-trailer trains. On a normal 80,000 lb tractor-trailer, legal payload is about 22 to 26 tons, like an end dump. Side dumps unload in seconds, handle everything from fine sand to boulders and broken concrete, and can dump on the move or beside a trench. They need clear space to the side and good footing. They're popular for rock, riprap, demo concrete and base on highway and site jobs.
field.title: Side dump trailer capacity
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Truck & Trailer Guide, 'MSB Excavating relies on SmithCo' (SX3-4234: 23 CY water level, 31 CY heaped); ForConstructionPros (side dump train about 150,000 lb)

field.text: Live-bottom trailers unload with a belt or chain conveyor in the floor. Walking floor (moving floor) trailers unload with sliding aluminum slats. Neither raises a box, so they unload under power lines, bridges and low trees and won't tip over, which helps in neighborhoods and under overhead utilities. Live-bottoms are common for hot mix asphalt, aggregate and sand going into pavers, spreaders or slow windrows. Legal payload on an 80,000 lb tractor-trailer is about the same as an end dump (roughly 22 to 26 tons); one trade source says the Northeast allows them 'almost as much payload' as a dump trailer. Big walking-floor chip and refuse vans hold about 90 to 108 CY (KEITH compares 108 CY walking floor to 90 CY belt), but with dirt or stone they weigh out far below that. KEITH lists unloading at about 4 to 8 minutes for a walking floor and 2 to 4 for a belt.
field.title: Live-bottom and walking floor trailers
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: KEITH Walking Floor, Belt Trailer Comparison flier; ForConstructionPros; Heavy Equipment Guide (Titan live floor)

field.text: Manufacturer ratings (heaped SAE 2:1). Cat: 725 26.5 tons / 19.6 CY; 730 31 tons / 23 CY; 740 40 tons / 29.7 CY; 740 EJ (ejector) 42 tons / 30.1 CY; 745 45.2 tons. Deere: 260 about 26.7 tons (53,334 lb) / 19.6 CY; 310 31 tons (62,005 lb) / 22.9 CY; 410 41.1 tons (82,157 lb) / 30.0 CY; 460 46.1 tons (92,197 lb) / 32.9 CY. Volvo (metric tonnes; short tons and CY by conversion): A25 25.4 t (28 tons) / 15.3 m3 (20 CY); A30 29 t (32 tons) / 17.8 m3 (23.3 CY); A40 39 t (43 tons) / 24 m3 (31.4 CY); A45 42 t (46.3 tons) / 25.5 m3 (33.4 CY); A60 55 t (60.6 tons) / 33.6 m3 (43.9 CY). These bodies are sized for about 1.35 tons per loose CY, so heavier wet clay, sand-gravel or rock fills them by weight before the heap is full. Off-road only: crossing public roads needs a permit or flaggers.
field.title: Articulated haulers (ADT, rock truck): payload and yards by size
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Western States Cat (Cat ADT specs); John Deere ADT page; Volvo CE articulated haulers page (conversions computed)

field.text: Rigid-frame off-highway trucks ('rock trucks', 'haul trucks', 'Euclids') are for mass excavation, quarries and big site jobs with good haul roads. Cat's nominal payloads (dealer list): 770 about 41 tons; 772 about 52 tons; 773 and 775 about 70 to 72 tons; the 777 class is roughly 100 tons. Mining trucks go far bigger. Get heaped body yards from the dealer spec sheet for your body; rock bodies hold less volume than dirt bodies. They need wide, maintained, watered haul roads and a big loader or excavator: the usual target is about 3 to 6 passes per truck. They're rarely used on utility pipe jobs except on big interceptors, ponds and mass grading packages. They're not street legal and are far over road weight limits, and their blind spots are huge, so light vehicles stay off the haul road.
field.title: Rigid off-highway haul trucks: payload by size
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Cleveland Brothers Cat dealer (770, 772, 773, 775 nominal payloads); 777 class and volume ratio are industry typical

field.text: Roll-off sizes are 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 30 and 40 CY. One national hauler's approximate outside dimensions and included weight: 10 yd about 14 x 7.5 x 3.5 ft, 1 to 2 tons; 15 yd 16 x 7.5 x 4.5 ft, 1 to 2 tons; 20 yd 22 x 7.5 x 4.5 ft, 2 to 3 tons; 30 yd 22 x 7.5 x 6 ft, 2 to 4 tons; 40 yd 22 x 7.5 x 8 ft, 4 to 5 tons. The tons are pricing limits; overage is billed per ton. Dirt, concrete, asphalt and brick are heavy: 10 CY of dirt at about 1.3 tons per CY is about 13 tons, far over the included tons and often more than the hauler will carry. Haulers put dense debris in 10-yd (sometimes 'dirt box' or low-side) containers and tell you to fill them only partway. Ask before loading spoil or broken concrete into a roll-off. Set boxes on asphalt, concrete or gravel with boards, not soft dirt, and keep them clear of overhead lines.
field.title: Roll-off containers: 10, 20, 30, 40 yard dumpster sizes and weight limits
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Dumpsters.com roll-off size guide; Wikipedia 'Roll-off (dumpster)' (sizes, dense debris, placement); weight math computed

field.text: Ready-mix trucks commonly carry 8 to 11 CY; the average load is about 10 CY. Front-discharge mixers run about 10 to 12, and compact mixers 2 to 3 CY. Concrete weighs about 145 to 150 lb per cubic ft, about 3,900 to 4,050 lb per CY, so 10 CY is about 40,000 lb of load. Legal yards depend on axles and length. Bridge-formula mixers are longer, with a booster (tag) axle at the rear; one spec guide says a 36 ft bridge needs at least 427 in from steer to booster. Lighter trucks and fewer axles carry fewer yards, and plants short-load trucks on posted roads or during frost laws. Flowable fill (lighter, about 90 to 145 lb per cubic ft) usually ships at the same 8 to 10 CY because the drum, not weight, is the limit. Order in full truckloads when you can; short loads (often under 3 to 5 CY) carry fees. Wet concrete burns skin: gloves, boots, eye protection.
field.title: Concrete mixer truck capacity: yards per load by axles
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Everything About Concrete (8 to 11 CY, about 4,000 lb/CY); Equipment World, 'Spec'ing a mixer truck' (bridge-formula booster, 427 in); weight math computed

field.text: On-road water trucks usually carry 2,000 to 4,000 gallons; Custom Truck's LK 4000 is rated 4,000 US gal with front, side and rear spray valves and a 4x3 pump. Water weighs about 8.34 lb per gallon, so: 2,000 gal = 16,680 lb = about 8.3 tons; 3,000 gal = about 12.5 tons; 4,000 gal = 33,360 lb = about 16.7 tons. A 4,000-gal tank is too heavy for a single-axle chassis and needs a tandem; 33,360 lb of water plus the truck puts many tandems near or over legal gross, so check the plate and scale it full. Off-road water wagons and articulated-chassis tanks carry about 5,000 to 20,000 gal. For a fill or test water estimate: gallons needed / tank size = loads, then add the fill and travel cycle. Hydrant filling usually needs a city meter and backflow device. A partly full tank surges on turns and slopes, so use baffled tanks and slow down.
field.title: Water truck capacity: gallons and weight (2,000 to 4,000 gal)
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Custom Truck LK 4000 water truck spec sheet; weight of water 8.34 lb/gal (computed)

field.text: Typical specs from a trade directory: Vactor 2100i combination sewer cleaner, 5 to 15 CY debris body, 1,000 to 1,500 gal water. Hydro-excavators: TRUVAC HXX 12 or 15 CY with 1,200 gal; Super Products Mud Dog 1200, 12 CY and 1,500 gal; Mud Dog 1600, 16 CY and 2,000 gal; Hi-Vac X-Vac 12 to 15 CY and 1,450 gal; Huber Baron 12 CY and 1,500 gal; Kaiser CV 11 to 13 CY and 1,800 to 2,250 gal; Supervac Hercules 15 to 18 CY. Compact and city units have 7 to 8 CY and 575 to 800 gal; trailer vacs have 2.5 to 4 CY and 200 to 400 gal. Air movers and air-excavation Guzzlers are 16 to 18 CY with little or no water. Debris body yards are volume only. Wet slurry is heavy (about 1.4+ tons per CY), so a full 12 to 15 CY body can be 17 to 22 tons, often more than legal payload. Many hydrovacs weigh out before the tank is full; ask the operator.
field.title: Vacuum and hydro-excavation trucks: debris body yards and water gallons
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Pumper magazine vacuum excavation equipment directory; Vactor TRUVAC HXX sell sheet; weight math computed

field.text: To plan dump trips for a hydro-ex or vac truck: (1) find the volume dug: a 1 ft x 1 ft x 6 ft deep potholing hole is 6 cubic ft = 0.22 CY in place; (2) add the water you put in. Hydro-ex slurry is often more water than soil, so the debris body fills faster than the soil volume suggests. Many operators plan 1.5 to 2+ CY of debris per CY of soil removed; check yours. (3) Divide the usable debris volume (body size, or less if the truck weighs out) by debris per hole. Example: 12 CY body, holes of 0.22 CY soil at 2x bulking = 0.44 CY debris each, so 12 / 0.44 = 27 holes in theory. Plan about 20 because of weight and spillover. Decant only where your permit allows; slurry usually goes to an approved dump site, not the storm drain. Water also runs out: 1,200 gal at about 10 to 20 gpm wand flow is about 1 to 2 hours of digging.
field.title: Hydrovac and vac truck: how many holes or yards per load
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Industry practice (bulking factor varies); volumes computed; pump rates from TRUVAC HXX sell sheet (10 to 25 gpm options)

field.text: One maker's loading chart for gasketed PVC sewer pipe (DR 35 and SDR 26, 14 ft lengths), feet per skid x skids per truck: 4 in, 938 ft x 18 = 16,884 ft (about 1,206 sticks); 6 in, 462 x 18 = 8,316 ft (594 sticks); 8 in, 196 x 24 = 4,704 ft (336 sticks); 10 in, 112 x 24 = 2,688 ft (192 sticks); 12 in, 42 x 36 = 1,512 ft (108 sticks); 15 in, 42 x 18 = 756 ft (54 sticks). Big plastic pipe 'cubes out' (fills the trailer by volume) long before it reaches the weight limit. Counts change with brand, length (13, 14 or 20 ft), SDR and trailer, so get your supplier's truckload quantity before ordering. Order full truckloads or full skids when possible; broken skids cost more. Unload with forks or a spreader bar, not chains, and stack no higher than the maker allows.
field.title: PVC sewer pipe per truckload: feet and sticks by size
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Charlotte Pipe TG-IR technical guide, PVC sewer pipe loading charts (totals computed)

field.text: HDPE (IPS sizes, straight lengths), from Chevron Phillips' truckload table, feet per truck on 40 / 50 / 53 ft trailers: 14 in DR 11, 1,680 / 1,950 / 1,855; 24 in DR 13.5, 640 / 800 / 848; 36 in, 160 / 200 / 212; 54 in DR 15.5, 80 / 100 / 106. Some loads need a 47,000 lb hauling rating. Ductile iron is weight-limited: McWane's goal is about 40,000 lb of pipe per truck (each row about 5,000 lb), with bundles no taller than 102 in or wider than 96 in, under a 13 ft 6 in truck height limit. Sticks per load = about 40,000 to 45,000 lb / weight per stick from the submittal. For example, if an 18 ft stick weighs 450 lb, that's about 89 to 100 sticks. Get exact counts from the supplier or sales rep. Fittings, gaskets and lube ride on the same truck and use up weight.
field.title: HDPE and ductile iron pipe per truckload
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Chevron Phillips Chemical (Performance Pipe) HDPE truckload table T.1.3; McWane Ductile, 'How much ductile iron pipe can ship on one truck'

field.text: A 5-axle tractor and 48 to 53 ft flatbed or step-deck at 80,000 lb gross typically weighs about 30,000 to 33,000 lb empty, leaving roughly 47,000 to 50,000 lb (23.5 to 25 tons) of legal payload. Ductile iron and concrete pipe load to that weight limit; PVC and HDPE fill the deck by volume first. Precast manholes, structures and RCP are counted by pieces and weight: a load is often only a few large pieces, so get piece weights from the precaster's ticket. Width is limited to 8.5 ft (102 in) without a permit, and height is typically 13.5 to 14 ft depending on the state. Self-unloading boom trucks and knuckle-boom trailers carry less (the crane weighs a lot) but unload without your excavator. Plan the unloading spot: firm, level ground, out of traffic, with the pipe strung where the excavator can reach it.
field.title: Flatbeds and pipe trucks: legal payload for pipe, precast and material
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: FHWA (80,000 lb gross; 102 in width per 23 CFR 658.15); tare and payload ranges are industry typical

field.text: A common 7 x 14 ft tandem dump trailer (for example a Big Tex 14LX) is rated 14,000 lb GVWR with about 10,340 lb payload (5.2 tons) and a 168 x 83 x 24 in box, about 7.2 CY struck. Weight governs fast: 5.2 tons of #57 stone at about 1.4 tons per CY is only about 3.7 CY, so a level-full box of stone or wet dirt is overloaded. Light material (mulch, dry topsoil) can fill the box. Your pickup's towing rating, hitch rating and GCWR must cover the loaded trailer. Federal CDL rules: a combination over 26,000 lb GCWR towing a trailer rated over 10,000 lb needs a Class A CDL in commercial use (49 CFR 383.91). A 1-ton pickup plus a 14,000 lb trailer usually crosses that line. Spread the load evenly with about 10 to 15% tongue weight, and tarp it.
field.title: Pickup and dump trailer: how many yards and tons it can haul
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Rentz Trailers Big Tex 14LX spec listing; 49 CFR 383.91 (vehicle groups); volumes computed

field.text: Use loose (in the truck) weights for truck math, not bank or compacted. Caterpillar's loose weights in tons per loose CY: dry packed earth about 1.28; loam about 1.05; natural or wet clay about 1.40; clay and gravel, dry, about 1.20; pit-run gravel about 1.63; damp sand about 1.43; wet sand about 1.55; wet sand and gravel about 1.70; crushed stone about 1.35; topsoil about 0.80. Supplier numbers: #57 and clean stone about 1.35 to 1.5 (use 1.4); dense-graded base (crusher run, DGA, CA-6) loose about 1.4 to 1.6; riprap about 1.5 to 1.7; broken concrete and RCA about 1.2 to 1.4; asphalt millings (RAP) about 1.1 to 1.4. Sticky wet clay and saturated spoil can run about 1.5 tons per loose CY or more. Moisture swings these a lot; your scale tickets are the best number.
field.title: Tons per loose yard for truck loads: dirt, clay, sand, stone, concrete, millings
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Caterpillar Earthwork Volumes Reference Tables (lb/LCY converted /2,000); existing KB aggregates-estimating-2/3/5 supplier values

field.text: Every truck has two limits: body volume (yards) and legal payload (tons). The load it can actually carry is whichever runs out first. Loose CY per load = the smaller of (a) heaped body CY and (b) legal payload tons / tons per loose CY. Tons per load = loose CY per load x tons per loose CY. Loads needed = total loose CY / loose CY per load, or total tons / tons per load, always rounded up. To convert trench (bank) yards: loose CY = bank CY x (1 + swell), for example 1.25 for common earth. Break-even = legal tons / body CY: about 0.7 to 0.8 tons per CY for a tandem or semi end dump, about 1.3 for a super dump. Above that the truck weighs out first, so stone, sand, clay, dirt, concrete and millings weigh out most on-road dumps; only mulch or light topsoil fill by volume. Scale tickets show the real tons; a truck that keeps scaling over is overloaded, not 'efficient'.
field.title: Loads per truck rule: is it weight or volume that limits the load?
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Standard earthmoving method (Caterpillar load factor and swell); arithmetic

field.text: Job: 400 bank CY of moist common earth to haul off. Swell 25%, so 400 x 1.25 = 500 loose CY; loose weight about 1.3 tons per CY. Tandem: 14 tons legal / 1.3 = 10.8 CY by weight, body about 16 to 20 CY, so weight governs at 10.8 CY (8.6 bank CY) and 500 / 10.8 = 46.4, so 47 loads. Super 10 / super dump: 26 tons / 1.3 = 20 CY, body about 20 CY heaped, so about 20 CY per load and 500 / 20 = 25 loads. Semi end dump: 24 tons / 1.3 = 18.5 CY, tub 30+ CY, so weight governs at 18.5 CY and 500 / 18.5 = 27.1, so 28 loads. So one super dump or semi does the work of nearly two tandems. Check whether the dump site, the street and the trench edge can take a semi; the super dump often wins on tight utility jobs. Use your own legal tons and tickets.
field.title: Worked example: hauling spoil in a tandem vs Super 10 vs semi end dump
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Computed with Caterpillar swell and loose weights; payloads from this file (Strong Industries, ForConstructionPros)

field.text: #57 stone (clean rock, 3/4 to 1 in washed) weighs about 1.4 tons per loose CY. Tri-axle at 20 tons legal: 20 / 1.4 = 14.3 CY, and the body holds about 16 to 18 CY struck, so weight governs. At 18 tons it's 12.9 CY; at 22 tons, 15.7 CY. To order 300 tons in quads: at 25 tons per load, 300 / 25 = 12 loads; at 22 tons, 300 / 22 = 13.6, so 14 loads; at 27 tons, 300 / 27 = 11.1, so 12 loads (the last one short). In tri-axles at 20 tons, 300 / 20 = 15 loads. Going from tons to yards in the trench: 300 tons / 1.4 = about 214 CY of stone. Order in tons, but plan and check placement by yards. Tell the quarry the truck type so they load to legal weight, and check the first tickets.
field.title: Worked example: #57 stone in tri-axles and quads (how many loads for 300 tons)
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Computed; unit weight from KB aggregates-estimating-2; payloads from this file

field.text: Wet, sticky clay is about 1.4 tons per loose CY (Caterpillar) and often 1.5 or more when saturated. A tandem with 14 tons legal: 14 / 1.5 = 9.3 CY, even though the 16 ft body holds about 17 CY struck. If the loader fills it level, that's about 17 x 1.5 = 25.5 tons, about 11 to 12 tons overweight. Fix: count passes. With a 2 CY bucket at about 85% fill (1.7 CY per pass), 9.3 / 1.7 = 5.5, so stop at 5 to 6 passes, not 'until it's full'. Compare topsoil at about 0.8 tons per CY: level-full 17.4 CY is about 13.9 tons, right at the limit, so light material fills by volume, but heaping it (20.8 CY, 16.6 tons) still overloads. Wet clay also sticks in the bed and can tip trucks when it hangs up during dumping, so dump on level ground and keep people clear. Weigh the first loads and set the pass count for the day.
field.title: Worked example: wet clay weighs out before the bed is full
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Caterpillar loose weights; computed; fill factor practice (Cat handbook ranges, KB heavy-trucks-haul-9)

field.text: Federal Interstate limits: 20,000 lb on a single axle, 34,000 lb on a tandem (axles more than 40 in and up to 96 in apart), 80,000 lb gross, and the Bridge Formula W = 500 x [LN/(N-1) + 12N + 36]. Here W is the maximum lb on any group of axles, L the feet between the outer axles of the group, and N the number of axles. Two tandems may carry 34,000 lb each if the first and last axles are 36 ft or more apart. Computed values (rounded to 500 lb): 3 axles at 22 ft, 52,500; 4 at 22 ft, 56,500; 5 at 24 ft, 63,000; 4 at 34 ft, 64,500; 7 at 34 ft, 80,000; 5 at 51 ft, 80,000. That's why lift axles, trailing axles and long trailers raise payload. Payload = legal gross minus the truck's empty (tare) weight. States set limits off the Interstate, some are grandfathered higher, and local roads and bridges can be posted lower.
field.title: Legal truck weight basics: 80,000 lb and the federal bridge formula
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: FHWA, Bridge Formula Weights; formula values computed

field.text: Weight limits are state law, so the same truck carries different tons in different states. Michigan allows up to 164,000 lb on 11 axles (axle-based rules). Pennsylvania and other Northeast states allow heavier straight trucks, like quads and tri-axles (a PA hauler reports 73,280 lb on a 4-axle). Strict bridge-formula states (for example Texas) hold a tri-axle to about 16 tons. Spring frost laws cut limits while roads thaw. Michigan reduces axle loads 25% on concrete and 35% on other roads during March to May, on dates the agencies post. A Minnesota county example: 5 tons per axle on gravel roads and 10 tons on paved roads unless posted. City streets, county roads and bridges can be posted lower year-round. Overweight loads need state permits, and divisible loads like dirt and stone generally can't be permitted over the limits. Check your state DOT's weight page and seasonal map, and ask your hauler for 'legal tons on this route'.
field.title: State weight exceptions, frost laws and permits: check before you haul
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck

field.text: Legal payload = the lowest of (1) the legal gross for that axle setup and route (state law and bridge formula), (2) the sum of the axle limits, and (3) the truck's own GVWR and axle ratings, minus the empty (tare) weight with fuel, driver and tarp. Steps: weigh the empty truck on a certified scale and write the tare on the door or in the app; know the registered gross (some states make you register for the weight you haul); know which axles must be down to be legal. Example: a tandem legal at 52,500 lb gross with 27,000 lb tare carries 25,500 lb = 12.75 tons. The same truck with a pusher at 56,500 lb carries about 14.75 tons, less the pusher's own weight. Lift axles only count when down and carrying weight. Track scale tickets: if loads keep coming in over, cut passes per truck; if they come in light, you're paying for air.
field.title: How to find your truck's real legal payload
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: FHWA axle and gross limits; arithmetic; industry practice

field.text: Truck cycle = load + haul + dump + return + wait/spot. Loads per truck per day = working minutes / cycle minutes, rounded down. Trucks needed = loads needed per day / loads per truck per day, rounded up. To keep a loader busy: trucks = cycle time / load time. Typical load times: Caterpillar puts a wheel loader's basic cycle (load, dump, maneuver) at 0.45 to 0.55 minutes (27 to 33 seconds), and two to three passes is optimal for on-highway trucks, so a loader with a 3 to 5 CY bucket loads a tandem or tri-axle in about 1.5 to 3 minutes. A 20 to 30-ton excavator with a 1.5 to 2 CY bucket at 18 to 25 seconds per pass needs about 6 to 10 passes, about 2.5 to 4 minutes. In a deep trench (25 to 40 s cycles) it's 4 to 6 minutes. Add 0.5 to 1 minute to spot each truck, plus scale and ticket time at the pit. Time a few real cycles on your job.
field.title: Trucking cycle math: loads per truck per day and how many trucks
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: ForConstructionPros, 'Wheel loader production tips' (Cat 0.45 to 0.55 min); Construction Business Owner, 'Your manual to effective truck loading' (2 to 3 passes); KB heavy-trucks-haul-8 cycle times

field.text: Job: haul 40 loads of spoil a day to a dump site with a 1-hour round trip. Cycle: load 5 min + haul 25 + dump 3 + return 22 + wait/spot 5 = 60 min. Day: 8 hours = 480 min, minus about 30 min for start-up, fuel and breaks = 450 working minutes. Loads per truck = 450 / 60 = 7.5, so 7 full trips. Trucks needed = 40 / 7 = 5.7, so 6 trucks. If the excavator could load nonstop at 5 minutes per truck, it could fill 12 trucks an hour (60 / 5), so 12 trucks would keep it busy. But a pipe crew digs only part of the hour, so 5 to 6 trucks is usually right. Output: with tandems at about 10.8 loose CY each, 7 loads x 6 trucks x 10.8 = about 450 loose CY a day (about 360 bank CY at 25% swell). Shorten the cycle (closer dump, staged trucks) before adding trucks.
field.title: Worked example: trucks needed with a 1-hour round trip
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Standard cyclic method (computed); swell from Caterpillar

field.text: Truck tickets are loose yards or tons, but trench quantities are bank (in-place) yards. Bank CY per load = loose CY per load x load factor, where load factor = 1 / (1 + swell). Caterpillar's load factors: common earth about 0.80 (25% swell); clay about 0.80 to 0.82; sand and gravel about 0.89 (12%); crushed or blasted rock about 0.60 (67%). Examples: a tandem carrying 10.8 loose CY of earth = 10.8 x 0.80 = 8.6 bank CY; a super dump with 20 loose CY = 16 bank CY; blasted rock in a 20 CY body = 12 bank CY. Trench check: a 3 ft wide, 9 ft deep trench is 1.0 bank CY per foot (3 x 9 / 27), so a tandem hauls about 8.6 ft of trench spoil and a super dump about 16 ft. Use these to sanity-check haul-off tickets against footage laid.
field.title: Bank yards per truckload: converting truck loads back to trench yards
field.topic: Truck hauling capacity: yards, tons and loads per truck
field.source: Caterpillar, Swell & Void Percentage, Load Factors; computed

field.text: A drinking water distribution system carries treated water from the plant or wells to customers. Parts: transmission mains (large pipes, often 16 inch and up, with few or no service connections) from the plant to storage and pressure zones; distribution mains (typically 6 to 12 inch) in streets that feed hydrants and services; service lines from the main to each customer meter and building; storage tanks and towers; booster pump stations; pressure-reducing valve stations; and valves, hydrants, air valves and blow-offs. Mains are laid in loops (gridded) where possible so water can reach any point from two directions, which keeps pressure up during fire flow, lets crews isolate a break without cutting off many customers, and avoids stagnant dead ends. Pipe materials and sizes are covered in the pipe files (ductile iron, PVC C900/C909, HDPE, concrete pressure pipe, steel).
field.title: Water distribution system overview: transmission, mains, services
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: General distribution system practice

field.text: Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Water Works), as summarized by WSB, call for distribution systems to keep at least 20 psi at ground level at all points under all flow conditions, including fire flow; normal working pressure of about 60 to 80 psi and not less than 35 psi. Illinois rules (35 IAC 604.1415) match: 20 psi minimum at all points under all flow conditions, normal working pressure at least 35 psi on distribution mains, and pressure-reducing devices on mains or individual services where static pressure exceeds 100 psi. Most plumbing codes also limit building pressure to about 80 psi, so homes on high-pressure streets get a PRV at the meter. The 20 psi floor exists because below it, backsiphonage and contamination through leaks and cross connections become likely; a main shut down or depressurized below 20 psi often triggers a boil water notice under state rules.
field.title: Water system pressure: 20 psi minimum, 35 psi normal, 60 to 80 psi typical
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: WSB summary of Ten States Standards (water distribution); Illinois 35 IAC 604.1415

field.text: Water pressure comes from elevation (head). 1 psi = 2.31 ft of water; 1 ft of water = 0.433 psi. A tank water level 150 ft above a street gives about 150 x 0.433 = 65 psi static at that street. Every 10 ft you go downhill adds about 4.3 psi; every 10 ft uphill loses 4.3 psi. That's why hilly towns have several pressure zones. Static pressure is what a gauge reads with no flow; residual pressure is what's left while water flows (friction loss lowers it). Field uses: estimating test pressure at the low point versus the high point of a test section (a 100 ft elevation difference changes the reading by 43 psi); checking a hydrant gauge reading against the tank level; and knowing that a service at the bottom of a hill may see 100+ psi and need a PRV. Gauges should be read at a known elevation.
field.title: Pressure and elevation: 2.31 ft per psi, 0.433 psi per ft
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Computed from the unit weight of water (62.4 lb/cu ft)

field.text: A pressure zone is an area served at one hydraulic grade line, usually set by the overflow elevation of a tank or a PRV setting, sized so customers stay within roughly 35/40 to 80/100 psi. Zones are separated by closed valves (zone valves), booster pump stations (pumping from a lower zone up to a higher one) and pressure-reducing valve (PRV) stations (dropping pressure from a higher zone to a lower one). Field cautions: never open a closed zone valve shown on the utility map without the utility's OK; it can over-pressure or drain a zone. PRV stations sit in vaults (confined spaces) with a main PRV, a smaller low-flow bypass PRV, isolation valves, pressure gauges and often a pressure-relief valve. Booster stations have pumps with check valves, suction pressure protection (cutting off pumps before suction drops too low), and often backup power. Tie-ins near these structures need utility coordination.
field.title: Pressure zones, booster stations and PRV stations
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: General distribution system practice; Ten States Standards concepts

field.text: Distribution storage (elevated tanks/water towers, standpipes and ground-level reservoirs) does three things: sets pressure in its zone (the water level is the hydraulic grade), stores water for peak demand and fire flow so the plant and wells can run at a steady rate, and supplies water during power or pump outages. Elevated tanks (spheroid, pedestal, multi-column, composite) and standpipes (tall cylinders) give pressure by height; ground tanks need pumps. Tanks have screened overflows that discharge to an air gap and splash pad (never connected to a sewer), screened vents, locked hatches, inlet/outlet piping often with a mixing system so water doesn't age (chlorine loss, nitrification), and drains. Tanks are inspected and cleaned periodically (often every 3 to 5 years) and disinfected after (AWWA C652). Climbing towers is fall-protection work.
field.title: Water storage tanks and towers: types and why they matter
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: General distribution system practice; Ten States Standards storage concepts

field.text: Minimum main sizes come from state rules and local standards. Ten States Standards (per WSB's summary of the current edition): 8 inch minimum for mains providing fire protection; 3 inch minimum where no fire protection is provided (older editions and many state rules use 6 inch for hydrant mains). Illinois (35 IAC 604.1415): mains serving fire hydrants at least 6 inch, or larger as needed for fire flow; 4 inch minimum in towns and subdivisions; 3 inch in rural systems with widely spaced services. Virginia (12VAC5-590-1120): 4 inch minimum distribution main, 2 inch allowed for runs under 300 ft and 3 inch for 300 to 600 ft, and no fire hydrant on pipe smaller than 6 inch. Many cities require 8 inch minimum in residential streets and 12 inch in commercial areas to meet fire flow. The plans govern; if you're asked to hang a hydrant on a 4 inch line, stop and ask.
field.title: Minimum water main sizes and hydrant main size rules
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: WSB Ten States summary; Illinois 35 IAC 604.1415; Virginia 12VAC5-590-1120

field.text: Dead-end mains let water sit, lose chlorine residual and collect sediment, so rules say minimize them and give each one a way to flush. Illinois (35 IAC 604.1425) requires flushing hydrants or devices sized to produce at least 2.5 ft/s velocity in the main being flushed, and flushing devices may not be connected directly to any sewer; Ten States Standards (per WSB) also uses 2.5 ft/s for dead-end flushing. Use a fire hydrant or a blow-off at the end of the line (see water-appurtenances-7). For an 8 inch main, 2.5 ft/s needs about 2.448 x 64 x 2.5 = 392 gpm. Plan future extensions so the end can be looped later: install a valve and a restrained plug or cap with a blow-off, so the extension can be tied in without a shutdown. Record dead-end locations for the utility's flushing program.
field.title: Dead ends, flushing hydrants and blow-off rules
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Illinois 35 IAC 604.1425; WSB Ten States summary; flow formula from Open Exam Prep

field.text: Valves on water systems (installation in water-appurtenances-1 and -2): Gate valves (resilient wedge, AWWA C509 /C515) are the standard isolation valve on 4 to 12 inch and often up to 16 to 24 inch mains; full open, no flow restriction. Butterfly valves (AWWA C504) are common 16 inch and larger; shorter and lighter, with a disc in the flow path (can't be pigged or swabbed through). Check valves stop reverse flow at pumps and some connections. Ball and plug valves are used for some large or high-pressure lines and pump stations. Tapping valves are gate valves with a flange that fits a tapping sleeve and a full-size bore for the cutter. Altitude valves close a tank inlet when the tank is full. Pressure-reducing, pressure-sustaining and flow-control valves (pilot-operated, often Cla-Val type) control pressure between zones. Know whether valves open left or right in your utility.
field.title: Water valve types: gate, butterfly, check, ball, plug, altitude
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: AWWA valve standards as commonly summarized; general practice

field.text: Valves let crews isolate a section for repair while keeping most customers in service. Common utility standards (check yours): at intersections, valves on all but one leg (a cross gets 3 or 4 valves, a tee gets 2 or 3); at each hydrant lead (auxiliary valve); maximum spacing along a main often about 500 ft in commercial areas and 800 to 1,000 ft in residential areas, or so that a shutdown affects no more than a set number of customers; valves on both sides of stream, rail and highway crossings; and at connections to transmission mains. Set valves outside the wheel path when possible, in line with property lines or a set offset so they're easy to find, with valve boxes centered on the nut and tied to the as-builts by measurements. Ten States Standards and state rules also require valves at both ends of underwater crossings (Virginia 12VAC5-590-1180).
field.title: Valve placement and spacing on water mains
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Common utility design standards; Virginia 12VAC5-590-1180

field.text: Air valve and blow-off rules aimed at keeping contamination out (installation in water-appurtenances-6 and -7): Virginia's waterworks rule (12VAC5-590-1160) requires the open end of an air relief pipe to extend at least 1 ft above ground with a screened, downward-facing elbow. Ten States Standards and most state rules prohibit connecting air relief valve vents, blow-offs, flushing devices or chamber drains directly to a sanitary or storm sewer, and don't let air valve chambers flood, because a flooded or sewer-connected vent can suck contaminated water into the main when pressure drops. Illinois prohibits connecting flushing devices to any sewer. Valve and meter pits should drain to daylight or a sump, not to a sewer. Field check: when you see a blow-off or air valve vent piped into a storm inlet on old work, report it.
field.title: Air relief and blow-off vents: no sewer connections, vent above grade
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Virginia 12VAC5-590-1160; Illinois 35 IAC 604.1425; Ten States Standards principles

field.text: Dry-barrel hydrants (AWWA C502) are used wherever it freezes: the main valve sits at the bottom of the barrel below frost, and when it closes a drain valve opens so the barrel empties into drain stone around the shoe. Wet-barrel hydrants (AWWA C503) are full of water all the time with a separate valve for each outlet; they're used only in warm climates (much of California, Hawaii, parts of the South). Dry-barrel hydrants come in compression type (valve closes with pressure, so it stays shut if the barrel is knocked off) and gate type. Typical outlets: two 2.5 inch hose nozzles and one 4.5 inch pumper (steamer) nozzle, with thread and operating nut pattern set by the local fire department. Traffic (breakaway) models have a flange and stem coupling that break on impact so the main valve stays closed. Parts: bonnet, operating nut, upper and lower barrel, shoe (foot piece), main valve, drain valve, nozzles and caps.
field.title: Fire hydrant types: dry barrel vs wet barrel
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Open Exam Prep ABC Water Distribution guide 3.2: Fire Hydrants; AWWA C502/C503 as commonly summarized

field.text: Illinois (35 IAC 604.1425) gives typical state rules: hydrant leads at least 6 inch in diameter; an auxiliary valve on every hydrant lead; hydrant drains kept at least 10 ft from sanitary sewers, storm sewers and storm drains and never connected to them; drains above the seasonal groundwater table. Where drains are plugged (high groundwater), the barrel must be pumped dry after use in freezing weather; where unplugged, provide a gravel pocket or dry well unless natural soil drains well. Open Exam Prep notes the cross-connection risk: in saturated ground, dirty water can enter through an open drain port, so utilities plug drains or use drain backflow devices there. Virginia doesn't allow fire hydrants on mains under 6 inch. Setting details (bury depth, breakaway flange height, thrust restraint) are in water-appurtenances-3.
field.title: Hydrant leads, auxiliary valves and hydrant drains: rules
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Illinois 35 IAC 604.1425; Open Exam Prep fire hydrant guide; Virginia 12VAC5-590-1120

field.text: Rules for anyone opening a hydrant (contractors filling trucks, flushing or testing): get permission and a hydrant meter or permit from the utility; use the correct hydrant wrench, not a pipe wrench; open the hydrant fully, then back off a fraction of a turn, because a partly open dry-barrel hydrant lets water blast out the drain port and wash out the soil around the shoe; never throttle flow with the hydrant main valve, use a gate valve on the outlet instead; close slowly, especially the last turns, to avoid water hammer; after closing in freezing weather, put your hand over the nozzle to feel suction (draining) or check that the barrel empties, because a barrel that holds water freezes and won't work in a fire. Report hydrants that won't open, leak, or don't drain. Keep at least 3 ft clear around hydrants; never block a hydrant with equipment or materials.
field.title: Hydrant operation: open fully, close slowly, check it drains
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Open Exam Prep hydrant and flushing guides; common utility hydrant use rules

field.text: Conventional flushing just opens hydrants until water runs clear. Unidirectional flushing (UDF) closes valves to force flow in one direction through each pipe segment toward one open hydrant, working outward from the source so clean water pushes into dirty pipe. Target velocity is at least 5 ft/s, preferably 6+ ft/s, to scour sediment. Flow needed: Q (gpm) = 2.448 x d squared x V (d = inside diameter in inches, V = ft/s); an 8 inch main at 5 ft/s needs about 783 gpm, a 16 inch main about 3,132 gpm, more than one hydrant can pass, so big mains are cleaned by pigging. Steps: plan segments on an accurate valve and hydrant map, notify customers (discolored water), monitor chlorine and turbidity at the flowing hydrant until both are good, dechlorinate discharge headed to storm drains or streams, control erosion, traffic and icing, and record volume and readings.
field.title: Unidirectional flushing (UDF) and flushing velocity
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Colorado operator guide: Fire Hydrants, Flow Testing and Flushing

field.text: Flow from a hydrant outlet measured with a pitot gauge: Q (gpm) = 29.83 x C x d squared x square root of P, where d is the outlet inside diameter in inches, P is the pitot pressure in psi, and C is the outlet coefficient (about 0.90 for smooth rounded outlets, 0.80 square-edged, 0.70 projecting into the barrel). Example: 2.5 inch outlet, C = 0.90, pitot 25 psi: 29.83 x 0.90 x 6.25 x 5 = about 839 gpm. Test results (static, residual and flow) are used to estimate available flow at 20 psi residual using the 0.54-power relationship in NFPA 291; the operator guide's example of 74 psi static, 58 psi residual while flowing 597 gpm works out to about 1,150 gpm at 20 psi (597 x (54/16)^0.54). The procedure and NFPA color codes are in water-operations-1. Use a diffuser to protect property and dechlorinate if required.
field.title: Hydrant flow test math: pitot reading to gpm
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Open Exam Prep, Colorado operator guide: Fire Hydrants, Flow Testing and Flushing

field.text: A typical small water service from main to building: the corporation stop (corp, AWWA C800) threaded into the main or into a service saddle at the tap; the service line (copper Type K, PE CTS tubing, PEX, or older galvanized or lead) to the property line; a curb stop (curb valve) with a curb box to grade, usually at or near the property line, so the utility can shut off the service; then the meter setter (yoke or copper setter with a meter, an angle meter valve on the inlet, often a check valve or dual check on the outlet) in a meter pit, vault or the building basement; then the customer's line into the building, with a PRV if pressure exceeds about 80 psi. Larger services (2 inch and up) use tapping sleeves or tees with gate valves and meter vaults. Who owns which part varies; many utilities own to the curb stop or meter. Taps and saddles: see water-appurtenances-4.
field.title: Water service line parts: corp stop, curb stop, meter setter
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: AWWA C800 and common utility service details, as commonly summarized

field.text: Meter installations follow the utility's standard detail exactly. Common points: meter pits (plastic or concrete, often 18 to 24 inch diameter for 5/8 to 1 inch meters) set to the depth the detail shows so the setter sits below frost, with the lid flush with finished grade and out of driveways where possible (or traffic-rated); setters set level so the meter reads correctly and can be removed without strain; insulated frost lids in cold climates; inlet and outlet on the correct side (flow arrow on the meter); no bends or fittings right at the meter that cause turbulence on large meters; bypass with a locked valve on large commercial meters so service can stay on while the meter is tested; and backflow assemblies after the meter when required. Virginia requires metering of all new service connections in community waterworks. Don't backfill until the utility inspects.
field.title: Meter pits, setters and meter vaults: installation points
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Common utility meter details; Virginia 12VAC5-590-1230

field.text: Small service taps are usually made with the main in service using a tapping machine (Mueller B-101 type or similar). Steps in common practice: expose and clean the main; confirm pipe material, OD and class (and the utility's DR limits for direct tapping PVC); install the saddle if required; thread the corporation stop into the saddle or main (closed corp, tap-through type) or attach the machine and drill-tap through the open corp; drill and tap in one operation, then retract the boring bar and close the corp before removing the machine; flush the shavings out through the corp before connecting the service. Never direct-tap PVC with a standard twist drill; use the shell cutter that retains the coupon. Keep taps apart from each other and from joints by the utility minimum. Disinfect the corp and fittings (AWWA C651 swabbing). Larger wet taps use a tapping sleeve and valve (water-appurtenances-5).
field.title: Tapping a live main for a service (hot tap with a tapping machine)

field.text: Main water main materials and where to find details: ductile iron (AWWA C151, cement-mortar lined, push-on or mechanical joints, polyethylene encasement in corrosive soils; pipe-ductile-iron.json); PVC (AWWA C900 for 4 to 60 inch pressure pipe, DR 18 common, DR 14 for higher pressure; C909 PVCO; pipe-pvc.json); HDPE (AWWA C906, PE 4710, butt-fused, DIPS or IPS OD; pipe-hdpe.json); concrete pressure pipe and steel (AWWA C300-series and C200) for large transmission mains (pipe-concrete.json, pipe-other-materials.json). Old systems also have cast iron (gray iron) and asbestos-cement (AC/transite) pipe; cutting AC pipe releases asbestos fibers and needs wet methods, proper tools (no power saws without controls) and trained workers under OSHA's asbestos rules. All materials in contact with drinking water must be certified to NSF/ANSI/CAN 61, and brass must meet lead-free limits.
field.title: Water main materials quick guide (see pipe files)
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Summary pointing to existing pipe files; AWWA standards as commonly summarized; OSHA asbestos rules

field.text: Three water main topics are covered in their own files; this is a pointer. Thrust restraint: concrete thrust blocks against undisturbed soil and restrained joints (MJ wedge glands, restrained push-on gaskets) at bends, tees, plugs, reducers and valves: thrust-restraint.json. Hydrostatic pressure and leakage testing under AWWA C600 (ductile iron) and C605 (PVC): test pressure rules, the allowable make-up formula L = S x D x square root of P divided by 148,000, filling and air removal: testing-water-1 through -5. Disinfection of new mains under AWWA C651 (tablet, continuous feed and slug methods, flushing, dechlorination, bac-T sampling, connections and repairs): testing-water-6 through -12. In short, a new main is laid clean, restrained, pressure tested, disinfected, flushed and sampled, and goes into service only after the lab results come back acceptable and the utility releases it.
field.title: Thrust restraint, pressure testing and disinfection: where to look
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Pointer to thrust-restraint.json and testing-water.json (AWWA C600/C605/C651 summaries)

field.text: Plain-language order of work under AWWA C651 as utilities apply it (numbers in testing-water-6 to -12): keep pipe clean during storage and laying (plugs in open ends, no trench water in the pipe); swab or spray fittings with chlorine solution; after pressure testing (or before, per spec), fill the main with chlorinated water by the method the spec names, typically about 25 mg/L held about 24 hours with a residual of at least 10 mg/L at the end; flush the heavily chlorinated water out until residual is back to normal system levels, dechlorinating discharge to protect streams; take bacteriological samples per the spec (often two sets, at set intervals along the line and at the ends); and only after passing results does the utility connect and open the new main to customers. Fill through an approved backflow-protected temporary connection, not a hose stuck in a hydrant.
field.title: Disinfecting new mains (C651) in plain terms: the sequence
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Summary of AWWA C651 as given in testing-water chunks (Open Exam Prep study guide)

field.text: Backflow is water flowing the wrong way, from a customer or a construction setup back into the public main. Two causes: backsiphonage, when supply pressure drops and creates a partial vacuum (a main break, heavy fire flow, a shutdown for a tie-in, or a hose left in a chemical tank, ditch or tank truck); and backpressure, when the downstream side is at higher pressure than the main (boilers, booster pumps, fire pumps, pressurized tanks). A cross-connection is any actual or possible link between potable water and a non-potable source. Construction examples: a hose from a hydrant into a water truck tank or into a fresh pour; filling a test section from an existing main; flushing hoses lying in a muddy trench; jetter or hydro-excavation trucks filling from hydrants. Every one needs an air gap or approved backflow assembly.
field.title: Backflow: backsiphonage vs backpressure
