field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Open Exam Prep, California operator guide: Cross-Connection Program

field.text: Device choice depends on hazard (Open Exam Prep summary): Air gap: physical separation of at least two pipe diameters, never less than 1 inch, between the supply outlet and the flood rim; best protection, any hazard. Reduced pressure principle assembly (RP, RPZ): two check valves with a relief valve between that dumps water if the zone pressure gets too close to supply pressure; for high hazards and both backsiphonage and backpressure; installed above grade, never in a pit that can flood. Double check valve assembly (DC, DCVA): two checks; low hazard only. Pressure vacuum breaker (PVB): backsiphonage only, installed at least 12 inches above the highest downstream outlet, not where backpressure is possible. Atmospheric vacuum breaker (AVB): point-of-use, no downstream shutoff, not testable. Dual checks at residential meters give limited low-hazard protection. Testable assemblies are tested at installation, at least yearly, and after repair, by a certified tester.
field.title: Backflow devices: air gap, RPZ, double check, vacuum breakers
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Open Exam Prep, California operator guide: Cross-Connection Program

field.text: Utilities usually require contractors to get a hydrant meter (construction meter) with an approved backflow assembly, often an RPZ, before taking water from a hydrant, and many rent the meter-and-RP assembly as a unit that the utility tests. Rules commonly include: use only designated hydrants; use a hydrant wrench and open fully; fill water trucks through an air gap (fill pipe ending above the tank opening by at least 2 diameters and 1 inch) or through the RP; never let a hose end sit in a tank, trench or mud; protect the RP from freezing and damage; and report the meter readings. High-hazard uses (chemical mixing, dust control with additives, hydroseeding, herbicide trucks, sewer jetters) always need an RP or air gap. A water truck connected without protection during a pressure drop can siphon its tank back into the main. Virginia requires an air gap or RPZ at loading station fill connections.
field.title: Backflow on construction: hydrant meters and filling trucks
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Open Exam Prep cross-connection guide; Virginia 12VAC5-590-1235; common utility hydrant use rules

field.text: The basic 10 ft horizontal and 18 inch vertical rules are in separation-cover-marking-1 and -2. Special cases from Ten States-based rules: force mains get at least 10 ft horizontal separation from water mains (Ten States wastewater force main section) and many states don't allow the 'closer if 18 inches higher' exception for force mains; water mains must not pass through or contact sewer manholes; Virginia requires 10 ft from septic tanks and drainfields; Illinois keeps hydrant drains 10 ft from sanitary and storm sewers. Where the water main is closer than 10 ft under the Ten States exception, it goes in a separate trench or on an undisturbed earth shelf with its bottom at least 18 inches above the sewer top. Storm sewers are treated like sanitary sewers in many states and less strictly in others. Reclaimed water lines have their own separation rules (often 4 to 10 ft). Check your state rule.
field.title: Water-sewer separation: special cases (force mains, septic, storm, manholes)
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Ten States Standards wastewater 2014 (38.31, 49.5); Virginia 12VAC5-590-1150; Illinois 35 IAC 604.1425

field.text: Lead service lines were installed mainly from the late 1800s through the 1940s, and some places allowed them into the 1980s (the 1986 SDWA amendments banned lead pipe and solder in new potable work). Also watch for lead goosenecks/pigtails (short lead connectors at the corp) and galvanized lines that sat downstream of lead ('galvanized requiring replacement'). EPA's identification approaches: records review (when lead was last allowed locally), historical records and interviews with crews and plumbers, visual, scratch and magnet tests, water sampling, and excavation (most accurate, most expensive). Scratch test: lead is dull gray, soft, non-magnetic, and scratches shiny silver with a key or coin; copper scratches yellow-orange or penny colored; galvanized steel is gray, hard, and a magnet sticks. Lead pipe often has a bulbous 'wiped' joint. Utilities must keep service line inventories, so record material on both sides of the curb stop whenever you expose a service.
field.title: Lead service lines: where they are and how to identify them
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: U.S. EPA Science Matters: approaches to identify lead service lines; general practice

field.text: EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (final rule October 2024) require water systems to replace all lead and 'galvanized requiring replacement' service lines, generally within 10 years. Florida DEP's schedule summary: the compliance date is November 1, 2027; a baseline inventory of all service lines and connectors and a service line replacement plan are due then; inventories are updated yearly after that; and full replacement is due by November 1, 2037 (some systems may qualify for deferred deadlines). AWWA's summary notes the lead action level drops from 15 to 10 micrograms per liter, first- and fifth-liter samples are both analyzed, and systems with repeated exceedances must make filters available. Status as of late 2026: a water-utility challenge (AWWA v. EPA) is pending in the D.C. Circuit with briefing complete and oral argument expected in fall 2026; the rule remains in effect and EPA has defended it. Check your state primacy agency for current deadlines.
field.title: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI): what utilities must do
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: Florida DEP LCRI schedule summary; AWWA LCRI summary; NRDC case page, AWWA v. EPA (LCRI) (checked Nov 2026)

field.text: Field practice for lead service line replacement (check the utility's LSLR procedure and state rules): replace the full line, public and private side, since partial replacement (cutting a lead line and connecting new copper to the remaining lead) can spike lead levels and is discouraged or restricted under the newer rules; get owner access agreements for private-side work; methods include open cut, pulling new pipe through with a cable puller, or boring; disturbing lead pipe releases particles, so after replacement flush the premise plumbing per the utility's protocol (often at least 30 minutes from the highest-flow taps after removing aerators) and give the resident a certified filter and information; handle removed lead pipe as scrap metal or per the utility's disposal rules; protect workers from lead dust (no cutting with abrasive saws without controls, wash hands before eating). Record materials and dates for the inventory.
field.title: Lead service line replacement: field practice
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: General LSLR practice; AWWA and EPA LCRI summaries

field.text: Typical main break response (follow the utility's procedure): locate and close the nearest valves to isolate the break (count turns, note valves that won't close); notify affected customers and fire department; call in utility locates before digging; keep the pipe under some positive pressure if possible, or pump the excavation down below the pipe so dirty water can't get in; expose the break and repair with a full-circle repair clamp, coupling or a new section of pipe; swab the repair parts and pipe ends with hypochlorite (AWWA C651 swabbing for repairs); flush from the repair to a hydrant until clear with normal chlorine residual; take bacteriological samples if the utility or state requires (often when pressure was lost or contamination was possible); and issue or lift a boil water notice per state rules. Trench safety rules apply even in an emergency.
field.title: Water main breaks and repairs: steps and contamination control
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: AWWA C651 repair provisions as summarized in testing-water-11; general utility practice

field.text: Utilities lose water through leaks, breaks, overflowing tanks, theft and meter errors. AWWA's water audit method separates real losses (physical leaks) from apparent losses (meter under-registration, data errors, unauthorized use such as unmetered hydrant use by contractors). Leak detection methods: acoustic listening on valves and hydrants, ground microphones, leak noise correlators that use two sensors to pinpoint a leak between them, permanently installed acoustic loggers, satellite and in-pipe tools, and district metered areas with night flow analysis. Signs of a leak in the field: water surfacing in dry weather, constant hiss at a curb stop or valve, sinkholes or soft spots, unusually green grass strips, and chlorine residual in ditch water. Contractors help by using metered hydrant water, reporting leaks found while digging, and fixing service leaks on new work before backfill.
field.title: Water loss and leak detection
field.topic: Drinking water distribution: pressure, storage, valves, hydrants, services, backflow, separation, lead service lines
field.source: AWWA water audit concepts as commonly summarized; general practice

field.text: Public water comes from surface water (rivers, lakes, reservoirs) or groundwater (wells into aquifers), and some systems use both or buy treated water wholesale from a neighbor. CDC notes surface water generally needs more treatment because it carries more sediment, germs, chemicals and toxins (including cyanobacteria toxins from algae blooms), while groundwater generally needs less, though some aquifers carry nitrate, arsenic, radionuclides, iron, manganese or hardness that need special treatment. Big cities mostly use surface water with large conventional plants; most small systems use wells with disinfection and maybe iron or arsenic removal. Source water protection (wellhead protection areas, watershed rules) limits activities like fuel storage and septic systems near intakes and wells, which can affect construction staging and spill plans near a wellfield or reservoir.
field.title: Drinking water sources: surface water vs groundwater
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: CDC, How Water Treatment Works

field.text: Some wells, springs and infiltration galleries draw water that is really surface water in disguise: shallow wells near rivers, wells in fractured rock or karst, springs that turn cloudy after rain. Regulators call this groundwater under the direct influence of surface water (GWUDI), decided case by case under state criteria (EPA tells private well owners to check whether their groundwater is under direct influence of surface water). Signs include changes in turbidity, temperature or bacteria that track rainfall or river levels, and the presence of algae, insects or Giardia-sized particles (microscopic particulate analysis). A GWUDI source must be treated like surface water, with filtration and higher disinfection requirements, not just chlorination. For crews: wells near construction can be affected by dewatering, blasting and spills; report any wellhead damage right away.
field.title: Groundwater under the direct influence of surface water (GWUDI)
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: U.S. EPA private wells guidance; Surface Water Treatment Rule concepts as commonly summarized

field.text: CDC's description of how community water treatment works, in order: Coagulation: chemicals such as aluminum (alum) or iron salts are added and rapidly mixed to neutralize the charge on dirt and tiny particles so they stick together. Flocculation: gentle mixing grows those into larger, heavier floc. Sedimentation: floc settles out in basins (sludge goes to solids handling). Filtration: clear water passes through filters of sand, gravel and anthracite or activated carbon to remove remaining particles and germs; activated carbon also takes out taste and odor, and some plants use membranes (ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis). Disinfection: chlorine, chloramine, chlorine dioxide, UV or ozone kills remaining germs, and a residual disinfectant is kept in the water to protect it through the pipes to the tap. Final adjustments: pH and corrosion control, and commonly fluoride.
field.title: Conventional water treatment train: coagulation to disinfection
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: CDC, How Water Treatment Works

field.text: Water filters in treatment plants: rapid sand or dual/mixed media filters (anthracite over sand over gravel) are the workhorse of conventional plants, cleaned by backwashing water upward through the bed; slow sand filters (very low rate, biological layer on top) serve some small systems; direct filtration skips sedimentation for clean sources; pressure filters (enclosed tanks) are common at wells for iron and manganese; membranes (micro- and ultrafiltration) physically strain out particles and pathogens. Turbidity (cloudiness, measured in NTU) is the key filter performance measure. Under EPA's surface water rules as commonly summarized, conventional and direct filtration plants must have combined filter effluent turbidity of 0.3 NTU or less in at least 95% of monthly readings and never over 1 NTU. Filter backwash water goes to lagoons or recycle, and its discharge may need an NPDES permit.
field.title: Filtration types and turbidity limits
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: EPA Surface Water Treatment Rules (IESWTR/LT1) as commonly summarized; general practice

field.text: Under the federal Surface Water Treatment Rule as adopted by states (example: Michigan R 325.10611a), the disinfectant residual in water entering the distribution system can't be below 0.2 mg/L for more than 4 hours, and residual must be detectable in the distribution system in at least 95% of samples each month (a heterotrophic plate count of 500 per mL or less counts as detectable). Many states set higher minimums (some require 0.2 mg/L or more free chlorine everywhere in the system). The maximum residual disinfectant level (MRDL) is 4 mg/L for chlorine and chloramine; CDC notes levels up to 4 mg/L are considered safe to drink. For crews this explains why flushed water must show normal residual before a new main goes into service, and why stagnant dead ends and oversized new mains cause residual complaints.
field.title: Disinfection residual rules: 0.2 mg/L entering, detectable in the system
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: Michigan Admin. Code R 325.10611a (state adoption of the federal SWTR); CDC chlorine/chloramine page

field.text: CDC: utilities first used chlorine in 1908 and chloramine (chlorine plus ammonia) in 1929. Free chlorine is a strong disinfectant that helps loosen biofilm in pipes, but it gets used up quickly and makes more disinfection byproducts (DBPs). Chloramine lasts longer in long pipe systems and makes fewer DBPs, so many large utilities use it as the residual disinfectant; EPA gives guidance to systems switching because it can affect lead and copper corrosion. Both are considered safe up to 4 mg/L. Many chloramine systems do a periodic 'chlorine burn' (temporary switch to free chlorine) to control nitrification. A field crew should know which one their system uses: chlorine test kits and dechlorination chemicals differ in how they handle total vs free chlorine, and new-main disinfection under AWWA C651 uses free chlorine even in chloramine systems.
field.title: Chlorine vs chloramine: why utilities use each
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: CDC, About Water Disinfection with Chlorine and Chloramine

field.text: CDC cautions: dialysis centers must remove all chlorine and chloramine from water before use, and home dialysis patients should check their equipment; fish, turtles, frogs and other aquatic animals absorb disinfectant directly and even low levels can sicken them; letting water sit out removes chlorine but not chloramine, so aquarium owners need a product that neutralizes chloramine. For construction: flushing water from chloraminated mains (and from new main disinfection) must be dechlorinated before it reaches a storm drain or stream, using products (such as sodium thiosulfate, ascorbic acid or sodium sulfite) that neutralize chloramine and its ammonia properly; test for total chlorine, not just free. In chloramine systems, nitrification in dead ends and tanks can drop residual and raise nitrite, which is another reason for flushing and turnover.
field.title: Chloramine cautions: fish, dialysis, discharges and nitrification
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: CDC, About Water Disinfection with Chlorine and Chloramine; general practice

field.text: Treatment plants get credit for killing pathogens using CT: disinfectant concentration (C, mg/L) times contact time (T, minutes, at the 10th percentile, called T10, from tracer tests). EPA tables give the CT needed for a given log inactivation at a given temperature and pH; colder water and higher pH need more CT. Surface water systems must achieve, through filtration plus disinfection combined, at least 99.9% (3-log) removal or inactivation of Giardia and 99.99% (4-log) of viruses, with filtration getting most of the Giardia credit; Cryptosporidium (resistant to chlorine) is handled by filtration, UV or ozone under later rules. Groundwater systems with fecal contamination risk need 4-log virus treatment under the Ground Water Rule. That's why clearwells and contact tanks have baffles and why changes to plant piping need engineer review.
field.title: CT and log removal: how disinfection credit is figured
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: EPA Surface Water Treatment Rule and Ground Water Rule, as commonly summarized

field.text: When chlorine reacts with natural organic matter in water it forms disinfection byproducts. EPA's Stage 1 and Stage 2 DBP rules limit total trihalomethanes (TTHM) to 80 micrograms per liter (ppb) and the five haloacetic acids (HAA5) to 60 ppb, calculated as locational running annual averages at monitoring sites in the distribution system; bromate (from ozone) is limited to 10 ppb and chlorite (from chlorine dioxide) to 1.0 mg/L. DBPs increase with water age, temperature and chlorine dose, so they're highest at the far ends of systems and in tanks with poor turnover. Utilities control them by removing organics before chlorination (enhanced coagulation, carbon), switching to chloramine, and reducing water age (tank mixing, flushing, right-sizing new mains). Oversized mains in new subdivisions can create DBP and residual problems.
field.title: Disinfection byproducts (DBPs): TTHM and HAA5
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: EPA Stage 1/Stage 2 Disinfectants and Disinfection Byproducts Rules, as commonly summarized

field.text: Most lead in tap water comes from lead service lines, lead solder and brass fixtures, not from the source water. Utilities control corrosion by adjusting water chemistry: raising pH and alkalinity, and adding orthophosphate, which forms a protective scale inside pipes (optimized corrosion control treatment under the Lead and Copper Rule). Changing source water, disinfectant (chlorine to chloramine) or chemistry without care can strip that scale and release lead, which is what happened in Flint, Michigan, in 2014 when corrosion control wasn't used after a source change. Physical disturbance (meter replacements, main work, partial service replacement) also knocks loose lead scale, so utilities flush and notify residents after work near lead lines. The LCRI lowers the lead action level to 10 micrograms per liter starting with the 2027 compliance date.
field.title: Corrosion control in drinking water (lead and copper)
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: Lead and Copper Rule concepts as commonly summarized; Florida DEP LCRI summary

field.text: Small and mid-size systems on wells typically pump from the aquifer into a treatment building or straight into the system. Common treatment: disinfection with sodium hypochlorite (or gas chlorine at larger plants), with contact time before the first customer; iron and manganese removal by oxidation and pressure filters or greensand (stops orange and black staining); arsenic removal (adsorption media, coagulation-filtration); nitrate removal (ion exchange, reverse osmosis); radium and uranium removal; softening; and corrosion control (pH adjustment, orthophosphate). Wellhead parts: casing and grout seal, pitless adapter or well house, sanitary well seal, screened vent, sampling tap, flow meter, check valve and pump-to-waste line. Public wells have state-set protection zones and setbacks from sewers and septic systems, and work inside a wellhead protection area often needs extra spill controls.
field.title: Well-based (groundwater) system treatment
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: General groundwater system practice

field.text: The Safe Drinking Water Act (1974, major amendments in 1986 and 1996) is the federal law that protects public drinking water. EPA sets national primary drinking water regulations: maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) or treatment techniques for more than 90 contaminants (microbes, disinfectants and byproducts, inorganics like arsenic, lead and nitrate, organics, radionuclides), plus monitoring, reporting and public notice rules; secondary standards cover taste, odor and color. The 1986 amendments banned lead pipe, solder and flux in new potable plumbing; the 1996 amendments added source water assessments, operator certification, consumer confidence reports and the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF), which funds many water main and lead line projects. The SDWA also regulates underground injection (UIC) to protect aquifers. It covers public water systems, not private wells.
field.title: Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) basics
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: Safe Drinking Water Act summary as commonly given by EPA

field.text: Under the SDWA, a public water system (PWS) provides water for human consumption through pipes or other constructed conveyances to at least 15 service connections, or serves an average of at least 25 people at least 60 days a year; it can be publicly or privately owned. Three types: Community water systems serve the same people year-round (cities, towns, mobile home parks, subdivisions). Non-transient non-community systems regularly serve at least 25 of the same people at least six months a year but not where they live (schools, factories, offices, hospitals with their own wells). Transient non-community systems serve people briefly (gas stations, campgrounds, rest stops). EPA counts over 148,000 public water systems, and public systems serve about 90% of Americans. A construction camp or jobsite well serving 25 or more workers for 60+ days can itself become a regulated PWS.
field.title: Public water system definition and types (CWS, NTNC, TNC)
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: U.S. EPA, Information about Public Water Systems (archived 2021)

field.text: EPA writes the national drinking water rules, but states, territories and tribes can apply for primacy (primary enforcement authority) if their rules are at least as strict. Nearly every state has primacy (Wyoming and the District of Columbia are the notable exceptions where EPA runs the program directly). The primacy agency is often the state health department or the environmental agency (names like Division of Drinking Water, Bureau of Safe Drinking Water, Office of Drinking Water). It approves plans and specifications for new mains, tanks, wells and treatment (often against Ten States Standards or its own design rules), issues construction and operating permits, certifies operators and labs, receives sample results, and enforces violations. For contractors, the primacy agency's rules are where separation distances, disinfection requirements and boil-water notice triggers come from.
field.title: Primacy: state drinking water programs vs EPA
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: EPA primacy program as commonly summarized

field.text: Water and sewer service in the U.S. is run by many kinds of owners: city or county utility departments (the most common for larger systems); special districts and authorities (water districts, sanitary districts, municipal utility districts, regional sewer authorities, water and sewer authorities) with their own boards and bonding power; investor-owned private utilities (regulated by the state public utility or public service commission for rates); nonprofit water cooperatives and rural water associations (common in rural areas, often funded by USDA Rural Development); homeowners associations, mobile home parks and businesses running small systems; and wholesale providers selling to other utilities. A regional authority may own the interceptors and plant while cities own the local collection pipes. For crews, this decides whose standards, inspectors, permits and shutdown procedures apply on a given street.
field.title: Who runs water and sewer: utility and district structures
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: General U.S. utility structure

field.text: Public water systems collect routine bacteriological samples from sites throughout the distribution system each month (number based on population served). Under the Revised Total Coliform Rule (effective 2016), total coliform is an indicator: a positive result triggers repeat samples, and too many positives in a month (or an E. coli event) trigger a Level 1 or Level 2 assessment to find and fix the cause (a sanitary defect such as a cross-connection, open tank hatch or main break). E. coli presence indicates fecal contamination; an E. coli MCL violation requires prompt public notice, often a boil water order. Sampling taps are dedicated stations or approved taps, flamed or disinfected, using sterile bottles with sodium thiosulfate. Field connection: construction is a common cause of positives (unsanitary tie-ins, contaminated new mains put in service early, backflow from hydrant use), so follow C651 and backflow rules.
field.title: Total coliform and E. coli monitoring (Revised Total Coliform Rule)
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: EPA Revised Total Coliform Rule, as commonly summarized

field.text: Utilities must notify customers when water may be unsafe. A boil water notice (boil water advisory or order) is issued when contamination is possible or confirmed: E. coli positives, loss of pressure (often below 20 psi) after a main break or during a shutdown, a treatment failure, or flooding of a wellhead. Customers are told to boil water for at least 1 minute (3 minutes at high elevations, per CDC practice) or use bottled water, until the utility flushes, restores residual and gets clean bacteriological results, typically at least one or two rounds of samples over 24 to 48 hours. Notice tiers under EPA's Public Notification Rule set how fast notice must go out (Tier 1 within 24 hours for acute risks). Construction shutdowns that drop customers to zero pressure often trigger a precautionary notice, so plan tie-ins with the utility to keep pressure where possible.
field.title: Boil water notices and public notification
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: EPA Public Notification Rule and common state boil-water practice, as commonly summarized

field.text: States require certified operators to run public water systems and wastewater plants, under SDWA operator certification guidelines and state law (many states also certify collection and distribution system operators). Licenses are graded by system size and complexity (often Class I to IV, or A to D) for water treatment, water distribution, wastewater treatment and wastewater collection, with separate backflow tester and cross-connection licenses. Certification needs education and experience hours plus an exam (ABC or state exams) and continuing education to renew. Each system must have an operator in responsible charge at the right grade. For construction crews: the utility's certified operators, not the contractor, usually must operate existing system valves, hydrants for shutdowns, and plant equipment, and they decide when a new main or facility goes into service.
field.title: Water and wastewater operator certification
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: General state operator certification practice

field.text: Private household wells (serving fewer than 15 connections and 25 people) aren't covered by the Safe Drinking Water Act; the owner is responsible for water quality. EPA points owners to state private well programs and local health departments. EPA's advice: test every year for total coliform bacteria, nitrates, total dissolved solids and pH; test for other contaminants common in your area (arsenic, radon, uranium, manganese, PFAS, pesticides) as the health department suggests; test more often with infants, pregnant or nursing women, or older adults in the home; and test right away after flooding, nearby construction or land disturbance, well repairs, or changes in taste, odor or color. Use a state-certified lab. A positive coliform result usually means shock chlorinating the well and retesting. Crews working near private wells should know where they are and avoid fueling or storing chemicals nearby.
field.title: Private wells: who regulates and how often to test
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: U.S. EPA, Protect Your Home's Water (private wells)

field.text: Most states license well drillers and require a permit (often from the county health department or state environmental or water resources agency) before drilling a private water well, with a well log filed afterward. Typical construction rules: steel or PVC casing extended at least 12 inches or more above finished grade (never buried in a pit in most states), grout sealing the annular space to a minimum depth to keep surface water out, a sanitary (vermin-proof) well cap with screened vent, a pitless adapter below frost for the buried line to the house, grading so water drains away from the casing, and disinfection after construction or repair. EPA advises installing a well cap or sanitary seal and periodically checking for a broken cap, cracked or corroded casing, and settling or cracked surface seals. Water rights or withdrawal permits may also be needed in western states.
field.title: Private well construction and permits
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: U.S. EPA private wells guidance; general state well code practice

field.text: Wells have minimum distances from contamination sources set by state well codes and county health rules. Examples in practice: septic tanks often 50 to 100 ft, drainfields 100 ft, seepage pits 150 ft (Kern County, CA uses 100 ft from tank and field and 150 ft from a seepage pit); sewer lines often 10 to 50 ft depending on pipe type; animal yards, fuel tanks and chemical storage farther. EPA advises keeping contaminants and hazardous chemicals away from wells and sinkholes and checking with the local health department about safe distances. Abandoned wells are direct paths for contamination into aquifers and a fall hazard: EPA says hire a certified driller to close them, don't dump waste in dry or abandoned wells, and don't cut the casing off below ground. If excavation uncovers an unknown casing, stop, protect it from runoff and debris, and report it.
field.title: Well setbacks and abandoned wells
field.topic: Drinking water sources, treatment and regulation (SDWA, EPA, primacy states, utilities, private wells)
field.source: U.S. EPA private wells guidance; Kern County (CA) setback table

field.text: Dampproofing and waterproofing are not the same job. Dampproofing (often a sprayed or rolled tar/asphalt coat, typically under 10 mils cured) slows moisture wicking through concrete when there is NO water pressing on the wall. It is brittle and will not bridge cracks or bug holes. Waterproofing resists liquid water UNDER hydrostatic pressure (water table, perched water, clay that holds water against the wall). Waterproofing coats are usually 40 mils or thicker, flexible enough to bridge cracks, or are sheet membranes, bentonite or crystalline systems. Rule of thumb: if groundwater will sit against the structure at any time of year, dampproofing is not enough. Both need clean, prepared surfaces, the maker's temperature limits, and careful backfill so rock doesn't puncture the coating. Check the spec section (usually 07 11 00 dampproofing, 07 13 00 / 07 14 00 waterproofing).
field.title: Waterproofing vs dampproofing: what is the difference
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: NPCA, Damp-proofing vs. waterproofing (citing ACI 515.1); IRC R406 summary (InterNACHI)

field.text: The International Residential Code requires dampproofing on foundation walls that hold back earth and enclose space below grade, from finished grade down to the higher of the top of the footing or 6 inches below the top of the basement floor. On masonry walls, first parge with at least 3/8 inch of portland cement, then apply one of: a bituminous coating, 3 lb per square yard of acrylic-modified cement, 1/8 inch of surface-bonding cement (ASTM C887), or any listed waterproofing. Poured concrete walls skip the parging and take any listed dampproofing or waterproofing product. Wood foundations get 6-mil polyethylene lapped 6 inches and sealed. Commercial work follows the IBC and the project spec, which are often stricter. Check your local code edition.
field.title: Building code dampproofing for basement and below-grade walls (IRC R406.1)
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: IRC R406.1 as summarized by InterNACHI

field.text: Where a high water table or other severe soil-water condition is known, the IRC requires waterproofing instead of dampproofing, over the same area (finished grade down to top of footing or 6 inches below basement floor top). Accepted materials include: 2-ply hot-mopped felts, 55-lb roll roofing, 6-mil PVC, 6-mil polyethylene, 40-mil polymer-modified asphalt, 60-mil flexible polymer cement, 1/8 inch cement-based fiber-reinforced waterproof coating, or 60-mil solvent-free liquid-applied synthetic rubber. Sheet joints are lapped and sealed with adhesive compatible with the membrane. Precast wall panel joints get ASTM C920 sealant full height. On insulated concrete forms (EPS foam) no solvent-based products, and hot asphalt must be under 200 F. Commercial and civil structures (vaults, wet wells, tunnels) follow the project spec.
field.title: Building code waterproofing where there is a high water table (IRC R406.2)
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: IRC R406.2 as summarized by InterNACHI

field.text: Self-adhered sheet membranes (rubberized asphalt or modified bitumen on a plastic film, often called peel-and-stick, Bituthene-type or blue skin) are the most common below-grade sheet. Typical install: concrete cured and dry, fins and form ties ground off, bug holes filled; prime the surface with the maker's primer and let it tack; start at the bottom and lap upper sheets over lower (shingle fashion) so water runs off the laps; side and end laps typically 2.5 to 3 inches, ends staggered; roll every sheet firmly with a hand roller; detail inside corners and cold joints with a strip or mastic fillet first; terminate at the top with a termination bar and mastic. Most self-adhered sheets need about 40 F or warmer to stick (low-temp versions exist). Cover with protection board or drainage board before backfill. Follow the maker's guide; laps and termination are where they leak.
field.title: Sheet membrane waterproofing (self-adhered / peel and stick / mod-bit) on walls and vaults
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice and typical manufacturer instructions; verify with your product's installation guide

field.text: Fluid-applied membranes (polyurethane, polymer-modified asphalt emulsion, rubberized asphalt hot-applied, polyurea, cementitious polymer) are sprayed, rolled or troweled on to a specified dry thickness, commonly 40 to 60 mils for below-grade waterproofing. Check it in the field with a wet-film gauge: required wet mils = dry mils divided by the percent solids (example: 60 dry mils at 75% solids needs about 80 wet mils). Two coats in opposite directions reduce pinholes. Reinforce cracks, cold joints and inside corners with fabric or a detail coat first. Respect cure time before backfill and keep rain off uncured product. Solvent-based and spray products give off vapors that collect in trenches and pits, which is both a fire and breathing hazard: ventilate, keep ignition sources away, and treat deep excavations as a possible confined space. Read the product data sheet and SDS.
field.title: Fluid-applied waterproofing membranes: thickness, wet mils and cure
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice; wet-to-dry mil conversion is simple arithmetic; check the product data sheet

field.text: Bentonite waterproofing uses sodium bentonite clay locked between geotextiles (or in panels). When wet and confined it swells into a dense gel that blocks water and self-heals small punctures. It ONLY works when confined: by concrete poured against it or by compacted backfill. Example manufacturer rules (CETCO Voltex): substrate compacted to at least 85% Modified Proctor and smooth, crushed stone 3/4 inch or smaller; overlap edges at least 4 inches and stagger ends at least 12 inches; fasten with washer-head fasteners about 24 inches on center (12 inches at grade terminations); backfill promptly and compact to at least 85% Modified Proctor with soil or angular stone 3/4 inch or smaller, no debris or sharp rock. Under slabs, place woven side up under a reinforced slab at least 4 inches thick. Product rules differ: follow your maker's manual.
field.title: Bentonite waterproofing (Voltex-type panels and sheets): how it works and install basics
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: CETCO Voltex product manual

field.text: Bentonite must not swell before it is confined. Don't install it in standing water or over ice, pump rain off it right away, and tape or seal exposed edges if backfill will be delayed. Wet, unconfined bentonite washes out and fails. Groundwater with salt, strong acids or alkalis, or high conductivity (CETCO asks for a water test at about 2,500 micromhos/cm or higher) can stop ordinary bentonite from swelling; contaminant-resistant grades or a different system are used then, so get a groundwater sample tested before you buy. At pipe penetrations, cut the sheet tight to the pipe and trowel a bentonite mastic fillet at least 3/4 inch thick, carried about 1.5 inches up the pipe and onto the sheet; clustered pipes get granular bentonite plus mastic. Bentonite is not used for expansion joints. Follow the manufacturer's detail drawings.
field.title: Bentonite waterproofing problems: early wetting, salt water, penetrations
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: CETCO Voltex product manual

field.text: Crystalline waterproofing (Xypex, Penetron, Kryton-type products) reacts with water and cement to grow crystals in the concrete's pores and hairline cracks, lowering permeability. It comes two ways: an admixture added at the batch plant or precast plant, or a cementitious slurry brushed onto damp, clean, open-pored concrete (it can work from the inside, the negative side). Admixtures are classed as permeability-reducing admixtures for hydrostatic conditions (PRAH) under ACI 212.3R, and makers say they self-seal hairline cracks over time; they do not fix wide or moving cracks, honeycomb or bad joints, which still need waterstops or injection. Trial mixes are recommended since dosage and set time vary by product. Brush-on slurries need the surface kept damp while curing. The powder is alkaline like cement: gloves and eye protection, wash skin promptly. Follow the product's data sheet.
field.title: Crystalline waterproofing (admixture or brush-on slurry) for vaults, tanks and manholes
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: Penetron Admix product page; general practice for surface-applied crystallines

field.text: Cementitious waterproof coatings (Thoroseal-type polymer-modified cement slurries) are brushed or troweled on concrete and masonry, usually in two coats, often about 1/8 inch total. Parging is a 3/8 inch or thicker portland cement plaster coat on block or brick, used as a base for dampproofing. Rules that apply to all cement coatings: remove laitance, form oil and dirt (pressure wash or abrade), pre-wet the surface to saturated-surface-dry (damp, no standing water), fill bug holes and voids first, cure damp and protect from freezing for the period the maker states. They resist moderate water pressure and can be used on the inside of a manhole, but rigid coatings crack if the structure moves, and they do not stand up to H2S acid attack in sanitary sewers (use a corrosion-rated liner there). Wet cement causes chemical burns: gloves, sleeves, eye protection.
field.title: Cementitious coatings and parging on manholes, vaults and walls
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice; IRC parging thickness from IRC R406.1 summary

field.text: Positive-side waterproofing goes on the face where the water is (the outside of a buried wall, vault or manhole). Water pressure pushes the membrane against the structure, and it also protects the concrete and rebar from wet soil. It needs access, so it is installed before backfill: sheets, fluid membranes, bentonite, exterior joint wraps. Negative-side waterproofing goes on the dry face (inside), where water pushes the coating away from the wall. Only products made for it work: crystalline slurries, cementitious coatings, some epoxies, and injection grouts. It is the usual fix for existing structures you cannot dig up, but the concrete itself stays wet. Blindside waterproofing is positive-side membrane placed against shoring or lagging before the wall is poured, used on tight sites. Ask what side the spec calls for before ordering material.
field.title: Positive-side vs negative-side waterproofing
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General waterproofing industry practice

field.text: Drainage board (dimpled HDPE sheet or a geocomposite of plastic core with filter fabric, brand names like Mirafi, J-Drain, Delta-MS) goes against the wall over the waterproofing before backfill. It gives water a free path down to the footing drain so hydrostatic pressure does not build against the wall, and it protects the membrane from rocks during backfill. Install points: fabric side faces the soil (not the wall); lap or shingle seams so soil cannot get in; fasten only at the top or with the maker's adhesive so you don't punch through the membrane; tie the bottom into the footing drain or collector pipe with fabric wrapped around so the core does not fill with fines; cap the top edge so backfill doesn't drop into the core. Drainage board is only as good as the outlet: the footing drain must reach daylight, a storm structure or a sump.
field.title: Drainage board / drainage composite against foundation and vault walls
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice; check the manufacturer's installation guide

field.text: Waterstops are strips cast across a concrete joint so water can't follow the joint through the wall or slab. Sika/Greenstreak's guide groups PVC profiles by joint movement. Non-moving joints (construction joints, cold joints): ribbed flat (seals better than dumbbell), dumbbell, labyrinth (vertical joints, no split bulkhead needed), base seal (on the form face of slabs and backfilled walls), split (avoids split forms but hard to splice). Moving joints (expansion and contraction joints): ribbed with center bulb (the most versatile), dumbbell with center bulb, and tear-web for big movement. Sizing guidance from Corps of Engineers testing: width at least 6 times the largest aggregate plus the joint gap, and clear distance to rebar at least 2 times the largest aggregate. Common profile widths are 6 and 9 inches. Use what the drawings call for.
field.title: Waterstops: PVC profiles and which one goes where
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: Sika PVC Waterstop Design Guide

field.text: PVC waterstops must be held exactly in position before the pour: tie them to the rebar with wire through factory grommets, punched holes or hog rings on the outer edge (Sika says this applies to every PVC install; many specs want ties about every 12 inches). Field splices are straight butt joints only, thermally welded with a thermostatically controlled splicing iron; tees, ells and crosses should be factory-made because field-mitered intersections are often done badly. Never lap PVC waterstop. Hydrostatic rupture is rare: Sika calculates a safety factor of about 17 for a 3/8 inch waterstop in a 1/2 inch joint at 200 ft of head. Most leaks come from water migrating AROUND the waterstop: wrong profile, folded or bent waterstop, bad splices, honeycomb from poor vibration under horizontal waterstops. Vibrate well around it and lift the edge of horizontal waterstops so concrete fills underneath.
field.title: Installing PVC waterstops: tying, splicing and why they leak
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: Sika PVC Waterstop Design Guide; tie spacing and vibration points are common spec practice

field.text: Where a PVC waterstop wasn't cast in or can't be (pipe penetrations, joints in precast, retrofit), crews use: hydrophilic rubber strips that swell when wet (often several times their volume); bentonite-rubber strips (Waterstop-RX type) nailed or glued to the first pour; and re-injectable hoses laid in the joint and later injected with resin if it leaks. Rules: put swelling strips on clean, sound concrete, with the cover the maker requires (often about 2 to 3 inches from the face) so the swelling doesn't crack the edge; keep them dry until the pour because early swelling ruins them (some have a time-delay coating); butt ends tightly with no gaps. They are good for construction joints and pipe penetrations, not for expansion joints that open and close a lot. Check the product sheet for cover and minimum concrete strength.
field.title: Hydrophilic swelling waterstops, bentonite strips and injection hoses
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice; bentonite strip coverage example from CETCO Voltex manual

field.text: External sealing bands wrap the outside of joints in concrete pipe, manhole sections and precast box (often called heat-shrink wraps, joint wraps, Infi-Shield or MacWrap type). ASTM C877 has three types: Type I rubber and mastic band, stretched about 8 to 12% and overlapped at least its own width; Type II plastic film and mesh-reinforced rubberized mastic, cut to the joint perimeter plus 8 inches and held with straps; Type III butyl adhesive on a plastic or rubber backing, cut to the perimeter plus at least twice the band width and applied without stretching. Band widths run from about 6 to 7 inches on small pipe and manholes up to 12 to 13 inches on very large pipe. Properly installed bands are meant to hold external water pressure up to about 13 psi (about 30 ft of head). Many sanitary specs require a wrap on every manhole joint, including the frame-to-cone chimney.
field.title: Exterior joint wraps for manholes and box culverts (ASTM C877 sealing bands)
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: ASTM C877-21 scope and summary (public sample)

field.text: Typical field steps for an exterior manhole joint wrap (always follow the band maker): set the sections with the gasket or butyl and let them seat; brush or wire-wheel the outside of the joint clean and dry, removing loose mortar and mud; fill large chips or gaps at the joint with non-shrink grout so the band is fully supported; apply primer if the product uses it and let it tack; center the band over the joint and wrap it around, keeping it tight to the concrete with no wrinkles or bridges; overlap ends as the maker says (often 6 inches or the band width); for heat-shrink bands, heat with a propane torch evenly until it shrinks and the mastic flows out at the edges, working the overlap last. Backfill by hand around wrapped joints so rock doesn't tear the band. Torches near fresh solvent primer or in a confined trench are a fire risk; have an extinguisher and keep the flame moving.
field.title: How to install a manhole joint wrap (heat-shrink or butyl band)
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice and typical manufacturer instructions; band types per ASTM C877

field.text: The chimney, meaning the adjusting rings or brick between the cone top and the cast iron frame, is one of the biggest sources of groundwater and surface water getting into manholes because frost and traffic loads crack the mortar. Common fixes: internal chimney seals (a flexible rubber sleeve with stainless steel expansion bands that clamps to the frame and the cone, bridging the rings; Cretex-type); external chimney seals or heat-shrink wraps over the rings before backfill; butyl mastic between every adjusting ring instead of mortar; and using HDPE or rubber adjusting rings that are sealed with the maker's sealant. Internal seals can be installed later from inside without digging. Make sure the frame is bedded and the rings are clean and smooth where the seal bands land. Check your agency's standard detail; many require an exterior wrap AND butyl between rings on sanitary manholes.
field.title: Manhole chimney seals (frame-to-cone) to stop inflow
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry and municipal standard-detail practice

field.text: Field checklist for a watertight precast structure (vault, wet well, manhole): check sections on delivery for cracks, chipped tongues and grooves, and correct opening locations; joint sealant per spec (butyl rope to ASTM C990 or rubber gasket to ASTM C443), warmed in cold weather; set sections straight down so sealant isn't rolled off; pipe connections through flexible boots or seals to ASTM C923, or Link-Seals in cored holes; fill lifting holes with the supplied plugs or non-shrink grout from both sides if reachable; exterior joint wraps if specified; exterior coating if specified (bituminous dampproofing or coal tar epoxy is common on sanitary structures); interior joints pointed with non-shrink grout; vacuum test (ASTM C1244) before backfill where required, and again after if the agency says. Backfill evenly so the structure doesn't shift and open a joint.
field.title: Making a precast vault or manhole watertight: field checklist
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General practice; standards named are those commonly cited in municipal specs

field.text: Link-Seal (and similar modular seals) is a chain of rubber links joined by bolts and pressure plates that fills the gap between a pipe and a sleeve or cored hole. Tightening squeezes each link so it bulges and seals. Install per the PSI guide: center the pipe in the hole and support it on both sides, because the seal does not carry pipe weight; keep surfaces clean and avoid weld beads; loosen the nuts, wrap the belt around the pipe and connect the ends with ALL bolt heads facing you (do not remove links to take up slack); slide it into the gap, on big belts starting at 6 o'clock and working both sides up; tighten starting at 12 o'clock going clockwise, no more than about 4 turns per bolt per pass, then 2 to 3 more passes until all links bulge evenly. Hand tools only; no impact or power tools at 450 rpm or more; 316 stainless bolts hand-tighten only. Size the seal from the maker's chart for pipe OD and hole ID.
field.title: Link-Seal modular seals for pipe through a wall, sleeve or cored hole
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: PSI/GPT Link-Seal installation guide

field.text: Ways to seal a pipe through a manhole, vault or wall: cast-in rubber boot or gasket to ASTM C923 (best for sewer manholes, allows movement); Link-Seal type modular seal in a cored hole or sleeve (good for larger pipe, ductile and steel, also used as a temporary seal); wall sleeve with a puddle flange or waterstop collar cast in, then Link-Seal inside; hydrophilic swelling ring or waterstop gasket on PVC pipe before grouting it in (smooth PVC does not bond to grout, so plain grout around PVC leaks); non-shrink grout packed into a roughened hole, used only where the spec allows rigid connections (often storm, not sanitary). Avoid regular mortar, which shrinks and cracks. Whatever the method, support the pipe outside the structure with compacted bedding so settlement doesn't shear the seal. Check your standard detail for which is required.
field.title: Sealing pipe penetrations through concrete: options compared
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General practice; ASTM C923 is the common flexible connector standard

field.text: Elastomeric joint sealants for concrete are usually polyurethane or silicone meeting ASTM C920. Basic rules: joint must be clean, dry, sound and primed if the maker says; push in closed-cell backer rod about 25% larger than the joint width so it stays put and sets the depth; the sealant should bond to the two sides only, not the bottom (the backer rod or bond-breaker tape prevents three-sided adhesion so the bead can stretch); typical shape is width-to-depth about 2:1 for joints up to about 1/2 inch, with a minimum depth around 1/4 inch; tool the bead concave so it is pressed against the sides. Don't seal in rain or below the maker's minimum temperature. Sealants submerged full time need a product rated for immersion. Fresh polyurethane contains isocyanates: gloves, avoid skin contact.
field.title: Joint sealants and backer rod (caulking concrete joints, vault tops, precast panels)
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice; check the product data sheet for joint design

field.text: Hydraulic cement (Water Plug, Waterplug, Quikrete Hydraulic Water-Stop type) is a fast-setting, slightly expanding cement used to plug running leaks in concrete or masonry. It sets in a few minutes (often about 3 to 5 minutes, faster in warm water). How to use: chisel the crack or hole out to at least about 3/4 inch wide and deep, undercut so it is wider at the back than the face; flush out loose material; mix a small handful to putty stiffness; shape it into a plug and push it into the leak, starting at the top of a crack and working down, holding firm pressure until it sets. It is a quick, rigid patch: it cracks again if the joint or crack moves, and quick-set patches can weaken the bond of a structural liner put on later. For moving cracks or joints, chemical grout injection is the better repair. Wear gloves and eye protection; it is caustic.
field.title: Hydraulic cement for plugging active leaks in manholes and vaults
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice; liner-bond caution from Trenchless Technology, Chemical Grouting and Manholes

field.text: Polyurethane chemical grouts stop infiltration through cracks, joints and pipe penetrations in manholes, vaults and wet wells. Hydrophilic (water-loving) foams react with water, expand about 5 to 8 times, and stay flexible, so they tolerate joints that move. Hydrophilic gels don't expand, can be mixed with up to 15 parts water to 1 part resin, but shrink if they dry out, so they are only for structures that stay wet below grade, and should not be used in moving joints because they can split. Hydrophobic (water-repelling) grouts need a catalyst, expand up to about 29 times, cure rigid, and penetrate loose soil well, so they are used to stop gushing leaks and fill voids outside the wall, but alone they are a temporary fix for minor cracks. Common approach on a gusher: hydrophobic first to cut the flow, then back it up with hydrophilic. Manholes are a major infiltration source in most systems, so grouting them often pays off quickly.
field.title: Chemical grout for leaks: hydrophilic vs hydrophobic polyurethane
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: Trenchless Technology, Chemical Grouting and Manholes

field.text: Typical crack and joint injection: drill holes at an angle (often about 45 degrees) beside the crack or joint so they cross it partway through the wall, staggered on alternate sides, spaced roughly 6 to 12 inches depending on wall thickness; install mechanical packers (injection ports) and tighten; flush with water; pump resin with a hand or electric injection pump starting at the lowest port and moving up as resin shows at the next port or the crack face. If the leak is too weak to pull grout in, inject straight into the defect. Curtain grouting means drilling clear through the wall and pumping grout into the soil outside to form a blanket over a joint or penetration. Activated oakum (oakum soaked in hydrophilic resin) is packed into gushing holes and pipe penetrations. Afterward remove packers and patch holes. Resins and catalysts irritate skin, eyes and lungs: goggles, nitrile gloves, follow the SDS and confined space rules.
field.title: How chemical grout injection is done on a leaking manhole or vault
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General industry practice; injection approach and oakum per Trenchless Technology

field.text: For leaking joints in sewer mains, crews use a CCTV-guided packer: a sleeve-shaped inflatable tool pulled through the pipe, centered on a joint, inflated to isolate it, then air or water tested. If the joint fails, chemical grout (acrylamide, acrylate gel or urethane) is pumped through the packer into the joint and the soil outside, the packer stays inflated until it gels, then the joint is retested. ASTM F2304 (sewers) and F2454 (laterals) cover the practice. It works on joints, not on cracked, broken or badly offset pipe, which need lining or replacement. Root control and cleaning come first. Lateral connections can be sealed with a lateral packer. Results depend on groundwater being present and soil the grout can mix with. Agencies usually require pre and post test records per joint. Check the contract spec for grout type and test pressure.
field.title: Sewer main joint test-and-seal (packer grouting) for infiltration
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General practice; standards named are those commonly cited for sewer chemical grouting

field.text: Signs of H2S attack: rotten-egg smell; soft, pasty or crumbly concrete above the waterline that you can scrape with a screwdriver; exposed aggregate and rebar; white crust; corroded frames, steps and ladder rungs; worst at force main discharge manholes, drop manholes, lift station wet wells and junctions with turbulence. Report it so the owner can plan lining or replacement, and don't stand on corroded steps. Safety: H2S is toxic and heavier than air, collecting in manholes, wet wells and trenches near sewers. At high levels it deadens your sense of smell, so 'it stopped smelling' is a warning, not relief. Never enter a structure without atmospheric testing, ventilation and a confined space permit as required. See the confined space files for entry procedures and alarm levels.
field.title: Recognizing H2S damage in the field and staying safe
field.topic: Below-grade waterproofing, structure sealing and corrosion protection
field.source: General field practice; H2S chemistry from biogenic sulfide corrosion summary

field.text: Trench volume in cubic yards (bank, in place) = length (ft) x average width (ft) x average depth (ft) / 27. Example: 400 ft of trench, 3 ft wide, 9 ft deep: 400 x 3 x 9 / 27 = 400 CY per day of digging. With sloped sides: average width = (bottom width + top width) / 2. Example: 10 ft deep, 4 ft bottom, sides sloped 1:1 (top width 4 + 2 x 10 = 24 ft): average width 14 ft; per foot 14 x 10 / 27 = 5.19 CY per foot, versus 1.48 CY per foot in a 4 ft wide boxed trench. Add structure pits separately (for a manhole, roughly the box footprint times depth). This is bank volume; for trucking, convert to loose volume using a swell factor. Exact math.
field.title: Trench excavation volume
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Soil changes volume when dug and when compacted. Bank cubic yards (BCY): in place. Loose cubic yards (LCY): after digging, bigger because of air. Compacted cubic yards (CCY): after compaction. Formulas (standard earthmoving method): LCY = BCY x (1 + swell); CCY = BCY x (1 - shrinkage). Swell percentages from ProjectEngineer's table: clay 40%; clay and gravel 40%; common earth or loam 25%; gravel 12%; sand 12%; hardpan 50%; well-blasted rock 65%; shale and soft rock 65%; limestone 67%; sandstone 54%. Other references give somewhat different values (for example clay 30 to 40%, rock 50 to 80%), so use them as estimates and check against your own truck counts. Shrinkage (bank to compacted) for common soils is often 10 to 20%, but rock can bulk permanently. Swell table from ProjectEngineer; shrink range is a general estimate.
field.title: Swell and shrink: bank, loose and compacted yards
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: ProjectEngineer, Swell Factors for Various Soils (B. Roseke, P.Eng.)

field.text: To estimate haul-off loads: (1) compute bank yards dug; (2) subtract what goes back as backfill (bank yards needed to fill the trench above the imported embedment, adjusted for compaction); (3) convert the excess to loose yards with the swell factor; (4) divide by truck capacity. Example: 400 ft of 3 ft x 9 ft trench = 400 BCY dug. Pipe zone gets imported stone (about 0.25 CY per foot = 100 CY), so 100 BCY of spoil is excess (plus pipe volume), and the other 300 BCY goes back as backfill. If all spoil must go (bad material), 400 BCY x 1.25 swell (common earth) = 500 LCY; at about 12 to 14 LCY per tandem load that's roughly 36 to 42 loads; with tri-axles or semis, fewer. Truck capacity is often limited by legal weight, not volume: wet clay may max out on weight before the box is heaped. Check truck legal limits and your actual truck counts.
field.title: Haul-off: how many truckloads
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Granular materials are usually bought by the ton but placed by volume. Tons = cubic yards x unit weight in tons per CY. Typical crushed stone and gravel run around 1.35 to 1.5 tons per loose or placed cubic yard depending on gradation and compaction; sand somewhat less or similar; get the actual factor from your supplier's material data or weigh tickets. Example: 92 CY of bedding at 1.45 tons per CY = about 133 tons, or about 7 loads at 20 tons. Add waste (commonly 5 to 10%) for over-excavation and spillage. Track tickets against placed quantities: if you're using far more stone than estimated, the trench is probably wider or deeper than planned, or stone is going into areas that should be native. Unit weights are typical ranges; use supplier data.
field.title: Bedding stone and import tonnage
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Flowable fill, or controlled low-strength material (CLSM), is a fluid cement-based backfill that self-levels and needs no compaction. Per NRMCA's CIP 17: for future excavation by machine, keep ultimate strength below about 200 psi; for hand digging, below about 50 psi; structural fills are often 50 to 100 psi, similar to well-compacted soil. Unit weight usually 115 to 145 lb per cubic ft. Slump generally over 8 inches. Loads can usually be applied when penetration resistance reaches 500 to 1,500 psi, often within hours. High-water mixes can settle about 1/4 inch per foot of depth. It must be protected from freezing until hardened. Caution: fluid flowable fill pushes hard on forms and can float pipe and structures; place in lifts or anchor the pipe. Order by the cubic yard: volume = trench length x width x depth / 27, minus pipe volume. Tell the supplier if it must be excavatable.
field.title: Flowable fill (CLSM) basics
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: NRMCA Concrete in Practice CIP 17, Flowable Fill

field.text: Concrete volume in cubic yards = length (ft) x width (ft) x thickness (ft) / 27. Inches to feet: divide by 12. Examples: thrust block 3 ft x 2 ft bearing face x 2.5 ft deep = 15 cubic ft = 0.56 CY. Manhole collar or pad 6 ft x 6 ft x 8 inch: 6 x 6 x 0.667 = 24 cubic ft = 0.89 CY. Cylinder (pipe encasement or round pad): pi x radius squared x length. For irregular blocks poured against soil, add more waste (commonly 10% or more) because over-dig fills with concrete. Pre-mixed 80 lb bags of concrete yield roughly 0.6 cubic ft each (check the bag), so 1 CY needs about 45 bags; for more than a fraction of a yard, order ready-mix. Concrete testing typically includes slump (ASTM C143), air content, temperature and cylinders (ASTM C31 making, C39 testing) per your specs. Exact math; bag yield from typical product labels.
field.title: Concrete yardage for thrust blocks, collars and pads
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Hot-mix asphalt (HMA) is ordered by the ton. Compacted HMA weighs roughly 145 lb per cubic ft (typical; mixes vary about 140 to 150). That gives about 110 lb per square yard per inch of compacted thickness (9 sq ft x 1/12 ft x 145 = 108.75, commonly rounded to 110). Tons = square yards x inches x 110 / 2,000. Example: trench patch 600 ft long x 5 ft wide x 4 inches: 3,000 sq ft = 333 SY; 333 x 4 x 110 / 2,000 = 73 tons. Or by volume: 3,000 x 0.333 ft = 1,000 cubic ft x 145 / 2,000 = 72.5 tons. Add waste (commonly 5 to 10%) and account for uneven base. Use your mix design's density if known. Agency specs set minimum patch thickness, often matching or exceeding the existing pavement plus a set amount; check your permit.
field.title: Asphalt tonnage for trench patching
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Under trench patches, agencies often require compacted aggregate base (crushed stone base course) at a set thickness. Tonnage = area (sq ft) x thickness (ft) x compacted unit weight (lb per cubic ft) / 2,000. Compacted dense-graded base is often in the range of about 130 to 145 lb per cubic ft (roughly 1.75 to 1.95 tons per compacted CY); get your supplier's or the spec's value. Example: 3,000 sq ft x 8 inches (0.667 ft) = 2,000 cubic ft; at 140 lb per cubic ft that's 140 tons. Compact in lifts per spec and get density tests before paving. Sawcut the existing pavement edges straight and back from the trench edge (many agencies require a T-patch extending 6 to 12 inches beyond the trench wall onto undisturbed base; check your permit). Unit weight is a typical range; use supplier data.
field.title: Aggregate base for pavement restoration
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Handy constants: 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic ft. 1 square yard = 9 square ft. 1 cubic ft of water = 7.48 gallons and weighs 62.4 lb. 1 gallon of water weighs 8.34 lb. 1 psi = 2.31 ft of water head; 1 ft of water = 0.433 psi. 1 ton = 2,000 lb. 1 mile = 5,280 ft. Gallons per foot of pipe = 0.0408 x (inside diameter in inches) squared; so 8 inch = 2.61, 12 inch = 5.87, 24 inch = 23.5 gallons per foot. Area of a circle = 3.1416 x radius squared = 0.7854 x diameter squared. Flow: gallons per minute = 448.8 x cubic ft per second. These are exact or standard constants.
field.title: Pipe volume, water weight and handy conversions
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Empty pipe in a flooded trench or in fresh flowable fill can float out of grade, because it displaces more weight of water or slurry than it weighs. Buoyant uplift per foot = volume displaced by the pipe's outside (0.7854 x OD in ft squared) x unit weight of the fluid (62.4 lb per cubic ft for water; flowable fill often 115 to 145 lb per cubic ft per NRMCA) minus the pipe's weight per foot. Example: 24 inch corrugated HDPE (OD about 28 inches = 2.33 ft): displaced volume 4.28 cubic ft per foot; in water, uplift about 267 lb per foot, far more than the pipe weighs; in flowable fill at 130 lb per cubic ft, about 556 lb per foot. That's why light pipe needs backfill placed promptly, dewatering, or anchoring, and flowable fill placed in lifts. Exact physics; weights vary by product.
field.title: Pipe flotation: when empty pipe can float
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: Diesel fuel use depends on engine size and how hard the machine works. A common estimating method in construction equipment texts: fuel (gallons per hour) is roughly 0.04 gallon per horsepower-hour times rated horsepower times a load factor; load factors are often taken around 0.5 for moderate work and higher for hard digging. Example: a 150 hp excavator at a 0.5 load factor: 0.04 x 150 x 0.5 = about 3 gallons per hour; 8 hours = 24 gallons. Modern machines' telematics report actual burn, which is better than any estimate. Use actual fuel logs per machine for job costing and bids. The 0.04 factor is a textbook approximation; real values vary by engine and machine.
field.title: Estimating fuel for equipment
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Construction equipment estimating texts (approximation); telematics data

field.text: Restoration quantities to plan: Sawcut: linear feet = both edges of the trench patch, plus ends (for 600 ft of patch, about 1,200 LF plus ends); sawcut depth often full pavement depth per agency rules. Curb and gutter, sidewalk: by LF or SF removed and replaced, usually to the nearest joint per city rules. Topsoil: area x depth / 27 (4 inches over 1,000 sq ft = 12.3 CY). Seed: by area at the specified rate (lb per 1,000 sq ft or per acre), plus mulch or erosion blanket. Sod: by square yard or square ft. Driveway and lawn items: measure before you dig and take photos for the record. Restoration often runs behind the pipe crew; track it as its own cost code so it doesn't hide in pipe costs. Exact math; rates come from specs.
field.title: Sawcutting, seeding and restoration quantities
field.topic: Materials math and quantities
field.source: Standard construction math (worked examples)

field.text: NASSCO's Pipeline Assessment Certification Program (PACP) is the standard US system for coding sewer CCTV observations. Defect groups include structural (cracks, fractures, broken pipe, holes, deformation, joint offsets and separations), operation and maintenance (roots, deposits, debris, infiltration, obstacles), and construction features (taps, connections, intruding service connections). Each defect gets a code and a grade from 1 (minor) to 5 (most severe). On new construction acceptance videos, common problems flagged are sags (ponded water), joint offsets or gaps, protruding taps, cracks from poor bedding or rocks, debris, and infiltration. Operators must be PACP-certified on many projects. Ask for the coded report, not just the video.
field.title: Sewer CCTV defect codes (PACP basics)
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: NASSCO PACP

field.text: When new mains replace old ones, the old pipes are usually abandoned in place or removed per the specs. Typical abandonment practice: disconnect and cap or plug the old pipe at each connection to the active system (for water, at the tee or with a cut and cap so no dead end remains on the live system); fill abandoned pipes larger than a set size (often 8 inch or more) with flowable fill or grout so they can't collapse and cause sinkholes; remove valve boxes and hydrants or fill them per detail; and record the abandoned lines and plugs on the as-builts. Asbestos-cement pipe needs special handling under asbestos rules if cut or removed. Check your specs for size thresholds and fill requirements.
field.title: Abandoning old water mains and sewers
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Many older water mains and some sewers are asbestos-cement (AC or transite) pipe. Cutting, breaking or grinding AC pipe can release asbestos fibers. Rules are set by OSHA's asbestos standard for construction (29 CFR 1926.1101) and EPA and state asbestos rules: use trained workers, wet methods and non-powered cutting tools (snap cutters) where possible, avoid abrasive saws, bag waste in labeled containers, and dispose at an approved site. Many utilities have specific procedures and require certified crews. Don't break up AC pipe with the excavator bucket when removing it unless your asbestos procedure allows. Identify pipe material before cutting.
field.title: Asbestos-cement (AC) pipe: caution
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1101; EPA asbestos rules (summary)

field.text: Water service lines are commonly copper (Type K for underground) or polyethylene tubing (PE, often PE 4710 in copper tube size, CTS, with a pressure rating such as 200 psi at DR 9), and sometimes PEX. Field points: use compression fittings made for the tubing type; insert stainless steel stiffeners in PE tubing at compression fittings if the fitting maker requires; cut tubing square and deburr; leave a gooseneck or loop at the main; bed in sand; install tracer wire with plastic tubing if required; avoid kinking PE tubing; and use dielectric protection where copper meets dissimilar metals if specs require. Check your utility's approved material list and details.
field.title: HDPE and copper water service tubing
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Ductile iron fittings for water mains come in two common AWWA standards. AWWA C110 (full-body or standard) fittings are longer and heavier, in sizes from small to very large. AWWA C153 (compact) fittings are shorter and lighter, with pressure ratings commonly 350 psi in smaller sizes and lower in larger sizes (check the maker's rating). Both use MJ, push-on or flanged ends per AWWA C111 (flanges per C115 or C110). Compact fittings are common for typical water mains because they're lighter to handle. Both are usually cement-lined per C104. Use restraints rated for the fitting and the pipe material. Check the approved submittal.
field.title: Ductile iron fittings: C110 versus C153
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: AWWA C110 / C153 scopes as summarized by fitting manufacturers

field.text: Common construction contract types for utility work. Unit price: pay per measured unit installed; owner carries quantity risk; common for public pipe work. Lump sum (stipulated sum): a fixed price for defined work; contractor carries quantity risk; common for private site work and small projects. Cost-plus (time and materials, with or without a guaranteed maximum price): owner pays actual costs plus a fee; used where scope is uncertain, such as emergency repairs. Design-build: one contract for design and construction. On any type, scope changes go through change orders. Know which type you're signing, because it changes who absorbs overruns and how you document quantities.
field.title: Contract types: unit price, lump sum, cost-plus
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)
