field.text: Common insurance coverages owners require from utility contractors: commercial general liability (bodily injury and property damage to others, including underground utility damage, which some policies exclude or limit, so check for 'XCU' (explosion, collapse and underground) exclusions); workers' compensation and employer's liability; commercial auto; umbrella or excess liability; contractor's equipment (inland marine) for your machines; and sometimes pollution liability (for dewatering, contaminated soil or spills) and professional liability on design-build. Contracts often require naming the owner as additional insured and a waiver of subrogation. Read the insurance requirements before bidding; an XCU exclusion on underground work is a big gap. This is general information, not insurance advice.
field.title: Insurance basics for utility contractors
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: Many contracts set liquidated damages (LDs): a fixed dollar amount per day the contractor pays if the work isn't complete by the contract date (or milestone dates), in place of proving actual damages. LDs usually stop at substantial completion, when the work can be used for its intended purpose, even if punch list items remain. To protect yourself: know the LD rate and milestones, request time extensions in writing promptly for excusable delays with documentation, and push to get substantial completion recognized as soon as the work qualifies. Interim milestones (such as reopening a road) may carry their own LDs or lane rental charges.
field.title: Liquidated damages and substantial completion
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: For company owners running several pipe crews, a weekly dashboard might include for each job: percent complete versus percent of time elapsed; earned value cost and schedule indexes (CPI, SPI); cost per foot versus estimate on the main pipe items; production factor (earned hours over actual hours); change orders submitted, approved and pending (with dollars); billing versus earned (over or under billed); retainage held; safety incidents and near misses; equipment utilization; and backlog. Red flags: CPI or production factor below 1.0 for two weeks running, pending change orders growing, or underbilling. The point is to catch trouble while there's still time to act. General construction management practice.
field.title: Owner-level dashboard: what to watch weekly
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: Bank cubic yards per linear foot of vertical-wall trench = width x depth / 27. Width 2.5 ft: depth 4 ft 0.37; 6 ft 0.56; 8 ft 0.74; 10 ft 0.93; 12 ft 1.11. Width 3 ft: 4 ft 0.44; 6 ft 0.67; 8 ft 0.89; 10 ft 1.11; 12 ft 1.33; 14 ft 1.56. Width 4 ft: 6 ft 0.89; 8 ft 1.19; 10 ft 1.48; 12 ft 1.78; 14 ft 2.07; 16 ft 2.37. Width 5 ft: 8 ft 1.48; 10 ft 1.85; 12 ft 2.22; 16 ft 2.96. Multiply by footage for the day: 300 ft of 3 ft x 10 ft trench = 333 BCY. Multiply by the swell factor for loose yards to haul. Computed values.
field.title: Trench volume per foot table
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Standard construction math (computed values)

field.text: Approximate cubic yards of embedment stone per foot for a 6 inch bed and stone to 12 inches over the pipe, in a trench of the width shown, minus the pipe's outside area (computed; real pipe ODs vary slightly). 8 inch PVC (OD about 8.4 in), 2.5 ft wide: about 0.19 CY/ft; 3 ft wide: about 0.23. 12 inch PVC (OD about 12.5 in), 3 ft wide: about 0.25 CY/ft; 3.5 ft wide: about 0.30. 24 inch pipe (OD about 26 to 28 in), 4.5 ft wide: about 0.47 to 0.48 CY/ft. Method: stone depth = 0.5 + OD (ft) + 1.0; area = width x stone depth - 0.785 x OD squared; CY per ft = area / 27. Add 5 to 10% for over-dig and waste, and convert to tons with your supplier's factor.
field.title: Embedment stone per foot table (approximate)
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Standard construction math (computed values)

field.text: Steep sewers can slide downhill or erode their bedding. The Ten States Standards call for concrete anchors on sewers laid on slopes of 20% or more, with spacing commonly cited as not more than 36 ft center to center on grades of 20% up to 35%, not more than 24 ft for 35% up to 50%, and not more than 16 ft for 50% and over. High velocities on steep grades can also scour the pipe and manholes, so designers may require drop manholes or special materials. Trench plugs (clay or concrete cutoffs) are often used on steep trenches to keep groundwater from running along the stone bedding and washing it out. Follow the plans and your agency's details.
field.title: Sewers on steep slopes: anchors
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards)

field.text: Crushed stone bedding is very permeable, so groundwater can flow along the trench like a drain, washing fines, lowering groundwater on neighboring property or carrying water to low points. Trench plugs (cutoff collars or dams) made of compacted clay, flowable fill or concrete across the full trench width at intervals and on steep grades stop this flow. Specs may call for them at set spacing, at manholes, at the ends of runs and where the sewer passes wetlands or changes slope. Geotextile around the stone (where specified) keeps fine soil from migrating into the stone. Follow the plans and details.
field.title: Trench plugs and groundwater along bedding
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: New mains are usually filled and tested with water from the existing system through a hydrant meter supplied by the utility. Common rules: get the meter and permission from the utility; use a backflow preventer (often a reduced pressure or double check assembly) so construction water can't flow back into the public system; open the hydrant slowly; fill the new main slowly with air venting at high points (fill velocity low enough to avoid surges); and record meter readings for billing. Don't open existing system valves without the utility's direction. Some utilities provide a disinfected water tank or require the contractor to supply one for testing (Spotsylvania County, for example).
field.title: Hydrant meters and filling new mains
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Valve boxes, curb boxes and manhole frames often get buried or left high by paving. Practices: before paving, set boxes to the planned finished grade or slightly low and mark them; after paving, find and adjust any covered boxes (a metal detector helps), cut out the asphalt neatly, raise the box top flush, and patch; make sure the valve key still reaches the nut and the box isn't resting on the valve. Many agencies require all castings be adjusted and checked before acceptance. Record valve ties so they can be found under pavement.
field.title: Valve boxes and castings after paving
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Small PVC pipe (Schedule 40 and 80, and some sewer and drain fittings) is joined with primer and solvent cement rather than gaskets. Steps from manufacturer guidance: cut square and deburr; dry-fit to check the fit; apply primer to the fitting socket and pipe end if required by code or the maker; apply an even coat of solvent cement to the pipe and a thinner coat to the socket; push the pipe fully in with a quarter turn and hold for the time the maker gives (pipe can push back out); wipe excess; let it set and cure before handling or testing (cure time depends on size, temperature and humidity). Use cement rated for the pipe size and type. Solvent fumes cause laser refraction in pipe and are a health hazard in trenches; ventilate.
field.title: Solvent cement joints on small PVC
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Key excavator specs for pipe work: maximum digging depth (with the specified boom and stick; plan to work well short of maximum, especially for trench boxes and with long pipe); maximum reach at ground; dump height (for loading trucks); operating weight; bucket breakout and stick digging force; lift capacity charts; tail swing (conventional versus reduced or zero tail swing, important on streets); travel width (for working beside traffic); and hydraulic flow for attachments like hammers or compaction plates. A machine that can just reach the depth at full extension will dig slowly and lift poorly there. Compare the lift chart at your working radius with the box and pipe weights. Field practice.
field.title: Reading excavator specs for trench work
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Industry practice / field experience (not a measured study)

field.text: Short safety talks work best when tied to the work that week. Useful topics for pipe crews: trench protection and the competent person's inspection; ladders and egress within 25 ft; spoil setback; water in trenches; utility locates, tolerance zones and what to do if a line is hit; excavator swing radius and struck-by hazards; rigging inspection and keeping out from under loads; quick coupler checks; traffic control and working near live lanes; confined space and manhole entry; heat illness or cold stress; silica when cutting concrete pipe; hand and finger injuries when joining pipe; and backing trucks with spotters. Record attendance and topic in the daily report. Field practice.
field.title: Toolbox talk topics for pipe crews
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Industry practice / field experience (not a measured study)

field.text: An inverted siphon (depressed sewer) carries sewage under an obstacle such as a stream or large utility by dipping below the hydraulic grade line and coming back up. Design and construction points from Ten States Standards guidance: at least two barrels (to allow cleaning and to handle low and high flows), a minimum pipe size, enough velocity to keep solids moving, inlet and outlet structures arranged for flow splitting and cleaning access, and pressure-rated pipe and joints. Other special structures include junction chambers, flow splitters and drop structures. These are engineered; build exactly to the shop drawings and confirm elevations carefully because siphons are sensitive to inverts.
field.title: Inverted siphons and special sewer structures
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards)

field.text: Example daily report entry showing the level of detail that holds up: 'Date 6/12. Weather: 78 F, sunny, dry trench. Crew: foreman, operator (EX 245), pipelayer, 2 laborers, loader operator; 10 hrs. Equipment: excavator #12 (10 hrs operating), loader #4 (9 hrs), trench box 8x24 (on site), plate compactor. Work: laid 8 inch PVC SDR 35 from MH 7 (Sta 14+20) to Sta 17+35, 315 LF, average cut 11 ft; installed 3 wyes at Sta 15+10 R, 16+05 L, 16+90 R with 4 inch stubs capped. Materials: 92 tons #57 stone (tickets 4471 to 4475). Tests: 2 density tests at 15+50 and 17+00, 96% and 95% (passed). Delays: 1.5 hrs, unmarked 2 inch gas service at 16+40, utility notified 10:15, cleared 11:45. Visitors: inspector J.R. on site AM. Safety: toolbox talk on swing radius; trench inspection 7:00 and 13:00.' Format is an example of field practice.
field.title: Sample daily report entry for a pipe crew
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Industry practice / field experience (not a measured study)

field.text: Pay quantities must be measured the way the contract says, so read the measurement and payment section before measuring. Common methods for pipe: horizontal length along the centerline from center of manhole to center of manhole (some specs) or from inside face to inside face (others), with fittings either included or paid separately; depth ranges measured from existing or finished grade to invert at set intervals; manholes measured by each plus vertical feet beyond a base depth from invert to rim; services by each or by length; stone and select backfill by ticket weight within pay limits; rock by cubic yard within a pay line (often a set width and depth below the pipe). Agree on measurements with the inspector as work proceeds, not at the end.
field.title: Measuring pay quantities for pipe
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Construction management practice (contract governs)

field.text: Locates must cover every area you'll dig, before you dig. Planning practice: keep a map of active tickets with their areas and expiration dates; request tickets far enough ahead to cover the next week or two of work, given your state's notice time (Iowa: 48 hours excluding weekends and holidays); renew before expiration (Iowa tickets last 25 calendar days after the wait period); check positive response for all utilities before starting each area; request re-marks when marks fade (Iowa expects marks to last at least 5 working days on dirt and 10 on pavement) or are destroyed by work; and note ticket numbers in the daily report. A missing or expired ticket can stop the crew and creates legal liability if a line is hit. Check your state law.
field.title: Planning tomorrow's 811 coverage
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024 (example state)

field.text: Contracts usually treat weather in one of two ways: a set number of anticipated weather days built into the contract time (with extensions only for days beyond that), or time extensions for weather that's unusually severe compared to historical averages for that location and month, often shown with NOAA records. To protect your schedule: record weather and its effect on work every day in the daily report (rain amount, frozen ground, wet trench, unsafe conditions, which activities stopped); note days after heavy rain when the site was too wet to work even if it didn't rain that day; and submit weather delay requests in the time the contract requires. Weather delays are typically excusable (more time) but not compensable (no money).
field.title: Weather days and time extensions
field.topic: Miscellaneous field and business topics
field.source: Construction management practice (contract governs)

field.text: Raising or lowering existing manhole frames (for paving projects or grade changes): remove the frame, remove or add adjusting rings, set the frame on sealant or mortar to the new grade and cross slope, seal ring joints inside and out to keep groundwater out, and restore the surrounding pavement (often a concrete collar around the frame in asphalt streets). Rings should stay within the agency's maximum total height. Manhole rehab methods for leaking or corroded manholes include grouting leaks, cementitious or epoxy linings, and chimney seals (internal rubber sleeves sealing the frame-to-cone joint). NCDOT's contract time guidelines list manhole and valve adjustments at 8 to 10 per day on resurfacing work. Follow the agency's standard detail.
field.title: Manhole frame adjustment and rehab
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: NCDOT contract time guidelines; common municipal practice

field.text: Typical water service installation (utility standard details vary): tap the main with a corporation stop (direct tap or through a saddle), at the side of the main; run service tubing (copper or PE/PEX per utility) with a gooseneck or loop at the main to allow settlement and movement; bed and cover with sand or fine material; maintain the minimum cover for frost; install the curb stop and curb box at the property line or as detailed, plumb and to grade; install the meter setter or meter pit as detailed; pressure test and disinfect with the main or as the utility requires; and record the tap location (station, offset, depth) and curb box ties. Use compression fittings rated for the tubing and stiffeners for plastic tubing where required.
field.title: Water service installation details
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Many owners now want as-built locations captured with GPS coordinates instead of (or as well as) tape ties. Practices: use a survey-grade GNSS rover tied to the project's coordinate system (or a mapping-grade receiver if the owner allows lower accuracy); shoot each fitting, valve, bend, service tap, cleanout, manhole and utility crossing before backfill, with a point code and description (size, material, depth); shoot tops of pipe or inverts where depth matters; back up data daily and include photos with the point numbers. Owners load this into GIS. Check the owner's required accuracy, coordinate system and file format before starting.
field.title: GPS as-builts and utility mapping
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Flexible pipe deflection limits are set by the project specs. ASTM D2321 discusses a 7.5% deflection limit as a long-term design limit for thermoplastic pipe; many municipal specs set acceptance at 5% (as in Berkeley County's spec, using a mandrel at 95% of base ID), and some DOTs accept corrugated HDPE or PP at up to 5% with evaluation or price reductions between 5% and 7.5%, with removal above that. ADS notes poor backfill or compaction may cause deflection above 5% and may call for deflection checks. Testing methods: mandrel, laser profiling or measured video (for large pipe, direct measurement by a person in the pipe under confined space rules). Check your spec for the limit, timing (often 30 days after backfill) and method.
field.title: Deflection testing of HDPE and other flexible pipe
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: ASTM D2321 summaries; Berkeley County spec; ADS TN 2.01

field.text: The owner's inspector decides whether work is accepted, so a good working relationship saves time and money. Practices: know who the inspector is and how they want to be notified for tests and observations; walk the day's plan with them in the morning; let them see work before backfill (fittings, services, bedding) so there's no reason to dig it up later; keep test reports and density results organized; raise problems early instead of hiding them; get directions in writing (or confirm by email) when the inspector asks for something beyond the plans, since that may be extra work; and keep your daily report consistent with theirs. Disagreements go up the chain in writing, politely.
field.title: Working with the inspector
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: Construction management practice (general; contract governs)

field.text: Night work on utility jobs needs lighting for the work area, flagger stations and equipment without blinding drivers. Practices: light plants aimed down and away from oncoming traffic; flagger stations lit (the MUTCD requires flagger stations to be illuminated at night except in emergencies); retroreflective devices and Class 3 apparel (MUTCD recommends Class 3 at night); amber lights on equipment; extra attention to fatigue and to impaired or speeding drivers; noise limits in residential areas (check local ordinances and permit conditions); and a plan for emergencies with nighttime contacts. Check the agency's night work requirements.
field.title: Night work lighting and safety
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: FHWA MUTCD Part 6; common agency practice

field.text: Sewer lateral details to get right: wye placement at the station shown, rotated so the lateral comes off at the angle the detail shows (often 45 degrees above horizontal, not flat on the bottom); a riser or chimney for deep mains per detail, bedded and supported so it doesn't settle; minimum lateral slope per local code (commonly 1/4 inch per foot for 4 inch); cap or plug watertight at the end with a marker (stake, magnetic marker or tracer wire) and record depth at the end; cleanout at the property line if required; and never connect roof drains, sump pumps or foundation drains to sanitary laterals (inflow). Check for an existing service before connecting a new one so a live service isn't cut off. Follow local standard details.
field.title: Sewer laterals: field details
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Sewage force mains are usually hydrostatically tested much like water mains, but specs vary: test pressure is often set at a multiple of the pump's maximum operating or shutoff pressure, or a fixed value (for example 100 or 150 psi), held for a set time (often 2 hours), with allowable make-up water by the C600 formula or a stricter limit. Use clean water; disinfection is not required for sewage service. Make sure air valves are isolated or rated for the test pressure, and that the lift station check valves and pumps are not over-pressurized. Check the force main spec section for the exact pressure and allowance.
field.title: Pressure testing sewage force mains
field.topic: Miscellaneous field topics
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: ASTM C76 (AASHTO M170) reinforced concrete pipe (RCP) is rated by class, based on the three-edge-bearing D-load test (pounds per foot of length per foot of inside diameter). Per ACPA: Class I, 800 lb/ft/ft at the 0.01-inch crack and 1,200 ultimate; Class II, 1,000 and 1,500; Class III, 1,350 and 2,000; Class IV, 2,000 and 3,000; Class V, 3,000 and 3,750. Example: 24 inch (2 ft) Class III must hold 1,350 x 2 = 2,700 lb per foot before a 0.01 inch crack. The 0.01 inch crack is a designed behavior, not failure. ACPA notes that with at least 1 ft of cover under highway HL-93 loading, Class III or greater generally suffices; deeper fill or heavy traffic may need Class IV, V or special design. The class is set by the engineer; check the plans for class by run and depth.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe: ASTM C76 classes and D-loads
field.topic: Pipe materials: concrete pipe and box
field.source: American Concrete Pipe Association, design FAQs (ASTM C76 D-loads)

field.text: ASTM C76 RCP comes in three wall thicknesses: Wall A (thinnest), Wall B and Wall C (thickest). Minimum wall thickness examples (inches) from the C76 tables as reproduced by Engineers Edge: 12 inch pipe, A 1.75, B 2.0, C 2.75; 15 inch, A 1.875, B 2.25, C 3.0; 18 inch, A 2.0, B 2.5, C 3.25; 24 inch, A 2.5, B 3.0, C 3.75; 30 inch, A 2.75, B 3.5, C 4.25; 36 inch, A 3.0, B 4.0, C 4.75; 48 inch, A 4.0, B 5.0, C 5.75; 60 inch, A 5.0, B 6.0, C 6.75; 72 inch, A 6.0, B 7.0, C 7.75. A handy pattern: Wall B is about the inside diameter in feet plus 1 inch (for example 48 inch: 4 + 1 = 5 inches). Wall thickness matters for OD, trench width, boot and manhole opening size, and pipe weight. Ask the supplier which wall you're getting.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe: wall types A, B and C
field.topic: Pipe materials: concrete pipe and box
field.source: ASTM C76 wall thickness table as reproduced by Engineers Edge

field.text: RCP joints come in a few types. Tongue-and-groove joints are common on storm drain; they're sealed with mortar, preformed butyl or bitumen mastic sealant (ASTM C990), or wrapped with an external joint wrap (ASTM C877) or geotextile to keep soil out. Gasketed joints (O-ring or profile gasket in a bell-and-spigot or modified tongue-and-groove, ASTM C443) are used where watertight joints are needed, such as sanitary sewer and many storm specs. Field practice: clean the joint surfaces, place the gasket or sealant per the maker (gaskets lubed with the maker's lube, butyl rope sized and placed on the tongue or groove, often warmed in cold weather), line up and push home with a pipe puller or come-along so the joint closes evenly, and check the gap all around. Joint type is set by the specs; check them.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe: joints for storm and sanitary
field.topic: Pipe materials: concrete pipe and box
field.source: ACPA Concrete Pipe & Box Culvert Installation guidance; ASTM C443/C990/C877 scopes

field.text: Concrete pipe installation is covered by ASTM C1479 and ACPA's installation manual, using the Standard Installation types (Type 1 through 4) from AASHTO and ASCE 15. Per ACPA, Type 1 needs the best backfill and compaction and allows the lowest-strength pipe; Type 4 is for little or no control of fill or compaction and needs the strongest pipe; Types 2 and 3 fall between. The bedding should be uniform and slightly loose under the middle third of the pipe so the pipe beds in, with bell holes dug so the pipe doesn't rest on its bells. The haunch zone must be filled and compacted; that's where concrete pipe gets much of its support. Lay downstream to upstream with bells (grooves) upstream. The plans or specs state the installation type; the field crew must build it as designed.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe: installation per ASTM C1479 and ACPA
field.topic: Pipe materials: concrete pipe and box
field.source: American Concrete Pipe Association, design FAQs (ASTM C76 D-loads)

field.text: RCP is heavy, so handling must be planned. Lift with the producer's lifting devices (lift holes with a lifting pin/toggle, cast-in lift anchors) or with a sling or pipe hook rated for the load; get the weight per piece from the supplier's delivery ticket or catalog, and check the excavator lift chart at the working radius. Don't lift by putting a chain through the pipe bore over the joint ends in a way that chips the bell or spigot. Never drop or roll pipe off the truck. Inspect for cracks, chipped joints and exposed steel before installing; minor chips can sometimes be repaired with approved patching, but cracked or damaged joints should be rejected. Plug lift holes after setting with the plug supplied or approved mortar so soil and water can't get in. These points are standard concrete pipe industry practice.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe: handling and lifting
field.topic: Pipe materials: concrete pipe and box
field.source: ACPA installation guidance and producer handling instructions

field.text: RCP is commonly made in 8 ft lay lengths, with other lengths (such as 4, 6, 7.5, 12 or 16 ft) available from some producers; large-diameter pipe is often shorter so pieces stay within truck and crane limits. Because RCP is heavy, the excavator's rated lift at the actual radius often decides the pipe length and machine size. Example of planning: if a 48 inch Wall B pipe piece weighs several tons (get the exact weight from the producer), the excavator must be rated for that weight plus rigging at the reach you'll set it, which may require setting from closer or using a bigger machine. Ask the producer for a weight-per-piece sheet before ordering, and plan box length for one or two pipe lengths per move. Lay-length range is industry information; weights must come from the supplier.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe: lay lengths and weight planning
field.topic: Pipe materials: concrete pipe and box
field.source: Concrete pipe producer catalogs; ACPA

field.text: Precast concrete box culverts are made to ASTM C1577 (designed for highway loads) and older C1433 standards, in spans and rises listed by the producer. Installation is similar to large RCP: a level, uniform bedding course (often fine granular material) prepared to grade, sections set and pulled together with come-alongs or pipe pullers, joints sealed with butyl mastic sealant (C990) and often wrapped with external joint wrap, lift holes plugged, and backfill placed and compacted evenly on both sides. Heavy pieces need crane-sized lifts. The design shows fill height range and any special bedding. Check the approved shop drawings for section weights and joint details. Source: ASTM product standards as summarized by ACPA and precast producers.
field.title: Precast concrete box culverts
field.topic: Pipe materials: concrete pipe and box
field.source: ACPA; ASTM C1577 scope

field.text: Ductile iron pipe (DIP) for water and force mains is designed under AWWA C150 and manufactured under AWWA C151. Pressure classes are 150, 200, 250, 300 and 350 psi; DIPRA's suggested specification notes the minimum rated working pressure is 150 psi, with design including a 100 psi surge allowance and a 2 to 1 safety factor on working plus surge pressure. Every pipe is hydrostatically tested at the factory to at least 500 psi. Older specs use thickness classes (Special Class 50 through 56) instead of pressure classes. Pipe is marked with class or thickness, weight, casting period, maker, country, year, and 'DI' or 'Ductile.' Common lengths are 18 ft and 20 ft depending on maker and size. Installation and testing follow AWWA C600; disinfection follows AWWA C651.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: standards and pressure classes
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: DIPRA suggested specification for ductile iron pipe and fittings (AWWA C150/C151/C104/C111/C600)

field.text: Ductile iron water pipe normally has a cement-mortar lining to AWWA C104, with a thin asphaltic seal coat over it, and a thin asphaltic exterior coating. DIPRA's suggested spec calls for C104 cement lining and the standard exterior coating. Double-thickness cement lining is available. Sewer and force main pipe in corrosive service may use special linings such as ceramic epoxy or polyurethane instead of cement. Handle lined pipe gently: dropping or hard impacts crack the lining. Small hairline lining cracks are normal and heal when wet (autogenous healing), but loose or spalled lining must be repaired per the maker. Polyethylene encasement (AWWA C105) is the common field corrosion protection in aggressive soils; check your specs.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: linings and coatings
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: DIPRA suggested specification for ductile iron pipe and fittings (AWWA C150/C151/C104/C111/C600)

field.text: Polyethylene encasement ('polywrap') is a loose sleeve of polyethylene film put around ductile iron pipe in the trench to protect it from corrosive soils, per AWWA C105. Common materials are linear low-density film (8 mil) or high-density cross-laminated film (4 mil). Methods: tube (sleeve slid over each pipe and overlapped at joints), or sheet wrap. Field practice from C105 and DIPRA guidance: overlap at joints about 1 ft and secure with tape or straps; take up slack with a fold at the top so it fits loosely; repair rips, holes and cuts with tape or patches of the same film; wrap fittings, valves and appurtenances too; for taps, wrap tape over the film around the tap area before tapping and inspect after. Don't drag the wrapped pipe or dump rocks on it. Check your specs for the film type and method.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: polyethylene encasement (AWWA C105)
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: AWWA C105 as summarized by DIPRA guidance

field.text: Ductile iron joints are covered by AWWA C111. Push-on joints (brand names include Tyton and Fastite) use a rubber gasket in the bell; clean the bell and gasket seat, seat the gasket fully, lubricate the gasket inside face and the spigot, keep the pipe straight, and push home to the maker's stripe or depth. Mechanical joints (MJ) use a gasket squeezed by a ductile iron gland with T-bolts; they're mainly used on fittings and valves. MJ assembly: clean, lube the gasket and spigot, slide the gland and gasket on, insert the spigot fully, push the gasket into the bell, then tighten bolts evenly in a crisscross pattern to the maker's torque (C111 and C600 give torque ranges by bolt size). Restrained versions exist for both: gasket-integrated restraints, restrained push-on joints, and MJ wedge-action restraint glands. Use only restraints rated for the pipe material.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: push-on and mechanical joints
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: DIPRA suggested specification for ductile iron pipe and fittings (AWWA C150/C151/C104/C111/C600)

field.text: Ductile iron push-on joints allow deflection at each joint. McWane Ductile's push-on joint chart (18 ft pipe length) lists: sizes 3 through 30 inch, maximum 5 degrees, maximum offset about 19 inches per 18 ft length, approximate curve radius 205 ft; 36 inch, 4 degrees, about 15 inches offset, radius about 260 ft. Other makers and AWWA C600 list similar or more conservative values, especially for larger sizes (some show 3 degrees for the largest pipe). Always use the specific maker's chart for the joint you have; mechanical joints and restrained joints have their own, often smaller, limits. Common design practice is to plan curves using less than the full allowable deflection (DIPRA guidance commonly suggests about 80% of maximum) so there's room for field adjustment. Assemble the joint straight and fully homed, then deflect.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: push-on joint deflection table
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: McWane Ductile, push-on joint deflection chart

field.text: Ductile iron is cut in the field with an abrasive saw (cut-off saw), a wheel cutter or a milling cutter. After cutting: remove sharp edges, and for push-on joints, bevel the cut end to match the factory spigot so it won't damage the gasket (makers specify the bevel; it's roughly similar to the original), and mark the insertion depth line. Check that the pipe OD at the cut point fits the gasket (some makers mark 'gauged' or 'cut' pipe suitable for cutting anywhere; large-diameter pipe may only be cuttable within a certain range). Repair the cement lining at the cut end if damaged and coat the exposed iron per the maker. Cutting creates dust and sparks: wear eye, hearing and respiratory protection, and never cut near gas or flammables. Follow the pipe maker's field-cutting instructions.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: field cutting
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: Ductile iron manufacturer installation guides (DIPRA/McWane/American/U.S. Pipe)

field.text: At bends, tees, dead ends, reducers and valves, water pressure pushes on the fitting (thrust). Instead of concrete thrust blocks, the pipe joints for a calculated distance on each side of the fitting can be restrained so the friction and soil bearing along that restrained pipe resists the thrust. The required restrained length depends on test pressure, pipe size, fitting angle, depth of cover, soil type, trench type and whether the pipe is polywrapped (polywrap reduces friction, so longer lengths). DIPRA publishes the Thrust Restraint Design method and a free calculator; restraint makers (EBAA and others) publish tables. The engineer usually shows restrained lengths on the plans. Field rule: restrain every joint within the shown length, both directions, including the fitting's own joints. Don't mix thrust blocks and restraint unless the design says so; some agencies prohibit combining them.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: restrained joints and restrained length concept
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: DIPRA Thrust Restraint Design for Ductile Iron Pipe; VCMWD design standard 5.2

field.text: U.S. Pipe explains that the AWWA C600 'testing allowance' is the amount of make-up water you may add during the hydrostatic test to hold pressure, and it is not a leakage allowance: properly assembled ductile iron joints are bottle-tight. The allowance covers pressure loss from other causes, like trapped air working out, water absorbed by the cement lining, restrained joints taking up slack, small pipe movements in the soil and temperature changes during the test. In practice, if you need make-up water near the allowance limit, look for trapped air or a problem before accepting it. C600 requires test pressure not less than 1.25 times working pressure at the highest point of the test section and not less than 1.5 times working pressure at the lowest point (per U.S. Pipe's summary), held at least 2 hours. Local specs may set different pressures; check them.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: testing allowance is not a leak allowance
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: U.S. Pipe FAQ, testing allowance in AWWA C600

field.url: https://clvr.imiscloud.com/common/Uploaded files/1-PPI/Divisions/Municipal and Industrial/Division Publications/Potable Water/General/Position Paper on HDPE PE 4710 Distribution Potable Water Pipe Sizes and Pressure Classes.pdf
field.text: Solid-wall HDPE pressure pipe for water is commonly PE 4710 material made to AWWA C906 (4 to 65 inch) or ASTM D3035 (smaller sizes) and ASTM F714. PPI's position paper lists PE 4710 pressure classes: DR 17 = 125 psi (recurring surge 188, occasional surge 250); DR 13.5 = 160 psi (240 / 320); DR 11 = 200 psi (300 / 400); DR 9 = 250 psi (375 / 500). As with PVC, a lower DR means a thicker wall. HDPE comes in IPS (iron pipe size, steel OD) and DIPS (ductile iron OD) sizing; the two have different ODs, so fittings and couplings must match. PPI notes AWWA defines pressure class differently for different materials, so an HDPE pressure class is not directly comparable to a PVC or DI class number. Check your specs.
field.title: HDPE pressure pipe: PE 4710 pressure classes by DR
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: PPI position paper on PE 4710 potable water pipe sizes and pressure classes (AWWA C906)

field.text: HDPE is usually joined by heat fusion, which makes the joint as strong as the pipe. Butt fusion steps (summary of ASTM F2620 practice): secure and align both pipe ends in the fusion machine; face the ends square with the facer until continuous ribbons come off both sides; check alignment (high-low mismatch within the procedure's limit, commonly no more than 10% of wall thickness); heat both ends on the heater plate at the specified temperature until the bead forms; remove the plate quickly; bring ends together at the specified fusion pressure; hold under pressure and let it cool for the full cooling time before removing or stressing it. Fusion operators should be qualified, and many utilities require a datalogger record of each joint. Inspect beads for uniform roll-back. Never rush cooling. Follow the pipe maker's and machine maker's fusion parameters.
field.title: HDPE pressure pipe: butt fusion basics
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: ASTM F2620 practice as summarized by PPI and HDPE manufacturers

field.text: Besides butt fusion, HDPE can be joined by electrofusion and mechanical fittings. Electrofusion couplings and saddles have embedded heating wires; a control box applies power for a set time. Key steps: cut square, scrape the oxidized skin off the pipe surface in the fusion zone with a proper scraper (sanding is not a substitute), clean with the approved wipe, mark insertion depth, clamp to prevent movement, fuse, and leave clamped through the cooling time. Mechanical joints include MJ adapters (fused HDPE end with a ductile iron back-up ring), flange adapters with back-up rings, and compression couplings; for compression and MJ fittings on HDPE, use an internal stiffener insert if the maker requires it, because HDPE creeps under clamping load. Follow the fitting maker's instructions; these are common practices in PPI and manufacturer guides.
field.title: HDPE pressure pipe: electrofusion and mechanical joints
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: PPI Handbook of Polyethylene Pipe / PE pipe field practice

field.text: HDPE expands and contracts much more than metal pipe with temperature. A commonly used PPI figure for the coefficient of thermal expansion of PE is about 1 x 10^-4 inch per inch per degree F, which works out to roughly 1.2 inches of length change per 100 ft of pipe for every 10 degree F change in temperature. A 500 ft fused string that heats up 40 degrees F lying in the sun can grow about 2 ft and then shrink back when it cools in the trench. Practical tips: let the pipe reach trench temperature before making final tie-ins; make final connections in the cool part of the day; anchor or restrain ends at connections to rigid pipe or structures; snake pipe slightly in the trench if your specs allow. Check the pipe maker's literature for the exact coefficient.
field.title: HDPE pipe: thermal expansion and contraction
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: PPI Handbook of Polyethylene Pipe / PE pipe field practice

field.text: Solid-wall HDPE can be bent in the field to follow curves, within limits. PPI handbook guidance commonly cited for the minimum cold-bend radius (pipe with no fittings in the bend): DR 9 and lower, about 20 times the OD; DR above 9 up to 13.5, about 25 times OD; DR above 13.5 up to 21, about 27 times OD; DR above 21, about 30 times OD. Where a fitting or flange is in the bend, the radius must be much larger (often cited as 100 times OD). Example: 8 inch IPS DR 11 pipe (OD 8.625 inches) at 25 x OD = about 216 inches, or 18 ft radius. Bends tighter than allowed can kink or overstress the pipe. Confirm with the pipe maker's literature for your DR and temperature.
field.title: HDPE pipe: minimum cold bending radius
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: PPI Handbook of Polyethylene Pipe / PE pipe field practice

field.text: Dual-wall corrugated HDPE pipe (smooth inside, corrugated outside) is widely used for storm drains and culverts. Main standards: AASHTO M294 (12 to 60 inch) and ASTM F2306 (12 to 60 inch for gravity storm sewer), with ASTM F2648 for some profile products. Joints come in soil-tight and watertight versions; watertight joints use a gasketed bell and spigot meeting the ASTM D3212 lab test (10.8 psi). Some DOTs and cities require watertight joints in all storm sewer; check your specs. Typical lay length is 20 ft (shorter available). Corrugated polypropylene (PP) pipe (ASTM F2764 for sanitary, F2881 for storm) is a related product with higher stiffness. Installation follows ASTM D2321 with embedment and compaction controlling deflection; the usual post-installation deflection limit is 5% (check specs).
field.title: Corrugated HDPE storm pipe: standards and joints
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: ADS and AASHTO/ASTM product standards summary

field.text: ADS Technical Note TN 2.01 gives cover limits for corrugated HDPE pipe made to AASHTO. Minimum cover in traffic areas (H-20, H-25 or HL-93 loads): 1 ft over the crown for 4 to 48 inch pipe, and 2 ft for 54 to 60 inch. Rigid pavement may count toward minimum cover; flexible (asphalt) pavement thickness does not. Maximum cover depends on backfill class and compaction; examples from the ADS table (feet): 12 inch pipe, Class 1 compacted 35, Class 2 at 95% 24, Class 2 at 90% 17, Class 3 at 95% 17; 24 inch pipe, Class 1 compacted 28, Class 2 at 95% 20, Class 2 at 90% 13; 48 inch, Class 1 compacted 25, Class 2 at 95% 17, Class 2 at 90% 11. Values assume no groundwater above the pipe and standard Proctor compaction. Construction equipment loads over shallow pipe must be considered too. Use the full table and your project design.
field.title: Corrugated HDPE storm pipe: minimum and maximum cover
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: ADS Technical Note TN 2.01, Minimum and Maximum Cover Heights for HDPE per AASHTO

field.text: Corrugated HDPE pipe is light and flexible, so its strength comes from the soil around it. Field cautions from manufacturer guidance: bed on a uniform, slightly loose layer so the pipe sits evenly; get backfill into the haunches; place and compact embedment in lifts on both sides at the same time so the pipe doesn't shift or float; don't drive heavy equipment over the pipe until enough cover is placed (ADS notes construction loads must be considered even if less than design loads); watch for flotation in wet trenches and when using flowable fill (pour flowable fill in lifts or weight the pipe). Lower-quality backfill or compaction can push deflection past the 5% limit, so check deflection on larger pipe or as specs require. Keep joints clean and gaskets lubricated; push home with a bar and block, not the bucket directly.
field.title: HDPE corrugated pipe: installation cautions
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: ADS Technical Note TN 2.01, Minimum and Maximum Cover Heights for HDPE per AASHTO

field.text: Vitrified clay pipe is fired clay pipe used for gravity sanitary sewer, valued for chemical and abrasion resistance. Pipe is made to ASTM C700, with compression joints to ASTM C425 (factory-applied polyurethane or similar joint seals on bell and spigot), and installed per ASTM C12 and the NCPI engineering manual. NCPI notes trenches are generally dug upstream and that trench width at the top of pipe must not exceed the design width, because widening adds load (widening a 2 ft trench by 6 inches adds about 50% load in their example). If a trench box rides below the top of pipe, protect the haunches from voids and don't let box movement pull joints apart (anchor the line back to a downstream manhole). Clay pipe is rigid and brittle: handle carefully, bed uniformly, and avoid point loads on rocks. Check the maker's literature (for example Logan Clay Products) for lengths and joint details.
field.title: Vitrified clay pipe (VCP) basics
field.topic: Pipe materials: clay, CMP, steel, selection
field.source: National Clay Pipe Institute (NCPI) Vitrified Clay Pipe Engineering Manual

field.text: Corrugated metal pipe is used for culverts and storm drains. Corrugated steel pipe is made to AASHTO M36 (ASTM A760), aluminum to AASHTO M196. Coatings include galvanized, aluminized Type 2 and polymer-coated; the coating and gauge are picked for design life and environment. Common corrugations are 2-2/3 x 1/2 inch for smaller sizes and 3 x 1 inch or 5 x 1 inch for larger; spiral rib pipe is also used. Joints are made with coupling bands (annular, hugger, dimple bands) and gaskets where soil-tight or watertight joints are needed. Installation follows ASTM A798 (steel) and NCSPA guidance: uniform bedding shaped or loosened to fit, well-compacted backfill in layers on both sides, and enough cover before heavy equipment crosses. CMP is flexible, so like plastic pipe its strength depends on the backfill. Check your specs for gauge, coating and band type.
field.title: Corrugated metal pipe (CMP) basics
field.topic: Pipe materials: clay, CMP, steel, selection
field.source: National Corrugated Steel Pipe Association (NCSPA) installation guidance; AASHTO M36

field.text: Steel water pipe is designed under AWWA M11 and made to AWWA C200, usually with a cement-mortar lining (C205) and an exterior coating (for example tape coating or polyurethane). Joints are welded (lap or butt weld) or rubber-gasketed bell and spigot. Steel casing pipe is used for bores and jack-and-bore crossings under roads and railroads, with the carrier pipe pushed through on casing spacers (insulators) and the ends closed with end seals. Railroad and DOT crossings have their own casing wall thickness and depth rules (for example in AREMA guidelines and state DOT utility accommodation policies); check the permit. Welding requires qualified welders and coating repair at welds. Source: AWWA steel pipe standards and common specification practice.
field.title: Steel pipe for water and casings
field.topic: Pipe materials: clay, CMP, steel, selection
field.source: AWWA M11 / C200 / C205 scopes; common specification practice

field.text: Common field trade-offs between pipe materials (general guidance, not a design rule): PVC is light, cheap, easy to cut and corrosion-proof, but depends on good embedment, is sensitive to impact in cold weather and to UV during long storage. HDPE is flexible and fusible into leak-free strings for bores and bad ground, but needs fusion equipment and trained operators, expands a lot with temperature and needs care with mechanical fittings. Ductile iron is strong, takes rough backfill and high pressure and handles traffic loads at shallow cover, but is heavy and can need corrosion protection. RCP is strong and rigid for storm drains and large sewers, but heavy and joint-sensitive. Clay is very chemical-resistant for sanitary sewer but brittle. CMP is light for culverts but can corrode. The engineer selects material in the design; substitutions need written approval.
field.title: Choosing between pipe materials: field trade-offs
field.topic: Pipe materials: clay, CMP, steel, selection
field.source: Summary of manufacturer association literature (Uni-Bell, PPI, DIPRA, ACPA, NCPI, NCSPA)

field.text: Pipe is classed as flexible or rigid by how it carries load. Flexible pipe (PVC, HDPE, polypropylene, CMP, steel, and to a degree ductile iron) deflects slightly under load and pushes against the side soil, so the embedment beside the pipe carries much of the load; that's why compaction in the haunches and sides matters so much, and why deflection is tested with a mandrel. Rigid pipe (RCP, clay) carries load through the pipe wall's strength and the bedding under it; uniform bedding support and good haunching prevent cracking. Practical result: for flexible pipe, sidefill compaction controls performance; for rigid pipe, a uniform bed without hard points and well-filled haunches control performance. Installation standards follow this split: ASTM D2321 (thermoplastic), D2774 (pressure plastic), C1479 (concrete), C12 (clay), AWWA C600 (ductile iron) and C605 (PVC pressure).
field.title: Flexible versus rigid pipe: why it matters in the trench
field.topic: Pipe materials: clay, CMP, steel, selection
field.source: Pipe installation standards and manufacturer association literature

field.text: ASTM D3034 covers solid-wall PVC gravity sewer pipe and fittings, the green pipe most crews know as 'SDR 35' sewer pipe. Per Uni-Bell's summary, the 2024 consolidated D3034 covers sizes 3 to 60 inches: smaller sizes are classified by dimension ratio (DR or SDR, for example SDR 35 and SDR 26) and sizes 18 to 60 inches by pipe stiffness (PS 46 and PS 115). SDR 35 is the thinner, more common wall (pipe stiffness 46 psi); SDR 26 is heavier (pipe stiffness 115 psi) and is often required for deeper cover or under roads. Joints are integral bell and spigot with a rubber gasket (gaskets to ASTM F477, joint performance to ASTM D3212). Common lay lengths are 14 ft for small-diameter sewer pipe, with 20 ft lengths also made; check the supplier. Installation follows ASTM D2321. Check your project specs for which SDR is required at which depth.
field.title: PVC gravity sewer pipe: ASTM D3034 basics
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, ASTM D3034 and F679 combined summary

field.text: ASTM F679 was the standard for large-diameter (18 inch and up) solid-wall PVC gravity sewer pipe. Per Uni-Bell, F679 grew to 48 inches by the mid-1990s and 60 inches in 2013, added a PS 115 stiffness in 2003 and a 75 psi stiffness level in 2008, and was withdrawn in 2024 when it was consolidated into ASTM D3034. Older plans, specs and submittals still say 'F679 PS 46' or 'F679 PS 115'; the equivalent is now D3034 at that pipe stiffness. If a spec calls F679 and the supplier ships D3034 large-diameter pipe of the same stiffness, ask the engineer to confirm in writing that it's acceptable. PS 46 means the pipe deflects 5% under 46 psi in the parallel-plate test; PS 115 is stiffer.
field.title: PVC large-diameter gravity sewer: ASTM F679 history
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, ASTM D3034 and F679 combined summary

field.text: AWWA C900 covers PVC pressure pipe for water mains (the blue pipe, often called 'C900') in 4 to 60 inch sizes; the 2016 edition absorbed the old C905 large-diameter standard. Most C900 is made to cast-iron OD (CIOD, same as ductile iron OD, so DI fittings fit), and some is IPS OD. Per Uni-Bell, dimension ratio (DR) and pressure class (PC) pair as follows: DR 51 = PC 80 psi; DR 41 = PC 100; DR 32.5 = PC 125; DR 27.5 = PC 150; DR 26 = PC 160; DR 25 = PC 165; DR 21 = PC 200; DR 18 = PC 235; DR 17 = PC 250; DR 14 = PC 305. Lower DR means thicker wall and higher rating. DR 18 and DR 14 are the common water main choices in small sizes. Not every DR is made in every size or OD; check with the manufacturer. Typical lay length for PVC pressure pipe is 20 ft. Your utility's specs decide the DR.
field.title: PVC pressure pipe: AWWA C900 sizes and pressure classes
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, PVC pressure pipe standards summary

field.text: AWWA C909 covers molecularly oriented PVC (PVCO) pressure pipe. Orienting the PVC molecules during manufacture makes the pipe stronger, so a thinner wall gives the same pressure rating as thicker C900 pipe, and the bore is larger. Per Uni-Bell, C909 covers 4 to 30 inch pipe on cast-iron/ductile-iron OD, in pressure classes 165, 235 and 305 psi (C909 does not use DR classes). Joints may be unrestrained gasketed, or internally or externally restrained. Installation is the same family as other PVC pressure pipe (AWWA C605). Because the wall is thinner, take care with cutting, tapping and fittings: use tools and tapping saddles approved for PVCO by the pipe maker. Some utilities restrict PVCO; check your specs.
field.title: PVC pressure pipe: AWWA C909 PVCO
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, PVC pressure pipe standards summary

field.text: Gasketed PVC pipe (sewer and pressure) has a factory insertion or homing mark on the spigot showing how far it should go into the bell. Push the spigot in until the mark is at the bell face (or within the band the maker shows). Pushing too far (over-homing) can bottom the spigot in the bell, leave no room for expansion, and can crack bells; under-homing can leak or pull apart. Clean the spigot, bell and gasket, apply the maker's lubricant to the spigot (and gasket if the maker says), line up the pipe straight, then push home with a bar and block or a pulling tool. If using the excavator bucket, push through a timber block across the bell end, gently, and only if the maker allows. If you cut a pipe, mark a new homing line at the same distance from the end as the factory mark. These steps follow PVC manufacturers' installation guides.
field.title: PVC pipe: homing marks and how far to push the joint
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: General industry references (ASTM/AWWA standard scopes as summarized by manufacturers)

field.text: Use only the joint lubricant supplied or approved by the pipe or gasket manufacturer. On potable water pipe, lubricant must be NSF/ANSI 61 certified for drinking water contact. Never substitute grease, oil, soap of unknown type or petroleum products; petroleum can swell and ruin rubber gaskets and contaminate a water main. Apply a thin, even coat to the spigot end (and to the gasket if instructed), and keep the lubed end out of dirt; if it gets dirty, wipe it clean and re-lube. In cold weather, keep lubricant warm so it spreads. Keep the lube bucket closed so it stays clean. These are common requirements in PVC and ductile iron installation guides and potable water specs.
field.title: PVC pipe: lubricant rules
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: General industry references (ASTM/AWWA standard scopes as summarized by manufacturers)

field.text: When a PVC stick has to be cut in the field: mark a square cut line all the way around (wrap a straight paper or a pipe-cutting guide), cut square with a fine-tooth saw, wheel cutter or power saw rated for plastic, remove burrs inside and out, and bevel the spigot end so it doesn't roll or cut the gasket. Match the factory bevel's angle and depth, or use a beveling tool made for the purpose; many makers show a bevel of about 15 degrees. Then mark a new homing line at the same distance from the end as the factory mark. Never use the bell end of a cut piece without checking it's undamaged. Wear eye protection and dust protection when power cutting. Uni-Bell publishes a field-cutting guide (PUB-15); follow the specific pipe maker's instructions, which govern.
field.title: PVC pipe: field cutting and beveling
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: General industry references (ASTM/AWWA standard scopes as summarized by manufacturers)

field.text: Gasketed PVC joints allow a small angle at each joint to follow a gentle curve without bending the pipe. The allowed angle depends on the maker and joint type; check the pipe print line or literature. Example from Westlake: integral bell joints 1 degree; their restrained coupling 0.5 degree per side (1 degree total); solvent-weld joints none. Uni-Bell's offset numbers: 1 degree at a joint moves the far end of a 20 ft stick about 0.35 ft (4.2 inches); on a 10 ft stick, about 0.175 ft (2.1 inches). Radius of curve (ft) = 57.3 x lay length (ft) / deflection per joint (degrees); for 20 ft sticks at 1 degree, about 1,146 ft. A 1 degree vertical change equals a 1.75% change in slope. To deflect: lay and home the joint straight, then swing the free end. Gravity sewer joints are normally laid straight between manholes; check your project specs.
field.title: PVC pipe: axial joint deflection (curving through joints)
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell technical blog, Changing Direction: Axial Joint Deflection Explained (Handbook of PVC Pipe, 6th ed.)

field.text: Two ways to curve PVC pipe: joint (axial) deflection, where each joint is angled slightly, and longitudinal bending, where the pipe barrel itself is bent. Uni-Bell describes axial deflection for gradual direction changes without bending the barrel. Some makers allow a limited bend of the barrel for pressure pipe, with a minimum bending radius published by the maker and pipe size; follow that literature exactly. Rules of thumb in maker literature: bend only the barrel, keep the joint itself straight during bending, never bend at the bell, never force a bend with the bucket, and restrain the bent pipe with embedment as soon as it's placed. Gravity sewer pipe is not bent to make curves in typical municipal specs; use manholes for changes in direction. Check your specs and the maker's bending table.
field.title: PVC pipe: longitudinal bending versus joint deflection
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell technical blog, Changing Direction: Axial Joint Deflection Explained (Handbook of PVC Pipe, 6th ed.)

field.text: PVC pipe can be damaged by impact and by long sunlight exposure. Handling: lift with nylon slings or forklift with padded forks, don't drop or drag it, don't let bells bang on hard objects, and in cold weather handle with more care because PVC is less impact-resistant when cold. Storage: store on flat ground supported along its length, bells alternated or hanging free so they don't carry the load, stacked no higher than the maker allows, and capped to keep dirt and animals out. Sunlight: UV exposure gradually reduces impact strength; makers generally recommend covering pipe with an opaque, ventilated cover if stored outdoors for a long period (many guides cite more than about a year or two), and not using clear plastic, which traps heat. Inspect for cracks, gouges deeper than the maker's limit, and damaged bells before laying. Follow the specific manufacturer's guide.
field.title: PVC pipe: storage, handling and sunlight
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: General industry references (ASTM/AWWA standard scopes as summarized by manufacturers)

field.text: SDR (standard dimension ratio) and DR (dimension ratio) both mean the pipe outside diameter divided by its minimum wall thickness. A smaller DR number means a thicker wall relative to diameter: DR 14 is heavier than DR 18, which is heavier than DR 25. For pressure pipe, the same DR gives the same pressure rating at any diameter (C900 DR 18 is 235 psi whether 4 inch or 12 inch, per Uni-Bell's C900 table). For gravity sewer, the same SDR gives about the same pipe stiffness at any diameter: SDR 35 is about PS 46 and SDR 26 is about PS 115. Example: an 8 inch SDR 35 sewer pipe has an OD of about 8.4 inches, so its minimum wall is about 8.4 / 35 = 0.24 inch. Check the print line on the pipe: it shows size, DR or SDR, standard (D3034, C900), maker, and production code.
field.title: PVC pipe: what SDR and DR mean
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, PVC pressure pipe standards summary

field.text: Every stick of PVC sewer and water pipe carries a print line along its length. It typically shows the manufacturer, nominal size, OD base (for pressure pipe: CIOD/DIOD or IPS), material code, DR or SDR, pressure class or pipe stiffness, the standard it meets (for example ASTM D3034 or AWWA C900), certification marks such as NSF-61 for potable water, and a production code with date and plant. For sewer pipe you'll see something like '8 in SDR 35 PS 46 ASTM D3034.' For water: '8 in DR 18 PC 235 AWWA C900 NSF-61.' Use the print line to confirm you have what the plans and approved submittal call for before you lay it, and keep the print line on top so the inspector can read it. Uni-Bell recommends checking the print line for allowable joint deflection details.
field.title: PVC pipe: reading the print line
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: Uni-Bell technical blog, Changing Direction: Axial Joint Deflection Explained (Handbook of PVC Pipe, 6th ed.)

field.text: PVC sewer fittings (wyes, tees, bends, couplings, reducers, cleanout adapters) are made to D3034 dimensions with gasketed or solvent-weld joints; use gasketed fittings to match gasketed pipe. For connecting PVC to other materials (clay, cast iron, concrete, ductile), use a transition coupling made for the two ODs, such as a rubber coupling with stainless shear band. For C900 water main on CIOD, standard ductile iron mechanical joint fittings fit directly; use MJ glands and restraints rated for PVC (not wedge restraints designed only for ductile iron). PVC pressure fittings (C907 molded, or fabricated C900 fittings) are also used. Uni-Bell publishes a fittings design and installation guide (PUB-13). Confirm fittings and restraints are on the approved submittal.
field.title: PVC fittings and adapters for sewer and water
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC
field.source: General industry references (ASTM/AWWA standard scopes as summarized by manufacturers)

field.text: Floor plans usually carry two to four parallel strings of dimensions outside each side of the building. The string farthest from the building is the overall (end to end of the building or wall). The next string in gives major breaks (corners, jogs, grid lines). The string closest to the building gives partial dimensions to openings, wall centers and edges. Interior strings locate interior walls. A dimension is read from extension line to extension line; the tick marks, dots or arrows at each end show the exact points. The number sits above or inside the line it describes. Before using any partial, check that the partials in a string add up to the overall next to it; if they do not, there is a drafting error to resolve.
field.title: Dimension strings on floor plans: overall, intermediate and partial
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: The same wall can be dimensioned to different points, and the difference is often 1/2" to 2-1/2". Common conventions: wood and metal stud walls dimensioned to face of stud (FOS) or to centerline of stud; masonry to face of block; concrete to face of concrete; new work in remodels sometimes to face of finish (drywall). Exterior building dimensions on wood framing are often to the outside face of stud or of sheathing, and the foundation plan to the outside face of concrete. A general note usually states it ('All dimensions are to face of stud unless noted otherwise'). Look at where the extension line touches: wall edge or wall center. Never assume the convention when a 1/2" matters; read the note.
field.title: What a dimension points to: face of stud, centerline, face of finish, face of concrete
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Always add the partials before laying out. Add feet and inches separately, then carry every 12 inches into a foot. Example: partials 12'-4" + 8'-6 1/2" + 15'-1 1/2": feet 12 + 8 + 15 = 35; inches 4 + 6.5 + 1.5 = 12 = 1'-0"; total 36'-0". If the overall string says 36'-0", the string checks. If it says 36'-2", there is a 2" error somewhere: do not split the difference; ask which is right. Also check that a string's start and end match the overall's start and end (both to face of stud, not one to face of sheathing). In decimal feet the same check is 12.333 + 8.542 + 15.125 = 36.000 ft.
field.title: Checking that partial dimensions add up to the overall
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Architectural and structural plans write lengths as feet, dash, inches: 8'-6" = 8 feet 6 inches. The single mark (') is feet and the double mark (") is inches. A zero is usually written: 8'-0" means 8 feet even, 0'-8" means 8 inches. Fractions are of an inch: 8'-6 3/4". Civil and survey plans use decimal feet instead: 8.50' is 8 feet 6 inches, not 8 feet 5 inches. Misreads to avoid: reading 8.5' as 8'-5"; confusing ' and " on a blurry photo (6" slab vs 6' footing; check whether the size is reasonable); reading a dash as a minus sign; dropping the fraction. When a photo is unclear, say which reading you used and why.
field.title: Feet-and-inches notation: 8'-6", 8.5', and common misreads
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Decimal feet = feet + inches / 12. Inch to decimal foot: 1" = 0.083, 2" = 0.167, 3" = 0.25, 4" = 0.333, 5" = 0.417, 6" = 0.5, 7" = 0.583, 8" = 0.667, 9" = 0.75, 10" = 0.833, 11" = 0.917. Examples: 8'-6 3/4" = 8 + 6.75/12 = 8.5625 ft. 24'-10" = 24.833 ft. A 3-1/2" slab = 0.292 ft; 4" = 0.333 ft; 5" = 0.417 ft; 6" = 0.5 ft. Convert everything to decimal feet before multiplying for area or volume, then convert answers back to feet-inches for layout. Keep 3 decimals during takeoff math and round only the final answer.
field.title: Converting feet-inches to decimal feet: inches table
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Fraction to decimal inch: 1/16 = 0.0625, 1/8 = 0.125, 3/16 = 0.1875, 1/4 = 0.25, 5/16 = 0.3125, 3/8 = 0.375, 1/2 = 0.5, 5/8 = 0.625, 3/4 = 0.75, 7/8 = 0.875. Divide by 12 for decimal feet: 1/8" = 0.0104 ft, 1/4" = 0.0208 ft, 1/2" = 0.0417 ft, 3/4" = 0.0625 ft. Going back: decimal feet to inches, multiply the decimal part by 12; inches to nearest 1/8, multiply the leftover decimal by 8. Example: 15.37 ft: 0.37 x 12 = 4.44"; 0.44 x 8 = 3.52 eighths, which rounds to 4/8 = 1/2, so 15.37 ft is about 15'-4 1/2".
field.title: Fractions of an inch to decimals and to decimal feet
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: On the same project the architect dimensions the building in feet-inches (24'-6") while the civil engineer gives site distances, elevations and inverts in decimal feet (24.50', EL 102.35). Survey stakes and cut sheets are in decimal feet (and often in feet and tenths). Mixups cause real errors: 102.35 is 102 feet 4-1/4 inches (0.35 x 12 = 4.2"), not 102'-3 1/2". Finished floor on the architectural sheets is often '100'-0"' as a relative datum, while the civil grading plan gives the true FF elevation (for example FF 412.75). To tie them together, set architectural 100'-0" = civil FF elevation and convert. Ask should state which system each number is in.
field.title: Architectural feet-inches vs civil decimal feet on the same job
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend; Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Wall tags are small symbols (often a hexagon, diamond, rectangle or circle with a number or letter like 3A) placed on a wall line in plan. They point to a wall type legend or wall schedule, usually on an A0 or A5/A6 sheet, that shows each wall type as a small section: stud size and spacing (2x6 @ 16" O.C.), sheathing, insulation, gypsum layers, fire rating, and sometimes acoustic rating. The tag value is a type code, never a dimension or a count. A wall tag is different from a shear wall mark: shear wall marks are on the structural plan, point to a shear wall schedule, and usually have a length beside them. If one symbol shape is used for both on a set, the legend tells you which.
field.title: Wall types and wall tags
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Door tags are usually a circle, ellipse or rectangle at each door holding a number, often based on the room number (101, 101A). The number is a key to the door schedule (often on an A6 or A8 sheet), which lists for each door: size (3'-0" x 7'-0" or 3070), thickness, material, type, frame type, fire rating, hardware set and remarks. The swing arc on the plan shows which way the door opens. In '3068', the first two digits are width in feet-inches (3'-0") and the last two height (6'-8"). A door tag number is not a dimension; if a crew asks for a rough opening, get the door size from the schedule and the rough opening rule from the framing notes or manufacturer, not from the tag.
field.title: Door tags and the door schedule
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Window tags are often a hexagon, diamond or square holding a letter or number (A, W1, 12) beside the window in plan and on elevations. They key to the window schedule: rough opening or unit size (width x height, width first), type (casement, slider, fixed), head height, glazing (tempered, egress), material and remarks. Sizes in schedules may be nominal manufacturer codes such as 3050 (3'-0" wide by 5'-0" high). Head height is often shown on elevations or in a note ('window heads at 6'-8" AFF UNO'). Do not read a window tag or code as a dimension on the plan; the location of the window is given by dimensions to its centerline or rough opening edge in the dimension string.
field.title: Window tags and the window schedule
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Room tags show the room name and number (KITCHEN 104), sometimes with area in square feet and a ceiling height. The number links to the room finish schedule, which lists floor, base, wall and ceiling finishes and ceiling height for each room. A number such as 145 SF in a room tag is the room area, not a dimension. Room numbers usually follow floor level (100s first floor, 200s second floor). When a crew wants slab or floor quantities, use dimension strings to compute areas rather than the area printed in tags, which may be net of walls or rounded.
field.title: Room tags, room names and finish schedules
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: A floor plan is a horizontal section cut a few feet above the floor (commonly around 4 ft) looking down. Things cut through (walls, columns) are drawn heavy. Things below the cut (floor, counters, fixtures) are lighter solid lines. Things above the cut (upper cabinets, beams, soffits, roof overhangs, skylights) are dashed. Hidden items under the floor (footings on some plans, underground pipe) are dashed too. So a dashed rectangle on a floor plan is not a footing unless labeled; on a foundation plan, dashed lines along walls commonly show footing edges under a slab. Always read the line label or the legend.
field.title: Floor plan: where the cut is and what dashed lines mean
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: A reflected ceiling plan shows the ceiling as if reflected in a mirror on the floor, so it lines up with the floor plan below (not flipped). It shows ceiling materials, grid, soffits, light fixtures, diffusers, access panels and ceiling heights. Ceiling heights are written as a tag like 'CLG 9'-0" AFF' or a number in a box or ellipse, meaning height of finished ceiling above finished floor. A height tag is not a horizontal dimension. Different heights in one room are separated by lines with each area tagged. For structure, use plate heights and framing sections, not ceiling heights; dropped soffits and furred ceilings sit below the structure.
field.title: Reflected ceiling plan (RCP) and ceiling heights (CLG, AFF)
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Roof plans show ridges, hips, valleys, eaves, crickets, drains and roof slope. Sloped roofs are noted as rise:run in inches per 12 inches (4:12 or 4/12 = 4" of rise per 12" of run), often with a small slope triangle. Low-slope roofs are noted in inches per foot (1/4" PER FT) with an arrow; the arrow points downhill toward the drain or gutter. Convert: 4:12 = 33.3% = about 18.4 degrees; 1/4" per ft = 0.25/12 = 2.08%. A roof slope label is not a dimension. Overhang dimensions (1'-6" overhang) are measured horizontally from the wall face, not along the slope.
field.title: Roof plans: slope notations, arrows and ridges
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend; Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Slab and flatwork plans show slope with an arrow pointing downhill and a note like 'SLOPE 1/8"/FT' or '2% MIN'. To get fall over a distance, multiply: 1/4" per ft over 20 ft = 5" of fall; 1/8" per ft over 22 ft = 2.75". Converting: 1/8" per ft = 1.04%, 1/4" per ft = 2.08%, 1/2" per ft = 4.17%, 1" per ft = 8.33%. 2% = 0.24" per ft (about 1/4"). Garage slabs commonly slope toward the door; shower and drain areas slope toward the drain; walks slope away from the building. Check the arrow direction and where the high and low points are stated (spot elevations or 'DN' arrows). The slope applies to the top of slab; slab thickness usually stays constant unless noted.
field.title: Slope arrows on slabs and paving: 1/4" per foot, 1/8" per foot
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Exterior elevations show the outside of each face of the building: materials, openings, roof lines and vertical levels. Level markers along the side give heights such as F.F. 100'-0", T.O. PLATE 109'-1 1/8", T.O. RIDGE. On many residential sets 100'-0" (or 0'-0") is an assumed datum for finished floor, so T.O. PLATE 109'-1 1/8" means 9'-1 1/8" above the floor. Grade lines on elevations are often schematic; the civil grading plan governs finished grades. Elevation drawings rarely carry horizontal dimensions; get horizontal locations from the plans. Window and door tags on elevations key to schedules; they are not heights.
field.title: Exterior elevations: level lines, plate heights and what they are not
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: A building section is a vertical cut through the whole building, showing floor levels, plate heights, roof framing and footings together. A wall section is a larger-scale vertical cut through one wall from footing to roof, with every layer labeled (footing, stem wall, sill plate, studs, sheathing, insulation, finishes, headers, rafters). Read vertical dimensions from the level lines and dimension strings at the side, not by measuring. The footing at the bottom of a wall section is often schematic; the structural footing detail governs its width, depth and reinforcing. Section titles carry their own number and the sheets that reference them, so you can find where on the plan the cut was taken.
field.title: Building and wall sections: reading heights and assemblies
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Remodel and addition plans mark what is new and what is existing. (N) = new, (E) or (EX) = existing, (R) = relocate or remove depending on the legend, (D) = demolish. Existing walls are often shown with lighter lines or a different hatch; walls to be demolished are dashed. Demolition plans (AD sheets, or A1.0 'DEMO PLAN') show what is removed; the new plan shows the result. On civil plans, existing utilities and grades are lighter or dashed and labeled EX (EX 8" SS, EX GRADE) and proposed are heavy. Misread to avoid: taking a dimension to an existing wall as new construction layout, or quantity-counting existing work as new.
field.title: (N), (E), (R) and demolition notation on remodel plans
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Property lines are usually drawn as a long-dash short-dash (phantom) line, labeled with a bearing and distance from the survey, for example N 89 deg 12'30" E  120.00'. Distances on property lines are in decimal feet. Setback lines (dashed, labeled '20' FRONT SETBACK') show how close the building may come to each property line, measured square to the property line. Easements (utility, drainage, access) are dashed areas labeled with width and type; often no building or footing may go inside. Site plans locate the building by dimensions from property lines to a building corner. Those dimensions govern layout, not scaling, and a surveyor normally sets property corners and building corners.
field.title: Property lines, setbacks and easements on site plans
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
