field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend; Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Architectural and electrical plans place small symbols on walls that can be confused with dimensions or tags. A duplex receptacle is a small circle with two parallel lines; letters next to it are qualifiers: GFI or GFCI (ground-fault protected), WP (weatherproof), AFCI (arc-fault), and a number like 42" or +42 is mounting height above floor, not a wall dimension. 'S' is a switch, S3 a three-way switch. SD is a smoke detector, CO a carbon monoxide alarm, often a circle on the ceiling. A small triangle on a wall can be a phone or data outlet. Treat any text that sits at a symbol with no dimension line and no extension lines as a label, not a length.
field.title: Electrical symbols on architectural plans: GFI, WP, AFCI, SD are not dimensions
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: Commercial and many structural plans use a grid: lines running each way, labeled with bubbles at the ends (letters A, B, C one way and numbers 1, 2, 3 the other). Grid lines locate columns, footings and walls; dimensions are given between grid lines and from grids to features ('2'-0" from grid C to face of footing'). A grid bubble 'C' or '4' is a name, not a dimension or a detail number. A reference like 'C/4' means the intersection of grids C and 4 (a column or pad footing location), not detail C on sheet 4. Check whether a wall dimension is to the grid or to a face; grid lines often fall on the centerline of columns or the face of stud, as defined in the notes.
field.title: Column grid lines and grid bubbles
field.topic: Plan reading: architectural plans, dimensions, tags and schedules
field.source: Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend; Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: A typical civil set runs: C0.0 or C-001 cover and index; C1.x general notes, legend and abbreviations; C2.x existing conditions and demolition; C3.x site or horizontal control; C4.x grading and drainage; C5.x utility plans (sewer, water, storm), often plan and profile; C6.x erosion control (SWPPP); C7.x to C9.x details. Numbering differs between firms (C3.0 may be grading on one job and utilities on another), so read the sheet title and the index. Utility details and city standard details referenced on the plans are where pipe bedding, manhole, cleanout and service lateral dimensions are found. The civil legend shows line types (SS, SD, W, G, existing vs proposed).
field.title: Civil sheet set order: cover, notes, demo, grading, utility, details
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: A plan and profile sheet shows the pipe from above (plan view, usually the top half) and from the side (profile view, the bottom half). Stations run along the bottom of the profile grid and line up with stations on the plan, so a manhole at 12+50 in plan sits above station 12+50 on the profile. The plan shows horizontal location: alignment, offsets, structures, services, crossing utilities, property lines and easements. The profile shows vertical: existing ground, finished grade, the pipe with its inverts and slope, structure rims and inverts, and crossing utilities with elevations. Read lengths and slopes from labels, and check them against stations and inverts; do not measure.
field.title: Plan and profile sheet layout: plan on top, profile below, same stations
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Georgia DOT Basic Highway Plan Reading manual; NCDOT Plan Reading Book

field.text: Sometimes stationing restarts or shifts along a line, shown as a station equation such as 'STA 138+49.42 BK = STA 114+11.00 AHD'. The first number is where the old stationing ends (back) and the second is where the new stationing picks up (ahead); they are the same physical point. When computing a length across an equation, do it in two pieces: from the start to the back station, then from the ahead station to the end. Example: from 130+00 to the equation is 13,849.42 - 13,000 = 849.42 ft; from 114+11.00 to 120+00 is 589.00 ft; total 1,438.42 ft. Simply subtracting 120+00 minus 130+00 gives a wrong (negative) answer. Utility lines tied to road stationing can carry equations.
field.title: Station equations: when stationing jumps
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Georgia DOT Basic Highway Plan Reading manual

field.text: An offset is the distance square off the centerline or baseline, written as 'STA 2+00, 80' RT' or '12.5' LT'. Left and right are defined looking ahead, in the direction stations increase, not the left or right of the sheet. NCDOT's example: 'Sta. 2+00, 80' RT.' is 80 ft right of the line at station 2+00. If stationing increases right to left on the sheet, LT points toward the bottom of the sheet. On utility plans the baseline may be the road centerline with the sewer at, say, 6 ft LT; structures are then located by station and offset of the road. Always check whether a structure's offset is to its center (usual) and from which line.
field.title: Offsets: LT and RT are looking ahead up-station
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book

field.text: Profiles use a much larger vertical scale than horizontal scale so that small grade changes are visible. Example: horizontal 1" = 50', vertical 1" = 5': vertical exaggeration = 50 / 5 = 10 times. NCDOT and GDOT plan reading guides show similar pairs (1" = 100' horizontal with 1" = 20' vertical, a 5x exaggeration). Consequences: a 0.50% sewer looks like a noticeable slope; a 2:1 side slope looks like a cliff; pipes look like tall ovals or thick bands. Never read slopes by eye from the profile and never scale vertical and horizontal with the same scale. Use written inverts, slopes and stations.
field.title: Profile vertical exaggeration: why slopes look steep
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book; Georgia DOT Basic Highway Plan Reading manual; Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: On a profile, existing ground (EG) is usually an irregular dashed or light line; proposed or finished grade (FG, the new road or surface) is a heavier smooth line. The pipe is drawn as two parallel lines (top and bottom of pipe) or a single heavy line, with the invert (inside bottom) being the line that slopes at the labeled grade. Manholes and structures show as vertical rectangles from rim down to below the invert, with rim and invert labels. Labels give elevations in decimal feet. Where the pipe's crown gets close to finished grade, check minimum cover. Depth of cut at any station = surface elevation minus invert (plus bedding below the invert for trench depth).
field.title: Profile lines: existing grade, finished grade, pipe and invert
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Georgia DOT Basic Highway Plan Reading manual; Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Structure labels on profiles and plans list rim and inverts, for example: 'SSMH #3, STA 12+50.00, 6.0' RT, RIM 105.20, IE IN 8" (N) 98.45, IE IN 6" (W) 98.80, IE OUT 8" (S) 98.35'. IE = invert elevation. Each line gives pipe size, direction it comes from or goes to (compass direction or the upstream structure), and invert elevation. The drop across the manhole here is 98.45 - 98.35 = 0.10 ft for the through line. A lateral or side pipe often comes in higher (98.80). The rim is the lid elevation; manhole depth = rim minus lowest invert = 105.20 - 98.35 = 6.85 ft. Read the north arrow on that sheet before deciding which pipe is (N).
field.title: Inverts at structures: reading IE IN and IE OUT
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Pipe slope is written several ways: 'S = 0.0050' (ft per ft), 'S = 0.50%', '@ 0.50%', or '0.005 FT/FT'. 0.0050 ft/ft = 0.50% = 0.50 ft per 100 ft. Do not read S = 0.0050 as 5% or 0.50 as 50%. Check every run: slope = (upstream invert out - downstream invert in) / length. Example: IE OUT at MH 3 = 98.35, IE IN at MH 2 = 96.85, length 300 ft: 1.50 / 300 = 0.0050 = 0.50%. If the labeled slope, length and inverts disagree by more than rounding, flag it before laying pipe. Pipe lasers are set in percent.
field.title: Slope notation: S = 0.0050 ft/ft, 0.50%, and checking it from inverts
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: A typical pipe label on a profile or plan: '300 LF - 8" PVC SDR 35 @ 0.50%'. Read: length 300 linear feet (usually horizontal, measured center of structure to center of structure, unless the notes say otherwise); 8 inch nominal size; PVC material; SDR 35 wall class (dimension ratio, ASTM D3034 gravity sewer pipe); slope 0.50%. Other common callouts: '12" RCP CL III' (reinforced concrete pipe, Class III), '8" DIP CL 350', '8" C900 DR 18' (water), '6" SDR 26'. The length on the label may differ from the station difference if structures have offsets or if lengths are to inside wall faces; check against stations.
field.title: Pipe callouts: 300 LF 8" PVC SDR 35 @ 0.50%
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Instead of labeling every structure on the drawing, many utility and storm plans use a structure table: one row per structure with number (SSMH-3, CB-12, DI-4), type and size (48" MH, Type C inlet), station and offset or northing/easting coordinates, rim or grate elevation, each invert with direction and size, and sometimes depth and frame-and-cover model. Pipe tables list each run: from structure, to structure, size, material, length, slope. The table governs over a label that conflicts only if the contract precedence says so; flag any mismatch. When answering, name the table and row used (for example 'Storm structure table, CB-12, grate 101.45, IE OUT 15" 97.10').
field.title: Structure tables and data blocks
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book; Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Existing and proposed utilities that cross the pipe are drawn on the profile at their station, usually as a circle or ellipse (exaggerated by the vertical scale) labeled with size, type and elevation, for example 'EX 12" W, TOP EL 101.50 (APPROX)' or 'POTHOLED'. Clearance between pipes = bottom outside of the upper pipe minus top outside of the lower pipe. Outside top of pipe = invert + inside diameter + wall thickness; outside bottom = invert - wall thickness. Example: sewer invert 98.00, 8" PVC (ID about 0.66 ft, wall about 0.02 ft): outside top about 98.68. Water main outside bottom 100.20: clearance about 1.52 ft. 'APPROX' elevations are not reliable; pothole before trenching.
field.title: Utility crossings on the profile and clearance math
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes; Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Service laterals are shown in plan as short lines from the main to the property, labeled with size and sometimes station and invert, for example '4" SS LAT, STA 13+42, INV AT R/W 101.15' or by a lot number. Many plans just show a tick and a note 'TYP SERVICE PER STD DET SS-6', leaving depth and slope to the standard detail (often a minimum slope such as 2% for 4" laterals and a cleanout at the property line). Water services are similar ('1" SERVICE W/ METER BOX'). The station is along the main's stationing, not a distance from the last manhole. Record actual locations in the field (station, offset, depth) for as-builts.
field.title: Services and laterals on utility plans
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Contours join points of equal elevation. On grading plans existing contours are usually light dashed lines and proposed contours heavy solid lines. Every 5th contour (index contour) is heavier and labeled. The contour interval (difference between neighboring lines, commonly 1 ft on site plans, 0.5 or 2 ft on others) is in the notes or legend. Close contours = steep; wide = flat. Where proposed contours depart from existing ones, there is cut (proposed lower) or fill (proposed higher). Water flows square across contours, downhill. Contours that point uphill form a swale or channel; contours that point downhill form a ridge.
field.title: Grading plans: existing and proposed contours
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Spot elevations are points marked with a small x, cross or dot and a decimal elevation, often with a prefix: FG finished grade, EG existing grade, FS finished surface (paving), TC top of curb, BC bottom of curb, FL flowline, TP top of pavement, TW and BW top and bottom of wall, FF finished floor, HP and LP high and low point, GB grade break, INV invert, RIM rim, ME match existing. A pair like 'TC 105.42 / FL 104.92' at a curb means a 0.50 ft (6 inch) curb face. These are elevations, not dimensions; they are in decimal feet (104.92 is 104 feet 11 inches, not 104'-9.2").
field.title: Spot elevations and grading abbreviations: FG, EG, TC, BC, FL, FF
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Grading and paving plans use arrows with a percent to show the direction water runs and the slope, for example an arrow labeled 2.0% pointing toward a catch basin. Slope between two spot elevations = (high - low) / horizontal distance x 100. Example: FS 102.40 at the building and FS 101.80 at a point 30 ft away: 0.60 / 30 = 0.02 = 2.0%. Fall over a distance at a given slope = slope x distance: 1.5% over 48 ft = 0.72 ft. Check that arrows run from high spot to low spot; an arrow toward a higher number is a red flag. Accessibility routes and parking often have maximum slopes (for example 2% cross slope), so small numbers matter.
field.title: Flow arrows and slope between spot elevations
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: For a straight run, length between structures = difference in stations if both sit on the same line and baseline. Example: MH 2 at 10+25.00 to MH 3 at 13+25.00 = 300.00 ft. If structures have different offsets from the baseline, the true length is longer: use the right triangle: sqrt(station difference squared + offset difference squared). Example: 300 ft apart in station, offsets 6.0 RT and 16.0 RT: sqrt(300^2 + 10^2) = 300.17 ft. On curved alignments, stationing follows the baseline curve; a pipe at an offset on the curve is longer (outside) or shorter (inside). Pipe laid on slope is longer than its horizontal length by a negligible amount on sewers (at 2% only 0.02%).
field.title: Computing pipe length from stations, offsets and curves
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: A cut sheet (grade sheet) from the surveyor turns plan inverts into cuts from field stakes. It should match the plans exactly in station, invert and slope. Check the first lines yourself: stake elevation minus cut should equal the plan invert at that station, and inverts should change by slope x distance between stakes. If the cut sheet and plan disagree, stop and ask the surveyor and engineer; the cause may be a revision the crew has not seen, a different reference (cut to invert vs to bottom of trench or top of bedding), or an error. Do not build to an unverified number. Keep the cut sheet with the plan revision date it was based on.
field.title: Cut sheet vs the plans: which to build to
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Utility lines are labeled by letters along the line: SS or S (sanitary sewer), SD or ST (storm drain), W (water), FM (force main), G (gas), E or UGE (underground electric), T or C (telephone/communications), RW (reclaimed water), FO (fiber optic). Existing lines are usually light, dashed or labeled EX; proposed lines are heavy. Abandon or remove notes are added (ABAN, TO BE REMOVED). Sizes may be shown without units: '8" SS' or just '8 SS'. These letters are labels, not elevations or distances. Use the project's legend because line styles vary, and remember existing utility locations on plans are approximate unless potholed.
field.title: Utility plan line types and labels: SS, SD, W, G, existing vs proposed
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: Standard civil and utility plan practice (US); check the project's legend and notes

field.text: Storm plans label structures with abbreviations: CB (catch basin), DI (drop inlet), CI (curb inlet), JB (junction box), MH (manhole), FES (flared end section), HW (headwall), OS (outlet structure). Each has a number and is listed in a storm structure table with grate or rim elevation and inverts. Pipe callouts give size, material and class: '15" RCP CL III', '18" HDPE', '24" CMP'. NCDOT's example lists runs as station, length, size and class between numbered structures (88 ft of 15" RCP Class III from Structure 23 to Structure 22). Box culvert sizes are given span first, then height (5' x 4' = 5 ft wide, 4 ft tall).
field.title: Storm drainage structure labels: CB, DI, JB, FES, HW, and storm pipe classes
field.topic: Plan reading: civil and utility plans, profiles and grading
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book; Georgia DOT Basic Highway Plan Reading manual

field.text: Every quantity Ask works out from a plan should show its inputs: each dimension, where it was read (sheet, drawing or detail, and which dimension: for example 'footing width 12" - detail 3/S2.0, horizontal dimension; depth 24" - same detail, vertical dimension from top of slab'), the math, and the result with units. Never scale a photo or print to fill a gap; if a needed number is not written, say which one is missing and ask, or show the answer with that value clearly marked as an assumption. This lets the foreman catch a misread (like width and depth swapped) before ordering concrete or cutting pipe. Round only the final answer and state any waste factor separately from the neat quantity.
field.title: Takeoff rule: list every written dimension used and where it came from
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Cubic yards = cubic feet / 27. Area x thickness: convert thickness to feet first (inches / 12). Cubic yards per 100 sq ft of slab: 3.5" = 1.080 CY, 4" = 1.235 CY, 5" = 1.543 CY, 6" = 1.852 CY, 8" = 2.469 CY. Coverage of 1 CY: 81 sq ft at 4", 64.8 sq ft at 5", 54 sq ft at 6". Footings per 100 linear ft: 12" x 12" = 3.70 CY; 12" x 18" = 5.56 CY; 12" x 24" = 7.41 CY; 16" x 8" = 3.29 CY; 18" x 12" = 5.56 CY; 24" x 12" = 7.41 CY. Keep at least 3 decimals during the math. Note 12" x 24" and 24" x 12" give the same volume, so a width/depth swap does not show up in concrete volume but does matter for layout, excavation and rebar.
field.title: Volume conversions for takeoff: cubic feet, cubic yards, thickness in inches
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Slab volume = area (sq ft) x thickness (ft) / 27. Get the area from written dimensions, breaking odd shapes into rectangles; add rectangles, subtract notches. Example: slab 30'-0" x 40'-0" from the foundation plan overall dimensions, 4" thick per the slab note: 30 x 40 = 1,200 sq ft x 0.333 ft = 400 cubic ft / 27 = 14.81 CY neat. Different slab areas (garage 5", house 4") are figured separately. Use outside dimensions of the slab edge (usually outside face of concrete; check whether the plan dimension is to stud, sheathing or concrete). Add the footing volume below the slab separately (see the overlap chunk) and add waste at the end.
field.title: Slab concrete takeoff: area times thickness
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: For continuous footings, use the centerline length so corners are not counted twice or missed. For a rectangle: centerline length = outside perimeter - 4 x footing width. Example: building 30'-0" x 40'-0" to outside of footing, 12" wide footing: outside perimeter 140 ft; centerline 140 - 4 x 1.0 = 136 ft. Check: the centerline rectangle is 29 x 39 ft, perimeter 136 ft. For other shapes measured along the outside face, each outside corner subtracts one full footing width (half a width off each leg) and each inside (re-entrant) corner adds one full width back; an L-shape (5 outside, 1 inside corner) still nets outside perimeter - 4 x width. Add interior footings separately, running each between the inside faces of the footings they meet so the overlap is not counted twice.
field.title: Perimeter footing length: use the centerline, not the outside perimeter
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: When the slab sits on or is poured with the footing, count the slab over its full area and count the footing only below the bottom of the slab. Example: 30 x 40 ft slab, 4" thick; perimeter footing 12" wide, 24" deep measured from top of slab (detail 1/S2). Slab: 1,200 x 0.333 = 400 cubic ft. Footing below slab: depth 24 - 4 = 20" = 1.667 ft; centerline length 136 ft; 136 x 1.0 x 1.667 = 226.7 cubic ft. Total = 626.7 cubic ft / 27 = 23.21 CY neat. If the detail's 24" is footing thickness below the slab instead (read where the dimension line starts), use the full 2.0 ft: 272 cubic ft. Counting the footing full depth plus the slab full area overcounts by the slab-over-footing strip.
field.title: Footing and slab overlap: do not double count
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: For a thickened edge or interior thickened slab, add only what hangs below the slab. Rectangle part: width x (total depth - slab thickness). Sloped (45 degree) sides each add a triangle: 0.5 x drop x drop, where drop = total depth - slab thickness. Example: interior thickened slab under a bearing wall, 12" wide at bottom, 12" total depth, 4" slab, 45 degree sides both sides, 40 ft long: drop = 8" = 0.667 ft; rectangle 1.0 x 0.667 = 0.667 sq ft; triangles 2 x 0.5 x 0.667 x 0.667 = 0.444 sq ft; total 1.111 sq ft per ft x 40 = 44.4 cubic ft = 1.65 CY. A perimeter thickened edge with a taper on the inside only gets one triangle: 0.889 sq ft per ft for the same sizes.
field.title: Thickened slab edges and interior thickened slabs: volume with taper
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Count each pad footing mark on the foundation plan (F3 x 6, F4 x 2), take sizes from the footing schedule, and multiply. Example: F3 = 2'-6" SQ x 12" DP: 2.5 x 2.5 x 1.0 = 6.25 cubic ft each x 6 = 37.5 cubic ft. F4 = 3'-0" SQ x 18" DP: 3 x 3 x 1.5 = 13.5 x 2 = 27 cubic ft. Total 64.5 cubic ft = 2.39 CY. If pads sit under the slab and the depth is from top of slab, subtract the slab thickness as with continuous footings. Round piers: volume = 0.7854 x diameter squared x depth (12" dia x 4 ft = 3.14 cubic ft each). Double-check the count against the schedule and any 'TYP' notes.
field.title: Pad footings and piers: count from the plan, size from the schedule
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Deduct openings in the slab that are large and shown with written dimensions (for example a 6 x 8 ft area left out for a later pour, a pit, or a large blockout). Common practice is to ignore small penetrations, pipe sleeves and floor drains since they are less than the normal waste. Slab depressions (for example a 1-1/2" recess for tile or a shower) reduce volume slightly and are usually ignored unless large. Pits, sumps and elevator or equipment pits add volume (walls and floor) and need their own detail takeoff. Note each deduction with its source dimension, so the foreman can see what was removed.
field.title: Openings, blockouts and depressions in slab takeoff
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Add waste after the neat volume, as a separate line. Typical ranges: formed slabs and flatwork about 5 to 10 percent; footings poured against excavated soil about 10 to 15 percent or more (trench overdig, soft spots, uneven bottoms); add pump line and hopper waste, often about 1/2 yard per pump setup. Ready-mix is ordered in whole or half yards; check the supplier's short-load charges. Example: 23.21 CY neat x 1.08 = 25.1 CY, order 25 to 25.5 CY and call the last truck after measuring what remains. These are typical figures, not rules; company history, crew and site conditions decide. Running short means a cold joint, which costs far more than a half yard of extra.
field.title: Concrete waste factors: typical ranges
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Base rock volume = slab area x base thickness (from the slab note or detail). Example: 1,200 sq ft x 4" (0.333 ft) = 400 cubic ft = 14.81 compacted CY. Dense-graded base compacted in place is commonly about 130 to 145 lb per cubic ft (about 1.75 to 1.95 tons per compacted CY); at 140 lb per cubic ft: 400 x 140 / 2,000 = 28 tons. Clean crushed rock (for example 3/4" washed) runs about 1.35 to 1.5 tons per CY. Add 5 to 10 percent for waste and grade variation. Extend the base under thickened edges only if the detail shows base under them; many details show footings on native soil with base only under the slab field. Check your supplier's weights.
field.title: Base rock under slabs: compacted volume and tons
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Ask KB aggregates-estimating chunks (typical unit weights); Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Vapor retarder area = slab area plus laps, turn-ups and waste. Laps are usually at least 6 inches (IRC minimum for slabs), taped; turn-ups at walls or slab edges per the detail. A quick estimate is slab area x 1.10 to 1.15. Example: 1,200 sq ft x 1.12 = 1,344 sq ft, then round up to whole rolls of the size your supplier stocks. Add seam tape and pipe boots for each penetration (count plumbing and electrical stub-ups on the plumbing and electrical plans). Read the mil thickness from the slab note (6, 10 or 15 mil) and any product class required; a 10 mil callout cannot be swapped for 6 mil without approval.
field.title: Vapor retarder takeoff
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: IRC R506 slab-on-ground provisions, as summarized by Jaspector (IRC 2024); Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Number of bars in one direction = (width across the bars minus edge clearances) / spacing, rounded up, plus 1. Example: 30 x 40 ft slab, #4 @ 18" O.C. E.W., bars held 3" from edges. Bars running the 40 ft way: (30 - 0.5) / 1.5 = 19.67, round up to 20 spaces, 21 bars, each 39.5 ft. With 20 ft stock and a 20" (1.67 ft) lap, each run needs 3 pieces and 2 laps: 39.5 + 2 x 1.67 = 42.83 ft x 21 = 899.5 ft. Bars running the 30 ft way: (40 - 0.5) / 1.5 = 26.33, so 27 spaces, 28 bars, each 29.5 ft + 1 lap = 31.17 ft x 28 = 872.7 ft. Total 1,772 ft x 0.668 lb/ft = about 1,184 lb, plus chairs. Lap length comes from the general notes.
field.title: Rebar takeoff for a slab: bars each way
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: CRSI standard bar data and ACI 318 provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide; Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Footing bars run the centerline length times the number of bars, plus laps and corner bars. Example: 136 ft centerline, (2) #4 BOT CONT, 20 ft stock, lap 24" per general notes. Laps per bar line on a closed loop = 136 / (20 - 2) = 7.56, round up to 8 laps x 2 ft = 16 ft. Each line = 136 + 16 = 152 ft; two lines = 304 ft. Corner bars (bent L bars lapped both ways, commonly required at corners and intersections): 4 corners x 2 bars x 4 ft (2 ft each leg) = 32 ft. Total 336 ft x 0.668 = about 224 lb. For T&B callouts double the bar lines. Add dowels, step bars and bars around openings separately. Check the detail for required corner bars and lap lengths.
field.title: Rebar takeoff for continuous footings: bars, laps, corner bars
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies; CRSI standard bar data and ACI 318 provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide

field.text: Embedded items are counted, not measured. Dowels at a spacing: count = length / spacing, rounded up, for a closed loop (136 ft at 24" O.C. = 68), plus 1 for an open run. Anchor bolts: for each sill run, one within 12" of each end plus one every spacing between (for example a 22 ft wall at 6 ft O.C.: ends plus 3 between = 5 bolts); add extra pieces at every sill splice, door opening (each side), and use the closer spacing from the shear wall schedule along shear wall lengths. Holdowns and STHD straps: count every symbol or model name on the foundation and shear wall plans; note each model separately (HDU4 x 4, STHD14 x 6). Post bases: count from the plan and post schedule.
field.title: Counting dowels, anchor bolts, holdowns and straps from the plan
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: American Wood Council FAQ on IRC R403.1.6 sill plate anchorage; Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Footing excavation volume = length x excavated width x excavated depth. Depth runs from the existing or pad grade at the time of digging to bottom of footing (not from finished floor). Width: footings poured neat against the trench walls (common for 12" to 24" wide footings in firm soil) are dug to the footing width; formed footings need working room, often 1 to 2 ft each side. Example: 136 ft of 12" footing dug neat, bottom 18" below pad grade: 136 x 1.0 x 1.5 = 204 cubic ft = 7.56 bank CY. Spoils swell when dug (about 25 percent for common earth), so about 9.4 loose CY to haul or spread. Add pads, thickened edges and over-excavation if the soils report requires it.
field.title: Footing excavation quantities
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies; Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Pipe runs on plan and profile sheets are usually labeled center of structure to center of structure (for example 300 LF between MH 2 at 10+25 and MH 3 at 13+25). The pipe actually installed is shorter by about the inside radius of each structure: 300 - 2.0 - 2.0 = 296 ft for 48" manholes. Check the measurement and payment section: many contracts pay pipe C-C of structures, some measure to inside faces. To order, divide by the joint lay length and round up (PVC gravity sewer is commonly sold in 14 ft or 20 ft lengths; check). 296 / 14 = 21.1, so 22 joints, plus extra for cutting and stub-outs. Sum all runs per size and material using a list with run, stations, length and source sheet.
field.title: Pipe length takeoff from plan and profile
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Count from the plan, run by run: structures (manholes by diameter and depth range, cleanouts, inlets) from the structure table; fittings shown as symbols (tees, wyes, bends with angle, reducers, plugs, valves, hydrants); services (each tick or label is a service: wye or tee at the main, lateral pipe from station to property or R/W, cleanout, bends, plug or meter box per the standard detail). Lateral length = distance from main to the R/W or end point shown, often a typical length in the notes. Water fittings need restraint or thrust blocks per detail; count them too. Present the count by sheet and station so it can be checked, for example 'SS services: 14 on C5.1 (STA 10+40 to 15+90).'
field.title: Fittings, services and structures takeoff from utility plans
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: For excavation and bedding quantities you need trench depth along the run: depth = ground surface elevation - invert + bedding depth below the invert. At structures read rim or finished grade and invert from the profile labels; between structures, read ground at station gridlines where elevations are labeled. Example: at MH 3 ground 105.20, IE 98.35; at MH 2 ground 103.00, IE 96.85; 0.5 ft bedding: depths 7.35 ft and 6.65 ft; average about 7.0 ft if ground is fairly even between. Uneven ground: split into station segments and average each. Then volume = length x trench width x average depth (see the trench excavation volume chunk in the materials math file), plus manhole excavation.
field.title: Trench depth and excavation from the profile
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: Civil and DOT sets often include a summary of quantities or bid quantity sheet listing each pay item with quantity and unit (LF of pipe by size, EA manholes, CY concrete, TON base). GDOT's plan reading manual lists it near the front of the set. Use it as a check against your own takeoff, not as a substitute: engineer's quantities are estimates and may be measured differently from how you order or build (C-C lengths, pay limits). Quick sanity checks for building jobs: slab CY should be close to area x thickness; rebar for a 4" slab with #4 @ 18" E.W. runs roughly 0.9 to 1.0 lb per sq ft; footing CY per 100 ft for common sizes (12" x 24" = 7.41 CY). Big differences mean a misread dimension.
field.title: Summary of quantities sheets and checking your own takeoff
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Georgia DOT Basic Highway Plan Reading manual; Standard quantity takeoff practice (worked here); company and spec practice varies

field.text: Stem wall concrete = centerline length x wall thickness x height. Height runs from top of footing to top of wall (T.O.F. to T.O.W.), read from the wall section or elevations, not from grade. Example: rectangle 30 x 40 ft outside, 8" (0.667 ft) wall, 2'-0" high: centerline = 140 - 4 x 0.667 = 137.3 ft; 137.3 x 0.667 x 2.0 = 183.1 cubic ft = 6.78 CY. Form contact area = outside face (140 x 2.0 = 280 sq ft) + inside face ((140 - 8 x 0.667) x 2.0 = 269.3 sq ft) = about 549 sq ft, plus bulkheads at ends and steps. Stepped walls: figure each step separately. Count anchor bolts, holdown anchors and STHD straps that land in the wall rather than the footing.
field.title: Stem walls and formed foundation walls: volume and forms
field.topic: Quantities from plans: concrete, base, rebar, excavation and pipe takeoff
field.source: Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: The first letter of a sheet number tells you the discipline. Under the US National CAD Standard (NCS): G = general (cover, sheet index, symbols, code summary), V = survey/mapping, B = geotechnical, C = civil, L = landscape, S = structural, A = architectural, I = interiors, F = fire protection, P = plumbing, M = mechanical (HVAC), E = electrical, T = telecom, Z = contractor or shop drawings. A sheet number like A-201 or AD101 is discipline letter(s), then a sheet type digit, then a two-digit sequence. When a crew sends a photo, read the sheet number in the title block first: it tells Ask whether the numbers on it are architectural (feet-inches, to face of stud), structural (concrete, rebar, holdowns) or civil (decimal feet, stations, elevations).
field.title: Sheet numbers by discipline: what A, S, C, G, M, E, P mean (National CAD Standard)
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: U.S. National CAD Standard (NCS) sheet identification, as summarized by Archtoolbox

field.text: In NCS-style numbering the digit right after the discipline letters says what kind of drawing the sheet holds: 0 = general (symbol legend, abbreviations, general notes), 1 = plans, 2 = elevations, 3 = sections, 4 = large-scale views (enlarged plans, elevations, sections, but not details), 5 = details, 6 = schedules and diagrams, 7 and 8 = user defined, 9 = 3D views and photos. So S-501 is a structural detail sheet, A-201 is an architectural elevation sheet, A-601 holds schedules (doors, windows, finishes). Sequence numbers run 01 to 99 and may skip numbers to leave room for added sheets, so a gap in the set (A-101, A-103) is not proof a sheet is missing; check the sheet index on the cover sheet.
field.title: Sheet type digit: 0 general, 1 plans, 2 elevations, 3 sections, 5 details, 6 schedules
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: U.S. National CAD Standard (NCS) sheet identification, as summarized by Archtoolbox

field.text: Many sets, especially small residential and commercial jobs, do not follow NCS exactly. Common patterns: A2.1 = architectural, group 2 (often elevations), sheet 1; S1, S2 = structural sheets in order; SD1 or S5.1 = structural details; C3.0 = civil, often grading or utility sheet. Under strict NCS a second letter is a modifier (AD = architectural demolition), so SD could mean structural demolition on a big project, while on a house set it almost always means structural details. The sheet index on the cover or first general sheet (G-001, T1, A0.0, C0.0) is the only sure answer. If a crew asks about a callout pointing to a sheet, look up that sheet's name in the index before assuming what is on it.
field.title: Non-standard sheet numbers: A2.1, S1, SD1, C3.0 and how to decode them
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: The first sheet (cover, title sheet, G-001, T1, C0.0) usually holds: project name and address, owner, architect and engineer of record, the sheet index (every sheet number and title), vicinity map, code and design data, and often the project-wide abbreviations and symbol legend. Check the index against the sheets you actually have; plan photos from the field are often from an old or partial set. On DOT and utility sets the title sheet also lists the governing standard specifications edition and the project length. If a sheet is referenced (for example detail 5/SD1) and not in the index, the reference may be to a standard detail book or another set (city standard plans, manufacturer details). Ask the crew which set and date they are holding before reading numbers.
field.title: Cover sheet and sheet index: start here when reading a plan set
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book

field.text: The title block runs along the right edge or bottom of every sheet. It holds the sheet number (usually the large text in the bottom right corner), sheet title (FOUNDATION PLAN, SHEAR WALL DETAILS), project name and number, the design firm and engineer's stamp, drawn/checked initials, the issue date and a revision block listing each revision number, date and description. Before using any number from a sheet photo, read: sheet number, sheet title, latest revision number and date, and scale if printed there. An unstamped or 'NOT FOR CONSTRUCTION', 'PRELIMINARY', 'BID SET' or 'PERMIT SET' sheet may be superseded; field crews should build from the latest issued-for-construction set or as directed by the super.
field.title: Title block: where it is and what to read in it
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: When a sheet is revised, the designer draws a wavy 'revision cloud' around the changed text or linework and places a small triangle (delta) with the revision number next to it. The delta number matches a line in the title block revision block, which gives the date and a short description (for example 'Rev 2 - Addendum 2, footing F2 widened'). On the next reissue older clouds are often removed but the delta and the revision block history stay. Reading tips: a number inside a triangle near a cloud is a revision number, not a dimension, a detail number or a shear wall mark; a shear wall mark is a triangle or other symbol on the wall line itself, usually with a length next to it. If the crew's printout shows a revision number lower than the latest issue, the numbers may be out of date.
field.title: Revision clouds and delta triangles: what changed on a sheet
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: ARE study guide 17.2: drawing cross-referencing, coordination and revision control (open-exam-prep)

field.text: General notes are numbered paragraphs (often on the first sheet of each discipline, like S0.1 or C1.0) that apply to the whole set or discipline unless a sheet says otherwise: concrete strength, rebar grade, soil bearing pressure, cover, compaction, 'all dimensions to face of stud', and so on. Sheet notes apply only to that sheet. Keynotes are short numbered or lettered tags (a number in a hexagon, square or circle, or a code like 03 30 00.A) placed on the drawing with a leader; the matching text is in a keynote list on the side of the same sheet. A keynote number is never a dimension or a quantity. When a dimension or rebar size is missing on a plan, the answer is often in the general notes ('typical footing reinforcement: (2) #4 continuous').
field.title: General notes, sheet notes and keynotes: how they differ
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: Symbols differ from firm to firm. A triangle may mean a revision, a shear wall type, a window tag or a keynote depending on the office. Every set should have a legend: a symbol list on the cover or first sheet of each discipline (G-002, A0.1, S0.1, C0.1) and often a small legend on the sheet itself, especially on civil sheets (line types for existing and proposed sewer, water, storm, contours). Before Ask interprets any symbol from a photo, it should ask for or look for the legend. If no legend is in the photo, say what the symbol most commonly means, say it is an assumption, and ask the crew to photograph the legend or the general notes sheet.
field.title: Legends and symbol lists: always read them before reading a sheet
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: TYP = typical (the same condition repeats wherever it applies; it does not mean 'approximately'). UNO / UON = unless noted otherwise. SIM = similar (same idea, details may differ; check). NTS = not to scale. VIF = verify in field. EQ = equal spacing. CLR = clear (dimension between faces, inside to inside). AFF = above finished floor. O.C. = on center. E.W. = each way. E.F. = each face. T&B = top and bottom. CONT = continuous. ALT = alternate. T.O. / B.O. = top of / bottom of (T.O.F. top of footing, B.O.F. bottom of footing, T.O.S. top of slab or steel, T.O.W. top of wall). F.F. = finished floor. N.I.C. = not in contract. (N) / (E) = new / existing. Each set's own abbreviation list governs.
field.title: Common plan abbreviations: TYP, UNO, SIM, NTS, VIF, EQ, CLR, AFF
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: There is no single universal order; the contract general conditions decide. Common patterns: change orders and addenda govern over the documents they change; project-specific items govern over standard ones (special provisions over standard specs, job-specific plan sheets over standard plans); written (figured) dimensions govern over scaled ones. Whether specs beat drawings varies: federal construction contracts (FAR 52.236-21) say the specifications govern over the drawings, while TxDOT puts special provisions over plans and plans over standard specifications. Many private contracts (AIA style) treat documents as complementary with no ranking. If a crew finds a conflict, Ask should point it out, say which way the typical rule leans, and tell them to get an answer from the super/engineer (RFI) before building.
field.title: Which governs when sheets and specs conflict: typical order of precedence
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: TxDOT PS&E Preparation Manual 4.5.8, Hierarchy of PS&E elements; FAR 52.236-21, Specifications and Drawings for Construction (federal contracts); NICET highway construction inspection study guide 2.2: plans vs specifications and order of precedence

field.text: A dimension written on the drawing (figured dimension) governs over anything you get by measuring the drawing with a scale. TxDOT states numerical dimensions govern over scaled dimensions, and plan reading guides say the same. Reasons: prints shrink or stretch when copied, half-size sets are common, PDF zoom and phone photos distort scale, and drafters do not always draw exactly to size. If the dimension you need is not written, do not scale it and treat it as contractual: add up other written dimensions to get it, or ask the engineer. Ask should never give a measured-off-the-photo number as a building dimension; at most it can give a clearly labeled rough check and say a written dimension or RFI is needed.
field.title: Written dimensions govern over scaled dimensions
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: TxDOT PS&E Preparation Manual 4.5.8, Hierarchy of PS&E elements

field.text: A common rule in general conditions and spec front ends is that larger-scale drawings govern over smaller-scale ones, and specific details govern over general or typical ones, because the detail is where the designer drew the condition carefully. Example: the foundation plan at 1/4" = 1'-0" shows a footing labeled F1, and detail 3/S5.1 at 3/4" = 1'-0" shows F1 as 18" wide; the detail wins over anything you would read off the plan. A detail marked for a specific location also governs over a 'TYP' detail. This is typical, not universal: the contract governs, and a real conflict (detail says 18", schedule says 24") is an RFI, not a judgment call for the crew.
field.title: Large-scale details govern over small-scale plans (typical rule)
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: When a footing width, invert, rebar size or length differs between sheets: 1) Check revision numbers and dates; the later revision usually wins. 2) Check whether one value is in an addendum, bulletin, ASI or change order. 3) Apply the contract's precedence clause if known (project-specific over standard, written over scaled, large-scale detail over small-scale plan). 4) Do not average or pick the cheaper one. 5) Write it down with sheet numbers (for example 'S1.1 footing schedule F2 = 24" wide; detail 4/S5.1 = 18" wide') and send it to the super or engineer as an RFI before pouring or laying. Ask should list the conflicting values with their sheet and detail references, say which one the usual rule favors, and flag that the crew needs a written answer.
field.title: What to do when two sheets disagree
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: Each drawing on a sheet has its own scale note under its title, for example 'FOUNDATION PLAN  SCALE: 1/4" = 1'-0"'. Architect's scales are fractions of an inch per foot (1/8", 1/4", 1/2", 3/4", 1", 1-1/2", 3" = 1'-0"); common for building plans and details. Engineer's (civil) scales are 1" = 10', 20', 30', 40', 50', 60', 100'; common for site, grading and utility plans. Profiles have two scales: horizontal (for example 1" = 50') and vertical (for example 1" = 5'). One sheet can hold drawings at different scales; a detail at 3/4" = 1'-0" next to a plan at 1/8" = 1'-0". 'NTS' means not to scale. A scale note tells you how the drawing was made, not permission to measure it for construction.
field.title: Scale notes: architect's scale vs engineer's scale
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Georgia DOT Basic Highway Plan Reading manual

field.text: Do not measure a phone photo, a screenshot, or a reduced print to get a construction dimension. Photos have perspective distortion (the sheet is not flat or square to the camera), PDFs get zoomed, and plan sets are often printed half size (an 11x17 print of a 22x34 sheet): NCDOT's plan reading book notes that on half-size sheets drawn at 1" = 50', 1/2" = 50 ft, so a ruler reading is off by a factor of 2 if you trust the scale note. Use written dimensions. If none exist, add up written dimensions, use stationing or coordinates, or ask. If a rough check is useful, use the graphic bar scale on the same sheet, label the result as approximate, and never use it for layout, forms, or ordering.
field.title: Never scale a photo or a reduced print
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book

field.text: A graphic scale is a printed bar marked in feet (for example 0, 10, 20, 40 ft) placed near the drawing title or north arrow. Because it shrinks or grows with the print, it stays correct on half-size prints, while a written scale note (1" = 20') only holds on a full-size sheet. NCDOT tells plan readers to measure against the graphic scale for reduced sheets. Still, a graphic scale gives only a rough check: photo distortion, line thickness and print shrinkage all add error. Use it to sanity-check that a written number is the right order of magnitude (is that pipe run about 200 ft or about 20 ft?), not to set forms, cut pipe, or order material.
field.title: Graphic (bar) scale: why it survives reduction
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book

field.text: The north arrow shows which way north is on the sheet. Civil and site plans usually show true or grid north; property bearings (N 45 deg 12'30" E) are referenced to it. Building plans sometimes use a 'plan north' (rotated so the building sits square on the sheet) with a second arrow for true north. Plans are often, but not always, drawn north-up. Elevation names (NORTH ELEVATION) and invert labels like 'IE IN (N)' mean compass direction, so read the north arrow on that same sheet before telling a crew which pipe is the north inlet. Stationing direction is independent of north: on DOT plans stations commonly increase south to north or west to east, but curves and project layout can change that.
field.title: North arrow, plan north and true north
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: NCDOT Plan Reading Book

field.text: A match line is a heavy line, often labeled 'MATCH LINE STA 15+00 - SEE SHEET C3.2', where a long plan or utility run is cut and continues on another sheet. Everything on one side is on this sheet; the continuation is on the named sheet. On utility plans the match line is usually at a station, so stations, pipe runs and structure numbers carry across. Reading tips: the match line is not a wall, property line or pipe; its station is a location, not a length; when adding up a pipe run across sheets, use stations at structures, not lengths measured on each sheet. On building plans match lines split large floor plans into areas (Area A, Area B) with key plans showing which part of the building each sheet covers.
field.title: Match lines: where one plan sheet continues on another
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: A section cut is shown on a plan by a line through the building or footing with a symbol at one or both ends: a circle split by a horizontal line, the section number (or letter) in the top half and the sheet number where the section is drawn in the bottom half, plus an arrow or solid triangle showing which way you are looking. Example: a bubble with 3 over S3.1 means section 3 is drawn on sheet S3.1. The arrow direction matters: the section shows what you see looking that way, so left and right in the section depend on it. On civil sets sections are often letters (A-A, B-B). The numbers in the bubble are references, not dimensions or elevations.
field.title: Section markers: circle with a number over a sheet, arrow shows view direction
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: ARE study guide 17.2: drawing cross-referencing, coordination and revision control (open-exam-prep)

field.text: Exterior elevations are usually titled by direction (NORTH ELEVATION, EAST ELEVATION) or numbered from the plan. Interior elevations are called out with an elevation marker: a circle or square with arrows (often up to four) pointing at the walls being shown, each arrow with a number, and the sheet number in the center or bottom (for example arrows 1-4 with A4.1 means interior elevations 1 to 4 on sheet A4.1). Level markers on elevations and sections (a circle with quadrants or a triangle on a horizontal line) give heights like 'T.O. PLATE 9'-1 1/8"' or 'F.F. 100'-0"'. A level datum of 100'-0" is often an assumed reference for finished floor, not a real site elevation; check the civil plan for the actual FF elevation.
field.title: Elevation markers: exterior and interior elevation references
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: ARE study guide 17.2: drawing cross-referencing, coordination and revision control (open-exam-prep); Standard architectural drawing practice (US); symbols vary by firm, check the legend

field.text: A detail callout bubble is a circle split by a line: the top is the detail number, the bottom is the sheet where it is drawn. Written inline, '5/SD1' means detail 5 on sheet SD1 (on small sets SD1 is usually the first structural details sheet; confirm in the sheet index). A dash or the same sheet number in the bottom means the detail is on this sheet. A leader or a box around part of the plan shows what area the detail covers. Go to that sheet, find the drawing whose title bubble shows 5, and read its title and scale. The letters always belong to the sheet, the bare number to the detail. Some details are standard plans from a city or DOT book (for example 'SEE STD DWG SS-4'), not in the set at all.
field.title: Detail callouts like 5/SD1: detail number over sheet number
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: ARE study guide 17.2: drawing cross-referencing, coordination and revision control (open-exam-prep)

field.text: Busy areas (kitchens, restrooms, stairs, mechanical rooms, wet wells, manhole clusters) are often drawn again at larger scale on an enlarged plan. On the main plan a dashed or chain-line box surrounds the area with a callout bubble or a note like 'SEE ENLARGED PLAN 1/A4.1'. Dimensions and details inside the box should be read from the enlarged plan, which typically governs over the small-scale plan. Large sets also carry a small 'key plan' near the title block, shading the part of the building or site that the sheet shows. If a photo shows only part of a sheet, the key plan and match lines tell you which part.
field.title: Enlarged plan references and key plans
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: ARE study guide 17.2: drawing cross-referencing, coordination and revision control (open-exam-prep); Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: 'TYP' on a detail or note means it applies at every similar location on the job, not that the value is approximate. A footing section titled 'TYP EXTERIOR FOOTING' applies to all exterior footings unless a different detail or schedule mark is shown. 'SIM' means similar: use the detail's concept but check for differences (opposite hand, different bar size called out). 'UNO' or 'UON' means unless noted otherwise: the general rule applies except where a plan or detail gives a specific value, and the specific value wins. Example: general note '#4 @ 18" O.C. E.W. UNO' plus a plan note '#4 @ 12" O.C. E.W. at garage slab' means 12" spacing in the garage and 18" everywhere else.
field.title: TYP, SIM and UNO: how far a note reaches
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: Utility and site plans often reference standard drawings that are not in the plan set: city or district standard details (manhole, cleanout, service lateral, trench patch, thrust block), DOT standard plans, or manufacturer details. They appear as a note or bubble like 'PER CITY STD 401' or 'SEE STD PLAN D73'. The standard detail is part of the contract if referenced; project-specific sheets usually govern over standard ones where they conflict (TxDOT, for example, puts job-specific sheets over standard sheets). When a crew asks about a referenced standard, Ask should say which standard book it is, ask for the edition or year named in the notes, and not invent the detail's numbers.
field.title: Standard details and standard plans referenced from outside the set
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: TxDOT PS&E Preparation Manual 4.5.8, Hierarchy of PS&E elements; Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: Before answering from a photographed sheet, Ask should: 1) Read the sheet number and title (discipline and drawing type). 2) Find the drawing title and its scale note under that drawing. 3) Note the revision number. 4) Identify what each number is attached to: dimension line with arrows or ticks, tag symbol, keynote, elevation, station, or schedule mark. 5) Check the legend and general notes if visible. 6) Use only written dimensions; never scale the photo. 7) State each value used and where it came from (for example 'footing width 12" from detail 3/S2, horizontal dimension under the footing'). 8) If something is cut off, blurry or ambiguous, say so and ask for a closer photo instead of guessing.
field.title: Reading a plan photo: checklist before giving a number
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: 'NTS' (not to scale) means the drawing is a diagram; no measurement off it means anything, and only written values count. 'VIF' (verify in field) means the designer did not know the exact value (often existing conditions or tie-in points); the crew must measure the real condition before building, and the written number is a starting assumption. A dimension with '+/-' (for example 12'-6" +/-) is approximate, usually existing work; do not lay out new work to it without checking. 'HOLD' or 'H' next to a dimension, or a dimension in a cloud marked 'HOLD', means that number is fixed and other dimensions should adjust to it. Ask should repeat these qualifiers when quoting such numbers.
field.title: NTS, VIF and dimensions marked with plus-minus
field.topic: Plan reading: sheets, symbols and which sheet governs
field.source: Standard US construction drawing practice; conventions vary by firm, so check the sheet legend and general notes

field.text: The first structural sheet usually holds the structural general notes. They set values that apply everywhere unless a plan or detail says otherwise: design code (IBC/IRC year), allowable soil bearing pressure (for example 1,500 psf), concrete strength by use (footings 2,500 or 3,000 psi, slabs 3,000 psi), rebar grade (Grade 60, ASTM A615), clear cover, lap length rule, anchor bolt size and spacing, lumber grades, nailing, holdown and connector manufacturer, and special inspection requirements. When a footing detail shows bars but no lap length, or a slab note gives no concrete strength, the answer is usually in these notes. Ask should check or request the general notes before saying a value is missing.
field.title: Structural general notes (S0, S0.1, S1): where the missing numbers live
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: A foundation plan is a view looking down at the foundation with the building above removed. It shows: outline of slab and slab edges, perimeter and interior footings (often dashed lines showing footing edges under the slab), pad footings at posts and columns, grade beams, thickened slabs, step locations, slab notes (thickness, reinforcing, vapor retarder, base), anchor bolt and holdown locations, shear wall marks, post bases, slab depressions and slopes, and section and detail callouts pointing to footing details. Dimensions locate walls and footings, usually to the outside face of concrete or to grid lines. Each footing type has a mark (F1, F2) or a detail callout; the detail or footing schedule gives width, depth and bars.
field.title: Foundation plan: what it shows and how to read it
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: A typical slab note reads like: '4" CONC SLAB W/ #4 @ 18" O.C. E.W. AT MID-DEPTH OVER 10 MIL VAPOR RETARDER OVER 4" BASE ROCK OVER COMPACTED SUBGRADE.' Read it top down: slab thickness 4 inches; #4 bars (1/2 inch) spaced 18 inches on center, each way (one set of bars running each direction, forming a grid); bars located at mid-depth (on chairs, about 2" up); a 10 mil plastic vapor retarder directly under the concrete; 4 inches of base rock (crushed aggregate) under that; then compacted subgrade. 'E.W.' does not mean two layers top and bottom. Thickened areas, depressions and different slabs (garage, porch) usually have their own notes.
field.title: Reading a slab-on-grade note: thickness, rebar, vapor retarder, base rock
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: The International Residential Code (R506) sets minimums for concrete floor slabs on ground inside the building: at least 3-1/2 inches thick; a base course of at least 4 inches of clean graded sand, gravel or crushed stone under the slab (with exceptions for suitable native soils); and a vapor retarder of at least 6 mil polyethylene (or approved equal) between the base and the slab, with laps of at least 6 inches. Plans often exceed these: 4" or 5" slabs, 10 or 15 mil retarders, and rebar or fiber reinforcement. The plan and the local code govern; some jurisdictions (for example under California rules) require more. Use these only to sanity-check a plan reading, never to replace a plan value.
field.title: Residential slab minimums in the IRC (3.5" slab, 4" base, 6 mil)
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: IRC R506 slab-on-ground provisions, as summarized by Jaspector (IRC 2024)

field.text: Plan notes call for a vapor retarder (often called vapor barrier, visqueen, poly) under interior slabs. Common callouts: '6 MIL POLY' (code minimum on many houses), '10 MIL VAPOR RETARDER' or '15 MIL' (common on commercial work and where floor finishes are moisture sensitive), sometimes with a product class (for example meeting ASTM E1745 Class A). Read laps (typically 6" minimum, taped) and whether it sits directly under the slab or under a sand or rock layer; the note or detail decides. Turn up at walls and sealing around pipe penetrations are often in the detail. The mil number is plastic thickness (1 mil = 0.001 inch), not a dimension or a rebar spacing.
field.title: Vapor retarder notes under slabs: 6 mil, 10 mil, 15 mil
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: IRC R506 slab-on-ground provisions, as summarized by Jaspector (IRC 2024); Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: Foundation plans often label footings with a mark instead of drawing full information at every footing: F1, F2 for footing types, or CF (continuous footing) and PF / SF (pad or spread footing) with a number. The footing schedule (a table on the foundation sheet or on S0/S5) lists each mark with width, length (for pads), depth or thickness, reinforcing, and sometimes top of footing elevation. A pad footing entry like '3'-0" SQ x 1'-6" DP W/ (4) #5 E.W.' means 3 ft by 3 ft, 18 inches thick, four #5 bars each way (8 bars total). Schedules may list size as width x length x depth or with headed columns; read the column headings, do not assume order.
field.title: Footing marks and footing schedules: F1, F2, CF, PF
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: In a footing section (a vertical slice through the footing), the horizontal dimension under or across the footing is the WIDTH; the vertical dimension at the side is the DEPTH or thickness. Example: a detail with 12" written along the bottom and 24" written up the side is a footing 12 inches wide and 24 inches deep, not 24 wide. Check by orientation of the dimension line (horizontal line = width), by which side of the drawing it is on, and by the soil hatching and grade line (depth is measured from grade or slab down). Sanity check: a narrow, deep perimeter footing (12" wide x 24" deep) is very common on wood houses and in frost or expansive-soil areas. When stating the answer, say 'width 12" (horizontal dimension), depth 24" (vertical dimension)'.
field.title: Reading a footing section: width is across, depth is down (do not swap them)
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: Footing details give vertical numbers that measure different things: 1) depth below lowest adjacent grade to bottom of footing (embedment, 'MIN 18" BELOW GRADE'); 2) total depth from top of slab to bottom of footing (for monolithic slab and footing); 3) footing thickness (top of footing to bottom of footing, for a separate footing under a stem wall). Read where the dimension line starts: the finished grade line outside, the top of slab, or the top of footing. Also look for elevation tags: T.O.F. (top of footing) and B.O.F. (bottom of footing). For quantities, depth below slab is what you add to the slab volume; for excavation, use depth below existing grade. Always state which depth you are using.
field.title: Footing depth: below grade, below slab, or footing thickness?
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: For houses under the IRC (R403), concrete footings must be at least 12 inches wide and 6 inches thick, bear on undisturbed soil or engineered fill, and the bottom must be at least 12 inches below undisturbed ground surface, and below the local frost depth unless frost protected. Footing bottoms may slope up to 1 in 10 (10%); steeper sites need stepped footings. Actual widths depend on soil bearing and number of stories (IRC tables) and the engineer's design; plans commonly show wider and deeper footings than the minimum. Use these numbers only to sanity check a reading (a footing read as 6" wide is almost certainly a misread) and follow the plan and local building department.
field.title: IRC footing minimums: 12" wide, 6" thick, 12" below undisturbed ground
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: IRC R403 footing provisions, as summarized by InterNACHI

field.text: Footing and slab details show cover as a small dimension from the bar to the concrete face, labeled 'CLR' (clear) or 'COVER', for example '3" CLR' at the bottom and sides of a footing cast against soil. ACI 318's baseline is 3 inches for concrete cast against and permanently exposed to earth, 1-1/2 to 2 inches for formed surfaces exposed to earth or weather depending on bar size, and 3/4 inch for interior unexposed. Cover is measured to the outside of the bar (or stirrup), not to its center. A '3" CLR' label is not a footing dimension. For bar layout: a 12" wide footing with 3" side cover leaves 6" between outside bar faces; the bottom bars sit 3" up on dobies or chairs.
field.title: Clear cover in footing details: 3" CLR against earth
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: CRSI standard bar data and ACI 318 provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide

field.text: Rebar callouts on details give count, size, location and extent. '(2) #5 T&B CONT' = two #5 bars at the top and two #5 bars at the bottom, continuous, for 4 bars total in the footing. '(1) #4 T&B' = one top, one bottom, 2 total. '(3) #4 BOT' = three bottom bars only. 'CONT' means run the bars the full length of the footing, lapping where needed and turning corners with corner bars. The number in parentheses is the bar count; the # number is the bar size in eighths of an inch (#5 = 5/8"). In the section view, bars running along the footing show as dots (circles) and bars running across show as lines; count the dots to confirm the callout.
field.title: Rebar callouts: (2) #5 T&B CONT and how many bars that is
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: '#4 @ 12" O.C.' = #4 bars spaced 12 inches center to center. 'E.W.' (each way) = a set of bars in both directions. 'E.F.' (each face) = a set at each face of a wall, so double the bars. 'T&B' = top and bottom layers. 'ALT' = alternate (for example alternate dowels hooked left and right, or alternate bar lengths). 'DWLS' or 'DOWELS' = short bars that stick out of one pour to tie into the next (footing to stem wall, slab to slab). 'HORIZ' and 'VERT' give direction in walls. Example: '#5 @ 16" O.C. VERT, #4 @ 12" O.C. HORIZ, E.F.' is two curtains of steel in a wall. The '@' number is spacing, never a bar count or length.
field.title: Bar spacing callouts: @ 12" O.C., E.W., E.F., ALT, DWLS
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: Bar size number = diameter in eighths of an inch for #3 to #8. #3: 0.375" dia, 0.376 lb/ft. #4: 0.500", 0.668 lb/ft. #5: 0.625", 1.043 lb/ft. #6: 0.750", 1.502 lb/ft. #7: 0.875", 2.044 lb/ft. #8: 1.000", 2.670 lb/ft. Stock lengths 20, 40 and 60 ft. Bars carry rolled-on marks (mill, size, steel type, grade). Use these to sanity-check a callout: #3 and #4 are common in residential slabs and footings, #5 in footings and grade beams, #6 and up in larger structural members. A callout read as '#14' on a house footing is probably '(1) #4'; check the parentheses and ask for a clearer photo.
field.title: Rebar sizes and weights for reading and takeoff (#3 to #8)
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: CRSI standard bar data and ACI 318 provisions as summarized in NICET reinforcing steel study guide

field.text: Dowels are bars cast in the footing that stick up into the stem wall, pier or next pour. Callouts read like '#4 DWLS @ 24" O.C. W/ STD HOOK, 18" MIN EMBED, LAP 24" W/ VERT'. Read: bar size, spacing, hook type at the bottom (a standard 90 degree hook is drawn as an L at the bottom of the bar), how far it goes into the footing (embedment), and how far it laps with the bars above. Commonly summarized ACI standard hook geometry: a 90 degree hook has a straight extension of 12 bar diameters past the bend; a 180 degree hook extends at least 4 bar diameters or 2-1/2", whichever is more. The detail governs. Dowels must be set before or during the pour, not pushed into stiff concrete unless the detail allows.
field.title: Dowels and hooks in footing details
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules; ACI 318 standard hook geometry as commonly summarized

field.text: Details often state laps and embedment as a multiple of bar diameter (db): '30 db', '40 BAR DIA', '48d'. Multiply by the bar diameter: #4 (0.5"): 30 db = 15", 40 db = 20", 48 db = 24". #5 (0.625"): 30 db = 18.75" (use 19"), 40 db = 25", 48 db = 30". #6 (0.75"): 30 db = 22.5", 40 db = 30", 48 db = 36". Round up, never down. ACI 318 development length depends on concrete strength, steel grade, bar location, cover and spacing, with a 12 inch minimum for straight bars and a minimum of 8 db or 6 inches for hooked bars; the engineer's number on the plan or general notes governs. Lap length is usually longer than development length.
field.title: Development length and laps in bar diameters: 30 db, 40 db, 48 db
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: ACI 318-19 development length provisions as summarized in Bentley RAM Concept documentation; Standard construction math (worked here)

field.text: On structural plans a shear wall is marked with a small symbol (often a triangle, hexagon, diamond or circle) holding a letter or number, placed on the wall line, with a length written beside it or a dimension or arrow lines showing the wall's extent, for example a triangle with 'A' and '8'-0"'. The letter is the shear wall TYPE, which keys to the shear wall schedule. The length is the length of that shear wall segment (the sheathed, nailed and held-down piece), NOT a building dimension, wall-to-wall dimension or room size. Holdowns are usually shown at each end of the segment. Do not add shear wall lengths into dimension strings, and do not read the triangle as a revision delta (deltas sit beside clouds) or as a window tag.
field.title: Shear wall marks on foundation and framing plans: symbol + letter + length
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules

field.text: The shear wall schedule (on the shear wall or framing sheet) has one row per wall type (A, B, C or 1, 2, 3). Typical columns: sheathing (for example 15/32" structural I plywood or 7/16" OSB, one side or both sides), edge nailing (for example 8d @ 4" O.C.) and field nailing (8d @ 12" O.C.), framing at panel edges (2x or 3x studs where nailing is tight), sill plate size and treatment, anchor bolt size and spacing in the sill (for example 5/8" dia @ 32" O.C.), top plate connection (A35 clips or nails), and allowable load (plf). Tighter nailing and closer anchor bolt spacing mean a stronger wall. The schedule's anchor bolt spacing overrides the general anchor bolt spacing along that shear wall length only.
field.title: Shear wall schedule: what each column means
field.topic: Plan reading: structural and foundation plans, footings, rebar, shear walls
field.source: Standard structural drawing practice (US); check the project's structural general notes and schedules
