Practical tip: when laying water main across a sewer, center a full stick on the crossing. Check your state and utility rules, which can differ.
field.title: Water and sewer separation: crossings and the 18 inch rule
field.topic: Installation: separation, cover, tracer wire, warning tape
field.source: Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities, 2014) 38.31, 38.32 for the common 10 ft / 18 in rule; the fallback details are one state's rule written on that approach: 12VAC5-590-1150, Separation of water mains and sanitary sewers

field.text: Minimum cover is the depth from finished grade to the top of the pipe. For water mains, cover is set mainly to keep the pipe below frost (the depth the ground freezes) and away from traffic loads; local utility specs set it, often around 3 ft in mild climates and 5 ft or more in cold northern areas. Frost depth varies widely by location and year; local building codes and utility standards publish design frost depths. For gravity sewers, cover is usually set by grade and service depth, with shallow pipe needing protection (stronger pipe, insulation or concrete cap) if below a minimum the specs set. For plastic storm pipe under traffic, makers set structural minimums (ADS: 1 ft for 4 to 48 inch corrugated HDPE, 2 ft for 54 and 60 inch). Check your project plans and specs; don't guess cover in the field.
field.title: Minimum cover and frost depth basics
field.topic: Installation: separation, cover, tracer wire, warning tape
field.source: Utility specification practice; ADS TN 2.01

field.text: PVC and HDPE pipe can't be found with a metal locator, so specs usually require tracer wire laid with the pipe so locators can trace it later. Typical spec practice: insulated solid copper or copper-clad steel wire (often 12 or 10 AWG, with HDPE or HMWPE insulation rated for direct burial; the insulation color often follows APWA colors: blue for water, green for sewer), taped to the top of the pipe or laid alongside it, brought up into valve boxes, hydrant areas, cleanouts or test stations, spliced only with waterproof direct-bury connectors, and grounded at ends per specs. Run a continuity test before acceptance; many utilities test with a locator and reject breaks. Don't wrap wire around the pipe. Requirements vary by utility; check your specs.
field.title: Tracer wire for nonmetallic pipe
field.topic: Installation: separation, cover, tracer wire, warning tape
field.source: Common municipal specification practice

field.text: Underground warning tape is laid in the trench above the pipe so a later excavator hits the tape before the pipe. Typical specs: tape in APWA color for the utility (blue water, green sewer, purple reclaimed, red electric, yellow gas, orange communications) printed with a caution message, laid flat about 12 to 24 inches below finished grade or a set distance above the pipe; detectable (metallic foil core) tape where the utility requires it. Electronic marker balls or disks (tuned to a utility-specific frequency) may be required at fittings, valves, service ends and bends for later locating. Record their locations on the as-builts. Exact depths and types vary by utility; check your specs.
field.title: Warning tape and marker balls
field.topic: Installation: separation, cover, tracer wire, warning tape
field.source: APWA uniform color code; common utility specification practice

field.text: Small water services (copper, PEX, HDPE tubing) and small sewer laterals need the same care as mainline pipe: no rocks against the pipe, uniform bedding, and compacted backfill. Common spec practice: sand or fine granular bedding and cover around copper or plastic tubing; a gooseneck or slack in copper service lines at the main to allow for settlement; sleeves where services pass through walls or under structures; and tracer wire on nonmetallic services if required. Curb stops and meter pits set to the grade shown in the utility's standard details. Sewer laterals usually need a minimum slope (commonly 1/4 inch per foot for 4 inch building sewers under plumbing codes, check local code and utility standards) and cleanouts as detailed.
field.title: Bedding and backfill for water services and small pipe
field.topic: Installation: separation, cover, tracer wire, warning tape
field.source: Plumbing code and utility standard details practice

field.text: Culvert installation steps (DOT and manufacturer practice): set line and grade so the inlet and outlet match the ditch flowlines (most culverts are set at or slightly below stream bed grade, with fish-passage rules where streams carry fish); prepare a uniform bedding (shaped for rigid pipe, loosened under the middle for flexible pipe); place pipe sections with bells upstream; joints as specified (bands for CMP, gaskets or sealant for concrete, gasketed bell and spigot for HDPE); haunch and backfill in equal lifts on both sides with compaction; provide at least the minimum cover before equipment crosses; build end treatments (headwalls, flared ends, riprap) per detail to prevent erosion and undermining. Long culverts may be cambered (set higher in the middle) so they settle to grade under high fills, if the design calls for it. Check your DOT standards.
field.title: Culvert installation basics
field.topic: Storm drainage, culverts and underdrains
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Culvert and storm outfall ends need protection against erosion and undermining. Headwalls (cast-in-place or precast concrete) hold the embankment and protect the pipe end; flared end sections (concrete or metal) fit the slope and are tied to the pipe. At outlets, riprap aprons or energy dissipators slow the water: riprap size, thickness and apron length come from the plans or DOT standard (typically based on outlet velocity and pipe size) and are placed over geotextile so soil doesn't wash out from under the stone. Toe walls or cutoff walls at the end of the apron prevent undercutting. Inspect after the first storms. Follow the plans and DOT standards.
field.title: Headwalls, end sections and outlet protection
field.topic: Storm drainage, culverts and underdrains
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Storm and sanitary sewers are built similarly but differ in key ways. Sanitary sewers carry sewage, so they must be watertight: gasketed joints, flexible manhole connectors, air and vacuum testing, CCTV, and separation from water mains. Storm sewers carry surface runoff: they often use larger pipe (RCP, corrugated HDPE or PP), may allow soil-tight joints where specs permit (many now require watertight), have inlets and catch basins with sumps, and outfall to streams or ponds with erosion protection. Storm grades are often steeper and less critical than flat sanitary grades, but low spots still hold sediment. Testing for storm may be CCTV or mandrel only, depending on the agency. Never connect storm to sanitary (it causes overflows), and vice versa. Check your specs.
field.title: Storm sewer versus sanitary sewer: field differences
field.topic: Storm drainage, culverts and underdrains
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Underdrains are perforated pipes in a stone trench that collect groundwater from under pavements, behind walls or in wet areas. Typical construction: a trench lined with geotextile (wrapped around the stone so fines don't clog it), a layer of clean drainage stone, perforated pipe (often corrugated HDPE or PVC with perforations), more stone, then the geotextile folded over before backfill. Perforations are usually placed down (holes at the bottom) so water enters from below, unless the maker or spec says otherwise. Outlets go to a structure or daylight with a rodent screen. Grade must be continuous to the outlet. Follow the spec detail for pipe type, stone gradation and fabric.
field.title: Underdrains and perforated pipe
field.topic: Storm drainage, culverts and underdrains
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Many sites now use underground stormwater detention: large pipe arrays (corrugated HDPE, CMP or concrete), arch chambers or precast vaults that store runoff and release it slowly through an outlet control structure (orifice or weir). Field points from manufacturer guides: build the foundation stone bed level and to grade, often over geotextile; install the units in the pattern on the shop drawing; wrap stone with fabric as detailed; place stone embedment evenly and in lifts so units don't shift; respect the maker's minimum cover before equipment crosses and the maximum cover limit; install inspection ports and the outlet structure exactly as detailed, since the orifice size controls release rate. Get the maker's installation guide and any required certification before starting.
field.title: Detention and underground storage systems
field.topic: Storm drainage, culverts and underdrains
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Precast concrete sewer manholes are made to ASTM C478. Parts from bottom up: base (a monolithic base with the first riser and pipe openings cast or cored in, or a flat base slab), riser sections (common inside diameters 48, 60, 72 and 96 inches; 48 inch is the usual minimum for sewer), a cone (eccentric, with the opening over the steps on one side, or concentric) or a flat top slab for shallow manholes, adjusting rings to bring the frame to grade, and the cast iron or ductile iron frame and cover. Section joints are sealed with preformed butyl mastic sealant (ASTM C990) or rubber gaskets (ASTM C443), often with an external joint wrap. Pipe connects through flexible connectors (ASTM C923 boots). Larger manhole diameters are needed for larger pipe or many connections; the plans and the manhole maker's opening charts govern. Check your local standard details.
field.title: Precast concrete manholes: parts and standards
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: NPCA / ASTM C478 precast manhole practice

field.text: The manhole base must sit level and on firm, uniform support so the structure doesn't settle or tilt and break the pipe connections. Common practice: excavate to the depth for the base plus a granular leveling course (commonly 6 to 12 inches of compacted crushed stone; check your standard detail), compact and fine-grade the stone level, set the base with the pipe openings oriented to the pipe lines (check the shop drawing for which opening is which and the invert elevations), and check level and elevation before setting risers. Over-excavate and replace soft soil like a pipe foundation. Heavy bases need a planned lift: get the base weight from the supplier and check the excavator lift chart. Set the downstream manhole base first so the pipe crew can lay upstream from it.
field.title: Manhole base: setting and bedding
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Setting precast riser sections: clean the joint surfaces; place the butyl mastic rope (ASTM C990) or the rubber gasket (ASTM C443) as the maker shows (butyl usually on the tongue or the shoulder, in one continuous piece with ends overlapped or butted per maker; warm it in cold weather so it compresses); lower the section straight down without dragging so the sealant isn't pushed off; let the weight of the section compress the joint. Line up steps vertically (if steps are used) and keep the cone opening over the steps and on the side the plans show. Check that the joint is closed evenly all around. Many specs then require an exterior joint wrap or grout on the inside joint. Plug lift holes with mortar or the supplied plugs. Vacuum test after assembly (ASTM C1244).
field.title: Manhole riser joints and setting sections
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: NPCA / ASTM C478 precast manhole practice

field.text: Pipes connect to precast manholes through flexible, watertight connectors to ASTM C923 (rubber boots cast into the wall, compression gaskets in cored holes, or similar). They let the pipe move slightly as the ground settles without cracking the manhole or leaking. Installation tips: core holes at the right elevation and angle for the pipe; clean the pipe and boot; center the pipe in the connector; tighten the stainless steel band clamp to the maker's torque; don't push the pipe so far into the manhole that it blocks the channel (trim flush with the inside wall, or as detailed); and keep the pipe supported outside the manhole with well-compacted bedding so it doesn't hang on the boot. Grouting pipes into holes without a connector is not allowed by many specs for sewers. Check your standard details.
field.title: Manhole pipe connections: boots and flexible connectors
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: ASTM C923 scope; common sewer specifications

field.text: Inside a sanitary manhole, the flow is carried through a formed channel (the invert) from each inlet pipe to the outlet, with a sloped bench (shelf) on each side. Common practice: channels formed of concrete or grout (or precast inverts supplied by the manhole maker), smooth and shaped as a half-pipe matching the pipe diameter, curved smoothly where the flow turns; channel depth commonly to at least the springline (half the pipe) and often to three-quarters or the full crown depth, per local standards; benches sloped toward the channel (commonly about 1 inch per foot or as detailed) so solids wash back into the flow. Set channel inverts to the plan invert-in and invert-out elevations. Rough channels catch debris and cause odor and blockages, and inspectors look at them closely. Check your standard detail for channel depth and bench slope.
field.title: Manhole invert channels and benches
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: A drop manhole is used when an incoming sewer is much higher than the manhole outlet, so the flow doesn't fall freely onto the bench and splash, erode concrete and release gases. Ten States Standards call for a drop pipe when a sewer enters a manhole at 24 inches or more above the manhole invert. Outside drop: the incoming pipe continues straight into the manhole wall (for cleaning access) and a tee drops vertically outside the manhole, entering near the bottom; the drop pipe is encased in concrete or well-supported. Inside drop: a drop bowl or pipe fastened to the inside wall; many agencies now allow these with a larger manhole diameter. Where the difference is under 24 inches, the invert channel is usually filleted to prevent solids from piling up. Follow your local standard detail.
field.title: Drop manholes
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), sewer chapter

field.text: Manhole frames and covers are typically gray cast iron or ductile iron, rated for highway traffic (commonly AASHTO H-20 or HS-20 or heavier) in roadways. Many standards call for a clear opening around 24 inches, with some agencies requiring larger openings (30 to 32 inches) for confined space entry and rescue; check your details. Adjusting rings (precast concrete, HDPE or rubber composite) bring the frame to grade; standards usually cap the total adjustment height (often around 12 inches; check yours) and require the rings to be sealed with butyl or mortar to keep groundwater out. Set the frame on a full bed of sealant or mortar, centered, and to the final pavement elevation and cross slope. Use the cover with the right lettering (SEWER, STORM) and pick holes as specified; watertight or bolted covers may be required in flood areas.
field.title: Manhole frames, covers and adjusting rings
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Manholes are placed at every change in pipe size, slope or direction, at pipe junctions, at the ends of lines, and at maximum spacing along straight runs. Ten States Standards set maximum spacing of 400 ft for sewers 15 inches and smaller and 500 ft for 18 to 30 inch sewers, with greater spacing allowed for larger pipe if cleaning equipment can handle it; many agencies set their own limits. Pipe between manholes is laid straight in line and grade in most sanitary specs, so cleaning and TV equipment can pass. Manholes are kept out of low spots where surface water ponds, or are given watertight covers. These are design rules; the field crew builds to the plans, but it helps to know why a manhole is where it is.
field.title: Manhole spacing and location
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (Ten States Standards), sewer chapter

field.text: Many manholes have steps cast or installed into the wall in a vertical line under the cover opening. Steps are typically polypropylene-encapsulated steel rebar, spaced evenly (many specs use 12 to 16 inches on center) and projecting a set distance from the wall. Some agencies have dropped steps entirely because they corrode and give a false sense of safety; workers then use portable ladders or a retrieval system. Never trust a step without testing it. Entry into a sewer manhole is usually a permit-required confined space entry under OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA (construction) or 1910.146 (general industry): atmospheric testing, ventilation, attendant, retrieval equipment and a permit. Check your company's confined space program and the app's permit tool before entry.
field.title: Manhole steps and access
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Common municipal standards; OSHA confined space standards

field.text: Catch basins and inlets collect surface water into the storm sewer. Types: curb inlets (opening in the curb face), grate inlets (in the gutter or a paved area), combination inlets, and yard or area drains. A catch basin has a sump below the outlet pipe to trap sediment; an inlet usually doesn't. Setting tips: set the frame and grate elevation to the gutter flowline or pavement grade shown on the plans, usually slightly below the surrounding pavement so water flows in; orient grates bike-safe (bars perpendicular to traffic) where required; make pipe connections watertight or grouted per specs; and protect inlets with sediment control (inlet protection) until the site is stabilized. Precast inlet boxes come from the supplier per the plan type number; cast-in-place inlets need forming and reinforcing per the detail. Check your DOT or city standard drawings.
field.title: Catch basins and storm inlets
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Cleanouts give access for rodding or jetting a sewer where a manhole isn't needed. Common uses: on building sewers and laterals at the property line, right-of-way or building wall, at changes in direction on laterals, and sometimes at the end of a short main if the agency allows. Typical construction: a wye fitting on the line with a riser pipe of the same size brought up to grade, a watertight cap or plug, and a cast iron frame and lid or box at grade in paved or traffic areas so the riser isn't crushed. Two-way cleanouts allow rodding in both directions. The local plumbing code and sewer utility standard details set cleanout spacing, size and location. Record each cleanout location for the as-builts.
field.title: Cleanouts on sewer lines
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Precast concrete vaults house water meters, pressure reducing valves, air release valves, backflow devices and other equipment. Installation tips: set on a compacted granular base to grade; orient the vault so the access hatch is over the equipment and the pipe penetrations line up; seal joints and penetrations (link-seal type modular seals or grout per specs); provide drainage (a sump or drain to daylight) if the detail calls for it; install ladders, steps or hatches per specs; and backfill evenly around the vault. Vaults in traffic areas need traffic-rated lids. Entry into a vault may be a confined space. Get the vault weight from the supplier for lift planning. Follow the approved shop drawings and utility standard details.
field.title: Precast vaults for meters, valves and air release
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: The low-pressure air test checks gravity sewer pipe (PVC, HDPE, PP and others) for leaks by plugging a section between manholes, pressurizing it with air and timing the pressure drop. It's covered by ASTM F1417 for plastic pipe (with similar methods for concrete, C924, and clay, C828) and Uni-Bell's UNI-B-6. Typical procedure (Berkeley County spec): plug both ends and any services; add air slowly to 4.0 psig above the average groundwater back pressure (never over 9 psig; a 9 psi relief valve is required); hold at least 2 minutes to stabilize; let pressure fall to 3.5 psig (above groundwater back pressure) and start timing; the section passes if the pressure drops less than 1.0 psig in the table time (or less than 0.5 psig in half the time). Use oil-free air, a 0 to 10 psi gauge readable to 0.1 psi. Never stand in front of plugs while the line is pressurized. Your specs govern.
field.title: Low-pressure air test for gravity sewer: what it is
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: Minimum time for a 1.0 psig drop (Q = 0.0015), from the UNI-B-6/F1417 table as published in Berkeley County's spec. Each line: diameter, minimum time (min:sec), length at which the minimum time applies, and time for longer lengths (seconds, L in feet). 4 inch: 3:46, up to 597 ft, 0.380 L. 6 inch: 5:40, 398 ft, 0.854 L. 8 inch: 7:34, 298 ft, 1.520 L. 10 inch: 9:26, 239 ft, 2.374 L. 12 inch: 11:20, 199 ft, 3.418 L. 15 inch: 14:10, 159 ft, 5.342 L. 18 inch: 17:00, 133 ft, 7.692 L. 21 inch: 19:50, 114 ft, 10.470 L. 24 inch: 22:40, 99 ft, 13.674 L. 27 inch: 25:30, 88 ft, 17.306 L. 30 inch: 28:20, 80 ft, 21.366 L. 36 inch: 34:00, 66 ft, 30.768 L. Example: 8 inch, 350 ft: 1.520 x 350 = 532 seconds = 8:52. For a 0.5 psig drop, use half these times. Check your spec, which may use a different table.
field.title: Low-pressure air test: time table for a 1.0 psi drop
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: Ready values for a 1.0 psig drop from the UNI-B-6/F1417 table (Berkeley County spec), by test length 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450 ft. 6 inch: 5:40 through 350 ft, 5:42 at 400, 6:24 at 450. 8 inch: 7:34 through 250 ft, 7:36 at 300, 8:52 at 350, 10:08 at 400, 11:24 at 450. 10 inch: 9:26 through 200 ft, 9:53 at 250, 11:52 at 300, 13:51 at 350, 15:49 at 400, 17:48 at 450. 12 inch: 11:20 at 100 and 150, 11:24 at 200, 14:15 at 250, 17:05 at 300, 19:56 at 350, 22:47 at 400, 25:38 at 450. 15 inch: 14:10 at 100 and 150, 17:48 at 200, 22:15 at 250, 26:42 at 300, 31:09 at 350, 35:36 at 400, 40:04 at 450. 18 inch: 17:00 at 100, 19:13 at 150, 25:38 at 200, 32:03 at 250, 38:27 at 300. Times are minutes:seconds; the line passes if the drop is under 1.0 psig in at least that time.
field.title: Low-pressure air test: worked lengths for 8 to 15 inch
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: The air test times come from the formula T = 0.085 x D x K / Q, where T is the shortest time in seconds for a 1.0 psig drop, D is nominal diameter in inches, K = 0.000419 x D x L but not less than 1.0, L is test length in feet, and Q = 0.0015 cubic ft per minute per square ft of internal pipe surface (Berkeley County spec, per UNI-B-6). For a 0.5 psig drop, use half of T. Groundwater: if groundwater stands above the pipe, raise the test pressure by the groundwater back pressure. Common method: back pressure (psi) = height of water above the pipe invert or crown (per your spec, in feet) divided by 2.31 (because 1 psi = 2.31 ft of water); with 4.6 ft of water above the pipe, add 2.0 psi, so start at 6.0 psig and time from 5.5. Never exceed the spec's maximum pressure. Check your spec for how groundwater height is measured.
field.title: Low-pressure air test: formula and groundwater adjustment
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: When a sewer section fails the air test, common causes are: a leaking plug (check plugs first with soapy water around the seal; re-seat or replace), an unplugged service or wye, a leaking joint (gasket rolled, not homed, dirt in joint), a cracked pipe or fitting, a bad connection at the manhole boot, or temperature change in the pipe during the test (warm air cooling drops pressure). Steps: let the air stabilize longer before timing; re-test; if it still fails, pull the plug and move it to isolate shorter sections, or use a joint tester or CCTV to find the leak; repair and retest. Specs generally say the contractor repairs and retests until the section passes. Safety: release pressure fully before removing any plug, and keep people out of the manhole and in-line with plugs while pressurized; plugs can blow out with deadly force.
field.title: Low-pressure air test: troubleshooting a failure
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Common municipal specification practice

field.text: Flexible gravity pipe (PVC, HDPE, PP) is tested for deflection by pulling a mandrel (a rigid 'go/no-go' gauge with fins or a proving ring) through each run. Berkeley County's spec, typical of many: mandrel diameter 95% of the pipe's inside diameter (5% deflection limit); pulled by hand, no mechanical pulling devices; initial test after final backfill and compaction have been in place at least 30 days and before the line is put in service; a final test in the 12th month before the warranty expires; deflection test done before the air test and CCTV. Mandrel sizes listed in that spec: SDR 26 D3034 sewer pipe at 5%: 14 inch 12.40, 16 inch 14.09, 18 inch 15.78, 24 inch 20.84 inches. Where the mandrel won't pass, dig up and re-embed or replace the pipe, then retest. ASTM D2321 discusses a 7.5% long-term design limit; most municipal acceptance tests use 5%. Check your specs.
field.title: Mandrel deflection test for flexible sewer pipe
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: The mandrel diameter for a 5% deflection test is 95% of the pipe's base inside diameter (for 7.5% it would be 92.5%). Base ID is usually computed from the pipe standard's average OD minus twice the minimum wall (with allowances per the standard), so mandrel sizes are specific to pipe type and SDR. Examples from Berkeley County's spec (5%): C900 DR 18: 6 inch 5.64, 8 inch 7.37, 10 inch 9.01, 12 inch 10.70 inches. SDR 26 D3034 sewer: 18 inch 15.78, 20 inch 17.47, 24 inch 20.84. Uni-Bell and pipe makers publish mandrel tables for SDR 35 and other pipe. Use a mandrel built for the exact pipe (many are adjustable with pins or interchangeable fins), have the inspector check its dimensions with a proving ring, and pull it through every run. Check your spec for which table to use.
field.title: Mandrel sizing: how to figure a mandrel diameter
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: Precast concrete manholes are commonly tested by vacuum per ASTM C1244. Procedure (City of Corpus Christi spec): plug all pipes into the manhole with pneumatic plugs (sealing length at least the pipe diameter) and brace them; place the test head at the top per the maker's instructions; draw a vacuum of 10 inches of mercury (Hg); close the valve and shut off the pump; time how long the vacuum takes to drop from 10 to 9 inches Hg; the manhole passes if the time meets or exceeds the table value for its diameter and depth. Testing may be done before or after backfill, but final acceptance tests the finished structure including adjusting rings and frame. If it fails, repair (usually joint, lift hole or boot) and retest until it passes. Your local spec governs timing and whether backfill must be in place.
field.title: Vacuum test of sewer manholes (ASTM C1244)
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: City of Corpus Christi spec 027203, Vacuum Testing of Wastewater Manholes (ASTM C1244 table)

field.text: Minimum test times in seconds for the vacuum to drop from 10 to 9 inches Hg, by depth and manhole diameter, as published in Corpus Christi's spec per ASTM C1244. Format: depth: 42 inch / 48 inch / 54 inch / 60 inch / 72 inch. 8 ft: 17 / 20 / 23 / 26 / 33. 10 ft: 21 / 25 / 29 / 33 / 41. 12 ft: 25 / 30 / 35 / 39 / 49. 14 ft: 30 / 35 / 41 / 46 / 57. 16 ft: 34 / 40 / 46 / 52 / 67. 18 ft: 38 / 45 / 52 / 59 / 73. 20 ft: 42 / 50 / 53 / 65 / 81. 22 ft: 46 / 55 / 64 / 72 / 89. 24 ft: 51 / 59 / 64 / 78 / 97. 26 ft: 55 / 64 / 75 / 85 / 105. 28 ft: 59 / 69 / 81 / 91 / 113. 30 ft: 68 / 74 / 87 / 98 / 121. A few entries in this published table (for example 54 inch at 20 and 24 ft) don't follow the pattern of neighboring values; check against your spec's copy of ASTM C1244 before relying on those.
field.title: Manhole vacuum test time table (ASTM C1244)
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: City of Corpus Christi spec 027203, Vacuum Testing of Wastewater Manholes (ASTM C1244 table)

field.text: Before air testing became common, sewers were tested by measuring water leaking in (infiltration, when groundwater is above the pipe) or out (exfiltration, by filling the pipe and manhole with water to a set head). Many specs still allow or require these tests. Berkeley County's limit is a maximum leakage of 200 gallons per inch of pipe diameter per mile per day, in or out; the Ten States Standards use the same 200 gallon figure as a maximum. Example: 1,000 ft of 8 inch pipe: 200 x 8 x (1,000 / 5,280) = about 303 gallons per day allowed. Exfiltration tests typically fill the upper manhole to a set height above the pipe crown or groundwater (commonly 2 ft or more, check your spec) and measure the drop over a set time. Visible leaks must be fixed even if under the allowance in many specs.
field.title: Infiltration and exfiltration testing
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: Most agencies require a closed-circuit TV (CCTV) inspection of new sewers before acceptance, usually after the line is cleaned and after air and deflection testing (Berkeley County's sequence: deflection, then air test, then CCTV). Common spec items: flush and clean the line first; run water down the line just before televising so sags show as ponded water; move the camera at a limited speed (many specs cap it around 30 ft per minute) and stop at every joint, service and defect; record footage, distance counter and observations; code defects using NASSCO's PACP system; and deliver video and reports in the agency's format. Defects that typically need repair: cracks, broken pipe, offset or open joints, protruding services, debris, infiltration, and sags deeper than the spec allows. Check your spec for camera requirements, speed and sag limits.
field.title: CCTV inspection of new sewers
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Common municipal specs; NASSCO PACP

field.text: A typical new sanitary sewer acceptance sequence (varies by agency): pipe laid and backfilled, manholes complete with channels, frames set; lines cleaned; deflection (mandrel) test, often no sooner than 30 days after final backfill; low-pressure air test of each run; vacuum test of each manhole (after frames and rings are set, for final acceptance); CCTV inspection; punch list repairs and retests; then acceptance and start of the warranty period, often with a final deflection test or CCTV near the end of the warranty (Berkeley County requires a final mandrel test in the 12th month). Berkeley County also requires retesting if a line passes but isn't permitted to operate within a year. Schedule the 30-day wait in your plan so testing doesn't delay paving or closeout. Check your project's spec for order and timing.
field.title: Testing order and timing for new sewer lines
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: Berkeley County (SC) Water & Sanitation spec 02731, Sanitary Gravity Sewer Line Testing (air test tables per UNI-B-6 / ASTM F1417)

field.text: For large-diameter gravity pipe (commonly 27 or 30 inch and up, where testing the whole run with air takes very long), many specs allow or require testing individual joints instead. A joint tester is an inflatable packer device placed across one joint from inside the pipe; it isolates the joint, which is pressurized with air or water, and the pressure drop is timed. For concrete pipe, ASTM C1103 covers joint acceptance testing; plastic pipe makers and specs have similar methods. Typical requirements give a test pressure and an allowable pressure drop over a set time per joint (check your spec; values vary). Joint testing also helps find the leaking joint after a failed run air test. Confined space entry rules apply when people enter the pipe to place testers.
field.title: Joint testing for large-diameter sewer pipe
field.topic: Testing: gravity sewer and manholes
field.source: ASTM C1103 scope; common spec practice

field.text: Water mains are pressure tested with water after laying and restraint. Test pressure rules differ by source, so follow your spec. AWWA C600 (per U.S. Pipe): not less than 1.25 times working pressure at the highest point of the test section and not less than 1.5 times working pressure at the lowest point. American Water's spec: for working pressure 200 psi or less, at least 100 psi above normal operating pressure; above 200 psi, 1.5 times operating pressure; never above the rating of pipe and appurtenances; measured at the low point, with a separate test if the high point is below 85% of test pressure. Spotsylvania County: 150 psi or 1.5 times working pressure, whichever is greater, at the high point. All three hold test pressure at least 2 hours (American Water and others allow plus or minus 5 psi). Never exceed the rating of closed valves in the test section.
field.title: Hydrostatic test for water mains: test pressure (sources differ)
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C600 via U.S. Pipe; American Water; Spotsylvania County (compared)

field.text: The allowable make-up water (testing allowance) during a water main hydrostatic test under AWWA C600, and used for PVC under C605 by many specs, is: L = S x D x square root of P / 148,000, where L is allowable leakage in gallons per hour, S is length of pipe tested in feet, D is nominal pipe diameter in inches, and P is average test pressure in psi. For mixed sizes, compute each size and add. Multiply by the test duration in hours for the total allowed. Worked example (Spotsylvania County): 1,000 ft of 12 inch at 150 psi = 1,000 x 12 x 12.25 / 148,000 = 0.993 gallon per hour, or 1.986 gallons for a 2-hour test. Some older specs use a formula based on number of joints; use the one in your spec. U.S. Pipe stresses this is a testing allowance, not permission to leak.
field.title: Hydrostatic test: allowable leakage formula
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: Spotsylvania County (VA) Utilities, Pressure Testing of New Mains

field.text: Allowable make-up water from L = S x D x square root of P / 148,000, per 1,000 ft of pipe, in gallons per hour (multiply by 2 for a 2-hour test). At 150 psi: 4 inch 0.33; 6 inch 0.50; 8 inch 0.66; 10 inch 0.83; 12 inch 0.99; 16 inch 1.32; 24 inch 1.99. At 200 psi: 4 inch 0.38; 6 inch 0.57; 8 inch 0.76; 10 inch 0.96; 12 inch 1.15; 16 inch 1.53; 24 inch 2.29. At 100 psi: 6 inch 0.41; 8 inch 0.54; 12 inch 0.81. Example: 2,400 ft of 8 inch at 150 psi, 2-hour test: 0.66 x 2.4 x 2 = about 3.2 gallons allowed. Values computed from the formula used in AWWA C600 and many C605-based specs; check your spec's formula and test pressure.
field.title: Hydrostatic test: allowable leakage per 1,000 ft
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: Computed from the AWWA C600 allowance formula (as given in American Water and Spotsylvania specs)

field.text: Trapped air is the most common reason water main tests fail or give confusing results. Common practice (American Water and Spotsylvania specs): fill each section slowly, expelling all air through hydrants, air valves or corporation stops at high points; restrain all caps and plugs before filling; let the line stand full (American Water requires at least 24 hours before testing; this also lets cement lining absorb water); tap high points to vent air if needed, then plug the taps; close valves between the existing system and the test section; pressurize with a hand or motor pump; add only enough water to hold pressure within 5 psi of test pressure, measuring the make-up water with a meter or calibrated container. Fill using a hydrant meter or approved source with backflow protection. Don't operate existing system valves unless the utility directs.
field.title: Hydrostatic test: filling and getting the air out
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: American Water spec 33 01 10.13, Pressure Leakage Tests (AWWA C600)

field.text: If a water main won't hold pressure: re-bleed air at high points and hydrants (air compresses and slowly dissolves, so pressure keeps sagging); check the test pump, hoses, gauge and test fittings for leaks; check that blow-off and hydrant valves are fully closed and not passing; walk the line looking for wet spots; check thrust blocks and restraints for movement; isolate shorter sections with valves to narrow the location. Temperature changes during the test also move pressure. Use a calibrated gauge (Spotsylvania requires a calibrated gauge; American Water wants gauges in no more than 5 psi increments) placed at a known elevation. Thrust blocks must be cured first (American Water: at least 5 days). Tapping sleeves get their own 15-minute test before tapping. Record start and end pressure, times, make-up water and gauge location on the test report.
field.title: Hydrostatic test: tips and troubleshooting
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: American Water spec 33 01 10.13, Pressure Leakage Tests (AWWA C600)

field.text: New water mains are disinfected under AWWA C651 before going into service. Three common methods (summary of C651): Tablet method: calcium hypochlorite tablets attached to the inside top of each pipe section during laying, for an average dose of about 25 mg/L held about 24 hours; fill slowly (no more than about 1 ft per second) so tablets don't wash away; not suitable where the line must be flushed first. Continuous feed: water entering the main carries at least 25 mg/L free chlorine; hold at least 24 hours; at the end, free chlorine must be at least 10 mg/L throughout the main (checked at the end and at branches). Slug method: a slug of at least 100 mg/L free chlorine passed through so every part of the pipe sees it for at least 3 hours; if the residual drops below 100 mg/L, stop and re-dose. Your utility's spec chooses the method.
field.title: Disinfection of new water mains: AWWA C651 methods
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

field.text: To figure how much chlorine to add for a target dose: pounds of chlorine = gallons of water x 8.34 x dose (mg/L) / 1,000,000. Pipe volume (gallons per foot) is about: 4 inch 0.65; 6 inch 1.47; 8 inch 2.61; 10 inch 4.08; 12 inch 5.87; 16 inch 10.4. Example from the C651 study guide: 12 inch, 1,800 ft, 25 mg/L: 5.87 x 1,800 = 10,566 gallons; 10,566 x 8.34 x 25 / 1,000,000 = 2.20 lb of available chlorine; with 12.5% sodium hypochlorite at 10.0 lb per gallon (1.25 lb chlorine per gallon), that's about 1.76 gallons. Per 100 ft at 25 mg/L: 6 inch about 0.031 lb; 8 inch 0.054 lb; 12 inch 0.122 lb. For calcium hypochlorite (HTH, about 65% available chlorine) divide pounds of chlorine by 0.65. Math is exact; product strength varies, so read the label.
field.title: Disinfection: chlorine dose calculation
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

field.text: New mains are flushed before disinfection (except with the tablet method) to remove dirt, and after disinfection to remove heavily chlorinated water. AWWA C651-14 (Sec. 4.4.2) calls for flushing at 3.0 ft per second or more; the 2005 edition said about 2.5 ft per second, and specs written on it still say that. Flow needed for 3.0 ft per second (computed from pipe area): 4 inch about 120 gpm; 6 inch about 265 gpm; 8 inch about 470 gpm; 10 inch about 735 gpm; 12 inch about 1,060 gpm; 16 inch about 1,880 gpm (at 2.5 ft per second, 8 inch is about 390 gpm). Your spec or the water agency governs. A single 2-1/2 inch hydrant outlet may not deliver enough for larger mains, so use more outlets or the pumper nozzle. Flush until the water runs clear and, after disinfection, until the chlorine residual is no higher than the normal distribution system level. Control discharge to prevent erosion and dechlorinate per permit. Flow values are computed from area times velocity.
field.title: Disinfection: flushing velocity and flow
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

field.text: Heavily chlorinated flush water can kill fish and is regulated, so it usually must be dechlorinated before discharge to storm drains, ditches or streams (check your state and stormwater permit). C651 lists approximate amounts of neutralizing chemical per mg/L of chlorine residual (per pound basis): sulfur dioxide 1.0; sodium bisulfite about 1.5; sodium sulfite about 1.8; sodium thiosulfate about 1.5 to 2.0. Field crews often use dechlorination diffusers with tablets (sodium sulfite or ascorbic acid) on hydrant outlets. Test the discharge with a chlorine test kit to confirm no detectable chlorine before it leaves the site. Also control erosion where flush water lands. Discharging to the sanitary sewer may need the sewer utility's permission.
field.title: Disinfection: dechlorination before discharge
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

field.text: After disinfection and final flushing, new mains must pass bacteriological tests before going into service. Common C651 practice (per the study guide): take samples every 1,200 ft of new main, plus one at the end of the line and one at each branch; require two consecutive sets of acceptable samples; the 2005 edition separates the sets by 24 hours, and later editions allow other options (such as a set after a standing period followed by a second set), so check which edition your spec cites. Bottles must contain sodium thiosulfate (to neutralize chlorine) and come from a certified lab; samples go to a state-certified lab within the holding time. Don't take samples from hydrants or hoses unless the spec allows; use a sampling tap or corporation stop with a gooseneck. If samples fail (coliform present), re-flush, re-chlorinate if needed and resample.
field.title: Disinfection: bacteriological (bac-T) sampling
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

field.text: For tie-ins and repairs where the full C651 procedure isn't practical, C651 calls for swabbing or spraying the interior of pipe and fittings with a 1 to 5 percent hypochlorite solution before installation, and flushing after. Preventive practice during construction: keep pipe ends capped, keep trench water out of the pipe, and swab joints and gaskets with hypochlorite if they get dirty. The study guide cites a 20 psi pressure drop example as a trigger for treating water as potentially contaminated after a break (utilities set their own rules). After a repair or cut-in, the utility may require bac-T samples. Wear eye protection and gloves when handling hypochlorite, and never mix it with acids or ammonia.
field.title: Disinfection: connections, repairs and swabbing
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

field.text: The tablet method puts calcium hypochlorite tablets inside the main during laying, so it has extra cautions. Attach tablets to the inside top of each section with an approved adhesive (NSF-61 for potable water) so they stay at the top; place tablets in hydrants and branches too; keep the pipe clean and dry until filled, because the method doesn't allow pre-flushing; fill slowly (no more than about 1 ft per second per the C651 summary) so tablets aren't washed to the end; hold the water about 24 hours (longer in cold water per C651) and check the residual. Don't use the tablet method if the pipe got dirty or if trench water entered; switch to continuous feed after flushing. Never use tablets with solvent-welded or screwed joints where the adhesive or chlorine could cause problems, or where the spec prohibits it. Tablet counts per section come from the C651 table for your edition.
field.title: Disinfection: tablet method cautions
field.topic: Testing: water main pressure test and disinfection
field.source: AWWA C651 summary, Open Exam Prep water operator study guide

field.text: In a pressurized water main, water pushes outward at every place the flow changes direction or stops: bends, tees, dead ends, plugs, reducers and closed valves. That push (thrust) can pull joints apart if nothing resists it. Two ways to resist: concrete thrust blocks that transfer the force to undisturbed soil, or restrained joints that tie a length of pipe together so soil friction and bearing along the pipe resists the force. Thrust grows with pressure and with pipe size squared. Thrust must hold during the hydrostatic test, which is the highest pressure the line usually sees, so blocking and restraint must be designed for the full test pressure (Oregon DOT's standard requires blocking 'adequate to withstand full test pressure'). The engineer designs the restraint; the crew builds it as shown.
field.title: Thrust: why fittings need blocking or restraint
field.topic: Water: thrust blocks and restrained joints
field.source: Oregon DOT standard drawing RD250, thrust blocks

field.text: Standard thrust formulas (as given in VCMWD's design standard, units pounds, psi and inches): dead ends, tees (on the branch) and closed in-line valves: T = 0.25 x pi x P x d squared, where P is internal pressure in psi and d the pipe outside diameter in inches. Bends: T = 0.50 x pi x P x d squared x sin(angle / 2). Reducers: T = 0.25 x pi x P x (D squared - d squared). Example: 8 inch C900 at 150 psi test pressure, OD 9.05 inches: dead-end thrust = 0.785 x 150 x 81.9 = about 9,650 lb. For a 90 degree bend, multiply the dead-end value by 1.414 (about 13,600 lb); 45 degree x 0.765; 22.5 degree x 0.390; 11.25 degree x 0.196. Use the actual test pressure and pipe OD from the maker. The design engineer's calculation governs.
field.title: Thrust force formulas
field.topic: Water: thrust blocks and restrained joints
field.source: Vista Irrigation/VCMWD water design standard 5.2, Thrust Restraint and Anchor Blocks

field.text: To size a thrust block's bearing face: required bearing area (square ft) = thrust (lb) / allowable soil bearing (lb per square ft), often multiplied by a safety factor (VCMWD uses 1.5). Oregon DOT's worked example: a 14 inch tee has 37,320 lb thrust at 250 psi; at 150 psi design pressure that's 37,320 x 150 / 250 = 22,392 lb; in sand at 2,000 psf, area = 22,392 / 2,000 = about 11.2 square ft. VCMWD adds: make the bearing face as close to square as field conditions allow, key at least 12 inches into undisturbed soil, and round up to the next half square foot. The bearing face must be against undisturbed soil, not backfill. When block height is more than half the depth to its bottom, passive soil pressure methods are used. Check the plans and the utility's thrust block table first.
field.title: Thrust block bearing area method
field.topic: Water: thrust blocks and restrained joints
field.source: Oregon DOT standard drawing RD250, thrust blocks

field.text: Thrust block tables use an assumed allowable soil bearing value when no geotechnical data is available, and published tables differ, so use your utility's table. Oregon DOT RD250 (psf): hard shale 10,000; sand and gravel cemented with clay 4,000; sand and gravel 3,000; sand 2,000; soft clay 1,000; muck, peat 0. VCMWD Table 5.2.2 (psf): granite 10,000; hard shale 5,000; cemented sandy gravel 4,000; sandy gravel 2,000; decomposed granite 1,500; fine sand 1,000; soft clay 500; muck, peat 0. Note the disagreement: soft clay is 1,000 psf in one and 500 in the other; hard shale 10,000 versus 5,000. Using the lower value gives a bigger, safer block. In muck or peat, a thrust block won't work: remove and replace with ballast or use restrained joints per an engineer's design. When in doubt, ask the engineer, and use geotechnical values if provided.
field.title: Soil bearing values for thrust blocks (tables differ)
field.topic: Water: thrust blocks and restrained joints
field.source: Oregon DOT RD250 and VCMWD Standard 5.2 (compared)

field.text: Field rules for pouring thrust blocks (from Oregon DOT RD250 notes and common specs): pour against undisturbed earth on the bearing side; use the concrete strength specified (commercial grade per ODOT; many utilities specify a minimum compressive strength); wrap pipe and fittings with polyethylene film where they touch concrete (ODOT says two layers) so the fitting can be removed later; keep concrete clear of joints, bolts and glands so they can be reached; form the sides so concrete doesn't spill around the pipe; place the block so its bearing face is centered on the line of thrust; and let concrete cure before pressure testing (American Water's spec requires thrust blocking cured at least 5 days before the hydrostatic test; others use different times or high-early concrete). Don't backfill against fresh blocks with heavy compaction. Follow the standard detail.
field.title: Thrust block construction tips
field.topic: Water: thrust blocks and restrained joints
field.source: Oregon DOT RD250; American Water spec 33 01 10.13

field.text: Where a water main bends downward and then back up (going under a culvert or utility), the upward thrust at the bottom bends (upward-pointing thrust) and the downward thrust at the top bends need anchoring. For bends whose thrust pushes upward, a gravity anchor block uses concrete weight to hold the fitting down. VCMWD's method: required block volume = thrust / (concrete unit weight, about 140 lb per cubic ft x a safety factor), using buoyant weight if groundwater can rise above the block, with fittings tied into the block by reinforcing rods (minimum two #4 bars in their standard). Many utilities now prefer restrained joints for vertical offsets. Build exactly what the plans or standard detail show; vertical anchors are a common spot for failures during testing.
field.title: Vertical bends and anchor (gravity) blocks
field.topic: Water: thrust blocks and restrained joints
field.source: Vista Irrigation/VCMWD water design standard 5.2, Thrust Restraint and Anchor Blocks

field.text: When the plans show restrained joints instead of thrust blocks, they give a restrained length on each side of each fitting (for example '36 ft each side of 45 degree bend'). Field rules: restrain every joint within that length, measured from the fitting, on every leg; include the fitting's own joints; use the restraint type on the approved submittal (MJ wedge-action glands, restrained gasket, restrained push-on joint), rated for the pipe material (PVC versus DI); tighten wedge bolts until the twist-off heads break off if that's the design; don't deflect restrained joints beyond the maker's (usually lower) limit; and if a tie-in or extra fitting is added in the field, ask the engineer for new lengths. Restrained length increases with test pressure, larger pipe, shallower cover, weaker soil and polywrap. VCMWD notes restraint systems should not be combined with thrust blocks unless designed together.
field.title: Restrained joint lengths: field rules
field.topic: Water: thrust blocks and restrained joints
field.source: Vista Irrigation/VCMWD water design standard 5.2, Thrust Restraint and Anchor Blocks

field.text: The MUTCD divides a temporary traffic control zone into four parts. Advance warning area: signs telling drivers what's ahead (ROAD WORK AHEAD, ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD, FLAGGER AHEAD). Transition area: tapers of cones or drums that move traffic out of its normal path. Activity area: the buffer space (empty space for errant vehicles, no equipment or materials) and the work space where the crew works, plus any traffic space. Termination area: a short downstream taper and END ROAD WORK sign returning traffic to normal. Typical layouts for common situations (shoulder work, lane closures, flagging on two-lane roads) are in MUTCD Part 6 typical applications and state DOT standard drawings. Most agencies require an approved traffic control plan for work in the right of way. Note: FHWA issued the MUTCD 11th edition in December 2023; section and table numbers changed from the 2009 edition.
field.title: Work zone layout: the four areas
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: FHWA Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, Part 6

field.text: MUTCD taper lengths are based on speed and lateral shift. For speeds of 40 mph or less: L = W x S squared / 60. For 45 mph or more: L = W x S. L is taper length in feet, W is the width of offset (lane shift) in feet, S is the posted speed limit, off-peak 85th percentile speed, or expected operating speed in mph. Examples: 12 ft lane closure at 35 mph: L = 12 x 35 x 35 / 60 = 245 ft. At 55 mph: L = 12 x 55 = 660 ft. At 30 mph: 12 x 900 / 60 = 180 ft. The study guide notes the MUTCD doesn't directly address 41 to 44 mph; many agencies use the higher-speed formula there as policy. Check state DOT standards, which may require longer tapers.
field.title: Taper length formulas
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: MUTCD taper formulas, summarized by IMSA work zone study guide

field.text: Different tapers use different fractions of L (from the formulas L = WS squared / 60 or L = WS). Merging taper (closing a lane on a multilane road): at least L. Shifting taper (moving traffic sideways without closing a lane): at least 1/2 L. Shoulder taper: at least 1/3 L. One-lane, two-way traffic taper (flagger or signal controlled on a two-lane road): 50 ft minimum to 100 ft maximum, not based on L. Downstream (termination) taper: 50 ft minimum to 100 ft maximum (optional; devices about 20 ft apart). When two lanes are closed in succession on a multilane road, a tangent of about 2L separates the two merging tapers. Check your state DOT standard drawings.
field.title: Taper types: merging, shifting, shoulder, flagger and downstream
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: MUTCD taper formulas, summarized by IMSA work zone study guide

field.text: Table 6B-1 gives the recommended minimum spacing for a three-sign series. A is from the taper or point of restriction back to the first sign, B is from the first sign to the second, C is from the second to the third. Urban low speed: 100 ft, 100 ft, 100 ft. Urban high speed: 350, 350, 350 ft. Rural: 500, 500, 500 ft. Expressway or freeway: 1,000 ft, 1,500 ft and 2,640 ft. The national table does not put mph numbers on low speed and high speed; the footnote says the road agency decides the speed category, and several state manuals do it by speed. Section 6B.04 adds rules of thumb: on urban streets the sign nearest the work should be about 4 to 8 times the speed limit in feet (use the high end for higher speeds); on rural highways the first sign should be 8 to 12 times the speed limit in feet, and a multi-sign series should cover 1,500 ft or more; on freeways signing may reach half a mile or more; a single sign on a low-speed residential street may be as close as 100 ft. Lengthen them for hills, curves and queues, and sign any side street that enters inside the series. ROAD WORK AHEAD should be the first sign a driver sees. The approved plan governs.
field.title: Advance warning sign spacing: city street, rural road, freeway (Table 6B-1, A B C)
field.topic: Traffic control: advance warning signs
field.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Table 6B-1 and footnotes; Section 6B.04 paras. 3-8; Sections 6H.02, 6H.03

field.text: The longitudinal buffer space and the distance from the flagger station to the work space are based on stopping sight distance. MUTCD table (2003 Chapter 6E values for flagger stations, also used for buffer space): 20 mph, 115 ft; 25 mph, 155 ft; 30 mph, 200 ft; 35 mph, 250 ft; 40 mph, 305 ft; 45 mph, 360 ft; 50 mph, 425 ft; 55 mph, 495 ft; 60 mph, 570 ft; 65 mph, 645 ft; 70 mph, 730 ft; 75 mph, 820 ft. Use the posted off-peak speed, the 85th percentile speed before work starts, or the expected operating speed; increase for downgrades. Flagger stations must be preceded by advance warning signs and lighted at night, except in emergencies. Keep the buffer empty: no trucks, materials or spoil in it. Check your edition and state standards.
field.title: Buffer space and flagger station distance
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: FHWA MUTCD Part 6, Chapter 6E Flagger Control (2003 edition text)

field.text: Per MUTCD flagger guidance: the STOP/SLOW paddle is the preferred hand device over flags. The paddle is octagonal on a rigid handle, retroreflective for night, STOP face red with white letters and SLOW face orange with black letters; the 2003 edition required at least 18 inches wide with 6 inch letters, and many states now require 24 inch paddles, so check your state. Flags (emergency use) at least 24 inches square, red, on a staff about 36 inches long. High-visibility apparel: ANSI/ISEA 107 Class 2 day and night as a minimum, with Class 3 recommended at night; fluorescent orange-red or yellow-green, retroreflective material visible at least 1,000 ft. Many states require flagger training or certification (for example ATSSA or state DOT courses). Flaggers should stand on the shoulder, visible, never in the open lane, with an escape route planned.
field.title: Flaggers: equipment and apparel
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: FHWA MUTCD Part 6, Chapter 6E Flagger Control (2003 edition text)

field.text: MUTCD flagger signals with a STOP/SLOW paddle: To stop traffic: face road users, aim the STOP face toward them with the arm extended horizontally away from the body, and raise the free arm with palm toward approaching traffic. To let traffic proceed: aim the SLOW face toward stopped traffic and motion with the free hand for drivers to go. To alert or slow traffic: aim the SLOW face toward traffic; optionally move the free hand up and down, palm down. With a flag (emergencies): to stop, extend the staff horizontally across the lane with the flag hanging below and raise the free palm; to proceed, stand parallel to traffic with the flag out of view and motion with the free hand (never signal 'go' with the flag); to slow, sweep the flag from shoulder level down, without raising the arm above horizontal. Coordinate flaggers at each end with radios or a pilot car.
field.title: Flaggers: hand signals
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: FHWA MUTCD Part 6, Chapter 6E Flagger Control (2003 edition text)

field.text: Channelizing devices (cones, tubular markers, drums, barricades) guide traffic through work zones. MUTCD rules widely followed: cones at least 18 inches tall for daytime low-speed use, and at least 28 inches tall on freeways and high-speed roads and at night, with retroreflective bands at night; drums at least 36 inches tall and 18 inches wide with orange and white retroreflective stripes. MUTCD guidance for spacing: in tapers, maximum spacing in feet equal to the speed limit in mph (for example 35 ft at 35 mph); along tangents (parallel to traffic), maximum spacing equal to twice the speed limit (70 ft at 35 mph). Closer spacing is used near flaggers, at night, and where needed. Keep devices upright and replace knocked-over ones promptly; assign someone to check them. Check your state standards.
field.title: Channelizing devices: cones, drums and spacing
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: FHWA Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, Part 6

field.text: Order matters when setting up and removing traffic control. Common practice in state DOT guidance: set up signs and devices in the direction traffic travels, starting with the first advance warning sign farthest upstream, then the next signs, then the taper, then the buffer and channelizing along the work; remove them in the reverse order (work area devices first, then the taper, then the advance signs last) so drivers are always warned before they meet devices. Use a truck with flashing lights or arrow board behind the workers placing devices on higher-speed roads, and on high-speed roads a truck-mounted attenuator may be required. Cover or remove signs when work isn't active so drivers don't learn to ignore them. Inspect the zone at the start, during and end of each shift, and at night. Follow your approved traffic control plan.
field.title: Traffic control: setting up and taking down safely
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: State DOT work zone practice consistent with MUTCD Part 6

field.text: When work closes a sidewalk or crosswalk, the MUTCD requires providing pedestrians with a reasonably safe, accessible path, either a temporary walkway or a detour, with advance signing at intersections so people don't walk up to a closed sidewalk mid-block. Accessibility: temporary routes should match the features of the existing route as much as practical (firm surface, width for wheelchairs, ramps, no abrupt edges); detectable barriers (continuous, with a bottom edge low enough for a cane to detect) are used to channelize pedestrians, not cones and tape alone. Cover or fence open trenches next to walkways. Many cities require pedestrian plans in the traffic control permit. Check local requirements.
field.title: Pedestrians and sidewalks in work zones
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: FHWA Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, Part 6

field.text: Steel trench plates let traffic use the road over an open trench outside work hours. Agency specs commonly require: plate thickness adequate for the span and traffic (often 1 inch or more for typical trench widths, check your agency's table), at least 12 inches of bearing on solid pavement on each side (many agencies say 12 to 18 inches), plates pinned or anchored so they can't slide, edges ramped with cold mix asphalt or ramp material, a skid-resistant surface, and 'STEEL PLATE AHEAD' or 'BUMP' signs, with motorcycle warnings in some states. Plates must not rock; shim or level them. Check them regularly, especially after heavy truck traffic. Requirements vary widely by agency; use the permit conditions.
field.title: Steel plates over trenches in roadways
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: Common city and state DOT permit conditions

field.text: Under OSHA's excavation standard (29 CFR 1926.652), workers in an excavation must be protected from cave-ins by a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring or a shield/trench box) unless the excavation is made entirely in stable rock, or is less than 5 ft deep and a competent person has examined the ground and found no sign of a potential cave-in. Excavations 20 ft deep or more need a protective system designed by a registered professional engineer (or based on tabulated data approved by one). OSHA's trenching page stresses that trench collapses kill workers every year and that a cubic yard of soil can weigh as much as a car. Never enter an unprotected trench 5 ft or deeper, and don't assume shallow trenches are safe; a state plan can set a shallower depth, so check the job's state. Some state plans are stricter than federal OSHA; your competent person and company program decide. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: when a protective system is required
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA Trenching and Excavation safety topic page

field.text: OSHA requires a competent person for excavation work: someone trained to recognize trench hazards and with authority to fix them immediately, including stopping work. Under 1926.651(k), the competent person inspects excavations, adjacent areas and protective systems daily before work starts, as needed during the shift, and after every rainstorm or other event that increases hazards. If they find signs of a possible cave-in, protective system failure, hazardous atmosphere or other hazard, workers must be removed until it's made safe. Signs to watch: cracks parallel to the trench edge, bulging walls, sloughing, water seeping, spoil sliding back, nearby vibration from traffic or equipment, and changes in soil. Record inspections in the daily report or the app's trench inspection log. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: the competent person and daily inspections
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651, Specific excavation requirements

field.text: OSHA Subpart P Appendix A classifies soil for sloping and shoring decisions. Type A: cohesive soil (clay, silty clay, hardpan) with unconfined compressive strength of 1.5 tons per square foot (tsf) or more; soil can't be Type A if it's fissured, subject to vibration from traffic or equipment, previously disturbed, or has seeping water. Type B: cohesive soil from 0.5 to less than 1.5 tsf, plus granular cohesionless soils like angular gravel, silt and silt loam, previously disturbed soil that isn't Type C, and Type A soil that is fissured or vibrated. Type C: cohesive soil at 0.5 tsf or less, granular soils like gravel, sand and loamy sand, submerged soil or soil with freely seeping water, and submerged rock that isn't stable. The competent person classifies soil using at least one visual and one manual test (such as thumb penetration, pocket penetrometer, ribbon test). When in doubt, treat it as Type C. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: soil types A, B and C
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652 and Subpart P Appendices A and B

field.text: OSHA Appendix B gives maximum allowable slopes (horizontal to vertical) for excavations less than 20 ft deep: stable rock, vertical (90 degrees); Type A, 3/4 to 1 (53 degrees); Type B, 1 to 1 (45 degrees); Type C, 1-1/2 to 1 (34 degrees). A short-term exception allows 1/2 to 1 (63 degrees) in Type A soil for excavations 12 ft or less deep that are open 24 hours or less. Example: a 10 ft deep trench in Type C soil sloped at 1-1/2 to 1 needs each side to lay back 15 ft horizontally, so the top is 30 ft plus the bottom width. That's why trench boxes are usually used in streets. Excavations 20 ft or deeper need an engineer-designed system. Slopes must be flattened if there are signs of distress. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: maximum allowable slopes
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652 and Subpart P Appendices A and B

field.text: Benching means cutting the trench walls in steps. OSHA Appendix B allows benching in Type A and Type B cohesive soils, not in Type C soil. In Type A, the overall bench profile must stay within the 3/4 to 1 slope; in Type B cohesive soil, within 1 to 1. Benches must be cut so the steps fit within the allowed slope line, with the bottom vertical cut limited (Appendix B shows a maximum 4 ft vertical bottom cut for multiple benches in Type A, and limits on unsupported vertical lower portions, commonly 3-1/2 ft). Benching takes a lot of room and is mostly used in open areas. Follow the Appendix B diagrams exactly or use another protective system. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: benching rules
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652 and Subpart P Appendices A and B

field.text: Trench boxes (shields) protect workers inside them but don't hold up the trench walls. OSHA 1926.652(g) and the manufacturer's tabulated data set the rules: use the box only within its rated depth and soil type per the maker's tabulated data (keep a copy on site); workers must stay inside the box while in the trench and must not be in it while it's being installed, removed or moved vertically; the box must be installed so it can't move sideways dangerously (backfill or block the sides if needed); excavation up to 2 ft below the bottom of a shield is allowed only if the shield is designed for the full trench depth and there's no sign of soil loss behind or below it. When the box is used in a sloped or benched trench, Appendix B shows the box must extend at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side. Inspect boxes for damage before use. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench boxes and shields: OSHA rules
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652 and Subpart P Appendices A and B

field.text: OSHA 1926.651(c)(2) requires a stairway, ladder, ramp or other safe means of exit in trench excavations 4 ft or more deep, located so workers have no more than 25 ft of lateral travel to reach it. In practice: put a ladder in the trench box (or within the protected area) and move it with the box; for long boxes or several workers spread out, use more ladders. Ladders should extend at least 3 ft above the landing (top of trench) per OSHA's ladder rules (1926.1053) and be secured. Never climb out on the box struts or pipe. Ramps used by workers need to be designed by a competent person. Keep the ladder area clear of spoil. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: ladders and access within 25 ft
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651, Specific excavation requirements

field.text: OSHA 1926.651(j)(2) requires that excavated material (spoil), tools, pipe and equipment be kept at least 2 ft back from the edge of the excavation, or held back with retaining devices, or both, so they can't fall or roll in. Heavier loads near the edge also add pressure on the trench wall, so keep heavy equipment and trucks back as far as practical, especially in Type B and C soils. Spoil can also slide back in when wet; watch it after rain. Practical tips: dig with the spoil side away from the work crew's access, use a spoil board or wall, and keep the 2 ft clear zone free of loose rocks. Pipe strung along the trench must be chocked so it can't roll in. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: spoil pile and material setback
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651, Specific excavation requirements

field.text: OSHA 1926.651(g) requires testing the atmosphere before workers enter excavations deeper than 4 ft where an oxygen-deficient or hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected, such as near landfills, sewers, gas lines, fuel tanks or contaminated soil. Oxygen below 19.5% is deficient and needs precautions such as ventilation or respiratory protection. Flammable gas must be kept below 20% of its lower flammable limit (LFL or LEL). Test again as often as needed to make sure the air stays safe. Sewer work adds hydrogen sulfide and other gases: use a calibrated multi-gas meter (O2, LEL, H2S, CO), and remember gases can settle in low trench areas. Emergency rescue equipment must be available where hazardous atmospheres could exist. Manhole entry is a separate confined space issue. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: hazardous atmospheres over 4 ft
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651, Specific excavation requirements

field.text: OSHA 1926.651(h) says workers must not work in excavations with accumulated water or where water is accumulating unless adequate precautions are taken, such as special support or shield systems, water removal, or safety harness and lifeline. If water removal equipment is used, a competent person must monitor it. If ditches, dikes or other diversions are used to keep surface water out, the excavation must be inspected after heavy rain. Water weakens trench walls quickly, especially in sandy (Type C) soils where seeping water automatically makes the soil Type C. Practical: keep a pump running at the low end, lay pipe downstream to upstream so water drains away from the work, and stop work if water is undermining the walls. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: water in the trench
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651, Specific excavation requirements

field.text: Other OSHA 1926.651 requirements: workers exposed to vehicle traffic must wear high-visibility vests or garments (d); no one may stand under loads being lifted or dug by equipment, and workers must stay away from vehicles being loaded or unloaded (e); when mobile equipment works near the edge and the operator can't see the edge clearly, use a warning system such as barricades, hand signals or stop logs (f); walkways are required wherever people or equipment cross an excavation, with guardrails when the walkway is 6 ft or more above the lower level (l); underground installations must be located before digging (b)(2). OSHA's 24-hour clause in (b)(2) does not override your state one-call law: nearly every state requires a valid ticket, the full notice period and a response from every operator before machine digging, so the state law and your company program decide, not the OSHA clause; adjacent structures must be protected from undermining (i). Your state 811 law may be stricter than OSHA on locates. This is a plain-language explanation, not the regulation; the OSHA text governs.
field.title: Trench safety: other OSHA excavation rules crews forget
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651, Specific excavation requirements

field.text: Open trenches left overnight are a hazard to the public and to the crew next morning. Common practice: backfill or plate trenches in roadways before leaving; barricade and fence open excavations off-road; cover or fence manhole openings and pits; leave no open trench next to sidewalks without fencing; keep the trench box in the trench if it's protecting a section that will be entered first thing; make sure pumps that run overnight are fueled and won't flood a neighbor's property. In the morning, the competent person inspects before anyone enters, especially after overnight rain (OSHA 1926.651(k)). Steel plates over trenches in traffic must be sized and anchored or ramped per the agency's requirements.
field.title: Trench safety: walking away from a trench at day's end
field.topic: Trench and excavation safety (plain-language guidance)
field.source: OSHA 1926.651(k); common agency practice

field.text: Trenchless construction installs or renews pipe with little or no open trench. Main methods and typical uses: horizontal directional drilling (HDD) for pressure pipe (water, force mains, conduit) under roads, rivers and yards, usually HDPE or fusible or restrained PVC, with limited grade accuracy; auger boring (jack and bore) for steel casings under roads and railroads, with moderate line and grade control; pipe ramming for casings in soft ground; microtunneling and guided boring for gravity sewers needing accurate grade; pipe bursting to replace an old pipe with a new, often larger HDPE pipe along the same path; and cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) lining to renew existing sewers from the inside. Method choice depends on pipe use, grade accuracy needed, soil, groundwater, length and access. NASTT publishes good practice guidelines for each method.
field.title: Trenchless methods overview
field.topic: Trenchless methods and casings
field.source: North American Society for Trenchless Technology (NASTT) educational resources

field.text: HDD installs pipe along a steered curved path. Steps: drill a small pilot bore from the entry pit to the exit following a planned profile, tracking the drill head with a walkover locator or wireline system; ream the hole larger in one or more passes (a common rule of thumb is to ream to about 1.5 times the product pipe OD; check your designer's or NASTT guidance); then pull back the product pipe, usually fused HDPE, attached to the reamer with a swivel so it doesn't twist. Drilling fluid (bentonite or polymer mix) stabilizes the hole, carries cuttings and lubricates.
