Risks: hitting utilities (pothole every crossing utility and keep the bore at the required clearance), inadvertent returns (frac-outs) of drilling fluid to the surface or into streams, and exceeding the pipe's safe pull force or bending radius. Record the bore path (depth and location) for as-builts.
field.title: Horizontal directional drilling (HDD) basics
field.topic: Trenchless methods and casings
field.source: North American Society for Trenchless Technology (NASTT) educational resources

field.text: Auger boring, often called jack and bore, pushes a steel casing pipe through the ground with hydraulic jacks from a launch pit while augers inside the casing remove the soil back to the pit. It's the standard method for crossing under highways and railroads, which usually require a casing with the carrier pipe installed inside on casing spacers and the ends sealed. Key points: the launch pit must be large enough for the boring machine, casing lengths and thrust block, and must have proper shoring; set the track on line and grade accurately, because steering is limited; keep the auger head slightly behind the casing lead edge in loose soils to prevent voids and settlement under the road; and monitor the road surface. Railroad crossings follow the railroad's permit conditions (often AREMA-based) for casing thickness, depth and grouting. Check the permit.
field.title: Jack and bore (auger boring) basics
field.topic: Trenchless methods and casings
field.source: North American Society for Trenchless Technology (NASTT) educational resources

field.text: Pipe bursting replaces an old pipe (clay, cast iron, concrete, some PVC) by pulling or pushing a bursting head through it, breaking it outward into the surrounding soil, while pulling in a new pipe (usually fused HDPE, or restrained-joint PVC or ductile iron in some systems) behind the head. It can install the same size or upsize the line. Steps: CCTV and clean the old line; dig insertion and receiving pits; reroute flow with bypass pumping; burst and pull in the new pipe; reconnect services by excavating at each lateral; test and TV the new line. Risks: heaving or damaging nearby utilities and structures if they're too close (keep clearances and pothole crossings), and repairs or concrete encasement on the old line that stop the head. NASTT publishes a pipe bursting good practices guide.
field.title: Pipe bursting basics
field.topic: Trenchless methods and casings
field.source: North American Society for Trenchless Technology (NASTT) educational resources

field.text: Cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) renews an existing sewer by inserting a resin-saturated felt or fiberglass tube into the host pipe (by water or air inversion or by pulling it in), expanding it against the old pipe and curing it with hot water, steam or UV light into a new pipe inside the old one. Standards include ASTM F1216 (inversion) and F1743 (pulled-in place). Steps: clean and CCTV the host pipe, remove roots and protruding taps, bypass flow, install and cure the liner, cut the ends, reinstate service laterals from inside with a robotic cutter, then CCTV the finished liner. Watch resin and styrene odor concerns near homes and businesses (notify residents), and handle cure water per permits. Lateral reinstatement and liner wrinkles are the usual quality issues.
field.title: Cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) lining basics
field.topic: Trenchless methods and casings
field.source: North American Society for Trenchless Technology (NASTT) educational resources

field.text: Where a pipe crosses under a road or railroad in a casing, the carrier pipe (water main or sewer) is installed inside the casing on casing spacers (insulators) that center it, keep it off the casing wall, protect its coating, and for gravity sewers hold it at the right grade. Typical practice: spacers spaced per the maker and specs (often within a couple of feet of each joint and at set intervals between), restrained joints on the carrier pipe inside the casing for pressure pipe so it can't pull apart, end seals (rubber boots or brick and mortar) at both casing ends, and sometimes grouting or sand fill of the annulus if the permit requires. For gravity sewer, check the carrier invert at both ends after installation. Railroad and DOT permits often dictate casing size, wall thickness and depth.
field.title: Casings, carrier pipe and casing spacers
field.topic: Trenchless methods and casings
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: 811 is the national call-before-you-dig number; it routes to your state one-call center, which also takes online requests. Basic process: (1) pre-mark the dig area in white paint or flags (white lining) unless your state allows describing it; (2) contact 811 the required number of days ahead; (3) the center notifies member utilities, which send locators to mark their lines; (4) check responses (many states have a positive response system showing each utility's status); (5) respect the marks and dig carefully within the tolerance zone. Wait times vary by state: most require 2 to 3 business days' notice (Iowa: 48 hours, not counting weekends and holidays, starting at 6 am the next business day). Tickets expire (Iowa: 25 calendar days after the 48-hour wait), so renew for long jobs. Check your state's one-call law.
field.title: 811 call before you dig: how the process works
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

field.text: Utility locate marks follow the APWA uniform color code: Red: electric power lines, cables, conduit and lighting cables. Yellow: gas, oil, steam, petroleum or other gaseous or flammable material. Orange: communication, alarm or signal lines, cables or conduit (phone, cable TV, fiber). Blue: potable water. Purple: reclaimed water, irrigation and slurry lines. Green: sewers and drain lines (sanitary and storm). White: proposed excavation limits or route (marked by the excavator). Pink: temporary survey markings. Marks are usually paint and flags, with the utility owner's initials and sometimes the size, material or number of lines (for example 'ATT FO' or '8 in W'). Iowa One Call's manual lists blue as water, irrigation and slurry, so some states group irrigation with blue; check your state.
field.title: APWA uniform color code for utility marks
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: Open Exam Prep water distribution guide: underground locating and APWA colors

field.text: The tolerance zone is the area on each side of a marked utility where mechanized digging isn't allowed, because marks are only approximate. Width depends on state law: many states use 18 inches either side of the outside edge of the utility, others 24 inches, and some use half the facility width plus 24 inches. Within the zone, expose the line by hand digging or vacuum excavation (or other nondestructive methods your state allows) to find its exact location and depth before digging nearby with a machine. Locators don't mark depth (Iowa's manual notes operators don't mark depth), so never assume a line is deep. Once exposed, support and protect it. Check your state's tolerance zone rule.
field.title: Tolerance zone: hand digging near marked lines
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

field.text: Potholing means digging a small test hole to expose a utility and confirm its exact location, depth, size and material. Vacuum excavation (hydro-excavation with water or air-excavation with compressed air, then vacuuming the spoil) is the preferred method near utilities because it's nondestructive and fast; many state laws recognize it as an acceptable method inside the tolerance zone. Tips: pothole every crossing utility ahead of the crew, ideally days ahead, so design conflicts get resolved before the crew arrives; record depth to top, size, material and station/offset; backfill and compact potholes per specs; use low water pressure near fragile lines and fiber; and remember hydro-excavation produces slurry that must be disposed of properly. Pothole data also supports change orders when utilities aren't where the plans show.
field.title: Potholing and vacuum excavation
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: State one-call laws (e.g., Iowa One Call manual); common industry practice

field.text: White lining means marking the proposed dig area with white paint, flags or stakes before calling 811, so locators know where to mark. Many states require it; a typical law requires white lining unless the location can be clearly described on the call or at a preconstruction meeting, electronic white-lining is used, or physical premarking is impractical (that is how the Iowa law puts it). Good tickets: give exact addresses and cross streets, describe the dig area (for example 'entire right of way, both sides of Main St from 1st Ave to 3rd Ave'), the type of work, depth and equipment, and the start date. Too-large tickets slow locates and may be rejected. Keep ticket numbers in the daily report and on site. Request re-marks when marks fade; Iowa's manual expects marks to last at least 5 working days on dirt and 10 on pavement.
field.title: White lining and good locate tickets
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

field.text: If a line is hit or damaged, even a scrape, dent or nicked coating: For gas or hazardous liquid: stop work, shut off equipment if safe (one state one-call manual says in an emergency leave equipment where it is), evacuate people away and upwind, call 911, then the utility owner; don't try to stop the leak, don't operate switches or anything that can spark. For electric: stay away and keep others away; if on equipment touching a line, stay on it unless there's fire, then jump clear with feet together. For all damage: notify the utility owner as soon as practical with the type and extent, report to the one-call center where required, and don't backfill the area until the owner has inspected (unless they approve). Small coating damage on a steel gas line can cause corrosion leaks later, so report it. Document with photos and the ticket number.
field.title: If you damage a utility line
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

field.text: Most state one-call laws allow emergency excavation without waiting the normal notice period when there's a clear and immediate danger to life, health, essential services or significant property (a typical state definition), but you must still notify the one-call center as soon as practical and dig with extra care. Emergency tickets go to utilities immediately. Lack of marks is not permission to dig: if a utility hasn't responded by the end of the waiting period, check the positive response system and contact the utility; OSHA 1926.651(b)(2) only allows proceeding without a locate after 24 hours (or longer if state law says) with caution and detection equipment. Many states require you to wait for all responses. Abandoned lines and private lines (service lines past the meter, private electric, irrigation) aren't marked by 811 members; hire a private locator for those.
field.title: Emergency locates and working without marks
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

field.text: 811 member utilities usually mark only their own facilities up to the meter or property line. Not marked by 811 in most states: private water and sewer services on private property, private electric lines (to outbuildings, signs, lights), private gas lines after the meter, irrigation systems, private fiber, septic systems, and abandoned lines. On sewer and water jobs, sewer laterals are often not marked because many sewer utilities don't mark laterals. Plan for these: review as-builts, ask property owners, hire a private locate company, use ground-penetrating radar or electromagnetic locators, and pothole. Record any unmarked utility you find on the as-builts and daily report.
field.title: Private utilities and unmarked lines
field.topic: Utility locates, 811 and damage prevention
field.source: Common one-call practice

field.text: When someone sends a photo and asks 'what rock is this?', check five things in order. (1) Size: is there something in the shot for scale (glove, boot, tape, coin, hand)? Without it, size is a guess. (2) Shape: sharp broken faces and corners mean crushed stone; smooth, rounded, egg-like pieces mean river or pea gravel. (3) Fines: is there dust, sand or mud between the stones, or are the stones clean with open gaps? (4) Color and rock type: gray, tan, pink speckled, black, white chunks, black coated pieces. (5) Wet or dry: wet stone looks darker and shinier, and dust on wet clean stone shows as a gray film. Then name the likely product and its look-alikes. A photo can narrow it to a family (clean stone, base with fines, sand, recycled); only the delivery ticket or a sieve test confirms the exact size number or spec class.
field.title: How to identify rock or gravel from a photo: what to look at first
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Everyday objects to judge stone size in a picture: a US quarter is a little under 1 inch across (0.955 in); a golf ball is about 1.7 in; a tennis ball about 2.6 in; a baseball about 2.9 in; a closed fist is roughly 3.5 to 4 in; a basketball about 9.5 in. A dried pea is about 1/4 to 3/8 in and a glass marble about 5/8 in. Field shorthand: #8 chip is pea size, #57 is mostly marble to grape size with a few quarter-size pieces, #4 is walnut to golf ball, #3 is golf ball to hen's egg, #2 is egg to baseball. Cobbles (3 to 12 in) run from a baseball up to a basketball; boulders are bigger than 12 in. Ask the crew to drop a glove, tape measure or coin on the pile and shoot straight down for a better call. Size by eye is about the biggest pieces you see; the spec size also depends on what passes the smaller sieves, which only a gradation test shows.
field.title: Size comparisons for stone in a photo (pea, marble, golf ball, fist)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region); ASTM D2487/D2488 particle size limits as used in USCS (public summaries); general field practice

field.text: #57 is the most common clean crushed stone in the East and Midwest; in other regions the same look is sold as '3/4 clean', '3/4 washed' or '1 inch drain rock'. By eye: angular crushed pieces, mostly marble to grape size (about 1/2 to 3/4 in) with some up to a quarter or a little bigger (1 in) and a few pea-size bits (down to about 3/16 in). No sand or dust filling the gaps: you can see dark open voids between stones. In a pile it forms a steep, loose cone and the stones rattle and slide underfoot; in a bucket it pours and does not clump. Wet, it looks darker and glossy but the water drains straight through; a dusty unwashed load leaves a gray film or milky runoff. Color depends on the quarry (gray limestone, pinkish or salt-and-pepper granite, dark trap rock). Look-alikes: #67 (smaller top size), #4 (bigger), 3/4 minus (gaps filled with fines). The ticket confirms the size number.
field.title: What #57 stone looks like (3/4 inch clean, 3/4 inch washed, 1 inch clean)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate size table (public reproduction, Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: #67 runs about 3/4 in down to 3/16 in (#4 sieve); #6 is 3/4 to 3/8 in. In a photo they look like #57 with the biggest pieces missing: mostly grape and marble size, nothing much bigger than a quarter's width. Side by side, #57 shows a scattering of 1 inch pieces and looks coarser and more open; #67 looks tighter and more even, and the pile surface is smoother. Both are clean (no dust filling voids), angular and free-draining. #67 is common as concrete coarse aggregate and pipe bedding where a spec caps stone size near 3/4 in. In the hand, a fistful of #67 holds 20 or more stones; #57 holds fewer, chunkier ones. You cannot reliably split #57 from #67 in a phone photo without a scale object; check the ticket. Spec gradation is in the existing aggregate size chunks.
field.title: What #67 and #6 stone look like (and how to tell them from #57)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate size table (public reproduction, Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: #4 stone is about 1 1/2 in down to 3/4 in: walnut to golf ball size, angular, clean, big open voids you could poke a finger into. #3 is about 2 in down to 1 in: golf ball to hen's egg. Both pour noisily, stack in a steep rough pile and roll under boots; walking on them is unstable. Wet, the faces shine and water vanishes into the voids. Uses: foundation stone under pipe in soft or wet bottoms, construction entrances, drainage blankets, stabilization under a manhole base. Look-alikes: #57 (much smaller, pieces mostly under 3/4 in), riprap (bigger than a fist, often irregular slabs), river cobble (rounded). 'Inch and a half clean', '2 inch clean' and 'ballast' are common yard names for these sizes; railroad ballast has its own AREMA sizes. Exact size number comes from the ticket.
field.title: What #4 and #3 stone look like (1 1/2 inch and 2 inch clean rock)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate size table (public reproduction, Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: #2 stone runs about 2 1/2 in (a few pieces up to 3 in) down to 1 1/2 in: egg to baseball size, angular and clean. In a bucket the pieces bridge and leave gaps big enough to see daylight through; the pile is very rough and coarse. It is used for construction entrances, stabilizing mucky trench bottoms (often over fabric) and as 'shot rock' or 'surge stone' in some regions. Look-alikes: #3 (smaller, golf ball to egg), light riprap or Class A riprap (bigger, many pieces fist size up to a basketball), crushed concrete in large sizes (gray paste, rebar bits), cobbles (round). 'Surge', 'shot rock' and '3 to 6 inch' are local names that are not standard sizes; their range varies by quarry, so ask what the ticket says.
field.title: What #2 stone and 3 inch clean rock look like (big shot rock vs riprap)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate size table (public reproduction, Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: #8 stone (3/8 in down to about 3/32 in, #8 sieve), also called 3/8 chip, chip stone, 'pea stone' or 'birdseye' in some yards, is crushed: small angular chips about pea size with sharp corners and flat faces. It is clean, so there is little dust. In the hand it feels sharp and grabs your palm slightly; it packs in place under a boot and leaves a crisp print. Pea gravel is the same size but rounded and smooth, often multi-colored and polished, and it rolls like ball bearings and squeezes out underfoot. Quick tell in a photo: zoom in on edges. Sharp facets and flat faces mean #8 chip; smooth, egg-shaped pebbles mean pea gravel. Many sewer bedding specs accept crushed chips but limit or exclude rounded pea gravel; the ticket and spec decide.
field.title: What #8 stone / 3/8 inch chip looks like (and how it differs from pea gravel)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate size table (public reproduction, Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: #89 runs about 3/8 in down to #16 (about 1/24 in); #9 is about 3/16 in down to #16. By eye these are tiny crushed chips, rice to small pea size, angular and fairly clean, often with a coarse-sand look at the fine end. They look like coarse sand mixed with small chips. Uses: chip seals and seal coats, masonry fill, joint fill for pavers (some specs), and filter layers. Look-alikes: screenings or stone dust (much more powder, packs into a crust), coarse concrete sand (rounded natural grains, no chips bigger than about 3/16 in), #8 (noticeably bigger, mostly pea size). Wet #89 looks dark and gritty and drains quickly; screenings stay damp and pasty. Exact size class needs the ticket.
field.title: What #89, #9 and chip seal chips look like (1/4 inch chips, grit)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: ASTM D448 / C33 standard aggregate size table (public reproduction, Govt of Bermuda tender Annex C); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Washed stone looks bright and crisp when dry, with clean faces; rinse a handful in a bucket and the water stays fairly clear. Unwashed or 'dry screened' stone carries a coat of rock dust: the faces look dull and powdery, your hand comes out gray, and rain or a hose gives milky runoff. A thin dust coat is normal for many quarry products and specs limit it by percent passing #200; heavy coats, mud streaks, clay balls (lumps that smear when squeezed wet) or roots mean contamination from the stockpile floor or loader. Clay balls in drain stone are a reject item on many specs because they plug the voids. In a photo, note dull surfaces, brown smears and lumps that are not stone. Whether the dust is within spec (for example 0 to 1 or 0 to 2 percent passing #200) needs a washed sieve test.
field.title: Washed vs unwashed clean stone: dusty #57, dirty rock and clay balls
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Pea gravel is natural, water-worn gravel screened to about 1/4 to 3/8 in (sometimes up to 1/2 in). By eye: smooth, rounded, egg- or bean-shaped pebbles, often a mix of colors (tan, white, gray, brown, rose, black) because it comes from river or glacial deposits of mixed rock. Washed pea gravel has a slight polish and almost no sand. In a pile it slumps to a low, flat cone and spreads like a liquid; underfoot it rolls and your boots sink and slide; in a bucket it pours and settles without voids you can see. Wet, the colors pop and it looks glossy. It is easy to mistake for #8 crushed chips in a blurry shot: zoom in for broken faces. Look-alikes: #8 chip (angular), small river rock (bigger, 3/4 in plus), coarse sand with gravel (pit run). Whether it meets a spec for crushed faces needs the ticket and, if in doubt, a fractured-face count.
field.title: What pea gravel looks like (rounded 3/8 inch river pebble)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: River rock is natural rounded stone sold in sizes like 3/4 to 1 1/2 in, 1 to 3 in, 2 to 4 in and up to cobble sizes. It is smooth, often polished, with mixed colors and no fresh broken faces. In the trench or ditch you may also hit natural rounded gravel in the ground (stream or glacial deposits). Crushed stone from a quarry is one rock type and color with sharp edges, flat broken faces and rough texture. Field tests: stones that roll and spin when kicked are rounded; crushed stone locks and stays. Crushed gravel (gravel run through a crusher) is a mix: rounded pebbles with one or two fresh broken faces showing a lighter interior. In bedding and base, angular stone interlocks; rounded gravel shifts. Specs often set a minimum percent of fractured faces; that count, not the look, decides acceptance.
field.title: What river rock and rounded gravel look like (vs crushed stone)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Crushed (quarried or crushed gravel): sharp corners, flat faces that meet at edges, rough or sugary texture, one dominant color, dust in the corners. In a heap it stands steep and rough. Rounded (natural gravel, pea gravel, river rock): no corners, smooth worn surfaces, mixed colors, often a slight shine, and it slumps flat. Hand test: roll a handful between your palms. Crushed stone grinds and catches; rounded stone slides past itself. Boot test: crushed stone locks under a boot; rounded rolls and slides. Sound: crushed stone crunches when walked on, rounded clatters and shifts. Mixed products exist (crushed gravel with a few broken faces). Many pipe embedment and base specs require crushed or a minimum fractured-face percent, measured by lab count, not by eye.
field.title: Crushed vs rounded: how to tell from a photo or in your hand
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: California Class 2 aggregate base (Class II AB, 'base rock', 'Class 2 base') is a dense-graded mix: crushed rock from about 3/4 in (or 1 1/2 in) down to sand and dust. By eye it looks like gravel and coarse sand blended with gray or tan dust, no open voids. Virgin Class 2 is usually gray to blue-gray or tan depending on the quarry. Recycled Class 2 and CMB (crushed miscellaneous base, a Greenbook product) often show white or light-gray chunks of old concrete with paste, black asphalt-coated bits and the odd red brick fleck. Dry it looks dusty and light; wet it darkens and turns cohesive, holding a squeezed lump and a sharp boot print. In a pile the sides are steep and slightly crusted. Compacted, it forms a hard, tight, smooth surface that rings under a shovel. Look-alikes: 3/4 clean (no fines), DG (sandier, no coarse rock), pit run (rounded). Ticket confirms Class 2 vs recycled vs CMB.
field.title: What Class 2 base / Class II AB / CMB looks like (California base rock)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Crusher run (Mid-Atlantic and Southeast), DGA (dense-graded aggregate, KY, NJ), ABC (aggregate base course, NC, SC, AZ), GAB, 21A / 21B (Virginia), 'road base' and '3/4 minus' all look alike: crushed stone from about 1 to 1 1/2 in down to rock dust, with the gaps filled by sand-size grit and powder. Gray (limestone, granite) or tan to brown depending on source. Dry, it looks dusty and pale and a handful leaves your palm gray; damp, it darkens, clumps and holds a squeezed ball. In a pile it stands steep and forms a skin; underfoot loose material crunches, compacted material feels like pavement. Water ponds or runs off rather than soaking in fast. Look-alikes: #57 clean (open voids, no dust), screenings (no coarse stone), recycled base (white concrete or black asphalt pieces). Which regional spec it meets (21A vs 21B, ABC vs CABC) needs the ticket and a gradation.
field.title: What crusher run, DGA, ABC, 21A / 21B and road base look like
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Same top size, opposite products. 3/4 clean (washed #57 or #67 look): separate stones with dark open gaps, bright faces, pours from a bucket like marbles, never clumps, water vanishes into it. 3/4 minus (crusher run, Class 2, road base): stones floating in gray or tan grit and dust, no visible voids, dusty to the touch, damp material clumps when squeezed, holds a boot print and a vertical cut face. Simple field checks: (1) Pour a little water on it: clean drains instantly; minus soaks slowly, darkens and ponds. (2) Squeeze damp: clean falls apart; minus balls up. (3) Look at the pile toe: minus leaves fines and dust; clean leaves only stones. A photo shot from a few feet away of the pile face usually shows the difference. Which one the spec calls for, and percent passing #200, is on the ticket and plans.
field.title: 3/4 minus vs 3/4 clean: telling them apart by eye, bucket and water
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Loose dense-graded base (Class 2, crusher run, ABC) looks rough and fluffy with stones standing proud and dust on top. Well compacted it turns tight and smooth: stones flattened into a mosaic, fines filling between, a slight sheen from the roller, and a boot or truck tire leaves little or no mark. Wet compacted base looks dark and slick and may pump (squeeze water and fines up under a wheel); pumping or a soft, rutting surface means too wet or a weak subgrade. Dry, overworked base shows a loose dusty skin and raveling stones. A 'rock face' surface with no fines on top suggests segregation or fines washed out. Look only tells you the surface; density versus Proctor needs a nuclear or sand-cone test, and the inspector's numbers rule. Dust from dry base is silica-bearing: wet it down.
field.title: What compacted base looks like vs loose base (and wet vs dry)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Screenings (#10, 'stone dust', 'rock dust', 'quarry fines', 'crusher dust', 'manufactured sand' in some yards) are the fines left after screening crushed stone: about 1/4 in or 3/16 in down to powder. By eye it looks like a gray, tan or pinkish coarse sand mixed with flour-like dust, with small sharp chips. Dry it is very dusty and puffs when dumped; damp it packs into a hard, smooth crust that can be troweled and holds a crisp footprint. In a pile it stands steep and forms a crust; it does not drain well once compacted. Look-alikes: concrete sand (rounded, washed, little dust), DG (granite, coarser, earthier, often tan or gold), #89 chips (more chips, less powder). Fresh screenings dust is high in respirable crystalline silica when the parent rock is granite or quartzite; wet it and wear a respirator as your silica plan requires.
field.title: What screenings, stone dust and rock dust look like
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Decomposed granite is granite weathered into a coarse, gritty sand with small rock fragments, usually sold as 1/4 or 3/8 in minus. Supplier descriptions put DG at up to about 3/8 in down to very fine particles, typically brown or gray (in California and the Southwest often tan, gold or reddish). You can see glittering mica flakes and glassy quartz grains. It feels gritty and crumbles in the hand; natural DG has a looser, more natural texture and does not compact as hard as screenings; stabilized DG has a binder added and sets firm. Granite screenings are a crusher product, about 1/4 in to fines in gray, brown, tan or pink, and pack into a smoother, harder surface. In a trench wall, DG is the weathered rock itself: it may still show the old granite texture and turn harder with depth. Whether a delivered product is natural, crushed or stabilized is on the ticket.
field.title: What decomposed granite (DG) looks like (and how it differs from screenings)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: GravelShop: decomposed granite vs granite screenings; Geology.com: Granite

field.text: Pit run or bank run is natural sand and gravel dug and loaded with little or no screening. By eye: a messy mix of rounded stones from pea to fist size or bigger (some specs allow up to 6 in or more), sand, and some silt or clay, often brown, tan or orange. Sizes are uneven from scoop to scoop, and you may see the odd cobble or root. It packs and compacts reasonably well when the fines are moderate, and drains poorly if it is clay-dirty. Wet, it darkens and may go soupy if silty. Look-alikes: crusher run (all angular, uniform gray), native glacial till (tighter, harder, more clay, cobbles), 'fill dirt' (fewer stones). Pit run can be close to the native soil in the same valley, so a photo alone cannot tell imported pit run from native ground. Max size and percent fines need the ticket or a gradation.
field.title: What pit run and bank run gravel look like (unprocessed sand and gravel)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: In soil classification, cobbles are rock pieces about 3 to 12 in and boulders are over 12 in. Field comparisons: a cobble is baseball to basketball size; a boulder is bigger than a basketball, from a 5 gallon bucket up. Natural cobbles from streams or glacial deposits are rounded or sub-rounded and mixed in color; cobbles from a quarry or blasting are angular. In a trench wall, cobbles sticking out of the face can loosen and fall; boulders change bucket work, shoring and pay. Logs and reports estimate cobbles and boulders by volume percent because a sieve sample cannot capture them. In a photo, judge size against the bucket teeth (often 3 to 5 in wide), a boot (about 12 in long) or a person. Pay as rock or boulder excavation depends on contract definitions, not on a photo.
field.title: Cobbles and boulders by size: what crews mean in the trench
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: ASTM D2487/D2488 particle size limits as used in USCS (public summaries); general field practice; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Riprap is large angular quarry stone placed to stop erosion at outlets, ditches and banks. By eye, good riprap is blocky, angular, hard and sound, with pieces of mixed sizes so the smaller ones fill between the big ones. Rough size feel: light or Class A riprap runs about fist to basketball (most around 6 in); medium classes have many stones the size of a basketball or a 5 gallon bucket (about 9 to 18 in); heavy classes have stones like a beach ball or a car tire and up, each one needing a machine. Bad signs: flat slabs or long thin pieces, rounded field stone (rolls out), cracked or layered rock that splits, soft shale, crushed concrete with exposed rebar (often banned). To check size, measure the long, middle and short dimensions of several stones or use the d50 your spec gives. Class sizes vary widely by state; the class comes from the ticket and spec, not the photo.
field.title: What riprap looks like by size (light, Class I to Class III) and bad riprap
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Crushed concrete (RCA, recycled concrete, 'recycled #57', 'crushed concrete base') is made from old slabs, curb and structures. FHWA notes it is 100 percent crushed and very angular. By eye: mostly light gray to white chunks, each piece often two-toned: original stone (gray, tan or dark) stuck in lighter gray cement paste with sand grains visible. Look for telltales: a short rebar or wire stub, red brick bits, black asphalt-coated pieces, tile, wood or joint sealant strips. Dust is light gray and chalky; it feels rough and chalky in the hand and makes your skin dry. Wet, the paste darkens unevenly. RCA fines absorb much more water than natural stone (4 to 8 percent vs 2 percent or less per FHWA) and the runoff can be high pH; tufa (white crust) can clog drains. Steel is magnet-removed at good plants. Product size and allowed contaminant limits come from the ticket and spec.
field.title: What recycled concrete aggregate (RCA, crushed concrete) looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 User Guidelines: reclaimed concrete material, granular base; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Both are gray and both fizz with acid (cement paste and limestone both contain calcium carbonate or react with acid), so the vinegar or acid test does not separate them. Look instead at each piece: limestone is one uniform rock through the whole piece, sometimes with fossils or fine layers, and breaks with clean, even faces. Crushed concrete pieces show two materials: rounded or crushed aggregate stones embedded in a lighter, sandy paste, and you can see sand grains in the paste with a hand lens. RCA usually has stray items (rebar, mesh wire, brick, asphalt, glass, wood). RCA dust is whiter and chalkier; limestone dust is gray to buff. RCA tends to be lighter in the hand and more absorbent: drop water on a piece and paste soaks it up and darkens. The ticket names the source; specs often limit where RCA can go (not against galvanized or aluminum pipe, not in underdrains).
field.title: Crushed concrete vs crushed limestone: telling them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: Geology.com: The acid test for carbonate minerals and rocks; FHWA-RD-97-148 User Guidelines: reclaimed concrete material, granular base; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Millings (RAP, reclaimed asphalt pavement, grindings, 'recycled asphalt') come from milling or crushing old asphalt pavement. FHWA says nearly all processed RAP is 1 1/2 in or smaller and contains about 3 to 7 percent asphalt by weight, with the rest stone. By eye: black to dark gray granular material, pieces coated in old asphalt, with some clumps of two or more stones stuck together; aged RAP turns gray and dull on top while fresh cuts are black. It smells of asphalt or oil, especially on hot days, and feels slightly tacky in the sun. Milled RAP is finer and denser than crushed RAP. In a pile it can bind and crust; compacted with a roller it can glue together in summer. Look-alikes: crushed basalt or trap rock (dark but clean, no tar smell or coating), slag (gray, porous), coal or cinders (light, brittle). Asphalt content and gradation need a lab test.
field.title: What millings, RAP and asphalt grindings look like
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 User Guidelines: reclaimed asphalt pavement, material properties; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Both look black or dark gray in a photo. Checks: (1) Break or scratch a piece with a knife: millings have a black skin over a lighter stone inside (gray limestone, tan gravel, pink granite); basalt or trap rock is dark all the way through. (2) Smell: millings smell like asphalt, especially warm or freshly turned; stone has no smell. (3) Touch on a hot day: millings feel tacky and leave a smudge; stone is dry. (4) Clumping: millings have glued clusters; trap rock is separate clean pieces. (5) Rub with a rag of diesel or solvent (where allowed): the black coat comes off millings and nothing comes off stone. Specs often limit RAP in base and backfill and some agencies restrict it near water lines or in drainage stone, so confirm with the ticket before placing.
field.title: Millings vs dark crushed stone (trap rock, basalt): quick field checks
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: Geology.com: Trap rock; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Air-cooled blast furnace slag (iron-making slag), per FHWA, crushes into angular, roughly cubical pieces with surfaces from rough, porous (vesicular, full of small bubble holes like a sponge) to glassy and smooth with curved, shell-like fractures. It is often light to medium gray, sometimes tan or with a whitish crust. It is lighter than you expect for its size: compacted unit weight is typically 70 to 85 lb per cubic foot. Foamed or expanded slag is even more porous and lighter. Granulated slag is a glassy sand with popcorn-like coarse grains. Telltale: water standing in contact with blast furnace slag can turn yellow-green and smell of sulfur (rotten eggs), with a pH as high as 12.5. Look-alikes: lava rock or scoria (red or black, natural), pumice, lightweight aggregate, RCA. Slag source and type need the ticket.
field.title: What blast furnace slag looks like (porous gray rock, sulfur smell)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials: blast furnace slag

field.text: Steel furnace slag (from steelmaking, not iron-making) is dark gray to black, dense and heavy in the hand, often with rusty orange-brown staining, small metallic bits or droplets that a magnet grabs, and a mix of dense and pitted pieces. It is much heavier than ordinary stone (specific gravity about 3.2 to 3.6 vs 2.5 to 2.7, per FHWA). Look-alikes: trap rock or basalt (no rust, no magnetism, not as heavy), millings (asphalt coating, smell), blast furnace slag (lighter, porous, sulfur smell). Why it matters: steel slag can swell as free lime and magnesia hydrate, and FHWA warns against it in trenches, behind walls and in confined base. It can also form tufa that clogs drains. A magnet and heft test suggest steel slag; the ticket and spec decide if it is allowed.
field.title: What steel slag looks like (heavy, dark, rusty, metallic) and why it matters
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: FHWA-RD-97-148 User Guidelines: steel slag (as summarized in materials/aggregates-backfill-18); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Lightweight aggregate (expanded shale, clay or slate, ESCS; brand names include Haydite, Stalite, Norlite and others) is made by firing shale, clay or slate in a rotary kiln above 1000 C (about 1830 F) until it bloats. ESCSI describes it as a ceramic aggregate with a porous interior inside a strong glassy shell. By eye: brown, reddish-brown, gray or charcoal pieces, either rounded pellets or crushed angular pieces, with a rough, bubbly or speckled surface; broken faces show tiny pores. In the hand it feels surprisingly light, like a stone that weighs about half what it should; dry pieces may float for a while in a bucket of water. Uses: lightweight fill behind walls and over soft ground or pipes, structural lightweight concrete, chip seal. Look-alikes: lava rock or scoria, blast furnace slag, pumice. Product and density come from the ticket and manufacturer.
field.title: What expanded shale / lightweight aggregate looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: Expanded Shale, Clay and Slate Institute (ESCSI): ESCS lightweight aggregate; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Red or black porous stones in a photo can be several things. Lava rock or scoria (volcanic cinder, common in the West, sold for landscaping and some fills): red, rust, purplish or black, natural and irregular, full of bubble holes, very light, with no flat crushed faces unless crushed. Blast furnace slag: usually gray, porous or glassy, may smell of sulfur when wet. Expanded shale: brown to gray, uniform product, pellets or crushed, light. Coal cinders and boiler ash (old fills, rail beds): black to gray, brittle, crumble under a boot, may leave black on your hands and smell burnt; often a sign of old urban fill. Pumice: white to light gray, floats easily. A photo narrows it; if it shows up in the ground unexpectedly, treat it as possible old fill and tell the super.
field.title: Lava rock, scoria and cinders vs slag and lightweight aggregate
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Crushed limestone is the most common aggregate in much of the East, Midwest and Texas. By eye: light to medium gray, blue-gray, buff, tan or near white; one fairly uniform color per piece, dull to slightly sugary texture, sometimes small fossils (shells, stems) or thin layers. Dust is light gray to buff and chalky. Fresh broken faces look sharp but limestone is softer than granite: a steel knife or nail scratches it. A drop of 10 percent hydrochloric acid on limestone fizzes strongly; dolomite (dolostone) barely fizzes unless you powder it first. Vinegar gives only a weak reaction. Wet limestone darkens to a blue-gray. Look-alikes: crushed concrete (two-toned pieces, paste and sand visible), marble (crystalline sparkle). Use acid only with eye protection and gloves, and rinse after; rock type and source come from the ticket.
field.title: What limestone aggregate looks like (gray, buff, fizzes in acid)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: Geology.com: The acid test for carbonate minerals and rocks; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Granite (and the similar gneiss and granodiorite products often sold as 'granite') is usually pink, red, gray or white with dark specks: visible mineral grains you can see without a lens. Geology.com notes feldspar shows white, gray, pink or reddish; quartz is clear to gray with a glassy shine; mica forms thin shiny flakes; black grains are biotite or hornblende. Crushed granite looks salt-and-pepper or pink-speckled, glitters in sun from mica and quartz, and breaks sharp and hard; a steel knife will not scratch the quartz and feldspar. It does not fizz in acid. Dust is light gray to pinkish and high in crystalline silica. Weathered granite turns tan to orange and crumbles into DG. Look-alikes: trap rock (dark all through, no visible grains), limestone (uniform, fizzes), pea gravel with granite pieces (rounded).
field.title: What granite aggregate looks like (speckled pink, white and black)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: Geology.com: Granite; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Trap rock is an industry term for dark igneous rock crushed for aggregate, most often basalt, diabase or gabbro (per Geology.com). By eye: dark gray, green-black or black, fine-grained so you cannot pick out mineral grains (diabase and gabbro are coarser and look dark speckled), sharp, blocky fragments, and heavy in the hand. Fresh dust is medium to dark gray. Weathered faces turn brown or rusty. It is valued for toughness and freeze-thaw resistance and common in the Northeast, Mid-Atlantic, Pacific Northwest and parts of the West. No fizz in acid; a knife does not scratch it. Look-alikes: millings (asphalt skin and smell, lighter inside), steel slag (rusty, magnetic, heavier), wet limestone (lighter when dry, fizzes). Confirm the source on the ticket.
field.title: What trap rock / basalt aggregate looks like (dark gray to black)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: Geology.com: Trap rock; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: A fabric-wrapped drain in an open cut or a test pit usually shows: a band of clean stone (#57, 3/4 or 1 1/2 in drain rock) with open voids, wrapped in geotextile that is most often white, gray or black felt-like nonwoven fabric (it looks fuzzy, like a dryer sheet or felt) with the edges overlapped on top. Inside there may be a perforated pipe (black corrugated HDPE with slots, white or green PVC with holes). Old drains may show fabric stained orange or brown, silt caked on the outside, or stone choked with fines, meaning the filter has blinded. Woven fabric (slit-film tape, shiny, like a tarp) under a road base is a separator, not a drain wrap. If you cut through a drain, tell the super: it must be repaired or rerouted per plans. Fabric type (woven vs nonwoven, weight) is on the roll label and submittal.
field.title: What drain rock wrapped in fabric looks like in a trench (French drain, burrito)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: In California and much of the West, clean stone is sold by top size rather than ASTM number: '3/4 inch drain rock', '1 inch drain rock', '1 1/2 inch drain rock', '3/8 pea gravel', 'washed gravel'. By eye these are clean, washed, screened stone with open voids and little dust; '1 inch drain rock' looks like #57 with slightly more big pieces; '3/4' looks like #67. Crushed products show sharp faces in one color; 'washed gravel' or 'river gravel' drain rock may be rounded and multicolored. 'Permeable material' Class 1 or Class 2 is a Caltrans drain material spec that is not the same as Class 2 aggregate base, despite the name. The look tells clean versus minus, crushed versus rounded; the ticket and spec give the exact product and grading.
field.title: '1 inch drain rock', '3/4 drain rock' and 'washed gravel': West Coast names by eye
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: From a photo Ask can usually tell: clean vs fines-filled, crushed vs rounded, rough size range, rock family (limestone, granite, trap rock, recycled concrete, millings, slag), and obvious contamination. A photo cannot confirm: (1) the exact size number (#57 vs #67) or percent passing each sieve; (2) percent passing #200 (fines); (3) the spec class (Class 2 vs Class 3, 21A vs 21B, ABC vs CABC); (4) quality tests like LA abrasion, soundness, sand equivalent, R-value, plasticity index, fractured faces; (5) recycled content percent or asphalt content; (6) whether it meets the project's approved source. For those, check the delivery ticket (product code and name), the supplier's gradation sheet or submittal, and the inspector's tests. If the material looks wrong for the ticket, stop placing and call the super before it goes in the hole.
field.title: What a photo cannot tell you about aggregate (ticket and lab only)
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: A pile of dense-graded base or a blended product can look like two products if it segregated: big stones roll to the toe and sides, fines stay in the middle and top. In a photo you see a ring of coarse stone at the bottom and a dusty core, or loads that are rock-heavy then sand-heavy. Placed, segregation shows as rock pockets (open, voided patches with no fines) and smooth fine patches next to each other. Clean single-size stone does not segregate much. Before calling a load wrong, look at the whole pile and how it was built (conical piles from a stacker segregate most). Remix with the loader by taking cuts across the face. If the material on site does not match the ticket after remixing, keep the ticket, take photos with a scale object and call the supplier and the super.
field.title: Segregated stockpile vs bad material: what uneven stone looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Quick color cues for crushed stone in a photo (dry): light to medium gray, blue-gray, buff or white, uniform: limestone or dolomite. Pink, red or gray with black and white speckles and glitter: granite or gneiss. Dark gray to black, fine grained, uniform: basalt, diabase, trap rock. Gray chunks with a lighter sandy coating and stray rebar: recycled concrete. Black with a tar coating and smell: millings. Rusty dark and very heavy: steel slag. Light gray, porous, light weight: blast furnace slag. Mixed colors, rounded: river gravel, pea gravel, glacial gravel. Tan to orange gritty sand with mica: decomposed granite. Red to black bubbly and light: lava rock or scoria. Brown to charcoal pellets, light: expanded shale. Wet stone is darker and hides these cues, so compare a dry piece if you can.
field.title: Rock types by color in a pile: quick color guide
field.topic: Visual ID: aggregates and stone by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Bends are named by degrees or by fraction of a full circle. 1/4 bend = 90 degrees, 1/5 = 72, 1/6 = 60, 1/8 = 45, 1/16 = 22-1/2, 1/32 = 11-1/4. Sewer suppliers often use fractions ('eighth bend', 'sixteenth bend'); water (DI MJ) fittings are cast with degrees ('45', '22 1/2', '11 1/4'). To judge one in a photo or the trench: a 90 turns the line square; a 45 is half that, the two legs form a wide V; a 22-1/2 looks like a gentle kink; an 11-1/4 is barely bent, easy to mistake for a straight coupling. In the hole, run a string along the incoming line and measure how far the outgoing leg moves away from it per foot of run along the string (the tangent of the angle): a 45 moves about 1.00 ft per ft, a 22-1/2 about 0.41 ft, an 11-1/4 about 0.20 ft. Long-sweep or long-radius bends have a longer curve than short-radius ones of the same angle. Read cast or printed marks on the fitting first: angle, size, material standard and maker.
field.title: Pipe bend angles: 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 bends and how to tell the angle by eye
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: Geometry: bend fraction = angle / 360 degrees; offset per foot = tangent of the bend angle

field.text: Tee: the branch leaves the run at a square 90 degrees, all three openings in a T shape. Used on water mains (for valves and hydrant leads) and on sewer only where the code allows. Wye: the branch leaves at about 45 degrees, so the fitting looks like a Y or a slanted letter; the normal sewer lateral fitting because flow enters in the direction of the main flow. Tee-wye (sanitary tee or combination wye-and-eighth bend): the branch starts as a wye but curves to 90 degrees, so it looks like a tee with a swept branch. Cross: two branches opposite each other, four openings. Reducing versions have a smaller branch, marked like '8 x 6' (run x branch). On a photo, check which way the wye branch points: it should lean downstream. A tee in a gravity sewer main where a wye was called for is a common inspection reject. DI water tees are marked with size, 'DI', and the standard (C110 or C153); PVC sewer fittings print SDR and size.
field.title: Tee, wye, tee-wye and cross: how to tell sewer and water branch fittings apart
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: PVC sewer fittings come in two builds. Molded (injection-molded) fittings have uniform thick walls, smooth curves and raised molded lettering with maker, size, 'SDR 35' and the ASTM standard. Fabricated fittings are made by cutting and solvent-welding or heat-forming pieces of pipe; you see seams, a pipe print line on the body and often a fiberglass or glued overwrap at the joint. Gasketed fittings have a bell with a rubber gasket on each hub (the green pipe pushes in); solvent-weld fittings have smooth glue sockets and are for glued systems. Common items: wyes, tee-wyes, 1/16, 1/8 and 1/4 bends (also called 22-1/2, 45 and 90), couplings (double bell, no stop or with a stop), cleanout adapters with a threaded plug, reducers, end caps, and adapters to other materials. Green fittings match green D3034 pipe; white fittings are usually Schedule 40 DWV and won't fit D3034 OD without an adapter. Check the size: 6 inch sewer (6.275 OD) and 6 inch Schedule 40 (6.625 OD) do not mix.
field.title: Green PVC sewer fittings by eye: molded vs fabricated, gasketed vs glue
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Mechanical joint (MJ) fittings for water mains are black (asphaltic or epoxy coated) ductile iron with a flared bell on each opening. Around each bell is a flange ring with bolt slots; a separate gland (follower ring) slides on the pipe, and T-head bolts pass through both and are tightened with nuts on the gland side. Cast into the body you'll find size, angle ('45', '1/8'), 'DI' or 'DUCTILE', pressure rating, the standard (AWWA C110 full-body or C153 compact) and maker or country. C153 compact fittings are shorter and lighter than C110 full-body fittings of the same size, which matters for lay length. Inside is a cement-mortar lining or a fused epoxy lining (often blue or black). Look-alikes: flanged fittings (flat faces, full bolt circle, no gland), push-on fittings (no bolts, smooth bells). MJ fittings fit CIOD pipe: C900, ductile iron and DIPS HDPE with a stiffener. Use glands and restraints rated for the pipe material.
field.title: Ductile iron MJ fittings: how to recognize them and read the cast marks
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: You can often tell the size of an MJ joint, valve or fitting by counting the T-bolts around the gland. Common AWWA C111 mechanical joint bolt counts (3/4 inch bolts for 4 to 24 inch): 4 inch = 4 bolts, 6 inch = 6, 8 inch = 6, 10 inch = 8, 12 inch = 8, 14 inch = 10, 16 inch = 12, 18 inch = 12, 20 inch = 14, 24 inch = 16. Because 6 and 8 inch both have 6 bolts, and 10 and 12 inch both have 8, check the size by a second clue: the cast size mark on the fitting, the gland, or the pipe circumference (6 inch CIOD about 21.7 in around, 8 inch about 28.4 in, 10 inch about 34.9 in, 12 inch about 41.5 in). A restraint gland has the same bolt count plus extra wedge or set-screw lugs between bolts. Missing or badly rusted T-bolts on an old valve are a sign to replace with stainless or coated bolts per the utility spec.
field.title: MJ bolt count: estimating pipe size from a photo of the gland
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: A wedge-action restraint gland replaces the plain MJ gland and grips the pipe so the joint can't pull apart. On EBAA's Megalug Series 1100 (for ductile iron) you see a thick follower gland with multiple pockets around it, each holding a toothed wedge pressed against the pipe by an actuating bolt with a torque-limiting twist-off nut. You tighten the twist-off nuts until the top hex shears off, leaving a smaller hex head (5/8 inch on the 1100) so the wedge can be loosened later. The number of wedges rises with size (2 on 3 inch, 36 on 54 inch). Ratings run 350 psi for 3 to 16 inch and lower for bigger sizes. Megalug glands are commonly coated red (EBAA's MEGA-BOND coating), and other brands use other colors, so color is only a clue. PVC pipe needs a PVC-rated version (EBAA's 2000PV series); using a DI-only wedge on PVC can crack it. Clues it is installed right: all twist-off nuts sheared, wedges seated, gland square to the bell.
field.title: Wedge-action MJ restraint glands (Megalug style): how to recognize them
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: EBAA Iron MEGALUG Series 1100 brochure

field.text: Restraint isn't always a wedge gland. Things you may see on water and force mains: Bell restraint harness for PVC: a split serrated ring clamped on the spigot behind the joint, tied to a second ring behind the bell by steel rods, so two rings and rods straddle each joint. Restrained push-on gaskets: a normal looking push-on joint whose gasket has stainless steel teeth molded in (for example Field Lok style); from outside it looks unrestrained, so read the gasket package or as-builts. Proprietary DI restrained joints (TR Flex, Flex-Ring, Lok-Ring styles): an extra lip or weld bead on the spigot and a locking segment or ring at the bell face. Tie rods and all-thread: rods with nuts and lugs or eye bolts running across valves or fittings. Mega-flange or flange adapters with set screws. Restraint length is set by design; if you uncover restrained pipe, don't remove rods or loosen glands with the line under pressure.
field.title: Other restrained joints by eye: bell harnesses, restraining gaskets, tie rods
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Push-on joint (Tyton, Fastite, gasketed PVC bell): a smooth bell with no bolts or flange; the gasket is hidden inside. You see only a bell and pipe going into it, and spigot stripes at the bell face if it is fully home. Mechanical joint (MJ): a bell with a flange ring, a separate gland on the pipe and a ring of T-bolts; you can see the gasket edge between gland and bell. Flanged joint: two flat machined faces bolted together through a full circle of round holes with regular hex bolts, a flat ring or full-face gasket between; used in vaults, pump stations, meter settings and on tapping valves, rarely buried. ANSI Class 125 flanges have 4 bolts on 3 inch and smaller, 8 bolts on 4 to 8 inch, 12 bolts on 10 and 12 inch. Flange-by-MJ and flange-by-push-on adapters join them. Grooved joints (Victaulic style) have a two-piece clamp in a groove near each pipe end, mostly in plant piping.
field.title: Push-on joint vs MJ joint vs flanged joint: telling them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Flexible rubber couplings join plain pipe ends on laterals and building sewers. Unshielded coupling: a black flexible rubber (elastomeric PVC) sleeve with a stainless worm-drive hose clamp at each end; many people call any of these a 'Fernco' after the brand. Shielded coupling: the same rubber sleeve with a corrugated stainless steel shear band or shield wrapped around it, often with four clamps; the shield stops the joint from sagging under soil load, and many plumbing codes require shielded couplings underground. Transition coupling: one end is a different ID than the other (molded step in the rubber, or bushings), for joining PVC to clay, cast iron, Orangeburg replacement, or ABS. The rubber is usually printed with the sizes and pipe types it fits (for example '4 in clay x 4 in PVC/CI'). In a photo, a bare rubber sleeve with two clamps is unshielded; a steel band covering most of the rubber is shielded. Check the code and utility spec for which one is allowed.
field.title: Rubber couplings for sewer laterals: unshielded, shielded and transition (Fernco style)
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Full-circle repair clamp: a wide stainless steel band (one, two or three sections) lined with a rubber gridded gasket mat, closed by bolts through lugs along one side; it wraps around a pipe with a hole or crack. Dresser-style (sleeve-type) compression coupling: a smooth center sleeve with a flared follower ring at each end, and long bolts running end to end between the two followers; used to join two plain ends, including different ODs with transition versions. Wide-range or transition couplings (brands include Romac, Smith-Blair, Ford, JCM) have big gaskets that cover a range of ODs, so they can join PVC, DI, cast iron, AC or steel; the OD range is printed on the coupling body or tag. DI solid sleeve: a long MJ coupling with a gland and T-bolts at each end. Tapping sleeves look like repair clamps but have an outlet branch. Before ordering, measure the OD of both pipes (circumference / 3.1416); old cast iron and AC pipe often need a specific range.
field.title: Repair clamps and repair couplings for water mains: how to recognize them
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: A tapping sleeve and valve (TS&V) is how a new branch is cut into a live main. The sleeve wraps around the main and has an outlet nozzle; the tapping valve bolts to that outlet. Sleeve types per one utility spec: all-stainless steel (4 to 12 inch) with a cast stainless flange, a heavy stainless armor plate in the gasket, welded lugs and pass-through bolts; fabricated carbon steel with fusion-bonded epoxy (often blue or black, 16 inch and up); and two-piece ductile iron split sleeves with MJ ends that bolt around the main. A 3/4 inch NPT test plug on the sleeve lets you pressure test it before tapping. The outlet flange is recessed to center the tapping valve (MSS SP-60). The tapping valve is a resilient-seated gate valve (AWWA C509) with a flanged inlet bolted to the sleeve and an MJ outlet for the new pipe; it has a full-size opening so the cutter passes through. Test before tapping; the referenced spec requires no leakage for at least 15 minutes.
field.title: Tapping sleeve and valve (TS&V): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: American Water specification 33 12 16.17, tapping sleeves and valves

field.text: Service saddle: a body that sits on the main with one or two straps (double-strap is common on PVC) around the pipe and a threaded outlet; bronze, epoxy-coated ductile, or stainless with a wide band (wide bands are used on PVC and AC to spread the load). Corporation stop ('corp'): a brass or bronze ball or plug valve threaded into the saddle or directly into a DI main, with an inlet thread (AWWA/CC taper or IPT) and an outlet for copper or PE tubing (flare, compression or pack joint), operated with a small tee-head key. Curb stop: a similar brass valve near the property line on the service, set in a narrow curb box (a 1 to 2-1/2 inch riser pipe with a lid at grade, sometimes called a Buffalo box) and turned with a long curb key. Meter setter or yoke: the brass assembly that holds the meter with valves on each side. Marks on brass parts give size, maker and 'NL' or lead-free mark for potable water. Old services may have lead goosenecks at the corp.
field.title: Service saddles, corporation stops and curb stops by eye
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Buried water gate valves (resilient wedge, AWWA C509 or C515) are tall-bodied iron valves: a round or oval bonnet sits on top of the body, with a 2 inch square operating nut on a non-rising stem (NRS) pointing straight up. Ends are MJ (gland and T-bolts), flanged, or push-on. Bodies are usually fusion-epoxy coated, often blue or black depending on maker. Cast marks show size, maker, pressure rating, 'OL' or 'OR' (open left or open right) or an arrow, and the standard. Above the nut a cast iron valve box rises to a lid at grade. OS&Y (outside screw and yoke) gate valves have a handwheel and a threaded stem that rises when open; they are used in vaults and fire service so you can see if the valve is open. Large gate valves may have a bevel or spur gear case. Look-alikes: butterfly valves (short body with a side gearbox), tapping valves (flange one end, MJ the other). Count turns to open: roughly 3 turns per inch of size plus 2 or 3.
field.title: Gate valve by eye: buried NRS and OS&Y valves
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Butterfly valves (AWWA C504) are common on water mains 12 inch and larger. They are much shorter end to end than a gate valve, so they look like a thick ring or short spool in the line, with MJ or flanged ends. A gearbox (actuator) is bolted to one side of the body, and the 2 inch operating nut is on top of the gearbox, so the nut is often offset from the pipe centerline; a valve box goes over the gearbox nut. Inside is a disc on a shaft that turns 90 degrees; when open you can see the disc edge-on in the middle of the bore, which is why you can't pig or tap through one. Gear cases are marked with turns to close and open direction. Look-alikes: gate valves (tall bonnet straight up), plug valves (eccentric body, used on sewage), check valves (external lever and weight or a cover plate, no nut). Close butterfly valves slowly; quick closing causes water hammer.
field.title: Butterfly valve by eye: short body and side gearbox
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Valve boxes are cast iron, ductile or plastic tubes (two-piece or three-piece, screw or slide type, commonly about 5-1/4 inch shaft) running from the valve to a round lid at grade. The lid usually has cast letters: 'WATER' or 'W' for water valves, 'GAS' or 'G' for gas valves, 'SEWER' or 'S' for force main valves, and 'RECLAIMED' or a purple painted lid for reclaimed water. Some utilities paint lids (blue water, yellow gas, green sewer, purple reclaimed) or use special shapes (triangle or square lids). Small round lids marked 'CURB STOP', 'CS' or with a pentagon plug are service curb boxes. A tracer wire may run up inside the box. In a photo, read the cast word first, then the color and size, then the location: water valves usually line up with the main near tees and hydrants; gas valves are often near regulators. A valve box sitting crooked or filled with dirt usually means the box shifted off the nut: dig it out and recenter it before operating.
field.title: Valve boxes and lids: water, gas, sewer, reclaimed (how to read them)
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: A dry-barrel hydrant (AWWA C502, used where it freezes) has one operating nut on top of the bonnet that opens a single main valve deep in the ground; the nozzles all share it, and the barrel drains when closed. A wet-barrel hydrant (AWWA C503, warm climates) has a separate valve and operating stem behind each outlet, so you see an operating nut over or next to each nozzle and none on top. Parts visible above ground: bonnet and operating nut (often a pentagon), hold-down nut, upper barrel, nozzle section with two 2-1/2 inch hose nozzles and one 4-1/2 inch pumper (steamer) nozzle with chained caps, and the breakaway (traffic) flange or ground ring just above grade. Cast marks on the barrel give maker, model and year, and on many models the direction to open. Bag or tag out-of-service hydrants (MUD Omaha requires vivid orange 'Not in Service' bags). Body and cap colors are set by the utility and fire department.
field.title: Fire hydrant by eye: dry barrel vs wet barrel and the parts you see
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: Metropolitan Utilities District (Omaha) fire hydrant standard 3.0.1

field.text: Bury depth is the vertical distance from the ground line to the bottom of the hydrant lead pipe connection, and hydrants are ordered by it (for example MUD Omaha's standard is a 5 ft 6 in bury). Many makers cast or stamp the bury depth on the lower barrel or shoe, or mark a ground line on the barrel; tags may also show it. The traffic or breakaway flange (with frangible bolts or a breakable ring and a stem coupling) must sit just above finished grade: MUD Omaha says ground level to no more than 2 inches above; other utilities allow a few more inches. If the flange is buried or sits high, the hydrant was set at the wrong depth or the grade changed; fix it with a hydrant extension kit or a different bury rather than mounding dirt. Clues in a photo: a flange buried in soil, a lower barrel showing above grade, or a nozzle too low for a hose wrench all mean a depth problem. Check your utility's detail for nozzle height and clearances.
field.title: Fire hydrant bury depth and traffic flange: where to look on the barrel
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: Metropolitan Utilities District (Omaha) fire hydrant standard 3.0.1

field.text: Air valves sit at high points on water mains and force mains. They look like a cast iron or stainless cylinder or dome, roughly 1 to 3 ft tall, with a small vent outlet on top or side, mounted on a riser with an isolation valve (often a ball or gate valve) below. Air release valves have a small orifice; air/vacuum valves have a large orifice; combination valves combine both, often as two bodies side by side. Sewage air valves are taller and slimmer, with a long body so sewage doesn't reach the float, and backflush connections with hoses and valves. They sit in a precast vault or round manhole, or above ground in a vented 'candy cane' pipe or locked enclosure. Lid marks may say 'AIR VALVE' or 'ARV'. Look-alikes: blow-offs (no float body), backflow devices (two checks and test cocks). Sewage air valves and vaults can hold hydrogen sulfide and are confined spaces; ventilate and test the air before entering.
field.title: Air release and air/vacuum valves: how to recognize them
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Blow-offs let crews flush or drain the end or low point of a main. Common looks: an in-ground blow-off with a 2 inch riser pipe or hose connection inside a valve box or small vault, closed with a cap or plug; a post-type flushing hydrant, a short above-ground standpipe with a single 2 or 2-1/2 inch nozzle and no pumper nozzle, often painted differently from fire hydrants; or a full-size hydrant at the end of a dead-end main. Below ground there is a valve on the main, a riser and sometimes a drain. Lids may read 'BLOW OFF', 'BO' or 'FLUSH'. Look-alikes: air valves (vent body with float), fire hydrants (pumper nozzle), irrigation quick-couplers (small brass valve in a green box). A blow-off must not connect to a sewer or storm drain; discharge goes to the surface. When flushing, dechlorinate if required and control the discharge so it doesn't erode or flood.
field.title: Blow-offs and flushing hydrants: how to recognize them
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Reduced pressure zone assembly (RP or RPZ): a body with two check valves in series, a relief valve between them with a discharge port facing down (it can spit water), four small test cocks on the side, and a shutoff valve at each end; must be installed above grade, often in an insulated 'hot box' enclosure. Double check valve assembly (DC or DCVA): two checks, four test cocks and two shutoffs but no relief port, so it is slimmer and can be in a vault where allowed. Double check detector assembly (DCDA) on fire lines adds a small meter bypass loop. Pressure vacuum breaker (PVB): one check and an air inlet with a bonnet on top, two test cocks, used on irrigation, mounted at least 12 inches above the highest outlet. Atmospheric vacuum breaker: a small bonnet on a riser with no test cocks. Each assembly has a nameplate with maker, model, size and serial number; the tester records these. Which device is required is set by the hazard level and local code.
field.title: Backflow preventers by eye: RPZ, double check and vacuum breakers
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: A cleanout is a riser pipe off the lateral that comes up to grade so the line can be rodded or jetted. You see a pipe (usually 4 or 6 inch, the same size as the lateral) ending in a threaded plug with a square or recessed head, a gasketed cap, or a test cap, often inside a small cast iron or plastic box with a lid at grade. A two-way cleanout has two openings or a special double-wye fitting so you can clean upstream and downstream. Lids are often cast 'CO', 'C.O.', 'SEWER' or 'SEWER CLEANOUT'; plastic ones may be green. In lawns the riser may simply end at grade with a cap. Look-alikes: water meter boxes (bigger, 'WATER METER'), irrigation valve boxes (green plastic, rectangular), gas risers (yellow or steel, never open them), downspout drains. A broken or open cleanout lets storm water into the sewer (inflow) and is a trip hazard; replace caps right away.
field.title: Sewer cleanouts by eye: one-way, two-way, plugs and caps
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Water meter boxes sit near the property line or curb. Shallow-climate boxes are rectangular plastic or concrete boxes with lids marked 'WATER METER' or 'WATER', often with a small reading lid or a hole for a radio (AMR/AMI) antenna. Cold-climate meter pits are deeper round pits (plastic or concrete, often 18 to 24 inch diameter, 3 to 6 ft deep) with a frost lid and a smaller inner lid. Inside you see the meter on a setter or yoke, valves on either side, and sometimes a backflow check. Large meters sit in precast vaults with hatches. Look-alikes: irrigation valve boxes (green plastic lids), sewer cleanout boxes ('CO' or 'SEWER'), electric or telecom pull boxes (gray polymer concrete, 'ELECTRIC' or 'TELEPHONE'), gas meters (above ground on the building). Reclaimed meter boxes often have purple lids. Don't drive over plastic meter boxes; most are not traffic rated.
field.title: Water meter boxes and pits: how to recognize them
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Cap: fits over the outside of a pipe end (spigot), so the pipe goes into it. Plug: fits into a bell or opening. On DI water mains, an MJ cap goes over a plain end with a gland and T-bolts; an MJ plug goes into an MJ bell and is held by the bell's bolts; a push-on plug pushes into a bell. Caps and plugs may have a tapped 2 inch outlet for testing or flushing. Dead-end caps must be restrained or blocked; never remove one under pressure. On sewers you see PVC gasketed caps or plugs on stubs, and temporary test plugs: mechanical plugs (rubber between two plates squeezed by a wing nut, often with a bypass) and inflatable plugs (rubber bladders with a hose and gauge). Inflatable plugs under pressure can shoot out like a cannon: stay out of the line of the pipe, use the rated pressure and a restraint, and never stand in the manhole in front of a pressurized plug. Lateral stubs are capped and marked with a stake or 2x4 at the end.
field.title: Caps, plugs and test plugs: telling them apart on water and sewer
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: A thrust block is a mass of concrete poured between a water main fitting (bend, tee, cap, plug, reducer or valve) and undisturbed soil, so internal pressure can't push the fitting off.
