When you dig near an existing main, a thrust block looks like rough, unformed concrete wrapped against the back of a fitting, often with the fitting still visible on the front side and plastic film between concrete and pipe. Vertical bends may have a gravity block (a big block underneath) or straps and rods anchoring the fitting to a block. Things not to do: don't undermine, break or dig out the soil behind an active thrust block; don't remove one while the line is pressurized; and expect restrained joints or tie rods instead on newer work. Problems you may see: concrete poured over bolts or joints (bad: the joint can't be serviced), a block poured against loose fill, or a block too small for the fitting. Check the utility detail for block size and bearing area.
field.title: Thrust blocks by eye: what you're looking at when you uncover one
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: How a lateral can join the main: In-line wye: a wye fitting cast in the main during construction, the cleanest connection. Strap-on saddle (wye or tee saddle): a curved PVC, clay or rubber saddle fitted over a cored hole in the main and held by stainless bands or glue; the branch rises at 45 or 90 degrees. Insert tap (Inserta Tee style): a black rubber sleeve pushed into a cored hole in the main with a PVC hub inserted and clamped with a stainless band, common on PVC, concrete and clay mains. Break-in connection (just a hole and the pipe jammed in with grout): an old practice, a source of leaks and roots, not allowed on new work. Stubs are capped and the end is marked with a stake, painted 2x4, green or white post, or 'S' stamped in the curb. CCTV shows the connection type from inside. Use the connection the utility details allow and seal it.
field.title: Sewer lateral connections by eye: wyes, tee saddles and insert taps
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Reducers join two sizes. Concentric reducer: tapered like a cone, both ends on the same centerline. Eccentric reducer: one side straight and the other tapered, so the centers are offset; on sewers set it with the flat side up (crowns matched) or as specified, and on pump suctions with the flat side on top to avoid air pockets. MJ reducers are marked with both sizes ('8 x 6'). Adapters you may find: PVC sewer to cast iron or clay adapters (one gasketed end per material), C900 to DI with standard MJ fittings, HDPE MJ adapter (a fused stub with a steel ring and MJ gland), flange adapters, and PVC 'C900 x sewer' adapters. Bell reducers on sewer fittings look like a big bell with a smaller hub. In a photo, check the size marks on each end and which way the taper faces. A reducer installed backwards on a gravity sewer (smaller pipe downstream) is a defect; most sewer codes do not allow downsizing downstream.
field.title: Reducers and adapters by eye: concentric, eccentric and transition fittings
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: In lift station valve vaults you'll usually find check valves and isolation valves. Swing check valve: a body with a cover plate on top and, on many, an external shaft with a lever arm and a weight or spring that moves as the pump starts and stops; the lever shows if the valve is open. Ball check: a smaller body with a rubber-coated ball, no lever. Plug valve (eccentric plug, common on sewage): a body with an offset bulge and a gear actuator or a 2 inch nut on top; preferred on sewage because it passes solids. Gate valves (resilient wedge) also appear. Flanged joints with flat gaskets and bolt circles connect everything. Pipes are often DI with red-primer sewer lining or epoxy lining. Valve vaults are confined spaces that can collect hydrogen sulfide and are often wet. Ventilate and test the air before entering, and lock out pumps before opening any check valve cover.
field.title: Check valves and plug valves at pump stations and force mains
field.topic: Visual ID: fittings and valves by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Utility locate marks come in three common forms. Paint: short dashes or lines sprayed on pavement, grass or dirt. Flags: small vinyl flags (about 4 x 5 inch) on wire staffs pushed into the ground, often printed with the owner's name, the utility type and a phone number. Whiskers: a bundle of colored plastic strands held by a nail or spike driven into pavement or a crack, used where paint wears off or isn't wanted; stakes or lath with colored tops are also used. The color says what's buried (APWA uniform color code): red = electric power, yellow = gas, oil, steam, petroleum, orange = communications, alarm, signal, cable TV, traffic loops, blue = potable water, purple = reclaimed water, irrigation and slurry lines, green = sewer and storm drain, white = proposed excavation, pink = temporary survey marks. Some one-call centers add their own notes (Gopher State also uses pink for unknown or unidentified facilities), so check your state's chart. Faded or chewed-up marks: request a re-mark.
field.title: Locate paint, flags and whiskers: what each looks like and what the colors mean
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: APWA Uniform Color Code chart (2021); Gopher State One Call, Locator language: decoding utility markings; Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: operator facility field delineation

field.text: Per the CGA marking guide, operator locate marks are about 12 to 18 inches long and about 1 inch wide, spaced roughly 4 to 50 ft apart, closer where the terrain or the dig needs it. A single facility is marked one of two ways: dashes along the centerline of the line, or marks along both outside edges joined by a short crossbar, which looks like a row of letter 'H' shapes; the H shows the width of a wide facility such as a big pipe or duct bank. Marks are the approximate location; the line can be anywhere in the tolerance zone set by your state law (commonly 18 to 24 inches either side of the outside edge of the marks), so hand dig or vacuum to expose it. Where marks stop, the locator either reached the end of the ticket area or the end of the facility; look for an end mark or 'END' before assuming. Paint marks on hardscape should be small and neat; overspray is a common complaint.
field.title: Locate mark size, spacing, and center line vs H marks
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: operator facility field delineation

field.text: Locators write text next to their marks in a set order: owner first (name, initials or abbreviation, at the top or left), then size or count, then material. Examples from Gopher State One Call and CGA: 'GASCO 12" STL' = the gas company's 12 inch steel line. '4/4" PLA' = four 4-inch plastic lines or ducts. '12" CDR' = a corridor 12 inches wide with an unknown number of lines (marked at the center with total width). '6" PLA in 12" STL' = a 6 inch plastic carrier inside a 12 inch steel casing. Common material abbreviations: STL steel, PLA or PL plastic, CI cast iron, DI ductile iron, PVC, PE or HDPE, AC asbestos cement, CU copper, FO fiber optic, CATV cable TV, ELEC or E electric, TEL telephone, D (distribution) and T (transmission). The owner ID goes at the start and end of the work area and where a line crosses another facility of the same color. If text is unclear, call the operator on the ticket before digging.
field.title: Reading locate abbreviations: owner, size, material, count and width
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Gopher State One Call, Locator language: decoding utility markings; Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: operator facility field delineation

field.text: When an operator has no facilities in the marked dig area, they mark or flag 'no conflict' instead of a line. Per CGA: for one facility type, the word 'NO' followed by the operator identifier in that utility's color, for example 'NO TELCO' in orange. Where an operator has several facility types, a slash code is added: 'NO GASCO/G/D' (no gas distribution), /G/T gas transmission, /E/D electric distribution, /E/T electric transmission. Gopher State notes a letter with a slash through it (a G with a slash) also means no conflict for that utility. No-conflict flags are clear or translucent, printed 'No Conflict' in the APWA color, with the operator's name, phone number, a blank for the ticket number and the date. Operators may also clear the ticket electronically through the 811 positive response system; check positive response before digging. 'No conflict' only covers that operator and the area on the ticket; it doesn't cover private lines.
field.title: No-conflict and 'clear' locate marks: NO TELCO, slashes and clear flags
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: operator facility field delineation; Gopher State One Call, Locator language: decoding utility markings

field.text: Locate marks show direction as well as position. Per CGA guidance, a change in direction or a lateral (service or branch) is marked at the exact point it happens, with an arrow showing which way the line goes; a curve is marked with arc marks following the radius. Termination points and dead ends are indicated, often with a short perpendicular bar across the line, a 'T' or the word 'END'. Arrows at the edge of the marked area point toward where the line continues beyond the ticket limits. Boundaries of buried vaults, inlets and lift stations that extend past what you can see at the surface are marked too. In a photo, follow arrows rather than assuming the line runs straight between flags; a gas or water service often turns 90 degrees at the main and runs toward the house meter. If a lateral arrow points into your dig but you can't find its continuation, call for a re-mark before excavating there.
field.title: Arrows, turns, laterals and dead ends in locate marks
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: operator facility field delineation

field.text: Sometimes the locator can't paint directly over the line, so they set offset marks on a uniform line nearby and show the distance and direction to the actual facility. Michigan's damage prevention board lists the reasons: pavement that will be removed, areas where grading will wipe out flags, landscaped or decorative areas where paint isn't wanted, and places where water would wash marks away. An offset mark typically shows the utility color, an arrow pointing toward the facility, the distance (for example '5 FT' or 'O/S 5''), and the owner ID; some locators add 'OS' or 'OFFSET' in front. Read it as 'the line is X ft from this mark in the arrow direction'. Measure at right angles to the line of marks, and pothole before you dig. Formats vary by state and locator; ask the operator if an offset isn't clear. Don't confuse locate offsets (APWA colors) with survey offset stakes (lath with station and cut, usually pink or another survey color).
field.title: Offset locate marks: when they're used and how to read them
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Michigan Damage Prevention Board, Best practices: offset staking

field.text: Conduit and duct systems are marked differently from single pipes. Gopher State One Call explains that a diamond symbol marks a conduit; their example shows four 4-inch plastic conduits with the telecom owner's ID. CGA says to mark the outer edges of the located duct structure and write the count and size, for example '4/4" PLA' with marks 16 inches apart showing the real left and right edges. A 'CDR' (corridor) note means several lines bundled where the exact count isn't known, with total width given. Duct banks may also show 'DB' or 'DUCT'. Expect electric duct banks to be concrete-encased and much wider than one pipe, sometimes 2 to 4 ft. In a photo, two parallel lines of red or orange paint with a diamond and a count between them mean a duct bank, not a single cable. Treat every duct in a bank as energized or carrying live fiber; expose by hand or vacuum and keep the bucket away.
field.title: Conduit and duct bank locate marks: diamonds, edges and counts
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Gopher State One Call, Locator language: decoding utility markings; Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: operator facility field delineation

field.text: White paint, flags or stakes are put down by the excavator (that's you) to show the proposed dig area before calling 811. Common white-lining shapes: a solid or dashed line around the dig area, dots or dashes along the centerline of a trench route with the width noted, or an arrow and 'TO' for a run continuing to a point. Writing the company name and ticket number in white helps locators. Pink (fluorescent pink) is for temporary survey markings, for example control points, lot corners, pavement cut lines, curb and gutter offsets, and grade marks the surveyor paints on the ground. Gopher State also uses pink for unidentified facilities. Don't use pink or white for anything else, and never paint over another utility's marks. Surveyors also use other colors by company practice, so read the text, not just the color. If you see white marks you didn't make, someone else is planning to dig there; coordinate.
field.title: White marks and pink marks: excavator white-lining and survey paint
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: APWA Uniform Color Code chart (2021); Gopher State One Call, Locator language: decoding utility markings

field.text: Not every line can be located. Clues you'll see: pink paint (Gopher State uses pink for unidentified facilities), question marks, or notes like 'UNLOC', 'UNLOCATABLE', 'NO TRACE', 'ABAND' or 'TBD' next to a utility color. 'TBD' and similar words are not part of the APWA color code; they mean the locator couldn't finish or is waiting on records, and the meaning varies by company. A ticket may also show 'marked from records' or 'potholes required'. What to do: check the positive response for the ticket, call the operator for the status, and don't treat an incomplete mark as clear. Nonmetallic pipe without working tracer wire (PVC, PE, clay, AC) is often unlocatable; the owner may send a crew to pothole or provide maps. Abandoned lines are not always dead; treat them as live until the owner confirms. Write down what you see in your daily report with photos and the ticket number.
field.title: Unknown, unlocatable and 'TBD' style locate marks
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Gopher State One Call, Locator language: decoding utility markings; Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: operator facility field delineation

field.text: Construction staking uses several kinds of wood. Hub: a short square stake (the Navy Engineering Aid manual describes 2 x 2 inch by about 12 inch) driven nearly flush with the ground, often with a tack or nail marking the exact point; its top is the elevation reference. Guard stake (lath or flat stake): a taller flat stake driven beside a hub, slanted toward it, with flagging; it protects and finds the hub and carries the writing. Lath: thin rough plaster lath, 18 to 48 inches long, used for offset and grade information. Witness stake: a stake set near a buried or hard-to-see point (a monument, iron pin, PK nail) to show where it is. Survey crews write on the stake faces with keel (lumber crayon) or permanent marker; the Navy manual says station goes on the front and other data on the back. Flagging tape is tied on top. Never pull or move a stake; report disturbed stakes and get them reset.
field.title: Survey stakes by eye: hubs, lath, guard stakes and witness stakes
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: US Navy Engineering Aid training manual (TPUB), construction stakes

field.text: A 'C' on a stake means cut (dig down) and 'F' means fill (build up), measured from the top of the hub or from a mark on the stake. Units are usually feet and tenths, but writing styles vary: the Navy manual's example 'C35' means cut 3.5 ft, while other crews write 'C 3.5', 'C 3.50' or feet and inches like 'C 3'-6"'. Always ask your surveyor how they write it. A crowfoot (a line with short marks like a bird's foot) marks the exact point or height the number refers to. Baseline Equipment notes a single slash separates two values from the same hub (for example cut to top of footing / cut to bottom), and a double slash on a slope stake shows a grade then a slope ratio, such as 'F 0.4 to toe // F 6.0 at 2:1'. On sewer jobs the stake usually gives cut to invert (or to a stated reference) and the station and offset; a cut sheet lists the same numbers. Check the reference before you set grade.
field.title: Reading cut and fill on a stake: C, F, slashes and crowfoot
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: US Navy Engineering Aid training manual (TPUB), construction stakes; Baseline Equipment, How to read land survey stakes

field.text: Abbreviations you'll see on stakes and paint (styles vary by survey company; ask for their legend): CL centerline; OS or O/S offset (with distance and side, L or R, or an arrow); STA station (for example 12+50); RP reference point; BM, BMK or TBM benchmark or temporary benchmark; HUB or TOP for the hub elevation reference; C and F cut and fill; INV or IE invert elevation; FL flowline; TC top of curb; BC back of curb or bottom of curb; FG finish grade; SG subgrade; EP edge of pavement; ROW right of way; LOD limit of disturbance; PC and PT point of curve and point of tangency; MH manhole; CB catch basin; CO cleanout; FH fire hydrant; GV or WV gate or water valve; SS sanitary sewer; ST or SD storm; W water; G gas; E electric; LP or HP low point or high point. A number like '3 MH 5' may be a structure ID from the plans. Match stake IDs to the plan sheet before you dig.
field.title: Common survey stake abbreviations for utility and site work
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Baseline Equipment, How to read land survey stakes; US Navy Engineering Aid training manual (TPUB), construction stakes

field.text: Flagging (ribbon) color on survey stakes is not standardized nationally. Survey firms and agencies set their own colors, and many use one color for each purpose on a job, for example one color for clearing limits, another for slope stakes, another for utility offsets and another for property corners. Hub tops may be painted: the Navy Engineering Aid manual mentions red and blue tops for finished grade work, and many crews call finish-grade hubs 'blue tops' and subgrade hubs 'red tops', but practice varies. APWA's color code covers utility locate marks, not survey flagging, except that pink is the APWA color for temporary survey markings; fluorescent pink and orange are common survey ribbon colors. So don't read survey ribbon as a utility color: a blue ribbon on a grade stake does not mean water. Ask the surveyor or the PM for the staking legend at the start of the job and keep it in the truck.
field.title: Survey ribbon and stake top colors: why they vary by company
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: US Navy Engineering Aid training manual (TPUB), construction stakes; APWA Uniform Color Code chart (2021)

field.text: Tracer wire is the locate wire laid with plastic pipe. It looks like a single insulated solid copper or copper-clad steel wire (often 10 or 12 AWG) with thick direct-burial insulation in the APWA color: blue for water, green for sewer, purple for reclaimed, yellow for gas, orange for telecom. It is taped to the top of the pipe or laid beside it, and comes up at valve boxes, hydrants, cleanouts and test stations. A tracer wire test station (access point) is a small round box at grade with a lid marked 'TRACER WIRE', 'TW' or 'TEST STATION', with one or more wire ends and terminals inside; some are on hydrant or valve box adaptors. Splices use waterproof connectors (gel-filled or grease-filled caps). Gas cathodic protection test stations look similar but are for steel pipe; don't disconnect wires in them. A broken or missing tracer wire means the line may be unlocatable later; repair any damage and tell the inspector.
field.title: Tracer wire by eye: colors, test stations and where it comes up
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Underground warning tape is a plastic ribbon laid in the backfill above a utility, usually 2, 3 or 6 inches wide, in the APWA color with black printing repeated along it, such as 'CAUTION BURIED WATER LINE BELOW', 'CAUTION SEWER LINE BURIED BELOW', 'CAUTION BURIED ELECTRIC LINE BELOW', 'CAUTION FIBER OPTIC CABLE BURIED BELOW' or 'RECLAIMED WATER'. Detectable tape has an aluminum foil core sandwiched in the plastic (you can see a shiny metal layer at a torn edge), so a metal detector or locator can find it; non-detectable tape is plain plastic film. If you dig up warning tape, stop and expose the line below by hand or vacuum; the utility is usually 1 to 2 ft below the tape, but not always. Colors: blue water, green sewer and storm, purple reclaimed, red electric, yellow gas, orange telecom. Some old tapes have faded to gray or white. Replace any tape you remove during backfill.
field.title: Warning tape by eye: colors, detectable vs non-detectable
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Electronic markers (EMS marker balls, disks or full-range markers) are passive radio tuned circuits buried at fittings, valves, service ends, bends and crossings so a marker locator can find them. They come in plastic shells color-coded and frequency-coded by utility. Per Hexatronic's listing of the industry frequencies: gas = yellow, 83.0 kHz; telephone = orange, 101.4 kHz; sewer = green, 121.6 kHz; water = blue, 145.7 kHz; electric power = red, 169.8 kHz; cable TV = black and orange, 77.0 kHz; reclaimed and general purpose = purple, 66.35 kHz. Balls (about 4 inch) self-level so they can be dropped in the trench; disks are flat and set level; long-range markers are bigger. Some markers can store data (ID, depth, owner). In the trench, a colored plastic ball sitting by a fitting is a marker, not debris: leave it in place and backfill over it. Record each marker location on the as-builts.
field.title: Electronic marker balls and disks: colors and frequencies by utility
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Hexatronic, Marking and locating your network (EMS marker colors and frequencies)

field.text: The words cast into a lid are the fastest way to tell what's below. Common lettering: 'SANITARY', 'SANITARY SEWER' or 'SEWER' (sanitary); 'STORM', 'STORM SEWER', 'DRAIN' or 'DRAINS TO RIVER / DUMP NO WASTE' (storm); 'WATER' or 'W' (water valve, meter or vault); 'GAS'; 'ELECTRIC', 'HIGH VOLTAGE' or the power company name; 'TELEPHONE', 'BELL', 'TELCO', 'COMMUNICATIONS', 'CATV', 'FIBER OPTIC'; 'TRAFFIC SIGNAL', 'STREET LIGHT', 'FIRE ALARM'; 'STEAM'. Many lids also carry the city or owner name, the foundry name and sometimes the year. Fort Wayne's sanitary lid detail, for example, specifies 'SANITARY' (Neenah) or 'SANITARY SEWER' (East Jordan) lettering with closed and concealed pick holes. A lid can be wrong: frames get swapped, and old lids say only 'SEWER' even on storm lines. Confirm by what's inside, by flow and by the maps before connecting or entering.
field.title: Manhole and utility lid markings: SEWER, STORM, WATER, ELECTRIC and more
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: Fort Wayne City Utilities standard detail C-1-1, sanitary manhole frame and lid

field.text: Above ground, buried lines are often marked by posts and signs. Pipeline markers are yellow, orange or other colored posts, flat fiberglass (Carsonite style) markers or domed caps at road and fence crossings, printed 'WARNING' or 'CAUTION', the product ('PETROLEUM PIPELINE', 'NATURAL GAS', 'HIGH PRESSURE GAS'), the operator's name and an emergency phone number. Telecom and fiber routes use orange posts or 'FIBER OPTIC CABLE' signs; power uses red or yellow markers; water and sewer sometimes use blue or green posts at valves, air valves or force main crossings. A marker shows that a line is somewhere near, not exactly under the post, and not its depth. Test station posts (often with a small cap and wire terminals) on gas and petroleum lines are for cathodic protection. If you see a pipeline marker near your dig, call 811 and the operator's number on the sign; transmission lines may need a standby inspector before you dig.
field.title: Pipeline markers and marker posts: reading the signs above buried lines
field.topic: Visual ID: locate marks, survey stakes and markings
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Green PVC gravity sewer pipe (ASTM D3034, the 'SDR 35 green pipe'; 4 to 15 inch is the usual SDR range; since 2024 D3034 also covers the big sizes once made under F679) looks like this: bright to olive green outside (some makers' shades differ; older pipe can be tan, white or faded), smooth glossy wall, white or off-white inside, and a thin wall you can see at the cut end. One end has an integral bell, a visible bulge a few inches long holding a black rubber gasket; the other end is a plain beveled spigot, often with a painted or printed homing line. Common lay lengths are 14 ft (also 20 ft). Sewer OD is smaller than water pipe of the same name: about 4.215 in for 4 inch, 6.275 in for 6 inch, 8.400 in for 8 inch, 12.500 in for 12 inch. The print line runs the full length, e.g. '8 IN SDR 35 PVC SEWER PIPE ASTM D3034 PS46' plus maker, plant and date code. Look-alikes: green C900 force main (much thicker wall, CIOD size, 'AWWA C900' and a pressure class printed) and green corrugated PVC or PP (ribbed outside). Westlake notes no governing body requires pipe colors; read the print line.
field.title: Green PVC sewer pipe (SDR 35, ASTM D3034): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, ASTM D3034 and F679 combined summary; Westlake Pipe & Fittings technical FAQ: PVC pipe color coding

field.text: SDR 35 and SDR 26 PVC sewer pipe (both ASTM D3034) look almost the same: same green, same bell, and the same outside diameter, so they fit the same fittings. The only differences are wall thickness and the print line. Wall = OD divided by SDR. For 8 inch (OD 8.40 in): SDR 35 wall is about 8.40 / 35 = 0.24 in (just under 1/4 inch); SDR 26 is about 8.40 / 26 = 0.32 in (about 5/16 inch). For 6 inch (OD 6.275 in): SDR 35 about 0.18 in, SDR 26 about 0.24 in. SDR 35 is about pipe stiffness PS 46; SDR 26 is about PS 115 and is the 'heavy wall' often called for deep cuts or under roads. To check a stick in the field, read the print line ('SDR 26' or 'PS 115') or measure the wall at a cut end with a tape or caliper. Some makers use a slightly different shade for SDR 26, but never rely on color alone. Check the plans for which SDR goes where.
field.title: SDR 35 vs SDR 26 green sewer pipe: how to tell them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, ASTM D3034 and F679 combined summary

field.text: Big green PVC sewer pipe from 18 to 60 inch was made under ASTM F679, which Uni-Bell reports was withdrawn in 2024 and merged into D3034, so newer pipe prints D3034 and older pipe F679, and is classed by pipe stiffness, PS 46 or PS 115, printed on the pipe instead of an SDR. It is solid-wall: smooth inside and out, thick at the cut end, with a gasketed bell. Uni-Bell notes the older F679 'T-1' and 'T-2' wall types; you may still see those marks on existing pipe. A different family is profile-wall PVC sewer: ribbed PVC (ASTM F794, closed or open ribs running around the outside) and corrugated dual-wall PVC (ASTM F949, corrugated outside, smooth inside). Profile pipe looks like corrugated plastic storm pipe but is PVC: harder, glossier, and printed with the PVC standard. Look-alikes: black corrugated HDPE (waxy, softer, dull black), corrugated polypropylene (print says PP). Always read the print line for the standard number before ordering fittings or couplings.
field.title: Large-diameter green PVC sewer (ASTM F679, 18 to 60 inch) and profile-wall PVC: how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, ASTM D3034 and F679 combined summary

field.text: A typical PVC sewer print line reads something like: MAKER 8 IN SDR 35 PS 46 PVC SEWER PIPE ASTM D3034 12454 [plant] [date code]. Decode it: '8 IN' is nominal size (sewer OD 8.40 in). 'SDR 35' is OD divided by wall. 'PS 46' is pipe stiffness in psi at 5% deflection (PS 115 for SDR 26). 'ASTM D3034' (older 18 inch and up pipe may say F679) is the product standard. A five-digit number like 12454 is the PVC compound cell class (material properties). Then come plant number, extrusion line or shift and a production date code, which helps trace a bad batch. Gasketed pipe may also show 'F477' (gasket) or 'D3212' (joint). The line repeats every few feet along the pipe. Keep it on top when laying so the inspector can read it. If the print says DWV, D2665, F891 or 'cellular core', it is building drain pipe, not a sewer main pipe. Date code formats vary by maker; ask the supplier to decode one.
field.title: PVC sewer pipe print line: what each code means (SDR, PS, D3034, cell class, date code)
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, ASTM D3034 and F679 combined summary

field.text: C900 PVC water pipe is the thick-wall pressure pipe crews call 'C900' or 'Blue Brute' (a JM Eagle brand). Look for: blue color (white is also common), a heavy wall at the cut end, a thick integral bell with a factory-locked gasket, 20 ft lay length, and a print line like '8 IN CIOD DR18 PC235 AWWA C900 NSF-61' plus maker and date code. CIOD means cast-iron OD: about 4.80 in for 4 inch, 6.90 for 6 inch, 9.05 for 8 inch, 11.10 for 10 inch, 13.20 for 12 inch, the same OD as ductile iron, so DI MJ fittings fit. Pressure classes by DR: DR 14 = 305 psi, DR 18 = 235 psi, DR 25 = 165 psi; DR 18 is the common municipal class. NSF-61 on the print means it is certified for drinking water. Look-alikes: blue IPS PVC (smaller OD, says IPS or D2241), blue PE water service tubing (soft, coiled), blue-striped HDPE (waxy black). Read the print line to be sure.
field.title: Blue PVC water main (AWWA C900, DR 18): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Utility Pipe Supply, C900 pipe explained (JM Eagle Blue Brute data); Miami-Dade Water and Sewer, PVC C900 pipe requirements

field.text: C900 PVC is not always blue. Westlake says no governing body requires PVC colors; the industry convention is blue for potable water, green for sewer (gravity and force main), purple for reclaimed (non-potable) water, white and gray for general use. Utility Pipe Supply lists blue for potable water, green for sewer force main and purple for reclaimed water. Some utilities write color into their specs: Miami-Dade requires green for sanitary sewer and blue for potable water. White C900 is common in many areas and is perfectly good water pipe if the print says AWWA C900 and NSF-61. So in a photo: blue or white thick-wall bell pipe printed AWWA C900 is usually water; green thick-wall C900 is usually a force main; purple is reclaimed. Color can fade in sunlight and shades vary by maker. Confirm by the print line and the plans, never color alone, before you tap or connect.
field.title: White, green or purple C900 PVC: what the color means
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Westlake Pipe & Fittings technical FAQ: PVC pipe color coding; Utility Pipe Supply, C900 pipe explained (JM Eagle Blue Brute data); Miami-Dade Water and Sewer, PVC C900 pipe requirements

field.text: C900 pipe of the same nominal size has the same OD in every DR, so you tell DR 14, 18 and 25 apart only by wall thickness or print. Wall = OD / DR. For 8 inch CIOD (OD 9.05 in): DR 14 wall about 0.65 in, DR 18 about 0.50 in, DR 25 about 0.36 in. For 6 inch (OD 6.90 in): DR 14 about 0.49 in, DR 18 about 0.38 in, DR 25 about 0.28 in. For 12 inch (OD 13.20 in): DR 14 about 0.94 in, DR 18 about 0.73 in, DR 25 about 0.53 in. Pressure classes: DR 14 = 305 psi, DR 18 = 235 psi, DR 25 = 165 psi; DR 14 and DR 18 carry FM approval for fire service per the supplier data, DR 25 does not. In the field, measure the wall at a cut end with a caliper or tape, or read 'DR18 PC235' on the print line. Fire lines and some utilities require DR 14; check the spec before using leftover pipe from another job.
field.title: C900 DR 14 vs DR 18 vs DR 25: telling the wall by eye
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Utility Pipe Supply, C900 pipe explained (JM Eagle Blue Brute data)

field.text: Since the AWWA C900 revision that absorbed the old C905, C900 covers big transmission sizes too (the current standard goes to 60 inch per supplier literature) and higher DR numbers. JM Eagle Blue Brute listings show DR 14, 18, 25, 32.5, 41 and 51, in both CIOD (ductile-iron OD) and IPS (steel-pipe OD) sizing. So 'C900' on a pipe does not prove it is CIOD: look for 'CIOD' or 'IPS' on the print line. A DR 41 or DR 51 pipe (100 psi or 80 psi class) has a thin wall for its size and is used for low-pressure transmission or force mains, not normal distribution. In a photo, a big blue bell pipe with a thin wall is likely a high-DR C900; a big blue pipe with a thick wall is likely DR 18 or 25. CIOD and IPS are not interchangeable; IPS needs IPS fittings or transition couplings. Old C905 print lines may still be found on existing pipe.
field.title: Large C900 PVC (14 inch and up, DR 25 to 51) and IPS-sized C900
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Utility Pipe Supply, JM Eagle Blue Brute C900 product listings (CIOD and IPS, DR 14 to 51); Utility Pipe Supply, C900 pipe explained (JM Eagle Blue Brute data)

field.text: C909 PVCO pipe is PVC that has been stretched during manufacture to make it stronger, so it carries the same pressure class as C900 with a noticeably thinner wall. It usually comes in blue and in CIOD sizes, so it fits DI fittings like C900. Clues in the field: the bell looks like C900 but the wall at a cut end is thinner than you expect for the pressure class, the pipe is lighter to carry, and the print line says 'PVCO' and 'AWWA C909' with a pressure class (common classes 150, 165, 200 and 235 psi). Some makers stamp a brand name such as IPEX Bionax. Look-alikes: high-DR C900 (also thin wall but the print says C900 and a DR number) and IPS PVC (smaller OD). Tapping, cutting and restraint rules differ for PVCO; check the maker's guide and use restraints and saddles approved for PVCO.
field.title: PVCO pipe (AWWA C909, molecularly oriented PVC): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Purple marks reclaimed, recycled or non-potable water. You may see purple PVC (C900 or IPS gasketed), purple Schedule 40 or 80 irrigation pipe, black HDPE with purple stripes, and purple tracer wire, warning tape and valve box lids. Many makers print 'RECLAIMED WATER' or 'DO NOT DRINK' along the pipe. Westlake lists purple as reclaimed (non-potable) water, and the APWA locate color code uses purple for reclaimed water, irrigation and slurry lines; blue is potable water only. Why it matters: a cross-connection between reclaimed and potable water is a public health hazard, so never connect, tap or repair a purple line with potable fittings without the utility's okay, and keep your separation distances. Purple can fade to pinkish or gray-lavender in sun. Confirm with the print line, plans and locate marks.
field.title: Purple pipe: reclaimed or recycled water lines (PVC, HDPE, tape)
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Westlake Pipe & Fittings technical FAQ: PVC pipe color coding; APWA Uniform Color Code chart (2021)

field.text: Schedule 40 and Schedule 80 PVC are iron-pipe-size (IPS) pressure pipe used for small services, irrigation, plant piping and vault piping. Schedule 40 is usually white; Schedule 80 is usually dark gray, made gray so it can be told apart. Both have the same OD for a given size (for example 4 inch is 4.50 in OD, 6 inch 6.625 in), but Schedule 80 has a thicker wall and smaller bore. Example pressure ratings: 4 inch Schedule 40 about 220 psi, Schedule 80 about 320 psi. Joints are usually solvent-weld (glued sockets, often with purple primer stains) or threaded on Schedule 80. Print line shows size, 'SCH 40' or 'SCH 80', 'PVC 1120' material code, ASTM D1785, and NSF-pw or NSF-61 if potable. Look-alikes: gray electrical conduit (says 'ELECTRICAL CONDUIT' or UL 651), white DWV or cellular-core drain pipe (says D2665 or F891, lighter, not pressure rated). Read the print before using it on water.
field.title: White Schedule 40 vs gray Schedule 80 PVC (IPS): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: PVC Fittings Online, Schedule 40 vs Schedule 80 PVC

field.text: Gray PVC is not always Schedule 80 water pipe. Electrical conduit (Schedule 40 or 80 rigid nonmetallic conduit) is gray and is printed 'ELECTRICAL CONDUIT', 'UL 651', 'SCH 40' or 'SCH 80', often 'SUNLIGHT RESISTANT' and a wire temperature rating; it comes in 10 ft and 20 ft lengths with one belled (glue) end and uses long-sweep electrical bends. White DWV pipe (ASTM D2665) and cellular-core pipe (ASTM F891) are for gravity drains; cellular core shows a foam middle layer at the cut end and feels light. Neither conduit nor DWV is rated for pressure. Water pressure pipe says D1785, D2241 or AWWA C900 and has NSF-61 or NSF-pw. If you expose gray PVC in a trench, treat it as a possible live electric line until proven otherwise: power conduit is often in concrete-encased duct banks, and red or orange warning tape may lie above it. Call the owner before cutting.
field.title: Gray PVC electrical conduit vs white DWV pipe vs pressure pipe: telling them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: IPS gasketed PVC (ASTM D2241) is the white, blue or purple bell pipe used for irrigation mains, rural water and some private systems. It looks like C900 but is a little smaller in OD for the same nominal size, because it uses steel-pipe OD: 4 inch is 4.50 in, 6 inch 6.625 in, 8 inch 8.625 in (C900 CIOD is 4.80, 6.90, 9.05). Common ratings are SDR 21 (Class 200 psi) and SDR 26 (Class 160 psi), with thinner walls than C900 DR 18. The print line shows 'IPS', 'SDR 21' or 'SDR 26', 'PR 200' or 'Class 200', and ASTM D2241. Many cities do not allow D2241 for public water mains, so if you dig up white bell pipe on a public main, read the print before ordering repair parts: IPS repair couplings will not fit CIOD pipe and vice versa. Measure the OD or circumference to be sure.
field.title: IPS gasketed PVC pressure pipe (ASTM D2241, SDR 21 and 26, Class 200 and 160)
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: When you need repair parts for an unknown pipe, wrap a tape around it, read the circumference, and divide by 3.1416 to get the OD. Then compare. 4 inch: sewer D3034 4.215 in (circumference 13.2 in), IPS 4.50 in (14.1 in), CIOD/ductile 4.80 in (15.1 in). 6 inch: sewer 6.275 (19.7 in), IPS 6.625 (20.8 in), CIOD 6.90 (21.7 in). 8 inch: sewer 8.40 (26.4 in), IPS 8.625 (27.1 in), CIOD 9.05 (28.4 in). 12 inch: sewer 12.50 (39.3 in), IPS 12.75 (40.1 in), CIOD 13.20 (41.5 in). C900, ductile iron and DIPS HDPE share the CIOD column; Schedule 40/80 PVC, D2241 PVC, IPS HDPE and steel share the IPS column. Old cast iron and asbestos-cement pipe often fall between these numbers, so measure and give the OD to the supplier. A pi tape gives the OD directly.
field.title: Telling pipe OD systems apart with a tape: sewer, IPS, and CIOD/ductile
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, ASTM D3034 and F679 combined summary; Utility Pipe Supply, C900 pipe explained (JM Eagle Blue Brute data)

field.text: Solid-wall HDPE (polyethylene) pressure pipe is dull black with a waxy, slightly soft feel; scratches look lighter and fingernails can mark it. It has no bells: joints are butt-fused, leaving a rolled double bead of plastic all the way around at each joint, or electrofusion couplers (a sleeve with wire terminals and a fusion indicator), or mechanical fittings. Small sizes come in coils; larger sizes come in 40 or 50 ft sticks. It bends in long sweeps and floats when empty. Print line example: 'MAKER 8 IN DIPS DR11 PE4710 PC200 AWWA C906 NSF-61' plus date code. PE4710 is the material designation; DR is OD divided by wall; DIPS or IPS tells the OD system. HDPE for water often carries blue stripes; all-black can be water, sewer force main or industrial, so read the print. Look-alikes: black corrugated storm pipe (ribbed), black ABS drain pipe (hard, glossy, glue joints), black poly-wrapped ductile iron (loose plastic bag over iron).
field.title: Solid black HDPE pressure pipe: how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: HDPE pipe and conduit are often black with three or four colored stripes running lengthwise, spaced evenly so one shows from any angle, or made in a solid color or a colored outer layer. The colors follow the APWA uniform color code: blue = potable water, green = sewer and drain (often force main), purple = reclaimed water, yellow = gas, oil, steam, orange = telecom and signal, red = electric power. PPI follows APWA and recommends reserving yellow for gas piping. Black alone is used where pipe will see long sun exposure, because carbon black protects it from UV; colored pipe fades. Telecom owners also use stripe colors to tell their own ducts apart in a shared trench, so a stripe color on conduit may identify an owner rather than a utility type. Examples: gas pipe can be black with yellow stripes; PPI notes power conduit as red or black with a red stripe. Always read the print line and locate marks to confirm.
field.title: HDPE pipe stripe colors: what blue, green, purple, yellow, orange and red stripes mean
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: United Poly Systems, HDPE color code guide (APWA-based; PPI reserves yellow for gas); Plastic Pipe Institute, About HDPE conduit (types, colors, DR)

field.text: HDPE pressure pipe comes in two OD systems that look identical except for size. DIPS (ductile iron pipe size) has the same OD as ductile iron and C900: 6 inch 6.90 in, 8 inch 9.05 in, 12 inch 13.20 in. IPS (iron pipe size) has steel-pipe OD: 6 inch 6.625 in, 8 inch 8.625 in, 12 inch 12.75 in. The print line says 'DIPS' or 'IPS'. You cannot butt-fuse DIPS to IPS directly; you need a reducer or a transition fitting, and couplings, stiffeners and MJ adapters must match the OD system. Because wall = OD / DR, an 8 inch DIPS DR 11 wall is about 9.05 / 11 = 0.82 in, while 8 inch IPS DR 11 is about 0.78 in; the inside bore of HDPE is much smaller than PVC of the same name because the wall is thick. Measure the circumference if the print is worn: about 28.4 in for 8 inch DIPS, 27.1 in for 8 inch IPS.
field.title: HDPE DIPS vs IPS: how to tell the OD system
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Yellow plastic pipe in a trench is almost always natural gas or propane. Performance Pipe's gas line shows the common looks: solid yellow medium-density PE (PE2708) from 1/2 inch CTS (copper tube size, small services) up to 12 inch IPS; yellow with three black stripes (PE4710 HDPE); and black with four yellow stripes (PE4710 HDPE). Gas PE is made under ASTM D2513, which requires a 16-character code (per ASTM F2897), printed both as text and as a barcode, that identifies maker, plant, run, date, pipe type and material grade. Services are small (1/2 to 2 inch), often coiled and joined with fused or mechanical couplings, with a copper tracer wire alongside. Older gas plastic can be tan or orange-tan (some older materials are prone to cracking). If you expose, nick or scrape gas pipe: stop, don't cover it, call the gas company and 911 if it is leaking, and keep ignition sources away. Never repair gas pipe yourself.
field.title: Yellow PE gas pipe: how to recognize it (and what to do)
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Performance Pipe (Chevron Phillips Chemical) gas piping brochure, Dec 2023

field.text: Dual-wall corrugated HDPE storm pipe, best known by the ADS brand N-12, is black with deep annular corrugations outside and a smooth wall inside. Joints are an integral bell (a smooth, wider sleeve that covers the corrugations) with a rubber gasket seated in a corrugation valley on the spigot; plain-end pipe uses split or snap couplers. ADS lists sizes 4 to 60 inch, 13 ft and 20 ft lengths, soil-tight (ST, to 30 inch) and watertight (WT, to 60 inch, rated to ASTM D3212). Standards on the print line: AASHTO M252 (4 to 10 inch), AASHTO M294 (12 to 60 inch), ASTM F2306 and F2648. The print usually sits on a corrugation crest or inside the bell. Look-alikes: corrugated polypropylene (print says PP or F2881; often a lighter color), profile-wall PVC (harder, glossier), CMP (metal, rings with a magnet), single-wall drain tile (corrugated inside too). Check the specs: many agencies require WT joints in storm sewers.
field.title: Black corrugated dual-wall HDPE storm pipe (ADS N-12): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: ADS N-12 dual wall pipe product page

field.text: Single-wall corrugated polyethylene pipe (drain tile, 'black flex pipe', 'perf pipe') is corrugated both outside and inside: look into the end and you see ridges. It comes in coils (3 to 6 inch, often 100 to 250 ft) or sticks, solid or perforated (rows of slots in the valleys), sometimes with a fabric sock. Joints are snap or split couplers, not gaskets. AASHTO M252 uses letter types: Type C corrugated inside and out, Type CP perforated; Type S has a smooth interior liner (dual-wall), Type SP smooth and perforated. Dual-wall pipe is smooth inside, much stiffer and is what storm sewers and culverts use. In a photo, check the inside: ridges inside means single-wall underdrain or downspout pipe, not storm sewer pipe. Single-wall pipe crushes easily under traffic loads and deep fill. If a storm line on the plans shows HDPE but you find single-wall, flag it to the engineer.
field.title: Single-wall corrugated drain pipe vs dual-wall smooth-interior pipe
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: ADS N-12 dual wall pipe product page

field.text: Corrugated polypropylene pipe looks like dual-wall or triple-wall corrugated HDPE (corrugated outside, smooth inside, integral gasketed bell) but is made of PP, which is stiffer. Storm pipe is made to ASTM F2881 or AASHTO M330; sanitary sewer versions to ASTM F2764. Brand examples include ADS HP Storm and SaniTite HP. Clues: the print line says 'PP', 'polypropylene', F2881, F2764 or M330; the color is often lighter than jet-black HDPE (gray, white-lined or another maker color; it varies); and the walls feel harder. Why it matters: PP and HDPE are not interchangeable for fittings, couplings or repair parts, and PP sanitary pipe has its own testing rules. A 'triple-wall' PP sanitary pipe has a smooth outer wall too, so it can look like solid-wall pipe from outside; look at the cut end for the hollow corrugation core. Read the print before ordering parts.
field.title: Corrugated polypropylene (PP) storm and sanitary pipe: how to tell it from HDPE
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Ductile iron (DI) water and force main pipe has a black asphaltic outer coating over a raised, pebbly 'peen' texture on the barrel. Inside you see a gray cement-mortar lining (sometimes with a thin black seal coat) or, on sewer pipe, a special lining such as ceramic epoxy. The bell is smoothly contoured (push-on) or flanged with bolt holes (MJ), and lengths are usually 18 or 20 ft. AWWA C151 requires cast-in marks on or near the bell: maker's mark, country where cast, year, the letters 'DI' or 'DUCTILE', and the size. A sticker near the bell gives size, pressure class, joint type, lining and coating, and cast date. OD matches C900 and DIPS HDPE (8 inch is 9.05 in). Look-alikes: old gray cast iron (smooth exterior, box-like hub, lead joints, raised maker names on the barrel); steel (smooth, welded seams); black-wrapped pipe (DI inside poly encasement). Magnets stick to DI and cast iron alike; the peen texture and markings tell them apart.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe: how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: McWane Ductile, Ductile iron pipe markings: what do they mean; McWane Ductile, What did I dig up: gray iron or ductile iron pipe?

field.text: Painted marks on ductile iron pipe, per McWane: Spigot stripes on the plain end show insertion depth: two even stripes for Tyton push-on joints, one stripe on American's Fastite. Assemble until the stripe is at the bell face, and deflect only after the joint is fully home. Green paint on the bell face marks 'gauged full length' (GFL) pipe, usually 14 inch and up, meaning it can be field cut anywhere along the barrel; 12 inch and smaller is considered GFL, but measure the OD before cutting anyway. Blue paint on the bell face means a zinc coating under the topcoat (often also a 'Zinc' sticker). Red primer on the bell and spigot identifies Protecto 401 lined pipe for sewer only, often stenciled 'For Sewer Use Only': never use it on potable water. White tick marks on the bell face show foundry trims, each up to 6 inch, maximum four (24 inch). Color codes or mark numbers may match a lay schedule on complex jobs.
field.title: Ductile iron paint marks: spigot stripes, green, blue and red paint, tick marks
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: McWane Ductile, Ductile iron pipe markings: what do they mean

field.text: Ductile iron pipe of one size has the same OD in every pressure class; the wall gets thicker inside as the class goes up, so you can't tell class by looking at the outside. Find it on the sticker near the bell (size, pressure class, joint, lining, cast date) or on older pipe on stenciled paint. Current AWWA C151 pressure classes are 150, 200, 250, 300 and 350 psi. Older pipe used thickness classes such as Class 50, 51, 52, 53 and so on, often stenciled 'CL 52'; McWane notes class designations changed over the years, which can help date pipe but don't identify the material. On a cut end you can measure the wall: subtract the lining. When a spec says 'Pressure Class 350' or 'thickness Class 52', confirm the sticker before laying. Fittings (C110 full-body, C153 compact) carry their own pressure rating cast on the body, often 250 or 350 psi.
field.title: Ductile iron pressure class: finding it on the pipe
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: McWane Ductile, Ductile iron pipe markings: what do they mean; McWane Ductile, What did I dig up: gray iron or ductile iron pipe?

field.text: If you dig up a pipe that looks like a big black (or clear, white or other colored) plastic bag taped around it, it is almost always ductile or cast iron in polyethylene encasement (AWWA C105), a loose tube of 8 mil linear low-density or 4 mil high-density film used as corrosion protection in aggressive soils. The film is loose, not bonded; overlaps are taped with plastic adhesive tape at joints and every few feet. Under it you find the black asphaltic DI coating. Look-alikes: HDPE pipe (solid plastic all the way through, no iron) and tape-wrapped steel (tight, spiral-wound, bonded wrap). When you tap, repair or connect to encased pipe, cut the film neatly, then rewrap and tape any damaged or opened film per C105 and the utility's spec. Some encasement is printed with the maker, 'AWWA C105' and the film type. Don't strip it off and leave the iron bare.
field.title: Plastic-bagged ductile iron (polyethylene encasement, AWWA C105): what it looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Old gray cast iron water main, McWane's field clues: the barrel exterior is smooth (pit-cast gray iron lacks ductile iron's pebbly peen texture); the hub is box-like or square-shouldered rather than contoured; the OD can vary, even along one length; maker names may be cast raised on the barrel; and joints are packed with oakum (tarred jute twine) and sealed with a ring of poured lead at the hub face, which looks dull gray and soft. Installation date helps: before 1965 likely gray iron, 1975 and later ductile, 1965 to 1975 check other clues. The sound test is unreliable on buried pipe. Gray iron is brittle: it cracks around the circumference (circle breaks) or splits lengthwise, and old mains can break from nearby excavation, vibration or loss of support. Handle lead joints as lead work (no torch cutting, wash hands, lead rules apply). Confirm material with the utility before buying repair clamps; OD varies.
field.title: Old cast iron (gray iron) water main with lead-and-oakum joints: how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: McWane Ductile, What did I dig up: gray iron or ductile iron pipe?

field.text: Cast iron soil pipe is the black, heavy drain pipe you meet where a building sewer leaves a structure. Hub-and-spigot pipe has a bell (hub) on one end; old joints are lead and oakum, newer ones a black neoprene compression gasket inside the hub. No-hub pipe has plain ends joined by a stainless steel band coupling (a corrugated stainless shield with two or four worm-drive clamps over a neoprene sleeve). Pipe is usually marked with the maker, size, country of origin and often 'CISPI' or ASTM A74 (hub) or A888 / CISPI 301 (no-hub). It is gray iron, so it breaks under point loads and cuts with a snap cutter. Look-alikes: ductile iron (thicker, pebbly coat, much bigger bell), Orangeburg (black but soft and layered, not metal), ABS (black plastic, glued). When you tie a new PVC lateral to cast iron, use a transition coupling sized for both ODs and approved by the plumbing code.
field.title: Cast iron soil pipe on building sewers: hub and spigot vs no-hub
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Reinforced concrete pipe is gray, heavy and thick-walled (wall roughly 1/12 of the inside diameter or more), with a bell and spigot or tongue and groove at the ends. You may see one or two lift holes (Iowa DOT allows no more than two, each no more than 2-1/2 inch diameter) or cast-in lift anchors, plugged after setting. Marks are stenciled or painted inside the pipe near the tongue or spigot: class, design or spec (for example ASTM C76 Class III), date of manufacture and the maker's trademark, plus a plant code; Iowa requires marking within 24 hours of casting. Common lay lengths are 8 ft (also 4, 6, 7.5 and 12 ft depending on maker and size). A rubber gasket on the spigot means a gasketed joint; a plain stepped tongue means mortar, mastic or wrap. Look-alikes: precast manhole risers (no spigot), asbestos-cement (thin, smooth, lighter), nonreinforced concrete pipe (small, no class III-V marks). Check the class on every pipe against the plans.
field.title: Reinforced concrete pipe (RCP): how to recognize it and read its marks
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Iowa DOT Standard Specifications Section 4145, Concrete Culvert Pipe (marking and lift holes)

field.text: Some round concrete pipe has its steel cage formed in an ellipse (elliptical reinforcement) or quadrant steel, so its strength depends on which way it is turned. That pipe must be marked to show the top; Iowa DOT requires the mark at least once on the inside and once on the outside, on opposite walls. In the field you will see 'TOP' stenciled, a painted line or arrow, or a letter at the crown, and often a matching mark at the bottom. Lift holes are usually at the top too. Set the pipe so the top marks are straight up at the crown. If the pipe is rolled 90 degrees, the weak axis of the cage carries the load and the pipe can crack under fill. Horizontal elliptical (HE) pipe is easy to see because the pipe itself is oval and wider than tall; round pipe with an elliptical cage looks round, so read the marks before you set it. If marks are missing, stop and ask the supplier.
field.title: RCP 'TOP' marks and elliptical reinforcement: why the pipe must be set right side up
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Iowa DOT Standard Specifications Section 4145, Concrete Culvert Pipe (marking and lift holes)

field.text: How to tell an RCP joint by looking at the spigot: O-ring joint: a round rubber ring sits in a groove cut into the spigot; used on all sanitary and some storm RCP where leak-resistant joints are required (ASTM C443, C1628, or C361 for low-head pressure). Profile (single offset) gasket joint: the spigot has a single step, and a wedge or profile-shaped gasket is stretched onto the step; common on storm sewers and culverts. Mortar or mastic joint: no gasket; a bead of mastic, butyl rope (black, sticky) or mortar goes on the bottom half of the bell and the top half of the spigot (ASTM C990 covers butyl/mastic sealant); used on storm and culverts and on horizontal elliptical pipe. External wrap: a rubber-and-mastic band wrapped around the outside of the joint (ASTM C877). Gasketed leak-resistant joints hold at least 13 psi (30 ft of head) in the lab test. If a sanitary line shows mastic joints, question it.
field.title: Concrete pipe joints by eye: O-ring, profile gasket, mastic and external wrap
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Georgia Concrete Pipe Association, concrete pipe joints

field.text: Precast concrete drainage comes in several shapes. Round RCP: the usual circle, with bell and spigot or tongue and groove. Horizontal elliptical (HE) pipe: an oval wider than it is tall, used where cover is shallow; ASTM C507. Vertical elliptical (VE): taller than wide, used where space is narrow. Arch pipe: flat-ish bottom and arched top (ASTM C506). Box culvert: a rectangle with square or chamfered inside corners and tongue-and-groove ends, often 6 to 8 ft long sections, marked with span x rise and design (ASTM C1577 for many sizes). Three-sided or bottomless arches sit on footings. In a photo, a rectangular concrete opening at a road crossing is a box culvert or a headwall; an oval opening is elliptical pipe; a round opening is RCP. Each shape needs its own fittings, joints and bedding details. Read the stenciled marks inside each section for span, rise, design load and date.
field.title: Concrete pipe and box shapes by eye: round, elliptical, arch and box culvert
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Corrugated steel pipe (CSP, 'CMP') is identified by its metal ripples and its coating. Galvanized: zinc coating, bright and spangled when new, dull gray when older, rust-red where zinc is gone, usually at the invert. Aluminized Type 2: steel hot-dip coated in aluminum on both sides; a dull, matte silver-gray, smoother looking than galvanized. Polymer-coated (polymer laminate, for example Trenchcoat): a plastic film bonded over galvanized, usually black or another solid color, smooth to the touch. Corrugation pattern: annular corrugations are separate rings around the pipe; helical corrugations spiral along the pipe and show a continuous lock seam. Helical pipe often has re-rolled annular ends for the coupling band. Common profiles: 2-2/3 x 1/2 inch (68 x 13 mm) for smaller pipe, 3 x 1 or 5 x 1 inch (125 x 25 mm) for big pipe. Couplers include bolted annular bands, dimple bands and Hugger bands with O-rings. A magnet sticks to steel CMP.
field.title: Corrugated metal pipe (CMP): galvanized, aluminized, polymer-coated, annular vs helical
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Armtec corrugated steel pipe catalog (profiles, coatings, couplers)

field.text: Not all corrugated metal is the same. Aluminum corrugated pipe (AASHTO M196) is lighter, dull silver-white, doesn't rust red, and a magnet will not stick. Spiral rib pipe (for example Armtec Ultra Flo) has small square box-shaped ribs running in a spiral on the outside and a smooth interior, which gives better flow; from inside it looks almost smooth with a spiral seam. Structural plate pipe and arches are big (often 5 ft and up) built from curved corrugated plates bolted together on site; you see rows of bolts along the seams. Nestable pipe comes in half-round corrugated sections bolted at flanges. Pipe-arch shapes are wider than tall with a flatter bottom. In a photo, look for bolts (structural plate), a lock seam (helical CSP), rivets (older riveted annular CSP), a magnet test (steel vs aluminum) and the coating color. Check the plans for gauge, coating and coupling band before ordering repairs.
field.title: Aluminum CMP, spiral rib pipe and structural plate: how to tell them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Armtec corrugated steel pipe catalog (profiles, coatings, couplers)

field.text: Vitrified clay pipe is fired clay sewer pipe: hard, brittle, and brown, reddish-brown, orange-tan or buff in color. Older pipe is often salt-glazed with a shiny brown skin; much modern pipe is unglazed with a matte finish. Old installations (roughly pre-1960s) used short lengths, about 2 to 3 ft, with bell and spigot joints packed with mortar, jute or bituminous compound; these joints crack and let roots in. Modern VCP (ASTM C700, Extra Strength and Standard Strength) uses factory-applied compression joints (ASTM C425), usually a polyurethane or plastisol ring cast inside the bell and on the spigot, in longer lengths (often 5 to 10 ft); plain-end pipe joins with rubber bands with stainless shields. Some pipe is stamped with maker, 'ES' or 'EXTRA STRENGTH' and the standard. NCPI notes allowed joint deflection ranges from 1/2 inch per foot (3 to 12 inch) down to 1/8 inch per foot (48 inch). Look-alikes: terra cotta drain tile (no bell, porous) and RCP (gray). Use a snap cutter to cut it.
field.title: Vitrified clay pipe (VCP): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: National Clay Pipe Institute, VCP engineering manual chapter 1

field.text: Asbestos-cement pipe (AC, ACP, 'transite') is used in many older water mains and some sewers. Look for: light to medium gray color, sometimes weathered off-white or tan; a dense, cement-like surface that can look slightly fibrous where worn; a thick wall for its bore; a dull, stony sound when tapped (not a metallic ring); separate sleeve couplings with rubber rings instead of bells; and stenciled or stamped text such as 'Transite', 'Johns-Manville', 'J-M', 'Class 150' or 'Class 200', size and date. It is heavy for its size and the OD does not match PVC or DI sizes. Visual clues raise suspicion but only lab analysis confirms asbestos. Do not cut, break, saw, grind or drill it, and don't crush it with the bucket. Disturbing AC pipe can release asbestos fibers; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1101 and state rules apply, so only a crew trained for AC pipe work under those rules, with a competent person in charge (some states also require licensed workers), may cut, remove or dispose of it. Stop, keep it wet and intact, and call your supervisor.
field.title: Asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe: how to recognize it and why you must not cut it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Inspect and Test, Asbestos-cement pipe guide; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1101

field.text: Orangeburg is bituminized fiber pipe: layers of wood pulp fiber (some formulas with asbestos) soaked in coal-tar pitch. It was used for building sewers and laterals mainly from the late 1940s to the early 1970s (Ann Arbor removed it from approved materials in 1970; the Orangeburg company closed by 1974). It looks black or dark brown, dull and tarry, sometimes with a tar smell, and it is soft enough to cut with a handsaw or dent with a shovel. Joints are tapered sleeve or plain friction joints of the same material, sealed by the sticky tar, with no gasket. Failed Orangeburg is often oval or flattened, bowed up from the bottom, delaminated or blistered inside, crumbly, and full of roots at joints. Look-alikes: cast iron soil pipe (metal, magnet sticks), ABS (black plastic, hard, glued), clay (brown, hard). Replace it; don't connect new pipe to it. Treat crumbly material as possibly asbestos-containing until tested.
field.title: Orangeburg pipe (black fiber sewer pipe): how to recognize it
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: City of Ann Arbor, Orangeburg sewer piping; Wikipedia, Orangeburg pipe

field.text: Steel pipe is smooth (no peen texture), has a straight or spiral weld seam, a magnet sticks, and ends are welded, flanged, grooved, threaded or gasketed bell and spigot. Water transmission steel (AWWA C200) is usually cement-mortar lined inside and coated outside with tape wrap (black or gray spiral-wound tape), polyurethane, or cement mortar. Fusion-bonded epoxy (FBE) coating on gas and oil pipelines is often green, blue, maroon or tan, colors vary by maker. Casing pipe for bores is bare black steel with the carrier pipe inside on spacers and rubber end seals. Older gas mains can be bare or coal-tar wrapped steel. Galvanized steel water services are gray with threaded joints. If you find coated steel with a test station or cathodic protection wires nearby, it may be a gas or petroleum line under cathodic protection: don't damage the coating, and report any scrape so it can be repaired. Treat unknown steel as live gas until the owner says otherwise.
field.title: Steel pipe: bare, coated, wrapped and cement-lined (how to recognize it)
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Copper water service tube is penny-colored when cut or scratched, turns brown or green (patina) in the ground, and a magnet won't stick. Underground services are normally Type K, the thickest wall, often soft annealed in coils so it bends by hand. The Copper Development Association color code for the printed marking: Type K = green, Type L = blue, Type M = red, DWV = yellow; medical gas tube is K or L. Look for the colored ink line or incised marks with type, size and maker. Coils of Type K come in 60 or 100 ft (1/4 to 1 inch) and 40 or 45 ft (2 inch); straight lengths are usually 20 ft. Joints you'll see: flare fittings and compression (pack-joint) fittings on corp stops and curb stops, and soldered joints inside buildings. Look-alikes: lead service pipe (dull gray, soft, scratches silver), galvanized steel (gray, threaded, magnet sticks), brass (yellowish). Check whether your utility allows Type L underground.
field.title: Copper water service: Type K, L and M color codes
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Copper Development Association, copper tube types and color code table

field.text: PEX (cross-linked polyethylene) tubing is flexible, slightly translucent or colored plastic, usually red, blue, white, orange or black. Color is a convention for hot and cold inside buildings, not a rule, so read the print. The print stream gives: nominal size in CTS (copper tube size, so 3/4 inch PEX has the same OD as 3/4 inch copper), SDR 9, ASTM F876 / F877, fitting systems it is approved for (F1960, F1807, F2159 and others), a four-digit material code such as 5306 (chlorine resistance, UV resistance, then hydrostatic design stress; 06 = 630 psi), pressure ratings at temperature (for example 160 psi at 73 F), NSF-61 or NSF-pw for potable water, and a date code. For underground water services, utilities more often use blue or black PE CTS tubing (PE4710, ASTM D2737) or PEX rated for burial. Look-alikes: yellow gas PE (never use for water), black poly irrigation pipe (low pressure, insert fittings). Use stiffener inserts in compression fittings.
field.title: PEX and plastic water service tubing: how to recognize it and read the print
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: PEX House, How to read a PEX pipe print stream

field.text: Conduit you may dig into: gray PVC Schedule 40 or 80 electrical conduit (printed ELECTRICAL CONDUIT, UL 651), orange or gray smoothwall HDPE duct for telecom and fiber, red or black-with-red-stripe HDPE for power (PPI's example), and older fiber or clay duct. Multiple conduits run together in a duct bank, often held by plastic spacers and encased in concrete; some electric utilities color the top of the encasement red or lay red warning tape or a red concrete cap over it, but practice varies. Telecom duct banks may have orange tape. Ducts end in handholes, pull boxes, vaults or riser poles. Signs it is power, not water: no bells or pressure ratings, long sweeping bends, pull string inside, and cables visible at broken ends. Never cut, pry or drill an unknown conduit or duct bank: assume it is energized high voltage. Expose it carefully by hand or vacuum, support it, and call the owner and 811 if it is damaged.
field.title: Electric and telecom conduit and duct banks: how to recognize them
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Plastic Pipe Institute, About HDPE conduit (types, colors, DR)

field.text: Innerduct is smaller HDPE tubing pulled inside a larger conduit (or buried directly) to give fiber cables separate paths. It is usually orange, but also comes in other colors and with colored stripes (for example orange with a red or blue stripe) so a carrier can tell its ducts apart. Types per PPI: smoothwall, ribbed (longitudinal ridges inside to cut cable friction), corrugated (flexible, mostly inside buildings), with tracer wire, and cable-in-conduit (cable already inside). Multi-way bundles (2-way, 3-way, 4-way) are several ducts joined side by side with a web, often in different colors. Typical sizes are 1 to 2 inch, DR 9 to 17 (SDR 11 and 13.5 common), on big reels with a pull tape inside. Broken innerduct shows glass fiber cable (thin, often black or yellow jacket) inside. A fiber cut can cost thousands of dollars an hour: stop, don't splice or tape it, and call the owner. Orange locate marks and orange warning tape go with it.
field.title: Fiber optic innerduct: orange, striped, ribbed and multi-way bundles
field.topic: Visual ID: pipe by eye
field.source: Plastic Pipe Institute, About HDPE conduit (types, colors, DR)

field.text: Concrete sand (ASTM C33 fine aggregate, 'washed concrete sand', 'C33 sand', 'coarse sand') is a washed sand with grains from about 3/16 in down to fine, with very little silt or clay. By eye: tan, gray or brownish, visibly gritty with a range of grain sizes including small pebbles the size of a match head; individual grains are easy to see. Dry it pours freely and leaves little dust on your hand; damp it holds a loose shape but crumbles when poked; it drains fast and a footprint fills in at the edges. Rub some between your fingers: it feels sharp and gritty and leaves your hands almost clean. Look-alikes: mason sand (finer, smoother, more even), fill sand (dirtier, leaves a stain), screenings (angular chips and dust, packs hard). Gradation and fineness modulus need the ticket and a sieve test.
field.title: What concrete sand looks like (coarse washed sand, C33 sand)
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Mason sand (mortar sand, ASTM C144, 'masonry sand', 'plaster sand' in some yards) is finer and more uniform than concrete sand. By eye: light tan, beige or off-white, smooth-looking with no visible pebbles, grains like table salt or finer. It feels soft and almost silky between your fingers compared to concrete sand, and a damp handful molds into a smoother shape. It is used for mortar, paver joints, playground or volleyball sand, and in some places as pipe bedding for small lines. Dry it can blow around; wet it packs and drains more slowly than concrete sand. Look-alikes: beach or blow sand (very uniform, rounded, often lighter colored), silt (feels like flour and is not gritty at all), fine fill sand. Which spec it meets is on the ticket.
field.title: What mason sand looks like (fine, uniform, smooth)
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Pinch and rub test: concrete sand feels coarse and gritty, with grains you can see and feel individually, and some tiny pebbles; mason sand feels fine and smooth, closer to sugar or salt. Pour test: concrete sand forms a rougher, slightly steeper pile with visible coarse grains at the toe; mason sand forms a smooth, even cone. Color: both vary by pit, but mason sand is often lighter and more uniform. Water: concrete sand drains almost immediately; mason sand drains more slowly and stays damp longer. Hand: both leave hands fairly clean if washed; a brown stain or flour-like dust means silt or clay (fill sand or dirty sand). The supplier's product name on the ticket confirms it; an inspector's sieve test confirms the gradation if the spec requires it.
field.title: Concrete sand vs mason sand: side by side and hand test
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Bedding sand, 'shading sand' (California term for sand placed around and over the pipe up to about a foot above the crown), 'pipe zone sand' and 'utility sand' are names for whatever clean sand the spec or agency allows in the pipe zone: often concrete sand, a clean SP or SW sand, or a sand with a sand equivalent minimum (30 is common in Southern California specs). By eye good bedding sand is clean, granular, free of clods, rocks over about 3/4 in, roots and trash, and fairly uniform in color. It is placed loose, then compacted or jetted where allowed. Problems to spot in a photo: dark lumps (clay balls), rocks touching the pipe, sticks, broken asphalt. The look is not enough to prove compliance; sand equivalent and gradation come from the supplier certificate and the inspector.
field.title: What bedding sand, shading sand and pipe zone sand look like
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Fill sand (dirty sand, structural sand in some areas, 'bank sand') is an unwashed natural sand with silt and sometimes clay. By eye: tan, yellow, orange, red or brown, with fine dust between the grains. Dry it looks slightly crusty; when damp it holds a firm squeezed ball and a sharp boot print, and water soaks in slowly and may pond. Rub it wet in your palm and it leaves a muddy stain; shake a damp pat and water may come to the surface if silty. A handful in a jar of water clouds and takes a while to clear. It compacts well near optimum moisture but goes soft and pumpy when wet. Look-alikes: concrete sand (washed, clean hands), silty native soil. Whether it meets 'select fill' or 'structural fill' requirements depends on percent fines and plasticity from lab tests.
field.title: What fill sand and dirty sand look like (silty sand, utility fill)
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Natural pit or river sand has rounded to sub-rounded grains, often mixed colors (clear quartz, black, pink, tan), and feels smooth-gritty. Manufactured sand (M-sand, crushed sand, made from crushing rock) has angular, sharp grains of one rock color (gray from limestone, pink-gray from granite), more dust, and feels harsher; it packs tighter and stands steeper. Beach sand and wind-blown (dune) sand are very uniform, fine to medium, well rounded and often light tan or white, sometimes with shell bits; they run like an hourglass and do not hold a cut face when dry. Uniform blow sand (AASHTO A-3) is hard to compact without confinement. A hand lens shows grain shape best. Whether any of these meets a bedding or backfill spec is a lab and ticket question.
field.title: Natural sand vs manufactured sand vs beach or blow sand
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: 'Select fill', 'select material', 'select backfill' and 'structural fill' have no single national definition: each agency or geotech report sets limits on max size, percent fines and plasticity. In practice delivered select fill is often a sandy or gravelly soil, tan to brown or red, with some fines, that compacts into a firm, dense layer and does not get sticky or shiny when wet. In Texas and the South, 'select fill' often means a sandy clay with a low plasticity index (for example PI 6 to 20 in many building pad specs). Visual red flags: shiny, sticky clay lumps; roots, wood or trash; rocks over the size limit; dark organic soil. A photo can show whether it is sandy, clayey or rocky, but not whether it meets PI or gradation limits; check the geotech report, the ticket and the test results.
field.title: What select fill looks like (and why the name means different things)
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: 'Import' means soil brought onto the job from elsewhere, versus native (on-site) soil. In a photo, imported fill often stands out as a different color or texture from the trench wall: a uniform tan or brown sandy layer over gray clay, or red clay dumped on a sandy site. It may contain stuff from its source: gravel, brick bits, roots, asphalt pieces or seams of different colors from several loads.
