Many agencies and projects require import to be tested and certified clean (not contaminated, within spec) before delivery, and some require a source letter. Signs of a problem: odd odors, oily stains, debris, different colors in streaks, or loads that do not match. Do not place unknown import until the super confirms the source paperwork and test results.
field.title: What 'import' or imported fill looks like vs native soil
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Flowable fill (CLSM, controlled low strength material, 'slurry', 'K-Krete', unshrinkable fill, controlled density fill, lean-mix backfill) comes from a ready-mix truck as a soupy gray to tan mortar-like fluid. NRMCA CIP 17 says it is very fluid, usually over 8 in slump, self-leveling, and needs no vibration or tamping. In a photo: a flat, smooth, gray or brownish surface filling the trench wall to wall, flowing around the pipe, sometimes with a sheen of water and fines collecting on top (bleed water), and occasional bubbles if it is a high-air or foam mix. Fly ash mixes look darker gray; sand-rich mixes look tan. Look-alikes: concrete (stiffer, has coarse stone, holds a slope), drilling mud or bentonite (slick, gray-brown, does not set). Wet CLSM is caustic like concrete: wear gloves and boots and wash skin promptly. Pipe flotation is a risk; follow the plan for lifts or anchoring.
field.title: What fresh flowable fill (CLSM, slurry) looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: NRMCA CIP 17 Flowable Fill; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Set CLSM looks like a pale gray to tan weak concrete or hard sandstone with no large stones (most mixes have only sand), often with a smoother, slightly crusted top where bleed water and fines settled. NRMCA CIP 17 says excavatable mixes should stay under about 200 psi long term for a backhoe and under 50 psi for hand digging; most mixes are under 300 psi. A low-strength mix scratches with a shovel and comes out in chunks; a hot (high cement) mix rings and needs a breaker. Readiness for load is judged by how hard it is to indent once surface water and fines are scraped off. Look-alikes: lean concrete or sand-cement slurry (harder, may have stone), caliche (natural, white, irregular), old soil-cement. Only a strength test or the mix ticket confirms strength; ask before you plan to hand dig it.
field.title: What hardened flowable fill looks like and how it digs
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: NRMCA CIP 17 Flowable Fill; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Fresh: flowable fill is soupy and self-leveling with no coarse stone; concrete is stiffer (typical slump 3 to 6 in), holds a slope and shows gravel or crushed stone; sand-cement slurry ('one-sack' or 'two-sack' sand slurry in California) is sandy grout, thicker than CLSM, gray. Hardened: break a piece. CLSM is uniform fine sand and paste, crumbly to firm, often marked by a shovel; concrete shows coarse aggregate in a hard paste and rings under a hammer; sand slurry looks like hard mortar. Fly ash CLSM is darker gray and lighter weight. Old trenches filled with slurry often show a gray band under the pavement and up the sides of the pipe. The ticket names the mix (sacks of cement per yard, design psi); in old work, a core or strength test is the only sure answer.
field.title: Flowable fill vs concrete vs sand-cement slurry: how to tell them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Topsoil is the top few inches to a foot or so of natural ground, rich in organic matter. By eye: dark brown to black (darker when moist), loose and crumbly with small rounded clumps, roots, rootlets, leaves and sometimes worms. It smells earthy, like a garden, not sour or rotten. It feels soft and light underfoot, compresses and springs back a bit. Screened topsoil from a yard is uniform dark brown, with no rocks or roots, and fluffy in a pile. Topsoil belongs on top as a growing layer: it is not suitable for trench backfill under pavement or structures because it compresses and rots. Look-alikes: organic soil or peat (wetter, spongy, sour or rotten smell), black fill with cinders, dark clay (sticky and shiny, no roots). Strip and stockpile it separately where the plans call for restoration.
field.title: What topsoil looks like (dark, crumbly, roots, earthy smell)
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Dark soil in a trench wall or spoil pile can be several things. Topsoil: dark brown, crumbly, roots, earthy smell, only near the surface. Organic silt or clay: dark gray to black, soft, may smell musty or sour, smears, often deeper in low or wet areas. Peat: dark brown to black, spongy, fibers and plant bits you can see, very wet, light when dry. Black fill: dark from cinders, ash, coal, asphalt or burnt material, with a gritty or sharp texture, debris and a burnt or chemical smell. Fuel-stained soil: gray-black with an oily sheen on water and a fuel or solvent smell. Each has a different response: topsoil is stockpiled, organics are usually unsuitable, fuel smell or sheen means stop and report. When in doubt, take a sample, photo with scale and tell the super.
field.title: Topsoil vs organic clay vs peat vs dark fill: telling dark soils apart
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: WisDOT Geotechnical Manual 4-2 (organic soils, peat, marl); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: In older towns trench spoils often contain fill: mixed soil colors in streaks or lumps, broken brick (red-orange chunks), concrete pieces, asphalt slabs, cinders and coal ash (black, gritty, light), glass, ceramic, metal, wood, old pipe pieces, wire and plastic. The pile looks patchy with no consistent layers. Debris fill compresses and settles, so it is usually not reusable as trench backfill and may need to be hauled. Some old fill holds contamination: black stained soil, an oily sheen on water, odors of fuel, solvent or rotten eggs, drums, tanks, asbestos-looking pipe or insulation, medical or industrial waste. If you see those, stop work in that spot, keep people out, and call the super; do not dig through or sort it by hand. The project's contaminated-soil plan and a qualified person decide what happens next.
field.title: What spoils mixed with debris look like (urban fill, buried trash)
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Dry sand is light colored, flows freely and will not hold a cut face. Damp (moist) sand turns noticeably darker, holds a footprint and a short vertical face for a while (apparent cohesion from water films), and fluffs up: damp sand can occupy up to about 20 to 30 percent more volume than dry (bulking), which matters when measuring by volume. Saturated sand looks glossy, water pools in footprints, and it can run, boil or flow into the trench when water is moving. Drying sand at the top of a cut lightens first and may start to dribble down the face. A sand face that stood fine in the morning can ravel as it dries or slump when it gets wet. Short-term standing of damp sand is not strength: the competent person classifies the soil and the protective system, never a photo.
field.title: Wet vs dry sand: how moisture changes the look and the volume
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Bucket and pile behavior gives fast clues. Clean stone (#57, drain rock): pours like marbles, rattles, steep loose pile, no clumps, water disappears. Base with fines (Class 2, crusher run): pours in a stream with dust, damp material clumps, steep pile with a crusted skin. Clean sand: pours smoothly, slumps to a medium-angle cone, damp sand holds a rough shape. Fill sand: clumps when damp, sticks a little to the bucket, crusts. Silt: dusty dry, flows like batter when wet, slumps flat. Clay: comes out in solid chunks with cut faces, sticks to the bucket and cleats, does not flow. Peat or muck: soft, wet, flops and oozes. Rock: clatters, blocky pieces. These describe tendencies; moisture changes everything, so look at a dry and a wet sample if you can.
field.title: How sand, base, clay and clean stone behave in a bucket and pile
field.topic: Visual ID: sand, fill, slurry and spoils by eye
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: A photo can suggest what a soil probably is (clay, silt, sand, gravel, fill, organic, wet) and point out warning signs, but it cannot classify soil for trench safety. OSHA requires the competent person to classify soil as stable rock, Type A, B or C using at least one visual and at least one manual test on site, for example a thumb penetration, plasticity or dry strength test, or a pocket penetrometer or shear vane, and to reclassify when conditions change (rain, seepage, vibration, drying, cracking). Ask will never say a trench is safe, unsafe, Type A, B or C, or OK to enter from a picture. What Ask can do: describe what the photo appears to show, list the on-site tests the competent person may run, and flag things to point out to them, such as cracks, seepage, layers, old backfill or sloughing.
field.title: Can Ask classify trench soil from a photo? (No: the competent person does)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

field.text: Clay in a trench wall usually cuts clean and smooth, often leaving a shiny, polished face where the bucket teeth dragged. Colors run gray, blue-gray, brown, red, yellow or mottled. Spoil comes out in solid chunks and slabs with sharp edges rather than crumbling, and sticks to the bucket, boots and tires. Dry clay crusts and shrinks into blocky clods with cracks (desiccation cracks); dry clods are hard to break by hand. Wet clay is slick, sticky and glossy and holds footprints with smooth sides. In the OSHA visual test, soil that stays in clumps when excavated is cohesive. Look-alikes: silt (dull face, crumbles, dusty dry, gets soupy when shaken), wet sandy clay (gritty), fill with clay lumps. Feel tests (ribbon, thread, dry strength) narrow it down; classification for shoring is the competent person's call.
field.title: What clay looks like in a trench wall and spoil pile
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Hand tests for clay (USDA texture by feel and OSHA manual tests): Wet a walnut-size lump to putty consistency and squeeze it between thumb and forefinger into a ribbon. Per USDA NRCS, a ribbon under 1 in is weak, about 1 to 2 in is moderate, and 2 in or longer is strong; strong ribbons that feel smooth mean clay, gritty ones mean sandy clay. Rub a wet pinch: clay feels sticky and smooth and leaves a shine when you rub it with a thumbnail or knife blade. OSHA's plasticity test: roll a moist sample into threads about 1/8 in diameter; if a 2 in thread can be held by one end without tearing, the soil is cohesive. Dry strength: dry clay lumps break only with real force. These tests describe the soil; they do not by themselves set the OSHA soil type, which also depends on strength, fissures, water and history.
field.title: Clay by feel: ribbon, shine, sticky and the thread test
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: USDA NRCS Soil Quality Test Kit Guide, ch. 11 Soil texture by feel; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

field.text: Silt (and very fine sandy silt, loess, rock flour) has grains too small to see but it is not sticky like clay. In a trench wall it looks dull and matte, light tan, buff, gray or olive, sometimes with fine layering. Dry it is dusty and powdery and puffs under a boot; a dry lump crumbles easily between fingers. Moist silt may stand in a vertical face for a while (loess is known for this), then slab off or collapse when wet. Wet silt quickly turns soupy and quick when vibrated or walked on: it bleeds water to the surface, footprints fill with water, and spoil flows like batter. Silt is frost-susceptible and hard to compact when wet. Look-alikes: clay (shiny cut, sticky, hard dry lumps), fine sand (gritty, individual grains visible). Use the shake test to separate silt from clay.
field.title: What silt looks like in a trench (dull, dusty, turns to soup)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Rub a pinch of moist silt between your fingers: it feels smooth and floury, like talc or flour, not gritty like sand and not sticky like clay; dry silt dusts off your hands easily. Shake test (dilatancy): make a pat of moist soil about the size of a golf ball, soft but not sticky, in your open palm. Shake it hard sideways, tapping the heel of the hand. Silt or very fine sand shows water on the surface quickly and turns glossy; squeeze the pat and the water disappears and the surface dulls or cracks. Clay shows no water and no change. Silt forms only a weak ribbon (under 1 in) and threads crumble. Dry strength of silt is low: dry lumps powder with light finger pressure. These are field description tests; they do not replace the competent person's classification or lab tests.
field.title: Silt by feel: flour feel and the shake (dilatancy) test
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: USDA NRCS Soil Quality Test Kit Guide, ch. 11 Soil texture by feel; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Take a handful of moist soil. Look: can you see individual grains? Yes means sand. Rub wet: gritty means sand, floury-smooth means silt, sticky-smooth means clay. Ribbon: clay makes a long ribbon (2 in or more is strong per USDA texture by feel), silt barely ribbons, sand will not. Shake a wet pat: water rises fast in silt and fine sand, nothing happens in clay. Dry a lump on the dash or in the sun: clay dries hard and needs force to break, silt crumbles to powder, sand falls apart. Wash your hands: sand rinses off, silt rinses easily, clay smears and needs scrubbing. Most soils are mixes (sandy clay, silty sand), so describe the main part first. Never taste or bite soil near sewer or contaminated work. Classification for protective systems is the competent person's job.
field.title: Clay vs silt vs fine sand: a 60 second field check
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: USDA NRCS Soil Quality Test Kit Guide, ch. 11 Soil texture by feel; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Sand in a trench wall shows visible grains, usually tan, gray, yellow, orange or white, often in layers with slightly different colors. Clean sand does not hold together: spoil falls into a loose pile with smooth sloping sides and no chunks. Damp sand may hold a near-vertical face briefly because of moisture, then the face dries pale from the top and starts to dribble or ravel; a ledge of sand at the toe of the wall or a slope of fallen grains shows the face is moving. Wet, running sand flows into the trench and can boil up from the bottom where water is pushing in. OSHA's visual test treats soil that breaks up easily and does not hold together as granular. Look-alikes: silt (no visible grains, floury), sandy fill with debris. Classification and protective system are set by the competent person on site.
field.title: What sand looks like in a trench wall (grains, runs, dries pale)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Gravelly soils show rounded or angular stones from pea to fist size set in sand, silt or clay. Glacial till: dense, gray or brown, mixed sizes from clay to boulders, often very hard to dig and with stones that pop out of the face. River or outwash gravel: rounded stones in layers with sand, often loose and water-bearing. Colluvium on slopes: angular rock pieces in soil. Stones sticking out of the wall can fall as the face dries or vibrates; holes left by fallen cobbles and a pile of loose stones at the toe are warning signs to point out to the competent person. Gravelly soils with little fines drain and cave easily; gravel in a clay matrix may stand but sheds stones. Percent gravel, max size and fines content need a sample and lab test.
field.title: What gravelly and cobbly soil looks like in a trench wall
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Most topsoils and many natural soils are mixtures named by the USDA texture triangle: sand, loamy sand, sandy loam, loam, silt loam, sandy clay loam, clay loam, silty clay loam, sandy clay, silty clay and clay. The USDA NRCS texture by feel method: moisten soil to putty, squeeze a ribbon, note its length (weak under 1 in, medium about 1 to 2 in, strong 2 in or more), then rub a very wet pinch and judge whether it feels very gritty, very smooth or neither. Examples: weak ribbon and gritty is sandy loam; weak ribbon and smooth is silt loam; medium ribbon and neither is clay loam; strong ribbon and smooth is silty clay; strong ribbon and neither is clay. These agriculture names are common in septic and landscape work; engineering reports use USCS (CL, SM and so on) or AASHTO. Lab sieve and hydrometer tests give the exact class.
field.title: Loam, sandy loam and clay loam by feel (USDA texture classes)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: USDA NRCS Soil Quality Test Kit Guide, ch. 11 Soil texture by feel

field.text: Organic soils (organic silt and clay, OL and OH) are dark gray to black, soft and spongy, and often wet. WisDOT describes organic silt, sand or clay as dark gray to black, mostly mineral soil with about 5 to 15 percent organic matter. Signs: a musty, sour or rotten-egg smell when freshly dug (from decaying plant matter in low-oxygen water), bits of wood, roots or leaves, a weak, mushy feel that compresses and springs back, and color that may lighten as a sample dries. They shrink a lot on drying and compress under load, so they are usually treated as unsuitable under pipe and pavement. Look-alikes: wet clay (sticky, no fibers, no smell), black fill with ash (gritty), fuel-stained soil (oily sheen, fuel smell). Organic content is confirmed by a lab (loss on ignition). Report it to the super; over-excavation is the engineer's call.
field.title: What organic soil looks like (dark, spongy, musty smell)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: WisDOT Geotechnical Manual 4-2 (organic soils, peat, marl); General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Peat is soil made mostly of plant remains. WisDOT describes peat as olive green to black in its natural state and often odorous; fibrous peat is dark brown to black with visible stems, leaves, seeds, roots and twigs and is soft and spongy; woody peat has twigs, branches and even trunks; sedimentary peat is fine-textured and somewhat gelatinous when wet. NRCS splits organic material by rubbing: fibric (most fibers still recognizable), hemic (in between), sapric or muck (well decomposed, less than about a sixth recognizable fiber). In the field peat is very wet, squeezes water like a sponge, weighs little when dry, and may float. It settles badly and can produce methane and hydrogen sulfide in confined spaces and deep trenches. Report it; removal depth and replacement are an engineering decision.
field.title: What peat and muck look like (fibers, spongy, very wet)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: WisDOT Geotechnical Manual 4-2 (organic soils, peat, marl)

field.text: Marl is a soft lime-rich deposit formed in old lake beds and wetlands, common in glaciated states such as Wisconsin, Michigan and Minnesota and in parts of Florida and Texas. WisDOT describes marl as gray to white, odorous, often with small shells and some plant remains. In a trench it looks like a pale, pasty, chalky soil that smears like putty when wet and dries to a crumbly white crust; it fizzes strongly with dilute acid because it is mostly calcium carbonate. It is often found with or below peat in old wetland areas and is soft and compressible. Look-alikes: white silt (no fizz), caliche (hard cemented, dry climates), lime-treated soil (uniform, in a road subgrade). Report it like other soft organic and compressible soils; the geotech decides on removal.
field.title: What marl looks like (gray-white, shells)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: WisDOT Geotechnical Manual 4-2 (organic soils, peat, marl); Geology.com: The acid test for carbonate minerals and rocks

field.text: Caliche is soil or gravel cemented by calcium carbonate, common in arid and semi-arid areas such as Arizona, New Mexico, Nevada, Texas and California. Geology.com gives typical colors as white, gray, brown and reddish-brown. In a trench it shows as a whitish or pale band that is harder than the soil above and below, often densest at the top and weaker downward; it may start as white coatings and nodules on stones and grains and in advanced cases forms a rock-like layer over 3 ft thick. Firm caliche rings under a bucket and may need a ripper or breaker; poorly cemented caliche crumbles. A drop of dilute acid fizzes on it. Look-alikes: concrete or CLSM rubble (has paste and sand, man-made shape), limestone bedrock, gypsum-rich soil (does not fizz). Rock pay and digging method depend on contract definitions.
field.title: What caliche looks like (white, hard cemented layer in desert soils)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: Geology.com: Caliche; Geology.com: The acid test for carbonate minerals and rocks

field.text: OSHA defines fissured soil as material that tends to break along definite planes of fracture with little resistance, or that shows open cracks such as tension cracks on an exposed surface. In a trench wall it looks like clay broken into blocks or wedges by thin cracks, sometimes with shiny, polished, grooved faces (slickensides) where the blocks slid against each other, often in old expansive clays. Spoil breaks into angular blocks along those cracks rather than tearing. OSHA's drying test: dry a sample about 1 in thick and 6 in across; cracks during drying indicate significant fissures, and dry clumps that break easily into smaller clumps indicate fissured material. Fissured clay can drop blocks without warning. A photo may show cracks, but the competent person decides whether the soil is fissured and what that means for the protective system.
field.title: What fissured clay looks like (cracks, blocky, slick planes)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

field.text: OSHA treats previously disturbed soil as unable to be Type A, so spotting it matters to the competent person. Undisturbed native ground usually shows consistent layers that run level or follow the land, natural color changes, roots that thin with depth, and a firm, uniform face. Disturbed soil (old trench backfill, fill, utility crossings) shows: mixed colors in lumps and swirls, chunks of different soils jumbled together, sharp vertical boundaries (the edge of an old trench), loose or softer zones, sand or gravel bedding, warning tape, old pipes, concrete or asphalt pieces, bricks, trash, or a different smell. Water often seeps along old trench lines. In a photo, an old trench often shows as a rectangle or V of different-colored soil in the wall. Point it out to the competent person; the call is theirs.
field.title: Previously disturbed soil vs undisturbed ground: what to look for
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Layers show as bands of different color or texture across the trench wall: sand over clay, gravel lenses, silt seams, peat bands. OSHA's visual test asks the competent person to examine layers and judge whether they slope toward the excavation and how steeply. Things to look for: a weaker layer (sand, silt, gravel) under a stiffer one, which can undercut and drop the layer above; water seeping out at the top of a clay layer (a perched water line, often with orange staining); layers dipping toward the trench; thin slick seams. In a photo, use a tape or rod in the shot to show depth and thickness. OSHA's rule for layered systems is that the soil is classified by the weakest layer in many cases; that classification is the competent person's job, done on site.
field.title: Layered soils in a trench wall: what layers look like and why they matter
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Signs of water in a trench wall or bottom: dark, glistening wet bands or patches on the face; water weeping, dripping or trickling from a layer; small fans of washed sand or silt at the toe; a muddy pool or standing water in the bottom; soft, pumping ground under a compactor; sand boiling or bubbling up from the bottom; sloughing or slumping of the wall below a wet zone; and spoil that slumps and runs. OSHA's visual test includes looking for surface water, water seeping from the sides and the water table level, and the soil classification must be revised when the excavation gets wet. Submerged or freely seeping soil generally cannot be treated as Type A or B. Tell the competent person right away; dewatering and protective changes are their call. Ask cannot say a wet trench is safe.
field.title: What saturated or seeping soil looks like in a trench
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Soil color shows where water sits. Orange, red, yellow-brown and black spots or streaks (iron and manganese concentrations) mixed with gray patches (depletions where iron was removed) form a mottled look; this pattern means the soil has been saturated often enough for iron to move, typically the zone where the water table rises and falls. A uniform gray, blue-gray or greenish soil that may turn brown when exposed to air for a while suggests soil that stays saturated with little oxygen. Bright, uniform brown, red or yellow usually means well-drained soil. Mottles can be old (relict) features in some soils, so they suggest, not prove, a water level. When you see a change from brown to gray in the wall, expect water near or below that depth and plan for dewatering; borings and observation wells give the real numbers.
field.title: Groundwater clues in soil color: mottling, gray and orange (redox features)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: Onsite Installer: soil mottles and redoximorphic features; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: OSHA's visual test lists what the competent person looks for, and these are worth pointing out if they show in a photo: tension cracks parallel to the trench edge back from the top; chunks spalling off the vertical face, which can mean fissuring or moving ground; bulging, sloughing or a toe of fallen soil; layers that slope toward the trench; water on the surface, seeping from the walls, or standing in the bottom; utilities, old structures or signs of previously disturbed soil; vibration sources such as traffic or equipment near the edge; and spoil or equipment too close to the edge (OSHA requires spoil at least 2 ft back). Ask can describe these from a photo, but it cannot decide whether the trench is safe or what protective system is needed. Stop and get the competent person if you see them.
field.title: Warning signs in a trench photo to point out to the competent person
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(j)(2) (spoil at least 2 ft from the edge)

field.text: OSHA's visual test includes watching samples and spoil as they are dug. Clues: soil that comes out in clumps and holds together is cohesive; soil that falls apart and runs is granular; mostly fine-grained material points to cohesive soil, coarse sand or gravel to granular. Other spoil clues: big blocky slabs that break along shiny cracks suggest fissured clay; mixed colors, trash, brick or asphalt mean previously disturbed fill; wet, flowing spoil that spreads flat means saturated silt or sand; black, smelly spoil points to organics or contamination; white hard lumps in dry country point to caliche. Change from one kind of spoil to another tells you the ground changed and the classification may need to change. Report changes to the competent person; they run the manual tests.
field.title: Spoil pile clues: what the dirt coming out tells you
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: The thumb penetration test is one of OSHA's manual tests for cohesive soil. As OSHA describes it, a Type A soil (unconfined strength about 1.5 tons per square foot) can be indented by the thumb only with great effort, while a Type C soil (about 0.5 tsf) can be penetrated several inches by the thumb and molded by light finger pressure. The test is done on an undisturbed clump as soon as it is dug, and the soil must be rechecked if it gets wet. A pocket penetrometer or hand shear vane gives a number for the same idea. These tests need the soil in hand, done by the competent person. A photo of someone's thumb in a soil face does not tell Ask the soil type, because the force used and the condition of the sample are unknown.
field.title: Thumb penetration and pocket penetrometer: what they are (not a photo test)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

field.text: Not all black soil is organic. Natural organic soil: dark gray to black, musty or rotten-egg smell (from decaying plants in wet ground), fibers or roots, no sheen. Fuel or oil contamination: gray to black staining that may follow a layer or pipe, an oily rainbow sheen on water in the trench (organic sheens break into flakes when poked, oil sheens swirl and rejoin), a petroleum, gasoline or solvent smell. Industrial fill: unnatural colors (green, blue, bright orange or white streaks), chemical odors, slag, ash, drums. Sewage leaks: gray-black, sewage smell, toilet paper. If you suspect contamination: stop digging in that spot, keep people out and upwind, do not enter a trench with strong vapors (hydrogen sulfide, fuel vapors and low oxygen are possible), and call the super. A photo cannot confirm what it is; sampling does.
field.title: Dark or stained soil: organic vs fuel or chemical contamination look-alikes
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: On directional drilling jobs, gray or tan slick slurry showing up at the surface, in a trench, a storm inlet or a creek is usually drilling fluid (bentonite clay mixed with water, sometimes with polymers) escaping through the ground, called a frac-out or inadvertent return. It looks like smooth, shiny, gray-brown to tan mud, often oozing up through cracks or around poles, spreading in a thin film and staying slick and gelatinous rather than settling into sand and water. Natural clay in place is firm, cut, layered and not flowing. Dried bentonite forms a cracked, light gray crust. Frac-outs near water must be contained and reported under the drilling plan and permits; stop pumping per the plan and tell the driller and super. A photo can suggest a frac-out; the crew on site confirms by tracking returns.
field.title: Bentonite and drilling mud vs natural clay (HDD and bore frac-outs)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Expansive clay (high plasticity clay, gumbo, adobe, black cotton soil) can swell when wet and shrink when dry. Visual clues: wide, deep shrinkage cracks in dry ground forming polygons, often over 1/4 in wide and several inches deep; a cracked crust that curls; a 'popcorn' crumbly texture on the dry surface; shiny slickensides on faces in the trench; dark gray to black or brownish clay that is very sticky and makes a long ribbon when wet; cracked sidewalks, curbs and foundations nearby; and heaved pavement. Wet, it is extremely sticky and balls up on boots and tracks. Swell potential is measured by lab tests (plasticity index, swell tests); a photo can only raise the flag. The existing soils-behavior chunks cover how to build in it.
field.title: Expansive clay signs you can see (cracks, slick faces, popcorn surface)
field.topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Clues that a manhole is sanitary sewer: a solid lid lettered 'SANITARY' or 'SEWER' (often with gaskets or concealed pick holes to keep water out), flow at the bottom even in dry weather, a sewage odor, gray-brown wastewater, toilet paper or rags, a formed U-shaped channel with benches, and smaller pipes (8 to 15 inch common on collectors). Storm manhole clues: lid lettered 'STORM' or 'DRAIN', sometimes vented or with an open grate; dry or clear water in dry weather; leaves, sediment, trash and road grit; bigger pipes (12 inch and up, often RCP or corrugated); and nearby inlets in the gutter. A combined sewer (in older cities) mixes both. A manhole lid can be mislabeled, so use several clues and the maps. Never connect a storm drain or sump to sanitary or a sanitary line to storm. Look from the surface only; entering any manhole is permit-required confined space work with air testing.
field.title: Sanitary vs storm manhole: how to tell them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Grate inlet: a cast iron grate set in the gutter or a paved area, with a shallow box below and the outlet pipe at the bottom (no sump). Catch basin: looks the same from the top, but the box goes deeper than the outlet pipe, leaving a sump that holds sediment and water; some have a hood or trap over the outlet. Area or yard drain: a small grate (often 12 to 24 inch, sometimes plastic or green) in lawns or landscaped areas. Manhole: a round solid lid, no grate, on a round or cone-topped structure, at a junction or change in grade or direction. Junction box: a structure where pipes meet with no surface inlet, usually a square or round solid lid lettered 'STORM'. In a photo, look down through the grate: standing water below the outlet pipe means a sump (catch basin); a pipe flush with the floor means an inlet. Catch basin sumps need vacuum cleaning; full sumps send sediment downstream.
field.title: Catch basin vs inlet vs manhole: what you're looking at
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: A curb inlet takes water through an opening in the face of the curb. What you see: a long horizontal slot (the throat) in the curb, often 4 to 6 inches tall and 3 to 20 ft long, sometimes with a cast iron curb hood or face plate; a depressed gutter in front of the opening so water drops in; and behind the curb, in the sidewalk or parkway, a concrete top slab with a round or square cast iron manhole lid (lettered 'STORM') for access. Combination inlets also have a grate in the gutter in front of the curb opening. Many cities add a medallion or cast message: 'NO DUMPING, DRAINS TO RIVER' or a fish symbol. In a photo, a slot in the curb with a lid behind it is a curb inlet; a grate only is a grate inlet. Curb inlets are storm structures; nothing from a sanitary line should ever enter them. Look out for missing hoods: a person or child can fit through some throats.
field.title: Curb inlet by eye: throat, hood, top slab and medallions
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Small boxes at the property line are easy to mix up. Sewer cleanout: a small round lid (about 6 to 10 inch) cast 'CO', 'C.O.', 'SEWER' or 'CLEANOUT', or a bare plastic cap at grade; under it a 4 or 6 inch riser with a threaded plug. Water meter box: a rectangular or round plastic, concrete or iron box (often 12 x 17 inch or bigger), lid 'WATER METER' or 'WATER', with a reading lid or radio antenna hole. Curb stop box: a tiny round lid (about 2 to 3 inch) on a narrow riser, sometimes with a pentagon plug, marked 'WATER' or 'W'. Irrigation valve box: green plastic (purple for reclaimed), rectangular or round, often marked 'IRRIGATION'. Gas: no small box at the curb in many areas; a gas curb valve box may say 'GAS', often painted yellow. Electric or telecom pull box: gray polymer concrete, lettered 'ELECTRIC', 'TELEPHONE', 'CATV', 'FIBER'. Read the cast or molded word first.
field.title: Lateral cleanout box vs water meter box vs irrigation box: telling small lids apart
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Round lids around 5 to 8 inches across in the street or sidewalk are usually valve boxes. Water valve box: cast iron lid lettered 'WATER' or 'W', sometimes painted blue; below is a 5-1/4 inch shaft down to a 2 inch square operating nut, 3 to 7 ft deep. Gas valve box: lid lettered 'GAS', often painted yellow or with a yellow ring; below, a gas valve that must only be turned by gas company personnel. Sewer force main valve: 'SEWER' or 'S', sometimes green. Reclaimed water: 'RECLAIMED' or purple. Monument boxes (survey control points) have lids marked 'MONUMENT', 'SURVEY' or a city benchmark name; don't disturb them. Fire service or fire line valves may say 'FIRE'. Clues: water valves line up along the main near hydrants and tees; gas valves are near regulators and branch points. If the lid is unmarked, look down with a light, then check the maps. Never operate a valve you don't own.
field.title: Water valve box vs gas valve box vs curb box: small round lids in the street
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Vaults are big rectangular or square precast concrete boxes with an access hatch or several lids at grade. Clues to what's inside: an aluminum or steel diamond-plate hatch (single or double leaf, often with a lifting handle and lock, sometimes brand-stamped like Bilco or Halliday) is typical of water meter, PRV (pressure reducing valve), backflow and air valve vaults; vent pipes with screened goosenecks nearby suggest an air valve or PRV vault; a vault next to a lift station holds the pump discharge valves; vaults lettered 'ELECTRIC', 'HIGH VOLTAGE' or with grates in the sidewalk are power vaults (often hot and vented); 'TELEPHONE' or 'BELL' vaults hold cable splices. Hatch rating matters: sidewalk hatches aren't for traffic. Every vault is a confined space; many can hold low oxygen, hydrogen sulfide or flammable gas. Don't enter without the permit, air test and ventilation your program requires, and never enter an electrical vault.
field.title: Precast vaults by eye: meter, PRV, air valve and electrical vaults
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: A sewage lift (pump) station is usually a small fenced site with: one or more round or square wet well lids or aluminum hatches (often lettered 'WET WELL' or 'LIFT STATION'); a separate valve vault with check and plug valves; a control panel on a pedestal or rack with a red or amber alarm light on top (a flashing light means high level or pump failure); a vent pipe with a screened gooseneck; electric service and often a generator or a generator receptacle (manual transfer switch) for portable backup; and sometimes an odor control unit or chemical feed. Wastewater stations smell of sewage and H2S. A grinder pump station for one house is much smaller: a fiberglass or HDPE basin with a green or black lid at grade and a small panel on the house. If you see the alarm light on, call the utility. Wet wells are permit-required confined spaces with H2S, explosive gas and drowning hazards; lock out pumps before any work.
field.title: Sewage lift station by eye: wet well, panel, alarm light and generator
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Pull boxes and handholes are small underground enclosures where conduit runs are pulled and spliced. They are commonly gray polymer concrete (Quazite is a well-known brand) or plastic, rectangular (from about 12 x 12 inch to 4 x 8 ft), with a bolted lid. The lid logo tells the use: catalog cover logos include ELECTRIC, HIGH VOLTAGE, LIGHTING, STREET LIGHTING, TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC SIGNAL, CONTROLS, TELEPHONE, COMMUNICATIONS, C.A.T.V., FIBER OPTICS, GROUND and WATER. The lid is also marked with its load tier under ANSI/SCTE 77: Tier 5 (5,000 lb design, sidewalks), Tier 8 (8,000 lb), Tier 15 (15,000 lb, driveways and parking lots with occasional vehicles) and Tier 22 (22,500 lb, occasional heavy vehicles). None of these tiers is for full-time roadway traffic. If you need to put a box in a drive lane, use a box rated for it per the spec. Treat every electric box as energized; don't open it.
field.title: Electric pull boxes and handholes: polymer concrete lids and tier ratings
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: Hubbell Quazite underground enclosures catalog (ANSI/SCTE 77 tiers, cover logos)

field.text: Telecom and cable TV structures you'll see: green or beige pedestals (short posts or boxes about 1 to 4 ft tall) holding cable splices and service drops, often stickered with the company name; larger metal cabinets on concrete pads (fiber or DSL equipment, sometimes with air vents and batteries); and handholes or vaults with lids lettered 'TELEPHONE', 'BELL', 'TELCO', 'COMMUNICATIONS', 'CATV', 'FIBER' or the carrier's name. Fiber vaults often have large polymer or iron lids in pairs. Locate marks near these are orange; buried cable or innerduct may be orange or black with orange stripes. Don't move, open or back into pedestals; they often sit right on the property line where laterals and services cross. If you damage one, call the number on the sticker and the 811 center. A pedestal close to your trench route usually means a service drop crossing your trench; pothole it.
field.title: Telecom pedestals, cabinets and handholes: how to recognize them
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Pad-mounted transformers are green (sometimes gray or tan) locked steel cabinets on a concrete or fiberglass pad, with 'DANGER HIGH VOLTAGE' or 'WARNING' stickers and an ID number. Smaller green or gray boxes nearby are switchgear, junction cabinets or secondary pedestals. Underground power vaults show up as steel or concrete lids lettered 'ELECTRIC', the utility's name or 'HIGH VOLTAGE', sometimes vented, and sidewalk grates that let heat out. Primary and secondary cables run out of the pad in conduits, so there are always buried lines all around a transformer, often shallower than you expect. Keep equipment, spoil and stockpiles off pads and lids, and keep the clearance in front of doors your utility requires. Never open, enter or dig under these; smoke, a buzzing noise or a burning smell from a vault means call 911 and the utility and keep people back. Red locate marks will run to and from every transformer.
field.title: Electric transformers and vaults: how to recognize them and stay clear
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Gas facilities you'll see on utility jobs: district regulator stations, either above ground (a fenced set of steel pipes, valves and regulators painted gray or yellow, often with a vent stack and signs) or below ground in a vault with lids lettered 'GAS' or 'REGULATOR'; gas valve boxes (small round lids 'GAS', often yellow); service risers coming up beside buildings to the meter, usually yellow-coated or bare steel, with an anodeless riser where the plastic service turns up; and pipeline markers and test stations along transmission lines. A hissing sound, a rotten-egg smell (mercaptan), dead grass, bubbling in puddles or blowing dust near a gas line can mean a leak. If you hit or suspect a gas leak: stop, shut off equipment if it's safe, evacuate upwind, no smoking, phones or switches near the leak, call 911 and the gas company. Never try to shut a gas valve or crimp a line yourself.
field.title: Gas structures by eye: regulator stations, meters and gas valve boxes
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: To identify an unknown lid or structure in the field: 1) Read the casting: utility word (SEWER, STORM, WATER, GAS, ELECTRIC, TELEPHONE), owner name or initials, foundry and year. 2) Check the shape and size: big round (24 inch and up) is usually sewer, storm, electric or telecom manhole; small round is a valve, curb stop or cleanout; rectangle is a meter, pull box, handhole, vault or inlet. 3) Check the color and material: blue, yellow, green, purple or red paint follows the APWA colors on many systems; gray polymer concrete is usually electric or telecom. 4) Look at location: in line with hydrants (water), at gutters (storm), at property lines (services), at transformers (electric). 5) Look down without entering: flow, smell, cables, valves. 6) Compare with locate marks and the plans or GIS maps. 7) Still unsure: call the city or 811. Never open or enter electric, gas or telecom structures, and never assume a mislabeled lid is right.
field.title: Who owns this lid? A step-by-step way to identify a utility cover
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: When precast manhole parts arrive, here's what each looks like. Base section: a round section with a cast floor, often with pipe openings and rubber boots or flexible connectors already cast in, and sometimes a formed invert channel. Riser: a plain round ring (commonly 48 inch inside diameter; 60 and 72 inch for big pipes or deep holes) with tongue and groove or gasketed ends, in heights of about 1 to 4 ft, often with steps cast in (orange or gray plastic-coated steel rungs). Cone (reducer): tapers from riser diameter to the 24 to 32 inch frame opening; an eccentric cone has one straight vertical side over the steps, a concentric cone tapers evenly all around. Flat top slab: a thick round lid with an offset opening, used where depth is too shallow for a cone. Adjusting rings: thin concrete, HDPE or rubber rings (2 to 6 inch) to bring the frame to grade. Check each piece's stenciled ID against the shop drawings and set the steps in line with the opening.
field.title: Precast manhole sections by eye at delivery: base, riser, cone, flat top, rings
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Older sewers and storm drains (often pre-1960s) have structures built of red clay brick or concrete block laid in mortar instead of precast rings. From inside you see courses of brick corbelled inward near the top to form a cone, mortar joints, sometimes a plastered surface, and pipes grouted into the walls; steps may be cast iron rungs set in the brick. Problems to look for: missing mortar, loose or fallen bricks, roots and groundwater coming through joints (infiltration), corroded steps, and H2S damage in sanitary manholes. Brick structures can collapse when you dig next to them, cut into them for a new pipe or run heavy equipment close by; support the excavation and don't undermine the base. Many utilities rehab them with liners or coatings or replace them with precast. Steps in old manholes may be unsafe; use a ladder and fall protection per your confined space program, never trust old rungs.
field.title: Old brick and block manholes and inlets: what they look like and what to watch
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Not every lid in a yard or parking lot is a public sewer manhole. Septic tank lids: rectangular or round concrete lids or green or black plastic risers with screwed-down covers, often two (inlet and outlet ends), about 2 to 4 ft apart, in a yard on rural or suburban lots; a distribution box and drain field nearby. Grease interceptor (grease trap) lids: usually behind restaurants, two or three cast iron lids in a row over one big tank, sometimes lettered 'GREASE TRAP' or 'GREASE INTERCEPTOR', with a strong rancid smell. Sampling or control manholes for businesses may be lettered 'SAMPLING'. Public sewer manholes are round, 24 inch or bigger, lettered with the city or 'SANITARY' and line up along the street or easement. Private structures belong to the property owner, and their condition is the owner's job. All of these can hold toxic gas and are deep enough to drown in: never stand on a broken lid, and keep lids closed and secured.
field.title: Septic tank and grease interceptor lids vs sewer manhole lids
field.topic: Visual ID: structures and lids by eye
field.source: General field practice and manufacturer literature; varies by maker, utility and region

field.text: Asphalt (blacktop, AC, HMA, bituminous) is black when new and fades to gray; surface shows small stones held in a black binder, no regular joints, and edges that crumble or ravel. It is flexible, so it ruts, shoves, and cracks in alligator patterns. Concrete (PCC, Portland cement concrete) is light gray to white, sometimes tan, with straight sawed or tooled joints every 10 to 20 ft on roads (closer on sidewalks), broom or tined texture, and cracks that are straight or form corner breaks; edges break in chunks, not crumbs. Check a cut edge: asphalt shows black throughout; concrete shows gray paste with stone. Watch for composite pavements: asphalt overlay on old concrete or brick, which shows reflective cracks in a grid pattern on the asphalt. Thickness and layers show only in a core or sawcut.
field.title: Asphalt vs concrete pavement: how to tell from a photo
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Freshly placed hot mix asphalt is deep black and glossy with a uniform texture, steams on cool days, and smells strongly of hot asphalt. Behind the paver it may be over 250 F; plant mixes are typically produced around 275 to 325 F (warm mix lower). The surface is soft enough to dent under a boot until rolled and cooled. Segregation shows as coarse, rough, open-textured streaks or patches; bleeding or flushing shows as shiny, sticky, binder-rich spots; tearing behind the screed shows as torn, open streaks. A sheen with a strong diesel smell can mean release agent overuse. Hot mix causes serious burns: wear long sleeves, gloves and boots, stay clear of the screed and the truck bed, and cool burns with water right away, never by peeling off stuck asphalt. Exact temperature and mix type come from the ticket and a thermometer.
field.title: What fresh hot mix asphalt looks like (and burn safety)
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Aged asphalt turns from black to medium or light gray as the binder oxidizes in sun, and the surface loses fine material so the stones stand out (raveling), giving a rough, pebbly look. Common distresses visible in a photo: alligator or fatigue cracking (interconnected cracks like a reptile hide, usually in wheel paths, a sign of base or subgrade failure), block cracking (large rectangles from age), longitudinal and transverse cracks, potholes, rutting in wheel paths, shoving near stops, and patches of different colors. Crack sealant shows as black rubbery bands or 'tar snakes'. Water often pumps up fines through cracks, leaving light-colored stains. These signs help explain why a pavement is failing; the pavement section and base condition need a core or cut to confirm.
field.title: What old and aged asphalt looks like (gray, raveling, cracked)
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Fresh plastic concrete is gray, wet-looking and glossy, and may show bleed water as a thin sheen on top shortly after finishing. Once set, the surface goes dull gray, then lightens as it dries, often with darker damp patches over the first days. A white or tinted coating means curing compound was sprayed. Cured, sound concrete is uniform light gray with crisp joints and edges; old concrete may be darker, stained, or show exposed aggregate where the paste wore off, scaling (flaking top layer), spalling at joints, map cracking, rust stains from corroding steel, or efflorescence (white powdery or crusty deposits). Wet cement and fresh concrete are caustic: cement burns can be severe and painless at first, so wear gloves and boots, keep it off skin and out of eyes, and wash it off promptly. Strength and age come from the mix ticket and cylinder or core tests, not the look.
field.title: What fresh, cured and old concrete looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: A chip seal (seal coat, oil and chip, tar and chip) is a surface treatment, not new pavement: the crew sprays asphalt emulsion on the road and spreads single-size stone chips that are rolled in with a rubber-tire roller and later swept. By eye: a rough, uniform, stony surface where you see individual chips (often 1/4 to 1/2 in) side by side, usually the color of the stone (gray, tan, red, brown) rather than black, unless a fog seal was sprayed over it. Fresh chip seal has loose chips that fly from tires and collect along the curb; over time the chips embed and the surface darkens. Chips missing in patches show bare black binder; bleeding shows shiny black wheel paths. Look-alikes: open-graded friction course (porous asphalt), slurry seal (smooth and sandy). Under a chip seal there is usually old asphalt or a gravel road.
field.title: What a chip seal looks like (stones glued on with emulsion)
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: Ergon Asphalt & Emulsions field guide: Chip seal defined; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Slurry seal and micro-surfacing are thin layers of asphalt emulsion, fine aggregate, mineral filler (cement or lime), water and additives spread with a squeegee box. Caltrans notes that the mix darkens as it breaks and cures, and a rule of thumb is that it can open to traffic once it has turned black; a fresh mix is brownish. Caltrans Type I aggregate is finest (passing the #4 sieve), Types II and III go up to 3/8 in, with Type III the coarsest. By eye cured slurry looks smooth, sandy and dark black to charcoal, without visible large stones, with a fine sandpaper texture, and it fills small cracks; you often see drag marks at the edges and a lip at joints. Over time it wears gray and the old pavement cracks may reflect through. Look-alikes: sealcoat (smoother and paint-like), chip seal (rough single-size chips).
field.title: What a slurry seal or micro-surfacing looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: Caltrans Maintenance Technical Advisory Guide ch. 8 Slurry seals; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Sealcoat (pavement sealer, refined coal tar or asphalt emulsion based, often with fine sand) is a thin black paint-like coat brushed or sprayed on parking lots and driveways. It looks very black, even and smooth, with a slight sheen when new, and it wears off first in traffic lanes and turns gray. It has no visible aggregate beyond fine sand. Coal tar sealers have a strong tar odor and are restricted in some states and cities. A fog seal is a light spray of diluted emulsion on roads or shoulders (often over chip seals) that darkens the surface without adding texture. A slurry seal is thicker, sandy and has visible fine aggregate. None of these add structural strength; an asphalt overlay or patch is a different layer you can see in a cut.
field.title: Sealcoat and fog seal vs slurry seal (parking lot black coat)
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Interlocking concrete pavers are uniform molded units, usually about 2 3/8 in (60 mm) thick for patios and 3 1/8 in (80 mm) for streets and driveways, with crisp or chamfered edges, consistent color (often dyed), a slightly sandy face and sand in the joints. Clay brick pavers are fired brick: red, brown or buff, denser and slightly irregular in color, often with rounded edges and older patterns in historic streets. Stone pavers (granite setts, cobbles, flagstone) are natural, irregular and heavy. Under concrete pavers you usually find 1 in of bedding sand (often concrete sand) over a compacted aggregate base; permeable pavers have open joints filled with small chips (#8 or #89) over clean stone layers. Mark pavers before removal, and save and reinstate them per the plans; replacement colors rarely match.
field.title: What pavers look like: concrete pavers, clay brick and stone
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: A typical road cut shows, top to bottom: asphalt (black) a few inches to a foot thick, often in two or more lifts with visible lines between them and sometimes old layers or a buried chip seal; aggregate base (gray or tan dense-graded rock with fines, Class 2, crusher run, ABC); sometimes a subbase (coarser rock, pit run, sand or recycled material); then subgrade (native soil or fill). Old streets may show concrete or brick buried under the asphalt, or a gravel road base under a thin surface. A thin or missing base, black and wet subgrade, or base contaminated with clay explains pavement failure. Measure each layer with a tape on a fresh, straight face for restoration: most agencies require matching or exceeding the existing section. The plans and permit define the restoration section.
field.title: What you see under pavement in a cut: asphalt, base, subbase, subgrade
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: A sawcut edge is straight, vertical and clean, with smooth, slightly grooved faces where the blade cut, stones sliced flat through their middle, and often a gray slurry stain or dried white dust line beside it from wet cutting. A broken or torn edge (from a breaker, bucket or plate) is jagged and irregular, leans or undercuts, has stones pulled out rather than cut through, and shows cracks running back into the slab. Many permits require straight sawcut edges, often set back from the trench wall (a T-cut), so that the patch bonds and the cut does not unravel. If edges were broken during digging, recut them before paving. Concrete and asphalt cutting produce respirable crystalline silica: use water to suppress dust or a vacuum system and follow the silica plan.
field.title: Sawcut edge vs broken edge in asphalt or concrete
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Rebar shows as round steel bars with raised ribs (deformations), usually 3/8 to 3/4 in diameter in slabs, in a grid or running lengthwise, often at mid-depth or near the bottom in sidewalks and driveways, near top and bottom in heavier slabs. Fresh cut ends are bright steel; old ones are rusty brown. Welded wire mesh (WWF) is thin smooth wire in a square grid, often 6 by 6 in, frequently found lying near the bottom where it was not lifted. Dowel bars at transverse joints are smooth, about 1 to 1 1/2 in thick, about 18 in long; tie bars along longitudinal joints are ribbed. Post-tensioned slabs have plastic-sheathed cables: never cut into a PT slab without engineering approval because a released tendon can whip violently. Rust staining and cracked concrete over a bar line show corroding steel. Ticket and plans confirm reinforcement.
field.title: Concrete with rebar or wire mesh: what it looks like in a cut or break
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Fiber-reinforced concrete contains short fibers mixed into the batch. ACI describes synthetic microfibers (very fine, 0.01 to 0.3 mm diameter, 3 to 50 mm long) used mainly against plastic shrinkage cracking, and synthetic macrofibers (0.3 to 1.0 mm, 12 to 65 mm long, stick, rope or tape shapes) used for post-crack strength. In the field, fresh or broken concrete with fibers shows thin white, gray or colored plastic strands sticking out of fractured faces and a fuzzy or hairy surface where fibers poke through, especially in broom finishes; macrofibers look like short stiff plastic sticks. Steel fibers look like short wires, often with hooked ends, that rust to brown specks at the surface. Fibers hold broken pieces together, so demolition leaves a frayed edge. Fiber type and dosage come from the batch ticket.
field.title: Concrete with fibers: what fiber-reinforced concrete looks like
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: ACI FAQ: synthetic microfibers and macrofibers; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Liquid membrane curing compound (ASTM C309) is sprayed on fresh concrete to hold in moisture. ASTM C309 Type 1 is clear or translucent, Type 1-D has a fugitive dye (often red, pink or blue) so the crew can see coverage and that fades in days, and Type 2 is white pigmented, which also reflects sun and is common on highway paving. In a photo: a uniform white or milky film on new pavement, or a pink or reddish tint fading over the next days, or a slight sheen if clear. Streaks, bare patches and puddles mean uneven spraying. White curing compound can be mistaken for efflorescence or concrete dust, but it is even and covers the whole surface. Curing compounds can interfere with bonding of later coatings or patches; check the spec before overlaying.
field.title: Curing compound: white, clear or red-tinted coating on new concrete
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Hot mix patches are placed hot and compacted: they look like the surrounding asphalt but darker and fresher, with crisp edges if sawcut, a tight, smooth, rolled surface, and they become hard within hours as they cool. Cold patch (stockpile patch, cold mix, bagged patch) is made with cutback or emulsion binder: it looks loose, dull black to brown, often with rounded or pea-size coated stones; a CDOT study noted one proprietary mix 'resembles coated pea gravel'. Cold patch stays soft and sticky in warm weather, can be dented with a boot, smells of solvent or oil, and gets shoved, pushed out or picked out by tires; feathered edges wear away. CDOT also found patches lasted longer when edges were squared, holes cleaned and dry, and tack used. Many permits allow cold patch only as a temporary patch until a hot mix restoration.
field.title: Cold patch vs hot mix patch: how to tell them apart
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: Colorado DOT research report 1993-9: cold patch materials evaluation; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Utility trench patches show as long rectangles or strips of different-colored pavement: darker newer asphalt, or concrete in asphalt, with straight sawcut edges. A T-cut patch shows a wider top layer that laps a few inches to a foot past each trench wall onto undisturbed pavement. Problem signs in a photo: a dip or bowl along the patch (settled backfill), a bump (patch too high or heaving), cracks along the edges (poor tack, edge breakdown), raveling or pushed patch (cold patch or low density), water ponding over the patch, and alligator cracking inside it. Settlement often means backfill was not compacted in lifts. Agencies may require repair within a warranty period. Photos with a straightedge or level show how much it settled.
field.title: What a trench patch or utility cut patch looks like (T-cut, settlement)
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Many older streets have brick, granite block or concrete under one or more asphalt overlays. Signs before you cut: reflective cracks in the asphalt in a straight grid (concrete joints every 10 to 20 ft) or a fine rectangular pattern (bricks or blocks), crown or curb line that looks too high, and potholes showing red brick or gray concrete at the bottom. In a sawcut, buried brick shows as a row of red rectangles on a sand or concrete bed; buried concrete shows a gray slab, often 6 to 9 in thick, possibly with dowels. This changes cutting (deeper sawcut, breaker), hauling (heavier, recyclable or regulated debris) and restoration (some cities require reinstating brick). Note it on the daily report and tell the super, since it can be a changed condition.
field.title: Old brick or concrete street under asphalt: spotting buried pavements
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Pervious concrete looks like gray popcorn or rice cake: coarse aggregate (often #8 or #89 size) glued together with thin paste, with visible holes between stones and no sand in the surface. Water poured on it disappears immediately. Porous asphalt looks like open, coarse, black asphalt with visible voids and little fine material; it also swallows water. Both are usually placed over a deep bed of clean stone (often #57 or #2) wrapped or underlain by fabric, which is a stormwater storage layer. In a cut you see the open-graded surface, then a choke course and clean stone reservoir. Clogged pervious surfaces turn smooth and stained and pond water. Cutting into these requires matching the layers and keeping fines out of the stone; check the stormwater plan for repair details.
field.title: Pervious concrete and porous asphalt: what they look like
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Black rubbery bands along cracks are crack sealant or crack filler (hot-poured rubberized asphalt), not a defect themselves; they can be shiny when new and soft in heat ('tar snakes'). In concrete, joints may be filled with black or gray silicone or hot-poured sealant, or preformed compression seals; missing sealant lets water and grit in. White or yellow lines are paint or thermoplastic markings; thermoplastic is thick, raised slightly and has glass beads that sparkle at night. Utility locate marks are spray paint dashes, arrows and letters in APWA colors (red electric, yellow gas, orange communications, blue water, green sewer, purple reclaimed, pink survey, white proposed excavation). Do not confuse locate marks with pavement markings or old marks; locates must be current under your ticket.
field.title: Crack sealant, joint sealant and paint markings vs pavement defects
field.topic: Visual ID: pavements, surfaces and placed materials
field.source: General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

field.text: Water main gate valves (resilient wedge, AWWA C509 or C515) are set plumb with the operating nut straight up, on firm bedding or a support block so the valve doesn't settle and load the pipe. Common practice: restrain the valve per the plans (MJ restraints or thrust blocking); install the valve box (two- or three-piece adjustable cast iron screw or slide type) centered over the nut, supported on its own base or a box adaptor so it doesn't rest on the valve bonnet or the pipe; adjust the box top to final grade (flush in pavement); install an extension stem if the nut is deeper than the utility's maximum (often a few feet below grade, check yours); and check that a valve key drops onto the nut without binding. Note the turning direction (open left or open right) the utility uses; it varies. Operate fully before backfill. Record valve location ties.
field.title: Gate valves: setting and valve boxes
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Butterfly valves (AWWA C504) are common on larger water mains (often 16 inch and up) because they're shorter and lighter than large gate valves. Field points: the disc swings into the pipe when opened, so make sure adjacent fittings or tapping sleeves don't block it; install with the actuator (gear operator) oriented as the plans show; support large valves on a concrete pad or blocks; set valve boxes or vaults per the detail; and never use a butterfly valve as the test head against more than its rated differential pressure (American Water's spec notes test pressure must not exceed the rated pressure of closed resilient-seated gate or butterfly valves in the test). Count turns to open and record them. Follow the maker's installation guide.
field.title: Butterfly valves and large valves
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: American Water specification 33 01 10.13, Pressure Leakage Tests

field.text: Dry-barrel fire hydrants (AWWA C502) are set on a hydrant lead (branch) from the main, with an auxiliary gate valve on the lead so the hydrant can be shut off. Common setting rules from utility standard details: set plumb; set the bury depth so the breakaway (traffic) flange is a small distance above finished grade (many standards say about 2 to 6 inches; check yours); face the large pumper nozzle toward the street or as the fire department requires; restrain the lead and hydrant shoe (restrained joints or thrust block against the shoe back, not covering the drain holes); place clean drain stone around the hydrant shoe so the barrel drains after use, and keep concrete off the drain holes; where groundwater is high, the utility may require drains plugged. Check clearances from curbs, sidewalks and obstructions per local fire code.
field.title: Fire hydrants: setting basics
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Small water services connect to the main with a corporation stop (AWWA C800), either threaded directly into the main or into a service saddle. On PVC main, use a saddle with a wide band or double strap designed for PVC, or direct-tap only if the pipe maker and utility allow it for that DR and size (Uni-Bell publishes direct-tapping guidance with limits on DR, pipe size and corporation size). On ductile iron, direct taps are common in thicker pipe; saddles otherwise. Field practices: tap on the side of the main (often between the 10 and 2 o'clock position, not the top or bottom); keep taps apart from each other and from joints by the minimum the utility sets; use a tapping machine with the right cutter for the pipe material and keep the coupon; use the right threads (AWWA CC taper) and thread tape or sealant per specs. Check your utility's details.
field.title: Water service taps: corporation stops and saddles
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: AWWA C800 scope; Uni-Bell tapping guidance; utility standards

field.text: A wet tap connects a new main to a live main without shutting it down, using a tapping sleeve and tapping valve (TS&V) and a tapping machine. Steps in common practice: expose and clean the main, confirm its OD and material so the sleeve fits; install the sleeve centered and level, tighten bolts evenly to the maker's torque; restrain or thrust-block the sleeve per plans; bolt on the tapping valve; pressure test the sleeve-valve assembly before tapping (American Water's spec: test at the required pressure with no pressure drop in 15 minutes); mount the tapping machine, open the valve, cut, retract the cutter with the coupon, close the valve and remove the machine. Disinfect the sleeve interior and cutter per AWWA C651 (swab with hypochlorite solution). The new main can then be connected to the tapping valve. Follow the utility's procedure; many require their own crew or witness.
field.title: Wet taps: tapping sleeve and valve
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: American Water specification 33 01 10.13, Pressure Leakage Tests

field.text: Air collects at high points in pressure pipelines and reduces flow, causes surges and gives false test readings. Air valves (AWWA C512) are placed at high points and where the plans show: air release valves vent small amounts of air while the line is under pressure; air/vacuum valves let large volumes of air out during filling and in during draining (preventing vacuum collapse); combination valves do both. Sewage force mains need sewage-rated air valves. Installation: tap at the high point, install an isolation valve below the air valve, put it in a vault or box per detail with venting and drainage, and make sure the vent can't let surface water or contamination back in. Lay pipe so high points are where the air valves are, not between them. Check the plans for exact locations.
field.title: Air release valves on water and force mains
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: AWWA C512 scope; utility standard details

field.text: Blow-offs let crews flush water mains, especially at dead ends and low points where sediment collects. Types: a hydrant at the end of the line, a flushing hydrant, or a blow-off assembly (a valve, riser pipe and cap in a box at grade). Size is usually set by the utility so flushing can reach the velocity AWWA C651 asks for when flushing new mains. During construction, temporary blow-offs are installed at the end of each test section for filling, flushing, chlorination and sampling. Install with restraint, a valve box or meter-style box, and drainage so the riser doesn't freeze. When flushing, control the discharge: dechlorinate if required and protect against erosion and sediment discharge per your stormwater permit. Check utility standards for blow-off details and sizes.
field.title: Blow-offs and flushing connections
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Connecting new water main to an existing main either with a wet tap (no shutdown) or a cut-in (shutdown). For a cut-in: coordinate the shutdown date and time with the utility, which notifies customers; locate and exercise the valves that will isolate the work area ahead of time (old valves may not close fully); have every fitting, coupling, sleeve, restraint and pump on site and checked against measurements before shutting down; pump the excavation; swab new fittings and the cut pipe ends with hypochlorite solution per AWWA C651 for connections; restore service and flush. Plan for a valve that won't close tight: have a plan B and the utility on call. Many utilities require their staff to operate existing valves. Follow the utility's shutdown procedure.
field.title: Water main connections to existing mains: shutdown planning
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: AWWA C651 connection practices; utility practice

field.text: Sanitary sewer services (laterals) connect buildings to the main.
