On new mains, a wye (or tee-wye) fitting is installed in the main at each service location shown, with the lateral angled up at the slope the standard detail shows, often with a riser for deep mains and a cap or plug at the property line or end. On existing mains, connections are made with saddles (strap-on or gasketed tap saddles cored into the main) or by cutting in a wye with couplings. Rules from typical specs: no break-in connections without approved fittings; core with a proper hole saw, not a hammer; don't let the lateral protrude into the main; bed and haunch the lateral like the main; mark the end with a marker stake or tracer per specs; record station, offset, depth and length for the as-builts. Minimum lateral slope is set by local code (commonly 1/4 inch per foot for 4 inch).
field.title: Sewer service laterals and wyes
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: Common municipal standard details and specification practice

field.text: Hydrant flow tests measure how much water the system can deliver. Procedure under NFPA 291: put a pressure gauge on a test hydrant to read static pressure, open one or more nearby flow hydrants, measure flow with a pitot gauge at the outlet, and read the residual pressure at the test hydrant; the results are used to calculate available flow at 20 psi residual. NFPA 291 recommends painting hydrant tops and caps by rated flow: Class AA, light blue, 1,500 gpm or more; Class A, green, 1,000 to 1,499 gpm; Class B, orange, 500 to 999 gpm; Class C, red, less than 500 gpm. Many utilities use their own color schemes. Coordinate flow tests with the utility and fire department, flush slowly to avoid water hammer, and control discharge.
field.title: Hydrant flow testing and color codes
field.topic: Water system operations on construction jobs
field.source: NFPA 291 (fire flow testing and marking of hydrants), as commonly summarized

field.text: Water hammer is a pressure surge caused by changing flow quickly, such as slamming a valve or hydrant shut or filling an empty main fast. Surges can be several times normal pressure and can break pipe, blow joints or damage valves. Field rules: open and close valves and hydrants slowly, especially the last few turns; fill new mains slowly with air venting at high points (the C651 tablet method summary limits fill velocity to about 1 ft per second); when flushing, open and close hydrants gradually; never use a hydrant as an on-off switch. Air trapped in a line makes surges worse. Utilities often require their own staff to operate system valves.
field.title: Water hammer: opening and closing valves slowly
field.topic: Water system operations on construction jobs
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Valves that sit unused for years can seize or fail to close fully. Utilities exercise valves on a schedule, opening and closing them fully and counting turns. On construction projects: operate every new valve fully before backfill and again before acceptance; record the number of turns to open and the direction (open left or open right, which varies by utility); confirm the valve box is centered and the key reaches the nut; and report any existing valve that won't operate when you need it for a shutdown, so the utility can plan. Count turns slowly and stop if torque spikes, which can mean debris or a broken stem. Follow the utility's valve operation procedure.
field.title: Valve exercising and turn counts
field.topic: Water system operations on construction jobs
field.source: Common industry and specification practice

field.text: Read a lath top to bottom. Top: the offset and what it is set to, often above a line ("10 / SD" = 10 ft off the storm drain; "5 / WALL / WF" = 5 ft off the wall face; "15' RT CL" = 15 ft right of centerline). Middle: the station and the point ("STA 12+50", "MH-4", "BCR", "CB #2"). Bottom, nearest the ground: the cut or fill and what it is to ("C 6.09 FL", "F8.11 TW"). The hub, a short stake driven near flush beside the lath, is the reference the cut or fill is measured from unless the lath names another mark (a crowfoot line, top of stake). Two grades are split by a slash or put on separate lines, each with its own target. Read the whole stake, then say it in plain words: "5 ft off the wall face; fill 8.11 ft to top of wall; cut 4.68 ft to top of footing."
field.title: How a stake is laid out, top to bottom
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Surveyors write grades in feet and hundredths, not inches. Common shortcuts: the decimals written small, raised or underlined after the whole feet ("C 4" with a small underlined "68" = cut 4.68 ft; "F 8" with a small "11" = fill 8.11 ft); a dot or dash right after the C or F is only a separator ("F. 8 11" = fill 8.11, never 0.8); a value is under 1 ft only when no whole-feet digit is written (".85"); the Navy style "C35" with the 5 small = cut 3.5 ft. Short bars or underlines under digits are decimal marks, not inch marks. A stake is in feet and inches only when written that way (6'-01 1/8", 4' 8 1/4") or with IN. To convert: 0.68 ft x 12 = 8.16 in, about 8 3/16 in; 0.11 ft = 1.32 in, about 1 5/16 in. When a crew wants it on a tape, give both: "cut 4.68 ft (4 ft 8 3/16 in)."
field.title: Decimal feet on stakes: .8, raised and underlined digits
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: C or CUT = the design grade is below the reference: dig down that much. F or FILL = the design grade is above the reference: build up that much. O/G, ON GRADE, GRADE or 0.00 = the reference is at design grade. A minus sign after C ("C-6.09") is just a separator, not a direction change; "C" alone decides it. A plus or minus ("±", "+/-") means close to grade. An arrow pointing down means cut, up means fill; an arrow along the lath can also point toward the hub or the face it describes. When a stake shows several values, each has its own target (FL, TC, TW, FG): never apply a cut meant for one target to another.
field.title: Cut, fill, O/G and grade arrows
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: The cut or fill is measured from a reference, and which one matters. Hub: the top of the hub (or the tack in it) unless the lath says otherwise; TOH or T/H = top of hub. Top of stake (TOS, sometimes TOL top of lath): measured from the top of that stake. A crowfoot line drawn on the lath: measured from that line, so the cut is from the mark, not the hub. A nail or PK/MAG nail in pavement, or a chiseled X in concrete: from the top of that nail or mark. A hub elevation is seldom written on the stake; only use one that is written (EL 2400.09, TOH 2400.09). If a hub has been hit or pulled, its grade is gone: don't set from it, get it reset.
field.title: Reference: hub, top of stake, crowfoot mark, nail
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Example lath: "10' / SS", "STA 3+25", "C 8.42 FL". Reading: 10 ft offset to the sanitary sewer line, station 3+25, cut 8.42 ft from the hub to the pipe flowline (invert). To get the invert elevation, hub elevation minus 8.42 if the hub elevation is known. To set pipe: measure 10 ft back to the pipe line at right angles to the alignment, and transfer the grade with a level, laser or grade rod. Some surveyors stake cut to top of pipe, bottom of trench or top of bedding instead; the stake or cut sheet says which ("TO TP", "BOT TR"). If it isn't written, the default on most sewer and storm jobs is cut to flowline, but confirm on the first stake of the job.
field.title: Pipe grade stake: station, offset, cut to flowline
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Structure stakes usually carry the structure ID and every invert. Example: "8' / SDMH-4", "STA 6+10.50", "C 9.12 IE IN (N)", "C 9.32 IE OUT (W)", "F 0.35 RIM". Reading: 8 ft off storm manhole 4 at station 6+10.50; cut 9.12 ft to the north inlet invert; cut 9.32 ft to the west outlet invert (0.20 ft drop through the structure); fill 0.35 ft to the rim. Manholes are often staked with two reference points (RPs) on different sides so the center can be found after excavation: the stakes give each RP's distance to the center ("RP 10' N CTR MH4"). Catch basins and inlets often show TG (top of grate) or TC and FL at the grate.
field.title: Manhole and structure stakes
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Curb stakes are normally offset behind the back of curb (often 2 to 5 ft). Example: "3' / BC", "STA 1+40", "C 0.42 TC", "C 0.92 FL". Reading: 3 ft offset from the back of curb; cut 0.42 ft to top of curb; cut 0.92 ft to flowline, so the curb face is 0.50 ft (6 in) tall. TC top of curb, FC face of curb, FL flowline of gutter, LIP lip of gutter (the edge where gutter meets pavement), BC back of curb (or begin curve on alignment stakes: context decides), BCR and ECR begin and end of curb return, PCR point on curb return. A curb return is staked at BCR, ECR and the midpoint or radius point, often with the radius written ("R=25'").
field.title: Curb and gutter stakes: TC, FL, BC, lip
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Retaining and screen wall stakes give the wall line and the grades of the wall parts. Example: "5 / WALL / WF" with a crowfoot, then "F. 8 11 TW / C. 4 68 TF" with the 11 and 68 written small. Reading: 5 ft offset from the wall face; fill 8.11 ft to top of wall; cut 4.68 ft to top of footing (so top of footing to top of wall is 8.11 + 4.68 = 12.79 ft at that point). Other wall marks: BW or BOW bottom of wall (also back of walk on a sidewalk job), BF or BOF bottom of footing, FTG footing, TOC top of concrete, FW face of wall, BOW back of wall, KEY keyway. Walls usually step: each stake gives the grade at its own station, so read each one.
field.title: Wall stakes: TW, TF, BF, wall face
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A slope stake marks where a cut or fill slope meets existing ground (the catch point). Example: "CATCH", "F 6.0", "2:1", "28.0 CL". Reading: this is the toe of a fill slope; build up 6.0 ft at the hinge or shoulder above it; slope 2 horizontal to 1 vertical; 28.0 ft from centerline. On a cut slope the stake reads C for the depth at the top of cut. A double slash can separate the grade from the slope ratio ("F 0.4 to toe // F 6.0 at 2:1"). Terms: TOS or TOP top of slope, TOE toe of slope, HP hinge point (where the slope breaks from the roadway shoulder), SH shoulder, DT ditch. Slope ratio: 2:1 drops 1 ft for every 2 ft out, so 6 ft of fill at 2:1 runs 12 ft horizontally.
field.title: Slope stakes and catch points
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Rough grade stakes tell the dozer and grader operators how much to cut or fill to reach subgrade or finished grade across a pad or road. Blue tops are hubs driven so their tops are exactly at the design grade (often subgrade or top of base) and painted blue on top; the operator trims until the blade just shows the blue. Red tops or other colors may mark a different grade (for example finish vs subgrade): colors vary by company, so ask. Typical marks: "RG" rough grade, "FG" finish grade, "SG" subgrade, "PAD" or "PE" pad elevation, "FF" or "FFE" finished floor. A pad stake might read "PAD 1352.40 / C 1.2" = pad elevation 1352.40, cut 1.2 ft from the hub to reach it.
field.title: Rough grade and blue tops
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: On asphalt and concrete there is often no lath. The point is a PK or MAG nail, a nail and shiner (washer), a drilled hole, or an X or + chiseled in concrete, with the information spray-painted beside it (station, offset, cut or fill, target), often with an arrow to the point. Read it the same way as a stake: the reference is the top of the nail or mark. Paint can be sideways or upside down relative to you; read it in its own direction. Old marks get painted over; use the freshest, clearest set that points to the nail. Don't confuse survey paint (usually pink or orange) with utility locate marks (811 colors with owner initials, arrows and line widths).
field.title: Paint marks on pavement and concrete
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Stakes are set off the work so the dig doesn't destroy them. Typical offsets: 5, 10 or 15 ft for pipe; 2 to 5 ft behind curb; 5 ft from a wall face; slope stakes at the catch. The offset is measured at right angles to the alignment at that station. To bring grade to the pipe: measure the offset back square to the line, set a grade rod or batter board, and carry the elevation over with a hand level, builder's level or laser. If the stake is on a curve, measure along the radius. An offset of 0 or "ON LINE" means the stake is on the line itself, usually a hub to be dug out once it's been transferred.
field.title: Offsets: why, how far, and how to bring grade over
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A station is distance along the alignment: 12+50 = 1,250 ft from 0+00; 12+50.25 = 1,250.25 ft. To find a point between stakes, subtract stations (13+00 minus 12+50 = 50 ft). Grade between stakes on a straight grade: invert at a point = invert at the upstream stake minus slope x distance. Example: invert 100.95 at 12+50, slope 0.0040 ft/ft, the invert at 12+80 = 100.95 - 0.0040 x 30 = 100.83. Stakes may also show an equation ("STA 10+00 BK = 9+87.42 AH") where two alignments' stationing meet: use the right one for the plan sheet you're on.
field.title: Stationing on stakes and how to use it
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: LT and RT are taken looking up-station (in the direction stationing increases). A stake marked "10' LT" sits 10 ft to the left of the alignment when you face up-station. Sewer and storm plans usually station upstream from the outlet, but not always; check the arrow on the plan. AH means ahead (up-station), BK means back (down-station). On a curve, LT and RT stay relative to the direction of stationing, and the offset is measured on the radius.
field.title: Left and right, ahead and back
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A guard stake is a lath driven next to a hub to flag it and carry the writing. A witness stake (WIT) is set near a point that will be destroyed or is hard to find, with the distance and direction to it ("WIT 10' N"). A reference point (RP) is a stake set at a known distance from a point so the point can be re-found after it's dug out; manholes often get two RPs. A monument (MON), iron pin (IP), iron rod or rebar (IR, RB), or a cap stamped with a surveyor's license number (LS, PLS, RCE) is a permanent survey point; never disturb it, and report it if it's in the way.
field.title: Witness stakes, guard stakes and reference points
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A crowfoot is a short line with three toes like a bird's foot; it points to the exact point, line or height the writing refers to. An arrow on a lath points toward the hub, the line or the face named on the stake. A horizontal line drawn across a lath with a value beside it is a grade mark: the cut or fill is from that line, not the hub. A triangle (Δ) marks a control point or, in curve data, the delta angle. A circle with a dot (⊙) marks a point or center. ℄ is centerline. Colored tape or paint bands around a lath usually code the line or the kind of stake on that job; ask the surveyor rather than guessing.
field.title: Crowfoot, arrows and other marks on lath
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Some stake abbreviations mean two things, and the rest of the stake decides. BC: back of curb on a curb stake, begin curve on an alignment stake. TOS: top of slope on a slope stake, top of stake as a reference. BOW: back of walk on a sidewalk, bottom of wall on a wall stake. TOC: top of curb or top of concrete. PCC: Portland cement concrete or point of compound curve. RW: retaining wall or recycled water. WM: water main or water meter. CO: cleanout (almost always on utility jobs). CP: control point or catch point. If the stake really doesn't show which, say both meanings and ask the surveyor; don't guess.
field.title: Two meanings: abbreviations that depend on the job
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: TC or TOC top of curb; BC back of curb; FC or FOC face of curb; FL flowline; LIP lip of gutter; G or GUT gutter; C&G curb and gutter; BCR and ECR begin and end of curb return; EP or EOP edge of pavement; ETW edge of traveled way; CL or ℄ centerline; CR crown; SH shoulder; MED median; XG cross gutter; DW or DWY driveway; SW or S/W sidewalk; BW or BOW back of walk; CR or RAMP curb ramp; EG existing ground; FG finished grade; FS finished surface; FP finished pavement; TP top of pavement; AC asphalt concrete; PCC portland cement concrete; AB, CAB or CMB aggregate base; SG subgrade; HP high point; LP low point; GB grade break; ROW or R/W right of way; PL property line.
field.title: Street and pavement abbreviations
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: STA station; PI point of intersection (where two tangents would meet); PC point of curvature (begin curve); PT point of tangency (end curve); BC and EC begin and end curve; PRC point of reverse curve; PCC point of compound curve; POC point on curve; POT point on tangent; POL point on line; AP angle point; R radius; L length of curve; Δ delta (the curve's central angle); T tangent length. Vertical curves: BVC or BVCS begin vertical curve (station or elevation), EVC or EVCS end, PVI vertical point of intersection, PVC and PVT begin and end of vertical curve, K rate of vertical curvature, HP or LP high or low point on the curve.
field.title: Alignment and curve abbreviations
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: RG rough grade; FG finish grade; SG subgrade; PAD or PE pad elevation; FF or FFE finished floor (elevation); GFF garage finished floor; TOS or TOP top of slope; TOE or BOS toe or bottom of slope; CATCH or CP catch point; SS slope stake; HP hinge point; 2:1, 3:1 slope ratio (horizontal:vertical); TOB and BOB top and bottom of bank; DT ditch; SWALE or V-DITCH; BERM; KEY keyway (trench cut at the toe of a fill slope); BENCH (steps cut into a slope before filling); OX overexcavation; RCP on a grading job can mean a remedial limit, but on utility work it is reinforced concrete pipe.
field.title: Grading, pad and slope abbreviations
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: TW or TOW top of wall; BW or BOW bottom of wall; TF or TOF top of footing; BF or BOF bottom of footing; FTG footing; WF, W/F or FW wall face; COL column; CMU concrete block; RW retaining wall; TOC top of concrete; BOC bottom of concrete; TS top of slab; TG or TOG top of grate; TFR top of frame; HW headwall; WW wingwall; EW endwall; FES flared end section; RIP or RIPRAP; VAULT; BOX; JB or JS junction box or junction structure; INV invert.
field.title: Wall, structure and concrete abbreviations
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: SS or SAN sanitary sewer; SD or ST storm drain; W or WL water; RW, RCW or RWL recycled water (purple pipe); IRR irrigation; FM force main; FS fire service; G or GAS gas; E or ELEC electric; UGE underground electric; OHE overhead electric; T or TEL telephone; CATV or TV cable; FO fiber optic; COMM communications; SL street light; TS traffic signal; JT joint trench (several dry utilities in one trench). Structures: MH, SSMH, SDMH manholes; CB catch basin; DI drop inlet; GI grate inlet; CI curb inlet; CO cleanout; FH or HYD hydrant; WV or GV gate valve; BV butterfly valve; ARV or AV air release valve; BO or BOV blow-off; WM water meter; SVC service; LAT lateral.
field.title: Utility line abbreviations on stakes
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: INV or IE invert elevation; FL flowline; BOP bottom of pipe; TOP or TP top of pipe; SPL spring line; OD and ID outside and inside diameter; ⌀ or DIA diameter; LF linear feet; S= slope in ft/ft (S=0.0040); % percent grade; TEE, WYE, CROSS; BEND or ELL with angle (11 1/4, 22 1/2, 45, 90); RED reducer; CAP; PLUG; TB thrust block; RJ restrained joint; MJ mechanical joint; FLG flange; CPLG coupling; CORP corporation stop; CS curb stop; STUB or STUB-OUT; CONN connection; POC point of connection; EX or EXIST existing; PROP proposed; ABAN abandoned; RELOC relocate; R&R remove and replace; POT or PH pothole; XING crossing. Materials: PVC, C900, C905, SDR, DR, DIP, CIP, RCP, CMP, HDPE, VCP, ACP, STL, CU.
field.title: Pipe and fitting abbreviations on stakes and cut sheets
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: BM benchmark; TBM temporary benchmark; CP control point; RP reference point; REF reference; WIT witness; HUB; TOH or T/H top of hub; TOS top of stake; GS grade stake; ELEV or EL elevation; SP set point; MON monument; IP iron pipe; IR iron rod; RB rebar; CAP (with license number, LS or PLS for a land surveyor, RCE for a civil engineer); PK nail or MAG nail; N&S nail and shiner; N&T nail and tag; X or + chiseled in concrete; LOD limit of disturbance; NTS not to scale; TYP typical; W/ with; W/O without; U/S and D/S upstream and downstream; BEG and END.
field.title: Control and reference abbreviations
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Lath: "12 / SD", "STA 4+80", "C 7.15 FL / C 5.47 TOP". Reading: 12 ft offset to the storm drain line at station 4+80; cut 7.15 ft to flowline (inside bottom); cut 5.47 ft to top of pipe. The difference, 1.68 ft, should equal the pipe's inside diameter plus one wall thickness when TOP is the outside top: an 18 in RCP has a 1.50 ft inside diameter and about a 2 to 2.5 in wall, so 1.68 ft fits. If the two values don't fit the pipe on the plan, ask before digging. Trench bottom = flowline cut + wall thickness + bedding depth from the plan.
field.title: Working a full stake example: storm drain with two grades
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Water mains are pressure pipe, usually staked for line and for depth of cover instead of an exact invert. Example lath: "10' / W", "STA 8+00", "FG" or "C 1.2 FG" and a note like "42 IN COV". Reading: 10 ft off the water line; cut 1.2 ft from the hub to finished grade; keep at least 42 in of cover from finished grade to top of pipe. Fittings, valves and hydrants get their own stakes ("GV", "FH", "45° BEND", "TEE 8x6") with stations. Where the plan has a profile, the stake may give cut to top of pipe instead.
field.title: Working a full stake example: water main
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Sewer laterals are often staked at the property line or the end of the lateral with the invert or a cut to it, and sometimes a depth. Example: "LOT 12", "SS LAT", "C 5.40 INV", "PL". Reading: lot 12 sewer lateral at the property line; cut 5.40 ft to the lateral invert there. The plan or a lateral table usually gives the station on the main where the wye goes, and the minimum slope (often 2 percent for a 4 in lateral). Water services: a stake at the meter box location, often with "WM" or "SVC" and the size.
field.title: Working a full stake example: lateral or service
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Read what is clearly written and say plainly what isn't. Common problems: faded or rain-washed marker, sun glare, a lath turned away, two stakes in one photo, old values crossed out beside new ones, dirt or paint over the bottom of the lath. Rules: never guess a digit; if a digit could be two values (8 or 3), say both. Crossed-out numbers are superseded; use the newest. If the hub is missing or the lath is broken off, the grade can't be trusted. A stake that doesn't match its neighbors (a jump in cut that doesn't fit the slope) may be a surveyor error or a disturbed stake: check it against the cut sheet before digging.
field.title: Hard-to-read stakes: what to do
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Before laying, check a few stakes: each hub elevation minus its cut should equal the design invert on the cut sheet or plan, and the inverts should change by slope x distance from stake to stake. Example: stakes 50 ft apart on a 0.50% grade should show inverts 0.25 ft apart. Cuts themselves can jump around because the ground isn't flat; it's the inverts that must line up. If one doesn't fit, recheck the reading, then call the surveyor. Note disturbed or missing stakes in the daily report and request a restake.
field.title: Checking stakes against each other and the cut sheet
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Survey stake and flagging colors vary by company and job, so no single color chart is universal; ask the surveyor's legend. Common practice: pink, orange or fluorescent flagging on survey stakes, and colored tops on grade hubs, but what each top color means changes by agency and region. On many jobs a blue top is a finished grade hub; WSDOT, for one, calls subgrade hubs blue tops, base rock hubs red tops and top course hubs yellow tops. Confirm which grade a top color means before you trim to it. Utility locate marks follow the APWA uniform color code: white proposed excavation, pink temporary survey marks, red electric, yellow gas, oil or steam, orange communications and CATV, blue potable water, purple reclaimed water and irrigation, green sewer and storm drain. Survey paint is not a utility locate.
field.title: Color of stakes, flagging, grade hub tops and paint
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: On a curb return, stakes are usually set at the BCR, the ECR, and points on the return (often the midpoint), each with its own TC and FL grades; the radius point (RP or CTR) may also be staked with the radius. Grades around the return are not always a straight line; use each stake's numbers. On a road curve, offsets are measured along the radius from the centerline, and LT and RT stay relative to the direction of stationing.
field.title: Grade on a curb return or curve
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Building corners are often set with offset hubs and batter boards rather than on the corner itself. Marks: "BLDG COR", "5' O/S", "FF 1352.50", "TF" top of footing, "BF" bottom of footing, "GRID A/3" grid line intersection. Batter boards carry string lines for the building lines, set at a known height (often finished floor or a round number above it); measure down from the string to grade. Pad stakes give the pad elevation and the cut or fill to reach it.
field.title: Building and footing stakes
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: If only a number shows with no C or F, don't assume. Clues: a minus sign before the number sometimes means cut on cut sheets written as differences (grade minus hub), but conventions vary; an arrow down means cut; a stake in a fill area where the ground is low is usually fill. The safe answer is: read what's written, say the C or F isn't visible, and check the cut sheet or the surveyor. Never dig on a guessed direction.
field.title: Telling cut from fill when the stake is unclear
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Inches to hundredths: divide inches by 12. 1 in = 0.083 ft; 2 in = 0.167; 3 in = 0.25; 4 in = 0.333; 5 in = 0.417; 6 in = 0.50; 7 in = 0.583; 8 in = 0.667; 9 in = 0.75; 10 in = 0.833; 11 in = 0.917. Eighths: 1/8 in = 0.010 ft. Hundredths to inches: multiply by 12, then the fraction by 16 for sixteenths. Example: 4.68 ft = 4 ft + 0.68 x 12 = 8.16 in = 8 in + 0.16 x 16 = 2.6 sixteenths, about 8 3/16 in. Example: 0.8 ft = 9.6 in, about 9 5/8 in.
field.title: Feet-inches to decimal feet and back
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: With a builder's level or laser: set up, read the rod on the hub (backsight). The design grade reading = hub reading + cut (a cut means the grade is lower, so the rod reads more) or hub reading - fill. Example: rod on hub reads 3.20; stake says C 6.09 FL; the rod on the flowline should read 3.20 + 6.09 = 9.29. With a grade rod (fixed-target): set the target so the laser hits it when the rod foot is at design grade, using the same math. Always re-shoot the hub before you rely on a setup that's been bumped.
field.title: Reading a grade from a stake to a rod
field.topic: Survey stakes: reading every kind of stake
field.source: Standard construction staking practice (US civil, utility and grading work); worked examples written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A joint trench carries several dry utilities (electric, gas, telephone, cable TV, fiber) in one trench, each placed to the serving utility's standard. The utilities' joint trench detail sets the trench width and depth, the position of each line, the clearances between them, the cover, and the backfill (often sand or slurry around conduits). Typical rules: electric is placed deepest or on the opposite side from gas, with a minimum horizontal and vertical separation set by the utility (often about 12 in between electric and gas, and more for primary voltage); telecom shares space with lower clearance needs. Follow the approved joint trench plan, not a general rule, and have each utility inspect before backfill.
field.title: Joint trench basics
field.topic: Dry utilities: joint trench, conduit, duct banks and vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Common underground conduit: PVC Schedule 40 (most direct-burial runs), PVC Schedule 80 (thicker wall, used where exposed, under roads, or where the utility requires it), DB-60/DB-100/DB-120 (direct-burial or encased duct; the number is a stiffness class), and HDPE (smooth or corrugated, coiled, common for fiber and bores). Electric utilities usually require gray PVC and specific sizes; communications often use orange or other colored HDPE innerduct. Use the utility's approved material and glue only with the matching cement. Long runs in trench usually join with solvent-weld bells; HDPE joins with couplers or electrofusion.
field.title: Conduit types: PVC Schedule 40, 80, DB and HDPE
field.topic: Dry utilities: joint trench, conduit, duct banks and vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Cable pulling tension rises fast with each bend, so specs limit bends between pull points. A common limit is 360 degrees of total bends between pull boxes (for example four 90s), and many utilities set tighter limits and require large-radius factory sweeps (36 in, 48 in or more for primary electric and fiber) instead of field bends. Heat-bent PVC must not kink or flatten. Count every bend including small offsets. Install a pull rope or mule tape in each conduit, and prove the conduit with a mandrel or test ball before the utility accepts it. If a run needs more bend than allowed, add a pull box.
field.title: Conduit bends, sweeps and pull limits
field.topic: Dry utilities: joint trench, conduit, duct banks and vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Primary electric duct banks are often encased in concrete with spacers holding the conduits apart, and the concrete is dyed red (red top or full red) so a future excavator knows it's electric. Typical details: spacers every 5 to 8 ft, conduits tied down so they don't float in the pour, a minimum concrete cover around the outside conduits, and warning tape above. Pour against undisturbed trench walls or forms as detailed. Don't drive equipment over fresh encasement. Check the utility's detail for cover, separation from other utilities and whether rebar is required.
field.title: Electric duct banks and red concrete
field.topic: Dry utilities: joint trench, conduit, duct banks and vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Pull boxes and handholes are small access boxes at bends, splices and service points; vaults are larger structures for transformers, switches and splices. Set them level and to finished grade (or the utility's specified height above grade in landscaping), on a compacted base of rock as detailed, with the lid rated for the traffic (for example a traffic-rated or H-20 lid in driveways and roads). Conduits enter through knockouts or bell ends at the specified height, sealed against dirt and water. Lids are marked by utility (ELECTRIC, TELEPHONE, CATV, SIGNAL).
field.title: Pull boxes, handholes and vaults
field.topic: Dry utilities: joint trench, conduit, duct banks and vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Before a utility accepts a conduit run, it is usually proved: a mandrel or test ball sized close to the conduit's inside diameter is pulled through to show there are no crushed, kinked or offset joints, and a pull rope or flat mule tape (marked in feet) is left in for the cable pull. Leave extra rope tied off at each end, and cap or plug the conduit ends so dirt and water stay out. A mandrel that won't pass means a crushed or misaligned section: find and fix it before backfill or before paving.
field.title: Mandrel, pull rope and conduit proving
field.topic: Dry utilities: joint trench, conduit, duct banks and vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Distribution gas mains and services are usually yellow PE (polyethylene) pipe, joined by heat fusion or approved mechanical fittings, with tracer wire. The gas utility or its qualified contractor does the tie-ins and fusion; only operator-qualified people work on gas facilities. In a joint trench, keep the gas line at the utility's specified position, cover and separation from electric. Never use a gas line or its tracer wire as a ground. If you hit or nick any gas line: stop, get everyone away, don't try to stop the leak, eliminate ignition sources, call 911 and the gas company.
field.title: Gas line installation basics for crews
field.topic: Dry utilities: joint trench, conduit, duct banks and vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Gravity sewer PVC (ASTM D3034, 4 to 15 in; ASTM F679 for 18 to 60 in) is usually green and rated by SDR (standard dimension ratio, outside diameter divided by wall thickness). SDR 35 is the common sewer wall; SDR 26 is thicker and stiffer (often required under roads, at deeper cover, or near water mains); SDR 41 is thinner and less common. Lower SDR = thicker wall = stiffer pipe. Profile-wall and corrugated PVC (ASTM F794, F949) save weight on larger sizes. Laterals are often 4 or 6 in SDR 35 or Schedule 40 where a building code applies.
field.title: PVC sewer pipe: SDR 35, SDR 26 and wall types
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC (sewer, storm and pressure)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: AWWA C900 PVC pressure pipe (4 to 60 in under the 2016 standard, which combined the old C900 and C905) is usually blue for water and comes in DR (dimension ratio) classes. Pressure class depends on DR: DR 25 is 165 psi, DR 18 is 235 psi, DR 14 is 305 psi under current C900 ratings. It has cast-iron outside dimensions so it fits standard ductile iron fittings. Purple C900 is recycled water. Use the DR on the plans; it's not interchangeable with sewer pipe.
field.title: PVC pressure pipe: C900 DR 25, 18 and 14
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC (sewer, storm and pressure)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Push-on PVC joints seal with a rubber gasket in the bell. To make one: clean the bell, gasket and spigot; check the gasket is seated the right way; lube the spigot (not the bell groove behind the gasket) with the manufacturer's lubricant; line the pipe up straight; and push until the spigot reaches the insertion (homing) mark. Field-cut pipe needs a new homing mark measured from the factory one and a bevel ground on the cut end, about the same as the factory bevel. Push with a bar and block or a come-along, not the bucket against the pipe end. Overinsertion past the mark can crack the bell or leave no room for expansion.
field.title: PVC gasketed joints: homing, lube and insertion marks
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC (sewer, storm and pressure)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: PVC gasketed joints allow only a small angle, set by the manufacturer (often about 1 degree or less at the joint for sewer pipe, a little more for some pressure pipe joints). Bigger direction changes need fittings or longitudinal bending of the barrel within the manufacturer's minimum bending radius (for C900, a radius of several hundred times the diameter). Don't pull a joint off-line to make a curve; it can leak or the gasket can roll. Check the manufacturer's installation guide for the exact allowed deflection and bending radius for the size and DR.
field.title: PVC joint deflection and bending
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC (sewer, storm and pressure)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: PVC loses impact strength in cold weather; handle it more carefully below freezing and don't drop or throw it. Long sun exposure (UV) can chalk the surface and reduce impact strength over months; store under cover or rotate stock if it will sit for a long time. Keep pipe supported along its length so it doesn't bow, keep gaskets clean and out of sun and oil, and keep the bells from getting dirt packed in them. Inspect for gouges deeper than about 10 percent of the wall and cut them out.
field.title: PVC handling, sun and cold
field.topic: Pipe materials: PVC (sewer, storm and pressure)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Ductile iron pipe (AWWA C151) is sold by pressure class (150, 200, 250, 300, 350 psi; 350 is the standard minimum for many small sizes) or by older thickness classes (50 to 56). Joint types: push-on (Tyton, Fastite style gasketed bell), mechanical joint (MJ: gland, gasket and T-bolts, mostly on fittings and valves), flanged (above ground and in vaults), and restrained joints (TR Flex, Field Lok gaskets, MJ with wedge-action retainer glands) where thrust must be held without blocks. Pipe is usually cement-mortar lined inside.
field.title: Ductile iron pipe classes and joints
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Push-on and MJ ductile iron joints allow some deflection, set in AWWA C600 tables and the manufacturer's literature. Rough figures for push-on joints: about 5 degrees for 3 to 12 in pipe and about 3 degrees for 14 to 48 in; at 5 degrees on an 18 ft or 20 ft length, the offset is roughly 19 to 21 in per length. Restrained joints often allow less. Make the joint straight first, then deflect, and don't exceed the table value. Check the manufacturer's numbers for the exact pipe and joint.
field.title: Ductile iron joint deflection
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Where soils are corrosive, ductile iron pipe and fittings are wrapped in loose polyethylene tube or sheet (AWWA C105) to keep soil off the iron. Install it loose, overlap the joints about 1 ft, tape the overlaps and the ends, repair any tears with tape or patches, and keep it intact during backfill. Wrap fittings, valves and the first part of any copper service tap, and use a tapping method that doesn't leave bare iron. The plans or the agency standard say where it's required.
field.title: Polyethylene encasement (poly wrap) on ductile iron
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Cut ductile iron with an abrasive saw or a pipe cutter, keep the cut square, and grind a bevel on the spigot end for push-on joints like the factory one; mark a new insertion depth. Watch silica and iron dust and use the dust controls and respirator required. Direct tapping of ductile iron for services depends on wall thickness and pipe size; many agencies require a tapping saddle. Clean and repair the lining at taps as the standard requires.
field.title: Cutting and tapping ductile iron
field.topic: Pipe materials: ductile iron
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: HDPE (high-density polyethylene) pressure pipe is rated by DR (outside diameter divided by wall): DR 11 is common for water and gas services and mains, DR 17 and DR 21 for lower pressures; lower DR = thicker wall = higher pressure rating. Pipe is made in IPS (iron pipe size) and DIPS (ductile iron pipe size) outside diameters, which are not the same, so match fittings to the sizing system. Black with stripes: blue for water, green for sewer, purple for recycled, yellow for gas. Corrugated HDPE (ADS N-12 style, AASHTO M294) is gravity storm drain pipe, joined with gasketed bells.
field.title: HDPE pipe: DR, colors and uses
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Butt fusion joins two HDPE pipe ends by heating them on a plate and pressing them together. Steps: clamp and align the pipes; face the ends square with the facer; check alignment (high-low no more than about 10 percent of the wall); heat to form a bead of the specified size; remove the heater quickly; bring the ends together at the specified joining pressure; hold and cool under pressure for the specified time. The fusion machine settings come from the pipe maker and PPI TR-33 or ASTM F2620, and many owners want each joint logged by a data logger. Only qualified operators fuse.
field.title: Butt fusion basics
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: HDPE grows and shrinks with temperature far more than steel or PVC: about 1 in per 100 ft for every 10 degrees F of temperature change. Pipe laid hot in the afternoon will pull back as it cools in the trench, so let it reach ground temperature before final tie-ins, or snake it in the trench. HDPE bends: minimum cold-bending radius is roughly 20 to 25 times the outside diameter for DR 11 and lower DRs, more for thinner pipe and when a fitting is in the bend; check the manufacturer.
field.title: HDPE expansion, contraction and bending
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Electrofusion fittings (couplings, tees, saddles) have heating wires built in; a processor heats them for a set time read from the fitting's barcode. The pipe surface must be scraped clean of the oxidized skin, kept clean and dry, marked for stab depth and clamped still while fusing and cooling. Mechanical fittings for HDPE need a stiffener insert in the pipe end. Never fuse wet or dirty pipe.
field.title: Electrofusion and mechanical fittings on HDPE
field.topic: Pipe materials: HDPE
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Gravity sewer and storm pipe is normally laid starting at the downstream structure and working upstream, with the bells facing upstream, so the spigot of each new pipe pushes into the bell of the last one and flow runs over the joints, not into them. Check grade on every joint (laser target, grade rod or string line), keep the trench bottom and bedding shaped so the pipe bears evenly along its length (dig out bell holes so the bell doesn't carry the pipe), and plug the open end at the end of the day so dirt, water and animals stay out.
field.title: Laying gravity pipe upstream, bells upstream
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Pipe should rest on the bedding along its barrel, not on its bells or on rocks. Shape a bell hole at each joint, place and level the bedding to the specified depth (often 4 to 6 in of rock or sand under the pipe), and after the joint is made, place haunch material and work it under the sides (shovel slicing or tamping) before covering. Uneven support causes bellies, joint deflection and, in flexible pipe, too much deflection. Check grade again after haunching; pipe can lift if haunch material is forced in hard.
field.title: Bedding the pipe and checking it isn't sitting on the bell
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: When joining new pipe to existing, measure the outside diameters of both pipes first (old clay, asbestos cement, cast iron and PVC all differ) and use a coupling made for those two ODs: flexible rubber couplings with stainless shear bands (Fernco style with a shear band for buried use), transition couplings, or repair couplings for pressure pipe. Cut the existing pipe square, support both sides so the joint doesn't sag, and keep the flowlines matched. Asbestos cement pipe needs certified handling and wet cutting; don't saw it dry.
field.title: Tying into an existing pipe with a coupling
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Dirt in a gravity line becomes a blockage or a failed CCTV inspection. Keep pipe ends capped until installed, wipe bells and spigots clean before joining, and set a test plug or watertight cap in the open end at night and during rain. Never let trench water run into new pipe. Before tying into an existing live sewer, plan the connection so construction water and debris can't get into the existing system.
field.title: Keeping pipe clean and plugs at night
field.topic: Laying procedures, joints and couplings
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A precast manhole is built from a base (often with the channel and shelf cast in, or poured in place after), risers (barrel sections, commonly 4 ft or 5 ft inside diameter in 1 to 4 ft heights), a cone (eccentric or concentric) or flat top slab, grade rings, and the frame and cover. Joints between sections are sealed with butyl rope (preformed mastic) or a rubber gasket, and often wrapped outside. Set the base level on compacted rock to the elevation that puts the inverts right, and set sections plumb with the steps lined up as detailed.
field.title: Precast manhole parts and how they stack
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Grade rings (concrete or HDPE adjusting rings) bring the frame to the final rim elevation. Many agencies limit total adjustment height (often 12 to 18 in) and want the rings sealed with mortar or butyl. In paved streets the frame is often set low, then raised to final grade after paving, or set to the final paving slope. The rim elevation on the plan is the top of the frame. Check rim against the street grade both ways so the lid doesn't rock or catch a plow or blade.
field.title: Grade rings and setting the frame to grade
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Pipes enter precast manholes through cored or cast holes fitted with flexible connectors (rubber boots clamped with stainless bands) or grouted connections where allowed. The pipe should stick in only as far as detailed, cut flush or slightly past the inside wall. Inside, the channel (invert) is shaped in concrete or grout to carry flow smoothly from inlet to outlet, at least to the springline for sewer, with the shelf sloped toward the channel. Drop connections are used when an incoming pipe is much higher than the outlet (commonly 2 ft or more); the plan shows inside or outside drop.
field.title: Pipe connections at manholes: boots and channels
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Precast manholes are often tested by vacuum (ASTM C1244) before backfill or after, as the spec says: plug all pipes, seal a test head on the top, pull a vacuum of 10 in of mercury, and time how long it takes to drop 1 in to 9 in of mercury. The minimum time depends on manhole diameter and depth from the standard's table (deeper and larger manholes need longer). If it fails, find the leak (joints, boots, lifting holes), fix it and retest. The agency's spec may change the times or require a hydrostatic test instead.
field.title: Manhole vacuum test
field.topic: Structures: manholes, inlets, cleanouts, vaults
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Ways to keep a trench dry: open sump pumping (water runs to a low hole with a pump, fine in stable clays and small inflows); wellpoints (rows of small wells jetted along the trench on a header pipe with a vacuum pump, good for sands to about 15 to 20 ft of drawdown per stage); deep wells (larger pumped wells for deep drawdown or large areas); and sock or rock trench drains. The goal is to lower the water below the trench bottom before digging, commonly at least 2 ft below, so the bottom stays firm. A geotech report or dewatering designer sets the system on bigger jobs.
field.title: Dewatering methods: sumps, wellpoints and wells
field.topic: Groundwater and dewatering
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Watch for: sand boiling up through the bottom, water bubbling at the base of the walls, soft pumping bottom that won't hold the bedding, sand running in behind the shield, and settlement around the trench. These mean water pressure is moving soil, which can undermine the trench, the pipe grade and nearby structures. Stop, keep people out, and fix the dewatering (more points, deeper, or stabilization rock and fabric per the engineer) before laying.
field.title: Signs the trench bottom is failing from groundwater
field.topic: Groundwater and dewatering
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Pumped groundwater usually can't just go to the street or storm drain. California and most states need a permit or coverage (a dewatering or construction general permit, or a sanitary district permit to discharge to sewer), sediment removal (baker tanks, filter bags, sediment basins), and sometimes testing if the site has contamination. Keep discharge off traffic and away from slopes, and log volumes if the permit requires it.
field.title: Discharging dewatering water
field.topic: Groundwater and dewatering
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Before digging near a marked utility, expose it by hand or vacuum excavation (potholing) to confirm its exact location and depth, especially before crossing it with a new pipe. Record the depth, size, material and location, and compare it to your grade: if your new pipe hits it or doesn't keep the required clearance, stop and get a design answer before you dig the run. In California the tolerance zone is the width of the facility plus 24 in on each side; within it, dig by hand or with vacuum excavation (or another method the operator allows).
field.title: Potholing before you cross or parallel a line
field.topic: Working around existing utilities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: An exposed line crossing the trench must be supported so it doesn't sag or break: hang it from a beam across the trench with straps, or support it from below, as the owner allows. Don't let backfill drop onto it; compact under and around it in lifts so it's supported when the trench is closed. Old clay, cast iron and AC pipe can break if disturbed; tell the owner if it's damaged. Never use an exposed line as a step or ladder.
field.title: Supporting exposed utilities in a trench
field.topic: Working around existing utilities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Gas: stop the equipment, don't try to stop the leak, get people away and upwind, keep ignition sources out, call 911 and the gas company. Electric: stay on the machine if you can, warn others to stay away, call 911 and the utility; if you must leave, jump clear with both feet together and shuffle away. Water main: shut down the area, call the water utility to isolate, watch for washouts under pavement. Any damage, even a scrape on coating or a nicked tracer wire, must be reported to the owner (California 4216 requires notifying the operator and calling 911 if there's danger).
field.title: If you hit a utility
field.topic: Working around existing utilities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Older water and sewer lines may be asbestos cement (AC or ACP), gray and smooth with a slightly fibrous edge when broken. Cutting, breaking or removing it releases asbestos fibers. Only trained workers should handle it, using wet methods, hand tools or snap cutters (not dry abrasive saws), with proper disposal as asbestos waste, and the work may need notification to the air district. When you find unknown gray pipe, assume AC until it's identified.
field.title: Asbestos cement pipe on the job
field.topic: Working around existing utilities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Every soil has an optimum moisture content where it compacts densest; the lab Proctor test (ASTM D1557 modified, or D698 standard) gives the maximum dry density at that moisture. Relative compaction is field dry density divided by that maximum, as a percent. Specs usually ask for 90 percent under landscaping and most fills, and 95 percent in the top part under pavement and in the pipe zone where specified. Too dry, the soil won't compact; too wet, it pumps and won't hold. Add water or dry it back (disc, aerate) to get near optimum before rolling.
field.title: Optimum moisture and relative compaction
field.topic: Earthwork: compaction, moisture and quantities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Compact backfill in thin, even lifts: commonly 6 to 8 in loose for hand-operated plates and rammers, and up to 12 in for larger rollers, but the spec and the testing decide. Rammers (jumping jacks) suit clays and tight trenches; vibratory plates suit sands and gravels; trench rollers and sheepsfoot rollers suit larger areas and clays. Don't run heavy compactors directly over the pipe until there's enough cover above the pipe (often 1 to 2 ft, more for big vibratory rollers).
field.title: Lift thickness and compaction equipment
field.topic: Earthwork: compaction, moisture and quantities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Soil volume changes as it's dug and placed. Bank (in-place) yards swell when excavated into loose yards: common factors are about 10 to 15 percent for sand and gravel, 20 to 30 percent for clay, and 30 to 60 percent or more for blasted rock. Compacted yards are usually smaller than bank yards (shrink) for most soils. Truck counts use loose yards; pay quantities often use bank or compacted yards. Use the geotech report's factors when they're given.
field.title: Shrink and swell: bank, loose and compacted yards
field.topic: Earthwork: compaction, moisture and quantities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A proof roll is driving a loaded water truck or dump truck over prepared subgrade to find soft spots: the ground should not rut or move in waves (pumping) under the tires. Soft areas get dug out and replaced, dried and recompacted, or stabilized (lime, cement, rock and fabric) as the engineer directs. Don't place base or pipe bedding on pumping soil.
field.title: Proof rolling and pumping subgrade
field.topic: Earthwork: compaction, moisture and quantities
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Elevation at a point = starting elevation + grade x distance (grade as a decimal, negative when falling). Example: invert 352.40 at station 2+00, falling at 0.50 percent (-0.0050), the invert at station 3+35 = 352.40 - 0.0050 x 135 = 351.725, written 351.73. Percent grade = rise over run x 100: a 1.2 ft drop over 240 ft = 0.5 percent. Inches per foot: 1/4 in per ft = 2.08 percent; 1/8 in per ft = 1.04 percent.
field.title: Elevation at any point on a straight grade
field.topic: Survey math for crews: grades, curves and offsets
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: On a parabolic vertical curve, elevation at distance x from the BVC = BVC elevation + g1 x x + (g2 - g1) / (2L) x x^2, with g1 and g2 the grades in and out (as decimals) and L the curve length. The high or low point is at x = -g1 x L / (g2 - g1). Example: BVC elevation 100.00, g1 = +2 percent, g2 = -1 percent, L = 300 ft: at x = 100 ft, elevation = 100 + 0.02 x 100 + (-0.03 / 600) x 10,000 = 100 + 2 - 0.5 = 101.50.
field.title: Vertical curve elevations
field.topic: Survey math for crews: grades, curves and offsets
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Curve terms: R radius; Δ (delta) central angle; L arc length = R x Δ in radians (Δ degrees x pi / 180); T tangent length = R x tan(Δ/2); chord = 2R x sin(Δ/2); external E = R x (1/cos(Δ/2) - 1); middle ordinate M = R x (1 - cos(Δ/2)). Example: R = 200 ft, Δ = 30 degrees: L = 200 x 0.5236 = 104.72 ft; T = 200 x 0.2679 = 53.59 ft. Stations run along the arc. Offsets on a curve are measured along the radius.
field.title: Horizontal curve basics
field.topic: Survey math for crews: grades, curves and offsets
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: To turn a right angle in the field without an instrument: from the point on the line, measure 3 ft along the line and 4 ft out, and adjust until the diagonal is 5 ft (or use 6-8-10, or 30-40-50 for longer layouts). Then measure the offset distance along that square line. For long offsets or when accuracy matters, use the instrument. A small error in the angle grows with distance: 1 degree off over a 15 ft offset is about 3 in sideways.
field.title: Offset at right angles: the 3-4-5 check
field.topic: Survey math for crews: grades, curves and offsets
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Merging taper length L (feet) for a lane closure, from the MUTCD: for speeds 40 mph or less, L = W x S^2 / 60; for 45 mph or more, L = W x S, where W is the lateral shift in feet (usually the lane width) and S is the posted speed or 85th-percentile speed in mph. Example: 12 ft lane at 35 mph: L = 12 x 1225 / 60 = 245 ft. At 55 mph: L = 12 x 55 = 660 ft. Shifting tapers use 1/2 L, shoulder tapers 1/3 L. The agency's approved traffic control plan governs.
field.title: Taper length formulas (MUTCD)
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: MUTCD guidance: in a taper, space channelizing devices no more than the speed limit in feet apart (35 mph, 35 ft); in the tangent along the work area, no more than about twice the speed limit in feet. Closer spacing is common in urban areas, at night and around turns. Add a buffer space before the work where possible. Devices must be retroreflective at night. Follow the approved plan and the agency's standard plans (in California, the CA MUTCD and Caltrans standard plans).
field.title: Cone and channelizer spacing
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Flaggers stand on the shoulder next to the lane they control, or in the closed lane, and step into the open lane only after traffic has stopped (MUTCD flagger procedures); clearly visible well ahead, with an escape route, wearing high-visibility apparel (class 2 or 3), using a STOP/SLOW paddle (not a flag, except in emergencies). Signs warn ahead of the flagger ("Flagger Ahead" symbol). Flaggers must be trained and certified where the state requires it. Never turn your back on traffic, and coordinate with the flagger at the other end by radio or sight.
field.title: Flagger basics
field.topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A fire service is a dedicated line from the water main to a building's fire sprinklers or a private hydrant system, usually with a gate valve at the main, a backflow assembly (double check detector assembly, DCDA, or reduced pressure detector assembly, RPDA, as the water purveyor requires), and a fire department connection (FDC) nearby. The backflow assembly is tested when installed and every year by a certified tester. Underground fire lines are often built and inspected to NFPA 24 and the fire marshal's standards, with their own flush and hydrostatic test.
field.title: Fire service lines and backflow devices
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A hot tap connects a new line to a live main without shutting it down: a tapping sleeve is bolted around the main, a tapping valve is bolted to the sleeve, the sleeve is pressure-tested, then a tapping machine drills through the main with the valve open and is withdrawn before the valve is closed. The cut coupon must be kept and shown to the inspector. Many water agencies do their own taps or require their inspector present. Size-on-size taps need a full-encirclement sleeve made for it.
field.title: Hot taps (tapping sleeve and valve)
field.topic: Water: valves, hydrants, taps, air valves, blow-offs, services
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A crowfoot is a short horizontal line with three short toes (like a bird's foot) drawn on the lath or a guard stake. The flat line marks the exact height or point the cut or fill is measured from, instead of the top of the hub. Cut is measured down from the crowfoot line, fill up from it. On an on-grade stake (GRADE, GRD, O/G) the crowfoot line is at design grade itself. On pavement paint a crowfoot or a line with a tick points to the nail or mark it describes.
field.title: Crowfoot on a stake or lath
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: A horizontal line with an arrow pointing down = cut (dig down from the line); arrow pointing up = fill (build up from the line); arrows at both ends of a line or a line with GRADE = finish grade at that line. An arrow along the length of the lath or on pavement points toward the hub, the face or the point described. Arrows are a common surveyor habit, but the written C or F always wins over an arrow if they seem to disagree; ask the surveyor if they do.
field.title: Arrows and lines drawn on stakes
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: A stake at design grade is marked GRADE, GRD, O/G, ON GRADE, 0.00, C=F, or C 0.00 / F 0.00, often with a crowfoot at grade. A mark like "C=F" is read as cut equals fill, which means on grade. Daylight stakes (DAY, D/L) mark where cut changes to fill or the end of a cut or fill.
field.title: On-grade marks
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: The offset distance is usually written at the top of the lath, above the description: "10 / SD", "5 / WALL / WF". Many surveyors draw a circle around the offset number (a circled 5 = 5 ft off whatever the stake names); others write O/S or OS, or underline the offset twice, or put it above a line. L/O usually means line only: the stake is good for line, not for distance. Some surveyors write L/O for lath offset instead, so check the staking legend. A number in front of a slash on a utility lath is an offset distance, never a pipe size.
field.title: Offset marks: circled or underlined numbers
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: Cut and fill are in feet to the hundredth (Caltrans marks distances, elevations and cuts/fills to the nearest 0.01 ft; slope stakes, abutment fill stakes and rough grade stakes to the nearest 0.1 ft). Common styles: C-4.68 and F+8.11; C 4.68; a short dash or dot after the C or F as a separator ("C. 4 68", "F- 8 11"), with the decimals written small, raised or underlined after the whole feet. Never drop the small digits: "F- 8 11" with the 11 small is fill 8.11 ft, not 0.8. Some crews write F-1 for fill 1 ft, so the letter C or F decides cut or fill, not the sign. Feet and inches only when written with ' and " (4'-8 3/16").
field.title: How cut and fill numbers are written
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual, Chapter 12 Construction Surveys (Nov 2012) and standard construction staking practice

field.text: The reference point is what every cut, fill, distance and elevation on the stake is measured from. It can be a wooden hub (Caltrans calls a 1x1 hub a ginnie), a hub with a tack (the tack is the exact point), a spike, a concrete nail or PK/mag nail in asphalt, a scribed or chiseled X or + on concrete, or the marker stake itself. Distances are measured from the RP away from the face of the marker stake (the side with the writing). RPSS = reference point for a slope stake: the stake is a reference to the slope point, not the slope point itself.
field.title: Reference point (RP) kinds
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual, Chapter 12 Construction Surveys (Nov 2012) and standard construction staking practice

field.text: Caltrans stake and flagging colors: horizontal and vertical control (benchmarks) white/red; clearing limits yellow/black; grading stakes (slope, rough grade, final grade) yellow; structure stakes white; drainage stakes blue; right of way and fencing white/yellow; miscellaneous orange. Pink, white or orange flagging may be added for contrast. Private surveyors often use their own colors and tape bands per line or stake type, so read the writing first and describe a color band without guessing what it codes on that job.
field.title: Survey stake color codes (Caltrans)
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual, Chapter 12 Construction Surveys (Nov 2012) and standard construction staking practice

field.text: ABUT abutment; AHD ahead; BAR barrier face; BC / EC begin / end curve; BCR / ECR begin / end curb return; BEN bench; BEG / END begin / end; BSR / ESR / MSR begin / end / mid slope rounding; BL base line; BK back (with WALL or SW); BR bridge; BSW back of sidewalk; C / F cut / fill; CGS contour grade stake; CHNL channel; CL centerline (a dot is also used); CONFM conform; CONT contour; CNTRL control stakes; CP catch point; CS curb stake; DAY or D/L daylight; DI drainage inlet; DIT ditch; DS drainage stake or system; EL / ELEV elevation; EP edge of pavement; ES edge of shoulder; ETW edge of traveled way; EW end wall; FDN foundation; FNC fence; FG finish grade; FGS final grade stake; FL / FLC flow line / flow line of curb; FSW front of sidewalk; FWALL face of wall.
field.title: Caltrans stake abbreviations A to F
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual, Chapter 12 Construction Surveys (Nov 2012) and standard construction staking practice

field.text: GRT grate; GTR gutter; HP hinge point (top of slope within the design surface); ISS intermediate slope stake; INV invert; L length; L/2, L/4 mid and quarter point of a long facility such as a pipe; LIP lip of gutter; L/O line only; LOL layout line for retaining, sound or wing walls; LT / RT left / right; ML match line (grade break); MON survey monument; OG original ground; O/S offset; PCC point of compound curve; PG profile grade; PPP pavement plane projected to a point (also SL); PRC point of reverse curve; QSR, 1/2 SR, 3/4 SR quarter, mid and three-quarter points of slope rounding; R radius; RGS rough grade stake; RP reference point; RPSS reference point for a slope stake; RSP rock slope protection; R/W right of way; S/C saw cut line; SE superelevation; SG subgrade; SHLD / SHO shoulder; SL stationing line; SR slope rounding; SS slope stake; STR structure; SW sidewalk; TBC / TC top back of curb / top of curb; TBERM top of berm; TDITCH top of ditch; TOE toe of slope or fill; TOP top of berm, ditch or wall; TW traveled way (on Caltrans stakes; on wall stakes TW is usually top of wall); WALL / WW wall / wingwall; TBM temporary benchmark; delta/2, delta/4 fractions of a curve length for cul-de-sacs and curb returns.
field.title: Caltrans stake abbreviations G to W
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual, Chapter 12 Construction Surveys (Nov 2012) and standard construction staking practice

field.text: A slope stake (SS) or its reference (RPSS) gives the distance and cut or fill from the reference to the catch point, then each slope segment in turn: cut or fill, distance and slope ratio, each measured from the previous point ("point to point" or "then" staking). Example: C 16.9 on 1:1 to the bench toe, then F 1.0 on 10:1 to the bench lip, then C 30.0 on 1:1 to the hinge point. Slope ratios are horizontal to vertical (2:1 = 2 ft out for 1 ft up or down) and carry no sign. Slope stakes are marked to 0.1 ft.
field.title: Slope stakes and 'then' staking
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual, Chapter 12 Construction Surveys (Nov 2012) and standard construction staking practice

field.text: Caltrans wall stakes give the horizontal offset to the wall layout line (LOL) and elevations only, no cut or fill. Private site work often writes the wall grades as cuts and fills from the hub, with an offset to the wall face: "5 / WALL / WF" then "F 8.11 TW / C 4.68 TF" = 5 ft off the wall face, fill 8.11 ft to top of wall, cut 4.68 ft to top of footing. Major structure stakes name the part (Abutment 1, wingwall), the layout line, the RP elevation and the distance along the layout line, with no cut or fill. Curb stakes (CS) give the RP elevation and the cut or fill and distance to the curb flow line, e.g. 0.11 below at 3.00 ft.
field.title: Wall, structure and curb stakes
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
