field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual, Chapter 12 Construction Surveys (Nov 2012) and standard construction staking practice

field.text: On hardscape there is often no lath. The point is a PK or mag nail, a nail and shiner (washer), a drilled hole, or a chiseled or scribed X or + in concrete, often with a painted circle, dot or triangle around it. The station, offset, description and cut or fill are spray painted next to it with an arrow or crowfoot pointing to the point. A painted triangle often marks a control point; a painted circle with a dot or cross marks a set point. Utility locate paint (811: color lines, arrows, owner letters, W, G, E) is not a grade mark.
field.title: Marks on concrete and pavement
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: Typical plan symbols (they vary by agency; the sheet legend wins): triangle = control point or benchmark (BM, TBM); circle with a dot or cross = found or set survey monument; open circle = iron pipe or rebar set; filled circle = found monument; x with a number = spot elevation; + = point or station mark; small square = PK or nail; double circle = well monument. Bearings and distances along lines are written like N 45°12'30" E 125.50'. A circled number over another number (5/C3) points to detail 5 on sheet C3.
field.title: Survey point and monument symbols on plans
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: Utilities are drawn as lines broken by letters: —W— water, —SS— or —S— sanitary sewer, —SD— storm drain, —RW— recycled water, —G— gas, —E— or —UGE— underground electric, —OHE— overhead electric, —T— telephone, —FO— fiber, —TV— cable, —IRR— irrigation, —FM— force main. Proposed lines are usually drawn heavy and solid; existing lines lighter, dashed or labeled (E) or EX; abandoned lines with x marks or ABAN. The pipe size and material are written along the line (8" PVC SDR 35). Flow arrows on sewer and storm lines point downstream.
field.title: Utility line types on plans
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: Typical plan symbols (check the legend): circle = manhole (SSMH, SDMH), often with a number; square or rectangle on the curb line = catch basin or curb inlet; small square = cleanout, meter box or junction box; bowtie (two triangles point to point) = valve (gate or butterfly); filled bowtie = closed valve; triangle on a line pointing toward the small side = reducer; T shape = tee; short perpendicular bar at the line end = cap or plug; hydrant drawn as a circle with side nozzles or a star-like symbol; small circle with a line to the main = service or lateral; zigzag or angled jog = bend with its angle written (22.5°, 45°); hatched block behind a fitting = thrust block. Wye laterals are drawn at 45° off the main.
field.title: Utility structure and fitting symbols on plans
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: Contours: thin dashed lines = existing ground, solid heavier lines = proposed grade, every fifth one darker with its elevation (index contour). Spot elevations: a small x or + with the elevation, often FS, FG, TC, FL, TW or BW written after it (TW 1256.40 / BW 1248.20 at a wall). Flow arrows show drainage direction with the slope written on them (1.0%). Slope arrows point downhill. Hatched or stippled areas mark pavement, concrete or rip-rap; the legend says which. Daylight or catch lines show where the cut or fill meets existing ground. GB grade break, HP high point, LP low point, FF finished floor, PAD pad elevation.
field.title: Grading symbols on plans
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: A section cut is a line with arrows or flags at each end and a letter or number (A–A) showing which way you are looking; the matching section is drawn elsewhere with the same label. A detail callout is a circle split by a line: the top number is the detail, the bottom is the sheet it is on (5 / D2). A match line (ML) with a sheet number means the drawing continues on that sheet. A north arrow shows plan north; plan stationing increases in the direction the alignment is drawn. A cloud with a triangle and number marks a revision.
field.title: Section, detail and match line symbols
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: Surveyors and companies add their own marks: tick marks, scribbles, check marks, initials, crossed-out old numbers, or a symbol that means something only to that survey crew. When a mark on a stake is not a standard symbol, say what it looks like in one line and that the surveyor who set it can say what it means; do not guess. Read the standard parts of the stake (offset, description, cut and fill) as normal. A number or word crossed out with an X or a line was usually voided and replaced by the writing next to it.
field.title: A mark you cannot identify
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard construction staking and plan drafting practice (US civil and utility work); symbols vary by agency and surveyor

field.text: On mass grading, grade checkers tie colored ribbon (flagging) on the lath so an operator can read the cut or fill from the seat without reading the writing. The common Southern California code, taught by Operating Engineers Local 12 grade-checker trainers and first used by a California earthmoving contractor: BLUE = grade; WHITE = 1 ft cut; RED = 2 ft cut; RED + WHITE = 3 ft cut; YELLOW = 4 ft cut; YELLOW + WHITE = 5 ft cut; YELLOW + RED = 6 ft cut. Deeper than that, cut down and have it restaked. FILL: blue added to a cut color turns it into fill: BLUE + WHITE = 1 ft fill, BLUE + RED = 2 ft fill, BLUE + RED + WHITE = 3 ft fill, BLUE + YELLOW = 4 ft fill. Trainers say the most common mistake by a new grade setter is forgetting the white ribbon 1 ft above the blue on a fill stake. When one lath carries two sets of ribbons (a lot split or a stake between two pads), the knot faces the side that ribbon is for.
field.title: Grade-checker ribbon color code for mass grading (cut and fill by the foot)
field.topic: Survey flagging and ribbon colors: grade-checker codes, agency colors, control points
field.source: Operating Engineers Local 12 grade-checker training code as described by grade checkers (heavyequipmentforums.com threads 33582 and 62002); a Southern California practice, not a national standard

field.text: Grade-checker ribbon codes vary by region, company and crew. Other versions in use: yellow = 3 ft, yellow + red = 5 ft, blue + white = top of slope (a Texas recollection), and many places use no code at all and tie whatever ribbon is handy. Before cutting off ribbons alone, confirm the code with the grade checker or foreman on that job, and check at least one ribboned stake against its written cut or fill. The writing on the lath and the cut sheet always win over a ribbon. When reading a photo, give the ribbon meaning under the common Southern California code and say it is that code.
field.title: The ribbon code is not universal: check it on the job
field.topic: Survey flagging and ribbon colors: grade-checker codes, agency colors, control points
field.source: Operating Engineers Local 12 grade-checker training code as described by grade checkers (heavyequipmentforums.com threads 33582 and 62002); a Southern California practice, not a national standard

field.text: Common grade-checker marks on grading lath (Southern California practice): the lath is painted BLUE below the crowfoot and ORANGE above it, so the grade line shows from the machine. Break lines get streamers: a SINGLE ORANGE streamer marks hinge points and tops of slope; a DOUBLE ORANGE streamer marks toes of slope and centerline. Blue tops are hubs driven to finished grade with the top painted blue. Grade checkers and surveyors do not always use the same break-line marks, so ask.
field.title: Lath paint and streamers on grading stakes
field.topic: Survey flagging and ribbon colors: grade-checker codes, agency colors, control points
field.source: Operating Engineers Local 12 grade-checker training code as described by grade checkers (heavyequipmentforums.com threads 33582 and 62002); a Southern California practice, not a national standard

field.text: For finish grading without a laser or GPS, some grade checkers lay ribbons on the ground and notch them in with a hatchet, using the same colors to mean TENTHS of a foot instead of feet: white 0.1, red 0.2, red + white 0.3, yellow 0.4, and blue added = fill (blue + red = 0.2 ft fill). Whether ribbons mean feet or tenths depends on the stage of the work: rough grade ribbons are feet, finish ribbons on the ground are tenths. Ask if it is not clear.
field.title: Ribbons for finish grade in tenths
field.topic: Survey flagging and ribbon colors: grade-checker codes, agency colors, control points
field.source: Operating Engineers Local 12 grade-checker training code as described by grade checkers (heavyequipmentforums.com threads 33582 and 62002); a Southern California practice, not a national standard

field.text: Agencies set flagging colors for their own jobs. Orange County Public Works (California) construction staking guide: red = clearing and grubbing, ESA and limits of grading; orange = slope staking, terrace drains, rough grade, retaining walls, storm drains and drop inlets, levees, major structure rough grade; fluorescent green = pavement final grade, curb and gutter, driveways, curb ramps, sewer lines and sewer manholes; blue = water lines; white = gas and dry utilities, minor structures, bridge parts, building final grade, channel bottom and top; yellow = fences; BLACK flagging added = a restake. Caltrans: control white/red, clearing yellow/black, grading yellow, structure white, drainage blue, right of way and fence white/yellow, miscellaneous orange. Private surveyors often use their own colors: read the writing and the job legend.
field.title: Stake and flagging colors by feature: agency standards
field.topic: Survey flagging and ribbon colors: grade-checker codes, agency colors, control points
field.source: Orange County Public Works, OC Survey Construction Staking Guide (2021 edition); Caltrans Surveys Manual Chapter 12

field.text: Control points, benchmarks and monuments are usually guarded by a lath with bright flagging and often a painted circle or triangle; Caltrans uses white/red for horizontal and vertical control. Many private surveyors use pink, red/white striped or 'glo' flagging on control, but there is no national rule. Treat any flagged hub, nail, pin or cap with no grading writing as possible control: don't disturb it, don't use it for grade unless the surveyor says so, and report it if it's in the way. A knocked-out control point must be reset by the surveyor.
field.title: Flagging on control points and benchmarks
field.topic: Survey flagging and ribbon colors: grade-checker codes, agency colors, control points
field.source: Caltrans Surveys Manual Chapter 12; standard construction staking practice

field.text: Small flags and paint lines from 811 locators follow the APWA / Common Ground Alliance uniform color code: white = proposed excavation; pink = temporary survey markings; red = electric power lines, cables, conduit and lighting cables; yellow = gas, oil, steam, petroleum or gaseous materials; orange = communication, alarm or signal lines, cables or conduit; blue = potable water; purple = reclaimed water, irrigation and slurry lines; green = sewers and drain lines. Locate flags often carry the owner's initials. A utility flag is not a survey or grade flag.
field.title: Utility locate flags and paint (811 color code)
field.topic: Survey flagging and ribbon colors: grade-checker codes, agency colors, control points
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines

field.text: A control point (CP), benchmark (BM) or temporary benchmark (TBM) is the point the whole job's line and grade come from. The actual point is small: a hub and tack, a rebar or iron pipe with a plastic or aluminum cap (often stamped with the surveyor's license number, LS or PLS, or RCE), a brass disk in concrete, a PK or MAG nail with a washer (shiner) in asphalt, a chiseled X or square on concrete, a drill hole, or a spike. Everything around it (lath, flagging, paint, posts) is only there to find it and protect it. The writing on a control guard lath is usually CP or TBM with a number, sometimes an elevation or coordinates, and often DO NOT DISTURB or DND. It has no cut or fill.
field.title: What a control point looks like
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: Surveyors protect a point with lath around it, not on it. Common setups: one or two flagged guard lath beside the point; three lath driven around the point and tied together at the top like a teepee or tripod, with the point in the middle under the peak; four lath in a square with flagging strung between them (a lath box or flagging fence). The point is the hub or nail in the center, not any of the lath. Don't pull the lath to get a machine through: the point is usually lost when the guard goes. A lath tripod or box is never a grade stake.
field.title: Guard lath, lath tripods and lath boxes
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: Whiskers (also called feathers) are a short bundle of plastic flagging strips held down by a nail, driven into pavement, a road shoulder or dirt so the point can be seen. The nail under the whiskers is the point. Whiskers are used for control, for points in pavement and for points that would be lost under a lath. They look like trash or a utility flag: don't kick them out or sweep them up. Utility locate flags are small flags on wire stems in the 811 colors; whiskers are loose strips under a nail head.
field.title: Whiskers and feathers
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: On pavement and concrete a control point is often marked with a painted circle, triangle or square around the nail or disk, with CP, TBM, BM or the point number, and sometimes DO NOT DISTURB, DND or arrows pointing to it. A painted dot or X next to a nail, or arrows on a curb pointing to a mark, also show where a point is. WSDOT uses pink paint for survey marks and white for stationing on paved shoulders. Survey paint is not a utility locate mark, and painting over or grinding a control mark destroys it.
field.title: Paint around control points
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: A witness post is a flexible fiberglass or carsonite post, or a steel fence post, set near a monument or control point to help find it and keep machines off it. It often has a decal like PLEASE DO NOT DISTURB NEARBY SURVEY MARKER. The post is NOT on the point: the point is nearby, usually flush with the ground and within a few feet. Some points also have a sign, cones, barricades or orange fence around them on busy sites.
field.title: Witness posts and signs
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: Surveyors expect points to get destroyed, so they reference them: ties (distances from the point to three or more nearby permanent objects such as a curb corner, power pole or hydrant), offset hubs set well outside the work, and backup control points and TBMs in safe spots. Ties are often painted on the curb, pole or wall with the point number, a distance and an arrow (CP 5 12.45 ft). An RP or reference hub is a backup to find a point again; it is not the point itself. Don't remove or pave over ties.
field.title: Reference ties, offset hubs and backup points
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: Benchmarks and control are often set where they will survive, which can confuse a crew: a spike or nail in a power pole, a nail in a tree, a bolt on a fire hydrant bonnet or flange (a common TBM), a chiseled square or drill hole on top of a curb or headwall, a brass disk set in a sidewalk, bridge, wall or building foundation, a rebar and cap set in concrete, a buried monument in a monument well with a round lid marked SURVEY or MONUMENT, or a point under a flush cover found with a metal detector. Treat any marked nail, disk, cap or chiseled mark as a survey point until the surveyor says it isn't.
field.title: Control points in odd places
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: Don't move, cover, pave over or reset a control point yourself, and don't set grade from a point that has been bumped (a hub that wobbles, a bent rebar, a cracked disk or a nail with a fresh scrape). Stop work at that point, flag it, and tell the foreman and surveyor so it can be checked or reset. In California, Business and Professions Code 8771 requires that monuments be located and referenced by a licensed surveyor before construction that may disturb them, and reset with a corner record after; whoever destroys one without that can be held responsible for the cost of resetting it. Plan the work so control is out of the way, and ask the surveyor to move control before you need that ground.
field.title: If a control point is in the way or gets hit
field.topic: Survey control points: how they are marked and protected, and what not to confuse them with
field.source: Standard survey practice; WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97 Ch. 15-16; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12; Calif. Business and Professions Code 8771

field.text: Centerline is written CL or with the centerline symbol, a C and an L drawn over each other (the L's upright through the middle of the C), printed as ℄. By hand it can look like a C with a line through it, a cent sign, a crossed C, or a C next to an L. On a stake, 'CL' or the symbol means the offset or station is measured from the centerline of the road, pipe or structure named (15 LT CL = 15 ft left of centerline). Caltrans also uses a dot for centerline, and on plans the centerline is drawn as a long-short-long dashed line, often labeled with the street or line name. Other line symbols: PL property line (a P and L overlapped by hand), R/W or ROW right of way, ML match line, BL base line, SL stationing line.
field.title: Centerline symbol
field.topic: Survey and plan symbols: stake marks, colors and plan symbols
field.source: Standard survey and drafting practice; Caltrans Surveys Manual Ch. 12

field.text: USA marks are the paint, flags, stakes and whiskers utility owners (or their locators) put down after an 811 ticket. USA is Underground Service Alert, California's 811 center (USA North 811 in the north, DigAlert in the south). The color says what kind of utility it is; the writing says who owns it and what it is. 811 marks show the approximate location of the line, not its depth: you still have to find it by hand inside the tolerance zone. Colors (APWA): white = proposed excavation (put down by the excavator); pink = temporary survey marks; red = electric; yellow = gas, oil, steam, petroleum; orange = communication, alarm, signal, CATV, fiber; blue = potable water; purple = reclaimed water, irrigation, slurry; green = sewer and storm drain.
field.title: What USA marks are
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines (APWA color code)

field.text: A locate mark is usually a dash about 12 to 18 in long and 1 in wide, repeated every 4 to 50 ft along the line, drawn over the center of the line or over its outside edges joined by a connecting line. The owner's initials or name (PG&E, SCE, SDG&E, SOCALGAS, ATT, a water district's initials) go at the start and end of the marked area and where it crosses another owner's line of the same color. Size and material are written at intervals: 12" STL = 12 in steel; 4" PLA = 4 in plastic; 6" PLA/12" STL = a 6 in plastic pipe in a 12 in steel casing. An arrow shows the direction the line runs, a change in direction, or where a lateral or service branches off; a curved arc shows a radius. A line ending in a T, a bar or the word END marks a dead end or termination.
field.title: Reading a locate mark: lines, dashes and arrows
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines (APWA color code)

field.text: When several lines run together, the mark shows the count and size over the center: 4/4" PLA = four 4 in plastic ducts; 9/4" CAB = nine 4 in cables or ducts. Conduit and duct banks may be marked at their outside edges to show the real width. A corridor mark (CDR) is used when the count isn't known: two outside lines with the width written, such as 12" CDR, mean everything is somewhere inside that width. Vaults, inlets and other structures are outlined to show their size. Dig carefully across the whole width, not just the center line.
field.title: Multiple lines, duct banks and corridors
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines (APWA color code)

field.text: When a line can't be marked over the top (a road, a wall, a busy street), the locator paints or stakes an offset: an arrow toward the line with the distance, like 5' → or OFFSET 10' LT, meaning the line is that far away in that direction. 'NO' plus the owner's initials in that owner's color means that owner has no lines in your marked area (NO TELCO, NO SCE; a multi-utility owner may add the type, like NO PGE/G for no gas). Clear or translucent 'No Conflict' flags mean the same. Some owners give the no-conflict answer by phone, email or the 811 positive response instead of paint. No marks and no response is not a clear: call the owner or 811 before digging.
field.title: Offsets, no-conflict and clear marks
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines (APWA color code)

field.text: E or ELEC electric; P or PRI primary electric; S or SEC secondary electric; SL street light; TS traffic signal; G gas; HP high-pressure gas (or HP on any high-pressure line); T, TEL or TELCO telephone; FO fiber optic; CATV or TV cable TV; C or COMM communications; W water; RW reclaimed water; IRR irrigation; S or SS sewer; SD storm drain; FM force main; STL steel; PLA or PL plastic; PE polyethylene; PVC; CI cast iron; DI ductile iron; AC or ACP asbestos cement; CU copper; CAB cable; CDR corridor; DB duct bank; CSG casing; ABAN abandoned; SVC service; LAT lateral; D or DIST distribution; TR or TRANS transmission (/G/D gas distribution, /G/T gas transmission, /E/D, /E/T for electric). The owner's name or initials are always on the marks somewhere.
field.title: Common locate abbreviations
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines (APWA color code)

field.text: White paint, white flags or white stakes mark where the excavator plans to dig, before the 811 ticket goes in. In California, white delineation is required (unless the area can't be marked and the 811 center is told the boundaries another way). Styles: a continuous white line or dashes around the dig area; dots or corner marks for small sites; for trenching or boring, a white centerline with arrows showing the direction of the work. A single white stake with the company name and a radius (up to 50 ft) can mark a small round dig. White marks often include the company name or initials. White is not a utility.
field.title: White paint: marking your own dig
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines (APWA color code); California Government Code 4216 et seq. (Dig Safe Act); USA North 811 and DigAlert (Underground Service Alert of Southern California)

field.text: Under California Government Code 4216 (the Dig Safe Act): call 811 (USA) at least 2 working days before digging, not counting the day you call, and no more than 14 calendar days before; mark the area in white first; the ticket is good for 28 days and must be renewed if work continues; owners must locate and mark or say no conflict within 2 working days; the tolerance zone is 24 in on each side of the field marking (from a single mark, treated as the centerline; from each outside edge mark when the width is shown), measured horizontally, and inside it you expose the line with hand tools or vacuum excavation (or another method the operator allows) before using power equipment; if marks are gone or faded, ask for a remark through 811 before continuing; high priority lines (like high-pressure gas and large petroleum lines) need an on-site meeting with the owner before digging near them; report any damage, even a scrape, to the owner right away and call 911 if anything is leaking or there's danger. Check the current law and your ticket; rules and timelines change.
field.title: California dig rules that go with the marks
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: California Government Code 4216 et seq. (Dig Safe Act); USA North 811 and DigAlert (Underground Service Alert of Southern California)

field.text: 811 locate marks don't give depth, and depth changes along a line (private locators may write an estimated depth). They are only accurate to within the tolerance zone, they can be off where lines bend, and they don't show private lines the owner doesn't own (private sewer laterals, irrigation, site lighting, private fire lines, abandoned lines that are no longer on maps). Survey paint (pink, or the surveyor's own colors) and grade marks are not locates. Before trenching a long run, pothole every marked crossing and anything parallel and close, and ask the owner of the property about private lines.
field.title: Things locate marks don't tell you
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Standard damage-prevention practice; Common Ground Alliance Best Practices, Appendix B: Uniform Color Code and Marking Guidelines (APWA color code)

field.text: 811 (USA) locates are free to the excavator: the 811 center notifies the member utility owners, and each owner (or a contract locator working for it, such as USIC or another locating company wearing the owner's name) marks only the lines it owns, usually up to the meter, the property line or the point of service. Everything past that point belongs to the property owner and is NOT marked by 811: private sewer laterals, private water and fire lines, gas yard lines past the meter, electric past the meter, site lighting and parking lot power, irrigation, storm drains on private sites, communication lines between buildings, and abandoned lines. A private locate is a paid service the contractor or owner hires to find those lines, using electromagnetic locators, ground penetrating radar (GPR), and sondes or cameras in sewer and storm lines. Private locators use the same APWA colors but mark with their own company name and are responsible only under their contract. Private locators can also write an estimated depth on their marks (for example D 4.2' or 4' DPTH), read from the locator's depth function; it is an estimate (less reliable near other lines, on deep lines and on bends), so pothole before trusting it. A private locate never replaces the 811 ticket: in California you still need a valid USA ticket and white marks. On private sites (schools, plants, shopping centers, campuses, older industrial sites), assume there are unmarked private lines until a private locate and potholing say otherwise.
field.title: Public (811/USA) locates vs private locates
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Calif. Government Code 4216 et seq.; Common Ground Alliance Best Practices; standard damage-prevention practice

field.text: In practice, 811 marks are not complete. Sewer and storm drain are often NOT marked: many cities, sewer districts and flood control agencies don't mark their gravity lines, mark them only on request, or just send a no-conflict or a map; find them from the plans and as-builts, manholes, inlets and cleanouts, and with a camera or sonde. Irrigation: when a water or irrigation district marks purple or irrigation lines, it usually marks only the irrigation MAIN, not laterals, valve wiring, drip or sprinkler lines. 811 only marks public (member) utilities up to their point of service; private lines are never marked by 811. Unmarked does not mean nothing is there: on every job, check the plans for sewer, storm and irrigation, look for manholes, inlets, valve boxes and cleanouts, and hire a private locator or pothole where lines are likely.
field.title: What 811 (DigAlert / USA) often doesn't mark: sewer, storm drain, irrigation, private
field.topic: USA / 811 utility locate marks: flags, paint, abbreviations and what they mean
field.source: Field experience of DIG Civil Construction (Southern California); Calif. Government Code 4216 et seq.

field.text: Most locating is done with an electromagnetic (EM) locator: a receiver that picks up the magnetic field around a metal line carrying current. Metal lines (steel, cast and ductile iron, copper, cables) or plastic lines with a tracer wire can be traced; plain plastic, concrete, clay and AC pipe without a wire give no signal. The receiver shows a peak (strongest signal right over the line) or a null (weakest right over it, depending on mode); good locators confirm with both. Passive mode picks up signals already on lines (60 Hz power, radio), which finds live power cables but can't tell lines apart. Active mode uses a transmitter to put a known frequency on one line, so the locator can follow that specific line.
field.title: How an electromagnetic locator works
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: Standard utility locating practice (electromagnetic locator, GPR and sonde manufacturers' guidance, CGA Best Practices); ASCE 38 for quality levels

field.text: Ways to put signal on a line: DIRECT CONNECT (clip a lead onto the line, a valve, meter, riser, tracer wire or test station, and ground the other lead to a stake in the dirt): the cleanest, most accurate signal on that line. CLAMP or coupler (a ring clamped around a cable or small pipe at a pedestal or riser): good for cables you can't clip onto. INDUCTION (set the transmitter on the ground over the line; it broadcasts signal into anything metal below): fast but less selective, and the signal jumps onto nearby lines. Plastic water and gas lines are traced through their tracer wire at test stations, valve boxes or meters; a broken or missing tracer wire means the line can't be located electronically.
field.title: Hooking up the transmitter: direct connect, clamp and induction
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: Standard utility locating practice (electromagnetic locator, GPR and sonde manufacturers' guidance, CGA Best Practices); ASCE 38 for quality levels

field.text: Low frequencies (about 512 Hz to 1 kHz) travel far on one line with little bleed onto others: best for long, well-grounded runs. Middle frequencies (about 8 to 33 kHz) are the general choice. High frequencies (about 65 to 200 kHz) jump across gaps and insulating joints and onto nearby lines (bleed-over): useful on poor connections, but they can light up the wrong line. Marks can be off when lines run close together or cross, near bends, tees and services, under rebar, fences, guardrail or overhead power, and where the signal splits at a tee. A good locator checks the signal strength both ways and walks the whole line. This is why marks are only trusted within the tolerance zone.
field.title: Frequencies, bleed-over and why marks can be wrong
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: Standard utility locating practice (electromagnetic locator, GPR and sonde manufacturers' guidance, CGA Best Practices); ASCE 38 for quality levels

field.text: A locator's depth readout compares the signal at the bottom and top antennas in the receiver; it reads to the center of the signal, not the top of the pipe, and only works when the receiver is right over a single clean signal. Field checks: the 45 degree method (find the null at 45 degrees off each side; half the distance between them is about the depth) and the peak-width method. Depth is less reliable near other lines, at bends and tees, on deep lines, and with induction or high frequencies. 811 owners don't usually give depths; private locators may write an estimate. A depth reading is never a substitute for a pothole before digging close.
field.title: How locators estimate depth
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: Standard utility locating practice (electromagnetic locator, GPR and sonde manufacturers' guidance, CGA Best Practices); ASCE 38 for quality levels

field.text: GPR sends radar pulses into the ground and shows reflections from anything with different properties: plastic, concrete and clay pipe, voids, rebar, and metal lines. It is how private locators find non-metal lines with no tracer wire. It works best in dry sand and gravel and poorly in wet clay, saline soil or under wet concrete, where the signal dies within a foot or two. Typical useful depth is a few feet, deeper in good soil. GPR shows something is there, not what it is, so the locator ties it to manholes, valves, cleanouts and plans. Treat GPR marks as approximate and pothole them.
field.title: Ground penetrating radar (GPR)
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: Standard utility locating practice (electromagnetic locator, GPR and sonde manufacturers' guidance, CGA Best Practices); ASCE 38 for quality levels

field.text: Gravity sewer and storm lines are usually plastic, concrete, clay or AC with no tracer wire, so they can't be traced from the surface the normal way. Methods: a SONDE (a small battery transmitter) pushed into the pipe on a rodder, snake or jetter hose, or on a CCTV camera crawler, then followed from above with the locator set to the sonde frequency (commonly 512 Hz, 640 Hz or 33 kHz); the locator marks its path and reads its depth at each point. A TRACEABLE RODDER (a fiberglass rod with a copper wire inside) pushed through the pipe and hooked to the transmitter, then traced like a cable. Straight-line between structures: open the manholes or inlets, measure the direction of the pipes and the depth from the rim to each invert, and mark the straight line between them (gravity mains usually run straight between structures, but laterals and old lines may not). GPR in good soil. Dye tests or flow tests to confirm which line connects where. Plans and as-builts show the stationing, inverts and sizes to compare against.
field.title: Locating sewer and storm drain
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: Standard utility locating practice (electromagnetic locator, GPR and sonde manufacturers' guidance, CGA Best Practices); ASCE 38 for quality levels

field.text: Sewer laterals are found by pushing a sonde or camera up from the main (lateral launch cameras) or down from a cleanout at the house, then tracing it; the camera footage shows the distance to the wye. Water services are traced from the meter or curb stop with a direct connect to copper or the tracer wire on plastic. Valve boxes, manhole lids, meter boxes and monuments are iron, so a magnetic locator (magnetometer) finds them when they're paved or buried. Abandoned lines, dead services and lines with broken tracer wire may only show on GPR, old maps or by potholing.
field.title: Finding laterals, cleanouts and services
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: Standard utility locating practice (electromagnetic locator, GPR and sonde manufacturers' guidance, CGA Best Practices); ASCE 38 for quality levels

field.text: Engineers grade utility information by quality level (ASCE 38): QL-D comes from records and memory only; QL-C adds a survey of visible features (manholes, valves, poles) matched to records; QL-B adds surface geophysics (EM locators and GPR) to designate the line's horizontal position; QL-A exposes the line by potholing and surveys its exact horizontal and vertical position, size and material. 811 marks are roughly QL-B for horizontal location only. Only QL-A (a pothole) gives a reliable depth. Plans that show utilities as 'approximate' or from records are QL-C or QL-D.
field.title: Quality levels: how sure is the location (ASCE 38)
field.topic: How utility locating works: locators, frequencies, GPR, sondes, sewer and storm locating
field.source: ASCE/UESI/CI 38 Standard Guideline for Investigating and Documenting Existing Utilities; standard subsurface utility engineering practice

field.text: Push-on (Tyton, Fastite style) bell: a smooth flared bell with the gasket inside and no bolts; the spigot slides in. Mechanical joint (MJ): the bell has a flat face with a ring of T-bolt holes; a loose iron gland pulls a wedge-shaped gasket into the bell with T-bolts and nuts, tightened evenly in a star pattern to the maker's torque. Flanged: two flat flanges bolted face to face with a flat gasket between, used above ground, in vaults and at valves; never buried unless the spec allows. Ductile iron fittings are usually MJ (AWWA C110 full body or C153 compact), marked on the casting with size, angle, 'DI' and the maker.
field.title: Telling joint types apart: push-on, MJ, flanged
field.topic: Identifying fittings, joints and couplings on sight
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA C110/C111/C153, manufacturer installation guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Restrained joints hold the pipe in against thrust without blocks. On MJ fittings, a wedge-action restraint gland (Megalug style) looks like a thick MJ gland with a row of wedge screws around it whose heads twist off at the right torque: twisted-off heads mean they were tightened. For PVC there are PVC-rated restraint glands (Series 2000PV style), and split-ring 'bell restraint' harnesses that clamp behind the bell and tie across the joint with rods. Restraining gaskets (Field Lok style) have metal teeth in the gasket and look like a normal push-on joint from outside: check the spec or the tag. Restrained joints (TR Flex style) have a welded bead or ring on the spigot and a locking segment in the bell. The plans give the length of pipe to restrain on each side of a fitting.
field.title: Restraint you can see: wedge glands, restraining gaskets, harnesses
field.topic: Identifying fittings, joints and couplings on sight
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA C110/C111/C153, manufacturer installation guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Repair or straight couplings join two pipes of the same OD: a steel or ductile body with a gasket and follower ring at each end, bolted (Dresser or Smith-Blair style), or a full-circle repair clamp with a gasket mat and bolted lugs for patching a hole. Transition couplings have different-sized ends for joining different ODs (cast iron to PVC, AC to ductile); the OD range is stamped on each end. Flexible rubber couplings with stainless band clamps (Fernco style) are for gravity sewer and drain, not pressure; buried ones should have a stainless shear band. Ordinary bolted couplings don't restrain pulling apart unless they're the restrained type or harnessed. Always measure both ODs and match the coupling's stamped range.
field.title: Couplings: repair, transition, flexible, and how to tell them apart
field.topic: Identifying fittings, joints and couplings on sight
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA C110/C111/C153, manufacturer installation guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A tapping sleeve is a two-piece body bolted around a main with an outlet flange for a tapping valve: used for hot taps of new mains or large services. A service saddle is a smaller strap or band with a threaded outlet for a corporation stop (corp), used for 3/4 to 2 in services: the corp goes into the saddle (or straight into the pipe wall on direct-tap ductile iron where allowed), then the service line runs to a curb stop and the meter. Saddles for PVC must have wide straps or full-circle bands so they don't crush the pipe. The corp's inlet thread is usually AWWA (CC) taper thread or iron pipe thread; the outlet is compression or flare for copper or PE.
field.title: Tapping sleeves, saddles and corp stops
field.topic: Identifying fittings, joints and couplings on sight
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA C110/C111/C153, manufacturer installation guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Wye: the branch comes off at 45 degrees (used for laterals so flow joins in the direction of the main); tee-wye or sanitary tee: a curved 90 degree branch (vertical risers and cleanouts); plain tee: a square 90 (rarely used for gravity sewer entries). Bends are 11 1/4, 22 1/2, 45 and 90 degrees; long-sweep 90s are used in gravity lines and cleanouts. Clean-outs have a riser to grade with a threaded plug or cap in a box. Saddle wyes or Inserta-Tee style connections are used to add a lateral to an existing main. Gasketed sewer fittings are green like the pipe; check the SDR matches.
field.title: Gravity sewer fittings by shape
field.topic: Identifying fittings, joints and couplings on sight
field.source: Standard industry practice (AWWA C110/C111/C153, manufacturer installation guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: Survey and grade rods are usually in feet, tenths and hundredths: big red numbers are feet, black numbers are tenths (0.1 ft), and each black or white block (the E shapes) is 0.01 ft; the middle bar of each E sits at the 0.05. Read the foot, then the tenth below the line, then count hundredths. A fixed-target grade rod is set once (target at hub reading + cut) so the laser beeps on grade when the rod foot is at design grade. Some rods are in feet-inches-eighths (builders' rods): check the face before reading, and never mix them on one job. Keep the rod plumb (use a rod level): a tipped rod reads high.
field.title: Reading a grade rod in feet and tenths
field.topic: Grade rods, levels and pipe lasers: reading them in the field
field.source: Standard construction surveying and pipe laser practice (manufacturer guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A pipe laser sits in the pipe or on a stand in the manhole or trench at the downstream end and shoots a beam up the pipe at the set grade in percent (for example 0.40 percent = 0.0040 ft/ft). Set it with its bottom on the flowline (or a known height above it), dial in the grade from the plans, and aim the line with the line-scope or the alignment arrows at a line target or a plumb bob over the upstream stake. A target in the end of each new pipe shows where the beam hits: centered means on line and grade. A high beam on the target means the pipe end is low; low beam means the pipe is high. Recheck the laser against a stake every morning, after any bump, and when the sun or heat shimmer makes the beam bend. Most lasers show warnings when they're off level or bumped.
field.title: Pipe lasers: setting grade and reading the target
field.topic: Grade rods, levels and pipe lasers: reading them in the field
field.source: Standard construction surveying and pipe laser practice (manufacturer guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: A rotating laser sends a level or sloped plane; a receiver on the rod or the machine shows where the beam is. The display shows an arrow up (move the receiver up, meaning the rod foot is low: cut less or fill), an arrow down (move the receiver down, meaning the rod foot is high: cut more), and a center line or solid tone for on grade. Fast beeps usually mean high, slow beeps low, and a steady tone on grade, but this varies by brand; check the receiver's setting. Deadband (fine, medium, coarse) sets how close counts as on grade. On a machine receiver, the bars show the bucket or blade relative to grade. Check the rotating laser's height of instrument against a benchmark at setup and during the day.
field.title: Machine and rod laser receivers: what the arrows mean
field.topic: Grade rods, levels and pipe lasers: reading them in the field
field.source: Standard construction surveying and pipe laser practice (manufacturer guides); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

field.text: The Greenbook (Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction, SSPWC) is the standard spec most Southern California cities, counties and water and sewer districts adopt for public works, updated every few years (2021 and 2024 editions are in use). The contract's Special Provisions change or add to it, and agency standard plans and their own standards (for example San Diego's Whitebook, or a water district's standards) can override it, so the order is: Special Provisions, then plans, then the agency's standards, then the Greenbook. Key sections for pipe crews: 201 concrete and slurry, 203 asphalt, 207 gravity pipe, 208 pipe joints, 209 pressure pipe, 217 bedding and backfill materials, 300 earthwork, 302 roadway surfacing, 306 open trench conduit construction, 307 jacking and tunneling, 308 microtunneling, 309 monuments, and Part 4 (400s) existing improvements and utilities.
field.title: What the Greenbook is and how it's used
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Greenbook 306-3: a Cal/OSHA (DOSH) permit is required before digging a trench 5 ft or deeper that a person must enter. Trench width (306-3.4) is measured at the top of the bedding zone, 1 ft above the pipe crown, with minimum and maximum widths by pipe type and size in Tables 306-3.4 (A) and (B) (read the table in your edition; plastic and corrugated pipe have tight maximums, ductile iron a 12 in minimum value per AWWA C600); if the maximum width is exceeded the contractor must add bedding, change bedding type or use stronger pipe as the engineer approves. Open trench (306-3.5): no more than 500 ft or one day's pipe laying, whichever is greater, unless the Special Provisions say otherwise. Ladders (306-3.6): in trenches over 4 ft deep, every 50 ft, with no more than 25 ft of travel to a ladder. Check the extension height in your edition: the ladder safety rules (29 CFR 1926.1053(b)(1); Cal/OSHA 8 CCR 1675) require the side rails to extend at least 3 ft above the landing, so use 3 ft whatever the spec says.
field.title: Greenbook trench excavation: permit, width, open trench length, ladders
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Greenbook 306-6: the bedding zone runs from the material under the pipe to 1 ft above the top of the pipe. Minimum bedding below the barrel (unless the plans say otherwise): 4 in for ferrous, concrete, clay and plastic pipe; 6 in on rock; and at least 1 in below a projecting bell. Shape the trench bottom so the pipe bears evenly along its length, never on bells or collars; remove and replace unsuitable subgrade as directed. Plastic pipe bedding material per 217-1.2. Laying (306-7.1): bells or collars laid upgrade unless directed otherwise; maximum invert offset at a joint is 1 percent of the inside diameter or 3/8 in, whichever is smaller. Narrow trenches (10 in wide or less) get owner-specified bedding and slurry or CLSM backfill.
field.title: Greenbook bedding zone and laying
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Greenbook 306-12.3 mechanically compacted backfill: relative compaction 85 percent in the bedding zone, outside the traveled way and under sidewalks; 90 percent in the upper 3 ft within the traveled way, in engineered embankments and where lateral support is needed; 95 percent where 301-1.3 requires it (usually the upper part of the road section under pavement, per the Special Provisions). Maximum loose lift before compaction: 24 in for impact or stomping equipment, 18 in for vibratory equipment, 8 in for rollers (sheepsfoot, grid, smooth-wheel), 4 in for hand-directed compactors. Jetting (306-12.4) only when the Special Provisions allow it: 1 1/2 in jet pipe, at least 40 psi, to within 2 ft of the bottom of the lift; no flooding. Many agencies and geotech reports are stricter (90 percent everywhere and 95 percent in the top 1 to 3 ft under pavement); the contract wins.
field.title: Greenbook backfill, lifts and compaction
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Greenbook 306-7.8.2: leakage tests and CCTV must be done and approved before permanent resurfacing. Sanitary sewers 24 in and smaller with 10 ft or less invert difference: water exfiltration or infiltration test; over 10 ft difference or 24 in and larger: air or infiltration test. Water exfiltration: fill to 4 ft above the upper manhole invert (or above groundwater); allowable leakage in gal/min = 0.00002 x L x D x sqrt(H) for gasketed joints (0.0001 for mortared joints), L = ft tested, D = inside diameter in inches, H = head in ft. Air test (306-7.8.2.4): raise the pressure, hold between 2.5 and 3.5 psi for at least 2 minutes, never over 5 psi, then time the drop from 2.5 to 1.5 psi and compare with Table 306-7.8.2.4; soap-check the plugs first. Storm drains are tested only if the plans or Special Provisions require it.
field.title: Greenbook sewer acceptance tests: leakage and air
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Greenbook 306-7.8.3: flexible sewer pipe is deflection tested no sooner than 30 days after backfill and compaction. Maximum deflection (percent of nominal ID) for solid-wall PVC, HDPE, ABS and FRPM sewer: 5.0 percent for 12 in and smaller, 4.0 percent over 12 to 30 in, 3.0 percent over 30 to 60 in (composite ABS/PVC 3.0 percent); larger pipe tighter. Pipe 24 in and smaller: pull a rigid, nonadjustable, odd-numbered-leg (at least 9 legs) certified mandrel through by hand, at least as long as its diameter (example: 8 in PVC SDR 35 mandrel at least 7.282 in). Laser profiling may replace the mandrel. Over-deflected pipe is dug up and re-bedded if undamaged, otherwise replaced.
field.title: Greenbook deflection (mandrel) test
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Greenbook 306-8.9.2 hydrostatic test: at least 4 hours per AWWA C600 or C605, at 50 psi over the working pressure on the plans unless the contract says otherwise; test sections up to 2,500 ft or between valves; fill slowly, hold operating pressure 24 hours and soak 48 hours before testing; leakage allowances from Table 306-8.9.2.3 (none allowed for welded steel or HDPE); retest after compacting with equipment over 100 lb. Disinfection (306-8.9.4): chlorinate at 50 to 100 mg/L, hold at least 24 hours, and end with at least 25 mg/L residual; dechlorinate flushing water (AWWA C655) and meet discharge rules; bacteriological samples must pass on 2 consecutive days (no total or fecal coliform, HPC under 500 CFU/mL) from each end and every 1,200 ft on mains over 2,400 ft; put the main in service within 4 weeks of sampling or resample.
field.title: Greenbook water main pressure test and disinfection
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Greenbook 306-13: temporary resurfacing at least 2 in thick (1 in in sidewalks); permanent asphalt resurfacing 1 in thicker than the existing pavement; concrete pavement replacement 1 in thicker than existing. Maximum compacted asphalt lift: 1 1/2 in with a vibratory plate, 2 in with a pneumatic plate or vibratory rammer, 2 1/2 in with a steel-wheel roller, 3 in with a vibratory roller (no pneumatic-tired rollers). At least 95 percent compaction, finished flush to 1/8 in above the adjacent pavement on trenches under 3 ft wide. Narrow trench slurry or CLSM is cut back 1 to 8 in below the pavement before paving. Many cities add a T-cut: sawcut the pavement back beyond each trench wall (often 12 in) so the new asphalt sits on undisturbed base; check the city's trench repair standard plan.
field.title: Greenbook trench resurfacing
field.topic: Greenbook: Standard Specifications for Public Works Construction (SSPWC)
field.source: Greenbook (SSPWC) 2021 edition, Section 306; check the edition and Special Provisions in your contract (California)

field.text: Ductile iron (AWWA C600) and PVC (AWWA C605) water mains are pressure tested after backfill (or with joints exposed if the spec allows): fill slowly, bleed all air at hydrants, air valves and taps, raise to the test pressure (commonly 1.5 times working pressure or 150 psi minimum, or the agency's rule, such as Greenbook's working pressure plus 50 psi) and hold for at least 2 hours (Greenbook: 4 hours). Measure the makeup water pumped in to keep the pressure. Allowable leakage in gallons per hour L = S x D x sqrt(P) / 148,000, with S = length tested in ft, D = nominal diameter in inches, P = average test pressure in psi. Example: 1,000 ft of 8 in at 150 psi allows about 0.66 gal/hr. Pressure that keeps dropping usually means air in the line, a valve passing, or a leaking joint or tap.
field.title: Water main pressure and leakage test (AWWA C600 / C605)
field.topic: Testing water and sewer lines
field.source: AWWA C600 and C605; Greenbook 306-8.9.2

field.text: Plug both ends, pressurize to about 4.0 psi, let it stabilize, then start timing at 3.5 psi and record the time for a 1.0 psi drop (some specs time a 0.5 psi drop for half the time). Minimum times for a 1.0 psi drop (ASTM F1417 / Uni-Bell): 4 in 1:53; 6 in 2:50; 8 in 3:47; 10 in 4:43; 12 in 5:40; 15 in 7:05. These apply up to about 597, 398, 298, 239, 199 and 159 ft; for longer runs the time is 0.190 x L (4 in), 0.427 x L (6 in), 0.760 x L (8 in), 1.187 x L (10 in), 1.709 x L (12 in), 2.671 x L (15 in) seconds. Raise the test pressure by groundwater head (0.43 psi per ft of water above the pipe). Never stand in front of a plug under pressure, use a relief valve, and never exceed the spec maximum (Greenbook: 5 psi). The agency's spec (Greenbook times 2.5 to 1.5 psi) governs.
field.title: Sewer low-pressure air test (ASTM F1417 for plastic pipe)
field.topic: Testing water and sewer lines
field.source: ASTM F1417; Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association; Greenbook 306-7.8.2.4

field.text: Keep pipe clean during laying, then disinfect before connecting to the system. AWWA C651 methods: continuous feed (water with at least 25 mg/L free chlorine fills the main, held 24 hours, ending with at least 10 mg/L), tablet (25 mg/L, 24 hours, water above 41 F), or slug (100 mg/L passed through for at least 3 hours). Agency specs can be stronger (Greenbook: 50 to 100 mg/L, 24 hours, 25 mg/L residual). Flush until the water is at system chlorine levels, dechlorinate the flush water before discharge, then take bacteriological (bac-T) samples: two sets that both pass, taken as the spec says (AWWA C651-14: a second set at least 16 hours after the first, or let the main sit 16 hours and take two sets 15 minutes apart; specs written on the 2005 edition say 24 hours apart), or per the agency; all must show no coliform. Don't connect until samples pass, and resample if the main isn't put in service in time.
field.title: Water main disinfection and bac-T samples (AWWA C651)
field.topic: Testing water and sewer lines
field.source: AWWA C651; Greenbook 306-8.9.4

field.text: Flexible sewer pipe (PVC, HDPE) is mandrel tested, usually 30 days after backfill, to a 5 percent deflection limit for most sizes (see the agency spec). CCTV inspection is run after backfill and before paving to find sags (bellies), joint offsets, cracks, debris and lateral problems; inspectors grade defects with NASSCO PACP codes. Water mains also get a conductivity or tracer wire continuity test, valve exercising and hydrant flow checks as the agency requires. Manholes get vacuum or water tests. Record all tests in the daily report with time, pressure, length, readings and inspector.
field.title: Deflection, CCTV and other acceptance checks
field.topic: Testing water and sewer lines
field.source: Greenbook 306-7.8; NASSCO PACP; standard agency practice

field.text: California Waterworks Standards, 22 CCR 64572: new water mains must not be in the same trench as, and must be at least 10 ft horizontally from and 1 ft above, pipelines carrying sewage (treated or untreated), disinfected secondary recycled water, or hazardous fluids. For disinfected tertiary recycled water and storm drains: at least 4 ft horizontally and 1 ft above. The 1 ft vertical rule applies when the horizontal distance is under 10 ft. Crossings: a new water main crossing a sewer, recycled water or storm line must cross at no less than 45 degrees and at least 1 ft above it, with no joints in the water main within 8 ft horizontally of the other pipe (center a full pipe length over the crossing). Distances are measured between the nearest outside edges of the pipes. New mains must be 100 ft from landfills, sewage ponds and hazardous waste sites and 25 ft from septic tanks, leach fields, seepage pits and underground hazardous tanks.
field.title: California water main separation (Title 22, section 64572)
field.topic: Water and sewer separation (California)
field.source: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 22, section 64572 (California Waterworks Standards)

field.text: If the plan or field conditions can't meet Title 22 separation, stop and get a written answer from the engineer and the water agency before laying. Common approved fixes (State Water Board alternatives and agency standards): higher-rated pipe for the sewer or water line (pressure-rated sewer pipe, C900 or ductile iron), sleeving or encasing one pipe across the crossing, a full length of pipe centered on the crossing, concrete encasement, or a replacement-main exemption under 64572(h) (under 1,320 ft, same location, not more than 6 in larger, installed to reduce risk). Many water districts publish their own separation standard drawing with zones showing what pipe is allowed at each distance. Never shave separation in the field without approval.
field.title: When separation can't be met
field.topic: Water and sewer separation (California)
field.source: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 22, section 64572; California State Water Resources Control Board Division of Drinking Water separation criteria

field.text: California's outdoor heat rule (Title 8, section 3395): provide fresh, cool drinking water close to the work, enough for at least 1 quart per worker per hour for the whole shift, and encourage drinking it; provide shade when it's over 80 F, close enough and big enough for everyone on break, and allow cool-down rests in the shade whenever someone asks (at least 5 minutes); watch new and newly returned workers closely for their first 14 days (acclimatization); at 95 F and above use high-heat procedures (effective communication, observing workers, reminding them to drink, pre-shift meetings); have a written heat illness plan, training and an emergency response plan with directions to the site. Signs of heat illness or stroke: call for help and cool the person right away.
field.title: Cal/OSHA heat illness prevention (section 3395)
field.topic: Cal/OSHA rules crews run into
field.source: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 8, section 3395 (California)

field.text: Cutting, drilling, breaking or grinding concrete, asphalt, block, AC pipe and some soils makes respirable crystalline silica. Cal/OSHA's construction silica standard (Title 8, section 1532.3, Table 1) sets controls by tool: walk-behind and handheld saws must use integrated water (wet cutting); handheld saws outdoors with water need no respirator up to 4 hours a shift and an APF 10 respirator over 4 hours; walk-behind saws with water outdoors need no respirator; jackhammers with water spray or dust collection outdoors need no respirator up to 4 hours. Also: a written exposure control plan, no dry sweeping or compressed air for cleanup, and medical exams for workers who must wear respirators 30 or more days a year. AC (asbestos cement) pipe has its own asbestos rules.
field.title: Silica dust when cutting concrete, asphalt and pipe
field.topic: Cal/OSHA rules crews run into
field.source: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 8, section 1532.3 (Table 1) (California)

field.text: Water pressure pushes on every bend, tee, reducer, dead end and valve. Thrust on a bend T = 2 x P x A x sin(angle / 2); at a dead end or tee branch T = P x A; P = test pressure in psi (use the test pressure, not working), A = area of the pipe's outside diameter in square inches. Bearing area of the block = T x safety factor / allowable soil bearing (psf). Example: 8 in C900 (OD 9.05 in, A = 64.3 sq in) at 200 psi: a 90 degree bend pushes about 18,200 lb; a 45 about 9,850 lb; a dead end about 12,900 lb. In soil allowing 2,000 psf, the 90 needs about 9.1 sq ft of bearing face (before any safety factor). Typical allowable bearing (check the geotech or agency standard): soft clay about 500 to 1,000 psf, sand about 2,000, gravel and hard clay 3,000 to 4,000 psf.
field.title: How thrust works and how a block is sized
field.topic: Thrust blocks and restraint
field.source: AWWA M41 (ductile iron) and M23 (PVC) thrust design; standard practice

field.text: Pour thrust blocks against undisturbed soil, never against backfill, with the bearing face square to the direction of thrust (outside of a bend, end of a dead end, back of a tee branch). Keep concrete off the joints, bolts and glands so they can be reached later (wrap fittings in poly). Size and shape from the agency's standard plan for the pipe size, pressure and fitting, adjusted if the soil is weak. Let the block cure before the pressure test (often several days; high-early mix if the spec allows). Vertical bends need gravity blocks or restraint with anchors. Where blocks won't fit or soil is poor, use restrained joints for the length the plans give.
field.title: Pouring thrust blocks right
field.topic: Thrust blocks and restraint
field.source: Agency water standards; AWWA M41 and M23

field.text: Slurry (sand-cement trench backfill) and CLSM (controlled low-strength material, flowable fill) fill a trench without compaction: good for narrow trenches, around tight utilities and when the agency wants quick paving. Greenbook covers trench backfill slurry in 201-1 and CLSM in 201-6; agencies often call out a sack content (like 1-sack or 2-sack slurry) and a maximum strength so it can be dug again later. Place it in lifts if the pipe can float, block or weight the pipe, and keep it off fresh joints until set. Slurry is cut back below the pavement surface before the final paving (Greenbook: 1 to 8 in).
field.title: Trench backfill slurry and CLSM
field.topic: Trench resurfacing and slurry
field.source: Greenbook 201-1, 201-6, 306-12.2 (California)

field.text: Typical city trench repair: sawcut the existing pavement straight and clean, compact the backfill and base, then sawcut back beyond each trench wall (a T-cut, often 12 in each side) so the new asphalt bears on undisturbed base; tack the edges; pave at least the existing thickness or thicker (Greenbook: 1 in thicker than existing) in compacted lifts; roll to 95 percent; finish flush with the existing street. Temporary paving (cold patch or hot mix, at least 2 in) holds until permanent paving. Many cities also require crack seal on the joints, restriping and a final grind and overlay when several trenches are close. Steel plates over open trenches need ramps or recessing and a pin-down, per the agency.
field.title: T-cut and paving a trench
field.topic: Trench resurfacing and slurry
field.source: Greenbook 306-13; typical city trench repair standards (California)

field.text: Jack and bore (auger boring) pushes a steel casing pipe through the ground from a jacking pit to a receiving pit while an auger inside removes the spoil; used under roads, railroads and channels. Then the carrier pipe (water, sewer) is pushed through the casing on casing spacers (plastic or stainless runners that hold the pipe centered and at grade) and the ends are sealed with end seals; some agencies require the annular space to be grouted. Line and grade are only as good as the first few feet: set the boring machine track carefully on grade and line, and check often. Railroad and Caltrans crossings need their own permits, casing thickness and depth rules.
field.title: Jack and bore with a steel casing
field.topic: Trenchless crossings: bore and jack, HDD
field.source: Greenbook 307; standard trenchless practice

field.text: HDD drills a steerable pilot hole along a planned arc from the surface, tracked by a walkover locator reading a sonde in the drill head, then reams it larger (usually about 1.5 times the pipe OD) and pulls back the product pipe (HDPE or fusible PVC, sometimes restrained-joint ductile iron) with drilling fluid (bentonite or polymer) holding the hole open. Watch for frac-outs (inadvertent returns of drilling fluid to the surface or into a waterway) and have a plan to contain them. Don't exceed the pipe's safe pull strength or minimum bend radius. HDD is not precise enough for gravity sewer grade in most cases. Pothole every crossing utility before drilling and keep the required clearance.
field.title: Horizontal directional drilling (HDD) basics
field.topic: Trenchless crossings: bore and jack, HDD
field.source: Standard HDD practice; pipe manufacturer pullback guidance

field.text: Sewer CCTV reports use NASSCO PACP codes, each with a distance from the start manhole, a clock position and a grade from 1 (minor) to 5 (most severe, needs attention soon). Structural codes: CL / CC / CM crack longitudinal, circumferential or multiple; FL / FC fracture; B broken; H hole; D deformed; X collapse; JOM / JOL joint offset medium / large; JSM / JSL joint separated. O&M codes: RFJ / RMJ / RBJ roots fine, medium or ball at a joint; DAE deposits attached encrustation; DS settled deposits; IR / ID / IG / IW infiltration runner, dripper, gusher, weeper; MWL water level (a high water level in new pipe can mean a sag). Laterals: TF factory tap, TB break-in tap. A new line should show no structural defects, no offsets beyond spec, and no standing water over the allowed depth.
field.title: Reading a NASSCO PACP sewer video report
field.topic: CCTV inspection reports (NASSCO PACP)
field.source: NASSCO Pipeline Assessment Certification Program (PACP) coding

field.text: Trench volume per foot (cubic yards) = width (ft) x depth (ft) / 27. Example: 2 ft wide x 5 ft deep = 0.37 cy per foot, 370 cy per 1,000 ft (bank yards; add swell for trucks). Bedding per foot = width x (bedding below the pipe + pipe OD + cover over the pipe in the bedding zone, all in ft) / 27, minus the pipe's volume (pi x OD squared / 4 / 27 per foot). Slurry per foot = width x slurry depth / 27 minus pipe volume. Always add waste (about 5 to 10 percent) and round up to full loads.
field.title: Trench, bedding and slurry quantities
field.topic: Quantity math for pipe crews
field.source: Standard estimating practice

field.text: Typical weights (use the supplier's ticket weight when known): crushed aggregate base compacted about 1.9 to 2.0 tons per cy (loose about 1.5 to 1.6); 3/4 in crushed rock loose about 1.35 to 1.45 tons per cy; sand loose about 1.3 to 1.4; native soil about 1.3 to 1.5 loose. Hot mix asphalt compacted about 145 lb per cubic ft (about 1.96 tons per cy): one ton covers about 55 sq ft at 3 in thick, about 83 sq ft at 2 in, about 41 sq ft at 4 in. Tons of asphalt = area (sq ft) x thickness (ft) x 145 / 2,000. Concrete: about 4,000 lb per cy (2 tons).
field.title: Tons per yard and asphalt yield
field.topic: Quantity math for pipe crews
field.source: Standard estimating practice; supplier data varies

field.text: NFPA 291 color code: the bonnet (top) and caps show flow class at 20 psi residual: light blue = class AA, 1,500 gpm or more; green = class A, 1,000 to 1,499 gpm; orange = class B, 500 to 999 gpm; red = class C, under 500 gpm. NFPA recommends reflective chrome yellow barrels for public hydrants unless another color was adopted locally, and red for private hydrants on private property. In practice the barrel (body) color is set by the water agency, so it often tells you which water district or city owns the hydrant, or whether it's public, private, a reclaimed or non-potable hydrant (often purple or violet), or out of service (often bagged or marked). Check the local agency's color standard; don't assume flow from the body color.
field.title: Fire hydrant colors: flow class and owner
field.topic: Fire hydrants, valves and boxes
field.source: NFPA 291 Recommended Practice for Fire Flow Testing and Marking of Hydrants; local water agency standards

field.text: Valve cans and box lids are marked with the utility (WATER, GAS, RECLAIMED), and some agencies paint the lid or a curb mark to show valve type or status (for example a painted lid or a tag for a normally closed valve on a zone boundary). Valves open either left (counterclockwise) or right (clockwise) depending on the agency: the direction is often cast on the nut or the lid (OPEN LEFT, OL, OR) and must be confirmed before operating. Count and record turns. Never operate an existing system valve without the water agency's approval; closing the wrong valve or closing it fast causes water hammer, outages and main breaks.
field.title: Valve boxes and valve operation marks
field.topic: Fire hydrants, valves and boxes
field.source: AWWA M44 (distribution valves); agency standards

field.text: Alabama (AL) construction rules for pipe and site work. State DOT spec: ALDOT Standard Specifications for Highway Construction (used for state highway work and often referenced by cities). Local and regional public works specs: most cities and water boards (e.g., Birmingham Water Works) have their own standard specs and details. Water and sewer design and separation: ADEM rules for water and sewer design; AWWA standards (C600, C605, C651 and others) are used nationwide for water mains. Dig law: call Alabama 811 before digging; notice time, ticket life and tolerance zone are set by Alabama law, so check the current rules. Excavation safety: federal OSHA (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P for excavations). On any job the contract's special provisions and the owner's standard plans govern; always ask which spec book and edition the contract names.
field.title: Alabama: which spec books, 811 center and safety rules apply
field.topic: Construction specs by state and region
field.source: State DOT, regional public works and 811 center publications; OSHA state plan directory. Check current editions.

On any job the contract's special provisions and the owner's standard plans govern; always ask which spec book and edition the contract names.

Ladders within 25 ft of travel at 4 ft deep, same as federal. Your competent person and company program decide how this applies on your job.
