field.text: Michigan's dig law is the MISS DIG Underground Facility Damage Prevention and Safety Act, 2013 PA 174 (MCL 460.721 to 460.733), enforced by the Michigan Public Service Commission. One center: MISS DIG 811. Notice: "at least 72 hours, but not more than 14 calendar days, before the start." Hours on non-business days do not count. A ticket is "valid for 21 days from the start date," or 180 days when the notice says the work will take longer. Past that, or if digging did not start in time, get a new ticket. Caution zone: 48 inches on either side of the marks. Before digging there, expose every marked line by soft excavation (hand or vacuum). Check positive response. No response on a ticket is a reason to stop near there and give additional notice. Hit a line: notify the owner right away; gas or liquid escaping or danger to life, call 911.
field.title: Michigan 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (MISS DIG 811)

field.edition: MCL compilation complete through PA 91 of 2026

field.text: Minnesota's dig law is Minn. Stat. chapter 216D, enforced by the Minnesota Office of Pipeline Safety. One center: Gopher State One Call (GSOC). Notice: at least 48 hours, not counting the day you file, weekends and holidays, and not more than 14 calendar days ahead. A ticket is good for 14 calendar days from the start date and time on it (up to six months when a marking schedule is agreed and written down). To go past 14 days, file an Update at least 48 hours (weekends and holidays not counted) before it expires; an Update gets a new ticket number and its own 48-hour wait. White marks are required: "without exception." Electronic white marks count from January 1, 2026. Check GSOC's positive response before you dig. "Not Yet Responded" and no marks: contact that operator directly. Hand dig zone: 2 feet (24 inches) from each side of the line. Hand tools or vacuum only there. Hit a line: notify the owner right away; gas or liquid escaping, call 911. Never bury a damaged line.
field.title: Minnesota 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Gopher State One Call)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone

field.text: Mississippi's dig law is Miss. Code 77-13-1 and after, amended by HB 1191 effective July 1, 2025. One center: Mississippi 811 (MS811). Ticket life went "from 14 to 20 calendar days" for Normal, Emergency, Impending Emergency, Short Notice and Design tickets. Update at least 3 working days before a ticket expires so there is no gap. (MS811's older portal guide says an update adds 14 calendar days; whether that is now 20 is not confirmed.) The wait before digging was not on the page read and is not confirmed here: go by the dig date on your ticket. Tolerance zone: 18 inches plus one-half of the diameter of the line when the diameter is shown at the marks, measured from the outside edge of the marks. Use non-invasive methods there (hand digging, vacuum), support the line, and keep machines a safe distance away. Pre-mark in white unless you own the property and described it clearly, or you drew the dig area on the web portal map after MS811's short training. Emergency tickets: operators respond within 2 hours, and you must name a contact who will be on site. Large projects (can't be finished in 20 calendar days): optional preconstruction meeting and a signed agreement before work.

field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone

field.text: Missouri's dig law is the Underground Facility Safety and Damage Prevention Act, RSMo 319.010 to 319.050 (amended August 28, 2025). One center: Missouri 811. Notice: "at least two working days, but not more than ten working days, before the expected date" of starting. A notice is good until 11:59 p.m. 21 consecutive calendar days from the start date of work on the ticket (RSMo 319.025, amended by 2025 SB 133); work while the marks can be seen until then. If you can't start within ten working days, make a relocate request before digging. Marks unusable: ask the center for a remark. White lining (paint, stakes, whiskers) may be used when the site can't be clearly described. Find a line unmarked or marked wrong: notify the center; the owner must contact you or mark it correctly within two hours. Hand or soft digging "shall be used as a best practice when possible"; no hand-dig distance is given in this section. Hit a line: notify the center. Gas or hazardous liquid pipeline release: "immediately contact 911." Do not hide or repair damage without the owner's OK.
field.title: Missouri 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Missouri 811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: RSMo 319.025, 319.026 (revisor.mo.gov, effective Aug 28, 2025; 2025 SB 133 truly agreed text)

field.text: Montana's dig law is Mont. Code Title 69, Chapter 4, Part 5 (underground facility protection). One center: Montana 811. None of Montana's numbers could be opened in an official source in this pass, so they are not confirmed: the wait before digging, how long a ticket lasts, the tolerance zone and the fines. Do not use another state's numbers. What to do: call 811 or go online at montana811.org before any digging, start only on or after the dig date printed on the ticket, check that every utility on the ticket has marked or cleared, and ask Montana 811 how long the ticket is good for on a long job. The federal rule applies everywhere for pipelines: use one-call first, wait for the marks, dig with care, report any pipeline damage to the operator, and call 911 if gas or hazardous liquid is released (49 CFR 196).
field.title: Montana 811: not confirmed yet: what to check with Montana 811
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: Mont. Code 69-4-501 to 69-4-530 (not opened); 49 CFR 196.103 to 196.109
field.edition: Not confirmed; federal rule current to Oct 22, 2026

field.text: Nebraska's dig law is the One-Call Notification System Act, Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-2301 to 76-2334. Since September 1, 2024 the State Fire Marshal investigates complaints and the Underground Excavation Safety Committee sets penalties. One center: Nebraska 811. Notice: the app's table has 2 full business days and not more than 10 business days; operators must respond "no later than two business days after receipt of a dig ticket." Do not call in an area where digging can't reasonably start "within seventeen calendar days after the ticket start date." Marks must be "within 18 inches on either side of the marking, plus one half of the width of the underground facility." Hand dig inside that strip. Hit a line: "the excavator shall immediately notify the center." Do not hide the damage or repair the line without the operator's OK. Penalties: up to $10,000 per day per event for pipeline and fiber optic violations (cap $500,000); up to $5,000 per day per event for other utilities (cap $50,000). Farm tilling and gardening for seeding are not excavation. How long a ticket lasts once digging has started was not confirmed.

field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone

field.text: Nevada's dig law is NRS 455.080 to 455.180 with rules in NAC 455. One center: USA North 811. Call at least 2 working days (7 AM to 5 PM, not weekends or holidays, call day not counted) and not more than 28 calendar days before digging (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). Mark the dig area in white first. Wait for every operator: the handbook says excavators "are required by law to wait until all operators" have given a positive response, even if the start time on the ticket has passed. A ticket is good for 28 calendar days from the date and time of the notification. It can be extended twice, 28 days each; after that the regulation requires a new notification (NAC 455.165). That is 84 days at most on one ticket. Hand tools only within 24 inches on either side of the outside of the line. Hit a line: notify the operator right away; in an emergency also 911.

Pre-mark the dig area in white (paint, flags, stakes or whiskers), then call at least 72 hours ahead, not counting weekends and holidays, and not more than 30 days ahead. Ticket life: tickets expire 30 days from the day of issue. In every Dig Safe state a ticket expires if digging does not start within 30 days. Renew with at least 72 hours' notice (weekends and holidays not counted) so there is no gap; if the scope of work changes, get a new ticket instead. Whether a renewal prints a new number is not confirmed. Tolerance zone: the width of the line plus 18 inches on each side. Hand dig or use vacuum equipment there; no machines until the line is verified. Power equipment may remove pavement only to the depth of the pavement. Dig Safe only notifies its members. Call non-member owners (often town water and sewer) yourself.

field.text: New Jersey's dig law is the Underground Facility Protection Act (N.J.S.A. 48:2-73 and after) with rules in N.J.A.C. 14:2, enforced by the Board of Public Utilities. Call 811 (New Jersey One Call). Notice: "no less than three business days before the beginning of the excavation." Start within 10 business days of the notice. The notice "shall remain valid for 45 business days from the notification." Digging after that needs a new notification with the normal wait. Operators must post an electronic positive response within three business days and mark out or tell you they have no lines there. You may mark the edge of the site in white; it is optional. Marks are paint, at intervals of 25 feet or less. Hit a gas, petroleum or hazardous liquid line: "immediately call 911," then the operator, or the One-Call center at 811 if you can't reach the operator. Fines: $1,000 to $2,500 per day, up to $25,000 for a related series. The hand-dig distance (2 feet in the statute) was not confirmed in the text read.

field.text: New Mexico's dig law is the Excavation Damage to Pipelines and Underground Utility Lines Act (NMSA 62-14) with rule 18.60.5 NMAC, enforced by the Public Regulation Commission's pipeline safety bureau. One center: NM811. Notice: 2 working days, not counting the day you call (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day); operators must mark "within two full working days from the effective date of the ticket." Marks are good for 15 working days from the end of the notice period. Marks gone with no offsets: stop and ask for a relocate, only for the part still to dig, and say why. Jobs longer than 15 working days: ask for a wide area conference at least two working days ahead, write a work plan signed by all, and reaffirm the wide area ticket every 15 working days. Pre-mark in white: it shows the actual dig, not the limits of construction. Before digging, check that every operator has marked or cleared. If one has not, call for a warning locate. Within 18 inches either side of a mark, expose the line first by non-mechanical means or vacuum. Hit a line: stop, call 911 if needed, the operator and 811, secure the site, and stay until released.
field.title: New Mexico 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (NM811)

field.text: New York's dig rules are 16 NYCRR Part 753 ("Code Rule 753") under General Business Law Article 36, enforced by the Public Service Commission. Two centers: UDig NY upstate and New York 811 for New York City and Long Island. Notice: "at least two but not more than ten working days, not including the date of the call." (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) There is no ticket expiry date. If you put the start off by more than ten working days, give a new notice. Do not start until you have heard from "each and every operator" that its lines are marked or that it has none. Use the Automated Positive Response system where there is one. Tolerance zone: half the known diameter plus two feet on each side of the center line (two feet each side if the size is not known). Verify the line's exact location before power equipment goes in the zone; gas and liquid petroleum lines must be found with hand-dug test holes. Hit a line: tell the operator right away; gas, liquid or electric emergency, clear the area and call 911.

field.text: North Carolina's dig law is the Underground Utility Safety and Damage Prevention Act, G.S. Chapter 87, Article 8A (amended in 2025). One center: NC811. Notice: at least 3 full working days before the start date (10 to 20 for work near underwater lines). Working days are every day but Saturday, Sunday and State holidays. A notice expires 28 calendar days after the work start date. To keep digging, give a new notice the same way; NC811 calls it an update and it gets a new ticket number. Check positive response before you dig. Tolerance zone: 24 inches on each side of the outside edge of the mark, or half the diameter plus 24 inches from the centerline when the size is known. No mechanized equipment in the zone until you can see the line. Hit a line: notify NC811 and the operator right away; gas, electricity or danger, call 911 first. No backfill until cleared.
field.title: North Carolina 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (NC811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.edition: Statute as amended by Session Law 2025-21

field.text: North Dakota's dig law is N.D.C.C. chapter 49-23. One center: North Dakota One Call (811). Notice: the handbook says "at least 48 hours (excluding weekends and holidays)" before digging. A ticket is good for 21 calendar days from the start time on it. The law says an excavator "may not use a location more than twenty-one days" after the planned dig date without arrangements with the operators; if no digging happened in the first 21 days, ask for a relocate first. After expiry, get a new ticket. There is no blanket ticket. One request covers at most three city blocks in town, or four quarter sections or five linear miles in the country. Show the site with white marking, digital white lining or project staking. Operators mark a strip two feet on either side of the line. Dig by hand within 24 inches of a located line. Emergency: call 911 first, then the utility, then the center. Hit a line: notify the operator promptly; danger, call 911 and keep people away. Knowing of damage and not reporting it, or backfilling over it, is a class A misdemeanor. Civil penalty up to $25,000. Farm work shallower than 18 inches and gardening shallower than 12 inches are not excavation.

field.text: Ohio's dig law is O.R.C. 3781.25 to 3781.38 (amended June 9, 2026); complaints go to the Underground Technical Committee at the PUCO. One center: OHIO811. Oil and gas producers answer through a separate group reached by the same call. Notice: "at least two working days, not including the day of the notification," and "not more than sixteen calendar days before commencing excavation." (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) The law and the June 2026 manual give no ticket expiry date. Keep the ticket for the whole job and ask for a remark when marks fade. Premark the dig in white paint unless an exception applies. Check Positive Response before you go to the job; code 999 means an owner has not answered by the legal start. Tolerance zone: the width of the line plus 18 inches on each side. Dig there carefully, with a second person watching the bucket. Hit a line: get everyone safe, stop, notify the utility and OHIO811; anything flammable, toxic or corrosive escaping, call 911.
field.title: Ohio 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (OHIO811)

field.source: OHIO811 Excavator Manual (rev. June 2026) pp. 5-7, 10-17, 20-24, 40; O.R.C. 3781.25 to 3781.32

field.text: Oklahoma's dig law is the Underground Facilities Damage Prevention Act, 63 O.S. 142.1 to 142.13 (last amended November 1, 2024). The Corporation Commission enforces it for oil and gas pipelines. One center: OKIE811. Notice: at least 48 hours before digging, not counting the day you call, Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. Demolition: 7 business days. "Notice shall expire fourteen (14) calendar days from the excavation start date." To keep going, update the ticket (Extend, or Re-Mark if marks are gone) at least 4 business days before it expires; operators get 48 hours to respond. A ticket covers no more than 500 linear feet in a city or town, or one linear mile outside. White line the dig area before you call. Check positive responses before starting. Operator missing: send a Second Notice. Approximate location: a strip two feet on either side of the line. Only hand digging there until the line is exposed; machines may remove pavement only. Hit a line: notify the operator and OKIE811 immediately; gas escaping, leave and call 911. Hold the backfill until repairs are done.

field.text: Oregon's dig rules are ORS 757.542 to 757.562 and OAR chapter 952, written by the Oregon Utility Notification Center (Oregon 811). Pre-mark the dig area in white, then call at least 2 full business days and not more than 10 business days before digging (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). Do not start until you have "received a response from each operator of underground facilities in the area." Ticket life: 30 calendar days. The Center's 2026 Addendum says the rule was changed "from 45 days to 30 days," effective January 8, 2026, and Oregon 811's own homeowner page says marks should no longer be used after 30 days. Older copies of the rule still say 45. Past ticket life, call in a new locate request. Tolerance zone: 24 inches around the outside of the line on all sides. Use hand tools or other non-invasive methods there. Hit a line: tell the operator right away; gas or hazardous liquid release, call 911. Don't bury it without the operator's OK.
field.title: Oregon 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Oregon 811)

field.text: Pennsylvania's dig law is the Underground Utility Line Protection Law (Act 287 of 1974, as amended by Act 50 of 2017 and Act 127 of 2024), 73 P.S. 176 and after. The Public Utility Commission enforces it through its Damage Prevention Committee. One center: Pennsylvania One Call (PA 811). Notice: "not less than three nor more than ten business days in advance of beginning excavation." Complex projects: at least ten business days. The law gives no number of days a ticket lasts. It says to call again if you leave the site for more than two business days (unless you made other arrangements with the owners). Ticket life is not confirmed; go by PA One Call. Tolerance zone: within eighteen inches of the outside wall or edge of the line. Use prudent techniques there, such as hand-dug test holes or vacuum. Check the owners' responses (KARL) before digging. If an owner fails to respond you may proceed on the lawful start date, with due care. Hit a line: tell the owner right away; gas or liquid escaping, call 911.

field.text: Rhode Island uses Dig Safe as its one-call center (call 811); the Division of Public Utilities and Carriers enforces the state's Dig Safe law. Pre-mark the dig area in white (paint, flags, stakes or whiskers), then call at least 72 hours ahead, not counting weekends and holidays, and not more than 30 days ahead. Ticket life: "tickets do not expire provided that the marks are maintained." In every Dig Safe state a ticket expires if digging does not start within 30 days. Renew with at least 72 hours' notice (weekends and holidays not counted) so there is no gap; if the scope of work changes, get a new ticket instead. Whether a renewal prints a new number is not confirmed. Tolerance zone: the width of the line plus 18 inches on each side. Hand dig or use vacuum equipment there; no machines until the line is verified. Power equipment may remove pavement only to the depth of the pavement. Dig Safe only notifies its members. Call non-member owners (often town water and sewer) yourself.

field.text: South Carolina's dig law is the Underground Facility Damage Prevention Act, S.C. Code Title 58, Chapter 36. One center: SC811. Wait: operators "have three full working days to mark," not counting the day you call. A normal request is good for 15 working days from its start time. Send an Extension any time before it runs out; an Extension does not refresh the paint. Marks gone: send a Remark, which makes a new ticket with a new number and gives operators three full working days. Once a request has expired you need a new one. Pre-mark in white paint, flags or stakes when the site can't be clearly identified. Before digging, verify that every operator has answered in Positive Response. No answer and no sign of a line: you may proceed. Signs of a line: request a No Show; the operator has three hours. Tolerance zone: 24 inches on either side of the mark plus half the diameter if known. No machines there until you can see the line; machines may remove pavement only. Hit a line: notify SC811 and the operator right away; danger or a release, call 911 first.
field.title: South Carolina 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (SC811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone

field.text: South Dakota's dig law is SDCL chapter 49-7A, with the One-Call Notification Board writing the rules. One center: South Dakota 811. Notice (49-7A-5, 2026 Senate Bill 9): "at least forty-eight hours prior to the commencement of the excavation." The 48 hours start at 12:01 a.m. the day after you send the notice and skip Saturdays, Sundays and state legal holidays. Operators mark within "eighteen inches horizontally from the exterior sides of the underground facilities." Keep "a minimum horizontal clearance of eighteen inches" between the marked line and the cutting edge of any machine. If you must dig closer than 18 inches, expose the line first with hand tools or an approved noninvasive method, then protect and support it before using the machine again. How long a ticket lasts, the damage steps and the fine amounts were not in the text read and are not confirmed here: go by the ticket and South Dakota 811.
field.title: South Dakota 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (South Dakota 811)

field.source: SDCL 49-7A-5 and 49-7A-8 as amended by 2026 Senate Bill 9 (enrolled)

field.text: Tennessee's dig law is the Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, T.C.A. 65-31-101 and after, with an Enforcement Board at the Tennessee Public Utility Commission. One center: Tennessee 811. Notice: "at least three (3) working days prior to the actual date of excavation" and not more than ten full working days ahead. A ticket is good for "fifteen (15) calendar days from the actual date specified to start." To keep digging, give a new notice at least three working days before the fifteenth day runs out; Tennessee 811 says you are then "given a new ticket number." When the digging is done, stop updating. Mark the dig area "with white paint, or by electronic white lining" unless an exception applies (for example the ticket gives a precise location). A property owner using non-mechanized tools on their own property is exempt. Within 100 feet of the edge of a street or highway, if an operator fails to locate in time the excavator is authorized to proceed. The tolerance zone (24 inches in 65-31-108) and penalty amounts were not re-read today and are not confirmed here.
field.title: Tennessee 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Tennessee 811)

field.text: Texas has two layers: Utilities Code chapter 251 (the one-call law for all lines) and Railroad Commission rule 16 TAC chapter 18 for pipelines (gas, hazardous liquid, CO2). Call 811 or use the Texas811 portal. Notice: at least 48 hours before digging, not counting weekends and legal holidays, and not more than 14 days ahead. Ticket life: 14 working days for pipeline locates unless you and the operator agree otherwise in writing. Not done: refresh the ticket for the area still to dig. Texas811 sends updates with a 2 business day notice. Tolerance zone for pipelines: half the pipe diameter plus at least 18 inches on each side. Wait for a positive response (marks, "all clear" or "no conflict"). None: give a second notice; if there is still none after 4 hours you may begin. Hit a pipeline: notify the operator through 811 within 1 hour, call 911 for a release, and file a damage report with the Railroad Commission within 30 days.
field.title: Texas 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Texas811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone

field.edition: 16 TAC ch. 18 as in effect Feb 12, 2018 (latest amendment shown)

field.text: Utah's dig law is Utah Code Title 54, Chapter 8a. One center: Blue Stakes of Utah 811. Notice: not "less than 48 hours before excavation begins" and not "more than 14 days before." The 48 hours count business days only; business hours are 8 AM to 4 PM, Monday to Friday, not holidays. A notice is "valid for 21 days from the day on which the notice is given." To keep going, renew at least 48 hours and no more than 7 calendar days before it expires. Blue Stakes gives an update a different ticket number. Tolerance zone: 24 inches on either side of the outside edge of the mark (or half the marked diameter plus 24 inches from the center). No power equipment inside the zone until you have found the exact location with hand tools. Operator did not mark or answer in 48 hours: file a no response notice; the operator then has 4 business hours. Hit a line: tell the operator right away; gas, electric or danger to life, call 911. No backfill until the operator says so.
field.title: Utah 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Blue Stakes of Utah 811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.edition: Utah Code as amended by the 2024 General Session (ch. 369)

field.text: Vermont uses Dig Safe as its one-call center (call 811); the Department of Public Service enforces the state's Dig Safe law. Pre-mark the dig area in white (paint, flags, stakes or whiskers), then call at least 72 hours ahead, not counting weekends and holidays, and not more than 30 days ahead. Ticket life: tickets expire 30 days from the day of issue. In every Dig Safe state a ticket expires if digging does not start within 30 days. Renew with at least 72 hours' notice (weekends and holidays not counted) so there is no gap; if the scope of work changes, get a new ticket instead. Whether a renewal prints a new number is not confirmed. Tolerance zone: the width of the line plus 18 inches on each side. Hand dig or use vacuum equipment there; no machines until the line is verified. Power equipment may remove pavement only to the depth of the pavement. Dig Safe only notifies its members. Call non-member owners (often town water and sewer) yourself.
field.title: Vermont 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Dig Safe)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: Dig Safe Excavator Manual (version Aug 2025; laws table updated 6/5/25) pp. 4-5, 9, 11, 14-19, 25-27, 31

field.text: Virginia's dig law is the Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, Va. Code 56-265.14 to 56-265.32, enforced by the State Corporation Commission. One center: Virginia 811. Wait: operators have 48 hours beginning at 7:00 a.m. the next working day after your locate request, so a Monday request is good Thursday at 7 AM. You may start sooner only when every operator has marked or posted a positive response that allows digging. A notice is "valid for 15 working days" from 7:00 a.m. the next working day after the request (or the scheduled date, if later). Three working days before it runs out, or when marks can't be read, request an update; Virginia 811 gives an update or re-mark a new request number. A re-mark is good for another 15 working days. Mark the site boundary in white paint, if practical, when you can't give an exact location. One request covers no more than one-third of a mile and only what can be dug in 15 working days. The hand-dig distance (2 feet in section 56-265.24) and fine amounts were not confirmed in this pass.
field.title: Virginia 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Virginia 811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: Va. Code 56-265.17 (2023 amendments); Virginia 811 "Ticket Types" sheet (May 15, 2026)

field.text: Washington's dig law is RCW 19.122, enforced by the Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC). Mark the boundary of the dig "with white lining or, when necessary, white pin flags," then call 811. Notice: "not less than two full business days and not more than 10 full business days" before the work-to-begin date (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). Since January 1, 2026 you "may not commence excavation until the excavator has received positive response" from every operator with lines in the area. Marks expire 45 calendar days after you gave notice; to dig after that, give a new notice. Marks are accurate to within 24 inches of the outside of the line on both sides. Find the exact location before digging there: hand digging when practical, vacuum or air tools. Hit a line: tell the operator and 811, call 911 if it is an emergency, don't bury it, and report the damage to the UTC within 45 days.
field.title: Washington 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Washington 811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.edition: RCW as amended through Laws of 2025 chapter 292

field.text: West Virginia's dig law is W. Va. Code Chapter 24C. One center: West Virginia 811. Notice: "Not less than forty-eight hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and federal or state legal holidays," and not more than ten work days before work begins. Changing the start date or time: tell the one-call system at least 24 hours ahead, not counting weekends and holidays. West Virginia 811's 2026 training, quoting the statute: a ticket is valid no more than 15 business days (no weekends or holidays) and the tolerance zone is 2 feet from the outside edge of the line (not confirmed in the statute text). Each equipment operator must be told to avoid damage, "including hand digging, when necessary," to keep a clearance "as may be reasonably necessary" from lines given the reach of the cutting edge, to protect marks and stakes, and to support lines during work and backfill. Line hit: report it immediately and give the operator reasonable time to repair. An emergency: alert the public and call 911. Damage that is not an emergency: notify the one-call system within 24 hours. Failing to notify or to report is a misdemeanor with a fine of "not more than $5,000," and you owe the repair cost.
field.title: West Virginia 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (West Virginia 811)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: W. Va. Code 24C-1-5 (code.wvlegislature.gov); West Virginia 811, 2026 excavator training slides (gowv.com)
field.edition: W. Va. Code 24C as read 2026-11-20; WV811 2026 training

field.text: Wisconsin's dig law is Wis. Stat. 182.0175. One center: Diggers Hotline (811). A Public Service Commission panel hears complaints. Notice: "not less than 3 working days before the start of nonemergency excavation." Working days are days other than Saturday, Sunday and legal holidays. There is no set ticket life. Give a new notice if the dig does not start "within 10 days of the scheduled start date," if marks are destroyed or covered, or if work stops for more than 10 days. Keep "an estimated minimum clearance of 18 inches" between a marked, unexposed line and the cutting edge of the machine. Once the line is exposed the clearance can drop to twice the machine's limit of control or 12 inches, whichever is greater. Owners mark within 3 working days in the ANSI uniform colors. Before backfilling, inspect any line you exposed. If a line may be damaged, notify the owner immediately and do not backfill until it has been inspected. Gas or liquid that may endanger life: call 911. Emergency: take all reasonable precautions and notify owners as promptly as possible. Fine amounts were not confirmed.
field.title: Wisconsin 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Diggers Hotline)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: Wis. Stat. 182.0175(1), (2), (2m), (3) (docs.legis.wisconsin.gov)

field.text: Wyoming's dig law is the Wyoming Underground Facilities Notification Act, Wyo. Stat. 37-12-301 to 37-12-307. One center: One-Call of Wyoming (811). Notice: "at least two (2) full business days, but not more than fourteen (14) business days prior to any excavation." (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) A job that runs longer than 14 business days needs the notice given again for each following 14 business day period. Mark the dig area before the locator comes, unless one operator can find the site from the address, there was a site meeting, or it is an emergency. Operators mark "within twenty-four (24) inches horizontally" of the outside of the line, in APWA colors, within two full business days. Reasonable care is always required, and it calls for hand or soft digging where needed to protect the line. Hit or touch a line: notify the operator and the center immediately. Gas or hazardous liquid released: call 911 first. Do not hide damage or repair it without authorization. In a dispute the excavator has to prove reasonable care. If the operator missed its deadline or marked wrong, an excavator who used reasonable care is not liable. Penalty amounts were not confirmed.
field.title: Wyoming 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (One-Call of Wyoming)
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: Wyo. Stat. 37-12-302 (Counsel Stack copy, 2026)

field.text: Every state has a one-call law and 811 reaches the right center from anywhere in the country. The steps are the same everywhere: mark your dig area in white, call or go online before you dig, wait the legal notice time, check that every utility has marked or answered, dig by hand or vacuum inside the tolerance zone, keep the marks visible, and renew the ticket before it runs out. What changes by state is the numbers. No federal law sets the wait, the ticket life or the tolerance zone. The wait runs from 48 hours to 5 working days; ticket life runs from about two weeks to 60 days, counted in working days in some states and calendar days in others, and from the call in some and from the legal dig date in others; the tolerance zone is 18 or 24 inches each side in nearly every state, measured from the mark in some and from the outside edge of the line in others. The 811 by-state tables list each state's numbers. So never carry one state's numbers to the next job: ask for your job's state by name (for example 'how long is a ticket good for in Texas'), or open Locates and tap Rules for the state. Federal OSHA adds its own duty in every state: find out where underground lines are before opening an excavation, and protect, support or remove them while it is open (29 CFR 1926.651(b)). The ticket, the 811 center and the state law govern; this is a plain-language summary.
field.title: 811 before you dig: what is the same everywhere and what changes by state
field.topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
field.source: State one-call laws as listed in the app's state rules table (51 rows, checked 2026-11-19); 29 CFR 1926.651(b)

field.text: Michigan does not use the federal excavation rule or OSHA's Type A, B and C soils. MIOSHA Construction Safety Standard Part 9, Excavation, Trenching and Shoring (R 408.40901 to R 408.40953, last amended effective January 3, 2024) says: "The side of an excavation more than 5 feet deep shall be sloped as prescribed in table 1, unless supported as prescribed in this part" (R 408.40941(1)). A shallower excavation is protected too "when examination of the ground indicates hazardous earth movement may be expected" (R 408.40941(2)). Support systems are designed by a qualified person and the design is kept at the jobsite (R 408.40942(2)). "Protective systems for use in excavations more than 20 feet in depth must be designed by a registered professional engineer" (R 408.40942(8)). An ongoing inspection by a competent person is required, and after every rainstorm (R 408.40932(4)). Federal OSHA starts at 5 ft or more (29 CFR 1926.652); this state's rule starts above 5 ft and uses its own table. Rule text read by an earlier check on 2026-11-20.
field.title: Michigan trench protection: its own rule, MIOSHA Part 9
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation

field.text: Oregon uses one confined space rule for general industry and construction, OAR 437-002-0146; Subdivision AA of its construction rules is reserved. As read on November 19, 2026: the permit must carry "The signature of the original supervisor authorizing entry" ((6)(b)(I)), a signature and not initials; "The date, start, and stop times" ((6)(b)(C)); and "Any problems, if any, encountered during the entry" as a permit item ((6)(b)(P)). Entrants get access to the completed permit before entry ((5)(e)). Cancelled permits are kept 1 year ((13)). Excavation and underground construction work is excluded, except entry into sanitary sewers large enough to enter ((2)). The federal construction rule allows the supervisor's signature or initials (29 CFR 1926.1206(g)). On an Oregon job, print the app's permit and have the supervisor sign it. The rule was not re-read on 2026-11-20.
field.title: Oregon confined space rule (OAR 437-002-0146): what differs on the permit
field.topic: State safety plan: confined space

field.note: Adds the 296-809-099 definitions (read 2026-11-21). "Not re-read on 2026-11-20" replaced by the dates in edition.
field.text: Washington has one confined space rule for all industries, chapter 296-809 WAC, instead of the federal construction rule; OSHA's adoption table lists it as different but at least as effective. Oxygen and flammable limits match federal: flammables over 10 percent of the LFL or LEL, oxygen below 19.5 or above 23.5 percent (296-809-099); carbon monoxide is stricter in Washington, 35 ppm (WAC 296-841-20025). Its definitions add: any physical hazard (electrical shock, moving parts) makes a space permit-required; where the opening is big enough to fully enter, a permit is needed even for partial body entry; excavations and pits are among its examples. Permit (read 2026-11-19): the same 15 items as the federal general industry list, in another order (296-809-50004), with equipment to detect a rise in hazard if ventilation stops (federal construction item (e)); available at entry (50002(5)); problems noted on it (50002(7)); kept 1 year (50006(2)). Air is tested with a calibrated, direct-reading instrument (60004(3)(a)). The app's permit form covers these items.
field.title: Washington confined space rule (chapter 296-809 WAC): one rule for all industries
field.topic: State safety plan: confined space

field.note: Supersedes plan-trench-depth-1 (same ord). Takes the trench facts of sp-in-trench-1 and sp-mn-trench-1 (both retired).
field.text: Twenty-one states run their own OSHA plan for private construction crews. A plan must be at least as protective as federal OSHA (protection from 5 ft, 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)) and may be stricter, so name the plan as the source. Use only the line for the job's state. As checked by 2026-11-20. The plan adopts the federal excavation rule, so 5 ft: Alaska, Arizona (R20-5-601), Kentucky (803 KAR 2:415), Minnesota (MNOSHA trenching fact sheet: no state difference), Nevada, New Mexico (11.5.3.9 NMAC), Tennessee, Utah (R614-1-4), Indiana (620 IAC 1-1-30 items 7 and 18 adopt 29 CFR 1926.650-652, in force March 5, 1990, with no Indiana depth or permit of its own; OSHA's page lists an Indiana excavation standard that was not identified, not confirmed: ask IOSHA). No excavation rule of their own on the list (agency pages, not each code read line by line), so 5 ft: Hawaii, North Carolina, Virginia. Differ, each has its own card: Washington, California, Michigan, Maryland, South Carolina, Oregon. Not checked: Iowa, Vermont, Wyoming: federal 5 ft is the floor; ask the state plan.
field.title: State OSHA plans and the trench rule: which plan states follow federal 5 ft, which differ, which are not checked
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules: which states follow federal OSHA
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); osha.gov/stateplans; AZ R20-5-601; UT R614-1-4; NM 11.5.3.9 NMAC; KY 803 KAR 2:415; 620 IAC 1-1-30 (54 FR); MNOSHA trenching fact sheet; checked 2026-11-20

field.text: California, line hit or found damaged (Gov. Code 4216.4(c)): 1) Call 911 right away if the damage is to a gas or hazardous liquid line and there is an "escape of any flammable, toxic, or corrosive gas or liquid" (also for high priority lines). 2) Call the operator right away for any damage, even a nick or scraped coating. 3) Notify the regional 811 center within 48 hours. Keep people away, do not try to fix or pinch the line, do not cover it up. Emergency digging: the 2 working day notice does not apply in an emergency, defined as "a sudden, unexpected occurrence, involving a clear and imminent danger, demanding immediate action" to prevent loss of life, health, property or essential public services (4216(f)). Call 811 for an emergency ticket as soon as you can. An expired ticket or marks you can no longer see are not emergencies: stop and call for a renewal or remark.
field.title: California 811: emergencies and what to do when a line is hit
field.topic: 811 emergencies and what to do when a line is hit
field.source: Cal. Gov. Code 4216, 4216.2, 4216.3, 4216.4, 4216.6 (FindLaw copy, current as of Jan 1, 2026)

field.note: Merges dig-ca-penalties-1 (this ord) and ca-dig-alert-4216-9 (retired): the same section said twice.
field.text: California fines for breaking the dig law (Gov. Code 4216.6(a)): a negligent violation, up to $10,000; a knowing and willful violation, up to $50,000; a knowing and willful violation that damages a gas or hazardous liquid line and lets flammable, toxic or corrosive gas or liquid escape, up to $100,000. Who enforces (4216.6(c) to (e)): the Contractors State License Board for licensed contractors (a license can be on the line); the Public Utilities Commission for gas, electric and water corporations; the State Fire Marshal for hazardous liquid pipeline operators; local boards for local agencies; and, since July 1, 2020, the Underground Facilities Safe Excavation Board (the Dig Safe Board, under the Office of the State Fire Marshal) for everyone else. The Board also investigates damages and near misses reported to it and recommends. The Attorney General or a district attorney can also sue. Repair costs and injury claims are separate. Typical: no valid ticket, digging before every operator has responded, machine digging in the tolerance zone, no delineation, not reporting damage. Keep the ticket number on the daily report, photos of the marks, and a record of hand-dug potholes.
field.title: California 811: the fine for digging without calling 811, and who enforces (Gov Code 4216.6, Dig Safe Board)
field.topic: 811 penalties, exemptions and design tickets
field.source: Cal. Gov. Code 4216.6(a), (b), (c), (d), (e)

field.text: Arizona ticket life: "The marking required by subsection B of this section is valid for fifteen working days from the date of the marking" (A.R.S. 40-360.22(J)). To keep digging past that, notify "at least two working days before the end of the validity period." The Corporation Commission's page says to call 811 "to have your marks refreshed." Whether the refresh gets a new ticket number is not confirmed. Landlords (apartment communities, mobile home parks) get up to 10 working days to mark their own lines. Operators answer through the interactive positive response system; check it before digging. If an operator can't finish marking in time it must tell you promptly and send someone to the site. A line is not abandoned until the operator tells you it is: "the excavator shall not treat the underground facility as abandoned until the excavator has received notification." New in 2026 (SB 1137, Laws 2026 ch. 147): for a large project, notify the one-call center "not less than 15 business days or 21 calendar days" before the start to set a coordination meeting, with a phased ticket plan agreed in the system. The effective date was not confirmed in the summary read.
field.title: Arizona 811: marks good 15 working days, renewals, large projects (2026 law)
field.topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
field.source: A.R.S. 40-360.22 (azleg.gov); 2026 SB 1137 House summary; azcc.gov AZ 811 page
field.edition: Statute as posted on azleg.gov, read Nov 20, 2026
field.unconfirmed: new ticket number on refresh; SB 1137 effective date

field.text: Arizona has no section called "tolerance zone." The rule is in the definition of "carefully" (A.R.S. 40-360.21): within 24 inches of a marked facility, the facility is "carefully exposed with hand tools, and the uncovered facility is supported and protected." Having the marks "does not excuse any person making any excavation from doing so in a careful and prudent manner" (40-360.23(A)). If you find a line that was not marked or was marked wrong, tell the operator (40-360.23(B)). White lining: you "shall clearly and carefully mark with white lining the area that is requested to be excavated" (40-360.22(C)). Marking colors follow the Commission's color code (A.A.C. R14-2-106), the same as the national APWA colors. Landscape irrigation lines 2 inches or smaller are not "underground facilities" under this law, and private lines past the meter are not marked by the utility.
field.title: Arizona 811: careful digging within 24 inches, white lining
field.topic: 811 marks: tolerance zone, hand digging, white lining, positive response
field.source: A.R.S. 40-360.21 to 40-360.28 (azleg.gov; statute copy in Southwest Gas "Arizona Dig Law" booklet, rev. Aug 2017)
field.edition: Statute text as printed in the Aug 2017 booklet; 40-360.22 checked on azleg.gov Nov 20, 2026

field.text: Arizona, line hit (A.R.S. 40-360.24): gas or hazardous material line damaged: "immediately notify the underground facilities operator and 911 or the local emergency response agency." Any other damage: tell the operator right away and do not try to repair it. "The excavation shall be left open until the arrival of representatives of the underground facilities operator." Fines (40-360.28): "a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed five thousand dollars," and the violator owes the repair cost (40-360.26) and the other side's attorney fees if it loses (40-360.27). The fine section does not apply (40-360.28(F)): during "an emergency which involves danger to life, health or property" if reasonable precautions are taken; to farm operations and resource extraction; to hand-tool gardening or tilling on your own lot. There is no depth below which you may dig without calling.
field.title: Arizona 811: line hits, emergencies, the fine for not calling 811, exemptions
field.topic: 811 emergencies and what to do when a line is hit
