OSHA's letter of March 23, 1992 says added shoring and pumping may not always be enough: it depends on the site. Water also changes the soil: submerged or freely seeping soil is Type C.
field.title: Water in the trench: when you can work in it
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(h)(1)-(3); OSHA interpretation 1992-03-23

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.651(i) covers the stability of adjacent structures. Where the stability of adjoining buildings, walls or other structures is endangered by the excavation, provide support systems such as shoring, bracing or underpinning. Digging below the base or footing of a foundation or retaining wall is limited to cases the rule lists, such as a support system that protects the structure, stable rock, or a registered professional engineer's decision that the structure will not be affected. Sidewalks, pavements and similar structures are not undermined unless a support system protects people from their collapse. Surcharge from structures also matters for sloping: Appendix B sends structure loads back to this paragraph. The exact wording of the listed cases was not confirmed on 2026-11-20 (only the paragraph headings were read), so read 1926.651(i) before relying on an exception.
field.title: Digging next to buildings, walls, sidewalks and pavement
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.651(j)(2): "Employees shall be protected from excavated or other materials or equipment that could pose a hazard by falling or rolling into excavations. Protection shall be provided by placing and keeping such materials or equipment at least 2 feet (.61 m) from the edge of excavations, or by the use of retaining devices that are sufficient to prevent materials or equipment from falling or rolling into excavations, or by a combination of both if necessary." (j)(1) also requires protection from loose rock or soil that could fall or roll from the face: scale it off, or use barricades or other protection. The 2 ft covers the spoil pile, pipe, fittings, tools and equipment. Spoil and equipment near the edge are also a surcharge load: the competent person may have to flatten the slope (Appendix B).
field.title: Spoil pile and materials: at least 2 ft back from the edge
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.651(k)(1): "Daily inspections of excavations, the adjacent areas, and protective systems shall be made by a competent person for evidence of a situation that could result in possible cave-ins, indications of failure of protective systems, hazardous atmospheres, or other hazardous conditions. An inspection shall be conducted by the competent person prior to the start of work and as needed throughout the shift. Inspections shall also be made after every rainstorm or other hazard increasing occurrence. These inspections are only required when employee exposure can be reasonably anticipated." (k)(2): when the competent person finds such evidence, "exposed employees shall be removed from the hazardous area until the necessary precautions have been taken to ensure their safety." Federal OSHA does not require the inspection to be written down, but a written daily log is the usual proof.
field.title: Daily trench inspections by the competent person
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.651(l): "Walkways shall be provided where employees or equipment are required or permitted to cross over excavations. Guardrails which comply with 1926.502(b) shall be provided where walkways are 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above lower levels." So people do not jump a trench: if they have to cross, there is a walkway, and at 6 ft or more it has guardrails (top rail 42 inches plus or minus 3 inches, able to take 200 pounds). Some state plans use a lower height or add a width, so check the job's state.
field.title: Crossing over a trench: walkways and guardrails
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1): "Each employee in an excavation shall be protected from cave-ins by an adequate protective system" except when (i) the excavation is made entirely in stable rock, or (ii) it is "less than 5 feet (1.52m) in depth and examination of the ground by a competent person provides no indication of a potential cave-in." So: 5 ft or deeper always needs sloping, benching, shoring or a shield unless it is all stable rock. Under 5 ft needs it too if the competent person sees any sign the ground could move. Under 5 ft is not an automatic pass: someone competent has to look. Depth is taken where the person is: OSHA's letter of September 30, 2004 says an average depth cannot be used and protection is "required at each point where the excavation is 5 feet or deeper." State plans can be stricter.
field.title: The 5 ft rule: when a trench needs a protective system
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)(i)-(ii); OSHA interpretation 2004-09-30

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.652(b) sloping and benching, four options: (1) slope no steeper than 1 1/2 horizontal to 1 vertical (34 degrees), the Type C slope, with no soil classification needed; (2) classify the soil and use Appendices A and B; (3) written tabulated data approved by a registered professional engineer; (4) a design by a registered professional engineer. 1926.652(c) shoring, shields and other systems, four options: (1) Appendices A, C and D; (2) the manufacturer's tabulated data, with any deviation approved in writing by the manufacturer; (3) other tabulated data; (4) a registered engineer's design. Tabulated data and engineered designs are in writing and a copy stays at the jobsite while the system is built. Appendix B and the appendix tables stop at 20 ft: deeper than 20 ft, sloping or benching is designed by a registered professional engineer.
field.title: Ways to design trench protection, and when an engineer is needed
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(b)(1)-(4), (c)(1)-(4); Appendix B to Subpart P

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.652(d): materials and equipment used for protective systems are free of damage or defects; a competent person examines damaged material and it is pulled from service until evaluated. (e)(1) Members of a support system are securely connected; systems are installed and removed so people are protected from cave-ins and from being struck; members are not overloaded; removal starts at the bottom and works up, and backfilling goes along with removal. (e)(2)(i): "Excavation of material to a level no greater than 2 feet (.61 m) below the bottom of the members of a support system shall be permitted, but only if the system is designed to resist the forces calculated for the full depth of the trench, and there are no indications while the trench is open of a possible loss of soil from behind or below the bottom of the support system." (f) No one works on a sloped or benched face above other people unless those below are protected.
field.title: Installing and removing shoring; digging below the bottom of the support
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.652(g)(1): a shield is not loaded beyond what it was designed for; it is installed so it cannot move sideways if the trench wall lets go; people are protected from cave-ins when getting in and out of the box; and no one is inside the box while it is being installed, removed or moved vertically. (g)(2): "Excavations of earth material to a level not greater than 2 feet (.61 m) below the bottom of a shield shall be permitted, but only if the shield is designed to resist the forces calculated for the full depth of the trench, and there are no indications while the trench is open of a possible loss of soil from behind or below the bottom of the shield." Appendix B: when the box sits in the vertical lower part of a sloped trench, it extends at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side. Use the box by its manufacturer's tabulated data and keep that data at the jobsite (1926.652(c)(2)).
field.title: Trench boxes (shields): the OSHA rules
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(g)(1)-(2), (c)(2); Appendix B to Subpart P

field.text: Appendix A to Subpart P. Type A: cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength of 1.5 tons per square foot (tsf) or more, such as clay, silty clay, sandy clay, caliche and hardpan. Soil is never Type A if it is fissured, subject to vibration from traffic or pile driving, previously disturbed, or part of a layered system that dips into the excavation at 4 horizontal to 1 vertical or steeper. Type B: cohesive soil above 0.5 tsf but under 1.5 tsf; granular cohesionless soils such as angular gravel, silt and loams; previously disturbed soil unless it is Type C; soil that would be Type A but is fissured or vibrated; dry rock that is not stable. Type C: cohesive soil at 0.5 tsf or less; granular soils including gravel, sand and loamy sand; submerged soil or soil with water freely seeping; submerged rock that is not stable. Stable rock is natural solid mineral that can be cut with vertical sides and stay intact. Most trench work along existing utilities is previously disturbed soil: Type B at best.
field.title: OSHA soil types A, B and C in plain words
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (b)

field.text: Appendix A (c): each soil and rock deposit is classified by a competent person as Stable Rock, Type A, Type B or Type C, based on at least one visual and at least one manual analysis. A layered system is classified by its weakest layer (a layer can be classed on its own when a more stable layer lies under a less stable one). If conditions change, such as rain or water, the competent person looks again and reclassifies. Manual tests in (d)(2): Plasticity: roll moist soil into a thread 1/8 inch thick; if a 2 inch length holds without tearing, the soil is cohesive. Thumb penetration: Type A soil (about 1.5 tsf) can be dented by the thumb but only penetrated with very great effort; Type C soil (about 0.5 tsf) can be penetrated several inches by the thumb. Pocket penetrometer or hand shearvane. Dry strength and drying tests tell granular soil from fissured clay. Test a fresh, undisturbed sample right after it is dug. A photo cannot classify soil.
field.title: How the competent person classifies soil: visual and manual tests
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (c)(1)-(5), (d)(2)

field.text: Appendix B to Subpart P, Table B-1, maximum allowable slopes (horizontal to vertical) for excavations less than 20 ft deep: stable rock, vertical (90 degrees); Type A, 3/4 to 1 (53 degrees); Type B, 1 to 1 (45 degrees); Type C, 1 1/2 to 1 (34 degrees). Short-term exception: a Type A excavation open 24 hours or less and 12 ft or less deep may be sloped 1/2 to 1 (63 degrees). Each side is cut back, so top width = bottom width + 2 x depth x the ratio: a 10 ft deep Type B trench with a 3 ft bottom is 23 ft across the top. The actual slope may never be steeper than the table. If there are signs of distress, cut the slope back at least 1/2 horizontal to 1 vertical flatter than the table. With surcharge loads (spoil, equipment, traffic) the competent person decides how much flatter. Over 20 ft deep a registered professional engineer designs the slope. The app's Trench Sloping calculator uses these numbers.
field.title: OSHA maximum slopes for trenches by soil type (Table B-1)
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B (b), (c)(2)-(3), Table B-1 and its notes

field.text: Appendix B figures, all for excavations 20 ft or less. Type A: simple slope 3/4 to 1; benched excavations held to an overall 3/4 to 1; a trench 8 ft or less deep may have an unsupported vertical lower portion up to 3 1/2 ft high; from more than 8 ft to 12 ft deep the vertical lower portion is still 3 1/2 ft at most and the slope above it is 1 to 1. Type B: simple slope 1 to 1; benching allowed within an overall 1 to 1 (the figures allow benching only in cohesive Type B soil). Type C: simple slope 1 1/2 to 1; the figures show no benching for Type C. In any soil, when the lower portion is vertical and is supported or shielded, the support or shield extends at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side, and the slope above it follows the soil type. Layered soils: each layer is cut to its own slope. Bench step heights are pictures in the rule and are not confirmed here; look at the figure before cutting benches.
field.title: Benching and combination cuts under OSHA Appendix B
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Figures B-1.1 to B-1.4

field.text: Subpart P has six appendices. A: soil classification. B: sloping and benching. C: timber shoring for trenches, used after the soil is classified under Appendix A. D: aluminum hydraulic shoring for trenches: "information that can be used when aluminum hydraulic shoring is provided as a method of protection" where the employer does not have manufacturer's tabulated data. E: alternatives to timber shoring (pictures of hydraulic shoring, trench jacks, trench shields). F: selection of protective systems, "a graphic summary of the requirements contained in subpart P for excavations 20 feet or less in depth": a flow chart that starts with whether the excavation is all stable rock and whether it is under 5 ft with no sign of cave-in. The tables in C and D are for trenches up to 20 ft deep. The table values were not checked on 2026-11-20 (they are images on the pages read); use the tables in the rule or the manufacturer's data on site.
field.title: OSHA excavation Appendices C, D, E and F: what each one is for
field.topic: Trench and excavation rules (OSHA Subpart P)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendices C, D, E, F

field.note: Takes in confined-space-silica-1 (retired: the plain overview; its program items are in osha-pl-cs-first-steps-1 / -program-1).
field.text: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA (1926.1201 to 1926.1213, in effect since August 3, 2015) protects employees doing construction work at a site with one or more confined spaces. The rule's own examples include manholes, sewers, storm drains, pits, vaults, tanks, lift stations and pipe; on utility jobs manholes, vaults, wet wells and large pipes are typically confined spaces, and sewer manholes are usually permit spaces because of hydrogen sulfide, methane and low oxygen. It does not apply to construction work regulated by Subpart P (excavations), Subpart S (underground construction, caissons, cofferdams and compressed air) or Subpart Y (diving) (1926.1201(b)). So an open trench is under the excavation rule, but a manhole, a vault or the inside of a pipe is a confined space even when it sits in an excavation. Where another OSHA rule also covers a hazard in the space, follow both (1926.1201(c)). Maintenance work that is not construction is under the general industry rule, 29 CFR 1910.146. Before any entry use the company's written program and the app's confined space permit. A state with its own OSHA plan may have its own rule: see the confined space state tables.
field.title: When the construction confined space rule applies, and when it does not
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.1201(a)-(c); OSHA Confined Spaces in Construction FAQ

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1202. A confined space (1) is large enough and so configured that an employee can bodily enter it, (2) has limited or restricted means for entry and exit, and (3) is not designed for continuous employee occupancy. A permit-required confined space has one or more of: a hazardous atmosphere or the potential for one; material that could engulf an entrant; walls that converge inward or a floor that slopes down to a smaller cross-section so a person could be trapped or asphyxiated; or any other recognized serious safety or health hazard. Hazardous atmosphere means: flammable gas, vapor or mist over 10 percent of its lower flammable limit (LFL); combustible dust at or above its LFL; oxygen below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent; a substance above its OSHA dose or permissible exposure limit; or any other condition immediately dangerous to life or health. Entry happens when any part of the body breaks the plane of the opening.
field.title: Confined space, permit space and hazardous atmosphere: the OSHA definitions
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.1202 (definitions)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1203(a): "Before it begins work at a worksite, each employer must ensure that a competent person identifies all confined spaces in which one or more of the employees it directs may work, and identifies each space that is a permit space" by looking at the space and testing as needed. (b) If there is a permit space, tell exposed employees by posting danger signs or another equally effective way; a sign reading "DANGER--PERMIT-REQUIRED CONFINED SPACE, DO NOT ENTER" or similar wording satisfies the sign requirement. Also tell the employees' representatives and the controlling contractor where each permit space is and what the danger is. (c) An employer who decides its people will not enter takes effective measures to keep them out. (d) An employer who decides its people will enter has a written permit space program, kept at the site and available to employees.
field.title: Before work starts: finding and marking permit spaces
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.note: Takes in confined-space-field-numbers-6 (retired). The reclassification sentence moved to osha-pl-cs-reclass-1.
field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1203(e)(1): alternate procedures (no full permit) only when the employer shows all physical hazards are eliminated or isolated so the only hazard is the atmosphere, and continuous forced air ventilation alone keeps the space safe, backed by documented monitoring data available to entrants; an entry to get that data is a full permit entry. (e)(2): make it safe to open the cover and guard the opening; test before entry "for oxygen content, for flammable gases and vapors, and for potential toxic air contaminants, in that order"; no hazardous atmosphere while anyone is inside; forced air at the work area from a clean source, from before entry until all are out; continuous monitoring (periodic only under the exception); all out at once on a hazard; safe access; a written certification (date, location, signature) at the entrance. Any engulfment, machinery, electrical or other physical hazard, such as sewer flow that can surge, means a full permit. The entry supervisor and the company program decide; Ask does not.
field.title: Alternate procedures: ventilation-only entry into a permit space, and when it is not allowed
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1202 and 1926.1203(h). Host employer: the employer that owns or manages the property where the construction work is taking place. Controlling contractor: the employer with overall responsibility for construction at the worksite. Entry employer: any employer who decides that an employee it directs will enter a permit space. Before entry, the host employer gives the controlling contractor what it knows: where each permit space is, its hazards, and precautions others have used. The controlling contractor gets that information, passes it to each entity entering the space and to any other entity whose work could create a hazard in the space. Each entry employer gets the information and tells the controlling contractor its permit program and the hazards it expects. The controlling contractor and entry employers coordinate when more than one entity works in the space at once or when work outside could create a hazard inside. After entry they debrief. With no controlling contractor, the host employer or the employer who arranges the work does that job (1926.1203(i)).
field.title: Host employer, controlling contractor and entry employer duties
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1204. Each entry employer must: (a) prevent unauthorized entry; (b) identify and evaluate the hazards before entry; (c) set the procedures for safe entry: acceptable entry conditions, a chance for entrants to watch the testing, isolating the space, purging, flushing or ventilating, monitoring that warns in time to get out if ventilation fails, barriers against traffic and pedestrians, and checking that conditions stay acceptable; (d) provide at no cost, maintain and make sure people use: testing and monitoring equipment, ventilation, communications, PPE, lighting, barriers, ladders, and rescue equipment; (e) test and monitor; (f) "Provide at least one attendant outside the permit space" for the whole entry; (h) name who has each role and train them; (i) have procedures to summon rescue, rescue entrants and prevent unauthorized people from attempting a rescue; (m) review entry operations when the program may not have protected people; (n) review the program with the cancelled permits within 1 year after each entry (one yearly review can cover all).
field.title: What a permit space program has to cover
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.note: Takes in confined-space-field-numbers-2 and confined-space-silica-2 (retired). The state test-order cite (8 CCR 1953(a)(5)) is in sp-ca-confined-1.
field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1204(e). Test from outside before entry with a calibrated, bump-tested direct-reading meter, in this order: "oxygen first, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors" ((e)(3); the LEL sensor needs oxygen to read right; 1910.146(d)(5)(iii) is the same). Test top, middle and bottom: H2S and CO2 settle low, methane rises. Then monitor continuously where entrants work, or periodically if continuous equipment is not commercially available or periodic is shown to be enough ((e)(2)). Ventilate with fresh air; get out at once on an alarm. Entrants may watch the testing, get a re-test on request and get the results right away ((e)(4) to (e)(6)). A sewer that cannot be isolated: test to the extent feasible and use an early-warning system that watches for engulfment and alerts entrants and attendants in time to get out ((e)(1)). Log readings on the permit at its interval; the app blocks check-in until a fresh good test is logged.
field.title: Working in a live sewer that could flood: OSHA early-warning system, air testing order, continuous monitoring
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.note: The 1926.1205 process sentences moved to osha-pl-cs-permit-keep-1.
field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1206 lists what the permit identifies: (a) the space; (b) the purpose of entry; (c) the date and authorized duration; (d) the entrants, by name or by a roster or tracking system; (e) how a rise in air hazard is detected if ventilation stops; (f) each attendant by name; (g) each entry supervisor by name, with the signature or initials of each supervisor who authorizes entry; (h) the hazards of the space; (i) the isolation and control measures; (j) the acceptable entry conditions; (k) test results with the tester's name or initials and when; (l) rescue and emergency services and how to summon them; (m) communication procedures; (n) equipment: PPE, testing, communications, alarms, rescue; (o) other information needed for safety; (p) other permits, such as hot work. The supervisor signs before entry and "The entry employer must retain each canceled entry permit for at least 1 year" (1926.1205(b), (f)); the permit process card has posting, duration, cancel or suspend and problems noted.
field.title: The entry permit: the 16 items and how long to keep it
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1207. (a) The employer trains each employee whose work is regulated by the standard, at no cost, in a language and vocabulary the employee understands, so the employee has the understanding, knowledge and skills for the assigned duties, including the hazards of the permit space and how they are isolated or controlled. (b) Training happens before the employee is first assigned duties, before there is a change in assigned duties, whenever a change in permit space operations brings a hazard the employee was not trained on, and whenever there is evidence of a deviation from entry procedures or that the employee's knowledge is inadequate. (c) The training establishes proficiency. (d) Training records show the employee's name, the trainer's name and the dates of training, and are kept for the period the employee works for the employer. Roles to train: entrants, attendants, entry supervisors, and the employer's own rescue team if it has one.
field.title: Confined space training: who, when and the records
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1208 to 1926.1210. Entrants know the hazards and the signs of exposure, use the equipment properly, keep in contact with the attendant, alert the attendant at any warning sign or prohibited condition, and get out fast when ordered, when an alarm sounds or when they notice a warning sign. Attendants know the hazards and the behavioral effects of exposure, keep an accurate count of entrants, stay outside the space until relieved by another attendant, keep in contact with entrants, watch conditions inside and outside, order evacuation when needed, summon rescue as soon as entrants may need help getting out, keep unauthorized people away, do non-entry rescue as the employer's procedure says, and take on no duty that interferes. Entry supervisors know the hazards, check that the permit is complete and tests are done before signing, verify rescue services are available and can be reached, remove unauthorized people, end the entry and cancel or suspend the permit when required, and check conditions when responsibility is handed over. One person can be supervisor and attendant, or supervisor and entrant, if trained and equipped for each role (OSHA FAQ).
field.title: Duties of entrants, attendants and entry supervisors
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.1208, 1926.1209, 1926.1210; OSHA Confined Spaces in Construction FAQ

field.note: Takes in confined-space-field-numbers-5 (retired). Retrieval detail moved to osha-pl-cs-retrieval-1; the state rescue section (8 CCR 1960) is in the state cards.
field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1211(a): an employer who names an outside rescue service (fire department, contract team) first evaluates whether it can respond in a timely manner for this space's hazards and can rescue from this type of space (a vertical manhole, a deep wet well); picks one that can; tells it the hazards; gives it access to plan and practice; and has it agree to say right away when it is unavailable. OSHA's Appendix F to 1910.146: posting the number or relying on 911 at the time of an emergency does not comply, so 911 is not a plan unless that service was evaluated and agreed. (b) An own rescue team: PPE, training, first aid and CPR (one member certified), a practice rescue every 12 months. (d) The SDS for any substance an injured entrant met goes to the medical facility. In practice: call the station before the job, confirm confined space rescue and response time, write it on the permit, keep retrieval set up, know the address and cross street (the app's EMERGENCY button shows a script). If they cannot respond in time, entry waits.
field.title: Confined space rescue: rescue has to be arranged before entry; 911 alone is not a plan
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.text: OSHA's FAQ on Subpart AA lists five ways the construction rule goes beyond the general industry rule (29 CFR 1910.146): (1) more detailed rules for coordinating when several employers are at the site; (2) a competent person evaluates the site and identifies confined spaces, including permit spaces; (3) continuous atmospheric monitoring whenever possible; (4) continuous monitoring of engulfment hazards, for example an upstream warning in a storm sewer where a storm could cause flash flooding; (5) a permit may be suspended instead of cancelled when conditions change, and the space is brought back to the permit's entry conditions before re-entry. Which rule applies depends on the work: building new or upgrading (construction) is Subpart AA; maintenance is 1910.146. OSHA says an employer doing both kinds of work in confined spaces meets its duty by following Subpart AA. The permit item lists are nearly the same: 16 items in 1926.1206 against 15 in 1910.146(f).
field.title: Construction confined space rule compared with general industry 1910.146
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)
field.source: OSHA Confined Spaces in Construction FAQ; 29 CFR 1926.1206; 29 CFR 1910.146(f)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1): "Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems." (b)(15) is the catch-all with the same 6 ft for surfaces not otherwise addressed. (b)(6) ramps, runways and other walkways: guardrails at 6 ft or more. (a)(2): the employer first determines that the surface is strong enough to hold the people on it. Training: each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards is trained by a competent person, and the employer keeps a written certification record (1926.503). Some state plans use a different height, so check the job's state.
field.title: The 6 ft fall protection rule in construction
field.topic: Fall protection around trenches, holes and manholes

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(7): "(i) Each employee at the edge of an excavation 6 feet (1.8 m) or more in depth shall be protected from falling by guardrail systems, fences, or barricades when the excavations are not readily seen because of plant growth or other visual barrier; (ii) Each employee at the edge of a well, pit, shaft, and similar excavation 6 feet (1.8 m) or more in depth shall be protected from falling by guardrail systems, fences, barricades, or covers." So an ordinary open trench that everyone can see does not need a guardrail along its edge under federal OSHA, but a hidden one does at 6 ft, and a well, pit, shaft, manhole excavation or bore pit 6 ft or deeper needs a guardrail, fence, barricade or cover. Crossings: 1926.651(l) requires a walkway where people cross, with guardrails at 6 ft or more. Protecting the public around an open excavation is usually a contract, traffic control or local code matter on top of this.
field.title: Fall protection at the edge of excavations, wells, pits and shafts
field.topic: Fall protection around trenches, holes and manholes

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(4): protect each employee from falling through holes more than 6 ft above lower levels with personal fall arrest, covers or guardrails; protect from tripping in or stepping into or through holes with covers; and protect from objects falling through holes with covers. 1926.502(i) covers: (1) covers in roadways and vehicular aisles, steel road plates over a trench included, support at least twice the maximum axle load of the largest vehicle expected to cross; (2) all other covers support at least twice the weight of the employees, equipment and materials that may be on them at one time; (3) "All covers shall be secured when installed so as to prevent accidental displacement by the wind, equipment, or employees." (4) Covers are color coded or marked with the word "HOLE" or "COVER". Cast iron manhole covers and steel grates used on streets are exempt from the marking rule. A sheet of plywood laid loose over an open manhole frame does not meet this.
field.title: Covers and steel road plates over a hole or trench in the road: how strong (twice the axle load), secured, marked
field.topic: Fall protection around trenches, holes and manholes

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.502(b): the top edge of the top rail is 42 inches, plus or minus 3 inches, above the walking or working level. Midrails, when used, go midway between the top rail and the walking level. The guardrail system can take, without failure, a force of at least 200 pounds applied within 2 inches of the top edge in any outward or downward direction. Toeboards used for falling object protection are at least 3 1/2 inches high and take 50 pounds (1926.502(j)). These are the numbers for a guardrail on a trench walkway, around a shaft or pit, or on a bridge over an excavation.
field.title: Guardrail numbers: 42 inches and 200 pounds
field.topic: Fall protection around trenches, holes and manholes

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.502(d). Anchorages for personal fall arrest are independent of any anchorage used to support or suspend platforms and hold at least 5,000 pounds per employee attached, or are designed and installed under a qualified person with a safety factor of at least two (d)(15). The system limits the arresting force on a body harness to 1,800 pounds, is rigged so the employee cannot free fall more than 6 feet or contact a lower level, and brings the employee to a complete stop within a deceleration distance of 3.5 feet (d)(16). "The employer shall provide for prompt rescue of employees in the event of a fall or shall assure that employees are able to rescue themselves" (d)(20). Inspect the system before each use and remove damaged parts (d)(21). A fall arrest harness and lanyard is not the same as a confined space retrieval harness and line; each has its own rule.
field.title: Personal fall arrest numbers: 5,000 lb anchor, 6 ft free fall
field.topic: Fall protection around trenches, holes and manholes

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.501(c): when an employee is exposed to falling objects, the employer has each employee wear a hard hat and does one of these: (1) puts up toeboards, screens or guardrail systems to keep objects from falling from higher levels; (2) puts up a canopy and keeps objects far enough from the edge that they would not go over if knocked; or (3) barricades the area where objects could fall, keeps employees out of it, and keeps objects back from the edge. For trench work the matching excavation rules are the 2 ft setback for spoil, pipe and tools (1926.651(j)(2)) and no one under a load handled by lifting or digging equipment (1926.651(e)).
field.title: Protection from falling objects on a jobsite
field.topic: Fall protection around trenches, holes and manholes

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.20(b): (1) "It shall be the responsibility of the employer to initiate and maintain such programs as may be necessary to comply with this part." (2) "Such programs shall provide for frequent and regular inspections of the job sites, materials, and equipment to be made by competent persons designated by the employers." (3) Machinery, tools, material or equipment that does not comply is not used: it is tagged or locked as unsafe or physically removed. (4) "The employer shall permit only those employees qualified by training or experience to operate equipment and machinery." 1926.20(f): PPE and training duties are owed to each employee, and each employee not given PPE or not trained can be a separate violation. Federal OSHA does not require a written safety program for construction in general, but several state plans do (written programs, safety committees), so check the job's state.
field.title: The basic OSHA duties on every construction job (1926.20)
field.topic: General jobsite safety duties and training (OSHA Subpart C)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.21(b)(2): the employer instructs each employee in the recognition and avoidance of unsafe conditions and in the regulations that apply to the employee's work environment, to control or eliminate hazards or other exposure to illness or injury. This is the general training rule behind toolbox talks. Specific rules add their own training: excavation (competent person), confined space (1926.1207, before first assignment, with records), fall protection (1926.503, with a written certification), silica (1926.1153(i)), hazard communication (1910.1200(h)), powered industrial trucks (1910.178(l)). Federal OSHA does not require an OSHA 10-hour card; some states and some owners do. Training has to be in a language the worker understands for the confined space rule (1926.1207(a)), and OSHA applies the same idea to other training.
field.title: OSHA training duty for construction workers (1926.21)
field.topic: General jobsite safety duties and training (OSHA Subpart C)
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.32. (f) Competent person: one who is capable of identifying existing and predictable hazards in the surroundings or working conditions which are unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous to employees, and who has authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them. (m) Qualified: one who, by possession of a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing, or who by extensive knowledge, training, and experience, has successfully demonstrated the ability to solve or resolve problems relating to the subject matter, the work, or the project. (d) Authorized person: a person approved or assigned by the employer to perform a specific type of duty or to be at a specific location on the jobsite; (i) designated person means the same. Federal OSHA issues no competent person card: the employer designates the person, and the test is knowledge plus authority to fix or stop.
field.title: Competent person, qualified person, authorized person: the OSHA definitions
field.topic: General jobsite safety duties and training (OSHA Subpart C)

field.text: Section 5(a)(1) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act requires each employer to furnish employment and a place of employment free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm to employees. OSHA uses this clause where it has no specific standard. Heat is the main example for outdoor crews: there is no final federal heat standard, so federal heat citations are written under this clause. State plans have their own version of the clause. The wording of the Act was not re-read on 2026-11-20; it is unconfirmed here only in that sense.
field.title: The General Duty Clause: hazards with no specific OSHA rule
field.topic: General jobsite safety duties and training (OSHA Subpart C)
field.source: OSH Act of 1970, Section 5(a)(1) (29 U.S.C. 654)
field.edition: OSH Act of 1970; OSHA heat page read 2026-11-20

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.50. (b) Arrange for prompt medical attention before the project starts. (c) "In the absence of an infirmary, clinic, hospital, or physician, that is reasonably accessible in terms of time and distance to the worksite", a person with a valid first aid certificate (American Red Cross or equivalent that can be shown on paper) is available at the worksite. (d) First aid supplies are easy to reach; the kit is in a weatherproof container with individually sealed packages and is checked before it goes out and at least weekly. (e) Have equipment to get an injured person to a doctor or hospital, or a way to call an ambulance. (f) Where 911 is not available, post the phone numbers of doctors, hospitals or ambulances. Where 911 is available but does not get the caller's location automatically, post the latitude and longitude of the worksite or other location information. (g) Where eyes or body may be exposed to corrosive materials, provide quick drenching or flushing facilities in the work area.
field.title: First aid on the job: when a trained person must be on site
field.topic: Jobsite health: first aid, water, toilets, noise

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.51. (a) An adequate supply of potable water in all places of employment; portable containers close tightly and have a tap; no dipping; containers are marked and used for nothing else; no common drinking cup. (c) Toilets, Table D-1: 20 employees or less, 1; 20 or more, 1 toilet seat and 1 urinal per 40 workers; 200 or more, 1 toilet seat and 1 urinal per 50 workers. Under temporary field conditions at least one toilet facility is available. The toilet table does not apply to mobile crews that have transportation readily available to nearby toilets (c)(4). (f) Washing facilities where people handle paints, coatings, herbicides, insecticides or other harmful contaminants. OSHA sets no number of quarts of water per hour; the state heat rules do.
field.title: Drinking water and toilets on a construction site
field.topic: Jobsite health: first aid, water, toilets, noise
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.52, Table D-2, permissible noise exposure (dBA, slow response): 8 hours at 90; 6 hours at 92; 4 hours at 95; 3 hours at 97; 2 hours at 100; 1 1/2 hours at 102; 1 hour at 105; 1/2 hour at 110; 1/4 hour or less at 115. Impulsive or impact noise should not exceed 140 dB peak. When levels exceed the table, use feasible engineering or administrative controls first; if they do not bring the level down, provide and use hearing protection. Where levels exceed the table, a continuing, effective hearing conservation program is required (1926.52(d)(1)). 1926.101: ear protection is provided and used where levels cannot be reduced; ear inserts are fitted by a competent person; plain cotton is not acceptable. Saws, breakers, vac trucks and compactors are commonly over 90 dBA.
field.title: Noise limits in construction: 90 dBA for 8 hours
field.topic: Jobsite health: first aid, water, toilets, noise
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1153 covers respirable crystalline silica in construction, except where exposure stays below 25 micrograms per cubic meter as an 8-hour average under any foreseeable conditions. Action level: 25. Permissible exposure limit (PEL): 50 micrograms per cubic meter, 8-hour average. The employer has two ways to comply: follow Table 1 fully for the task (the listed tool, water or vacuum control and the listed respirator), and then no air sampling is needed; or, for tasks not in Table 1 or where its controls are not fully used, measure exposure and keep it at or under the PEL. With wet methods, apply water at flow rates sufficient to minimize the release of visible dust. Housekeeping: no dry sweeping or dry brushing where it could add to exposure unless wet sweeping or HEPA vacuuming is not feasible; no compressed air for cleaning clothing or surfaces unless used with a ventilation system that captures the dust or no other method is feasible.
field.title: Silica rule basics for construction: limits and Table 1
field.topic: Silica dust rules (OSHA 1926.1153)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1153 Table 1 (respirator shown for 4 hours or less / more than 4 hours per shift; APF 10 means at least a tight N95 or half mask). Handheld power saw, any blade diameter, with an integrated water feed to the blade: outdoors none / APF 10; indoors or in an enclosed area APF 10 / APF 10. Walk-behind saw with integrated water feed: outdoors none / none; indoors APF 10 / APF 10. Rig-mounted core saw or drill with water to the cutting surface: none / none. Handheld and stand-mounted drills with a shroud and dust collector, and a HEPA vacuum to clean holes: none / none. Jackhammers and handheld powered chipping tools with a continuous stream or spray of water at the point of impact, or a shroud and dust collector: outdoors none / APF 10; indoors APF 10 / APF 10. Heavy equipment used to abrade or fracture silica material (hoe ram, rock ripping) or for demolition: operator in an enclosed cab, and water or dust suppressant when people outside the cab are involved: none / none. Heavy equipment for grading and excavating: water or dust suppressant as needed, or an enclosed cab when the operator is the only one on the task: none / none.
field.title: Silica Table 1 for pipe crews: saws, drills, jackhammers, equipment
field.topic: Silica dust rules (OSHA 1926.1153)
field.source: 29 CFR 1926.1153(c)(1), Table 1 rows (ii), (iv), (vi), (vii), (x), (xvii), (xviii)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1153. (g) The employer has a written exposure control plan that describes the tasks with silica exposure, the engineering controls, work practices and respirators for each task, the housekeeping measures, and how access to the work area is restricted when needed to limit exposure, including dust made by other employers. The plan is reviewed at least once a year. (g)(4) The employer designates a competent person to make frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials and equipment to carry out the plan. (h) Medical surveillance is offered at no cost to each employee who is required by this section to use a respirator 30 or more days per year. (i) Each covered employee can show knowledge of the health hazards, the tasks that could expose them, the controls, the contents of the rule, who the competent person is, and the purpose of the medical program. An enclosed cab used as a control is kept as free as practicable from settled dust, has working door seals, positive pressure, filtered intake air (95 percent efficient, MERV-16 or better) and heating and cooling.
field.title: Silica written plan, competent person, medical exams and training
field.topic: Silica dust rules (OSHA 1926.1153)

field.text: As of November 20, 2026 there is no final federal OSHA heat standard. OSHA published a proposed rule, Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings, in the Federal Register on August 30, 2024. The comment period closed January 14, 2025; the informal public hearing ran June 16 through July 2, 2025; the post-hearing comment period ended October 30, 2025. OSHA's rulemaking page lists no later step and no final rule. Until a rule is final, federal OSHA enforces heat hazards under the General Duty Clause and its heat emphasis program, and the rules with real numbers are state rules. State plans with their own heat rule set the water, shade, rest and written plan duties for jobs in those states, so check the job's state.
field.title: Federal heat rule status: still a proposal
field.topic: Heat illness rules
field.source: OSHA, Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings Rulemaking page

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.95(d): protective equipment used to comply with the construction rules is provided by the employer at no cost to employees, with listed exceptions. The employer does not have to pay for non-specialty safety-toe footwear (steel-toe boots) or non-specialty prescription safety eyewear, if the employee is allowed to wear them off the jobsite. The employer does not have to pay for everyday clothing such as long-sleeve shirts, long pants, street shoes and normal work boots, or ordinary clothing and items used only for weather. 1926.95(a): PPE is provided, used and kept in a sanitary and reliable condition wherever hazards make it necessary. (c) PPE is of safe design and is selected so it properly fits each affected employee. Where an employee brings their own, the employer still has to make sure it is adequate and maintained (b). Some state plans require the employer to pay for all required PPE.
field.title: Who pays for PPE under OSHA
field.topic: Personal protective equipment (OSHA Subpart E)
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.100(a): employees working where there is a possible danger of head injury from impact, falling or flying objects, or electrical shock and burns are protected by protective helmets, meeting one of the ANSI Z89.1 editions the rule lists. 1926.102(a): appropriate eye or face protection when exposed to flying particles, molten metal, liquid chemicals, acids or caustics, chemical gases or vapors, or injurious light; side protection when there are flying objects; devices meet one of the listed ANSI Z87.1 editions. 1926.28(a): the employer is responsible for requiring appropriate PPE wherever there is exposure to hazardous conditions. High visibility: employees exposed to public vehicular traffic at an excavation wear warning vests or other reflective or high-visibility garments (1926.651(d)), and flaggers' garments follow MUTCD Part 6 (1926.201(a)). Safety-toe footwear is covered by 1926.96.
field.title: Hard hats, eye protection and high-visibility vests
field.topic: Personal protective equipment (OSHA Subpart E)
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart G. 1926.200(a): signs and symbols are visible at all times when work is being performed and are removed or covered promptly when the hazard is gone. Danger signs are used only where an immediate hazard exists (red upper panel); caution signs warn of potential hazards or unsafe practices (yellow). (g)(1) "At points of hazard, construction areas shall be posted with legible traffic control signs" and protected by traffic control devices. (g)(2) Traffic control devices for the protection of construction workers conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD. 1926.201(a): flagger signaling and use, including warning garments, conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD. (h) Accident prevention tags are a temporary warning of an existing hazard, such as defective tools or equipment, and are not a substitute for signs. So OSHA does not write its own taper or sign spacing numbers: it points to the MUTCD, and the state's own MUTCD or supplement applies on that state's roads.
field.title: OSHA signs, tags and traffic control: the MUTCD link
field.topic: Other OSHA construction rules

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.416(a): (1) no employee works so close to an electric power circuit that they could contact it, unless protected by deenergizing and grounding the circuit or guarding it by insulation or other means. (2) "In work areas where the exact location of underground electric powerlines is unknown, employees using jack-hammers, bars, or other hand tools which may contact a line shall be provided with insulated protective gloves." (3) Before work begins the employer finds out, by asking or by looking or with instruments, whether any energized circuit, exposed or concealed, is where people or tools could contact it, posts warning signs and tells the crew where the lines are and what to do. (e) Worn or frayed cords are not used; extension cords are not stapled, hung from nails or suspended by wire. 1926.417: controls being deactivated are tagged; deenergized equipment or circuits are made inoperative and tagged at every point where they could be energized.
field.title: Electric lines underground and energized parts: the OSHA basics
field.topic: Electrical safety and lockout
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1910.147, the general industry lockout rule, covers servicing and maintenance of machines and equipment where unexpected start-up or release of stored energy could injure someone. It does not cover construction (1910.147(a)(1)(ii)). It requires an energy control program with written procedures, employee training and an inspection of each procedure at least annually. The lockout sequence: (1) prepare for shutdown, (2) shut the machine down, (3) isolate it from its energy sources, (4) apply the lock or tag, (5) release or restrain stored energy, (6) verify isolation before work. Before locks come off: inspect the area, make sure people are clear, notify affected employees. On construction work the lockout duties come from 1926.417 (tag and make circuits inoperative), the equipment rules, and for confined spaces the duty to isolate the space (1926.1204(c)(3)): pumps, valves, flow and gates are locked, blanked or plugged before entry. Work at an operating plant or lift station that is maintenance is under 1910.147 itself.
field.title: Lockout/tagout: which OSHA rule applies on a pipe job
field.topic: Electrical safety and lockout

field.text: 29 CFR 1910.1200 applies to construction through 1926.59. The employer has a written hazard communication program for the site, a list of the hazardous chemicals present, a label on each container, a safety data sheet (SDS) for each hazardous chemical that employees can get to during the shift, and training for employees when they are first assigned and when a new chemical hazard comes into their work area. For a pipe crew that means SDS on hand for primer and solvent cement, fuels, form oil, concrete and grout, epoxy, pipe lube and disinfectant (chlorine). On a site with several employers, each employer's program says how the others get the SDS and are told about the labels. Several state plans add right-to-know rules, such as yearly training.
field.title: Hazard communication: SDS, labels and training
field.topic: Other OSHA construction rules
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.601(b) motor vehicles on the jobsite: service, emergency and parking brakes in operable condition; no vehicle with an obstructed view to the rear is backed up unless it has "a reverse signal alarm audible above the surrounding noise level" or an observer signals that it is safe; haul vehicles loaded by crane, shovel or loader have a cab shield or canopy; seat belts and anchorages are installed; dump trucks have a permanently attached support that locks to hold the body up during maintenance; and vehicles are checked at the beginning of each shift, with all defects corrected before the vehicle is placed in service. 1926.600(a)(3)(ii): whenever equipment is parked, set the parking brake; on an incline, chock the wheels and set the brake.
field.title: Trucks on site: backup alarms, seat belts, daily checks
field.topic: Equipment, vehicles, rigging and cranes

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.602(a) earthmoving equipment (scrapers, loaders, dozers, tractors, graders and similar): seat belts are provided, with rollover protection under Subpart W; equipment moves only on access roads and grades built and kept to carry it safely; service brakes can stop and hold the loaded machine. (a)(9)(i): bidirectional machines such as rollers, compactors, front-end loaders and bulldozers have a horn that can be heard above the surrounding noise. (a)(9)(ii): no earthmoving or compacting equipment with an obstructed view to the rear is used in reverse unless it has a reverse signal alarm that can be heard above the surrounding noise or an employee signals that it is safe. 1926.600(a)(3)(i): bulldozer and scraper blades, end-loader buckets, dump bodies and similar equipment are fully lowered or blocked when being repaired or when not in use. 1926.20(b)(4): only employees qualified by training or experience operate equipment. Forklift operators are trained under 1910.178(l) (1926.602(d)).
field.title: Excavators, loaders and dozers: OSHA equipment rules
field.topic: Equipment, vehicles, rigging and cranes

field.text: The crane standard, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC, excludes "Power shovels, excavators, wheel loaders, backhoes, loader backhoes, track loaders" and says this machinery is also excluded "when used with chains, slings or other rigging to lift suspended loads" (1926.1400(c)(2)). So setting pipe, structures or a trench box with an excavator is not crane work under Subpart CC, and the operator does not need crane operator certification for it. What still applies: no employee under a load handled by lifting or digging equipment (1926.651(e)); the rigging rules in 1926.251 (inspect slings and hardware before use each shift, pull damaged gear, stay within rated capacity); only qualified operators (1926.20(b)(4)); and the machine maker's lifting chart and lift points. A forklift is excluded from Subpart CC too, unless it is set up to hoist and lower a suspended load with a winch or hook. State plans may have their own rule for lifting with excavators.
field.title: Lifting pipe or a trench box with an excavator: which rules apply
field.topic: Equipment, vehicles, rigging and cranes

field.text: Cranes (29 CFR 1926.1408): before work, find out whether any part of the equipment, load line or load could get closer than 20 feet to a power line. If so, choose one: (1) have the utility confirm the line is deenergized and visibly grounded at the site; (2) keep everything at least 20 feet away; or (3) find the line's voltage and keep the Table A distance: up to 50 kV, 10 feet; over 50 to 200 kV, 15 feet; over 200 to 350 kV, 20 feet; over 350 to 500 kV, 25 feet; over 500 to 750 kV, 35 feet; over 750 to 1,000 kV, 45 feet. Other equipment: 1926.600(a)(6) sets clearances for mechanized equipment near power lines, 10 feet for lines rated 50 kV or below. Excavators, dump trucks raising a bed and concrete pump booms are the usual contact. Assume every line is energized until the utility says otherwise, and use a spotter whose only job is the line.
field.title: Overhead power lines: 20 ft, or 10 ft up to 50 kV
field.topic: Equipment, vehicles, rigging and cranes
field.edition: eCFR as of 2026-09-30 (the 29 CFR text already in the Ask library)

field.text: 29 CFR 1904.39(a): report to OSHA within 8 hours after the death of any employee from a work-related incident, and within 24 hours after the in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, an amputation, or the loss of an eye. How: call or go to the nearest OSHA Area Office, call 1-800-321-OSHA (1-800-321-6742), or use the online form at osha.gov. A voicemail, fax or email to a closed office does not count. A death is reportable only if it occurs within 30 days of the incident; a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss only if it occurs within 24 hours of the incident. If you learn of it later, the clock starts when you or your agent learn. In-patient hospitalization means formal admission for care or treatment; admission only for observation or tests is not reportable. Sent home from the emergency room (ER) without being admitted: no OSHA call for that (it may still go on the 300 log). A motor vehicle crash on a public road is reportable only if it happened in a construction work zone. All employers report, even those exempt from keeping the OSHA 300 log. Many state plans use shorter times or longer lists, so check the job's state.
field.title: Reporting a death, a worker admitted to the hospital, an amputation or eye loss to federal OSHA: 8 and 24 hours
field.topic: Injury reporting and OSHA recordkeeping

field.text: 29 CFR 1904.7: a work-related injury or illness is recordable on the OSHA 300 log if it results in death, days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or a significant injury or illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional (cancer, chronic irreversible disease, a fractured or cracked bone, a punctured eardrum). First aid, which does not make a case recordable, is a complete list: non-prescription medication at non-prescription strength; tetanus shots; cleaning, flushing or soaking surface wounds; bandages, gauze, butterfly bandages or Steri-Strips; hot or cold therapy; non-rigid supports such as elastic wraps; temporary immobilization for transport; drilling a nail or draining a blister; eye patches; removing something from the eye with irrigation or a cotton swab; removing splinters with tweezers or irrigation; finger guards; massage; drinking fluids for heat stress. Stitches, prescription drugs and rigid splints are medical treatment. Days away can be capped at 180.
field.title: What makes an injury OSHA recordable; the first aid list
field.topic: Injury reporting and OSHA recordkeeping

field.text: OSHA lists 29 State Plans. 22 cover private employers and state and local government: AK, AZ, CA, HI, IN, IA, KY, MD, MI, MN, NV, NM, NC, OR, SC, TN, UT, VT, VA, WA, WY and Puerto Rico. 7 cover state and local government workers only: CT, IL, ME, MA, NJ, NY and the U.S. Virgin Islands; private crews there are under federal OSHA. Everywhere else federal OSHA covers private employers. A State Plan must be at least as effective as federal OSHA, and it can be stricter or have rules federal OSHA does not. Even inside a plan state, federal OSHA usually keeps jobs on military bases, tribal lands, some federal enclaves and national parks, and maritime work. For a pipe crew the things that most often change by state are the trench protection depth, heat rules, injury reporting times, written safety program and training card rules, and fall protection heights.
field.title: Which states run their own OSHA plan
field.topic: State safety plans: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA State Plans page

field.text: Puerto Rico has an OSHA-approved State Plan (PR OSHA) covering private employers and state and local government, so a job there follows PR OSHA's rules. The U.S. Virgin Islands plan covers state and local government workers only; private employers there are under federal OSHA. American Samoa, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands have no approved State Plan: federal OSHA covers most private employers there. Federal OSHA's 29 CFR 1926 rules, including the 5 ft trench rule and the confined space rule, are the floor in all of them. Which Puerto Rico rules differ from the federal text was not checked: it is not confirmed here whether PR OSHA is stricter on trenching, heat or reporting, so ask PR OSHA for a job there.
field.title: OSHA in Puerto Rico and the U.S. territories
field.topic: State safety plans: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA State Plans page

field.text: OSHA letter of September 30, 2004, "Permissibility of using average excavation depth to determine protective system requirements for the excavation." The question: a trench has some spots deeper than 5 ft and some shallower, and the average is under 5 ft. OSHA's answer: no. The exception in 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)(ii) is not based on an average. "Protective measures are required at each point where the excavation is 5 feet or deeper." Shallower stretches need protection only if the competent person's examination shows a potential cave-in. The letter adds that the definition of an excavation has no minimum length, because the danger at 5 ft or more does not depend on how long the cut is. So a short deep spot at a tie-in or a service crossing needs a box, shoring or a slope even if the rest of the run is shallow.
field.title: OSHA letter: you cannot average trench depth to stay under 5 ft
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 2004-09-30 (1926.652(a)(1)(ii))

field.text: Short answer: no. OSHA does not require every box in a stack to be rated for the whole trench depth; each box must be used no deeper than the depth it is designed for. OSHA letter of October 29, 1991 (stacking trench boxes): stacked shields "do not all have to be designed to resist the forces calculated for the deepest part of the trench." "The standard only requires that the shields be used at a depth not greater than that for which they are designed." So the bottom box must be rated for the full trench depth in the soil type the competent person classified, and a box higher in the stack only for the depth where it sits; put the deeper-rated box at the bottom. OSHA suggested a marking system that shows the maximum depth of each shield so a lighter box does not end up on the bottom. Stack only as the manufacturer's tabulated data allows (its box combinations, stacking pins or connectors and depth limits), keep that data at the jobsite, and get the manufacturer's written approval for anything outside it (29 CFR 1926.652(c)(2)). Do not mix this up with 1926.652(g)(2), which is not a stacking rule: digging up to 2 ft below the bottom of a shield is allowed only if the shield is designed for the full trench depth and there is no sign of soil loss from behind or below it. Where a box sits in the vertical lower part of a sloped trench, it must extend at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side (Appendix B). No one may be in a shield while it is installed, removed or moved vertically (1926.652(g)(1)(iv)).
field.title: Stacked trench boxes: does the top box in a stack need the full-depth rating? (OSHA: no)
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 1991-10-29 (1926.650, 1926.652); 29 CFR 1926.652(c)(2), (g)(1)(iv), (g)(2); Appendix B to Subpart P
field.edition: OSHA letter of interpretation and eCFR 1926.652 (current), read 2026-11-20

field.text: OSHA letter of March 23, 1992, "Construction standards addressing excavations." The question: may employees enter a trench with water in it if they are protected from cave-in by shoring, shields or sloping and the water level is controlled? OSHA's answer: 29 CFR 1926.651(h) allows it "provided adequate precautions have been taken to protect employees against the hazards posed by water accumulation." The precautions depend on the situation, and OSHA said extra shoring and controlling the water level may not always give the protection required. So there is no fixed number of inches of water that is allowed: the competent person decides, watches the pumps, and treats soaked or seeping soil as Type C.
field.title: OSHA letter: working in a trench that has water in it
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 1992-03-23 (1926.651(h))

field.text: OSHA letter of May 21, 1992 on 29 CFR 1926.652(c) Option 2. OSHA agreed that trench protective systems may be designed using the manufacturer's tabulated data "without additional certification from a registered professional engineer", because tabulated data is by definition already approved by a registered professional engineer, so "additional certification is not necessary." What the crew needs: the tabulated data for the box or shoring actually in the trench, on site, and use that stays inside it (depth, soil type, spacing). Any deviation needs the manufacturer's written approval (1926.652(c)(2)).
field.title: OSHA letter: manufacturer's tabulated data needs no extra engineer stamp
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 1992-05-21 (1926.652(c), 1926.650(b))

field.text: OSHA letter of December 22, 2003, on combination trench shield and sloping systems deeper than 20 ft. A shield manufacturer's tabulated data said to slope above the shield "per OSHA requirements." OSHA's answer: that is not enough over 20 ft, because Subpart P gives no sloping criteria beyond 20 ft: "Sloping or benching for excavations greater than 20 feet deep shall be designed by a registered professional engineer." The letter also says an engineer who approves tabulated data used in many states does not have to be registered in each state, but the engineer who approves an employer's own sloping design under 1926.652(b)(4) must be registered in the state where the work is done.
field.title: OSHA letter: trenches deeper than 20 ft and the engineer
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 2003-12-22 (1926.652(b)(3)-(4))

field.text: OSHA letter of June 15, 1992 to a utility contractors association, "Soil testing for excavations and confined spaces." Three answers. (1) The thumb penetration test may be used to identify Type B soil. (2) A storm sewer manhole that is not connected to a raw sewage line is still a confined space, because rain can wash contaminants in: such manholes "must be considered confined spaces" and the atmosphere "must be tested before an employee enters it." (3) A trench usually has natural ventilation and is not a confined space unless the factors in 29 CFR 1926.651(g) are present, while other enclosed areas with limited access generally are. The letter predates the 2015 construction confined space rule (Subpart AA), which now covers manholes and sewers directly.
field.title: OSHA letter: a storm sewer manhole is a confined space
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 1992-06-15 (1926.651(g), 1910.146)

field.text: OSHA letter of August 10, 2000, "Trench shield must extend 18 inches above excavation walls when below grade." A shield manufacturer asked whether the 18 inch extension applies when it would put the top of the box above ground level. OSHA's answer: no, "the standard does not require trench shields to extend above grade." The 18 inches in Appendix B applies where the box sits in the vertical lower part of a trench with a sloped cut above it: there the box extends at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side so material from the slope cannot roll in. The 2 ft setback for spoil and materials (1926.651(j)(2)) still applies at the surface.
field.title: OSHA letter: the 18 inch rule for a trench box at ground level
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 2000-08-10 (1926.652(b), 1926.651(j)(2))

field.text: OSHA letter of March 17, 2009, "Removing ladders during trenching activities; compliance with 29 CFR 1926.651(c)(2)." An employer asked to pull the ladder out of a trench box after workers go in, keep it at the exit point, and have two trained workers outside ready to lower it. OSHA's answer: 1926.651(c)(2) requires a safe means of egress in trench excavations 4 ft or deeper that employees can use at all times, and "the system you describe would not be considered an 'other safe means of egress'", because it delays getting out and can fail. OSHA said it knew of no hazard from leaving the ladder in that outweighs the hazard of not having it.
field.title: OSHA letter: the ladder stays in the trench
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, 2009-03-17 (1926.651(c)(2))

field.text: OSHA memo of January 9, 1991, "Clarification of Excavation Standards." OSHA told its field offices that the competent person's duties vary with the protective system option used under 29 CFR 1926.652. Under 1926.651(k) a competent person inspects before work starts and daily, and 1926.651(k) is cited when no competent person is available to do those inspections. For the options that depend on soil type, the competent person does the visual and manual soil tests, and a manual test is expected whenever the soil looks like it is getting worse, because dug soil "can only deteriorate." If employees are in an excavation said to comply with 1926.652(b) or (c) and no competent person is present, both 1926.651(k) and the 1926.652 paragraph are cited. The federal rule does not say in so many words that the competent person must stay at the trench all day; some state plans do.
field.title: OSHA memo: no competent person at the trench is a citation
field.topic: OSHA interpretation letters on trenches and manholes

field.note: Takes in ca-cal-osha-trench-and-confined-1 and cal-1 (both retired: the same permit).
field.text: California (Cal/OSHA) requires a protective system unless the excavation is entirely in stable rock, or under 5 feet with no sign of a potential cave-in on a competent person's examination (8 CCR 1541.1(a)(1)): the same 5 ft test as federal, with the same slopes (1541.1 Appendix B). What California adds is a permit: 8 CCR 1539 sends excavation permits to 8 CCR 341, which requires a Cal/OSHA permit before building a trench or excavation 5 ft or deeper into which any person is required to descend (341(d)(5)(A)). It is an annual permit or a one-job project permit from the district office (application and fee, 341.1); an annual holder notifies the Division before each new site. Exempt (341(e)): government bodies, PUC-regulated utilities, emergency repair of underground facilities, excavations nobody has to enter, graves and pools. Greenbook 306-3.1 repeats the requirement. Keep the permit number with the job paperwork; the permit does not replace the competent person or the protective system. Shields: dig no more than 2 ft below the bottom of the support (1541.1(e)(2)(A)).
field.title: California trench protection depth (5 ft, same as federal) and the Cal/OSHA excavation permit (8 CCR 341)
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.edition: Title 8 as posted on dir.ca.gov, read 2026-11-20

field.text: California's excavation rule, 8 CCR 1541(b), goes further than the federal utility paragraph. Before digging starts: the excavation area is marked by the excavator as Government Code 4216.2 requires, the regional notification center (811) and any non-member owners get at least 2 working days' notice, and the excavator has a positive response from all known owners or operators inside the project boundaries. Within 10 feet of a high priority subsurface installation (high pressure natural gas, petroleum pipelines and similar) the owner or operator notifies the excavator and the two hold an onsite meeting. Only qualified persons do the locating. Employees exposed to excavation work are trained in the notification and digging practices. If a line is damaged, the excavator notifies the owner or operator or the notification center right away, and calls 911 for a gas or hazardous liquid release from a high priority line. Federal OSHA only says to contact owners within local response times (29 CFR 1926.651(b)).
field.title: California excavation rule on locating utilities before digging
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.edition: Title 8 CCR, last amended operative 5-31-2012 (Register 2012, No. 18)

field.note: Takes in ca-cal-osha-trench-and-confined-2 (retired). Its 1541(b) one-call sentence is in sp-ca-trench-dig-1.
field.text: California's excavation standard is Title 8 Construction Safety Orders Article 6: 1539 (permits), 1540 (definitions), 1541 (general requirements) and 1541.1 (protective systems, Appendices A to F matching the federal ones; appendix options to 20 ft, an engineer beyond). It keeps the federal numbers: a stairway, ladder or ramp in trenches 4 feet or deeper within 25 feet of lateral travel (1541(c)(2)); air testing before entry deeper than 4 feet where a hazard could exist, limits 19.5 percent oxygen and 20 percent of the LFL (1541(g)(1)(A)); spoil and equipment at least 2 feet from the edge (1541(j)(2)); daily competent-person inspections before work, as needed and after rain (1541(k)(1)). Crossings differ: walkways or bridges with standard guardrails where people or equipment cross excavations more than 6 feet deep and wider than 30 inches (1541(l)(1)); remote excavations, wells, pits and shafts barricaded or covered (1541(l)(2)). The federal crossing rule has no width (29 CFR 1926.651(l)). The 5 ft permit is in section 341.
field.title: California trench rules that match federal (ladders, air, spoil, inspections) and the crossing rule (Title 8 Article 6)
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.edition: Title 8 as posted on dir.ca.gov, read 2026-11-20

field.note: Takes in ca-cal-osha-trench-and-confined-4 (retired: the same Article 37 summary) and the Cal/OSHA cites of the retired confined-space-field-numbers cards.
field.text: California's construction confined space rule is 8 CCR 1950 to 1962 (Article 37), in effect since December 30, 2015, amended January 1, 2026 (see the 2026 card). It mirrors federal Subpart AA: 1951 definitions, 1952 general requirements, 1953 program, 1954 permitting, 1955 permit, 1956 training, 1957 to 1959 entrant, attendant and supervisor duties, 1960 rescue. The 1955(a) permit items are the same 16 as 1926.1206; supervisor signs before entry (1954(b)), permit available at entry (1954(c)), kept 1 year (1954(f)). Test from outside: oxygen, flammable, toxic (1953(a)(5)(C)); monitor continuously unless periodic is shown enough (1953(a)(5)(B)); a sewer gets continuous monitoring and an engulfment early warning (1953(a)(5)(A)). Not for Article 6 excavations, tunnels, diving or pressurized work (1950(b)); its note lists manholes, sewers, tanks and vaults. Maintenance (not construction) is 8 CCR 5157; 5158 was the construction rule before 2015. CO and H2S limits are stricter than federal (air limits card).
field.title: California confined space rule for construction (8 CCR 1950 to 1962, Article 37), not federal Subpart AA
field.topic: State safety plan: confined space
field.edition: Title 8 CCR Article 37 operative 12-30-2015 (Register 2016, No. 1); permit cites read 2026-11-19, 1950 read 2026-11-20

field.text: California's outdoor heat rule is 8 CCR 3395; construction gets the full rule including high-heat procedures. Water: fresh, cool, free and close to the work; where it is not plumbed, at least 1 quart per employee per hour for the whole shift. Shade: when the temperature is above 80 F, shade is up at all times while employees are present, close to the work, with room for everyone on a rest or recovery period to sit fully in the shade without touching each other; at or below 80 F, shade is provided or available on request. Anyone may take a preventative cool-down rest in the shade at any time, is watched and asked about symptoms, and is not ordered back to work until symptoms are gone, with at least 5 minutes in the shade plus the time to get there. Temperature here means the dry-bulb air temperature in the open. The employer has a written heat illness prevention plan, in English and the language most employees understand, available at the worksite. Federal OSHA has no heat standard in force.
field.title: California outdoor heat rule: water, shade at 80 F, cool-down rest
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.edition: Title 8 CCR 3395, last substantive amendment operative 5-1-2015 (Register 2015, No. 14)

field.text: California's 8 CCR 3395(e) high-heat procedures start when the temperature is 95 F or more, for construction and the other listed industries: keep voice, sight or phone contact so employees can reach a supervisor; observe employees for alertness and signs of heat illness by one of these: a supervisor watching 20 or fewer employees, a mandatory buddy system, regular contact with anyone working alone, or another effective way; name who is authorized to call emergency medical services; remind people to drink water; and hold a pre-shift meeting on the procedures. Acclimatization (3395(g)): all employees are closely observed during a heat wave, meaning a day predicted to reach at least 80 F and at least 10 degrees hotter than the average high of the last five days; and an employee newly assigned to a high heat area is closely observed for the first 14 days. Emergency response (3395(f)): act on symptoms at once, never leave a sick worker alone or send them home without first aid, and give responders clear directions to the site.
field.title: California high-heat procedures at 95 F, heat waves and new workers
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.edition: Title 8 CCR 3395, last substantive amendment operative 5-1-2015 (Register 2015, No. 14)
