field.text: California employers report to Cal/OSHA (the Division of Occupational Safety and Health) immediately, by telephone or the online mechanism, any serious injury or illness, or death, of an employee at work (8 CCR 342(a)). "Immediately means as soon as practically possible but not longer than 8 hours after the employer knows" or with diligent inquiry would have known. Only if the employer can show exigent circumstances may the report be made within 24 hours of the incident. Serious injury or illness (8 CCR 330(h)) means a hospital admission as an inpatient for more than observation or tests, an amputation, the loss of an eye, or serious permanent disfigurement; a crash on a public road counts only in a construction zone. Taken to the emergency room (ER) and admitted: call Cal/OSHA within 8 hours; an ER visit only for observation or tests is not by itself a serious injury. The report gives the time and date, employer name and contact, the site address, the injured person's name, the nature of the injury, where the person was taken, and a description of the accident and whether the scene was changed. The federal 24 hours for a hospitalization does not apply to a job covered by Cal/OSHA.
field.title: California injury reporting: serious injury or worker in the hospital, immediately and no later than 8 hours
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting

field.text: California's construction fall protection rule, 8 CCR 1670(a), requires approved personal fall arrest, personal fall restraint or positioning systems when work exposes an employee to falling more than 7 1/2 feet from the perimeter of a structure, unprotected sides and edges, leading edges, through shaftways and openings, from steep roof surfaces, or other sloped surfaces not otherwise protected. That is a different height from the federal 6 feet (29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)); on a job covered by Cal/OSHA use California's rule and check the specific order for the work (guardrails, openings, roofing and steel have their own sections). System numbers match the federal ones: anchorages 5,000 pounds per employee, arresting force 1,800 pounds with a harness, free fall no more than 6 feet, deceleration distance 3.5 feet (1670(b)). Fall arrest systems are inspected at least twice a year by a competent person, with the dates documented.
field.title: California fall protection trigger in construction: more than 7 1/2 feet
field.topic: State safety plan: fall protection

field.note: Takes in sp-wa-trench-other-1 (retired). The Table N-1 sentence moved to sp-wa-trench-slope-1, which already says it in full.
field.text: Washington (L&I, DOSH) requires a protective system for each employee in an excavation unless it is made entirely in stable rock, or it is "less than 4 feet (1.22m) in depth and examination of the ground by a competent person provides no indication of a potential cave-in" (WAC 296-155-657(1)(a)). So the depth is 4 ft, one foot shallower than the federal 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)). The 2 ft rules match federal: dig no more than two feet below the bottom of a support system or a shield, and only if it is designed for the full depth and no soil is being lost (657(5)(b), (7)(b)). An engineer designs slopes over 20 ft. Guardrails are required "where walkways are four feet or more above lower levels" (296-155-655(12)); federal uses 6 ft (1926.651(l)). Utilities are located before opening the excavation and found exactly by safe means as digging gets close (655(2)). Same numbers as federal: a way out within 25 ft at 4 ft deep (655(3)(b)), air testing over 4 ft (655(7)(a)(i)), equipment 2 ft from the edge (655(10)(b)), daily inspections and after every rainstorm (655(11)(a)).
field.title: Washington trench protection starts at 4 feet (stricter than federal 5 ft); walkway guardrails at 4 ft
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.edition: WAC 296-155-657, WSR 16-09-085, effective 5/20/2016; WAC 296-155-655 as amended eff. June 1, 2026

field.text: Washington added new trench rules effective June 1, 2026 (WSR 26-09-113, Order 21-20). WAC 296-155-655(13)(a): "A competent person must remain on the job site any time trench excavation work is being performed." (13)(b): the employer must have a competent person complete a written trench excavation work plan for any trench excavation an employee may enter where a protective system is required under WAC 296-155-657(1)(a), that is, from 4 ft. (13)(d): before employees go into such a trench, they are trained on the plan. The plan covers items such as soil classification, underground installations, the protective system and the way out, and is available on site for the department. L&I publishes a form, Trench Excavation Evaluation and Work Plan (F417-324-000); an employer may use its own plan if it covers the same items. Definitions moved to a new section, WAC 296-155-652. Federal OSHA requires neither a written trench plan nor, in so many words, a competent person on site all day.
field.title: Washington written trench work plan and competent person on site (June 1, 2026)
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation

field.text: Washington's outdoor heat rule (WAC 296-62-095 through 296-62-09560) applies all year whenever the outdoor temperature is at or above the action level: 80 F for most clothing, 52 F for non-breathable clothing such as vapor barrier suits. Workers who are not required to be outdoors more than 15 minutes in any 60-minute period are exempt. At the action level the employer provides at least one quart of suitably cool drinking water per worker per hour, shade or another way to cool down at all times, and paid preventative cool-down rest whenever a worker feels the need. New workers, workers back from an absence, and everyone during a heat wave are closely observed; the acclimatization period is 14 days. Training for employees and supervisors is before outdoor work and every year. The heat procedures are written into the employer's Accident Prevention Program. Numbers here are from L&I's own Be Heat Smart page; the WAC subsections were not read section by section.
field.title: Washington outdoor heat rule: 80 F, or 52 F in non-breathable clothing
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.source: WAC 296-62-095 through 296-62-09560; L&I Be Heat Smart page

field.text: Washington's outdoor heat rule adds mandatory paid cool-down rest in high heat (WAC 296-62-095 through 296-62-09560, as explained on L&I's Be Heat Smart page): at 90 F or hotter, at least 10 minutes every 2 hours; at 100 F or hotter, 15 minutes every hour. These breaks are not required if engineering or administrative controls keep the exposure below 90 F; cooling vests and similar wearables do not count as engineering controls. A meal break can cover a rest break but is not paid for that reason. Emergency work to restore or maintain critical infrastructure is exempt from the mandatory breaks. Supervisors and workers must be able to reach each other at all times, and there are written emergency steps for a worker with symptoms. The state measures by air temperature, not heat index. Federal OSHA has no heat standard in force.
field.title: Washington high heat: paid cool-down breaks at 90 F and 100 F
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.source: WAC 296-62-095 through 296-62-09560; L&I Be Heat Smart page

field.text: Washington employers report to L&I's Division of Occupational Safety and Health within 8 hours of a work-related incident that results in a death or the inpatient hospitalization of any employee (WAC 296-27-031(1)), and within 24 hours for an amputation or the loss of an eye that does not need inpatient hospitalization (2). Call 1-800-4BE-SAFE (1-800-423-7233) or go to the nearest DOSH office. For a death or hospitalization, secure the scene and do not move equipment involved, including tools, machinery and PPE, "unless it is necessary to remove the victim or prevent further injuries." The clock starts when the employer learns of the event. A death counts if it happens within 30 days of the incident. The federal rule gives 24 hours for a hospitalization (29 CFR 1904.39), so this state is stricter on that point.
field.title: Washington injury reporting: a worker admitted to the hospital, report within 8 hours
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting

field.text: Oregon OSHA adopts the federal excavation rules, 29 CFR 1926.650, 1926.651 and 1926.652 with Appendices A to F, in Division 3, Subdivision P (OAR 437-003-0001; read by an earlier check on 2026-11-20). So protection is required from 5 ft, or shallower when a competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in, and the federal sloping table applies. The one Oregon-initiated rule in the subdivision is OAR 437-003-0096, Underground Installations: in addition to the federal utility paragraph, the Public Utility Commission's one-call law and rules apply, ORS 757.541 through 757.571 and OAR 952-001-0050 and 860-024-0007. In practice that makes the state's locate law (call before you dig, marks, hand digging near marks) enforceable by the safety agency too. Oregon OSHA's Division 3 page lists no other state trench rule.
field.title: Oregon OSHA trench and excavation rule: federal Subpart P plus the state utility-locate rules
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.source: OAR 437-003-0096; OAR 437-003-0001 (adopting 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P)
field.edition: OAR chapter 437 Division 3, current through Register Vol. 63, No. 12 (Dec. 1, 2024); read 2026-11-20

field.text: Oregon's heat illness prevention rule, OAR 437-002-0156 (effective June 15, 2022), applies indoors and outdoors when the heat index is 80 F or higher. Exempt: exposure when work is not required for more than 15 minutes in any 60-minute period, and buildings with mechanical ventilation that keeps the heat index under 80 F. At a heat index of 80 F: shade that is immediately and readily available, open on at least three sides or mechanically ventilated, close to the work, and big enough for everyone on a break to sit fully in it; and drinking water that is cool (66 to 77 F) or cold (35 to 65 F), free, and enough for each employee to drink up to 32 ounces per hour. The employer has a written heat illness prevention plan available at the worksite, a written acclimatization plan, an emergency medical plan that covers heat (construction also follows 29 CFR 1926.50), and yearly training with a record of each employee's name, the date and the trainer. This rule measures by heat index, not air temperature. Federal OSHA has no heat standard in force.
field.title: Oregon heat rule: shade and water from a heat index of 80 F
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness

field.text: Oregon's OAR 437-002-0156(5) adds high-heat practices when the heat index is 90 F or higher and controls do not bring the exposure below that: (a) employees can reach a supervisor at any time, in a language they understand (a cell phone counts only with reliable reception); (b) employees are observed for signs of heat illness by regular contact with anyone working alone, a mandatory buddy system, or an equally effective way; (c) someone at each worksite is designated and equipped to call emergency medical services; (e) the employer adopts a written heat illness prevention rest break schedule, choosing one of three options: its own schedule built on the rule's Table 1, the NIOSH work and rest schedule in Appendix A, or the simplified schedule in Table 2. Only time in the shade counts toward a break, and the breaks are paid unless they fall in an unpaid meal period. The break lengths in Tables 1 and 2 were not confirmed on 2026-11-20 (the tables are not in the page text read), so read the tables before quoting minutes.
field.title: Oregon high-heat practices at a heat index of 90 F
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.source: OAR 437-002-0156(5)(a)-(g), Tables 1 and 2, Appendix A

field.text: Oregon employers report to Oregon OSHA within 8 hours of a work-related fatality or catastrophe, in person or by telephone only (OAR 437-001-0704). A catastrophe is an incident in which two or more employees are fatally injured or three or more are admitted to a hospital. Within 24 hours they report any in-patient hospitalization, loss of an eye, and any amputation or avulsion that includes bone or cartilage loss. Amputation here includes a fingertip. A death counts if it occurs within 30 days of the incident. Deaths and in-patient hospitalizations from a motor vehicle accident during the work shift, or from a heart attack at work, are reportable. Admission only for observation, or emergency room treatment without admission, is not reportable. The times match the federal rule (29 CFR 1904.39); the avulsion wording and the 8-hour catastrophe report are the state's own. The phone numbers are in the rule's Table 1, which was not in the page read.
field.title: Oregon injury reporting: 8 hours and 24 hours, with a wider amputation rule
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting

field.text: Oregon's construction fall protection rule is its own, OAR 437-003-1501, in place of the federal 1926.501. (1) Employees exposed to falling 6 feet or more to a lower level are protected. (3) "Regardless of height," employees are protected from tripping in or stepping into or through holes, including skylights, by covers. (4) Wall openings whose inside bottom edge is less than 39 inches above the walking surface and whose outside bottom edge is 6 feet or more above lower levels are protected. (5)(a) At the edge of an excavation 6 feet or more deep that is not readily seen because of plant growth or another visual barrier: guardrails, fences or barricades. (5)(b) Wells, pits, shafts and similar excavations 6 feet or more deep: guardrails, fences, barricades or covers. (6) Employees less than 6 feet above dangerous equipment are protected by guardrails or equipment guards. Fall protection systems follow 1926.502 and the state's restraint, warning line and safety monitor rules. The 6 ft and the excavation edge rules match federal OSHA.
field.title: Oregon construction fall protection: 6 feet, holes regardless of height
field.topic: State safety plan: fall protection

field.text: Michigan's slope table is Table 1 of R 408.40941 (MIOSHA Part 9), listed by soil and not by Type A, B or C. As printed on MIOSHA's own card CET-0204 (dated 8/2026) and matching a University of Michigan safety page: solid rock 90 degrees; fractured rock 75 degrees (1/4 to 1); stiff clay 63 degrees (1/2 to 1); firm clay 56 degrees (2/3 to 1); previously disturbed soil 45 degrees (1 to 1); wet granular soil 34 degrees (1 1/2 to 1); saturated granular soil 26 degrees (2 to 1); running soil 18 degrees (3 to 1). The table in the official standard is an image that could not be opened, so these values are not confirmed against the standard itself: look at Table 1 in Part 9 before cutting a slope. Other Part 9 numbers: spoil not less than 2 feet from the edge (R 408.40933(2)); a ladder from 48 inches deep, extending 3 feet above the top, within 25 feet of travel (R 408.40933(4)); bench rise not more than 5 feet (R 408.40944(2)). Saturated and running soils need flatter slopes than the federal Type C 1 1/2 to 1.
field.title: Michigan trench slopes: MIOSHA Part 9 Table 1 angles
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation

field.text: Michigan employers report a work-related death to MIOSHA within 8 hours by calling 1-800-858-0397 (Mich. Admin. Code R 408.22139). Within 24 hours they report the inpatient hospitalization of 1 or more employees, an amputation, or the loss of an eye: by phone or in person at the nearest MIOSHA office, by phone at 1-844-464-6742 (the Severe Injury Report Line), or online through MIOSHA's incident report form. A death is reportable if it occurs within 30 days of the incident; a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss if it occurs within 24 hours of the incident. If the employer learns late, the time runs from when it learns. A crash on a public road is reportable only in a construction work zone. An answering machine, fax or email to a closed office does not count. The times are the same as the federal rule (29 CFR 1904.39); the phone numbers are the state's.
field.title: Michigan injury reporting to MIOSHA: 8 hours and 24 hours
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: Mich. Admin. Code R 408.22139 (MIOSHA Part 11)

field.text: Michigan runs its own plan, MIOSHA, for private and public employers. OSHA's page for the plan says MIOSHA has adopted many federal standards by reference and lists construction subjects where its requirements differ from federal OSHA, including: first aid, sanitation, illumination, hazard communication, personal protective equipment, fire protection, signals and barricades, hand and power tools including lockout/tagout, electrical, scaffolds, mobile equipment, excavations, concrete, underground construction, stairways and ladders, cranes and derricks, walking-working surfaces and confined spaces. Only the excavation standard (Part 9) and the reporting rule (R 408.22139) were read for this library. For the other subjects it is not confirmed here what differs: check the MIOSHA construction standard for the subject. No state heat rule was found for this state, and that too is not confirmed. Federal OSHA covers maritime work and tribal employers on reservations.
field.title: Michigan: which construction subjects MIOSHA handles differently
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA Michigan State Plan page

field.text: Minnesota (MNOSHA) lists these differences from federal OSHA on its own page. AWAIR, A Workplace Accident and Injury Reduction program: employers in the industries on the state's list must have a written safety and health program (Minn. Stat. 182.653, subd. 8; Minn. R. 5208.1500); the list is revised every five years, and whether a given construction code is on it was not confirmed on 2026-11-20. Safety committees: employers with more than 25 employees must have a joint labor-management safety committee; smaller employers only if they are subject to AWAIR (Minn. Stat. 182.676). PPE: the employer provides and pays for all personal protective equipment required for the job (Minn. Stat. 182.655, subd. 10a); federal OSHA lets the employer skip paying for ordinary safety-toe boots. Recordkeeping: employers with more than 10 employees keep the injury records whatever their industry. The state also enforces the 1989 exposure limits where there is no separate standard.
field.title: Minnesota written safety program (AWAIR), safety committees and PPE costs
field.topic: State safety plan: written programs and training
field.source: Minn. Stat. 182.653 subd. 8; Minn. R. 5208.1500; Minn. Stat. 182.676; Minn. Stat. 182.655 subd. 10a; MNOSHA differences page

field.text: Minnesota keeps its own Employee Right-to-Know rules (Minn. R. chapter 5206) on top of the federal hazard communication standard, which the state adopted on September 10, 2012. MNOSHA's page says the state keeps annual training for all hazardous chemicals, harmful physical agents and infectious agents, where the federal rule requires training at first assignment and when a new hazard arrives, and keeps a three-year recordkeeping requirement for that training. Harmful physical agents include heat, noise and vibration in the state's rules. The state also has its own construction lockout rule, Minn. R. 5207.0600, in addition to 29 CFR 1926.417; its text was not read on 2026-11-20, so its details are not confirmed here.
field.title: Minnesota Employee Right-to-Know: yearly training
field.topic: State safety plan: written programs and training
field.source: Minn. R. ch. 5206; Minn. R. 5207.0600; MNOSHA differences page

field.note: New id in the ord of sp-mn-trench-1. The trench fact also sits in osha-pl-trench-states-2. "Injury reporting times not read" dropped: sp-mn-report-1 now has them.
field.text: Minnesota (MNOSHA) uses the federal confined space in construction rule, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA: the old state construction rule, Minn. R. 5207.0300 to 5207.0304, is marked repealed (42 SR 1015; read 2026-11-19). MNOSHA's page of differences from federal OSHA lists nothing for confined space or excavation. Trenches in this state follow the federal excavation rule, 29 CFR 1926.651 and 1926.652: protection from 5 ft, or shallower when a competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in; MNOSHA's trenching fact sheet states no state difference (read by an earlier check on 2026-11-20).
field.title: Minnesota confined space in construction: the federal rule (old state rule repealed)
field.topic: State safety plan: confined space
field.source: Minn. R. 5207.0300-.0304 (repealed, 42 SR 1015); MNOSHA differences page; MNOSHA trenching fact sheet; 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA, 1926.651-652

field.text: Virginia employers report to the Virginia Department of Labor and Industry within eight hours any work-related incident resulting in a fatality, and "within 24 hours any work-related incident resulting in (i) the inpatient hospitalization of one or more persons, (ii) an amputation, or (iii) the loss of an eye" (Va. Code 40.1-51.1(D), last amended 2016). The same section requires a workplace free of recognized hazards, posting of citations at the site of the violation, and keeping employees informed of their rights. The times match the federal rule, 29 CFR 1904.39; the report goes to the state agency (VOSH), not federal OSHA, for a job covered by the state plan.
field.title: Virginia injury reporting to DOLI: 8 hours and 24 hours
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting

field.text: Virginia has no heat illness standard in force as of November 20, 2026. A 2026 law, Va. Code 40.1-44.2, requires the Safety and Health Codes Board to adopt one, and the state agency's page says the deadline is May 1, 2028. The agency is still developing it: a regulatory advisory panel met on October 15, October 29 and November 12, 2026, with trigger temperatures, water, cooling, rest, acclimatization, training and emergency response under discussion. The planned topics are drinking water, shade or climate-controlled areas where practicable, rest breaks, acclimatization, training, emergency response and added protections in high heat; no numbers are set. Until the standard is adopted, heat is enforced through the general duty to keep the workplace free of recognized hazards (Va. Code 40.1-51.1(A)).
field.title: Virginia heat illness standard: required by law, not yet written
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.source: Va. Code 40.1-44.2; Va. Code 40.1-51.1(A); DOLI heat illness prevention standard page (modified 2026-11-17)

field.text: Virginia runs its own plan, VOSH, under the Department of Labor and Industry. OSHA's page for the plan says VOSH adopted the majority of federal standards and lists its unique construction rules: Reverse Signal Operation Safety Requirements for Vehicles, Machinery and Equipment for the Construction Industry; medical services and first aid; sanitation; steel erection; and the Overhead High Voltage Line Safety Act. It also has a rule making manufacturer's specifications and limitations enforceable for machinery, vehicles, tools and equipment. Excavation and confined space are not on the unique list: the state's old construction confined space rule, 16VAC25-140, was repealed when the board adopted the federal rule effective January 1, 2016 (read 2026-11-19), and trench protection is the federal 5 ft rule. The texts of the reverse signal and first aid rules were not read on 2026-11-20; their details are not confirmed here. Federal OSHA covers military bases and other federal enclaves.
field.title: Virginia: what VOSH has that federal OSHA does not
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA Virginia State Plan page; Virginia Register notice on 16VAC25-140

field.text: Nevada OSHA's heat illness regulation (R131-24AP, approved by the Legislative Commission on November 15, 2024) applies to employers that must have a written safety program, which Nevada OSHA's guidance describes as employers with more than 10 employees. It sets no temperature trigger. The employer does a one-time written job hazard analysis of heat for each job where most employees are exposed to heat for more than 30 minutes of any 60-minute period, and redoes it when the task changes materially or after an accident. Where the analysis finds heat exposure, the written safety program covers: potable water, a rest break for an employee showing signs or symptoms of heat illness, means of cooling, monitoring of working conditions, work processes that add heat or humidity, employee training, and procedures for a medical emergency. The employer names a person with the authority to monitor conditions and respond. Work in a climate-controlled space, including a vehicle with working air conditioning, is generally exempt. For enforcement the agency treats a day at or above 90 F as a heat priority day. Federal OSHA has no heat standard in force.
field.title: Nevada heat illness rule: job hazard analysis and written program
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.source: Nevada OSHA Updated Heat Illness Prevention Guidance (2026-05-21); R131-24AP; NRS 618.383; NAC 618.538, 618.540

field.text: Nevada law requires training cards on construction sites. NRS 618.983: "Not later than 15 days after the date a construction worker other than a supervisory employee is hired, the construction worker must obtain a completion card for an OSHA-10 course", and a supervisory employee must obtain a completion card for an OSHA-30 course within the same 15 days. The employer keeps proof of the card (NRS 618.987), and penalties are in NRS 618.990. Whether a card expires and has to be renewed was not confirmed on 2026-11-20: the regulation on card renewal (NAC 618.9923) is marked repealed, and the definition of a valid completion card (NAC 618.9912) was not read. Federal OSHA does not require a 10-hour or 30-hour card.
field.title: Nevada OSHA 10 and OSHA 30 cards: how long a new construction worker has to get one (15 days)
field.topic: State safety plan: written programs and training

field.text: Nevada OSHA has incorporated most federal OSHA standards by reference, according to OSHA's page for the state's plan. Its unique standards listed there are, for construction, cranes, steel erection and asbestos, and for general industry, safety programs, explosives, sanitation and hazard communication. Excavation and confined space are not on the list, so trench protection is the federal 5 ft rule (29 CFR 1926.652) and confined space in construction is 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA. A written safety program is required of employers with more than 10 employees (NRS 618.383, as described in Nevada OSHA's heat guidance). Injury reporting to Nevada OSHA uses the federal times: a death within 8 hours; a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss within 24 hours (Nevada OSHA's report page). Federal OSHA covers military bases, land under exclusive federal jurisdiction and tribal land.
field.title: Nevada: federal rules by reference, plus state safety program rules
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA Nevada State Plan page; NRS 618.383

field.text: Arizona's plan, ADOSH, "has adopted federal OSHA standards and incorporates them by reference", according to OSHA's page for the plan. The unique state standards listed there are few: for construction, fall protection; for general industry, compressed gas and air receivers and commercial diving; for agriculture, field sanitation. Excavation and confined space are not on the list, so trench protection is the federal 5 ft rule (29 CFR 1926.652), confined space in construction is 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA, and reporting follows 29 CFR 1904.39 (8 hours for a death, 24 hours for a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss). What the state's construction fall protection rule changes was not read, and whether the state has adopted a heat rule since its heat emphasis program was not checked: both are not confirmed here. Federal OSHA covers tribal reservations, copper smelters and land under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
field.title: Arizona: ADOSH uses the federal rules
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA Arizona State Plan page

field.text: Utah employers must notify Utah OSHA (UOSH) "within 8 hours of occurrence" of any work-related fatality, "of any disabling, serious, or significant injury and of any occupational disease incident" (Utah Admin. Code R614-1-5(B)(1)). The number is (801) 530-6901. Tools, equipment, materials or other evidence that might pertain to the cause of the accident are not removed or destroyed until UOSH authorizes it (B)(2). The employer investigates all work-related injuries and occupational diseases (B)(3). The rule does not define serious or significant by a list, so treat any hospitalization, amputation or eye loss as within it. That is stricter than the federal rule, which gives 24 hours for a hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye (29 CFR 1904.39).
field.title: Utah injury reporting: 8 hours for any serious injury
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: Utah Admin. Code R614-1-5(B)(1)-(3)

field.text: Utah's plan, UOSH (Utah Labor Commission), adopts the federal construction rules: the app's state table, checked November 19, 2026, records that UOSH adopts the federal trench rule, a protective system from 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652), and OSHA's adoption table lists the state as identical on the construction confined space rule (29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA). The state's own difference found for this library is injury reporting: 8 hours for any disabling, serious or significant injury (R614-1-5). OSHA's page for the plan was not read on 2026-11-20, so any other unique state standard is not confirmed here. No state heat rule was found for this state.
field.title: Utah trench and confined space rules: the federal text
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: App state table (checked 2026-11-19); OSHA adoption table 2015-05-04; Utah Admin. Code R614-1-5

field.text: New Mexico OSHA "has adopted all OSHA standards, incorporated by reference", and OSHA's page for the plan says "the state and federal standards are identical." The unique state standards listed are hazard communication (all sectors), state and local government firefighting, workplace violence in convenience stores, and agriculture rules. So for a pipe crew: trench protection from 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652), confined space under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA, fall protection at 6 ft, and reporting under 29 CFR 1904.39 (8 hours for a death, 24 hours for a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss). Federal OSHA covers military installations and tribal land in the state.
field.title: New Mexico: state and federal standards are identical
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA New Mexico State Plan page

field.text: New Mexico has no heat rule in force as of November 20, 2026. The Occupational Health and Safety Bureau proposed a Heat Illness and Injury Prevention Rule (to be 11.5.7 NMAC) on March 12, 2025 and asked the Environmental Improvement Board for a hearing; the hearing has been reset several times, most recently by a fourth motion to vacate and reschedule on August 11, 2026, and the bureau's page shows no adoption and no effective date. The March 16, 2026 draft would apply above a heat index of 80 F: at least one quart of drinking water per hour, a paid 15-minute rest for every two hours of work below a heat index of 100 F and a stricter work and rest table from 100 F, shade or cooling areas, acclimatization starting at 20 percent of the usual time in heat on day one, a written plan, yearly training, and reports of heat illness within 24 hours. None of that is enforceable until the board adopts it.
field.title: New Mexico heat rule: proposed, not adopted
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness
field.source: NMED OHSB heat rule page; proposed 11.5.7 NMAC, draft of 2026-03-16
field.edition: NMED page and draft rule, read 2026-11-20

field.text: Kentucky changed its reporting rule in 2026. 803 KAR 2:181, effective February 3, 2026 (52 Ky.R. 312), now says "an employer shall comply with 29 C.F.R. Part 1904", so the federal times apply: a work-related death within 8 hours, and an in-patient hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye within 24 hours (29 CFR 1904.39). The state's older text, which gave 72 hours for an amputation, loss of an eye or hospitalization and listed the state phone number (502) 564-3070, is struck from the rule. The change follows House Bill 398 of 2025 (KRS 338.062, effective June 27, 2025), which the regulation cites as its basis. Where the report is phoned in now was not confirmed on 2026-11-20: the current text gives no number, so use the state OSH office or 1-800-321-6742.
field.title: Kentucky injury reporting: now the federal 8 and 24 hours
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting

field.text: Kentucky's plan (Kentucky OSH, Education and Labor Cabinet) adopts the federal excavation rule: 803 KAR 2:415 adopts 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P with only definitions added (read by an earlier check on 2026-11-20), so trench protection is required from 5 ft. OSHA's page for the plan lists state-specific construction standards: fall protection in residential construction, in steel erection and on cranes and derricks; safety and testing of supply lines in excess of 600 volts; receiving and unloading bulk hazardous liquids; bloodborne pathogens; and recordkeeping and reporting. A 2025 law, House Bill 398 (KRS 338.062), is the stated basis for the state bringing its reporting rule in line with the federal one in 2026. Whether the state fall protection rules listed on OSHA's page are still in force after that law was not confirmed on 2026-11-20. Federal OSHA covers military bases and Tennessee Valley Authority sites.
field.title: Kentucky trench rule and the state-specific construction standards
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: 803 KAR 2:415; OSHA Kentucky State Plan page; KRS 338.062

field.text: Tennessee's plan, TOSHA, has adopted the federal standards for private and public employers. TOSHA's own page of differences lists, for construction (29 CFR 1926), only that four administrative sections are not adopted (1926.1 to 1926.4); nothing differs for excavation, confined space or fall protection. So trench protection is from 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652) and confined space in construction is 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA. The state rules that go beyond federal are the Hazardous Chemical Right to Know rule (Rule 0800-01-09) on top of hazard communication, a sharps injury rule, and the state's own air contaminant limits (Rule 0800-1-1-.07(2)(b)) in place of 29 CFR 1910.1000. The state's injury reporting times and any heat rule were not read; they are not confirmed here. Federal OSHA covers Tennessee Valley Authority facilities, military bases and railroad employment.
field.title: Tennessee: TOSHA uses the federal construction rules
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: TOSHA, Differences in TOSHA and Federal OSHA Standards; OSHA Tennessee State Plan page; Tenn. Rules 0800-01-09, 0800-1-1-.07

field.text: North Carolina's plan (NC Department of Labor, OSH Division) publishes a list of its state-specific standards. For construction they are 13 NCAC 07F .0202 (general safety and health provisions), .0203 (occupational health and environmental controls), .0204 (personal protective and life saving equipment), .0205 (steel erection) and .0207 (toxic and hazardous substances), plus communication tower and blasting rules. Rule .0202 rewords 29 CFR 1926.28(a): the employer is responsible for requiring appropriate personal protective equipment in all operations where there is an exposure to hazardous conditions. The state also has rules on safety and health programs and committees (13 NCAC 07A .0600 to .0606) and a Hazardous Chemical Right to Know Act. Excavation and confined space are not on the list, so trench protection is the federal 5 ft rule (29 CFR 1926.652). Who must have a safety committee, the state's reporting times and any heat rule were not read; they are not confirmed here.
field.title: North Carolina: state-specific standards and the trench rule
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: NCDOL, North Carolina State-Specific Standards; 13 NCAC 07F .0202

field.text: South Carolina OSHA has identically adopted the federal standards, according to OSHA's page for the plan, with two unique construction items: excavations and general safety and health requirements. The state's list of changes to 29 CFR 1926 shows the excavation change in the definition of competent person (1926.650(b)): besides being able to identify existing and predictable hazards and having authority to correct them, the competent person "must have specific training in, and be knowledgeable about, soils analysis, the use of protective systems" and the requirements of the excavation rule. Federal OSHA says that only in its preamble. Everything else is the federal rule: protection from 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652), ladder at 4 ft within 25 ft, spoil 2 ft back. The comparison document shows two versions of the definition side by side; reading the first as the state's is our reading of its column order, so that point is not confirmed with the agency. Injury reporting to SC OSHA uses the federal times: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss (SC OSHA's report page).
field.title: South Carolina trench rule: federal text, with training written into competent person
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.source: SC OSHA, SC 1926 standard modifications (1926.650(b)); OSHA South Carolina State Plan page

field.text: Maryland's Heat Stress Standards, COMAR 09.12.32 (effective September 30, 2024), apply indoors and outdoors where employees are exposed to a heat index that equals or exceeds 80 F. Exempt: emergency operations, employees not required to work in the heat for more than 15 consecutive minutes per hour, and buildings with mechanical ventilation that keeps the heat index below 80 F. The employer has a written heat-related illness prevention and management plan, available to employees and to MOSH. Water: at least 32 ounces of drinking water per hour for each exposed employee, free and close to the work (.07). Shade: as close to the work as practicable, outside, open and exposed to air on at least three sides (.06). Acclimatization: up to 14 days for newly exposed employees and those back after 7 or more consecutive days away, on a written schedule, for example a gradual increase over 5 to 14 days with at most a 20 percent increase each day (.05). Training before first exposure, every year, and right after any suspected heat illness at the site; training records kept one year (.10). Federal OSHA has no heat standard in force.
field.title: Maryland heat stress standard: plan, water and shade from a heat index of 80 F
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness

field.text: Maryland's COMAR 09.12.32.08 requires high-heat procedures when the heat index in the work area reaches or exceeds 90 F. Unless the employer uses the alternatives below, the rest schedule is: heat index above 90 and below 100 F, "A minimum rest period of 10 minutes for every 2 hours worked"; heat index above 100 F, "A minimum rest period of 15 minutes for every hour worked." The employer may follow current NIOSH work and rest recommendations instead, or show effective heat management through alternative cooling and control measures. Employees are monitored for signs of heat illness in high heat, and the plan has emergency response steps: communication, monitoring and care, who to contact, and how the person is transported. The numbers are heat index, not air temperature.
field.title: Maryland high-heat rest breaks at a heat index of 90 F and 100 F
field.topic: State safety plan: heat illness

field.text: Maryland's plan, MOSH, lists its state-specific regulations in COMAR Title 09, Subtitle 12: employee injury and illness records (09.12.21), fall protection in steel erection (09.12.25), crane safety (09.12.26), tower crane operator certification (09.12.27), tree care (09.12.28), heat stress (09.12.32), access to information on hazardous and toxic substances (09.12.33), field sanitation (09.12.36) and personnel platforms on cranes (09.12.38). The same MOSH page lists Maryland supplements to federal standards, including 29 CFR 1926.651 (excavations), 29 CFR 1926.1201 to 1213 (confined spaces in construction), 29 CFR 1926.62 (lead) and Subpart CC (cranes). The excavation amendments keep the federal 5 ft trench rule and add that protective system records (tabulated data, designs) are kept at the jobsite (see Maryland's trench card); MOSH adopted the federal confined space in construction rule by reference effective January 2, 2017 and repealed the old state rule (COMAR 09.12.35); MOSH's list entry for that supplement links to the federal Subpart AA text itself and the adoption page names no Maryland change, so the federal rule applies as written (read 2026-11-21).
field.title: Maryland: MOSH-specific rules and supplements to the federal trench rule
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: MOSH, Maryland-specific standards page; COMAR 09.12.21-09.12.38

field.text: Alaska employers report an employment accident that is fatal to an employee or that results in an in-patient hospitalization, the loss of an eye or an amputation "immediately but in no event later than eight hours after receipt by the employer" of information that the accident occurred (AS 18.60.058(a)). Report by telephone or in person to the nearest office of the Division of Labor Standards and Safety. If the employer learns of it later but within 30 days of the accident, the 8 hours run from when it learns. After an accident with one or more deaths or the in-patient hospitalization of two or more employees, equipment, material or product related to it is not moved or altered until the department clears it, unless waiting would interfere unreasonably with work or create more hazards (b). Federal OSHA gives 24 hours for a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss (29 CFR 1904.39); the state did not adopt that federal section (8 AAC 61.1010(a) skips 1904.39).
field.title: Alaska injury reporting: hospitalization, amputation or eye loss within 8 hours
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting

field.text: Alaska's plan, AKOSH, "has adopted all federal OSHA standards and incorporates them by reference", per OSHA's page for the plan. 8 AAC 61.1010(c) adopts 29 CFR 1926.10 through 1926.29, 1926.31 through 1926.1153, 1926.1200 through 1926.1213 and 1926.1400 through 1926.1442 as amended, with state exceptions in 8 AAC 61.1145 through 61.1170. That range includes the excavation rule (5 ft, 29 CFR 1926.652), fall protection, silica and the construction confined space rule. OSHA's page lists the additional state construction standards as gases, vapors, fumes, dusts or mists; steel erection and wood framing; and electric power transmission and distribution. The exception sections were not read on 2026-11-20, so it is not confirmed that none of them touches trenching. No state heat rule was found for this state. Federal OSHA covers Denali National Park, several military sites and the Metlakatla Indian Community.
field.title: Alaska: federal construction rules adopted by reference
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: 8 AAC 61.1010(a)-(e); OSHA Alaska State Plan page

field.text: Hawaii employers report to HIOSH within 8 hours after the death of any employee from a work-related incident, and within 24 hours of the inpatient hospitalization of an employee, an amputation, the loss of an eye, or property damage in excess of $25,000 from a work-related incident (HAR 12-52.1-1, the state's amendments to 29 CFR 1904.39). Report by telephone at (808) 586-9102 or in person at the HIOSH office in Honolulu; a phone message left when the office is closed counts only if it gives all the required information. The state defines amputation to include fingertip amputations with or without bone loss, medical amputations from irreparable damage, and body parts that are reattached. The property damage report and the wider amputation definition go beyond the federal rule (29 CFR 1904.39).
field.title: Hawaii injury reporting: includes property damage over $25,000
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: HAR 12-52.1-1 (state amendments to 29 CFR 1904.39)

field.text: Hawaii's plan, HIOSH, has adopted the majority of federal standards; OSHA's page for the plan says some of its standards have significant differences and some have no federal counterpart. The unique construction standards listed are signs, signals and barricades; steel erection; cranes and derricks; and worker intoxication. For general industry they include a safety and health program standard, noise and toxic substances. Excavation and confined space are not on the unique list, so trench protection is taken to be the federal 5 ft rule (29 CFR 1926.652); the state's own construction rule text was not read on 2026-11-20, so that is not confirmed. No state heat rule was found for this state. Federal OSHA covers private employers inside secured military installations and contractors in the national park.
field.title: Hawaii: HIOSH unique standards and the trench rule
field.topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs
field.source: OSHA Hawaii State Plan page

field.text: Connecticut has an OSHA-approved State Plan that covers state and local government workers only, according to OSHA's list of State Plans. Private employers there, including a contractor working for a city or a water district, are under federal OSHA: trench protection from 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652), the construction confined space rule (29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA), fall protection at 6 ft (29 CFR 1926.501), and reporting a death within 8 hours and a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss within 24 hours to federal OSHA at 1-800-321-6742 (29 CFR 1904.39). The city's or district's own employees on the same job are under the state plan. The public-sector plan's rules were not read for this library; it is not confirmed whether they differ from the federal text.
field.title: Connecticut: federal OSHA for private crews, a state plan for public workers
