A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
field.title: Do hours laying pipe count against a driver's 14 hours? What "on duty" means
field.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

field.text: FMCSA lists the drivers who do not have to use an electronic logging device (ELD): drivers using the short-haul exception ("Drivers who use the short-haul, timecard exceptions are not required to keep records of duty status (RODS) or use ELDs."); drivers who have to keep a log on no more than 8 days in any 30 day period (they can use a paper log on those days); driveaway-towaway operations where the vehicle driven is the thing being delivered; and trucks "manufactured before the model year 2000". A crew truck that normally stays inside 150 air miles and gets back within the short-haul hours needs time cards, not an ELD. If that truck goes outside the exception more than 8 days in any 30, it needs an ELD. The FMCSA page was issued as guidance in 2018 and marked rescinded on March 10, 2022 only because the same rules are in the regulation itself (49 CFR 395.8 and Part 395 Subpart B); the regulation text was not re-read for this chunk.
field.title: Electronic logs (ELD): which crew trucks do not need one
field.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
field.source: FMCSA, "Who is exempt from the ELD rule?" (guidance 2018; 49 CFR 395.8(a)(1)(iii))

field.text: Before driving: 49 CFR 396.13 says "Before driving a motor vehicle, the driver shall" "Be satisfied that the motor vehicle is in safe operating condition", review the last inspection report if one was required, and sign it. End of day: 396.11 requires a written report "at the completion of each day's work on each vehicle operated" covering at least brakes (including trailer brake connections), steering, lights, tires, horn, wipers, mirrors, coupling devices, wheels and emergency equipment. But: "Drivers are not required to prepare a report if no defect or deficiency is discovered by or reported to the driver." The company must fix safety defects before the truck goes out again, certify it on the report, and keep it "for three months from the date the written report was prepared." The trailer is part of the inspection. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
field.title: Pre-trip and post-trip truck inspection (DVIR): what the driver must do
field.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

field.text: 49 CFR 396.17: "Every commercial motor vehicle must be inspected as required by this section." In a combination each unit counts on its own: "the tractor, semitrailer, and the full trailer (including the converter dolly if so equipped) must each be inspected." A commercial vehicle may not be used unless each part of it "has passed an inspection in accordance with the terms of this section at least once during the preceding 12 months" and "documentation of such inspection is on the vehicle." The proof can be the inspection report itself or a sticker or decal showing the inspection date, who did it, the vehicle it belongs to, and that it passed. What crews miss: the equipment trailer and the tilt-deck need their own inspection and their own sticker, not just the truck. This applies from the 10,001 lb commercial vehicle line, not only to CDL trucks. A roadside officer will ask for the sticker or report on both units. These are the federal (interstate) rules. A truck that never leaves the state follows that state's version, usually close: check with the state.
field.title: Annual DOT inspection: every truck AND trailer, proof on the vehicle
field.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

field.text: When hauling equipment, pipe or plates, the driver has to stop and check the chains, binders and straps. 49 CFR 392.9: a commercial truck may not be driven unless the cargo is "properly distributed and adequately secured", and the "tailgate, tailboard, doors, tarpaulins, spare tire and other equipment used in its operation" are secured, and nothing blocks the driver's view or movement. The driver must make sure of that before driving, then "Inspect the cargo and the devices used to secure the cargo within the first 50 miles after beginning a trip" and adjust or add tie-downs as needed. After that, re-check whenever the driver changes duty status, or the truck "has been driven for 3 hours", or "has been driven for 150 miles, whichever occurs first." For a crew this means: after loading the excavator, pipe, plates or a trench box, stop within the first 50 miles (chains and binders settle), and again at the fuel stop. Heavy equipment over 10,000 lb has its own tie-down rule (49 CFR 393.130: at least four tie-downs, see the library chunk on tying down equipment).
field.title: Hauling the excavator: stop and check chains and binders in the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles
field.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

field.text: On the Interstate system and reasonable access to it, 23 CFR 658.17 sets the weight limits a state must allow without a special permit: "The maximum gross vehicle weight shall be 80,000 pounds." One axle: 20,000 pounds. "The maximum gross weight on tandem axles is 34,000 pounds." Groups of axles must also meet the bridge formula, W = 500 x (LN / (N - 1) + 12N + 36), where W is the weight allowed on the group, L is the distance in feet between the outer axles of the group, and N is the number of axles. Two sets of tandems may each carry 34,000 lb when the first and last axles are at least 36 ft apart. Anything heavier, such as a large excavator on a lowboy, moves on a state overweight permit, and the permit sets the route, the hours and the escorts. States also have their own limits on state and local roads, bridge postings, and seasonal (frost) load limits, which can be lower. Axle weights are what get a dump truck ticketed: a truck can be under its gross and still be over on the rear tandem if the load sits too far back.
field.title: Federal truck weight limits: 80,000 lb gross, 20,000 single axle, 34,000 tandem
field.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

field.text: Fuel a crew carries for its own saws and pumps is a "material of trade": under 49 CFR 173.6 no placards or shipping papers are needed inside these limits. Gasoline (a Class 3 flammable liquid, Packing Group II): each container no more than "30 L (8 gallons)". All materials of trade on the truck together: no more than "200 kg (440 pounds)" gross weight. "For gasoline, a packaging must be made of metal or plastic" and meet the OSHA safety can rules (29 CFR 1910.106(d)(2) or 1926.152(a)(1)) or DOT packaging rules. Cans must be closed, secured and marked "gasoline". The driver "must be informed of the presence of the hazardous material" and of these limits. Diesel: a liquid with a flash point at or above 100 F "may be reclassed as a combustible liquid" (173.150(f)(1)), and the hazardous materials rules "do not apply to a material classed as a combustible liquid in a non-bulk packaging" (173.150(f)(2)). A large diesel transfer tank is bulk packaging and has marking and placard rules. The gallon size where a tank becomes bulk is in 49 CFR 171.8 and was not confirmed for this chunk, so check before buying a tank.
field.title: Hauling gas cans and diesel on the crew truck: the materials of trade rule
field.topic: DOT rules for crew trucks: CDL, medical card, hours of service, inspections, loads
field.source: 49 CFR 173.6 (materials of trade); 49 CFR 173.150(f) (combustible liquids)
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20
field.unconfirmed: the gallon figure that separates non-bulk from bulk packaging (49 CFR 171.8) was not read

field.text: Federal rule of thumb: a job that will disturb one or more acres of land needs stormwater permit coverage before dirt moves, and so does a smaller job that is part of a larger common plan (a phase of a subdivision, for example) that will disturb an acre or more in total (EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, Part 1.1.2). A long trench adds up: width disturbed times length. In most states the state environmental agency issues the permit, with its own name, forms and fees. EPA's own permit (the CGP) is used only where EPA is the permitting authority (Part 1.1.3, Appendix B): all of Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the Pacific territories, plus Indian country in most states and many federal facilities and lands of exclusive federal jurisdiction. On an EPA job the Notice of Intent goes in "At least 14 calendar days before commencing construction activities." The 2022 CGP expires at 11:59 pm on February 16, 2027. EPA proposed a 2027 CGP on August 3, 2026; as of EPA's page dated November 17, 2026 it was not final. On a tribal or federal job in any state, ask which permit covers the site before assuming it is the state one.
field.title: How big a job needs a stormwater permit and SWPPP: 1 acre. And where EPA's own permit applies
field.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
field.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 1.1.2, 1.1.3, 1.4.3, Appendix B; EPA proposed 2027 CGP page (updated 2026-11-17)
field.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

field.text: Under EPA's 2022 Construction General Permit the site picks one inspection schedule (Part 4.2): either "At least once every seven (7) calendar days", or once every 14 calendar days plus within 24 hours of a storm of 0.25 inches or more in 24 hours (or snowmelt that causes a discharge). Sites draining to sensitive waters inspect every 7 days and within 24 hours of such a storm (Part 4.3). Fewer are allowed for stabilized areas, arid areas in the dry season, and frozen ground (Part 4.4). The inspector must be a "qualified person": for projects covered on or after February 17, 2023, someone who has passed EPA's construction inspection course and exam or holds a current equivalent certification (Parts 4.1, 6.3). Fixes have a clock: a new or replaced control or a significant repair within 7 calendar days; routine maintenance by the close of the next business day (Part 5.2.1). These are EPA's own permit numbers. Most states issue their own permit, usually close to this, and the state permit governs there.
field.title: How often the SWPPP inspection is due: every 7 days, or 14 days plus after a 0.25 inch rain
field.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
field.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 4.1 to 4.4, 5.2.1, 6.3
field.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

field.text: Three field rules from EPA's 2022 Construction General Permit. Stabilization (Part 2.2.14): where earth work has stopped for good, or will sit idle for 14 or more days, start stabilizing right away (seed and mulch, blanket, rock, pavement) and finish "as soon as practicable, but no later than 14 calendar days" after starting, on sites with 5 acres or less disturbed at one time. Sites with more than 5 acres open at once, and sites draining to sensitive waters, get 7 calendar days. Perimeter controls (Part 2.2.3): silt fence, wattles and berms go in before the dirt work upslope; remove built-up sediment "before it has accumulated to one-half of the above-ground height of any perimeter control." Concrete washout (Part 2.3.4): wash chutes, pumps and tools only into a "leak-proof container or leak-proof and lined pit"; never onto the ground, into a storm drain inlet, a ditch or the trench. Let it harden and haul it off. Paint, form oil and curing compound wash water are handled the same way. These are EPA's own permit numbers. Most states issue their own permit, usually close to this, and the state permit governs there.
field.title: Stabilization deadline (14 days), silt fence clean-out at half height, concrete washout
field.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
field.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 2.2.3, 2.2.14 (Table 2), 2.3.4
field.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

field.text: Pumping water out of a trench or excavation to a ditch, creek or storm drain (dewatering) is a regulated discharge under EPA's 2022 Construction General Permit. What the water must look like (Part 2.4): "Do not discharge visible floating solids or foam", and the discharge must not cause "a visible sheen on the water surface". Run the discharge through a sediment control (dewatering bag, weir tank, basin or thick vegetation) and do not let it erode where it lands. Inspection (Part 4.3.2): the dewatering operation is inspected "once per day on which the discharge occurs." If it shows a plume, sheen or foam, stop or cut the discharge right away and fix the cause before pumping again (Part 5.2.2). Sites that pump to sensitive waters must also sample the dewatering discharge for turbidity against a benchmark of 50 NTU (Part 3.3). Water that smells of fuel or has a sheen is not ordinary trench water: stop pumping and call the office. These are EPA's own permit numbers. Most states issue their own permit, usually close to this, and the state permit governs there.
field.title: Pumping the trench out to a ditch or storm drain: what to check (daily, no foam, no sheen, 50 NTU)
field.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
field.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 2.4, 3.3, 4.3.2, 5.2.2
field.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

field.text: OSHA letter of May 29, 2007 on tapping and tying in to asbestos-cement (AC, transite) water pipe under 29 CFR 1926.1101. A competent person must classify the work. OSHA said removal of AC pipe "is normally Class II asbestos work." It can be Class III only when it is repair or maintenance work that disturbs a small amount, no more than fits in one glove bag or waste bag. If it is not clear, the employer "should assume the higher class applies." Required: wet methods, HEPA vacuums, prompt cleanup and bagging of waste. Prohibited: high-speed abrasive disc saws without controls, compressed air, dry sweeping. In practice that means a snap cutter or a wet hand method, never a dry cut-off saw. Training: Class III workers need training that "shall take at least 16 hours" in the usual case; Class II workers need training with hands-on practice for the material and method. Being under the exposure limit does not exempt the work: a consultant "was in error when he stated that when an activity is below the PEL it is exempt". State rules can be stricter.
field.title: OSHA on tapping, cutting or removing asbestos-cement water pipe: Class II work, no "below the limit" exemption
field.topic: Asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe: federal rules for cutting, removing and bursting
field.source: OSHA Standard Interpretation, May 29, 2007 (29 CFR 1926.1101(b), (g), (k)(9), (o)(4))
field.edition: OSHA letter of interpretation dated May 29, 2007

field.text: EPA's asbestos air rule (the Asbestos NESHAP, 40 CFR Part 61 Subpart M) can apply to a job that removes or breaks up asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe. The amounts that trigger the full notice and work-practice rules in 40 CFR 61.145 are "At least 80 linear meters (260 linear feet) on pipes", or 160 square feet on other components. Above the line, written notice goes to the air agency "At least 10 working days before asbestos stripping or removal work or any other activity begins". Work practices: "Adequately wet the material and ensure that it remains wet until collected and contained", and no visible dust to the outside air. EPA describes the normal way to take out AC pipe as open trench: expose it, and it is "wet-cut into 6- and 8-foot sections using a snap cutter or similar tool", wrapped, and hauled to a landfill that takes asbestos waste. "All ACWM must be kept adequately wet and sealed in leak-tight containers." A short tie-in on one stick is normally under the 260 ft line, but OSHA's worker rules apply at any length. State and local air agencies often have lower thresholds.
field.title: EPA asbestos rule for AC pipe jobs: the 260 ft line, 10 working day notice, keep it wet
field.topic: Asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe: federal rules for cutting, removing and bursting
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

field.text: Pipe bursting or reaming an old asbestos-cement (AC, transite) main breaks the pipe into fragments and leaves them in the ground. In its Federal Register notice of June 10, 2019 (84 FR 26852) EPA said it "neither approved pipe bursting nor pipe reaming as AWPs to replace A/C pipe" (AWP means alternative work practice). EPA said bursting or reaming more than the threshold amount of AC pipe has to follow the Asbestos NESHAP, including the standards for an active asbestos waste disposal site (40 CFR 61.154) and, where the broken pipe is left in the ground, the standards for an inactive site (40 CFR 61.151). In the same notice EPA approved one trenchless method, "close tolerance pipe slurrification (CTPS)", which grinds the old pipe into a wet slurry that is pumped out and disposed of as asbestos waste; it was approved on May 30, 2019 with required inspections, wetting, sampling and landfill disposal. So before bidding or starting a burst on an AC main, get the owner's and the air agency's position in writing. Some states have their own written policy on AC pipe bursting.
field.title: Pipe bursting asbestos-cement pipe: EPA has not approved it as an alternative (2019 notice)
field.topic: Asbestos-cement (AC, transite) pipe: federal rules for cutting, removing and bursting
field.source: EPA, Notice of Final Approval: Alternative Work Practice Standard for Asbestos Cement Pipe Replacement, 84 FR 26852 (June 10, 2019)

field.text: Federal rule (40 CFR Part 110, the "sheen rule"): an oil discharge to water must be reported when it is a harmful quantity, which EPA explains as oil that "violates state water quality standards, causes a film or sheen on the water's surface" or "leaves sludge or emulsion beneath the surface". Oil means diesel, gasoline, hydraulic and motor oil. There is no gallon minimum: a sheen on a creek, a lake, or a ditch or storm drain that leads to one is enough. The person in charge must notify the National Response Center "immediately after he or she has knowledge of the discharge": "1-800-424-8802 or 1-202-267-2675", staffed 24 hours by the Coast Guard. On the job: stop the source, keep it out of inlets and water with booms, pads or a dirt berm, and call the foreman and the office. Most states also require a call to the state spill line, often for spills on dry ground over a set number of gallons. Never wash a spill down or bury it.
field.title: Fuel or oil spill that reaches water: call the National Response Center, 1-800-424-8802
field.topic: Fuel and oil on the job: spill reporting and fuel storage rules
field.source: EPA, 40 CFR Part 110 Discharge of Oil regulation FAQ ("When must I report an oil discharge to NRC?")
field.edition: EPA FAQ page read 2026-11-20 (rule: 40 CFR Part 110)

field.text: EPA's Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure (SPCC) rule, 40 CFR Part 112, generally applies to a site that stores oil and has a "total aggregate capacity of aboveground oil storage containers greater than 1,320 gallons" and that "Has the potential to discharge oil in quantities that may be harmful into navigable waters or adjoining shorelines." Oil includes diesel, gasoline, hydraulic and motor oil, and used oil. Count the capacity of the containers, not what is in them today: a 1,000 gallon diesel tank plus a 500 gallon tank is 1,500 gallons and is over the line. A covered site needs a written SPCC plan, secondary containment for bulk containers (a double-wall tank or a dike or tub that holds the contents), regular inspections, and trained people. An engineer must certify the plan if "total oil storage capacity exceeds 10,000 gallons"; at or below that the owner may be able to self-certify. For a pipe company this usually comes up at the yard. Which small containers count toward the 1,320 gallons (EPA's rule text counts containers of 55 gallons and up) was not confirmed from the rule text for this chunk.
field.title: When a yard or job site needs an SPCC plan: more than 1,320 gallons of oil in tanks and drums
field.topic: Fuel and oil on the job: spill reporting and fuel storage rules
field.source: EPA Region 9 SPCC compliance fact sheet (September 2025); 40 CFR Part 112
field.unconfirmed: the 55 gallon minimum container size for counting capacity (40 CFR 112.1) was not read in the rule text

field.text: Laying pipe across a stream, a wetland or some ditches is work in "waters of the United States" and needs authorization from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under the Clean Water Act (Section 404), usually through a nationwide permit (NWP) that the owner or engineer obtains before the job. The nationwide permits were reissued in 2026: the Corps published them in the Federal Register on January 8, 2026 ("The 56 reissued and one new nationwide permit in the final action"). "The nationwide permits in this action take effect March 15, 2026." "The 2021 permits are set to expire March 14, 2026." What this means on the job: the crossing has a permit with conditions that the crew has to follow, such as the limits of disturbance at the crossing, how the trench is backfilled and the bank restored, where spoil can go, and fish timing windows. Ask for the permit and its conditions before working at a crossing, and do not widen the work area on your own. A job permitted under the 2021 permits that was not finished may need its authorization checked against the 2026 permits; the terms of the 2026 utility line permits were not read for this chunk and are not confirmed here.
field.title: Creek, ditch and wetland crossings: Corps of Engineers nationwide permits were reissued for 2026
field.topic: Working in or near streams and wetlands: Corps permits
field.source: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers news release, January 8, 2026 (2026 nationwide permits; 91 FR, Jan. 8, 2026)
field.unconfirmed: terms and acreage limits of the 2026 utility line nationwide permits were not read

field.text: On Davis-Bacon (federally funded or assisted) construction, each contractor and subcontractor turns in a weekly certified payroll with a signed statement of compliance. 29 CFR 3.4 sets the deadline: the statement is delivered "within 7 days after the regular payment date of the payroll period". The 7 days run from the regular payday for that week, not from the end of the work week. It goes to the agency's representative at the site; if there is none, it is mailed or sent another reliable way to the agency contracting for or financing the work, inside the same 7 days. On most jobs the subcontractor sends it up through the prime contractor, who is responsible for all tiers, and many agencies now require their own online system. Records: the certified payrolls are kept for 3 years after all the work on the prime contract is completed, and the contractor keeps its own payroll records for the same time. A week with no work on the job is commonly reported as a "no work" payroll so the numbering stays continuous; check what the agency wants. State prevailing wage jobs have their own forms and deadlines (see the state chunks in the library).
field.title: Certified payroll deadline on federal jobs: 7 days after payday, keep 3 years
field.topic: Prevailing wage paperwork: certified payroll and payment bonds
field.source: 29 CFR 3.4 (submission of weekly statements and preservation and inspection of weekly payroll records)
field.edition: eCFR text as shown on law.cornell.edu, read 2026-11-20

field.text: AWWA C651-14 gives three main ways to disinfect a new main. Tablet method (Sec. 4.3): calcium hypochlorite tablets glued in the top of each pipe as it is laid, for a dose of 25 mg/L; fill slowly, no faster than 1 ft per second; hold at least 24 hours, or 48 hours when the water is colder than 41 F; a free chlorine residual of at least 0.2 mg/L must still be found at every sample point at the end. Continuous feed (Sec. 4.4): first flush the main at 3.0 ft per second or more, then refill while feeding chlorine for 25 mg/L throughout; hold 24 hours; at least 10 mg/L free chlorine must remain at the end. Slug method (Sec. 4.5): move a slug of water dosed to 100 mg/L slowly down the main so every part of the wall sees it for at least 3 hours; if it falls below 50 mg/L, stop and bring it back to 100. Then flush to normal system chlorine, dechlorinate the flush water before it reaches a drain or stream, and take bacteriological samples. From the 2014 edition; a 2023 edition exists and was not read, so any change there is not confirmed. The spec, the water agency and state health rules govern.
field.title: Chlorinating a new water main: tablet, continuous feed and slug doses and hold times (AWWA C651-14)
field.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
field.source: AWWA C651-14, Sections 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6 (our summary; facts only)
field.edition: ANSI/AWWA C651-14 (effective Feb. 1, 2015); a C651-23 edition exists and was not read
field.unconfirmed: whether the 2023 edition changed these numbers

field.text: After final flushing, AWWA C651-14 (Sec. 5.1) requires two sets of bacteriological samples that both pass, taken one of two ways. Option A: take a first set, then take a second set at least 16 hours later. Option B: let the flushed main sit for at least 16 hours with no water use, then take two sets at least 15 minutes apart with the sample taps left running and without flushing the main first. Where to sample: a set for every 1,200 ft of new main, plus one at the end of the line and at least one from each branch longer than one pipe length. If trench water or a lot of dirt got into the main during laying, sample about every 200 ft. If a sample fails: flush and sample again; if it still fails, chlorinate again by the continuous feed or slug method and repeat until both sets pass. Older specs written on the 2005 edition ask for two sets 24 hours apart. No tie-in or service until the agency releases the main. From the 2014 edition; a 2023 edition exists and was not read, so any change there is not confirmed. The spec, the water agency and state health rules govern.
field.title: Bac-T samples on a new water main: two sets, 16 hours, every 1,200 ft (AWWA C651-14)
field.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
field.source: AWWA C651-14, Sections 5.1.1, 5.1.4, 5.1.6 (our summary; facts only)
field.edition: ANSI/AWWA C651-14 (effective Feb. 1, 2015); a C651-23 edition exists and was not read
field.unconfirmed: whether the 2023 edition changed these numbers

field.text: AWWA C651-14 on tie-ins and repairs. Final connection to the existing main (Sec. 4.10): tie-in piping up to one pipe length, generally 20 ft or less, may be sprayed or swabbed inside with at least a 1 percent chlorine solution just before it goes in. A longer connection must be set up above ground, disinfected and pass bacteriological samples before it is installed. Repairs (Sec. 4.11): if the main stayed under pressure and the leak was controlled (a clamp on a live main), swab or spray the parts with 1 percent chlorine and flush; no samples are needed. If the main was shut down and depressurized but kept clean: 1 percent chlorine on the exposed pipe, reachable inside surfaces and new parts, flush about three pipe volumes until clear, and take a sample set downstream; it may go back in service before results. If dirty water got in, disinfect like a new main where practical and get passing samples before service. Keep the trench pumped below the pipe while it is open. From the 2014 edition; a 2023 edition exists and was not read, so any change there is not confirmed. The spec, the water agency and state health rules govern.
field.title: Disinfecting a cut-in, repair or final tie-in: 1 percent chlorine swab and the 20 ft rule (AWWA C651-14)
field.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
field.source: AWWA C651-14, Sections 4.10, 4.11, 5.1.2 (our summary; facts only)
field.edition: ANSI/AWWA C651-14 (effective Feb. 1, 2015); a C651-23 edition exists and was not read
field.unconfirmed: whether the 2023 edition changed these numbers

field.text: Texas issues its own construction stormwater permit through TCEQ: the Construction General Permit, TXR150000. The current permit took effect March 5, 2023 and "expires on March 5, 2028." It covers construction that discharges stormwater to surface water in the state and will "disturb an acre or more of soil", including smaller sites that are part of a larger common plan. Small sites: "Small construction activities which disturb at least 1 but less than 5 acres" need a stormwater pollution prevention plan (Texas calls it the SWP3) and a signed site notice posted at the site; no Notice of Intent is filed with the state. Large sites: "Large construction activities which disturb 5 or more acres" need the SWP3, a Notice of Intent filed online through STEERS (or with an electronic reporting waiver), and the large-site notices posted. In every case operators must "develop and implement a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWP3) prior to commencing construction." Sites under 1 acre that are not part of a larger plan are "not regulated by this general permit", though the city may have its own rules. TCEQ began work on the 2028 renewal in June 2026.
field.title: Texas construction stormwater permit TXR150000: 1 acre, small and large sites, SWP3
field.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
field.source: TCEQ, Stormwater General Permit for Construction Activities (TXR150000), page modified 2026-11-16

field.text: In California, any work in, under or over a state highway right of way needs a Caltrans encroachment permit before it starts: trenches, bores, potholing, driveways, surveys, even tree trimming. The law treats "any tower, pole, pole line, pipe, pipeline, fence, billboard, stand or building" placed in the right of way as an encroachment. How to apply: the Standard Encroachment Permit Application, form TR-0100, with plans and traffic control, goes to the Caltrans district the job is in. Caltrans says "Effective January 1, 2025, you will be required to submit all permit applications through CEPS", its online Encroachment Permit System. Time: under Streets and Highways Code section 671.5, Caltrans must approve or deny a complete application "within 60 calendar days"; an incomplete package restarts the wait. Cost: a deposit at submittal, then actual review and inspection time at the Standard Hourly Rate, $181 per hour effective January 1, 2026. On the job: keep the permit and approved plans on site, call the Caltrans inspector named on the permit before starting, and follow its work hours and lane closure charts. City and county streets need the city or county permit instead.
field.title: California state highway encroachment permit (Caltrans): form TR-0100, CEPS, 60 days
field.topic: Working in the state highway right of way: encroachment and utility permits
field.source: Caltrans Encroachment Permits program page; Streets and Highways Code 671.5(a); read 2026-11-20

field.text: In Texas, putting a utility line in, under or across a state highway right of way goes through TxDOT's Utility Installation Review (UIR) system. TxDOT describes UIR as "a web-based system that automates the submission, review, approval, inspection, and post-construction processing" of "utility installation requests on the state right of way (ROW)". TxDOT calls the request a notice of proposed installation (NOPI). The utility owner, not the pipe contractor, is the applicant: it files the request with plans in UIR, and the TxDOT district reviews and approves it. The rules for where and how a line can go are in TxDOT's Utility Accommodation Rules and its Utility Manual. For the crew: do not start in TxDOT right of way without the approved request in hand; keep a copy on site; give the district office the advance notice the approval calls for; and build what was approved, since changes go back through UIR. Review times and the exact notice period before starting were not confirmed from the TxDOT pages read for this chunk; get them from the approval and the district utility coordinator. County roads and city streets have their own permits.
field.title: Texas state highway utility permit: the TxDOT UIR system and notice of proposed installation
field.topic: Working in the state highway right of way: encroachment and utility permits
field.source: TxDOT Utility Installation Review (UIR) help pages, About UIR; read 2026-11-20
field.unconfirmed: review time and the start-of-work notice period

field.text: In Florida, utility work in a state road right of way needs an FDOT utility permit. Rule 14-46.001 of the state administrative code says its purpose is to "regulate the location and manner for installation and adjustment of utility facilities" on FDOT right of way, and that FDOT issues permits for the "construction, alteration, operation, relocation, removal, and maintenance of utilities." The rule adopts the FDOT Utility Accommodation Manual (UAM), "2017 edition", effective July 30, 2017. FDOT says utilities must be installed "in accordance with the 2017 Utility Accommodation Manual (UAM)", the permit and any agreement with the department. The permit is issued to the utility owner (FDOT calls it the utility/agency owner, UAO); the contractor works under it. For the crew: have the approved permit and plans on site, give the notice before starting that the permit states, and follow the permit's lane closure and restoration conditions. How to file (FDOT's online permitting site) and the review time were not confirmed from the pages read for this chunk; the FDOT district utility office will say. County and city roads have their own right-of-way permits.
field.title: Florida state road utility permit (FDOT): the Utility Accommodation Manual
field.topic: Working in the state highway right of way: encroachment and utility permits
field.source: Fla. Admin. Code R. 14-46.001 (amended 7/30/2017); FDOT Utilities FAQ; read 2026-11-20
field.unconfirmed: how to file online and the review time

field.text: Florida sets its own sampling rule for new and altered public water mains in Rule 62-555.340 of the state administrative code (Department of Environmental Protection). Disinfection must follow "AWWA Standard C651, C652, or C653" (C651 is the one for water mains). Then, at each sampling location, the rule requires "a total of at least two samples - each taken on a separate day and taken at least six hours apart from the other sample(s)". If any sample shows total coliform, sampling goes on "until two consecutive samples at each sampling location show the absence of total coliform." The sampling locations are the ones called for in the AWWA standard (for mains: along the line at set spacing, at the end, and on branches). So in this state the two sets cannot both be pulled the same day, even though the 2014 edition of AWWA C651 has an option for two sets 15 minutes apart after the main sits 16 hours. The main cannot be placed in service until the department or county health unit clears it based on the results. The rule text read was last amended August 28, 2003; check with the permitting office for any newer requirement in the construction permit.
field.title: Florida bac-T rule for new water mains: two samples on separate days, 6 hours apart
field.topic: Disinfecting new water mains and repairs (AWWA C651): doses, sampling, cut-ins
field.source: Fla. Admin. Code R. 62-555.340 (amended 8-28-03); read 2026-11-20

field.text: Washington's trench sloping table is Table N-1 in WAC 296-155-66403 (Part N, Appendix B). Maximum allowable slopes, horizontal to vertical, for excavations less than 20 ft deep: stable rock vertical (90 degrees); Type A soil 3/4 to 1 (53 degrees); Type B soil 1 to 1 (45 degrees); Type C soil 1 1/2 to 1 (34 degrees). Sloping or benching for an excavation deeper than 20 ft must be designed by a registered professional engineer. Where it differs from the federal table: the federal table (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Table B-1) has a note allowing a steeper short-term slope of 1/2 to 1 in Type A soil for excavations 12 ft or less that are open 24 hours or less. Table N-1 has no such note and the Washington appendix has no short-term allowance, so on a Washington job Type A is 3/4 to 1 no matter how short a time the trench is open. In the app's Trench Sloping screen, pick plain Type A (0.75:1) on a Washington job; its 'Type A, short-term' choice (0.5:1) is the federal note and is not in Washington's table. The competent person classifies the soil and picks the slope.
field.title: Washington trench sloping by soil type (Table N-1): no steeper short-term slope in Type A
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.source: WAC 296-155-66403 Table N-1 and notes (WSR 16-09-085); 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Table B-1 note 2

field.text: Where a flagger stands (MUTCD Part 6, flagger procedures, Guidance): on the shoulder next to the lane of traffic being controlled, or in the closed lane, before stopping traffic. A flagger should only stand in the lane that moving traffic uses after the vehicles have stopped. The flagger should stand alone, be clearly visible to approaching traffic the whole time, and not stand among other workers or equipment. The flagger station itself goes far enough ahead of the work that approaching drivers can stop at the stopping point (Section 6D.06, Standard), with advance warning signs ahead of it and lighting at night except in an emergency; the flagger picks an escape route before starting. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
field.title: Where the flagger stands: on the shoulder next to the lane, or in the closed lane (never in the open lane)
field.topic: Traffic control: flaggers
field.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Sections 6D.05 (flagger procedures) and 6D.06 (flagger stations)

field.text: "Short duration" is the traffic control manual's term: work that occupies one location for up to 1 hour (MUTCD Section 6N.01). The other work durations: short-term stationary is daytime work at one location for more than 1 hour within a single daylight period; intermediate-term stationary is more than one daylight period up to 3 days, or night work over 1 hour; long-term stationary is more than 3 days; mobile work moves along. For short-duration work the manual allows simplified traffic control built around a vehicle with high-intensity warning lights. Do not mix this up with OSHA's "short term exposure" in the trench sloping appendix, which means an excavation open 24 hours or less and only matters for the Type A short-term slope. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern on the job.
field.title: Short duration work in traffic control: up to 1 hour (MUTCD); not OSHA's 24-hour short-term soil term
field.topic: Traffic control: short jobs and mobile work
field.source: MUTCD 11th Edition (FHWA, Dec 2023; Rev. 1 Dec 2025), Part 6, Section 6N.01; 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B (b) definition of short term exposure

field.text: Under EPA's 2022 Construction General Permit, keep a copy of every SWPPP inspection report at the site or at an easily accessible location (Part 4.7.3), and retain all inspection reports "for at least three (3) years from the date that your permit coverage expires or is terminated" (Part 4.7.4). The corrective action log follows the same rule: a copy at the site or easily accessible (Part 5.4.3), kept at least three years after coverage expires or is terminated (Part 5.4.4). Keep a current copy of the SWPPP itself at the site or an easily accessible location (Part 7.3), with the dates of every change to it (Part 7.4.2). These are EPA's own permit numbers. Most states issue their own construction stormwater permit; where the state permit asks for longer, the longer period applies.
field.title: How long to keep SWPPP inspection reports and the corrective action log: 3 years after coverage ends
field.topic: Stormwater on the job: construction general permit, SWPPP, inspections, dewatering
field.source: EPA 2022 Construction General Permit, as modified April 2025, Parts 4.7.3, 4.7.4, 5.4.3, 5.4.4, 7.3
field.edition: 2022 CGP as modified (effective April 8, 2025); expires February 16, 2027

field.text: On a California job, steel plates over an open trench in a road follow the road owner's encroachment permit. Caltrans' Encroachment Permits Manual (section 602.1) gives minimum A-36 plate thickness by trench width for highway loading: 1/2 inch for a 10 inch trench, 3/4 inch to 1 ft 11 in, 7/8 inch to 2 ft 7 in, 1 inch to 3 ft 5 in, 1 3/4 inch to 5 ft 3 in, and an engineered design for anything wider. Plates extend at least 12 inches past the trench edges, are pinned or recessed, ramped with asphalt at no more than 8.5 percent, and may be signed Rough Road (W8-8). Cities copy or tighten these in their permits. OSHA's cover rule applies too: at least twice the maximum axle load (1926.502(i)(1)).
field.title: California steel road plates over a trench: Caltrans plate thickness by trench width (Encroachment Permits Manual 602.1)
field.topic: Trench crossings, walkways, loads, traffic and public protection
field.source: Caltrans Encroachment Permits Manual section 602.1 (steel plate bridging), as summarized in the live library chunk trench-crossings-fall-public-4; city encroachment permit conditions
field.edition: as carried in the live library (moved, not re-read)

field.text: Appendix D vertical shores (no sheeting needed). Vertical spacing is 4 ft in every row. Cylinder size by trench width: up to 8 ft wide, 2 inch; over 8 to 12 ft, 2 inch with full-length steel tube oversleeves (3.5 x 3.5 x 0.1875) or the maker's oversleeves; over 12 to 15 ft, 3 inch. Maximum horizontal spacing, Type A (Table D-1.1): over 5 to 10 ft deep, 8 ft; over 10 to 15 ft, 8 ft; over 15 to 20 ft, 7 ft. Type B (Table D-1.2): over 5 to 10 ft, 8 ft; over 10 to 15 ft, 6.5 ft; over 15 to 20 ft, 5.5 ft. Over 20 ft deep: not from the tables; manufacturer's data or a registered professional engineer. Rules: 2 inch cylinders at least 18,000 lb and 3 inch at least 30,000 lb safe working capacity at full extension; spacing is center to center; shores in groups of at least three, equally spaced; rails at least 0.40 cubic inch section modulus; plywood (1.125 in softwood or 0.75 in 14-ply birch) only stops ravelling and is not structural. Type C is never on these tables: it needs a waler system with sheeting (Table D-1.4).
field.title: Aluminum hydraulic shores (vertical shores) Type A and Type B: spacing and cylinder size, Tables D-1.1 and D-1.2
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D, Tables D-1.1, D-1.2 and notes (g)(1)-(g)(7)
field.edition: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D (1989, unchanged); values read from the identical 8 CCR 1541.1 Appendix D text

field.text: Appendix D Table D-1.3, waler systems, Type B. Wales at 4 ft vertical spacing. Maximum horizontal cylinder spacing by wale section modulus (3.5 / 7.0 / 14.0 cubic inches): over 5 to 10 ft deep, 8.0 / 9.0 / 12.0 ft; over 10 to 15 ft, 6.0 / 8.0 / 10.0 ft; over 15 to 20 ft, 5.5 / 6.0 / 9.0 ft. Cylinders: with the 3.5 wale, 2 inch up to 8 ft wide, 2 inch with oversleeves over 8 to 12 ft, 3 inch over 12 to 15 ft; with the 14.0 wale, and with the 7.0 wale below 10 ft, 3 inch at every width. Timber uprights (3x12) behind the wales: 3 ft apart for 5 to 10 ft deep, 2 ft apart for 10 to 15 ft, solid sheeting for 15 to 20 ft. Over 20 ft deep: manufacturer's data or a registered professional engineer. Ask the shoring supplier which wale sizes they have (the table assumes the wale modulus you pick).
field.title: Aluminum hydraulic waler system in Type B soil: cylinder spacing by wale size and depth, Table D-1.3
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D, Table D-1.3 and notes
field.edition: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D (1989, unchanged); values read from the identical 8 CCR 1541.1 Appendix D text

field.text: Appendix D Table D-1.4, waler systems, Type C. Type C always gets solid sheeting (3x12 timber) behind the wales; wales at 4 ft vertical spacing. Maximum horizontal cylinder spacing by wale section modulus (3.5 / 7.0 / 14.0 cubic inches): over 5 to 10 ft deep, 6.0 / 6.5 / 10.0 ft; over 10 to 15 ft, 4.0 / 5.5 / 8.0 ft; over 15 to 20 ft, 3.5 / 5.0 / 6.0 ft. Cylinders: with the 3.5 wale, 2 inch up to 8 ft wide, 2 inch with oversleeves over 8 to 12 ft, 3 inch over 12 to 15 ft; with the 14.0 wale, and with the 7.0 wale below 10 ft, 3 inch at every width. Example: an 8 ft deep, 4 ft wide Type C trench with 7.0 wales: cylinders at most 6.5 ft apart, 2 inch, wales every 4 ft, solid sheeting. Over 20 ft deep: manufacturer's data or a registered professional engineer.
field.title: Aluminum hydraulic waler system in Type C soil: cylinder spacing by wale size and depth, solid sheeting, Table D-1.4
field.topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
field.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D, Table D-1.4 and notes
field.edition: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix D (1989, unchanged); values read from the identical 8 CCR 1541.1 Appendix D text

field.text: No. The US survey foot is about 2 parts per million longer than the international foot (0.3048 m exactly), about 0.01 ft per mile, so a cut, a fill, a rod reading or a pipe grade over a run is not changed. Where it matters is state plane coordinates (northings and eastings in the millions of feet), where the two feet can differ by several feet. NGS, NIST and the other federal agencies deprecated the US survey foot on December 31, 2022: from January 1, 2023 it should not be used, and the next state plane system (SPCS2022) supports only the international foot. It stays in older plans and records, and some agency manuals still set up projects in survey feet, so a plan set or data file may still be in survey feet. If a coordinate file and a plan disagree by a few feet over a long distance, ask the surveyor which foot each one uses.
field.title: US survey foot vs international foot: does it change my grade?
field.topic: Survey units: survey foot and international foot
field.source: Federal Register, Deprecation of the United States (U.S.) Survey Foot, 85 FR 62698 (Oct. 5, 2020), final determination

field.text: Elevations are measured from a vertical datum. Most current plans use NAVD 88; older plans, old record drawings and some local agencies use NGVD 29 (also written NGVD 1929) or a city datum. NGS found NAVD 88 minus NGVD 29 heights range from about -40 cm to +150 cm across the lower 48 states (about -1.3 ft to +4.9 ft), and +94 cm to +240 cm in Alaska. So an invert from an old as-built and a benchmark on the new datum can be off by feet, while every row on the cutsheet still adds up. Before tying into existing pipe or setting up on a benchmark, check that the plans, the cutsheet and the benchmark name the same datum. If they do not, or the benchmark has no datum on it, stop and ask the surveyor or engineer for the conversion. Never convert it yourself from a rule of thumb.
field.title: NAVD 88 vs NGVD 29: how far apart are the elevations, and why it matters on a pipe job
field.topic: Survey: vertical datum
field.source: Zilkoski, Richards and Young, Results of the General Adjustment of the North American Vertical Datum of 1988, Surveying and Land Information Systems Vol. 52 No. 3 (1992), abstract (published by NGS)

field.text: Washington: the WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual (M 22-97, chapter 15) sets flagging colors for construction stakes on WSDOT jobs: clearing and grubbing white, right of way red, slope stakes blue, centerline yellow, drainage blue, signing and illumination white, references and control multicolor, selective thinning orange, trees remaining blue. Spray paint: white is acceptable for stationing along the paved shoulder; pink for all other survey markings, per the national utility color code. Grade hubs (15-02.9): subgrade hubs are called blue tops, base rock hubs red tops, and top course hubs yellow tops. That is different from many other places, where blue top means finish grade, so on a Washington job a blue top may be subgrade. Private surveyors and cities can use their own colors: read the writing on the lath and get the job staking legend. The copy read was dated January 2005 with a draft footer; whether the current WSDOT edition is the same is not confirmed.
field.title: Washington WSDOT stake flagging colors and blue tops, red tops, yellow tops
field.topic: Survey: stake and flagging colors
field.source: WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97, Chapter 15 Construction Survey Procedures, 15-02.9 and 15-06

field.text: North Carolina: the NCDOT Manual for Construction Layout (revised 9/01/2018) gives flagging colors by stake type: centerline orange, slope stakes orange, intermediate grade stakes orange, fine grade hubs orange, clearing limits blue and white striped, ditch stakes blue, pipe stakes blue, minor structure and endwall stakes blue, fence line white, right of way markers white, sign stakes pink, curb stakes orange on the guard stake. Pipe stakes give the cut or fill from the hub to the invert (8.5); pipe stationing starts at 0+00 at the outlet end (8.2). On slope and ditch stakes the manual writes the offset difference with a sign: plus means the offset stake is higher than the intercept point, minus lower (6.5, 7.4). So on NCDOT work a plus or minus on a slope stake is not the same as fill or cut to grade: read the letters and the legend. Private surveyors may use other colors.
field.title: North Carolina NCDOT construction stake flagging colors and pipe stake cut to invert
field.topic: Survey: stake and flagging colors
field.source: NCDOT Manual for Construction Layout, revised 9/01/2018, chapters 3-17 (flagging), 6.5, 7.4, 8.2, 8.5

field.text: Florida, Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Department (WASD) Section 01031 Grades, Lines and Levels (rev. 5/2017): elevations may be on NGVD 1929, NAVD 88 or the City of Miami datum. WASD accepts NAVD 88 with a conversion factor on each page; it notes FDOT uses NAVD 88 and that City of Miami datum needs a conversion factor to NAVD 88 (3.01-D.8). Stations are set along the pipe centerline (or a stationed offset line) at most 100 ft apart (3.01-B.4), with control points at the start, the end and at least every 1,400 ft (3.01-B.2). For crews: a Miami-Dade plan, an old as-built and a benchmark can be on different datums. Check the datum note and conversion factor on each sheet before tying into existing pipe, and ask the surveyor if they differ.
field.title: Florida Miami-Dade water and sewer jobs: NGVD 1929, NAVD 88 and City of Miami datum on plans
field.topic: Survey: vertical datum
field.source: Miami-Dade WASD Design and Construction Standard Specifications, Section 01031 Grades, Lines and Levels, rev. 05/2017, 3.01-B.2, 3.01-B.4, 3.01-D.8

field.text: Federal pipeline safety rules say that if damage to a pipeline from excavation activity causes the release of any PHMSA regulated natural and other gas or hazardous liquid, "the excavator must promptly report the release to appropriate emergency response authorities by calling the 911 emergency telephone number" (49 CFR 196.109). Get people out and upwind first, keep ignition sources away, then call 911 and the pipeline operator. State one-call laws also require telling the operator about any damage, even a nick; check your state's damage notice rule.
field.title: Gas or hazardous liquid escaping after you hit a pipeline: the excavator calls 911
field.topic: Utility strike response
field.source: 49 CFR 196.109 (Protection of Underground Pipelines From Excavation Activity)

field.text: Maryland employers report a work-related death to MOSH (Maryland Occupational Safety and Health) within 8 hours, and an in-patient hospital stay, an amputation or the loss of an eye within 24 hours. COMAR 09.12.21 adopts the federal recordkeeping and reporting rule, 29 CFR Part 1904, by reference, with MOSH in place of OSHA. MOSH Central Office toll-free number: 1-800-759-6297. Maryland's text words the amputation item as an amputation involving bone or cartilage loss; when in doubt, call. The 8 and 24 hour times are the federal 1904.39 times that COMAR 09.12.21 adopts. Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
field.title: Maryland injury reporting to MOSH: deaths in 8 hours, hospital stays in 24 hours
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: COMAR 09.12.21, Employee Injury and Illness Records and Reports (adopts 29 CFR 1904; amends 1904.39(a)(2))
field.edition: COMAR 09.12.21 as posted by MOSH, read 2026-11-20

field.text: Minnesota employers report every work-related death to MNOSHA within 8 hours, and every work-related in-patient hospitalization, amputation and loss of an eye within 24 hours. Call MNOSHA Compliance at 651-284-5050 or 877-470-6742 from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday to Friday; outside those hours, on weekends and holidays, call federal OSHA at 800-321-6742. Minnesota adopted federal OSHA's revised reporting rule effective October 1, 2015. Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
field.title: Minnesota injury reporting to MNOSHA: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for hospital, amputation, eye
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry, MNOSHA Compliance: Report an accident, fatality or serious injury

field.text: Nevada employers report to Nevada OSHA (NVOSHA) every workplace accident with an employee death within 8 hours of learning of it, and every in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours. Phone: Southern Nevada (702) 486-9020, Northern Nevada (775) 688-3700. These are the same times as the federal rule (29 CFR 1904.39). Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
field.title: Nevada injury reporting to Nevada OSHA: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for hospital, amputation, eye
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: Nevada Division of Industrial Relations, Nevada OSHA: Report an Accident or Fatality

field.text: South Carolina employers report a work-related fatality to SC OSHA within 8 hours, and an in-patient hospitalization, an amputation or an eye loss within 24 hours. Call the SC OSHA office at (803) 896-7672, or report online through the SC OSHA eService portal. These are the same times as the federal rule (29 CFR 1904.39). Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
field.title: South Carolina injury reporting to SC OSHA: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for hospital, amputation, eye
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: SC Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, SC OSHA: Report a Severe Injury

field.text: Iowa employers report a work-related death within 8 hours and an in-patient hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye within 24 hours: 875 IAC chapter 4 adopts the federal rule, 29 CFR 1904.0 to 1904.46, by reference. Rule 875-4.3(2) adds ways to report on top of the federal ones: call Iowa OSHA at 877-242-6742, fax or email the completed incident report form, or go to 6200 Park Avenue, Suite 100, Des Moines. Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
field.title: Iowa injury reporting to Iowa OSHA: federal times, phone 877-242-6742
field.topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
field.source: Iowa Administrative Code 875 chapter 4 (adopts 29 CFR 1904; rule 4.3(2) reporting methods)

field.text: California requires a Cal/OSHA permit before building a trench or excavation 5 feet or deeper into which any person is required to descend (8 CCR 341(d)(5)(A)); descend means entering any part of it once it reaches 5 feet. The Project Administrator gets a Project Permit for the project (341(c)(1)); other employers doing the permit work hold an Annual Permit, good for any jobsite that year (341(c)(2)). An Annual Permit holder must notify the Division each time it starts permit-required work at a new site (341(c)(2)(B)). Exempt (341(e)): federal, state, county, city and district government agencies; public utilities under the Public Utilities Commission; trenches for emergency repair of underground facilities; excavations nobody has to enter; graves; swimming pools. Cal/OSHA says annual permit holders must hold a valid contractor's license.
field.title: California Cal/OSHA trench permit: 5 feet or deeper, annual or project permit, who is exempt
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.source: 8 CCR 341 (c)(1), (c)(2), (c)(2)(B), (d)(5)(A), (e); Cal/OSHA enforcement FAQ on construction activity permits

field.text: California construction employers must have supervisors hold toolbox or tailgate safety meetings, or equivalent meetings, with their crews at least every 10 working days to emphasize safety (8 CCR 1509(e)). The same section requires an Injury and Illness Prevention Program under 8 CCR 3203 (1509(a)) and a written Code of Safe Practices for the employer's operations (1509(b)), posted at a conspicuous place at each job site office or given to each supervisor, who keeps it readily available (1509(c)).
field.title: California toolbox or tailgate safety meetings: at least every 10 working days
field.topic: State safety plan: written programs and training
field.source: 8 CCR 1509 (a), (b), (c), (e), Construction Safety Orders

field.text: Washington construction employers must hold crew leader-crew safety meetings at the beginning of each job and at least weekly after that (WAC 296-155-110(5)(a)), tailored to the operation. Each meeting covers walk-around inspections, citations and accident investigations since the last meeting (6), and the employer documents attendance (6)(d) and the subjects discussed (6)(e). Minutes of each meeting are prepared and a copy is kept where most of the site's employees report each day (7), and the minutes are kept at least one year (8). Every 2 weeks is not enough in Washington.
field.title: Washington crew safety meetings: start of each job and at least weekly, minutes kept 1 year
field.topic: State safety plan: written programs and training
field.source: WAC 296-155-110 (5)(a), (6), (7), (8), Accident prevention program
field.edition: WAC 296-155-110 as posted by the Legislature, read 2026-11-20

field.text: Washington requires a person or persons holding a valid first-aid certificate at worksites with a crew (WAC 296-155-120(1)), and crew leaders, supervisors and persons in direct charge of one or more employees must have a valid first-aid certificate (296-155-120(2)). A crew is two or more employees at any worksite (3). A note allows a crew leader to work up to 30 days in an emergency without the certificate if another trained employee or crew leader is in the immediate work area. For a pipe crew this means the foreman carries a current first-aid card.
field.title: Washington first aid card: every crew leader and supervisor needs one
field.topic: State safety plan: first aid training and emergency numbers
field.source: WAC 296-155-120 (1), (2), (3), First-aid requirements

field.text: California construction employers must make sure a suitable number of appropriately trained persons are available to give first aid (8 CCR 1512(b)); employers on a shared site may pool them. At least one first-aid kit in a weatherproof container is provided, inspected regularly and restocked (1512(c)(1)); no drugs or medicines unless a physician approves in writing (1512(c)(3)). The phone numbers of a physician and an alternate, hospitals, ambulance services and fire protection services in the area are posted near the job telephone, or otherwise made available where there is no job phone (1512(e)). Section 1512 sets no ratio of first aiders per crew.
field.title: California first aid on construction jobs: trained people, a kit, and emergency numbers posted
field.topic: State safety plan: first aid training and emergency numbers
field.source: 8 CCR 1512 (b), (c)(1), (c)(3), (e), Emergency Medical Services
field.edition: Title 8 section 1512 as posted (last amended 2012), read 2026-11-20

field.note: Rewritten from the OAL-approved text (read 2026-11-21); keeps every fact of the FSOR-based card.
field.text: California amended 8 CCR 1951, 1952, 1953, 1955, 1956 and 1960 (and 5156) effective January 1, 2026 (filed November 4, 2025). Text approved by OAL (read 2026-11-21): a competent person must "conduct an initial survey of its work area for confined spaces existing at the time work begins" (1952(a)(1)) and inspect often enough to find new ones (1952(a)(2)); evaluation includes testing (1952(a)(4)); if flammables cannot be brought under 10 percent LFL, entry only after inerting, with PPE (1953(a)(3)(D)); the permit says how to summon rescue and emergency medical services (1955(a)(12)); and "the rescue services at the site are trained, immediately available, properly equipped" (1960(a)), with a note on a standby person able to rescue at once. Federal 1926.1211(a) accepts an evaluated service that can respond in a timely manner: follow California's stricter wording. Which words are new is not confirmed from the text (no underline); the Final Statement of Reasons (2025-09-18) shows no permit item change.
field.title: California confined space changes from January 1, 2026: site survey, testing, inerting and rescue at the site
field.topic: State safety plan: confined space
field.source: OSHSB rulemaking Confined Spaces in Construction: Text Approved by OAL; Final Statement of Reasons updated 2025-09-18; 8 CCR 1952, 1953, 1955, 1960

field.note: Adds the Part 90 pointer (MIOSHA page read 2026-11-21).
field.text: Michigan's Construction Safety Standard Part 35, Confined Space in Construction, adopts 29 CFR 1926.1202 (definitions) through 1926.1212 (employee participation) by reference, except as amended in the rules (R 408.43510, via the scope rule R 408.43501(4)). That includes the federal permit items in 1926.1206, so a federal-style entry permit covers Michigan. Part 35 does not apply to work covered by Part 9 (excavation, trenching and shoring), Part 14 (tunnels, shafts, caissons, cofferdams), Part 504 (diving) or Part 665 (underground construction and compressed air); where another standard also covers a confined space hazard, both apply (R 408.43501(2), (3)). Part 35 has three rules: scope, provision of documents, and adopted standards. Work that is not construction (an owner's plant or utility staff) falls under MIOSHA's general industry rule, which MIOSHA lists as Part 90, Permit-Required Confined Spaces (read 2026-11-21; its text was not read here).
field.title: Michigan confined space in construction: MIOSHA Part 35 adopts the federal rule
field.topic: State safety plan: confined space
field.source: Mich. Admin. Code R 408.43501, R 408.43505, R 408.43510 (MIOSHA Part 35); MIOSHA confined spaces page
field.edition: Part 35 as posted by Cornell LII, read 2026-11-20; MIOSHA page read 2026-11-21

field.text: Maryland (MOSH) uses the federal excavation rule: a protective system from 5 feet unless the trench is entirely in stable rock (29 CFR 1926.652). Maryland amends 1926.652 on records: the tabulated data used for a protective system, a slope design, the manufacturer's data and any approval to deviate from it, and an engineer's design are kept at the jobsite while the system is being built and after that until it is no longer used; then they may be kept off site but available to the Commissioner of Labor and Industry on request (Maryland amendments to 1926.652(b)(4)(iii), (c)(2)(iii), (c)(4)(iii)). Confined space in construction is the federal rule, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA, adopted by reference effective January 2, 2017, with no Maryland change found (MOSH adoption page and supplement list, read 2026-11-21).
field.title: Maryland trench rule: federal 5 feet, plus protective system records kept at the jobsite
field.topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
field.source: MOSH, Maryland amendments to 29 CFR 1926.652; MOSH-specific standards list

field.text: Colorado law requires all new underground facilities installed on or after August 8, 2018 to be electronically locatable, including laterals up to the building they serve (C.R.S. 9-1.5-103(10)). The Colorado Underground Damage Prevention Safety Commission says the install method does not change this (pipe bursting counts), planned replacement or rehab is treated as new work, and routine repairs are not included. For PVC and other pipe a locator cannot find, a tracer wire or another locating method is part of the design and install; the Commission does not pick the method. If a tracer wire is cut, repair it or otherwise keep the line locatable. Your project spec sets the wire type, splices and test stations.
field.title: Colorado: new underground lines must be electronically locatable (tracer wire on PVC)
field.topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
field.source: C.R.S. 9-1.5-103(10), as quoted in Colorado UDPSC Best Practice "Electronically Locatable" (approved 2019-11-14)

field.text: Indiana law (IC 8-1-26-18.5) covers any new or replacement underground facility installed after June 30, 2020, in public right-of-way or on private property. The operator (whoever installs it or has it installed) must make sure it can be detected from above ground. If the material cannot be found with standard locating equipment, as with PVC or HDPE, the facility must be encased in conductive material or equipped with an electrically conducting wire or other means of locating it underground. In practice that means tracer wire on plastic water and sewer pipe unless the plans call for another method. The section does not list exceptions such as sewer laterals in the text read; check with the owner or engineer.
field.title: Indiana: new or replacement underground lines must be detectable (locating wire on nonmetallic pipe)
field.topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
field.source: Indiana Code 8-1-26-18.5 (read at FindLaw; verify the current text at iga.in.gov)

field.text: West Virginia law (W. Va. Code 24C-1-11) says underground facilities owned by an operator and installed on or after July 1, 2018 must be installed so they are locatable using a generally accepted locating method. The law does not name a method; for PVC, HDPE and other nonmetallic pipe that usually means tracer wire or another method the owner accepts. The project spec and the utility owner set the wire, splices and test points.
field.title: West Virginia: underground lines installed since July 1, 2018 must be locatable
field.topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
field.source: W. Va. Code 24C-1-11 (West Virginia Legislature)

field.text: Nebraska law (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-2320.02) says plastic or nonmetallic underground facilities installed on or after January 1, 2021 must be installed so the operator can locate them under the One-Call Notification System Act, either by mapping or by tracer wire. The owner picks which; ask before you lay plastic pipe whether tracer wire is required. This was read from a 2020 compilation, so the current wording is not confirmed; check it on the Nebraska Legislature site.
field.title: Nebraska: plastic and nonmetallic lines installed since 2021 must be locatable (mapping or tracer wire)
field.topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
field.source: Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-2320.02 (2020 compilation read at Justia; current text at nebraskalegislature.gov not read)

field.text: Minnesota Rule 7560.0150, subpart 2: for each nonconductive underground facility installed in a public right-of-way after December 31, 2005, the operator must install a locating wire (tracer wire) or an equally effective means of marking where it is. Minor repairs, meaning repairs to or partial replacement of existing service laterals for routine upkeep, are not covered. Subpart 1 also has operators keep records (map, drawing or GIS) of facilities they install in public right-of-way. This is the 2014 version of the rule as read; the current version is not confirmed, so check it at revisor.mn.gov.
field.title: Minnesota: nonconductive lines in public right-of-way need a locating wire (Rule 7560.0150)
field.topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
field.source: Minnesota Rules 7560.0150, subparts 1 and 2 (version of 2014-01-18 at revisor.mn.gov)

field.text: Federal gas pipeline rule 49 CFR 192.321(e): "Plastic pipe that is not encased must have an electrically conducting wire or other means of locating the pipe while it is underground." Tracer wire may not be wrapped around the pipe, contact with the pipe should be kept small, and the wire must resist corrosion (coated copper or another means). This rule is for gas transmission lines and mains. Water and sewer tracer wire comes from state law in some states and from the project spec everywhere else.
field.title: Gas lines: plastic pipe must have a tracer wire or other way to locate it (49 CFR 192.321(e))
field.topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
field.source: 49 CFR 192.321(e), Installation of plastic pipe (eCFR / LII)

field.text: Minnesota: wait at least 48 hours before digging, and the 48 hours do not count the day you file the ticket, Saturdays, Sundays or holidays (Minn. Stat. 216D.04). Gopher State One Call says the 48 hours begin at 12:01 a.m. on the business day after the request. So a ticket filed on a Tuesday can be dug on Friday, and one filed on a Friday can be dug the next Wednesday, when there is no holiday in between. File no more than 14 calendar days ahead. The ticket is good for 14 calendar days from the start date and time printed on it. An Update gets a new ticket number and its own 48-hour wait, so send it early enough to keep digging without a gap. Go by the start date and time on your ticket.
field.title: Minnesota 811: when can I dig after I file a ticket (48 hours, the filing day not counted)
field.topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
field.source: Gopher State One Call web page "when can I dig" (read Nov 20, 2026); Minn. Stat. 216D.04

field.text: Iowa: the law defines the forty-eight-hour wait as beginning at 6:00 a.m. on the next business day after Iowa One Call receives the notice, and it skips Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays (Iowa Code 480.1(6), 480.4). So a notice given on a Monday can be dug from 6:00 a.m. Thursday, and one given on a Friday from 6:00 a.m. the next Wednesday, when there is no holiday in between. The notice is valid for 25 calendar days beginning on the day the 48-hour period ends. There is no renewal: ask for a new ticket before the old one runs out, and it has the same wait.
field.title: Iowa 811: when can I dig after I call (the 48 hours start 6 AM the next business day)
field.topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
field.source: Iowa Code 480.1(6) and 480.4 (Iowa Code 2026, chapter 480)

field.text: Indiana: call at least two full working days and not more than ten calendar days before digging (Ind. Code 8-1-26-16). The day you call is not a full working day. Work may start at 7 a.m. on the next working day after the two full working days, so a Monday call can be dug from 7 a.m. Thursday when there is no holiday in between. You may start sooner only if every operator has posted a positive response. A notice expires at 11:59 p.m. twenty days after it is received.
field.title: Indiana 811: when can I dig after I call (2 full working days, then 7 AM)
field.topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
field.source: Ind. Code 8-1-26-16

field.text: South Dakota: give notice at least 48 hours before digging. Under SDCL 49-7A-5 as amended in 2026 (Senate Bill 9), the 48 hours start at 12:01 a.m. on the day after the notice and skip Saturdays, Sundays and state legal holidays. So a notice given on a Monday can be dug Thursday, when there is no holiday in between. Marks are good while clearly visible, but not more than 21 calendar days from the start date on the ticket.
field.title: South Dakota 811: when can I dig after I call (the 48 hours start 12:01 AM the next day)
field.topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates

field.text: Oklahoma: give notice at least 48 hours before digging, not counting the day of the notice, Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. So a notice given on a Monday can be dug Thursday when there is no holiday in between. Demolition needs 7 business days.

field.text: South Carolina: operators have three full working days to mark, not counting the day you call, so a Monday call can be dug Friday when there is no holiday in between. SC811's 2026 holiday list adds days that do not count toward the three full working days even though the center is open: Confederate Memorial Day (May 11, 2026), Christmas Eve (December 24) and the day after Christmas (observed December 28, 2026); the notice is counted from the next business day. Its other 2026 holidays are New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day (July 3), Labor Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and the day after, and Christmas. field.text: Air limits for a permit space under the construction rule (29 CFR 1926.1202, hazardous atmosphere): oxygen below 19.5 percent is deficient and above 23.5 percent is enriched (a fire hazard); flammable gas, vapor or mist over 10 percent of its lower flammable limit (LFL, also called LEL); combustible dust at or above its LFL; any substance above its OSHA permissible exposure limit; or anything immediately dangerous to life or health. Subpart AA sets no H2S or CO number; the exposure limit tables do: H2S 10 ppm 8-hour average (1926.55 Appendix A), CO 50 ppm (federal construction PEL; NIOSH recommends 35 ppm, which most monitor alarms use). NIOSH IDLH: H2S 100 ppm, CO 1,200 ppm. App permit defaults: O2 19.5 to 23.5 percent, LEL 10 percent, H2S 10 ppm, CO 25 ppm (stricter than federal); a state plan or company program may be stricter. An open excavation uses 20 percent of the LFL (1926.651(g)(1)(iii)); a confined space, 10 percent. These numbers do not by themselves make a space safe: the entry supervisor signs only when testing at all levels, ventilation, attendant, communication, retrieval and rescue are in place.
field.title: Confined space air limits for manhole and vault entry: oxygen, LEL, hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and carbon monoxide (CO)
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1205. The entry employer documents the measures on a permit (a); the entry supervisor named on it signs before entry (b). It is available to entrants at entry, posted at the portal or an equally effective way (c), for no longer than the task needs (d). The supervisor cancels it when the work is done, or suspends or cancels it and fully reassesses before re-entry when a temporary condition not allowed arises; any other such condition means cancel (e). "The entry employer must retain each canceled entry permit for at least 1 year", with problems met noted on it so the program can be fixed (f); the program review uses them within 1 year after each entry; one yearly review can cover all (1926.1204(n)). Entry is any body part breaking the plane of the opening (1926.1202): a head in a manhole counts. The app keeps every closed permit in Records. A new condition (alarm, weather, new hazard): out, cancel, re-evaluate.
field.title: Confined space permit process: sign before entry, post it, cancel or suspend, keep canceled permits 1 year
field.topic: Confined space rules (OSHA Subpart AA)

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1211(c): "Non-entry rescue is required unless the retrieval equipment would increase the overall risk of entry or would not contribute to the rescue of the entrant." Otherwise the employer designates an entry rescue service; with non-entry rescue it confirms before entry that help is available if it fails. Each entrant wears a chest or full body harness, line at the center of the back near shoulder level or above the head (wristlets or anklets only if a harness is infeasible or more hazardous). The other end goes to a mechanical device or fixed point outside, and "A mechanical device must be available to retrieve personnel from vertical type permit spaces more than 5 feet (1.52 meters) deep": a tripod and winch or davit, so every manhole and most vaults. No lines that could tangle. The attendant stays outside and does non-entry rescue only (1926.1209(d), (i)); a trained team does entry rescue. No retrieval set up, no entry.

field.text: 29 CFR 1926.1203(g): a permit space may be reclassified as a non-permit confined space only when a competent person determines that the space has no actual or potential atmospheric hazard and every hazard in it is eliminated or isolated without entry (unless that is shown infeasible), and only while they stay that way. An entry needed to eliminate or isolate them is a full permit entry. Forced air ventilation does not count as eliminating or isolating a hazard (ventilation-only entry is 1203(e), not a reclassification). The basis is documented in a certification with the date, the location of the space and the signature of the person deciding, available to each entrant (g)(3). If hazards arise, everyone exits and the space is re-evaluated and reclassified as a permit space as needed (g)(4). The other way: when use or configuration changes might increase the hazards, or the first evaluation may have been inadequate, a competent person re-evaluates the non-permit space and reclassifies it if necessary (1203(f)).
